chapters.html:
Opening poem

The Yangtze rolls east in endless flood; its churning waves scour away heroes as time goes by. Victories and defeats turn empty in an instant: green mountains remain, and the setting sun burns red again and again. White-haired fishermen and woodcutters on the river islets, have long watched autumn moonlight and spring wind. A jar of cloudy wine meets us in glad reunion: of all things past and present, all are laid into easy talk.

Now the great affairs of the realm follow a general course: after long division comes unity, and after long unity comes division. At the end of Zhou, seven states contended until Qin united them. After Qin fell, Chu and Han contended until Han united them. The Han dynasty began when Emperor Gaozu raised his cause after slaying the white serpent and brought all under Heaven under one rule. Later Emperor Guangwu restored the dynasty, which passed down to Emperor Xian and then divided into three kingdoms. Tracing the origins of the disorder, they began chiefly under Emperors Huan and Ling. Emperor Huan proscribed worthy men and placed his trust in eunuchs. When he died and Emperor Ling ascended, General-in-Chief Dou Wu and Grand Tutor Chen Fan assisted the throne. The eunuch Cao Jie and others were then manipulating power. Dou Wu and Chen Fan plotted to execute them, but the plan was not kept secret, and they themselves were killed. From then on, the palace eunuchs grew still more overbearing.

In the second year of Jianning, on the full-moon day of the fourth month, the emperor entered Wende Hall. Just as he took his seat, a sudden gale tore through a corner of the hall; a great green serpent flew down from a roof beam and coiled upon the throne. The emperor fainted in terror. His attendants hurried him into the inner palace, and all the officials fled. Soon the serpent vanished. Then came violent thunder, rain, and hail, which did not cease until midnight and destroyed countless houses.

In the fourth year of Jianning, second month, Luoyang suffered an earthquake. Again the sea overflowed, and along the coast residents were swept away by the flood waves. In the first year of Guanghe, hens turned into roosters. On the first day of the sixth month, more than ten zhang of black vapors flew into Wende Hall. In autumn’s seventh month, a rainbow appeared in Yutang Hall; the banks of Wuyuan Mountain split apart. These signs were many and grave.

The emperor issued an edict asking ministers about the omens. Court advisor Cai Yong submitted a memorial, arguing plainly that the fallen rainbow and hens changed into roosters came from the inner-court women and eunuchs meddling in government. The emperor read it, sighed, and rose to change his robes. Cao Jie looked from behind, reported what he had heard to everyone nearby, and by another pretext charged Cai Yong with a crime and sent him home. Soon afterward Zhang Rang, Zhao Zhong, Feng Xu, Duan Gui, Cao Jie, Hou Lan, Jian Shuo, Cheng Kuang, Xia Yun, and Guo Sheng—ten in all—banded together as the “Ten Eunuchs.” The emperor trusted Zhang Rang deeply and called him “Ah Father.” Court government went wrong day by day; popular minds turned toward disorder and brigands and bandits rose.

At that time, in Julu Commandery, there were three brothers: one named Zhang Jiao, one Zhang Bao, and one Zhang Liang. Zhang Jiao was a scholar who had failed the examinations. Entering the mountains to gather medicinal herbs, he met an old man with blue eyes and a youthful face, holding a staff of goosefoot. The old man called him into a cave and gave him three volumes of a heavenly book. “This is called the Essential Arts of Great Peace. Once you receive it, you must proclaim the Way on Heaven’s behalf and bring salvation to all people. If any disloyal thought arises in you, you will surely meet with retribution.” Jiao bowed and asked his name. The old man answered, “I am the Old Immortal of Nanhua.” Having spoken, he changed into a clear breeze and vanished.

Once Jiao had obtained the book, he studied and practiced day and night. He learned to summon wind and rain and took the title “Daoist of Great Peace.” In the first month of the first year of Zhongping, an epidemic spread. Zhang Jiao distributed talisman water and treated the sick, calling himself “the Great Worthy and Good Teacher.” He had more than five hundred disciples who traveled in every direction, all able to write talismans and recite incantations.

As his followers multiplied, Jiao organized thirty-six divisions. A large division had more than ten thousand members; a small one, six or seven thousand. Each had a leader whom they called a general. He spread the saying: “The Blue Heaven is dead; the Yellow Heaven shall rise. In the year jiazi, great fortune will come to the realm.” He ordered every household to write the two characters jiazi (甲子) on its main gate with white clay. Throughout the eight provinces of Qing, You, Xu, Ji, Jing, Yang, Yan, and Yu, household after household revered the name of Zhang Jiao, the Great Worthy and Good Teacher.

Jiao sent his follower Ma Yuanyi secretly bearing gold and silk to win over the eunuch Feng Xu as an agent within the palace. Jiao and his two brothers discussed: “Nothing is harder to obtain than the people’s hearts. Now their hearts already turn to us. If we do not seize the moment and take the realm, it will be truly regrettable.” He secretly made yellow banners and fixed a date for the uprising.

At the same time he sent his disciple Tang Zhou with a dispatch to Feng Xu. Tang Zhou instead rushed to the capital and reported the plot. The emperor ordered General-in-Chief He Jin to arrest Ma Yuanyi and execute him; then Feng Xu and the rest were also arrested and imprisoned.

When Zhang Jiao heard the affair was exposed, he raised troops overnight and proclaimed himself “General of Heaven”; Zhang Bao proclaimed himself “General of Earth”; Zhang Liang proclaimed himself “General of Men.” He told the band: “The Han order is ending, and the Great Sage has appeared. All of you should follow Heaven’s will and move uprightly, to delight in peace.” Four or five hundred thousand commoners in the realm bound yellow cloth on their heads and rose with him. The rebels’ force was vast, and the official troops, by the wind of fear, scattered.

He Jin petitioned the emperor to issue urgent commands ordering every district to prepare its defenses and win merit by suppressing the rebels. At the same time, Colonels Lu Zhi, Huangfu Song, and Zhu Jun were each sent with elite troops along separate routes to attack them.

Now Zhang Jiao’s army advanced into the territory of You Province. Its administrator, Liu Yan, was a native of Jingling in Jiangxia and a descendant of Prince Gong of Lu of the Han house. When he heard that the rebel army was approaching, he summoned Colonel Zou Jing for counsel. Zou Jing advised, “Their troops are many and ours few. My lord, you should recruit men at once to meet them.” Liu Yan agreed and immediately posted notices calling for volunteers.

The notices reached Zhuo County and drew out a hero from there. He cared little for reading; his nature was generous and mild, and he spoke little. Neither joy nor anger showed on his face. He had long harbored great ambitions and delighted in befriending the realm’s heroes. He stood seven chi and five cun tall; his ears hung to his shoulders, his hands reached below his knees, and when he looked straight ahead he could glimpse his own ears. His face was like fine jade and his lips as though painted with rouge. He was Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, a descendant of Liu Sheng, Prince Jing of Zhongshan, and a remote descendant of Emperor Jing of Han. Liu Sheng’s son Liu Zhen had been enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhuolu Village under Emperor Wu, but lost his marquisate for failing to contribute the proper ceremonial gold. This branch of the family therefore remained in Zhuo County.

Liu Bei’s grandfather was Liu Xiong, his father Liu Hong. Liu Hong once passed as filial and served as an official, but died young. Liu Bei was orphaned early and filial to his mother. Poor, he sold sandals and mats for his livelihood. His house stood in Lou-sang village of the county. To the southeast, a tall mulberry tree rose more than five zhang, looking from afar like a wagon canopy. Fortune-tellers said, “A noble man will come from this house.” As a boy, Liu Bei played with village children beneath it and said, “I will one day be Son of Heaven and ride this canopy.” His uncle Liu Yuanqi saw and said, “This child is not ordinary,” and because the family was poor, he often supplied him. At fifteen, his mother sent him to study. He once studied under Zheng Xuan and Lu Zhi and was friend to men like Gongsun Zan. When Liu Yan called for volunteers, Liu Bei was already twenty-eight.

On seeing the announcement, he sighed deeply. Immediately a man raised his voice: “A real man does not waste effort on the state and then sigh so long. Why this?”

Liu Bei looked at him. The man was eight chi tall, with a tiger-bearded face and bold eyes like a leopard, chin like a swallow’s head, voice like thunder, and a gait like a war horse. Liu Bei asked his name.

“The surname is Zhang, name Fei, courtesy name Yide. We live in Zhuo Commandery, hold some broad fields, and make a living selling wine and meat. I enjoy befriending heroes across the land. I only saw you reading and sighing and thus asked.”

Liu Bei said, “I am of the Han imperial kin, surname Liu, name Bei, courtesy name Xuande. Hearing that the Yellow Turbans have risen, I desire to break them and bring the people peace, but my strength is small, so I sigh.”

“Good,” said Fei. “I have some resources. Let me recruit village fighters and join you.” Liu Bei was very glad. They entered an inn and drank together.

While they drank, a big man came pushing a cart and halted at the tavern gate. Sitting down, he called the server: “Quickly pour wine. I must hurry into the city to enlist.” Liu Bei saw him. He was nine chi tall, with a beard nearly two feet long, a face like a ripe jujube, and lips like painted rouge. His eyes were like dark phoenixes, brows like curled silk. He looked grand and imposing. Liu Bei invited him to sit and asked his name.

“My surname is Guan, my given name Yu, and my courtesy name was Changsheng, later changed to Yunchang. I come from Xieliang in Hedong. A local bully relied on his power to mistreat others, so I killed him and fled abroad for five or six years. Hearing of this call to arms, I came to volunteer.”

Liu Bei explained his purpose. Guan Yunchang rejoiced greatly. The three men went to Zhang Fei’s village homestead and discussed the matter.

“Behind my farm is a peach garden in full blossom,” Zhang Fei said. “Tomorrow we will hold sacrifice to Heaven and Earth there. The three of us shall become brothers and unite in intent and strength before we attempt anything great.” Liu Bei and Guan Yu answered, “That is excellent.”

The next day in the Peach Garden they prepared rituals with white ox, white horse, and incense. The three burned incense and knelt twice, swearing:

“Take Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei: though our surnames are not one, once we have sworn brotherhood we shall join heart and mind, rescue those in distress and help those in danger, serve the state above and bring peace below. We do not ask to be born same year, month, or day; we only ask to die in one same year, month, and day. Heaven and Earth know this heart. Those who betray loyalty and forget gratitude, let Heaven and men together slay them.”

After the oath, Liu Bei was declared elder brother, then Guan Yu, then Zhang Fei. After worshiping Heaven and Earth, they slaughtered an ox, set out wine, gathered villagers with courage, and more than three hundred arrived. The three drank till the Peach Garden rang with cheers. The next day they arranged their arms and armor and regretted they had no horses.

While they were thinking this over, news came that two guests had arrived leading a troop and horses at full pace. Liu Bei said, “Heaven is helping us.” The three men met them at the gate. The two were great merchants from Zhongshan: Zhang Shiping and Su Shuang, who annually sold horses northward and had returned because of raids.

Liu Bei treated them well, shared wine, and told them of his wish to defeat rebels and comfort the people. The two were glad and offered fifty fine horses, five hundred taels in gold and silver, and one thousand jin of iron for supplies.

Liu Bei thanked them and had local smiths forge a pair of swords. Guan Yu had a Green Dragon Crescent Blade made, also called the “Cold-Beauty Saw,” weighing eighty-two jin. Zhang Fei had a one-zhang-eight-chi pointed steel spear made. All three donned full armor. Gathering more than five hundred village fighters, they came to see Zou Jing, who presented them to Administrator Liu Yan.

The three introduced themselves. Liu Yan rejoiced and welcomed Liu Bei as nephew.

Not long after, reports came that Cheng Yuanzhi, a rebel commander under Zhang Jiao, was leading fifty thousand men to attack Zhuo Commandery. Liu Yan ordered Zou Jing to take Liu Bei and the two in charge of five hundred troops. He had them go first to fight. Liu Bei took command with joy and advanced to the foothills of Daxing Mountain, where the rebels stood.

The rebels had unbound hair and yellow cloth bound around their brows. The two armies faced each other. Liu Bei mounted, with Guan Yu on his left and Zhang Fei on his right, raised his whip, and shouted, “You traitors who have rebelled against the state, why do you not surrender now?”

Cheng Yuanzhi raged and sent his deputy Deng Mao to battle. Zhang Fei thrust his long snake spear forward, and with one motion he drove it into Deng Mao’s heart. The rebel tumbled from the saddle. Seeing Deng Mao dead, Cheng Yuanzhi whipped his horse and drew his blade to charge Zhang Fei. Guan Yu mounted and swung his great sword. Shocked, Cheng Yuanzhi could not respond and was cut in two.

A later poem praised them:

A hero shows his edge in this hour: first test of spear, first test of sword. From the first clash his might is revealed, and in three notes his name is set to remember.

Seeing their commander cut down, the rebels all threw aside their weapons and ran. Liu Bei sounded the charge and gave chase. Captured men were countless; they returned in a great victory. Liu Yan met them in person and rewarded the troops.

The next day came a memorial from Gong Jing, Administrator of Qing Province, saying the city was besieged and about to fall, imploring help. Liu Yan discussed it with Liu Bei.

“I am willing to go,” said Liu Bei.

Liu Yan ordered Zou Jing to take five thousand troops and send Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei to Qing Province. The rebels saw the rescue force and split and fought hard. Liu Bei’s force was too small and withdrew thirty li to camp.

“There are too many rebels and not enough of us. We need a surprise force to win,” Liu Bei told Guan Yu and Zhang Fei. He posted Guan Yu with one thousand troops on the mountain left, Zhang Fei with one thousand on the right, and used gongs and struck metal as the signal for all to come out and support.

The next day Liu Bei and Zou Jing marched forward with drums and horns. The rebels met and fought. Liu Bei then withdrew his lines. When the rebels pursued past the ridge, all Liu Bei’s army rang metal at once, and both flanking detachments emerged together. Liu Bei turned his whole host and struck back.

Encircled on three sides, the rebels collapsed and fled. They were chased to the foot of Qing Province’s wall, where Administrator Gong Jing also led citizen troops out to help. The rebel force suffered terribly; the siege of Qing Province was lifted.

Later, people composed a poem praising Liu Bei:

His planning and calculations had divine merit; one dragon could still make two tigers yield. From his first charge he already left great achievements; in due course he should share in the partition of the realm.

After feeding the troops, Gong Jing had them rewarded. Zou Jing wished to return. Liu Bei said, “I have heard that General-in-Chief Lu Zhi and rebel head Zhang Jiao are contesting in Guangzong. I once studied under Lu Zhi and want to go to his aid.” Zou Jing then withdrew with the main force. Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei set out with their own five hundred to Guangzong.

When they entered Lu Zhi’s camp, they came to his tent, made proper bows, and stated their intent. Lu Zhi was very pleased and kept them there while making plans.

At that time Zhang Jiao’s force was one hundred and fifty thousand; Lu Zhi had only fifty thousand. They stood at Guangzong with no winner yet. Lu Zhi told Liu Bei: “I am besieging them here; Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao are in Yingchuan, opposing Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun. You bring your own men; I will add one thousand soldiers of the court and send you to Yingchuan to gather intelligence and set a date to destroy them.”

Liu Bei took the order and rode through the night to Yingchuan. There Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun were already repelling rebels. The rebels were not winning in open battle and had fallen back into Changshe to build camp in grass. Song and Jun concluded, “They are camping among grass; we should attack by fire.” So they had each soldier carry a bundled sheaf of grass in secret. After the second watch, with wind suddenly rising, all the troops set fire together. Song and Jun then attacked the camp in turn.

Fire rose into the sky. The rebels panicked—no one could saddle horses, no one buckle armor—so they scattered. By dawn, Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao, leading remnants, fled. Suddenly they saw a body of horsemen ahead, all displaying red banners, closing the road. At their fore a general appeared: seven chi tall, narrow eyes and a long beard. He was a Cavalry Commandant from Qiao County in the state of Pei: Cao Cao, whose courtesy name was Mengde.

Cao Cao’s father, Cao Song, was originally surnamed Xiahou; because he had been adopted by Grand Eunuch Cao Teng, he took Cao as his surname. Cao Cao’s childhood name was A-Man, and he was also called Jili. As a boy he loved hunting, roaming, singing, and dancing; he was resourceful and quick-witted. An uncle often grew angry at his wandering ways and reported them to Cao Song, who would reprimand him. Cao Cao then devised a plan: when he saw his uncle approaching, he fell to the ground and feigned a seizure. The uncle, alarmed, reported this to Cao Song. Cao Song hurried to see his son and found him perfectly well. “Your uncle says you suffered a seizure,” he said. “Are you recovered?”

“I have never had such an illness,” Cao Cao replied. “My uncle no longer cares for me, so he deceived you.”

Cao Song believed him, and after that, even when the uncle kept blaming Cao, Cao Song no longer listened. So Cao Cao was allowed to enjoy himself as he wished.

At that time Qiao Xuan said to him, “The world is about to fall into disorder. Only one endowed with the talents to command an age can save it. Could that man be you?” He Yong of Nanyang saw Cao Cao and said, “The Han house is about to fall. The man who can bring peace to the realm must be this one.” Xu Shao of Runan, famed for his ability to judge character, also met Cao Cao. Cao Cao asked, “What kind of man am I?” Xu Shao did not answer. Asked again, he said, “In times of peace, you would be a capable minister; in times of disorder, a treacherous hero.” Cao Cao was delighted.

At age twenty, Cao passed the filial official test and became a court gentleman; he was appointed Northern Capital Captain of Luoyang. Soon after, he placed more than ten-colored rods at the four gates of the commandery. If any transgressed, whether rich or poor, he could punish them with the rods. One night eunuch Jian Shuo’s uncle walked with drawn sword; Cao caught him on patrol and punished him with rods. Thus no one dared to offend inside or out, and his fame was powerful.

Later he became Magistrate of Dunqiu. Because of the Yellow Turban uprising, he was appointed Cavalry Commandant and brought five thousand cavalry and infantry to Yingchuan to assist. Just as Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao had been defeated and were fleeing, Cao Cao intercepted them, beheaded over ten thousand men, and took many banners, drums, and horses. Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao fought hard and slipped away.

Cao then met Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun and immediately pursued them.

Returning now to Liu Bei and his men: they rode into Yingchuan hearing cries and seeing fire light the sky. They arrived to find the rebels already dispersed. Liu Bei reported to Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun that Lu Zhi had asked, and Song said, “Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao are near ruin and exhaustion; they must flee to Guangzong and connect with Zhang Jiao. Liu Bei, go at once by night and aid.”

Liu Bei took command and marched. Halfway, he saw horsemen guarding a barbed cage-cart; inside was Lu Zhi. Liu Bei dismounted and asked what had happened.

Lu Zhi answered, “I surrounded Zhang Jiao and nearly won. Yet because he used sorcery, I could not take him immediately. The court sent Palace Attendant Zuo Feng to inspect and demand bribes. I replied, ‘Army rations are still lacking. Where can I find extra silver to flatter messengers from Heaven?’ He resented it and reported that I sat idle on the high wall and was lazy and harming the troops’ spirit. The court grew furious and sent General Zhonglang Dong Zhuo to replace me and bring me back for charges.”

Zhang Fei, hearing this, grew furious and wanted to execute the escort immediately to free Lu Zhi. Liu Bei restrained him: “The court has official process. How could you act rashly?” The escortmen carried Lu Zhi onward.

Guan Yu said, “Middle Gentleman Lu has been seized. If another takes command now, we will have nowhere to rely. Better return to Zhuo Commandery.” Liu Bei agreed. They moved north.

Before two days passed, they heard a great shout from behind from the hills. Liu Bei rode with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei to a high knoll and looked out. Han troops had been badly beaten; behind them rebel forces covered hills and fields, their flags marked “General of Heaven.”

“This is Zhang Jiao,” Liu Bei said. “We must attack at once.” The three spurred forward with their force. Zhang Jiao had just defeated Dong Zhuo and was pressing the pursuit when the three charged into him. His army fell into confusion and fled more than fifty li.

The three rescued Dong Zhuo and brought him back to camp. He asked their rank. Liu Bei answered, “Common soldiers.” Dong Zhuo made no courtesy and offered little respect. Liu Bei stepped away. Zhang Fei was enraged and said, “We rode straight into bloodshed and saved this man, and he answers without honor! If we do not kill him, my anger cannot settle.” He reached for his blade and entered his tent to kill Dong Zhuo.

The narrator says:

The world’s gains and losses and men’s motives are the same now as in old times. Who can tell at once which is truly a hero and which is but a common man? If only there were a quick-handed man like Yide, all traitors in the world should be erased at once.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Oath of the Three Heroes in the Peach Garden: The First Deed of Merit Against the Yellow Turbans

chapters.html:
Now Dong Zhuo, whose courtesy name was Zhongying and who came from Lintao in Longxi, was appointed Administrator of Hedong Commandery. He had long been arrogant. One day he slighted Liu Bei. Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, flew into a rage and wanted to kill him.

Liu Bei and Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, quickly restrained him. “He is an officer appointed by the Court. How can we take a man’s life on our own?”

Zhang Fei replied, “If I do not kill this fellow, then I would have to serve under him among his troops, and I cannot endure that!”

Liu Bei said, “The three of us have sworn to live and die together. We cannot be separated. Why not all leave for another place at once?”

Zhang Fei said, “If it is so, at least part of my anger will be relieved.”

Thus the three rode through the night and brought their troops to Zhu Jun. Zhu Jun treated them with great respect, gathered all the soldiers in one force, and marched to attack Zhang Bao.

At that time, Cao Cao had accompanied Huangfu Song in the campaign against Zhang Liang, where a fierce battle had already been fought at Quyang.

Here Zhu Jun besieged Zhang Bao. Zhang Bao brought eighty or ninety thousand raiders and posted them behind the hills. Zhu Jun appointed Liu Bei as advanced guard and put them opposite the rebels.

Zhang Bao sent his deputy commander Gao Sheng to engage. Liu Bei ordered Zhang Fei forward. Zhang Fei rode with spear in hand; he clashed with Gao Sheng, and within moments he skewered him and sent him falling from his horse.

Liu Bei drove the army straight on. Zhang Bao, with hair unbound and sword raised, began his incantations. A violent wind and thunder rose. A stream of black smoke came down from the sky. In the blackness it seemed as though endless riders and horses were bearing down.

Liu Bei wheeled his horse and withdrew in haste. The army collapsed into confusion and fell back in defeat. He consulted with Zhu Jun.

Zhu Jun said, “He has used sorcery. Tomorrow I will have the soldiers pour out pig, sheep, and dog blood, along with refuse, and lie in ambush on the hilltops. When the rebels rush up, we will douse them from above. The method should dispel his trick.”

Liu Bei followed the order. He sent Guan Yu and Zhang Fei each with one thousand men to hide behind the ridge on the hill, preparing jars of animal blood and filth.

On the next day, Zhang Bao beat drums and raised his banners to draw troops into battle. Liu Bei rode out to meet them. In the clash, Zhang Bao again began his ritual; wind and thunder roared, sand and stones flew, black fog filled the sky, and masses of riders and infantry seemed to descend from above.

Liu Bei turned his horse and withdrew. Zhang Bao’s troops rushed after him. As they passed the rise, Guan and Zhang’s ambushing force sounded horns and drums and loosed the prepared foulness in one pour.

Paper men and straw horses that had been in the air tumbled down as if collapsing. The storm stilled. Sand and stones stopped flying. Zhang Bao saw that the spell had been broken and tried to retreat at speed.

With Guan on the left and Zhang on the right, both flanking armies surged out. Liu Bei and Zhu Jun closed in from the rear, and the bandit force was routed. Liu Bei saw the banner of the Dìgōng General (地公將軍) and spurred forward. Zhang Bao broke and fled. Liu Bei loosed an arrow into his left arm.

Zhang Bao escaped with the wound, riding toward Yangcheng, and made a hard stand there.

Zhu Jun surrounded Yangcheng and pressed the attack. He also dispatched scouts to seek word of Huangfu Song.

The scouts returned and reported: “Huangfu Song won a major victory. In the imperial court, since Dong Zhuo had repeatedly failed, they replaced him with Huangfu Song. When he arrived, Zhang Jiao had already died; Zhang Liang inherited the rebels and met our army, but Huangfu Song defeated him in seven engagements and beheaded Zhang Liang at Quyang. They opened the coffin of Zhang Jiao, executed the corpse, sent his severed head to the capital, and the rest surrendered.

The court has promoted Huangfu Song as General of Chariots and Cavalry and appointed him Governor of Ji Province. Huangfu Song also petitioned that Lu Zhi had no crime and deserved restoration; the Court has restored Lu Zhi to his former office. Cao Cao was likewise commended and made Administrator of Jinan and ordered to return from campaign at once.”

When Zhu Jun heard this, he urged the horses onward and redoubled his assault on Yangcheng.

The rebels’ situation grew desperate. Their general Yan Zheng killed Zhang Bao and presented his head in surrender.

Zhu Jun then pacified several commanderies and submitted a report of victory.

Again three former followers of the Yellow Turbans—Zhao Hong, Han Zhong, and Sun Zhong—gathered several ten-thousands, and, smelling opportunity, burned and plundered villages. They claimed they were avenging Zhang Jiao.

The Court issued orders for Zhu Jun to take this victorious army and destroy them. Zhu Jun obeyed the edict and advanced.

At that time the rebels occupied Wancheng. Zhu Jun besieged it. Zhao Hong sent Han Zhong to battle. Zhu Jun ordered Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei to attack the southwest corner of the city.

Han Zhong brought all his elite men and came to the southwest to resist. Zhu Jun led two thousand armored horsemen straight for the northeast corner. Fearing the loss of the city, the rebels hurriedly abandoned the southwest and returned.

Liu Bei struck from behind. The rebels were routed and fled back into Wancheng. Zhu Jun divided his troops to encircle the city on four sides. Supplies inside were cut. Han Zhong sent envoys out of the gates to surrender.

Zhu Jun refused.

Liu Bei said, “When Emperor Gaozu first won all under heaven, it was because he could turn enemies into followers and keep them in line. Why then does the prefect forbid Han Zhong’s surrender?”

Zhu Jun answered, “That was one age, this is another. In the days when Qin and Xiang contended, the realm was in chaos and the people had no ruler, so turning foes was useful to coax them. Now the realm is unified; only the Yellow Turban rebels stand against us. If we accept their surrender, we will teach brigands that they may rob and burn, then surrender only when they are cornered. That is the custom of hardened bandits, not the way of statecraft.”

Liu Bei said, “You are right that we should not accept them as such. But with all four sides blocked like an iron cask, they cannot ask for clemency, so they will fight to the last breath. Ten thousand men with one purpose are not easily broken. And inside are many who will rather die than flee. Why not withdraw your southeast line and strike only the northwest. The rebels will abandon the city to escape. They will not stand to die if escape remains open, and we can catch them all.”

Zhu Jun agreed and withdrew two sides to the southeast, then drove all three columns at once toward the northwest.

Han Zhong indeed led his men to abandon the city and run. Zhu Jun, Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei pursued in threefold formation and killed Han Zhong with arrows. The rest scattered in all directions.

Just as the pursuit was underway, Zhao Hong and Sun Zhong arrived with their rebels and fought Zhu Jun. He saw their overwhelming force and pulled the army back for a moment.

Zhao Hong used the opening to retake Wancheng.

Zhu Jun moved ten li away to encamp and was just preparing to attack when a band of riders came in from the east. Leading them was a general with a broad forehead and wide face, with a frame like a tiger and waist like a bear.

He was from Fuchun in Wu Commandery: surname Sun, personal name Jian, courtesy name Wentai. He was a descendant of Sun Wuzi. At seventeen he traveled with his father to Qiantang, saw more than ten pirates seize merchants’ goods on the shore, and split the loot there.

Jian told his father, “These men can be taken.” He snatched up a broad sword and leaped ashore, bellowing and waving in all directions, as though he were rallying his men.

The raiders took him for official troops and threw their loot away before they ran.

Jian chased them down and killed one.

Because of this, he gained fame in the counties. He was recommended and made a colonel.

Later, in Kuaiji, a demon-mad uprising rose in Xuchang led by one who claimed to be Emperor Yangming. It drew tens of thousands. Jian and the county clerk recruited over a thousand brave men, joined forces with the commanderies and prefectures, and crushed them, beheading the rebel and the rebel’s son, Xu Shao.

Inspector Zang Min submitted a memorial and he was appointed magistrate of Yandu, then magistrate of Xuyi, then of Xiapi.

Now, when the Yellow Turban raiders rose again, Sun Jian assembled village youths and merchants, plus over fifteen hundred seasoned fighters from the Huai and Si regions, and marched to aid the army.

Zhu Jun rejoiced and commanded Sun Jian to strike the south gate, Liu Bei the north gate, and himself the west gate, leaving the east gate open for the enemies to run toward.

Sun Jian first climbed the wall and beheaded more than twenty rebels. The bandits broke and fled.

Zhao Hong, with lance couched on horse, rushed straight for Sun Jian. Sun Jian sprang from the wall, snatched the lance from him, and stabbed him off the horse. He then mounted Zhao Hong’s horse and leaped through the melee, mowing down rebels.

Sun Zhong brought his men out of the north gate. They collided with Liu Bei and had no wish to stand in battle. They just sought to escape.

Liu Bei drew a bow and shot Sun Zhong with one arrow. The man flipped and fell from his horse.

Zhu Jun’s main force arrived hard behind and mopped up, taking thousands of heads; no count of surrendering men could be kept. From Nanyang through a dozen commanderies, peace returned.

Zhu Jun withdrew to the capital. He received appointments as General of Chariots and Cavalry and Prefect of Henan.

He reported Sun Jian’s and Liu Bei’s merits. Sun Jian, whose reputation had spread, was later appointed to another commandery as its clerk and took up his post; Liu Bei, however, was never appointed despite waiting many days.

The three were uneasy and walked idly through the city streets. By chance, the Court clerk Zhang Jun’s carriage happened by. Liu Bei presented his case.

Zhang Jun was startled and immediately entered the audience chamber.

He said to the Emperor: “The Yellow Turban rebellion began in part from the ten eunuchs selling offices and noble ranks, entrusting only whom they favored, failing to punish the disloyal. That is why the realm has fallen into great disorder. The Court should execute the eunuchs, hang them at the southern suburbs, send envoys to announce this across the empire, reward merit with generous gifts, and in this way the Four Seas will return to peace.”

The ten eunuchs told the emperor, “Zhang Jun is deceiving Your Majesty.” The emperor ordered the guards to eject him.

The ten eunuchs together discussed and said, “He must be one of those who won merits against the Yellow Turbans but still has not yet been appointed; therefore he has such complaints. For now, cut him down a little in household records and defer full punishment.”

Thus Liu Bei was appointed Magistrate of Anxi County in Zhongshan Commandery of Dingzhou. On an appointed day he took up his post.

Liu Bei dispersed his troops and returned home, keeping only twenty or so attendants. He arrived in Anxi with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei. He administered the county for a month; neither officials nor soldiers harmed the people in even a hair’s breadth, and the people were deeply moved.

When he took up his post, he and Guan Yu and Zhang Fei ate at the same table and slept on the same bed. As Liu Bei sat among crowds and many people, Guan and Zhang stood in attendance before him, tireless all day.

Before four months had passed, a Court edict arrived: all civil officials promoted for military merit were to be purged. Liu Bei suspected he would be removed.

At that moment the district inspector rode in. Liu Bei went out to meet him and offered formal welcome. The inspector gave him a brief salute from horseback and answered him with a cane and pointing gesture alone.

Guan Yu and Zhang Fei both grew angry.

At the guesthouse, the inspector sat facing south while Liu Bei stood in attendance below the steps.

After a while, the inspector asked, “Who is the Anxi magistrate by birth and station?”

Liu Bei answered, “I am descended from the King Jing of Zhongshan. From Zhuo Commandery, I helped wipe out the Yellow Turbans in thirty-odd engagements, large and small, and won some minor merit; I obtained this office because of that.”

The inspector shouted, “You claim imperial kinship falsely and exaggerate your exploits! The Court has just decreed that corrupt officials who took office without merit be purged!”

Liu Bei nodded repeatedly and withdrew.

Back in the county, he consulted with the county clerks. They said, “The inspector’s show of authority means only one thing—he is demanding a bribe.”

Liu Bei said, “I have wronged no one in my dealings with the people. How could I produce gifts for him?”

The next day the inspector dragged the clerks away first and forced them to claim that the magistrate had harmed the people.

Liu Bei made repeated appeals to have the matter waived, but he was always stopped by gate guards and not allowed inside.

Zhang Fei had had several cups of wine. He mounted and rode by the guesthouse, passing six or so old men weeping at the gate.

He asked why. They answered, “The inspector has pressured the clerks to accuse Liu Gong; we all came here to complain, but we are refused entry and are beaten back by the gatekeepers!”

Zhang Fei, furious, fixed his eyes like coins, clenched his teeth, leaped from the saddle, and went straight in. No gatekeeper could stop him.

He went at once to the rear hall and found the inspector still seated in the hall, with the county clerks already bound on the floor.

“Traitor who harms the people! Do you know me?” Zhang Fei shouted.

Before the inspector could answer, Zhang Fei seized his hair and dragged him out to the county front.

He tied him to a post and, seizing willow rods, struck the inspector’s two legs hard and repeatedly until more than ten rods snapped.

While Liu Bei was still perplexed at the commotion, he heard the noise outside the county and asked what it meant. He was told, “General Zhang has bound a man and is beating him before the county gate.”

Liu Bei hurried there and saw the bound man was the inspector.

He asked in shock what had happened.

Zhang Fei said, “Such a man who harms the people—how could he be left alive?”

The inspector cried out, “Liu Bei, lord, I would have died without your rescue!”

Though generous by nature, Liu Bei ordered, “Stop!” and Zhang Fei relented.

Guan Yu stepped from one side and said, “You have earned great service, elder brother, yet after all your merit you obtained only this magistracy. Now this inspector insults you. I think thorns and briars are not a place for dragons and phoenixes. It would be better to kill the inspector, cast off office, return home, and pursue greater plans elsewhere.”

Liu Bei took his insignia and put it around the inspector’s neck. He said, “For abusing the people you deserved death; I spare you this time. Keep your insignia and leave!”

The inspector returned to Dingzhou and reported to the commandery chief, Shen Wen. Shen Wen summoned the provincial office and sent men to arrest Liu Bei.

Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei went to Dai County and sought out Liu Hui.

When Liu Hui saw Liu Bei and recognized him as a scion of the Han house, he concealed and sheltered him at home.

The ten eunuchs, now in full control, met together. Any official who would not obey was executed. Zhao Zhong and Zhang Ràng sent officers to demand bribes from former Yellow Turban soldiers. Those who refused were dismissed.

Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun both refused to cooperate with them. Zhao Zhong and the others dismissed those two officials. The eunuchs then granted all thirteen of Zhang Ràng’s associates the rank of marquis.

State administration worsened, and the people sighed in complaint.

At once, in Changsha, bandits under Qu Xing rose; and in Yuyang, Zhang Ju and Zhang Chun rebelled. Zhang Ju proclaimed himself Son of Heaven; Zhang Chun called himself General-in-Chief. Their memorials from the hills came down in urgent dispatches.

The ten eunuchs hid everything and did not report.

One day, at a garden banquet with the eunuchs, the Censor Liu Tao strode straight before the emperor and wept loudly.

The emperor asked why.

Liu Tao said, “The realm is in danger before dawn. Your Majesty still shares your cup with eunuchs?”

The emperor replied, “The kingdom is peaceful. What danger can there be?”

Liu Tao said, “Bandit raiders rise in all four directions and plunder states and commanderies. Their troubles all spring from the ten eunuchs selling offices and titles, harming the people, deceiving the throne and misleading the court. The upright officials have gone; ruin is now at the gate.”

The eunuchs themselves removed their caps and knelt before the emperor, saying, “The senior ministers cannot endure one another with Your Majesty, and thus we cannot live. Permit us to return to our villages. We will give all our wealth to help with the campaign.”

Then they wept bitterly.

The emperor, angry, said to Liu Tao, “You yourself are near the inner attendants. Why do you alone oppose me?” He ordered guards to execute him.

As Liu Tao was carried out with the soldiers, one high minister shouted, “Do not lay hands on him yet. Let me offer counsel first.”

All eyes turned; it was the Minister over the Masses, Chen Dan. He entered the hall and remonstrated:

Liu Tao, who obtained what crime, merits execution?”

The emperor said, “He slandered those near Your Majesty and dared to presume before me.”

Chen Dan said, “The people, seeing these eunuchs, want only their blood. You honor them as mother and father, yet they have done nothing for the realm and are only rewarded with peerage titles. Now they conspire with the Yellow Turbans and seek inner turmoil. If Your Majesty does not introspect now, the state will fall apart.”

The emperor replied, “Feng Xu and his associates are in revolt. The facts are not clear. Are there not one or two loyal men among the eunuchs?”

Chen Dan tried to reason and even struck his head against the stair in grief.

The emperor grew angry, ordered him and Liu Tao in chains, and both went to prison.

That same night the eunuchs plotted in the jail to kill them. Using a forged imperial edict, they ordered Sun Jian appointed Governor of Changsha to suppress Quxing.

Not fifty days later news of victory came: Jiangxia had been pacified.

The Court made Sun Jian Marquis of Wucheng, and Liu Yu Governor of Youzhou with command to march to Yuyang and punish Zhang Ju and Zhang Chun.

Liu Hui of Dai County wrote a memorial recommending Liu Bei to Liu Yu.

Liu Yu rejoiced and made Liu Bei a duwei. Liu Bei marched directly to the rebel nest and fought them for several days, shaking their edge and spirit.

Zhang Chun was cruel and arbitrary. His soldiers’ hearts turned from him. One of his captains and lieutenants stabbed him and brought his head as a gift, then led the band together into surrender.

Zhang Ju saw his position fail and hanged himself. Yuyang was fully pacified.

Liu Yu reported Liu Bei’s major merit. The Court pardoned Liu Bei’s beating of the inspector, removed him from office as a lower assistant in Xia-mi, and transferred him to Gaotang Wèi.

Gongsun Zan then submitted a memorial praising Liu Bei’s earlier service and recommending him as a separate unit’s staff officer and later Magistrate of Pingyuan County.

In Pingyuan, Liu Bei had both money and horses, and he gradually restored his old vigor.

Liu Yu’s success against the raiders brought him promotion to Grand Commandant.

In the sixth year of the Zhongping era, in the fourth month, Emperor Ling fell mortally ill and called General-in-Chief He Jin into the palace to discuss succession.

He Jin, being born into a family elevated by office and connected to the palace through his sister, had by then gained heavy authority. The sister entered as an imperial consort, became empress, and bore a son, Liu Bian. Soon after, another beauty from the Wang household gained favor and bore a son, Liu Xie.

She was the empress. Jealousy drove her to poison the Wang beauty. Liu Xie was raised in Empress Dowager Dong’s palace.

Empress Dowager Dong, the mother of the emperor, had been wife of Liu Chang, Marquis of Jiedu Pavilion. In earlier times, when Emperor Huan had no sons, the court brought in Liu Chang’s son and enthroned him as Emperor Ling. When he inherited the great charge, he brought his mother into the inner palace and honored her as empress dowager.

Dowager Dong had urged the emperor to appoint Liu Xie as crown prince, and the emperor also loved him and wished to do so.

While the emperor was still gravely ill, the middle-ranked eunuch Jian Shuo said, “If Your Majesty is to enthrone Liu Xie, He Jin must first be executed, to remove future danger.”

The emperor accepted and summoned He Jin into the palace.

When he arrived at the gate, the Sima officer Pan Yin told him, “Do not enter. Jian Shuo means to kill you.” He Jin was startled, returned home at once, and summoned ministers, intending to execute the eunuchs.

At that table, one man stepped forward and said:

“The eunuchs’ power began under Qiang and Zhi. Their roots now spread through the Court. How can they all be cut away at once? If the operation is clumsy, entire clans may be destroyed. It is best to investigate thoroughly before moving.”

He Jin looked and recognized him as Military Adviser Cao Cao.

He Jin barked, “What does a youth like you know of major affairs of state?”

While he still hesitated, Pan Yin returned and reported, “The emperor has died. Jian Shuo has already confederated with the ten eunuchs and is withholding the news of the mourning. He has forged edicts to summon you, He Jin, into the palace and to eliminate your followers, securing the succession for Liu Xie and making him emperor. A messenger has arrived. He says: enter quickly and settle the succession.”

Cao Cao said, “Before we do anything else, we must first set the ruler right; only then can we deal with the brigands. A wrong throne cannot be corrected later.”

He Jin asked, “Who will stand with me to set the ruler and punish these villains?”

A man stood: “Grant me five thousand picked soldiers; I will cut through the gates, enthrone a new Son of Heaven, execute the eunuchs, clear the Court, and settle the realm.”

He Jin recognized him as Yuan Shao, son of Yuan Feng and nephew of Yuan Wai, serving as Colonel of the Capital. He was pleased and gave him command of the Palace Guards, five thousand men.

He Jin then brought over He Yong, Xun You, Zheng Tai, and more than thirty ministers, and one after another they entered and stood before the emperor’s bier. They raised the crown prince, Liu Bian, to the imperial throne.

After all officials had completed their salutes, Yuan Shao entered the palace and arrested Jian Shuo. Jian Shuo fled in panic into the shadows of the imperial garden and was killed by the inner attendant Guo Sheng. His whole garrison turned to the victor.

Yuan Shao said to He Jin, “The eunuch clique has conspired as one. Today the moment is ripe—execute them all.”

Zhang Ràng and the others learned this and hurriedly informed the empress Dowager.

“Originally, it was only Jian Shuo who plotted against the General-in-Chief; we had no hand in it,” they said. “Now He Jin listens to Yuan Shao and intends to wipe us all out. I beg your mercy.”

Empress Dong answered, “Do not fear. I will protect you.” She sent an order summoning He Jin.

In private she said, “He Jin and I came from poor origins. Without men like Zhang Ràng we could never have had such wealth or power. Jian Shuo was cruel. He has already been executed; why do you now believe slander when people claim you will exterminate the eunuchs?”

He Jin listened and then told the assembly, “Jian Shuo plotted against me. His whole line should be exterminated. As for the rest, do not slay them out of hand.”

Yuan Shao said, “If we do not pull out the roots now, this will become a source of death.”

He Jin answered, “My decision is made. Do not press further.”

All officials withdrew.

The next day, the empress dowager asked He Jin to co-administer the central secretariat and appointed him to other offices.

He told Zhang Ràng and the others to come into the palace to confer:

“He Jin’s sister, when I first entered this court, she raised him. Now his younger brother stands as emperor, and ministers inside and out are his intimates. His authority is too great. What are we to do?”

Zhang Ràng said, “Your Majesty should rule behind a screen and hear affairs from behind the curtain. Appoint Liu Xie as a king; appoint Dong Chong, your brother-in-law, as Piaoqi General, and restore military control to you. If the great officers are employed, we can accomplish much.”

Empress Dowager Dong was delighted.

On the next day, at court, she issued an edict: Liu Xie was made Prince of Chenliu, and Dong Chong was made Piaoqi General. Zhang Ràng and others entered into shared administration of Court affairs.

Dowager He then saw that Empress Dong dominated too openly. She hosted a banquet inside the palace and invited Empress Dong.

At mid-drinking, Dowager He stood, raised her cup, bowed twice, and said:

“We are all women and should not involve ourselves in state governance. Former Empress Lü’s clan was annihilated with a thousand mouths after she wielded great power. We should now remain within the inner chambers. Let ministers and veterans conduct state affairs. That is best for the country. Please grant that.”

Empress Dong was furious: “You killed Lady Wang by poison. Now you dare speak for this realm with your brother’s power behind you! I order your command in the cavalry to sever your brother’s head as easily as clapping hands.”

Dowager He also replied angrily, “I spoke out of concern. Why do you rage?”

Empress Dong spat back, “Your family are but butchers and fishmongers. What knowledge do you claim?”

The two courts fiercely competed for power. Zhang Ràng and the others each urged each other to leave the palace.

He Jin was summoned by his sister through the night and told of the matter. He Jin then convened three fellow officials and planned:

“We should summon an early audience and have the ministers state that Empress Dong, initially just a palace consort from another household, should not stay in the palace indefinitely. She must be moved back to Hejian and ordered to leave the capital within days.”

At the same time he sent men to escort Empress Dong out and ordered troops to surround Piaoqi General Dong Chong’s mansion to seize his seal and insignia.

Dong Chong saw the danger and hanged himself in the back hall.

His household wailed. The soldiers dispersed.

Zhang Ràng and Duan Gui saw that Empress Dong had been formally removed. They cultivated He Qu and his family with gold and jewels, and arranged for regular visits to Empress Dowager He from He Qu and his mother, Lady Wuyang.

Through words they protected their influence, and so the ten eunuchs won favor at court again.

In the sixth month He Jin secretly had Empress Dong poisoned at Hejian station, had her coffin returned to the capital, and buried her at Wenling.

Feigning illness, He Jin did not leave his quarters. Yuan Shao arrived and warned him:

“Zhang Ràng, Duan Gui and others spread stories outside that Your Grace poisoned Empress Dong and is planning great trouble. This is not the time to forgo action against the eunuchs; if we do not act, a catastrophe will follow.

Dou Wu once sought to execute inner palace personnel. The stratagem was careless and he himself suffered for it. Now all your brothers, subordinate commanders, and clerks are people of ability. If they all exert themselves, success is in hand. This is Heaven’s support; we must not miss it.”

He Jin replied, “Let us discuss it first.”

Zhang Ràng and the others quickly informed He Miao and poured gifts.

He Miao entered and reported to the empress dowager:

“The General-in-Chief now, as advisor to the new emperor, uses no leniency and focuses only on killing. He wants also to kill the eunuchs, which is the path to disorder.”

The empress accepted his words.

Soon after, He Jin entered to petition the empress dowager on executing the eunuchs.

She said, “The eunuchs command the inner court. In Han custom they are old retainers. The previous emperor left no peace to the land. You would kill old ministers as if they were enemies of the ancestral temple.”

He Jin, not firm enough by nature, nodded and withdrew.

Yuan Shao asked when he saw him, “What is the state of matters?”

He Jin said, “The empress dowager will not agree. What can we do?”

Yuan Shao said, “Send messengers to the generals and commanders in all corners, summon them to the capital, and execute all eunuchs. The moment is urgent; we cannot wait for the dowager’s consent.”

He Jin said, “This is excellent.” He then sent mobilization edicts to each commandery.

Clerk Chen Lin objected:

“Do not do it. The saying goes, ‘to blindfold oneself and catch a sparrow’—that is self-deception. If you cannot even trick a small thing, how will you manage state destiny? You now hold imperial might and command troops. If you truly wish to execute eunuchs, the work is like burning hair in a kiln’s flame—quick and complete.

But to issue broad commands to ministers while we are still moving so swiftly is dangerous. Outside forces arriving at the capital will gather with weapons, each with his own designs. That is like placing arms in hands already bent against you. Your success will fail, and chaos will follow.”

He Jin laughed, “That is the view of a coward.”

At his side one man clapped and laughed loudly. “This matter is as easy as turning a hand; why deliberate?”

It was Cao Cao.

The chapter closed:

To remove corruption by courtiers beside the Son of Heaven, heed the counsel of the wise ministers in court.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhang Fei Whips the Inspector in Anger; Imperial Uncle He Plots to Execute the Eunuchs

chapters.html:
Cao Cao, whose courtesy name was Mengde, told He Jin that day, “The catastrophe caused by the eunuchs has happened in all ages. The ruler should not have given them such power and favor, for that is how this came to pass. If they are to be punished, remove the original evil, but one jailer would suffice. Why summon troops from outside in such a clamorous way? If you aim to execute everyone, the matter will certainly be exposed. I think they are doomed.”

He Jin grew angry. “Mengde also harbors private intent?”

Cao Cao withdrew. “The one to bring disorder to the realm is you, He Jin.”

He Jin sent secret envoys with a secret edict through the night.

Dong Zhuo, Former General and Marquis of Lixiang, was Inspector of Liang Province. He had once won no merit in suppressing the Yellow Turbans. The court intended to punish him, but he bribed the Ten Eunuchs and was spared. Later he attached himself to court magnates and rose to high office, commanding two hundred thousand troops in the western provinces and always harboring disloyal thoughts. At this point, when he received the edict, he rejoiced, raised his forces, and prepared to depart. He left his son-in-law, General of the Household Niu Fu, to hold Shaanxi, while he himself led Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, Fan Chou, and others toward Luoyang.

His strategist Li Ru said, “Though we now obey the edict, there is much uncertainty. Why not send someone to court with a memorial, giving us the appearance of righteousness? A larger matter is available.”

Dong Zhuo rejoiced, then submitted a memorial. It read:

I have learned that the repeated rebellions and turmoil of the realm stem from Zhang Rang and the other eunuchs of the inner court. If one wants to stop boiling water, one should remove the firewood, not just remove the boiling surface. A spreading abscess, though painful, is better to lance than to nurse poison. I dare to beat bell and drum and ride into Luoyang to request their removal. May the state be fortunate! May the world be fortunate!

When He Jin presented the memorial to the ministers, Attendant Censor Zheng Tai remonstrated, “Dong Zhuo is a jackal and a wolf. If he is admitted into the capital, he will certainly devour men.”

He Jin said, “You are too suspicious and not fit to plan great affairs.”

Lu Zhi also remonstrated, “I have long known Dong Zhuo’s nature. He has a kind face and a hard heart. Once he enters the inner court, calamities will surely arise. We should stop him from entering to avoid fresh disorder.”

He Jin ignored them, and Zheng Tai and Lu Zhi both left office. Most of the ministers at court also left. He Jin sent men to receive Dong Zhuo at Mianchi Pool, where Dong Zhuo held his troops in place.

When Zhang Rang and the others learned that outside troops were arriving, they held counsel together. “It is He Jin’s plot. If we do not strike first, our clans will be exterminated.”

They first stationed fifty men with knives and axes inside Jia-de Gate of Changle Palace. They burst into the inner palace and petitioned the Empress Dowager: “The Grand General has falsified an edict and called outside troops to the capital, intending to destroy us. Please have pity and save us.”

The Empress Dowager said, “You may go to the Grand General’s residence and make your amends.”

Zhang Rang said, “If we go before the Prime Minister, our bones will be ground to paste. Command His Majesty to summon him, tell him to stop here, and keep him from proceeding. If he refuses, we and our men will come here to die before you.”

The Empress Dowager issued an edict and summoned He Jin. He Jin acted on it.

Chief Clerk Chen Lin remonstrated, “This edict from the Empress Dowager must be the Ten Eunuchs’ scheme. You must not go. If you go, disaster follows.”

He Jin replied, “The Empress Dowager has commanded me. What danger can there be?”

Yuan Shao said, “The plan is already exposed and the plot known. Do you still intend to enter the palace?”

Cao Cao said, “First summon out the Ten Eunuchs, and then enter.”

He Jin laughed. “That is a child’s view. I hold power over the realm. How can the Ten Eunuchs dare to do anything?”

Yuan Shao said, “If you must go in, we will have armored troops to protect you in case of contingencies.”

So Yuan Shao and Cao Cao each selected 500 elite soldiers. He placed Yuan Shao’s brother Yuan Shu in command. Yuan Shu armoured himself fully and deployed his men outside Qingsuo Gate. Yuan Shao and Cao Cao, both with unsheathed swords, escorted He Jin to the forecourt of Changle Palace.

A palace attendant of the Yellow Gates brought an order from the Empress Dowager: “The Empress Dowager specifically summoned the Grand General; the others are not to enter.”

Yuan Shao, Cao Cao, and those with them were halted outside the gate.

He Jin strode in directly.

At the gate of Jia-de Hall, Zhang Rang and Duan Gui came out to welcome him, and their men surrounded him. He Jin was struck with alarm. “What are you doing?” Zhang Rang cried sharply.

“What crime did Empress Dong commit that you dare to speak of poisoning her? You claim she is only sick and absent from mourning, yet you treat this as cause enough to act? You began as a petty butcher, and it was through our recommendation that you rose to honor and wealth. Yet now you mean to destroy us! You call us corrupt—but who among us is clean?”

He Jin panicked and searched for an escape. The palace gates were fully closed. Armored men came out all at once and cut He Jin in two.

Someone later lamented in verse:

The Han realm tottered, heaven’s signs ending, and He Jin, without counsel, made three lords his own. Again and again the loyal ministers advised, yet he could not avoid the sword’s edge in the palace.

When Zhang Rang and the others had killed He Jin, Yuan Shao remained long without seeing him emerge. He then shouted from outside the gate, “Bring the general out in a carriage!”

Zhang Rang and the others threw He Jin’s severed head over the wall and announced: “He Jin plotted rebellion and has already been executed. All others coerced with him are all pardoned.”

Yuan Shao shouted, “The eunuchs killed a major minister! All who punish evil are summoned to rise and aid in battle!”

Wu Kuang, one of He Jin’s captains, set fire at Qingsuo Gate. Yuan Shu led his men in sudden assault into the palace. Where there were eunuchs, whether high or low, he killed them all.

Yuan Shao and Cao Cao cut through the gates and entered. Zhao Zhong, Cheng Kuang, Xia Yun, and Guo Sheng were driven to Cuihua Tower and chopped to paste.

Fire rose to the sky from the palace. Zhang Rang, Duan Gui, Cao Jie, and Hou Lan seized the Empress Dowager and the crown prince and Prince of Chenliu, carrying them into the inner court by the northern passage.

At that time Lu Zhi had not yet left office, and seeing the confusion in the palace, he donned armour and took up his halberd, standing beneath the pavilion. At a distance he saw Duan Gui dragging the Empress Dowager forward, and he shouted, “Duan Gui, traitor, how dare you seize the Empress Dowager?” Duan Gui turned and fled.

The Empress Dowager leapt from a window; Lu Zhi quickly rescued and saved her. Wu Kuang burst into the inner courtyard and saw He Miao coming out with drawn sword.

Wu Kuang shouted, “He Miao conspired to kill his brother. He must die!”

All replied, “We are willing to execute the one who conspired against his brother!”

He Miao tried to flee; surrounded on all sides, he was chopped to paste.

Yuan Shao again ordered his soldiers in different directions to kill the Ten Eunuchs’ household, without distinguishing rank or age. Many, including beardless men by mistake, were also killed.

At the same time, Cao Cao extinguished the palace fire, and begged the Empress Dowager to take authority over state affairs. He sent troops to pursue Zhang Rang and his men and to continue searching for the young emperor.

As for Zhang Rang and Duan Gui, who had taken the young emperor and Prince of Chenliu, they fled through smoke and flame northward in desperation. Around the third watch, shouts rose behind them, and mounted men closed in.

Ahead, the middle clerk of the commandery Min Gong shouted, “Treachous ones, do not run!”

Seeing the urgency, Zhang Rang threw himself into the river and died. The emperor and Prince of Chenliu, uncertain whether they were in danger, did not cry out. They crouched among thicket by the riverbank, while riders dispersed in pursuit and failed to know where the emperor had gone.

At the fourth watch, the two remained hidden there. Dampness was falling, and hunger gnawed at their bellies. They clung together and wept in whispers, afraid to raise their voices in the weeds.

The Prince of Chenliu said, “We cannot stay here. We must separate and find some way to survive.”

So the two tied their clothing together and climbed to the bank. The ground was all thorny with no visible path. As they despaired, hundreds of fireflies gathered in a cluster, and only their light moved in front of the emperor. The prince said, “Heaven aids us, brothers.”

They followed the fireflies and gradually found a way.

By dawn, their feet ached so much they could not continue. They lay down by a heap of grass at the side of a knoll. Before it stood a farmhouse. The householder had dreamed that night of two red suns falling behind his home, awoke startled, dressed, and came out to look around. He saw a red light rising to the sky above the grass heap behind the house and hurried over to see the two youths lying there.

The householder asked, “Which house are these two boys from?”

The emperor did not answer. The Prince of Chenliu pointed and said, “This is the present emperor, who has escaped the Ten Eunuchs’ chaos. I am Prince of Chenliu, brother of the emperor.”

The man was shocked and knelt again: “I am Cui Yi, younger brother to Cui Lie, former Minister over the Masses of the old court. I have hidden here because I saw the eunuchs selling offices and excluding worthy men.”

He carried them in, helped the emperor inside, and knelt to present food and wine.

Min Gong soon caught Duan Gui and seized him, then asked where the Son of Heaven was.

Duan Gui answered that he had lost contact midway and did not know where the emperor had gone.

Min Gong killed Duan Gui and hung the head under the horse’s collar, then sent soldiers in four directions to search. Alone, he mounted and kept riding.

By chance he reached Cui Yi’s estate. Cui Yi saw the head and asked. Min Gong explained everything.

Cui Yi brought Min Gong before the emperor and the Prince. Both lord and minister wept.

Min Gong said, “The state cannot be without a ruler for even a single day. Please, Your Majesty, return to the capital.”

In Cui Yi’s house there was only one thin horse for the emperor to ride. Min Gong and Prince of Chenliu shared one horse.

After they left, less than three li away came out Minister over the Masses Wang Yun, Grand Commandant Yang Biao, Left Army Colonel Chunyu Qiong, Right Army Colonel Zhao Meng, Rear Army Colonel Bao Xin, and Central Army Colonel Yuan Shao, along with hundreds of men and horses. They followed the imperial carriage; all wept as they traveled.

Before anything else they sent Duan Gui’s head to the capital and gave orders.

Then they exchanged mounts and gave fresh horses for the emperor and Prince of Chenliu, and began escorting them back to the capital.

A children’s saying in Luoyang was already known: “The emperor is no emperor, the king is no king. A thousand chariots and ten thousand riders run toward Bei Mang.” Its fulfillment came in full.

When the procession had not gone far when banners covered the sky and dust blocked heaven, a unit of horsemen appeared at once. Officials turned pale, and even the emperor trembled.

Yuan Shao rode forward and asked aloud who was coming.

Behind embroidered banners, a general jumped from horseback and shouted, “Where is the Son of Heaven?”

The emperor trembled and could not answer. The Prince of Chenliu scolded, “Who are you, who comes here?”

It was Dong Zhuo, Inspector of Xiliang: “I am Dong Zhuo of Xiliang.”

The prince said, “You came to escort the carriage, did you? Yet you came to seize it, did you not?”

Dong Zhuo answered, “I came to protect the carriage.”

The prince said, “If you have come for that, and the Son of Heaven is here, why do you not dismount?”

Dong Zhuo was astonished. He hastily dismounted and knelt on the left side of the road.

The Prince of Chenliu spoke in controlled tones all the way, calming Dong Zhuo with words and never missing a phrase.

Dong Zhuo admired him in secret, and already held thoughts of enthronement.

That day they returned to the palace. Dong Zhuo and the Empress Dowager both wept together. He checked the palace and found the Heirloom Imperial Seal missing.

Dong Zhuo stationed his troops outside the city. Each day he brought iron-armoured cavalry into Luoyang and roamed the streets. The people were terrified and uneasy. He moved through the palace as if he feared no one.

The Right Army Colonel Bao Xin went to Yuan Shao and warned that Dong Zhuo surely had ulterior motives and should be removed at once.

Yuan Shao replied, “The court has only just been restored; we should not act rashly.”

Bao Xin also spoke to Wang Yun. Wang Yun said, “Let us discuss this first.”

Then Bao Xin took his own troops and withdrew toward Mount Tai.

Dong Zhuo attracted soldiers from He Jin’s men and drew them under his control.

Dong Zhuo asked Li Ru privately, “I intend to depose the emperor and enthrone the Prince of Chenliu. What do you think?”

Li Ru said, “The court has no master now. We should act now; if we delay, changes will come. Tomorrow in Wenming Garden we should summon all ministers and announce deposition and enthronement. Those who refuse should be executed. Then your authority will be established today.”

Dong Zhuo was glad.

The next day he arranged a grand banquet and invited all the ministers. Since Dong Zhuo was frightening, no one dared not appear. When the ministers had assembled, Dong Zhuo dismounted at the garden gate and entered slowly before all, sword at his side.

After several rounds of serving wine, he ordered the music to stop and said, “I have one matter to state. Let all officials keep still.”

The ministers hushed.

Dong Zhuo said, “The Son of Heaven is lord over the ten thousand families, but without dignity one cannot serve at ancestral and state temples. The present Son of Heaven is feeble; the Prince of Chenliu is clever and studious and can bear the Great Seat. I intend to depose the emperor and enthrone the Prince of Chenliu. What do you think all this?”

No one among the ministers dared to speak.

One man pushed the table aside and stood in front of the feast.

He shouted, “Impossible! Impossible! Who are you to speak so? The Son of Heaven is the elder son of the late emperor and has no fault. By what ground do you dare to speak of deposing and enthroning? Do you seek to usurp?”

Dong Zhuo saw him and knew him as Ding Yuan, Inspector of Jing Province.

Dong Zhuo shouted, “Those who follow me shall live; those who oppose me shall die!” He drew his waist sword to behead Ding Yuan.

Li Ru said, “This is no place at a banquet to discuss state affairs. Let this be handled tomorrow in the hall for full deliberation.”

After others urged, Ding Yuan mounted and left.

Dong Zhuo asked the ministers, “Was what I said in accord with public truth?”

Lu Zhi replied, “Illustrious lord is mistaken. In former times, when King Taijia was unclear, Yi Yin exiled him to the Hall of Tong. When King of Changyi ascended and ruled for twenty-seven days only, he amassed more than three thousand offenses. Huo Guang presented a memorial in the ancestral hall and deposed him. Though the present Son of Heaven is young, he is intelligent and benevolent and bears no fault. You are a provincial inspector from far away and have long never entered state affairs; yet you do not have the capacity of Yi Yin or Huo Guang. How can you force this deposition and enthronement? The sages said, “He who has Yi Yin’s will may do this; he who lacks it is a usurper.””

Dong Zhuo grew angry and drew his sword to kill Lu Zhi.

Shangshu Lu Zhi was consulted by Councillor Peng Bo: “Shangshu Lu Zhi is widely esteemed across the realm. If you first harm him, the whole empire will be shaken by terror.”

Dong Zhuo stopped.

The Minister over the Masses Wang Yun said, “Matters of deposition and enthronement should not be settled after drinking. On another day we should discuss them.”

The ministers all dispersed.

Dong Zhuo kept his sword at the gate and then saw a man riding in and out of view beyond the gate, carrying a halberd.

He asked Li Ru, “Who is that man?”

Li Ru replied, “It is the one called Ding Yuan’s sworn companion: a man surnamed Lü, named Lü Bu, courtesy name Fengxian. My lord must avoid him.”

Dong Zhuo moved quietly into the garden to avoid him.

The next day they heard that Ding Yuan had brought out his army and challenged battle. Dong Zhuo grew angry and rode with his troops, Li Ru at his side.

The two formations arrayed opposite each other. Lü Bu rode in with his hair tied up under a cap, a hundred-flower war robe, tiger-leopard armour, and a lion-marten-jeweled belt. He rode hard and came forward with Ding Jianyang.

Ding Jianyang pointed at Dong Zhuo and shouted, “The state has not been blessed; eunuchs have usurped authority, and all under heaven burns in distress. You have no merit of even an inch. How dare you speak of deposition and enthronement and seek to disrupt the court?”

Dong Zhuo had not yet answered when Lü Bu charged at him on horseback.

Dong Zhuo hurriedly fled. Ding Jianyang’s units covered and killed the enemy. Dong Zhuo’s army was routed, falling back more than thirty li before setting a camp, then gathering the men for consultation.

Dong Zhuo said, “I have seen that Lü Bu is no ordinary man. If I gain him, what has the world to fear?”

A man came before the tent and said, “My lord, do not worry. I am from the same homeland as Lü Bu. He is brave but without stratagem; he sees profit and forgets righteousness. By my long and smooth tongue I can make him lay down his arms and surrender to us. Can that be done?”

Dong Zhuo looked at him, and it was Li Su of the Tiger Guards. Dong Zhuo asked, “How will you do it?”

Li Su said, “I have heard my lord has a famous horse called Chitu, a thousand li a day. If one first obtains this horse and then gives gold and pearls, Lü Bu’s heart can be won. I can speak more to him. He will surely turn from Ding Yuan and come to my lord.”

Dong Zhuo asked Li Ru, “Is this feasible?”

Li Ru answered, “If my lord wishes to take the world, why should one horse matter?”

Dong Zhuo gladly gave him one thousand taels of gold, several bright pearls, and a jade belt.

Li Su took the gifts and came to Lü Bu’s camp. Soldiers ringed the road.

Li Su said, “Take this to General Lü quickly: a familiar man has come.”

The soldiers informed him. Lü Bu asked to receive him.

Li Su told him, “Respected younger brother, is all well with you, since we have not met?”

Lü Bu bowed and asked, “It has been long. Where have you been?”

Li Su said, “I have accepted office as Tiger Guard Commander. I heard of your loyalty in guarding the realm and am happiest than words can say. There is a splendid horse, able to run a thousand li a day, cross rivers and climb mountains as though on level ground. Its name is Chitu. I present it to you, to help your martial grandeur.”

Lü Bu had it brought. Truly, the horse was red like hot embers, with not one strand of odd hair. Its length was a full ten chi and it was eight chi from hoof to withers. Its neigh and roar seemed as if it could leap into the sea.

Later people recited a poem:

It rushes a thousand li, flinging up dust. Through water and over mountains, violet mist parts. It snaps loose the silk reins and sways the jade bit; A fire-dragon descends from the ninth heaven.

Lü Bu rejoiced to see it and said, “Brother, you have gifted this good horse. How shall I repay?”

Li Su replied, “I came from brotherly loyalty, not for repayment.”

Lü Bu set wine before him.

When the wine had taken effect, Li Su said, “You and I have rarely had a chance to meet, worthy brother, but I often see your honored father.”

Lü Bu said, “Brother, you are drunk! My father died many years ago. How could you meet him?”

Li Su laughed. “No, no. I meant Inspector Ding, whom you serve today.”

Lü Bu said uneasily, “I remain with Ding Jianyang only because I have no alternative.”

Li Su said, “You have talent to hold heaven and steer the seas; who among the four seas does not revere you? Fame and rank can be as easy as reaching into a sleeve. Why call yourself one without remedy?”

Lü Bu said, “I regret not meeting one’s lord.”

Li Su said, “A worthy bird chooses its tree. A worthy minister chooses his lord. To see the moment too late leads to regret.”

Lü Bu asked, “In the court, who among these is the age’s true hero?”

Li Su said, “I have reviewed all officials. None compare with Dong Zhuo. Dong Zhuo honors the worthy and punishes the guilty clearly. He will become one of the great achievers.”

Lü Bu said, “I want to follow him, but have no route.”

Li Su laid out the gold, pearls, and jade belt before him.

Lü Bu was astonished. “How did these come here?”

Li Su sent everyone away and said to Lü Bu, “This is Dong Gong’s long-coveted gift, sent by my lord to present to you. The horse Chitu is also given by Dong Gong.”

Lü Bu said, “If my lord Dong honors me so much, how should I report gratitude?”

Li Su said, “Though I lack talent, I am still a Tiger Guard Commander. If you come to my lord, your status will be beyond words.”

Lü Bu said, “I regret having no trace of merit by which I could make proper presentation.”

Li Su said, “The deed lies within a turn of your hand; the only question is whether you are willing.”

After long thought Lü Bu said, “I wish to kill Ding Yuan and return with my troops to Dong Zhuo. What of this?”

Li Su said, “If you can do this, it is a great achievement indeed. Do it at once; do not delay.”

They agreed to surrender the next day, and Li Su departed.

At the second watch of the night, Lü Bu entered Ding Yuan’s tent with his blade drawn. Ding Yuan was reading by lamplight when he saw him arrive.

Ding Yuan asked, “My son, what brings you here?”

Lü Bu answered, “I am a man of honor and stature. How could I consent to be your son?”

Ding Yuan asked, “Why has your heart changed?”

Lü Bu stepped forward and in one stroke cut off Ding Yuan’s head. He shouted, “Guards! Ding Yuan was not loyal. I have killed him. Those who follow me, stay; those who do not, go their own way.”

Most soldiers scattered.

The next day Lü Bu rode with Ding Yuan’s head to Li Su. Li Su then brought him before Dong Zhuo.

Dong Zhuo rejoiced and set out wine in welcome. He bowed first and said, “Now that I have gained you, General, I am like a parched seedling receiving sweet rain.”

Lü Bu did not take his own seat and, kneeling, said, “If my lord does not reject me, I request to call you my father by righteousness.”

Dong Zhuo gave him golden armour and embroidered robes and bestowed on him honours, appointing him Commander of the Cavalry and Gentleman Attendant of the Palace, and granting him the marquisate of Tuting.

From then Dong Zhuo’s authority grew; he took charge of the former general command. He made his brother Dong Min Left General and Marquis of Hu, and made Lü Bu Commander of Cavalry and an Internal Cavalry Gentleman, Marquis of Tuting.

Li Ru urged Dong Zhuo to settle deposition and enthronement at once. Dong Zhuo again held a banquet in the court and gathered all ministers, placing more than a thousand armed soldiers in guard around him. That day Grand Tutor Yuan Kui and all officials came.

After several rounds of wine, Dong Zhuo drew his sword and said, “The present Son of Heaven is feeble and cannot serve the ancestral temple and state altars. I will follow Yi Yin and Huo Guang, depose the emperor and make him King of Hongnong, and enthrone the Prince of Chenliu as emperor. Those who do not obey will be beheaded.”

The ministers were terrified and did not dare to speak.

Yuan Shao, Central Army Colonel, stepped out: “His Majesty ascended not long ago and has shown no wrongdoing. You seek to depose the legitimate son and enthrone a collateral line. Is that not treason?”

Dong Zhuo shouted, “State affairs are in my hands. If I do this, who dares not follow? Do you think my sword is not sharp?”

Yuan Shao drew his sword too: “Your sword is sharp; mine has never been dull.”

The two faced each other on the feast, ready for clash.

Ding Yuan stood for justice and was first to lose his life; How will Yuan Shao’s life end?

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Deliberation at Wenming, Dong Zhuo Rebukes Ding Yuan, and Li Su Gifts Red-Jewel Treasures to Persuade Lü Bu

chapters.html:
When Dong Zhuo wanted to kill Yuan Shao, Li Ru restrained him and said, “The matter is not settled yet. Do not kill in haste.”

Yuan Shao left with his sword in hand, bidding farewell to the hundred officials and walking out. He hung his travel tally at the East Gate and rode for Jizhou. Dong Zhuo said to Grand Tutor Yuan Kui, “Your nephew has no propriety. Looking at your face, I will forgive him for now. What should be done about the issue of deposition and enthronement?” Yuan Kui replied, “What the Grand Commandant saw is the way it should be.”

Dong Zhuo said, “If anyone blocks this great decision, punish them by military law.”

The other ministers, trembling, all said, “We will obey your command.”
