After the banquet, Dong Zhuo asked the Court Attendant Zhou Bi and Colonel Wu Qiong, “What will come of Yuan Shao’s departure?” Zhou Bi said, “Yuan Shao left in anger. If you press him too hard, he is certain to rebel. The Yuan family has dispensed favors for four generations; their former pupils and officials are everywhere under heaven. If he gathers bold men and raises a following, heroes will rise with him, and the lands east of the passes will no longer be yours. Better to pardon him and appoint him administrator of a commandery. He will rejoice at escaping punishment, and there will be no danger.”

Wu Qiong said, “Yuan Shao likes to scheme but cannot carry things through to judgment. No need to worry overmuch about him. Better still, appoint him one commandery governor and win the people’s heart.”

Dong Zhuo followed their suggestions and that very day sent an order appointing Yuan Shao as Governor of Bohai. On the first day of the ninth month he asked the emperor to go to Jia De Hall for a grand assembly of civil and military officers.

Dong Zhuo drew his sword and said to all, “The Son of Heaven is dim in nature and unfit to rule the world. I have now a memorial draft to be read.” He then ordered Li Ru to read it:

The late Emperor Ling of Han abandoned his people too early; after him, the world looked up to the successor of the throne. Yet the present Emperor was born light-minded and lacked dignity, and in his mourning period he was lazy and negligent. When his faults are so clearly manifest, he is unworthy of the great seat. The Empress Dowager has not governed by maternal guidance, and state administration has become disorderly. When Empress Dowager Yongle suddenly died, all men were confused.

Are not the Way of the Three Bonds and the order of Heaven and Earth now in question?

The Prince of Chenliu, Liu Xie, possesses lofty and abundant virtue and observes the rules of conduct with solemn care. In mourning he has shown grief; his words have never strayed from what is right. His excellent reputation is known throughout the realm. He should inherit the Great Enterprise and establish the succession for ten thousand generations.

Therefore the Emperor is hereby deposed and made King of Hongnong, and the Empress Dowager shall return authority to the throne. Let the Prince of Chenliu be received as emperor, in accord with Heaven and the people, to answer the hopes of all living souls.

When Li Ru finished reading, Dong Zhuo shouted for attendants to help the emperor down from the hall. He removed his seals and ribbons and, facing north, knelt long and said he was Your servant and would obey. Then he ordered the Empress Dowager to put away formal mourning attire and wait for an imperial command.

Emperor and Empress Dowager wailed together. No minister in the hall was without grief.

A major official from the steps below shouted in rage, “Treacherous minister Dong Zhuo, how dare you attempt a plot against Heaven? I will spray your face with my own blood from my throat!” He raised an ivory baton in hand and struck straight at Dong Zhuo.

Dong Zhuo was furious. He shouted for soldiers, who hauled the man out. He was none other than Shangshu Minister Ding Guan. Dong ordered him seized and beheaded. Ding Guan kept cursing without ceasing and never changed expression until death.

Later people composed a poem of lament:

The traitor Dong long hid a design to depose and enthrone; The Han’s temples and ancestral halls were cast to rubble. All the ministers of the court looted the court for themselves, Yet in them all only Ding Gong kept the stature of a true man.

Dong Zhuo invited the Prince of Chenliu to ascend the throne.

After the ministers had offered their congratulations, Dong ordered Empress Dowager He, the King of Hongnong, and the emperor’s consort Lady Tang confined in Yongan Palace. He sealed the palace gates and forbade the ministers to enter without permission.

The pitiful young emperor had ascended the throne in the fourth month and was deposed by the ninth. The man Dong Zhuo enthroned was Liu Xie, the King of Chenliu, whose courtesy name was Bohe. He was Emperor Ling’s second son—the Emperor Xian of Han—and was nine years old at the time.

The era name was changed to Chuping. Dong Zhuo became Chancellor of State; in the audience hall he came without ritual deference, with sword and boots on, and none could match his power to grant favor or inflict punishment.

Li Ru advised Dong to recruit famous men in order to gather popular trust. He recommended Cai Yong for his talents. Dong summoned him, but Cai Yong did not come. Dong grew angry and told him, “If you do not come, I will exterminate your family.” Frightened, he had to obey the summons and arrive.

Dong met Cai Yong and rejoiced greatly. Within one month he promoted him three times and appointed him Court Attendant, treating him with unusual warmth.

In the meantime, the young emperor and Empress Dowager He and Empress Consort Tang were trapped in Yongan Palace, with food and clothing growing scarce. The young emperor had not once stopped weeping.

One day, he happened to see two swallows flying together in the courtyard and so composed a poem:

New green grass stiffened in the mist; twin swallows rose, light and high. The Luo River ran as a blue-green ribbon, and passersby on the road praised it with envy. Far away, under deep blue clouds, stood my old palace. Who was loyal and righteous and carried out his heart’s grievance so openly?

Dong Zhuo often had people listening. That day they obtained this poem and brought it to him.

Dong Zhuo said, “A poem of grievance is enough for murder. Kill him openly and make it famous.” He ordered Li Ru with ten armed men to enter the palace and kill the emperor.

The emperor, Empress Dowager, and consort were on an upper floor when a palace maid announced Li Ru’s arrival. The emperor was deeply frightened. Li Ru offered him poisoned wine. The emperor asked, “What is this for?” Li Ru said, “In this warm springtime, the Chancellor Dong offers celebratory longevity wine.”

The Empress Dowager said, “If it is truly celebratory, then you may drink first.”

Li Ru snapped, “Do you refuse to drink?” He held out a short knife and a white cord before him and said, “If you will not drink this longevity wine, you may receive these two things.”

Consort Tang knelt and said, “I will drink in the emperor’s place. Spare my son and me.”

Li Ru barked, “Who are you to die in the emperor’s place?” Then he held out the cup to Empress Dowager He and said, “You should drink first.”

The emperor then sang:

Heaven and earth are now changed, and the sun and moon are turned over. As a servant reduced to this, I know my life is not long. The great current passes by, and I can only weep with empty tears.

Consort Tang also sang:

The Son of Heaven will collapse and Earth Mother will fall; As an imperial consort, I regret I cannot follow. Life and death now take different paths from this parting; How can my grief be so quick to fade?

After the songs, the two embraced and wept together.

Li Ru barked, “The Chancellor ordered you to return and report right away. You delayed; who will save you now?”

The Empress Dowager shouted harshly that He Jin had lacked judgment and let a villain into the capital, bringing this day’s catastrophe. Li Ru’s anger rose. He and his men dragged her down from the stairs, then ordered soldiers to strangle Tang Consort and force poison wine down the throat of the young emperor before reporting back to Dong Zhuo.

Dong Zhuo ordered the boy emperor buried outside the city wall.

From then on Dong entered the palace every night, violated palace attendants, and slept in the Dragon Bed.

At one point he led troops out of the city to a place near Yangcheng in the second month. Villagers were gathering for the spring festival. Men and women all assembled. Dong ordered the soldiers to surround them, slaughtered everyone, plundered women and goods, loaded them on carts, hung more than one thousand heads beneath the carts, then drove straight back to the capital and boasted they had crushed the rebels. At the city gate he burned heads of the dead and distributed women and goods among the troops.

Wu Fu, Colonel of the Horse-Archers, style name Deyu, saw Dong’s cruelty and was unable to bear it. He once wore thin armor beneath his court robes and concealed a short sword, waiting for a chance to kill Dong.

One day, when Dong entered court, Wu Fu came up to the chamber stairs and drew his sword to stab him. Dong had great strength; he gripped him with both hands. Lü Bu ran in and dragged Wu Fu down.

Dong said, “Who taught you to rebel?”

Wu Fu stared and shouted, “You are not my lord, and I am not your retainer. How can there be rebellion between us? Your crimes fill heaven, and everyone wishes to execute you! I’d rather be torn apart by a cart than fail to answer to the world for not punishing you.”

Dong, furious, ordered him seized and cut open and quartered. Wu Fu cursed without pause to the end of his life.

Later men made a poem praising him:

In late Han, the loyal and upright called Wu Fu the true man. No sky-reaching pride in this age was greater than his. His name remains for striking a villain in the court, And across ten thousand ages he is worthy of the name “great man.”

From then on Dong Zhuo left and entered in the company of armored men at all times.

Yuan Shao was then in Bohai. Hearing that Dong Zhuo was manipulating power, he sent a secret letter to Wang Yun.

The traitor Dong has defied Heaven and deposed the ruler; the people cannot bear to speak it. Yet you, in your own authority, allow him to run wild. If you do not hear and respond, are you truly a loyal minister serving the realm?

Yuan Shao now gathers men and drills troops. I wish to clear the royal house of this danger, but have not dared to move quickly. If you are willing, seize this chance and strike. If you can order soldiers, command me and I will obey.

When Wang Yun received the letter he pondered for a long while and could think of no answer.

One day he told the old ministers all assembled in the inner court pavilion, “I, this old servant, have descended in humiliation today. Tonight I ask all of you to come to my home for a small drink.” All the ministers said they would certainly come.

That evening Wang Yun held a banquet in the rear hall, and all court ministers arrived. After several rounds of drink, he suddenly covered his face and wept. The assembly cried out in surprise, “Your Excellency the Minister over the Masses, why this grief?”

Wang Yun said, “Today this old servant is not truly humiliated. I wanted to gather you only to have a quiet exchange. Dong Zhuo now upholds this usurpation; if he sees our hearts are set elsewhere he may suspect us. So I used this as a pretext for laughter before tears.”

He continued: “Dong Zhuo has betrayed the ruler and seized command; the state and ancestral hall are one step from ruin tomorrow. Think: from the High Emperor who beheaded Qin and crushed Chu, who once held all under heaven, to this day we have fallen into Dong’s hand. This is why I cry.”

Immediately the whole assembly wept.

Someone in the hall then slapped his hand on his thigh and laughed aloud: “The entire court is crying until dawn, dawn to dusk and dusk to dawn. How can crying kill Dong Zhuo?”

Wang Yun looked up and saw it was the Cavalry Captain Cao Cao. He was furious and said, “Your ancestors and yours have all eaten the Han court’s salaries. How can you, instead of thinking of service to the state, laugh at the others?”

Cao Cao said, “I did not laugh for another reason. I laughed because none here has one plan to kill Dong Zhuo. Though I am mediocre, I would gladly cut off Dong’s head now, hang it over the city gate, and offer that to the world.”

Wang Yun withdrew and asked, “What stratagem do you, Mengde, have?”

Cao Cao said, “Of late I have humbled myself serving Dong Zhuo only in order to seize the moment. He now trusts me well, so I can stand near him. I have heard that Your Excellency the Minister over the Masses possesses a treasured seven-star sword. Lend it to me. I will enter the Chancellor’s residence and stab him. Even if I die, I will have no regret.”

Wang Yun said, “If Mengde truly bears this intent, heaven is fortunate on behalf of the land.” He then personally poured him wine. Cao Cao sipped and took oath. Wang Yun then took out the treasured sword and gave it to him.

Cao Cao concealed the sword. After he finished drinking, he stood, took leave of the assembly, and left. The ministers sat once more, then all gradually dispersed.

Next morning, wearing the broadsword at his side, Cao Cao came to the Chancellor’s office and asked where the Chancellor was.

A servant answered, “He is in the small pavilion.” Cao Cao went straight in.

Dong Zhuo sat on a bed; Lü Bu stood beside him. Dong said, “Why are you late, Mengde?” Cao Cao replied, “My horse is lame, so my progress is slow.”

Dong turned to Lü Bu and said, “I have fine horses from Xiliang. Fengxian, you may choose one and give it to Mengde.”

Lü Bu obeyed and went to pick one. Cao Cao thought, “This villain deserves to die.” He prepared to draw his sword and stab him but, fearing Dong’s strength, did not dare to move lightly.

Dong was fat and could not remain seated long; he turned and lay down, facing inward. Cao Cao thought again, “This villain has just taken his rest.” He quickly drew out his broadsword. At the moment he was about to stab, Dong happened to glance into a mirror, saw Cao Cao behind him with the blade already drawn, and turned quickly.

“Mengde,” Dong asked, “what is this?”

Lü Bu had already led out the horse and was outside the pavilion. Cao Cao, alarmed, knelt and held out the sword.

“Thank you, my lord, a treasured broadsword, offered to the favored Chancellor.”

Dong took a good look and saw it was over a chi long, inlaid with seven jewels, extremely sharp. It was truly a treasured sword. He handed it to Lü Bu for safekeeping. Cao Cao put the scabbard back on and gave it to him.

Dong then led Cao Cao out of the pavilion to inspect horses. Cao Cao said with thanks, “May I test one of them?”

Dong told him to take a saddle and reins. Cao Cao led the horse out of the Chancellor’s office, whipped it, and rode toward the southeast.

Lü Bu said, “Cao Cao came in as if to strike you, but, being called out, he gave this as a presentation.”

Dong said, “I also had my suspicions.”

Just as they were speaking, Li Ru arrived. Dong related this to him. Li Ru said, “Cao Cao has no wife or children in the capital and lives alone in his rented house. If men are sent to summon him and he comes at once, that would support your claim that this is an offering. If he resists coming, then he certainly attempted to strike.”

Dong approved this plan and sent four jail guards to summon Cao Cao.

A long time passed. The men returned saying, “Cao Cao has not come back to his lodgings. He mounted a horse and fled out through East Gate. When the gate guard asked, he said: ‘The Chancellor has an urgent official matter for me,’ and he rode off.”

Li Ru said, “Cao’s bandit heart has already fled. This is certainly an attempted assassination.”

Dong Zhuo was enraged: “I trusted this man so heavily, and he now wants to kill me!”

Li Ru said, “There must be confederates. Once we seize Cao Cao, we can know the truth.”

Dong issued warrants across the city, posted sketches and descriptions, and ordered Cao Cao arrested. Whoever delivered him would be rewarded a thousand pieces of gold and made a marquis of ten thousand households; those hiding him shared the same guilt.

At that time Cao Cao had fled beyond the city and rode hard toward Qiao commandery. When passing through Zhongmou County, he was caught by gate soldiers and brought before the county magistrate.

Cao Cao said, “I am a travelling merchant. My surname is Huangfu.”

The magistrate stared hard at Cao Cao and was silent a while, then said, “I recognized you in Luoyang when I once sought office. You are Cao Cao. Why hide your name? Bring him to custody and tomorrow bring him toward the capital with your report for reward.” He gave the guard soldiers wine and food and left.

By midnight the magistrate had his attendants secretly summon Cao Cao for questioning in the back courtyard.

He said, “I hear the Chancellor did not treat you badly. Why did you bring this trouble on yourself?”

Cao Cao replied, “How can a sparrow know the ambition of a wild goose?”

He added, “Now that you have captured me, you will release me and bring a reward back to the capital. Move the attendants away.”

The magistrate dismissed those present and said, “Do not disdain me. I am not an ordinary petty official; only that I have not yet met the lord to whom I belong.”

Cao Cao said, “My ancestors and family have eaten the Han stipend for generations. If I did not think to repay the state, how am I any different from beasts? I only bent my body to serve Dong Zhuo in order to strike when a moment opened, so the realm might be cleared of him. Now that matter failed, it is the will of Heaven.”

The magistrate asked, “Where does Mengde now intend to go?”

Cao Cao said, “I go to my home county, issue a forged edict, and summon the lords of the world to rise together and execute Dong Zhuo. This is my wish.”

Hearing this, the magistrate immediately untied him and helped him to his seat. He bent twice in obeisance and said, “You are truly a loyal and righteous man of all under heaven.”

Cao Cao also bent and asked the magistrate’s name. He said, “My surname is Chen. My personal name is Gong, my courtesy name is Gongtai. My old mother and wife and children are in Dong Commandery. Moved by your righteousness, I am willing to abandon my office and flee with you.”

Cao Cao rejoiced.

That night Chen Gong packed provisions, changed clothes with Cao Cao, and the two mounted horses and rode toward their hometown. After three days they reached Cheng Gao.

At dusk, Cao Cao pointed his whip toward the deep wood and said to Chen Gong, “There is a man there, surname Lü, named Bo She. He was my father’s sworn-brother. Go ask about his family and whether we might stay one night.”

Chen Gong said, “That is best.” They dismounted before Bo She’s homestead and entered.

Bo She said, “I have heard court notices all over seeking you in earnest. Your father has fled to Chenliu. How did you come here?”

Cao Cao explained earlier events and said, “If not for the magistrate of Zhongmou, I would already have been pulverized to dust and bone.”

Bo She bowed to Chen Gong and said, “Had the young gentleman not been Your Excellency, the Cao household would already be exterminated. Young master, sit at ease; tonight you may lodge in my thatch.”

He rose immediately and went inside. After a while he returned and told Chen Gong, “This old man has no good wine. Let me go to Xiang village and buy a jar for your reception.” Saying this he hurriedly mounted a mule and left.

Cao Cao and Chen Gong sat awhile. Suddenly they heard in the rear of the compound the sound of sharpening blades. Cao Cao said, “Lü Bo She is no intimate. This is suspicious. We should try to overhear.”

They moved stealthily behind the thatch hall. They heard voices saying, “Shall we tie him and kill him?”

Cao Cao said, “That is so. If we do not strike first, we will surely be seized.” So he and Chen Gong drew their swords and entered directly, killing without distinction of man or woman. They killed eight people in a row.

Searching in the kitchen, they saw a tied pig being readied to be killed. Chen Gong said, “Mengde’s heart is hard. He has just killed good people by mistake.” He hurried out of the homestead and mounted.

They had gone less than two li when they saw Bo She returning on his mule, with two jars of wine hanging from his saddle-bow and fruits and greens in his hands.

He called out, “How could this worthy nephew and Your Excellency leave so quickly?”

Cao Cao said, “A man pursued by guilt cannot linger.”

Bo She replied, “I have already ordered my household to butcher one pig for your hospitality. Why would worthy nephew and Your Excellency hate a single night’s lodging? Turn back quickly.”

Cao Cao ignored him and spurred his horse on.

After only a few strides he pulled out his sword and turned back, crying, “Who is this newcomer?” As Bo She looked over his shoulder, Cao Cao slashed him from horseback.

Chen Gong exclaimed in alarm, “You misjudged him a moment ago. Why do this now?”

Cao Cao said, “Bo She has come to his own home and has seen many killed. Why would he remain calm? If he gathers many men and pursues, we will be ruined.”

Chen Gong said, “To know and then kill is too unjust.”

Cao Cao answered, “I’d rather bear blame before all under heaven than let all under heaven bear blame against me.” Chen Gong was silent.

That night, after riding several li, they reached an inn under moonlight and knocked open the door to stay the night. They fed their horses. Cao Cao lay down first and slept.

Chen Gong thought to himself, “I took Cao Cao for a good man and gave up office to follow him. He is actually pitiless indeed. If I keep him here, he will bring trouble later.” He reached for his sword, intending to kill Cao Cao.

The proper saying of the chapter is:

If a heart is cruel and vicious, it is no fit character for a worthy man. As for Cao and Zhuo, they were men of one ilk.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Han Emperor Is Deposed and the King of Chenliu Made Emperor; Cao Cao Offers the Treasured Sword

chapters.html:
False edicts are issued to summon provincial stations to Cao.
Three heroes at the Guan Pass break Lü Bu.

Chen Gong, who had been about to strike Cao Cao down, suddenly reconsidered. “I came this far with him for the sake of the state. To kill him now would be wrong. Better I leave and go elsewhere.” He sheathed his sword, mounted, and left before dawn, heading straight for Dong Commandery.

When Cao Cao, whose courtesy name was Mengde, woke and did not see Chen Gong, he thought, “This man heard me speak these two words and suspected my intent. He thought me unvirtuous and left. I must move at once and not linger.” He rode through the night to Chenliu and found his father. He explained everything from the beginning and asked to disburse family resources and raise just-war troops. His father replied, “Your funds are too small to sustain this; success is unlikely. There is in this region a filial and able man named Wei Hong. He is austere with money and proud of his integrity, and his household is very wealthy. If we gain his help, matters may be arranged.”

Cao Cao prepared wine and tables, invited Wei Hong to his house, and said, “The Han court is without a true master. Dong Zhuo monopolizes power, cheats the Son of Heaven, and harms the people. The realm spits with grief and anger. I wish to uphold the state, but my strength is not enough. You are a man of loyalty and justice. Dare you give aid?”

Wei Hong said, “I have carried this will for long and have only lamented not having met a true hero. Since Mengde has such grand intent, I will put my family resources behind it.” Cao Cao rejoiced. He first issued counterfeit edicts and sent them flying to all the commanderies, then gathered volunteer troops. He raised a white recruitment banner with the word “Loyalty” above it. In a few days the volunteers came thick as rain.

One day, Le Jin, a man from Yángpíng named Le, with given name Jin and courtesy name Wenqian, came to serve Cao Cao. Soon afterward, another man arrived: Li Dian, from Julu in Shanyang, surname Li, given name Dian, courtesy name Mancheng. Cao Cao kept both as clerks at the main command tent.

Another arrived as well: Xiahou Dun, courtesy name Yuanrang, from Qia of Pei state, a descendant of Xiahou Ying. He had trained with spear and staff since childhood. At fourteen he studied arms under a master, and when someone insulted his teacher, Xiahou Dun killed the culprit and fled into the outside territories. Learning that Cao Cao had raised the army, he and his clan-brother Xiahou Yuan, each leading a thousand sturdy men, came to join. These two were in truth related to Cao Cao’s household: Cao Song, Cao Cao’s father, had been a son of the Xiahou clan by a collateral connection, so there was kinship.

Not long after, Cao Cao’s brothers, Cao Ren and Cao Hong, came each with more than a thousand troops. Cao Ren’s courtesy name was Zixiao and Cao Hong’s was Zilian. Their soldiers and mounts were well trained, and both were highly skilled in arms. Cao Cao was delighted and arranged their horse and foot around the camp.

Wei Hong spent the entire family wealth and equipped armor, standards, and banners. Supplies came in from all directions, too many to count.

At that time Yuan Shao learned of Cao Cao’s false edicts, gathered his civil and military officers, and brought thirty thousand troops from Bohai to meet Cao Cao. Cao Cao had his proclamation carried to all the commanderies:

Cao and the others, with reverence to great righteousness, now announce to the realm: Dong Zhuo deceives Heaven and earth, has destroyed the state, and murdered the Son of Heaven; he has defiled the palace and slaughtered the living. Fierce, reckless, and without humanity, his crimes are beyond counting. Now, under a secret order of the Son of Heaven, we have raised forces for loyal duty and swear to sweep across the Central Plains and put the violent crowd to death. Let all those of upright feeling rise together, vent the public grievance, support the imperial house, and save the common people. When this edict arrives, follow it without delay.

After the proclamations spread, lords from many commanderies rose and responded:

  1. The First Position: Grand General and Administrator of Nanyang Commandery, Yuan Shu.
  2. The Second Position: Han Fu, Inspector of Ji Province.
  3. The Third Position: Kong Zhou, Inspector of Yu Province.
  4. The Fourth Position: Liu Dai, Inspector of Yanzhou.
  5. The Fifth Position: Wang Kuang, Administrator of Henan Commandery.
  6. The Sixth Position: Zhang Miao, Administrator of Chenliu.
  7. The Seventh Position: Qiao Mao, Administrator of Dong Commandery.
  8. The Eighth Position: Yuan Yi, Administrator of Shanyang.
  9. The Ninth Position: Bao Xin, Minister of Jibei.
  10. The Tenth Position: Kong Rong, Administrator of Beihai.
  11. The Eleventh Position: Zhang Chao, Administrator of Guangling.
  12. The Twelfth Position: Tao Qian, Inspector of Xuzhou.
  13. The Thirteenth Position: Ma Teng, Administrator of Xiliang.
  14. The Fourteenth Position: Gongsun Zan, Administrator of Beiping.
  15. The Fifteenth Position: Zhang Yang, Administrator of Shangdang.
  16. The Sixteenth Position: Sun Jian, Marquis of Wucheng and Administrator of Changsha.
  17. The Seventeenth Position: Yuan Shao, Marquis of Qixiang and Administrator of Bohai.

Their troop strengths varied; some brought 30,000, some 10,000 to 20,000, and each arrived with both civil officials and military commanders, all converging on Luoyang.

Now hear of Gongsun Zan, Administrator of Beiping, commanding fifteen thousand elite soldiers, passing through P’ingyuan County in Dezhou Prefecture. As he rode, he saw a yellow banner rise among a clump of mulberry trees and several riders coming out in greeting. It was Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande.

Gongsun asked, “Elder brother, what brings you here?”

Liu Bei said, “I used to serve under your protection as magistrate of P’ingyuan County. Hearing that your main army is passing this way, I came to offer my regards and to invite you to enter the city and rest your horses.”

Gongsun pointed at Guan and Zhang and asked, “Who are these two?”

Liu Bei answered, “This is Guan Yu and Zhang Fei. They are sworn brothers with me.”

“Did they help break the Yellow Turbans, then?”

“By their efforts alone.”

“What offices do they hold now?”

Guan Yu answered, “Guan Yu serves as mounted archer. Zhang Fei serves as foot archer.”

Gongsun sighed. “Then your heroes have been buried in small posts. Dong Zhuo has ruined the realm. All lords are going against him. You should leave this petty office, go now with us, restore the Han court, and uphold the state.”

Liu Bei replied, “I am willing.”

Zhang Fei said, “If I had had room then to kill this robber, we would not have reached this day.”

Yunchang said, “The matter has already arrived at this point; we shall gather our strength and follow.”

Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei brought a few riders and came with Gongsun Zan. Cao Cao met them and they all camped. The lords came in over the next days and each established camp and stockades, linked in a line for more than two hundred li. Cao Cao held a grand sacrifice, slaughtering oxen and horses, and convened the lords to discuss advancing the army.

Wang Kuang said, “Since this is righteous duty, we must name an alliance leader. If the lords all accept common discipline, we can advance.”

Cao Cao said, “Yuan Shao was formerly Benchu, four generations from high office, descendant of a great minister of Han. He can serve as alliance leader.”

Yuan Shao demurred repeatedly. The assembly cried, “No one else but Benchu is possible.”

Only then did Yuan Shao assent. The next day they built a three-tiered platform, hung five directional banners, and raised white-mane lances with yellow battle standards and the seals of command. They invited Yuan Shao up onto the platform. He adjusted his robes, strapped on his sword, climbed up with feeling, burned incense, and bowed twice.

Their alliance oath read:

The Han house is unfortunate; the imperial thread has lost its order. The treacherous minister Dong Zhuo has exploited disorder, unleashed harm upon the Supreme Ruler, and oppressed the common people. We fear the state will collapse and the altar will fall. Therefore we have gathered righteous troops and come in response to the national emergency. We who enter this alliance are one in spirit and one in labor, to preserve our official loyalty; there shall be no divided intent. Whoever violates this oath shall lose life and have no descendants spared. Heaven and Earth, ancestors, and the bright spirits of previous rulers all bear witness.

After they read this, all drank blood and swore. Their emotion was such that tears flowed down many faces.

Once the oath was done, they descended. The lords helped Yuan Shao into the reception tent and sat according to rank and age in two rows. Cao Cao went around with cups and said, “Now that we have chosen our alliance leader, all will obey deployment orders and together support the state. Do not measure one another by strength.”

Yuan Shao said, “Though I lack talent, having accepted your appointment as leader, any merit shall be rewarded and any guilt punished. The state has regular punishment, and the army has discipline; each must obey it, and none may transgress.”

They all replied, “We will do as ordered.”

Yuan Shao said, “My brother Yuan Shu now supervises provisions. He will answer each camp so there is no shortfall. We still need one man for the vanguard to ride straight to Sishui Pass and provoke battle. The rest should hold difficult terrain for support.”

Sun Jian stepped forward: “I, Wentai of Wucheng, will take the vanguard.”

Yuan Shao said, “You are brave and fierce, Wentai; you can bear this task.”

Thus Sun Jian led his own men and rode hard to Sishui Pass.

The officers at the pass sent mounted couriers to the Prime Minister’s Office in Luoyang to report the alarm. Since Dong Zhuo had seized great power, he was hosting drinking sessions each day. Li Ru received the urgent memorial and came straight to Zhuo.

Dong Zhuo was greatly startled. He gathered all his generals and consulted. Wenhou Lü Bu stepped forward and said, “Do not worry, Your Highness. The lords from beyond the passes are no more than weeds and grasses to me. Let me take a tiger-and-wolf army and cut all their heads, hanging them at your gate.”

Dong Zhuo rejoiced. “Since we have Fengxian, we may rest easy!” he said.

Before he finished, a tall man behind him shouted in a loud voice, “Why cut a chicken with an ox knife?” The speaker continued, “There is no need for the Wenhou to ride there in person. I can cut down the lords’ chiefs as easily as removing a plum from a basket.”

Dong Zhuo turned and saw him: he was nine chi tall, with a tiger’s chest and wolflike waist, a leopard face and ape-like arms; he was a man of Guanzhong. His surname was Hua, given name Xiong. Dong Zhuo rejoiced again and promoted him to Assistant Cavalry Commander, assigning him fifty thousand horse and foot with Li Su, Hu Zhen, and Zhao Cen to ride through the night and meet the lords at the pass.

Among those lords there was Bao Xin, Minister of Jibei. He thought, “Since Sun Jian has taken the vanguard, he may seize all the glory. I will secretly send my brother Bao Zhong with three thousand mounted infantry by a short route straight under the pass to force hand-to-hand contact before the vanguard gets there.”

Hua Xiong led five hundred iron cavalry and thundered down the pass with a cry: “Rebel commanders, do not run!” Bao Zhong tried to fall back, but Hua Xiong struck instantly and beheaded him from horseback. He took many officers alive. He sent Bao Zhong’s head back to Dong Zhuo as a message of success, and Dong Zhuo promoted Hua to Chief Commander.

Now Sun Jian arrived with four generals, and straightened out the front. They were:

The first was Cheng Pu, from northeastern Beiping in Tiyin, surname Cheng, given name Pu, courtesy name Demou, who carried a long iron-serpentine spear.

The second was Huang Gai, surname Huang, given name Gai, courtesy name Gongfu, from Lingling, and he used an iron flail.

The third was Han Dang, surname Han, given name Dang, courtesy name Yigong, from Liao-Xi Ling; he wielded a great sabre.

The fourth was Zu Mao, surname Zu, given name Mao, courtesy name Darong, from Fuchun in Wu Commandery, and he used a pair of swords.

Sun Jian wore torn silver armor, a red helmet beneath it, and a broad old mace. He rode a mane-maned horse, pointed at the pass, and shouted, “Assist those villains? Why did you not surrender earlier?”

Hu Zhen, Hua Xiong’s second-in-command, brought five thousand men out to meet him.

Cheng Pu, riding hard and lifting his spear, charged straight for Hu Zhen. After only a few engagements, he skewered Hu Zhen in the throat; Hu Zhen fell dead from his horse. Sun Jian drove the troops straight to the pass mouth, where arrows and stones rained down.

He brought his men back to camp on the east of the Ridge and sent word to Yuan Shao of his success and then to Yuan Shu urging him for supplies.

A courtier said to Yuan Shu, “Sun Jian is a ferocious tiger of Jiangdong. If we break through to Luoyang and kill Dong Zhuo, this is removing a wolf and taking its tiger. If you do not provide supplies now, his army will scatter.”

Yuan Shu believed him and sent no grain.

Sun Jian’s army soon had a shortage, and confusion spread. Hu Zhen then informed Dong Zhuo. He advised, “Tonight I will lead one unit by a side track down the pass and strike behind Sun Jian’s camp. Once our general swings his forward camp down, Jian can be taken.”

Hua Xiong followed this plan. He ordered all soldiers to eat to fullness and ride down the pass during the night.

That night the moon was clear and the wind mild. When he reached Jian’s camp, it was past midnight. The drums and cries drove straight forward. Sun Jian hastily buckled on his armor and mounted. He met Hua Xiong immediately. The two horses clashed; after only a few engagements, a second wave of Li Su’s soldiers arrived and sent fire rising from the camps. Sun Jian’s men scattered in panic. The commanders fought in mixed confusion; only Zu Mao stayed fixed on Sun Jian and broke through with him. They ran.

Hua Xiong pursued.

Sun Jian shot two arrows, both dodged by Hua. When he released a third, he pulled too hard and snapped the Qiehua bow, so he abandoned the bow and fled at speed.

Zu Mao said, “My lord, your face is visible through the red helmet and can be recognized from afar. Take it off and give it to me to wear.”

Sun Jian removed it and switched helmets. Then they split on two routes and escaped. Hua Xiong’s troops chased only the red helmet. Sun Jian slipped away by a small path. Zu Mao, seeing the pursuit close, hung the red helmet on a courtyard pillar that still had burning soot and then disappeared into the woods.

At the pass the moonlight revealed that red helmet among the shadows. They encircled him from all sides, too afraid to close in closely. They shot arrows until they realized the trick, and then moved to recover the helmet.

Zu Mao broke out behind the trees, swinging his twin swords and trying to cleave Hua Xiong.

Hua shouted once and cut Zu Mao down from horseback.

It was dawn before he led his troops back up the pass. Cheng Pu, Huang Gai, and Han Dang found Sun Jian and helped him reform and set up camp once more.

Because Zu Mao had fallen, Sun Jian was deeply shaken. That night he sent word to Yuan Shao. Yuan Shao was alarmed: “I never expected Sun Wentai to be defeated at the hand of Hua Xiong!” and gathered the lords for counsel. All came except Gongsun Zan, who arrived last; Yuan Shao asked him in.

“Sun Wentai violated our orders and advanced of his own choosing. He was hit and killed many of our men and has fallen. Now he has been defeated again by Hua Xiong. Morale is bruised. What are we to do?” he asked.

No one spoke.

Yuan Shao looked around and saw three unusual men standing behind Gongsun Zan, who were smiling coldly. He asked, “Who are those men behind the Governor?”

Gongsun lifted up Liu Bei and said, “They are my childhood housemates and sworn brothers, including the magistrate of P’ingyuan named Liu Bei.”

Cao Cao said, “Could it be Liu Bei, the one who once broke the Yellow Turbans?”

Gongsun nodded. “Yes.”

He then ordered Liu Bei to bow and present himself. Gongsun recounted Liu Bei’s service and background in full. Yuan Shao said, “Since you are from the Han imperial household, come take a seat.” He ordered him to sit. Liu Bei thanked him.

Yuan Shao said, “I do not honor your title; I honor you as a scion of the imperial house.”

Liu Bei sat at the end position, while Guan Yu and Zhang Fei knelt with hands crossed behind him.

Then a messenger came: “Hua Xiong has ridden down from the pass with a long spear, holding aloft Sun Wentai’s red helmet, and has come to the camp to taunt our front-line struggle.”

Yuan Shao asked, “Who goes to fight him?” Yuan Shu emerged from behind with his brave man Yu She. “This junior officer wishes to go.”

Yuan Shao was pleased and gave Yu She leave to ride.

The immediate report came back: “Yu She fought Hua Xiong for less than three engagements. Hua Xiong has beheaded him.”

The camp was greatly startled.

Wang Kuang said, “I have Han general Pan Feng; he can behead Hua Xiong.” Yuan Shao ordered him forward at once.

Pan Feng carried a great axe and went up on horseback. Not long after, a rider returned: “Pan Feng was also cut down by Hua Xiong.”

Again the camp lost color.

Yuan Shao said, “It is a pity that my top generals Yan Liang and Wenchou have not yet arrived. A single brave man in this place—why should we fear Hua Xiong?” Before he could finish, someone shouted from the steps below, “I, a junior officer, volunteer to behead Hua Xiong and offer him under your camp!”

All looked. The man was near nine chi tall, with a beard two chi long, darting Danfeng eyes, broad eyebrows like a curled silkworm, a face like a ripe date, and a voice like a bronze bell. He stood before the tent.

Yuan Shao asked, “Who is this?”

Gongsun said, “He is Guan Yu, brother of Liu Bei.”

Yuan Shao asked, “What office does he hold?”

Gongsun said, “He serves Liu Bei as mounted archer.”

Yuan Shu shouted from the rank, “Do you dare boast before our lords as if no general stood above you? A mere archer, how dare you challenge! Fight with me!”

Cao Cao hastened to stop him. “Calm down,” he said. “He has spoken boldly; he must have courage and skill. Let him ride and test it. If he cannot win, it is no later to hold him accountable.”

Yuan Shao said, “If one archer goes out, Hua Xiong will mock him.”

Cao Cao said, “This man has uncommon bearing. How would Hua Xiong know he is only an archer?”

Guan Yu said, “If I fail, I will submit my head.”

Cao Cao handed him a cup of warmed wine, drank with him, and then sent him up.

Guan said, “Set the cup aside and pour it down; I will return shortly.”

He stepped from the tent, took up his saber, and vaulted onto his horse. The other lords heard the war drums and shouts outside the passes like a sky collapsing and the earth opening. Just as they strained to learn what was happening, a jangling bell sounded and he entered the center, Yun chang lifted Hua Xiong’s head and flung it to the ground while the wine was still warm.

Later someone composed a verse in praise:

He alone restrains heaven and earth with the first of deeds, Drumskins in Yüan Gate thunder in the gate-way’s roar. Yunchang set down the cup and displayed valor, With his wine still warm, he cut down Hua Xiong.

Cao Cao rejoiced greatly.

From behind Liu Bei, Zhang Fei stepped out, shouting at full voice, “My brother has beheaded Hua Xiong. Shall we not ride into the pass and seize Dong Zhuo alive now? How long can we wait?”

Yuan Shu was furious and shouted, “My lord is still yielding in humility. How can a foot soldier under a county magistrate dazzle and display arms here? Send him out of camp at once!”

Cao Cao said, “Reward follows merit, not rank.”

Yuan Shu said, “If the lords honor only a county magistrate, then I withdraw.”

Cao Cao said, “Can we let one word ruin major business?” and ordered Gongsun Zan to escort Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei back to camp.

The officers dispersed. Cao Cao quietly sent men with ox and wine to soothe the three.

Now Hua Xiong’s defeated forces carried news back to Dong Zhuo. Li Su quickly wrote an urgent memorial and presented it. Dong Zhuo convened Li Ru, Lü Bu, and others and consulted.

Li Ru said, “We have now lost our senior general Hua Xiong; the rebel forces are vast. Yuan Shao is alliance leader, and Yuan Wai, now Grand Tutor, serves in our heartland. If inside and out there is collusion, it would be deeply troublesome. First remove him. I suggest the Chancellor should personally lead the great army to divide and hunt the rebels.”

Dong Zhuo accepted this view. He called Li Jue and Guo Si and ordered each to lead five hundred men to surround the home of the Grand Tutor Yuan Wai, killing old and young alike and leaving no survivors, and then sending Yuan Wai’s head to the pass front as a warning. Dong Zhuo then raised 200,000 troops and split into two columns. One column, first, sent Li Jue and Guo Si with 500 men to hold Sishui Pass and avoid close battle; Dong Zhuo himself led 150,000 with Li Ru, Lü Bu, Fan Chou, Zhang Ji, and others to guard Hulao Pass, which was fifty li from Luoyang. When the host arrived at Hulao Pass, Dong Zhuo ordered Lü Bu to take 30,000 and set a great encampment before the pass. Dong Zhuo himself stayed on the pass.

A messenger who had watched from starry horse patrols reported to Yuan Shao’s main camp. Yuan Shao gathered the lords again to discuss.

Cao Cao said, “Dong Zhuo is now stationed at Hulao, blocking the middle route of our lords. We should send half the army out to meet him now.”

Yuan Shao then assigned eight lords—Wang Kuang, Qiao Mao, Bao Xin, Yuan Yi, Kong Rong, Zhang Yang, Tao Qian, and Gongsun Zan—to go to Hulao to meet Dong Zhuo. Cao Cao brought his own troops in support. The eight lords separately raised their forces.

The Administrator of Henan, Wang Kuang, arrived first with his troops. Lü Bu then brought three thousand heavy cavalry and came rushing to meet him. Wang Kuang drew up his men in battle formation and held them beneath the horse-banner gate when he saw Lü Bu take command. Lü Bu appeared with a triple-braided black-gold crown, a Sichuan red brocade robe in a hundred-flower pattern, beast-faced overlapping mail, and an elaborate leopard-patterned belt of armor at his waist. A bow and arrows hung at his side. He sat astride a wind-whistling Chìtù horse. Truly, among men he was Lü Bu, and among horses he was Chìtù.

Wang Kuang turned to ask, “Who dares to take the field?” A commander rode out behind him and presented a spear.

Wang Kuang recognized him as Fang Yue, a famous general of Henan. Their horses clashed; within fewer than five exchanges, Lü Bu skewered him so he fell from the saddle. Wang Kuang’s army collapsed badly and broke in all directions.

Lü Bu rode east and west as if crossing an empty place. By good fortune, Qiao Mao and Yuan Yi arrived with both armies and came to save Wang Kuang. Lü Bu then withdrew.

The three roads of lords, each losing some men and horses, withdrew thirty li south to reestablish camp. Soon the other five contingents arrived and they gathered to debate. All praised Lü Bu as an unmatched hero.

In the midst of this, a junior adjutant reported, “Lü Bu is offering battle.” The eight lords mounted as one and split their armies into eight divisions. Lü Bu stood atop a high mound. From afar his horse and men and embroidered banners were seen, and he first crashed into the line.

The commander of Zhang Yang’s column, Mu Shun, rode forward and met him with a spear; Lü Bu thrust once and felled him in the saddle.

The crowd gasped. The Officer of Beihai’s command, Wu An’guo, rode out with a hammer and an iron maul. Lü Bu struck and then swept with his halberd in reply. Their fight lasted over ten exchanges before Lü Bu cut off Wu An’guo’s wrist with one stroke; he dropped his hammer and fled.

The eight armies surged together and rescued Wu An’guo. Lü Bu rode back.

The lords returned to camp and deliberated. Cao Cao said, “Lü Bu is valiant and invincible in close combat. Let us gather all eighteen allied forces and craft a better plan. If we can capture him, Dong Zhuo will be easy to kill.”

While they were still discussing, Lü Bu once more brought his force out to fight. The eight lords advanced together. Gongsun Zan wielded his long spear and engaged Lü Bu in person. Within only a few passes, Gongsun fled. Lü Bu prised his red-horse forward to pursue.

That horse could run a thousand li a day, and flew like the wind. When it nearly caught him, Lü Bu raised his painted halberd and aimed at Gongsun’s back. At that moment another commander beside him, with round eyes and upright tiger whiskers and a tall snake-spear in hand, spurred on and shouted, “Three-surname houseman, do not run! Zhang Fei of Yan is here!”

When Lü Bu saw this, he dropped Gongsun and turned to Zhang Fei.

Zhang Fei stirred his resolve and fought Lü Bu in full force. After more than fifty rounds they clashed without clear victory.

Yunchang saw this, struck his horse once, and came with his eighty-two-lb Green Dragon Crescent Blade to flank Lü Bu. Three horses whirled and clashed like a turning lantern pattern.

After thirty exchanges, none could yet bring Lü Bu down.

Liu Bei drew his double-edged sword, reined his gold maned horse sharply, and rode in with a slanting stroke to join.

The three then closed around Lü Bu and fought as if whirling lanterns. No one could stay apart from the press for long. Lü Bu tried to force gaps in their lines. Turning from one flank to another, he made a feint with one stroke of the halberd and made Liu Bei move to avoid it. Lü Bu then whipped the flank aside and wheeled, dragging his painted halberd, and sped his horse back.

The three refused to yield. They spurred after him. The armies of all eight lords shouted so loudly it shook the air as they moved to cover the encirclement.

Lü Bu’s army turned and ran toward the pass. Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei followed.

An old saying was written of this three-man fight with Lü Bu:

The stars of the Han have ordained this age for Huanling. The blazing sun slants toward the west. The treacherous minister Dong Zhuo deposed a young emperor, Liu Xie, timid and weak, dreams in alarm. Cao Cao sent a memorial to all beneath the sky and lords throughout the realm rose in wrath to raise troops. They chose Yuan Shao as alliance leader, swearing to uphold the Wang house and set peace at last. Lü Bu, called Wenhou, is unmatched under heaven; his lion-like talent draws praise from the four seas. He shields his body in silver scales like dragon scales, binds his hair with a golden crown crowned by peacock feather tail. Gemmed belts hang askew across the saddle, his brocade robes flutter like flying phoenixes. His dragon steed leaps and kicks up a wind from heaven, its painted halberd gleams and throws winter-water light. Out of the pass to brawl—who can bear him? Every lord’s heart quails in fear. Zhang Fei of Yan springs forth, gripping a snake spear the length of eight chi. Tiger whiskers bristling, eyes round as a wheel, they flash like lightning. Their fierce battle could not decide one side, while at the frontline Guan Yunchang’s rage swelled. The Green Dragon blade flashed with frost-white brilliance; his parrot-patterned battle robe flew like a scarab. Horse-hooves screamed everywhere and ghosts and spirits screamed back; when anger peaked, blood was to run. He who seemed a wolf, Liu Bei, drew his twin blades, shook out heavenly awe and displayed his martial valor. Three men circled and fought long, guarding and interposing with no rest. Their battle cry made heaven and earth move, killing breath filling the air with a cold of stars and ladles. Luo Bu, his strength exhausted, sought a road to escape, looked to the mountain pass and rode, turning back. Dragging back his painted halberd, the Fāngtiān spear, he scattered and disordered the five-colored banners. He snapped the red reins and rode the Chìtù in a turning leap back to Hulao Pass. The three chased Lü Bu all the way to the foot of the pass, and saw to the west wind a blue gauze parasol flapping above the gate. Zhang Fei cried out, “That must be Dong Zhuo. Where is there strength in chasing Lü Bu? Better to seize the bandit first. Then we truly remove the root.” he spurred up the pass to seize Dong Zhuo.

Then:

If we seize the bandit, we must first seize the bandit’s head. Great merit waits only for a rare man. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: False Edicts Summon the Provinces to Aid Cao; Three Heroes at Guan Gate Defeat Lü Bu

chapters.html:
Fire the Golden Hall as Dong Zhuo commits violence. Hide the Imperial Seal, while Sun Jian breaks his vow.

Zhang Fei pressed on at full speed and reached the pass gate. Arrows and stones fell like rain, and he could not force his way through before retreating.

The eight lords together praised Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei for their service, and sent men to Yuan Shao’s camp with the news.

Yuan Shao then sent a summons to Sun Jian, ordering him to advance. Sun Jian came with Cheng Pu and Huang Gai to meet Yuan Shu.

With a staff Sun Jian drew lines on the ground and said, “Dong Zhuo and I had no feud. Today I threw myself into danger, risking life and body, and came to fight a desperate battle: above is the state’s duty, to punish the traitors; below is the private grievance of this general’s household. Yet you, general, have listened to slander, withheld grain, and caused me to be defeated and disgraced. How can you still be at peace?”

Yuan Shu, alarmed and speechless, ordered the man who had brought the slander to be executed in apology to Sun Jian.

Just then someone came to report, “A general is waiting outside the gate on horseback and asks to see you, General.”

Sun Jian left Yuan Shu and returned to his own camp, then asked him to come in. It was Dong Zhuo’s favored general Li Jue.

“Why have you come?” Sun Jian asked.

Li Jue replied, “My only one favored by the Chancellor is you, General. I was sent now solely to forge a bond: the Chancellor has a daughter and wishes to marry her to your son.”

Sun Jian’s face darkened. “Dong Zhuo is a rebel against Heaven and has no righteousness. He has overturned the court and trampled the royal house. I would wipe out his nine clans to answer the world. Would I ever agree to make alliance with such a traitor? I will not kill you. You should go quickly and report at the gate. If you do so, your life may be spared. If you delay, your bones will be ground to dust!”

Li Jue lowered his head and fled in fear like a mouse, then returned to Dong Zhuo and reported Sun Jian’s offense.

Dong Zhuo, furious, asked Li Ru. Li Ru said, “Wenhou has just been defeated, and the soldiers have no will to fight. Better to draw the troops back to Luoyang and move the Son of Heaven to Chang’an, in line with the street couplet. Recently in the market, people are chanting: ‘A Han in the west, a Han in the east. When a deer enters Chang’an, the trouble will cease.’ I believe ‘a Han in the west’ refers to Gaozu rising in western Chang’an to pass on twelve emperors, and ‘a Han in the east’ to Guangwu rising in eastern Luoyang, also to pass on twelve emperors. Heaven’s turn is now so; if the Chancellor returns to Chang’an, there will be peace.”

Dong Zhuo rejoiced. “Without your words, I might not have understood this.” He sent Lü Bu back by night to Luoyang to begin discussing a change of capital.

He gathered ministers and commanders in the hall and said, “Luoyang has been Han’s eastern capital for two hundred years, and its mandate is spent. I can feel the vital force at Chang’an; I intend to ride west and go there. All of you should make ready at once.”

Yang Biao, the Chancellor, said, “The lands of Guanzhong are in ruins and scattered. To abandon ancestral temples and imperial tombs without cause would alarm the people; they are easily stirred and hard to soothe. I beg Your Excellency to deliberate carefully.”

Dong Zhuo shouted, “Do you obstruct the great plan of the state?”

Grand Commandant Huang Wan said, “Yang Biao speaks truly. In the time of Wang Mang and the Chimei uprising, Chang’an was burned and left in ruin; the people were displaced and nothing remained. To abandon palace and buildings for waste land is not right.”

Dong Zhuo said, “Bandits from the eastern regions have already raised havoc. Chang’an has the defensive heights of Xiao and Han. It is nearer to Longyou, and timber, stone, and tiles can be prepared in a few days. Build the palaces and halls; do not disturb me with disruptive talk.”

Xun Shuang remonstrated, “If Your Excellency moves the capital, the people will be agitated and unrestful.”

Dong Zhuo answered in anger, “I act for all under Heaven. Would I care so much for commoners?”

That day he demoted Yang Biao, Huang Wan, and Xun Shuang to commoners.

As Dong Zhuo climbed into the carriage, two men bowed as he approached the gate: Zhou Bi, Minister of the Masters of Writing, and Wu Qiong, the gate captain.

Dong Zhuo asked what they wanted, and Zhou Bi said, “We heard Your Excellency intended to move the capital to Chang’an, so we came to remonstrate.”

Dong Zhuo roared, “At first I heard you both and trusted you to guard against Yuan Shao; now Yuan Shao has already revolted, so you are his faction!” He ordered the guards to drag the two out and behead them at the city gate.

He ordered the move immediately, and said all troops must depart by the next day.

Li Ru said, “Funds and grain are now lacking, and Luoyang has too many wealthy households. We can confiscate their property. As for those under Yuan Shao’s following, kill their kin and seize their household stores; we will obtain vast sums.”

Dong Zhuo then dispatched five thousand cavalry, who swept through Luoyang and seized thousands of wealthy households. Poles were tied to them with the inscription “Rebel ministers and traitor factions,” and they were all beheaded outside the city and stripped of gold.

Li Jue and Guo Si drove the people of Luoyang forward by the hundreds—up to several million mouths—interspersed with military units.

As many as those dying in ditches and ravines could not be counted. The troops also raped the wives and daughters, seized grain; the cries of weeping shook heaven and earth. If anyone lagged on the road, three thousand soldiers behind carried white blades and cut people down.

When Dong Zhuo departed, he ordered each gate set aflame and set fire to household houses, along with ancestral temples and palace offices.

The northern and southern palaces burned into one sheet of flame; Luoyang’s palace courts were left a blackened waste.

He also sent Lü Bu to exhume the tombs of former emperors and empresses and seize their jewels.

Taking advantage, the troops dug through officials’ and civilians’ graves almost to exhaustion.

Dong Zhuo loaded thousands of wagons with gold, pearls, silk cloth, and fine goods, carrying off the Son of Heaven and empresses as he headed for Chang’an.

Afterwards Dong Zhuo’s general Zhao Cen, seeing his master had already abandoned Luoyang, surrendered Sishui Pass.

Sun Jian first drove in with troops; Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei smashed into Hulao Pass, and the lords each brought forces in.

Then Sun Jian dashed to Luoyang and from afar saw flames leaping heavenward and smoke spreading for two to three hundred li, with no sign of people, chickens, or dogs. He first sent out troops to extinguish the fires, and ordered the lords to camp their men and horses on the wasteland.

Cao Cao came to see Yuan Shao and said, “The traitor Dong has gone west; now is the moment for strike and pursuit. Why does Benchu hold back?”

Yuan Shao replied, “The troops are exhausted and advancing may do no good.”

Cao Cao said, “The traitor Dong burned the palace and moved the Son of Heaven, and the realm is shaking without place to return. This is a time when Heaven has withdrawn support; one battle will settle the empire. Why do the lords hesitate?”

All the lords spoke against moving too quickly.

Cao Cao was furious, saying, “You are not fit to advise.” He then took more than ten thousand troops himself, with Xiahou Dun, Xiahou Yuan, Cao Ren, Cao Hong, Li Dian, and Yue Jin, and rode through the night in pursuit of Dong Zhuo.

When Dong Zhuo reached Xingyang, Superintendent Xu Rong came out to receive him.

Li Ru said, “Your Excellency has just abandoned Luoyang and there may be pursuit. Tell Xu Rong to station his troops in ambush by the hills by the outer stockade of Xingyang. If any army pursues, let it pass through; after I crush it here, block and ambush it. Then those who come after will not dare pursue.”

Dong Zhuo followed his counsel and ordered Lü Bu to lead chosen cavalry to hold the rear.

Lü Bu was moving ahead when Cao Cao’s army caught up to him.

Lü Bu laughed. “This is exactly what Li Ru predicted.”

Cao Cao rode forward and shouted, “Traitor! You looted the Son of Heaven, moved the people, and now what do you seek to do?”

Lü Bu spat back, “Lord-abandoning coward! How dare you speak this way?”

Xiahou Dun raised his spear and leapt onto his horse, charging straight at Lü Bu.

Before they had traded more than a few blows, Li Jue brought one force in from the left, and Cao Cao rushed Xiahou Yuan to meet it.

A shout rose again from the right as Guo Si led in troops. Cao Cao urgently sent Cao Ren to meet him.

The combined three lines of horse were overwhelming.

Xiahou Dun could not hold against Lü Bu for long and wheeled back to rally.

Lü Bu moved his iron cavalry forward and ambushed, and Cao Cao’s force was heavily defeated. He turned back and ran for Xingyang.

When they reached the foot of a barren hill, it was about the second watch; the moon was bright as day. They had only just gathered the survivors.

They were just about to dig a field pot and cook when cries came from every side. Xu Rong’s ambush troops all surged out.

Cao Cao rushed his horse in panic, cut across and fled. He met Xu Rong, wheeled and ran on.

Xu Rong loosed an arrow that struck Cao Cao in the shoulder. Cao Cao kept riding with the arrow still in him.

Around the bend of a slope, two soldiers lay in the grass. As Cao Cao’s horse came, both spears were thrown together. The horse was struck and collapsed.

Cao Cao tumbled from the saddle and was seized by two infantrymen.

A general suddenly rode in, slicing down the two infantrymen with his sword, then dismounting, lifted Cao Cao.

It was Cao Hong.

Cao Cao said, “I die here; worthy younger brother, go at once!”

Cao Hong said, “Your servant must mount at once. I will walk.”

Cao Cao said, “Bandits are on us. What will you do?”

Cao Hong answered, “The realm may do without Hong, but not without Your Excellency.”

Cao Cao said, “If I live again, it is because of your strength.”

Cao Cao mounted again; Cao Hong stripped off his garments and armor and followed the horse, dragging the sword.

By the time they had gone a little further, it was past the fourth watch. Ahead lay a great river blocking the way; from behind the shouting drew near.

Cao Cao said, “My life is at this end; I cannot survive.”

Cao Hong quickly helped him down, took off his own robe and armor, and carried him through the water.

Only when they had crossed to the far bank did the pursuers arrive and fire arrows across the river. Cao Cao pressed on through the water.

By dawn they had gone more than thirty li and rested briefly below an earthen rise. Suddenly cries sounded, and a mass of riders came on. It was Xu Rong crossing from upstream to continue pursuit.

In Cao Cao’s panic, Xiahou Dun and Xiahou Yuan appeared with a dozen riders and shouted, “Xu Rong, do not harm our lord!”

Xu Rong immediately charged at Xiahou Dun. Dun lowered his spear and met him in close combat, killing him on horseback and scattering the rest.

Then Cao Ren, Li Dian, and Yue Jin each arrived with troops. Seeing Cao Cao, their fear and joy mingled. They gathered the broken survivors, five hundred or more, and returned together toward Henei.

Dong Zhuo’s army continued on to Chang’an.

The other lords separately camped around Luoyang.

Sun Jian quenched the remaining palace flames, camped his troops inside the city, and set his tents on the foundations of Jianzhang Hall.

He ordered his soldiers to clear away the debris of roof tiles from the palace.

All tombs that Dong Zhuo had dug were fully re-buried.

On the ancestral hall platform, he hastily built three rooms, invited all the lords to line up, raised the spirit tablets of the ancestral gods, and performed the great sacrificial rite.

After the sacrifice, all dispersed.

Sun Jian returned to camp. That night, under starlight and moonlight, he sat with sword unsheathed, looking up at the heavens.

He saw a long white vapor in the Purple Forbidden Enclosure. He sighed, “The star of Heaven’s mandate is unclear. The traitorous ministers have ruined the state; the multitude is in torment; and the capital lies empty!”

When he finished speaking, tears came unbidden.

A soldier pointed out, “Master, in the well south of the hall, five-colored brilliant light rises.”

Sun Jian ordered men to light torches and send down to recover what was in the well.

They brought up a woman’s corpse. Though long dead, the body had not putrefied. She wore court dress, and a silk knot was around her neck.

Opening it they found a vermilion lacquer box locked with gold. Within was an imperial seal, four cun across.

Its top had five coiled dragons; one corner was missing and inlaid with gold. On it were eight seal-script characters: “受命於天，既壽永昌.”

Sun Jian asked Cheng Pu.

Cheng Pu said, “This is the Heirloom State Seal. This jade was first seen by Bianhe under Jing Mountain, where a phoenix rested on a stone. He brought it to King Wu of Chu, and when he opened it, it proved to be true jade.

In the twenty-sixth year of Qin, it was cut into this seal by court jade craftsmen, and Li Si engraved those eight characters. In the twenty-eighth year, Emperor Shi Huang’s southern tour reached Dongting Lake, winds and waves rose, the ship nearly capsized, and he threw this seal into the lake to save the boat.

In the thirty-sixth year, Emperor Shi Huang made a tour to Huayin. Someone raised the seal on the road and said to attendants, “Take this to Ziying.” Then he disappeared. The seal returned to Qin.

The following year, Emperor Shi Huang died. Later, Ziying passed the seal to Emperor Gaozu of Han. In Wang Mang’s usurpation, Empress Dowager Xiao Yuan ordered the seal presented to Wang Xin and Su Xian, broke one corner, and set it with gold.

Emperor Guangwu won this treasure at Yiyang, and it has come down to this day.

I recently heard the ten eunuchs had mutinied, dragged the young emperor out to Bei Mang, and while returning to court the seal was lost. Since this charge is now in your hands, your fate is to rise to the ninth rank. You cannot stay here long. Go quickly back to Jiangdong and seek another great design.”

Sun Jian said, “What you said matches my thought exactly. Tomorrow I will feign illness and ask permission to leave.”

After discussion they settled it. He secretly told his men not to leak a word.

Then, unexpectedly, one soldier of Yuan Shao’s home district slipped out by night to use this for his own advancement and reported to Yuan Shao.

Yuan Shao rewarded him and kept him secretly in the ranks.

The next day, Sun Jian asked leave of Yuan Shao, saying, “I have a small illness, and wish to return to Changsha; I came only to bid farewell.”

Yuan Shao laughed. “I know your illness is a pretext for hiding the Heirloom State Seal.”

Sun Jian turned pale. “How did that thought come from?”

Yuan Shao said, “You rose with the people to expel the bandits and remove evil from the land. The Heirloom State Seal is a court treasure. Since you have obtained it, you should show it to the coalition chief, wait to punish Dong Zhuo, and then return it to court. If you hide it and leave, what are you aiming at?”

Sun Jian said, “How could this treasure be in my possession?”

Yuan Shao said, “Where is the one from Jianzhang Hall’s well?”

Sun Jian said, “I did not have it at all. Why do you force this?”

Yuan Shao said, “Bring it out now, and avoid creating trouble for yourself.”

Sun Jian raised his hand to heaven and swore, “If I truly possessed this treasure and concealed it privately, I will die without blessing, under blade and arrow.”

The lords said, “Wen Tai has sworn so; surely he did not.”

Yuan Shao called for a soldier and asked, “Was there anyone there when you dredged it up?”

Sun Jian grew furious, pulled his sword, and stepped to behead the man.

Yuan Shao likewise drew his sword and said, “If you behead a soldier, you cheat me.”

Behind Yuan Shao, Yan Liang and Wen Chou drew their swords.

At Sun Jian’s back, Cheng Pu, Huang Gai, and Han Dang also had blades out in hand.

All the lords together restrained him.

Sun Jian immediately mounted and lifted camp, then left Luoyang.

Yuan Shao was furious and wrote a letter, then in the night sent a trusted man to Jing Province to deliver it to Inspector Liu Biao, commanding him to intercept and seize Sun Jian on the road.

The next day, word came that Cao Cao had pursued Dong Zhuo, fought at Xingyang, and returned after a great defeat.

Yuan Shao sent men to summon Cao Cao to camp and gathered everyone to drink and ease grief.

During the banquet Cao Cao sighed, “My first intention was to do what was right and rid the realm of bandits. Since all of you came with upright purpose, my first plan was to ask Benchu to bring the troops of Henei to Mengjin and Suanzao. You all should hold Chenggao, occupy the granaries, block Huan-yuan and Dagu, and control the strategic points. Gonglu should lead the Nanyang troops, station at Danxi and Xixi, and enter Wuguan to shake the Three Divisions:

Make deep trenches and high earthen walls; do not seek open battle. Use feigned reinforcements so the outside can read the situation, then move steadily to punish the traitor and set the realm right. Your present hesitation and delay have failed the world. It shames me.”

No one had an answer.

When the banquet ended, Cao Cao saw that everyone carried divided intent and could not accomplish anything together, so he took his troops to Yang Province.

Gongsun Zan said to Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei, “Yuan Shao cannot achieve this. He will change eventually. We should withdraw now.”

They lifted their camps and rode north. At Pingyuan, he appointed Liu Bei as Inspector of Pingyuan and withdrew to defend and strengthen the army.

Liu Dai, Administrator of Yanzhou, asked Qiao Mao, Administrator of Dongjun, for grain. Qiao Mao refused. Liu Dai rode in and charged Qiao Mao’s camp, killing him; all his men surrendered.

Yuan Shao saw everyone dispersing and took his own forces, lifted camp, left Luoyang, and went toward Jiangdong.

At that time, Liu Biao, style name Jingsheng, was from Gaoping in Shanyang. He was a collateral branch of the Han house. As a youth he liked gathering with notable men and had seven famous friends, and they were known as the “Eight Worthies of Jiangxia.”

Those seven were: Chen Xiang of Runan, style Zhonglin; Fan Pang, a fellow-countryman, style Mengbo; Kong Yu of Lu State, style Shiyuan; Fan Kang of Bohai, style Zhongzhen; Tan Fu of Shanyang, style Wenyu; Zhang Jian, a fellow-countryman, style Yuanjie; and Cen Zhi of Nanyang, style Gongxiao.

Liu Biao was also friendly with Kua Liang and Kua Yue, both from Yanping, and Cai Mao, who was from Xiangyang.

When Liu Biao saw Yuan Shao’s letter, he immediately ordered Kua Yue and Cai Mao, with ten thousand troops, to intercept Sun Jian.

As soon as Sun Jian’s army arrived, Kua Yue set the formation and rode out first.

Sun Jian asked, “Kua Yue, why do you bring troops to block my road?”

Kua Yue replied, “You are a Han minister. How can you hide the Heirloom Seal and keep it to yourself? Leave it at once and I will let you go.”

Sun Jian was enraged and ordered Huang Gai to fight.

Cai Mao came on, brandishing his sword.

They fought several exchanges. Huang Gai struck him with a whip directly into the breastplate. Cai Mao turned his horse and fled. Sun Jian pressed on through the gate.

From behind the hills drums and gongs sounded together, and Liu Biao himself arrived with troops.

From horseback, Sun Jian saluted, saying, “Why, Jingsheng, did you trust Yuan Shao’s letter and pressure a neighboring commandery like this?”

Liu Biao asked, “You are hiding the Heirloom State Seal and plotting rebellion?”

Sun Jian said, “If I had this object, I would have died by blade and arrow.”

Liu Biao replied, “If you want me to believe you, place your baggage under my authority and let me inspect it.”

Sun Jian said angrily, “What power do you think you have to look down on me!”

As he moved to engage, Liu Biao withdrew.

Sun Jian drove after him. Behind the hills both sides rose with ambushes. Kua Yue and Cai Mao came from the rear and drove Sun Jian into a surrounded position.

It was this:

The Heirloom State Seal brought no benefit, but this treasure stirred all the blades and the bloodshed.

How Sun Jian might escape this trap, How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Jade Hall Burns as Dong Zhuo Turns Violent, and Sun Jian Conceals the Imperial Seal, Then Breaks His Word

chapters.html:
Yuan Shao clashes with Gongsun at Pan River. Sun Jian crosses the river and strikes at Liu Biao.

Earlier, Sun Jian is besieged by Liu Biao. Thanks to Cheng Pu, Huang Gai, and Han Dang, who risk their lives to save him, Sun Jian breaks out, though his force suffers heavy losses, and forces a road open to return to Jiangdong. From then on, Sun Jian and Liu Biao become enemies.

Elsewhere, Yuan Shao camps in Henei. He is short of provisions. Han Fu, Governor of Jizhou, sends supply grain to support the army. Adviser Feng Ji says to Yuan Shao: “A man of broad ambitions under heaven should not have to wait for others to send him food to eat. Jizhou is a land of broad and abundant grain and wealth. Why does the General not take it?” Yuan Shao says, “I have no good plan yet.” Feng Ji says, “You can send a secret courier to Gongsun Zan, ordering him to move in with his troops and attack Jizhou. Strike from both sides, and he will certainly raise his forces. Han Fu has no strategic sense; he will ask you to take over provincial administration. In that arrangement, taking what is needed from him is easy.”

Yuan Shao is delighted and immediately sends a sealed dispatch to Gongsun Zan. Gongsun receives it and orders his troops to mobilize at once, thinking Jizhou can be divided after they attack together. Yuan Shao then sends a trusted agent with secret news to Han Fu. Han Fu panics and gathers his counselors Xun Shen and Xin Ping for counsel.

Xun Shen says, “Gongsun Zan brings troops from Yan and Dai as his leading force, and their momentum is hard to withstand. Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei also support him. Yuan Shao is beyond ordinary in wisdom and valor; he has many famous generals. Ask him to govern the province under you. He will certainly treat you well. No threat from Gongsun Zan.” Han Fu sends his officer Guan Chun at once to invite Yuan Shao.

Chancellor Geng Wu remonstrates: “General Yuan Shao is a lone guest and an impoverished army, drawing breath from us. It is like an infant in our palm—if its nursing is cut off, it will soon die of hunger. Why would we entrust the province to him? This is like leading a tiger into a flock of sheep.” Han Fu replies, “I am an old retainer of the Yuan house, and I am not as capable as Benchu. In former times, the worthies were invited and entrusted with office; why are you all resentful?” Geng Wu sighs, “Jizhou is doomed!”

So more than thirty officials leave office. Only Geng Wu and Guan Chun wait outside the city to receive Yuan Shao. After several days, Yuan Shao arrives with his troops.

Geng Wu and Guan Chun draw their swords and rush out to stab Yuan Shao. Yuan Shao’s general Yan Liang immediately beheads Geng Wu, and Wen Chou kills Guan Chun with his saber.

Yuan Shao enters Jizhou, appoints Han Fu as General Who Expands the Might of the Army, and places Tian Feng, Ju Shou, Xu You, and Feng Ji to share control of provincial administration, stripping Han Fu of authority. Han Fu repents too late. He gives up wife and family and, on one horse, rides to Chenliu to surrender himself to Governor Zhang Miao.

Later, Gongsun Zan hears that Yuan Shao has already taken Jizhou and sends his brother Gongsun Yue to request a division of the land. Yuan Shao answers, “Let your brother come here in person. I have a matter to discuss.” Gongsun Yue departs.

Not yet fifty li from home, a band of horsemen appears from the roadside and shouts: “I am an armed retainer from Chancellor Dong’s household!” Arrows flew and killed Gongsun Yue. The survivors return to Gongsun Zan with the news of Yue’s death. Gongsun Zan is furious and says, “Yuan Shao lured me to raise troops against Han Fu, then took this place in his own hands. Now he sent Dong’s household soldiers in disguise and killed my brother! How can such a grievance go unavenged?” He raises all his forces and rides toward Jizhou.

When Yuan Shao learns that Gongsun Zan is approaching, he also leads the army out. The two forces meet at Pan River.

Yuan Shao takes his camp east of the bridge at the river; Gongsun Zan stays west of it. Gongsun Zan mounts on the bridge and shouts: “You traitorous man of loyalty and righteousness! How dare you sell me out!” Yuan Shao also rides to the bridge edge and says, “Han Fu has no talent. I have offered to take Jizhou into my charge; what concern have you?” Gongsun Zan replies, “You once were counted loyal and upright, and you were made alliance leader. What you do now is the conduct of a heart with a wolf’s heart and dog’s gait. How can you still face this world?”

Yuan Shao is furious: “Who can seize him?”

Before he finishes, Wen Chou spurs his horse with spear raised and rides straight onto the bridge. Gongsun Zan closes with him at the bridge edge. The two fight for less than ten exchanges. Gongsun Zan cannot withstand the pressure, and he breaks from the line to flee.

Wen Chou pursues hard. Gongsun Zan runs into the main formation. Wen Chou gallops directly into the rear rank, weaving through and clashing again and again. Four of Gongsun Zan’s strongest captains rush forward together, but Wen Chou with one spear thrust slays one and makes that captain fall from his horse; the other three give way. Wen Chou presses on in pursuit after Gongsun Zan breaks away from the host. Gongsun Zan runs toward a valley in the hills; Wen Chou yells, “Dismount and yield!” and shouts at him. Gongsun’s helmet falls and his arrows are spent. He lets his hair stream, wheels his horse on the slope, and the horse stumbles. Gongsun tumbles down the hillside.

Wen Chou quickly turns his horse and lifts his spear to strike. Suddenly, from the left side of the grass slope, one young commander appears on horseback. He rides in, spear raised high, and attacks Wen Chou directly. Gongsun climbs up after him. He is tall, broad-shouldered, with thick brows and bright eyes, a wide face, and a heavy jawline. He has a majestic air. For five or six dozen passes, he and Wen Chou trade blows, and victory is still undecided.

Gongsun’s rescue force arrives. Wen Chou wheels his horse away and pulls back. The young man does not give chase. Gongsun hurries down from the slope and asks his name. The young man bows and says, “My surname is Zhao, my personal name is Yun, and my courtesy name is Zilong. I am from Zhen Ding in Changshan, and was once under Yuan Shao’s command. Seeing that Yuan Shao has no loyalty to his lord or compassion for the people, I abandoned him and came under your banner; I did not expect to meet you here.”

Gongsun rejoices and takes him back to camp to arrange the troops.

The next day, Gongsun deploys his cavalry in matching left and right wings, like wings to a bird in flight. He has over five thousand horses, most of them white. Because Gongsun once fought the Qiang, he chose white horses for the vanguard, bearing the title “White Horse General.” The Qiang fled at the sight of the white horses, so he had many of them.

Yuan Shao appoints Yan Liang and Wen Chou as the vanguard, each bringing one thousand bowmen, arranged again in two wings: the left to shoot at Gongsun Zan’s right wing, the right to shoot at his left. He also orders Qiu Yi to lead eight hundred crossbowmen and fifteen thousand infantry to form the main formation. Yuan Shao himself brings several thousand cavalry and foot soldiers in the rear.

Gongsun, just now reinforced by Zhao Yun, trusts him no more than before and assigns him to a separate force in the rear. He sends the general Yan Gang to lead the vanguard. He leads the center himself, mounting on the bridge and setting a broad red banner marked with a gold-ringed Shuai in front of his horse.

From the Chén period through the Sì period, drums thunder and Yuan Shao’s army does not advance.

Qiu Yi orders the bowmen to lie below the arrow screens and hold fire until the signal. Yan Gang bellows and rushes forward, striking straight for Qiu Yi. Qiu Yi’s men freeze as they see Yan Gang arrive. When he is close enough, the signal sounds and all eight hundred bowmen fire together.

Yan Gang, forced to turn back, is cut down when Qiu Yi beats his horse and swings his saber. He beheads him at the horse’s foot. Gongsun’s force is routed.
