Both left and right wings try to come to its aid, but Yan Liang and Wen Chou’s bowmen hold them at bay. Yuan Shao’s army advances, pressing to the bridge edge when Qiu Yi’s horse arrives. The first to fall is the flag-bearer, and the embroidered banner falls.

When Gongsun Zan sees the banner fall, he turns his horse and rides back across the bridge to retreat. Qiu Yi chases toward the rear and crashes directly into Zhao Yun. Zhao Yun lifts his spear, leaps from the saddle, and drives it home. In no more than a handful of exchanges, Qiu Yi falls from his horse.

Zhao Yun flies into Yuan Shao’s host on his own horse, cutting left and right like entering empty land.

Gongsun rallies his men and turns to strike back. Yuan Shao’s army collapses.

Yuan Shao had already sent scouts; they returned reporting that Qiu Yi had killed the flag-bearer and captured the banner, and had pursued the routed troops. In overconfidence he makes no further preparations and rides out with Tian Feng and several hundred halberdiers and a handful of mounted bowmen, riding hard. “Look at this wretched Gongsun Zan, he is good for nothing!” he laughs. Before the words are done, Zhao Yun bursts in before him.

The mounted bowmen move to shoot, but Zhao Yun spears several of them and the others scatter. Behind him Gongsun Zan’s whole army closes in all around.

Tian Feng panics and says to Yuan Shao, “My lord, hide behind the wall for a moment.” Yuan Shao throws down his helmeted weight and roars, “A man of honor goes into battle and dies; how could I hide behind a wall and hope to live?”

The soldiers all stand as one and fight to the death. Zhao Yun cannot break through to the far side. Yuan Shao’s main force arrives in depth, then Yan Liang also brings his force; the two strike together. Zhao Yun protects Gongsun Zan through the heavy encirclement and returns to the border bridge.

Yuan Shao presses in and presses them to cross the bridge again. Men fall into the water, beyond counting. Yuan Shao himself chases within five li before shouts rise from behind the hill and a company of horsemen bursts forth. Three riders lead them: Liu Bei (Xuande), Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei.

They had learned in Pingyuan that Gongsun and Yuan Shao were fighting and come in aid. On three horses with three kinds of weapons, they charge straight at Yuan Shao.

Yuan Shao is struck with shock and his cherished sabre falls from his hand. He turns and rides off in panic, and his men fight hard to cover him as they carry the crossing of the bridge in haste.

Gongsun also gathers his army and returns to camp. Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei ask after him. Gongsun says, “If Xuande had not come all this way to save me, I would have been reduced to misery.” He has them receive Zhao Yun.

Liu Bei is deeply respectful of him and not willing to part.

Yuan Shao, after losing a hard battle, holds his ground and does not sortie. For a month the two armies stare across each other. Someone goes to Chang’an and reports to Dong Zhuo. Li Ru says, “Yuan Shao and Gongsun Zan are both prominent heroes now. Since they are fighting at Pan River, we should use the emperor’s edict to send envoys and make peace between them. If they receive the Great Tutor’s command, they will yield.” Dong Zhuo is delighted.

The next day he sends Grand Tutor Ma Ridi and Master of the Stable Zhao Qi with an imperial edict. The two arrive in Hebei; Yuan Shao receives them one hundred li out and bows to them twice. The following day they go to Gongsun Zan’s camp and read the edict.

Gongsun then sends a memorial to Yuan Shao and agrees to reconciliation talks. The envoys return and report in the capital.

That same day Gongsun dismisses his army and recommends Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, for the office of Pingyuan Administrator.

Liu Bei and Zhao Yun part ways, clasping hands and crying, reluctant to separate. Zhao Yun says, “I only just mistook Gongsun Zan for a hero; now that I have seen him, he is no different from men like Yuan Shao.”

Liu Bei says, “For now, submit and serve him. We will meet again.” They part in tears.

Yuan Shu in Nanyang hears that Yuan Shao has just taken Jizhou. He sends a request for one thousand horses. Yuan Shao refuses, and Yuan Shu is angry. From then on, the brothers are estranged.

Yuan Shu sends another envoy to Liu Biao asking for two hundred thousand rations. Biao refuses as well.

Yuan Shu, still resentful, sends a secret letter to Sun Jian saying:

Formerly, Liu Biao cut off my return route—that was Benchu’s design. Now Benchu is secretly in counsel with Biao and intends to attack Jiangdong. You should quickly raise troops and strike Liu Biao. I will capture Benchu for you; then the two grudges can be repaid together. You take Jingzhou, and I will take Jizhou. Do not miss the moment.

Sun Jian reads the letter and says, “I cannot bear Liu Biao! Earlier he blocked my route, and that was Benchu’s plot. He did not take vengeance then, and now the time still comes. Why do we wait?” He gathers Cheng Pu, Huang Gai, and Han Dang to discuss.

Cheng Pu says, “Yuan Shu is full of deceit and cannot be trusted.” Sun Jian replies, “I already mean to repay this injury. I need not wait for Yuan Shu’s help.” He orders Huang Gai to the river first, preparing ships. The boats are loaded with weapons and grain, and the largest vessels carry warhorses. He fixes an auspicious day and raises troops.

Scouts on the water report to Liu Biao. Liu Biao is greatly alarmed and gathers his civil and military officers to discuss. Kuai Liang says, “No reason for alarm. Have Huang Zu’s unit lead the troops of Jiangxia as vanguard, while you lead Jing and Xiang forces in support. Sun Jian crosses river and lake and cannot really bring force here.” Liu Biao accepts this and orders Huang Zu to make preparations while he mobilizes a major army.

Now Sun Jian has four sons by Lady Wu: his eldest is Sun Ce, courtesy name Bo Fu; second is Sun Quan, courtesy name Zhongmou; third is Sun Yi, courtesy name Shubi; fourth is Sun Kuang, courtesy name Jizuo. Lady Wu’s younger sister is Sun Jian’s second wife. She bore him one son and one daughter as well: a son named Lang, courtesy name Zao'an, and a daughter named Ren.

He also had another son by Lady Yu named Shao, courtesy name Gongli. He has a younger brother, Jing, whose courtesy name was Youtai.

As Sun Jian leaves, Jing brings the sons before the horses and remonstrates: “Dong Zhuo now monopolizes power. The Son of Heaven is weak, and the realm is in turmoil under competing lords. In Jiangdong, things are still relatively calm. To raise troops for a private grievance is not fitting. Consider this carefully.” Sun Jian says, “Do not urge me further. A man who means to stride through the world does not let an injury go unavenged.”

His eldest son Sun Ce says, “If my father must go, I will go with him.” Sun Jian grants permission, and they both board and sail for Fancheng.

Huang Zu deploys bowmen along the bank. As the boats approach shore, his men pour out arrows all together. Sun Jian orders the troops not to move recklessly. They stay aboard and bait them in and out. For three days, the ships come by the bank repeatedly. Huang Zu’s men keep firing until their arrows are spent.

Sun Jian has his men haul out the arrows from the ships, around ten-thousand or more in number. That day the wind is favorable, and Sun Jian orders the troops to fire all at once from the boats. Huang Zu’s men break and fall back.

Sun Jian’s forces land. Cheng Pu and Huang Gai divide and advance in two directions, striking directly at Huang Zu’s camp. Han Dang leads the support behind. With the army pressed from three sides, Huang Zu is routed, abandons Fancheng, and retreats into Dengcheng.

Sun Jian leaves Huang Gai to guard the ships and personally leads the pursuit. Huang Zu takes the field to meet him and arrays his troops in open ground. Sun Jian arranges formations and appears under the gate banner. Sun Ce, fully armed, raises his spear and mounts at his father’s side.

Huang Zu brings out two commanders: one Zhang Hu of Jiangxia and the other Chen Sheng of Xiangyang.

Huang Zu cracks his whip and shouts, “Mouse thieves of Jiangdong, how dare you invade Han ancestral territory!” He orders Zhang Hu into battle.

Han Dang rides out to meet him. The two horses clash; they fight for more than thirty exchanges. Seeing Chen Sheng stronger than Zhang Hu, Chen Sheng rides up to assist. Sun Ce sees this, braces his spear, nocks an arrow, and shoots it into Chen Sheng’s face. Chen Sheng is knocked from his horse.

Seeing Chen Sheng fall, Zhang Hu is startled and unsure what to do; Han Dang’s blade cuts through half his skull at once. Cheng Pu rides directly toward Huang Zu’s front. Huang Zu drops both helmet and war horse and flees into the infantry ranks.

Sun Jian pursues the defeated enemy to the Han River and orders Huang Gai to bring the ships into the Han River harbor.

Huang Zu gathers his broken host and reports to Liu Biao that Sun Jian is now beyond check. Liu Biao swiftly asks Kuai Liang for counsel.

Kuai Liang says, “The army has no fighting heart after this defeat. Open deep ditches and build high ramparts to avoid his thrust; meanwhile, secretly request help from Yuan Shao. This siege can then be relieved.” Cai Mao says, “The matter that Kuai Liang proposes is a narrow plan. If the army is already at the walls and the riverbank, can we stand and die there waiting for rescue? Though I am unfit, I ask to lead soldiers out and force a decisive engagement.” Liu Biao grants permission.

Cai Mao leads over ten thousand men out of Xiangyang and sets a camp on Xianshan. Sun Jian charges with his victorious troops. Cai Mao comes out too.

Sun Jian says, “This man is a brother of Liu Biao’s newly acquired wife. Who among us can capture him?” Cheng Pu rides with his iron-backed halberd and clashes with Cai Mao. After only a few exchanges, Cai Mao breaks and runs. Sun Jian’s army continues slaughter until the plain is covered with bodies.

Cai Mao escapes into Xiangyang. Kuai Liang says Cai Mao ignored his counsel and brought disaster; by military law he should be beheaded. Liu Biao, having recently taken a new wife, refuses to punish him.

Sun Jian then divides forces in four and besieges Xiangyang. One day, a raging wind rises and breaks the banner staff of the command center.

Han Dang says, “This is inauspicious. We should suspend the attack briefly and retreat.” Sun Jian says, “I have won battle after battle. Xiangyang will fall tomorrow or the day after. We do not stop because a banner staff broke.” He refuses and presses harder.

Kuai Liang tells Liu Biao, “Last night I observed the skies and saw one general star about to fall. Judged by where it falls, the star should strike Sun Jian. Your lordship should quickly send a letter to Yuan Shao and ask for his help.” Liu Biao sends the letter.

The question is who can break through the lines to the enemy. Veteran Lu Gong volunteers immediately.

Kuai Liang advises: “You go out and keep five hundred horses with you, plus as many good archers as possible. Ride to Xianshan. He will pursue when he sees you. Send one hundred men to the ridge with stones prepared. Keep another hundred among the trees with bows and crossbows in ambush. If there is a pursuer, do not run straight away. Turn in winding paths, drawing him to the ambush. Then fire all together. If you win, fire the chain cannon and the city will send support. If no pursuer comes, do not fire; leave quickly while dusk remains.”

Lu Gong takes this plan and tightens the reins. At dusk he secretly opens the east gate and brings out troops.

Sun Jian is in his tent when he hears the commotion and rides out with more than thirty riders to investigate. The troops report: “A band of mounted men has broken out and is moving toward Xianshan.” Sun Jian does not wait for his whole command and chases with only thirty riders.

Lu Gong is already in position in mountain thickets, and he and his men are concealed for ambush in the brush. Sun Jian rides hard and closes in fast, alone with his vanguard close behind.

Sun Jian shouts, “Do not flee!” Lu Gong rears his horse and turns toward Sun Jian. Their horses clash once. Lu Gong then turns and slips into a mountain path.

Sun Jian chases after him and is suddenly struck by drum, gong, and stone. Stones crash from the hill and arrows pour out of the woods. A stone-arrow pierces Sun Jian. His brain bursts and both he and his horse die at Xianshan. He is thirty-seven.

Lu Gong intercepts thirty of Sun Jian’s riders and kills them all, then sounds the linked cannon. In the city, Huang Zu, Kuai Yue, and Cai Mao each lead troops out in separate directions, and Jiangdong troops are thrown into confusion.

Huang Gai hears the sky-filling cry, drives his water troops in and blocks Huang Zu. They fight for less than two exchanges, and Huang Gai captures Huang Zu alive.

Cheng Pu protects Sun Ce and searches for a way out. He meets Lu Gong. Cheng Pu spurs forward and in a few exchanges drives a spear into Lu Gong at his horse’s side. The two armies clash until dawn, then withdraw.

Liu Biao’s army returns to the city. Sun Ce returns to the Han River and learns his father’s body has been shot by random arrows; Liu Biao’s soldiers carried the corpse inside with a bier. He cries out.

All his men weep together.

Sun Ce says, “My father’s body is there. How can we return home?” Huang Gai says, “We have Huang Zu alive in camp. Send one man into the city as envoy to negotiate. Return Huang Zu, and in exchange recover our lord’s body. Let both sides stop and never cross this boundary again.”

Before he finishes, the officer Huan Kai steps forward: “I have old ties with Liu Biao and ask leave to enter the city as envoy.” Sun Ce grants it.

Huan Kai enters Xiangyang and reports all. Liu Biao says, “I have placed Lord Wentai’s body in a coffin here. Return Huang Zu at once. Let both sides stand down and never invade each other again.”

Huan Kai bows to leave. On the stair below, Kuai Liang appears and cries out, “No! No! I have one plea: if we wish all Jiangdong soldiers not to return, first execute Huan Kai, and only then set the plan in motion.”

So it is written:

Sun Jian dies as he gives chase, and Huan Kai is punished while seeking peace. Unknown is Huan Kai’s fate.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Yuan Shao Battles Gongsun at Pan River; Sun Jian Crosses the River to Strike Liu Biao

chapters.html:
Later Kuai Liang said, “Sun Jian has fallen, and all his sons are still young. Seize this hour of weakness, and advance the army at once. In one drumbeat, Jiangdong can be taken. If we return after receiving the body and then dismiss our soldiers, they will gather their strength, and that will be a threat to Jing Province.”

Huan Kai replied, “I have Huang Zu with me in camp. How could I endure to abandon him?”

Kuai Liang said, “What is there wrong in letting Huang Zu go and taking Jiangdong?”

Huan Kai said, “You and Huang Zu are intimate close friends. To abandon him is unjust.”

He sent Huan Kai back to camp, and the two agreed to exchange Sun Jian’s body for Huang Zu. Liu Biao got Huang Zu returned, while Sun Ce received the body, halted the war, returned to Jiangdong, and buried his father on the plain of Quya. The mourning rites completed, he moved his troops to Jiangdu, where he recruited able men and received scholars and heroes with humility. Men of renown from all four directions gradually came to him.

Later, Dong Zhuo in Chang’an heard that Sun Jian was dead, and said, “A heart’s-most-troublesome enemy has been removed.”

He asked, “How old is the son?”

Someone answered, “Seventeen.”

Dong Zhuo gave it no further thought. From then on he grew more arrogant and rampant. He began to style himself “Shangfu” and moved in and out as if he were sharing the emperor’s ceremonial train. He made his brother Dong Min a Left General and marquis of Hu; his nephew Dong Huang a chamberlain, in charge of the imperial guards. The Dong clan, without regard to age, were all made marquises.

Two hundred and fifty li from Chang’an, a separate stronghold, Meiwu, was built. Two hundred and fifty thousand laborers were conscripted for its construction; its walls and buildings were raised to heights and thicknesses like those of Chang’an. Inside stood palace rooms and storehouses, with twenty years’ grain stockpiled. They installed eight hundred handsome young maidens from the villages, and heaps of gold, silk, and pearls beyond count. His family all lived within.

Dong Zhuo traveled back to Chang’an, sometimes every two weeks, sometimes monthly. All the ministers waited to receive him outside Heng Gate.

Dong Zhuo often pitched a pavilion on the road and drank with the ministers. One day, when he came out through Heng Gate, all officers escorted him. After he kept the banquet running, several hundred surrendered soldiers from Beidi who had submitted were brought in. Dong Zhuo ordered them to the front of the seat, and then had some have hands and feet cut off, some have their eyes gouged out, some have their tongues severed, and some boiled in great cauldrons. Their cries shook the heavens; the ministers trembled and dropped their chopsticks, while Dong drank and joked as if nothing had happened.

Another day, Dong Zhuo assembled the ministers in the audience hall and lined them in two rows. After wine had gone back and forth several times, Lü Bu entered directly and whispered a few words into Dong Zhuo’s ear. Dong Zhuo laughed and said, “Aha, I understand.” He ordered Lü Bu on the spot to seize Zhang Wen, Minister of Works, and drag him from the hall. The ministers’ faces drained of color.

Not long after, an attendant stepped forward carrying a red tray bearing Zhang Wen’s head and presented it. The ministers were stunned.

Dong Zhuo laughed. “Do not be alarmed, gentlemen. Zhang Wen had secretly linked with Yuan Shu and plotted to harm me. A letter was sent and came misdelivered to my son Fengxian’s quarters, so I executed him. You have no reason to fear.”

The officials agreed politely and dispersed.

Grand Chancellor Wang Yun returned home and kept thinking about the events of the hall, unable to sit still. Late at night under bright moonlight, he took a cane and walked into the rear garden. He stood beside the peony trellis and looked up at the sky, tears falling. Suddenly he heard someone at the side of the peony pavilion sighing in long, bitter gasps. Wang Yun stepped softly to peer inside. It was Diaochan, a singer-dancer of the house.

She had been selected from childhood for the household, taught song and dance, and at eighteen, with all the graces of an accomplished beauty. Wang Yun treated her as if she were his own daughter. That night he listened for a long while before calling out, “Girl, do you have feelings of your own?”

Diaochan started and knelt. “How could I, your slave, have any private feeling?”

Wang Yun said, “If not, why long sighing and crying in the deep of night?”

She said, “Permit me, Master, to lay bare my heart.

“Do not hide anything from me; tell me truly.”

“Greatly honored by your kindness, trained in song and dance, and treated with every courtesy, I could tear my body to powder and still fail to repay you even once.”

“Recently I saw the furrow above your brows; there must be a great matter of the state, and I dared not ask. Tonight I found you unable to remain seated, and so I sighed. It was no intention of disloyalty, only to be caught by you by chance. If there is any use for me, I will die ten thousand times without complaint.”

Wang Yun struck the ground with his cane and cried, “Who would have thought Han’s realm now rests in your hands? Come with me into the Painted Pavilion.”

Diaochan followed Wang Yun to the pavilion, and he ordered all maidservants out and had her seated. She knelt and prostrated herself. Diaochan said from the floor, “Why this, Great Minister?”

Wang Yun said, “Have pity on the lives of the people of the Great Han.” His voice broke with tears.

Diaochan said, “Just now I said this: if there is an order, I dare not refuse, even to the end of my life.”

Wang Yun knelt and said, “The common people stand in peril as if hanging in midair; the throne and ministers have an emergency as precarious as eggs stacked together. No one can save this but you.”

“The traitorous courtier Dong Zhuo will seize the throne. The ministers and military men of the court have no plan left.”

“Dong Zhuo has a man of loyal heart, surname Lü, name Bu. He is extraordinary in valour. I see that both men are lovers of desire. We will use a linked stratagem: first promise you to Lü Bu, and then present you to Dong Zhuo. In the middle, set father and son at odds, have Bu slay Zhuo, and cut off the great evil. Then the realm will rise again and the state be restored. It will all be through your strength.”

“What do you say?”

Diaochan replied, “I give my word to you, my life will be spent in no hesitation. I will be offered to him at once. I have my own way to do it.”

Wang Yun said, “If word of this leaks, my whole house will be wiped out.”

Diaochan answered, “Do not worry. If I fail the great cause, let me die under ten thousand blades.”

Wang Yun gratefully accepted her loyalty.

The next day he took several radiant pearls from his hidden stores and had a master goldsmith set one gold crown. He sent it secretly to Lü Bu.

Lü Bu rejoiced, and came in person to Wang Yun’s residence to offer thanks. Wang Yun prepared refined food and wine and, when he saw Lü Bu arrive, went out to welcome him and brought him into the rear hall, seating him above. Lü Bu said, “Lü Bu is a general of the Chief Minister’s office, and you, Wang, are a high minister of court. Why do you show this much respect?”

Wang Yun said, “Today there is no hero under heaven besides the General.”

“Wang does not honor the general’s rank but the general’s worth.”

Lü Bu smiled broadly. Wang Yun made him drink carefully and praised Dong Tai-shi and Lü Bu’s virtues as one stream without end. Lü Bu laughed and drank freely. Wang Yun dismissed the attendants, leaving only a few servants to urge him on with wine.

When he was half drunk, Wang Yun said, “Call the girl.”

A short while later, two blue-clad attendants brought out Diaochan in vivid beauty. Lü Bu asked, surprised, who she was.

Wang Yun said, “She is my daughter, Diaochan. I care for the general like a dear elder brother, so I let her meet the general.”

He then ordered Diaochan and Lü Bu to raise their cups together. Diaochan offered wine to him, and eyes met across it.

Wang Yun feigned drunkenness. “My girl begs you, General, to drink a few more cups. My household now depends on you.”

Lü Bu invited Diaochan to sit. She made as though she wished to leave.

Wang Yun said, “You are my truest friend, why should my daughter not sit here?”

Diaochan then sat at Wang’s side. Lü Bu’s gaze never moved.

After several more cups, Wang Yun said, “My wish is to give this girl to you as a concubine. Will you still accept?”

Lü Bu said with ceremony, “If this is granted, Bu will repay with the loyalty of a hound and horse.”

Wang Yun said, “Choose a fine day soon, and I will send her to your household.”

Lü Bu was boundless with delight and kept looking at Diaochan. Diaochan too returned glances with her eyes.

After a while the banquet ended. Wang Yun said, “I had wanted to keep you here for the night, but the Grand Master might grow suspicious.”

Lü Bu thanked him again and left.

A few days later, Wang Yun saw Dong Zhuo in court and, while Lü Bu stood not at his side, he knelt to the ground and requested, “I ask of the Chief Minister permission to host the Grand Master in my thatched residence and present this banquet. I do not know whether this pleases him.”

Dong Zhuo said, “If Chancellor Wang invites, of course I will come.”

Wang Yun thanked him and returned home. He gathered troops and vessels by land and water, and arranged a central seat in the front hall, with brocade spread on the floor and curtains inside and out. The next midday Dong Zhuo arrived.

Wang Yun came out in court robes and received him with a second bow. Dong Zhuo stepped down from the chariot; two dozen halberd-bearers in armor accompanied him into the hall and lined up to either side. Wang Yun bowed in the hall again; Dong Zhuo ordered him raised and gave him a place at his side.

Wang Yun said, “Great Master, your virtue is lofty beyond comparison, beyond even Yi and Zhou.”

Dong Zhuo was greatly pleased.

They moved from wine to music. Wang Yun honored him to the fullest. Late into the evening he invited Dong Zhuo into the back hall and ordered his guards dismissed.

Wang Yun raised the cup and said, “Since youth I have read some astronomy. Nightly I have watched the Milky Way stars, and the fate of the Han house is nearly spent. Great Master, your merit and virtue resound across the realm, like Yao receiving Shun, like Yu succeeding Yao. It matches heaven’s will and the people’s mind.”

Dong Zhuo said, “How could I dare to expect such a thing?”

Wang Yun said, “Since old times, one who has the Way may punish one without it, and one with virtue should yield to one with greater virtue. Is that excessive?”

Dong Zhuo laughed. “If heaven’s mandate truly returns to me, the Chancellor will become a primary contributor of this age.”

Wang Yun bowed. In the hall they lit painted candles and left only women to bring wine and food. Wang Yun said, “Music from the court academy is not enough for proper reception; I have a household performer who can respond to your wishes.”

Dong Zhuo said, “Very fine.”

He ordered the curtains lowered, and music of reed pipes coiled through the hall as attendants presented Diaochan through the draped screen to dance.

The words praising her were sung:

Once she had been a woman of Zhaoyang Palace,
A startled swan-like beauty turned within the palm,
As though she had flown over spring at Dongting.
In rhythm she moved with a steady lotus-step,
A fresh flower swaying in the wind, a new blossom,
The painted hall was warm with fragrance, overwhelmed by spring.

Another poem:

Red-toothed hands beat the rhythm, and swallows fly in haste, A streak of drifting cloud reaches the painted hall. Dark brows and eyeliner sharpen the homesick ache of a traveler; Her face first cuts the old companion’s heart. A pair of willow-wreath charms mocks money worth a thousand gold; Why spend rich ornaments on this beauty. After the dance, she watched from behind the screen as if stealing glances, Not knowing which is king of Chu and lord Xiang.

When the dance ended, Dong Zhuo ordered her nearer. Diaochan returned through the curtain and knelt deeply. He saw her and asked, “Who is this woman?”

Wang Yun replied, “She is the singing and dancing slave Diaochan.”

Dong Zhuo asked, “Can she sing?”

Wang Yun told Diaochan to strike the clappers softly and sing a single piece.

It was this:

A single cherry point opens vermilion lips, Two lines of broken jade fling out the spring sun. A lilac tongue looses a cross-guarded sword, Wanting to cut down treacherous ministers and restore order in the realm.

Dong Zhuo praised her without end.

Wang Yun ordered Diaochan to pass the cup, and Dong Zhuo raised his and asked, “How old are you?”

Diaochan answered, “The slave is only eighteen, still young.”

Dong Zhuo laughed, “Truly, you are a spirit from paradise.”

Wang Yun spoke, “I wish to present this girl to Great Master, if he can accept.”

Dong Zhuo said, “For such kindness, how should I ever repay your favor?”

Wang Yun replied, “The fortune she has in serving Great Master will be slight.”

Dong Zhuo thanked him repeatedly.

Wang Yun ordered a felt carriage prepared and first sent Diaochan to Dong Zhuo’s residence. Dong Zhuo rose and took leave. Wang Yun personally escorted him to his residence and then returned.

Riding onward, he had not yet gone halfway when two lines of red lanterns lit the way and Lü Bu rode up with an uplifted halberd. He met Wang Yun face to face and jerked him to a stop, grabbing his robe collar and crying out in a rough voice,

“First Wang promised her to me as a wife; now you have sent her to Great Master. Is this some mockery?”

Wang Yun hurriedly said, “This is no place to talk. Let us go to the thatched pavilion.”

Lü Bu accompanied him home and entered the rear hall. After the formal courtesy, Wang Yun asked, “General, why do you accuse this old man?”

Lü Bu said, “Someone reported to me that you sent a felt carriage with Diaochan to Dong Zhuo’s residence. Why was this done?”

Wang Yun said, “General, you do not know. Yesterday Great Master said in court: ‘I have a matter to deal with at your house.’ So I prepared and waited for Great Master. Over wine I said, ‘I have heard you have a girl named Diaochan already promised to my son Fengxian. I fear what you hear may be uncertain, so I came to ask for one audience with her.’ The old man had no choice. I brought Diaochan out and had her bow to the great lord. Great Master said, ‘Today is an auspicious day. I shall take this woman and return her to be matched with Fengxian.’

“General, think this over. When Great Master came in person, how dare I resist?”

Lü Bu said, “Wang, forgive the error. By forceful wrong, I have erred once and will shoulder the guilt tomorrow.”

Wang Yun said, “My girl has only some preparation. After she passes your home gate, I will send her on.”

Lü Bu thanked him and left.

The next day, Lü Bu inquired all over the household, but he heard nothing of her. He strode into the hall and directly questioned the maidservants.

A waiting maid said, “Last night Great Master slept with the new bride in the same chamber. She has not yet risen.”

Lü Bu raged, and sneaked into Dong Zhuo’s bedchamber and looked from behind. At that moment Diaochan had risen and was combing her hair at the window. She suddenly saw his figure reflected from the pool outside, tall and shadowed, wearing a bundled-hair crown. She feigned a frown and an air of sorrow, then with thin silk repeatedly dabbed tears from her eyes.

Lü Bu watched for a long while and then withdrew. After a short while he entered again.

Dong Zhuo had already sat in the central hall. Seeing Lü Bu come in, he asked, “No trouble outside, I think?”

Lü Bu replied, “No trouble.”

He stood beside Dong Zhuo. As Dong was eating, Lü Bu stole glances into the embroidered screen and saw a woman going in and out, half her face exposed, sending eye signals of attachment. Lü Bu knew it was Diaochan and his spirit wandered.

Dong Zhuo saw Lü Bu in this state and felt suspicion in his heart. He said, “Fengxian, if you have no business, then leave.”

Lü Bu left unwillingly.

From the time Dong Zhuo took Diaochan as his own, he fell into lust and ignored affairs for the whole of a month. One day he fell mildly ill. Diaochan did not unfasten her girdle and continued to turn him with softness and favour; his pleasure only increased.

Lü Bu went into the inner chamber just as Dong Zhuo slept. Diaochan leaned half her body behind the bed; she put her fingers to her heart and then to Dong Zhuo, weeping without ceasing.

Lü Bu’s heart broke apart.

Dong Zhuo, half clouded with sleep, saw Lü Bu staring at the back of the bed, his eyes unblinking. He turned and saw Diaochan standing there. Dong Zhuo, furious, shouted at Lü Bu, “How dare you make sport with my cherished concubine! Call the guards and drive him out. From now on he is no longer to enter the main hall.”

Lü Bu left in anger and met Li Ru on the road, telling him what had happened.

Li Ru rushed in to see Dong Zhuo and said, “Great Master wants the realm, why punish Wenhou for a minor fault? If his heart should turn, a great matter will be lost.”

Dong Zhuo said, “What should I do?”

Li Ru said, “Summon him again, give him gold and silk, and soothe him with good words. Naturally there will be no trouble.”

Dong Zhuo complied. The next day he ordered men to summon Lü Bu to the hall and say, “I was still sick and dazed when I spoke, my spirit dim and words mistaken; do not hold it in your heart.” He at once gave ten catties of gold and twenty bolts of brocade. Lü Bu thanked him and left, but although he remained beside Dong Zhuo in appearance, his heart was still bound to Diaochan.

When Dong Zhuo recovered, he entered court for matters of state. Lü Bu carried his halberd at his side. Seeing Dong Zhuo in talk with the Son of Heaven, he found a moment to leave through the inner gate, mounted his horse, and rode straight to Dong Zhuo’s residence. He tied his horse before the gate and entered the rear hall with halberd drawn, then found Diaochan.

Diaochan said, “Wait for me at the Fengyi Pavilion by the rear garden.”

Lü Bu went straight there and stood under the arched rail by the pavilion.

Some time later, Diaochan came along the flower-laden path, like an immortal from the moon palace. Looking up and weeping, she said to Lü Bu,

“I may not be Grand Chancellor Wang’s own daughter, but I was raised as if I were his child. Since I first saw the General, I have been willing to serve him even in the most humble tasks, and this has been my wish all my life. Who could have imagined the Great Master would take such evil intent and defile me? I should have died at once, but because I had not yet once met the General, I endured this hidden shame.”

“Now that you have come at last, I can die fulfilled. This body is already tainted and cannot again serve a hero. Let me die before you and clear my resolve.”

When she finished, she gripped the pavilion rail and turned toward the lotus pool as if to leap.

Lü Bu hurriedly caught her and cried, “I have known your heart long ago! I only regret that we could not even truly speak together.”

Diaochan pulled at his sleeve and said, “In this life I cannot be your wife; let us meet in a future life.”

Lü Bu replied, “In this life I am unable to take you as wife; then I am not worthy to be called a hero.”

She said, “Day by day I count each as a year. I beg you, be pitiful and rescue me.”

Lü Bu said, “I have come in stolen moments. I fear the old villain may grow suspicious, so I must go at once.”

Diaochan held his garment and said, “If General is this afraid of the old villain, there will be no day to see the sky.”

Lü Bu stopped. “Let me devise a better plan first.”

Then he said these words and, spear in hand, he turned to leave.

Diaochan said, “In the deep inner chambers I heard your name like thunder in my ear, thinking you alone among this age. Who could have imagined you would become subject to another man’s control?”

Her words done, tears poured like rain. Shamed and ashamed, Lü Bu stood with full face and, leaning again on his halberd, turned and embraced Diaochan, comforting her with soft words. The two clung close, reluctant to part.

Dong Zhuo, in the audience hall, looked back and could not see Lü Bu. Suspicious, he took leave of the Son of Heaven in haste, climbed into his cart, and returned home. He saw Lü Bu’s horse tied before the gate and asked the gate guard. The guard said, “Wenhou has gone into the rear hall.”

Dong Zhuo dismissed his guards and went straight into the rear hall, searching and not finding her. He called Diaochan, but she was absent as well. He asked the maidservants in haste. One said, “Diaochan is in the rear garden, looking at flowers.”

Dong Zhuo entered the garden and saw, exactly there, Lü Bu and Diaochan talking together under the Fengyi Pavilion while a painted halberd leaned at one side. He roared with fury.

Lü Bu, seeing Dong Zhuo arrive, startled, turned and bolted. Dong Zhuo snatched the painted halberd and gave chase. Lü Bu ran fast; Dong, too broad and fat, could not keep up. He threw the halberd at Lü Bu. Lü Bu’s spear-tip struck the ground. Dong picked it up and chased on, but Lü Bu had gone far.

Dong pursued out through the garden gate. A man came running and collided with him in the chest. Dong fell to the ground.

Upward flew rage a thousand cubits high, then collapsed into a mounded mass of heavy flesh upon the earth.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Minister Wang the Grand Strategist Wields a Linked Stratagem; Master Dong Roils Fengyi Pavilion

chapters.html:
It was then that the man who had knocked down Dong Zhuo was Li Ru. He helped Dong Zhuo up and brought him to sit in the study hall.

Dong Zhuo said, “Why did you come here?”

Li Ru said, “I have only just reached the gatehouse. I heard the Grand Tutor was angry in the rear garden and was asking for Lü Bu. I ran here in haste. I happened to meet Lü Bu running out, crying, ‘The Grand Tutor is about to kill me!’ I rushed into the garden to intervene, and by bad luck I struck your favorite minister. I beg your pardon! I beg your pardon!”

Dong Zhuo said, “How can a rebel behave so shamefully? After I have joked with my favorite concubine, I swear I will kill him!”

Li Ru said, “Your Honor is mistaken. In the old meeting of King Zhuang of Chu, when the knotted ties were cut, he did not pursue punishment for joking with his cherished beauty; later, when he was trapped by Qin troops, the very same man’s strength saved him. Diaochan is only one woman, but Lü Bu is your Grand Tutor’s trusted and ferocious general. If Your Grace seizes this moment and gives her to Lü Bu, he will be moved by your great kindness and repay you with his life. Grand Tutor, think again.”

Dong Zhuo stood silent for a long while. “What you say is reasonable; I will think it over.”

Li Ru thanked him and withdrew.

Dong Zhuo entered the back hall and called Diaochan: “Have you been secretly close with Lü Bu?”

Diaochan wept. “My lord, I was in the rear garden watching the flowers when Lü Bu suddenly rushed in. I tried to step away in alarm. He said, ‘I am your lord’s son. Why should I avoid you?’ and grabbed me with a halberd in hand, dragging me to the Fengyi Pavilion. When I saw his intent was not right, I feared he would force me and tried to cast myself into the lotus pool to die, but this fellow held me. At the very edge of life and death, your Grace arrived and saved me.”

Dong Zhuo said, “I will give you to Lü Bu now. What say you?”

Diaochan cried out in dismay, “I have already served a noble lord. If I am suddenly to be granted as household slave, I will die rather than dishonor myself!” She drew the jewel-hilted sword from the wall and tried to cut her own throat.

Dong Zhuo hurriedly snatched the sword away and held her in his arms. “I was only playing with you.”

Diaochan collapsed into Dong Zhuo’s chest and covered her face, crying greatly. “This must be Li Ru’s scheme. Li Ru and Lü Bu are close to each other; therefore he laid this trap, without regard for your Grace’s dignity or this lowly concubine’s life. I should have borne his flesh in my teeth and bitten him to death!”

Dong Zhuo said, “How can I bear to send you away?”

Diaochan said, “Though your Grace has been merciful and affectionate, I fear this place is no longer safe for me; I will surely be harmed by Lü Bu.”

Dong Zhuo said, “Tomorrow I will return with you to Meiwu, and we will share our pleasures. Do not harbor fear.”

At last Diaochan wiped her tears and knelt in thanks.

The next day, Li Ru came to report, “The hour is auspicious today; your concubine may be sent to Lü Bu.”

Dong Zhuo said, “Lü Bu and I share a father-and-son bond. I cannot give him what he is not mine to give. I will not judge his fault for now. You carry my mind to him and comfort him with gentle words.”

Li Ru said, “My lord must not be led astray by a woman.”

Dong Zhuo's face darkened. “Will your wife go with Lü Bu? About Diaochan, say no more. If you speak, I will execute you.”

Li Ru left and lifted his face to heaven in a sigh: “We will all die at the hand of a woman.”

A reader later wrote, with a poem:

By the Chancellor’s red-sleeved stratagem, no spears were raised and no blades were drawn; Though Hulao was fought three times at great cost, the victory cry sounded at Fengyi Pavilion.

That same day Dong Zhuo ordered a return to Meiwu and all officials came out to escort him. In her carriage Diaochan saw Lü Bu standing in a dense crowd and looked at him from inside the curtains. She half-closed her face to look hidden, as if she were weeping in grief.

The cart moved far away. Lü Bu drew in the reins on a rise of earth and watched the cloud of dust behind, sighing in regret and rage. Suddenly someone behind him asked, “Why does Lord Wen Hou not go with the Grand Tutor, but stand here staring from afar in sorrow?”

Lü Bu turned and saw it was Wang Yun, the Chancellor.

When they met, Wang Yun said, “I have been slightly ill and stayed indoors these past days, so we have gone long without meeting. As I could only venture out despite my malaise to see the Grand Tutor return to Meiwu, I was glad to meet you. Tell me, why are you sighing so long?”

Lü Bu said, “It is all for your daughter.”

Wang Yun feigned surprise. “How, when we have not met for so long?”

Lü Bu said, “The old villain has long shown me his favor.”

Wang Yun feigned surprise again. “I do not believe such a thing.”

Lü Bu told Wang Yun, piece by piece, what had happened before.

Wang Yun raised his face, stamped his feet, and stayed silent for a while. After some time he said, “I never thought the Grand Tutor could do this beastly thing.” He grasped Lü Bu’s arm and said, “Come to my humble house so we may confer.”

Lü Bu followed him home. Wang Yun brought him into the inner chamber and set wine in waiting. Lü Bu once again recounted in full the affair at Fengyi Pavilion.

Wang Yun said, “The Grand Tutor touched my daughter, then took your wife. It is a disgrace before all under heaven—none laughs at Dong, all at you and at me. But I am old and powerless, too feeble to be a matter for record; yet it is a pity that you, a hero for the ages, should be shamed.”

Lü Bu was livid with rage and struck the table.

Wang Yun said quickly, “Forgive my rash words. Calm yourself, General.”

Lü Bu said, “I swear I will kill this old villain and wash away my disgrace.”

Wang Yun quickly covered his mouth. “General, do not say it. I fear it will implicate my poor old life.”

Lü Bu said, “A true man cannot live long beneath another. Should he keep silence while he is buried in resentment?”

Wang Yun said, “With your ability, the Grand Tutor Dong can never truly limit you.”

Lü Bu said, “I want to kill this old villain, but because of father-and-son sentiment, I fear later generations will criticize me.”

Wang Yun smiled faintly. “Your family name is Lü, and his is Dong. When the halberd was first cast, was there any father-and-son feeling then?”

Lü Bu cried out, “Without your words, General, I might have erred.”

Wang Yun saw his mind was fixed and said, “If General aids the Han house, he is a loyal minister, his name will endure across a hundred ages. If he aids Dong Zhuo, he is a traitor, and history will leave him a stench forever.”

Lü Bu bowed from his seat. “My intention is firm, Chancellor. Do not doubt.”

Wang Yun said, “I only fear this may fail and bring calamity.”

Lü Bu drew a belt knife, sliced his arm, and let the blood flow as an oath.

Wang Yun knelt in thanks. “The Han sacrifice must not be cut off; all this comes through your generosity. Keep this secret. At the appointed moment we will respond in kind.”

Lü Bu promised and departed.

Wang Yun then asked Palace Attendant Shisun Rui and Inspector Huang Wan to consult.

Rui said, “The Son of Heaven has only just recovered from illness. We can send someone eloquent to Meiwu to discuss matters with Dong Zhuo. At the same time, send a sealed imperial edict to Lü Bu so that armored troops wait within the palace gate and draw Dong Zhuo in for execution. This is the best stratagem.”

Huang Wan said, “Who would dare to go?”

Rui said, “Lü Bu and Li Su, the cavalry commander of their commandery, was deeply resentful because Dong Zhuo kept him from his post. If that man goes, Dong Zhuo will not suspect.”

Wang Yun said, “Good.” They sent for Lü Bu to discuss.

Lü Bu said, “It was this man who once urged me to kill Ding Jianyang. If he does not go, I will first execute him.”

He had a man quietly summon Li Su.

Lü Bu said, “That day you told me to kill Ding Jianyang and then cast me before Dong Zhuo. Dong now mocks the Son of Heaven and torments life itself; his crimes are full and complete, and men and spirits alike resent him. You can convey an imperial order to Meiwu, summoning Dong Zhuo to court. Let hidden troops be ready there and kill him, preserving the Han and acting as loyal ministers together. What is your view?”

Li Su said, “I have long wished to remove this villain, but there are no like-minded men. Now that your intent is this, Heaven has granted it. How could Li Su harbor divided intention?”

He then broke an arrow to swear. Wang Yun said, “If you can carry this through, why should you not rise to rank and honors?”

The next day Li Su led ten riders and arrived at Meiwu. A report announced that an edict of the Son of Heaven had come; Dong Zhuo summoned him in.

Li Su entered and paid respects.

Dong Zhuo said, “What is the emperor’s order?”

Li Su said, “The Son of Heaven has just recovered from illness and wishes to gather officials and soldiers in Weiyang Hall to discuss transferring the Mandate to the Grand Tutor. That is the purpose of this edict.”

Dong Zhuo said, “What does Chancellor Wang Yun intend?”

Li Su said, “Chancellor Wang has already ordered the platform for receiving abdication to be built. He waits only for the emperor to arrive.”

Dong Zhuo rejoiced. “I dreamt a dragon draped over my body this very night; now I have received this joyful command. The time is ripe and must not be missed!”

He then ordered his inner men to take Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou, each commanding three thousand of the Flying-Bear troops, to guard Meiwu. He himself left for the capital that very day. He told Li Su, “When I am emperor, you shall be the Chief Commander of the Golden Guards.”

Li Su bowed and declared himself a subordinate.

Dong Zhuo went to bid his mother farewell. She was past ninety. She asked, “Where is my son going?”

Dong Zhuo said, “I go to receive the transfer of the Han mandate. Mother will soon become the empress dowager!”

His mother said, “These days my flesh trembles and my heart is frightened. I fear it is not an omen of good.”

Dong Zhuo said, “Soon to be the mother of the state is not without terrifying signs.” Then he said farewell and departed.

He told Diaochan, as he left, “I will be emperor. I will raise you as noble consort.”

Diaochan already understood what was coming and feigned joy, then bowed in thanks.

Dong Zhuo left the encampment in his carriage. Men pressed at the front and guarded him at the rear as he headed toward Chang’an. After they had not gone even thirty li, the carriage wheel broke. He dismounted and mounted a horse. After another ten li, the horse screamed and snapped its rein.

Dong Zhuo asked Li Su, “A broken wheel, a broken rein—what omen is this?”

Li Su said, “It means the Grand Tutor will receive the Han abdication and cast aside the old for the new; a sign of advancing in jade sedan and golden saddle.”

Dong Zhuo rejoiced and believed him.

The next day, while traveling, a wild wind rose suddenly and dense fog covered the sky.

Dong Zhuo asked Li Su, “What blessing or warning is this?”

Li Su said, “When the lord ascends the dragon throne there must be red light and purple mist to amplify heavenly majesty.”

Dong Zhuo, again delighted, set this aside.

When they reached the outskirts, all officials came out to receive him. Only Li Ru was ill at home and could not go out. Dong Zhuo arrived at the Chancellor’s residence and Lü Bu came to congratulate.

Dong Zhuo said, “I have reached the Nine-Five. You shall oversee military affairs across the realm.”

Lü Bu bowed his thanks and rested in the front tent for the night.

That same night some dozen children sang beyond the outskirts. The wind carried their song into the tent.

They sang: “The grass runs a thousand li, how vivid it is! For ten days it never yields life!”

The song was sharp with sorrow. Dong Zhuo asked Li Su, “What fortune or misfortune does this children’s rhyme hold?”

Li Su said, “It is only saying that the Liu house will perish and the Dong house will rise.”

The next morning before dawn Dong Zhuo assembled his ceremonial attendants and entered court. He suddenly saw a lone Daoist, blue robe and white headcloth, carrying a long staff, on which a strip of cloth was tied a full zhang long with the character kou written on each end.

Dong Zhuo asked Li Su, “What does this man mean?”

Li Su said, “A man of troubled heart.” He ordered soldiers to drive him off.

When Dong entered court, the ministers in ritual robes lined the way and prostrated to him. Li Su walked with a sword in hand by the carriage.

At the Beiye Gate, all the troops halted outside, only two dozen imperial guards entered with the carriage. Dong Zhuo saw Wang Yun and others standing at the hall doors, each with a sword in hand. He cried out sharply, “The rebel has arrived here! Where are the guards?” Two hundred or more men emerged on both sides, halberds raised, spears out, charging.

Dong Zhuo, armored, did not move into the hall. He was struck and thrown from the carriage with an arm wound. He shouted, “Where is my son Fengxian?”

Lü Bu stepped out from behind the carriage and in a loud voice cried, “There is an edict to punish the rebels!”

With one strike he drove a halberd straight at Dong Zhuo’s throat. Li Su, already behind him, had decapitated him and held the head in his hand.

Lü Bu held a halberd in his left hand and drew the imperial edict from his robe with the right, crying, “By decree, punish the traitorous minister Dong Zhuo. Ask nothing else!”

The officials all shouted, “Ten thousand years!”

A poet later sighed for Dong Zhuo:

When success is near, why did he not become emperor? Lacking it, he is merely a wealthy householder. Who could know Heaven’s will is never partial? The moment Meiwu was complete, his ruin had already begun.

Lü Bu now roared, “The one who enabled the Grand Tutor’s cruelty is Li Ru! Who can capture him?”

Li Su answered at once that he would go.

Just then a call came from outside the gate: Li Ru had been bound by his household slave and brought in as tribute.

Wang Yun ordered him taken bound to the city office and executed. He then ordered that Dong Zhuo’s head be displayed through the streets.

Dong Zhuo’s corpse was fat and massive. The soldiers took tallow and set it in oil at his navel to burn it like a lamp; melted fat spread across the ground. Those who passed by trampled it with their feet and kicked at the body. Wang Yun also ordered Lü Bu, together with Huangfu Song and Li Su, to take fifty thousand soldiers and sweep Meiwu for Dong Zhuo’s property and households.

Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou heard that Dong Zhuo had died and that Lü Bu would be coming. They fled overnight with the Flying-Bear army to Liang Province.

When Lü Bu reached Meiwu, he first recovered Diaochan.

Huangfu Song ordered all the respectable sons and daughters kept in the camp to be released.

But all of Dong Zhuo’s own kin, not distinguishing old and young, were all executed. Dong Zhuo’s mother was killed as well. Dong Ming and nephew Dong Huo were both beheaded.

They collected from the encampment tens of thousands of taels of gold, silk bolts, brocades, jewels, vessels, and grain beyond count and reported them to Wang Yun.

Wang Yun then gave generous rewards to the troops and set a feast in the Great Hall, summoning all officials and raising cups in celebration.

In the midst of the banquet, a report came in: “Dong Zhuo’s exposed corpse lies in the city, and a man has thrown himself at it and wept loudly.”

Wang Yun was angry. “Dong Zhuo has been beheaded. The common people all rejoice. Who is this who dares to wail?” He ordered, “Seize him.”

Soon the man was brought.

All the officials were stunned to see it was not another, but Court Attendant Cai Yong.

Wang Yun shouted, “Dong Zhuo was a traitor and today he has fallen. It is this realm’s great good fortune. You are a minister of Han—yet you do not rejoice for the state and instead weep for the traitor. Why?”

Cai Yong knelt and confessed his guilt. “Though I am untalented, I also know what is righteous. Would I ever turn my back on the state and side with Dong Zhuo? I was moved by a moment of personal gratitude and, without thought, wept once. I know my fault is great. Let this be my plea for mercy: if the penalty is to have my nose branded and my feet cut, so I may continue the Han history and redeem my crime, that is my good fortune.”

All the officials, moved by his talent, pleaded strongly for him.

Grand Tutor Ma Ridi said privately to Wang Yun, “Bó Jié is a brilliant talent beyond this age; if he is allowed to continue writing the Han history, that would be an honor indeed. His filial conduct is well known. If he is put to immediate death, we may lose public esteem.”

Wang Yun said, “When Emperor Wu spared Sima Qian and then had him write history, later abuse and slander filled later ages. Now state fortune has declined and court governance is in chaos. We cannot let a flattering courtier hold the brush beside a young ruler and make this court subject to his malicious judgment.”

Ma Ridi had no argument and withdrew.

Privately he said to the assembled officials, “Could Wang Yun have no descendants? A good man is the thread of a state; rite and record are its rules. If thread is broken and rite discarded, can it endure?”

At that moment, Wang Yun did not follow Ma Ridi and ordered Cai Yong to prison, where he was strangled.

All scholars who heard this wept. Later people judged that Cai Yong’s lament for Dong Zhuo had not been beyond blame, but Wang Yun’s killing of Cai Yong was also excessive.

They sang:

Dong Zhuo hoarded power and gave himself to cruelty, How came the Court Attendant to lose his life so? If that noble Zhuge in Longzhong still lay at his mat, Would he ever have traded his life for a traitor of disorder?

Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou, fleeing to Shaanxi, sent envoys to Chang’an petitioning clemency. Wang Yun said, “Dong Zhuo’s arrogance was enabled by these four. Even if I grant a general amnesty, I will not pardon these four.”

The envoy returned with this reply to Li Jue. Li Jue said, “If clemency is denied, we can only save ourselves one by one.”

His strategist Jia Xu said, “If each of you abandons your troops and goes alone, a single village chief can bind you all. Better draw in the people of Shaanxi and your core forces, then march into Chang’an and strike in vengeance for Dong Zhuo. If fortune favors us, we will restore right under the court. If not, we may still withdraw later.”

Li Jue and the rest accepted his counsel. They spread word in Xiliang: “Wang Yun intends to purge the people of this land.” All were thrown into fear. Then they proclaimed: “To die idly is no gain. Will you not rise with us against him?” All were willing to follow.

They gathered tens of thousands, divided into four routes, and hurried toward Chang’an.

On the way they met Dong Zhuo’s son-in-law, Lieutenant Colonel Niu Fu, commanding five thousand, also intent on avenging his father-in-law. Li Jue joined hands with him for the vanguard and the four men set out in stages.

Wang Yun heard from the west of Liang that Li Jue’s troops were coming. He conferred with Lü Bu.

Lü Bu said, “Chancellor, be at ease. What are these rats compared to us?”

He then led Li Su out with troops.

Li Su took the first encounter and met Niu Fu, slashing through one battle at once. Niu Fu could not hold and turned and fled.

Unluckily at the second watch of that same night, Niu Fu slipped through Li Su’s unprepared lines and raided the camp. Li Su’s army scattered in confusion and fled more than thirty li, half the formation lost. He came to Lü Bu.

Lü Bu raged: “Why did you blunt my edge?” He decapitated Li Su and hung his head on the city gate.

The next day Lü Bu marched out again against Niu Fu.

How could Niu Fu resist Lü Bu? He was routed once more.

That night Niu Fu and his intimate Hú Chier (Hu Chi’er) discussed: “Lü Bu is fierce and brave; he is impossible to match. Better deceive Li Jue and the three others, hide our gold and pearls, and with three to five close men abandon the army and flee.”

Hu Chi’er agreed.

That night they packed jewels and pearls and left camp by the night with three or four companions.

When they reached a river crossing, Hu Chi’er sought to seize all the jewels by killing Niu Fu. He severed Niu Fu’s head and brought it to Lü Bu.

When Lü Bu asked about the matter and heard it, he burned with anger and immediately executed Hu Chi’er.

He then took command to march, just as he came in contact with Li Jue’s cavalry.

Lü Bu did not wait for formation. He raised his halberd, leapt to horseback, and drove his army forward in direct charge.

Li Jue’s forces could not withstand him and withdrew over fifty li, then camped below a mountain. They called Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou for council and said, “Though Lü Bu is brave, he has no strategy and is nothing to fear. I will hold the army at Rengukou each day, baiting him into close fight. General Guo should lead troops striking at his rear, using the old method of Peng Yue to trouble Chu, sounding brass and then beating the drums to recall our men. Zhang and Fan, you two should split forces on two routes and take Chang’an directly. If he tries to defend both front and rear, he will be unable to respond and will be completely defeated.”

The men accepted the plan.

Back at the mountain foot, Lü Bu pressed Li Jue’s men in a close battle. Li Jue withdrew and climbed the heights. Arrows and stones fell like rain overhead; Lü Bu’s men could not advance.

Just then word came: Guo Si had turned from the rear to charge.

Lü Bu hurried back to fight. Loud drumbeats sounded and Guo Si’s troops withdrew.

As Lü Bu moved to reform, the sound of gongs rang out and Li Jue’s army came again. Before he could engage them, Guo Si once again led troops and crashed against him from the rear. By the time Lü Bu arrived, Guo Si also sounded drums and withdrew, leaving Lü Bu’s fury surging in his chest.

The pattern repeated for several days: he could not fight; he could not rest. While he burned with anger, a mounted messenger arrived. He reported that Zhang Ji and Fan Chou, from both wings, had already broken into Chang’an; the capital was in grave danger.

Lü Bu led troops back at once. Behind him, Li Jue and Guo Si attacked as he fled.

He had no mind to continue battle and only focused on running, breaking through many men and horses.

By the time he reached the foot of Chang’an’s walls, rebel troops filled the hills and valleys and surrounded the city. Lü Bu’s army met them in skirmish and was at a disadvantage.

Several soldiers, fearing Lü Bu’s ferocity, defected. Lü Bu’s concern grew great.

After several days, Dong Zhuo’s remaining accomplices Li Meng and Wang Fang opened the city gates as inside agents, and the four columns of rebels surged in together.

Lü Bu surged left and right to block, but could not hold them back. He led several hundred riders out of the gate called Qingsuo and cried to Wang Yun: “The situation is urgent! Please, Chancellor, mount and ride out with me. We must leave the pass and seek another plan.”

Wang Yun said, “If Heaven and the state altar allow the kingdom to be stabilized, this is my wish. If it cannot be, then I, Wang Yun, will offer my life in death. I will not survive by cowardly escape in calamity. Go and inform the gentlemen east of the river. Think always of the state.”

Lü Bu pleaded repeatedly, but Wang Yun would not leave.

Not long after, flames rose from many gates, climbing to the sky. Lü Bu was forced to abandon his household, lead out barely a hundred riders, and flee through the pass to Yuan Shu.

Li Jue and Guo Si loosed their soldiers to plunder. Grand Master of Ceremonies Zhong Fu, Great Equerry Lu Kui, Grand Envoy Zhou Huan, gate magistrate Cui Lie, and cavalry colonel Wang Qi all died in the national disaster.

Rebel troops ringed the inner court so tightly that the attendants prayed the Son of Heaven should issue a command from Xuanping Gate to quiet the turmoil.

When Li Jue and Guo Si saw Huang Gai, they restrained the soldiers and cried, “Long live the lord!”

The Emperor, leaning from the tower, asked, “Without waiting to submit a petition, you entered Chang’an. What do you intend?”

Li Jue and Guo Si looked up and replied, “Dong Taishi was the Son of Heaven’s Grand Tutor and was beheaded without cause by Wang Yun. We have come only to avenge him, not to rebel. If we can see Wang Yun, we will withdraw our armies.”

Wang Yun was at the emperor’s side when he heard this and said, “I have only acted for the realm. Now that matters are this far, Your Majesty should not spare your servant if the state is endangered. I ask permission to meet the two rebels.”

The emperor hesitated and could not bring himself to answer.

From the Xuanping gate tower, Wang Yun jumped down and shouted, “Wang Yun is here!”

Li Jue and Guo Si drew swords and shouted, “What crime did Dong Taishi commit to deserve death?”

Wang Yun said, “Dong the traitor’s crimes fill the sky and earth. To recount them would be endless. On the day he was executed, the people of Chang’an all celebrated. Did you not hear?”

Li Jue and Guo Si said, “Dong Taishi had guilt. What guilt did we have, that we should not be pardoned?”

Wang Yun yelled, “Traitor rebels, no more words. I, Wang Yun, am to die today.”

The two traitors moved their hands at once and killed Wang Yun below the tower.

A court historian later praised in verse:

Wang Yun laid the scheme in motion, and Dong Zhuo, the evil minister, was removed. His heart held the state in grief, His brows were furrowed with sorrow. His righteous spirit rose to the Milky Way, His loyalty ran through the stars of the Northern Dipper, Even now, his spirit and body still circle the Phoenix Tower.

The rebels killed Wang Yun and then sent men in every direction to kill the whole of his clan, old and young. The people of the realm all wept. Li Jue and Guo Si then thought, “Now that we have reached this far, if we do not kill the Son of Heaven and make great plans, when else?”

They raised their swords and shouted, then rushed inside.

It was as if to say:

Our crime confessed, we have only just eased one disaster; Yet again evil from the rebels spreads through the land. Who knows what fate awaits the Son of Heaven? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Lü Bu Dismantles a Tyrant, Assists the Chancellor, and Li Jue Hears Jia Xu

chapters.html:
Now Li Jue and Guo Si, the two villains, sought to murder Emperor Xian. Zhang Ji and Fan Chou advised against it.

“Do not do that. If we kill him at once, the people will likely not submit. Better keep him as our lord for now, lure the lords into passing the passes, strip away his support first, and then kill him; then the realm might be won.”

Heeding this counsel, Li Jue and Guo Si put back their weapons. From the tower, the emperor announced, “Wang Yun has already been executed. Why have your troops not withdrawn?”

Li Jue and Guo Si replied, “We have done service for the royal house and have not yet been rewarded with noble rank, so we dare not pull back our troops.”

The emperor asked, “What titles do you ask for?”

Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou each submitted written petitions for offices and ranks. The emperor yielded. He made Li Jue General of Chariots and Cavalry, Marquess of Chiyang, and Inspector of the Capital with imperial command token and axe. He made Guo Si Rear General, with the same token and axe, to share oversight of court affairs. He made Fan Chou Right General and Marquess of Wannei. He made Zhang Ji General of Agile Cavalry and Marquess of Pingyang, and ordered him to garrison Hongnong. Li Meng and Wang Fang and the rest were all made Colonels. They offered thanks and then led their troops out of the city.

He then issued orders to recover Dong Zhuo’s remains. They collected scattered bits of skin and bone, carved a likeness from aromatic wood, arranged him with decent ceremony, held an elaborate funeral, clothed him in royal robes, prepared coffin and lid, chose an auspicious day, and moved him to be buried at Meiwu.

On the day of interment, tremendous thunder and rain fell. The flat ground was flooded to several chi. Thunder split open the coffin, and the body was thrown out. Li Jue waited for clear weather and tried to rebury him again. The same thing happened again that night.

They tried three times and still could not bury him. The scraps and bones were all consumed by thunder and fire. The anger of Heaven against Zhuo was truly extreme.

Now that Li Jue and Guo Si held authority, they were cruel toward the people. They placed intimate men near the emperor and watched his movements closely. Court officials rose and fell at their whim. Because of public sentiment, they singled out Zhu Jun and made him Master of the Stables, sharing control of state affairs with him.

One day, news came that Ma Teng, Governor of Longxi, and Han Sui, Inspector of Bing Province, were leading over one hundred thousand troops, hastening to Chang’an and claiming they were coming to punish bandits.

In truth, the two commanders had previously sent men into Chang’an to make secret connections with Court Attendant Ma Yu, Censor Zhong Shao, and Left General Liu Fan. The three had become insiders and advised the emperor in private. The emperor then secretly commissioned Ma Teng as General Who Conquers the West and Han Sui as General Who Guards the West, and ordered them to unite and attack the rebels.

When Li Jue, Guo Si, Zhang Ji, and Fan Chou heard that the two armies were coming, they discussed together how to repel the threat. Jia Xiu advised, “The two armies have traveled far. We should dig deep trenches and raise high ramparts, hold fast and resist. In no more than a hundred days, their grain will run out, and they will be forced to retreat. Then we can pursue and capture both commanders.”

Li Meng and Wang Fang said, “That is not a good plan. Give us ten thousand picked troops. We can execute Ma Teng and Han Sui on their own and bring their heads to you.”

Jia Xiu said, “If we fight now, we will surely be defeated.”

Li Meng and Wang Fang together said, “If we two fail, we will submit our heads to be cut off. If we win, you must give us your heads as promised.”

Jia Xiu then told Li Jue and Guo Si, “Two hundred li west of Chang’an is Zouzhi Mountain. The roads are rough and perilous. Station Generals Zhang Ji and Fan Chou there to hold a fortified wall. Let Li Meng and Wang Fang draw out their army and meet the enemy.”

Li Jue and Guo Si accepted this plan and sent fifteen thousand men and horses with Li Meng and Wang Fang. The two men departed happily and set camp two hundred and eighty li from Chang’an.

When the Western troops arrived, both sides rode out to meet each other. The Western army formed its lines and blocked the road. Riding side by side, Ma Teng and Han Sui came out, and they pointed at Li Meng and Wang Fang and shouted, “Traitors to the realm! Who will capture them?”

Before the words were done, a young general burst forth from within the formation. His face was like a crown jewel, his eyes like shooting stars, his build like a tiger, his arms like those of an ape, with a barrel chest and wolf-like waist. He held a long spear, his horse was swift, and he flew across the front line.

He was Ma Chao, courtesy name Mengqi, son of Ma Teng, seventeen years old and invincible in courage. Wang Fang mocked him for his youth and leapt from his horse to engage him. In only a few thrusts, Ma Chao skewered Wang Fang while he was still mounted. Ma Chao checked his reins and rode back.

Li Meng saw Wang Fang wounded, and he rode hard from a distance to pursue. Ma Chao did not seem to notice, and he purposely delayed. When Li Meng came close and thrust with his spear, Ma Chao sidestepped, Li Meng thrust into empty air, and the two horses came close together. Ma Chao then, with a light swing of his ape-strong arm, took him alive.

With no commander above them, the soldiers panicked and ran for their lives. Ma Teng and Han Sui pressed on with pursuit and won a full victory, pressing down to the camp by the pass and giving the order to behead Li Meng.

When Li Jue and Guo Si learned that both Li Meng and Wang Fang had been killed by Ma Chao, they at last understood Jia Xiu’s foresight. They held strictly to his plan, keeping the passes and forcing him to fight, without riding out themselves. As he had predicted, in less than two months the Western army was short on grain and decided to withdraw.

At that moment in Chang’an, a household servant of Ma Yu exposed his own house and reported it to Liu Fan and Zhong Shao. In truth, they were already in outer alliance with Ma Teng and Han Sui to serve as insiders. Li Jue and Guo Si were furious. They captured all three families and beheaded them in the market, then set the three severed heads in front of the city gate as a public signal. Ma Teng and Han Sui, seeing that supplies had run out and their insiders had failed, had no choice but to lift camp and retreat.

Li Jue and Guo Si ordered Zhang Ji to chase Ma Teng, and Fan Chou to chase Han Sui. The Western-Land force was routed. Ma Chao fought in the rear and drove back Zhang Ji. Fan Chou rode on in pursuit of Han Sui; soon he caught up near Chen Cang.

Han Sui reined up beside him and said, “We are from the same homeland. Why are you so merciless today?”

Fan Chou also pulled his horse up and replied, “The emperor’s command cannot be disobeyed.”

Han Sui said, “I came only for the realm. Why must you press me so hard?”

After hearing this, Fan Chou turned his horse, drew back his men, and returned to camp, letting Han Sui go.

Without warning, Li Jue’s nephew Li Bie saw Fan Chou letting Han Sui pass and reported it to his uncle. Li Jue became furious and wanted to raise troops against Fan Chou. Jia Xiu said, “At present the people’s minds are unsettled; frequent calls to arms are highly unfit. Why not hold a banquet? Invite Zhang Ji and Fan Chou to celebrate the victory, and while they are still on the mat, seize and behead Fan Chou with no cost.”

Li Jue agreed immediately and set a banquet for Zhang Ji and Fan Chou. The two generals came gladly. By mid-session, Li Jue suddenly changed color and said, “Why did Fan Chou communicate with Han Sui and intend rebellion?”

Startled, Fan Chou had not yet answered when the executioners marched out and immediately beheaded him before the hall. Zhang Ji, frightened, fell to the ground. Li Jue raised him and said, “Fan Chou plotted rebellion, and therefore he was executed. You are one of my intimate men. Why should you panic?” He handed command of Fan Chou’s troops to Zhang Ji, and Zhang Ji withdrew to Hongnong.

After Li Jue and Guo Si had defeated the Western army, no lord dared oppose them. Jia Xiu repeatedly urged pacification and recruitment of worthy men. There was then a little vitality again at court. Unexpectedly, Yellow Turbans in Qingzhou rose again: tens of thousands assembled, with all ranks mixed, plundering good households.

The Master of the Stables, Zhu Jun, presented one man who could crush the bandits. Li Jue and Guo Si asked who he was.

Zhu Jun said, “To defeat the rebel bands in Shandong, no one but Cao Mengde can do it.”

Li Jue asked, “Where is Mengde now?”

Zhu Jun replied, “He is the Governor of Dong Commandery. If he is ordered, he commands many troops and can break this rebel force by dawn.”

Li Jue rejoiced and in the night issued an edict. He sent it to Dong Commandery with orders for Cao Cao and Bao Xin to destroy the rebels together.

Cao Cao accepted the imperial decree, joined Bao Xin, and raised troops. At Shouyang they struck the rebels. Bao Xin pressed deep and was killed by the enemy. Cao Cao pursued the enemy to Jibei, where many surrendered.

He employed the surrendered bandits as his vanguard, and his soldiers and horsemen spread everywhere, bringing all others to submit. In just over a hundred days, over three hundred thousand surrendered soldiers and more than one million men and women came to him. He selected the finest and called them “Qingzhou troops”; the rest were sent back to farming.

From then onward, Cao Cao’s fame grew daily. When the victory report arrived in Chang’an, the court promoted him to General Who Guards the East.

While in Yanzhou, Cao Cao recruited men of talent. An uncle and nephew came to surrender to him: Xun Yu, surname Xun, given name Yu, courtesy name Wenruo, son of Xun Kun. He had served Yuan Shao, and now had abandoned Yuan Shao and submitted to Cao Cao. Cao Cao was delighted with their conversation and said, “You are my Son of Heaven’s advisor!” He made Xun Yu Army Marshal.

His nephew Xun You, courtesy name Gongda, a famous gentleman of the realm, had once served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gates. He had left office and returned home, and now came with his uncle to submit to Cao Cao. Cao made him Army Instructor.

Xun Yu said, “I have heard there is a worthy man in Yanzhou, but I do not know where he is now.” Cao asked who it was.

“He is from Dong’e in Dong Province: surname Cheng, given name Yu, courtesy name Zhongde.”

Cao Cao said, “I have heard his name for a long time.” He sent men to ask around the district. They found him studying in the mountains. Cao then invited him.

When Cheng Yu arrived, Cao Cao was greatly pleased.

Cheng Yu told Xun Yu, “I am limited in learning and talent; I do not deserve the recommendation you gave. In your area there is a worthy man, surname Guo, given name Jia, courtesy name Fengxiao. He is one of the greatest among living worthies. Why do you not gather him and bring him?”

Xun Yu suddenly realized, “I nearly forgot him.” He petitioned Cao to summon Guo Jia to Yanzhou to discuss matters of the world.

Guo Jia then recommended Liu Ye, a true-line descendant of Emperor Guangwu, from Chengde in Huainan, surname Liu, given name Ye, courtesy name Ziyang. Cao immediately recruited him. Liu Ye then recommended two men: one from Changyi in Shanyang, surname Man, given name Chong, courtesy name Boning; one from Wucheng, surname Lü, given name Qian, courtesy name Zike.

Cao Cao had long known both of their reputations and recruited both as attendants. Man Chong and Lü Qian together recommended another, a man from Pingqiu in Chenliu, surname Mao, given name Jie, courtesy name Xiaoxian. Cao also recruited him as an attendant.

A commander then arrived with several hundred cavalrymen to serve Cao Cao. He was from Juping in Taishan, surname Yu, given name Jin, courtesy name Wenze. Cao saw that he was exceptionally skilled in horsemanship and martial arts and appointed him Assistant Army Commandant.

One day Xiahou Dun brought a huge man before Cao Cao. When Cao asked who he was, Dun said, “He is from Chenliu: surname Dian, name Wei, very strong in strength. He formerly followed Zhang Miao and quarreled with men under him, killing dozens; then he fled to the mountains. In a hunt, I saw him chasing deer through a ravine, so I brought him into the army. I now recommend him especially.”

Cao said, “I see in him a broad face and powerful form. He must be greatly brave.”

Dun said, “He once avenged a friend by killing a man, and he walked the market with the severed head on a pole, so hundreds dared not go near him. Now he carries two iron halberds, each weighing eighty jin, and with them mounted he moves like the wind.”

Cao ordered Wei to be tested.

Wei fastened the halberds on horseback and rode back and forth at full speed. Suddenly a large standard in camp was blown by the wind and nearly fell. The soldiers nearby could not hold it. Wei dismounted and shouted them back, then with one hand gripped the pole and stood in the wind, unmoving.

Cao said, “Such force comes from the old ages.” He made him Colonel Before the Canopy, stripped off his embroidered robe, and granted him a fine horse with carved saddle.

From then on, Cao Cao had in his army both brilliant strategists and fierce generals. He was feared in Shandong.

He then sent Ying Shao, Governor of Taishan, to Langye to bring his father Cao Song forward. Cao Song had been avoiding danger in Chenliu and was living in hiding in Langye. He received the letter, then with his younger brother Cao De and over forty attendants of his household, plus more than a hundred followers and over a hundred wagons, set off straight for Yanzhou.

Passing through Xu Province, he met Tao Qian, courtesy name Gongzu, a man of warm and honest nature. Tao Qian had wanted to welcome Cao Cao but had not found a way. Learning that Cao Song was coming, he came out to receive him at the gate, bowed repeatedly and honored him, then hosted him in a grand banquet for two days.

When Cao Song prepared to depart, Tao Qian personally saw him out of the gate and assigned County Commandant Zhang Kai with five hundred men to escort him.

Cao Song and his household arrived at the Hwa-Fei pass, and in late summer and early autumn a sudden heavy rain came, so they were forced to seek shelter in an old temple. The monk there admitted them. Cao Song settled his household and ordered Zhang Kai’s soldiers to take up positions in both corridors.

Their garments were soaked through and all the soldiers complained in one voice. Zhang Kai then summoned his lieutenants to a quiet place and said, “We were once the remnants of the Yellow Turbans and have only weakly submitted to Tao Qian. There is little to gain in that. Now Cao Song has an endless train of wagons and baggage. If you want fortune and rank, it is not difficult. At the third watch tonight, we all break in together, kill Cao Song and his family, seize their goods, and flee to the mountains as bandits. What do you think?”

All approved.

That night the rain and wind did not cease. Cao Song was seated when he heard shouts erupting around the temple walls. Cao De drew his sword to look out and was stabbed to death.

Cao Song rushed with one concubine into the rear of the abbot’s chamber to flee over the wall. The concubine was heavy and could not pass. In haste, Cao Song and the concubine hid in a latrine and were killed by the raiders. Ying Shao escaped at the risk of his life and eventually went to Yuan Shao.

Zhang Kai killed Cao Song’s entire family, took their property, set the temple ablaze, and fled with five hundred men toward Huainan.

A poem later was said:

Cao Cao’s treacherous cleverness was praised under heaven; he once killed the entire Lü household. Now his own household meets killers of strangers at home, and Heaven’s justice circles back without fail.

A soldier under Ying Shao who escaped and ran reported to Cao Cao. When Cao heard, he collapsed to the ground in tears. They pulled him back.

Through clenched teeth he said, “Tao Qian’s troops slaughtered my father. This feud can be shared by none under heaven. I will now raise a full army, scour Xu Province, and at last settle this grudge!”

He left Xun Yu and Cheng Yu with thirty thousand men to guard Jucheng, Fan County, and the three counties of Dong’e, while the rest moved into Xu Province. Xiahou Dun, Yu Jin, and Dian Wei went as vanguard.
