Cao Cao ordered that wherever a city was taken, its inhabitants should all be slaughtered to avenge his father.

At that time, Bian Rang, governor of Jiujiang and close associate of Tao Qian, heard of the danger in Xu Province. He came with five thousand men to help. When Cao heard this, he flew into anger and ordered Xiahou Dun to intercept and kill him on the road.

At that moment, Chen Gong, an attendant of Dong Commandery and likewise close to Tao Qian, heard that Cao Cao had raised an army to take revenge and intended to kill the citizens, and he came late at night to see Cao Cao. Cao knew he was speaking as Tao Qian’s envoy. Though he wanted not to see him and could not fully forget former favors, he invited him into camp.

Chen Gong said, “I have heard, my lord, that with your great army you have entered Xu Province to avenge your honored father, and you now mean to exterminate the civilians. Here is what happened, however: it was the evil of Zhang Kai. It is not Tao Qian’s fault. And what grievance do the people of the counties have against you? Killing them is inauspicious. Please reflect once more.”

Cao replied angrily, “You abandoned me before and now have no shame to return to me? Tao Qian has slaughtered my household. I swear to tear out his heart and wash away my hatred! Even if you speak on his behalf, why should I heed your words?”

Chen Gong stepped back and said in grief, “I too have no face with which to meet Tao Qian.” He then rode off to Chenliu Governor Zhang Miao.

Now, where Cao Cao’s army arrived, it left slaughter among the people and even dug up graves. In Xu Province, Tao Qian, hearing that Cao had raised troops to avenge his father and was slaughtering commoners, looked to Heaven and cried out, “My guilt to Heaven is what has made the people of Xu Province suffer this great calamity!”

He quickly gathered officials and deliberated. Cao Bao said, “Cao’s army has arrived. We cannot stand and wait for death. I will help my lord break them.”

Tao Qian had no choice but to bring troops out. From afar, Cao’s army looked like frosted earth becoming snow. In the central command he raised two white banners, each with four characters, “Avenge and wash away resentment” (“Avenge and Wash the Grudge”).

The horse and foot formed in line.

Cao Cao rode out of his ranks in plain white robes, whip raised, and yelled out abuses. Tao Qian also rode out beneath the city gate and, bowing low, spoke: “I had wanted to be on good terms with you, my lord, so I entrusted Zhang Kai. I cannot claim he has changed to villainy by his own heart. It was not Tao Qian’s doing; please examine this carefully.”

Cao shouted back, “Old fool! You killed my father, and you still dare to speak out of turn! Who can capture that old villain alive?”

Hearing this, Xiahou Dun stepped forward at once. Tao Qian panicked and rode into formation. Xiahou Dun chased him. Cao Bao thrust a spear and leapt onto his horse to meet him. As the horses came near each other, a furious wind rose, flying sand and stones everywhere. The two armies were thrown into confusion and each withdrew its men.

Tao Qian entered the city and discussed with the crowd: “Cao’s force is vast and hard to withstand. I should bind myself and ride to Cao’s camp to let them cut me open if needed, saving the people of Xu Province.” Before he had finished, a man stepped forward and said, “For many years you have ruled Xu Province, and the people are grateful. Though Cao’s army is large, it has not yet broken through our walls. You should hold the city and do not ride out. Though I am unworthy, I can offer a small stratagem: we can make it so that Cao Cao has no place to be buried alive.”

Everyone was shocked and asked how to avoid this fate. Exactly then:

To welcome and admit allies only to have them turn to enemies, who would have guessed that at the very edge of destruction one might yet meet life again?

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Loyal Vassals of the Court, Ma Teng Rises in Righteous Valor, and Cao Cao Raises the Army to Avenge His Father

chapters.html:
Liu the Imperial Uncle goes to Beihai to save Kong Rong. Lord Lü Wen of Puyang smashes Cao Cao.

Then there was the man who had offered the scheme. He was from Qu County in Donghai. His surname was Mi, given name Zhu, courtesy name Zizhong. He came from an affluent household. Once he had gone to Luoyang on business and was returning in a cart. On the road he met a beautiful woman who asked to share the cart. Mi Zhu stepped down and walked, giving her his place. The woman asked him to ride together. He stepped onto the cart and sat upright, never letting his eyes wander. After a few li, she asked leave; as she was departing she said, “I am the Lord of Fire Virtue from the south, ordered by the Son of Heaven to burn your house. I came by because you treated me with courtesy, so I tell you plainly. Return home at once and remove your goods. I will come tonight.” She vanished.

Mi Zhu was greatly startled. He ran home and hastily moved everything from the house. That night, as promised, fire rose in the kitchen and burned the whole house. Because of this, Mi Zhu emptied his household stores and gave freely to the poor and the distressed. Later Tao Qian appointed him Biejia-attendant. On that same day he proposed: “I will go personally to Beihai Commandery, ask Kong Rong to raise troops for rescue. Also ask for a man from Qingzhou to seek aid from Tian Kai. If both horse columns arrive, Cao Cao must withdraw his army.” Tao Qian agreed and wrote two letters. He asked who among the retainers would dare to go to Qingzhou. One man stepped forward at once. It was a man from Guangling named Chen Deng, courtesy name Yuanlong.

Tao Qian first sent Chen Deng to Qingzhou. Afterward he sent Mi Zhu with letters to Beihai, and he himself gathered people to hold the city against attack.

Now Beihai’s Kong Rong, courtesy name Wenju, was from Qufu in Lu State. He was the son of Kong Zhou, governor over the Eastern Mountain commandery for the Han, and a great-great-great-grandson of Confucius. He was gifted from childhood. At ten, he went to pay respects to Li Ying, Inspector of Henan. The gatekeeper refused him; Rong said, “My house has long-standing ties to the Li house.” When he was admitted, Ying asked, “How were your ancestors tied to mine?” Rong answered, “Once Confucius sought rites from Laozi. Were not you and I of intertwined families for generations?” Li Ying was amazed.

Before long, Senior Master of the Secretariat Chen Wei arrived. Ying said, “This extraordinary child.” Wei replied, “A child may be intelligent early; a grown man is not always so.” Rong responded at once, “As you said: one who is bright in childhood is not always bright later?” Chen Wei and the others all laughed: “When this child comes of age, he will surely become a splendid instrument of his age.” From then on he became famous.

He later became a Zhong Lang general, then rose by turns to Administrator of Beihai Commandery. He delighted in welcoming guests. He used to say, “The hall should always be full of guests, and the cup in the jar should never be empty. That is my wish.” In six years at Beihai he won the people’s confidence.

One day he was with his guests when a report came that Mi Zhu of Xuzhou had arrived. Rong asked to receive him and inquired as to his errand. Mi presented Tao Qian’s letter and said, “Cao Cao’s assault is severe. I beg Your Excellency to render rescue.” Rong said, “My ties with Tao Gongzu are close, and your son came here personally; how could I not go? Yet Cao Mengde and I are not enemies. I should first send a letter offering peace. If he refuses, then we will raise troops.”

Mi said, “Cao Cao relies on force and will never consent to peace.” Rong ordered the troops to be mobilized and at the same time sent a messenger with a letter. In the middle of consultations, news came of a band of bandits led by Guan Hai with several ten thousand men charging in from the Yellow Turban side. Rong was alarmed. He quickly counted his troops and sallied out to engage the raiders.

Guan Hai rode up and called out: “I know Beihai has ample grain. Lend me ten thousand shi and I will withdraw; otherwise I will break this city and spare no old or young!” Rong shouted back, “I am a servant of the Great Han and defender of Han land. Shall grain be given to bandits?”

Guan Hai grew furious, struck his horse and swung his saber, charging straight at Kong Rong. Rong had Zongbao step forward with a spear. After a few exchanges they were in battle; with one slash Guan Hai cut Zongbao down from his horse. Kong Rong’s soldiers broke and ran back into the city. Guan Hai divided his men to surround the city on four sides. Kong Rong’s heart darkened. Mi Zhu’s face grew anxious and he said nothing.

The next day Kong Rong climbed the wall and looked out. The raiders were vast beyond measure. His unease doubled. He saw a man outside riding with spear high, leaping his horse into the enemy ranks, slashing right and left as if in a deserted field, coming right to the foot of the city and shouting, “Open the gate!” Kong Rong could not recognize him and did not dare to open.

The bandits chased him to the riverbank. The man wheeled back and shot down a score of them from the saddle. The rest withdrew. Rong at once ordered the gate opened and drew him in. The man dismounted, tossed aside his spear, and ascended to the wall to kneel before Kong Rong.

Rong asked his name. The stranger replied, “I am a man from Huang County, Donglai. My surname is Taishi, my given name is Ci, courtesy name Ziyi. My mother is deeply in your debt. Yesterday I returned from Liaodong to visit her at home and learned that rebels had surrounded Beihai. My mother said, ‘You have long received the Magistrate’s grace. You must go and save the city.’ So I came alone on one horse.”

Kong Rong rejoiced. Though he and Taishi Ci had not yet met, he knew him for a hero. Because he had gone far, with his elderly mother dwelling twenty li beyond the city, Rong often sent her grain and silk. Moved by Rong’s kindness, the mother had specifically dispatched Ci to save the city.

Kong Rong now treated Taishi Ci with special honor and gave him clothing, armor, saddle and horse. Ci said, “I ask to borrow a thousand picked soldiers and ride out to kill the bandits.” Rong said, “You are brave, but the raiders are many and you should not go out lightly.” Ci replied, “My mother is repaid for your kindness in sending me forth. If I cannot relieve the siege, I cannot show my face to her. I will accept a battle to the death.”

Rong said, “I have heard that Liu Xuande is the hero of this age. If we can bring him, this siege will dissolve on its own; but no man is available.”

Ci said, “Your Excellency has sent writing to him. I will go at once.”

Rong was pleased. He wrote a letter and handed it to Ci. Ci donned his armor, mounted, belted bow and arrows to his waist, and bore a stout iron spear. After a full meal and full equipment, he passed through the gate on a single horse.

Near the river, enemy commanders came with their men to fight. Ci shot and killed several in succession and broke through the encirclement. Guan Hai knew someone had ridden out and must be a messenger for aid, and with several hundred riders he gave chase. He surrounded Ci on all sides, but Ci steadied his spear, set arrow to bow, and loosed. The arrows struck and riders all toppled from their saddles. The raiders did not dare to pursue. Taishi Ci escaped by night and rode to Pingyuan to meet Liu Xuande.

After formal greeting, he explained Kong Rong of Beihai was besieged and showed the letters. When Liu had read them, he asked, “Who are you?”

Ci answered, “I am Taishi Ci, a humble man from Donghai. Kong Rong and I are not of one blood or one village; yet our sense of justice and kinship of fellowship is enough for us to share danger and help one another. Now Guan Hai has gone mad and Beihai is under siege. As I have no one to report to, and the crisis is immediate, I have come at great risk by breaking through the lines, for I heard that Your Grace is famed for benevolence and could save one in peril. So I came.”

Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, replied gravely, “Does the Lord of Beihai, Kong Rong, even know that Liu Bei exists?” Then he selected three thousand chosen men with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei and moved toward Beihai.

When Guan Hai saw the rescue force arrive, he personally led his men out to meet them. Thinking Liu’s army small, he made light of it. Liu rode with Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Taishi Ci to the front of the formation. Guan Hai flew into a rage and rushed out. Taishi Ci hung back, while Guan Yu charged first and went straight at Guan Hai. Their horses met and the crowd roared. No one knew how Guan Hai could be matched by Guan Yu. Within a few dozen exchanges, the Green Dragon Crescent Blade cut Guan Hai down from his horse.

Taishi Ci and Zhang Fei both charged forth together, spears raised in both hands, cutting into the raiders. Liu Bei led men in a supporting sweep and killed broadly. From the battlements Kong Rong watched Taishi Ci with Guan and Zhang as they drove through the host as if a tiger through sheep, moving in all directions untouchable. He then ordered his men out as well. The two-pronged assault crushed the rebels in a great rout, with innumerable surrenders and the rest scattered.

Kong Rong received Liu into the city with ceremony and, after formalities, made a grand feast of celebration. He then brought forth Mi Zhu and told him to present all: “Zhang Kai killed Cao Song. Now Cao Cao leads the men in mass plunder and has Tianzhou under siege. We came only for help.”

Liu said, “Tao Gongzu was a man of principle. It is unfortunate he has suffered such unjust humiliation.”

Kong Rong said, “You are a kinsman of the Han house. Cao Cao now destroys the common people, using his strength to bully the weak. Why not go with me to rescue him?”

Liu said, “I do not decline it. Yet my troops are few and my generals few. I fear I cannot move lightly.”

Rong said, “Rong’s wish to rescue Tao Gongzu is not only for old friendship; it is for justice itself. Do you, my lord, have no heart for justice?”

Liu replied, “If so, let Wenju go first; let Liu Bei go to Gongsun Zan and borrow three to five thousand horse and men. He will follow after.”

Rong said, “Do not fail in your word.”

Liu said, “How do you judge me? The Master of the Five Classics says, ‘From old times men have all died; the one with no trust cannot stand.’ Whether I can borrow soldiers or not, I will come in person.”

Rong assented. He asked Mi Zhu to return to Xuzhou first and report. Then Rong set out for home.

Taishi Ci bowing and thanking said, “I came by my mother’s command to help and now we are safe for now. There is Liu Yao, Inspector of Yang Province, from my commandery and he has written to summon me. I dare not disobey. Pray that we meet again.”

Rong rewarded him with gold and fine goods, which Ci refused and departed. His mother saw him and said joyfully, “I am glad you have repaid your debt to Beihai!” then sent him off to Yangzhou.

There is no account here of Kong Rong’s levying of troops. Meanwhile Liu Bei left Beihai for Gongsun Zan, still intending to save Xuzhou. Gongsun Zan said, “You and Cao Cao have no feud. Why spend your strength for another?” Liu said, “I have given my word and dare not fail.”

Gongsun Zan said, “I will lend you two thousand horse and foot.” Liu added, “I also ask leave to borrow Zhao Zilong and his company.” Zan consented. Liu then sent three thousand men under his own command as an advance, and Zhao Zilong led two thousand in support on the way to Xuzhou.

Mi Zhu returned to report to Tao Qian that Beihai had now also obtained Liu Bei’s help. Chen Deng also reported that Tian Kai of Qingzhou had gladly raised men and was coming. Tao Qian was at peace.

In truth Kong Rong’s and Tian Kai’s forces, fearing the ferocity of Cao’s host, camped under the mountain and did not advance lightly. When Cao saw the two columns arrive, he also split his troops and did not yet attack the city.

When Liu Bei's troops arrived and he saw Kong Rong, the older man said, “Cao’s force is immense, and Cao is skilled at war. We cannot begin by light fighting. Observe their movements first, then advance.”

Liu said, “I fear the city has no grain and cannot hold long. Guan Yu and Zhao Zilong should together lead four thousand men under your command as support. Liu Bei and Zhang Fei will take a thousand cavalry and strike the rear to run into Xuzhou and consult with Tao Gongzu.”

Rong was glad and then linked with Tian Kai, giving them a flanking formation, with Guan Yu and Zilong taking the two wings.

That day Liu Bei and Zhang Fei with one thousand men rode in to strike the edge of Cao’s camp. As they moved, a drum sounded inside the camp and cavalry and infantry surged out like waves. At their head was a great general, Yu Jin, who reined in and shouted, “What madmen are these, and where do you intend to go?” Zhang Fei rode straight at Yu Jin first and their horses met. After several rounds of battle, Liu drew both his paired swords and pushed his troops forward in a great charge, and Yu Jin broke through and fled.

Zhang Fei pressed on, pursuing to the foot of Xuzhou walls. On the wall they saw a red banner with white characters reading “Pingyuan Liu Xuande,” and Tao Qian immediately ordered the gate opened. Liu entered; Tao received him and together they went to the yamen. After ceremony, there was a feast and troops were comforted.

Tao Qian saw in Liu’s bearing and manner a dignified, openhearted man, and his heart rejoiced. He told Mi Zhu to fetch the seal of Xuzhou and hand it to Liu.

Liu asked in surprise, “What is Your Excellency’s intent?”

Tao said, “Under Heaven turmoil reigns and the state pillars are weak. You are of imperial blood and should uphold the realm. I am old and useless; I am willing to yield Xuzhou to you. Do not refuse. I will write memorial and request the court to ratify it.”

Liu knelt and stood again: “Though Liu Bei is of Han’s seed, my achievements are slight and my virtue thin. Even as Prefect of Pingyuan I fear I would not be worthy. I came here for righteousness. Does Your Excellency truly suspect that Liu Bei seeks to swallow a province? If such a thought arises, Heaven will not support him!”

Tao replied, “This is truly my mind.”

After repeated remonstration, Liu still would not accept.

Mi Zhu said, “With enemy men before the city and disorder in the empire, no one may step aside. Xuzhou is rich and has a million households. Should Liu Gongshu lead it, he cannot decline.”

Liu answered, “I will not accept this command.”

Chen Deng added, “Tao Gongzu is ill and cannot take charge. My lord, do not refuse.”

Liu said, “Yuan Gonglu, famed throughout the realm and near Shouchun, is one who is known across the empire. Why not give the province to Yuan Gonglu?”

Rong said, “Yuan Gonglu is just the dried bones in the tomb. What is there to bring up his name? What comes by Heaven this day cannot be regained by regret.”

Liu remained firm and refused.

Tao Qian wept, “If you leave me, I will not die in peace!”

Guan Yu said, “Since Tao Gong has bestowed the state, my brother may temporarily assume command.”

Zhang Fei said, “No one forced him. He offered from kindness. Why should he persist in refusing?”

Liu said, “Do you want to entangle me in unrighteousness?”

After repeated remonstrance, Tao again offered. Liu still refused.

Tao said, “If Liu Bei must not accept, there is an outer town nearby, Xiao Pei. It is enough to station troops. Please remain there temporarily and hold Xuzhou. Is that agreeable?”

All urged him to stay in Xiao Pei, and Liu obeyed. Tao had finished mustering the troops. Zhao Zilong asked leave to go. Liu grasped his hand with tears and parted. Kong Rong and Tian Kai also took leave separately and withdrew their commands.

Liu and Guan Yu and Zhang Fei brought their main contingent to Xiao Pei and repaired the walls, then spoke to the people to calm them.

Cao Cao returned homeward, and Cao Ren reported on following: “Lü Bu is powerful, and he now has Chen Gong supporting him. Yanzhou and Puyang are lost. Jucheng, Dong’e, and Fancounty have held only by the cunning defenses arranged by Xun Yu and Cheng Yu.”

Cao said, “I have judged Lü Bu: brave but not scheming, not to be feared.” He ordered the army to camp and consider again.

Lü Bu learned Cao had turned back after passing Teng County and summoned his deputies Xue Lan and Li Feng. “I have wanted to use you two for some time,” he said. “You may lead ten thousand men and hold Yanzhou. I will lead out myself to break Cao.”

They obeyed. Chen Gong hurried in at once and asked, “General, why leave Yanzhou?”

Bu said, “I intend to station at Puyang and create a three-legged balance.”

Chen Gong replied, “That is mistaken. Xue Lan will not hold Yanzhou long. It is one hundred eighty li to the south from here: the road past Mount Tai is difficult. A host of ten thousand can lie in ambush there. Cao’s men, when they learn of Yanzhou lost, will push ahead doubled, and when they are halfway through, one strike can seize him.”

Lü Bu said, “At Puyang I have another good plan. How can you know it?” He ignored Chen Gong and appointed Xue Lan to Yanzhou.

Cao’s troops moved to the hazardous pass of Mount Tai. Guo Jia said, “Do not advance yet. I fear ambush here.” Cao laughed, “Lü Bu is no master of planning and told Xue Lan to hold Yanzhou while he goes to Puyang. How could there be an ambush?” He ordered Cao Ren to occupy Yanzhou and himself pushed on to Puyang to strike him quickly.

When Chen Gong heard Cao had approached, he offered counsel: “Cao’s troops are far, weary, and short of strength. Speed wins here; do not let them gather strength.”

Lü replied, “I, who ride and cut through all under heaven, have no fear of Cao Cao. Once he camps, I will capture him myself.”

Cao’s force reached Puyang and made camp at the base of the ridge. The next day he brought out all commanders and deployed for battle in the field. Cao mounted beneath his gate-banner and watched Lü’s approach. At the front of Lü’s line, two horsesmen came out first.

The first was from Yanmeng, of Mayi, surname Zhang, given name Liao, courtesy name Wenyuan. The second was from Hua Yin in Mount Tai, surname Zang, given name Ba, courtesy name Xiangao. Each brought six fine captains: Hao Meng, Cao Xing, Cheng Lian, Wei Xu, Song Xian, and Hou Cheng.

Lü’s army was fifty thousand, and drums thundered loudly. Cao pointed to Lü and said, “Between us there was no old enmity. Why then did you seize my states and commanderies?”

Lü answered, “Han fortresses and cities are for all our share-holders; how can you alone take what belongs to everyone?” He then ordered Zang Ba to ride out.

Cao’s troops, with Yue Jin at the front, rode to meet him. The two horses met and two spears rose together. After more than thirty rounds, victory was not yet decided. Xiahou Dun struck and leapt from the saddle to join; on the field Zhang Liao intercepted and wrestled. Enraged, Lü sent his halberd hard and drove forward; Xiahou Dun and Yue Jin both turned away and fled. Lü then cut down in pursuit, and Cao’s army suffered heavy defeat and withdrew thirty to forty li. Lü gathered his men.

Cao, having lost an engagement, returned to camp and counseled with his generals. Yu Jin said, “I watched from the hill this morning. On the west of Puyang, Lü has only one outpost with few troops. Tonight he will think our force withdrew and prepare little. If we strike now, he cannot hold. This is the best stratagem.”

Cao followed this and took Cao Hong, Li Dian, Mao Jie, Lü Qian, Yu Jin, Dian Wei, and a select force of twenty thousand horse and foot through a side path by night.

In camp, Lü held a review. Chen Gong said, “The west stockade is a critical point. If Cao attacks there, what will we do?”

Lü said, “He lost one bout today. How could he dare?”

Chen Gong urged, “Cao is one who masters battle. You must prepare for an unguarded assault.”

Lü moved Gao Shun, Wei Xu, and Hou Cheng forward to hold the west stockade.

At dusk Cao reached the west stockade and burst in from all sides. The stockade men could not withstand him and scattered. Cao seized the camp. Not until the fourth watch did Gao Shun arrive with troops, cutting through and entering.

Cao rode out to meet him, and they entered a mixed melee. By dawn, at the sound of westward drums, word came that Lü was leading his main army himself.

Cao abandoned the camp and ran.

Behind him Gao Shun, Wei Xu, and Hou Cheng chased hard. Lü arrived at the front immediately, leading his men himself. Yu Jin and Yue Jin both fought Lü and could not hold him. Cao turned north.

Out from behind the ridge came another force: to the left, Zhang Liao; to the right, Zang Ba. Cao sent Lü Qian and Cao Hong against them, but the fight was not favorable. Cao headed west.

Again a shout rose and another unit arrived: Hao Meng, Cao Xing, Cheng Lian, and Song Xian blocked his road. All generals fought to the death. Cao himself broke into the line first. When the bronze clappers sounded, arrows fell in sudden rain.

Cao could not advance or find escape. He shouted, “Who will save me?”

From the cavalry ranks one general leapt out: it was Dian Wei. He held both iron halberds in hand and cried, “Master, do not worry!” He sprang from his horse, planted both halberds in the ground, took up ten short spears and carried them in his hands. He called to those around him, “When the enemy is ten steps away, then call me!” and he pressed forward in deliberate steps through arrows.

Nearly fifty riders of Lü’s horse closed on him. The men around him shouted, “Ten steps!”

Wei answered, “When they are five!” They shouted again, “Five!”

Wei lunged with his halberd. One stroke, one rider downed from his horse; none of his stabs missed. He killed ten or more at once. All around him turned and fled.

Wei mounted again and, lifting his two great iron halberds, broke through in a charge. Hao, Cao, Cheng, and Song could not meet him and each turned away and fled. Dian Wei scattered the enemy and rescued Cao. The other commanders arrived in turn; eventually they found the road back to camp.

By evening the light was near gone when shouts rose from behind. Lü Bu spurred and charged, halberd raised, crying, “Cao the traitor, do not run!”

The men were exhausted and their horses spent, and all cast their eyes about, each seeking flight. At this point:

Though he can for a moment break from the heavy encirclement, he may not endure the pursuit of such a determined foe.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Liu, the Imperial Uncle, Saves Kong Rong at Beihai; Lord Lü Wen of Puyang Breaks Cao Cao

chapters.html:
Cao Cao was already in a frantic withdrawal when a full troop came from the south. Xiahou Dun then led his force to aid him and blocked Lü Bu for a major fight. By dusk the battle was still raging when heavy rain poured down. The two sides pulled back their troops in different directions, and Cao Cao returned to camp, rewarding Dian Wei heavily and promoting him to Colonel of the Vanguard.

When Lü Bu reached camp he conferred with Chen Gong. Chen Gong said, “In the city of Puyang there is the wealthy Tian household, a great household of the commandery with a thousand retainers. Send a secret man to Cao Cao’s camp with a letter saying that Marquis Wenhou Lü is cruel and heartless, and the people have a deep grievance against him. He now intends to move troops to Liyang. There is only Gao Shun in the city, and I can serve as an insider. If Cao Cao comes, lure him in. Light fires at all four gates and station an ambush outside. Though Cao Cao has talent enough to govern heaven and earth, how can he get out once he is here?”

Lü Bu followed his plan and sent a man from the Tian house straight to Cao Cao’s camp. Cao Cao was still shaken by his recent defeat and in no hurry to decide when he was told that the Tian envoy had arrived and submitted a secret letter: “Lü Bu has gone to Liyang and the city is largely empty. Hurry and come. I will act as your insider. If you see a white banner with the character 義 (‘righteousness’) on the city wall, that is our signal.”

“Heaven has granted me Puyang,” Cao Cao said in delight. He rewarded the messenger and at once set his troops in order. Liu Ye said, “Lü Bu may lack strategy, but Chen Gong has many plans. Yet this may be a ruse, and we must not be careless. If you want to go, divide your army into three groups: two groups to wait outside the city, and one to enter the city.”

Cao Cao took his advice and divided the force into three columns, then came to Puyang’s walls. Looking up first, he saw banners raised all over the city; on the west gate turret a white flag with the character “義” appeared, and his heart warmed within him. At the midday watch the gate opened. Two generals led troops out to meet them: Hou Cheng in front, Gao Shun behind. Cao Cao sent Dian Wei forward to take Hou Cheng at once. Hou Cheng could not stand the attack and turned back toward the city. By the time Dian Wei reached the bridge, Gao Shun could not hold him either, and both retreated inside.

Then several soldiers forced their way through and came to see Cao Cao, saying they were men from the Tian household. They presented another secret letter: “Tonight at the first watch, when drums sound from the wall, it is time to advance. One of us will open the gate.” Cao Cao gave Xiahou Dun the left side and Cao Hong the right, while he himself led Xiahou Yuan, Li Dian, Yue Jin, and Dian Wei to enter.

Li Dian said, “Your Excellency should remain outside. Let us enter first.”

“If I do not go first, who will go ahead?” Cao Cao snapped, and led the van in.

At the first watch of night, with no moonlight yet, they heard shell-like clappers from the west gate and sudden shouts. Torchlight blazed at the gate; it was thrown wide, and the bridge was lowered. Cao Cao urged his horse forward and entered first. By the time they reached the yamen not a single person was in sight. Realizing the trick, he wheeled around and shouted, “Fall back!”

A loud blast sounded from the yamen. Flames shot up from all four gates and roared toward the sky; gongs and drums rang together; the shouting sounded like the sea in spate. Zhang Liao came out through the east alley and Zang Ba from the west, and the two pressed in together to butcher. Cao Cao ran for the north gate and was met by Haomeng and Cao Xing, who killed another group before him. He rushed on toward the south gate, where Gao Shun and Hou Cheng blocked him. Dian Wei bared his teeth and charged through. Gao Shun and Hou Cheng ran out of the city.

Dian Wei charged to the bridge and then found he could no longer see Cao Cao. He pivoted and rushed back into the city. There at the gate he struck against Li Dian.

“Where is the lord?”

“I have not found him either,” Dian Wei replied. “You stay outside and call in the rescuers. I will enter and search for the lord.” Li Dian left.

Dian Wei entered and searched but found no trace. He fought out again to the moat edge and met Yue Jin.

Yue Jin asked, “Where is the lord?”

“I entered twice and still cannot find him,” Dian Wei replied.

“Then I’ll ride in with you,” Yue Jin said.

The two rode to the gate. A cannon shot rattled down from above. Yue Jin’s horse could not enter. Dian Wei pushed through in smoke and flame and broke in again, searching all around.

Now Cao Cao saw Dian Wei ride out. He found horsemen cutting him off on every side and could not come out by the south gate. He turned to the north gate, and through the firelight saw Lü Bu come riding hard, halberd raised. Cao Cao covered his face, lashed his horse, and somehow leapt past.

Lü Bu thundered after him and struck the halberd on the top of Cao Cao’s helmet. “Where is Cao Cao?”

“The rider on the yellow horse out front is he,” Cao Cao said.

Hearing this, Lü Bu discarded caution and drove after the rider in pursuit. Cao Cao turned his horse toward the east gate and happened to meet Dian Wei. Dian Wei cleared a bloody way and shielded Cao Cao. At the gate the flames were fierce. Bundles of brushwood lay heaped under the wall, and fire covered the ground. Dian Wei used his halberd to shove open a path, his horse charging through smoke first and bursting out. Cao Cao followed immediately.

As they reached the gate pass a burning beam fell from above and struck Cao Cao’s horse in the haunch. It pitched and crashed to the ground. Cao Cao braced the beam with his hands and shoved it down, but his arms, beard, and hair were badly burned. Dian Wei turned back to help him at just the right moment, and Xiahou Yuan also arrived. The two brought Cao Cao out and dashed through the fire. Cao Cao mounted Xiahou Yuan’s horse, and Dian Wei cut a wide bloody road as they ran.

They fought in and out until dawn before Cao Cao finally returned to camp. The officers knelt and greeted him. Looking up, he laughed: “I have been outwitted by one coarse fellow, and I must repay it.”

Guo Jia said, “The plan can be carried out at once.”

Cao Cao answered, “Let us counter-plan with counter-plan. Publicly, say I was burned and that the fire and heat have taken me; by the fifth watch I am dead. Lü Bu will then come forward to attack. I have hidden my best troops in Maoling Mountain. When half his force had crossed the bridge and was mid-crossing, strike them. Lü Bu can be taken.” Guo Jia approved, “That is truly a good stratagem.”

So he ordered soldiers to hang mourning cloth and announce his death. Before long a man came to Puyang to report to Lü Bu that Cao Cao had been burned, that his limbs had been scorched, and that he had already died in camp. Lü Bu quickly mounted and rode for Maoling.

As his army drew near, one drum beat, and the hidden troops rose. Lü Bu barely fought his way out, though many men and horses were lost. He returned to Puyang defeated and held close to the city walls.

That year locusts suddenly swarmed up and stripped the grain. Across Guan Dong, a hu of grain fetched fifty guan, and people preyed upon each other to survive. Cao Cao, seeing his army’s grain gone, returned to Juancheng and withdrew briefly. Lü Bu also moved out and camped at Shanyang to forage. Thus both sides briefly stood down their campaigns.

Now Tao Qian, whose courtesy name was Gongzu, was in Xu Province. He was sixty-three, and suddenly his illness deepened. He summoned Mi Zhu and Chen Deng to deliberate. Mi Zhu said, “Cao Cao’s troops left only because they came to strike Yanzhou. Now because of the shortage this year they have ceased, but next spring they will come again. Lord Tao tried twice to give up his command to Liu Xuande, but at that time you were still strong, so he refused. Now your illness is grave, and this is the moment to do so openly; Liu Bei will surely not decline.”

Tao Qian was overjoyed and sent word to Xiaopei to summon Liu Bei to discuss military affairs. Liu Bei arrived with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei and several dozen riders, and Tao Qian invited him into his bedchamber. After Liu Bei offered his respects, Tao Qian said, “I ask Liu Gong to come not for anything else. I am old and gravely sick, and life is uncertain from dawn to dusk. If the lord values these Han cities, please take over the seal of command for Xu Province, so I may die at peace.”

Liu Bei said, “You have two sons. Why not pass the post to them?”

Tao Qian answered, “The elder is Shang, the younger Ying; neither has the talent for this station. Even after I die, I still hope you will guide them and not let them hold this command.”

Liu Bei said, “How can I, one man, carry such a heavy charge?”

Tao Qian said, “I can point to one man to be your assistant. He is from Beihai, surname Sun, given name Qian, courtesy name Gongyou. He can serve as congshi. Also tell Mi Zhu: Liu Gong is foremost among men now; you must serve him well.”

Liu Bei still hesitated. Tao Qian pointed to his chest and died. The officers wept and, after all mourning rites, presented the seal to Liu Bei. Liu Bei still resisted.

The next day the people of Xu Province crowded before the office and wept: “If Lord Liu does not take this commandery, we cannot live in peace!” Guan Yu and Zhang Fei again and again urged him. Liu Bei therefore agreed to assume authority, temporarily granting Sun Qian and Mi Zhu as assistants and Chen Deng as his secretary; he brought in the Xiaopei troops and posted the peace notice to calm the people. At the same time he arranged for the burial matters. Liu Bei and all officers and soldiers donned mourning cloth and held a grand memorial. After the rite he buried Tao Qian at the plain by the Yellow River and carried his testament to court.

At this time Cao Cao, in Juancheng, heard Tao Qian was dead and that Liu Bei had become Governor of Xu Province. He grew furious: “My grievance has not yet been repaid. You won’t spend even half an arrow’s worth, and yet you have come by Xu Province! I will first kill Liu Bei and only then hang Qian’s corpse to clear my father’s resentment.” He gave immediate orders to move out against Xu Province the next day.

Xun Yu interceded. “In former times, Emperor Gaozu held Guanzhong and Emperor Guangwu held Henan. Both rooted deeply and made their base secure; then they could win against enemies and stand firm in defense. So even when in hardship they still accomplished their great work. My lord began with Yanzhou, and the He and Ji region is the key of all under heaven, just as Guanzhong and Henan were in old days. If you take Xu Province and keep too many troops there, they are wasted; keep too few and Lü Bu will exploit the opening and raid, and you lose Yanzhou. If Yanzhou falls, where can my lord stand? Though Tao Qian is dead, Liu Bei already holds Xu Province and its people have submitted to him. They will fight to the death for Liu Bei. To abandon Yanzhou and go after Xu Province is to abandon the root for the branch, seeking the lesser when the greater lies at hand.”

Cao Cao said, “This year the land suffers from famine and my soldiers have no grain to guard long here. This is no sound policy.”

Xun Yu said, “Then march east and forage in Chen territory. In Yuzhou and Yingshan, Yellow Turban remnants like He Yi and Huang Shao are raiding commanderies and counties; they possess much gold and grain. Those bandits are easy to break. Breaking them and seizing their stores will feed three armies. The court will be satisfied and the people glad. That is the way of Heaven.”

Cao Cao agreed. He left Xiahou Dun and Cao Ren to hold Juancheng and nearby posts, and he led his force east to Chen land, then to Yu and Ying. He Yi and Huang Shao, hearing Cao’s troops approaching, came out with their followers and met at Mount Yang. Though their soldiers were many, they were a rabble, with no formation or line. Cao Cao ordered the heavy-bow and crossbowmen to pin them and had Dian Wei lead. He Yi sent his vice-general to fight; he could not withstand three exchanges, and Dian Wei pierced him once with a halberd at the horse’s base. Cao Cao drove the force across the mountain’s foot to camp.

The next day Huang Shao led troops in person. In the circular formation a single commander came out on foot, head wrapped in a yellow turban, body in a green jacket, iron bar in hand. He shouted, “I am He Man, the Night-Crushing Scourge. Who dares fight me?” Cao Hong saw him and gave a great shout, leaping from his horse and stepping out with his sabre.

The two clashed and fought in front of the lines for forty or fifty exchanges with no clear winner. Cao Hong feigned defeat and withdrew. He Man chased him, and Cao Hong turned the blade on its back and with one leap cut him down, then finished him with a second stroke. Li Dian then flew into the rebel ranks with his horse. Huang Shao could not recover in time and was taken alive by Li Dian.

The Cao troops slaughtered the bandits and seized a great quantity of gold, valuables, and grain. He Yi became isolated and led a few hundred riders to run toward Gefu. While running, a force emerged behind the mountain. The first of them was a broad-shouldered warrior, eight chi tall, waist ten fists around; he held a great sword and cut off their way.

He Yi thrust his spear and countered, but in one exchange the warrior lifted him cleanly over his shoulder and carried him. The rest dismounted at once and surrendered, and the warrior drove them all into the Gefu stockade.

Still, Dian Wei pursued He Yi to Gefu, where the warrior blocked him with his army.

Dian Wei said, “Are you a Yellow Turban rebel too?”

The warrior replied, “All the Yellow Turban riders—hundreds of them—I have all captured in the stockade.”

Dian Wei asked, “Why won’t you surrender them?”

The warrior said, “If you can win the precious sword in my hand, then I will yield.”

Dian Wei grew furious and thrust both his halberds forward to fight. They fought from morning to midday without either gaining advantage and taking little rest. Soon after, the warrior came out again and Dian Wei also entered the fray. The struggle continued to dusk, and then both temporarily withdrew when their horses grew exhausted. Before long the warrior broke off again, and Dian Wei’s men reported the battle’s progress to Cao Cao. Cao Cao was startled and quickly brought his commanders to see.

The next day the warrior returned to battle again. Cao Cao watched him and quietly rejoiced in his strength. He ordered Dian Wei to feign defeat for the day.

Dian Wei obeyed. After thirty exchanges he withdrew to the rear. The warrior chased him to the gate and returned arrows from his bow and crossbow. Cao Cao pulled his army back five li and quietly ordered soldiers to dig a pit, hiding hook-men within.

The next day he again sent Dian Wei out with about a hundred riders. The warrior laughed, “How could a beaten general dare come back?”

He spurred his horse and engaged. After only a few exchanges Dian Wei turned away and rode back. The warrior only chased forward, eyes fixed on him, not on the ground, and fell into the prepared pit with horse and rider. Hook-men dragged him in and brought him before Cao Cao. Cao Cao pushed the soldiers back from him, personally unbound him, put him in robes, seated him, and asked about his hometown and name.

The warrior said, “I am from Qiao County of Qiao State. My surname is Xu, my given name is Chu, and my courtesy name is Zhongkang. When bandit trouble struck, I gathered several hundred kinsmen and built a strong stockade here for defense. When the raiders came one day, I ordered everyone to gather stones. I threw stone after stone myself and never missed; the raiders withdrew.

Another day the raiders returned and we had no grain in the stockade, so we bargained with them: plow oxen for rice. When the rice arrived, the raiders drove the oxen outside the stockade. The animals bolted homeward, and I seized both tails with both hands, pulling them back a hundred steps. The raiders were startled; they did not dare take the oxen and fled. So we held this place in peace.”

Cao Cao said, “Your name has reached me long ago. Are you willing to surrender?” Xu Chu answered, “That has long been my wish.” He therefore called in several hundred of his clan at once.

Cao Cao appointed Xu Chu as Colonel, rewarding him richly. He then ordered He Yi and Huang Shao put to death. Yu and Ying were fully pacified.

When Cao Cao then returned from the campaign, Cao Ren and Xiahou Dun came and reported that intelligence said soldiers under Xue Lan and Li Feng from Yanzhou had gone out to plunder, leaving the cities open. One drum and one charge could take them. Cao Cao immediately marched straight for Yanzhou.

Xue Lan and Li Feng were caught off guard and had to ride out to meet him. Xu Chu said, “I wish to take both men as an offering in sacrifice.” Cao Cao approved and ordered him forward.

Li Feng raised a halberd and charged. Two exchanges of cavalry clashed, then Xu Chu cut Li Feng down beneath his horse. Xue Lan turned back to rejoin his lines; at the bridge edge Li Dian blocked him. Xue Lan did not dare return into the city and led his troops toward Juyê. But Lü Qian came riding and shot an arrow beneath his horse; the force was scattered.

Cao Cao recovered Yanzhou, and Cheng Yu asked to advance on Puyang. Cao ordered Xu Chu and Dian Wei as vanguard, Xiahou Dun and Xiahou Yuan on the left wing, Li Dian and Yue Jin on the right, and himself taking the center, with Yu Jin and Lü Qian covering the rear. When the army reached Puyang, Lü Bu wanted to lead a sortie himself. Chen Gong counseled him not to: “Do not go out yet; wait until all your commanders are assembled.” Lü Bu replied, “Who is there for me to fear?” and disobeyed, riding out to battle with his halberd raised.

Xu Chu charged out. After twenty rounds neither side had gained an edge. Cao Cao said, “Lü Bu is no opponent one man can beat,” and ordered Dian Wei to assist. The two joined and attacked together. Xiahou Dun and Xiahou Yuan came on the left, Li Dian and Yue Jin on the right, and the six together pressed Lü Bu. He could not hold and rode back to the city. Atop the wall, the Tian family saw him return, and at once called to haul up the bridge. Lü Bu shouted, “Open the gate!”

“I have already surrendered to General Cao,” they replied.

Lü Bu shouted curses and rode to Dingtao. Chen Gong quickly opened the east gate to protect Lü Bu’s household. Cao therefore took Puyang and pardoned the old crimes of the Tian household.

Liu Ye said, “Lü Bu is a fierce tiger. Though exhausted today, he should be given no room.”

Cao left Liu Ye and others in Puyang and led his own troops to Dingtao. Lü Bu, Zhang Miao, and Zhang Chao were all in the city then. Gao Shun, Zhang Liao, Zang Ba, and Hou Cheng had gone out to gather provisions and had not yet returned.

Cao’s army reached Dingtao and, without battle for several days, drew back forty li to encamp. It was ripening season in Jizhou, so Cao ordered the troops to cut and eat the wheat. Spies told Lü Bu of this. Lü Bu came with speed toward Cao’s camp. As he neared, he saw lush woods on the left side and, fearing ambush, pulled back.

Cao Cao saw that Lü Bu had turned back and said to his commanders, “Lü Bu only suspects soldiers in the woods. Let him suspect still: place many banners in the trees. Along the western line the long dike is dry and has no water; conceal our finest troops there. Tomorrow Lü Bu will surely come and burn the trees. We will cut him off from the rear at the dike and take him.”

He left fifty drummers inside camp beating through the night and rounded up men and women from the village and forced them to cry out inside the camp. The best troops lay hidden in the dike.

Lü Bu returned to report to Chen Gong. “Cao uses too many tricks. Do not challenge him lightly,” Chen Gong said.

“I will use fire attack and break the ambush,” Lü Bu said. He left Chen Gong and Gao Shun to guard the city and drew up his army the next day.

From afar Lü Bu saw banners in the woods and drove his men forward in one huge press, burning on four sides. No one answered; when he tried to drive into camp, drumming sounded with a tremendous shock. Lü Bu was still in doubt, and suddenly a large force burst out behind the camp. He drove forward at once. As cannon boomed in answer, the hidden force in the dike came out together: Xiahou Dun, Xiahou Yuan, Xu Chu, Dian Wei, Li Dian, Yue Jin, all bursting from horseback to strike.

Lü Bu judged he could not match them and broke and ran. In the mêlée one of his lieutenants, Cheng Lian, was killed by a shot from Yue Jin. Lü Bu’s army withdrew three times, and on two of those his men were beaten back. A few survivors reported to Chen Gong. He said, “A city empty is hard to hold. Better to leave at once.” He and Gao Shun protected Lü Bu’s household and withdrew, abandoning Dingtao.

Cao Cao’s victors surged in like a split bamboo and cut their way through the city. Zhang Chao set himself on fire, and Zhang Miao fled to Yuan Shu. Shandong as a whole came under Cao’s grasp. The pacification and repair of the city is not recounted here.

Now Lü Bu was again on the move and all his generals were returning in order. Chen Gong had found them as well. Lü Bu said, “Though my force is small, we can still break Cao.” He then led out his army again. It is said:

In war, victory and defeat remain uncertain as ever; a reformed host can return when none expected it.
Who knows how Lü Bu will fare? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Tao Gongzu Gives Up Xu Province Three Times; Cao Mengde Fights Lü Bu

chapters.html:
Now Cao Cao, whose courtesy name was Mengde, had inflicted a major defeat on Lü Bu at Dingtao. Lü Bu gathered his shattered soldiers and horses on the seashore, and his officers all came to him to muster for another battle with Cao Cao. Chen Gong said, “Now Cao Cao’s forces are too strong; we should not contend with him yet. First, we should seek a place where we can secure ourselves, and only then return.”

Lü Bu said, “I want to go over to Yuan Shao. What do you think?” Chen Gong said, “First send someone to Jizhou to gather news, and then we can depart.” Lü Bu followed his advice.

At that time Yuan Shao was in Jizhou. When he heard that Cao Cao and Lü Bu were engaged, his adviser Shen Pei proposed, “Lü Bu is like a jackal and tiger; if he gains Yan Province, he will surely move against Jizhou. Better to aid Cao Cao and strike him first, then we can avoid trouble.” Yuan Shao therefore dispatched Yan Liang with fifty thousand men to assist Cao Cao. A spy discovered this and quickly reported to Lü Bu. Lü Bu was greatly alarmed and conferred with Chen Gong. Chen Gong said, “I hear that Liu Bei has newly taken command of Xu Province. You may go and submit there.” Lü Bu took the advice and, in fact, came to Xu Province.

Someone informed Liu Bei. He said, “Lü Bu is among the most heroic men of the age; we should ride out and greet him.” Mi Zhu objected: “Lü Bu is a beast of the tiger and wolf sort; we cannot keep him. If we accept him, he will hurt others.” Liu Bei replied, “Did he not previously raid Yan Province? Then how would this commandery have escaped ruin? Now he is desperate and has come to me; how could he harbor any other intention?” Zhang Fei added, “Brother, your heart is too tender. Even so, we must be prepared.”

Liu Bei led his men out thirty li from the city, met Lü Bu, and then went in with him by horse. They arrived at the prefectural hall, completed formal greetings, and sat down.

Lü Bu said, “Since I joined with Chancellor Wang in plotting Dong Zhuo’s death, I was then undone by the upheaval of Jue and Si, and I have since drifted in and out of the provinces of Guandong. Most lords could not tolerate me. Recently, Cao the usurper, through his cruelty, invaded Xuzhou, so the Xuanjun governor had to come to the rescue of Tao Qian. I then marched on Yan Province to split his forces, but unexpectedly I fell into a cruel stratagem and lost men and officers. Now I have come to you, my lord, to plan matters together. I do not yet know your heart’s intent.”

Liu Bei said, “Marquis Tao Qing [Tao Qian] died recently, and no one is in charge of Xu Province; I have therefore ordered Bao Quan to act in his place. Now that the commanding general has come here, it is proper that I defer.” He gave him his seal and tokens of command. Lü Bu seemed about to receive them, but saw that Guan Yu and Zhang Fei stood behind him with angry faces. Lü Bu therefore affected a laugh and said, “How can a lone brave like me serve as Governor of a Province?” Liu Bei insisted on yielding again. Chen Gong said, “The honored guest must not suppress the host. Please, my lord, make no suspicion.” Liu Bei then stopped.

They held a feast in Lü Bu’s honor and made arrangements to settle him into a residence.

The next day Lü Bu called Liu Bei to his side. Liu Bei went with Guan and Zhang. When wine had reached half intoxication, Lü Bu asked him into the back hall. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei entered with him. Lü Bu told his wife and children to come and bow to Liu Bei. Liu Bei refused repeatedly out of courtesy. Lü Bu said, “You need not insist on calling your brother-in-arms a humble subordinate.” Hearing this, Zhang Fei glowered and shouted, “My brother is gold-blooded and jade-bloomed; who are you to call him a humble subordinate? You come! I will fight you three rounds!” Liu Bei quickly ordered Guan Yu to restrain him. Liu Bei said to Lü Bu, “My younger brother was mad with wine; brother, do not reproach him.” Lü Bu remained silent. When the feast eventually broke up, Lü Bu saw Liu Bei out. Zhang Fei leaped from his horse and came charging forward with his spear, shouting, “Lü Bu! I will settle this against you in three rounds of combat!” Liu Bei again hurriedly ordered Guan Yu to calm him.

The next day Lü Bu came to take leave of Liu Bei. He said, “Thanks to your lordship for not abandoning me, but I fear my younger men may not accept each other. I shall seek another place to go.” Liu Bei said, “If you leave, your brother has committed a grave offense. The younger brother’s insolence should be answered another day in private conversation. This nearby Xiao Pei was once a place where I quartered troops. If your excellence does not mind that it is narrow, stay there for now. As for grain and military supply, I will see that all is arranged.” Lü Bu thanked Liu Bei and withdrew with his men to Xiao Pei. Liu Bei then withdrew, grumbling at Zhang Fei in silence.

Meanwhile, Cao Cao pacified Shandong and reported to the court. He was advanced to General of Jian-de and made Marquis of Feiting. At that time Li Jue had made himself Grand Commandant and Guo Si General-in-Chief. They ran rampant without restraint, and no one in court dared to speak. Grand Commandant Yang Biao and Minister of Agriculture Zhu Jun secretly reported to the Son of Heaven: “Now Cao Cao commands more than twenty thousand troops and has a host of dozens of advisers and generals. If this man could be supported to shore up the dynasty and eliminate the traitors, the realm would be safer.” The emperor wept and said, “I have been oppressed by the two violent chiefs for so long. If they can be executed, the joy would be immeasurable!” Yang Biao said, “I have one stratagem. First we let the two bandit chiefs destroy one another. Then we issue an edict for Cao Cao to bring troops, slay them, and clear the traitors for the court.” The emperor asked, “How will this be done?” Yang Biao said, “I have heard that Guo Si’s wife is extremely jealous. If one were to plant rumors at Guo Si’s wife’s ears, the two chiefs would come to mutual ruin.”

The emperor therefore wrote a secret edict and gave it to Yang Biao. Yang Biao immediately sent his wife on other pretexts to Guo Si’s household and told Guo Si’s wife at an opportune moment, “People are whispering that Guo Si has grown intimate with the wife of Sima Li, and that the relation is widely known. If her husband hears of it, he will surely kill you. Your wife should cut off such contact at once as best.” Guo Si’s wife was startled: “How is it that he has not returned home for many nights, yet does such a shameless thing? I would not know it unless you told me of it. I will be on guard.” Yang Biao’s wife returned and reported this; Guo Si’s wife thanked her repeatedly and left.

After several days, Guo Si again prepared to go to Li Jue’s home for a banquet. His wife said, “Jue’s temper is uncertain, and now these two lords cannot both remain in power together. If he slips poison into the wine after drinking, what can I do?” Guo Si would not yield to repeated counsel and insisted on going. By evening Li Jue sent the banquet to Guo Si’s house. Guo Si’s wife secretly placed poison in the wine and only then offered it. Guo Si was about to eat when his wife said, “This came from outside; why should you eat it at once?” She offered it first to a dog, which died standing. From then on Guo Si was suspicious.

One morning after court, Li Jue urgently invited Guo Si to his home to drink. By nightfall, after the feast had broken up, Guo Si returned drunk and suddenly suffered abdominal pain. His wife said, “It must have been the poison!” and ordered him to drink excrement-water. After one expulsion he calmed. Guo Si became furious and said, “I and Jue together planned great matters. Now no cause has been given to me except to attempt my murder. If I do not act first, I will surely meet with venomous hands.” He then quietly readied all his troops and prepared to attack Li Jue. His plan was reported early. Li Jue grew enraged as well: “How dare Guo Ya-di do this!” He immediately mustered his troops and came to kill Guo Si. Under the city gates there was wild fighting; they took opportunity to plunder the residents.

Li Jue’s nephew Li Xian surrounded Chen Gong’s residence with troops and used two wagons, one for the Son of Heaven and one for the Empress Fu, with Jia Xu and Zuo Ling in charge of escorting the carriage. The rest of the palace attendants and eunuchs, all on foot, followed behind. As they came out through the main gate, Guo Si’s troops arrived and a rain of arrows fell. Palace attendants were shot dead beyond counting. Li Jue then followed and slaughtered everyone behind, while Guo Si’s men retreated. The carriage rode through the city in extremity with no chance for refusal and was carried all the way to Li Jue’s camp. Guo Si entered the palace with his troops, robbed all palace women and singing-maids into camp, and set fire to the hall. The next day Guo Si learned Li Jue had seized the Son of Heaven. He marched out with his main forces to fight before the camp. The emperor and empress were stricken with fear. Later someone later wrote this verse in lament:

光武中興興漢世，上下相承十二帝。 桓靈無道宗社墮，閹臣擅權為叔季。 無謀何進作三公，欲除社鼠招奸雄。 豺獺雖驅虎狼入，西州逆賊生淫凶。 王允赤心託紅粉，致令董呂成矛盾。 渠魁殄滅天下寧，誰知李郭心懷憤。 神州荊棘爭奈何，六宮饑饉愁干戈。 人心既離天命去，英雄割據分山河。 後王規此存兢業，莫把金甌等閒缺。 生靈糜爛肝腦塗，剩水殘山多怨血。 我觀遺史不勝悲，今古茫茫歎黍離。 人君當守苞桑戒，太阿誰持全綱維？

At once Guo Si’s troops arrived. Li Jue rode out to engage. Guo Si’s force was at a disadvantage and withdrew for the time being. Li Jue then moved the emperor and empress and the carriage to Meiwu and put Li Xian in charge, cut off all inner attendants, and let food and supplies stop. The ministers all showed the look of hunger. An attendant asked the emperor to request five hu of rice and five carcasses of cattle to be given to aides. Li Jue was furious: “I have provided the daily meal; why does he ask again?” He then gave them decayed flesh and rotten grain, all foul and inedible. The emperor cursed, “Such rebel monsters are now deceitful in this way.” Sergeant-at-Arms Yang Biao immediately reported: “Grand Commandant Li Jue is cruel and violent. Under the circumstances, Your Majesty must bear it for now; do not oppose his momentum.” The emperor lowered his head in silence, tears filling the sleeves of his robe.

Suddenly an attendant reported, “A body of mounted troops is coming, spear and saber shining in the sun, bronze and drums filling the sky, and they have come to rescue the emperor.” The emperor inquired: it was Guo Si. His worry deepened. From outside the camp shouts rose. Li Jue had sent soldiers to meet Guo Si and pointed and lashed out, cursing, “I treated you generously; how can you scheme to harm me?” Guo Si said, “You are a rebel against the throne; why should I not kill you?” Li Jue replied, “I have the Son of Heaven under my protection here; how can they call me a rebel?” Guo Si said, “This is an abduction of the throne-carriage. How can you claim to protect it?” Li Jue said, “No need to speak more. Each of us is to decide no to the use of soldiers; we decide this by strength alone. If I win, I take the emperor.” The two then began close combat before the line. After ten exchanges, victory was still unclear. At once Yang Biao rode in at a gallop and shouted, “Both commanders, spare an interval. The old one has invited more than sixty court officers to come and talk peace with you.” Li Jue and Guo Si each returned to their camps.

Yang Biao and Zhu Jun met with more than sixty officials and first came to Guo Si’s camp to urge reconciliation. Guo Si nevertheless placed all those officials under guard. One of them said, “We have come in friendship. Why do you receive us so?” Guo Si said, “Li Jue abducted the Son of Heaven; he alone did not seize the ministers.” Yang Biao asked, “He seized the Son of Heaven, and he seized the ministers. What do you intend?” Guo Si was so angry that he drew his sword to kill Biao. Middle Gentleman Yang Mi begged him to stop, and Guo Si then released Yang Biao and Zhu Jun but kept the others confined in camp. Yang Biao told Zhu Jun, “As ministers of the realm, we cannot right the ruler and save the lord. We have come merely to waste away in this world.” After speaking, he and Zhu Jun embraced each other and wept, then lost consciousness. Zhu Jun returned home and became bedridden and died. After this, Li Jue and Guo Si fought each other daily; for more than fifty days, the number of dead could not be counted.

It was said that Li Jue most enjoyed left-way sorcery and often let shamanesses beat drums and summon spirits in the camp. Jia Xu repeatedly remonstrated but was ignored. Middle gentleman Yang Qi secretly reported to the emperor, “Though Jia Xu is near Li Jue’s heart, he has never forgotten the Son of Heaven. Your Majesty should consult him.” While he spoke, Jia Xu arrived. The emperor dismissed attendants and with tears said to Jia Xu, “Can you pity the Han court and save my life?” Jia Xu knelt and said, “This is my fixed wish. Your Majesty should not say more; I will devise a way.” The emperor dried his tears and nodded in thanks.

After a short while Li Jue came to court, entering with a drawn sword. The emperor’s face had turned clay-colored. Li Jue said to the emperor, “Guo Si is disloyal; he has imprisoned the ministers and intends to abduct Your Majesty. Without me, the carriage would have already been seized.” The emperor clasped his hands and thanked him. Li Jue then left. At that moment Huangfu Li came before the emperor. The emperor noticed Li's eloquence and that he was from the same commandery as Li Jue. He issued an order asking him to reconcile both sides. Li carried the command to Guo Si’s camp and relayed it. Guo Si asked, “If you are sent from Li Jue, then he intends to release the ministers?”

Li immediately appeared before Guo Si. He said, “The Son of Heaven commanded me, a native of Xiliang, and your fellow countryman, to urge both lords to reconcile. Guo Si has obeyed the command. What is your view?” Li Jue replied, “I had great merit in defeating Lü Bu and for four years of assisting the court I achieved many meritorious accomplishments; all under heaven knows this. Guo Si is no more than a horse-thief who dares to seize ministers and oppose me. I swear I will execute him. Will your forces and tactics be enough to beat Guo Si?” Li Pu said, “No. In former times, the impoverished Hou Yi boasted of his excellent archery and thought no misfortune could touch him, and so he perished. In these recent times, you yourself have seen Daoshi Dong too [Dong Zhuo] rise in force, Lü Bu received grace and then plotted treachery in an instant and came to hang over the gate of the realm. Therefore mere strength cannot be relied upon. As upper general, you wield the axe and banner; your kin and descendants are all in distinguished rank. The court’s grace toward your clan is not light. If Guo Si seizes the ministers while your lordship seizes the Son of Heaven, who can say who is lighter, who is heavier?”

Li Jue grew furious, drew his sword and shouted, “The Son of Heaven sent you to humiliate me? I will first behead your head!” Cavalry Captain Yang Feng advised, “Guo Si is not yet removed; if we kill the Son of Heaven’s envoy, Guo Si will have a pretext to raise troops, and all the lords will aid him.” Jia Xu also urged him strongly. Li Jue’s anger eased a little. Jia Xu then pushed Huangfu Li out. Li Pu shouted, “Li Jue does not obey the imperial order and wants to assassinate the Son of Heaven and set himself up!” Middle gentleman Hu Miao hastened to stop him: “Do not utter such words; it may harm your body.” Li Pu yelled, “Hu Jingcai! You too are a minister of the court; how can you attach yourself to bandits? Better to say, ‘A minister should die for his lord’s humiliation.’ If I am killed by Li Jue, that is my division of life!” He kept cursing without end. The emperor learned this and hurriedly ordered Huangfu Li to return to Xiliang.

Now Li Jue’s troops were mostly men from Xiliang, and his army relied heavily on Qiang troops. Yet when Li Pu spoke among those men and said, “Li Jue intends rebellion; anyone who follows him will become a bandit associate with deep future harm,” many Xiliang soldiers listened and the army’s spirit gradually broke. Li Jue heard of what Li Pu had said and became enraged. He sent Tiger-Guarded Wang Chang to pursue him. Wang Chang knew Li Pu was a loyal and righteous man, so he did not pursue him; he only returned and reported, “Li Pu’s destination is unknown.” Jia Xu then secretly told the Qiang men, “The Son of Heaven knows your loyalty and long hardship. He has issued a secret edict ordering you home; later he will reward you greatly.” The Qiang men had long resented Li Jue for withholding noble titles and gifts, so they took Jia Xu’s words, and all drew away with their forces.

Jia Xu then memorialized the emperor in secret: “Li Jue is greedy and without strategy; now his soldiers are scattered and afraid. It is possible to entice them with high rank as bait.” The emperor therefore issued an edict and made Li Jue Grand Commandant. Li Jue rejoiced, saying, “It is the favor of the witch whose spirit-offering and prayers prevailed!” He greatly rewarded the shamaness but gave no reward to army officers. Yang Feng, the Cavalry Commander, was enraged. He said to Song Guo, “We were born together and died together, braving arrows and stones, and our merit is less than that of a witch?” Song Guo replied, “Why not kill this brigand and save the Son of Heaven?” Yang Feng said, “You set fire in the center army as the signal; I shall draw troops outside.” The two agreed to act at the second watch of the night. But the matter leaked. Someone reported it to Li Jue. Li Jue was furious and ordered Song Guo seized and killed first. Yang Feng brought his troops outside but saw no signal fire. Li Jue led troops out himself and happened upon Yang Feng; a brawl broke out among the stockade through the fourth watch of the night. Unable to prevail, Yang Feng withdrew and rode toward Xian. From this Li Jue’s force progressively weakened. As if in addition, Guo Si kept attacking often, and many men were killed. Suddenly there was a report: “General Zhang Ji commands a large army coming from Shaanxi and seeks to reconcile both lords; if not, he will advance with troops.” Li Jue then made a courtesy gesture and first sent men to Zhang Ji’s army to ask for peace. Guo Si also had no choice but to assent. Zhang Ji submitted a memorial, requesting that the Son of Heaven ride the carriage east to Hongnong. The emperor rejoiced: “I have longed for the eastern capital. By this turn, to return there is a great blessing!” He issued an edict making Zhang Ji Commander of Agile Cavalry. Zhang Ji brought grain, wine, and meat and provisioned the hundred officials. Guo Si released the ministers from camp. Li Jue gathered the emperor’s carriage and moved eastward, sending a few hundred old guard cavalry, with spears raised, to escort.

The carriage passed Xinfeng and reached Bailing. It was autumn; the cold wind rose abruptly. Suddenly great shouts rose as hundreds of soldiers came to the bridge and blocked the carriage. They asked in ringing voices, “Who comes here?” Middle Gentleman Yang Qi rode up and cried on the bridge, “The sacred carriage has passed this way. Who dare block it?” Two officers replied, “We serve General Guo and hold this bridge to prevent hidden traitors. Since you claim to be the sacred carriage, we must see Your Majesty in person to verify.” Yang Qi raised the silk curtain high. The emperor ordered: “I am here in person. Why do you not withdraw?” The captains shouted “Long live the emperor!” and parted to both sides; the carriage passed through.

The two officers returned to Guo Si and said, “The carriage has already gone.” Guo Si said, “I meant to trick Zhang Ji and then abduct the carriage again to return to Meiwu. Why did you let it pass on your own?” He then beheaded the two officers and raised troops to give chase. When the carriage reached Huayin County, shouts from behind shook the sky. “Stop the carriage and stay put!” the emperor told ministers through tears, “I have just left a wolf’s den and again face a tiger’s mouth. What can I do?” All were pale. Bandit troops drew nearer. There was then one wave of drums. Around the hill behind came a commander with a great banner, upon which the characters “Yang Feng of Han” were written, bringing a thousand troops to charge. It was Yang Feng. Having been defeated by Li Jue and taking refuge beneath Mount Zhongnan, he had moved his troops there; when he learned the carriage had arrived, he came specifically to defend it.

They quickly arrayed for battle. Guo Si’s captain Cui Yong charged out. He shouted that Yang Feng was a rebel. Yang Feng grew furious and looked back through the ranks, saying, “Where is Gongming [Xu Huang]?” One officer with a great axe spurred his horse at breakneck speed and rode straight for Cui Yong. The two horses met; after one exchange Cui Yong was beheaded on his mount. Yang Feng took advantage and drove on, and Guo Si’s army suffered a great rout, retreating twenty-some li. Yang Feng then reformed and came to present himself to the Son of Heaven. The emperor encouraged him: “You saved my person; your merit is no small thing.” Yang Feng knelt and thanked him. The emperor asked, “Who is the commander that slew the bandit general?” Yang Feng introduced this commander before the carriage: “This man is Xu, a native of Hedong, Yang Commandery. His family name is Xu, his personal name was Huang, and his courtesy name is Gongming.” The emperor expressed gratitude. Yang Feng protected the carriage until it reached Huayin where it set camp. General Duan Wei came with clothing, drink, and food to present. That night the Son of Heaven lodged in Yang Feng’s camp.

Guo Si, defeated once, raised troops again the next day and attacked before the camp. Xu Huang was first to ride out. Guo Si’s main host surrounded them on eight sides, and the emperor and Yang Feng were trapped in the center of the field. At the moment of utmost crisis, a loud cry rose from the southeast. A commander spurred on with his mounted men and charged in. The bandit host broke and fled. Xu Huang seized the moment to attack and dealt Guo Si’s army a severe defeat. The man who came to the emperor was Dong Cheng, an imperial kinsman. The emperor, in tears, recounted what had happened. Dong Cheng said, “Let Your Majesty fear nothing. Your servant and General Yang have sworn to behead both brigands and bring peace under heaven.” The emperor ordered an early departure to the eastern capital. The carriage moved overnight and proceeded east to Hongnong.

Meanwhile, Guo Si, having suffered defeat, collided with Li Jue on the road and said, “Yang Feng and Dong Cheng have rescued the carriage and gone to Hongnong. Once they set root in Shandong, they will declare to all under heaven and induce the lords to attack us together; three clans cannot be preserved.” Li Jue said, “Zhang Ji’s army is now stationed in Chang’an and cannot yet be lightly moved. We shall wait for a moment and unite our troops, go to Hongnong and kill the Han ruler, then divide heaven and earth; is this not possible?” Guo Si assented. The two combined forces, looted along the way, and left each place empty as they passed. Yang Feng and Dong Cheng, knowing bandit troops were near, therefore halted and returned their troops. They engaged the brigands in great combat at Dongjians.

Li Jue and Guo Si deliberated together: “Our men are many and theirs are few; mixed battle is what wins this.” So Li Jue was on the left and Guo Si on the right, and their army pressed in over mountain and plain. Yang Feng and Dong Cheng fought deathly on both sides, barely shielding the emperor and empress’s carriage as it moved. Ministers, palace attendants, seals, registers, and all court implements were abandoned. Guo Si drew his men into Hongnong and looted. Dong Cheng and Yang Feng, defending the carriage, withdrew toward Shaanbei. Li Jue and Guo Si split detachments in pursuit. Dong Cheng and Yang Feng at once sent delegates to negotiate and, at the same time, sent secret edicts to Hedong to summon Han Xian, the former White Wave commander, Li Le, and Hu Cai from three commands to come to the rescue. Li Le’s army was also bandit origin from the mountains, now called in from necessity. When these three commands heard that the Son of Heaven had pardoned them and granted office, how could they refuse? They at once drew men from their camps and met with Dong Cheng, and together took Hongnong once more.

By then, Li Jue and Guo Si only plundered where they passed, killing the old and weak and pressing the strong into forced labor; when facing the enemy, they drove local militia before them under the name of a "death-strikers" corps, and the bandits’ force was vast. Li Le’s army arrived at Weiyang. Guo Si ordered his men to throw aside clothing and gear along the road. Li Le’s men saw the clothing strewn on the ground and rushed to grab it; formation shattered. Li Jue and Guo Si’s two armies then closed and in all-around fighting the Li Le army was badly defeated. Yang Feng and Dong Cheng could not hold the line to block, and had to protect the carriage northward while brigands chased from behind. Li Le said, “The matter is urgent. Ask the Son of Heaven to remount and go first!” The emperor replied, “I cannot leave the ministers behind.”

All shouted and wept as they followed. Hu Cai was killed by the confused crowd. Dong Cheng and Yang Feng saw the enemies pressing and asked the Son of Heaven to abandon the carriage, then go on foot to the Yellow Riverbank. Li Le found a small boat to serve as a ferry. The weather was bitterly cold. The emperor and empress, both struggling with effort, reached the bank. The far bank was high and they could not disembark, and the pursuing force was near. Yang Feng said, “We can unfasten the horse reins and knot them together, tying the emperor to his waist as he gets off the boat.” The crowd of attendants included the emperor’s brother-in-law Fu De, who carried ten bolts of white silk and said, “I found these cloths in the melee; we can tie a harness to pass the litter.” The field lieutenant Shang Hong wrapped the emperor and empress with silk and ordered the line first to lower the emperor and then others into the water; thus they got into the boat. Li Le stood at the bow with his sword. Behind him, Fu De bore the empress into the boat’s center. On the home bank, those unable to enter the boat pulled at the rope together; Li Le hewed many down in the water. After the emperor and empress were crossed, he sent the boat back for the rest. Those who still struggled over the crossing were cut, with fingers severed, and cries shook the sky.

Once across, only ten or so remained around the emperor. Yang Feng found a single ox-cart and carried the emperor to Dayang. They had eaten nothing; at night they slept in a tile-roofed shed. A rustic old man offered coarse millet gruel; he and the empress ate together, but it was too rough to swallow. The next day the Son of Heaven made Li Le General Conquering the North and Han Xian General Conquering the East, and moved forward. Two ministers arrived and knelt in tears before the carriage: Grand Commandant Yang Biao and Minister of Household Han Rong. The emperor and empress both wept. Han Rong said, “Li Jue and Guo Si, though rebels, have trusted my words. I will risk my life and go to bid them cease by force. Guard your dragon body well.” Han Rong left. Li Le invited the emperor to Yang Feng’s camp to rest briefly. Yang Biao asked the emperor to go to Anyi County. The carriage reached An yi. Lacking high halls, the emperor and empress both had to live in a grass hut; there were no gates or doors, and thorn branches were stuck through the four sides for barricade. The emperor and ministers discussed state matters beneath the hut while the generals held soldiers outside the fence to suppress threats. Li Le and his men held exclusive power; if the ministers made even slight offense, they even beat them before the emperor and deliberately brought muddied wine and coarse food for him, and the emperor barely accepted. Li Le and Han Xian then promoted two hundred and more men from bandits, escorts, and witch-doctors into posts such as Colonels and Censors. The seals were not even carved deeply; they were marked only by an awl, and none held proper form.

Han Rong again counselled Li Jue and Guo Si, and the two bandits from his words let ministers and palace attendants return. That year was full of famine; the people all ate wild greens and famine-bloated bodies lay everywhere. The commander of Henei, Zhang Yang, presented rice and meat; the commander of Hedong, Wang Yi, presented silk and silk bolts. The emperor was somewhat eased. Dong Cheng and Yang Feng deliberated. One sent men to repair the Luoyang palace and wished to bring the carriage back east. Li Le refused. Dong Cheng said, “Luoyang is the capital where the Son of Heaven built his court. Anyi is too small a place. How can it hold the carriage? It is proper to restore the carriage to Luoyang.” Li Le said, “If you take the carriage away, I stay here.”

Dong Cheng and Yang Feng then raised the carriage and set out. Li Le secretly sent men to connect with Li Jue and Guo Si to abduct the carriage again. Dong Cheng and Yang Feng and Han Xian learned of this plan and through the night positioned their soldiers to guard the carriage and send it onward to Jiguan at once. Li Le learned this and, before Li Jue’s and Guo Si’s forces could arrive, drew his own men and gave pursuit. At the fourth watch, on the left side, they reached below Mount Ji and shouted: “Do not move the carriage! Li Jue and Guo Si are here!” The emperor was frightened to heart and marrow. Flames rose all over the mountain.

前番兩賊分為二，今番三賊合為一。
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Li Jue and Guo Si Clash; Yang Feng and Dong Cheng Together Rescue the Imperial Carriage

chapters.html:
Earlier, Li Le marshaled troops and falsely announced that Li Jue and Guo Si were pursuing the imperial carriage, and the Son of Heaven was greatly alarmed. Yang Feng said, “It was Li Le.” He ordered Xu Huang to go out and receive him. Li Le rode out to face him himself. When their horses met, one clash was all it took for Xu Huang to strike him off his mount with an axe, break up the remnants of his band, and protect the carriage across Ji Pass. The commandery administrator Zhang Yang brought grain and silk to welcome the carriage on the Zhi road. The emperor enfeoffed Zhang Yang as Grand Marshal.
