After thanking the emperor, Zhang Yang withdrew and stationed his troops at Yewang.

The emperor entered Luoyang and saw the palace halls burned out, the streets desolate, and every patch of ground covered with mugwort and weeds. Within the palace compounds, only ruined walls and broken buildings remained. He ordered Yang Feng to construct a small temporary palace for residence. All officials came for audience, and all of them had to stand amid thorny brush. By edict, the era Xingping was changed to the first year of Jianan.

That year, calamity came again. Only a few hundred households were left in Luoyang, and there was nothing to eat. The people had all left the city to strip bark and dig out grass roots. From the minor clerks of the Secretariat down, all had gone out of the city to chop firewood, and many died among the collapsed walls and ruined foundations. No era in late Han had declined more harshly than this. Later writers composed a poem in grief:

Blood flooded Mang and Tang, and the white snake vanished.
Crimson banners ran crossing and intersecting through the four quarters.
Qin’s deer-hunt overturned and raised the altars of state; Chu’s noble steed overturned and reset the borders.
The Son of Heaven was soft and weak, and wicked men rose;
lineage shrank, the state withered, and thieves ran wild.
In the suffering of the two capitals, even men of iron did not shed tears without sorrow.

Grand Commandant Yang Biao reported to the emperor, “Your Majesty previously received the imperial summons but did not send troops. Now Cao Cao is in Shandong with strong armies and excellent commanders. You may announce this and summon him to court to assist the imperial house.” The emperor said, “I already issued a summons, and you need not report again. I now have men sent at once to carry out that order.” Biao understood the instruction and sent an envoy to Shandong.

At that time Cao Cao was in Shandong. When he heard that the carriage had returned to Luoyang, he gathered his advisors to deliberate. Xun Yu said, “In past times, Duke Wen of Jin accepted King Xiang of Zhou, and the lords all submitted. Han Gaozu carried Emperor Yì’s catafalque, and all of the world turned to him. Now the Son of Heaven is covered in dust and distress. If you truly rise now as champion of righteousness, carry the Son of Heaven with popular acclaim, and move the court, this would be a stratagem beyond compare. If you do not act at once, others will beat you to it.” Cao Cao was delighted. As he was about to raise his forces, news came that an emissary with a celestial edict had arrived. He accepted the edict and set a date to muster.

Back in Luoyang, still in ruin, the city had not been repaired, and collapsed lanes could not yet be restored. A report came that Li Jue and Guo Si were bringing their troops. The emperor was terrified and asked Yang Feng, “The envoy to Shandong has not returned, and Li and Guo are now coming. What are we to do?” Yang Feng and Han Xian said, “Your servant is prepared to fight the brigands to the death in order to protect Your Majesty.” Dong Cheng said, “The city walls are not firm, and we have no many armored men. If we do not prevail in battle, what then? Better to take the carriage to Shandong and evade this danger.” The emperor accepted their counsel and ordered departure that day, heading toward Shandong. No officials had horses, and all followed on foot.

Once outside Luoyang, there was no space for a single arrow to fly. Only dust covered the sky, drums clanged, and endlessly more men and horses arrived. The emperor and empress trembled and could not speak. Then they saw one rider fly in. It was the envoy to Shandong who had been sent earlier. When he arrived before the carriage, he knelt and announced: “General Cao has raised all the troops of Shandong and, in answer to your summons, has come. When he heard that Li Jue and Guo Si had violated Luoyang, he first sent Xiahou Dun as vanguard with ten commanders and fifty thousand elite soldiers to protect the carriage.” The emperor was eased somewhat. Before long, Xiahou Dun came with Xu Chu and Dian Wei and others to the front of the carriage and all rendered military homage. When the emperor had finished the audience words, a report came that another unit had arrived from the east. The emperor ordered Xiahou Dun to scout. He returned to report, “They are on foot from General Cao.”

Soon after, Cao Hong, Li Dian, and Yue Jin came to the carriage. After formal introductions, Hong said, “I know the enemy troops are near and I feared that Xiahou Dun alone could not hold them, so I too hurried with this force to aid him.” The emperor replied, “General Cao is truly a minister to the state.” He ordered them to lead the escort onward. A scout reported, “Li Jue and Guo Si have come at speed with their troops.” The emperor directed Xiahou Dun to meet them in two columns. Xiahou Dun divided with Cao Hong and took the cavalry forward while infantry followed behind, attacking with all power. Li Jue’s and Guo Si’s brigands were heavily defeated, with more than ten thousand heads taken. Then they returned to the old palace in Luoyang. Xiahou Dun stationarily garrisoned outside the city.

The next day, Cao Cao arrived with a great army. He finished camp, then entered the city and was presented at the base of the hall stairs. The emperor bade him dismount and spoke comfort and gratitude. Cao Cao said, “I, your servant, have long been covered by the state’s grace and have always sought this moment to repay it. Now Li Jue and Guo Si are criminals through and through. General Cao has more than two hundred thousand elite men and will subdue rebels in orderly pursuit and leave no enemy undefeated. Your Majesty should preserve your Dragon Body and place the state above all else.” The emperor enfeoffed him as Metropolitan Commandant (司隸校尉), gave him command tokens and authority seal, and entrusted him with the Secretariat affairs.

Li Jue and Guo Si, on hearing that Cao Cao had come from afar, discussed pressing battle. Jia Xu advised, “Do not. General Cao’s troops are elite, his officers brave; he is not one to be confronted by force. Surrender and ask that your lives be spared.” Li Jue was furious. “How dare you extinguish my fighting temper?” He drew his sword to behead Jia Xu, and other generals intervened to restrain him. That night Jia Xu rode alone and returned to his native place.

The next day, Li Jue and Guo Si sent forces to meet Cao Cao’s troops. Cao first ordered Xu Chu, Cao Ren, and Dian Wei to lead three hundred armored horsemen to clash with their formation three times before full formation was set. At an open stretch of field, Li Jue’s nephews Li Xian and Li Bie came forward in battle. Before either could speak, Xu Chu rode past and with one stroke cut down Li Xian. Li Bie started, jolted his horse, and fell from it; Xu Chu also cut him down and returned carrying both heads. Cao Cao patted Xu Chu’s back and said, “You are truly my Fang Kuaiji.” He then ordered Xiahou Dun to lead troops on the left, Cao Ren on the right, and Cao Cao himself to lead the center. At the first drumbeat, all three forces advanced together. The brigands could not withstand the clash and fled in a full rout. Cao Cao drew his treasured sword, seized the formation, and led a night pursuit and annihilation. The number of those killed was great, and the number of those captured was beyond counting. Li Jue and Guo Si fled westward in panic, running in disorder like dogs that had lost their homes. Knowing there was nowhere to hide, they retreated into the hills.

Cao Cao withdrew his army and still encamped outside Luoyang. Yang Feng and Han Xian met together and discussed: “Now that Cao Cao has achieved such merit, he will gather all authority. How can we endure this?” They then submitted an audience memorial to the emperor in the name of pursuing Li Jue and Guo Si, and moved their own troops to garrison at Daliang.

One day the emperor sent a request to Cao Cao’s camp for him to come to palace consultation. When Cao heard that an envoy had arrived, he asked for immediate audience. The man who stood before him was clear-faced and clear-eyed, full of vigor. Cao silently wondered, “In this land of great famine the officials, soldiers, and commoners all show hunger. How can this one man alone be so full-bodied?” He then asked, “You are handsome and well-nourished. By what regimen have you kept such a state for so long?” He replied, “I have no special method. I have only eaten a light diet for thirty years.” Cao nodded. He asked, “What position do you hold?” He answered, “I passed the Candidacy of Filial and Frugal Conduct. I formerly served Yuan Shao and was once attached to Zhang Yang. Now that the Son of Heaven has returned, I came to court to pay homage. My office is the title of Zhengyi-lang. I am from Jiyin, from Dingtao. My surname is Dong, my given name is Zhao, and my courtesy name is Gongren.” Cao rose and said, “Your fame has long been known. I am honored to meet you here.” He then offered him food in his own tent and had him meet Xun Yu. A report came in: “One unit is moving eastward, and no one knows whose it is.” Dong Zhao said, “This is Yang Feng, a former commander under Li Jue, and Han Xian, commander of Bai Bo. Since Your Excellency has now come here, they brought troops intending to leave for Daliang.” Cao asked, “Could you be suggesting I am to be doubted?” Zhao said, “They are men of no foresight. Why should Your Excellency worry?” Cao asked, “What of Li and Guo now?” Zhao replied, “A tiger without claws and a bird without wings will soon be captured by Your Excellency.”

Seeing Dong Zhao’s readiness to work at court advantage, Cao asked him about major court matters. Zhao said, “Your Excellency has raised a righteous army to eliminate disorder and entered court to support the Son of Heaven. That is the work of one of the five outstanding heroes. Yet the other commanders all have different thoughts and may not yet submit. For now, your remaining here is not convenient. The best choice is to move the carriage to Xuandu. Still, the court has only just returned to the capital, and near and far all expect security for one day of peace; if the carriage is moved again so soon, it will tire the people. Great deeds are done by extraordinary measures. I urge Your Excellency to resolve this.” Cao took Zhao’s hand and smiled. “That is precisely my intent. Yet Yang Feng and the ministers are in Daliang. Could there be unexpected changes?” Zhao said, “It is easy. Write to Yang Feng and first calm his thoughts. Then tell the great ministers plainly that there is no grain in the capital, so the carriage should move to Xuandu near Luyang to handle transportation, so shortages will not interrupt supplies. When they hear this, they will gladly agree.” Cao rejoiced. After Zhao took his leave, Cao said, “Whatever this servant still intends, you must guide me.” Zhao bowed and departed.

From that point, Cao held private consultation with his strategists about moving the court. At that time, the eunuch-officer of the Court Historians, Wang Li, told Liu Ai of the Ministry of Rites in private: “I have observed the heavens from above. Since spring, Great White has violated the Guardian Star at Dipper and Bull, has passed Tianjin, and Planet Mars has also run backwards. Now it has met Great White at Tian Gate, and metal and fire have converged. There must be a new Son of Heaven. I have seen that the Great Han’s mandate is ending, and in Jin and Wei the land that will rise is already prepared.” He also reported to the Son of Heaven: “Heaven’s mandate comes and goes. The Five Phases are never eternally prosperous. When Fire yields to Earth, it is Earth’s turn. He who replaces Han and governs the world will be of Earth.” Cao said to him, “I know your loyalty to the court, yet Heaven’s way is deep. I beg you not to speak too widely.” He told Xun Yu the matter. Xun Yu said, “Han is a fire-mandated kingdom, while Your Excellency is an Earth fate. Xuandu is Earth-ground. There Your fortunes must rise. Fire gives birth to Earth, and Earth nourishes Wood. This exactly matches Dong Zhao and Wang Li. One destined to rise will rise on another day.” Cao decided at once. The next day he entered court and proposed, “The Eastern capital has been neglected and ravaged for long and cannot be repaired. Moreover, transporting grain is difficult. Xuandu is near Luyang, and its palace and halls, money, grain, and goods are sufficient. Only Your Majesty may go there.” The emperor did not dare refuse. All ministers feared Cao’s power and dared not object. An auspicious day was then chosen. Cao escorted the escorting army and the court moved; all officials followed. After only a few stages, they came to a tall ridge. Suddenly a cry rose, and Yang Feng and Han Xian led troops blocking the road. Xu Huang rode first and shouted, “General Cao aims to seize the carriage! Where are you going?” Cao dismounted to see. At the sight of Xu Huang’s imposing bearing, he admired him in silence. Then he ordered Xu Chu out to confront Xu Huang. Sword and axe met for over fifty exchanges, with no winner determined. Cao then sounded the battle horn to recall and convened his strategists. “Yang Feng and Han Xian are not worth contending with. Xu Huang is a truly good commander. I will not force a decisive battle. We should win him by stratagem.” Camp-administrator Man Chong said, “Your lordship should not worry. I once had direct acquaintance with Xu Huang. Tonight I can disguise myself as a common soldier, slip into his camp, and persuade him. I will make him tilt his heart to surrender.” Cao approved and sent him.

That night, Man Chong disguised himself as a foot soldier, mixed into that army, and slipped to Xu Huang’s tent. He saw Xu Huang sitting in armor by candlelight. Chong moved up to him and said, “Old friend, are you still well?” Xu Huang startled and looked carefully. “Are you not Man Chong of Shanyang, Faning? How did you arrive here?” Chong said, “I now serve General Cao. At the front I saw an old friend and came to speak but one matter, so I risked my life to come.” Xu Huang invited him to sit and asked his intention. Chong said, “Your courage and stratagem are rare in the world. Why remain under Yang and Han? General Cao is the hero of this age, known everywhere for valuing worthy men and learned officers. In battle today I have seen your courage; I honor you all the more. I cannot bear to watch good commanders throw themselves into useless death. I have come to invite you. Why do you not leave the dark and enter the light to share a great enterprise?” Xu Huang stood and sighed long. Then he said, “I have long known Yang and Han are not men for establishing a cause, but I have followed them long and cannot easily leave.” Chong said, “Have you not heard, ‘A fine bird chooses its tree, and a worthy minister chooses a lord? When one has found a lord worth serving, it is not fitting that he lose him through a weak arm?’” Xu Huang rose and thanked him: “I will accept your counsel.” Chong said, “Then why not kill Feng and Han now and come as your way of presenting yourself?” Xu Huang answered, “To kill one’s lord is a grave injustice; I will never do that.” Chong replied, “You are truly a man of righteousness.” Xu Huang then brought out dozens of riders and, with Man Chong by night, rode to surrender at Cao’s camp. Someone had already informed Yang Feng. Yang was furious and led one thousand horsemen in pursuit, calling, “You rebellious Xu Huang, do not escape!”

In the middle of the pursuit, a cannon blast sounded. Torches flared on mountain and below, and concealed troops appeared from all sides. Cao himself rode out in front, leading the army, and shouted, “I have waited here too long; do not think to slip away!” Yang Feng was greatly shocked and hurried to turn back his army, but was quickly surrounded by Cao’s soldiers. Han Xian happened to bring troops in aid, and in the close melee Yang Feng managed to escape. Cao Cao took advantage of their disorder, attacked hard, and the soldiers of both sides mostly surrendered. Yang Feng and Han Xian were isolated, and with broken troops withdrew and took refuge with Yuan Shu.

Cao Cao withdrew his army and returned to camp. Man Chong brought Xu Huang before him. Cao rejoiced and treated him generously. Then he brought the court carriage to Xuandu, built halls, palaces, temples, altars, and court offices, and repaired city walls and granaries. He enfeoffed Dong Cheng and thirteen others as marquises. He meted out rewards and punishments and allowed Cao Cao to handle all appointments.

From then on, Cao Cao styled himself Grand General and Wuping Marquis. Self as Duke of Wuping, he was later known as Grand General. He appointed Xun Yu as Gentleman-in-Waiting and Prefect of the Masters of Writing, Xun You as military adviser, and Guo Jia as Sima Jiaozhi (司馬祭酒). He appointed Liu Ye clerk-assistant to the Minister of Works. Mao Jie and Ren Jun were made Dian Nong Zhonglangjiang, charged with urging and supervising grain and money. Cheng Yu became the Chancellor of Dongping. Fan Cheng and Dong Zhao were made magistrates of Luoyang. Man Chong was made Prefect of Xuandu. Xiahou Dun, Xiahou Yuan, Cao Ren, and Cao Hong were all appointed generals. Lü Qian, Li Dian, Yue Jin, Yu Jin, and Xu Huang were all made colonels. Xu Chu and Dian Wei were made captains. Other officers all received offices. From then on, all major power belonged to Cao Cao. Major court matters were first reported to Cao Cao, and only then to the Son of Heaven.

When Cao Cao had set matters in order, he held a banquet in the rear hall and gathered commanders to discuss: “Liu Bei has stationed troops in Xu Province and already governs provincial affairs. Recently Lü Bu, defeated in battle, came to him; Liu Bei has him housed at Xupei. If the two join hearts and raise armies together, they will become an inner disaster.” “What fine stratagem do you have?” Xu Chu said, “I wish for five thousand? no, fifty thousand elite soldiers and to cut off the heads of Liu Bei and Lü Bu for the Chancellor.” Cao repeated: Xu Chu asked for too many maybe? Actually says "借精兵五萬". Let's maintain 50,000. He then said to execute? we keep. Xun Yu said, “General Cao is brave, yes. But he does not yet know all stratagem. Xuandu is newly settled; now is no time for reckless campaigning. There is a plan called the Two-Tigers Competing-for-Prey stratagem. Although Liu Bei holds Xu Province, he has no commission. Your Excellency should request an imperial order giving him office as Xu Province Inspector, then send him a secret letter commanding him to kill Lü Bu. If it succeeds, Liu Bei will be left without a strong ally and can be dealt with gradually. If it fails, Lü Bu will surely kill Liu Bei. This is the Two-Tigers Competing-for-Prey stratagem.” Cao followed that counsel and at once offered a memorial requesting commission, sending an envoy with the edict. He enfeoffed Liu Bei as General Who Conquers the East, Marquis of Yicheng Pavilion, and confirmed him as Inspector of Xu Province, with a private letter sealed and sent.

Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, was in Xu Province when he heard the Son of Heaven had moved to Xuandu. He had just intended to submit an address of congratulations, when news arrived that an imperial envoy had come. He went out to the gate to welcome him. After the envoy was ushered in and received the imperial favor, Liu Bei set a banquet and hosted him. The envoy said, “My lord’s receiving of this favor is truly due to General Cao’s recommendation to the Son of Heaven.” Liu Bei thanked him. The envoy then presented a private letter. After reading it, Liu Bei said, “This still allows time for deliberation.” The gathering dissolved. The envoy was lodged in the official inn, and that night Liu Bei discussed with his retainers. Zhang Fei said, “Lü Bu has no loyalty; why should we hesitate to kill him?” Liu Bei said, “He came in desperation, and now he has placed his trust in us. If we kill him, that would also be unrighteous.” Zhang Fei said, “It is hard to be a good man!” Liu Bei did not yield.

The next day, Lü Bu came to congratulate. Liu Bei invited him in to meet. Lü Bu said, “I heard your lordship had obtained favor from court and came to congratulate.” Liu Bei replied with humble thanks. As soon as he entered, Zhang Fei drew his sword and entered the hall to strike Lü Bu. Liu Bei anxiously restrained him. Lü Bu was alarmed and said, “Yide, why do you now want to kill me?” Zhang Fei shouted, “General Cao calls you a man of no virtue and told my elder brother to kill you!” Liu Bei shouted him back twice. Then he took Lü Bu into the back hall and explained the whole matter from the beginning, showing the private letter from Cao. After reading it, Lü Bu burst into tears and said, “This is the bandit of Cao trying to set two people against each other.” Liu Bei said, “Brother, do not grieve. Liu Bei swears he will not do this unrighteous thing.”

Lü Bu repeatedly offered thanks and bowed. Liu Bei kept him at wine and he only returned late at night. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei said, “Brother, why did you not kill Lü Bu?” Liu Bei said, “Cao Mengde fears that Lü Bu and I might both conspire to strike at him. So he devised this plan to make the two of us devour each other while he profits. How can one move against what he has made?” Guan Yu nodded in assent. Zhang Fei said, “I only want to kill this robber and remove later danger.” Liu Bei said, “That is not an act of a true gentleman.”

The next day, Liu Bei sent back the envoy with thanksgiving and submitted a memorial of thanks, and sent back to Cao words that he needed time to consider. The envoy returned and reported to Cao that Liu Bei had not killed Lü Bu. Cao asked Xun Yu, “The stratagem failed. What next?” Xun Yu said, “There is yet another plan, called the Tiger Driving the Wolf into Being swallowed by the Tiger.” Cao asked, “What is this?” Xun Yu said, “Secretly send men to Yuan Shu and report that Liu Bei has submitted a memorial asking to seize the Southern Commanderies. When Yuan Shu hears it, he will rage and attack Liu Bei. Then issue a clear imperial order that Liu Bei is to punish Yuan Shu. When both sides advance, Lü Bu will surely develop divided loyalties. That is the Tiger Drives Wolf strategy.” Cao rejoiced. He first dispatched men to Yuan Shu, and then, under imperial edict, dispatched troops to Xu Province.

Liu Bei was in Xu Province when he heard an envoy had arrived. He came out of the city gate to welcome him and read the edict. It was an order to raise troops to attack Yuan Shu. Liu Bei accepted the command and sent the envoy on at once. Mi Zhu said, “This, too, is Cao Cao’s stratagem.” Liu Bei said, “Even if so, the command of the throne cannot be refused.”

He then selected thirty thousand horse and infantry and, on the appointed day, set out. Sun Qian said, “First fix the one who will hold the city.” Liu Bei asked, “Which of my two younger brothers can hold it?” Guan Yu said, “I would hold this city.” Liu Bei said, “Early and late I wish to confer matters with you both. How can we separate?” Zhang Fei said, “I will keep the city, my younger brother.” Liu Bei said, “You cannot hold this city. You are fierce in drink, you whip soldiers, and you act lightly and ignore advice. This is not to my taste.” Zhang Fei said, “From now on, younger brother will not drink, will not whip soldiers. Whatever men counsel, he will follow.” Mi Zhu said, “I only fear the words and heart do not match.” Zhang Fei got angry and said, “I have followed elder brother for so many years and never broke my word. How can you disparage me?” Liu Bei said, “Though you speak so, my heart cannot be at ease. Then ask Chen Deng to assist. In the coming days, have him restrain your wine and keep you from creating trouble.” Chen Deng agreed. Liu Bei issued instructions and then led thirty thousand horse-and-infantry southward toward Nanyang.

Yuan Shu heard that Liu Bei had submitted a memorial seeking to seize his southern commanderies and became furious: “You are one who makes straw mats and knotted sandals yet dares to occupy this great commandery and stand with the lords? I truly meant to attack you, and now you would take his lands! This is beyond endurance.” He ordered his senior general Ji Ling to raise one hundred thousand troops and attack Xu Province. The two armies met at Xuyi. Liu Bei’s troops were few and camped by river and hill.

Ji Ling was from Shandong and wielded a three-pronged spear weighing fifty jin. That day he led his troops out and shouted violently, “Rural Liu Bei, how dare you trespass my territory?” Liu Bei replied, “I carry an imperial edict to subdue unfaithful subjects. How can you come and resist me? Your offense is beyond punishment.” Ji Ling was greatly enraged, leapt on his horse and brandished his spear, charging straight for Liu Bei. Guan Yu shouted, “You rabble cannot win by force!” He came to horse and fought Ji Ling in full force for thirty rounds, without clear victory. Ji Ling called for pause, and Guan Yu wheeled his horse back into formation, standing at the line for him. Ji Ling then sent his deputy general Xun Zheng. Guan Yu said, “Let only Ji Ling come and settle this with me directly!” Xun Zheng said, “You are a nameless junior officer; you are not an equal for Commander Ji.” Guan Yu was furious and instantly took him. One horse-turn passed, and he cut Xun Zheng down from his mount. Liu Bei drove his troops over to kill the commander. Ji Ling was routed, withdrew in retreat, and took position at Huain Riverbank, refusing close battle. His soldiers were ordered to raid and plunder; each was cut down by Xu Province troops. The two armies then kept apart; their standoff needed no further telling.

After Liu Bei departed, Zhang Fei had all miscellaneous matters entrusted to Chen Deng, and he handled strategy on his own. One day he held a banquet and invited all officers. When all had taken their seats, Zhang Fei began: “When brother left, he told me to cut down my drinking, for fear of trouble. Tonight all of you should drink freely. Tomorrow each of you must abstain and help me guard this city. Yet today I require every man to drink his fill.” He rose and toasted each of them in turn. When the cups came before Cao Bao, the latter said, “I have an oath from Heaven: I do not drink.” Zhang Fei said, “How does a killer of Han men not drink? Take a cup.” Cao Bao, frightened, drank one cup only. Zhang Fei served everyone in turn and drank giant jugs himself until heavily intoxicated, then rose again to toast the rest. When cups came again to Cao Bao, Bao said, “I truly cannot drink anymore.” Zhang Fei said, “You just drank one!” Now that Bao refused again, Zhang Fei, drunk and incensed, shouted, “You disobey my command, and deserve one hundred blows!” He ordered soldiers to seize him. Chen Deng said, “How can you treat this man when Lord Liu Bei expressly forbade it?” Zhang Fei answered, “You are only a civil officer; mind civil matters and never police me!”

Cao Bao had no choice and begged: “Master Yide, spare me for my son-in-law’s sake.” Zhang Fei asked, “Who is your son-in-law?” Cao Bao said, “Lü Bu.” Zhang Fei said, “I did not want to beat you. You bring up Lü Bu to frighten me. If I beat you, then I am beating Lü Bu!” The others could not dissuade him. He lashed Cao Bao fifty times with his whip. Only after many repeated pleas was it stopped.

After the gathering dispersed, Cao Bao returned, deeply resentful of Zhang Fei. In the night he sent a sealed letter straight to Xupei, asking Lü Bu to come and saying that Zhang Fei had been dishonorable. He further wrote: “Liu Bei has gone to Huainan. Tonight he is drunk; take this chance with your troops and strike at Xu Province and do not miss this opportunity.” Lü Bu saw the letter and immediately asked Chen Gong for counsel. Chen Gong said, “Xupei has never been a permanent place to stay. Now Xu Province has an opening. If we lose this, we will later regret.”

Lü Bu agreed. He immediately donned his harness and rode out with five hundred cavalry as vanguard. Chen Gong led the main army behind; Gao Shun followed as well. Only forty to fifty li from Xu Province, after mounting and riding they arrived near evening. When Lü Bu reached the wall below the city gate, it was just the fourth watch. The moonlight was clear, and the gate watchmen had not noticed the approach. Lü Bu’s cry outside the gate said, “The Lord Liu has an intelligence agent come in.” Atop the city wall, Cao Bao’s troops reported it to Cao Bao. Bao climbed and looked and ordered his soldiers to open the gate. Lü Bu gave one covert signal, and all his troops rushed in; the shouting swelled.

Zhang Fei was drunk, asleep in the residence when his attendants quickly shook him awake. They reported, “Lü Bu has broken open the gate and his troops are coming in to kill the guards!” Zhang Fei was furious, hurriedly armed himself, and grasped his eight-foot snake-spearl. As he came out of the hall and mounted, Lü Bu’s horse and men had already arrived and were then greeting each other. Zhang Fei’s wine had not yet cleared. Lü Bu, who knew Zhang Fei’s courage, did not dare immediately close. An escort of eighteen mounted guards kept him while he cut his way through the East Gate. Liu Bei’s household, including the family, were inside and could not be protected.

It says that Cao Bao saw Zhang Fei with only ten-odd attendants and knowing his disorderly drunkenness, led about a hundred and ten men in pursuit. When he saw Bao, Zhang Fei grew furious and charged. They fought three rounds; Cao Bao was defeated and fleeing. Zhang Fei chased him to the riverbank and thrust a spear into Bao’s back, killing him with horse and rider in the water. Outside the city, Zhang Fei called to his soldiers. All who could leave the city followed him in retreat to Huainan. Lü Bu entered the city, calmed the residents, and ordered one hundred soldiers to guard Liu Bei’s residence, allowing no one to enter without permission.

Zhang Fei then left with several dozen riders to Xuyi and reported to Liu Bei that Cao Bao and Lü Bu were acting together inside and had mounted a night assault on Xu Province. Those present all went pale. Liu Bei sighed, “What is there to rejoice in? What is there to grieve?” Guan Yu asked, “Where is Sister-in-law?” Zhang Fei answered, “She is all trapped inside the city.” Liu Bei stayed silent. Guan Yu stamped the ground in frustration: “What did you say when you were told to guard the city? What instruction did elder brother give you? Now the city is lost and the women are trapped. How are we to face this?” Zhang Fei, hearing those words, had no place for himself, drew his sword, and prepared to commit suicide.

What use is drunken joy with a lifted cup?
A sword drawn to give up life, and regret comes too late.
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Mengde Moves the Imperial Carriage to Xuandu; Lü Fengxian Makes a Night Assault on Xuzhou

chapters.html:
And so it was said that Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, drew his sword and intended to die by it. Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, stepped forward, embraced him, snatched away the sword, and threw it down, saying, “The ancients said, ‘Brothers are like one’s hands and feet, and wife and children are like clothing. Clothing may be patched when torn; hands and feet, once severed, can never be made whole again.’

We three swore brotherhood in the peach garden, and we did not seek to live together, but wished to die together. Though I have now lost city and home and household, how can I allow one of my sworn brothers to die halfway through this journey? As for the city, it was never truly ours. Though our household was captured, Lü Bu will not intend to kill them; we can still devise a rescue. Why, for one brief error, should a worthy younger brother rush to throw away his life?”

He finished, and wept bitterly. Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, and Zhang Fei also wept.

Now Yuan Shu heard that Lü Bu had invaded Xuzhou. He sent men through the night to Lü Bu offering fifty thousand hu of grain, five hundred horses, one thousand taels of gold and silver, and one thousand bolts of silk, in exchange for a joint strike on Liu Bei. Lü Bu rejoiced and ordered Gao Shun to lead fifty thousand troops to strike Liu Bei from behind.

When Liu Bei heard this message, he withdrew in drizzling rain, abandoned Xuyi, and moved eastward to seize Guangling. By the time Gao Shun’s army arrived, Liu Bei had already gone. Gao Shun met Ji Ling and asked for the promised gift. Ji Ling said, “Please withdraw your troops; permit me first to put this before the lord.” Gao Shun withdrew separately and returned, then reported Ji Ling’s words to Lü Bu.

Lü Bu still hesitated, when a letter from Yuan Shu suddenly arrived. The letter said, “Though Gao Shun has come, Liu Bei is not yet gone. Wait until we have seized him, then send the promised gifts.” Lü Bu scolded Yuan Shu for breaking faith and was about to raise troops against him. Chen Gong advised, “No. Yuan Shu is in Shu-chun with many soldiers and abundant grain. Do not lightly engage him. Better call Liu Bei back to Xupei and make him our right wing. In time have Liu Bei lead the vanguard; then we can take Yuan Shu first and Yuan Shao after that, and sweep all under heaven.”

Lü Bu agreed and sent a letter inviting Liu Bei back.

Liu Bei had led his troops east to seize Guangling when Yuan Shu raided his camp and cut his army in half. Returning, he happened upon Lü Bu’s envoy with the letter and was greatly relieved. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei said, “Lü Bu is an unfaithful man and cannot be trusted.” Liu Bei replied, “He received me once as one treated with affection; how can I now doubt him?” So they returned to Xuzhou.

Lü Bu feared that Liu Bei might still harbor suspicion, so he first sent Liu Bei’s family back. Gan and Mi’s two wives met Liu Bei and reported in detail: Lü Bu had placed guards at the gate and forbidden anyone to enter the estate; his attendants regularly brought provisions, and nothing was ever missing. Liu Bei said to Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, “I know Lü Bu will not harm my family.” He entered the city to thank him.

Zhang Fei, bearing resentment toward Lü Bu, did not come with him and first escorted the two wives back to Xupei.

After Liu Bei paid his respects and thanked him, Lü Bu said, “I did not come to seize your city. I came only because my younger brother Zhang Fei, in his drunkenness, had killed a man here and might cause trouble. I came to hold it in guard.”

Liu Bei said, “I have long wished to yield my claim of elder brothership.” Lü Bu outwardly yielded again. Liu Bei pressed his refusals, then returned and resumed camp at Xupei.

Guan Yu and Zhang Fei inwardly remained unsettled. Liu Bei said, “One should bend and hold one’s place, and wait on Heaven’s timing; one should not contend with fate.” Lü Bu then sent grain and bolts of silk. From then on the two houses were reconciled. No further account of it is given.

Now Yuan Shu held a grand banquet for his officers at Shouchun. News came that Sun Ce had taken Lujiang’s Administrator Lu Kang and returned in victory. Yuan Shu summoned Sun Ce, and Sun Ce came and knelt before him. After the formalities, he was invited to sit and dine.

Previously, after Sun Jian’s death, Sun Ce had retired south, honoring learned men and gentlemen. Later, because of disputes between Tao Qian and his mother’s uncle Wu Jing of Danyang, Sun Ce moved his mother and household to Qu’e and entered the service of Yuan Shu. Yuan Shu loved him deeply and often said, “If Yuan Shu had a son like Sun Lang, what regret at death would matter!” So he appointed him as Huaiyi Colonel and sent him with troops against Jing County, where Tai Shi Zu Lang won a victory. Seeing Sun Ce’s valor, Yuan Shu again dispatched him against Lu Kang, and he returned once more in victory.

When the banquet ended, Sun Ce returned to camp. The courteous treatment he received from Yuan Shu on that evening’s hall seemed too proud to him; he brooded and walked the yard by moonlight. He remembered that his father Sun Jian had been such a hero, and he, Sun Ce, had now fallen to this state; he could not help but cry out aloud.

At that moment a man entered from outside, laughing, “Bofu, why this sorrow? While your father was alive, he often employed me. If you have matters undecided, why do you not ask me rather than weeping?”

Sun Ce saw him: he was a former retainer from Danyang, surname Zhu, given name Zhi, courtesy name Junli. Sun Ce wiped his tears and had him seated, saying, “I weep because I cannot carry on my father’s will.”

Zhu said, “Why do you not go to Yuan Gonglu, ask for troops, and cross to Jiangdong in the pretext of rescuing Wu Jing, while truly seeking your great enterprise, rather than remain long beneath another man’s hand?”

While they discussed this, another man suddenly entered: “I have learned all of what you are planning. I have one hundred stout and sturdy men. I can for a while add an arm to Bofu’s strength.” Sun Ce saw him and recognized him as Lu Fan, from Runan Xiyang, surname Lu, given name Fan, courtesy name Zi Heng. Sun Ce rejoiced and invited him to sit as they discussed together.

Lu Fan said, “I fear Yuan Gonglu will not be willing to lend troops.” Sun Ce answered, “I have my father’s Imperial Jade Seal. I can offer it as collateral.” Lu Fan replied, “Yuan Gonglu has long desired it. If you offer this as pledge, he will surely issue troops.”

The plan was settled. Next day Sun Ce appeared before Yuan Shu, weeping and kneeling, and said, “The grievance against my father cannot be avenged; now my mother’s uncle Wu Jing is also pressured by Liu Yao, the Inspector of Yangzhou. My aged mother and household are in Qu’e and will surely be harmed. I dare to ask for several thousand veteran soldiers to cross the river and rescue them. In case Your Excellency does not believe me, I give this inherited Imperial Jade Seal as collateral.”

When Yuan Shu saw the seal he took and examined it, then said joyfully, “I do not want your seal. Leave it here for now. I will lend you three thousand troops and five hundred horses. When you restore order, return quickly. Your position is low; you cannot yet hold great authority. I will list you as a Zhechong Colonel and General Who Exterminates Bandits. Move out on an auspicious day and take command.”

Sun Ce thanked him and then led troops and horse, taking with him Zhu Zhi, Lu Fan, his old general Cheng Pu, Huang Gai, Han Dang, and others. He moved out on the appointed day.

When he reached Liyang, another force was seen. First to come forward was a man with elegant bearing and handsome appearance. On seeing Sun Ce he dismounted and knelt. He was Zhou Yu, surname Zhou, given name Yu, courtesy name Gongjin, from Shucheng in Luyang. He had moved with Sun Jian to Luyang during the Dongzhou campaign against Dong Zhuo, and he and Sun Ce, being of the same age, had been close and treated as elder and younger brothers.

His uncle Zhou Shang had been administrator of Danyang. He had come east to visit his family and happened to meet Sun Ce there.

Sun Ce rejoiced at seeing him and spoke from his heart. Zhou Yu said, “I am willing to lend horse-and-saddle service and work together for this great undertaking.” Sun Ce said joyfully, “Now that I have Gongjin, this great matter will be complete.” He arranged for him to meet Zhu Zhi, Lu Fan, and others.

Zhou Yu said, “My lord seeks to accomplish a major undertaking and knows too that there are two men in Jiangdong called Zhang. One is Zhang Zhao, courtesy name Zibu, of Pengcheng. The other is Zhang Hong, courtesy name Zigang, of Guangling. Both have talent that measures Heaven and Earth and, to avoid trouble, are in seclusion here. Why does my lord not recruit them?”

Sun Ce rejoiced and immediately sent gifts to invite both. Both refused. He then visited their homes personally, spoke with them at length, and persuaded them. Both consented.

Sun Ce appointed Zhang Zhao as Chief Clerk, and simultaneously as Colonel Who Pacifies the Troops; Zhang Hong as Military Adviser, Master of Correct Counsel. They then discussed attacking Liu Yao.

Now Liu Yao, style name Zhengli, was from Mouping in Donglai. He too was related to the Han household, was nephew of Grand Commandant Liu Chong, and brother of Inspector Liu Dai of Ji Province. He had formerly served as Inspector of Yangzhou, was stationed at Shouchun, and, after being driven from Jiangdong by Yuan Shu, had come to Qu’e. As soon as he heard that Sun Ce’s army had arrived, he gathered his generals and discussed together.

His subcommander Zhang Ying said, “I have one army quartered at Niuzhu. Even if I had a hundred thousand troops, I still could not come close.” Before he had finished speaking, a man beneath the banner shouted, “I am willing to be the forward vanguard.”

The soldiers looked, and it was Taishi Ci, from Huang County in Donglai. After he had once broken through the Beihai encirclement and returned, he had come to see Liu Yao and been retained under the command tent. When he heard Sun Ce had arrived, he asked to be the forward vanguard. Liu Yao said, “You are still young and cannot yet be a great general. Stay at my side and obey orders.” Taishi Ci withdrew displeased.

Zhang Ying moved his soldiers to Niuzhu and stockpiled ten-thousand measures of grain in the command pavilion. Sun Ce marched in and Zhang Ying came out to meet him. The two armies met on Niuzhu bank.

Sun Ce took up position in full gear and dismounted his horse; Zhang Ying shouted abuse. Huang Gai stepped out and fought. After no more than a few exchanges, alarm erupted in Zhang Ying’s camp: there was fire in the stockade. Zhang Ying quickly turned back, and Sun Ce pressed in with his troops and cut down their chances. Zhang Ying abandoned Niuzhu and fled toward the deep hills.

Those who had set the fire were in fact two strong generals. One was Jiang Qin, from Shouchun in Jiujiang, surname Jiang, given name Qin, courtesy name Gongyi. The other was Zhou Tai, from Xiacai in Jiujiang, surname Zhou, given name Tai, courtesy name Youping. Both had been ruined by disorder and gathered followers; they survived by plundering on the Yangzi. For long they had heard Sun Ce in Jiangdong as a great man who could gather worthy men, and therefore brought over three hundred and more of their men to join him.

Sun Ce rejoiced and took them into service as Captains of the Chariot Front. He collected the grain and weapons at Niuzhu’s stronghouse, and over four thousand surrendered soldiers, then advanced toward Shenting.

Zhang Ying returned in defeat before Liu Yao and faced him. Liu Yao raged and wished to behead him. Counselor Zuo Rong and Xue Li urged mercy and stationed the troops at Lingling to block the enemy. Liu Yao himself led his own army to camp south of the Shenting ridge, while Sun Ce encamped on its north side.

Sun Ce asked local people, “Is there a Han Guangwu temple up the hill?” They answered, “There is one on the ridge.” Sun Ce said, “I dreamed last night that Guangwu summoned me. I will go offer incense there.”

Chief Clerk Zhang Zhao said, “No. The south side of this ridge is Liu Yao’s camp. What if there is an ambush?” Sun Ce said, “A divine spirit helps me; why should I fear?” He donned armor, took up spear, and with thirteen riders—Cheng Pu, Huang Gai, Han Dang, Jiang Qin, Zhou Tai—mounted and went up the ridge to burn incense.

After kneeling and offering worship he descended and looked over the men and said, “If I can establish my livelihood in Jiangdong and restore my father’s foundation, I will rebuild this temple and worship there in all four seasons.”

After worship he mounted and returned. Looking back over the troops, he said, “I will go past the ridge and inspect Liu Yao’s stockades.” All the commanders said this was not possible. Sun Ce would not yield and together they ascended the ridge and looked south toward village woods.

A forward detachment had already sent word back. Liu Yao declared, “This must be Sun Ce’s ploy to lure the enemy. We must not give chase.” Taishi Ci said energetically, “If not now, when can we catch Sun Ce?” He ignored Liu Yao’s order and immediately donned his armor, mounted, took up his spear, and cried out, “Who has courage, follow me!”

All other commanders remained still. Only one young general answered, “Taishi Ci is truly a fierce commander; I can aid him.” He rode beside him. The other generals laughed.

Sun Ce watched for a while and then turned. As he rode along the ridge, he heard from above, “Do not run, Sun Ce!” He turned and saw two horses coming down. He formed his thirteen riders and set them out. Sun Ce took his spear across the saddle and waited at the foot of the ridge.

Taishi Ci shouted, “Who is Sun Ce?” Sun Ce asked, “Who are you?”

The reply came, “I am Taishi Ci of Donglai. I have come to capture Sun Ce.”

Sun Ce laughed, “Then I am the one. You and two of yours come for one me. I do not fear you. If I feared you, I would not be Sun Bofu.”

Taishi Ci said, “You can come with all your men. I am not afraid.” He spurred forward with raised spear. Sun Ce answered with a raised spear. The two horses met and fought fifty exchanges, with no clear winner; Cheng Pu and the others marveled silently.

Seeing that Sun Ce’s spearwork was faultless, Taishi Ci feigned loss and drew him in. Sun Ce pursued, but Taishi Ci did not return by the same way. Instead he went around the back of the mountain. Sun Ce chased him on. “You run badly, you are not a true man!” Taishi Ci thought to himself, “This fellow has twelve followers. If I seize him, these men will snatch him away. I must lead him farther, to a place without refuge, then I can act.”

He fought while advancing and while withdrawing. Sun Ce would not relent and pursued to open ground. Taishi Ci wheeled and came back again; they fought another fifty exchanges. Sun Ce thrust; Taishi Ci dodged and caught hold of the spear. Taishi Ci thrust back; Sun Ce also dodged and caught hold of the spear. Both exerting hard strength, both horses tumbled off.

Their horses vanished in opposite directions. They dropped their spears, grabbed at each other, and their military robes were torn to pieces.

Sun Ce moved faster, drew the short halberd from Taishi Ci’s back. Taishi Ci drew Sun Ce’s helmet. Sun Ce thrust the halberd at him; Taishi Ci blocked it with his helmet.

Then cries rose from behind. It was Liu Yao’s relieving force, about one thousand strong. At once, as Sun Ce was in disarray, Cheng Pu and the other twelve riders came charging. Sun Ce and Taishi Ci only just let go.

Taishi Ci snatched a horse in the camp and took up a spear to remount. Sun Ce’s horse had been taken by Cheng Pu, and Sun Ce also took a spear and mounted another horse.

Liu Yao’s more than one thousand men and Cheng Pu’s twelve riders clashed hand to hand, pressing on to the foot of Shenting ridge in a drawn-out fight. At the height of uproar Zhou Yu arrived with troops. Liu Yao himself led the main force down the ridge. Near dusk the wind rose and rain broke, and both sides withdrew.

The next day Sun Ce brought his army before Liu Yao’s camp. Liu Yao brought troops out to meet him. As both formations circled, Sun Ce lifted Taishi Ci’s small halberd before the lines and ordered his men to shout, “Taishi Ci would already have been stabbed through had he not run so fast!”

Taishi Ci in turn raised Sun Ce’s helmet before the lines and ordered his men to shout, “Sun Ce’s head is right here!”

Both sides shouted, each side praising its own strength and claim of victory. Taishi Ci rode out, wishing to settle it with one-on-one combat. Sun Ce moved to do so.

Cheng Pu said, “My lord need not spend your strength. I will capture him myself.” Cheng Pu came forward to the line; Taishi Ci replied, “You are not my opponent. Let Sun Ce himself come out!” Angered, Cheng Pu charged him with spear. Their two horses met, and they fought thirty exchanges before Liu Yao sounded the recall.

Taishi Ci said, “I only intended to seize that bandit-general. Why recall now?” Liu Yao answered, “Messengers report Zhou Yu has entered with Chen Wu, style name Zilie, and has attacked Qu’e. Our family lands are already lost. Do not linger. Go at once to Moling to join Xue Li and Zuo Rong and bring their cavalry to reinforce.”

Taishi Ci followed Liu Yao in retreat. Sun Ce did not pursue; he held the men in order.

Chief Clerk Zhang Zhao said, “That army was struck at Qu’e by Zhou Yu; they no longer have desire to hold a prolonged battle. This night is ideal for a night raid on camp.” Sun Ce approved, split his army into five columns that night, and forced a rapid advance.

Liu Yao’s army was heavily defeated, and men scattered in all directions. Taishi Ci alone could not resist; he led a dozen riders through the night to Jing County.

Sun Ce then gained Chen Wu as an assistant. He was over seven chi tall, with yellow face and red eyes, and an odd aspect. Sun Ce respected him deeply and made him a captain, putting him in charge of the vanguard to attack Xue Li.

Chen Wu led ten or more riders in a sudden rush through the lines, beheading more than fifty men. Xue Li closed the gate and did not dare to come out.

As Sun Ce was still attacking, news came that Liu Yao was joining Zuo Rong to retake Niuzhu. Sun Ce was incensed and led the main army straight to Niuzhu.

Liu Yao and Zuo Rong rode out to meet him. Sun Ce said, “I am here now. How can you still refuse to submit?”

Behind Liu Yao, one officer, Yu Mi, came out. After fewer than three exchanges with Sun Ce, he was taken alive and dragged back into line. At that moment Liu Yao saw him captured and sent forth Fang Neng. Fang Neng’s spear-tip just thrust toward the back of Sun Ce’s heart.

An officer in Sun Ce’s ranks cried out from behind, “There is someone attacking from the rear!” Sun Ce turned. Seeing Fang Neng arrive at the horse, he roared like thunder. Fang Neng, startled and terrified, flipped backward and fell from his horse, breaking his head and dying.

Sun Ce threw Yu Mi beneath his standard; Yu Mi was dead. At that moment one general was choked to death, and another was killed at Sun Ce’s shout. From then on all called Sun Ce “the Little Overlord.”

That day Liu Yao’s army suffered a great defeat; nearly all horses and men were surrendered to Sun Ce. More than ten thousand were executed. Liu Yao and Zuo Rong fled to Yuzhang and sought Liu Biao.

Sun Ce returned, attacked Moling again, and personally went to the moat’s edge to invite Xue Li to surrender. From above the walls a cold arrow struck Sun Ce in the left leg, and he rolled off and fell from his horse.

His generals rushed to rescue him, lifted him, withdrew to camp, and pulled out the arrow and applied medicinal gold ointment. Sun Ce ordered his soldiers to feign that their commander had been mortally wounded and had died. They mourned, and the camp was raised in withdrawal.

When Xue Li heard Sun Ce was dead, he secretly raised the troops in the city through the night and with fierce commanders Zhang Ying and Chen Heng marched out to chase. Suddenly ambushes erupted all around. Sun Ce rode out first, crying aloud, “Sun Lang is here!”

The soldiers nearby were startled; all dropped their spears and swords and knelt on the ground. Sun Ce ordered no one to kill. Zhang Ying wheeled his horse back and was stabbed to death by Chen Wu. Chen Heng was shot dead by Jiang Qin. Xue Li died amid the confused melee.

Sun Ce entered Moling and set the populace in order. He then moved the troops to Jing County to seize Taishi Ci.

Taishi Ci had recruited just over two thousand stout men and his own unit and was on the way to seek revenge for Liu Yao. Sun Ce and Zhou Yu discussed catching him alive. Zhou Yu proposed attacking the county from three sides and leaving only the east gate open for flight; at twenty-five li from the city, one force should be hidden along each of three routes. When Taishi Ci arrived, exhausted and depleted, he and his horseflesh would surely be trapped.

Most of Taishi Ci’s recruited men were from fields and hills and unfamiliar with discipline. Jing County’s walls were not very high. At night Sun Ce ordered Chen Wu, in short military dress with a dagger, to climb first and set fire inside the city.

When Taishi Ci saw fire on the city walls, he mounted and rode out through the east gate. Sun Ce’s army, right behind, gave chase.

As Taishi Ci ran, the rear force came within thirty li but did not press too close. After running fifty li he was exhausted, horse and body both spent. In the reed marsh a shout rose at once. Taishi Ci ran on desperately. From both sides, horse snares closed together and tripped him. His horse was pulled down and Taishi Ci was captured alive and carried to the great stockade.

When Sun Ce heard that Taishi Ci had been taken, he personally came out, dispersed the troops, and released him. He clothed him in brocade robes and brought him into camp, saying, “I know you are truly a man of steadfast integrity. Liu Yao’s flock are fools, not fit to be used as generals; this is why they came to this ruin.”

Taishi Ci, seeing Sun Ce’s generosity, asked to submit. Sun Ce grasped his hand and laughed, “At Shenting when we fought, if I had been captured by you, would you still have harmed me?”

Taishi Ci laughed, “That cannot yet be known.”

Sun Ce laughed and asked him into his tent, invited him to sit, and gave him a feast.

Taishi Ci said, “Liu Yao has been recently broken and his soldiers are scattered. I want to go and gather my remaining men to help Your Excellency. I do not know whether you can believe this.”

Sun Ce rose and said, “This is truly what I wish. Let us make an agreement: come back tomorrow at midday.”

Taishi Ci assented and left. The other generals said, “Once he goes, he will not return.” Sun Ce said, “Taishi is a man of trust and integrity. He will not betray me.” Yet all still doubted.

The next day he set up a pole at the camp gate and watched the sun’s shadow. Right at midday Taishi Ci arrived with more than one thousand men to camp. Sun Ce rejoiced greatly. All praised Sun Ce’s gift of discernment.

So Sun Ce gathered tens of thousands, moved south of Jiangdong, and pacified the people, aiding them and setting them at ease. Countless came to him. Jiangdong’s people, hearing his army had arrived, all lost courage and fled. When his army arrived, he did not allow even one civilian to be plundered. Chickens and dogs did not know fear. The people rejoiced and brought cattle and wine to the camp in labor.

Sun Ce rewarded them with gold and silk; joy spread across the land. Of Liu Yao’s former troops, those who wished to join followed him. Those unwilling returned home after rewards and were sent to the fields.

The people of Jiangnan all praised him. So his strength grew greatly. He brought back his mother, his uncle, and his brothers to Qu’e, and made his younger brother Sun Quan stand watch with Zhou Tai at Xuanzheng. Sun Ce then led his army south to take Wu Commandery.

At that time Yan Baihu, styling himself the King of Virtue in Eastern Wu, occupied Wu Commandery and sent his detachments to guard Wucheng and Jiaxing. On the very day Sun Ce’s force arrived, he heard of it and sent his brother Yan Yu into battle to meet at Maple Bridge. Yan Yu rode across the bridge with crossed blade on his mount. News of this reached Sun Ce in the central camp, and Sun Ce was about to ride out.

Zhang Hong pleaded with him, “As commander, your life is tied to the threefold army; do not lightly dare this petty enemy. I beg my lord to be cautious.” Sun Ce said, “Your words are as firm as metal and stone; but if I do not personally face arrows and spears, my officers and soldiers will not obey.” So he sent Han Dang forward.

By the time Han Dang came to the bridge, Jiang Qin and Chen Wu had already quickly crossed by boat from the riverbank, firing arrows to bring down the troops on shore, and both leapt to shore to cut down men, causing Yan Yu to retreat.

Han Dang drove straight on with his troops to the gate under Chang Gate and cut into the city; the robbers fled back inside.

Sun Ce divided his forces and advanced by land and water, surrounding Wucheng. He besieged it for three full days and drew no enemy sortie.

That night Sun Ce marched and drew all troops to the gate’s outside, summoning them in parley. On the battlement above, an enemy auxiliary officer held his left hand on a supporting beam and pointed his right hand to the field below, hurling curses. Taishi Ci, mounted, drew bow and arrow and said to his officers, “Watch me strike this man’s left hand!”

Before he finished speaking, the bowstring snapped and the arrow flew true, passing through the man’s left hand and driving it hard through the guard beam.

Both above and below the walls, all who saw it cheered.

They pulled that man down. Yan Baihu, greatly startled, said, “How can this army withstand a man like that?” and then he discussed making peace.

The next day he sent Yan Yu to see Sun Ce. Sun Ce invited him into camp to drink. In the middle of the wine, he asked, “What does your master intend?” Yan Yu said, “To divide Jiangdong evenly with the general.”

Sun Ce became angry: “How dare a rat claim equality with me?” He ordered him beheaded.

Yan Yu drew his sword and rose. Sun Ce’s sword struck him down in an instant; he fell and his head was severed and sent back into the city.

Yan Baihu, realizing he had misjudged the strength, abandoned the city and fled.

Sun Ce pressed forward and pursued. Huang Gai took Jiaxing, and Taishi Ci took Wucheng; several districts came under control.

Yan Baihu fled to Yuhang, looting en route. He was then defeated and beaten by Ling Cao and his father among the local people; he turned and ran toward Kuaiji.

The father and son Ling Cao came out to meet Sun Ce. Sun Ce made him a Commander for an expeditionary campaign, and together they crossed the river in force.

Yan Baihu gathered bandits and deployed them at the western ford at western ford crossing. Cheng Pu engaged and routed them once more, then hurried through the night to Kuaiji.

In Kuaiji, Governor Wang Lang considered bringing troops to rescue Yan Baihu. Suddenly one man spoke up, “No. Sun Ce leads a force rooted in benevolence and propriety. Yan Baihu is nothing but violent marauders. It is better to capture Yan Baihu and present him to Sun Ce.”

Wang Lang recognized him as Yu Fan, from Yuyao in Kuaiji, surname Yu, courtesy name Zhongxiang, and a county officer there. Wang Lang shouted in anger at him, and Yu Fan sighed and withdrew.

Wang Lang then brought out his troops and joined Yan Baihu, forming battle lines on Shanyin plain.

The two armies faced each other. Sun Ce rode out and said to Wang Lang, “I have raised an army of benevolence and righteousness to bring peace to this land of the Great River. Why do you help thieves?”

Wang Lang shouted back, “Is your greed never satisfied? You have already gained Wu Commandery and now forcefully swallow my border. Today I come especially to exact revenge on the Yan clan!”

Sun Ce grew angry and was about to engage when Taishi Ci had already gone out.

Wang Lang wheeled his horse and swung his blade against Taishi Ci. Not long after, his officer Zhou Xing broke through to aid him. In Sun Ce’s ranks, Huang Gai mounted and met Zhou Xing. The drums thundered as they grappled in fierce duel.

Suddenly disorder broke first in Wang Lang’s rear ranks and one unit attacked from behind. In alarm Wang Lang returned on his horse; there appeared Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu leading troops to strike diagonally, coming against him from front and rear at once.

Unable to withstand the multitude, Wang Lang and Yan Baihu and Zhou Xing cut a blood trail and ran back into the city, hauling up the hanging bridge and shutting the gate tight.

Sun Ce’s main force followed to the city foot, arranged his men in spread formation, and attacked the four gates.

Inside the city Wang Lang wished to issue another sortie for a decisive death battle. Yan Baihu said, “Sun Ce’s army is enormous. Your Eminence should only dig deep ditches and raise high banks, hold your walls firmly, and do not come out. In no more than one month, their grain will run out and they will naturally retreat. Then, by surprise, we can take the city without battle.” Wang Lang followed his advice and held Kuaiji in place, never issuing a sortie.

Sun Ce repeatedly besieged for several days and failed to take it quickly. He discussed the matter with his officers. Sun Jing said, “Wang Lang’s fixed defense cannot be stormed at once. Most of Kuaiji’s grain is stored at Zha Du, which lies some tens of li away. Why not first seize that place with forces, by taking an unprepared point and striking unexpectedly?”

Sun Ce rejoiced and said, “My uncle’s plan is excellent. It will destroy these brigands.” He ordered fires lit at each gate, a pretense of loud forces, and withdrew the siege southward by night in feigned retreat.

Zhou Yu said, “With your great army moving, Wang Lang will certainly come out to pursue. Then we can win with an unusual force.” Sun Ce said, “I am ready. The taking of this city is for tonight.” He ordered the mounted troops to depart.

When Wang Lang heard that Sun Ce’s army had withdrawn, he went to the enemy wall tower with his men to watch. He saw smoke and fire below and banners uncoordinated. His heart wavered.

Zhou Xing said, “Sun Ce has left. This is only a stratagem to confuse us. You should sortie and strike.” Yan Baihu said, “Sun Ce’s move is likely toward Zha Du. I will send troops with Zhou Yu to pursue.”

Wang Lang said, “Zha Du is where I store grain. It must be protected. You must lead your men first.” He led five thousand troops out with Yan Baihu and Zhou Xing.

Yan Baihu and Zhou Xing advanced from the city in pursuit. Near dawn, roughly twenty li out, a drum sounded in dense forest and torchlight flashed as one. Yan Baihu was startled and turned his horse back. A single officer stood ahead to block him, and in the firelight he saw Sun Ce himself.

Zhou Xing danced with his blade to meet him. Sun Ce speared him to death. The rest surrendered.

Yan Baihu made a blood trail and fled toward Yuhang.

When Wang Lang heard that the advance force had collapsed, he did not dare return into the city but fled off to the edge of the sea.

Sun Ce returned with the main army, took the city in turn, and settled the people in peace. Not a day later, a man came before Sun Ce’s army bearing the severed head of Yan Baihu as tribute.

Sun Ce looked at him: he was eight chi tall, broad-faced, with a wide mouth. He asked his name. It was Dong Xi, from Yuhang in Kuaiji, surname Dong, given name Xi, courtesy name Yuandao. Sun Ce rejoiced and made him Commander of a separate detachment.

From then, the routes to the east were all pacified. He ordered Sun Jing to stand in governance, made Zhu Zhi prefect of Wu Commandery, and withdrew the army back toward Jiangdong.

Now Sun Quan and Zhou Tai were holding Xuanzheng. A band of mountain brigands suddenly rose and attacked from all sides. It was deep in the night, and they could not come to meet them in time, so Zhou Tai lifted Sun Quan onto his horse.

The brigands came with knives to slash. Zhou Tai, bare-bodied and on foot, lifted his sword and killed over ten men. Then one brigand leapt from horseback and drove his spear straight at Zhou Tai. Zhou Tai grabbed the spear, dragged him from horse to ground, took spear and horse, and by a line of blood cut a way out to rescue Sun Quan. The other brigands fled far.

Zhou Tai had been struck by twelve spear wounds; his wounds swelled with feverish heat, and life was at an end in moments.

When Sun Ce heard, he was greatly alarmed.

In his tent, Dong Xi said, “I once held with sea raiders and, though struck by many spears, recovered in half a month after Yu Fan, that worthy county officer in Kuaiji, recommended a physician.”

Sun Ce said, “Could Yu Fan be Yu Zhongxiang?” Dong Xi replied, “Yes.”

Sun Ce said, “He is a worthy man. I shall employ him.” He ordered Zhang Zhao and Dong Xi to invite Yu Fan.

Yu Fan arrived, and Sun Ce honored him as a distinguished guest, making him a Gongcao. Yu Fan said, “This man is from Qiao Commandery of Pei: surname Hua, name Tuo, courtesy name Yuanhua. He is truly a divine physician of this age. Bring him here.”

Within less than a day he was brought. Sun Ce saw him: he had a childlike face and white hair, and bore an otherworldly manner. Sun Ce hosted him as a top guest and asked him to attend to Zhou Tai’s wounds.

Hua Tuo said, “This is not hard.” He applied medicine, and in one month Zhou Tai recovered.

Sun Ce rejoiced and thanked Hua Tuo richly.

He then pressed onward to eliminate mountain bandits. Jiangnan was pacified. Sun Ce assigned troops to guard key passes, posted officers at strategic points, sent memorials to court, cultivated ties with Cao Cao, and sent envoys to Yuan Shu to retrieve the Imperial Jade Seal.

Yuan Shu, however, had secretly harbored thoughts of claiming the empire, so he wrote back with excuses and did not return it. He quickly gathered Chief Clerk Yang Dajiang, Commander Zhang Xun, Ji Ling, Qiao Rui, General-in-Chief Lei Bo, Chen Lan, and over thirty others and discussed:

“Sun Ce borrowed my troops and cavalry to raise his uprising, and now he has won all Jiangdong as if it had never been yours, then again comes to demand the seal. This is sheer impertinence. How should he be addressed?”

Chief Clerk Yang Dajiang said, “Sun Ce relies on the Yangtze’s natural barriers, has fine soldiers and ample grain. He cannot be targeted now. We should first attack Liu Bei and repay the old grievance of our unprovoked earlier clash; only then may we think on Sun Ce, and it will be timely if we act then. I submit a plan: let Liu Bei be taken at once.”

It was then:

They do not go to Jiangdong to chase tiger and leopard.
Yet they come to Xuzhou to wrestle with a dragon there.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Taishi Ci Fights the Little Conqueror; Sun Bofu Battles Yan Baihu

chapters.html:
Fengxian of Lü shoots the painted halberd at the gate. Cao Mengde is defeated at the Yi River.

Later, Commander Yang proposed the plan to attack Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande. Yuan Shu asked, “How is this plan to be carried out?”

Yang said, “Liu Bei’s army is camped at Xiaopei. It is easy to take, but there is still Lü Bu in Xuzhou, and he has a tiger’s grip. We promised him money, grain, and horses before, but he still has not delivered them, and he may well aid Liu Bei. If we send him grain now, we can secure his heart so he stays put. Then we can capture Liu first, and only afterward deal with Lü Bu. So we can take Xuzhou as well.”

Yuan Shu approved and prepared two hundred thousand hu of grain. He ordered Han Yin to take a sealed letter to Lü Bu. Lü Bu was very pleased and treated Han Yin with great courtesy. Han Yin returned with the report. Yuan Shu then appointed Ji Ling as commander, with Lei Bu and Chen Lan as deputy generals, and led forth several ten-thousands into Xiaopei.

When Liu Bei heard of this news, he assembled his men to deliberate. Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, wanted to ride out and fight. Sun Qian said, “Our supplies in Xiaopei are lean and our men are few. How can we stand against them? We should send an urgent letter to Lü Bu for aid.”

Zhang Fei said, “How would that wretch come?”

Liu Bei said, “Sun Qian’s counsel is sound.” He prepared a letter and sent it to Lü Bu.

The letter read:

“My general, I bow and beg your kindness. I now shelter at Xiaopei and survive by Heaven’s grace alone. Yuan Shu seeks to repay a private grievance and has sent Ji Ling with troops against this county. Catastrophe is near; none but you can rescue me. Please move an escorting force at once and save me from this peril hanging over my head. I am grateful beyond measure.”

Lü Bu read the letter and conferred with Chen Gong, saying, “Before, when Yuan Shu sent grain and provisions, he wanted me not to rescue Liu Bei. Liu Bei has now come asking for aid. I believe Liu Bei may not in fact be truly threatening me, though he camps at Xiaopei. If Yuan Shu swallows Liu Bei, then with the northern lords from Mount Tai he could still threaten me, and I would not sleep in peace. Better to rescue Liu Bei now.”

So he ordered soldiers forward.

Ji Ling marched with rapid stride and soon reached southeast of Pei County. He pitched camp there. By day he displayed banners and flags that overshadowed mountain and river; at night he set drums and fires that shook earth and sky. Only around five thousand men remained in Xiaopei, so Liu Bei could only take command and lead them out to hold camp.

Just then word came that Lü Bu had set out with his force and moved one li from the county toward the southwest to pitch his own encampment. Ji Ling understood that Lü Bu had come to rescue Liu Bei. In panic he sent a letter to Lü Bu accusing him of broken faith. Lü Bu laughed and said, “I have a way that will spare blame between the houses of Yuan and Liu. I will send envoys to both Ji Ling’s and Liu Bei’s camps and invite them to a banquet.”

When Liu Bei heard that Lü Bu had invited him, he prepared to go at once. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei said, “Elder brother, you must not go. Lü Bu surely has divided intentions.”

Liu Bei said, “I have not treated him poorly. He will not harm me.” So he mounted and rode out.

Guan Yu and Zhang Fei followed. Upon reaching Lü Bu’s encampment and entering, Lü Bu said, “I have come only to ease your emergency. If, at another time, we rise to power, let neither of us forget this.”

Liu Bei expressed his thanks. Lü Bu invited him to sit. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei drew their swords and stood behind him. News came that Ji Ling was arriving. Liu Bei was startled and tried to step away. Lü Bu said, “I called you both here for a joint consultation. Do not let suspicion rise.”

Liu Bei did not understand Lü Bu’s intention and felt uneasy. Ji Ling dismounted and entered camp, but when he saw Liu Bei already seated in the tent, he was deeply astonished and tried to withdraw at once. His guards could not restrain him.

Lü Bu strode forward and pulled him back as if he were lifting a child. Ji Ling said, “Does the general mean to kill me?”

Lü Bu said, “No.”

Ji Ling said, “Then is this to kill that big-eared one?”

Lü Bu said, “No.”

Ji Ling said, “Then for what?”

Lü Bu said, “Liu Bei and I are as brothers. He is now in distress, so I have come to save him.”

Ji Ling said, “If that is so, then kill me?”

Lü Bu said, “Not at all. I have always disliked fighting. I only like to settle fights.”

Ji Ling said, “Then tell me the method by which you intend to settle it today.”

Lü Bu replied, “I have one method, ordained by Heaven.”

He brought Ji Ling into the tent to meet Liu Bei. Each still suspected the other; Lü Bu took the middle seat, put Ji Ling on the left and Liu Bei on the right, and ordered a banquet and the passing of wine.

The wine went around several rounds. Lü Bu said, “You two look at my face, and both of you are to lay down arms.”

Liu Bei was silent. Ji Ling said, “I carry ten thousand troops by the master’s command solely to seize Liu Bei. How can I lay down arms?”

Zhang Fei grew furious and drew his sword. He shouted, “Though I am few in number, I look on you men as children at play! How do you dare to compare yourselves with a hundred-thousand Yellow Turban band? How dare you touch my brother!”

Guan Yu hastened to restrain him, saying, “Let us first see what General Lü intends. We can return to our camps and not start killing each other yet.”

Lü Bu said, “I invited the two of you to end this fighting and I mean you both to obey. Do not fight each other.”

Ji Ling was angry at this side; Zhang Fei at this side wanted to fight. Lü Bu became very angry and ordered, “My men, bring me the painted halberd!”

Lü Bu took the painted halberd in his hand. Ji Ling, Liu Bei, and all of them went pale. Lü Bu said, “I tell you both: do not fight each other. Heaven has decreed this. My men will take this halberd outside the gate-post and plant it there. If I strike the small branch on its top with one arrow, then both sides must stop fighting. If I miss, you may each return to your camps and kill as you will. If anyone disobeys me, then use all your strength to resist him.”

Ji Ling thought privately, “The halberd will be planted a full one hundred and fifty bu away. Can he really hit it? Let him answer once. If he misses, then I can do as I wish.” He agreed aloud.

Liu Bei agreed as well without objection. Lü Bu told everyone to sit and drink one more cup each.

When the wine was finished, Lü Bu called for bow and arrows. Inwardly Liu Bei prayed, “May he strike true.”

Lü Bu then rolled up his sleeves, nocked an arrow, drew his bow to full span, and cried, “Now!”

Like this:

The bow opens, a winter moon crossing heavenward; the arrow runs down like a meteor striking earth.

The arrow struck the small branch on the painted halberd. Officers and attendants alike in tent and out shouted in acclaim.

Later someone wrote a verse:

Wenhou’s marksmanship is rare beneath heaven; at the gate-post once he alone averted danger. When evening falls, it truly shames Hou Yi; the ape-cry roared as if still striving to outdo Youji. The tiger sinew twanged as he loosed the bow; the painted-beaked fletchings flew as the arrow arrived. His leopard-tail banner shook, and the painted halberd was pierced; ten thousand roaring soldiers shook loose their war-gear.

When Lü Bu’s arrow struck the branch, he laughed heartily and threw down his bow, took the hands of Ji Ling and Liu Bei, and said, “Heaven’s will is that both your armies cease.”

He ordered the officers to pour wine and each drank a large cup. Liu Bei quietly felt ashamed. Ji Ling was silent for a while, then told Lü Bu, “Your words, I dare not disobey. But when I return, how will the lord believe me?”

Lü Bu replied, “I will write it myself.” They drank through a few more rounds, and Ji Ling asked to return for a letter first.

Lü Bu said to Liu Bei, “Without me, your peril would have been great.” Liu Bei thanked him and withdrew with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei. By the next day all three bodies of troops and horses had dispersed.

Liu Bei no longer in Xiaopei, Lü Bu returned to Xuzhou.

Ji Ling later returned to Huainan to report to Yuan Shu, describing how Lü Bu had resolved the quarrel by shooting the halberd at the gate-post. He submitted written copies. Yuan Shu was furious.

“Lü Bu has taken so much grain and rice from me and then made this matter a mere child’s game while shielding Liu Bei! I myself will lead heavy troops and personally campaign against Liu Bei, while at once punishing Lü Bu too!”

Ji Ling said, “My lord, do not act in haste. Lü Bu has strength beyond ordinary men and has the land of Xuzhou. If Lü Bu links with Liu Bei, they will be hard to destroy. I have heard Lü Bu has a daughter of marriageable age and near maturity. Your lord has a son. Send someone to ask for her as bride. If Lü Bu marries her to your house, he will kill Liu Bei. This is the strategy of tying the knot so that the enemies cannot stand in-between.”

Yuan Shu followed this and that very day sent Han Yin as matchmaker with gifts to Xuzhou to ask for a marriage alliance.

When Han Yin reached Xuzhou and saw Lü Bu, he said, “My lord, the General, admires you and wishes to make your daughter his child’s wife, so that your bond with him shall be as Qin and Jin’s harmony.” Lü Bu consulted with his wife Yan Shi.

Lü Bu had two wives and one concubine: first he married Yan as his principal wife, then took Diaochan as concubine. Later, when he stayed at Xiaopei, he took Cao Bao’s daughter as his second wife. The household of Cao Bao’s line had already perished; Diaochan had also no further family ties; only Yan had borne him a daughter, whom Lü Bu loved most.

Yan Shi said at once, “I hear Master Gonglu has long held Huainan. He commands many soldiers and broad supplies, and surely he will soon be emperor. If this is fulfilled, then my daughter may become an empress. I only wonder: how many sons does he have?”

Lü Bu replied, “Only one.”

She said, “Then I consent at once. Even if not empress, I have no worry in Xuzhou.”

Lü Bu resolved firmly, lavished gifts on Han Yin, and accepted the betrothal. Han Yin returned to Yuan Shu. Yuan Shu immediately prepared bridal gifts and again sent Han Yin back to Xuzhou. Lü Bu received them, invited him to dine, and then kept him at an inn to rest.

The next day, Chen Gong entered the inn and paid his respects to Han Yin. After formalities were complete and they sat down, he snapped at the attendants and spoke directly to Han Yin: “Who proposed this plan? To have Master Gonglu marry into Fengxian is to aim at Liu Xuande’s head, is it not?” Han Yin was shaken and apologized.

He said, “Pray, General, reveal nothing of this.”

Chen Gong said, “I will not reveal it. But I fear if this drags on, someone else will discover it and the matter will turn.”

Han Yin asked, “Then what shall be done?”

Chen Gong said, “I have come to see Fengxian and urge him to send the bride at once.”

Han Yin rejoiced and thanked him: “If so, my lord will appreciate your brightness deeply.”

Chen Gong then left Han Yin and entered before Lü Bu, saying, “I am very happy your daughter is promised to Master Gonglu. But I do not know on which day the marriage will be concluded.”

Lü Bu said, “Let us discuss it.”

Chen Gong said, “In antiquity, from engagement to marriage there were fixed times: one full year for the Son of Heaven, six months for lords, three seasons for ministers, one month for common folk.”

Lü Bu said, “Yuan Shu is heaven’s gift of a treasure to the state and soon a future emperor. Might we follow the Son of Heaven’s rule?”

Chen Gong said, “No.”

Lü Bu asked, “Then follow the lordly rule?”

Chen Gong said, “No.”

Lü Bu said, “Then follow the ministerial rule?”

Chen Gong said, “No.”

Lü Bu laughed, “Do you want me to follow the commoner rule?”

Chen Gong said, “No.”

Lü Bu said, “Then what do you think is right?”

Chen Gong said, “Today, all lords contend for supremacy. If Fengxian weds with Gonglu now, which lord in the world will not resent it? If you delay the date too long, they may set an ambush along the way and seize her when she travels. What then? For this plan, do not wait and do not rest. Since it is accepted, send her to Shouchun at once and place her in a separate pavilion. Then choose the lucky day and complete the marriage. That will leave no room for error.”

Lü Bu agreed. “Your words are apt.” He informed Yan Shi at once, arranged the bride’s ornaments and conveyance overnight, and had Song Xian and Wei Xu send the woman along with Han Yin.

Drums and music rang loud as he escorted her out of the city gate.

At that time Chen Gui, Chen Yuanlong’s father, though old, came home. He heard the music and questioned his attendants, and they explained its source.

Chen Gui said, “This is the strategy called 疏不間親: a distant-marriage stratagem. Liu Bei is in danger.”

He came leaning on the hand to see Lü Bu.

Lü Bu asked, “Why have you come, Master?”

Chen Gui said, “I heard the General had died, so I came specially to mourn.”

Lü Bu, startled, said, “Why do you say that?”
