Chen Gui said, “Formerly Master Gonglu sent grain and silver to you to have Liu Bei killed, and you relieved him by shooting at the gate halberd. Now he suddenly asks for marriage. He means to use your daughter as a hostage, then come and seize Xiaopei soon after. If Xiaopei falls, Xuzhou is lost. He may come for grain, he may come for troops. If you comply, you will be running in exhaustion and making enemies. If he refuses, he has already broken betrothal and will take up arms. Moreover, it is known that Yuan Shu already intends to claim the throne; this is rebellion. If he rebels and you stand with him by marriage, will not all under heaven reject you?”

Lü Bu was greatly shocked and said, “Chen Gong deceives me!” He immediately ordered Zhang Liao to pursue. After about thirty li he brought the woman back. Han Yin himself was seized and imprisoned and was not allowed to return. Yet he sent word back to Yuan Shu saying the bride stock had not been fully prepared and would be sent when it was complete.

He also told Lü Bu of Chen Gui’s warning and had Han Yin sent to Xudu as escort. Lü Bu still hesitated.

Then a messenger arrived: “Liu Bei in Xiaopei is recruiting men and buying horses. Who knows why?”

Lü Bu said, “This is the business of a commander. Why should it be strange?”

Before longer speech, Song Xian and Wei Xu came and told Lü Bu: “By your order I and my comrade bought over three hundred fine horses in Shandong. Returning to the edge of Xiaopei, bandits robbed half of them. We traced the trail to Zhang Fei, who is Liu Bei’s younger brother. He disguised himself as a mountain bandit and robbed the horses.”

Lü Bu grew angry and immediately ordered troops toward Xiaopei to attack Zhang Fei. When Liu Bei heard this he was alarmed and hurried to lead his men out.

The two camps met. Liu Bei came out on horseback and said, “Brother, why did you bring your troops here?”

Lü Bu shouted back, “At my gate-post I shot the halberd and saved you in a dire emergency. Why have you stolen my good horses?”

Liu Bei said, “Because we lack horses, we have bought them in all directions. How could we dare steal your horses?”

Lü Bu said, “You accuse your brother of stealing my horses, and yet you dare keep a hundred and fifty good horses of mine in your custody!”

Zhang Fei thrust his spear and said, “I stole your horse, yes! What do you intend to do now?”

Lü Bu cursed, “You reckless brigand! You have long treated me with contempt!”

Zhang Fei said, “I stole your horse, and that has offended you. You stole my brother’s Xuzhou, and you have not said a word about it!”

Lü Bu rose with his halberd, charged out, and Zhang Fei also came forward with his spear. The two fought fiercely for more than a hundred bouts with no clear victor.

Liu Bei feared there was a gap in the situation and hastily sounded the gold-and-bell signal to withdraw into the city. Lü Bu split his troops and encircled it on all four sides.

Liu Bei summoned Zhang Fei and said, “You stole his horses and brought this trouble on us. Where are those horses now?”

Zhang Fei answered, “They are all stashed in monasteries.”

Liu Bei sent men out of the city to Lü Bu’s camp to seek peace and offer to return the horses, and asked that both sides disband. Lü Bu appeared willing.

Chen Gong said, “If Lü Bu does not kill Liu Bei now, he will later be a grave harm.”

Lü Bu did not agree to what was requested and made the siege still tighter.

Liu Bei deliberated with Mi Zhu and Sun Qian. Sun Qian said, “Cao Cao’s target of hatred is Lü Bu. Better than defend here, we should abandon the city and run to Xudu and seek Cao Cao. From there we may gather troops and break Lü Bu. That is the best plan.”

Liu Bei asked, “Who can break through first and lead us out?”

Zhang Fei said, “Your younger brother is willing to die in battle.”

Liu Bei put Zhang Fei in front and Yan Yun? maybe 云長 behind? Wait text: “飛曰:... 令飛在前；雲長在後；自居其中，保護老少。” So Guan Yu in back protecting children/elders.

Liu Bei gave Zhang Fei the fore, with Guan Yu behind, and placed himself in the center among the old and young.

Deep into the third watch, by moonlight they went out through the north gate and left. They happened upon Song Xian and Wei Xu, and Yide drove them back, forcing them off. The two brothers broke through the outer ring.

Zhang Liao arrived on the rear. Guan Yu held him at bay.

When Lü Bu saw Liu Bei gone, he did not pursue. He entered the city, settled his people, ordered Gao Shun to hold Xiaopei, and then returned to Xuzhou.

Liu Bei then hurried to Xudu, camped outside the gates, and sent Sun Qian to meet Cao Cao, saying he had been driven by Lü Bu and had come to submit. Cao Cao said, “Liu Bei is a brother of mine.” and invited him into the city.

The next day, Liu Bei left Guan Yu and Zhang Fei outside, and entered with Sun Qian and Mi Zhu. Cao Cao treated him with the courtesy of an honored guest. Liu Bei explained at length Lü Bu’s actions. Cao Cao said, “Lü Bu is a man without righteousness. I and my capable brother will join and punish him.” Liu Bei thanked him.

Cao Cao hosted a banquet and saw him off late. Xun Yu came and said, “Liu Bei is a hero. If not addressed early, he will later bring trouble.”

Cao Cao made no reply.

Xun Yu left, and Guo Jia entered. Cao Cao asked, “Xun Yu urges me to kill Liu Bei. How do you see it?”

Guo Jia said, “You should not. The lord raises armies for righteousness and to remove disorder from the people, and must rely on trustworthiness to attract talent. If it is truly as you fear, Liu Bei came in hard times and without treasure, yet if you kill him you do injury to a worthy man. The men of the realm who know him will doubt your intentions and halt their own steps. With whom will you settle the world then? To remove one man’s danger at the cost of the hopes of the four seas and your own security is beyond careless.”

Cao Cao was greatly pleased. “What you said exactly matches my heart.”

The next day he submitted a recommendation that Liu Bei be appointed Governor of Yu Province. Cheng Yu remonstrated, “Liu Bei will never remain beneath another man. Better to act early against him.”

Cao Cao said, “Now is the age when heroes are needed. One should not lose the heart of the world by killing one man. Guo Fengxiao and I share the same thought.” He ignored Cheng Yu’s advice and sent three thousand troops and ten thousand hu of grain with Liu Bei as he moved to Xiaopei to regroup, collecting his scattered troops and preparing to attack Lü Bu.

Liu Bei reached Yu Province and arranged a meeting with Cao Cao there.

Cao Cao was about to lead an army to punish Lü Bu when a fast horse messenger arrived with news that Zhang Ji had come from Guanzhong with troops to attack Nanyang and had been killed by a stray arrow. His nephew Zhang Xiu had inherited his troops and employed Jia XU as strategist. He linked with Liu Biao, stationed his men in Wancheng, and planned to rise and seize power.

Cao Cao was furious and wanted to campaign immediately, but also feared Lü Bu might attack Xudu. He asked Xun Yu for a plan.

Xun Yu said, “This is easy. Lü Bu has no planning mind. If profit appears, he rejoices. Your Lordship should send an envoy to Xuzhou with appointments and rewards, ordering him to reconcile with Liu Bei. If he is pleased, he will think no further of far plans.”

Cao Cao said, “Good.” He dispatched the Commander of the Imperial Guards, Wang Ze, with official decrees and a peace letter, and headed out with five hundred thousand troops to prosecute Zhang Xiu. He divided the force into three routes and made Xiahou Dun the vanguard. The army reached the banks of the Yi River and camped there.

Jia XU advised Zhang Xiu: “The Cao Cao host is immense. You cannot withstand it. Better to surrender the city.”

Zhang Xiu followed and sent Jia XU to negotiate terms at Cao’s camp. Cao Cao found Jia XU’s responses effortless and liked him greatly, wanting to appoint him as strategist.

Jia XU said, “I once served Li Que and earned the enmity of all under heaven. Now I serve Zhang Xiu and have seen and heard him faithfully. I can not abandon him now.” He then withdrew.

The next day he brought Zhang Xiu to meet Cao Cao, and Cao Cao treated him with highest honor. He led troops into Wancheng and pitched camp, placing the other forces at outposts connected across ten or more li.

They stayed several days. Every day Zhang Xiu held feasts for Cao Cao.

One day Cao Cao became drunk and returned to his sleeping quarters, then privately asked his attendants, “Is there a courtesan in this city?”

His brother’s son, Cao Anmin, sensing Cao’s intent, whispered, “Last night my nephew saw by the side of the guest-house a woman of extraordinary beauty. I asked who she was; she is, it is said, the wife of Zhang Ji, who is now known as my uncle Zhang Xiu’s spouse.”

When Cao Cao heard this, he ordered Anmin with fifty soldiers in light armor to fetch her. Soon they brought her to camp. Cao Cao found her indeed beautiful.

He asked her name. She answered, “I am Zou Shi, wife of Zhang Ji.”

Cao Cao said, “Lady, do you recognize me?”

Zhu Si said, “I have long heard of the Chancellor’s fame; tonight I am glad to bow and gaze on him.”

Cao Cao said, “I have taken you as my lady because I have accepted Zhang Xiu’s surrender. Had I not, I would have exterminated his clan.”

Zhu Si thanked him, saying, “I truly feel your kindness as a second life.”

Cao Cao said, “To meet a lady tonight is Heaven’s fortune. Tonight I hope to share a bed with you. Come with me to the capital and enjoy lasting rank and wealth.”

Zhu Si thanked him and retired. That night they lay together in his tent.

She said, “If I remain in this city, Zhang Xiu will surely grow suspicious, and outsiders will speak.”

Cao Cao said, “Tomorrow we move together to the camp at my command.”

The next day he moved her outside the city to rest. He ordered Dian Wei to stay outside the central command tent as outside guard. No one was to enter without a call, so the inside and outside were effectively sealed.

Cao Cao spent each day in pleasure with Zhu Si and did not return to the campaign schedule. Zhang Xiu’s household reported quietly and the message reached him. Zhang Xiu became furious and asked Jia XU for strategy.

Jia XU said, “This must not be leaked. Tomorrow, when Cao Cao leaves his tent for business, then we will do as follows.”

The next day Cao Cao was in his tent when Zhang Xiu came in and said, “Among the newly surrendered soldiers there are many deserters. I ask that you move them into the main camp.” Cao Cao agreed.

Zhang Xiu then moved his army and divided it into four camps, giving a set hour for action. He feared Dian Wei’s ferocity and kept away, then consulted Hu Che'er.

Hu Che'er could carry five hundred jin and walk seven hundred li a day, another of rare strength. He offered this strategy: “What makes Dian Wei formidable is his pair of iron halberds. Tomorrow the lord should invite him to drink to excess and have him return drunk. Then I will slip among his escort soldiers and steal his halberds. Without them this man will no longer intimidate us.”

Zhang Xiu was delighted and prepared bowmen, armor, and troops in advance, then told everyone in each camp. On the appointed day he had Jia XU send greetings to Dian Wei and treated him with much ceremony and wine. By evening Dian Wei returned inebriated. Hu Che'er blended into the men’s files and marched straight into the main camp.

That night Cao Cao, drinking with Zhu Si in the tent, heard horses whinny outside the camp. He ordered men to investigate. They reported it was Zhang Xiu’s troop patrol. Cao Cao did not suspect anything.

It was near the second watch when he heard shouting from the rear camp. “There is fire on the grass cart!”

Cao Cao said, “There is fire in camp. Do not let panic spread.”

Soon flames rose in every quarter, and Cao Cao grew alarmed. He called for Dian Wei. Dian Wei had fallen asleep drunk; in his half-dream he heard the drum and alarm of killing and rose at once, but his two halberds were gone.

The enemy were already at the gate. He grabbed his waist sword and dashed out. Around the gate there were countless enemy horsemen with long spears rushing in. Dian Wei pushed forward and struck down more than twenty at once.

As the horses withdrew, foot soldiers arrived; spears rose on both sides like rows of reeds. Dian Wei had no armor at all. He was pierced all over by dozens of spears and still fought to the death. His sword blade became too short and split, so he dropped it and held two soldiers up with both hands, killing eight or nine with those bare hands.

The raiders would not come near him, only shooting arrows from afar. The arrows came down like sudden rain, yet Dian Wei still held the gate through death. For half a while after, no one dared enter through the front gate.

It was Dian Wei’s stand at the gate that allowed Cao Cao to escape by horse from the rear. Only Cao Anmin could follow on foot.

Cao Cao’s right arm was struck by an arrow, and his horse had also taken three arrows. Fortunately the mount was a fine Dawan horse and, though hurt, ran swiftly. They had barely reached the bank of the Yi River when enemy troops caught them; Cao Anmin was cut down into meat and bone.

Cao Cao spurred forward across the water and gained the farther bank. As he mounted, an arrow struck the horse’s eye; it collapsed to the ground.

Cao Ang, Cao Cao’s eldest son, immediately offered his horse to his father. Cao Cao mounted and rode hard.

Cao Ang was then shot dead by a shower of arrows. Cao Cao escaped.

On the way he met generals and gathered the remains of the army.

At that time the troops of Qing Province under Xiahou Dun had been marching through the countryside, and looted civilian homes. The Suppression of Barbarians Colonel, Yu Jin, was now taking his core units on the road to suppress and punish them and console the villagers.

When the Qing troops returned, they came and bowed to Cao Cao, crying, while reporting Yu Jin’s insurrection and that he had cut down Qing horsemen. Cao Cao was greatly startled. Before long Xiahou Dun, Xu Chu, Li Dian, and Yue Jin arrived. Cao Cao said that Yu Jin had rebelled and they should draw up the army to meet him.

When Yu Jin saw that Cao Cao and the others had all arrived, he deployed his troops to hold the camp corners, dug ditches, and entrenched at once.

He said to the assembled leaders, “The Qing troops claim the general has rebelled. But the Chancellor is already here. Why did you build a camp first instead of arguing it out?”

Yu Jin replied, “The rebel pursuit force is behind me, and they can arrive at any time. If we do not prepare now, how shall we resist? A small dispute can be argued; a larger battle cannot.”

By the time the works were finished, Zhang Xiu’s army arrived by two columns.

Yu Jin rode out first to meet them. Zhang Xiu quickly withdrew.

When other generals saw Yu Jin charging forward, they likewise led soldiers against him. Zhang Xiu’s force was ruined and was driven over a hundred li.

Zhang Xiu, in dire straits, withdrew in defeat and fled to Liu Biao.

Cao Cao rallied the army and made the roll. Yu Jin entered and testified that Qing troops had raided and despoiled villages, losing the people’s trust, so he had therefore executed them. Cao Cao said, “Without telling me, why did you first descend to a camp?”

Yu Jin repeated his earlier explanation.

Cao Cao said, “A general in haste who can still organize men, strengthen defenses, and turn near ruin into victory—what great commander in old times does not deserve such praise!” He bestowed a pair of gilded vessels, ennobled him as Marquis of Yishu Ting, and blamed Xiahou Dun for failure in strictness of camp discipline.

He then ordered a ceremony and sacrificial rite for Dian Wei. Cao Cao himself wept and poured libation.

He said to the assembled generals, “I have lost my eldest son and a beloved nephew, but I carry no deep grief for that. I weep only for Dian Wei.”

All were moved by this.

The next day he ordered the army to disengage.

We need now return to Cao Cao’s mission to Xudu. Wang Ze arrived in Xuzhou with the edict. Lü Bu received him and brought him into the government hall.

He read the decree: Lü Bu was made General Who Conquers the East and granted seals and ribbons. Wang Ze then presented Cao Cao’s private letter. In front of Lü Bu, he explained the deep respect Cao Cao held him.

Lü Bu was very pleased. Then he was told that Yuan Shu had sent envoys. He called them in.

They said, “Yuan Shu is soon to take the imperial throne and has established the eastern palace. He urges the empress to come promptly to Huainan.”

Lü Bu grew furious: “A rebel dares speak so?” He killed the envoy and shackled Han Yin.

He sent Chen Deng with a memorial of thanks and told Han Yin be brought, after which they came with Wang Ze to Xudu to offer thanks.

They also sent a reply to Cao Cao seeking the actual appointment of Governor of Xuzhou.

Cao Cao knew Lü Bu had refused the marriage with Yuan Shu and was delighted. He had Han Yin publicly beheaded in the market court.

Chen Deng subtly remonstrated: “Lü Bu is a wolf among ministers. He is strong but without planning and light in changing loyalties. We should act against him early.”

Cao Cao said, “I have long known Lü Bu is a wolf cub with wild ambition. He is hard to keep long. No one but a father and son pair can know his full nature; you must work your counsel with me.”

Chen Deng said, “If the Chancellor takes action, I will serve as inner support.”

Cao Cao was greatly pleased. He rewarded Chen Gui with the office of zhizhong (with a 2,000-shi stipend), and made Chen Deng Administrator of Guangling Commandery.

Chen Deng withdrew. Cao Cao took his hand and said, “For the affairs in the east, let us entrust them to you together.”

Chen Deng nodded and returned to Xuzhou before Lü Bu.

Lü Bu asked, and Chen Deng explained that Chen Gui had been rewarded with zhizhong and that Chen Deng himself had become Administrator of Guangling Commandery.

Lü Bu became very angry. “Did you not seek Xuzhou for me? Instead you sought your own titles and salary! Your father taught me to break with Cao, and now what I seek is not one hair obtained, while both you and your father are advanced in rank. I was bought by you both.”

He drew his sword to behead him. Chen Deng laughed and said, “General, how blind you are.”

Lü Bu said, “How can I not be blind?”

Chen Deng said, “I saw Cao Cao and he said, to feed you is like feeding a tiger: you must feed it to keep it alive; unfed, it will bite people.”

Cao Cao smiled and added, “Not to say it like that, sir. I keep Wenhou as if keeping an eagle; a fox and rabbit have not ceased, and one must not feed it fully too early. If hungry, it is useful; if full, it flies away.”

“Who are those foxes and rabbits?” Chen Deng asked.

Cao Cao answered, “Yuan Shu of Huainan, Sun Ce of Jiangdong, Yuan Shao of Ji Province, Liu Biao of Jing Province, Liu Zhang of Yi Province, and Zhang Lu of Hanzhong are all foxes and rabbits.”

Lü Bu caught the fallen sword and laughed: “Cao truly knows me!”

Before he finished speaking, news came that Yuan Shu’s army was advancing on Xuzhou. Lü Bu was shocked.

Then it is said:

Qin and Jin are not yet reconciled, and Wu and Yue still contend in battle. It is marriage that has stirred out the clatter of armies.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Lü Bu, Fengxian, Shoots the Halberd at the Gate, and Cao Mengde Is Defeated at the Yi River

chapters.html:
Now Yuan Shu was in Huainan. He had broad lands and abundant grain, and he had the jade seal Sun Ce had handed over to him, so he began to consider claiming the imperial title. He called a large meeting of his followers and asked,

“It was only Liu Bang of Han who began as a district chief at Sishui, yet he gained all under Heaven. Four hundred years have now passed, Heaven’s pattern has spent its course, and all beneath Heaven is in turmoil. Our house has held rank for four generations with three high offices, and the people have long relied on our house. I wish to obey Heaven, follow the people, and set myself in the center imperial seat. What do you all think?”

The clerk Yan Xiang answered, “This must not be done. In the past, Zhou King Houji amassed virtue and merit until Wen Wang; even when he held two parts of the underworld? Not; even after three-quarters of the world, he still served the Yin. Your family is indeed noble, but not as flourishing as that of Zhou. The Han house has declined, but it is not as cruel as King Zhou of Yin. This matter is absolutely not feasible.”

Yuan Shu growled. “Our Yuan surname came from Chen. Chen was descended from Great Shun. By the order of earth receiving fire, this is exactly my age and destiny. Also there is a prophecy: ‘The one who will replace Han is Tu Gao.’ My courtesy name is Gonglu; it exactly fulfills that prophecy. And I still have the national jade seal: if I do not be king, I would oppose Heaven and Man. My mind is fixed. Anyone who keeps speaking too much will be executed.”

He therefore proclaimed the title Zhong, appointed officials from the court downward, rode in the dragon and phoenix sedan chair, performed sacrifices at the southern and northern suburbs, made Fengfang’s daughter his empress, and named his son crown prince. He then ordered Lü Bu’s daughter to be brought as consort to the crown prince. Then he learned that Lü Bu had already taken Han Yin to Xu and delivered him to Cao Cao, who had him executed. He was furious, so he made Zhang Xun a Great General and made him command more than twenty thousand men, dividing them into seven routes to campaign against Xu Province.

The first route, with Great General Zhang Xun, took the center. The second route, with Senior General Qiao Rui, went to the left. The third route, with Senior General Chen Ji, went to the right. The fourth, with Deputy General Lei Bo, went to the left. The fifth, with Deputy General Chen Lan, went to the right. The sixth, with the surrendered general Han Xian, went to the left. The seventh, with the surrendered general Yang Feng, went to the right. Each route took subordinate heroes, and they all set out that same day.

Yuan Shu made Jin Shang, Yanzhou Inspector, Grand Commandant, to supervise the transport of grain and silver for all seven routes. Jin Shang refused. Yuan Shu executed him and made Ji Ling the chief officer for relief coordination among the seven routes. Yuan Shu himself brought out thirty thousand troops and sent Li Feng, Liang Gang, and Yue Jiu as rapid-response messengers to aid the seven routes.

Lü Bu sent scouts and learned that Zhang Xun’s army would go straight on the Great Road into Xu Province, while Qiao Rui’s army would take Xiaopei, Chen Ji’s Yidu, Lei Bo’s Langye, Chen Lan’s Qihe, Han Xian’s Xiapu, and Yang Feng’s Junshan. The seven armies rode fifty li a day and robbed as they moved. In haste he summoned his advisers. Chen Gong and his father Chen Gui arrived.

Chen Gong said, “The disorder in Xu Province was invited by Chen Gui and his son. They flattered the court for rank and salary, and today they have shifted the calamity to the general himself. You should have the heads of those two beheaded and presented to Yuan Shu; his army will then withdraw.”

Lü Bu listened and immediately ordered Chen Gui and Chen Deng to be arrested. Chen Deng laughed aloud. “What kind of fool’s resolve is this? I see Yuan Shu’s seven routes of soldiers as seven mounds of rotting straw. Why should we pay this any mind?”

Lü Bu said, “If you can propose a way to break the enemy, then your death sentence will be set aside.”

Chen Deng said, “If the general were to heed a fool’s plan, Xu Province could be kept safe.”

Lü Bu said, “Explain it.”

Chen Deng said, “Yuan Shu’s army is large, but it is a disordered host and not one to trust itself. We can hold with our proper troops and then break it with unexpected forces; everything will succeed. There is one more plan: it not only preserves peace in Xu Province but can also capture Yuan Shu alive.”

Lü Bu said, “From where will that plan come?”

Chen Deng replied, “Han Xian and Yang Feng were old Han officials who fled because they feared Cao Cao and went to Yuan Shu without any home to rely on. Yuan Shu will lightly dismiss them, and they will not be happy serving him deeply. If, with forged tally letters, they become inside allies, and if Liu Bei links with them as an outside partner, Yuan Shu will surely be captured.”

Lü Bu said, “You must go to Han Xian and Yang Feng in person and deliver a letter.” Chen Deng agreed.

Lü Bu then issued a general order at Xu and, at the same time, sent written letters to Yuzhou, and then ordered Chen Deng to ride out with a few mounted men to meet Han Xian on the Xiapu road.

Han Xian arrived with his men, set up camp, and then entered for audience. He asked, “You are a man of Lü Bu. Why have you come here?”

Chen Deng laughed. “I am an officer of the Great Han. How can I be called a man of Lü Bu? If you, once an officer of Han, are now a retainer of rebel thieves, then all your former service in protecting Guan Zhong is now for nothing. I think, sir, that Yuan Shu is deeply suspicious by nature and in time will surely kill you. If you do not act now, you will repent too late.”

Han Xian sighed. “I wish to return to Han, but I have no gate to do it through.”

Then Chen Deng produced Lü Bu’s letter. Han Xian read it and said, “Now I understand. Return at once. Yang Feng and I will turn our spears and strike together. Watch for the signal fires, and Minister Wenhou can meet us with troops.”

Chen Deng left and quickly reported to Lü Bu.

Lü Bu split his force into five routes. Gao Shun led one to Xiaopei against Qiao Rui. Chen Gong led one to Yidu against Chen Ji. Zhang Liao and Zang Ba led one to Langye against Lei Bo. Song Xian and Wei Xu led one to Qihe against Chen Lan. Lü Bu led one himself along the Great Road against Zhang Xun.

Each route had ten thousand men, while the rest stayed to guard the city. Lü Bu camped his forces thirty li outside the city. When Zhang Xun’s army arrived, thinking that Lü Bu’s force was not that strong, he drew back twenty li and waited for the other four routes to join.

At the second watch that night, Han Xian and Yang Feng split their troops in various places and set fires, signaling Lü Bu’s army to enter the camp. Zhang Xun’s army was thrown into disorder. Lü Bu seized the opportunity to cut through and destroy them, and Zhang Xun ran.

At dawn, Lü Bu rode onward and in time collided with Ji Ling’s relieving force. Just as the two armies were about to meet, Han Xian and Yang Feng’s two routes came charging in. Ji Ling was heavily defeated and fled. Lü Bu gave chase, and his men captured him; they took countless horses and armor and arms.

When the mountain road opened, Yuan Shu’s banner-and-flag cluster appeared. At the front it revealed a line of mounted men beneath dragon-and-phoenix and sun-and-moon standards, four kinds of drum banners and five directional flags, golden gourd clubs and silver axes, yellow-yellow silk streamers and white horsehair plumes, and yellow gauze mantles with gold-spiked canopies. There stood Yuan Shu in polished golden armor, two sabers hanging on his wrists, in front of his formation, shouting at Lü Bu,

“Turncoat servant of one’s lord!”

Lü Bu flew into a rage and strode forward with his halberd raised. Liu Feng of Yuan’s side came running with a spear to meet him. In fewer than three bouts of combat, Lü Bu wounded Liu Feng’s hand with his spear. Liu Feng cast away his spear and ran.

Lü Bu led his men in a violent charge and slaughter and Yuan Shu’s army broke into utter confusion. Lü Bu pursued from the rear and captured many horses and many men, as well as robes and armor.

Yuan Shu withdrew with his broken troops, and after scarcely going a few li, a compact force appeared from behind the mountain and blocked the way. At its front was Guan Yu. He shouted, “Rebel! Face death if you dare not submit!” Yuan Shu panicked and ran. The rest of his men scattered. Guan Yu cut down many in a sweep of battle.

Yuan Shu gathered his broken force and fled back to Huainan.

Lü Bu won the victory and invited Guan Yu, and also Yang Feng and Han Xian with their men, into Xu Province, where he arranged a grand banquet and entertained them. The soldiers all received rewards.

The next day, Guan Yu took his leave and returned. Lü Bu kept Han Xian as Administrator of Yidu and Yang Feng as Administrator of Langye. They discussed leaving the two there in Xu Province.

Chen Gui said, “No. Han Xian and Yang Feng hold the east of Shandong. If the two remain for less than a year, all the cities and fortresses of Shandong will belong to that general.”

Lü Bu agreed. He settled the two for the time being at Yidu and Langye and left them awaiting orders.

Chen Deng privately asked his father, “Why did you not keep those two in Xu Province as the root for killing Lü Bu?”

Chen Gui said, “If those two help Lü Bu, they will become, instead of cutting him off, claws and teeth added to a tiger.” Chen Deng agreed with his father’s high judgment.

Yuan Shu, defeated, returned to Huainan and sent an envoy to Sun Ce in Jiangdong to ask for troops for revenge. Sun Ce was furious.

“You have relied on my jade seal to claim the imperial title, gone against the Han house, and committed great treason. I was preparing to strike you for this wrong. How could I now help a rebel traitor?”

He wrote a letter and cut all ties.

The messenger bore that letter back to Yuan Shu. After reading it, Yuan Shu shouted, “An insolent child with a loud mouth—who dares to answer me so! I will punish him first!” Chief Clerk Yang spoke up, remonstrating hard and nearly stopping him.

After sending the letter, Sun Ce organized defense and placed troops to guard the river mouth. Then Cao Cao arrived. He appointed Sun Ce Prefect of Kuaiji and ordered him to raise troops and campaign against Yuan Shu. Sun Ce conferred and wanted to mobilize, but Chief Clerk Zhang Zhao advised him first to send a letter to Cao Cao asking him to move south and, if so, Sun Ce would follow in support. If the two armies aided one another, Yuan Shu’s army would collapse. If any accident arose, Cao Cao might rescue them. Sun Ce took this advice and sent a message to Cao Cao with this intent.

Cao Cao came to Xu, and remembering Dian Wei, he ordered sacrifices in his honor. He made Dian Wan his son, title Zhonglang, and took him into the household. Then a report came that Sun Ce had sent an envoy with a letter. After reading it, word also arrived that Yuan Shu was short of grain and was raiding Chenliu, and planned to exploit the opportunity to attack. Cao Cao therefore raised his army southward. He kept Cao Ren in Xu and sent the remainder on campaign: one hundred and seventy thousand horse and infantry with over one thousand grain carts. He first sent men to join Sun Ce, Liu Bei, and Lü Bu.

When the army reached the boundary of Yuzhang, Xuande already drew out his own soldiers to welcome them, and Cao Cao ordered him to come into camp.

After they met, Liu Bei presented two severed heads.

Cao Cao said in astonishment, “Whose heads are these?”

Xuande said, “These are the heads of Han Xian and Yang Feng.”

Cao Cao asked, “How did you obtain them?”

Xuande answered, “Lü Bu put the two in charge at Yidu and Langye, and they unexpectedly unleashed their troops to loot the people. Everyone among the people came to resent them. So I set up a feast, invited them under pretense of debate, and in the middle of drinking used cups as our signal so that Guan and Zhang, my two brothers, slew them and all their men surrendered. I have come now to admit my guilt.”

Cao Cao said, “You have removed a danger to the state. That is great merit, not guilt.”

He then gave Xuande great reward and joined forces to the border of Xu Province. Lü Bu came out to receive him and Cao Cao spoke kindly, appointing him as Left General and promising that upon return to the capital he would exchange the seals and baton for him. Lü Bu was overjoyed.

Cao Cao placed Lü Bu’s troops on the left and Xuande’s on the right, and he took personal command in the center with Xiahou Dun and Yu Jin as vanguard.

Yuan Shu learned that Cao Cao’s army was arriving. He ordered Senior General Qiao Rui to lead fifty thousand as vanguard. The two armies met at the border gate of Shouchun. Qiao Rui charged first on horseback, and after fewer than three exchanges Xiahou Dun thrust him through to death.

Yuan Shu’s army broke and ran back to the city. Then news came that Sun Ce had sent ships to attack the west bank of the river. Lü Bu moved his force against the east bank, while Liu Bei with Guan and Zhang attacked the south. Cao Cao himself moved one hundred and seventy thousand men against the north.

Terrified, Yuan Shu quickly gathered his civil and military commanders to deliberate. Chief Clerk Yang advised:

“Shouchun has suffered years of drought and heat; everyone is short of grain. Now that soldiers are stirring the people again, the people all resent it, and it will not be easy to resist the enemy. It is better not to fight inside Shouchun. Keep the army there and do not make battle. Let time run and their grain run out, and change will surely come. Your Majesty should lead the troops across the Huai. First, this is ground we are accustomed to, and second, it briefly avoids their sharpness.”

Yuan Shu took that advice. He left Li Feng, Yue Jiu, Liang Gang, and Chen Ji in four groups totaling one hundred thousand to hold Shouchun. He moved out with the rest, and with him all the treasuries, gold, jade, and precious goods, and crossed the Huai.

Cao Cao’s army of one hundred and seventy thousand consumed vast amounts of grain each day. Many prefectures were in drought, and support from adjacent districts was impossible. Cao Cao pushed for a swift assault, but Li Feng and the rest kept their gates shut.

The armies faced each other for more than a month. Supplies neared exhaustion. Cao Cao wrote to Sun Ce and borrowed one hundred thousand hu of grain, which still did not cover their dispersing needs.

Supply officer Ren Jun and his subordinate warehouse captain Wang Hou reported to Cao Cao: “The army has great numbers and little grain. What are we to do?”

Cao Cao said, “Issue it in small measures for now to pass this immediate crisis.”

Wang Hou said, “If the soldiers complain, what then?”

Cao Cao replied, “I have a way.”

Following orders, Wang Hou distributed the grain in small measures. Cao Cao secretly sent agents into each camp to listen in. In every place the men lamented and said the Chancellor was deceiving the soldiers. Cao Cao then summoned Wang Hou privately and said, “I need to borrow one thing from you in order to settle the men’s minds. You must not spare anything.”

Wang Hou said, “Your Excellency is borrowing what from me for no fault of mine.”

Cao Cao said, “I know you are innocent, yet if I do not execute you, the army’s heart will change. When you die, your wife and children I will raise and support, so do not worry.”

Before Wang Hou could speak again, Cao Cao called for the executioner, who dragged him out the gate and executed him with one stroke. He hung the head on a high pole and posted a bulletin: “Wang Hou broke the small measures and stole official grain. He is punished by military law.”

From that moment the grumbling among the men began to ease.

The next day, Cao Cao gave this order to commanders of every camp: “If the city is not broken within three days, by joint assault, all of you will be executed!” Cao Cao rode to the foot of the walls, overseeing troops carrying earth and stone to fill the ditches and block the moats. From the city walls arrows and stones rained down. Two assistant officers, fearing the danger, turned back; Cao Cao drew his sword and executed both before the city wall, then dismounted and personally filled the pits.

At once all the troops surged forward, and the army’s strength surged high. The city defenses gave way. The Cao soldiers rushed to storm and opened the gates, cutting the locks. Large formations surged inside. Li Feng, Chen Ji, Yue Jiu, and Liang Gang were all captured alive.

Cao Cao ordered all of them executed in the market.

He burned fake palace buildings and halls and all prohibited objects of indulgence. Shouchun was emptied and stripped of its goods.

The commanders discussed crossing the Huai and pursuing Yuan Shu, when Xun Yu remonstrated: “This year has been drought-stricken and grain is hard to come by. If we push further we will waste the army and harm the people. It is not surely beneficial. Better to return to Xu and wait until next spring, when wheat ripens and supply is prepared before trying again.”

Cao Cao hesitated. At once a mounted messenger came:

“Zhang Xiu, relying on Liu Biao, has become unruly again; counties in Nanyang have risen again. Cao Hong cannot hold them and has been forced to yield over several engagements. They have come to give emergency warning today.”

Cao Cao immediately wrote to Sun Ce and ordered him to deploy across the river as a front against any force Liu Biao might send, so that he would not dare act rashly. Cao Cao then ordered a prompt return that day and planned separately how to campaign against Zhang Xiu.

Before leaving, he left Xuande to keep troops at Xiaopei and to conclude a brotherly pact with Lü Bu for mutual relief and no more raids on each other.

Lü Bu led his men back toward Xu Province.

Before departing, Cao Cao told Xuande privately: “I kept you at Xiaopei as a plan to dig a pit and wait for a tiger. You should only discuss things with Chen Gui and his son and avoid any loss. I will aid you from the outside.” They parted.

Then Cao Cao brought his army back to Xu. News arrived that Du Wei had killed Li Jue, Wu Xi had killed Guo Fan, and brought their heads. Du Wei also had brought Li Jue and over two hundred of his household alive and in chains to Xu.

Cao Cao ordered them divided among the gates and executed, posting proclamations with their head counts. The people praised the justice.

The Son of Heaven entered the hall, assembled civil and military officials, and held a peace banquet. He made Du Wei General Who Disturbs the Rebellious and Wu Xi General Who Crushes Distress, assigning both to command troops and station at Chang’an. The two offered thanks and withdrew.

Cao Cao then petitioned that Zhang Xiu had rebelled and requested orders for a campaign. The Son of Heaven personally arranged the phoenix carriage and sent Cao Cao out as chief commander in person. It was the summer of the third year of Jian’an, the fourth month.

Cao Cao left Xun Yu in Xu, reassigned troops and generals, and personally marshaled the main army.

Along the march he saw a stretch of wheat already ripe. Because of the army’s movement, villagers had fled outside and did not dare to reap.

He sent proclamations to village elders and officers everywhere along the route: “I am acting on the Son of Heaven’s explicit order to dispatch troops to punish rebels and clear dangers for the people. Though we were forced to march while wheat was ripe, all major officers and commanders should know: if any feet tread down any wheat in the field, the penalty is beheading. Army law is strict. The people need not be alarmed or confused.”

Hearing this, the people rejoiced and praised it. They stood in the dust and blocked the road to bow in respect.

Officer cavalry passed through the wheat with every unit dismounting to hold the stalks by hand, passing the grain down to each other so it would not be trampled.

As Cao Cao rode, a startled bird rose from the wheat and his horse went wild-eyed into the fields, trampling a wide swath of grain.

Cao Cao immediately called for the military clerk and inquired whether he should charge himself with the crime. The clerk said, “Can the Chancellor be investigated for a crime?”

Cao Cao replied, “I made the law; I have broken it. How can I ask the troops to obey if I do not uphold it?” Then he drew his side sword as if to cut his own throat. They rushed and saved him.

Guo Jia said, “In the rites of the Spring and Autumn, law did not apply to the honored one. The Grand Commander in charge of the whole army cannot choose self-harm.”

After long thought, Cao Cao said, “Since the ancient principle says law does not apply to the honored one, I will for now forgo death.” He drew his sword through his own hair and threw it to the ground, saying, “I cut my hair to substitute for my head.” He had the hair shown to the entire army and said, “The Chancellor trampled the wheat and would by law have been beheaded; instead he has given his hair in place.”

The whole army was now solemnly alert and strictly obeyed the order.

Later people commented in verse:

For ten thousand tiger-charged troops, ten thousand hearts can still be stirred, One man gives an order, but the multitude is hard to restrain. He drew his sword and cut his hair, exchanging it for his head— Now one can see how deep the arts of Cao Cao are.

Then Zhang Xiu learned that Cao Cao was arriving with his forces. He immediately sent a letter to Liu Biao asking for back-up support and at the same time sent Generals Lei Xu and Zhang Xian out of the city to meet him.

The two forces faced one another in a circle. Zhang Xiu rode out, pointed at Cao Cao, and shouted,

“You are one who pretends benevolence and has no sense of morality, no better than a beast!”

Cao Cao was furious and ordered Xu Chu to ride out. Zhang Xian met him in combat. In only three exchanges, Xu Chu beheaded Zhang Xian from horseback, and Zhang Xiu’s army suffered a major defeat. Cao Cao drove his forces to Nanyang and put the city under siege.

Zhang Xiu closed the gates and did not come out.

Cao Cao besieged and attacked. He saw the moat was very wide and deep and the waters strong, and it was hard to reach the walls in one stroke. So he ordered soldiers to carry earth to fill the moat, to use earth sacks and mixed brushwood and straw, and to make bench-like ladders at the city’s edge. He had observation ladders raised and then personally rode around the city.

After three days, Cao Cao ordered soldiers to stack brushwood at the southwest angle and, gathering his commanders there, directed his men to use that place to scale up. Within the city, Jia Xu saw this development and said to Zhang Xiu,

“I already understand Cao Cao’s intention. Now we can use strategy to counter strategy and proceed accordingly.”

The verse then ran:

Among the strong there are still stronger hands; If one uses deceit, then only one who knows deceit can meet it. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Yuan Gonglu Raises Seven Armies, and Cao Mengde Unites Three Generals

chapters.html:
Jia Xu, who understood Cao Cao’s intention, decided to turn the stratagem back upon him. He said to Zhang Xiu, “From the walls I watched Cao Cao circle and inspect for three days. At the southeast corner he studied the old and new bricks and the broken battlements, where he intends to break through. On the northwest he has secretly removed the packed grass and straw, making a show of force so that he may lure us into believing we must guard that side. In that way, while we stand ready there, he hopes to climb in at night through the southeast.”

Zhang Xiu asked, “What then?”

Jia Xu said, “That is easy. Tomorrow send your strongest and best men, well fed and lightly armed, into the buildings on the southeast and hide them there. Order the townspeople to pretend to be soldiers and hold only a show defense on the northwest. At night let him come up the southeast wall; as soon as he gets inside, sound one cannon and the ambush rises. Cao Cao will be captured.”

Zhang Xiu approved the plan. A courier soon reported to Cao Cao that Zhang Xiu had withdrawn all men from the southeast and posted them on the northwest, calling out to hold it, while the southeast was nearly empty. Cao Cao said, “This is exactly my thought!” He ordered the army to prepare climbing tools in secret and worked the wall with picks and pries in private. In the daytime he led assaults only at the northwest. At the second watch of the night he brought his picked men to the southeast and climbed in by the moat edge, hacking open the broken battlements.

The city made no response. All the ambush force surged in together. At the first cannonshot, the hidden men rose up. Cao’s force turned and fled. Zhang Xiu drove in personally with hard-fighting men and pressed the pursuit hard. Cao’s army was routed and burst from the city, running for dozens of li. Zhang Xiu gave chase until dawn before withdrawing back into the city.

When Cao Cao took stock, more than fifty thousand had fallen and much baggage was gone. Li Qian and Yu Jin were both wounded.

Then Jia Xu, seeing Cao Cao turn and run, hurriedly urged Zhang Xiu to send a dispatch to Liu Biao and raise troops to cut off his rear. Liu Biao, once he received it, almost immediately raised troops when a scout came to report that Sun Ce had encamped at Lukou. Kuiliang said, “Sun Ce’s camp at Lukou is Cao Cao’s plan. Cao Cao has only just suffered defeat; if we do not strike him now, he will become a later danger.”

Liu Biao ordered Huang Zu to hold the pass and himself moved with his army to Anzhong County to cut off Cao’s line of retreat, while at the same time signaling Zhang Xiu. Once Zhang Xiu heard Liu Biao was already in motion, he and Jia Xu jointly led troops to attack Cao.

Meanwhile Cao Cao’s army moved slowly to Xiangcheng and the You River. There, while still in the saddle, he suddenly burst out crying. The men were startled and asked why. “Last year, right here, I lost my general Dian Wei in combat,” he said. “How could I not weep?” He then ordered the army to halt and the mounts to be penned, and arranged a grand mourning banquet for Dian Wei’s soul. Cao Cao himself offered incense and knelt in tears.

All soldiers grieved. After sacrificing for Dian Wei, he sacrificed too his nephew Cao Anmin, his eldest son Cao Ang, and the soldiers killed in this battle. Even the Dawan horse that had been shot was laid in sacrifice as well.

The next day, Xun Yu informed him that Liu Biao had reached Anzhong with Zhang Xiu to block the road home. Cao Cao replied to Xun Yu, “I have only marched a few li at a time, and I know well that the enemy gives chase, but my plan is fixed. If we reach Anzhong, we will surely crush him. Doubt it not.” He then drove the army on to the border of Anzhong County.

Liu Biao’s force had already held the difficult ground, and Zhang Xiu followed close behind. Cao Cao ordered his men to cut a route in the night and conceal elite troops in ambush.

As dawn came, Liu Biao and Zhang Xiu joined forces and, seeing Cao’s army small, assumed he was fleeing. Both marched into the pass and attacked. Cao then released the hidden troops. He utterly broke the two armies together. Cao’s men withdrew from Anzhong’s border and camped beyond the choke point. Liu Biao and Zhang Xiu gathered their broken troops and faced each other.

Liu Biao said, “How could we have been deceived by Cao Cao’s trick?”

Zhang Xiu said, “Let us try again.”

So both armies gathered again at Anzhong.

Soon Xun Yu learned that Yuan Shao was preparing to move north against Gongsun Zan, and rode through the night with urgent news to Cao Cao. Cao Cao, uneasy at once, ordered the army back. Spies soon told Zhang Xiu. He wanted to pursue. Jia Xu said, “Do not pursue. To do so means defeat.”

Liu Biao said, “If we fail to pursue today we lose our chance.” He pressed hard for Zhang Xiu to lead over ten thousand men in pursuit. After ten or so li of march, they reached Cao’s rear guard. Cao’s men fought fiercely and Zhang Xiu and Liu Biao’s two armies were defeated and had to pull back.

Zhang Xiu said to Jia Xu, “I ignored your advice, and as you foretold this is what happened.”

Jia Xu said, “Now let us re-form and chase again.”

Zhang Xiu and Liu Biao both said, “We are already beaten. How can we chase again?”

Jia Xu said, “If we chase now, we shall certainly win; if not, cut off my head.”

Zhang Xiu believed him. Liu Biao, however uncertain, did not join. Zhang Xiu alone took one column and pursued.

Cao’s force was indeed defeated; horses, supplies, and baggage carts were abandoned as he ran in panic.

While Zhang Xiu pressed the chase, a mass of troops came bursting out from behind a hill. Zhang Xiu dared not continue, and withdrew and returned to Anzhong. Liu Biao asked Jia Xu,

“Earlier you said not to pursue, saying we would lose. Later, after we were defeated, you said we would surely win. How can both be true?”

Jia Xu said, “It is simple. My lord, you are a competent commander in one sense, but not a match for Cao Cao in the art of defeating enemies. Even when he is beaten, he has hardy fighters held in reserve to receive pursuers, and our sharp men cannot overcome them. So I knew we would lose then.

Now Cao’s forced retreat after our initial loss was because he had urgent business in Xu. Having broken our pursuing force, he returned at speed with light escort and little preparation. At that moment he was no longer ready. That is why we could catch him and win.”

Liu Biao and Zhang Xiu both accepted his reasoning. Jia Xu advised Liu Biao to return to Jing Province and Zhang Xiu to hold Xiangcheng as a forward wedge. The two armies dispersed.

As Cao Cao still marched onward, he heard that Zhang Xiu had pursued his rear and ordered all his generals to turn and return. He found that Zhang Xiu had already withdrawn. Cao’s beaten men reported, “If not for the force that blocked the mountain road behind us, all of us would have been captured.”

Cao immediately asked where they had come from. A man dismounted with lowered spear and knelt. It was Li Tong, courtesy name Wenda, Zhenwei Zhonglang-General, a native of Jiangxia Pingchun. “Where do you come from?” Cao asked.

Li Tong said, “I have recently been on garrison duty in Runan. Hearing that the Chancellor fought against Zhang Xiu and Liu Biao, I came to reinforce.”

Cao was pleased. He ennobled Li Tong as Marquis of Merit and ordered him to hold Runan’s western frontier against Liu Biao and Zhang Xiu. Li Tong thanked him and withdrew.

Cao returned to Xu, and Liu Biao reported Sun Ce’s meritorious service. Cao made Sun Ce a General Who Crushes Rebels and granted him the marquisate of Wu. He then sent an edict to Jiangdong ordering him to suppress Liu Biao.

When Cao returned to the hall, all officials had already paid their respects. Xun Yu asked, “How did you know they would certainly be defeated although you arrived slowly at Anzhong?”

Cao replied, “They had no way to return, so they had to die fighting. I tempted them forward and concealed my hidden plan. Therefore I knew they were bound to fail.”

Xun Yu offered obeisance. Guo Jia entered.

Cao said, “Why did you come so late, Counselor?”

Guo Jia drew out a letter and said, “Yuan Shao has sent an envoy to the Chancellor saying he wants to attack Gongsun Zan and asking for grain and troops.”

Cao said, “I have heard Yuan Shao wishes to strike Xu. Yet now that I have returned, he puts forward another request. I opened it and found the tone arrogant.”

He then asked Guo Jia, “Yuan Shao is so insolent. I want to punish him, but I do not yet have the power. What do you think?”

Guo Jia said, “You and I both know Liu and Xiang were not evenly matched. It was intelligence that won, not numbers. Even though Xiang Yu was formidable, he was captured in the end. Cao now has ten victories, and Yuan Shao ten defeats. Though Yuan Shao’s army is great, he is not to be feared.

Yuan Shao relies on ceremony and outward display; your natural steadiness is strength.

Yuan Shao sought fame through display, while you act with sincerity.

From Huan to Ling, policy has declined from indulgence. Yuan Shao governs by indulgence and thus fails in discipline, while you are severe when needed and precise.

Yuan Shao is outwardly generous and inwardly jealous; he appoints many kin, while you are outwardly plain and inwardly clear, choosing only the worthy. That is a decisive edge.

Yuan Shao makes many designs and few decisions, while you act at once on good counsel. That is a strategic edge.

Yuan Shao gathers reputation, while you keep loyalty through sincerity.

Yuan Shao cares for near relations and neglects distant ones; your concern is all-encompassing.

Yuan Shao is swayed by slander and confusion, while your judgment is clear.

Yuan Shao muddles right and wrong, while your laws are strict and obvious.

Yuan Shao delights in empty show and does not understand military essentials; you defeat a greater force with fewer men, and command your troops like one moved by the Way.

You have these ten advantages. Defeating Yuan Shao will not be difficult.”

Cao laughed. “If your words stand, how can I face him?”

Xun Yu said, “Guo Jia’s ten victories for your ten defeats fits exactly my view. Yuan Shao may be strong in number, but he is no fear.”

Guo Jia said, “Lü Bu in Xuzhou is our serious interior danger. Since Yuan Shao has gone north to confront Gongsun Zan, this is our chance. If we first take Lü Bu and sweep the southeast, then turn on Yuan Shao, that is best. If we go against Yuan Shao now, Lü Bu will exploit the opening and attack Xu. His damage to us will be deep.”

Cao accepted this and then discussed moving east against Lü Bu. Xun Yu said, “First send word to Liu Bei; wait for his return before mobilizing.” Cao agreed. He at once sent a letter to Liu Bei, and in full form he answered Yuan Shao’s envoy, appointing him Grand General and Grand Commandant and Chief Commander over the four states of Ji, Qing, You, and Bing. In a sealed private letter he added,

“Proceed against Gongsun Zan. I will give support.”

Yuan Shao was overjoyed and advanced to attack Gongsun Zan.

Now Lü Bu in Xuzhou was being repeatedly praised by Chen Gui and his son in every guest gathering. Chen Gong, displeased, took advantage of a chance to warn Lü Bu: “The father and son flatter your merit too much. Their hearts cannot be trusted. You must guard carefully.”

Lü Bu barked, “Why do you slander without cause and try to harm a good man?”

Chen Gong sighed, “Truthful counsel will never be welcomed here; if we speak it, we suffer with it.” He wished to leave Lü Bu and go elsewhere, but did not dare, and he was too ashamed to be laughed at. So he stayed, miserable all day.

One day he took several riders to the fields outside Pei for hunting to vent himself. A rider came galloping along the road. Suspicious, Chen Gong left the hunt and followed by a side path.

He asked, “What errand and from where do you come?”

The messenger, seeing him as a man from Lü Bu’s retinue, was flustered and could not answer at first. Chen Gong searched him and found a sealed letter from Liu Bei for Cao Cao. He took both man and letter to Lü Bu.

Lü Bu asked his reason for it.

The messenger said, “The Chancellor Cao sent me to Lord Liu of Yuzhou with this letter. I have now returned with your reply but do not know what is in it.”

Lü Bu tore open and read it.

In response to your commands, I dare not fail to apply myself night and day. Our own troops are light and few; I dare not make any rash move. If the Chancellor raises a great expedition, I shall be your vanguard. Tighten the ranks and keep the armor in order; I stand ready for your command.

When Lü Bu heard it, he was startled and said, “That bandit Cao dares speak this way!” He executed the messenger at once and then ordered Chen Gong and Zang Ba to join the bandits by Mount Tai: Sun Guan, Wu Dun, Yin Li, and Chang Xi. He sent them east to capture the commanderies of Yanzhou in Shandong.

He also ordered Gao Shun and Zhang Liao to take Pei City and attack Liu Bei. He ordered Song Xian and Wei Xu to move west and take Ru and Ying. Lü Bu kept the central army to provide reinforcement along three routes.

When Gao Shun and his men left Xuzhou and neared Xupei, someone reported the matter to Liu Bei.

Liu Bei quickly summoned his counselors. Sun Qian said, “Send urgent news to Cao Cao.”

Liu Bei said, “Who can go to Xu and ride for help?”

One man from below stepped forward: “I can.” He was Jian Yong, with courtesy name Xianhe, originally from Liu Bei’s own commandery.

Liu Bei wrote immediately and gave him the letter, ordering Jian Yong to ride through the night to Xu for aid. At the same time he had preparations made for the city’s defense.

Liu Bei held the south gate himself, Sun Qian the north gate, Yunchang the west gate, Zhang Fei the east gate. He ordered Mi Zhu and his brother Mi Fang to guard the center camp. Mi Zhu had a younger sister married to Liu Bei as a secondary wife, and Liu Bei had a sworn affinity with her brothers, so he entrusted them with the inner guard for his household.

When Gao Shun arrived, Liu Bei called out from the enemy-facing tower, “I hold no enmity with Fengxian. Why have you brought troops here?”

Gao Shun said, “You have joined Cao Cao and plan to harm my lord. Now your intent is known. Why do you not submit?”

With that, he waved his troops forward and attacked the city. Liu Bei stayed within the gate and did not come out.

The next day Zhang Liao led his men against the west gate. From the wall, Yunchang addressed him: “Your manner and bearing are not base. How did you come to fall into bandits’ hands?”

Zhang Liao lowered his head and said nothing. Yunchang saw this man had a true sense of loyalty and righteousness, and he added no insults, nor did he go out to fight.

Zhang Liao withdrew toward the east gate, and Zhang Fei rode out to meet him. Before Guan Yu came, one had reported matters.

Guan Yu hurried to the east gate. He saw Zhang Fei had just left and that Zhang Liao’s men had already pulled back. Guan Yu urged him to chase. “They withdrew out of fear; why not pursue?”

Guan Yu said, “This man is no weaker than either of us. From what he said I sense no bad spirit in him, and some remorse. For that reason he did not press battle.”

Zhang Fei understood and ordered the men to hold their own gate firmly, and not ride out again.

Now Jian Yong arrived in Xu and informed Cao Cao of what had happened. Cao then gathered his ministers.

Cao said, “I want to attack Lü Bu. I do not fear Yuan Shao’s interference. I am only concerned about Liu Biao and Zhang Xiu attacking our rear.”

Xun Yu said, “These two have only just been defeated and will not act lightly yet. Lü Bu is strong and bold. If he further joins with Yuan Shu and moves along Huai and Si, the danger will be hard and fast.”

Guo Jia said, “Now is the time. He has only just turned rebellious and the army has not fully settled to him. Strike quickly.”

Cao agreed. He ordered Xiahou Dun, Xiahou Yuan, Li Qian, and Li Dian to lead fifty thousand men ahead, while he himself followed with the main host in staggered echelons. Jian Yong went with them.

A scout soon reported to Gao Shun. Gao Shun sent the news to Lü Bu. Lü Bu first sent Hou Cheng, Hao Meng, and Cao Xing with more than two hundred riders to join Gao Shun, meet Cao’s army thirty li outside Pei, and then led his main force out to support in turn.

When Liu Bei saw that Gao Shun had turned from Xupei, he knew Cao’s army was near. He left Sun Qian to hold the city, and Mi Zhu and Mi Fang to guard the family in the center camp. He with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, raising all his troops, marched out and split camps to receive Cao’s army.

Xiahou Dun then led forward and met Gao Shun squarely, hurling his spear and horse forward to meet him. They circled and fought for forty to fifty exchanges. Gao Shun could not stand and broke and withdrew.

Xiahou Dun spurred after him; Gao Shun ran in circles to evade. Xiahou Dun did not relent and kept circling in pursuit.

From the line, Cao Xing saw them and from cover drew bow and arrow with a sure eye. He loosed one arrow that struck Xiahou Dun’s left eye. Xiahou Dun cried out and tried to pull it free with his hand; as he pulled, the eyeball came out with it. He cried out,

“By my father’s strength and my mother’s blood, I must not lose it!”

He put it in his mouth and swallowed it, then rode forward with spear in hand.

Cao Xing had no time to guard himself and was speared through the face and killed in the saddle.

The soldiers on both sides saw this and were all shaken.

After Xiahou Dun had killed Cao Xing, he turned his horse back. Gao Shun came from behind, raised his troops all at once, and pressed in. Cao’s army was crushed. Xiahou Yuan helped rescue his brother and withdrew. Li Qian and Li Dian withdrew with the broken army and camped south of Jibei.

Gao Shun gained the advantage, turned back, and moved to strike Liu Bei. Just then Lü Bu’s great army also arrived.

Lü Bu sent Zhang Liao and Gao Shun in three detachments, and they attacked Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei’s three camps from three sides.

Even a ferocious commander who fights well, once struck in the eye, cannot long hold the vanguard. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Jia Xu Reads the Enemy’s Moves and Decides Victory: Xiahou Dun Draws an Arrow Through His Eye and Swallows It

chapters.html:
Gao Shun led Zhang Liao against Guan Yu's stockade, while Lü Bu personally attacked Zhang Fei's stockade. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei each rode out to meet battle; Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, brought forces forward in two columns to support them. Lü Bu split his force and came on from behind. The armies of Guan Yu and Zhang Fei both broke. Liu Bei led a score or two riders back toward Pei City.

Lü Bu closed on him. Liu Bei rushed back to the wall to order the soldiers to lower the drawbridge. Lü Bu soon arrived. The men on the wall prepared to shoot arrows, but feared they might strike Liu Bei. Taking that opening, Lü Bu rushed through the gate. The gate guards resisted, but could not hold and scattered. Lü Bu called in his troops and entered the city. Realizing things had become urgent and home was beyond reach, Liu Bei abandoned his wife and children, slipped through the gate, rode out through the west gate, and fled on a single horse.

When Lü Bu arrived at Liu Bei's home, Mi Zhu came out to greet him and said, "I have heard that a true man does not cast aside another man's wife and children. Now the man contending with you for all under heaven is Cao Gong. Liu Bei always remembers his debt at Yuan Gate and the spear-thrust, so he dared not betray your favor. I have no choice but to have yielded to Cao Gong; I beg you to show pity to him." Lü Bu replied, "I am old friends with Liu Bei. How could I harm his wife and children?"

He told Mi Zhu to lead Liu Bei's wife and children out and settle them in Xuzhou. Lü Bu himself drew his force eastward into Shandong, to the boundary of Yanzhou, and left Gao Shun and Zhang Liao to hold Xiao Pei. By then Sun Qian had already escaped outside the city. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei each gathered some men and moved into the hills to hide.

Now Liu Bei, while fleeing on a single horse, was pursued from behind; as he rode he saw a man catch up. It was Sun Qian.

Liu Bei said, "I do not know whether my two younger brothers are alive, and my wife and children have become scattered. What should I do?" Sun Qian said, "Do not do anything rash. Go to Cao Cao for now and then think of a later plan."

Liu Bei followed his counsel and took back roads to Xuchang. On the road they ran out of grain. Whenever they entered a village in search of food, they heard of the arrival of the Governor of Yu Province, and everyone rushed to offer them wine and food.

One day they stopped at an inn. A young boy came out and bowed, asking his name. He was Liu An, a hunter.

When Liu An learned that the governor of Yu Province had arrived, he sought game for a meal but could not get any at once, so he killed his wife and prepared her for cooking. Liu Bei asked, "What meat is this?" An said, "It is wolf meat."

Liu Bei did not doubt him and ate a full meal. He stayed there overnight. At dawn he left, went to the rear court for his horse, and saw a woman dead in the kitchen, with flesh already cut from her arm. Liu Bei was startled, and then learned that the food he had just eaten was his wife's flesh. He could not hide his grief and mounted after tears.

Liu An said, "I meant to follow Your Lordship, but my old mother is in the hall. I cannot travel far with her."

Liu Bei thanked him and left, then took the road out of Liang City.

Suddenly dust darkened the sky and a mighty host came charging. Liu Bei recognized Cao Cao's army. He and Sun Qian rode straight to the main camp and met Cao Cao. They explained in full how Pei City was lost, how the two younger brothers had been separated, and how Liu Bei had lost his family. Cao Cao too was moved and shed tears. Liu Bei also described how Liu An had killed his wife for food. Cao Cao ordered Sun Qian to take one hundred taels of gold to reward him.

The army entered Jibei, and Xiahou Yuan and other officers met them on arrival, reporting that his brother Xiahou Dun had lost one eye, was bedridden, and had not yet recovered.

Cao Cao visited him at his sickbed, ordered him to return to Xuchang to recover, and at the same time sent men to find out where Lü Bu was.

A scouting rider reported, "Lü Bu has allied with Chen Gong and Zang Ba and the Mount Tai bandit bands, and together they are attacking the commanderies of Yanzhou."

Cao Cao immediately ordered Cao Ren to lead three thousand troops against Pei City. He himself marshaled the army and marched with Liu Bei to engage Lü Bu. They reached Shandong and near Xiaoguan, where they encountered bandits Sun Guan, Wu Dun, Yin Li, and Chang Xi from Mount Tai blocking the way. Cao Cao ordered Xu Chu to meet them. The four generals rode out together. Xu Chu fought fiercely, but all four could not stand and withdrew one by one. Cao Cao pressed the advantage and chased to Xiaoguan, and a courier galloped back to Lü Bu.

By then Lü Bu had returned to Xuzhou and wished to go out with Chen Deng to rescue Xiao Pei. He ordered Chen Gui to defend Xuzhou.

As Chen Deng mounted to leave, Chen Gui said, "Cao Gong once told me he had placed the eastern affairs entirely in your hands. If Bu is likely to be defeated, act while there is time." Chen Deng replied, "I can manage outside matters; if Bu loses and comes back, ask Father to hold the city with Mi Zhu and do not let Bu in. I myself will devise a way to get out." Chen Gui said, "Bu's wife and children are here, and you have many trusted men deep inside. What can be done in this case?" Chen Deng said, "I have a plan as well." He went in to report to Lü Bu.

"Xuzhou is under pressure from all four sides and Cao Cao will certainly attack with force. We must first think about withdrawing. Move the grain stores to Xiapi. If Xuzhou is besieged, Xiapi will still have supplies to help. My lord, should you not make arrangements now?" he advised.

Lü Bu answered, "Yuanlong's words are right. We should move the wife and children too." He then ordered Song Xian and Wei Xu to protect his wife, children, and grain, and to move them to Xiapi. At the same time he headed out with Chen Deng to relieve Xiaoguan. Midway, Chen Deng said, "Please let me go first and ride ahead to Xiaoguan to scout Cao's forces."

Lü Bu agreed. Chen Deng arrived there first. Chen Gong and the others met him.

Chen Deng said, "The Grand Commander is suspicious at heart that you have not advanced and is coming to blame you." Chen Gong replied, "Cao's force is now enormous. We must not challenge it lightly. Let us hold the pass tightly. We should advise my lord to hold Pei firmly; that is the best plan." Chen Deng nodded in assent.

That night he watched from the gate and saw Cao's force pressing hard against the gate below. He then wrote three letters in succession by lamplight, tied each to an arrow, and shot them down at the pass.

The next day he took leave of Chen Gong and rode hard to meet Lü Bu.

"The men at the pass—Sun Guan and the others—are all ready to surrender it. I have left Chen Gong in charge there. My lord should strike by dusk and ride out to relieve it."

Lü Bu said, "Without you, this pass is lost." He ordered Chen Deng to ride on ahead and contact Chen Gong inside, using a beacon fire as the signal.

Chen Deng reached the pass and reported immediately: "Cao's army has slipped in behind the lines and reached the pass. Xuzhou may fall. You had better return quickly." Chen Gong then withdrew the troops from the pass and ran.

Chen Deng set fire to the gate. Lü Bu moved by stealth through the dark. In the darkness, Chen Gong's men and Lü Bu's men in the confusion shot at each other.

When Cao's men saw the beacon fire, they all rushed forward and struck hard. Sun Guan and the others scattered in all directions.

Lü Bu fought on until daybreak and only then learned it was a ruse. He hurried back to Chen Gong and Xuzhou. As they reached the city gate, arrows rained down in panic.

On the enemy tower Mi Zhu shouted, "You seized my lord's city; return it now to him. You shall not enter this city again!" Lü Bu shouted back in rage, "Where is Chen Gui?" Mi Zhu replied, "I have already killed him." Lü Bu turned and asked, "Where is Chen Deng?" Chen Gong said, "My lord still asks that traitor after he has misled you so?"

Lü Bu ordered a full search through the camp, but could not find Chen Deng. Chen Gong urged him to hurry toward Xiapi. Lü Bu obeyed. Midway they encountered a massed force: Gao Shun and Zhang Liao.

Lü Bu asked how they had come. They replied, "Chen Deng came with word that the lord is besieged and we rushed to help." Chen Gong said, "This is another trick by that treacherous man." Lü Bu snapped, "I will kill that villain!" and drove on toward Xiapi.

When they reached the city, banners on the walls were all Cao's. Cao Cao had already ordered Cao Ren to storm the city and station troops.

Under the walls, Lü Bu cursed at Chen Deng. From the city Chen Deng pointed and shouted, "I am an officer of Han; how could I serve you, a rebel treacherous son?" Lü Bu became furious.

He was about to attack when a cry rose from the rear and another force arrived. In front, Zhang Fei rode out to confront him. Gao Shun engaged and could not gain an advantage. Lü Bu took to personal combat. While they fought, cries rose again from beyond the line: Cao Cao himself had led the main force and charged in.

Lü Bu judged he could not hold and drove eastward. Cao Cao's men pursued.

Lü Bu soon was exhausted and his horse spent. Suddenly a large force appeared at once to block his road. Their frontman, mounted, unsheathed his sabre and shouted, "Lü Bu, do not run! Here is Guan Yunlong!".

Lü Bu rushed into melee, and Zhang Fei came on behind him. Lü Bu had no wish to prolong the fight; he cut his way through with Chen Gong and bolted toward Xiapi. Hou Cheng came out to assist.

When Guan Yu and Zhang Fei finally met, both wept and spoke of their separation. Guan Yu said, "I had been bivouacking along the route to Hai Province. I caught wind of the news and came straight here." Zhang Fei said, "My brother has been camping on Mangdang Mountain for some time now. I am glad we met today."

After speaking a while they came together with their troops to meet Liu Bei and knelt on the ground to bow in grief and joy.

Liu Bei's sorrow and happiness mingled together. He brought both men before Cao Cao, then went with him to Xuchang.

Mi Zhu received them and reported that Liu Bei's family had been unharmed. Liu Bei was deeply relieved. Chen Gui and his son came as well to pay court to Cao Cao.

Cao Cao held a grand banquet and rewarded the generals. He sat in the center, with Chen Gui on the left and Liu Bei on the right; the other officers were seated in order.

After the banquet, Cao Cao praised Chen Gui and his son, granted him ten thousand households in stipend, and promoted Chen Deng to the General Who Subdues the Waves.

When Cao Cao had gained Xuzhou, he rejoiced and discussed raising troops to attack Xiapi. Cheng Yu said, "Lü Bu now has only Xiapi. If we press him too tightly he will fight to the death and then throw himself with Yuan Shu. If he combines with Yuan Shu, he will be hard to break. Keep people who can hold the Huainan route; defend inside against Lü Bu and outside against Yuan Shu. And as long as Zang Ba and Sun Guan and their men in Shandong have not submitted, they too must be watched."

Cao Cao said, "I will take all the roads in Shandong. The Huainan route should be entrusted to you, Liu Bei." Liu Bei replied, "As the Chancellor commands, dare I disobey?"

The next day Liu Bei left Mi Zhu and Jian Yong in Xuzhou and took Sun Qian, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei with troops to guard the Huainan route. Cao Cao himself led the army against Xiapi.

Now in Xiapi, Lü Bu trusted himself because he had enough grain and relied on Sishui's dangers and thought himself secure in defense. Chen Gong said, "Now that Cao's army has only just arrived, this is the moment to strike while he is unsettled. We should attack him while he is tired; there is nothing he cannot lose."

Lü Bu replied, "I have suffered too many defeats to charge recklessly. Wait until he attacks, and then we will fight. He will all fall in Sishui." He did not take Chen Gong's advice.

After several days, the Cao troops made their camp stable. Cao Cao and the assembled host moved to the base of the wall and called aloud for Lü Bu to answer. Lü Bu climbed the wall and stood there.

Cao Cao said, "I hear that you are seeking a marriage alliance with Yuan Shu. I led this force for that reason. Yuan Shu is a rebel against the state, yet you, who once won merit in punishing Dong Zhuo, have now abandoned your former accomplishments and joined with a rebellious villain. If this city falls, your regret will come too late. If you come now to submit and help restore the Son of Heaven, you need not lose your chance for a marquisate."

Lü Bu said, "Chancellor, withdraw for now and allow me time to negotiate."

Chen Gong, standing beside him, loudly denounced Cao Cao as a villain. One of Lü Bu's arrows struck his banner shelter. Cao Cao pointed at him and swore, "I swear I will kill you!" Then he ordered the attack.

Chen Gong said to Lü Bu, "Cao Cao has come from far off and cannot remain long. My lord can send out horse and foot to camp outside, while I will keep most of our men in the city. If Cao attacks your troops, I will strike at his rear. If he attacks the city, you will send men to relieve him from behind. In less than ten days his provisions will run out, and one push will break him. This is a favorable posture."

Lü Bu agreed and returned to make his final military preparations. The winter was already at hand, and he told his attendants to carry warm cloaks.

Lü Bu's wife Yan heard and came out to ask, "My lord, where will you go?" He told her of Chen Gong's plan.

Yan said, "You would abandon the whole city, cast aside wife and children, and ride out with a small force alone. If something goes wrong, how can I still be your wife?"

Lü Bu delayed three days and did not emerge. Chen Gong entered and said, "Cao's troops now encircle the city from every side. If we do not act early, we will be trapped." Lü Bu answered, "I think it would be better to remain and hold than to ride far." Chen Gong said, "I recently heard that Cao's grain is already running low. Send out your picked troops to cut his supply route. That is an excellent plan."

Lü Bu considered this, then returned inside and told Yan again.

Yan wept and said, "If you ride out, can Chen Gong, Gao Shun, and so on hold the city? If even one small lapse occurs, regret will be too late. Once I was in Chang'an, you once discarded me. I survived only because Pang Shu hid me; only then did I meet you again. Who is to say you will not cast me off again? My lord has ten thousand li ahead. Do not hold me back for his sake." She wept.

Lü Bu was weighed down with sorrow and uncertainty. He then went to Diaochan. Diaochan said, "We are one household. Do not ride out in reckless haste."

Lü Bu answered, "Do not worry. I have the Chi Mian horse. Who dares come near me?" He then told Chen Gong, "Cao's grain has arrived and all this is deception. Cao is full of tricks; I dare not move yet."

Chen Gong sighed, "If this is so, there is no place where we shall have proper burial."

So Lü Bu did not ride out all that day, drinking with Yan and Diaochan to dispel his gloom. Adviser Xu Si and Wang Kai came with a plan:

"Yuan Shu has now risen in Huainan with increasing momentum. Since Your Lordship once promised marriage, you should ask again. If his troops arrive, they can attack from both inside and out, and Cao will be hard to break."

Lü Bu accepted and the very same day had letters written, sending Xu Si and Wang Kai ahead with them.

Xu Si said, "You still need a force to lead the way out." Lü Bu ordered Zhang Liao and Hao Meng to lead one thousand men out through the pass.

At the second watch that night, Zhang Liao rode ahead and Hao Meng followed, escorting Xu Si and Wang Kai out of the city. They slipped past Liu Bei's stockade; pursuing commanders failed to catch them before they passed the gate.

Hao Meng led five hundred men to follow Xu Si and Wang Kai. Zhang Liao returned with half of his men and when he reached the pass, Guan Yu blocked him.

Before they could close, Gao Shun rode out and came to give relief. He then re-entered the city.

Xu Si and Wang Kai reached Shouchun and presented themselves to Yuan Shu, presenting their petition. Yuan Shu said, "You once killed my envoy, and yet relied on our marriage arrangement for protection. Why come now asking this again?"

Xu Si said, "It was all due to Cao Cao's treacherous stratagem. Your Grace should understand." Yuan Shu replied, "Your lord did not offer his daughter while under pressure from Cao's troops; why now?"

Wang Kai said, "If my lord is not rescued, your fortune too will be in danger. If the mouth is lost, the teeth grow cold; that would be no blessing for Your Excellency."

Yuan Shu said, "Lü Bu is utterly unsteady and untrustworthy. Send the woman first, and then send troops." Xu Si and Wang Kai had no choice but to bow and return with Hao Meng.

Back near Liu Bei's stockade, they made arrangements. They were not to travel by daylight. At midnight Xu Si and Wang Kai would go first, while Hao Meng covered their retreat.

Late in the night they crossed first. As Hao Meng then moved, Zhang Fei rode out from camp and blocked the way.

Hao Meng and his horse met for a single exchange, and Zhang Fei captured him alive. His five hundred men and horses were cut down. Zhang Fei brought Hao Meng before Liu Bei and took him to Cao Cao. Hao Meng explained the request about sending a wife to secure help.

Cao Cao was furious and beheaded him at the military gate. He then ordered notices sent to all camps: remain alert, hold your posts; if any of Lü Bu or his men escape through a breach, they are to be punished by military law. The camps were all startled.

Liu Bei returned to camp and instructed Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, "The Huainan route is now a critical crossing. You both must keep careful watch and not violate Cao Gong's military order."
