Zhang Fei said, "I captured one bandit officer, and Cao Cao did not reward him richly. He only came to terrify us. Why is that?" Liu Bei said, "No. Cao Cao leads much force. Without orders, how could he command men? Do not disobey him."

Guan Yu and Zhang Fei answered and withdrew.

Now Xu Si and Wang Kai returned to Lü Bu and reported all: Yuan Shu wanted the marriage first before moving troops. Lü Bu asked, "How can this be done?"

Xu Si said, "Hao Meng has now been captured, so Cao surely knows our purpose and has prepared. Unless Your Lord personally escorts her, who can break through the encirclement?"

Lü Bu said, "Can we send today?" Xu Si replied, "Today is an inauspicious day for spirits. Do not go." "Tomorrow is auspicious; use the hour of the Dog and Pig."

Lü Bu ordered Zhang Liao and Gao Shun to take three thousand horse and men, and to ready one small cart. "I will escort her out two hundred li and then let both of you take over."

At the second watch of the next night, Lü Bu wrapped the woman in padded cotton, packed her in armor, and carried her on his back before mounting. He opened the gate and rode out first; Zhang Liao and Gao Shun followed.

They had almost reached before Liu Bei's stockade when a drum sounded. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei blocked the road and shouted, "Do not run!"

Lü Bu was in no mood to linger in battle. He cut a path and pushed forward. Liu Bei led a column in pursuit, and the two forces collided in close combat.

Lü Bu was brave, but he had a woman bound on his back and feared harming her, so he did not force through the hardest fighting. Behind him Xu Huang and Xu Chu arrived, and the whole ranks shouted, "Do not let him slip away!"

Seeing the enemy come too swiftly, Lü Bu withdrew into the city. Liu Bei pulled back his troops. Xu Huang and Xu Chu returned to their camps. Not one broke through.

Lü Bu entered the city again and only drank in bitterness.

When Cao Cao had besieged the city for two months without success, a report came: "The Inspector of Henei, Zhang Yang, has marched out to Dongshi to aid Lü Bu. One of Cao's officers, Yang Chou, killed him and wished to present his head to the Chancellor. Yet Zhang Yang's trusted attendant Sui Gu killed him and then turned to Qun City."

Cao Cao heard it and immediately dispatched Shi Huan to pursue and execute Sui Gu.

He gathered his commanders and said, "Although Zhang Yang has ruined himself, there remain concerns to the north with Yuan Shao and in the east with Biao and Xiu, and Xiapi has not fallen despite long siege. I may return to the capital and rest from this campaign for now. What do you say?" Xun You urged against delay.

"No," he said. "Lü Bu has been defeated too often; his edge has dulled. When the commander fails, an army loses heart. Chen Gong's plan is clever but slow. Lü Bu has already lost momentum and Chen Gong's own plan is not settled. If we strike now, we can seize him."

Guo Jia said, "I have one stratagem; Xiapi can be broken and won more surely than with twenty ten-thousand armies." Xun Yu asked, "Could it be the waters of Yi and Si?" Guo Jia laughed. "You see it exactly."

Cao Cao rejoiced and ordered the troops to open and control the waters of both rivers. Cao's soldiers took the high ground and watched as Xiapi was submerged. In the city only the east gate remained un-flooded; all other gates were under water. The alarm sounded through the camps and reached Lü Bu.

Lü Bu said, "I have the Chi Mian horse. For me, crossing water is like level ground. What need I fear?" So the whole day he drank and caroused with wife and concubines. Overindulgence in wine and flesh weakened his appearance. The next day, seeing himself in a mirror, he said, "I have harmed myself by wine and women. From this day on, I must restrain myself." He then ordered that anyone drinking in the city be executed.

At this time Hou Cheng had fifteen horses, but rear guardsmen stole them and wanted to offer them to Liu Bei. When Hou Cheng discovered this, he pursued, killed the men, and recovered the horses. The other commanders met and congratulated him. Hou Cheng brewed six or seven hu of wine and wanted to drink with all the commanders. Fearing Lü Bu's wrath, he first presented five bottles at Lü Bu's headquarters: "By General's tiger-like might, I recovered the stolen horses. The officers all gathered to rejoice and brewed this much wine. We dared not drink it. Please accept it as our small regard."

Lü Bu raged. "I banned drinking, and you brew wine to drink in celebration. Are you conspiring to rebel against me?" He ordered Hou Cheng brought out and beheaded.

Song Xian, Wei Xu and the other officers went in together to plead. Lü Bu said, "You broke my order, so death is right. But seeing you all, I'll strike one hundred lashes and then release you."

He had him flogged fifty lashes and then let him go. The commanders all despaired.

Song Xian and Wei Xu went to visit Hou Cheng at home. Hou Cheng cried, "Without you men, I am already dead." Song Xian said, "General Lü is attached only to wife and children and sees us as weeds." Wei Xu said, "We are ringed below the city walls. With water around the moat, we have no end to our lives." Song Xian said, "Lü Bu has no kindness or justice. Why should we remain and follow him?" Wei Xu said, "You are no man. Better to capture Lü Bu and present him to Cao Cao."

Hou Cheng said, "I was blamed for chasing the stolen horses, and what Lü Bu relies on is the Chi Mian horse. If you two truly can capture him and surrender him through the gate, I will first take that horse and go to Cao Cao."

The three made their arrangements. That night Hou Cheng slipped quietly into the stable at the back, stole the horse, and rode out to the east gate. Wei Xu opened the gate and feigned pursuit as Hou Cheng left.

Hou Cheng reached Cao Cao's encampment and offered the horse, explaining that Song Xian and Wei Xu would raise white banners as signals and were preparing to surrender.

Cao Cao heard and ordered dozens of placards shot into the city. They read:

The Grand General Cao has this day carried down a clear imperial command to campaign against Lü Bu. Whoever opposes the main army and the day the walls are broken, his entire household will be exterminated. From the highest generals to commoners, whoever can capture Lü Bu and bring him in, or bring his severed head, will be richly rewarded. This edict is to be proclaimed to all.

At daybreak the next morning, shouts shook the ground outside.

Lü Bu started up in alarm, lifted his spear, and moved to the gate. He inspected each gateway and was still furious, cursing that Song Xian had broken through and Hou Cheng escaped, and that his battle horse was lost and punishment now awaited him.

The Cao troops saw white banners on the wall and redoubled their attack. Lü Bu had to lead his defense himself.

From dawn until noon they fought. Cao's troops withdrew slightly. Lü Bu took a brief rest in the gatehouse and, without realizing it, fell asleep in a chair.

Song Xian drove the attendants away, first stole his halberd, then together with Wei Xu wrestled him down. They wound him tight with rope and bound him in a tight bundle.

Lü Bu awoke with a start, calling out to his attendants, but they were all already dead, having been killed by the two. Seeing the white flags raised, Cao's men rushed to the wall.

Wei Xu cried, "Lü Bu has been captured alive!" Xiahou Yuan still did not believe it.

Song Xian then tossed Lü Bu's halberd out and flung the gates wide. Cao's troops surged in. Gao Shun and Zhang Liao were at the west gate. Water blocked their escape, and Cao's men captured them. Chen Gong ran to the south gate and was seized by Xu Huang.

Cao Cao entered the city, ordered the water released, and published calming proclamations. At once he sat beside Liu Bei on White Gate Tower with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei at his side as the captured men were presented.

Though Lü Bu was large and imposing, he was bound tightly in rope into one bundle. Lü Bu said, "The binding is too tight. I beg to have it loosened." Cao Cao answered, "To bind a tiger one must be quick."

Lü Bu saw that Hou Cheng, Wei Xu, and Song Xian stood nearby and said, "I was not unkind to the officers. How could you betray me then?" Song Xian said, "You would not heed wife and concubines or counsel from your advisers. How is that not neglect?"

Lü Bu was silent. In due time they brought Gao Shun in. Cao Cao asked, "Do you have any words?" Gao Shun did not answer. Cao Cao ordered him executed.

Xu Huang then brought in Chen Gong. Cao Cao asked, "Are you in good health, Master Gongtai?" Chen Gong answered, "Your heart is not upright. I left you for that reason." Cao Cao said, "My heart is not upright. Why did you alone stand by Lü Bu?" Chen Gong replied, "Lü Bu has no planning; he is not like your crooked villainy." Cao Cao said, "You claimed yourself full of wisdom. How has it proven itself now?"

Chen Gong looked at Lü Bu and said, "I hate that this man would not follow my words. If he had, he might not have been captured." Cao Cao asked, "What is to be done now?" Chen Gong raised his voice: "For today, there is only death."

Cao Cao asked, "If so, what of your aged mother and your wife and children?" Chen Gong answered, "I have learned that one who governs with filiality does not harm others' kin, and one who rules with benevolence does not sever ancestral rites. The fate of my mother and wife and children now rests with Your Excellency. Since I am already captured, ask only for my execution."

Cao Cao's heart still wavered. Chen Gong strode down the steps at once, but his attendants could not hold him back. Cao Cao rose and with tears accompanied him. Chen Gong did not look back.

Cao Cao told his attendants, "Take Master Gongtai's mother and wife back to Xuchang so they can live out old age. If you are lax, you die." Chen Gong heard it and spoke no more. He stretched his neck out to death.

The men around wept.

Cao Cao placed Chen Gong's body in a coffin and buried it at Xuchang. Later people composed a verse:

Life and death have no divided aims; how grand was this man! He refused to follow gold and stone, and in the end failed his beams and rafters. Truly worthy to assist the ruler, yet truly sorrowful in the matter of kinship. On the day Master Gongtai died at the White Gate, who could rival him?

As Cao escorted Chen Gong down the steps, Lü Bu said to Liu Bei, "You are the honored guest above, while I am the prisoner below. Why do you not speak one word and show me mercy?" Liu Bei nodded. When Cao returned to the upper floor, Lü Bu called out: "Your trouble is only Lü Bu. Now that he has submitted, the Great General is your master and Lü Bu your deputy. The world need not be difficult to settle."

Cao Cao asked Liu Bei, "What do you say?" Liu Bei answered, "Have you not seen what happened with Ding Jianyang and Dong Zhuo?" Lü Bu stared at Liu Bei and said, "You are the least dependable of all sons!"

Cao Cao ordered him hauled down and hanged.

Lü Bu turned to Liu Bei and cried, "Great-eared man! Do you not remember the spear thrust at Yuan Gate?"

There was another verse on Liu Bei:

To bind a starved tiger as prisoner and hold back is sheer slowness; Blood from Dong Zhuo and Ding Yuan had not yet dried. Now that Liu Bei already knows how to devour his father, why did he spare Cao and conceal it?

Suddenly a man shouted, "Lü Bu was a mere man to kill. If death is his fate, let him die. Why fear it?" The soldiers' eyes turned and saw the execution squad bringing in Zhang Liao.

Cao Cao pointed at Zhang Liao. "This man's face is fine." Zhang Liao said, "I met you in Puyang city. How could I forget?" Cao Cao said with a smile, "You still remember." Zhang Liao said, "It is a pity only." Cao Cao asked, "Why is that?" Zhang Liao said, "Only that on that day the flames were not fierce, else you could have burned this traitor of the state."

Cao Cao became angry and said, "How can a defeated general dare insult me?" He drew his sword in his own hand and came forward to kill Zhang Liao. Zhang Liao showed no fear and held out his neck to receive the stroke.

Cao Cao had an arm grabbed from behind and another man step before him. The man said, "Chancellor, do not strike yet!"

Then another verse was sung:

Beg for pity for Lü Bu and not a single man came to aid him. Yet he blamed and cursed, and Zhang Liao still survived. Who in the end will save Zhang Liao?
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: At Xiapi City, Cao Cao Waged Battle; Lü Bu Fell at the White Gate Tower

chapters.html:
Cao Cao raised his sword to strike Zhang Liao. Liu Bei stepped forward and grabbed his arm. Guan Yu knelt before him. Liu Bei said, “This is a man of true loyalty and sincerity. Such a one ought to be kept.” Guan Yu said, “I, Guan Yunchang, have long known Wenyuan to be a man of loyalty and righteousness, and I am willing to stake my life to protect him.” Cao Cao tossed the sword aside and laughed. “I knew Wenyuan was loyal and righteous, so I was only playing a trick.” He personally untied him, gave him fresh clothes, and invited him to take a seat beside him. Wenyuan understood his intent and submitted.

Cao Cao appointed him Zhonglang General and granted him the marquisate of Guannei. He ordered him to pacify Zang Ba. When Zang Ba heard that Lü Bu was dead and that Zhang Liao had submitted, he also led his main force to yield. Cao Cao rewarded him richly.

Zang Ba next persuaded Sun Guan, Wu Dun, and Yin Li to submit, but Chang Xi alone would not acknowledge him. Cao Cao made Zang Ba the Governor of Langye. Sun Guan and the others each received offices and were ordered to guard the coast in Qing and Xu. He had Lü Bu’s wives and children brought back to Xu.

After giving substantial rewards to the three armies, he ordered the encampment withdrawn and the troops to march back. When passing through Xu Province, the people burned incense and lined the road, begging Liu Bei to remain as administrator. Cao Cao said, “Liu Bei has great merit. Wait until I give him an appointment and title. To return later will not be delayed.” The people knelt in thanks.

Cao Cao summoned Che Zhi Quan, General of Chariots and Cavalry, and put him in charge of Xu Province. Cao Cao’s army then returned to Xuchang, where he distributed rewards among those who had gone out and campaigned, then left Liu Bei in a residence near the Chancellor’s house to recover.

The next day, the Former Emperor held court. Cao Cao submitted his account of Liu Bei’s services and sought audience for him.

Liu Bei, dressed in formal court robes, knelt on the altar terrace. The Emperor ascended the upper hall and asked, “Who is your ancestor?”

Liu Bei said, “Your servant is a descendant of the Emperor Jing of Han, of King Liu Sheng of Zhongshan. I am Liu Xiong’s grandson and Liu Hong’s son.”

The Emperor ordered the imperial genealogical register brought and had the Master of Lineages read it aloud:

Emperor Jing had fourteen sons. His seventh was Liu Sheng, King Jing of Zhongshan.

Liu Sheng had Liu Zhen, the Marquis of Lucheng Pavilion.

Liu Zhen had Liu Ang, the Marquis of Pei.

Liu Ang had Liu Luo, the Marquis of Zhang.

Liu Luo had Liu Lian, the Marquis of Yishui.

Liu Lian had Liu Ying, the Marquis of Qingyang.

Liu Ying had Liu Jian, the Marquis of Anguo.

Liu Jian had Liu Ai, the Marquis of Guangling.

Liu Ai had Liu Xian, the Marquis of Jiaoshu.

Liu Xian had Liu Shu, the Marquis of Zuyi.

Liu Shu had Liu Yi, the Marquis of Qiyang.

Liu Yi had Liu Bi, the Marquis of Yuanzhe.

Liu Bi had Liu Da, the Marquis of Yingchuan.

Liu Da had Liu Buyi, the Marquis of Fengling.

Liu Buyi had Liu Hui, the Marquis of Jichuan.

Liu Hui had Liu Xiong, the magistrate of Fanyu in Dongjun.

Liu Xiong had Liu Hong.

Liu Hong did not enter office. Liu Bei was the son of Liu Hong.

The Emperor checked the register and saw that Liu Bei was indeed his uncle. He rejoiced and invited him into the side hall for uncle-nephew audience. The Emperor thought inwardly, Cao Cao has taken control of the state. The affairs of the realm no longer proceed by my will. Now that I have found this hero as my uncle, he will surely help me. So he appointed Liu Bei as Left General and Marquis of Yicheng Pavilion.

A banquet was held. After honoring him, Liu Bei offered thanks and left court. From then on, everyone called him “Imperial Uncle Liu” (Liu Huangshu).

When Cao Cao returned home, Xun Yu and other advisors were ushered in and said, “Now that the emperor has recognized Liu Bei as his uncle, it may not do much for your benefit, my lord.”

Cao Cao replied, “If he is already recognized as the Imperial Uncle, then if I command it through an imperial edict, he will be even less likely to dare disobey. As for keeping him in Xuchang, he may be near me in name, but truly under my control. What should I fear?” He continued, “What I worry about is Grand Commandant Yang Biao. He is kin to Yuan Shu, and if he coordinates with the two Yuans, their inner collusion could do grave harm. Remove him at once.”

He then sent men secretly to accuse Biao of secret dealings with Yuan Shu. Biao was arrested and brought before the court, and Cao Cao ordered Man Chong to investigate.

At this time, Kong Rong, the Administrator of Beihai, happened to be in Xuchang and remonstrated with Cao Cao: “Yang Gong has kept himself pure through four generations. Can we punish him merely because of ties to the Yuans?” Cao Cao replied, “It is how this court works.”

Kong Rong said, “If King Cheng had killed the Shang Gong, could the Zhou Gong fail to speak out?”

With no better course, Cao Cao discharged Biao from office and sent him back to farming.

An adviser named Zhao Yin submitted a memorial, charging Cao Cao with usurping imperial authority and summarily arresting high ministers. Cao Cao grew furious, seized Zhao Yin, and had him killed. Then all officials were stricken with dread.

Cheng Yu advised Cao Cao, “My lord, your name and influence rise daily. Why not take this opportunity and act as a hegemon king?” Cao Cao answered, “There are still many in the court who act as the state’s shoulders and arms. It is not yet the moment for a light move. I will ask the emperor for a hunt, so we can observe how things stand.”

Cao Cao then chose excellent horses, renowned hawks, and swift hunting dogs, with bows and arrows in readiness. He first gathered troops outside the city and then petitioned to take the emperor on a hunt.

The Emperor replied, “A hunt can hardly be said to be the correct way.”

Cao Cao said, “The emperors of old practiced spring pasture, summer planting rites, autumn hunting, and winter drives. Four times in the year they rode out to the suburbs to display martial vigor before the realm. In these times when all under Heaven is in turmoil, this is exactly the moment to use a hunt to rehearse arms.”

The Emperor could not refuse. He mounted the Xiaoyao horse and set out with bow, jeweled-hawk quiver, and gold-tipped arrows in hand. Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei each bent their bows, nocked arrows, wore armor beneath their robes, took up weapons, and followed with several dozen cavalry.

Cao Cao rode a claw-yellow horse that flew like lightning and, with a host of one hundred thousand, hunted with the emperor at Xu Field.

The soldiers of the host opened a ring. The encirclement spread over more than two hundred li. Cao Cao and the emperor rode side by side, keeping only one horse-length between them. Behind came Cao Cao’s close officers and retainers. Ministers and military officials followed at a distance, and none dared come near.

That day, when the emperor reached Xu Field, Liu Bei was positioned by the roadside. The emperor said, “I wish to see the Imperial Uncle Liu shoot in the hunt.”

Liu Bei mounted on command. Suddenly a rabbit burst from the grass. He shot; the arrow struck dead-center. The emperor cheered.

After circling a mound of earth, they saw a large stag break from the thorns. The emperor shot three arrows, none of them true, and said to Cao Cao, “You try.” Cao Cao took the emperor’s prized hawk bow and the gold-tipped arrows and loosed one shot that struck the stag’s back and sent it down into the grass.

Officers and court guards saw only those gold-tipped arrows and assumed the emperor had made the kill. They shouted cheers and praised him.

Cao Cao drove straight through the line, placing himself in front of the emperor to receive the applause. The crowd turned white.

Behind, Guan Yu’s rage flared. He raised the ridged brows and eyes like vermilion phoenixes, drew his sword, and leaned into the saddle, ready to strike Cao Cao down.

Liu Bei saw this and frantically shook his hand and gestured. Seeing his brother so, Guan Yu did not move.

Liu Bei bowed to Cao Cao and said, “The Chancellor is an archer whose skill even history cannot match.”

Cao Cao laughed. “That was the emperor’s good fortune.” He turned back toward the emperor and offered congratulations. He did not return the hawk bow, but kept it on himself.

After the encampment was cleared, the party feasted at Xu Field, then returned to Xuchang and the participants dispersed.

Guan Yu asked Liu Bei, “Cao is a villain who deceives the throne and tramples on superior authority. I want to kill him and remove this danger to the realm. Why do you restrain me?”

Liu Bei replied, “Throwing a mouse into a crock makes one hesitate to use any vessel.” Cao Cao and the emperor were only a horse-length apart, and his trusted men ringed them closely. If you act on sudden anger and the matter fails, it will harm the emperor, and blame will fall on us.”

Guan Yu said, “If we do not kill this villain now, it will only become disaster later.”

Liu Bei said, “Keep this inside us. Do not speak of it lightly.”

When the emperor returned to the palace, he spoke in tears to Empress Fu: “Since I ascended the throne, one rogue tyrant after another has risen. First we suffered Dong Zhuo’s disaster, then the turmoil of Huo and San. No one else has borne this burden except you and me. We later accepted Cao Cao as a minister who would serve the state, yet he has seized the state’s power, arrogating authority and dispensing rewards and punishments without my command. Every time I face him, it is like a thorn scratching my back. Today, in the hunting grounds, he had me receive his compliments publicly and in person. That is the height of impropriety! He will surely scheme someday. You and I do not know when death will come for us!”

Empress Fu said, “All the high ministers at court eat Han stipends, and not one can rescue the kingdom from danger.”

Before they finished speaking, someone entered from outside and said, “Your Majesty and Empress, set aside your worries. I can produce one man who could eliminate this threat.”

The emperor looked up and recognized him as his father-in-law, Fu Wan. He said, wiping his tears, “Your Honor too knows how Cao, this villain, is overbearing?”

Fu Wan said, “Everyone saw the hunt at Xu Field. If there is any who is not of Cao’s family, it is his underling circles. If it is not my kin, who would remain to punish this villain with sincerity? I have no official power, and the task is hard. But General of Chariots and Cavalry, your Imperial Uncle Dong Cheng, can be entrusted.”

The emperor said, “Dong Cheng, the imperial uncle, has repeatedly gone out to my aid in trouble. I know him well indeed. Summon him inside so we can discuss major state matters.”

Fu Wan said, “Your Majesty is surrounded by ministers loyal to Cao. If this leaks, the disaster will be deep.”

The emperor answered, “Then what can be done?”

Fu Wan replied, “Make one robe and one jade belt. Give him the belt as an honor. Stitch inside the lining a secret edict for him. Let him return home by night and day and shape a plan; spirits and ghosts will not see it.”

The emperor accepted this plan. Fu Wan withdrew.

The emperor drafted a secret decree himself, bit the tip of his finger, and wrote it in blood. He secretly instructed Empress Fu to sew it inside a layer of purple brocade on the jade belt. He then donned the same brocade robe, tied the belt, and ordered the court usher to present Dong Cheng.

When Dong Cheng entered and paid respects, the emperor said, “My lord, last night I spoke with the empress about the hardships by the Bahe River. I know your great service to your uncle-by-marriage, so I have called you only to offer comfort and thanks.” Dong Cheng kowtowed and thanked him.

The emperor led him out of the audience hall to the ancestral temple, then into the Hall of Meritorious Ministers. After offering incense and ritual, he showed him the painted images there. In their midst hung the portrait of Emperor Gaozu of Han. The emperor said, “Where did our founding emperor begin his life, and how did he begin his undertaking?”

Dong Cheng answered, “How can your majesty mock your minister so?” Then, with composure, he said, “Your highness’s honored grandfather began at Sipang Pavilion, took up a three-foot sword, and rose in the Snake-Rebellion; he marched in all directions across the four seas. In three years he brought down Qin, and in five years he overthrew Chu, winning the realm and laying foundations for ten thousand generations.”

The emperor said, “Our ancestor was such a hero while his descendants are so cowardly. Is this not a matter for lament?” He pointed to two paintings near him and said, “Are these not Lord Liu, Zhang Liang, and Marquis Zang, Xiao He?”

Dong Cheng said, “Yes, your majesty.”

The emperor replied, “Han Gaozu built this realm and founded this state relying on those two men.”

Then the emperor glanced around and, in a low voice, said, “You should likewise stand at my side as those two once did.”

Dong Cheng said, “I have no merit. How can I stand at your side?”

The emperor said, “Your service in rescuing me at Xiadu has not been forgotten. I have nothing else worthy of giving you.” He touched his own robe and belt and said, “Wear this robe and belt and tie this belt often. Imagine I am by your side.”

Dong Cheng knelt deeply and thanked him. The emperor removed the robe and belt and presented them to him and whispered privately, “When you return home, examine this carefully and do not disappoint my intent.”

Dong Cheng understood, put on the robe, tied the belt, and, after thanking the emperor, withdrew from the hall.

Not long after, someone reported to Cao Cao: “His Majesty spoke with Dong Cheng in the Hall of Meritorious Ministers.” Cao Cao entered court at once.

When Dong Cheng came out of the hall and had just passed the palace gate, he chanced to meet Cao Cao. With no place to slip away, he stood to the side of the road and offered formal salutation.

Cao Cao asked, “Why is the imperial uncle here?”

Dong Cheng said, “The emperor had just summoned him, and this robe and jade belt were imperial rewards.”

Cao Cao said, “Why were you granted these?”

Dong Cheng said, “It was for the old service of rescue in Xiadu. That alone won me this gift.”

Cao Cao said, “Take off the belt so I can see it.”

Dong Cheng knew there must be a secret hidden there, and he feared Cao Cao might discover it, so he delayed. Cao Cao shouted at those nearby, “Unfasten it at once!” After looking for quite some time, he laughed and said, “It is indeed a fine jade belt. Take off the robe too; let me see.”

Dong Cheng, fearful in his heart, dared not refuse and removed the robe. Cao Cao lifted it with his own hands and, in the sunlight, studied it closely. After he had finished, he put it on himself and tied the jade belt. He turned to his attendants and asked, “How does it fit?” They praised it.

He said to Dong Cheng, “So the imperial uncle has returned these same robes and belt to me?”

Dong Cheng replied, “It is a gift from Your Excellency. I dare not return it as a favor. I can make another and give my devotion.”

Cao Cao said, “The imperial uncle received this robe and belt from the Son of Heaven. Why should I take them from him? It was just a joke.” He then removed and returned robe and belt to Dong Cheng.

Dong Cheng bowed farewell and returned home.

At night he sat alone in his study and examined the robe repeatedly. No object appeared. He thought, “The emperor gave me this robe and belt and ordered close inspection. Surely he did not do so without meaning. Why is there no sign now?”

He then checked the jade belt. It was milky white jade carved into small, delicate dragons set through the flowers, with purple-cotton backing and careful stitching. There was nothing there either.

Still doubtful, he laid it on the table and searched again and again. After a long time, exhaustion took him. As he was about to lie down, a lamp ember fell onto the belt and caught the lining alight. He put it out in alarm, but one patch had burned open, exposing a strip of plain white silk and a faintly visible blood mark. He quickly took up a knife, split it open, and found the emperor’s handwritten blood secret order.

The decree read:

*I know that in human relations, sonship comes first, and parent to child is first of all. Of hierarchical order, ruler and ministers are the most weighty. Of late, the bandit Cao has monopolized authority and oppressed the Son of Heaven and his father; he has formed a coterie and ruined the court order. He issues rewards and punishments without my command. I have worried through the night and day, fearing that all under Heaven will be imperiled. You are one of the state’s great ministers and my own closest relative. Recall how the High Emperor founded this state with such hardship. Join the loyal and upright with a single mind, annihilate the treacherous clan, and restore the peace of the realm. Our ancestors will take joy in this.

I broke my finger and wrote this in blood. I send this edict to you. Be doubly careful and do not fail my wish!

Edict, spring, third month, fourth year of Jian’an.*

Dong Cheng read it to the end. Tears of grief and rage rose; he could not sleep all night. At dawn he returned to the study, looked again and again at the edict, and found no way to act. He placed it on the desk, then sat in deep thought, trying to devise the means to kill Cao. He lay back, half asleep.

At that moment, Wang Zifu, the Court Gentleman, arrived. The gatekeeper, aware that Wang Zifu was close to Dong Cheng, did not block him and he entered directly into the study.

He saw Dong Cheng lying still in a half-nodding stupor, with plain silk from the edict tucked beneath his sleeve, peeking out with the character “朕” showing. He looked at it silently, then quickly slipped it into his sleeve and called out, “Imperial Uncle, how are you so comfortable? How can you sleep through this?”

Dong Cheng jolted awake and, seeing the edict gone, seemed to lose spirit in his limbs and body. Wang Zifu said, “If you want to kill Minister Cao, I will offer my head.”

Dong Cheng wept and said, “If you do that, the Han house will be lost.”

Wang Zifu said, “I am only jesting. Our ancestors all served the Han revenues for generations. Are we without loyalty? I am willing to lend one arm to brotherly aid. Let us together execute the state-destroying traitor.”

Dong Cheng said, “Brother, this means great fortune for the realm.”

Wang Zifu said, “Let us write a declaration of justice in private and each abandon three clans in common punishment for this, so that we may answer the Han lord.”

Dong Cheng was delighted. He took a strip of white silk and first wrote his name. Wang Zifu did the same.

Then Wang said, “General Wuzilan is very close to me and can conspire with us.”

Dong Cheng said, “Among all ministers, only Colonel Zhong Ji of the Changshui unit and Registrar Wu Shuo are trusted in my innermost circle; they can stand with me.”

As he was speaking, a house servant entered to report that Zhong Ji and Wu Shuo had come to call.

Dong Cheng said, “Heaven has assisted me.” He told Wang Zifu to hide for now behind the screen. He then received the two in the study. They sat, drank tea.

Zhong Ji said, “Do you still resent the incident at the Xu Field hunt?”

Dong Cheng said, “I do, but there is nothing I can do.”

Wu Shuo said, “I swear to kill this villain, yet no one else will aid me.”

Zhong Ji added, “If our task is to remove danger from the state, even dying brings no complaint.”

Wang Zifu came out from behind the screen and said, “You two would kill Cao the Chancellor! I will be the first to lead. Dong, the imperial uncle, has asked me to stand witness.”

Zhong Ji frowned, then said angrily, “A loyal minister does not fear death. We would prefer to become Han ghosts than to cling to the villain’s faction.”

Dong Cheng laughed and said, “We meet you for this matter. Master Wang’s words were made in jest.” He drew out the secret edict from his sleeve and showed it to both.

The two read it and could not stop weeping.

Dong Cheng asked that they sign. Wang Zifu said, “The two of you wait a little. I will go invite Wuzilan.”

He had not gone far before he returned with Wu Zilan, and all met together. He too wrote his name.

Dong Cheng invited everyone to the rear hall for a shared drink.

Then word came that Ma Teng, the Governor of Xiliang, had come to visit.

Dong Cheng said, “Say I am ill and cannot receive him.”

The gatekeeper conveyed this, but Ma Teng grew angry: “I just came through Donghua Gate at night and saw him leave in a robe and jade belt. How can he hide behind illness? I did not come for no business. Why refuse me?”

The gatekeeper reported Ma Teng’s rage. Dong Cheng stood up and said, “Gentlemen, wait a moment. Let me go out for a moment.” He immediately went out to receive him with courtesy.

After receiving him with ceremony, they sat.

Ma Teng said, “I returned from court audience and came to bid farewell. Why was I turned away?”

Dong Cheng said, “His household has a severe illness; I have failed in welcome and am at fault.”

Ma Teng said, “Your face still has the freshness of spring. I do not see you as sick.”

Dong Cheng had no answer.

Ma Teng swept his sleeve and rose, then sighed as he reached the lower step and said, “There are none among us who are true to rescuing the state!”

Dong Cheng hurriedly detained him and asked, “Who, then, do you mean is not rescuing the state?”

Ma Teng said, “At Xu Field’s hunt, my fury was still in my chest. You, imperial uncle foremost in the household, still linger in wine and women and do not think of punishing the traitor. How could you be a rescuer of disasters to the court?”

Dong Cheng, fearing deceit, feigned surprise: “Cao the Chancellor is a great minister and pillar of court. Why do you speak this way?”

Ma Teng snapped, “Do you still take this Cao-ruffian for a good man?”

Dong Cheng said, “I hear well enough from near and close. Please lower your voice.”

Ma Teng replied, “A man who clings to life and fears death is unfit to discuss major things.” He had only just stood when Dong Cheng said, “I know your loyalty and righteousness. Please stay. See this document,” and invited him to the study.

He showed him the edict.

After reading it, Ma Teng’s hair stood on end. He bit his teeth and chewed his lips until blood ran into his mouth.

He said to Dong Cheng, “If you now move, I will summon the Xiliang armies as outside support.”

Dong Cheng asked him to meet the others and showed him the oath register.

Ma Teng was asked to write his name.

He took wine and blood to swear, then said, “We swear by life itself: we will not fail this pledge.” He pointed among the five seated and said, “With ten men, the great matter can be accomplished.”

Dong Cheng replied, “A loyal man is not easy to gather. If those we take are unfit, we only hurt one another.”

Ma Teng ordered the family register known as the Yanxing Register brought and examined. When it reached the Liu clan, he clapped his hands and said, “Why do we not discuss this with this person?” All asked who that was.

Ma Teng, unhurried, named that person. It was as if to say:

It begins because the Imperial Uncle Dong had accepted the edict in full clarity, And now one sees Zonghuang serving and aiding the Han court.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao the Deceiver’s Encirclement at Xu Field and Chancellor Dong’s Reception of the Imperial Command

chapters.html:
Dong Cheng and the others asked Ma Teng, “Governor, whom do you intend to choose?” “See there is Liu Bei, Governor of Yu Province, here,” Ma Teng said. “Why not invite him?” Dong Cheng said, “This man is, though he is the Imperial Uncle, now attached to Cao Cao. Would he agree to this?” Ma Teng replied, “I observed him in the arena yesterday when Cao Cao rode out to receive all the congratulations. Yunchang stood behind Liu Bei with his knife raised, as if ready to strike Cao Cao. Liu Bei noticed it and motioned with his eyes to stop him. Liu Bei does not fail to dislike Cao Cao, but he saw that Cao Cao had too many blades around him and feared he could not win. Ask him to help, and he will certainly consent.” Wu Shuo said, “We should not move too quickly. We should discuss this at leisure.” All withdrew.

The next night, Dong Cheng entered the city at once with the imperial order tucked near his person and went straight to Liu Bei’s pavilion. The gate officer announced him, and Liu Bei came out to meet him and asked him into the small pavilion and had him seated. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, whose courtesy names were Yunchang and Yide, stood at the sides. Liu Bei said, “Your Imperial Uncle came here at this late hour. There must be a matter of consequence.” Dong Cheng replied, “If he had visited by day, Cao Cao might have become suspicious. So I came at night.” Liu Bei ordered wine to be brought. Dong Cheng said, “Yesterday in the arena, Yunchang wanted to kill Cao Cao. The General simply looked at him and shook his head for him to stop. Why was that?” Liu Bei’s expression changed in alarm. “How do you know that?” Dong Cheng said, “No one else saw it. I alone saw it.”

Liu Bei could not conceal the feeling and said, “My younger brother, seeing Cao Cao overreaching, could not restrain his anger.” Dong Cheng covered his face and wept. “If ministers of the court were all like Yunchang, how could there be unrest in the realm?” Liu Bei, fearing that Cao Cao had sent him to test, said with feigned casualness, “Why does the Chancellor of the Cao state fear disorder so much?” Dong Cheng’s color changed, and he rose. “You are the Imperial uncle of Han. How can you hide the truth in a heart that has offered up its liver and spleen? Why do you feign?” Liu Bei said, “Fearful you might be testing me, I only tested you.”

Then Dong Cheng showed him the folded order. Liu Bei could not hide his grief and resentment. He also produced the oath document. The names were only six: 1) Dong Cheng, General of Cavalry; 2) Wang Zifu, Minister of Works; 3) Zhong Ji, Colonel of Changshui; 4) Wu Shuo, Gentleman Secretary; 5) Wu Zilan, General Zhaoxin; and 6) Ma Teng, Governor of Xiliang. Liu Bei said, “You now bear an imperial order to punish traitorous rebels; how could I not labor like a hound and horse in your service?” Dong Cheng bowed and thanked him, then asked for a personal seal and order of rank. Liu Bei also wrote out “General of the Left Liu Bei,” signed and stamped it, and had him take it. Dong Cheng said, “You may still ask three more men and gather ten to plot against the bandit of the state.” Liu Bei said, “Do it slowly and cautiously. Do not disclose matters lightly.”

They discussed through the fifth watch and parted. Liu Bei himself, fearing Cao Cao’s designs, went to the back garden and personally watered the vegetable beds he had set there, as a stratagem of concealment. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei asked, “Brother, why neglect the great affairs of the state and busy yourself in such petty matters?” Liu Bei said, “This is no matter for your younger brother to know.” The two did not speak further.

One day, with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei absent, Liu Bei was tending the garden, when Xu Chu and Zhang Liao entered with several tens of soldiers. “By order of the Chancellor,” they said, “the lord must depart at once.” Liu Bei asked in alarm, “Is there an urgent matter?” Xu Chu said, “I do not know. They only told me to come and summon you.” Reluctantly Liu Bei followed the two men to the ruler’s residence. Cao Cao smiled. “You have done a fine thing at home.” Liu Bei turned ashen. Cao Cao took him by the hand and led him to the rear garden. “Your garden of vegetables is not an easy thing to keep.” Only then did Liu Bei finally relax. He answered, “Only idle amusement.” Cao Cao said, “Just now, seeing the green plums on the branches, I remembered last year when we marched against Zhang Xiu. The roads were dry and waterless, and all the men were thirsty. A plan came to me then. I pointed my whip at the air and said, ‘A plum grove lies ahead.’ Hearing that, every soldier moistened his mouth with saliva, and their thirst was lessened. To see these plums now is a moment we should celebrate. Also, now that the boiled wine is just at its best, I have invited you to this pavilion for a brief meeting.” Liu Bei, now at ease, followed him to the pavilion where casks and trays had already been set out: green plums arranged on a dish and one jar of boiled wine. The two sat across from each other and drank with good heart.

When half drunk, a dark bank of cloud spread at the horizon and a sudden storm was about to arrive. A servant pointed far off to a cloud shaped like a dragon, and Cao Cao and Liu Bei leaned over the balustrade to watch. Cao Cao asked, “Do you know the transformations of dragons?” Liu Bei said, “I do not know them in detail.” Cao Cao replied, “A dragon can grow great or small. It can rise and it can hide. Great, it raises clouds and exhales mist. Small, it hides and crouches close to the ground. When it rises, it soars through the spaces of heaven and earth; when it hides, it lies submerged within the waves. At this time of deep spring, a dragon follows the changes of season, like a man who gains command and ranges freely over the four seas. Dragons may be compared to heroes of the world. You have traveled in the world long enough and must know the heroes of the age. Please point them out and I will hear.”

Liu Bei said, “With eyes alone, how can I know heroes?” Cao Cao said, “Do not feign such modesty.” Liu Bei said, “By your grace and protection, I have been admitted to office. As for the heroes of all under Heaven, truly there are many I do not know.” Cao Cao said, “If you do not know their appearance, at least you know their names.” Liu Bei said, “In Huainan there is Yuan Shu, whose stores and grain are full. He can be called a hero.” Cao Cao said, “Bones waiting in a grave mound—sooner or later I will capture him.” Liu Bei said, “In Hebei there is Yuan Shao, who comes from four generations of the Three Dukes’ line and who has many old state men at hand. Now he has entrenched himself in Ji Province and has many capable men under him. He may be called a hero.” Cao Cao said, “Yuan Shao has a fierce face and thin courage. He can conceive plans but never finishes them. He undertakes great undertakings yet saves his own life, and for a small profit he forgets life and duty. He is no hero.” Liu Bei said, “There is a man called the Eight Halls, who holds power across the Nine Provinces: Liu Biao, courtesy name Jingsheng, might be a hero.” Cao Cao said, “Liu Biao is hollow fame without substance. He is no hero.” Liu Bei said, “There is a man whose blood and qi are vigorous and upright, a leader of Jiangdong: Sun Ce, whose sobriquet was the Little Conqueror, is a hero.” Cao Cao said, “Sun Ce hides behind his father’s reputation. He is no hero.” Liu Bei said, “What of Liu Zhang of Yi Province, courtesy name Jiyu? Could he be a hero?” Cao Cao said, “Though Liu Zhang is of imperial clan, he is a gate dog in a householder’s home. How could he be a hero?” Liu Bei said, “Then what of men such as Zhang Xiu, Zhang Lu, and Han Sui?” Cao Cao clapped his hands and laughed loudly. “Those are mere trifling men—surely not worth mentioning.” Liu Bei said, “Outside these, I truly do not know.” Cao Cao said, “A hero is one whose heart bears vast ambition and whose belly contains sound counsel: one who holds the stratagems of the cosmos and the will of heaven and earth.” Liu Bei asked, “Who can shoulder that?” Cao Cao pointed at Liu Bei with one hand, then to himself with the other and said, “As for heroes of the world today, only the lord and I.”

When Liu Bei heard this, he was startled and the spoon-and-chopsticks he held fell from his hand to the ground. At that very moment thunder rolled as the rain came. Liu Bei quietly stooped and picked up the fallen spoon. “The force of one clap of thunder can go so far,” he said. Cao Cao laughed. “Would a man not fear thunder?” Liu Bei said, “When a sage commands lightning and wind to rage, how can one not fear?” He used his dropped utensil as a light pretext to pass over the cause of his alarm. Cao Cao then harbored no more suspicion.

Later, someone wrote a verse praising him:

He steps from the tiger’s den but for a moment, Names the hero and startles those who would die. He shrewdly borrows the thunder for cover, And meets each turn of chance with a spirit like a god.

When the rain stopped, two men charged into the rear garden with sword in hand and forcefully pushed to the pavilion. Cao Cao and Liu Bei looked up and could not stop them. They were Guan Yu and Zhang Fei. Guan and Zhang had just returned from the city wall after shooting arrows. They had heard that Xu Chu and Zhang Liao had taken Liu Bei away and came hastily to his hall to inquire. Hearing he was in the garden, they feared delay and broke through the gate. There they saw Liu Bei drinking with Cao Cao. Both men drew their swords and stood upright. Cao Cao asked, “How did you come?” Guan Yu said, “Hearing that the Chancellor and my elder brother are drinking together, I came to dance my sword and join a laugh.” Cao Cao said, “This is no banquet at Hongmen. Why need Xiang Zhuang and Xiang Bo?” Liu Bei laughed as well. Cao Cao said, “Give the two of them wine to steady their nerves.” Guan Yu and Zhang Fei thanked him and withdrew.

A short while later, the meal ended and Liu Bei took his leave. He turned to Guan Yu and Zhang Fei with his voice low, “You nearly caused us to die, both of you.” Liu Bei explained to them the matter of the dropped chopsticks. Zhang Fei asked what it meant. Liu Bei said, “In tending my garden, I wanted Cao Cao to see that I had no great ambition. Yet he ended by pointing to me as a hero. So I was startled and dropped my chopsticks. Then, fearing Cao Cao might suspect me, I used the thunder as cover.” Both Guan Yu and Zhang Fei replied, “Brother’s vision is truly extraordinary.”

On the next day, Cao Cao invited Liu Bei again. While they were drinking, full and at ease, Man Chong returned from scouting Yuan Shao and report was made. Cao Cao summoned him in. Man Chong said, “Gongsun Zan has already been defeated by Yuan Shao.” Liu Bei urgently asked, “Tell me the details.”

Man Chong said, “Gongsun Zan and Yuan Shao could not contend well. He built a circular defense and a high tower ten zhang above it, calling it the Yijing Tower. He stockpiled 300,000 measures of grain and kept watch. No sooner did soldiers enter or leave than he sent them through. Some among Zhang’s men came under siege by Yuan Shao and petitioned rescue. Zhang said, ‘If we rescue one man, then every future battle man will wait to be rescued and will not dare to die in combat.’ So he would not send aid. Therefore many joined Yuan Shao’s forces. Gongsun grew isolated and sent letters to the capital asking for rescue, but they were intercepted on the way. He then sent a letter to Zhang Yan and made a secret signal of raising fire as a mark for inside and outside coordination. The man who carried that letter was captured by Yuan Shao anyway. He was brought out before the walls to set fire and lure the enemy outward. Zhang then rode out in battle. Hidden troops rose and the army horses broke into half. He fell back into the city. Yuan Shao burrowed through the earth floor and entered beneath Zhang’s dwelling tower, then set fire below it. With no way out, Zhang slew his wife and children and then hanged himself. The whole household was burned. Now Yuan Shao gained Gongsun’s army, and his prestige rose greatly. Yuan Shao’s younger brother Yuan Shu in Huainan had grown arrogant and extravagant; he neglected troops and the people, and all under him rebelled in spirit. Yuan Shu sent word submitting the imperial title to Yuan Shao. Yuan Shao wanted to take the Imperial Seal, and Yuan Shu promised to send it to him in person. Now he has abandoned Huainan and intends to return north to Hebei. If the two of them unite, this calamity could be recovered with difficulty. I beg your Highness, take emergency action.”

Hearing of Gongsun Zan’s death, Liu Bei could not hide his sorrow at remembering the old favor that had once recommended him. He was also anxious, not knowing how Zhao Zilong had fared. In thought, he said, “If I do not find a way to escape now, when can I?” He rose and said to Cao Cao, “If Yuan Shu submits to Yuan Shao, he must pass through Xuzhou. Grant me one army and I can intercept him halfway and capture him.” Cao Cao laughed. “Tomorrow I will report this to the emperor, then we shall raise troops.”

The following day Liu Bei presented himself before the Son of Heaven. Cao Cao ordered him to supervise fifty thousand men and horses and sent Zhu Ling and Lu Zhao with him. Liu Bei spoke before he left. The emperor wept and sent him off. When Liu Bei returned to his quarters, he packed his arms and horses in one night and, with his command seal hung, urged the army to speed. Ma Teng rode out ten li to send him off. Liu Bei said, “Please endure this, Imperial Uncle. I will someday repay this command.” Ma Teng said, “You should stay alert and never fail the mind of the emperor.” They parted. As they rode, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei asked while still mounted, “Brother, why such haste in this campaign?” Liu Bei said, “I have long been a bird in a cage and a fish in a net. This trip is like a fish entering the Great Sea or a bird up into broad sky, free from cage and chain.” So he ordered Guan Yu and Zhang Fei to urge Zhu Ling and Lu Zhao forward at speed.

At that time Guo Jia and Cheng Yu, having recently returned from calculating grain and silver accounts, learned that Cao Cao had already sent Liu Bei toward Xuzhou and hurried in remonstration. “Why did the Chancellor send Liu Bei to command troops?” Cao Cao asked. “Previously, when Liu Bei served as Governor of Yu Province, we urged him to be executed and the Chancellor refused. Now to send troops with him is to cast a dragon into the sea and let a tiger return to its mountain. When you later wish to bring it under control, how can you?” Guo Jia said, “Even if the Chancellor does not kill Liu Bei, he should not let him go. The old saying is true: one day of letting an enemy loose becomes trouble for ten generations. Please consider it.” After hearing them, Cao Cao wavered. “Let him go,” said Cheng Yu and Guo Jia. Cao Cao gave Xu Chu orders to go with five hundred men and bring Liu Bei back by force if he tried to leave; Xu Chu agreed and rode out.

Yet while Liu Bei was traveling onward, he saw dust rise behind them and told Guan Yu and Zhang Fei, “This can only be Cao Cao’s soldiers pursuing us.” He then broke camp and ordered Guan Yu and Zhang Fei each to hold weapons at their sides and stand on both flanks. Xu Chu arrived; seeing the strict array and full armor, he dismounted and went into camp. Liu Bei said, “Why have you come here?” Xu Chu replied, “I have an order from the Chancellor, summoning the general to return. There is other business.” Liu Bei said, “A general abroad can refuse what is not fit for him. I have already faced you and have the Chancellor’s words in my ears. I have no other matter. You can return quickly and report this to the Chancellor.” Xu Chu thought to himself, “The Chancellor and Liu Bei have always been close. This time he did not tell me to strike him. I should simply relay Liu Bei’s words and await the Chancellors’ final judgment.” So he took leave of Liu Bei and returned with his troops. When he reached Cao Cao, he reported Liu Bei’s words. Cao Cao still hesitated. Cheng Yu and Guo Jia said, “Since Liu Bei refuses to recall his army, we may know his heart has turned.” Cao Cao said, “I have Zhu Ling and Lu Zhao there. Liu Bei will not dare to change his heart. In any case, since I have sent him, how can I now repent and bring him back?” He gave no further order to pursue Liu Bei.

Later, someone wrote a verse praising him:

A swift departure with troops fed and saddled, Yet he carried Heaven’s mandate in his belt. He crashes the iron cage and escapes tiger and leopard, Opening suddenly a golden chain and departing like a river-dragon.

When Ma Teng learned that Liu Bei had left and fresh reports came from the frontier, he returned to Xiliang. Liu Bei’s army reached Xuzhou. The city commander Che Zuo came out to receive them. A banquet followed. Sun Qian, Mi Zhu and others came to pay their respects. After visiting the elders and the children at home, Liu Bei sent people to inquire after Yuan Shu. A scout returned and said, “Yuan Shu has overreached and become too luxurious. Lei Bo and Chen Lan have both gone to Songshan. Yuan Shu’s strength is now depleted, and he has abandoned Huainan and set his face toward Hebei. He has written to yield the imperial title to Yuan Shao. If the two of them work together, this emergency will be hard to repair. Yuan Shao has summoned him, and Yuan Shu has packed his men and beasts and palace goods and arrived at Xuzhou first.”

Knowing Yuan Shu was nearing, Liu Bei called forward Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Zhu Ling, and Lu Zhao with fifty thousand soldiers and rode out to meet him. They were met by the forward guard Ji Ling. Zhang Fei said nothing and rode straight at him. They fought fewer than ten passes before Zhang Fei roared once and stabbed Ji Ling beneath his horse. The enemy army broke and fled. Yuan Shu then came on in person. Liu Bei divided his force into three columns: Zhu Ling and Lu Zhao on the left, Guan Yu and Zhang Fei on the right, Liu Bei himself in the center. He met Yuan Shu beneath the gate and thundered, “You traitor act against the state with no sense of righteousness. I now come with an imperial order to suppress you. You should lay down your weapons and surrender, so your offense may be lessened.” Yuan Shu jeered, “A rag-plaited cobbler of a fellow dares speak so lightly of me!” He gestured for troops to charge. Liu Bei gave ground for a while to let the left and right wings cut through. They slew Yuan Shu’s men, filling the field with bodies and turning streams red with blood. When the enemy soldiers fled, they escaped in number beyond counting. Lei Bo and Chen Lan, now at Songshan, plundered their grain and forage. Attempting to return to Shouchun, they were attacked by bandits, so they could only halt at Jiangting. Only a little over a thousand remained, all old or weak. It was high summer. Supplies were exhausted. Only thirty hu of wheat remained. Liu Bei distributed what remained only among the soldiers; his household had no food, and many starved.

Yuan Shu disliked the coarse grain and could not swallow it. He ordered the cook to bring honey water to soothe his thirst. The cook said, “Only blood water remains. How can I bring honey water?” Yuan Shu sat up, shouted once, and collapsed to the ground, retching out blood before dying. It was the fourth year of Jian’an, sixth month. Later people made a verse:

At the end of the Eastern Han, weapons and war broke in four quarters, Yuan Shu rose too recklessly, with no cause. Forgetting generations of service in office, he sought in solitude the title of Son of Heaven, He boasted of the Imperial Seal and boasted of Heaven’s blessing. Thinking of honey water and finding none, he lay alone upon an empty bed and died after vomiting blood.

Yuan Shu was already dead. His nephew Yuan Yin brought his coffin and his family to Lujiang. Xu Qiu slew them all. He took the Imperial Seal and carried it to Xudu to present it to Cao Cao. Cao Cao rejoiced greatly and made Xu Qiu Governor of Gaoling. At this time the Imperial Seal returned to Cao Cao.

When Liu Bei learned that Yuan Shu was dead, he composed and presented a memorial to the court and delivered a copy to Cao Cao, instructing Zhu Ling and Lu Zhao to return to Xudu and leave the troops to hold Xuzhou while he himself went out of the city and summoned the scattered people to return to farming.

Zhu Ling and Lu Zhao came back to Xudu and told Cao Cao that Liu Bei had left troops in place. Cao Cao grew angry and wished to execute the two. Xun Yu said, “The authority now lies with Liu Bei; these two were in no position to refuse.” Cao Cao pardoned them. Xun Yu added, “Write to Che Zuo and set an inside plan.”

Cao Cao accepted the plan and secretly sent a man to Che Zuo with the Chancellor’s instructions. Che Zuo immediately asked Chen Deng to counsel with him. Chen Deng said, “The matter is easy. Liu Bei has gone out to summon civilians. He will soon return. You may post soldiers hidden at the edge of Weng City and let them merely receive him. When his horse arrives, one stroke can cut him down. I will stand atop the city walls and fire on his rear troops. Then the matter will be settled.” Che Zuo followed this.

Chen Deng then returned to his father, Chen Gui, and explained what had happened. Chen Gui ordered him to report it first to Liu Bei. Chen Deng rode hard and, upon reaching the road, encountered Guan Yu and Zhang Fei. He relayed it to them all. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei had already returned; Liu Bei was behind.

When Zhang Fei heard, he readied himself to fight. Guan Yu said, “He is waiting outside Weng City to receive me. If I go, I will walk into danger. I have one plan: we can kill Che Zuo. We will spend the night in the clothing and flags of Cao Cao’s army, ride to Xuzhou, and lure Che Zuo out to welcome us. Then we kill him.” Zhang Fei accepted. Their men already held Cao’s insignia, their armor matching. At the middle of the third watch, they called at the gate. Those above the city wall asked who came. The men shouted, “The troops of Chancellor Cao sent by Zhang Wenyuan.” Che Zuo was told. He quickly asked Chen Deng for counsel. “If we do not receive them, that is suspicious. If we go out to receive them, there may still be deceit.” Che Zuo then climbed the wall and shouted back, “Night makes it hard to distinguish faces. Let us meet in the morning.” From below, the voices answered, “Liu Bei may learn of this. Open at once!”

Che Zuo still hesitated. From outside there came many cries calling for the gate to open. Che Zuo finally donned his armor, mounted, and rode out with one thousand men. Crossing the hanging bridge, he cried, “Where is Zhang Wenyuan?” In the firelight Guan Yu was seen, sword in hand, driving straight from horseback to meet him. Guan Yu shouted, “How could a common man dare to plot deceit and come to kill my elder brother?” Che Zuo was shocked. Before the battle had gone even for a few exchanges, he could not block him, so he turned his horse away. At the hanging bridge, Chen Deng shot a storm of arrows from above the wall, and Che Zuo ran around the city. Guan Yu pursued and, with one stroke, severed him at the horse’s side, cutting off his head. He raised it high and called back to the wall, “The rebel Che Zuo has been killed. I have his head. The soldiers and townsfolk are innocent. If they surrender, they will not die.” The opposing forces turned their swords around and surrendered. Army and civilians all came to peace.

Guan Yu carried Che Zuo’s head to meet Liu Bei and explained the plot against him. It was already ended by the beheading. Liu Bei was stunned. “If Cao Cao comes, what then?” Guan Yu said, “My brother and Zhang Fei will meet him.” Liu Bei regretted deeply, then entered Xuzhou. The elders and old men met him in the roads and came to welcome him. When he reached his hall, he searched for Zhang Fei. Zhang Fei had already killed Che Zuo’s entire household. Liu Bei said, “Would one who had slain Cao Cao’s trusted officer ever be allowed to rest?” Chen Deng said, “I have a plan. It may send Cao Cao away.”

He slipped from the tiger’s den as a single man, then set a brilliant plan in motion to quiet the war-smoke. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Cao Weighs Heroes over Boiled Wine; Guan Yu Captures a City and Beheads Che Zuo

chapters.html:
Yuan and Cao each bring up horse and foot armies. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei together capture Generals Wang Zhong and Liu Dai.

Thereupon Chen Deng presented his plan to Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande: “Cao Cao fears Yuan Shao most. Shao sits on Ji, Qing, You, and Bing, commanding a million armed men, and he has many literati and generals. Why not write a letter and send envoys to ask for help?”

Liu Bei replied, “Shao has never traded greetings with me, and he just defeated his own younger brother. Why would he dare to assist now?”

Chen Deng said, “There is one man in all this world with three generations of family ties to Yuan Shao. If we can get one letter to him, Yuan Shao will certainly come to assist.”

Liu Bei asked who he was.

Chen Deng said, “It is the one you greet with bowing and careful ritual each day. How could you have forgotten him?”

Liu Bei said with a start, “Could it be Master Zheng Kangcheng?”

Chen Deng smiled and said, “It is.”

In truth, Zheng Kangcheng was named Xuan. He was eager to learn and skilled in many arts. He once studied under Ma Rong. Whenever Ma Rong lectured, he would set up a red pavilion, place his students in the front, and line his female attendants on both sides. Xuan listened for three years and never glanced askew; Ma Rong found this astonishing.

After he finished learning and returned home, Rong sighed, “Only one man, Zheng Xuan, has received the secret of my teaching.”

Zheng Xuan’s maids all knew the Classic of Poetry. One maid once offended him; Xuan ordered her to kneel on the stairs.

She joked, “Why stoop down into the mud?”

She immediately answered, “I had spoken a slight word in haste and met his anger.” So elegant was her diction.

In Emperor Huan’s reign, Xuan rose to Shangshu. Later, because of the Disturbance of the Ten Attendants, he left office, returned to the fields, and lived in Xu Province.

When Liu Bei had been in Zhuo Commandery, he had once been his disciple. Afterward, when Liu Bei served as Administrator of Xu Province, he came often to visit and seek instruction, and showed him singular respect.

At once Liu Bei vividly remembered this man and was overjoyed. He and Chen Deng together went to Zheng Xuan’s house to ask him to write a letter. Xuan gladly agreed and wrote one missive, then gave it to Liu Bei.

Liu Bei immediately sent Sun Qian at night to take it and deliver it to Yuan Shao. After reading it, Yuan Shao privately reflected, “Liu Bei has destroyed my brother; I should not help him. Yet because this is at the command of Shangshu Zheng, I have no choice but to go.”

He gathered his civil and military officers and discussed mustering troops to strike Cao Cao.

Advisor Tian Feng said, “War has continued for years. The people are exhausted, and the granaries have little reserve. It is not possible to raise a great army anew. First send men to report victory to the Son of Heaven. If he does not grant passage, then submit a memorial saying Cao Cao blocks our royal road. Then raise troops and station them at Liyang. Also in Hebei increase boats and transport craft, repair weapons, distribute selected troops, and post detachments along the border. In three years, major matters can be settled.”

Counselor Shen Pei said, “Not so. With your divine prowess, my lord, to pacify the north of the river and raise the army against Cao bandit is as easy as turning over your palm. Why delay by the months?”

Counselor Ju Shou said, “A strategy to conquer is not only a matter of strength. Now Cao Cao’s laws are implemented and his soldiers are disciplined; he is nothing like Gongsun Zan, who sat trapped and remained vulnerable. Abandoning a winning memorial and raising an army with no name is not what my lord should do.”

Counselor Guo Tu said, “This is not true. To raise an army against Cao Cao is no such thing as being nameless. My lord should secure a great undertaking at once. I would follow Shangshu Zheng’s words: join Liu Bei in upholding righteousness and exterminating Cao’s bandit. Heaven’s will is above and the people’s feeling below. This would truly be a heaven-sent blessing.”

The four could not agree. Yuan Shao hesitated. Just then Xu You and Xun Shen entered from outside.

Shao said, “The two of you have much discernment. Hear how you advise.”

After they had offered courtesy, Shao said, “Shangshu Zheng has written, ordering me to raise troops and aid Liu Bei in attacking Cao Cao. Should we raise troops, or not?”

Both answered together, “My lord can let numbers master numbers; let the strong attack the weak. Strike down the Han bandit and assist the imperial house. Raise troops.”

Shao said, “What you both have seen accords with my heart.” He decided to proceed with the campaign. He first ordered Sun Qian to report back to Zheng Xuan and arranged with Liu Bei for support preparations. At the same time he appointed Shen Pei and Feng Ji as commanders-in-chief, Tian Feng, Xun Shen, and Xu You as strategists, Yan Liang and Wenchou as generals, and raised 150,000 horse and 150,000 infantry, 300,000 selected soldiers in total, to advance on Liyang.

The assignments now made, Guo Tu said, “Since my lord will take a great campaign against Cao Cao, he must publicize Cao’s crimes by sending proclamations to every commandery, laying out each accusation, and thus make the war legitimate.”

Shao approved. He ordered his recorder, Chen Lin, to draft the edict. Lin was styled Kongzhang, already famed for talent; under Emperor Ling he had been a bureau official. After he had remonstrated with He Jin and was not heard, Dong Zhuo’s disorder later drove him to flee to Ji Province, where Shao employed him as a secretary. Now he was ordered to draft at once.

The text read:

It is well known that a wise ruler designs against peril to alter changing conditions, and a loyal minister worries over danger to found authority. Therefore extraordinary men come forth before extraordinary acts arise, and only then do extraordinary achievements appear. What is extraordinary is not sought by ordinary men.

In former times, the strong Qin pressed a weak ruler; Zhao Gao seized the reins of government, making power and rank all his own. The world feared coercion and dared not speak truly. At the end there came the fall of the Qin and the ruin of its ancestors, with humiliation lasting to this day as warning to posterity. When the empress dowager Lü and the Du Lu clan later monopolized government in their final years, they controlled both armies, ruled the two frontiers, made decisions on all matters, removed restraints, and punished officials; they insulted superiors while crushing subordinates, and the whole realm grew cold of heart. Therefore in response to this, Marquis Jiang and Zhu-Xu raised their prestige in righteous anger, eradicated the tyrants, and reestablished the Grand Ancestor. Thus kingly order revived and clear brilliance returned. This is the clearest demonstration of how ministers may rightfully seize authority.

Grand Commandant Cao Cao: his father’s father, Zhongchangshi Teng, together with Zuo Huan and Xu Huan, were wicked together, greedy and violent, harming the people and perverting the laws. His own father Song was raised from beggary; he bought office through bribes and carried golden chariots and jade tablets into office for the sake of gain. He stole from the Department of State Treasury and overturned great vessels. Cao, by inheritance and corruption, is base by nature. He is flashy, crafty, and likes trouble and disaster.

In the government, Dong Zhuo was bold and domineering. He swept away the murderous officials and overthrew those who confronted him, then continued the slaughter from Dong Zhuo onward, invading offices and plundering the state. Thus, with sword and drum he issued commands across Dongxia, gathering heroes, discarding the worthy and taking up power. So he and Cao conferred and plotted together; he gave Cao command as a second adviser, saying his skills were like those of a hunting hound and claw, fit to be entrusted. In time Cao proved shallow, cunning, and fickle, rushing in and withdrawing easily, wounding and killing men, losing soldiers and teachers again and again. Dong repeatedly sent fresh troops to replace losses, kept him in post after repairs, and eventually made him Inspector of Yanzhou in the Eastern Commandery, praising him with tiger-like insignia and honoring him to secure authority, hoping to reap a reward for Cao’s one decisive strike. In the end Cao inherited privilege and became arrogant, proceeding with outrage, stripping and seizing without mercy, harming the worthy and favoring the wicked.

Therefore Bojiang Prefect Bianrang, famed for talent and greatness, was famous throughout the world. He spoke plainly, spoke uprightly, and never flattered. He met death at the stake, while his wife shared him in the fire, for saying the truth against him. Since then the world of scholars burned with grief, and the people’s resentment only deepened. One man lifted up his arms, and the whole commandery rose with one voice. Thus Bianrang was driven from the western regions and land lost to Lü Bu; he wandered eastward, grasping only a few footholds and holding none in place. Dong Zhuo, in line with strengthening the strong and casting off the weak, did not even openly take the side of rebels, and so took up banner and armor, and swept away to campaign again. When drums and gongs sounded, rebel forces scattered. He rescued this suffering and restored the district lordship. For the people of Yanzhou, Dong Zhuo had no benevolence, yet caused him the greatest harm.

Later, he received the Son of Heaven in return and the realm was in turmoil. At this time Ji Province still faced danger on its northern frontiers, and he had neither time nor freedom to govern. Therefore he used Xu Hun as Director of Palace Affairs, sending him out to Cao and ordering him to repair ancestral temples and guard the young sovereign. Cao then seized his opportunity: he carried out forced transfers in turn, set himself above palace regulations, insulted the imperial house, broke the law and manners; while seated over the Three Platforms he monopolized court politics, gave rewards at his pleasure, and made punishment dependent on his tongue. Those he favored gained five kinships; those he hated were wiped out three generations. Men who spoke in gatherings were publicly executed; those who spoke privately were secretly punished. The great officers held back their words, and officials along the roads watched one another with narrowed eyes. At court, Shangshu clerks still attended assembly, and ministers and chancellors merely filled seats.

Thus Grand Commandant Yang Biao had administered two ministries and reached the highest post in the empire. Cao took advantage of a speck of resentment to wrong him; he brought him to trial through the fivefold tortures. Acting on impulse and ignoring order, he made himself tyrant. Another counsellor, Zhao Yan, loyal and straightforward, gave advice that ought to have been heeded, and because he spoke with reason in this holy court, he was rewarded and honored. Yet Cao sought to blind the times’ clarity and close all roads of counsel; he took people alive and dead by his own hand without waiting for petitions. He then despoiled the mother of the former Prince of Henei, Liang Xianwang’s mother, by excavating her tomb. Though her tomb, mulberry fields, and cypresses deserved reverence, Cao led officers, clerks, and soldiers to the grave, personally exposed coffins, stripped and robbed the corpse for treasures. Even now the sacred court weeps and the people of the realm lament.

Cao has also established a detachment called the Faqiu Zhonglang General and a "touch-gold" Colonel of the Bodyguard; wherever he goes, gates are smashed and no tomb is left unviolated. He holds the rank of one of the Three Excellencies, yet he behaves as a common thief and bandit, defiling the state and harming the people, spreading poison among the human and spirit worlds. He makes household regulations cruelly harsh and multiplies controls. Tax offices and checkpoints block roads with nets and traps; where one lifts a hand one is cast in a net, where one sets a foot down one trips a device. Therefore in Yan and Yu there are endless poor peasants and the Emperor’s capital has complaints and cries. Surveying the records, no ruler has been as wicked, greedy, cruel, and ferocious as Cao.

Dong Zhuo had begun to investigate outside traitors but had not yet finished training. He sought to patch over appearances. Yet Cao’s wolfish, wild ambition concealed disaster and plotting, desiring to break the pillars, leave the Han too weak and alone, remove loyal and upright men, and become the age’s sole predatory hero. Formerly, he marched north against Gongsun Zan, a ruthless and violent rebel, who withstood siege for a year. Cao, while Gongsun was not broken, secretly exchanged letters and orders, offering aid to the royal army while secretly striking a blow from the side. When this was exposed by couriers, Gongsun too was felled, so Cao’s sharpness was blunted and his plan failed.

Now he has established himself at Aocang, blocking the river and strengthening his base, hoping to use a mantis axe against the great chariot. The government that bears the spirit and mandate of Han has been shattered by this one man who claims authority over the universe: a hundred thousand spears, a thousand ferocious horsemen; he has gathered fierce men from Zhongyi, Yu, Huo and others; the force of good bows and taut crossbows; he crossed Taihang from Bingzhou and passed through Ji and Luo in Qingzhou. His great army moved down the Yellow River and formed its front there, then down to Wan and Ye to press behind from Anhwe, like striking with thunder-wolf pace. He would be like setting blazing fire to withered thistle or pouring burning coals across the blue sea. What could not be destroyed by such force?

Again, the officers and soldiers under Cao that can fight were mostly drawn from You and Ji, or former command staff, all homesick and longing for return, weeping as they looked north. The rest of Yanzhou and Yuzhou men were remnants of Lü Bu’s and Zhang Yang’s survivors, forced by collapse and threat into opportunistic obedience. Many were broken and embittered, each made enemy to all.

If they turn their banners and advance in return, if they climb high posts and beat drums and horns, if they raise white banners and open a path to surrender, they will collapse like a crumbling wall; no blade of blood need be drawn. The imperial house now declines and order frays; the court has not one loyal support, no ministers capable of mediating between ruler and world. In the close lands around the capitals, all polished officials keep head bent and feathers hidden, having no place to lean; though there are ministers of loyalty and righteousness, they stand under tyrants’ fear and cannot yet show their integrity. Cao keeps seven hundred chosen troops and surrounds the imperial palace, pretending imperial bodyguard while inwardly being kidnappers; fearing rebellion within grows like a sprout, this is why. This is the time when ministers pour out liver and brain for the state and heroes should win their merit.

Cao also forged orders, sending troops by his own command. If he sends demands to distant commanderies and officers and they can no longer provide grain and pay, he will treat refusal as rebellion and disgraceful surrender, and make the world laugh. Therefore a wise ruler would not do so.

From this day, all four commands of You, Bing, Qing, and Ji were ordered forward. When copies arrived in Jingzhou, troops were to be assembled and coordinated with the forces of Jianzhong. Each commandery was to mobilize its righteous soldiers, cover its borders, raise arms, and jointly support the ancestral state; in this way an extraordinary achievement would be made.

Whoever captures Cao’s head will be made a marquis of five thousand households and granted fifty million coins. For the soldiers, escorts, junior officers, and all officials who surrender, none should be questioned. Spread wide the promise of mercy, publicize the seal and rewards, and issue notices to all under heaven so they all know that the sacred court is constrained by coercion and helplessness. By imperial ordinance!

Shao was delighted by the edict and immediately ordered copies to be distributed through every commandery and posted at every gate, pass, and strait.

When the edict reached Xudu, Cao Cao was then afflicted with a severe headache, lying in bed. His attendants presented it to him. Cao saw it and felt his bones and hair rise; cold sweat poured down his body; in spite of himself his headache eased, and he sprang up from the bed in one leap. Turning to Cao Hong, he asked, “Who wrote this text?”

Cao Hong said, “It is said to be Chen Lin’s hand.”

Cao laughed. “A man of letters can only be judged by his strategy in arms. Chen Lin is talented in prose, but is his way of war enough for Yuan Shao?” He then gathered his officers and counsel and discussed how to meet the threat.

Kong Rong heard of it and came to see Cao: “Yuan Shao has such force; we cannot battle him. We can only make peace.”

Xun Yu said, “Yuan Shao is not a man fit for use. Why speak of peace?”

Kong Rong replied, “Yuan Shao is vast in land and strong in people. His subordinates, such as Xu You, Guo Tu, and Shen Pei, are all men of talent and plans. Tian Feng and Ju Shou are loyal ministers. Yan Liang and Wen Chou are the foremost of the three armies in courage. Others like Gaolan, Zhang He, and Chunyu Qiong are famous generals of the age. Why would one call Shao useless?”

Xun Yu laughed. “Yuan Shao has many soldiers but no order. Tian Feng is rigid and overbearing. Xu You is greedy and no wise. Shen Pei is single-minded and without plotting. Feng Ji is upright and of no use. These men cannot be coordinated; they are bound to internal discord. Yan Liang and Wen Chou are courage of common men; a single battle could catch them. As for the rest, if they are thousands of ordinary men, what is to be said?”

Kong Rong fell silent.

Cao laughed broadly. “None of this escapes Xun Wenruo’s calculations.” He then summoned the front commander Liu Dai and rear commander Wang Zhong, ordered them to lead fifty thousand each under the flag of the Chancellor, and advance from Xudu into Xu Province to strike Liu Bei.

Liu Dai, it should be said, had once been Administrator of Yanzhou. After Cao took Yanzhou, Dai surrendered and was made a subordinate general; this is why Cao now assigned him to lead together with Wang Zhong.

Cao himself, however, moved out with 200,000 troops to Liyang to resist Yuan Shao.
