Cheng Yu warned, “I fear Liu Dai and Wang Zhong cannot fulfill this commission.”

Cao said, “I also know that Liu Bei is no ordinary enemy. For now we will make only an empty show.”

He instructed, “Do not rush forward recklessly. Once I break Yuan Shao, then we return in full force and crush Bei.”

Liu Dai and Wang Zhong took the army out.

Cao led one main force to Liyang.

The two main armies stood eighty li apart and dug deep trenches and raised high ramparts, holding ground without fighting. From the eighth month to the tenth, they remained so.

In truth, Xu You did not enjoy that Shen Pei led the forces, and Ju Shou resented that Shao did not adopt his scheme. They never agreed and never sought active advance. Yuan Shao was full of doubt and did not intend to push forward. Cao therefore called forward the former subordinate of Lü Bu, Zang Ba, to guard Qing and Xu; Yu Jin and Li Dian were posted along the river; Cao Ren was made overall commander of the main army, which encamped at Guandu. Cao withdrew with one contingent back to Xudu.

Elsewhere, Liu Dai and Wang Zhong had left Xu Province and camped one hundred li out. Their middle camp, flying only a false Chancellorship banner, did not dare to advance and only listened for news from the north. Here in this place Liu Bei also did not know Cao’s true position and did not dare to move on his own; he only gathered intelligence from the north.

Suddenly Cao Cao sent men urging Liu Dai and Wang Zhong to engage in battle. The two discussed in camp.

Liu Dai said, “The Chancellor urges us to attack the city. You should go first.”

Wang Zhong said, “The Chancellor has sent you first.”

Liu Dai said, “I am the principal commander. How can I go first?”

Wang Zhong said, “I will go with you.”

Liu Dai said, “Let us draw lots. Whoever draws the ‘first’ goes.”

Wang Zhong drew the character for “first” and had to take only half his troops when he went to attack Xu Province.

When Liu Bei heard the horsemen had arrived, he asked Chen Deng to confer: “Although Benchu is encamped at Liyang, his ministers are not in accord and he has not yet advanced. We do not know where Cao Cao truly is. In Liyang’s army there is no Cao banner; why do we here see another banner?”

Chen Deng said, “Cao has a hundred schemes. He treats Hebei as vital and watches personally. He is deliberately not placing his banner here, only making a show of strength. I think Cao is not here.”

Liu Bei asked which of his two younger brothers could reconnoiter.

Zhang Fei said, “Your younger brother will go.”

Liu Bei said, “You are rash and hot-tempered; you may not go.”

Zhang Fei said, “Even if Cao Cao is there, I can seize him.”

Zhang Yun said, “Let this brother go observe their movements.”

Liu Bei said, “If Yunchang goes, I will be at ease.”

So Yunchang led three thousand horse and marched out from Xu Province. It was early winter. The sky was overcast, snow fell in whirls. All horsemen and cavalry were arrayed in snow.

Yunchang rode hard, sword drawn, and rode out, calling loudly for Wang Zhong to respond.

Wang Zhong came out and said, “Why has the Chancellor not yet surrendered here?”

Yunchang said, “Invite the Chancellor to the field; I have words to speak.”

Wang Zhong said, “Would the Chancellor step out to see you?”

Yunchang grew angry and spurred forward. Wang Zhong raised his spear to meet him. The two horses collided and Yunchang wheeled his mount away. Wang Zhong chased. They turned at a hillside. Yunchang turned again, shouted once, and then cut straight in with his blade.

Wang Zhong could not block him, so he bolted at speed. Yunchang with his left hand lowered his treasure sword, and with his right grabbed the chin strap on Wang Zhong’s armor; he dragged him from the saddle and carried him crosswise on his horse back to the original camp. Wang Zhong’s troops scattered in all directions in flight.

Yunchang took Wang Zhong captive and returned to Xu Province to see Liu Bei.

Liu Bei asked, “Who are you? What post do you hold? How dare you pretend to be Chancellor Cao?”

Wang Zhong said, “How could I fake it? I was ordered to create this false show and feint as an uncertainty. The Chancellor is not actually here.”

Liu Bei ordered him given clothes and food, kept him temporarily under watch, and said they would execute this after capturing Liu Dai and then confer. Yunchang said, “My elder brother has a wish for peace, so I brought the general alive.”

Liu Bei said, “I feared Yide was violent and rash, and might kill Wang Zhong, so I did not send him. There is no benefit in killing such men; keep him alive so that he may serve as ground for negotiation.”

Zhang Fei said, “Our second brother has captured Wang Zhong. I will go and capture Liu Dai alive.”

Liu Bei said, “Liu Dai formerly governed Yanzhou. In the campaign against Dong Zhuo at Hulao, he was also a commanding lord. He is now a vanguard general; we cannot underestimate him.”

Zhang Fei replied, “How important can such a man be? If I can capture him like Yide, all will be done.”

Liu Bei said, “I fear his life may be lost and our cause go awry.”

Zhang Fei said, “If it comes to killing, I will pay for his life.”

Liu Bei set out with three thousand soldiers.

When Liu Dai heard Wang Zhong had been captured, he held his camp tight and did not come out. Zhang Fei shouted abuse daily in front of the camp. Dai heard it was Zhang Fei and all the more dared not come out. Fei held out several days and planned: “Tonight at the second watch, break into their camp; by day, drink in the tent pretending to be drunk. Then seek out offences among the soldiers, beat someone, and tie them in camp, saying: ‘When I march out at night, bring me back our banners.’”

But he secretly allowed his men to slip out at once. They escaped and went straight to Liu Dai’s camp with a report of the planned raid. Liu Dai saw the surrendered soldier badly wounded and listened. He believed his words. He left camp seemingly empty and posted hidden troops outside.

That night, Zhang Fei divided his troops in three columns. In the center he sent just over thirty men to raid the camp and set it on fire. He also ordered two wings to swing out behind Liu Dai’s camp. When flames rose, that would be the signal to close and strike.

At the second watch, Zhang Fei with selected troops first cut off Liu Dai’s retreat. The middle column of thirty or so men burst into the camp and set it ablaze. Liu Dai’s ambush waited until they entered fully; then both wings came out together. Dai’s army descended into confusion, not knowing how many soldiers they faced, and scattered.

Liu Dai gathered a remnant force and tried to break out, only to run into Zhang Fei. In the narrow streets there was no space to avoid one another. They met horse to horse once, and at the first clash, Zhang Fei captured him alive. The rest surrendered.

Fei sent word to Xu Province at once.

When Liu Bei heard this he said to Zhang Fei, “Yide has always been rough; today he has used strategy too. I have no worries.” Then he rode out himself to greet him at the gate.

Zhang Fei said, “My older brother says I am violent and rash. How is this now?”

Liu Bei said, “Do not incite him with words; how would he not follow cunning?”

Zhang Fei laughed.

When Liu Bei saw them bring Liu Dai bound, he dismounted in haste and untied him, saying, “Younger brother Zhang Fei, I have committed an affront. Please forgive the offense.” He brought him into Xu Province and released Wang Zhong, then received them both.

Liu Bei said, “Formerly a cart guard wanted to harm me, so I had no choice but to strike him. Chancellor Cao misread my loyalty and sent two generals to come and question me. I have received great grace from the Chancellor and was ready to repay it; how could I rebel? If these two generals go to Xudu and petition for me with fair words, such is my hope.”

Liu Dai and Wang Zhong said, “We deeply owe your lordship for not killing us. When we return to the Chancellor, our entire households and the old and young of ours will protect and serve him.”

Liu Bei thanked them. On the next day he returned all their army mounts and sent them out beyond the city walls.

Liu Dai and Wang Zhong had not yet gone ten li when a drum sounded. Zhang Fei blocked their path and roared, “My brother was too careless! How can he capture bandit generals and then release them?”

Liu Dai and Wang Zhong trembled in their saddles.

Zhang Fei opened his eyes, held his spear out, and dashed toward them. From behind came another man on a flying horse shouting, “Do not be rude!” Looking back, it was Yunchang.

Only then did Liu Dai and Wang Zhong breathe.

Yunchang said, “Since elder brother has released them, how can my younger brother not follow law?”

Zhang Fei said, “This time they have been released. If they return again, it is no late to kill.”

Liu Dai and Wang Zhong retreated together, saying, “Even if the Chancellor orders our whole families punished, we will never return. Please show us mercy.”

Zhang Fei said, “Even if Cao Cao comes himself, not a sliver of his armor will leave! Let this time pass with the count of two heads marked.”

Liu Dai and Wang Zhong clutched their heads and fled like rats.

Zhang Fei and Guan Yu returned to Liu Bei and said, “Cao Cao will surely return.”

Sun Qian told Liu Bei, “The land around Xu Province is under enemy. It cannot be held long. Better divide troops and hold Xiao Pei, defend Pizhou, and become a projecting flank to guard against Cao Cao.”

Liu Bei accepted his counsel. He ordered Yunchang to hold Xiaopei. Lady Gan and Lady Mi were also placed at Xiaopei: Lady Gan was from Xiaopei; Lady Mi was the sister of Mi Zhu.

Sun Qian, Jian Yong, Mi Zhu, and Mi Fang were ordered to defend Xu Province. Liu Bei and Zhang Fei moved to Xiaopei.

Liu Dai and Wang Zhong returned to Cao Cao and reported everything about Liu Bei’s lack of rebellion. Cao Cao shouted in fury, “You have shamed the state by these tasks, what use are you?” and ordered his men to bring them out and behead them.

The verse that followed read:

Dogs and hogs do not hold in combat against a tiger. Fish and shrimp vainly contend with dragons.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Yuan and Cao Each Raise Horse and Foot Armies; Guan Yu and Zhang Fei Jointly Capture Generals Wang Zhong and Liu Dai

chapters.html:
Cao Cao then wished to execute Liu Dai and Wang Zhong. Kong Rong remonstrated: “Those two are no match for Liu Bei; if they are executed, the soldiers may lose heart.” Cao Cao therefore spared their lives, stripped them of rank and stipends, and intended to raise troops against Liu Bei himself.

Kong Rong said, “It is the severe and frigid middle of winter now, and it is not the time to move an army. Wait until spring; it will not be too late. First send envoys to induce Zhang Xiu and Liu Biao to submit, and then we can turn to Xu Province.” Cao Cao accepted this counsel and first sent Liu Ye to persuade Zhang Xiu.

When Liu Ye reached Xiangcheng, he first visited Jia X and presented Cao Cao’s renown. Jia kept him at his house.

The next day he came to present himself before Zhang Xiu and spoke of Cao Cao’s invitation. In the midst of their discussion, a messenger from Yuan Shao arrived. Zhang Xiu ordered him in. The envoy presented a letter. Zhang Xiu read it, and it too expressed a bid for surrender.

Jia X said, asking the envoy, “How have you lately fared in raising troops and breaking Cao Cao? What was the outcome?”

The envoy said, “In this bitter winter we hold back from battle for now. General and Liu Biao of Jing Province both carry the manner of men of worth, so I come at their request.”

Jia X laughed aloud. “Go back to Benchu and tell him: ‘You cannot even endure your own brothers, how can you tolerate the worthies of all under heaven?’” He tore the letter apart before him and shouted the envoy away.

Zhang Xiu asked, “Now Yuan Shao is strong and Cao Cao weak. If we ruin this letter and expel the envoy, what shall we do if Yuan comes?”

Jia X replied, “Do not join Yuan; join Cao Cao.”

Zhang Xiu said, “I already bear a feud with Cao Cao. How can I live in peace with him?”

Jia X said, “There are three reasons to follow him: first, Cao Cao bears the Son of Heaven’s decree and campaigns under imperial command to pacify all under heaven; one should follow him. Second, if you join the stronger one, Yuan Shao, you are few for him and he will not value you much, while Cao Cao, though weak, would welcome your service. Third, Cao’s ambition is that of a hegemon; he is likely to set aside private resentments and show virtue across the realm. Therefore, do not doubt him.”

Zhang Xiu accepted him, then asked Liu Ye to meet face-to-face. Liu Ye praised Cao’s virtues and said, “Would the Chancellor still wish me to come here and make peace if he kept one old grievance in his mind?”

Zhang Xiu rejoiced and together with Jia X and others went to Xu, where they formally presented themselves and submitted. Zhang Xiu knelt on the steps before Cao Cao.

Cao Cao hurried to help him up and held his hand, saying, “Let your small fault not be kept in the heart.” He made Zhang Xiu the General Who Uplifts Valor and Jia X the Commander of the Golden Guard.

Cao then ordered Zhang Xiu to compose a letter inviting Liu Biao to submit. Jia X objected:

“Liu Jingsheng likes to gather renowned men. He will submit only if a famed scholar comes to speak for us.”

Cao asked Xun You, “Who is fit?”

Xun You answered, “Kong Rong could bear that responsibility.”

Cao assented. Xun You sought out Kong Rong and said, “The Chancellor wants one famed scholar as a traveling envoy. Can your Excellency take that office?”

Kong Rong said, “My friend Ni Heng, whose courtesy name was Zhongping, is ten times more gifted than I am. He belongs at the Son of Heaven’s side; he can do more than merely serve as envoy. I will recommend him to the throne.”

He then submitted this memorial for the emperor’s approval:

I have heard that when floodwaters run wild, the Son of Heaven seeks order and reaches to all four quarters to recruit worthy men. In former times, each reigning ruler extended his ancestor’s foundation, and good men gathered from every side.

Your Majesty, though brilliantly wise, inherited the thread of the realm and has met grievous misfortune, your labor and humility continuing from dawn to dusk. Heaven’s great mountains have lowered their spirits, and strange men have arisen.

I have observed Ni Heng of Pingyuan, a man of the surname Ni and courtesy name Zhongping. He is twenty-four years old, of pure character, upright and bright, with towering talent. Early he entered literature and in the halls saw hidden things. Whatever he behold, he can recite at once; whatever he briefly hears, he does not forget. Nature accords with the Way in him, and his thoughts seem divine. He can quietly discern hidden intentions and the movements of the world as if by a single glance.

He is loyal, upright, and frank, with a heart like frost and snow. When he sees the good he is startled; when he sees evil he is a resentful foe. In office and in conduct he stands firm, and in duty and warning he has not been surpassed by Shi Yu. A hundred hawks in a flock are not equal to one eagle. If he stands in the audience hall, there is much to behold: his eloquence runs swift and his speech pours forth in abundance. He untangles doubt and unravelled knots; even opposite camp and opposing arguments he can answer with ease.

In former times Jia Yi sought to test Juxu by linking him to the Xiongnu; General Zhongjun desired a long thong to hold fast to the violent Yue. He was brave in youth and praised by the age before he had reached maturity. Recently, Luo Cui and Yan Xiang likewise raised unusual talent and were raised as Platform gentlemen. Zhongping is worthy to stand beside them. Like a dragon leaping the sky road, spreading wings in the clouds, he can raise his cry to Ziwei and cast light like a rainbow arch; he can illuminate the multitudes of near office and add gravity to the front gate. In great orchestras of the vaults he will provide a rare spectacle, and in the imperial household he will secure an extraordinary treasure. Men of his rank cannot be obtained often.

In pieces like The Stirring of the Ch'u and The Songs of Yang E he has mastery of exquisite posture and movement, so coveted by performers. As a hawk-footed rabbit or the swift-flying mare, he is without limit in his run and in the way of music and delight that the discerning call for.

How can we not report this, since we are unworthy servants? His Majesty should choose your officials with care and test them in practice. Grant that Zhongping be summoned in plain brown robes. If no one can find him worthy, let me bear the guilt of deceiving Your Majesty by showing his face in vain.

The emperor read the memorial and passed it to Cao Cao. Cao thus sent for Ni Heng.

After the ceremonial greeting, Cao Cao did not order him to sit. Ni Heng looked up and sighed, “Although Heaven and Earth are vast, why is there no one?”

Cao Cao said, “There are dozens under my command, all heroes of our age. Why do you say there is none?”

Ni Heng said, “I would hear you tell me.”

Cao said, “Xun Yu, Xun You, Guo Jia, and Cheng Yu are sharp of mind and far-sighted in intellect, though even they fall short of Xiao He and Chen Ping. Zhang Liao, Xu Chu, Yue Jin, and Li Dian are formidable in courage, though not equal to Cen Peng and Ma Wu. Lü Qian and Man Chong attend to affairs; Yu Jin and Xu Huang lead the vanguard. Xiahou Dun is a rare genius of heaven and earth; Cao Zixiao is a blessed commander of our age. How then could there be no one?”

Ni Heng laughed. “Your words are in error. I know all these men well:

Xun Yu may be sent to inquire after a funeral and to visit the sick; Xun You to watch a grave and tend tombs; Cheng Yu to shut the gate and bolt a door; Guo Jia to read a verse with clear wording; Zhang Liao to beat drums and strike bronze; Xu Chu to graze cattle and release horses; Yue Jin to copy documents and read an edict; Li Dian to carry letters and deliver summonses; Lü Qian to grind blades and cast swords; Man Chong to drink and feast; Yu Jin to carry timbers and build walls; Xu Huang to slaughter pigs and dogs.

Xiahou Dun is called the General of Complete Body, while Cao Zixiao is called the Money-Taking Magistrate. As for all the rest, they are merely cloth racks and grain sacks, wine vats and meat bags.”

Cao Cao grew angry: “What can you do?”

Ni Heng said, “Heaven and earth, astronomy and geography—I know none that I do not know. The Three Teachings and Nine Streams—I know none that I do not understand. I can make a ruler into Yao and Shun above, and I can equal Kong and Yan in virtue below. Why should I discuss such things with vulgar men?”

Only Zhang Liao stood at his side and drew his sword to execute him. Cao Cao said, “What I lack is only a drummer in the halls. At dawn and dusk in court banquets and rites, I can make Ni Heng serve in that role.”

Ni Heng did not decline and answered at once. Zhang Liao said, “His words are insolent. Why not kill him?”

Cao Cao said, “He has a reputation, broad and distant, heard near and far. If I kill him today, all under heaven will say I cannot bear talent. He thinks himself able; therefore I will place him in this post and humiliate him.”

The next day Cao Cao held a grand banquet in the hall and ordered the drumming attendant to strike the drum. An old attendant said, “The drummer should change into new clothing.”

Ni Heng entered in old clothes and played the drum to the tune Yuyang San Zhua. The notes were extraordinary, with depth like jade and stone striking together. No guest failed to be moved and to weep. Someone nearby shouted, “Why do you not change garments?”

Ni Heng took off his old torn robe before all and stood fully bare. Every onlooker covered his face. Ni Heng then slowly pulled up his trousers; his expression never changed.

Cao shouted, “How can you be so impolite in a place of ancestral halls?”

Ni Heng replied, “To deceive the ruler and mislead superiors is itself the true indecency. I stand bare of my mother-and-father’s form only to reveal the purity of my body!”

Cao said, “If you are pure, who is polluted?”

Ni Heng replied, “Your eyes are muddy, for you cannot distinguish the worthy from the base. Your mouth is muddy, for you do not study poetry and books. Your ears are muddy, for you ignore loyal counsel. Your body is muddy, for you know not past and present. Your belly is muddy, for you do not treat the princes and lords rightly. Your mind is muddy, for you constantly bear rebellious ambition. I, the famed scholar of the world, being made mere drumming attendant, is the same as if Yang Huo had mocked Confucius and Zang Cang had slandered Mencius. If one seeks the work of a hegemonic lord, why treat men so lightly?”

Kong Rong was present and feared Cao would order his death. He said calmly, “Ni Heng’s offenses are not beyond the common sort, and they are not fit to expose the Son of Heaven’s intentions.”

Cao gestured at Ni Heng and said, “Send him to Jing Province as an envoy. If Liu Biao submits, I will make him a minister of the court.”

Ni Heng refused to go. Cao prepared three fine horses and had two men hold him and lead him. At the same time he sent his civil and military officers to line up wine outside the East Gate.

Xun You said, “When Ni Heng comes, do not rise.”

Ni Heng arrived, dismounted, and entered to see Cao. All sat upright. Ni Heng burst into loud weeping.

Xun You asked, “Why do you cry?”

Ni Heng answered, “If I am already in a bier of death, how could I not weep?”

The others said, “We are all walking corpses. You alone are a headless madman!”

Ni Heng said, “I am an official of the Han; I am not a band of Cao Cao’s associates. How could I be headless?”

They wanted to kill him, but Xun You quickly stopped them, “What is this, mouse and sparrow alike, to dare defile the sword?”

Ni Heng said, “I am a mouse or sparrow, yes, but still with human nature. You, I can only call you mantises.”

With that the crowd turned away in resentment.

At Jing Province Ni Heng met Liu Biao. Though he praised his merits, he spoke in sarcasm. Liu Biao was not pleased and sent him to Jiangxia to meet Huang Zu.

Someone asked Liu Biao, “Ni Heng mocked Lord Liu. Why do you not execute him?”

Liu Biao said, “Ni Heng has insulted Cao Cao many times; Cao did not execute him, fearing he would lose public support. So he sent him here, hoping to let my hand take him and make me bear blame for killing a worthy man. I now send him to Huang Zu so Cao Cao may know that I recognized his trick.” All praised this.

Around the same time Yuan Shao also sent envoys. Liu Biao asked his strategist circle, “Yuan Benchu has sent messengers again, and now Cao Mengde has dispatched Ni Heng. Which side should we follow?”

Han Song, one of the Gentleman Attendants of the Household, said, “The two mighty men are now locked against each other. If the commander wishes to accomplish anything, this is a chance to break the enemy. If not, he should attach himself to the better side. Cao Cao commands troops well and many worthies gather to him; he will surely first take Yuan Shao and then move his force toward Jiangdong. Then the general may not hold it back. Therefore it is best to carry all of Jing Province to him; Cao will then treat the general with honor.”

Liu Biao said, “You go back to Xu, observe the situation, and then we shall again consult.”

Han Song replied, “Ruler and minister each has fixed duty. Now I serve this general; though I go through fire and boiling water, I must obey my command only. If the general can first accord with the Son of Heaven above and follow Cao above below, he may keep Han Song; if he remains uncertain, and then stands in the capital where he receives an appointment from the Son of Heaven, Han Song will be the Son of Heaven’s official and can no longer die as the general’s man.”

Liu Biao said, “Go and observe first. I have another design.”

Han Song withdrew and went to Xu, where Cao Cao received him. Cao made him Central Attendant and appointed him Administrator of Lingling Commandery.

Xun You said, “Han Song has come only to observe movements and achieved no real service, yet you have granted him this post. Ni Heng has provided no reports, and Cao Cao sent him and has not inquired again. Why?”

Cao Cao replied, “Ni Heng insulted me to the utmost, so I used Liu Biao’s hand to dispose of him; why press further?” He then sent Han Song back to Jing Province to speak with Liu Biao.

Han Song returned and praised the court’s grandeur and urged Liu Biao to send his son to attend audience. Liu Biao flew into rage. “Do you have a double heart?” he said, and he wanted to execute Han Song.

Han Song shouted, “General, you owe Song; Song owes no debt to the general.”

Kuai Liang said, “Before Song left, he already spoke this.” Liu Biao pardoned him.

A report arrived that Huang Zu had beheaded Ni Heng. Liu Biao asked why. The one present answered, “Huang Zu and Ni Heng drank together and became drunk. Huang asked him, ‘Who are the men of note in Xu in your eyes now?’

Ni Heng said, ‘My older child is Kong Wenju, my younger child is Yang Dezu; apart from these two, there are no other figures.’

Huang Zu asked, ‘How do I compare to you?’

Ni Heng said, ‘You resemble the spirit in a temple: though it receives sacrificial rites, one may regret there is no power in it.’

Huang Zu grew furious: ‘Do you take me for a puppet of earth and wood?’ He immediately beheaded him. To the end, Ni Heng did not cease his abuse.”

When Liu Biao heard of Ni Heng’s death he wailed long and ordered burial by the banks of Parrot Isle.

Later poets sighed:

Huanzu had no equal among true elders; Ni Heng lost his head at this riverbank. When I come now past Parrot Isle, only the cold water flows without feeling.

When Cao Cao heard that Ni Heng had been harmed, he laughed, “A corrupt scholar’s sword of tongue has killed itself!” He then said that since Liu Biao did not submit, he would raise troops to demand justice.

Xun You remonstrated, “Yuan Shao is not yet subdued and Liu Bei has not been destroyed. To move troops through Jianghan now is like abandoning one’s vital organs to defend the hands and feet. First destroy Yuan Shao, then destroy Liu Bei, and the lands along Yang and Han can be leveled and pacified at once.” Cao followed this counsel.

Meanwhile, after Dong Cheng had left, he and Wang Zifu and others discussed the matter day and night and had no workable plan. In the fifth year of Jian’an, on New Year’s day, they offered court salutations and saw Cao Cao becoming even more arrogant and overbearing, so they burned with anger and fell ill. The emperor learned his imperial uncle had grown sick and ordered the chief imperial physician to go with Dong to treat him.

That physician was from Luoyang, surname Ji, given name Tai, courtesy name Ping, and known as Ji Ping, a famed doctor. Ji Ping came to Dong’s estate and medicated him day and night without leaving. He often heard Dong’s deep sighs and laments but did not dare to question.

When the Lantern Festival came, Ji Ping asked leave to depart. Dong Cheng begged him to stay, and the two drank together. They drank until past the watch of night, and Dong Cheng grew weary and in sleep took up his robes and lay down.

Suddenly word came that Wang Zifu and four others were there. Dong Cheng went to receive them.

Wang Zifu said, “Great fortune has come to pass!”

Dong Cheng said, “Tell me what you propose.”

Wang Zifu said, “Liu Biao has aligned with Yuan Shao and raised 500,000 men. They are advancing in ten routes to kill us. Ma Teng has joined Han Sui and raised seven hundred and twenty thousand from the west, marching south. Cao Cao has called out all Xu Prefecture troops and divided forces to meet each enemy, leaving the capital bare. If we gather five household retainers, we can have a little over a thousand men. Tonight this house holds a grand banquet for Lantern Festival rewards and honors. If we seize the gates and break in, we can kill him. This is the moment; do not miss it.”

Dong Cheng rejoiced and immediately summoned all household slaves to ready arms. He donned armor, took up his spear, mounted and prepared; all agreed to meet at the inner gate, and then to advance in formation.

At second watch they all arrived.

Dong Cheng took up his treasured sword and on foot entered straight in and saw Cao Cao hosting a banquet in the main hall. He shouted, “Cao thief, do not run!”

He raised his blade and struck once, then collapsed. Suddenly he awoke as if from a dream of Nan-ke, and still cursed, “Cao thief!” with no end to it.

Ji Ping came forward shouting, “Did you intend to kill Cao Gong?”

Dong Cheng was frightened and could not answer.

Ji Ping said, “Uncle, do not be alarmed. Though I treat the sick, I have not forgotten Han. For several days I saw your uncle sighing and lamenting and did not dare to ask. The words just now, spoken in your dream, have revealed your true intent. Do not hide it from me. If there is a use for me, even if nine generations are annihilated, I have no regret.”

Dong Cheng covered his face and wept, “I only fear you are not sincere!”

Ji Ping then bit off a point of his finger and swore. Dong Cheng brought out the belt edict and asked Ji Ping to read it. He said, “The plan failed because Liu Xuande and Ma Teng had each departed, and no new method remained, and so I became sick from grief.”

Ji Ping said, “No need for your concern. Cao the thief’s life lies in my hands.”

Dong Cheng asked why.

Ji Ping replied, “Cao is habitually afflicted with wind in the head; it drives pain into the marrow. The slightest bout summons my visit. If there is a call from him in the morning or evening, one dose of poisonous medicine is enough to kill him. Why raise swords and troops?”

Dong Cheng said, “If this is so, this one man will save the Han and the realm.”

Ji Ping then took leave to return.

In his heart Dong Cheng was secretly glad. He entered the rear hall and saw his slave Qin Qingtong and his concubine Yun Ying whispering together in hiding.

Dong Cheng grew furious, shouted for guards, and had them seized, intending to kill them.

His wife interceded to spare their lives. Each was whipped forty lashes, and Qingtong was bound in the cold room.

Nursed with resentment, Qingtong twisted the iron shackles in the middle of the night, jumped over the wall, and fled directly to Cao Cao’s residence, reporting a matter of state.

Cao Cao summoned him to a private room and asked, “What have you seen?”

Qingtong said, “Wang Zifu, Wu Zilan, Zhong Ji, Wu Shuo, and Ma Teng met to discuss a secret matter at master’s estate. It must have been a plot against the Chancellor. The master was about to send out a strip of white silk; I do not know what was written on it. Recently Ji Ping bit his finger as oath; I saw it myself.”

Cao Cao hid Qingtong inside the compound and let Dong Cheng think he had fled elsewhere, so no one sought him.

The next day Cao Cao feigned a headache, and summoned Ji Ping for medicine.

Ji Ping thought inwardly, “This villain has finished,” and secretly hid poison in the pharmacy. Cao Cao lay on his bed and told Ji Ping to give the dose.

Ji Ping said, “This illness can be cured in one dose.” He took the medicine jar and brewed it before him. When half the decoction had dried, Ji Ping had already added poison and then gave it himself.

Cao knew poison was in it, and intentionally delayed drinking.

Ji Ping said, “If taken hot, only a little sweating and he will recover.”

Cao rose and said, “You have read the books, so you know propriety. ‘When one is ill, a subject tastes the medicine first; when one’s father is ill, a son tastes it first.’ You are my close officer; why do you not taste it first and only then give it?”

Ji Ping answered, “Medicine is to cure disease. Why does one need to taste first?”

Ji Ping saw that the matter was exposed, strode forward, gripped Cao’s ear, and forced it down his throat.

Cao thrust the medicine out to the ground; the bricks flew and shattered.

Cao had not spoken when guards seized Ji Ping and brought him below. Cao said, “I was not truly ill; I only tested you. If you would poison me, someone must have urged you. If you tell me that name, I will spare you.”

Ji Ping shouted, “You are the usurping bandit who deceives the Son of Heaven; all beneath the heavens want to kill you—why not me alone?”

Cao repeated the torture. Ji Ping grew angry: “I wanted to kill you myself. Who could have sent me? The plot failed, and only death remains.”

Cao grew angry and had prison guards beat him fiercely. For two hours his skin split and flesh opened, blood filling the steps. Fearing they had killed him before testimony, Cao ordered the guards taken to a quiet place and let him rest for the moment.

He ordered a banquet the next day and invited all senior ministers to drink. Dong Cheng only feigned illness and did not come. Wang Zifu and the others, fearing Cao’s suspicion, all came.

Cao set seats in the rear hall. The wine went around several rounds. “There is nothing here to make this banquet lively,” he said. “There is one person among us who can wake all others.” He ordered twenty guards, “Bring him.”

Soon the guards came with a long fetter and collar and chain and dragged Ji Ping to the steps.

Cao said, “My honored ministers do not know: this man joined evil rebels and plotted to overturn court and slay Cao. Heaven has turned against him. Hear his own words.”

He ordered a beating first; the man collapsed unconscious. They poured water on his face. Ji Ping revived, opened his eyes and with teeth clenched cursed,

“Cao thief! If you will not kill me, when else?”

Cao said, “There are six accomplices already, making seven with you. Tell me their names.”

Ji Ping only shouted more abuse. Wang Zifu and the others looked at each other like men seated on a bed of needles.

Cao commanded more blows and more water. Ji Ping made no plea for mercy. Seeing no confession, Cao ordered him dragged away.

After the ministers dispersed, Cao left only Wang Zifu and the four with him for the night banquet. The four were dazed, with no spirit in their bones.

Cao said, “I had no wish to keep you, but there remains something to ask. What did you all discuss with Dong Cheng?”

Zifu said, “Nothing of consequence.”

Cao said, “What was written on the strip of white silk?”

Wang Zifu and the other three all held back. Cao brought out Qingtong to confront them. Wang Zifu said, “This villain had adultery with your uncle’s maid and was punished for false reporting. Do not accept it.”

Cao said, “Ji Ping’s poison was not sent by Dong Cheng. Who else then?”

The four said, “We know nothing.”

Cao said, “If you confess tonight, you may still be pardoned. If we wait until the matter breaks out, this will be intolerable!”

Even then Wang Zifu and the others denied involvement.

Cao shouted and had guards seize all four and imprison them.

The next day he led those gathered and went straight to Dong Cheng’s house on the pretext of making inquiry into his illness. Dong Cheng had no choice but to come out.

Cao said, “Why did you fail to attend my banquet last night?”

Dong Cheng said, “A mild illness has not healed; I dared not venture out lightly.”

Cao said, “That is a grave illness of state.” Dong Cheng was stunned.

Cao said, “Do you know about Ji Ping?”

Dong Cheng said, “I do not.”

Cao laughed coldly, “How can my uncle not know?” He shouted for attendants: “Bring him, and let him rise with the uncle’s sickness.”

Dong Cheng had no place to stand.

Soon twenty guards dragged Ji Ping to the steps.

Ji Ping shouted, “Cao, bandit of the state?”

Cao pointed to him and told Dong, “This man has already linked up with Wang Zifu and three others, whom I have arrested and brought before the Censorate. One remains at large.”

Turning back, he asked, “Who sent you to give me medicine? Speak quickly and name him!”

Ji Ping said, “Heaven sent me to kill this treacherous lord!”

Cao ordered him beaten. There was no point on the body where there was no instrument for punishment.

Dong Cheng watched, his heart cut as with a knife.

Cao asked again, “You had ten fingers. How do you now have nine?”

Ji Ping said, “I chewed them off as an oath—to slay the rebel lord!”

Cao ordered a knife brought, and at the steps cut away his remaining nine fingers, saying, “One strike to cut, teach you the weight of oath.”

Ji Ping said, “I still have a mouth to denounce traitors and a tongue to curse them!”

Cao then ordered his tongue severed.

Ji Ping said, “Do not move yet. Punishment has done me no good; only confession can be had. Release my bonds.”

Cao asked, “What is the obstacle to release?” He ordered his fetters undone.

Ji Ping rose, stood facing the hall gate, and bowed.

“Your servant could not remove the criminal from the state,” he said. “Such is Heaven’s decree.”

When he finished, he threw himself against the steps and died.

Cao ordered his limbs separated and distributed.

It was the first month of the fifth year of Jian’an. A court poem was written:

Han has no sign of renewal; in this world, doctor Ping is praised by name. He swore to remove treacherous kin and gave his body for bright rule. The words of extreme punishment grew fiercer still. Blood from all ten fingers ran like threads; for ages to come he is revered for a name beyond ordinary.

After seeing Ji Ping dead, Cao had guards bring Qin Qingtong before him.

Cao said, “Can the imperial uncle recognize this man?”

Dong Cheng grew furious: “That was a runaway slave! He should be executed at once.”

Cao said, “He first accused a plot to rebel; now he bears witness to it. Who then dare execute him?”

Dong Cheng said, “Why does the Chancellor listen to the word of one escaped slave?”

Cao said, “Wang Zifu and the four have already been captured by me and their confessions are clear. Do you still deny?”

He called attendants and had Dong Cheng seized. He ordered men to enter Dong’s bedchamber and search out the belt edict and the written declaration of intention.

Cao read and laughed, “How dare common rats do this!”

He then ordered, “Arrest all of Dong Cheng’s household, both men and women. Let not one escape.”

He returned to his estate and showed the declaration to all advising ministers so they might discuss. He spoke of deposing the Son of Heaven and installing a new sovereign.

A handful of vermilion decrees make vain hopes, one sheet of alliance writing brings calamity. Who knows how the life of the offered Son of Heaven will fare? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Ni Heng, Bare of Garments, Curses the Traitor, and Master Ji Dies from His Failed Poisoning

chapters.html:
Later, Cao Cao, whose courtesy name was Mengde, saw the secret belt order and conferred with his ministers, wanting to depose Emperor Xian and enthrone another man of virtue. Cheng Yu, whose courtesy name was Zhongde, advised him, “My lord, your ability to strike fear across the four quarters and command all under heaven came from acting in the Han’s name. The lords are not yet pacified; if he now attempts to depose and enthrone in haste, troops will surely rise.” Cao Cao stopped.

He ordered Dong Cheng and four others, together with all their older and younger family members, sent on chains to the city gates and beheaded there. More than seven hundred perished. No officials or commoners in the city who saw it did not weep.

Later people wrote this verse in mourning for Dong Cheng:

A hidden edict was carried in the ribbon of a sash; heaven’s decree went out through the gate of the inner palace. He once saved the imperial carriage, and now on this day he again receives grace. To worry for the state became a sickness in his heart, purging treachery entered even his dreams and his soul. Faithful rectitude remains for all ages; who can now judge success or failure?

Another verse was written for Wang Zifu and the others:

On narrow paper and white silk we wrote an oath of loyal counsel, fierce at heart, we longed to repay our lord as one repays a father. A red-hearted man may be pitied when he offers a hundred lives, yet a cinnabar heart alone endures for a thousand autumns.

Now that Dong Cheng and the others had been killed, Cao Cao’s fury had not yet faded. He drew his sword and entered the palace to execute Lady Dong, who was Dong Cheng’s sister. The emperor had favored her and she was already five months pregnant. That day, Your Majesty was in the inner court, privately discussing the matter of Dong Cheng with Empress Fu. No report had yet reached them.

Suddenly Cao Cao arrived with a drawn sword and a face full of rage, and Your Majesty started in alarm and turned pale. Cao Cao asked, “Do You know that Dong Cheng plotted rebellion, Your Majesty?”

Emperor Xian replied, “Dong Zhuo was already executed.”

Cao Cao said loudly, “Not Dong Zhuo—Dong Cheng.”

The emperor trembled: “I truly did not know.”

Cao Cao said, “Do You forget the edict you had corrected by breaking your own finger?”

The emperor could not answer. Cao Cao shouted for the guards, who seized Lady Dong and brought her forward.

Your Majesty begged, “Lady Dong is five months pregnant. I beg Your Chancellor to show mercy.”

Cao Cao replied, “Had it not been for Heaven’s betrayal, I would already have been killed. How can I still keep this woman, to become a future danger to me?”

Empress Fu then said, “Demote her to the cold palace; after she gives birth, to kill her is not yet too late.”

Cao Cao snapped, “Would you keep this treacherous seed so her mother may take revenge?”

Lady Dong, crying, begged, “Let me die with my body whole, and do not expose what is inside me.”

Cao Cao ordered white rope brought before him. The emperor wept and said to her, “Under Nine Springs, do not blame me.” He had no more words, and tears fell like rain. Empress Fu also wept loudly.

Cao Cao shouted, “Still making a child’s show of grief?” He ordered the guards to drag her out and had her beheaded outside the palace gate.

Later people wrote of Lady Dong:

Even in the spring hall she had been honored, yet all was in vain; alas, the dragon seed was cast down and the time to mourn came together. Though an emperor’s lord and ruler, he could not save himself, and only covered his face while tears rose in sudden springs.

Cao Cao instructed the prison and palace officers: “Hereafter, if any in-law clan of the inner court enters the palace gate without my orders, execute them on the spot. If the guards fail in defense, they share the same guilt.”

He also assigned three thousand trusted men to the Imperial Guard under Cao Hong’s command for watch and protection.

Cao Cao said to Cheng Yu, “Though Dong Cheng has been executed, there are still Ma Teng and Liu Bei in these parts. They cannot be left alive.”

Cheng Yu replied, “Ma Teng is camped in Xiliang; he cannot be taken lightly. But send letters to soothe and honor him and never stir suspicion, then lure him to the capital to deal with him. Liu Bei is now in Xu Province, scattered in awkward, bent-formation posture; he too should not be underestimated. Besides, Yuan Shao keeps troops at Guandu and often has designs on Xuchang. If I one day go east against Liu Bei, Liu Bei will surely seek Yuan Shao’s aid. Yuan Shao, taking advantage of the opening, could strike. How would we answer that?”

Cao Cao said, “No. Liu Bei is a man of talent. If we do not strike now, when his wings have formed, matters will quickly become difficult. Yuan Shao may be powerful, but his plans are full of doubt and indecision. Why should we fear him?”

While they were in council, Guo Jia entered from outside. Cao Cao asked, “I want to campaign east against Liu Bei, yet I still worry about Yuan Shao. What should I do?”

Guo Jia, whose courtesy name was Fengxiao, replied, “Yuan Shao is slow and suspicious, and his advisors compete out of envy. There is no need to fear him. Liu Bei has only just reassembled his soldiers, and their loyalty is not yet settled. If the Chancellor leads troops east, one battle will settle him.”

Cao Cao was overjoyed. “That is exactly what I had in mind.” He therefore raised two hundred thousand troops and divided them into five columns toward Xu Province.

Spies later reported the movement to Xu Province. Sun Qian first rode to Xiapi and informed Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, then went on to Xiaopei to tell Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande.

Liu Bei and Sun Qian discussed: “We must surely seek help from Yuan Shao; only so can we end this danger.” So Liu Bei drafted one letter and sent Sun Qian to Hebei.

Sun Qian first visited Tian Feng and explained everything, asking him to plead on their behalf. Tian Feng then took Sun Qian to meet Yuan Shao and presented the letter. Yuan Shao looked withered and disheveled in dress and cap.

Tian Feng asked, “Why is Your Excellency so stricken today?”

Yuan Shao said, “I am as good as dead.”

Tian Feng said, “Why would Your Excellency say that?”

Yuan Shao answered, “I have five sons, and of them only the youngest is most distressing to my thoughts. I am now afflicted with scabies; my life is nearly gone. What other affairs could I still consider?”

Tian Feng said, “Now Cao Cao is marching east against Liu Bei. Xuchang is left open. If we enter with righteous troops at this moment, we can protect the Son of Heaven above and save myriads of people below. This is an opportunity not easily obtained. You alone must judge it.”

Yuan Shao said, “I know this would be best. Yet my mind wavers; I fear something may go badly for me.”

Tian Feng asked, “What is this uncertainty?”

Yuan Shao said, “Of my five sons, only this child’s illness in the cradle is enough to unsettle me.”

He then refused to dispatch troops. “I shall not leave,” he said, and turned to Sun Qian. “Return and tell Liu Bei the reason. If things go ill, he may come to me for alliance; I will surely have means to aid him.”

Tian Feng struck the ground with his staff and cried, “At a time when such a chance has appeared, to waste it over a sick infant is to let a great affair slip away. How regrettable!” He stamped his foot and sighed deeply as he left.

When Sun Qian saw Yuan Shao refused to send help, he had to return by night to Xiaopei to report to Liu Bei.

Liu Bei was greatly alarmed. “What can we do now?”

Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, said, “Elder brother, do not grieve. Cao Cao’s army has come from far off and will surely be exhausted and short of supply. If we strike its vanguard at first arrival and sack its camp, we can break Cao Cao.”

Liu Bei said, “I have always thought of you merely as a brave fighter, but when you once captured Liu Dai you used plans as well. That proposal now is also apt strategy.” He followed Zhang Fei’s advice and divided forces to raid the camp.

Now Cao Cao was leading his army toward Xiaopei. As they marched, a sudden gale came up, and just then there was a loud sound: a tusked banner was snapped. Cao Cao ordered the troops to halt at once and gathered his counselors to read the omen.

Xun Yu asked, “From which direction does this wind come, and what color was the banner it snapped?”

Cao Cao answered, “From the southeast. It snapped the one flag hanging at the point, a blue-and-red banner.”

Xun Yu said, “Do not attend other matters. This night Liu Bei will surely raid the camp.” Cao Cao nodded.

Then Mao Jie came in and said, “The southeast wind just rose and bent the same blue-and-red tusked banner. What do Your Lordship think this bodes?”

Cao Cao asked, “What is your meaning?”

Mao Jie said, “I only dare to say this: this night someone is certain to raid the camp.”

Alas, when the son of heaven stood alone and desolate, he relied fully on splitting his forces and raiding camp. Yet how can we endure this omen of the snapped banner? Why did Heaven let this crooked hero run wild?

Cao Cao said, “Heaven confirms my concerns. We will prepare at once.” He divided his troops into nine sections, leaving one section forward to make a sham encampment while the other eight lay hidden in ambush on every side.

That night the moon was faintly bright. Liu Bei was on the left, Zhang Fei on the right; they sent out two columns, leaving Sun Qian to hold Xiaopei.

Zhang Fei thought himself to have gained a good stratagem and led light horse in front, breaking into Cao Cao’s camp. He saw only scattered men and horses. From four sides firelight surged up and shouts rose in unison. Realizing he had been tricked, he hurried out of camp.

From the east came Zhang Liao, from the west Xu Chu, from the south Yu Jin, from the north Li Dian, from the southeast Xu Huang, from the southwest Yue Jin, from the northeast Xiahou Dun, and from the northwest Xiahou Yuan. Their mounted troops came charging from eight directions.

Zhang Fei charged and countercharged, covering front and rear at once. The troops he had brought were old soldiers of Cao Cao’s own men. Seeing the sudden danger, they all surrendered.

Just as Zhang Fei was still killing, Xu Huang smashed in with a great charge, and Yue Jin came up behind. Zhang Fei cut a bloody lane and burst through. Only a few dozen riders could keep up with him.

He thought of returning to Xiaopei, but the road was blocked. If he rushed to Xu Province and Xiapi, he feared Cao’s army would intercept him. Finding no way, he headed toward Mangdang Mountain.

Now Liu Bei led his troops in raiding the camp. As he neared the gate, his shouted battle cries thundered, and a force burst from behind, first cutting off half his men. Xiahou Dun was there again. Liu Bei broke through and escaped; Xiahou Yuan chased him from the rear.

Liu Bei looked back and saw only some thirty riders still with him. He wanted desperately to run back to Xiaopei, but there he saw flames rising from Xiaopei city. He had to abandon it and aim for Xu Province and Xiapi, but saw Cao troops flooding through ridges and hills, blocking every road.

Liu Bei thought there was no place to return. “Yuan Shao had said, ‘If things do not go as you wish, you may come to me for alliance.’ Rather than push straight onward, I should perhaps go to him for the moment and make another plan.” He headed toward the road to Qing Province, where at once Li Dian blocked him. Liu Bei fled northward in disorder on horseback. Li Dian captured him with pursuing riders.

Liu Bei reached Qing Province on a single horse, covering three hundred li in a day, and rushed beneath the city gate. After giving his name, Liu Bei sent word to the Inspector. The inspector was Yuan Tan, Yuan Shao’s eldest son. He had long respected Liu Bei and, when he heard that he had come in alone, immediately opened the gate to receive him, brought him into the public office, and inquired about his situation.

Liu Bei fully explained that he had been routed and sought alliance and refuge.

Yuan Tan lodged him at the relay station in the guest hall, sent a dispatch to Yuan Shao, and ordered local troops to escort him. At the edge of Pingyuan Commandery, Yuan Shao himself led people out from thirty li beyond Ye County to meet him.

Liu Bei knelt in thanks. Yuan Shao hurriedly replied with courtesies, “Yesterday I was taken ill and so failed to send aid. My heart has long held this resentment. I am now greatly relieved to meet You at last, for this is a long-desired sight.”

Liu Bei said, “I am Liu Bei, poor and destitute, long wishing to come under your protection. Yet chance never met us until now. Cao Cao attacks, and my wife and children are all in peril. You, who receive scholars and soldiers from all over the realm, I did not shrink from this shame to come directly to you for alliance. I beg that You receive me and I will swear to repay in full.”

Yuan Shao was delighted and treated him with great warmth. They stayed together in Ji Province.

Now Cao Cao took Xiaopei that very night and then advanced straight on Xu Province. Mi Zhu and Jian Yong could not hold the city gates and had to abandon the city and flee. Chen Deng submitted Xu Province. When Cao Cao’s main army entered the city and had pacified the people, he summoned his counselors to plan the seizure of Xiapi.

Xun Yu said, “Yun Chang is guarding Liu Bei’s wife and children and is holding this city to the death. If we do not take it quickly, he may be seized by Yuan Shao.”

Cao Cao said, “I have long admired Yun Chang’s military skill and talent, and I would like to bring him to my service. Better to send someone to persuade him and compel him to surrender.”

Guo Jia said, “Yun Chang’s loyalty is deep and righteous; he surely will not surrender. If we send someone to persuade him, they may be killed.”

A man from the tents stepped out and said, “I have at least some former acquaintance with Guan Yu and wish to go and speak with him.”

The men saw that it was Zhang Liao.

Cheng Yu said, “Though Wenyuan has old ties with Yun Chang, I judge this man can’t be won by words. I have a stratagem: make this man’s way of advance and retreat none at all; then have Wenyuan speak to him. He will then surely return to the Chancellor.”

Just so:

The bow is tuned and laid to send an arrow at the fierce tiger, fragrant bait to fish an ao fish. I do not yet know how this plan is to work. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Treacherous Court Scion's Outrage and the Death of the Imperial Consort; The Imperial Uncle Flees to Yuan Shao

chapters.html:
Cheng Yu, whose courtesy name was Zhongde, presented a plan: “Guan Yunchang could not be taken by strength alone, only by stratagem. At once send over several former soldiers of Liu Bei who have already surrendered. Send them to Xiapi to meet Lord Guan, telling him they are deserters who have turned back from the enemy and are now hiding in the city as an inside force. Then force Lord Guan into battle, feign defeat and partial rout, lure him into another position, and when he begins to retreat, cut off his path with an elite detachment. Then the matter can be accomplished.”

When Cao Cao heard the proposal, he ordered dozens of surrendering troops from Xu Province to ride straight to Xiapi and submit to him. Guan Yunchang took them for old soldiers and kept from doubting.

The next day Xiahou Dun took the vanguard with five thousand men and went to wrestle Lord Guan.

Guan did not come out, so Xiahou Dun sent men under the city walls to hurl insults. Guan flared with anger and brought out three thousand horse and foot, then engaged Xiahou Dun. After more than ten bouts, Dun wheeled his horse and turned back. Guan chased and Dun fought and withdrew as he ran. Guan drove him nearly twenty li. Fearing that Xiapi might be lost, he gathered his men and returned. He then heard a cannon-shot. Xu Huang came in from the left and Xu Chu from the right; two battalions interposed and blocked his path.

Guan broke for their flank, but both sides had hidden crossbowmen, one hundred great crossbows laid down, sending arrows like locusts. He could not pass. He ordered his troops to wheel back. Xu Huang and Xu Chu caught him and closed again. Guan cut down both sides and, turning the pursuit toward Xiapi, found Xiahou Dun blocking him again.

The engagement lasted through evening and into dusk. With no route home, Guan withdrew to a nearby earthen rise, and there he posted his troops and rested briefly. Cao’s troops then drew up in rings and enclosed the mound.

From the summit, Guan could see Xiapi in the city, flames leaping into the sky. It was then that those pretending to have surrendered had opened the gate from inside. Cao Cao had brought his main army into the city and had set the fires to confound Lord Guan’s mind.

Guan saw the fires and grew alarmed. Through the night he ran down from the mound several times, each time turned back by scattered arrows. At dawn he again sought to gather and rush down, when a rider came up the hill on horseback. It was Zhang Liao.

Guan greeted him and asked, “Wenyuan, have you come to cross swords with me?”

Zhang Liao replied, “No. I came because old friends remember old affection. I came to pay my respects.”

He threw his sword, dismounted, and completed formal salutations with Guan Yu. After they sat at the top of the mound, Guan said, “You did not come to bring an accusation, did you?”

Zhang Liao said, “No. In former days your mercy saved my brother; today, as his brother, how could I refuse you?”

Guan replied, “Then you intend to aid me?”

Zhang Liao said, “Not exactly.”

Guan said, “If you are not here to aid me, why have you come?”

Zhang Liao said, “Liu Bei does not know whether you still live, and your brother Zhang Fei has not heard of your life or death. Last night Cao’s army broke into Xiapi and harmed neither soldier nor civilian. It sent escorts to guard Liu Bei’s household and forbade all disturbance. In such treatment, I came only to report to you.”

Guan grew angry: “You have come with these words only for me. I am now trapped and regard death as return. Go at once. I will descend to fight.”

Zhang Liao laughed: “Would your words not make you laughable in all under Heaven?”

Guan replied, “I rely on loyalty and righteousness and am willing to die for it. Why should I be laughed at by the world?”

Zhang Liao said, “If you die now, you have three crimes.”

Guan said, “Then speak them.”

Zhang Liao answered, “First, when Liu Bei took the oath with you, you swore to share life and death; now my lord has been defeated, and you stand ready to die in battle. If he should rally again and seek your aid, and you cannot be found, is that not betraying the oath of your founding years? Second, Liu Bei entrusted his household to you. If you die now, the two madams have nowhere to lean and you betray that trust. Third, you excel at arms and know the Classics and histories, yet you do not join your lord to secure the Han. You only rush into flames and blades to display a mere man’s bravery. How then are you still called righteous?”

Guan held silence. “You have called my three crimes. What is expected of me?”

Zhang Liao replied, “You are ringed on all four sides by Cao’s troops. If you do not surrender, you will die. To die in vain gains nothing. Better to yield for a while, then inquire after Liu Bei. Where he is, then go to him. First, you can save both madams. Second, you do not break the Peach Garden pledge. Third, you preserve a useful body. If these three are fulfilled, then this is a good course.”

Guan said, “You spoke of three goods; I also have three terms. If the Chancellor accepts them, I will lay down my armor. If not, I accept those three crimes and choose death.”

Zhang Liao said, “The Chancellor is broad and generous. What terms?”

Guan said, “First, I submit to the Han emperor and do not submit to Cao Cao. Second, my two madams are to petition the Imperial Uncle for salary and stipends, and no household retinue under them may cross my gate. Third, once I hear where Liu Bei is, whether near or far, I may leave at once. If even one of the three is missing, I will never submit.”

He added, “Please tell Wenyuan to report this quickly.”

Zhang Liao agreed and rode out. He informed Cao Cao first that he would submit to the Han emperor but not to Cao. Cao smiled: “I am Chancellor of Han. In this I am Han. This can be done.”

Then Zhang Liao added, “The two madams seek to petition my lord for stipend; no retainers from within or without should be permitted to pass their gate.”

Cao said, “For the stipend to the Imperial Uncle, I will add extra. As for strict prohibitions at home, that is family discipline.”

Zhang Liao also said, “If he knows Liu Bei’s location he will go at once, even across ten thousand li.”

Cao shook his head. “Then why did I preserve Guan Yu in the first place? This is hard to grant.”

Zhang Liao said, “Do you not recall Yu Rang’s praise among all gentlemen? Liu Bei’s favors to him were only deep kindnesses. If Your Excellency adds deep grace, why should Guan Yu not be attached?”

Cao said at last, “Your words are well taken. I will grant all three.”

Zhang Liao returned to Guan Yu and gave the terms. Guan said, “If so, let the Chancellor first withdraw his lines so I may enter the city, visit the two madams, and tell them the matter before I submit.”

Zhang Liao repeated this to Cao. Cao ordered the troops to pull back ten li. Xun Yu said, “Do not; it may be a trick.”

Cao answered, “Guan Yunchang is a chivalrous man. He will not break faith.”

So he withdrew. Guan led his troops into Xiapi, found all people safe and still, and went straight to the hall to greet the two madams.

Lady Gan and Lady Mi heard that Guan had come and rushed out together. Guan knelt at the stair and said, “My fault is that the two madams were frightened. I beg pardon.”

Lady Gan asked, “Where is your Imperial Uncle now?”

Guan said, “I do not know his whereabouts.”

Lady Mi asked, “What will become of the younger uncle?”

Guan said, “I, Guan, went out to die in battle and became trapped on the earthen mound. Zhang Liao urged me to surrender. I bargained three conditions with him. The Chancellor accepted all three and withdrew his troops for me. I could not take up this matter myself without first hearing your decision.”

Lady Gan asked him for those three terms, and Guan repeated all three clearly.

Lady Gan said, “Yesterday when the Cao army entered Xiapi, we all believed it was certain to die. Who would have thought not a hair moved and not one soldier dared enter the gate. If you have already obtained the lord’s word, why should you ask me two women? Only for fear that Cao Cao will later not let you go seek the Imperial Uncle.”

Guan said, “Sister-in-law, trust me. Guan has a resolve.”

Lady Mi said, “Brother, your own judgment belongs to you. Do not seek counsel from women.”

Guan withdrew and led some tens of riders to Cao Cao. Cao came out to meet him at the outer court.

Guan dismounted and entered. Cao hurriedly replied with ceremonial courtesy.

Guan said, “I deeply owe the mercy of not being killed to a commander who has suffered defeat.”

Cao said, “I have long admired Yunchang’s loyalty and righteousness. To meet you today fully satisfies old hope.”

Guan said, “Wenyuan presented three conditions, and the Chancellor accepted them. I trust he does not break faith.”

Cao said, “Once my words are out, how could I ever fail in trust?”

Guan said, “If I learn where Liu Bei is, even through water and fire I would surely go to him. I cannot spend the moment properly bidding farewell. Please, grant me leave.”

Cao said, “If Liu Bei yet lives, you must go to him. I fear, however, if he does come, the army might fall into disorder. Hold your heart still and I will listen first.”

Guan thanked him and withdrew.

The next day Cao arranged a banquet and treated him as an honored guest. Officers, ministers, and soldiers were invited, and Guan was shown a seat above his rank. He also sent fine silk and gold and silver vessels as gifts. Guan sent everything to the two madams to store.

Guan divided the one household into two courtyards, and he posted ten seasoned soldiers at the inner gate. Guan lived in the outer court.

Cao introduced Guan to Emperor Xian, who ordered him to be made a general. Guan thanked him and returned home.

From the day Guan arrived in Xuchang, Cao had treated him with exceptional honor: three small feasts and five grand feasts, then sent ten beauties to attend on Guan.

Cao attempted to disrupt courtly propriety by having Guan share a room with the two madams. Guan sent all the women into the inner gate and ordered them to attend on Lady Gan and Lady Mi. He then stood outside the gate through the night with a torch in hand, from dusk until dawn, without showing the least fatigue. Cao noticed this and respected him all the more.

Yet every three days he went to the inner gate, bowed and kept his place, and asked after the two madams. Whenever they asked of the Imperial Uncle, they answered, “Uncle, see to your own course.”

Only then would Guan dare to return. Cao heard this and praised him still more.

One day Cao saw that the green-gold battle robe Guan wore was worn, and estimated his quality by his person. He had a robe of special patterned silk made and presented to him.

Guan received it, put it on below his old robe, and wore the old robe over it.

Cao said with laughter, “Why does Yunchang keep such thrift?”

Guan said, “I am not thrifty. This old robe was given by Liu Bei. To wear Liu Bei’s gift as though it were Your Excellency’s new gift would be like turning from elder to younger brother in person. I wear the old as one facing the elder’s face.”

Cao sighed, “Truly a man of righteousness. Yet though my mouth praised him, my heart was not joyful.”

One day, while Guan was in the mansion, a report arrived: “The two madams in the inner palace have collapsed in crying on the ground; no one knows why. Please have the general come quickly.”

Guan straightened his clothes, knelt outside the inner gate, and asked why they wept.

Lady Gan said, “I dreamed last night that the Imperial Uncle lay trapped in an earthen pit. When I woke, I discussed it with Lady Mi. I think he has gone below the Nine Springs, and I weep for this.”

Guan said, “Dreams should not be trusted. This is only sisterly longing. Do not grieve.”

At that very moment a messenger from Cao had already arrived to summon Guan to banquet. Guan informed the two madams and went to Cao.

Cao saw him with tears and asked what troubled him.

Guan said, “The two madams long for their brother and weep with grief, and that has shaken me.”

Cao smiled and tried to soothe him, repeatedly offering wine.

Guan drank until his beard loosened in speech: “One cannot repay the state and yet betray one’s elder brother. One becomes no man.”

Cao asked, “How many hairs has Yunchang’s beard?”

Guan said, “Perhaps three hundred. Each autumn I trim three or five. In winter I wrap it in a dark muslin bag so it does not break.”

Cao had a silk-brocade pouch made and gave it to Guan, to protect his beard.

The next morning at audience, he saw that the silk pouch hung at Guan’s chest. The emperor asked him.

Guan reported, “My Excellency’s beard is long, and the Chancellor presented me a pouch to hold it.”

The emperor ordered him to stand at the hall and let the pouch pass across his belly. He said, “You are truly a handsome-bearded general,” and from then everyone called him “Beautiful-Bearded General.”

One day Cao held Guan to banquet. At the close, he saw Guan’s horse was thin and said, “Why is your horse so lean?”

Guan answered, “This body is not light, and the horse cannot carry it.”

Cao ordered a horse prepared at once. A horse was brought: its body was like hot embers, its form mighty and bold.

Cao said, “Do you recognize this horse?”

Guan said, “Could this be Lü Bu’s Red Hare?”

Cao said, “It is.”

Then he presented the saddle and bridle, and gave them to Guan.

Guan knelt once more in thanks.

Cao was displeased and said, “I have long sent gifts of women and gold and silver; he had never bowed for them. For this horse, he bows twice. How can one so poor cherish a beast so much?”

Guan said, “I know this horse can run a thousand li in a day. If I knew where my elder brother is, we could see him in one day.”

Cao looked startled and repented. Guan then departed.

A poem was written afterward:

His prestige shakes the three kingdoms; his courage and nobility are renowned,
Though the evil prime minister grants him empty honors, how could one guess Yunchang would not submit to Cao?

Cao asked Zhang Liao, “I have not held Yunchang lightly, and yet he is always with a heart to leave. Why?”

Zhang Liao said, “Permit me to test him.”

The next day he went to pay visit to Guan. After formal greetings Zhang said, “I have recommended you to the Chancellor and did not let you fall behind.”

Guan said, “I am deeply grateful for the Chancellor’s kindness. But although my body is here, my mind still keeps to the Imperial Uncle.”

Zhang Liao replied, “You are mistaken. If one handles the world without weighing the light and heavy, he is not a man. Liu Bei’s favor for you is no greater than that of the Chancellor. Why hold only departure in your mind?”

Guan said, “I know the Chancellor’s kindness very well. Yet I received Liu Bei’s great kindness and swore to die together. I cannot abandon it. I will not remain. I must first render service and then leave.”

Zhang Liao said, “If Liu Bei is dead, where will you go?”

Guan said, “I would go to the earth below.”

Zhang Liao recognized he could not keep him, returned, and told Cao all of it.

Cao sighed, “A minister who never forgets his root is righteousness itself.”

Xun Yu said, “He says he must win merit before he goes. If no one compels him to win merit, he may never leave.”

Cao agreed.

Meanwhile Liu Bei, in the camp of Yuan Shao, worried day and night. Yuan Shao asked, “Why are you so troubled, Liu Bei?”

Liu Bei replied, “My second brother has no news. His wife and children are in the hands of Cao bandits. He cannot report to the realm nor protect his own house. How can he not be worried?”

Yuan Shao said, “I have wished to strike at Xuchang for long. Now that spring has warmed, this is a good time to raise troops.”

Then they discussed a plan to break Cao’s forces. Tian Feng warned, “When Cao attacked Xu Province, Xuchang was bare and open. This was the chance then and is gone. Now he has defeated Xu Province; his troops are sharp. Do not meet him rashly. Better hold long and wait for a gap.”

Yuan Shao said, “Let me think on it,” then asked Liu Bei, “How do you read Tian Feng’s counsel?”

Liu Bei said, “Cao is a bandit to Heaven’s court. If my lord does not punish him, he loses righteousness in the whole world.”

Yuan Shao said, “Liu Bei speaks well. We should move to raise troops.”

Tian Feng counseled again. Yuan Shao grew angry and said, “You play with writing and neglect arms, so my righteousness is obstructed.”

Tian Feng knelt: “If you do not heed my plain words, your campaign will fail.”

Yuan Shao grew furious and ordered him to be executed.

Liu Bei interceded, and Tian Feng was only confined to jail.

Ju Shou saw him brought low and then gathered his family. He distributed all his property and told his household, “I go with the army. If we win, honors will follow me; if we lose, one body cannot be kept.”

Everyone wept as he left.

Yuan Shao sent his great commander Yan Liang as vanguard to advance on Baima.

Ju Shou advised, “Yan Liang is narrow of temperament though brave and fierce. He should not be set alone.”

Yuan Shao said, “My senior commanders are not weighed by such men as you.”

As the army marched to Liyang, Liu Yan, the Administrator of Dong Commandery, came in haste to Xuchang with urgent news. Cao hurried to confer and raise troops.

When Guan Yu heard of it, he entered the Secretariat and told Cao, “I heard Your Excellency march. I volunteer to be the forward division.”

Cao said, “I will not trouble the General. There will be work again soon and I will then send for you.”

Guan retired.

Cao gathered one hundred fifty thousand troops and advanced in three columns. On the road he added Liu Yan’s emergency dispatch and sent fifty thousand personally to Baima, holding near the mound.

From afar he looked across the broad plain before the hill and saw Yan Liang’s vanguard: one hundred thousand picked troops in battle order.

Cao was startled. He turned and addressed Song Xian, a former underling of Lü Bu: “I hear you once rode as Lü Bu’s fierce commander. Go now and fight Yan Liang.”

Song Xian accepted and, with spear in hand, mounted his horse and rode straight out before the ranks.

Yan Liang stood under his banner with a broad blade. Seeing Song Xian arrive, he shouted and charged on his horse.

In fewer than three exchanges, with one stroke Song Xian was cut down before the lines.

Cao said in astonishment, “Truly a brave general.”

Wei Xu said, “I lost one comrade and wish to go for revenge.”

Cao allowed it.

Wei Xu mounted and galloped straight to the front, shouting at Yan Liang. Yan offered no words, clashed horse against horse once, and with one stroke of his blade he cleaved off Wei Xu at the top of his head.

Cao said, “Who now dares him?”

Xu Huang called out and went forward to battle Yan Liang. After twenty exchanges, he returned defeated to camp.

All the officers trembled. Cao withdrew his troops, and Yan Liang also drew back.

Seeing two commanders fallen in succession, Cao was heavy in mind. Cheng Yu said, “One person alone can oppose Yan Liang.”

Cao asked, “Who?”

Cheng Yu said, “No one but Guan Yunchang.”

Cao said, “I fear if he wins merit he may leave.”

Cheng Yu replied, “If Liu Bei is alive and returns, he will go to Yuan Shao; then Yuan Shao will suspect Liu Bei and kill him. If Liu Bei is dead, where can Guan go? Therefore he must go.”

Cao was pleased and ordered someone to summon Guan.

Guan came and made his leave to the two madams. The two madams said, “Uncle, on this trip find any word of the Imperial Uncle.”

Guan nodded and set out.

He raised the Green Dragon Crescent Blade, mounted Red Hare, and with several attendants rode directly to Baima to meet Cao.

Cao told him the situation: “Yan Liang has put down two commanders in one stretch. His bravery is beyond holding. I have asked you to discuss this with him.”

Guan said, “Please allow me to observe.”

Cao entertained him with wine and then word came that Yan Liang had met for battle. Cao brought Guan to the mound and gave him a place to sit. Generals stood about.

Cao pointed to the formations at the foot and said, “These Hebei horse and foot are so strong and showy.”

Guan said, “To me they are like chickens and dogs.”

Cao pointed again: “Under that standard and plume, in rusted robes and golden armor, the one with blade in hand mounted is Yan Liang.”

Guan looked up and said, “He is a marked man for head bounty.”

Cao warned him, “Do not be hasty.”

Guan stood: “Though I am not able, I will ride into the ten-thousand ranks and bring back his head for the Chancellor.”

Zhang Liao said, “No play-speech in the army. Even Yunchang should not be taken lightly.”

Guan leapt to his horse, raised the Green Dragon Crescent Blade, and flew down from the mound. His hawk-like eyes flared and his brows came up like caterpillars. He charged straight into the line. The Hebei troops parted like waves ripping open.

He charged straight at Yan Liang. Yan Liang was still beneath the command umbrella. Seeing Guan come, he asked what he should do. Guan’s horse reached him first. Yan did not have time.

One stroke from Guan, from below the horse, struck and cut him down. He dropped from the saddle and severed Yan Liang’s head. He tied it beneath the horse’s bridle, sprang back to the saddle, lifted his sword, and broke clear from formation as if entering an empty camp.

The Hebei troops were shocked and scattered in confusion without fighting.

Cao’s troops pressed in. Those who fell could not be counted; horses and equipment were taken in great number.

Guan wheeled to the hill as those men cheered all around. He presented the severed head before Cao.

Cao said, “The general is truly a man of spirit.”

Guan said, “What am I that I can boast? My brother Zhang Yide in a hundred-thousand host can take a foremost general’s head as easily as drawing from a purse.”

Cao was stunned. He turned to those around and said, “If you meet Zhang Yide in the future, do not ever take him lightly.” He ordered that line written upon the hem of his robe.

Yan Liang’s routed troops fled back. Halfway he met Yuan Shao and reported that one long-bearded, red-faced man on one horse had entered the host, beheaded him, and carried off the head, causing a total defeat.

Yuan Shao asked sharply, “Who is this man?”

Ju Shou said, “This must be Liu Bei’s brother, Guan Yunchang.”

Yuan Shao was furious. He pointed at Liu Bei and said, “Your brother has slain my prized general. You must have connived in it. What use to keep you?”

He called the executioners and ordered Liu Bei brought to the block.

At first he was a guest on the banquet bench; this day he nearly shared the ground below with other prisoners. Unknown is how the life of Liu Bei will end. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Guan Yu Camps on the Earthen Mound and Swears Three Conditions; Guan Yunchang Saves Baima and Cao Cao Relieves the Encirclement

chapters.html:
Yuan Benchu breaks his troops; Guan Yunchang hangs up his seal and seals his gold.

It was said that Yuan Shao wished to behead Liu Bei. Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, entered calmly and said, “My lord, are you listening to only one side while turning away from what your long acquaintance has shown you? Since I was scattered from Xuzhou, I do not know whether my second brother, Guan Yu, has survived. Many in the world share the same red face and long beard, yet not every such man is Lord Guan. Why not make sure?”

Yuan Shao, a man with little resolve, when he heard Liu Bei’s words, blamed Ju Shou and said, “You heard him and almost killed an honest man.” He then invited Liu Bei to climb into his canopy and discuss avenging Yan Liang.

A man from below answered at once and came in. “Yan Liang has been as a brother to me. Now he has been killed by the bandits of Cao. How can I fail to wash away this grief?”

Liu Bei looked at him: he was eight feet tall, with a face like the xiezhi beast. He was Wen Chou, the famous general of Hebei. Yuan Shao rejoiced greatly and said, “No one but you can repay Yan Liang’s blood-debt. I have a hundred thousand soldiers; we will cross the Yellow River and hunt down the Cao bandits.”

Ju Shou said, “No. It is better to hold Yanzin for now and split the army at Guandu. If you cross lightly in haste and some reversal comes, everyone will have no way to return.”

Yuan Shao grew angry and said, “It is because all of you are slow and weaken the army’s morale, delaying by day and by day and obstructing this great matter. Do we not hear, ‘In war, speed is precious’?” Ju Shou withdrew and sighed, “His lordship swells his intent, the men below carry out his work; with this broad Yellow River between us, can I cross it?” He then feigned sickness and stayed out of counsel.

Liu Bei said, “My lord, by your mercy I owe too much to repay. I wish to accompany Wen Chou. First, it will honor your virtue; second, I hope to discover firm news of Guan Yu.” Yuan Shao was pleased and called Wen Chou and Liu Bei to lead the vanguard together.

Wen Chou said, “Liu Bei has been a general who fails repeatedly and is not fortunate in war. Since the lord has ordered him away, I have assigned him thirty thousand men and made him command the rear.”

So Wen Chou set out first with seventy thousand men, and Liu Bei followed with thirty thousand.

When Cao Cao learned that Guan Yu had beheaded Yan Liang, his esteem grew even more. He submitted a memorial to court and enfeoffed Guan Yu as Marquis of Hanshou Ting, then had the seal cast and sent it to him.

That same moment came word that Yuan Shao had ordered the great general Wen Chou to cross the Yellow River and he had already taken the heights above Yanzin. Cao Cao first moved the local population to the western bank and then led out troops to meet him.
