His order to the command below was this: “Use the rear army as the vanguard, and the vanguard as the rear. Supplies march first; the soldiers follow.”

Lu Qian said, “Why are the supplies in front and the army behind?”

Cao Cao said, “Supplies are often plundered when they are behind. So put them first.”

Lu Qian said, “If the enemy troops come and steal them, what then?”

Cao Cao said, “Let them come. We will explain when they arrive.”

Lu Qian’s heart remained doubtful. Cao Cao ordered the grain train and baggage along the riverbanks to Yanzin. He stood with the rear army when he heard shouting from the vanguard. He hurriedly sent men to check, and they reported: “The great general Wen Chou has reached us. Our troops have abandoned the grain carts and are running in all directions. The rear army is still far away. What are we to do?”

Cao Cao pointed with his whip at two earth mounds and said, “This is a place to conceal ourselves for a while.” The horse and men rushed to the mounds. Cao Cao ordered the soldiers to remove their armor and loosen their coats for a short rest, and to dismount their horses. Wen Chou’s army came on in cover.

A commander cried out, “The enemy has arrived! Gather up the horses and run back to Baima!” Xun You stopped him in urgency: “This is exactly a chance to bait the enemy. Why turn back?” Cao Cao shot Xun You a glance and smiled. Xun You understood and said no more.

Wen Chou’s men had reached the grain carts and equipment and then came to seize the horses. The soldiers no longer kept formation and mingled into a chaos. Cao Cao, from the mounds, ordered his officers to descend all together and strike at them; Wen Chou’s army was thrown into confusion. Cao’s troops enveloped and wrapped around them, and Wen Chou stood upright to fight alone. The troops trampled over one another. Wen Chou could not hold back the rush of them and had to turn his horse and retreat.

From atop the mound, Cao Cao pointed and asked, “Wen Chou is a famed general of Hebei. Who can take him?” Zhang Liao and Xu Huang spurred their horses out together and shouted, “Wen Chou, do not run!”

When Wen Chou turned back and saw the two officers gaining, he pressed his iron spear, nocked an arrow, and aimed at Zhang Liao. Xu Huang shouted, “Bandit, do not loose your arrow!” Zhang Liao bent his head quickly and dodged. One arrow struck his helmet and tore away the feather plume. He recovered himself and dashed after Wen Chou again, then his horse reared and knelt on its front legs; Zhang Liao tumbled from the saddle.

Wen Chou wheeled his horse and came again. Xu Huang swung his great axe and closed in to melee. He then saw Wen Chou’s rear cavalry and horsemen arriving all together and judged he could not stand against them, so he wheeled away. Wen Chou chased along the river. Suddenly he saw ten or so riders, banners rippling in disorder, and at their head was a figure with a drawn knife charging on horseback. It was Guan Yu. He thundered, “Bandit general, do not run!” and struck in horse-to-horse combat with Wen Chou. They fought for less than three exchanges; Wen Chou grew faint with fear and wheeled away along the riverbank.

Guan Yu’s horse was quicker. He caught Wen Chou, drew back his blade and with one stroke to the back of the head cut Wen Chou down from his horse.

Cao Cao stood on the mound. Seeing Guan Yu hewed down Wen Chou, he drove all his horsemen forward to press the kill. Most of Wen Chou’s Hebei army drowned, and their grain carts and horses were recovered by Cao Cao.

Guan Yu wheeled a handful of riders, darting east and west. Just as he was still cutting, Liu Bei arrived with thirty thousand men in his wake. A forward scout rider reported to Liu Bei, “This time, a red-faced, long-bearded man has slain Wen Chou.”

Liu Bei wheeled hard to ride over. From across the river he saw a cluster of horse and men darting here and there; the banner read seven characters: “Marquis of Hanshou Ting, Guan Yu.” Liu Bei silently thanked heaven and earth: “Then my brother truly is at Cao Cao’s side!” He wished to call out and greet him, but masses of Cao’s soldiers crowded in. He had to withdraw his force.

Yuan Shao moved to support at Guandu and set camp fortifications. Guo Tu and Shen Pei entered before Yuan Shao and said, “Again it was Lord Guan who killed Wen Chou. Liu Bei pretends not to know.” Yuan Shao grew furious and cursed, “Scoundrel, how dare you do this?”

After a short while, Liu Bei arrived. Yuan Shao ordered him dragged out to be executed.

Liu Bei said, “What crime have I committed?”

Yuan Shao said, “You had your brother ruin another of my principal generals; how can this be without guilt?”

Liu Bei said, “Let me speak one brief answer before I die. Cao Cao has long feared Xuande. Now he knows I am in your service and fears I may aid the lord, so he specifically sent Guan Yu to execute two of his own generals. Your lordship would surely be angered. He has taken this chance through your hand to kill Liu Bei. Please reflect on that.”

Yuan Shao said, “Liu Bei speaks truly. You all have made me suffer the name of one who injures the worthy. Return the side-kick men and have Liu Bei sit in the canopy.”

Liu Bei offered thanks: “I am grateful for the lord’s broad clemency. I can never repay it. I wish to dispatch my one trusted man with a secret letter to Guan Yu, so he may know Liu Bei’s situation. He will come by star and night at once, aid the lord, and together punish Cao Cao for the deaths of Yan Liang and Wen Chou. What say you?”

Yuan Shao rejoiced and said, “I gain Guan Yu—ten times more than Yan Liang and Wen Chou together.”

Liu Bei drafted the letter, but none came forward to deliver it. Yuan Shao ordered him to withdraw to Wuyang. He chained successive camps for several tens of li and sat on the orders line, unmoving.

Cao Cao then put Xiahou Dun in command to hold the Guandu pass and then himself marched back to Xuchang. He held grand entertainment for his officials and congratulated Guan Yu on his achievement. Turning to Lu Qian, he said, “My putting the supplies in front before, that was the plan to bait the enemy. Only Lord Xun has understood my heart.” All there admired him.

While the banquet was still under way, a messenger burst in: “In Runan, the Yellow Turbans, Liu Bi and Gong Du, have become wildly rampant. Cao Hong has fought repeatedly without success and begs for troops.”

Hearing this, Guan Yu stepped forward and said, “Guan Yunchang is willing to offer his utmost service and break these rebels in Runan.”

Cao Cao said, “Guan Yu has done a great deed and has never yet been richly rewarded. How can we burden him again in campaign?”

Guan Yu said, “I have been idle for too long. If I stay still, illness will come. I will make one more expedition.”

Cao Cao praised him and raised fifty thousand troops, placing Yu Jin and Yue Jin as deputies. The next day they set out.

Xun Yu whispered to Cao Cao privately, “Guan Yu has a mind to return to Liu; if he learns the news, he will go. You should not send him out so often.”

Cao Cao said, “This time he has earned it; I will no longer send him to meet an enemy.”

As for Guan Yu, he drew near to Runan and drew up camp. In the middle of the night, at the camp gate, two spies were captured. Guan Yu examined them and recognized one as Sun Qian.

Guan Yu shouted to clear his men away and asked Qian, “Since the dispersal after our flight, your whereabouts were unheard. Why are you here now?”

Qian said, “I fled in disaster and drifted into Runan. By fortune I was sheltered by Liu Bi. Why does your Excellency remain at Cao Cao’s camp? Do you know whether Madam Gan and Madam Mi are safe?”

Guan Yu then recounted the above events and current state in detail.

Qian said, “Recently we heard that Xuande is at Yuan Shao’s camp and wants to submit to him but has found no path. Now Liu and Gong have submitted to Yuan Shao and aid him in attacking Cao. If the General arrives here, I have already ordered a detachment to guide the way and told someone as a secret agent to report to him. Tomorrow these two will feign defeat in one engagement. You can quickly guide the two wives into Yuan Shao’s camp to meet Liu Bei.”

Guan Yu said, “Since my brother is at Yuan Shao’s camp, I will come by night and by day. I regret only that I killed the two of your general-commanders; I fear matters have changed.”

Qian said, “I will first go to test the true state and then return to report.”

Guan Yu said, “If I can see my elder brother once, I will accept ten thousand deaths. From this day, I will soon leave Xuchang and bid Cao Cao farewell.”

He sent Sun Qian away that same night.

The next day Guan Yu led out his troops. Gong Du arrayed himself and went into the line. Guan Yu said, “Why have you turned your back on the throne?”

Gong said, “You are one who turns from your own lord. Why reproach me?”

Guan Yu said, “Why do you say I turn from my lord?”

Gong said, “Liu Bei is at Yuan Benchu’s camp, and yet you serve with Cao Cao. Why?”

Guan Yu did not answer further. He struck his horse and spun with sword.

Gong turned and warned him, “Do not forget your former lord’s kindness. If your pace is swift you will be lost. I yield Runan to you.”

Understanding, Guan Yu drove his troops to close and slay. Liu Bi and Gong Du put on a show of defeat and disorderly retreat, scattering apart. Guan Yu won the prefectures and counties, pacified the populace and set things firm, then returned to Xuchang.

Cao Cao received him at the city gate, praised the troops, and rewarded the soldiers.

After the banquet, Guan Yu returned home and knelt to pay respects to his two wives outside the gate. Gan said, “Uncle, you have gone out twice. Have you any word from the Imperial Uncle?” Guan Yu replied, “No.”

After Guan Yu withdrew, the two women wept in the inner chamber. Gan said bitterly, “The Imperial Uncle is dead, is he not? The younger uncle hides the trouble from my sister and me and never speaks.”

At that moment, an old soldier who had accompanied them heard the unending weeping and came to the gate to report, “Lady, do not weep. Master is alive in Yuan Shao’s camp in Hebei.”

She said, “How do you know this?”

The soldier said, “I followed Guan General on campaign. A man spoke this in the ranks.”

She called in urgency and scolded Guan Yu: “Did not the Imperial Uncle ever wrong you? You now receive Cao Cao’s grace and have forgotten the old obligations; why do you not tell me the truth?”

Guan Yu knelt and said, “My brother is truly in Hebei. I did not dare tell you, for fear of leakage. We must proceed carefully. Do not force the matter.”

Gan said, “Uncle, you must press this matter.”

Guan Yu withdrew and thought over a way to go; he was seated and restless.

Yu Jin had learned that Liu Bei was in Hebei and reported it to Cao Cao. Cao Cao sent Zhang Liao to probe Guan Yu’s intentions.

Guan Yu was deep in brooding when Zhang Liao entered to offer congratulations. “I hear, brother, that after this battle you learned Liu Bei’s report. I came to congratulate you.”

Guan Yu said, “My former lord is not yet face to face with me, what is there to rejoice at?”

Zhang Liao asked, “How does friendship between you and Xuande compare with that between brothers?”

Guan Yu replied, “With my own brother, it is friendship. With Liu Bei, it is brotherhood and, beyond that, lord and subject. How can it be discussed as equals?”

Zhang Liao said, “Now that Liu Bei is in Hebei, will you go with him?”

Guan Yu said, “The words spoken before, how could I repudiate them?”

Guan Yu said, “Wen Yuan must carry my words to the Chancellor.”

Guan Yu’s thought was reported to Cao Cao. Cao Cao said, “I have my own plan to keep him.”

While Guan Yu was still pondering, a messenger arrived: an old acquaintance sought an audience. When he was invited in, he turned out to be no one known. Guan Yu asked, “Who are you?”

He answered, “I am Chen Zhen of Nanyang, under Yuan Shao.” Guan Yu grew alarmed and hurriedly sent men away from the sides, asking, “This man certainly comes for a purpose.”

Chen Zhen presented one sealed packet and gave it to Guan Yu. He looked inside. It was Liu Bei’s letter. It read:

I and you made a brotherly alliance in the Peach Garden and swore to die together. Why now do we part in the middle and sever loyalty and righteousness? If you truly seek fame and wealth, offer up my head to complete your career. The letter cannot speak all; death waits upon your direction.

Guan Yu finished and wept. “It is not that I do not wish to seek my brother; I simply did not know where he was. How could I barter old oaths for ambition and wealth?”

Chen said, “Liu Bei misses you greatly. Since you do not betray old oaths, you should go swiftly and meet him.”

Guan Yu said, “One who lives in this world with no end is not a gentleman. I came when my way was clear; when I leave it must be clear. I will write now. Tell my brother first, and ask leave from Cao Cao and bring the two wives to him. If Cao Cao refuses, what could we do?”

He said, “I would rather die than remain here long.”

Chen said, “You should write a reply quickly to spare Lord Liu from suspended expectation.”

Guan Yu wrote back:

I have heard that righteousness is no betrayal of the heart and loyalty no willingness to die. Since youth I have read books and rough understanding of ritual and morality; each time I remember the stories of Yang Jiao and Zuo Botao I cannot help but sigh and cry. When I guarded Xiapi before, there was no grain stored within and no aid from outside; I wanted to die at once, but there were two madams who weighed on my conscience, and I dared not cut off my own head and body to the point of betraying what I was entrusted with. So I have for a while kept myself bound here, hoping for a later meeting. Only this afternoon I have reached Yunan and learned your letter. I will at once face you and leave Cao Cao, then take the two wives back. Yunchang harbors another heart, and Heaven and men alike will share the guilt. I have bared my entrails and drained my heart, yet brush and paper cannot capture the extent. I bow and await your judgment. Pray cast your light upon this.

Chen took the letter back as he returned. Guan Yu told his two wives and then immediately went to Cao’s Secretariat to bid farewell to the Chancellor. When Cao Cao understood his intent, he hung a notice of avoidance on the gate.

Guan Yu left in disgruntlement, ordered men from his old following to pack the wagons, and told them to wait by day and night. He instructed that all things granted by Cao should remain behind, not a single coin to be carried.

The next day he went again to the Secretariat to take his leave. Again a notice of avoidance hung at the gate. He went again, still not granted audience. Then he went to Zhang Liao to speak, hoping to tell him everything; Zhang Liao also gave excuses and was ill and stayed out.

Guan Yu thought, “This Chancellor Cao intends he not leave. My resolve to go is fixed; how can I remain?” He immediately wrote a letter of resignation to Cao:

I have served my imperial uncle and swore to live and die with him. Heaven and Earth have heard that vow. Earlier, when Xiapi fell, my three requests were met with imperial favor. Now I have learned that my former lord is among Yuan Shao’s troops. Remembering our old oath, how can I turn away? Though the new favor is deep, the old righteousness cannot be forgotten. I therefore respectfully send this letter to resign. Please consider carefully. For whatever grace still remains unreturned, I pray to repay it someday in different time.

After sealing it and sending it to the Secretariat, he sealed in one place after another the silver and gold he had received and placed them in the granaries. He hung the Hanshou Ting seal in the hall and asked the two madams to mount the carriage.

Guan Yu mounted his Red Hare horse, holding aloft the Green-Dragon Blade, led his old attendant men, and with them escorted the wagons directly through the north gate.

The gate guards blocked him. Guan Yu narrowed his eyes and brandished his sword, roaring once; the guards all withdrew.

Once beyond the gate, he told his followers, “You keep the wagons and baggage ahead. If anyone gives chase, I will handle it. Do not cause panic for the two madams.” They pushed the carriage and moved along the imperial road.

Now Cao Cao was still undecided about Guan Yu’s departure when one to his side reported that Guan Yu had submitted his letter. He read it and cried out in surprise, “Guan Yu has gone!”

A northern gate guard reported from the charge: “Guan Yu forced through the gate and left, with about twenty men of wagons and riding animals, all heading north.”

At the same time, one from Guan Yu’s household reported: “Guan Yu sealed all the gold and silver he had received. He has set ten beauties apart in the inner room. The Hanshou Ting seal still hangs in the hall. All the people sent by the Chancellor are not with him; only his original attendants and personal baggage are with him, and he has gone out through the north gate.”

Everyone was stunned.

A general stepped forward and said, “I will take three thousand iron riders to capture Guan Yuchang alive and present him to the Chancellor.”

It was Cai Yang.

It ended:

He wants to leave the dragon cave of ten thousand fathoms, but meets three thousand riders like wolves and tigers. Cai Yang will ride to chase Guan Yunchang; how it ends will be heard in the next part.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Yuan Shao Breaks His Army; Guan Yu Hangs Up His Seal

chapters.html:
Among Cao Cao’s subordinates, apart from Zhang Liao, only Xu Huang and Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, were close to him; the rest all respected him as well. Only Cai Yang did not. When he heard Guan had left, Cai Yang wanted to chase after him right away. Cao Cao said, “Not forgetting one’s former lord and leaving in plain sight—he is a true man. All of you should do the same.” So he snapped at Cai Yang and did not allow him to give chase.

Cheng Yu said, “His Excellency has favored General Guan greatly. He leaves without even asking leave, speaking reckless nonsense and daringly insulting your majesty. His crime is great. If we let him return to Yuan Shao, it would be like adding wings to a tiger. Why not pursue and kill him now, and end future trouble?” Cao Cao said, “I have already promised him. Can I then break my word? Each of us serves his own lord. Do not pursue.” Then he told Zhang Liao, “Guan has returned the seal and the gold. Bribes cannot move his heart, and rank and rewards cannot change his will. Such men I deeply respect. I suspect he will not be far from here. I will meet him once to settle this as a matter of feeling. Go ahead and ask him to wait. When I come, I will send him off and give him travel funds and a robe, so there will be no regret later.” Zhang Liao took the order and rode ahead alone. Cao Cao followed with several dozen riders.

From this point Guan Yu, whose red horse was Red Hare, normally could run a thousand li in a day, yet it was not possible now. Wanting to guard the carriage and supplies, he did not let the horse run free but held the reins and moved at a measured pace. Suddenly he heard someone from behind shout, “Guan, slow down!” He turned, saw Zhang Liao hurrying his horse.

Guan told the men of the carriage to keep pushing forward and keep the road clear. He himself pulled back Red Hare, gripped the Green Dragon Crescent Blade, and asked, “Is this not to bring me back, Wenyuan?” Liao said, “No. The Chancellor knows you have traveled far and wanted to see you off, so he only sent me to ask you to wait. Nothing else is meant.” Guan said, “If even iron cavalry from the Chancellor is coming, I am ready for a fight to the death.” He then rode back to stand on the bridge and wait. He saw Cao Cao and several dozen riders coming at speed. Behind them were Xu Chu, Xu Huang, Yu Jin, Li Dian, and others.

When Cao Cao saw Guan standing on horseback with sword across, he ordered the officers to rein in their horses and line their riders to either side. When Guan saw that the men before him were all unarmed, only then was he fully at ease. Cao Cao said, “Why does General Guan ride so fast?” Guan answered from horseback, “Formerly I informed the Chancellor. My former lord is in Hebei, so I cannot linger on the way. I returned to court many times and could not receive audience; therefore I sent him a formal letter to take leave, and I returned the seal and gold. I beg your Excellency not to forget your old words.” Cao Cao said, “Do you think I, who keeps faith with the world, would break my promise? I feared there might be shortages on the road, so I had travel provisions prepared for you.” A soldier handed a tray of gold down from horseback. Guan said, “Your gifts have been generous; I still have plenty left. Leave this gold here to reward your men.” Cao Cao said, “It is only a small return for your great merits, what need is there to refuse?” Guan said, “This is a trifling effort; how could it measure against this debt?” Cao Cao laughed and said, “Guan is a man of justice and virtue. Heaven has been unkind that I cannot keep you. Here is one brocade robe, a small token of my heart.” He ordered one of the men to dismount and hold out the robe with both hands.

Guan feared some trap and did not dismount. He lifted the robe with the tip of the Green Dragon Crescent Blade and flung it across his body, then turned the horse around and thanked him, saying, “I am grateful, Excellency, for the robe you have given. We shall meet again on another day.” He dismounted from the bridge and turned northward.

Xu Chu said, “This man is too impertinent. Why did we not arrest him?” Cao Cao said, “He is one man on one horse while I have scores of riders. How could he suspect me if I let him go? My word is already given. I must not pursue.” Cao Cao then led his officers back to the city and rode all the way, thinking about Guan without cease.

Now we set down Cao Cao’s return. Guan Yu drove on to keep ahead of the carriage riders and after about thirty li they disappeared from sight. Guan grew uneasy and rode out in all directions, searching. Suddenly a figure appeared on a hill and called out loudly, “General Guan, stop here!” Guan looked up and saw a youth in yellow brocade, spear in hand and mounted. A severed head hung under the horse’s neck. He rushed in with a little over one hundred soldiers. Guan asked, “Who are you?” The youth threw down his spear, dismounted, and knelt. Guan, still holding the Green Dragon Crescent Blade, reined in his horse and said, “Brave man, tell me your name.” The youth replied, “I am from Xiangyang. My surname is Liao, my given name Hua, courtesy name Yuanjian. When the world fell into chaos, I drifted on the rivers and lakes and gathered more than five hundred men to live by raiding. Just now my companion Duyuan was patrolling down the mountain and by mistake abducted the two wives. I asked my men and learned they were the two wives of the imperial uncle of the Great Han, Liu Bei. I heard the General was escorting them here, so I came to bring them down. Duyuan spoke insolently and I killed him. Now I present the head and beg your punishment.”

Guan asked, “Where is the second wife?” Liao Hua said, “She is still in the hills.” Guan told him to hurry and bring her down at once. Before long, over a hundred men came and surrounded the carriage. Guan dismounted, put down the saber, and crossed his arms before the carriage. “Were the second sister frightened?” he asked. The second wife said, “If not for General Liao, I would have been wronged by Duyuan.” Guan asked his men, “How did Liao Hua save the wives?” They said, “Duyuan lured them up the mountain to rob. He offered one woman as wife to me and one to Liao Hua. Liao Hua asked where the matter came from and paid him due respect. Duyuan refused and was killed by Liao Hua.” Guan thanked Liao Hua. Liao Hua wished to send his men to escort Guan, but Guan thought this man was surely some Yellow Turban remnant and not one to be kept as a companion. He declined. Liao Hua offered to give him gold and cloth, but Guan refused. Liao Hua knelt in farewell and withdrew with his men into the valley.

Guan told the wives of Cao’s gifted robe, then urged the carriage onward. At dusk, they reached a village and rested. The head of the household came out with hair white as silk and asked, “General, what is your surname and name?” Guan offered formal greeting and said, “I am Guan, brother of Liu Bei, courtesy name Xuande.” The old man said, “Are you not the Guan who slew Yan Liang and Wenchou?” Guan said, “I am.” The old man rejoiced and invited them in. Guan said, “There are two wives in the carriage.” The old man called his wife and daughters to welcome them. When the wives entered the thatched hall, Guan stood with his hands crossed at their side. The old man offered him a seat, and Guan said, “The honored elder sister is above. How could I dare to sit?” The old man told his wife and daughters to receive the wives in the inner room, and invited Guan to drink tea in the hall. Guan asked, “What is your name?” The old man said, “My surname is Hu, my name is Hua. In Emperor Huan’s reign I once served as a Gentleman-in-attendance. I later retired to the countryside. My son, Hu Ban, is a clerk under Governor Wang Zhi in Xingyang.” Guan promised to see him.

At the next day’s breakfast, after finishing his meal, he had the two wives mount the carriage, took out Hu Hua’s letter, and after giving farewell took the road to Luoyang. Before long they reached a checkpoint called Dongling Pass. Its gatekeeper was Kong Xiu, with five hundred soldiers posted on an earthen rise. When Guan’s party approached, the soldiers informed Kong Xiu. Kong Xiu came out and met him at the gate. Guan dismounted and greeted him. Kong said, “Where are you going, General?” Guan said, “This servant of the Chancellor has resigned. I go to Hebei to seek my elder brother.” Kong said, “Yuan Shao in Hebei is exactly the Chancellor’s rival. If you go there, you must have documents.” Guan said, “I am in too great a rush and did not manage to get them.” Kong said, “The law requires that I first report to the Chancellor, then permit passage.” Guan said, “If I wait for that, my schedule is ruined.” Kong said, “I am bound by law, and must do as required.” Guan asked, “Will you not let me pass?” Kong said, “If you insist on crossing, leave your elders and children as hostages.” Guan grew angry and killed Kong Xiu. Kong withdrew into the pass and sounded a drum, summoning soldiers to mount. He came out and shouted down at Guan, “Will you dare to pass?” Guan ordered the carriage back, then spurred forward with his horse raised for attack. The two horses met just once; when steel flashed, Kong Xiu’s body fell from the saddle. The soldiers started to run. Guan called, “Soldiers, do not run. I killed Kong Xiu only because I had to; this has nothing to do with you. Borrow your voices and tell the Chancellor of Wei that I had to kill Kong Xiu because Kong Xiu meant to do me harm.” All the soldiers knelt before their horses.

Guan then ordered the carriage out and toward Luoyang. Beforehand, the Administrator Han Fu already knew Guan had killed Kong Xiu and gathered men in haste. The discussion turned among them. Captain Meng Tan said, “Since he has no document from the Chancellor, this was a private action. If we do not block him, we all bear blame.” Han Fu said, “General Guan is fierce; he already killed Yan Liang and Wenchou. We cannot stand against him in open battle. We should devise a way to capture him.” Meng Tan said, “I have a plan. First set horns at the pass as a blockade. When he comes, let a young officer engage him and feign defeat, drawing him to pursue. Then hidden troops can fire arrows. If he falls from the horse, seize him and bring him to Xudu. We will get rich rewards.” The plan settled. A scout reported the carriage had arrived. Han Fu drew bow and arrow, and led one thousand horsemen to line the pass.

He asked, “Who goes there?” Guan inclined his body from the saddle and said, “I am the Marquis of Hanshou, Guan.” Han Fu said, “Do you have an order from the Chancellor?” Guan said, “Because of haste I did not obtain one.” Han Fu said, “I hold this pass under the Chancellor’s order, charged to ferret out traitors. Without an order, you are an absconding fugitive.” Guan shouted, “I have already killed Kong Xiu at Dongling, who meant to trap me. Do you also wish for your own death?” Han Fu said, “Who would capture you?” Meng Tan came out, twin blades drawn. Guan ordered the carriage back, then charged with his sword. Meng Tan and Guan fought less than three exchanges before Meng Tan wheeled and fled. Guan pursued. Meng Tan had meant only to lure him, but Guan was faster and caught him at once. With one stroke he cut him in two. Guan reined back toward Han Fu, who stood at the gate. As Han shot an arrow at him from that position, it struck Guan’s left arm. Guan pulled the arrow out with his mouth, though blood would not stop. He drove his horse onward at a breakneck speed and rushed through the soldiers. Han Fu did not dodge in time; Guan rose with his sword, striking him at the neck and shoulder, severing him from horse to saddle. He scattered the troops and protected the carriage.

Guan wrapped the arrow wound tightly with silk from his own store, and because enemies might be hidden in ambush he did not stay long, riding all night to Sishui Pass. The gatekeeper there was Bian Xi, surnamed Bian, name Xi, a man from Bing Province, skilled in the meteor hammer. He had once been a Yellow Turban remnant, then joined Cao Cao and had been posted there to guard the pass. When he learned Guan was coming, he set a trap. He hid over two hundred men with axes and halberds inside Zhen Guo Temple and used the sound of cups striking as a signal to strike when Guan arrived. He then came out to meet Guan. Guan dismounted and greeted Bian Xi. Bian Xi said, “General, who does not admire you under heaven? Now you have returned to your imperial uncle; your loyalty is clear.” Guan told him how he had killed Kong Xiu and Han Fu. Bian Xi said, “You did well to kill him. I have already reported to the Chancellor and explained the situation.” Guan rejoiced, then mounted again with him past Sishui Pass to the gate of Zhen Guo Temple and dismounted there. The temple monks rang their bell to welcome him.

Zhen Guo Temple had once been the incense and offerings court of Emperor Han Mingdi, and it had over thirty monks. Among them was one monk, Pujing, who was from the same region as Guan. When Pujing saw Guan, he stepped forward and asked, “General, how many years has it been since you left Pudong?” Guan said, “It has been almost twenty years.” Pujing asked, “Can you still recognize a poor monk?” Guan said, “Years away from home make one unable to recognize everyone.” Pujing said, “The poor monk’s home and yours are separated by just one river.” Bian Xi saw Pujing talk of old ties. Fearing disclosure, he shouted, “I invited the General to a feast. Why does a monk speak so freely?” Guan said, “It cannot be otherwise. Should fellow natives not recall old ties when they meet?”

Pujing asked Guan to wait in the abbot’s hall for tea. Guan said, “The two wives in the carriage should be offered tea first.” Pujing ordered tea brought for the wives and then invited Guan into the abbot’s hall. Pujing held up his戒刀 and looked at Guan. Guan understood and ordered his men to keep their blades close. Bian Xi invited Guan to a banquet in the Dharma Hall. Guan said, “Bian, this is kindness or treachery?” Before Bian could answer, Guan saw axe-and-hammer men among the wall hangings. He shouted, “I took you for a worthy man. How dare you do this?” Bian Xi saw through it and shouted, “Arms!” His men began to move, but Guan had already cut them down with his sword. Bian Xi fled through the corridor; Guan dropped his saber and took the great saber to give chase. Bian Xi threw a flying hammer at Guan. Guan blocked it with his blade, chased him in, and split Bian Xi in two with one stroke. Then he turned at once to check on the two wives.

Soldiers had already surrounded them, and when they saw Guan approach, they ran in panic. Guan drove them away and thanked Pujing, saying, “Had it not been for my teacher, this bandit would have harmed me.” Pujing said, “A poor monk has no place here. I will gather robe and bowl and wander elsewhere. We will meet again. Guard yourself.” Guan thanked him and escorted the carriage onward toward Xingyang.

Wang Zhi, the Administrator of Xingyang, was related by marriage to Han Fu. When he learned Guan had killed Han Fu, he consulted with others and planned a hidden strike. He ordered guards at the pass. When Guan arrived, Wang Zhi came out in smiling welcome. Guan explained he was traveling to find his brother. Wang Zhi said, “General, your road has been hard, and your wives are weary. Enter the city, rest one night at an inn, and set out tomorrow. There is still time.” Guan saw Wang Zhi’s courtesy and kindness and so brought the two wives into the city. The inn was laid out with care. Wang Zhi invited him to banquet; Guan declined. Wang Zhi had food trays sent to the inn. Because Guan had suffered from the road, he fed the wives, then had them rest each in their places and fed the horses. Guan unbuckled his armor and rested.

At that moment Wang Zhi secretly summoned his clerk Hu Ban and said, “Guan has run from the Chancellor and killed not only the Chancellor’s subordinate officers on the roads. This is not a slight offense. His valor is hard to oppose. If we do not strike now, he may escape. Set one thousand soldiers around the inn and give each a torch. At the third watch they should burn in unison; whoever is inside, regardless of who, should be burned to death. I will lead the reinforcements.” Hu Ban obeyed. He placed dry timber and fire-making materials near the gate and fixed the time. Hu Ban thought, “I have heard of Guan Yunchang for long, but never learned his form. I will go secretly to see.” He slipped into the inn and asked the inn attendant, “Where is General Guan?” The attendant said, “He is in the front hall, reading.” Hu Ban went to the hall, saw Guan with his left hand on his beard reading by lamplight. At the sight, he cried out involuntarily, “A man of heaven!” Guan asked who he was. Hu Ban knelt and said, “I am Hu Ban, clerk under the Administrator of Xingyang.” Guan said, “Are you the son of Hu Hua outside Xudu’s walls?” Hu Ban said, “I am.” Guan told him to bring out the letter from among the baggage. Hu Ban read it and exclaimed, “By a narrow turn I nearly killed an upright loyal man.” Then he whispered, “Wang Zhi’s heart is cruel and intends to kill you. He has surrounded the inn on all sides. At the third watch they will set fire. You must leave through the gate at once.”

Guan was greatly startled. He quickly donned armor, drew his blade, mounted, called the two wives aboard, and hurried out all at once. At the gate they saw soldiers with torches waiting. Guan reached the city edge and saw the gate already open. They drove out in haste. Hu Ban returned to light the fire.

After not many li, torchlight rose from behind as troops pursued. First came Wang Zhi himself shouting, “Guan, do not run!” Guan reined in his horse and shouted, “Base man! I have no grievance against you. Why do you have men burn me?” Wang Zhi raised his horse and drove his spear straight at Guan. Guan cut him at the waist, splitting him in two. The troops scattered. Guan pushed the carriage onward and felt Hu Ban pursuing still.

When they reached the head of Huzhou Commandery, a messenger brought Liu Yan. He rode out with tens of horsemen and came to receive them. Guan inclined forward from horseback and said, “Administrator, have you been well while I was absent?” Liu Yan said, “General, where are you now going?” Guan said, “I have left the Chancellor and am going to seek my elder brother.” Liu Yan said, “Xuande is with Yuan Shao; Yuan Shao is the Chancellor’s foe. How can he allow you to pass?” Guan said, “Formerly we were to meet.” Liu Yan said, “Now at the Yellow River crossing in the pass, Qinqi, a sub-commander under Xiahou Dun, holds the banks. He may not let you pass.” Guan said, “How can you make provisions for the boats?” Liu Yan said, “Boats are available, but I dare not risk providing them.” Guan said, “I once saved you from danger by killing Yan Liang and Wenchou. Why would I ask for a fordboat and be denied it?” Liu Yan said, “I fear only that Xiahou Dun will hold me responsible.” Guan saw Liu Yan could do nothing and pressed the carriage onward.

At the Yellow River ferry, Qin Qi came out with soldiers and asked, “Who are you?” Guan said, “I am the Marquis of Hanshou, Guan. I have come to ask to cross and go to Hebei in search of my elder brother.” Qin Qi said, “Where is the Chancellor’s written order?” Guan said, “I do not take orders from the Chancellor. What need do I have for an order?” Qin Qi said, “I serve under General Xiahou Dun and am assigned this pass. Even if you grew wings and tried to fly, you still could not pass.” Guan was furious and said, “Do you know how many blockers I have struck down on this road?” Qin Qi said, “You have only killed nameless minor officers. How dare you kill me too?” Guan charged and the two horses met at once. Guan’s blade flashed and Qin Qi’s head fell. Guan said, “Those who came out to block me are dead. Others need not panic. Make ready the boats and send me across at once.” The soldiers hurriedly steadied the boats at the bank. Guan put the two wives on board and crossed. They were already in Yuan Shao’s lands.

On the passes he had passed through, Guan had cut down six officers. Later people made a verse:

He returned the seal and gold and bade the Chancellor farewell, Then sought his brother and looked out upon a distant road. On the red horse Red Hare he rode a thousand li, with the Green Dragon Crescent Blade at rest after crossing five passes. Loyalty and righteousness surged through heaven and earth, and heroes have shaken kingdoms since this day. Though he walked alone and beheaded generals, he had no equal. For ages and across ages his name would remain in ink.

Mounted, Guan then sighed, “I did not wish to kill men along the way. But I had no choice. Cao Cao will think I have repaid his kindness with betrayal.” As he rode on, a rider came from the north and shouted, “General, stop!” Guan reined in and saw it was Sun Qian. Guan said, “Since we parted at Ruyang, how has the situation gone?” Sun Qian said, “Liu Pi and Gongdu, after the troops returned from your campaign, retook Ruyang and sent me north to make ties with Yuan Shao, asking Xuande to conspire against Cao. But in Hebei the officers are jealous of each other. Tian Feng is still imprisoned; Ju Shu is removed and unused; Shen Pei and Guo Tu each contest authority. Yuan Shao is suspicious and his leadership is unsettled. We discussed escape with the Imperial Uncle first. He has already gone to Ruyang to meet Liu Pi. I feared if you did not know this, you might go to Yuan Shao and be harmed. That is why I was sent to meet you on the road. I am fortunate to meet you here. Make haste to Ruyang to meet the Imperial Uncle.” Guan asked Sun Qian to bow to the wives. The two wives asked him what had happened. Sun Qian explained, “Yuan Shao has tried twice to execute the Imperial Uncle. Now he has escaped and gone to Ruyang. The wives should meet the Imperial Uncle there.” Both wives covered their faces and wept.

Following their words, Guan did not go to Hebei but turned straight toward Ruyang. As they moved, dust rose behind them and a mounted force came in. First came Xiahou Dun, who shouted, “Guan, stop!” The verse that follows is:

Six commanders barred the pass hoping for death as their plan, An army blocked the road and fought again. How Guan Yu will escape from this,
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Bearded Hero Rides a Thousand Li Alone

chapters.html:
Not long after, Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, rode south with Sun Qian guarding the two wives toward Runan. Unexpectedly, Xiahou Dun came after them with over two hundred riders. Sun Qian drove the ox-cart ahead. Guan Yu wheeled around, drew his horse up, and rested a hand on his sword.

“Why do you pursue me?” he asked. “You have overstepped the Chancellor’s generosity.”

Xiahou Dun replied, “The Chancellor sent no clear order. Yet on the road you kill men and severed the head of one of my officers. It is grossly improper. I have come specifically to capture you and present you to the Chancellor so he can decide your punishment.”

With that he reined his horse, cocked his spear, and moved to strike. A rider flashed up behind him, shouting, “Do not fight with Yunchang!” Guan Yu held his reins and did not move.

The new messenger drew the official document from his breast and said to Xiahou Dun, “The Chancellor esteems General Guan’s loyalty and righteousness. Fearing obstacles at the mountain passes, he sent me with this commission to pass through every post.”

Xiahou Dun asked, “Does the Chancellor know that Guan slew his officers on the road?”

The messenger said, “That is not yet known.”

Xiahou Dun replied, “I will only capture him alive and bring him to the Chancellor. He may then release him.”

Guan Yu said angrily, “Did I fear you?” and he spurred his horse forward with sword drawn.

Xiahou Dun thrust forward with his spear to meet him. When their horses closed, no more than ten exchanges apart, another rider broke in, crying, “Second General, pause!”

Xiahou Dun lowered his spear and asked the messenger, “Did the Chancellor order that you capture Guan?”

The messenger said, “No. The Chancellor feared that officers at the mountain passes might block Guan. He again sent me with this order to allow him to pass.”

Xiahou Dun asked, “Does he know Guan has killed men on the road?”

“Not yet known,” the messenger said.

“Since I do not know that his killing was not unjustified, he cannot yet be released.” Xiahou Dun ordered his soldiers to surround Guan Yu. Guan Yu, furious, swung his sword and charged to fight.

Just as the two were about to clash, another horseman came hard from the rear and cried, “Cloud-Long and Yuanrang, do not dispute this battle!”

The men turned and saw Zhang Liao. Both held their mounts.

Drawing nearer, Zhang Liao said, “By the Chancellor’s command: I have heard that Cloud-Long has severed men and blocked a guard post. The Chancellor feared you might be obstructed on the road and therefore dispatched me to carry instructions everywhere to let him pass.”

Xiahou Dun said, “Qin Qi was Cai Yang’s nephew. He had entrusted Qin Qi to my care, and now Guan has killed him. How can I stop?”

Zhang Liao said, “I know Commander Cai’s worth. Since the Chancellor is generous, he has commanded that Yunchang be released. It would be improper to refuse him.”

Reluctantly, Xiahou Dun withdrew his horse.

Zhang Liao then asked, “Where now does Yunchang intend to go?”

Guan Yu said, “I have heard that my elder brother is no longer at Yuan Shao’s side. I will now ride across the land and the world to find him.”

“Since you do not know where Xuande is,” Zhang Liao said, “perhaps you should return to the Chancellor first.”

Guan Yu laughed. “Is that reasonable? Let Wenyuan return to him and beg pardon on my behalf.”

When he had said this, he and Zhang Liao bowed briefly to each other and parted.

Then Zhang Liao and Xiahou Dun withdrew with their troops.

When Guan Yu overtook the carriage, he informed Sun Qian of what had happened. The two rode together at one pace. They had gone several days when a heavy downpour drenched everything they carried. Seeing a manor on a hillside in the distance, Guan Yu guided the cart there and sought shelter.

An old man came out to receive them. Guan Yu explained their errand.

“My surname is Guo,” said the old man, “my name is Chang. My family has long lived here. I have long heard of your fame and am glad to have paid my respects.” He slaughtered a sheep, poured wine, and treated them. He asked the two wives to rest in the rear hall. Guo Chang stayed with Guan Yu, while Sun Qian drank in the hall and worked the fire, while their baggage was dried and the horses fed.

Near dusk, they saw a youth arrive with several men and go straight into the hall. Guo Chang called, “My son has come to pay respects to the General.” Then he said to Guan Yu, “He is this foolish boy.”

Guan Yu asked where he came from.

“Back from hunting,” said Chang.

When he saw Guan Yu, the youth left the hall at once.

Guo Chang wept. “My family lived by farming and study for generations, and I have no sons but him. He refuses our occupation and wastes himself in hunting. This household has no fortune!”

Guan Yu replied, “In this age of disorder, a man skilled in arms can win rank and renown. Why call this misfortune?”

“Could he only become a worthy man,” Guo Chang said, “if he learns arms? He prefers to roam and do anything in turn. That is why I worry.”

Guan Yu sighed in pity.

Late that night, Guo Chang quietly took his leave. Guan Yu and Sun Qian were about to sleep when they heard horses neighing and voices from the rear compound.

Guan Yu called for his attendants, but none answered. He and Sun Qian drew swords and went to see.

They saw Guo Chang’s son lying on the ground crying out. The house guests were fighting with his attendants. Guan asked what had happened.

An attendant said, “This fellow came to steal the Red Hare. The horse kicked him down. When we heard him cry out, we came out to investigate. The other guests then fought us.”

Guan Yu said angrily, “What mouse-thief dares steal my horse?”

Before he could strike, Guo Chang came running and said, “My wayward son did this vile thing. The crime deserves ten thousand deaths! But my old wife dotes on him most. I beg Your General’s mercy.”

Guan Yu answered, “This son truly is not fit. As you said just now, a father knows his own son best. I look at your face, and I can at least spare him.”

He ordered the attendants to tend the horse well, and sent the house guests scattering, then withdrew with Sun Qian to the hall to rest.

The next day Guo Chang and his wife came to the front hall to give thanks.

“My son has committed a grave offense against Your General’s majesty, and we are deeply grateful for your mercy,” Guo Chang said. “My heart is in your debt for your clemency.”

Guan Yu called out to him, “I only instruct with righteous words.”

Chang said, “At the fourth watch, he brought several rascals again and has gone off somewhere. I do not know where.”

After thanking Guo Chang, Guan Yu loaded his two wives into the cart and set out with Sun Qian, escorting it on the mountain path.

In less than thirty li they saw, behind the mountain, more than a hundred men emerge, with two riders leading. The man in front had his head wrapped in yellow cloth and wore martial clothing; behind him was Guo Chang’s son.

The yellow-headed man shouted, “I am a subordinate of Zhang Jiao, the General of Heaven! If you want to pass, leave the Red Hare behind and continue.”

Guan Yu laughed. “You ignorant, wild brigand! If you once served Zhang Jiao as a robber, do you still know the names of Liu, Guan, and Zhang, the three brothers?”

The yellow-head said, “I have heard only of the red-faced bearded man named Guan Yunchang. I do not know his face. Who are you?”

Guan Yu stopped his horse and drawing his mount up, unfastened the bundle at his beard and let his full whisker show.

The man dropped from the saddle and knelt, head bowed, to offer him homage before his horse. Guan Yu asked his name.

He answered, “My surname is Pei, name Yuanshao. Since Zhang Jiao died, I have had no lord. I gathered mountain folk and hid in these hills. This morning this youth reported: ‘A guest has arrived and is staying at my house riding a thousand-mile horse.’ So I was invited here to seize it. Yet by mischance I met your General.”

Guo Chang’s son knelt and begged for his life.

Guan Yu said, “I look to your face, and because your father is respectable, I spare your life.”

Pei bowed and ran off, hiding his head.

Guan Yu asked him, “You do not know my face. How did you know my name?”

Pei said, “Some twenty li from here lies Woniu Mountain. On that ridge lives a man from Guanzhong named Zhou, surname Zhou, name Cang. Both arms could bear a thousand jin. His chest was broad, his curling beard thick, and his countenance imposing. He once served under Zhang Bao of the Yellow Turbans. After Zhang Bao died, he gathered men in the hills. He has spoken to me before about your fame and regrets that there was no way to present himself.”

Guan Yu said, “The Green Forest is no place for men of this caliber to settle. All of you should return to the right path and avoid your own ruin.”

Pei bowed in thanks.

As they were still speaking, they saw a troop ride up in the distance.

“That must be Zhou Cang,” Pei said.

Guan Yu held his horse fast and waited.

Indeed, one man came on, black-faced and tall, spear in hand. He urged his horse forward with a following band and saw Guan Yu. He delightedly shouted, “This is General Guan!” and jumped down quickly, kneeling at the roadside.

“Will this stalwart not have ever met General Guan before?” Guan Yu asked.

Zhou Cang said, “I once followed him under Yellow Turban Zhang Bao and recognized his august face then. I was unable to remain with him when he lost his band. Today I am fortunate to bow before him. If the General does not reject me, let him take me as a footsoldier. I would gladly take the lash and follow behind his stirrup, even at death.”

Guan Yu saw his sincerity and said, “If you follow me, what of your men?”

“I will go with them if he will take them too; if he will not, leave them as they wish,” Zhou Cang answered.

Then all spoke: “We will all follow.”

Guan Yu dismounted and asked the two wives.

Gan Furen said, “Since Uncle left Xu City, he has traveled alone since this road and has endured many hardships, never having demanded cavalry to accompany him. When Brother Liao offered to join him, Uncle refused. Why do you now allow Zhou Cang and his men?”

Guan Yu replied, “What my sister-in-law says is true.” He said to Zhou Cang, “It is not because this General is cold, but because the two wives do not consent. You all should return to the hills and wait. When I find my elder brother, he will surely summon you.”

Zhou Cang knelt again and said, “I am a rough man, and have fallen into banditry. To meet the General is as if seeing daylight again. Could I bear to miss this chance? If only having a crowd is inconvenient, they may all go with Pei Yuanshao. I alone can walk. I will follow the General on foot, even for ten thousand li.”

Guan Yu repeated this to the two wives.

Gan Furen said, “If there are only one or two men, it need not hinder the way.”

He ordered then Zhou Cang to send men with Pei Yuanshao and let Yuanshao go with them.

Yuanshao said, “I too wish to follow General Guan.”

Zhou Cang said, “Your men have dispersed, and if you are to go, they will come off this hill then return. I will follow the General, and return to fetch you wherever we halt.”

Yuanshao parted with resentment.

Zhou Cang followed Guan Yu toward Runan. After several days they saw in the distance a mountain city.

Guan Yu asked a villager, “What place is this?”

The villager said, “This is Gucheng. A few months ago an officer named Zhang Fei, surname Zhang, came with some dozens of riders, drove out the county official, and occupied Gucheng. He recruited troops and bought horses, storing hay and grain. He has now three to five thousand men and horses and no one in four directions dares oppose him.”

Guan Yu rejoiced. “My brother has been separated from me since we parted in Xuzhou. Never did I know where he was. So he is here, after all.”

He told Sun Qian to go into the city first and report, and ask them to receive the two wives.

Zhang Fei had been staying in Mangdang Mountain for more than a month. He had gone out to seek news of Xuande and by chance had passed through Gucheng, entered the county to buy grain, and been refused. Angered, he had forced the county magistrate out and seized the county seals before occupying the city as a temporary hold. So when Sun Qian arrived under Guan’s seal and saluted properly, he gave the message in full.

“Xuande has left Yuan Shao’s side and gone to Runan,” he said. “Now Yunchang escorts the two wives from Xu City directly here. He begs you to come out and meet him.”

When Zhang Fei heard, he said nothing but immediately donned his armor, took up a zhangba spear, mounted, and led more than a thousand men straight out the north gate.

Sun Qian was astonished and dared not ask anything. He had to follow out of the city.

When Guan Yu saw Zhang Fei arriving, joy burst from him. He handed his sword to Zhou Cang and trotted over in a mounted salutation.

Zhang Fei squinted wide-eyed, set his tiger whiskers upright, roared like thunder, and thrust with the spear straight at Guan Yu.

Guan Yu, startled, moved quickly to evade and cried, “Dear brother, why do this? Have you forgotten the oath we swore at the Peach Garden?”

Zhang Fei shouted back, “You have no loyalty. How dare you come before me?”

Guan Yu said, “How can I be called disloyal?”

Zhang Fei replied, “You abandoned our elder brother, accepted the title and fief from Cao Cao, and now you come to deceive me! Today I shall settle this as life and death!”

Guan Yu said, “You did not know and I can hardly explain it. My two wives stand before you now. Ask your dear brother yourself.”

The two wives heard this and pulled back the curtain.

“Why are you like this, Third Uncle?” Gan Furen called.

“Your sisters-in-law are present,” Zhang Fei said. “First, see me kill this perfidious man; afterward I will bring your wives into the city.”

Gan Furen replied, “The second uncle did not know where you were, so he temporarily lodged under Cao’s house to avoid danger. Knowing now that your elder brother is in Runan, he risked all to bring us here. Third Uncle, do not misread this.”

Mi Furen said, “The second uncle was in Xu City only because he had no other choice.”

Zhang Fei snapped, “Do not let him deceive you! A loyal retainer dies before dishonor. A true man does not owe service to two lords!”

Guan Yu said, “Dear brother, do not torment me.”

Sun Qian said, “Yunchang came only to seek his brother, the General.”

Zhang Fei shouted, “Why do you dare lie like that too? Where else would he have goodwill? He came to capture me!”

Guan Yu said, “If I wished to capture you, I would have come with cavalry and troops.”

Zhang Fei pointed and said, “So not now with cavalry then.”

Guan Yu looked back and saw dust rising ahead, a band of riders arriving. Flags whipped by wind: it was a Cao force.

Zhang Fei was furious. “Now do you still pretend?” He raised his spear and began thrusting.

Guan Yu stopped him quickly and said, “Dear brother, hold. Watch me decapitate this arriving general to show my true heart.”

Zhang Fei said, “If your heart is true, after three drumbeats I expect you to cut down this man.”

Guan Yu agreed.

Soon the Cao soldiers arrived. At their head rode Cai Yang, sword drawn and horse reared, shouting,

“You killed my nephew Qin Qi and were hiding here! By the Chancellor’s command, I have come to seize you!”

Guan Yu wasted no words. He lifted his sword and struck. Zhang Fei himself beat the drum.

Before one drumbeat had finished, Cai Yang’s head had already fallen from his shoulders.

The soldiers of the battalion all scattered.

Guan Yu captured a standard-bearer and asked him the reason for his coming.

The soldier said, “Cai Yang heard that General Guan had killed his nephew and was furious, then came to Hebei to do battle with the General. The Chancellor refused, and ordered him to go to Runan to attack Liu Bi. Not expecting to meet the General here, he came now.”

Guan Yu told him to report in Zhang Fei’s presence. Zhang Fei questioned the young soldier in detail about Guan’s affair at Xu City. The soldier repeated the sequence from start to finish before Zhang Fei finally believed it.

At that moment city soldiers reported that ten or more riders had come quickly to the south gate of the city.

Zhang Fei, still suspicious, rode out through the gate. It was indeed ten or so light-mounted archers and short-bow men. On seeing Zhang Fei, they dismounted at once.

They were Mi Zhu and Mi Fang.

Zhang Fei also dismounted and greeted them. Mi Zhu said,

“Since we parted at Xuzhou, my brother and I fled disaster and returned home. We have sent men everywhere to ask, and heard that Yunchang submitted to Cao Cao, while Xuande was in Hebei. We also heard Jian Yong had gone to Hebei as well. We did not know where the General was. Yesterday on the road we met a group of guests who said there was a general surnamed Zhang, such a face, now in Gucheng. The two brothers measured that this must be the General, so we came searching. Now we are fortunate indeed to meet him.”

Zhang Fei said, “Yunchang has just come with Sun Qian, bringing the two wives. He now knows where my brother is.”

The two Mi were delighted and came with Zhang Fei to greet Guan Yu, and then also paid their respects to the two wives.

Zhang Fei then invited the wives into the city.

Once seated in the yamen hall, they recounted what Guan Yu had gone through. Zhang Fei burst into tears and then paid homage to Yunchang. The two Mi were also moved.

Zhang Fei spoke himself of what had happened since their separation, and then held a banquet to celebrate.

The next day Zhang Fei planned to go with Guan Yu to Runan and meet Xuande. Guan Yu said,

“Dear brother, you should remain in this city and guard the two wives. Wait here for a while. Let me and Sun Qian first go to learn news of our elder brother.”

Zhang Fei agreed.

Guan Yu and Sun Qian rode out with a few men toward Runan. They were met by Liu Bi and Gongdu, and Guan asked,

“Where is the Imperial Uncle?”

Liu Bi said, “The Imperial Uncle has stayed here for several days. Lacking soldiers, he returned to Hebei and has gone to Yuan Shao’s encampment for counsel.”

Guan Yu was dissatisfied.

Sun Qian said, “Do not worry. Endure this one more tour of hardship; then we shall go to Hebei and report to the Imperial Uncle. We can meet at Gucheng there.”

According to that plan, Guan Yu informed Liu Bi and Gongdu and returned to Gucheng to tell Zhang Fei.

Zhang Fei wished to go at once to Hebei.

Guan Yu said, “With this one city we have a place to settle, and we should not abandon it lightly. I will go with Sun Qian to Yuan Shao and find our elder brother so that we may meet here. Brother must hold this city.”

Zhang Fei said, “You once beheaded Yanliang and Wen Chou. How can you manage it now?”

“No harm in that,” Guan Yu replied. “I can go to him when opportunity presents.”

He summoned Zhou Cang.

“How many men and horses does Pei Yuanshao command on Woniu Mountain now?”

Zhou Cang said, “About four or five hundred.”

“I will take a shortcut to find my elder brother,” Guan Yu said. “You must go up to Woniu Mountain, summon that force, and bring them to join us on the main road.”

Zhou Cang accepted and departed.

Guan Yu and Sun Qian continued toward Hebei with only some twenty riders.

At Jiushou boundary Sun Qian said, “General, you should not enter lightly yet. Let us rest here a while.”

He added, “I will go ahead first to see the Imperial Uncle and settle our plan.”

Guan Yu nodded and sent Sun Qian on.

In the distance he saw a manor at a village and, with his men, went there to lodge for the night.

An old man came out with a staff and greeted Guan Yu. The General explained everything frankly.

The old man said, “My surname is also Guan, my name is Ding. I have long heard your name and am glad to have seen you.” He ordered his two sons out and had them receive Guan Yu, and asked all of Guan’s attendants to stay in the house as well.

Meanwhile Sun Qian rode into Hebei alone and met Xuande.

He reported all that had happened.

Xuande said, “Jian Yong is also in this area. Invite him secretly to discuss.”

Not long after, Jian Yong arrived and after seeing Sun Qian, they discussed a way to break out.

Jian Yong said, “Tomorrow morning Xuande will meet Yuan Shao and tell him he plans to go to Jing Province, and to propose that Liu Biao and we will together break Cao Cao. After that he can slip away.”

Xuande said, “That is excellent. But can you truly follow me?”

Jian Yong said, “I have my own plan to break free as well.”

When that was settled, Xuande went the next day to meet Yuan Shao and said,

“Liu Biao, whose courtesy name is Jingsheng, holds Jing Province and occupies the nine commanderies. His troops are disciplined and his provisions abundant. It is fitting to form an agreement to attack Cao Cao together.”

Yuan Shao said, “I have sent an envoy to make terms before, but he refused to join.”

Xuande said, “Liu is your fellow clansman. If you send him and he hears my plea, he surely will not refuse.”

Yuan Shao said, “If we can secure Liu Biao, we can greatly defeat Liu Bei.”

He then ordered him onward.

Yuan Shao said, “I have also heard that Guan Yunchang has left Cao and comes to Hebei. I intend to kill him and settle my grievance for Yanliang and Wen Chou!”

Xuande replied, “You intended to employ him before, and I invited him for that reason. Why do you now want him dead? Yanliang and Wen Chou are only two deer; Yunchang is one tiger. If one loses two deer, one gains a tiger. What reason then to grudge?”

Yuan Shao laughed. “I do favor him indeed. These were but playful words. You may send someone again and order him to come quickly.”

Xuande said, “You may send Sun Qian.”

Yuan Shao rejoiced and agreed.

When Xuande left, Jian Yong said, “If Xuande goes to meet Liu Biao he will not return. I wish to accompany him. One to speak on Liu Biao, one to keep watch over him.”

Yuan Shao accepted this judgment.

Guo Tu remonstrated, “Xuande has gone to see Liu Biao and to no effect. Now you send him again with Jian Yong to Jing Province; he will not return.”

Yuan Shao said, “Do not over-suspect. Jian Yong has enough judgment.”

Guo Tu left with a sigh.

Xuande first ordered Sun Qian out of the city to ask about Guan Yu. Then he took leave of Yuan Shao and mounted.

On the road to Jiushou, Sun Qian met up and took him to Guan Ding’s estate.

Guan Yu greeted and took his hand, then could not stop crying.

Guan Ding brought his two sons and had them bow in the hall.

Xuande asked their names.

Guan Yu said, “This man shares our family name. He has two sons: the elder, Guan Ning, studies literature; the younger, Guan Ping, studies arms.”

Guan Ding said, “My foolish thought is to send the younger to follow General Guan. I do not know if he can take him.”

Xuande said, “How many years old?”

Guan Ding replied, “Eighteen.”

Xuande said, “Since you show such favor, and since my brother has no sons yet, I accept this good young man as my foster-son at once. What says he?”

Guan Ding was greatly pleased and had Guan Ping bow to Guan Yu as father and call Xuande uncle. Xuande, fearing Yuan Shao’s pursuit, hurried preparations for departure.

Guan Ping followed Guan Yu, and both mounted at once.

Guan Ding saw them off partway and returned.

Guan Yu instructed him to take the way toward Woniu Mountain.

As they were traveling, they suddenly saw Zhou Cang coming with some men wounded.

Guan Yu brought him before Xuande and asked why he was hurt.

Zhou Cang said, “Before I reached Woniu Mountain, a single rider came and engaged Pei Yuanshao in combat. He stabbed Pei Yuanshao in one exchange, and I persuaded all of Pei’s men to surrender, then occupied the stockade. When I went up the mountain to summon men, only these few followed me; the rest were afraid. I could not bear it, fought him again, and was repeatedly defeated several times. He pierced me with three spears. So I have come to report to you.”

Xuande asked, “What is he like? What are his surname and name?”

Zhou Cang answered, “He is extremely rugged and broad. I do not know his name.”

Guan Yu urged his horse forward first, with Xuande behind, and rode straight for Woniu Mountain.

At the foot of the mountain Zhou Cang shouted and cursed. They saw that warrior fully armed, spear in hand, riding hard, leading men down.

Xuande quickly drew his whip, dismounted, and called out,

“Are you not by any chance Zilong?”

The rider saw Xuande, dropped his reins, dismounted, and knelt beside the road.

It was indeed Zhao Yun.

Xuande and Guan Yu both dismounted and met him. They asked how he had come there.

“After I left the lord,” Zhao Yun said, “I found that Gongsun Zan did not listen to counsel, and so by battle lost and set himself ablaze. Yuan Shao invited me repeatedly. Since I thought him no true man of talent, I did not go. Later I intended to return to Xuzhou to serve the lord, but I heard Xuzhou had fallen and that Yunchang had returned under Cao Cao, while the lord was still at Yuan Shao. I tried many times to come, but feared Yuan Shao would be suspicious. A man of no place in all four seas, I had nowhere to stand. By chance I passed this way and happened to meet Pei Yuanshao when he came down the mountain to seize my horse. I killed him and used that as a chance to stay. I recently heard Yide was in Gucheng and planned to go to him, though I could not confirm it. I am fortunate indeed to meet you now!”

Xuande rejoiced and recounted former events. Guan Yu also told what had happened.

“From the first time I saw Zilong,” Xuande said, “I have never been able to let that attachment leave me. I am so glad we met.”

Zhao Yun said, “I have run four seas and five rivers, seeking a lord to serve, but none compared with you. Now to be able to serve you is the pride of my life. Even if my liver and brain are smeared in the dust, I have no regret.”

That day they burned the mountain stockade and gathered all troops and all men to follow Xuande immediately to Gucheng.

Zhang Fei, Mi Zhu, and Mi Fang came out to welcome them and all paid their respects. The two wives reported everything about Guan Yu; Xuande was deeply moved.

Then they slaughtered cattle and horses, offered thanks to Heaven and Earth, and then visited all the troops.

Xuande saw the brothers reunited, his counselors complete, and now gained Zhao Yun anew; Guan Yu had found Guan Ping and Zhou Cang. He rejoiced beyond measure and drank for several days in company.

People praised this with a verse:

Then the three brothers were as if separated apart, and messages between them were sparse and faint in the distance. Today lord and minister are reunited in righteousness, meeting like dragon and tiger in wind and cloud.

At that time Xuande, Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Zhao Yun, Sun Qian, Jian Yong, Mi Zhu, Mi Fang, Guan Ping, and Zhou Cang had command of roughly four to five thousand horse and foot, while marshaling officers.

Xuande wished to leave Gucheng and go north to garrison Runan. Liu Bi and Gongdu happened to send men then, asking him to do so.

He then led out his army to Runan, bought grain and horses, and slowly prepared for advance. It is not recorded further here.

As for Yuan Shao, he saw Xuande did not return and became enraged, ready to raise troops against him.

Guo Tu said, “Liu Bei is not one to fear. Cao Cao is a formidable foe and must be dealt with decisively. Liu Biao, though occupying Jingzhou, is not strong enough; Sun Bofu in the southeastern lands holds the Three Rivers and commands six commanderies, where ministers and soldiers are many. It would be possible to join with him and both attack Cao Cao.”

Yuan Shao accepted this advice and drafted a letter dispatching Chen Zhen to meet Sun Ce.

Then it was written,

Only because the heroes have gone from Hebei, Heroes from the Jiangdong lands have been drawn forth. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Guan Yu Beheads Cai Yang’s Kinsman and Reunites at Gucheng

chapters.html:
Now Sun Ce, whose courtesy name was Bofu and who was known as the Little Conqueror, had come to dominate Jiangdong. His army was well-drilled and his granaries were full. In the fourth year of Jian’an, he raided Lujiang, defeated Liu Xun, and sent Yu Fan to rush proclamations to Yuzhang; the Administrator of Yuzhang, Hua Xin, surrendered. From then on, his prestige surged. He sent Zhang Hong to Xuchang to present a report of victory.

Cao Cao, whose courtesy name was Mengde, realized how formidable Sun Ce had become and sighed, “I will not compete in direct contest with that lion-cub.” He then married his daughter, the daughter of Cao Ren, to Sun Ce’s younger brother Sun Kuang, and the two families formed an alliance. Zhang Hong was left in Xuchang.

Sun Ce asked to become the Grand Marshal, but Cao Cao refused. He resented it and often thought of raiding Xuchang. As a result, Xu Gong, the Administrator of Wu Commandery, secretly sent a messenger there with a memorial to Cao Cao. Its preface read:

Sun Ce is brave and strong, similar to Xiang Yu. The court should bestow him honors from afar and summon him back to the capital. He should not be left out in a frontier command, for he will become a later source of trouble.

The messenger carried the memorial across the river, but he was intercepted by soldiers guarding the river. They brought him to Sun Ce. When Sun Ce read it, he exploded in rage, beheaded the messenger, and sent men to ask Xu Gong to come under the pretext of discussion.

When Xu Gong arrived, Sun Ce presented the document and shouted, “Did you intend to send me to my death?” He then ordered soldiers to strangle him. Xu Gong’s family all scattered. Three retainers in his household wished to avenge him, but they lacked opportunity.

One day Sun Ce led his troops on a hunt in the western hills of Dantu. He chased a large deer at a gallop on horseback. As he was pursuing, he saw three men in the trees, each holding spear and bow. Sun Ce drew up and asked, “Who are you?”

They replied, “We are soldiers of Han Dang, out here to shoot deer.”

Sun Ce was just raising his reins to pass when one lunged a spear at his left leg. He was greatly startled, pulled out his sword from horseback and struck, but the blade came away from the hilt, leaving only the handle in his hand.

One of them swiftly nocked an arrow and shot. It struck Sun Ce squarely in the cheek. He drew out the arrow from his face and grabbed a bow to shoot the archer; the man fell as soon as the bowstring was drawn.

The other two men raised their spears and pressed wild against Sun Ce, shouting that they were retainers of Xu Gong come to avenge their master. Sun Ce had no other weapons. He used his bow to parry and kept retreating while he fought, but both men did not retreat. Sun Ce was pierced by several spears, and his horse was also wounded.

At the dangerous moment Cheng Pu arrived with a few men. Sun Ce shouted, “Kill the bandits!” Cheng Pu urged everyone forward, and the men from Xu Gong’s household were hacked down into scraps.

By then Sun Ce’s face ran with blood. He was badly wounded, so he cut through his own robes with a knife, bound his wounds, and returned to Wukui to recover. Later, a verse praised the three retainers of Xu’s household:

The little hero, brave in wit and courage, leads across the riverbank; while hunting in the mountains he was suddenly trapped in danger. The three retainers of Xu serve loyalty unto death; as for sacrificing themselves like Yu Rang, it is nothing strange.

Sun Ce came back from the hunt in pain, sent for a physician, and asked Huatuo to treat him. Unfortunately Huatuo had already left for Zhongyuan, and only his disciple remained.

The disciple said, “The arrowhead carried drug. The poison has entered the bone. He needs one hundred days of rest to avoid danger. If anger rises in him, the wound will never heal.”

Yet Sun Ce was impatient by nature and wished to recover at once. After only a little over twenty days of rest, he heard that a messenger from Zhang Hong had come back from Xuchang and called him to inquire. The messenger said, “Cao Cao fears the lord here, and all of his subordinate strategists are respectful of him. Only Guo Jia does not defer.”

Sun Ce asked, “What did Guo Jia say?”

The messenger dared not speak. Sun Ce pressed him again. The messenger finally replied honestly: Guo Jia had once told Cao Cao, “The lord has nothing to fear. He is rash and unready, few in strategy and merely brave like a common man. One day he will die at the hands of a petty man.”

Sun Ce grew furious and said, “How dare this commoner presume to appraise me! I swear I will take Xuchang!” Even before he had fully recovered, he began to discuss marching out.

Zhang Zhao advised him, “Your physician ordered a hundred days of rest; why move now over a sudden fury and risk this precious body worth ten thousand pieces of gold?”

As they were still discussing, word came that Chen Zhen had arrived, sent by Yuan Shao. Sun Ce summoned him. Chen Zhen reported that Yuan Shao wished to form an alliance with Eastern Wu as an external support and strike Cao Cao together.

Sun Ce was delighted and that same day summoned his officers to the city tower for a banquet to receive Chen Zhen. After many cups, he noticed his commanders exchanging whispers and dropping down from the tower in crowds. He asked what was wrong. They said, “A Daoist named Yu has just passed below the tower. The officers all want to go and pay respects.”

Sun Ce stood at the railing and saw an old man in a crane-feathered gown, carrying a staff of li bamboo, standing in the road. All the commoners were burning incense and prostrating themselves before him.

Sun Ce shouted, “What sort of demon is this? Bring him to me at once!”

His attendants said, “His surname is Yu, given name Ji. He lives in the east and comes and goes through Wukui. He offers talisman-water that cures all manner of illness, and people say it never fails. They call him a true immortal today. You should not offend him.”

Sun Ce’s anger rose further. He shouted, “Seize him at once. If anyone disobeys, execute them.”

With no choice, the men brought Yu Ji upstairs. Sun Ce shouted, “How dare you sorcerer incite the people!”

Yu Ji said, “I am a Daoist from the Langye Palace. In the reign of Emperor Shun (Shun-di), I entered the mountains to gather herbs and found a scripture on the waters of Quyang Spring. It was called The Way of Peaceful Blue-Grey Dao, hundreds of volumes, with methods for treating illness. I received it only to spread Heaven’s compassion and save the many people. I have never taken even a pin from anyone. How could I inflame the people, then?”

Sun Ce replied, “If you do not take money, then how do you sustain your clothes and food? You are among those followers of Zhang Jiao and the Yellow Turbans. If you are not punished now, you will bring disaster later.”

He shouted, “Cut him down!”

Zhang Zhao pleaded, “Yu Ji has practiced here in Jiangdong for decades with no misconduct. He should not be killed.”

Sun Ce said, “Such a charlatan—I strike him, and it is no different from butchering swine and dogs.” All the officials urged him to spare Yu Ji. Even Chen Zhen spoke. But Sun Ce did not relent and ordered Yu Ji confined.

The officials withdrew. Chen Zhen returned to his guest pavilion and rested.

When Sun Ce returned to the residence, his mother, the Lady Wu, had already been informed. She called him to the inner hall and said, “I have heard you have put Yu Ji under chains. He has treated many illnesses before; soldiers and commoners alike venerate him. Do not harm him.”

Sun Ce answered, “He is a demon. He can cloud men’s minds with sorcery. He must be removed.” The mother urged him again and again, but he said, “Do not heed other men’s words. My lord’s own judgment stands.”

He ordered the jailer to bring Yu Ji. Unknown to him, the jail staff revered Yu Ji. While in prison, they had taken off all his fetters, but when Sun Ce called for him, he came in shackled.

Sun Ce raged still more, blamed the jailer, and bound Yu Ji again for execution. Zhang Zhao and some thirty officials submitted a joint petition urging him to spare the Daoist. Sun Ce said,

You are all men of letters and can still not understand. In former times, the Inspector of Jiaozhou, Zhang Jin, believed in heterodox teachings, played qin and burned incense, and always wrapped his head in a red sash, claiming he could support troops in war. In the end he was killed by enemy armies. Such practices do nothing. You have yet to understand it. My intention in killing Yu Ji is to shut down demonic delusion.

Lu Fan added, “I have always known this Daoist can pray for wind and rain. At this drought, why not order him to pray for rain to atone?”

Sun Ce said, “I will watch this sorcerer now.”

He then commanded the prison staff to bring Yu Ji out, remove his shackles, and set him upon an altar to seek rain.

Yu Ji followed orders, bathed, changed clothes, and tied a rope around himself in the fierce noon sun. Crowds filled the streets and lanes. Yu Ji told them, “I can summon three chi of fine rain to save the ten thousand, but I know I cannot escape death.”

The crowd said, “If he proves efficacious, the lord will certainly trust him.” Yu Ji said, “My destiny is near, and I fear I cannot escape.”

Not long after, Sun Ce personally came to the altar and issued his command: if it were noon and still no rain, he would burn Yu Ji. Men were ordered to stack dry timber in readiness.

As noon neared, a violent wind rose. Dark clouds gathered all around. Sun Ce said, “The hour is near noon, only clouds and no sweet rain—this is exactly a demon.” He shouted for men to carry Yu Ji to the pyre and build flame on all four sides. The flames rose with the wind.

Then a single black column of smoke shot upward. A sharp crack sounded, lightning and thunder split together, and torrential rain poured. In moments, streets turned to streams and every gully filled; the rain ran three chi deep. Yu Ji lay supine on the pyre, let out a great cry, and at once the wind died, the rain stopped, and the sun reappeared.

Officials and commoners together carried Yu Ji down from the pyre, removed his cords, and bowed again in thanks. Seeing soldiers and officials kneeling in standing water, bareheaded and unconcerned for their clothes, Sun Ce flared in anger. He shouted, “Rain is ordained by Heaven; a sorcerer took the moment for show. How could you all be so bewitched?” He drew his treasure sword and ordered the nearest men, “Kill Yu Ji at once.”

The officials tried to intercede repeatedly, but Sun Ce said, “You all would join Yu Ji in rebellion, then?” none dared to speak.

He shouted for soldiers to behead Yu Ji. As the executioner’s blade fell, a line of green vapor rose and shot off to the northeast. Sun Ce ordered Yu Ji’s corpse publicly exposed in the market to establish the crime of sorcery.

That night rain and wind mixed. At dawn, Yu Ji’s severed head was gone.

A guard reported this to Sun Ce. Sun Ce began to order the guard executed, when a man quietly entered from the front hall. It was Yu Ji.

Sun Ce roared, drawing his sword to cut him down, but suddenly he collapsed in a faint.
