He recovered after some time, and Mother Wu came to see him. “By killing your own holy man, you invited this disaster,” she said.

Sun Ce laughed, “Since childhood I followed my father in campaign and killed as with chaff. Why would I ever bring a ruin upon myself? By killing this demon now, I have eliminated a great ruin; how can this become ruin for me?”

His mother replied, “The sages say, ‘The virtue of ghosts and spirits is truly magnificent.’ They also said, ‘Pray to the deities above and below.’ Matters of ghosts and spirits cannot be ignored. To kill Master Yu unjustly—how can there be no retribution? I have already arranged for a ritual to be prepared at the Yuching Hall of this commandery. You may go there yourself and offer prayers; then all will be set right.”

Sun Ce said, “My life is in Heaven’s hand; this demon cannot bring calamity. Why waste on appeasement?”

She realized he would not listen and secretly ordered good works to avert evil.

In the middle watch of that night, Sun Ce lay in the inner court when a sudden gust blew, the lamps went out and flared on again. In the lamp light he saw Yu Ji standing before him. Sun Ce shouted, “I have sworn to punish demons and sorcery to pacify the realm. Since you are now a ghost, how dare you come near me?”

He threw the sword from the bedside, but Yu Ji vanished at once.

Wu Mother heard this and grew deeply anxious. Sun Ce forced himself back up and went out to the Yuxing Palace at her command. The Daoist there took him in and asked him to burn incense. Sun Ce burned incense but offered no thanks.

From the incense burner rose a single column of smoke that would not dissipate, then formed a canopy beneath which Yu Ji sat. Sun Ce cursed him and left the hall. At the hall gate he saw Yu Ji again, glaring at him.

He told his attendants, “Do you all see this ghost?” All said they did not.

Sun Ce became even more furious. He drew his belt sword and hurled it at Yu Ji, but one soldier was struck and collapsed, his brain cleft and blood pouring from the seven openings. He had been one of the young soldiers who had killed Yu Ji. Sun Ce ordered that man buried.

As Sun Ce left the hall, Yu Ji again appeared at the gate and entered the monastery. Sun Ce said, “This monastery also harbors a demon’s place.” He sat before the temple entrance and ordered five hundred soldiers to tear it down.

The soldiers had just begun to lift roof tiles when Yu Ji appeared on the eaves and hurled tiles down. Sun Ce was infuriated and ordered all resident Daoists expelled and the buildings burned.

As flames rose, Yu Ji stood out in the firelight once more. Sun Ce returned to the residence and saw Yu Ji waiting by the gate. He did not return indoors; he called up three military camps, had everyone ride out beyond the city, and convened his commanders to discuss. He wanted to march immediately with Yuan Shao against Cao Cao.

The commanders said in one voice, “My lord’s body is out of balance; it is not time to move. Wait until you are fully recovered. A campaign can wait.”

That night Sun Ce slept at the camp and again saw Yu Ji, hair loose, coming toward him. He shouted in his tent without rest.

The next day, his mother summoned him home. Sun Ce returned and saw his mother. She cried, “My son, you have lost your bearing.” Sun Ce took a mirror and saw his own face was terribly gaunt. He looked at those around him and said, “How have I become so emaciated?”

Before he could finish, Yu Ji appeared within the mirror. He pounded the frame and shouted. The scar on his face split apart, and he fainted.

His mother had him carried indoors. He soon recovered, then summoned Zhang Zhao and the others and his younger brother Sun Quan to his bed, and spoke his charge:

“If you can gather the men of Jiangdong, decide your move between the two opposing ranks, and contend with all under Heaven, then you are not inferior to me. Appoint worthy and capable men and have each give his full strength to preserve Jiangdong. As for this, I am not as capable as you. My dear one, be mindful of the hardship my father and brothers endured to found this house.”

Sun Quan wept and accepted the insignia and silk credentials.

Sun Ce then said, “My years are fulfilled. I cannot serve our mother any longer. I now hand her the insignia and command seals to you. Guide her each day. Do not neglect your old companions and officers.”

His mother wept, “I fear your younger brother is still young and cannot shoulder great affairs. What then?”

Sun Ce replied, “My brother surpasses me tenfold and is fit for great burden. If domestic matters trouble you, ask Zhang Zhao. If matters of war trouble you, ask Zhou Yu. I regret that Zhou Yu is not here to hear my last words.”

He called his brothers and continued,

“After I die, all of you must assist Zhongmou [Sun Quan]. If any in our clan gives way to disloyal thought, execute him together. Bone and flesh that turn traitor shall not enter ancestral tombs.”

His brothers wept and accepted.

He called his wife, Lady Qiao, and said, “Though we were not destined to stay together, you must now honor and support our mother-in-law. In time, when my younger sister comes to see you, send her to Zhou Lang [Zhou Yu] and ask him to uphold what we have shared.”

After he finished, he lay still and passed away, saying nothing. He was twenty-six.

Later people spoke this poem of lament:

He alone fought in the southeast, and men called him the Small Conqueror. He planned operations like a crouching tiger, and his decisions flew like a soaring eagle. He pacified the three rivers, and his name was fragrant across the four seas. In death he left heavy state matters, yet his final trust was on Zhou Yu.

When Sun Ce died, Sun Quan fell across the bed and wept. Zhang Zhao said, “This is no time for only tears. You must manage mourning and at once the affairs of the state.” Sun Quan restrained himself.

Zhang Zhao ordered Sun Jing to oversee the funeral rites and then asked Sun Quan to appear in the hall and receive the formal greetings of the civil and military officials.

Sun Quan had a square jaw, wide mouth, blue eyes, and purple beard. In earlier times a Han envoy named Liu Wan visited the Sun clan and saw all the brothers. He said to someone, “I have observed all of the Sun brothers: each has keen talent and brilliance, and all of them are short-lived in blessing. Only Zhongmou has an uncommon countenance and extraordinary bearing, and he carries the marks of future eminence. He will enjoy long life. None of the others compare.”

At that time Sun Quan followed his brother’s charge and assumed charge in Jiangdong, but the realm was still unsettled. News came that Zhou Yu returned from Baqiu with troops. Sun Quan said, “Gongjin has returned; I have no more cause for fear.”

Zhou Yu had been stationed to guard Baqiu and heard Sun Ce had been wounded by arrow. He returned to inquire, but when he reached Wu Commandery he heard Sun Ce was dead, so he rode through the night to attend the mourning.

As he entered before Sun Ce’s coffin, he wept and kowtowed. Lady Wu came forth and recited Sun Ce’s dying instruction to him. Zhou Yu knelt at the ground and said, “I will do what a loyal horse and dog can do and follow it through with my life!”

Shortly after, Sun Quan entered. After Zhou Yu had paid his respects, Sun Quan said, “Do not forget your elder brother’s command.” Zhou Yu knelt and said, “I will bathe in my own blood and blood and flesh and repay his kindness to the core.”

Sun Quan asked, “What plan would you set so I can keep what my father and elder brother have built?”

Zhou Yu said, “As the old saying goes, one gains a ruler and loses one too. For now we need a counselor with great and far-seeing vision. Only then can Jiangdong be steadied.”

Sun Quan replied, “My elder brother’s final words place internal affairs under the charge of Zi Bu, and external affairs wholly on Gongjin.”

Zhou Yu said, “Zi Bu is a sensible and gifted officer; he can carry great responsibilities. I am not enough for that trust, and I am ashamed at the weight of it. I should recommend one man.”

Sun Quan asked who it was. Zhou Yu said,

He is Lu Su of the surname Lu, courtesy name Zijing, and native to Dongchuan of the Linhuai region. He has strategic depth in his chest and stratagems hidden in his heart. His father died young, and he served his mother with filial devotion. Their family is very wealthy; once he gave away two granaries of grain, each holding three thousand hu, to help people in poverty. When I, Zhou, governed Chao as a prefect, I marched with several hundred men through Linhuai. When our provisions ran short, I heard Su’s family had two granaries of rice, each of three thousand hu. I asked Su for aid. He indicated one and granted it. He was so generous.

He loves horse and bow so deeply and had long lived in Quya. When his grandmother died, he buried her in East City. His friend Liu Ziyang invited him to Chao Lake to meet and seek out Cheng Bao, but Su had been hesitant. Now, summon him quickly.”

Sun Quan was pleased and ordered Zhou Yu to invite him at once. Zhou Yu obeyed, met Lu Su, completed formal rites, and explained Sun Quan’s esteem. Lu Su replied, “Liu Ziyang has asked me to go to Chao Lake; I am due to go.”

Zhou Yu said, “In former times, in response to Emperor Guangwu, Ma Yuan said: ‘Today, the ruler chooses ministers no less than ministers choose ruler.’ My Sun Jiangjun honors worth and welcomes scholars; he treasures rare and strange people. This is rarer than one can find in these lands. You need not make your own plan. Come with me and offer yourself to Eastern Wu.’”

Lu Su followed this counsel and came with Zhou Yu to see Sun Quan. Sun Quan received him with great respect and spoke all night; he would talk until exhaustion.

One day, after everyone else had left, Sun Quan and Lu Su remained drinking together and lay side by side to rest. At midnight Sun Quan said, “Now the Han court totters and the four corners of the world are in disorder. As a son inheriting the enterprises of my father and brother, I wish to act like Huan and Wen. What can you teach me?”

Lu Su replied, “In the past, when Emperor Gaozu sought to honor Emperor Yi, he failed because of Xiang Yu. Today Cao Cao may be compared to Xiang Yu. How can a general become a Huan or a Wen? I suspect under Heaven that the Han court cannot be revived and Cao Cao cannot be removed in a day. For your benefit, General, there is only this path: establish a tripod balance with Jiangdong and observe the fractures under Heaven. Now, while the northern front is burdened with many tasks, you should first eliminate Huang Zu, then advance south to drive forth against Liu Biao until you hold the reaches at the end of the Yangtze. Thereafter take on a dynastic title and contend for the world. That is the Great Ancestor’s enterprise.”

When Sun Quan heard this, he sat up and thanked him. The next day he rewarded Lu Su richly and gave robe, canopies, and tenting goods, and sent gifts to Su’s mother as well.

Lu Su then recommended another man to Sun Quan: Zhuge Jin, whose surname was Zhuge, name was Jin, courtesy name Ziyu, and from Longzhong in Nanyang.

Sun Quan honored him as a distinguished guest. Zhuge Jin advised Sun Quan not to ally with Yuan Shao; follow Cao Cao first, then take advantage to strike. Sun Quan agreed and sent Chen Zhen away with a letter, severing ties with Yuan Shao.

Cao Cao, on hearing of Sun Ce’s death, intended to raise troops and descend to Jiangnan. Court censor Zhang Hong advised him, “To attack while they mourn is neither righteous nor wise. If he cannot be subdued, you will only turn good ties into enmity. Better to treat him well and gain him.”

Cao Cao accepted the counsel. He immediately proposed granting Sun Quan a military title and also the office of Administrator of Kuaiji Commandery. He further appointed Zhang Hong as Chief Commandant of Kuaiji and sent him with the seals to Jiangdong.

Sun Quan rejoiced and, when Zhang Hong returned, assigned him to work with Zhang Zhao on governing affairs.

Zhang Hong then recommended another man: one surnamed Gu, given name Yong, courtesy name Yuan-tan, a student of Cai Yong, formerly a gentleman of the zhonglang bureau.

He spoke little, drank no wine, and was strict and upright. Sun Quan made him his deputy and had him carry out the Administrator’s duties for the commandery. From then on, Sun Quan’s authority prevailed through Jiangdong, and he won deep loyalty among the people.

Chen Zhen then returned to Yuan Shao and reported that Sun Ce was dead and Sun Quan had succeeded him. Cao Cao had conferred the military title and made an external alliance, and Yuan Shao was furious. He raised more than seven hundred thousand men from Ji, Qing, You, and Bing commanderies and returned to take Xuchang once more.

The chapter closed with this verse:

In Jiangnan, military gear had just begun to rest; in Ji Province, the clash of war had risen again. No one yet knows how victory and defeat will turn.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Little Conqueror Strikes Yu Ji

chapters.html:
Now Yuan Shao, whose courtesy name was Benchu, raised his forces and set out toward Guandu. Xiahou Dun, whose courtesy name was Yuanrang, sent a dispatch in urgent alarm. Cao Cao, whose courtesy name was Mengde, raised seventy thousand men to go out and meet him, leaving Xun Yu, whose courtesy name was Wenruo, to guard Xuchang.

As Yuan Shao's army prepared to march, Tian Feng, still confined, submitted a memorial: "Now it is best to hold firm and wait for the times, not to raise a great army in haste, lest we invite harm." Feng Ji said, "My lord now has assembled an army for righteousness and virtue; how can Tian Feng speak such inauspicious words?"

Yuan Shao grew angry and ordered Tian Feng executed. The officers begged for clemency. Yuan Shao said, "After I have broken Cao Cao, I will rectify his crimes openly." and drove the army onward. Banners spread across the plain, and swords flashed like a forest. When they reached Yangwu they made camp. Ju Shu said, "Though our army is large, our courage does not exceed theirs; though theirs is smaller and their courage is stronger, their grain is weaker than ours. They have advantage in rapid battle; we have advantage in endurance. If we can hold on for days and months, they will break on their own. "

Yuan Shao snapped, "Tian Feng does not understand my soldiers' heart. When I return, I will execute him." He ordered Ju Shu chained in prison. "When I have defeated Cao Cao, I will deal with Tian Feng in the same action." He then ordered seven hundred thousand men to encircle on all sides and connect camps for over ninety li.

Scouts learned the truth and reported to Guandu. The Wei troops newly arrived there, hearing the news, were afraid. Cao Cao consulted his advisers. Xun You said, "Yuan Shao's army is large, but we need not fear it. Our soldiers are all elite men; one of ours can stand for ten. The advantage is for rapid battle. If we delay too long, grain will become insufficient, and that is troublesome."

"Your counsel is exactly what I thought," said Cao Cao. He ordered the officers to beat war drums and cry out and advance.

Yuan Shao rode out to meet him and both sides arranged in array. Shen Pei set ten thousand crossbowmen on both wings and five thousand bowmen behind the banners, with one order to shoot together.

After the third beat of drums, Yuan Shao appeared before the front in gold helmet and armor, silk robes and jade sash, mounted on horseback. At his sides stood Zhang He, Gao Lan, Han Meng, Chunyu Qiong, and other generals. Standards and halberd marks were arranged in strict order.

At the opening of Cao Cao's gate cloth, Cao Cao rode out. Xuchu, Zhang Liao, Xu Huang, and Li Dian held him with arms drawn at front and rear. Cao Cao pointed with his whip: "Before the Son of Heaven, I had your office recommended as Great General. Why do you now conspire to rebel?"

Yuan Shao replied, "You call yourself Chancellor of the Han, but in truth you are a traitor to the Han. Your crimes are vast and worse than those of Meng and Zhuo. You now slander innocence while you are already a rebel against the Son of Heaven." Cao Cao said, "I now go against you by imperial command." Yuan Shao barked, "I carry the command in my sash to strike rebels."

Cao Cao, angry, sent Zhang Liao out first. Zhang He rode out to meet him. The two fought four or five dozen passes without giving way. Cao Cao observed and praised silently. Xuchu spurred his horse and sword forward to aid. Gao Lan thrust forward his spear. Four commanders clashed in close struggle. Cao Cao sent Xiahou Dun and Cao Hong, each with three thousand men, to surge together into the formation.

Shen Pei saw Cao's force charging and ordered the signal horns and signal guns raised. Then in both directions ten thousand crossbows and the bowmen inside the wagons surged to the front and shot in disorder. Could Cao's army stand against it? They looked in panic and ran southward. Yuan Shao pressed with pursuing troops and cut them down. Cao Cao's force was badly beaten and withdrew all the way to Guandu. Yuan Shao moved his troops nearer and camped south of Guandu. Shen Pei advised, "Now send ten thousand to hold Guandu. Build an earthen mound before Cao Cao's camp and place soldiers to shoot down into it. If Cao Cao leaves, we can secure this chokepoint and break through to Xuchang."

Yuan Shao adopted this. In every camp he selected stout men, brought iron spades and earth baskets, and together marched to the edge of Cao's camp, heaping soil into mounds. Inside Cao's encampment, soldiers who wished to break out were blocked by Shen Pei's crossbowmen holding the throat roads.

Within ten days they had raised more than fifty earthworks and set high watchtowers, posting crossbowmen there. The Wei troops were deeply alarmed and held shields overhead. At each clapper sounded on a mound, arrows fell like rain.

Cao's men huddled low with shields, while Yuan's men shouted and laughed. Cao Cao called his advisers again. Liu Ye said, "We can make catapult carts to break this." Cao Cao ordered Liu Ye's design, and through the night had hundreds built and set along the camp wall opposite the earthen towers. When the bowmen shot, the men inside pulled in unison. Stone shots flew up wildly. Many of the enemy bowmen were killed. Yuan's soldiers called these engines "thunderclap carts."

From then on, Yuan's men could not climb high and shoot from the ridges. Shen Pei offered another plan: have soldiers dig a tunnel with iron spades through to the middle of Cao's camp, a "sapper company." The Cao troops saw Yuan's diggers making pits behind the earthworks and reported it.

Cao asked Liu Ye again. Liu said, "This means Yuan's army cannot attack openly; it attacks by digging. They want to tunnel through and enter the camp from below." "How to counter it?" Cao asked. "Dig a long trench around the camp," Liu replied. "Then their tunnel is useless." Cao ordered the trench dug that night. Yuan Shao's troops had reached to its edge but could not enter.

For the rest of the eighth month through the ninth month, Cao Cao held at Guandu. Strength declined, grain grew scarce. He intended to abandon and withdraw to Xuchang but hesitated, then sent for Xun Yu by letter. Xun Yu answered:

To resolve Your Excellency's doubts of advancing or withdrawing, I submit this. Yuan Shao has gathered all his force at Guandu and seeks to decide victory and defeat with Your Excellency. Though Your Excellency is now weaker against the strongest enemy, if you do not master him, he will certainly take the advantage. This is the great chance of the age. Yuan Shao's forces are many but cannot use their strength. With Your Excellency's divine valor and clear judgment, why should this not be resolved? Though ours are few, we are better than when Chu and Han opposed one another at Xingyang and Chenggao. Now hold your position and cut off his throat so he cannot advance. He seems depleted, but only then does change appear. This is the time for stratagem. It must not be missed. I beg Your Excellency to judge and decide.

Cao Cao rejoiced greatly at the letter and ordered the troops to hold fast to the end. Yuan Shao's troops withdrew slightly more than thirty li. Cao Cao sent detachments on patrol. A unit under Xu Huang captured a Yuan scout and brought him before Xu Huang. Xu Huang asked about enemy supplies. The captive answered: "Each morning and evening, General Han Meng brings grain to the front. He first sends us out to probe the roads." Xu Huang reported this at once.

Xun You said, "Han Meng has courage only for charge, not stratagem. Send one man leading a few thousand light cavalry by a back path to strike him. He has no grain now if we can cut it, and Yuan Shao will be in confusion." Cao Cao asked, "Who can go?" Xun You said, "Xu Huang can."

Cao Cao then ordered Xu Huang, with his subordinate Shi Huan and his men, to move out first. He sent Zhang Liao and Xuchu to come afterward for support. That night Han Meng moved with thousands of grain carts toward Yuan Shao's main camp. Midway, in a mountain valley, Xu Huang and Shi Huan cut off the way. Han Meng charged in battle. Xu Huang met him and they fought hand to hand. Shi Huan drove off the porters and set the grain carts burning. Han Meng could not stand and turned to flee. Xu Huang ordered the baggage burned completely.

In Yuan's camp, fire rose in the northwest and soldiers were still in wonder and doubt when they heard a broken messenger cry: "The grain was intercepted."

Yuan Shao, in alarm, sent Zhang He and Gao Lan to block the main road. They met Xu Huang as he returned with the grain burning. At the very edge of contact the two were about to engage when Zhang Liao and Xuchu arrived behind. Under pressure from both sides Yuan's force was scattered and the four commanders withdrew to Guandu.

Cao Cao rejoiced and awarded extra rewards. He then set his line before the camp in a cornered formation.

When Han Meng returned defeated, Yuan Shao wished to execute him, but officials begged for leniency. Shen Pei said, "A campaign depends on grain. Never neglect that. Wuchao is the granary. It must be guarded by heavy troops."

Yuan Shao said, "My plan is already made. You may return to Bei and supervise the grain transport; make sure there is no shortage." Shen Pei obeyed and left. Yuan Shao then sent Chunyu Qiong to command Sui Yuanjin, Han Juzi, Lü Weihuang, and Zhao Rui, with twenty thousand men and horses, to hold Wuchao. That Chunyu Qiong was a hard drinker and beloved by soldiers for their fear. He arrived and that day feasted all along with other commanders.

Cao Cao's grain stores now said near empty. He urgently sent word to Xuchang to tell Xun Yu to arrange rapid grain delivery through the night to the front. A messenger left with letters. Within less than thirty li he was seized by Yuan's troops, tied and brought before strategist Xun You. Xun You had once been Cao Cao's friend but was now serving Yuan Shao. Searching the packet, he showed the letter to Yuan Shao:

Cao Cao camps at Guandu and has for long held against me. Xuchang is surely vulnerable. If one body of troops can strike at Xuchang by night, then Xuchang can be taken and Cao Cao captured. As for him now, grain is already finished. This is the moment to act. If we do not strike now, we will later suffer from this chance.

Yuan Shao said, "Cao Cao's tricks are endless. This is only bait to lure us." Xun You said, "If we do not seize this now, we will later be repaid by it."

At that moment came a messenger from Ye Commandery presenting Shen Pei's report. First he spoke of grain movement. Then he said that when Xun You was in Jizhou he had repeatedly plundered the people, and allowed his sons and nephews to levy extra taxes and grain into his own hands. Their sons and nephews now stood in jail.

Yuan Shao shouted, "A low official abusing the people dares still to offer plans before me!" He added, "You were close to Cao Cao before; now you must be taking his money and making a traitorous scheme to profit from me. You should have been beheaded at once. For now I spare your head for a moment. Leave quickly now, and do not let us meet again."

Xun You stepped out, looked upward, and sighed. "Loyal advice that goes against the ear is rarely accepted. A base man has no place to counsel. My sons and nephews have already been harmed by Shen Pei's designs. How can I show my face in Jizhou?" He tried to draw a sword to commit suicide. Those near him took the sword away and begged, "Do not throw your life away. If Yuan Shao does not accept frank counsel, he will later be taken by Cao Cao. You had former intimacy with Cao Cao. Why not leave darkness and join the light?"

Those two lines awakened Xun You. He turned and came straight to Cao's camp. A later poem says:

Benchu's heroic zeal once covered all under Heaven, But at Guandu the stand turned to endless grief. If Xun You's counsel had been followed, Could the mountains and rivers have escaped the house of Cao?

Xun You slipped out in secret and reached Cao Cao's camp. He was caught by the sentries and brought in.

"Carry this word as a messenger from old times," he said, "I am Xun You of Nanyang, and I come to see the General of the Han."

The guards told Cao right away. At that moment Cao Cao had just removed his garments and was resting. Hearing that Xun You had deserted into the camp, he rushed out barefoot without boots. From a distance he saw him, clapped and laughed, and brought him in. He first knelt to the ground. Xun You drew him up and said, "You are Han Chancellor; I am but a commoner. Why thus with my old friend?"

Cao said, "You are my old companion. I cannot stand to place titles above old ties."

Xun You said, "I could not choose a lord. I went with Yuan Shao, but he did not hear my words; when my counsel was ignored he now is in danger. I now leave him and come to this old friend. I ask you to accept me."

Cao said, "If Xun You has come, my matter is resolved. Teach me the way to break Yuan Shao."

Xun You said, "I once advised Yuan Shao to send light cavalry and strike Xuchang from both front and rear." Cao gasped, "If Yuan Shao followed that, then I would have lost."

Cao then asked, "How much grain does Your Excellency still hold?" Xun You said, "As for a year, maybe enough." Cao admitted, "A year at most." Xun You laughed, "I do not believe it." Cao corrected, "Six months, at best."

Xun You rose in resentment: "I trusted in trust, yet I was deceived. Is this what I sought?" Cao replied, "Do not take offense. Your warning is still welcome. Our camp can truly support one month only." Xun You shouted, "Do not hide from me. The grain is already gone!"

Cao asked, "How do you know?" Xun You showed the letter between Cao and Xun Yu and asked, "Who wrote this?" He explained he had obtained it from the captured messenger.

Cao took his hand and said, "Because Xun You came with honest heart, teach me now." Xun You said, "Mengde fights great enemies with only a lean host and does not seek speed for victory; this is the road to death. I have one stratagem. In three days Yuan Shao's one-million-strong host will collapse without battle. Will Your Excellency hear?"

Cao replied, "Speak it." Xun You said, "Yuan Shao's grain and baggage are all stored at Wuchao. Chunyu Qiong guards it. That man loves wine and is careless. Now choose selected troops, announce that Jiang Qi has come with escorts to protect the grain, and at the right moment burn that grain and baggage. In three days Yuan Shao's force will collapse from within."

Cao Cao rejoiced and kept Xun You in honored quarters.

The next day Cao Cao selected five thousand horse and foot and prepared to raid Wuchao. Zhang Liao said, "Where Yuan stores grain, it cannot be without guard. Your Excellency should not go lightly. Xun You might deceive." Cao said, "No. Xun You has come to overturn Yuan Shao's fate. My own camp grain is exhausted and cannot hold. If I do not use his plan, we sit to be trapped by need. If he deceived, why would he stay in my camp? Besides, I have long wished to raid a camp. This must be done."

He ordered Xun Yu, Jia Xu, and Cao Hong to hold the main camp with Xun You. He placed Xiahou Dun and Xiahou Yuan with one force on the left, and Cao Ren and Li Dian with another on the right, as a guard against anything sudden. He sent Zhang Liao and Xuchu forward, Xu Huang and Yu Jin behind. Cao Cao rode in the center with his other officers. They were five thousand in all, carrying Yuan's banners. Each soldier carried bundled straw and firewood. Each rider held a torch in his mouth and reins in hand. At dusk they marched for Wuchao. That night the sky was filled with stars.

Ju Shu was still confined by Yuan Shao. That night, seeing the stars brilliantly set, he asked his guard to lead him to the courtyard. He looked up and saw the Great White Star moving backward, passing between Niu and Dou. He grew alarmed.

He sought immediate audience with Yuan Shao, but Yuan had fallen asleep in drink. When told of urgent astrological warning, Yuan Shao summoned him.

Ju Shu warned: "I have read the sky. The Great White Star travels backward between Niu and Dou, and its radiance enters the sector of Niu and Dou. There will be enemy raiders and robbery. Wuchao is where grain is stored; we must make heavy preparations. Dispatch bold troops now to patrol side paths and mountain roads, or Cao Cao will compute against us."

Yuan Shao shouted, "You are already in guilty standing. How dare you mislead the troops!" He turned to the guard and said, "Who let him out of prison?" He had the officer who had released him beheaded, then had another escort him back to prison.

Ju Shu came out, covered his eyes with tears, and sighed, "Our army will fall within a day or two. I do not know where my body will lie." Later people lamented in a poem:

Loyal advice is often repaid with hostility, Simple-minded Benchu lacks foresight. Wuchao's grain is gone from its roots, Yet he still seeks to hold Jizhou in name.

Cao Cao's army then moved at night. At every Yuan outpost, guards asked what force it was. He answered, "Jiang Qi has been ordered by my command to Wuchao to guard grain." Yuan's men saw their own banners and doubted nothing. From camp to camp, no obstacle stopped the same claim.

At the end of the fourth watch they reached Wuchao. Cao Cao ordered his soldiers to gather straw and set fires around. Commanders and captains blew horns and rushed straight in.

At that time Chunyu Qiong was still drinking with others and lay drunk in his tent. When he heard the noise he woke and asked, "What is this commotion?" Before he could finish, he was hooked and dragged down.

Sui Yuanjin and Zhao Rui were returning after carrying grain when they saw flames rise over Wuchao. They came in haste to aid. They sent a flying report to Cao Cao: "The enemy is at our back. Divide the forces and resist!"

Cao Cao shouted, "Do not worry about the rear yet. Push forward with all strength. When the enemy comes behind you, then turn and meet them!"

Every commander struggled to strike first. Suddenly flames rose in all directions and smoke blurred the sky. Sui and Zhao came to aid, but Cao wheeled back and struck. The two could not resist and were both killed by Cao's men. Wuchao grain was entirely burned.

Chunyu Qiong was captured and brought before Cao Cao. Cao ordered his ears, nose, and fingers cut off. He had him tied to a horse and sent back to Yuan's camp in humiliation.

Yuan Shao was in his tent when he saw fire covering the northern sky and knew Wuchao had fallen. He ran out, calling ministers and officers. They discussed and who should go to rescue.

Zhang He said, "I can go with Gao Lan." Guo Tu objected, "No. If Cao Cao has raided grain, he surely came in person. If he left his camp, the camp is empty and we can strike there first. Once he hears this, he must return. This is the stratagem of Sun Bin: surround Wei and rescue Zhao."

Zhang He said, "No. Cao Cao is cautious. If he goes out, he surely leaves men inside for sudden defence. If we attack his camp but do not take it, then Qiong and the others will be lost and our men too."

Guo Tu replied, "Cao Cao is absorbed in the raid and will leave no reserve men in camp." After repeated entreaty, Yuan Shao decided: Zhang He and Gao Lan, with five thousand, were sent to attack Guandu. Jiang Qi, with ten thousand, was sent to save Wuchao.

Cao Cao had already scattered Chunyu Qiong's men, seized all their uniforms and banners, and made his men feign a routed return. On a side road they met Jiang Qi's cavalry. Jiang Qi's men said they were retreating from Wuchao, and Jiang Qi did not suspect. He rode through.

Zhang Liao and Xuchu suddenly appeared shouting, "Jiang Qi, do not run!" Caught unprepared, he could not avoid it. Zhang Liao cut him down from the saddle. All of Jiang Qi's men were killed. Another officer was sent ahead to report, "Jiang Qi has scattered and returned from Wuchao."

Because of that report Yuan did not send additional troops to Wuchao but added force toward Guandu.

Zhang He and Gao Lan attacked Cao's camp. Xiahou Dun came on the left, Cao Ren on the right, Cao Hong in the center. They assailed three times and were deeply defeated. When reinforcements arrived, Cao attacked from behind, surrounding on all sides. Zhang He and Gao Lan cut their way out and fled.

Yuan Shao gathered the remains from Wuchao and the horsemen fleeing. Seeing Chunyu Qiong's severed ears and nose and hands and feet removed, he asked, "How was Wuchao lost?" The survivors said, "Chunyu Qiong was drunk in bed and could not resist."

Yuan Shao ordered immediate execution. Guo Tu feared that if Zhang He and Gao Lan returned they would clarify the truth. He slandered before Yuan Shao that "Zhang He and Gao Lan, hearing the lord's loss, were in secret happy. The two had long ago wished to defect to Cao. Now sent to Wuchao, they held back intentionally and caused so much loss."

Yuan Shao asked sharply, "How can that be so?" Guo Tu said, "The two have long been inclined to surrender to Cao. Now they were sent to attack; naturally they did not exert themselves."

Yuan Shao became furious and ordered a messenger to summon both at once. Guo Tu first sent ahead: "The lord intends to execute you." The envoy arrived before Gao Lan. Gao Lan asked, "Why does the lord call us?" The messenger replied, "I do not know."

Gao Lan drew his sword and killed the envoy. Zhang He was startled. Gao Lan said, "Yuan Shao believes slander and will surely be captured by Cao. Why should we wait and die? Let us go and submit at once." Zhang He said, "I have held this in my heart for some time."

So the two led their main troops and defected to Cao's camp.

Xiahou Dun said, "Two commanders have come over from Yuan's side. I cannot yet tell true from false." Cao said, "I will welcome them with favor. Even if they hold a divided heart, it can be turned." He opened the gate and commanded them in.

The two cast down their spears and removed armor, kneeling on the ground. Cao said, "If Yuan had listened to these two, he would not have met this defeat. Now they come to me. It is like Weizi leaving Yin and Han Xin returning to Han."

He titled Zhang He as General and Marquis of Tingting. He titled Gao Lan as General and Marquis of Donglai. They were greatly delighted.

By then Yuan Shao had lost Xun You, then Zhang He and Gao Lan, then Wuchao's grain. His army's spirit was shaken.

Xun You urged Cao Cao to advance at once. Zhang He and Gao Lan asked to be vanguard. Cao Cao agreed. He ordered both to lead five thousand for the first strike on Yuan's camp. At the third watch they moved out by three routes. They fought until morning and then withdrew by portions. Yuan Shao's army was split in half.

Xun You then offered one more plan:

Make the drums announce troop movements. Send one route for Suanzao and another toward Ye Commandery. A third should cut Yuan Shao's path of retreat. Yuan will be alarmed and split his forces. When his men move to resist, strike him then and break him.

Cao implemented it with small and large detachments and orders in all four directions. Yuan Shao heard the report in camp: "Cao Cao has split his army. One route to Ye Commandery; one route to Liyang."

Yuan Shao was shocked. He sent Yuan Shang with fifty thousand to defend Ye Commandery. Xin Ming left with fifty thousand for Liyang. Both moved at once through the night.

Cao Cao learned the movement and then sent his large teams in eight columns, all to strike Yuan's camp. Yuan's men had no spirit for fighting and scattered in all directions. It became a great rout.

Yuan Shao could not put on full armor in time. He rode out with only a light robe and a broad scarf. His eldest son Yuan Tan followed behind.

Zhang Liao, Xuchu, Xu Huang, and Yu Jin led the pursuit. Yuan hurried across the river, throwing away carts carrying books, ceremonial vessels, and silk and gold. Only about eight hundred and some riders escaped with him.

Cao Cao's men could not catch him but recovered all abandoned stores. More than eighty thousand were killed. Blood filled the channels, and those who drowned were beyond count.

Cao Cao won a complete victory. He distributed recovered gold and silk to reward soldiers.

Among documents seized from official baggage and records there was a bundle of letters showing secret communication between people in Xuchang and Yuan's commanders. An officer said, "Match each name and execute everyone implicated."

Cao Cao said, "When Yuan was this strong, I alone could not secure myself. How could others keep safe?" He ordered all letters burned and asked no more.

Yuan Shao's army routed and fled, Ju Shu still confined. He tried to run but could not evade. He was captured by Cao's troops.

Ju Shu was brought before Cao. Cao and Ju Shu had once known one another. When Ju Shu saw him, he shouted, "I do not surrender!" Cao said, "Benchu had no stratagem and did not use your words. How do you still persist in dark loyalty? If I had gained you earlier, there would be no concern in the realm."

He kept Ju in honorable custody. Yet Ju stole a horse in camp, wanting to return to the Yuan household. Cao was angry and executed him. Ju's expression did not change to the end.

Cao sighed, "I have killed a loyal and upright man in error." He ordered proper funeral rites and burial at a ford on the Yellow River, titling the mound "Tomb of the Loyal and Righteous Ju."

Later people praised him in verse:

Many eminent men were in Hebei, Loyal and true, they honored the Lord Ju. In the eye, he understood formations; Upward he could read the stars. To death his heart was iron, In peril his breath was like cloud. Cao valued his righteousness, and raised him a grave at once.

Cao Cao then ordered a march against Jizhou.

Weakness is not a vice if it is full of stratagems, while strength falls when strategy is absent. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Battle at Guandu: Benchu’s Reversal and Mengde Burns Wuchao’s Grain Stores

chapters.html:
Cao Cao, taking advantage of Yuan Shao’s defeat, set his mounts and horses in order and continued to pursue in a sweeping line. Yuan Shao, in a broad sash and a plain robe, led more than eight hundred riders and rushed to the north bank of Liyang. General Jiang Yiqu came out of the camp to receive him. Shao reported what had happened before, and Jiang then called out to the soldiers to disperse. When they heard that Yuan Shao had arrived, they gathered again in crowds and the army revived, and they resolved to return to Ji Province. On the next day’s march they camped for the night on a wild mountain. In his tent Shao heard distant weeping and went alone to listen. It was his former troops, clustered together, talking through their pain over the loss of brothers and companions, of abandoned comrades and dead relatives; each beat his chest and cried out. All of them said, “If we had listened to Tian Feng, how could we have come to this calamity?” Shao was consumed with remorse: “I should have listened to Tian Feng. The army has been broken and ruined. I return now, but with what face can I meet him?”

The next day, after mounting and setting out, Feng Ji came out with a detachment to receive him. Shao said to Feng Ji, “I should have listened to Tian Feng and now lost my army. I am returning to a face I no longer can show.” Feng Ji slandered him: “Tian Feng, in prison, heard of the Lord’s defeat; he slapped his hands and laughed, saying, ‘Just as I expected; it was no surprise to me.’” Shao, furious, said, “How dare that base scholar laugh at me! I will kill him myself!” He then ordered an envoy to carry a precious sword to the jail in Ji Province to take Tian Feng’s head.

Tian Feng was in prison. One day a jail officer came to him saying, “An assistant officer has come to offer congratulations.” Tian Feng said, “What is there to be congratulated for?” “Yuan General has suffered a great defeat and is returning,” said the jailer. “You will surely be honored.” Tian Feng laughed. “I am dead now.” The jailer asked, “Everyone rejoices on your behalf. Why do you speak of death?” “Yuan General,” Tian Feng replied, “is outwardly broad but inwardly jealous and distrustful, and does not honor loyalty and devotion. If he had won, he might have pardoned me. Now that he has lost, he is ashamed; I do not expect to live.”

The jailer did not believe him. Suddenly an envoy arrived with a sword, conveying Yuan Shao’s order to seize Tian Feng’s head. Only then did the jailer start in shock. Tian Feng said, “I knew I must die.” The jailers all wept.

“‘A man truly a gentleman should not serve a lord he does not know,’ Tian Feng said. ‘To live now and die under this one—what is there to lament?’ He slit his own throat in the prison.”

Later people composed a verse:

Yesterday Jushou died in the camp; today Tian Feng perished in prison. The pillars of Hebei are broken, and yet Benchu has not lost his clan and state?

When news of Tian Feng’s death spread, all who heard it lamented. Yuan Shao returned to Ji Province, restless and mentally shaken, and no longer attending to state affairs. His wife Liu Shi urged him to settle the matter of his heir. Shao had three sons: his eldest, Yuan Tan, courtesy name Xianzhong, served as Administrator of Qing Province; his second, Yuan Xi, courtesy name Xianyi, served as Administrator of You Province; the third, Yuan Shang, courtesy name Xianfu, was born to his later wife Liu Shi. Yuan Shang was handsome and imposing, and Shao loved him deeply, so he kept him at his side.

Since the defeat at Guandu, Liu Shi had urged Shao to appoint Shang as heir. Shao then consulted four men: Shen Pei, Feng Ji, Xin Ping, and Guo Tu. In truth, Shen and Feng favored Yuan Shang, while Xin and Guo favored Yuan Tan. Each man pushed his own candidate.

Shao then told all four, “The outer threat has not ended; internal matters must be settled quickly. I will now consider which son should succeed. The first son, Tan, is hard of nature, quick to kill; the second, Xi, is soft and timid, hard to bring to completion. The third, Shang, has the look of a hero, honors worthy scholars and men of virtue. I would have him set as heir. What is each of your opinions?”

Guo Tu said, “Among your three sons, Tan is the eldest and he is away. If Your Lordship were to set aside the elder for a younger brother, disorder will be sown in this root itself. At present military prestige is still diminished and enemy forces are pressing hard at the border. Can we now allow sons and brothers to contend with one another and throw the house into further strife? For the present, Lord, first settle strategy against the enemies at hand. Leave the question of succession for another time.”

Shao hesitated and did not decide. Suddenly word arrived that Yuan Xi was coming with sixty thousand from You Province, Yuan Tan with fifty thousand from Qing Province, and his nephew Gao Gan with fifty thousand from Bing Province. They all arrived in Ji Province to aid the coming fight. Shao rejoiced, then repaired his men and riders and prepared once more to fight Cao Cao.

By then Cao Cao had brought his victorious forces and arrayed them along the river. The local people offered him grain and food in rustic pitchers to receive him. Cao saw several elderly men, all with hair and beards entirely white, and ordered them into his pavilion, seating them and asking, “Sirs, how many years have you?” “They are nearly a hundred,” they answered. Cao said, “My troops disturbed your village. That sits badly with me.” The elders answered, “In the time of Emperor Huan, a yellow star appeared between Chu and Song. Yin Kui, a man from Liaodong who studied the stars, passed through this area at night and told old men like us, ‘The yellow star appearing in a dry pattern means its light points to this place. In fifty years, a true gentleman will arise between Liang and Pei.’ As we count years, it is exactly fifty now. Yuan Benchu has overtaxed and squeezed the people, and all the people resent him. The Chancellor now raises a principled army, to relieve the people and punish crime. In the battle at Guandu, he shattered Yuan Shao’s host of ten hundred thousand; this accords with Yin Kui’s words. Surely the common people can now hope for peace.”

Cao laughed: “How dare I presume to match such words?” He then offered wine, food, and silk, sent them off. He then ordered the three armies: “If anyone among the soldiers, once in the villages, kills a household’s chickens or dogs, he will be punished as if he had killed a man.” The soldiers and civilians were immediately subdued and respectful, and Cao was pleased within himself.

Reports came that Yuan Shao had gathered troops from four provinces, reaching two or three hundred thousand men, and had come to set camp before Cangting. Cao marched forward, and his camp was fixed. The next day, both armies faced each other and arrayed themselves.

Cao brought his generals into the ranks; Yuan Shao also brought out his three sons and his nephew with civil officials and military commanders before the lines. Cao said, “Benchu has spent every possible effort, and yet he still refuses to think of surrender? He waits only until the blade rests at his throat before regretting—too late.”

Shao, furious, looked back at the assembled commanders and shouted, “Who dares to ride out?” Yuan Shang wanted to show himself before his father. He swung his twin sabers and came out and spurred into battle, charging back and forth.

Cao asked the officers, “Who is this man?” One who knew him answered, “That is Yuan Shang, Yuan Shao’s third son.”

Before the answer was finished, one officer lowered his spear and came out fast. Cao recognized him as Shi Huan, a company leader under Xu Huang. The two riders met without three full exchanges. Yuan Shang turned his horse and cut away and fled. Shi Huan pursued. Shang drew his bow and set an arrow to the string, then turned back in the saddle and fired; it struck Shi Huan in the left eye. He fell from his horse and died.

When Shao saw his son victorious, he cracked his whip and pointed. “Now,” he shouted, indicating, and a great mass of horse and men surged forward to mix in close fight. They fought fiercely and in one round of hard combat, both sides blew the signal gongs and withdrew to camp.

Cao consulted with his commanders for a way to break Shao. Cheng Yu offered the stratagem of a ten-sided ambush. He urged Cao: “Withdraw the army to the riverbank, hide ten ambush columns there, and lure Shao to pursue. If he reaches us by the river, our army will have no way to retreat and must fight to the death. That is when we can beat him.”

Cao approved. Left side: one squad under Xiahou Dun, second under Zhang Liao, third under Li Dian, fourth under Yue Jin, fifth under Xiahou Yuan. Right side: one under Cao Hong, second under Zhang He, third under Xu Huang, fourth under Yu Jin, fifth under Gao Lan. In the center, Xu Chu led the vanguard. The next day the ten columns moved ahead and the ambushes were set in place on both flanks.

Toward midnight Cao ordered Xu Chu to advance with his men in the posture of a surprise assault on camp. The five hundred camps of Yuan Shao all rose together. Xu Chu then turned and gave the look of flight. Shao brought his army forward in pursuit, their cries unending. By dawn, they reached the river, where Cao’s army had no route to retreat.

Cao shouted aloud, “There is no way forward. What say you, soldiers? Why not fight to the death?” The troops wheeled and rushed with renewed strength. Xu Chu, leaping on horseback in front, cut down more than ten of Shao’s commanders. Yuan Shao’s army fell into disorder.

Shao hurriedly withdrew, but behind him Cao’s army pressed. As they moved, a drumbeat sounded, and Xiahou Yuan on the left and Gao Lan on the right burst out with both armies. Shao pulled together Yuan Shang and Gao Gan and charged madly along the blood-stained road. Less than ten li farther, Yue Jin on the left and Yu Jin on the right struck out; they killed so many that Yuan Shao’s army lay sprawled across the ground and blood ran in channels. Not yet five li farther, Li Dian on the left and Xu Huang on the right met and intercepted, slaughtering them in another hard bout.

Shao and his sons, their courage gone, terrified in heart, ran back into the old camp and ordered the three divisions to prepare food. Just as they were about to eat, Zhang Liao on the left and Zhang He on the right came straight and broke into camp. Shao scrambled onto a horse and pushed forward toward Cangting. Men and horses were tired and exhausted and wished to rest; behind them Cao’s whole army pursued, and Shao fled as if for life.

While in flight, Cao Hong on the left and Xiahou Dun on the right blocked his way. Shao shouted, “If we do not fight now to death, we will all be taken!” He drove forward with force and broke through the heavy ring. Yuan Xi and Gao Gan were both wounded by arrows. Their horses and mounts were nearly gone.

Shao embraced Yuan Shang and wept once, then suddenly fainted. His men quickly tried to revive him, but he spat blood continuously from his mouth. “I have seen more than ten battles in my life,” he sighed, “yet I did not expect to be brought to shame today. Heaven has stripped my life away! Each of you, return to your own province. Swear to settle this in combat against the Cao bandits.”

He then ordered Xin Ping and Guo Tu to hurry after Yuan Tan to Qing Province to reorganize there, lest Cao Cao violate the borders. He told Yuan Xi to return to You Province and Gao Gan to return to Bing Province, each to gather and reassemble their forces for possible deployment. Shao withdrew with Yuan Shang and entered Ji Province to recover his health, leaving Shang with Shen Pei and Feng Ji to handle military affairs temporarily.

Cao Cao, after his great victory at Cangting, gave rich rewards to the three armies and sent men to probe the conditions of Ji Province. His informants reported, “Shao is bedridden. Yuan Shang and Shen Pei hold the city tightly. Yuan Tan, Yuan Xi, and Gao Gan have returned to their home provinces.” All urged Cao to attack at once.

Cao replied, “Ji Province has enormous grain stores; Shen Pei also has military acumen. We should not force a quick capture. At present the crops are still in the fields; if we strike now, we risk ruining the people’s labor. Better to wait until after harvest in autumn.”

While they debated, a message arrived from Xun Yu: “Liu Bei is in Runan with tens of thousands gathered under Liu Pi and Gongdu. He heard that Your Excellency had led the army to campaign in the north, and set Liu Pi to guard Runan. Liu Bei himself is leading troops to exploit the opening and march on Xuchang. Excellency should return your army swiftly to oppose him.”

Cao was greatly startled. He left Cao Hong to garrison the riverbank and create an appearance of force. He personally brought the main army out toward Runan to meet Liu Bei.

That evening Liu Bei, with Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Zhao Yun, and others, marched with troops to strike Xuchang. Near the land of Rangshan they met Cao’s soldiers coming to kill them. Liu Bei camped below Rangshan.

The army divided into three groups: Guan Yu held men at the southeast corner, Zhang Fei at the southwest corner, and Liu Bei with Zhao Yun at the southern center. Cao’s troops arrived, and Liu Bei sounded a challenge. Cao formed battle lines and called for parley. Liu Bei rode out under his banner. Cao, with his whip raised, rebuked him: “I treated you as a high guest; how have you betrayed loyalty and forgotten kindness?”

Liu Bei answered, “You claim to be the Han Chancellor, but you are truly a traitor to the state! I am of Han imperial kin. I bear a secret imperial edict to come and suppress rebel traitors.” Then he recited on horseback the hidden edict.”

Cao flew into a rage and ordered Xu Chu into combat. Liu Bei rode out with Zhao Yun at his back, who took up a spear and rode with him. The two commanders met, and for more than thirty exchanges neither won. Suddenly a huge cry rose. From the southeast corner, Guan Yu charged in collision; from the southwest, Zhang Fei brought his army and charged. All three fronts converged to give the slaughter. Cao’s army, tired from traveling from afar, could not stand it and broke in retreat. Liu Bei won the day and returned to camp.

The next day Liu Bei sent Zhao Yun out to skirmish. Cao’s army did not leave camp for ten days. Liu Bei sent Zhang Fei again; Cao still did not come out.

Liu Bei grew suspicious. Suddenly word came that Gongdu had brought grain and was now surrounded by Cao’s army, and Liu Bei rushed to send Zhang Fei to relieve him. Soon after came word that Xiahou Dun had moved out and was marching behind to strike directly at Runan. Liu Bei was shocked and said, “If this happens, I will be attacked in front and back and have nowhere to turn to!” He dispatched Zhang Fei to save Runan.

Both armies then departed.

After less than one day, a rider arrived with the report that Xiahou Dun had already broken through Runan, that Liu Pi had abandoned the city and fled, and that Guan Yu was now himself enclosed. Liu Bei was deeply alarmed. In another message, he heard Zhang Fei sent to save Gongdu had also been surrounded. Liu Bei wished to turn back, but feared Cao’s force might strike from behind. Then he heard Xu Chu had come out to engage near camp. Liu Bei did not dare to ride out.

At first light he ordered the soldiers to eat fully; foot soldiers rose first and cavalry followed. He spread a false order in camp as the watch changed. After six or so li of movement from camp, they turned around a clay knoll. When the torchlights rose together, a shout sounded from the hilltop: “Let no one let Liu Bei get away! Your Excellency the Chancellor is waiting right here!”

Liu Bei looked for a path in alarm. Zhao Yun said, “My lord, do not worry. Follow me only.” Zhao Yun cast his spear, leapt into the saddle, broke a path with force, and Liu Bei followed behind him, gripping his twin swords.

As the fight went on, Xu Chu arrived and battled Zhao Yun at close range. Behind him Yu Jin and Li Dian came too. Liu Bei saw the danger and fled in disorder. Hearing the shouted voices behind them grow faint and distant, Liu Bei looked for a hidden deep-mountain path and fled on a lone horse.

He made it to dawn, when suddenly from the side burst out a band of soldiers. Liu Bei was startled; looking, he saw Liu Pi leading more than a thousand of his battered men and escorting Liu Bei’s household people. Sun Qian, Jian Yong, and Mi Fang also arrived and said: “Xiahou Dun’s force is sharp and keen, and for that reason we abandoned the city. Cao’s soldiers came pressing in; only because Guan Yu held the line were we able to escape.”

Liu Bei said, “Do you know where Guan Yu is now?” Liu Pi said, “General, ride on for the moment. We can think of him after.”

After some li, a drum sounded. In front came a clump of mounted men bursting out. At its front rode a great commander: Zhang He, shouting, “Liu Bei, dismount and surrender at once!”

Liu Bei, just about to turn back, saw a red standard stirring atop the hill, and an army pouring out from within a mountain fold, with Gao Lan at its head. Liu Bei saw no way forward and cried to heaven, “Why has Heaven brought me to this extreme plight? When the matter has come to this, I am better dead!” He reached for his sword to commit suicide.

Liu Pi rushed forward and checked him: “Allow me to die fighting and cut our way back to save you.” Once said, he went into collision with Gao Lan. They fought less than three rounds, and Gao Lan cut him down from his horse.

As Liu Bei stood in panic and was about to join the fight, Gao Lan’s rear troops suddenly faltered. One officer crashed into the formation; at the rise of his spear, Gao Lan flipped and toppled from his horse. When Liu Bei looked, it was Zhao Yun.

Liu Bei rejoiced. Zhao Yun spurred his horse and with spear drove apart the rear ranks, then rode forward again and fought Zhang He alone. Zhang He and Zhao Yun fought for more than thirty exchanges, then Zhang He wheeled his horse and withdrew in defeat. Zhao Yun pushed his advance, cutting and clearing, but Zhang He’s soldiers blocked the mountain pass and the trail narrowed too much to pass.

While trying to break through, Guan Yu, Guan Ping, and Zhou Cang arrived with three hundred men. They attacked from both sides and drove back Zhang He. Each of them then came out of the pass opening, occupying the mountain pass and setting camp below.

Liu Bei ordered Guan Yu to seek Zhang Fei. It turned out Zhang Fei had gone to save Gongdu. Gongdu had already been killed by Xiahou Yuan. Fei fought hard and drove Xiahou Yuan back, then pursued slowly, but was in turn surrounded by an army led by Yue Jin. Guan Yu met failed troops on the way, followed their trail and, after driving Yue Jin off, returned together with Fei to Liu Bei.

A report then came that a large body of Cao’s army was arriving, so Liu Bei ordered Sun Qian and the others to protect women and children and move first. Liu Bei, Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Zhao Yun held behind, fighting while retreating. When Cao saw Liu Bei had gone far, he withdrew and did not pursue. Liu Bei’s broken force numbered not a thousand; they fled in disorder.

Reaching a river, Liu Bei called to locals to ask what it was. It was the Han River. Liu Bei made a temporary camp.

The locals recognized Liu Bei and brought lamb and wine. They gathered together to drink on the riverbank. Liu Bei sighed, saying to them all, “My lords, all of you have the ability to be counselors of kings, and it is unfortunate to have followed Liu Bei. The fate of this man is grave and has drawn all of you in. Today I own no standing place to plant even a bodkin, and I truly fear I am ruining all of you. Why should you not abandon Liu Bei and enter service under the Son of Heaven to earn your own fame?”

All covered their faces and wept.

Guan Yu said, “Your words are mistaken. In former days, High Ancestor quarreled with Xiang Yu over the empire and was defeated by him many times; only after the battle at Jiu Li Mountain did he succeed and thereby open the foundation of four hundred years. Victory and defeat are constant in war. How can one destroy one’s own will?”

Sun Qian said, “Success and failure come by time. Do not abandon your spirit. We are not far from Jing Province now. Liu Jingsheng holds Jiuzhou with heavy troops and ample supplies, and he is of the same imperial line as you. Why not go to submit there?”

Liu Bei said, “I only fear he will not welcome me.”

Sun Qian replied, “Let me go first and explain; I will have Liu Jingsheng come out beyond the borders and receive Your Grace.”

Liu Bei was greatly heartened and at once sent Sun Qian under cover of the night to Jing Province. He entered the commandery and presented himself to Liu Biao. After formal greetings, Liu Biao asked, “General, why has Liu Bei come here?”

Sun Qian answered, “General Liu is among heroes of the age. Though his troops are few and his commanders few, his aim is to support and straighten the state. Liu Pi and Gongdu in Runan were once no intimates, yet they died to him all the same. Your Excellency and this general are kin under the Han court. This master was recently defeated and now wishes to go south to Jiangdong, to Sun Zhongmou. I have dared to remonstrate with him, saying: ‘It is not proper to turn against one’s kin and go to distant lands. In Jing Province, Liu General honors the worthy and lowers men of worth; men return there as waters return to the eastern sea. How much more can those of one generation relate by blood?’ Thus the general has sent me first to report and beg your command.”

Liu Biao was delighted. “Liu Bei is my younger brother. I have long wished to meet him, but could not. That he has honored us with his presence is truly a blessing.”

Cai Mao interposed slander: “He should not be admitted. Liu Bei first followed Lü Bu, then served Cao Cao, lately went over to Yuan Shao, and all times he did not persist. His character can be seen there. If we take him in, Cao Cao will certainly send forces against us and needlessly inflame war. Why not, instead, behead Sun Qian and present his head to Cao Cao. Cao will then treat Your Excellency richly.”

Sun Qian replied straight, “Sun Qian does not fear death. General Liu serves the state with loyal intent and is not like Cao Cao, Yuan Shao, or Lü Bu. His past following was only out of necessity. I now hear he is a Han branch descendant, with feeling as close as shared kinship. How can such a man slander one so upright as to be jealous of him and call forth betrayal?”

On hearing this, Liu Biao cried out at Cai Mao, “My decision is made. You need not speak further.” Cai Mao, ashamed and resentful, withdrew.

Liu Biao then ordered Sun Qian to report first to Liu Bei and at the same time personally rode out thirty li beyond the city gate to welcome him. Liu Bei saw Liu Biao and executed the rites with great deference. Biao in turn treated him generously. Liu Bei brought Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and others to bow and meet Liu Biao. Liu Biao then entered Jing Province with Liu Bei and assigned separate houses for each to stay in.

Cao Cao learned that Liu Bei had already gone to Jing Province, seeking refuge under Liu Biao, and he considered leading an army to attack it. Cheng Yu said, “Yuan Shao has not yet been eliminated, and if we now strike Jing Province in haste, and Yuan Shao rises from the north, we will not know where victory lies. Better to return to Xuchang, let the army recover its strength, and in spring next year break first Yuan Shao and then take Jing Province afterward. In one campaign, we can gather benefits in both north and south.”

Cao accepted this advice, then raised the army and returned to Xuchang.

By the eighth year of Jian'an, in the first month, Cao held another council to raise troops. First he ordered Xiahou Dun and Man Chong to garrison Runan to resist Liu Biao. He left Cao Ren and Xun Yu to guard Xuchang, then personally took command of the main army and marched back to Guandu to establish camp.

Now it is said that Yuan Shao, who had suffered coughing blood since the past year, had by now only partly recovered. He conferred and sought to attack Xuchang. Shen Pei remonstrated, “The defeat at Guandu and Cangting this past year has not fully recovered the morale of the army. We should still dig deep moats and build high stockades to rebuild the strength of men and people.”

While deliberating, a report came that Cao Cao was moving his forces toward Guandu, marching to attack Ji Province. Shao said, “If we wait until enemy troops stand at the foot of the wall and then move to the riverbank, it will be too late. I will myself lead the main army out to meet him.” Yuan Shang said, “Father is still unwell and not fully recovered. He should not campaign afar. I will lead troops to meet the enemy.” Shao allowed it and sent men to Qing Province for Yuan Tan, to You Province for Yuan Xi, and to Bing Province for Gao Gan, saying all four columns were to strike Cao together.

Now the war drums have only just sounded at Runan, and from north Ji the campaign drums are raised again.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: At Cangting, Cao Cao Defeats Benchu; In Jingzhou, Xuande Seeks Refuge with Liu Biao

chapters.html:
Yuan Shang seizes Jizhou in fraternal strife;
Xu You’s counsel turns the Zhang River against them.

After Yuan Shang executed Shi Huan, he grew proud of his courage. He did not wait for Yuan Tan and the others to bring their troops, but led several tens of thousands out of Liyang to meet Cao’s forward detachment. Zhang Liao rode out first. Yuan Shang charged in with his spear, and within three close rounds of fighting he could not hold the line and was routed. Zhang Liao pressed the attack into the rout, cutting down Yuan Shang’s men as Shang could not rally the field and hurried his men back toward Jizhou.

When Yuan Shao heard of Yuan Shang’s defeat, fear struck him anew. His old illness returned; he vomited blood for several dou, then sank unconscious. Lady Liu rushed in and carried him into his inner chamber, but his condition worsened. In panic she summoned Shen Pei and Feng Ji; they sat beside the sickbed to discuss matters after he died. Yuan Shao could only nod and point to his fingertips. He could not speak. Lady Liu asked, “Will Shang be able to continue the line?” Yuan Shao nodded once. Shen Pei wrote a will beside the sickbed.

Yuan Shao rolled onto his side, shouted once, and vomited blood again before he died. Later, someone wrote this poem:

Generations of ministers raised up a great name, a young man’s bold spirit strode unbounded. He drew in three thousand outstanding guests, and by mere talk amassed a hundred thousand soldiers. With a sheep’s form but tiger skin, his achievements came to little; with phoenix plumage and rooster’s heart, his enterprise never reached completion. Most to be pitied is this wound, when sorrow for the clan was borne only by two brothers.

After Yuan Shao’s death, Shen Pei and the others took charge of the funeral rites. Lady Liu then ordered the five favored concubines Yuan Shao loved to be all executed. Fearing their spirits might one day meet him beneath the earth again, she shaved their heads, pierced their faces, and disfigured their bodies. Her jealousy was that cruel.

Yuan Shang feared that concubine households might still hurt them, so he ordered all of them killed as well. Shen Pei and Feng Ji then installed Yuan Shang as Grand Marshal-General and appointed him governor of Jizhou, Qing Province, Youzhou, and Bing Province, and sent envoys to announce his father’s death.

At that time Yuan Tan had already set out from Qing Province with his troops. When he learned that his father had died, he conferred with Guo Tu and Xin Ping. Guo Tu said, “Your Lordship is not in Jizhou now. Shen Pei and Feng Ji will surely set Xianfu as lord. You should move at once.” Xin Ping said, “Shen and Feng have surely prepared a scheme already. If you go quickly, you will walk into their trap.”

Yuan Tan asked, “What should I do?”

Guo Tu answered, “We can station troops outside the city and observe how they move. I will go into the city to inspect myself.”

Yuan Tan followed this counsel. Guo Tu entered Jizhou and met Yuan Shang. After the formal exchange of ceremony, Shang asked, “Why did brother not come?”

“Because I was sick in camp and could not meet him,” Guo Tu said.

Shang said, “Our father gave me his command: he set me as lord and made you General of Chariots and Cavalry. Cao’s army is pressing on us. Go out as the forward commander; I will follow with troops and reinforce in time.”

Guo Tu said, “There is no one in the camp to discuss a good plan. I ask that you take Shen Pei and Feng Ji as advisers.”

Shang said, “I also want this and that pair of men to keep advising me day and night. How can I let them leave?”

Guo Tu said, “Then send one of them away. Let the two draw lots, and the one chosen goes.”

Shang had no choice. He ordered a lot to be drawn; Feng Ji was chosen. Shang immediately gave Feng Ji the seals and instructed him to go with Guo Tu to Yuan Tan’s camp.

When Feng Ji arrived with Guo Tu, he saw that Tan was not sick and felt uneasy. He presented the seals and ribbons of office. Tan flew into a rage and wished Feng Ji executed. Guo Tu spoke in private and counseled, “Cao’s army is still pressing in. Keep Feng Ji here only for now to calm Shang’s mind. Once we break Cao, we can still contend for Jizhou later.”

Tan accepted this and at once broke camp and moved toward Liyang, where he met Cao’s forces. He dispatched Wang Zhao to fight. Cao sent Xu Huang to meet him. The two generals fought only a few rounds; Xu Huang cut Wang Zhao down from under his horse. Cao’s troops then pressed their advantage and Yuan Tan suffered a heavy defeat.

Tan withdrew with his broken army into Liyang and asked for aid from Shang. Shang and Shen Pei discussed it and sent only more than five thousand soldiers.

Cao Cao learned that the relief force had arrived and sent Yue Jin and Li Dian with troops halfway to meet them. The two wings closed in and slaughtered the force.

When Tan saw that Shang had sent no more than five thousand and that they had been cut down en route, he was furious and had Feng Ji brought forward.

Feng Ji said, “Allow me to write to your lord, asking him to come himself and save us.”

Tan ordered Feng Ji to write. He sent a messenger to Jizhou with the letter.

Shen Pei and Shang discussed it. Shen said, “Guo Tu is a man with many plans. He did not contend with us earlier because Cao is pressing on us now. If we defeat Cao, he will surely contend for Jizhou. Better to hold back our relief and use Cao’s strength to remove him.”

Shang accepted this and refused to send help. When the messenger returned, Tan was furious and executed Feng Ji; he spoke of submitting to Cao.

A confidential informer had already reported this to Shang. Shang and Shen said, “If Tan were to submit to Cao and then unite with him in battle, Jizhou is in danger.” They therefore left Shen Pei and Grand General Su You to hold Jizhou and brought the main army to Liyang to relieve Tan.

Shang asked who would lead the vanguard. The two great generals, Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang, both volunteered. Shang selected thirty thousand men and made them the vanguard to go first to Liyang.

When Tan learned that Shang had come, he abandoned thought of surrender. He camped inside the city; Shang camped outside, setting a wedge form.

Not long after, Yuan Xi and Gao Gan each brought troops and camped outside in three separate positions, riding out each day to contest Cao’s army. Shang was defeated repeatedly, and Cao was victorious repeatedly.

By the spring of the eighth year of Jian’an, in the third month, Cao divided his forces and attacked. Yuan Tan, Yuan Xi, Shang, and Gao Gan all suffered major defeats and abandoned Liyang.

Cao pressed them and marched toward Jizhou. Tan and Shang entered the city and held firm, while Xi and Gan camped thirty li away, making a show of strength. Cao’s army attacked day after day without breaking through.

Guo Jia then said, “The Yuan family has displaced elders and raised youths; power has merged among brothers into rival camps. If pressed, they rush to each other’s aid; if given breathing room, they fight. Better to bring the army south into Jing Province and campaign against Liu Biao, waiting for the Yuan brothers to turn on one another. Then when the change comes, strike them and settle the matter in one stroke.”

Cao liked the argument and, appointing Jia Xu to command Liyang, ordered Cao Hong to guard Guandu. He then moved with the main army to Jing Province.

When Tan and Shang heard that Cao’s army had withdrawn, each rejoiced. Yuan Xi and Gao Gan took their leave.

Yuan Tan and Guo Tu and Xin Ping met again. “I was the eldest son, yet I could not inherit our father’s legacy; Shang is the son of the concubine and inherited the great rank,” Tan said. “My heart is not at peace with it.”

Guo Tu said, “Your Lordship should station your troops outside the walls and invite Xianfu and Shen Pei to drink. Hide swords and axe-men among the attendants and kill them. Then it is done.”

Tan followed this counsel.

At that time Wang Xiu arrived from Qing Province. Tan laid out this plan to him. Wang Xiu said, “Brothers are like right and left hands. To cut against one another and then claim I must prevail—can that ever succeed? If blood is denied in kinship, who will any longer count a father or brother? Let slanderers divide siblings for one day’s gain; stop your ears and do not listen.”

Tan grew enraged and sent him off in anger, then summoned Shang.

Shang and Shen Pei consulted. Shen said, “This is surely Guo Tu’s design. If you go, you will surely be caught in it. Better to seize the moment and strike.”

Shang agreed, so he donned armor and led fifty thousand men from the city.

When Tan saw Shang’s army advancing he knew the plot had leaked. He threw on armor and rode at once. They met with front lines and exchanged abuse.

Tan said, “You drugged our father to death, stole the rank, and now come to kill your brother!”

The two brothers fought in person. Tan was badly defeated. Shang rushed ahead amid darts and stones and pressed forward to kill as he pursued. Tan took his broken force back to Pingyuan and Shang withdrew.

Tan and Guo Tu discussed another advance and sent Cen Bi forward at the head of troops. Shang himself led his army out of Jizhou.

The two camps faced each other at distance, banners and drums answering across the field. Cen Bi rode forward, taunting the array. Shang wanted to fight him himself. Lü Kuang, spurring his horse, flourished his sword and came to meet him. The two met for many rounds, and Lü Kuang cut Cen Bi from underneath his horse.

Tan was defeated again and fled yet again to Pingyuan. Shen Pei urged Shang to press on and pursue to Pingyuan.

Shang pursued and reached Pingyuan. Tan could not withstand it, withdrew into the city, and held firm behind the walls. Shang then encircled it from three sides and attacked.

Tan and Guo Tu took counsel again. Guo Tu said, “Now grain is low inside the city, and their soldiers are hard-hit and keen. They are not our equal in force. My thought is to send men to surrender to Cao and ask him to move against Jizhou. When he comes, Shang will have to return and can be intercepted then. If Cao defeats Shang, we then absorb his army and hold it back to repel Cao. Cao’s men have come far and their grain is thin; he will soon have to withdraw. Then we can still hold Jizhou and work toward further gains.”

Tan asked, “Who can carry this?”

Guo Tu said, “Xin Pi, your brother Xin Pi, courtesy name Zuozhi, who serves as Magistrate of Pingyuan. He is a man of words and can carry your message.”

Tan summoned Xin Pi immediately, and Xin Pi’s face brightened at the summons. Tan handed him a sealed letter and sent him out with three thousand troops.

At night Xin Pi took the letter and rode out through the pass. He carried the dispatch to Cao’s camp.

At that time Cao had encamped at Xiping to attack Liu Biao. Liu Biao had sent Liu Bei, courtesy name Xuande, with troops as the vanguard to meet him. Before battle began, Xin Pi reached Cao’s camp.

After the formal courtesies, Xin Pi stated fully what Yuan Tan requested and presented the letter.

Cao read it and kept Xin Pi in camp while he and his ministers deliberated.

Cheng Yu said, “Yuan Tan has been struck by Shang too harshly and came to submit only because he had no choice. His request cannot be trusted.”

Lü Qian and Man Chong also said, “Since the Chancellor has brought the army here, how could he leave Liu Biao and then go to aid Tan?”

Xun You said, “The three above do not advise well. In my view: the world is in upheaval. Liu Biao sits between the Jiang and the Han waters and does not dare to step out. That shows he lacks great ambition. If the Yuan clans of four commanderies hold tens of thousands of armed men and the brothers still kept peace, the world is not yet secure. Now, as brothers and brothers attack each other, they are pressed and exhausted and throw themselves in. It is the hour for the house of Yuan to fall apart. We should first remove Shang, and then after events unfold, destroy Tan. This is the chance; do not miss it.”

Cao rejoiced. He invited Xin Pi to drink and asked, “Is Tan truly coming in surrender, or is he feigning? Can Shang’s army surely be overcome?”

Xin Pi said, “My lord, do not ask if it is true or false. Judge only its likelihood. The Yuan house has suffered losses for years; their military stores are exhausted by outside wars, and scheming ministers were executed at home. Brothers have become separated by slander; the state is split in two. On top of that famine and disasters strike together and people are hard-pressed; anyone, wise or not, can see collapse ahead. This is Heaven’s time to destroy the Yuans.

If Your Excellency advances to seize Ye and Shang does not return, he loses his nest; if he returns, Tan will then strike from the rear. Under Your Excellency’s pressure, the exhausted troops will fall like dry leaves in an autumn wind. This way is better than marching to Jing Province now. Jing is a rich and pleasant land, with order among state and people, and cannot be moved lightly. More than all the other dangers, Hebei is the greatest threat. If Hebei is pacified, the hegemonic enterprise is complete. Please consider this, my lord.”

Cao smiled, “I regret I meet Xin Zuo only now.”

He ordered the army to return that day and seize Jizhou.

Liu Bei feared Cao had designs and did not dare to press pursuit. He led his army back to Jing Province.

When Shang heard that Cao had crossed the river, he hurriedly brought his army back to Ye and ordered Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang to cover the rear.

When Tan saw Shang’s withdrawal, he mustered the Pingyuan troops in full and advanced in pursuit. In less than several dozen li, a cannon sounded once and both armies rushed out at once. Lü Kuang took the left, and Lü Xiang the right; the two brothers cut off Tan.

Tan reined in and said, “While our father was alive, I did not treat you as lesser generals. Why now do you, because you are with my brother, press in and block me?”

The two generals dismounted and surrendered to Tan.

Tan said, “Do not submit to me. Submit to Chancellor Cao.”

Tan had them follow him back into camp and sent word to Cao requesting aid in taking Jizhou.

Cao was delighted and offered to marry his daughter to Tan, then made Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang his mediators.

Tan asked Cao for help in taking Jizhou. Cao replied, “At present grain transport is not linked, and the labor is heavy. I have already cut a channel from the Ji River and blocked the Qi River into Bai Gou to open the grain road; after that I can move forward.” He ordered Tan to hold in Pingyuan for now.

Cao withdrew his army back to Liyang and made Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang marquises to serve with his force.
