Guo Tu advised Tan, “Cao’s marriage offer may not be sincere. He has rewarded and brought these two into his army to keep a cage over northern hearts. In time this will become our disaster. Your Lordship should immediately carve two generals’ seals, send them secretly to those two brothers, and make them an inside support. When Cao destroys Shang, strike immediately and make your move.”

Tan followed this advice. He had two general seals made at once and sent them secretly to Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang.

When the two received them, they carried the seals directly to Cao and presented them.

Cao laughed, “Tan has sent these seals in secret and expects you both to aid him from inside after he has broken Shang. He thinks to grab the matter for himself. Keep them for now. I have my own design.” From then on Cao came to bear a secret intention to kill Tan.

Shang and Shen Pei discussed: “Now that Cao’s army has set up grain logistics into Bai Gou, he will certainly move against Jizhou. How do we answer?”

Shen said, “Issue orders to Yin Kai, the commandant of Wuan, to garrison at Maocheng and secure the grain road through Shangdang; and ask Ju Hu, son of Ju Shou, to hold Handan for distant support. Your Lordship should march on Pingyuan and attack Tan quickly, first breaking him off, and only then strike Cao.”

Shang rejoiced. He left Shen Pei and Chen Lin to hold Jizhou, and sent Ma Yan and Zhang Yi as the vanguard for the first move. He then led troops out at night.

When Tan realized Shang’s army was near, he called in urgent aid from Cao.

Cao said, “This time, I will surely take Jizhou.”

As he spoke, Xu You came from Xuchang. Hearing that Shang had again attacked Tan, he entered and said to Cao, “My lord, why do you sit here? Do you wait to be struck by heaven and die with the two Yuans?”

Cao smiled and said, “I have already calculated it.” He ordered Cao Hong forward first against Ye, while he brought one army to attack Yin Kai.

When the troops arrived in range, Yin Kai rode out to meet them.

“Where is Xu Zhongkang?” Cao asked.

Xu Chu answered at once, and rode out, driving his horse straight at Yin Kai. He took him unprepared and struck him down under the saddle with one stroke. The rest of Yin Kai’s men broke and fled.

Cao offered all who would surrender clemency and then ordered his men to take Handan.

Ju Hu came forward in relief. Zhang Liao rode out to meet him. They fought fewer than three rounds, and Ju Hu was badly defeated. Zhang Liao pursued from behind.

The two horses did not separate far, and Zhang Liao took his bow quickly and shot him from under his saddle.

Cao signaled the horsemen to cover the kill. The rest of the men scattered.

Then Cao moved the main army forward to Jizhou. Cao Hong had already come near the wall. Cao ordered all three commands to circle the city and build an earthen embankment, then secretly dig a tunnel beneath it.

Shen Pei held the defense firm and imposed strict discipline. Feng Li, who commanded the east gate, became careless in drunkenness and neglected the watch, so Shen Pei sharply rebuked him. Feng Li nursed the grudge and slipped out by night to surrender to Cao.

Cao asked how to break in. Feng Li said, “The gate breach is deeply packed with earth. We should dig into the city through a tunnel.” Cao ordered Feng Li to lead three hundred stout men and dig at midnight.

After Feng Li had gone out and surrendered, Shen Pei climbed the city walls each night to inspect troops and horses himself. That night at the gate tower he looked out and saw no lights outside the walls. He said, “Feng Li will bring men in through a tunnel.” He urgently ordered the best troops to throw stones against the gate and close the gate shutters. Feng Li and his three hundred stout men died inside the earth.

Cao therefore gave up this tunnel plan and withdrew the army to the banks of the Huan River to wait for Shang to turn back. Shang was attacking Pingyuan. Hearing that Cao had broken Yin Kai and Ju Hu and had the city under heavy siege, he returned his army to rescue Jizhou.

Officer Ma Yan said, “If we take the main road, Cao certainly has an ambush. Take the smaller route through the Fushui mouth by way of the western hills and strike Cao’s camp at its rear; then the encirclement will be broken.”

Shang followed this and led the main force first, leaving Ma Yan and Zhang Yi to cover the rear.

A messenger quickly informed Cao.

Cao said, “If they come by the main road, we will evade; if they come by the smaller western-hill road, one battle may catch them. He will surely light signal fires for aid. I will divide my troops.”

As planned, Cao made his dispositions.

Shang left through the Fushui River mouth and moved east to Yangping, camping at Yangping Pavilion seventeen li from Jizhou, with one side anchored on the Fushui.

Shang had his soldiers pile wood and dry grass, and in the evening they were set alight as signal beacons. He sent his chief clerk Li Fu, disguised as Cao’s metropolitan commander, down toward the city and to shout, “Open the gate!”

Shen Pei recognized Li Fu’s voice immediately and said to him when he entered the city, “Shang has arrayed troops at Yangping Pavilion and waits for support; if troops from the city go out, raise beacon fires as well.” He then ordered fire signals to be prepared in the city.

Li Fu said, “There is no grain in the city. Send out the old and weak, invalid soldiers, and women with their households to surrender. Cao will not be prepared; once they have gone out, I will advance behind the people.”

Shen approved his argument.

The next day, a white banner flew over the city walls, bearing the words: “The people of Jizhou surrender.”

Cao said, “This is the city saying it has no grain and sending old and weak people down; afterwards soldiers will come out.” He ordered Zhang Liao and Xu Huang to bring three thousand horsemen and men each, and hide on both sides. Cao himself rode forward beneath his banner to the gate.

As expected, when the gate opened there came out old and young, old and weak men with women, carrying white flags and banners.

After all civilians had gone, soldiers surged out. Cao raised a red flag and the two wings under Zhang Liao and Xu Huang struck out in disorder and slaughtered. City soldiers had to run back in.

Cao remounted and rode to the Diao Bridge side. Crossbow bolts fell like rain from the city, one striking his helmet and nearly piercing through the top of it. His generals hurried him back into formation.

He changed his armor and horse, then returned with the commanders to attack Shang’s camp. Shang came out to meet him.

Meanwhile all columns converged; both armies charged together and mixed in close fighting. Shang was badly defeated. He withdrew and drew his men to camp under the western hills. He sent urgent orders for Ma Yan and Zhang Yi to arrive.

He did not know that Cao had already sent Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang to summon the two generals.

The two came down with them and surrendered. Cao likewise made them marquises.

That same day he advanced to assault the western hills, and first sent Lü Kuang, Lü Xiang, Ma Yan, and Zhang Yi to cut off Shang’s food route.

Shang knew the western hills could not hold. In the night he fled through Yikou. Before his camp was set, fires rose in every direction and ambush troops surged from every side; men had not put on armor and horses had not taken saddles. Shang’s army was in rout and ran fifty li before it broke.

In final desperation he sent Yin Kui, Inspector of Yuzhou, to Cao’s camp to petition surrender. Cao pretended to accept, then that night sent Zhang Liao and Xu Huang to seize Shang’s camp.

Shang threw away his seals, badges, armor, and military kit and fled toward Zhongshan.

Cao returned with the army to Jizhou.

Xu You offered this strategy: “Why not release the waters of the Zhang River and flood them?”

Cao approved the idea. He ordered men outside the city to dig a large channel and embankment around Jizhou, extending for forty li.

On the city wall Shen Pei saw Cao’s men digging shallow trenches and laughed to himself. “They mean to release Zhang River water into the city and drown it. But this is so shallow—can it serve?” he said and made no new preparation.

That night Cao added ten times the usual number of soldiers and labored through the night to dig. By dawn the trench was two zhang wide and deep, and water from the Zhang flowed in to several chi deep.

At the same time grain failed, and the men began to starve.

Outside the city, Xin Pi held up a spear and prodded the seals, robes, and garments of Yuan Shang to attract the city, inviting it to surrender.

Shen Pei grew furious and had more than eighty members of Xin Pi’s household, old and young, executed atop the city wall, their heads cast down.

Xin Pi wept without end. Shen Rong, Shen Pei’s nephew and long friend of Xin Pi, grieving over the deaths of Xin Pi’s household, secretly wrote a letter of surrender and tied it to an arrow, shooting it into the city.

A soldier picked up the message, and Xin Pi delivered it to Cao.

Before entering Jizhou, Cao issued this order first: once we are in, no one is to kill the elders or children of the Yuan household, and civilians who surrender are to be spared.

At dawn the next morning, Shen Rong opened the west gate and let Cao’s army in. Xin Pi sprang into the saddle first and entered. The captains followed and overran Jizhou.

From the southeast city tower Shen Pei saw Cao’s army had entered. He rode out with a few horsemen to die in battle. He met Xu Huang at close range and was captured alive; as he was led out he encountered Xin Pi.

Xin Pi ground his teeth and pointed with his whip to the head, saying, “Traitor! You brought Cao to break my Jizhou; today you die!”

Shen Pei growled back, “Traitorous cur! You brought Cao to destroy my Jizhou, and I regret I did not kill you sooner!”

Xu Huang presented Shen to Cao.

Cao asked, “Do you know who opened the gate for me?”

Shen said, “I do not know.”

Cao said, “It was your nephew, Shen Rong.”

Shen snapped, “Can a boy of mine do such a thing?”

Cao asked, “Why were there so many crossbow bolts outside the gate yesterday?”

Shen answered, “I regret it deeply, I regret it.”

Cao said, “You were loyal to the Yuan, and this is only what such loyalty demands. Will you submit to me now?”

Shen replied, “No. No.”

Xin Pi knelt and cried out, “My household of more than eighty was all killed by this traitor. I beg the Chancellor to have him executed, so this grudge is avenged.”

Shen said, “I was born to serve the Yuan and die a ghost of the Yuan. I am no like you, who slander and flatter. Kill me now!”

Cao ordered him bound out. At the end he shouted to the executioner, “Carry this out quickly!” He knelt facing north and said, “My lord is in the north; let me not die with my face turned south.” Then he held out his neck to the blade.

Later someone wrote this poem of lament:

Hebei has many worthy men; who is equal to Shen, the upright minister? Fate gave him an ignorant lord and a ruined house, and still his heart joined the ancients. Loyal and upright in speech, with no hidden schemes, his ambition knew no greed. Even at death he faced the north, and those who had surrendered were all ashamed.

After Shen died, Cao honored his loyalty and told him worthy burial north of the city walls.

Many officers asked Cao to enter the city. Just as he was about to move, an executioner arrived carrying one man. Cao saw it was Chen Lin.

Cao said, “You drafted a memorial for Benchu before; your crimes were by no means light. Why then would I bring disgrace on your ancestors and your parents as well?”

Chen Lin replied, “When an arrow is on the string, one cannot keep it from release.”

Many urged Cao to execute him, but Cao pitied his talent and spared him, appointing him to service.

Now Cao’s eldest son Cao Pi, courtesy name Zihuan, was eighteen years old. Since he had been eight he had already been able to compose texts of style, with uncommon talent. He was learned in ancient matters, adept at riding and archery, and good with the sword.

When Cao had taken Jizhou, Pi followed his father in the army. He first took command of his own bodyguard and rode straight to Yuan Shao’s household, dismounted, drew his sword, and entered.

A general stepped forward to block him: “My lord has ordered this, and no one may enter the Yuan household.”

Cao Pi shouted him away, then pressed forward with sword into the rear hall.

He saw two women embracing and weeping, and moved on as if to kill them.

Four generations of lords and nobles are only dreams now, and another household of blood and bone meets calamity once more. Who can know what fate now awaits? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Yuan Shang Contests Jizhou, and Xu You’s Stratagem by the Zhang River

chapters.html:
Then it is said that Cao Pi saw two women weeping. He drew his sword and meant to behead one. Suddenly a red glare filled his sight. He lowered the sword and asked, “Who are you?”

One woman said, “I am Lady Liu, wife of General Yuan.” Cao Pi asked, “And this one?”

Lady Liu said, “This is Lady Zhen, wife of Yuan Xi. When Xi was posted to garrison Youzhou, Lady Zhen refused to travel far and stayed behind.”

Cao Pi pulled this woman forward and saw her hair loose and face soiled. He wiped her face with his sleeve and looked closely. Lady Zhen’s skin had the smoothness of jade and a beauty of flowers, with a charm enough to overturn a state. He then told Liu, “I am the son of Chancellor Cao. I will keep your household safe. Do not worry.” He then set his sword down and sat in the hall.

Later, Cao Cao led the commanders into Jizhou and came to the city gate to enter it. Xu You urged his horse forward and with his whip pointed at the gate, cried out, “Aman, you cannot bar me; how can you enter this gate?”

Cao Cao laughed loudly. The commanders all heard and were inwardly upset. Cao Cao came beneath the gate of the Shao manor and asked, “Who has entered this gate?”

The gate commander replied, “The Heir Apparent is inside.” Cao Cao called him out and questioned him. Liu Shi knelt and spoke: “My lord the Heir Apparent is not here. I am able to protect the household only because of him. I offer Lady Zhen, to serve as household attendant to the Heir Apparent.”

Cao Cao ordered Lady Zhen brought out and presented.

When he saw her, he said, “She is truly a wife fit for our son.” Cao Cao then ordered Cao Pi to take her.

Cao Cao had by then secured Jizhou. He went personally to Yuan Shao’s tomb and offered sacrifice, bowing twice and weeping bitterly. Then he said to the commanders, “Long ago, when I and Bencu raised troops together, Bencu asked me: ‘If matters do not go well, what place can we hold?’ I asked him, ‘What is it that you wish to do?’ Bencu said, ‘I hold the south of the Yellow River, block Yan and Dai in the north, and unite the frontier tribes; with that, we can face south and contend for all under heaven. Could this be enough?’ I answered, ‘I command all intelligence in the realm and govern by the Way; there is nothing impossible.’ That is as clear as yesterday, and now Bencu is dead. I cannot help but weep.”

All of them sighed. Cao Cao gave Liu Shi of General Yuan’s wife gold, silk, grain, and rice. He then issued an order: “The people of Hebei have suffered through war. Remit this year’s taxes and grain levies entirely.” At the same time he drafted a memorial to court. Cao Cao took the post of Administrator of Jizhou.

One day, Xu Chu rode hard through the east gate and met Xu You. Xu You called out to Xu Chu, “Without me, how can you pass this gate?” Xu Chu was furious. “We have braved bloodshed a thousand times, risking our lives, stormed city walls and seized towns. How dare you boast?”

Xu You cursed, “You are all mere ordinary men. Why speak so much?”

Xu Chu in anger drew his sword and killed Xu You, then brought the head to Cao Cao and said, “Xu You was this rude. I have killed him.”

Cao Cao said, “You and I are old companions. It was only horseplay between us. Why did you kill him?” He sternly reprimanded Xu Chu, and ordered Xu You buried with honors.

Then he ordered men across Jizhou to search out worthy scholars. A local said: “Cui Yan, Master of the Cavalry Guards in office, courtesy name Jiqi, from Dongwu in Qinghe Commandery. He has offered plans to Yuan Shao several times; Yuan Shao did not adopt them, so Cui Yan feigned illness and stayed at home.”

Cao Cao immediately summoned Yan as his provincial deputy-attendant. Then he said, “I checked the household registers yesterday. This state has roughly three hundred thousand people; it may be called a great province.”

Yan replied, “Now the realm is divided and broken. The nine provinces are torn asunder. The two Yuan brothers contend; the people of Jizhou lie with bones scattered in the plains. If the Chancellor cares first for his own power and does not inquire after their ways and rescue them from this furnace and cauldron, what use is this first counting their households to the people here?”

Cao Cao, hearing this, changed his expression and apologized and treated him as an honored guest.

After stabilizing Jizhou, Cao Cao asked after Yuan Tan’s movements. Tan had taken troops to pillage Ganling, Anping, Bohai, and Hejian. On hearing that Yuan Shang had been defeated and fled to Zhongshan, he rallied and marched to attack Jizhou. Shang had no heart for battle; he rode straight away to Youzhou and surrendered to Yuan Xi. Tan absorbed all his men and wanted to cast another eye toward Jizhou. Cao Cao summoned him, but Tan did not come. Cao Cao was furious and, breaking the marriage tie, himself led the main army and marched straight to Pingyuan.

When Tan heard Cao Cao personally commanded a grand expedition, he sent to Liu Biao for aid. Liu Biao asked Liu Bei, courtesy name Xuande, to confer.

Liu Bei said, “Cao Cao has now taken Jizhou. His force is at full strength. Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang will not long avoid capture by him. To rescue them is fruitless. Besides, Cao Cao still has his eye on Jing and Xiang. I should only keep my troops and hold the ground, not move rashly.”

Liu Biao said, “Then what should I do for him?”

Liu Bei said, “Send letters to both Yuan brothers in the name of reconciliation, and politely offer thanks.”

Liu Biao agreed and first sent a letter to Tan. It read:

A gentleman must avoid disaster and avoid striking an enemy state. I hear you have knelt and yielded to Cao this morning. Then you have forgotten your forefathers, cast aside the bond of brothers, and let the shame of your alliance go uncovered.

If Jizhou cannot be held, lower your heart and join us in sincerity. Once affairs are settled and the world restored to order, will that not be righteousness of high order?

Liu Biao also wrote to Yuan Shang:

Qing Province is severe and hasty by nature and often lost in right and wrong. You should first remove Cao Cao, and for your soldiers to settle the grudge against the late Lord. Once affairs are in order, you can then reckon what is right and wrong. Is that not best?

If you remain lost and do not return, then Hanlu and Dongguo will dig themselves into a trap and leave Tianfu’s gain behind.

Tan received Liu Biao’s letters. Knowing Liu Biao had no intention to send troops and judging he could not match Cao, he abandoned Pingyuan and withdrew to defend Nanpi. Cao Cao pursued to Nanpi. The weather was cold and raw; every river was frozen, and grain-ships could not move. Cao Cao ordered the local people to chip the ice and drag the ships along. Upon hearing the order they fled. Cao Cao was furious and wanted to execute them, but when they heard, they came personally to the camp and offered their heads.

He said, “If I do not kill you, my orders will be worthless; if I kill you, I cannot bear it. Run quickly to the hills and hide. Do not fall into capture by my soldiers.”

The people all wept and left.

Tan brought his troops out of the city and opposed Cao Cao’s army. The two camps faced each other. Cao Cao mounted and pointed with his whip at Tan while cursing, “I treated you lavishly. Why do you harbor treachery?”

Tan replied, “You invaded my borders, took my cities, and then rely on my wife and son to argue that I have foreign intent?”

Cao Cao became enraged and sent Xu Huang forward. Tan sent Peng An to meet him. The two horses met and after only a few exchanges, Xu Huang cut Peng An down from the saddle. Tan’s army broke and ran back into Nanpi. Cao Cao sent troops to encircle from all sides.

Tan, panicked, sent Xin Ping to negotiate surrender with Cao Cao.

Cao Cao said, “Tan is a fickle youth and unsteady; I can trust him no more.”

“You are wrong, Chancellor. I have long served in the Yuan house; what I heard long ago was that when a lord is honored, his ministers are praised, and when a lord is in distress, his ministers are humiliated. Could I turn on my lord?” Xin Ping replied.

Cao Cao knew he could not be retained and sent him back. Xin Ping returned to Tan and said Cao Cao would not accept him. Tan shouted, “You have seen how I deal with Cao Cao and your mind is split in two.” Xin Ping heard, filled with resentment, and fell unconscious. After being carried out, he soon died. Tan regretted it deeply.

Guo Tu said to Tan, “Tomorrow, drive out all the townspeople first and then, with the army behind, decide one battle to the death with Cao Cao.”

Tan followed his advice. That night he drove all the people of Nanpi out in formation, each carrying knife and spear at command. At first light he opened all four gates. The army followed, the people in front. Shouting as one, they surged out and met Cao’s camp.

The two armies collided in close melee from morning to noon, victory and defeat still uncertain. Seeing he had not won outright, Cao Cao mounted a horse and climbed the slope, striking the war drum himself. The officers saw and surged forward. Tan’s forces were thoroughly broken; countless civilians were killed.

Cao Hong pressed hard, broke through the formation, and when Tan came straight at him, he swung his blade wildly. Tan was cut down in the melee. Guo Tu saw the formation in chaos and dashed into the city in haste. Le Jin saw him and loosed an arrow down into the city trench; horse and rider both sank.

Cao Cao led his troops into Nanpi and pacified the people. Then a detachment of troops arrived, led by Yuan Xi’s generals Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan. Cao Cao personally greeted them as they came. The two surrendered at once, casting down spears and armor. He made them lords of marquis rank.

Also Zhang Yan, the Black Mountain bandit, came with one hundred thousand men to surrender. Cao Cao made him General Who Pacifies the North.

He then ordered that whoever dared to cry over Yuan Tan’s head was to be beheaded, and he hung the severed head outside the northern gate. A man in a coarse cap and torn robe came and wept beneath it. They seized him and brought him before Cao Cao. He was Wang Xiu, the Deputy Provincial Governor of Qingzhou, who had once advised Tan and now came to mourn after hearing of Tan’s death.

Cao Cao asked, “Do you know my order?”

Wang Xiu said, “I do.”

“Are you not afraid to die?” Cao Cao asked.

Wang Xiu said, “I have long lived by receiving orders. If I live and do not cry, it is not righteousness. If I fear death and forget righteousness, how can I stand in this world? If I can bring in Tan’s body for burial, I can bear death without resentment.”

Cao Cao said, “Such many men of principle in Hebei—what a lot of them there are. If only the Yuan house had used you, would I dare to look this way with an unblinking gaze?” He ordered Tan’s body to be recovered and buried with honors. He treated Wang Xiu as an honored guest and appointed him Colonel of the Gold-in-Charge Office.

Then he asked, “Now that Yuan Shang has already fled to Yuan Xi, what strategy should we use to take them?”

Wang Xiu did not answer. Cao Cao said, “A loyal minister.” Guo Jia said, “You can use Yuan’s surrendered commanders Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan to attack them themselves.”

Cao Cao accepted the counsel. He ordered Jiao Chu, Zhang Nan, Lü Kuang, Lü Xiang, Ma Yan, and Zhang Yi, each with his own troops, to advance on Youzhou from three directions. At the same time he sent Li Dian and Le Jin to join Zhang Yan, strike Bingzhou, and attack Gao Gan.

Now Tan and Shang, hearing Cao’s troops would come, thought it hard to meet battle, so they abandoned the city and by night fled west to Liaoxi and then to the Wuhuan.

The Youzhou governor, Wuhuan Chu, assembled the leading officials, swore blood oaths, and held counsel over turning from the Yans to Cao. Wuhuan Chu spoke first: “I know Cao Chancellor is the hero of our age. Should anyone here fail to obey his summons when he comes in submission, he should be executed.” He passed the oath cup around until it came to Deputy Provincial Governor Han Heng.

Han Heng threw his sword to the ground and shouted, “I have received deep favor from Yuan and Father. Now my lord has fallen, my wisdom could not save him, my courage could not die in service. I have failed in rightness! If I bow north and submit to Cao, I will not.”

All were taken aback. Wuhuan Chu said, “To accomplish great matters one must stand on great righteousness. The success or failure of affairs does not rest on one man. Since Han Heng has resolved so, let him do as he pleases.” He pushed him out.

Wuhuan Chu then rode out of the city to meet the three columns and rode directly to Cao to surrender. Cao Cao was pleased and made him General Who Guards the North.

Soon a messenger came: “Le Jin, Li Dian, and Zhang Yan have attacked Bingzhou. Gan Gan holds Hupass and will not descend.”

Cao Cao drew up his forces and advanced. The three commanders arrived and reported, “Gao Gan blocks the pass and is hard to beat.” The officers met and debated breaking Gao Gan. Xun You said, “To break Gan, a stratagem of feigned surrender is required.”

Cao Cao accepted. He summoned surrendering commanders Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang and spoke in whispers. They led several tens of troops straight down to the pass and cried, “We were once commanders under the Yans. We had no choice but submit to Cao. Cao Cao is crafty and has treated us lightly. We return now to our old lord. Open the gate and receive us at once.”

Gao Gan did not believe them. He only sent the two commanders up to the pass to speak. The two shed armor, left their horses, and entered, telling Gan, “Cao’s troops are newly arrived and their hearts are unsteady. Come tonight, seize the camp. We are willing to lead first.”

Gan gladly accepted and ordered Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang to lead a force of more than ten thousand in first rank. As they reached Cao’s camp, shouts rose behind them and ambushes leapt up. Gan realized he had been trapped and hurried back to Huoguan City. By then Le Jin and Li Dian had already taken the pass.

Gan snatched a route of escape and fled to the Shanyu. Cao Cao ordered his men to hold the pass mouth and sent detachments to pursue Gan. Gan reached the Shanyu border and met the Left King Xianxian of the northern tribes. He dismounted and fell to the ground in homage, saying, “Cao Cao has absorbed the lands and now seeks to invade Your Majesty’s territory. I beg aid in all of your strength to join in recovering it and securing the north.”

The king said, “I have no enmity with Cao Cao. Why would you make me enemy to the Cao house?” He dismissed Gan angrily.

Gan found no road left and had to go submit to Liu Biao. He had gone as far as Shanglu when he was killed by Major Wang Yan, who took his head and sent it to Cao Cao. Cao Cao made Wang Yan a marquis of the columns.

With Bingzhou settled, Cao Cao discussed a western campaign against the Wuhuan. Cao Hong and others said, “Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang have been beaten and nearly ruined. They are on the edge, driving toward the desert. If we go west now, Liu Bei and Liu Biao may strike Xuchang while we are away. We may not return in time; the harm will be deep.”

Guo Jia said, “What you have said is wrong. Though the Chancellor’s fame shakes all under heaven, the desert tribes, far from the capital and trusting their remoteness, are not prepared. If we strike them suddenly while they are unready, we can break them. Besides, Yuan Shao had bonds with the Wuhuan, and Shang and Xi still remain. They must be removed. Liu Biao is but an entertainer of talking guests; he knows his ability is not enough to confront Liu Bei, so if he has him with heavy trust he cannot contain him; if he has him lightly, Bei will become useless. No matter: fear not a distant campaign.”

Cao Cao said, “Fengxiao speaks well.”

So he led ten thousand and many more, with three thousand carts, advancing forward. At once the land was only drifts of yellow sand, wild winds rose in every direction, and the roads were rough; men and horses struggled to travel. He wondered about turning back and asked Guo Jia. Jia, at this time ill from the land and unable to stand, lay sick in the cart.

Cao Cao said with tears, “Because I wished to pacify the desert and drove you over hardships until you took ill, how can my heart be at peace?”

Jia said, “I have received the Chancellor’s great grace. Even death cannot repay it.”

Cao asked, “I saw the roughness of the northlands and thought of turning back. What should be done?”

Jia answered, “In war, speed is prized. This long ride of a thousand li against scattered enemies, with many baggage wagons, cannot move swiftly for profit. Better to send a light force on multiple routes and break out. We only need a guide who knows the paths.”

Cao left Jia in Yizhou to recover and sought local guides. Someone recommended Tian Chou, an old commander under Yuan Shao who knew these lands well, and Cao Cao asked him.

Tian Chou said, “In summer and autumn there is water in this route, too shallow for horse and carriage; in depth one can carry no boats. It is hardest for movement. Better to turn back, cross from Lulong mouth past Baitan Pass through empty lands, come near Liucheng, and strike where they are least prepared. A man of the Xiongnu, Modu, could be won in one battle.”

Cao Cao followed this counsel, made Tian Chou General Who Pacifies the Northern Border, appointed him local guide and vanguard. Zhang Liao was second. Cao Cao stayed in rear and drove light cavalry by separate roads.

Tian Chou led Zhang Liao on ahead to BaLang Mountain and just met Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang, who had joined with Modu and several ten thousand horsemen. Zhang Liao raced back to report. Cao Cao reined and gained elevation to watch; he saw Modu’s troops without formation and badly arranged. He told Zhang Liao, “When the enemy is disorderly, he may be struck.”

He handed a signal and Zhang Liao. Zhang Liao then sent Xu Chu, Yu Jin, and Xu Huang in four directions down the mountain and attacked with all force. Modu’s force collapsed in disorder. Zhang Liao cut down Modu from horseback and the rest all surrendered. Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang withdrew with several thousand riders and fled toward Liaodong.

Cao Cao withdrew his army into Liucheng and made Tian Chou Lord of Liuting to guard Liucheng. Tian Chou wept and said, “I am one who fled in guilt. Your great grace let me live. To be so fortunate and then the fort at Lulong for reward and stipend—this I cannot do. I dare not accept marquis rank in death.”

Cao Cao valued his feeling and made him a Yilang. He comforted the Shanyu people, and obtained ten thousand fine horses. The same day he ordered the army home.

Now the weather was cold and dry. Two hundred li held no water. The army lacked grain and had to eat its horses. Men had to dig three to four zhang for water. Cao Cao returned to Yizhou and rewarded those who had first advised him. He told the commanders, “I only this time undertook a perilous distant campaign; by chance and luck I succeeded. Though there was victory, Heaven favored it. It cannot be a model for the future. What saved us was your counsel. I therefore reward it. In future, do not hold back in speaking.”

When Cao Cao reached Yizhou, Guo Jia had been dead several days; his coffin had been resting in the public hall. Cao Cao went to offer sacrifice and wept: “With Fengxiao dead, Heaven has robbed me.” He looked back at the gathered officers and said, “You all are older than I am; Fengxiao was the youngest. I wished to entrust him later matters, and now he has met an untimely death. My heart and intestines are torn apart.”

Jia’s attendants presented a sealed paper written in his final hand:

Guo Gong, before death, wrote this with his own brush and entrusted it: “If the Chancellor follows what is written herein, matters in Liaodong will be settled.”

Cao Cao opened the letter and nodded with sighing wonder. None of the others knew what it meant.

The next day, Xiahou Dun brought the assembly and said, “The Governor of Liaodong, Gongsun Kang, has long refused to submit. Now Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang have fled to him. He will become trouble after trouble. It is best to seize him now while he has not yet moved.”

Cao Cao laughed: “There is no need for your tiger-like might. In a few days Gongsun Kang will present the heads of both Yans to me.”

No commander believed him.

Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang then led several thousand horse toward Liaodong. Gongsun Kang, Governor of Liaodong, came from Xiangping and was the son of Wu-wei General Gongsun Du. When he heard the two brothers had come to surrender, he gathered his officers and discussed. Gongsun Gong said, “While Yuan Shao lived, he had long wished to seize Liaodong. Now that Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang are beaten and near death, they have nowhere to go and have come here to offer themselves. This is the act of a hawk and eagle seizing the magpie’s nest. If we host them, they will surely prey on each other and plot against us later. Better to lure them into the city and kill them, send their heads to Cao; then Cao will surely reward me.”

Kang said, “I only fear if Cao brings soldiers to Liaodong, it is better not to receive the two Yans and instead use them to help me.”

Geng said, “Send someone to scout. If Cao marches here, keep the two Yans. If he does not move, then kill both and send them to Cao.” Kang followed this and sent a scout.

When Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang arrived in Liaodong, the two spoke privately: “Liaodong has many thousands troops; it is enough to match Cao. We will pretend to submit now and later kill Gongsun Kang and seize his land, then build our strength and oppose the Central Plains to recover Hebei again.”

After deciding, they presented themselves to Gongsun Kang. Kang received them at a guest house but said he was ill and did not meet at once. Before a day passed, an informant reported, “Cao Cao’s army is stationed at Yizhou and has no intent to come to Liaodong.” Kang rejoiced. He placed his blade and axe men inside the wall curtains and brought the two Yans in.

After formal greetings, he ordered seats arranged. In severe cold, Shang saw no quilt or cushion on the couch and said, “I beg that seats be laid.”

Kang turned his eyes in rage and said, “Your heads traveled ten thousand li, and you ask for seats?”

Shang was startled. Kang shouted, “Why do your attendants not fall upon them?” Blade-men came out and with one motion climbed onto the seats, cutting off both heads. They placed the heads in a wooden chest and sent them to Yizhou for Cao Cao.

At that time Cao Cao sat at Yizhou, waiting without moving. Xiahou Dun and Zhang Liao reported: “If we do not go to Liaodong, we can return to Xuchang; fear that Liu Biao may seize the chance.” Cao Cao said, “Wait until the Yans’ heads arrive, then return.” All quietly smiled.

Soon a messenger announced that Gongsun Kang had sent the heads of Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang. The whole assembly was startled. The envoy offered a letter. Cao Cao laughed and said, “So Fengxiao’s prediction proves true.” He heavily rewarded the envoy and made Gongsun Kang Marquis of Xiangping and Left General.

The officers asked, “How was it not as Fengxiao predicted?”

Cao Cao brought out Guo Jia’s letter and showed it:

I hear Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang have gone to Liaodong. You must not send troops there. Gongsun Kang has long feared the Yans’ swallowing of this land. If the two Yans do arrive there, he will surely suspect them.

If you strike him at once, he and the Yans will surely combine and meet battle; delay will not do. If you wait, Gongsun Kang and the Yans will inevitably plot against one another. Their momentum is thus.

All praised him. Cao Cao gathered the officers again and made sacrificial offerings at Guo Jia’s spirit tablet. Jia had died at thirty-eight years of age; in ten years of campaigning he had earned many great merits.

Later men composed a verse:

Born of Heaven, Guo Fengxiao; a heroic figure among heroes,
The classics and histories in his belly, troops and weapons hidden in his breast;
He planned with the subtlety of Fan Li and decided with the decisiveness of Chen Ping.
Alas, he died too soon; the main beam of the Central Plains already tilts.

Cao Cao then led the army back to Jizhou and sent men ahead to place Guo Jia’s coffin in Xuchang for burial. Cheng Yu and others asked, “Now the north is settled. If we return to Xuchang, we can begin strategy for the lands south of the Yangtze.”

Cao Cao laughed, “I have long had this wish. What you say accords exactly with mine.”

That night he lodged on the eastern watchtower of Jizhou city and leaned on the balustrade watching the heavens. Xun You stood beside him. Cao Cao pointed and said, “The southern yang vitality is brilliant. Perhaps it is not yet time.”

Xun You replied, “With the Chancellor’s Heaven-borne majesty, what would not submit?”

As they watched, they suddenly saw a shaft of golden light rise from the ground. Xun You said, “This must be treasure hidden below.”

Cao Cao went down and ordered men to dig where the light had shown. So it was:

A star-trace points south toward the center; a turning of golden treasure rises from the northern earth.
What is obtained, we do not yet know. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Pi Took Lady Zhen in Turmoil, and Guo Jia's Plot Settled Liaodong

chapters.html:
Cao Cao had a bronze sparrow unearthed at Jinguang and asked Xun Yu what omen it signified. Xun Yu replied, “Long ago, Shun’s mother dreamed that a jade sparrow entered her womb, and she gave birth to Shun. Finding a bronze sparrow now is also an auspicious sign.” Cao Cao rejoiced greatly and ordered a high terrace built in celebration.

That same day he broke the ground, felled timber, burned tiles, and ground brick. He had the Bronze Sparrow Terrace erected above the Zhang River. In about a year the work was finished. Cao Zhi, his youngest son, then spoke up: “If the lofty platform is to be built, three towers should stand on it. Let the middle, highest one be named the Bronze Sparrow, the left one the Jade Dragon, and the right one the Golden Phoenix. Build two flying bridges that cross through the air, and it will be a grand spectacle.”

Cao Cao approved. “My son has spoken well. When the terrace is finished, it will be enough to please me in my old age.”

Cao Cao had five sons, and Cao Zhi alone was by nature quick and gifted, and skilled in writing. Cao Cao loved him the most in his daily life.

So he left Cao Zhi and Cao Pi in Ye Commandery to oversee the terrace, and made Zhang Yan keep watch over the northern stockade. He returned to Xu with the army he had captured from Yuan Shao—five or six hundred thousand men—reviewed the troops, and gave his merits to his officers with great rewards. He also submitted a memorial granting Guo Jia the title of Marquis Zhen, and took his son Yi into his household for care. He gathered strategists again and discussed a southern campaign against Liu Biao. Xun Yu said, “The main army has just come back from campaigning in the north; it ought not to move again yet. Wait half a year, restore strength and sharpen the edge. Liu Biao and Sun Quan can be brought down together when the time is right.”

Cao Cao agreed and therefore dispersed his troops to rotate into military farms while awaiting employment.

As for Liu Bei, when he arrived in Jing Province, Liu Biao treated him with great warmth. One day, while they were gathering together at table and drinking, there came news that the surrendered men Zhang Wu and Chen Sun were raiding the people of Jiangxia and plotting rebellion. Liu Biao was alarmed: “Those two villains have risen up again; this is no small calamity.”

Liu Bei said, “Do not have your brother worry. I beg to ride out and punish them.”

Liu Biao was delighted and immediately appointed thirty thousand soldiers, then set out with Liu Bei. Liu Bei took command at once and in no time reached Jiangxia. Zhang Wu and Chen Sun came out with their soldiers to meet him. Liu Bei, Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Zhao Yun rode out under the gate standards. They saw the horse that Zhang Wu rode, and it was extremely lofty and handsome.

Liu Bei said, “This must be a thousand-li horse.”

Before he finished speaking, Zhao Yun lowered his spear and rushed straight into their formation. Zhang Wu loosed his horse to receive him and, before they made three rounds, was knocked from the saddle by a single thrust from Zhao Yun. Zhao Yun snatched the rein and pulled the horse back toward his formation. Chen Sun came on after him to seize the horse. Zhang Fei bellowed once, lifted his spear, and drove it straight into Chen Sun, killing him. The men all broke and scattered.

Liu Bei pacified the remaining bands, restored order in the counties of Jiangxia, and returned with his army to report. Liu Biao rode out beyond the city gate to welcome him back, then held a banquet in celebration. Halfway through the wine, Liu Biao said, “My younger brother has such extraordinary talent; Jing Province has a pillar with which to rely. I worry only that, from the south, an invasion may come inopportunely. Zhang Lu and Sun Quan are enough to be causes for concern.”

Liu Bei said, “My brother has three commanders enough for this: send Zhang Fei to patrol the southern frontier; let Yunchang hold Zicheng to contain Zhang Lu; let Zhao Yun hold Sanjiang to oppose Sun Quan. What cause is there to worry?”

Liu Biao was pleased and wished to follow Liu Bei’s words. He had Cai Mao report to his sister, Lady Cai: “Liu Bei leaves only three of his generals outside and remains in Jing Province. If he stays there long, he will surely become a danger.”

So Lady Cai spoke to Liu Biao at night: “I have heard that Liu Bei has too much traffic with the people of Jing Province. He should not be taken lightly. Since he now lives in the city it helps him nothing; he should be sent away.” Liu Biao replied, “Liu Bei is a man of benevolence.”

Cai said, “I fear he is not as you are.” Liu Biao paused and did not answer.

The next day, Liu Biao came out of the city and saw Liu Bei’s horse, which was extremely fine, and heard that it was Zhang Wu’s horse. He praised it without measure. Liu Bei then presented this horse to Liu Biao.

Liu Biao rejoiced and mounted to ride back into the city. Kui Yue saw it and asked about it. “It was a gift from Liu Bei,” Liu Biao said.

Kui Yue replied, “Your elder brother Kua Liang was most skilled at judging horses, and I also know somewhat. This horse has tear-marked eyes and white spots on either side of the forehead, a marking known as Di Lu; it brings harm to the rider. Zhang Wu was killed because of this horse. Master, you should not ride it.”

Liu Biao listened. The next day he invited Liu Bei to banquet him and said, “Yesterday I gratefully received a fine horse. I am deeply moved by your kindness. Yet my worthy younger brother is not always in motion on campaign. He may still be put to use, so I will return it.”

Liu Bei rose and offered thanks. Liu Biao added, “My younger brother has lived here too long and may let his martial skills grow soft. In Xiangyang, the subordinate county of Xinye has some supplies and grain. He may bring his troops and horses there and encamp.”

Liu Bei acknowledged it.

The following day he thanked Liu Biao and withdrew with his main army and mounts straight to Xinye. As he passed through the gate, a man stepped forward and made a deep bow before his horse, saying, “Your lordship’s horse is not one to ride.” Liu Bei looked, and saw it was Ji Bo—Yi Ji of Jingzhou’s attendant office, surname Ji, from Shanyang.

Liu Bei dismounted at once and asked him. Ji said, “Yesterday I heard Kua Yi-duo tell Liu of Jingzhou, ‘This horse is named Di Lu; one who rides it is harmed.’ It was returned to you, so how could you ride it again?”

Liu Bei replied, “I deeply appreciate your concern. But the lives and deaths of ordinary men are a matter of destiny; can a horse truly bring one harm?”

Ji greatly admired his lofty view, and from that day he often went in and out with Liu Bei.

When Liu Bei arrived in Xinye, soldiers and civilians rejoiced, and the administration was transformed.

In the spring of the twelfth year of Jian'an, Lady Gan gave birth to Liu Shan. That night a white crane flew onto the county office roof, cried out more than forty times, then flew westward. At the onset of childbirth there was perfume filling the room. Lady Gan had once dreamed she drank in by gazing up and swallowed the Northern Dipper, so her milk name was A-Dou.

At this time Cao Cao’s main army was campaigning north. Liu Bei went to Jing Province and said to Liu Biao, “Now Cao Cao has gone north and Xu is empty. If we take the forces of Jing and Xiang and strike in the opening, a great undertaking can be accomplished.”

Liu Biao said, “I have a seat here in Jing Province and need not try for anything else.”

Liu Bei was silent. Liu Biao invited him into the rear hall to drink.

The wine rose to half-intoxication when Liu Biao suddenly drew a long sigh. Liu Bei said, “Brother, why such a long sigh?”

Liu Biao answered, “I have a matter in my heart that is not easy to speak plainly.”

When Liu Bei tried to ask again, Liu Biao fell silent. At that moment Lady Cai stepped out and stood behind the screen. Liu Biao lowered his head and still spoke nothing.

When the feast was over, Liu Bei returned to Xinye.

That winter, when Liu Bei heard that Cao Cao had returned from Liucheng, he lamented deeply that Liu Biao had ignored his advice. One day Liu Biao sent a messenger to ask Liu Bei to come and meet in Jing Province. Liu Bei followed the messenger.

When he arrived, Liu Biao greeted him, completed the formalities, and asked him into the rear hall for a drink. He said, “Recently I have heard that Cao Cao has returned to Xu with troops; his strength grows stronger each day, and he surely harbors the intention of swallowing Jing and Xiang. I regret I did not heed your words and missed this good chance.”

Liu Bei said, “The realm is divided and banners have risen. Are opportunities only ever abundant? If we can answer at the right later moment, this is not yet cause for regret.”

Liu Biao replied, “Your words were true.” The two drank together.

The wine ran deep, and Liu Biao wept thickly. Liu Bei asked why.

Liu Biao said, “I have had this in my heart. I wanted to tell my worthy younger brother before, but could not find the proper moment.”

Liu Bei said, “What is the matter that Brother cannot decide? If there is any service by me, I would refuse no charge, even life.”

Liu Biao said, “I have an elder son, Qi, born of my first wife, Lady Chen. Though he is a virtuous man, he is too soft and weak for great affairs. My younger son, Cong, born of Lady Cai, is relatively quick. I wish to depose the elder and elevate the younger, but that would offend law and ritual. If I uphold the elder, I fear Lady Cai’s clan will hold full command over military affairs and in time create disorder. Thus I have not resolved myself.”

Liu Bei said, “From ancient times, deposing the elder for the younger has been a route to chaos. If you fear Cai authority, reduce it gradually, but do not spoil yourself by enthroning the younger.”

Liu Biao was silent.

In fact, Lady Cai had long suspected Liu Bei, and whenever he and Liu Biao discussed matters, she always came and listened behind the screen. At this moment she was indeed behind it and heard Liu Bei’s words. Her heart was deeply resentful.

Liu Bei knew he had spoken badly, and so he rose as if to relieve himself. He saw, too, that flesh had returned to his thighs, and could not help but burst into tears. Shortly he returned to his seat.

Seeing tears on Liu Bei’s face, Liu Biao asked in surprise. Liu Bei sighed deeply and said, “Brother often says he has never left his saddle and my thigh flesh is all gone. For a long time now I have not ridden; flesh has returned in my thighs. Months and years are slipping away, and old age comes toward me while accomplishments are not built. This is what makes me mourn.”

Liu Biao replied, “I have heard that your younger self at Xu drank wine with Cao Cao, and he spoke with you of heroes. You named all the renowned men of the age, and Cao Cao allowed none, only saying, ‘Among the heroes of the age, only my lord and Cao Cao stand foremost.’ Even with Cao Cao’s power, he would still not place himself before you. Why would you fear that achievement is not for you?”

With drink on his breath, Liu Bei blurted, “If I have any real merit, those lesser men under heaven need not be worried about me.”

Liu Biao went silent at these words.

Liu Bei knew he had misspoken and pretended drunkenness to rise and go back to his quarters to rest.

Later people made a poem praising Liu Bei:

Cao Gong counted his fingers from the beginning and found that under heaven among heroes there was only you. Even my thigh flesh has returned, and I still lament; why should he not still strive to keep all under heaven from being divided three ways?

Later that day, Liu Biao heard Liu Bei’s words. His mouth said nothing, but his heart was not at ease. After sending Liu Bei away, he withdrew into the inner hall.

Lady Cai said, “I just heard him behind the screen. Liu Bei looked down on me, and by that I can see he intends to seize Jing Province. If we do not remove him now, he will be a trouble for the future.”

Liu Biao gave no answer and only shook his head.

So Lady Cai privately summoned Cai Mao and together they discussed the matter. Cai Mao said, “First, have him killed in his lodgings, then report it to our lord.”

Lady Cai agreed. Cai Mao left and raised troops that same night.

Liu Bei sat by his lamp in his lodgings and only after the third watch wanted to retire for the night when a man knocked at the door and entered. It was Yi Ji. Yi Ji had learned Cai Mao’s plot and had come in the middle of night to report it.

Yi Ji immediately told Liu Bei of Cai Mao’s plot and urged him to leave at once.

Liu Bei said, “I have not yet paid my farewell to Master Jingsheng. How can I leave at once?”

Yi Ji answered, “If you do not leave, Master, Cai Mao will surely kill you.”

Liu Bei thanked him, then hurriedly called his attendants and had them all mount.

Before dawn, he rode through the night back to Xinye. By the time Cai Mao arrived with troops at the lodgings, Liu Bei had already gone far.

Cai Mao regretted it too late and wrote a poem on the wall, then went directly in to see Liu Biao:

“Liu Bei means rebellion and has hung up a rebel poem on the wall. He has departed without leaving. Master, he is intent on treason,” he reported.

Liu Biao did not believe him. He himself came to the lodgings, and there was indeed a poem of four lines. It read:

For years I merely guarded the hardships, looking into old mountains and rivers in vain. Is a dragon a thing of a pond; can it ride a thunderbolt and rise toward heaven?

Liu Biao, seeing the poem, became enraged and drew his sword, saying, “I swear to kill this treacherous man!” He took a few steps, then suddenly thought soberly: “I have lived with Liu Bei for a long time and never saw him write poetry. This must be a scheme to incite discord.”

He returned, entered the lodgings, used his sword tip to scrape the poem off the wall, cast the sword back on the saddle, and mounted.

Cai Mao begged, “The soldiers are already lined up. We can go now and seize Liu Bei at Xinye.”

Liu Biao said, “Not yet. Do not act hastily; let this be handled with further thought.”

Cai Mao saw that Liu Biao delayed and hesitated, so he secretly advised with Lady Cai. That very day he assembled the senior officers at Xiangyang and planned there. The next day he informed Liu Biao, “There has been a bountiful harvest this year. Let us gather all the officials at Xiangyang to show them favor. I beg the lord to join the proceedings personally.”

Liu Biao replied, “Lately I have had what I think is a chest illness and truly I cannot travel. Let the two sons receive and host the guests.”

Cai Mao said, “The sons are young and may fail in ceremony.”

Liu Biao said, “Then ask Liu Bei to come to Xiangyang and host the guests.”

Cai Mao was secretly pleased that this struck his plan true and sent word for Liu Bei to come to Xiangyang.

Liu Bei hurried back to Xinye and knew that by his own mistaken words he had invited danger. Yet he did not speak of this to everyone. Soon an envoy arrived requesting his attendance in Xiangyang.

Sun Qian said, “Yesterday when I saw the lord return in such haste, he seemed not well in spirit. I suspect this is the beginning of trouble in Jing Province. To be suddenly invited now, we should not go lightly.”

Liu Bei had only just told the men the matter before. Zhang Fei said, “You doubt your own tongue from earlier. Liu of Jing has no intent to punish. Do not take outsiders’ words as true. Xiangyang is not far from here. If you fail to go, suspicion will rise in Jing Province.”

Zhao Yun said, “I will take three hundred cavalry and accompany you so that your safety may be secured.”

Liu Bei said, “This is good.” He and Zhao Yun then went to Xiangyang that day.

Cai Mao came out beyond the gate to receive him with deep courtesy. Behind him came Liu Qi and Liu Cong and a group of civil and military officials.

When Liu Bei saw both princely sons present, he did not suspect treachery.

That day Liu Biao asked Liu Bei to rest temporarily in the guest house, while Zhao Yun led three hundred troops to circle him in protection. Zhao Yun wore armor, hung his sword at his side, and moved with never leaving Liu Bei.

Liu Qi told Liu Bei, “My father has chest illness and cannot move. He has asked his uncle to receive guests and to urge the commanders from the counties and commanderies to carry out proper measures.”

Liu Bei replied, “I am not deserving of such a post. Since my older brother commands, I dare not refuse.”

The next day, officials from nine commanderies and forty-two counties had all arrived in attendance. Cai Mao had already asked Kui Yue to plan with him:

“Liu Bei is a mighty hawk among the age, and if he remains long in these lands he will become dangerous. He can be removed today.”

Kui Yue said, “I fear it will lose the confidence of the people.”

Cai Mao replied, “I already have a copy of Liu Biao’s words in this matter.”

Kui Yue said, “If so, make preparations in advance.”

Cai Mao said, “At Dongmen Xianshan we have ordered my brother Cai He to guard with troops. At the south gate outside we have ordered Cai Zhong to guard. At the north gate outside we have ordered Cai Xun to guard. The west gate need not be guarded: there is Tan Creek ahead, and even a host of tens of thousands cannot cross it easily.”

Kui Yue said, “I have seen Zhao Yun move never apart from Liu Bei. It will be difficult to take him.”

Cai Mao said, “I have five hundred troops quietly inside the city prepared.”

Kui Yue said, “Set out separate seats for Wen Pi and Wang Wei in the outer hall and have them wait for the military officers. Invite Zhao Yun first to take his seat, and only then may we act.”

Cai Mao accepted.

That day they slaughtered cattle and horses and set a grand banquet. Liu Bei arrived at the prefectural office on the Di Lu horse; he ordered it led into the rear courtyard and tethered. All the officers gathered in the hall. Liu Bei presided; Liu Qi and Liu Cong sat on either side, others in order.

Zhao Yun, with sword drawn, stood at Liu Bei’s side. Wen Pi and Wang Wei entered and asked Zhao Yun to join the banquet. Zhao Yun refused.

Liu Bei ordered him to take a seat, and Zhao Yun reluctantly obeyed and came out.

Cai Mao had brought an iron tub and something alike from outside and had it set up; he ordered Liu Bei’s three hundred guards to return to the guest house to await, so that at the height of wine they could make their move.

When the wine had made three rounds, Yi Ji lifted the cup and brought it before Liu Bei. He looked at Liu Bei with his eyes and said in a low voice, “Please change your clothing.”

Liu Bei understood at once and rose as if to relieve himself. As soon as Yi Ji had set down the cup, he ran into the rear garden and met Liu Bei, whispering in his ear: “Cai Mao has planned to kill you. On the east, south, and north outside the city there are troops stationed. Only the west gate remains open. You must flee at once!”

Liu Bei was greatly startled. He quickly broke the Di Lu horse, opened the rear garden gate, and pulled it out. He vaulted on the horse without regard for attendants and rode one horse toward the west gate. The gate sentry asked something, but Liu Bei gave no answer, only striking with his goad and leaving.

The gate attendant could not stop him and immediately reported to Cai Mao. Cai Mao mounted and led five hundred soldiers after him in pursuit.

Liu Bei burst out past the west gate and rode on for many li until a great stream blocked his road. That was Tan Creek, several yards wide, with water flowing into the Xiang River and swift current. When Liu Bei reached its bank and found he could not cross, he reined in and turned back. He looked far off to see a mass of dust rising in the west of the city; the pursuit was nearly there.

Liu Bei said, “I die today!” He turned the horse to the creek. Looking back, he saw pursuers still near.

In panic, he spurred into the creek. After only a few strides, the front hooves of the horse sank and his sleeves and robes became wet. He shouted with all his force, “Di Lu! Di Lu! Today, you ruin me!”

When he had uttered the words, the horse rose out of the water as if from the bottom, leapt three zhang high, and climbed the west bank.

As if rising from cloud and fog, Liu Bei escaped.

Later Scholar Su wrote an old-style poem solely on Liu Bei’s horse-leaping at Tan Creek. It ran:

Greying blossoms fall as spring’s dusk comes, and a guest-officer by accident reaches the road to Tan Creek. He halts the horse and stares afar, lingering alone while red petals drift down in air. Secretly he imagines Xianyang’s fire-luck withers; dragon and tiger wrestle and hold each other fast. At Xiangyang the prince gathers men for wine; in the hall Liu Bei stood near death. In flight for life he goes out only through the west gate, while from behind the horsemen give chase. Along the misted, swollen waters of Tan Creek he cried out and drove the riders ahead to leap. Hooves shattered turquoise-green glass as the sky wind roared; in that ringing he swung his golden whip. All he heard about his ears was a thousand riders running; in the water at once he saw twin dragons take wing. In the western lands, one true lord of valiant power—there he met the dragon mare and the hero lord. Tan Creek water runs eastward; where now is that heroic lord of the dragon horse? Looking at the stream he sighed three times, his heart turning bitter; slanting sunlight shone on empty mountains. The three-part tripodal power is but a dream-like vision; only traces remain in the world.

Liu Bei leapt past the creek to the west bank and looked back toward the east bank, where Cai Mao had already brought troops to the stream. Cai Mao shouted, “Why did you leave the feast and flee?”

Liu Bei answered, “I have no enmity with you. Why do you wish me harm?”

Cai Mao said, “I have no such thought. My lord, do not listen to others.”

Seeing Cai Mao reach for bow and arrow, Liu Bei at once turned and urged the horse toward the southwest.

Cai Mao said to those around him, “What spirit aided him!” He was about to pull his troops back to the city, when he saw Zhao Yun rushing in from the west gate with three hundred soldiers.

Then it was said:

The leaping dragon-horse saved its lord. The pursuing tiger-general came on to exact revenge. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Lady Cai Eavesdropped Behind a Screen, and Liu, the Imperial Uncle, Leapt His Horse Across Tan Creek

chapters.html:
Liu Bei meets a reclusive figure in South Nanzhang.
Dan Fu meets a worthy lord in Xinye.

Yet as Cai Mao was about to return to the city, Zhao Yun drove troops out of it.
Zhao Yun had been drinking when he suddenly noticed men and horses in motion, so he hurried inside to investigate. Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, was no longer at the seat. He was greatly startled. He rushed out to the inn and heard someone say, “Cai Mao has taken the troops westward.” Yun, in haste, snatched up his spear and mounted, leading three hundred soldiers he had brought with him. He galloped out the West Gate and met Cai Mao head-on. “Where is my lord?” he demanded.

“Your lord left the banquet in haste and disappeared. I do not know where he has gone,” Cai Mao replied.

Zhao Yun was meticulous and never hasty, so he kept his horse moving forward. From a distance he looked toward the great creek, saw no path of escape, and turned his horse back. “You invited my lord to a banquet,” he called. “Why did you come chasing with an armed force?”
“The officials from nine provinces and forty-two counties are all here,” Cai Mao replied. “As chief commander, how could I fail to give protection?”

“Where have you driven my lord to?” Yun asked.

“I heard His Lordship rode out the West Gate alone on a single horse,” Cai Mao said, “and then was no longer to be seen at this place.”

Zhao Yun was uncertain and alarmed. He had gone down to the creek and looked there himself and saw only a broad line of disturbed water on the far bank. “Could he have leapt with his horse across the creek?” he thought in silence. He ordered the three hundred to spread out and search, but no trace was found.
When he rode back, Cai Mao had already returned to the city. Yun seized a gate soldier and asked, and all said that Lord Liu had ridden out alone through the West Gate. He wanted to enter again, but fearing an ambush, he hurriedly brought the troops back to Xinye.

Liu Bei meanwhile had leapt his horse across the creek as if drunk and dazed, thinking: to clear such a broad ravine in one bound—was this not Heaven’s will? He proceeded slowly along Nanzhang, riding southward as the sun sank west.

While he was still on the road, he saw a shepherd boy riding astride a bull, blowing a short flute as he came. Liu Bei sighed, “I am no match for him.” He pulled up and watched. The boy stopped playing, turned the flute aside, and studied him closely.

“General, are you not Liu Bei, the one who crushed the Yellow Turbans?” the boy asked.

Liu Bei asked in surprise, “You are a village child. How do you know my surname and name?”

The boy said, “I did not know before. But whenever our master receives guests, many have spoken of a man named Liu Bei: tall about seven chi and five cun, with drooping hands past the knees, and eyes that can see his own ears. He is a hero of this age. Seeing you now, it must be he.”

Liu Bei said, “Who is your master?”

The boy replied, “My master’s family name is Sima. His given name is Hui, and his courtesy name is Decao. He comes from Yingchuan. People call him Master Water Mirror.”

Liu Bei asked, “Whom does your master count as friends?”

The boy said, “A Pang Degong and Pang Tong in Xiangyang.”

Liu Bei asked, “Who is this Pang Degong?”

“An uncle and nephew,” said the boy. “Pang Degong’s courtesy name is Shanmin; he is ten years older than my master. Pang Tong’s courtesy name is Shiyuan; he is five years younger. Once, my master was collecting mulberry leaves in a tree when Pang Tong happened to visit. The two sat under the tree and talked the whole day without tiring. My master loves Pang Tong deeply and calls him his younger brother.”

Liu Bei asked, “Where is your master now?”

The boy pointed toward the woods ahead. “There, in that grove, is his manor.”

Liu Bei said, “I am Liu Bei. Take me to your master so I can pay him my respects.”

The boy led him on. After more than two li they dismounted at the gate, entered the courtyard, and reached the inner gate. They heard exquisite zither music. Liu Bei told the boy to hold off the announcement and listened. The music stopped abruptly. A man laughed and came out.

“The tune of the zither was clear and pure,” he said. “Yet within it rose strains of high, penetrating force. There must have been a hero eavesdropping.”
The boy pointed at Liu Bei: “This is my master, Master Water Mirror.”

Liu Bei looked at him and saw a tall, upright body with a crane-like frame and a bearing beyond compare. He hurried forward and paid his respects, though his robe was still damp at the collar.

“Lord,” the master said, “you have escaped great peril today.”

Liu Bei was astonished.

The boy added, “This is Liu Bei.”

Master Water Mirror invited him into the thatched pavilion and seated guest and host. Liu Bei saw shelves piled with books, and outside the windows thickly planted pines and bamboos. A zither and chessboard stood on the stone bed, and an elegant fragrance floated about.

Water Mirror asked, “My lord, where do you come from?”

Liu Bei replied, “I passed this way by chance. Since your boy pointed me here, I have gained a chance to pay my respects and am deeply happy.”

Master Water Mirror smiled. “My lord, do not hide it. You are certain to have fled disaster and come here.”

Liu Bei told him about the affair at Xiangyang.

Water Mirror said, “From your color and presence I already understood.”

He asked, “For a long time I have heard of your reputation. Why are you still so poor and unrewarded?”

Liu Bei said, “My road has long been full of twists. That is why I am here.”

Water Mirror said, “Not so. It is because the men around the general are not the right men.”

Liu Bei answered, “Though I am limited, I have Sun Qian, Mi Zhu, and Jian Yong in civil matters and Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Zhao Yun in war. They are loyal and support me to the utmost. I owe much to their strength.”

Water Mirror said, “Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Zhao Yun are each worth ten thousand men, but no master can use them well. Men like Sun Qian and Mi Zhu are white-faced scholars, not strategists fit to govern and save the age.”

Liu Bei said, “I have often sought the worthy hidden in valleys and hills, but I have not yet met them.”

Water Mirror said, “Did you not hear what Confucius said: ‘In every town with ten households, there is at least one who is loyal and truthful’? How can you say there are none?”

Liu Bei replied, “I am ignorant. I would welcome instruction.”

Water Mirror said, “Have you heard the saying in the counties of Jing and Xiang?”

Liu Bei said, “No.”

Water Mirror recited:

“In the eighth and ninth years things first begin to decline;
by the thirteenth there is no one left.
In the end Heaven’s mandate returns to its home,
and the coiled dragon from the mud soars toward the sky.”

“This saying began at the start of Jian’an. In Jian’an eight, Liu Jingsheng lost his former wife and disorder came to his household—this is what is meant by ‘beginnings decline.’ ‘No one left’ means that Liu Jingsheng was about to die, and his civil and military retainers scattered with none left behind. As for ‘Heaven’s mandate returns’ and ‘the dragon rises from the mud,’ these point to the general.”

Liu Bei was startled and grateful. “I dare not presume I could receive such as this!”

Water Mirror said, “All the extraordinary talent under Heaven is concentrated in this one man. You must go and seek him.”

Liu Bei urgently asked, “Where is this singular talent? Who is he?”

Water Mirror clapped his hands and laughed. “Good! Good!”

When Liu Bei asked again, Water Mirror said, “If you can obtain one of the pair, the country can be set at peace: Fulong and Fengchui.”

Liu Bei asked, “Who are Fulong and Fengchui?”

Water Mirror laughed broadly and twice said, “Good! Good!”

Liu Bei asked yet again. Water Mirror said, “Night has fallen. Let the general stay here for one night. Tomorrow he shall hear the full answer.” He ordered the boy to prepare wine and dishes, and had the horses led to the rear yard to be fed.

After Liu Bei finished dinner, he stayed the night in the side of the pavilion. He could not sleep, thinking over what Water Mirror had said. Late in the night, he heard a knock and saw someone enter. Water Mirror asked, “What brings Yuan Zhi?”

Liu Bei rose and listened carefully. The man answered, “I have long heard that Liu Jingsheng, though he distinguishes between right and wrong, does not know how to use what is right, and though he knows evil, he cannot remove it. So I left him by letter and came here.”

Water Mirror said, “My lord has talent to stabilize the realm; you should choose men carefully and enter service. Why go personally to present yourself to Jingsheng? Heroic heroes are before your eyes, but you do not recognize them yourself.”

The man replied, “What my lord says is true.”

Liu Bei listened with joy and thought this must be one of Fulong and Fengchui, so he wished to step out and meet him, yet feared to act in haste. At dawn he asked Water Mirror who had come in the night.

Water Mirror said, “He is my friend.”

Liu Bei begged to be introduced. Water Mirror replied, “This man seeks to serve a great lord and has already gone to another place.”

Liu Bei asked again for his name. Water Mirror only laughed and repeated, “Good! Good!”

Liu Bei again asked, “So are Fulong and Fengchui the same men?”

Water Mirror answered only with, “Good! Good!”

Liu Bei implored, “Master, leave the mountains and aid me. Help me uphold the Han court together.”

Water Mirror said, “I am a reclusive man, given to life in field and mountain; I cannot be used by the world. There will be someone ten times better than I to assist you. You should go and seek him.”

While they were still speaking, someone outside the estate shouted and horses whinnied. A boy came to report, “A general and several hundred men have come to the estate.”

Liu Bei was greatly startled and stepped out; it was Zhao Yun. Liu Bei rejoiced.

Zhao Yun dismounted and entered, saying, “I returned to the county the other night and could not find my lord. I tracked him through the night and came here. My lord should return the county quickly. I fear men may come to slaughter there.”

Liu Bei thanked Water Mirror and departed with Zhao Yun, mounting to ride back to Xinye.

After going not far, a force arrived and turned out to be Guan Yu (Yunchang) and Zhang Fei (Yide). They rejoiced at meeting each other. Liu Bei explained how he had leapt the creek at Tanxi. All shared in wonder and regret.

Back in the county he conferred with Sun Qian and others.

Sun Qian said, “First send a letter to Jingsheng to report this matter.”

Liu Bei followed that counsel and ordered Sun Qian to carry the letter to Jing Province.
Liu Biao summoned him and asked, “I invited Liu Bei to meet in Xiangyang. Why did he flee the banquet?”

Sun Qian presented the letter. It stated clearly that Cai Mao had plotted to harm him and that Liu Bei had escaped only by leaping Tanxi. Liu Biao was furious and immediately ordered Cai Mao brought out and executed.

Cai’s wife came out and wept to spare him from death, but Liu Biao’s anger had not yet cooled. Sun Qian said, “If you kill Cai Mao, Imperial Uncle will never rest in this place.” Liu Biao then held him to account, blamed him, and finally released him, sending his eldest son Liu Qi and Sun Qian to Liu Bei with an apology.

Liu Qi arrived and carried out the order. Liu Bei received him and held a feast.

When the wine grew deep, Liu Qi suddenly burst into tears. Liu Bei asked why.

Liu Qi said, “Lady Cai has always harbored intent to harm him. As her nephew I have no way to avert the calamity. I am fortunate my uncle has taught me.”

Liu Bei urged him, “Keep dutiful devotion carefully, and naturally there will be no danger.”

The next day Liu Qi took leave in tears.

Liu Bei rode out of the city gate with him, and as he looked toward the horse he said, “If not for this horse, I would now be beneath the earth.”

Liu Qi replied, “It is not the horse’s strength; it is your uncle’s great good fortune.”

After parting, Liu Qi wept and returned. Liu Bei rode back into the city.

As he entered, he saw a man in the market wearing a coarse cap and hemp robe, black cord and dark leather boots, singing loudly:

The world turns and turns, and the fire is near to dying.
A grand hall begins to collapse; one beam cannot hold it.
The worthy in valleys and hills wish to offer themselves to a bright lord.
The bright lord seeks the worthy and does not know me.

Liu Bei silently thought, “Could this be one of the Fulong or Fengchui that Water Mirror spoke of?” He dismounted, approached, and brought him into the county yamen for questioning.

He asked his name. The man answered, “I am a man of Ying. My surname is Dan, my given name Fu. I have long heard that my lord receives men and recruits worthies, and I came to entrust myself here, but did not dare to enter directly. So I sang in the market to draw your honored hearing.”

Liu Bei was very pleased and treated him as a guest of honor.

Dan Fu said, “Your horse, which your lord has ridden, I ask to see once more.”

Liu Bei ordered its reins loosened and brought it beneath the hall. Dan Fu said, “Is this not a Dilu horse? Though it is a thousand-li horse, it hinders the lord and should not be ridden.”

Liu Bei said, “I have already made use of it.” He then explained the leap at Tanxi.

Dan Fu said, “This is a horse that saved your lord, not one that harmed him. It will certainly hinder another lord. There is a way to avert that.”

Liu Bei asked, “I would hear the way to avert it.”

Dan Fu replied, “If there is someone in your heart who bears you a grudge, give this horse to him. After this one is barred, then ride it again and there will be no mishap.”

Liu Bei’s face changed as he listened. “When you first came here, you did not teach me the righteous way, but now you counsel a practice of harming another for selfish gain. I dare not follow it.”

Dan Fu smiled and bowed in thanks. “I had heard that my lord had a reputation for benevolence, and so I did not dare to trust it fully at once. I spoke this only to test you.”

Liu Bei at once changed expression and thanked him. “I am not one who can claim mercy and benevolence toward others; it is my teacher who has taught it.”

Dan Fu said, “Since I came from Ying, I have heard the people of Xinye sing: ‘In Xinye live the pastoral officer, Liu the Imperial Uncle. Since he came here, the people are plenty and rich.’ It is proof of my lord’s benevolence and kindness.”

Liu Bei appointed Dan Fu as military adviser and organized training for the main force.

Later, Cao Cao returned from Ji Province to Xuchang. He often had intent to seize Jing Province, so he sent Cao Ren, Li Dian, and the defected commanders Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang with thirty thousand troops to hold Fan City, watch Jingxiang, and test conditions.

Lü Kuang and Lü Xiang reported to Cao Ren, “Liu Bei is now encamped in Xinye. He is recruiting soldiers and buying horses, storing grass and grain. His intent is not small, and it cannot be left unexamined. Since we both have not earned even a foot of merit since we submitted to the Chancellor, we ask for five thousand picked troops to take Liu Bei’s head and offer it to the Chancellor.”

Cao Ren rejoiced and, with the two Lü men and five thousand men, marched toward Xinye to engage them.

An envoy brought news to Liu Bei. He consulted Dan Fu.

Dan Fu said, “Since enemy troops have already arrived, do not let them enter the territory. Send Guan Yu with one force out to the left to cut them in the road of their approach. Send Zhang Fei with one force to the right to strike at their rear. The general should lead Zhao Yun out ahead of the vanguard to meet them first. Their force can be broken.”

Liu Bei did as he said. He had Guan and Zhang set out and then, with Dan Fu, Zhao Yun, and others, led two thousand horse and men out through the gate to meet them.

After only a short distance, dust billowed behind a mountain and the two Lü took command near the front. They aligned both battle lines.

Liu Bei rode into the flag gate and shouted, “Who comes? Who dares to violate my borders?”

Lü Kuang rode out and said, “I am Great General Lü Kuang, and by order of the Chancellor I have come to seize you.”

Liu Bei grew angry and sent out Zhao Yun. The two commanders fought not for long; in one lance thrust Zhao Yun struck Lü Kuang under the horse.

Liu Bei signaled his troops to surround and kill. Lü Xiang could not withstand the pressure and withdrew in disorder.

As they pressed onward, a force burst from the roadside. At its head was a great commander: Guan Yu. It split the formation in one charge. Lü Xiang lost over half of his men and broke through to escape.

Before they had gone ten li, another force blocked the road again. Its leading commander raised his spear and shouted, “Zhang Yide is here!”

He drove straight at Lü Xiang, who was caught unprepared, and Zhang Fei thrust him once through with a spear. Lü Xiang turned and fell from the horse, dead. The rest scattered in flight.

Liu Bei gathered and pursued. Most of them were captured.

Liu Bei returned to the county, gave ample reward to Dan Fu, and honored the troops.

The defeated troops reported to Cao Ren. They said both Lü men had been killed and many soldiers captured alive. Cao Ren was greatly startled and spoke with Li Dian. Li Dian said, “The two commanders were lost while engaging the enemy. Now we should hold position and report first to the Chancellor, then bring out large forces for an exterminating campaign. That is the best course.”

Cao Ren said, “No. Two commanders are dead and many troops are lost; this feud cannot wait to be answered. If Xinye is only a small territory no larger than a handful of bullets, why must I summon the Chancellor’s great army?”

Li Dian said, “Liu Bei is a person of outstanding talent. He should not be underestimated.”

Cao Ren replied, “Are you fearful?”

Li Dian said, “The Art of War says, ‘Know the enemy and know yourself, and you will be victorious in a hundred battles.’ I am not afraid of fighting, only fearful that we may not surely win.”

Cao Ren grew angry. “Do you have divided loyalty? I will take Liu Bei alive if I can.”

Li Dian said, “If the general goes, I will hold Fan City.”

“If you do not follow me,” Cao Ren said, “then you truly harbor divided loyalty.”

Unable to refuse, Li Dian agreed. Cao Ren raised twenty-five thousand horse and troops, crossed the river, and rode toward Xinye.

Thus it was said:

The attached contingent has already borne the shame of a litter-bound corpse,
And the main general rises again to lead troops and avenge the disgrace.
