How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Liu Bei Meets a Recluse in South Nanzhang, Dan Fu Meets the Hero-Lord in Xinye

chapters.html:
Then Cao Ren, furious, raised the whole of his own force and crossed the river by night, intending to trample down Xinye.
At that time Dan Fu had returned from a victory, and he said to Liu Bei: “Cao Ren has stationed his army at Fan City. Now that he knows the two generals have been executed, he will surely bring a large force to fight.”
Liu Bei asked, “How should we meet him?”
Dan Fu replied, “If he brings out all his soldiers, Fan City will be empty. We can strike then.”
Liu Bei asked for a stratagem, and Dan Fu leaned in and whispered the plan to him in detail. Liu Bei was overjoyed; he had already prepared in advance.
Suddenly a scouting horse arrived: “Cao Ren has crossed the river with a large army.”
Dan Fu said, “It is just as I predicted.” He then asked Liu Bei to lead out the troops to meet him.

The two formations faced one another. Liu Bei sent Zhao Yun out to call across to the opposing commander for words.
Cao Ren ordered Li Dian to form the front line, where he crossed spears with Zhao Yun. After ten or more bouts, Li Dian judged that their enemy force was too strong and reined his horse back into the ranks.
Zhao Yun spurred his horse in pursuit. Their two wings closed up, then both sides drew back and returned to camp.

Returning to Cao Ren, Li Dian said, “That enemy is all chosen soldiers; we must not treat it lightly. It would be better to fall back to Fan City.”
Cao Ren was furious. “You already weakened the army’s spirit before we were in battle, and now you ran from the line. The crime deserves execution.” He ordered the executioner and the axe-men to bring Li Dian out to behead him. The generals interceded so fiercely that only then was he spared.
He reassigned Li Dian to command the rear and led the troops forward himself.

The next day he beat the war drums and advanced the army, forming an array. He sent to Liu Bei: “Can you read my array?”

Dan Fu climbed to high ground and looked closely before saying, “This is the Eight-Gate Golden-Lock Formation. Its gates are Rest, Life, Harm, Obstruction, Splendor, Death, Alarm, and Opening. From Life Gate, Splendor Gate, or Opening Gate is auspicious; from Harm Gate, Alarm Gate, or Rest Gate, one is wounded; from Obstruction Gate or Death Gate, one is lost. Today the eight gates are set in perfect order, but the center still lacks a controller. If you strike through the Life Gate at the southeast corner and pass out through the west Splendor Gate, the formation will break.”

Liu Bei issued orders for the front to hold the gates of the array and told Zhao Yun to lead five hundred men in through the southeast, straight westward to break out.
Zhao Yun obeyed. He stood upright in the saddle, leapt forward, and with raised spear and horse dashed toward the southeast corner, crying out, then drove into the center. Cao Ren immediately turned northward in retreat.
Zhao Yun did not give chase. Instead he burst out through the west gate and then circled, coming back through the southeast corner from the west. Cao Ren’s army became a rout.

Liu Bei waved his troops forward in a renewed assault, and Cao’s soldiers suffered a crushing defeat and withdrew. Dan Fu ordered that pursuit cease, then gathered his men and withdrew homeward.

After losing that engagement, Cao Ren at last believed Li Dian’s warning. He again asked Li Dian to counsel him and said, “Liu Bei certainly has outstanding men with him; he has still broken my formation.”
Li Dian replied, “Though I stand here, I still fear for Fan City.”
“Tonight we raid the camp,” Cao Ren said. “If we win, we can discuss plans. If we fail, we will retreat and return to Fan City.”
Li Dian said, “No, we cannot. Liu Bei will be ready for us.”
Cao Ren snapped, “If you are always so suspicious, how should a man do battle?” He refused Li Dian’s advice. He led the troops in the front rank and made Li Dian the rearguard. They were to raid the camp at the second watch of the night.

Meanwhile Dan Fu and Liu Bei were still discussing matters in camp when a sudden gale rose.
Dan Fu said, “Tonight Cao Ren is surely coming to raid the camp.”
Liu Bei asked, “Why do you say so?”
Dan Fu smiled. “I have already made my reckoning.” He quietly apportioned their defenses in secret.
By the second watch, Cao Ren’s troops had drawn near the camp. They saw fires flaring around all sides of the stockade, the fences already burned. Cao Ren knew there had been preparation and ordered immediate withdrawal.

Zhao Yun’s men killed those coming too near. Cao Ren could not withdraw his whole force and return to camp in time and fled toward the north bank of the river. Reaching the bank, he tried to find a boat to cross, but a band of soldiers had already arrived on the bank. At their head was none other than Zhang Fei.
Cao Ren fought desperately. Li Dian protected him while he boarded and crossed. A great part of Cao’s force drowned in the water.

Crossing over, Cao Ren reached the bank and ran to Fan City to call the gate. A drum sounded on the wall, and one general rode out with troops and shouted, “I have held Fan City for long already!”
Everyone stared in astonishment; it was Guan Yu. Cao Ren was shocked and whipped his horse into flight. Guan Yu chased and cut down men around him. Cao Ren lost yet more horses and in the night rode for Xuchang. On the road he learned that Dan Fu had served as their strategist and had laid this plan in advance.

Nothing need be said of Cao Ren’s defeat as he withdrew to Xuchang.
Meanwhile Liu Bei had achieved a complete victory and brought his army into Fan City. The county magistrate Liu Bi came out to welcome him. Liu Bei pacified the local households quickly.

Liu Bi was from Changsha and a relative of the Han court. He invited Liu Bei home and served him a feast.
A man standing at his side caught Liu Bei’s eye by his commanding presence, so Liu Bei asked Bi who he was.
Bi said, “That is my nephew Kou Feng, son of the former Lord of Luo, Kou. Both his parents died, so he depends on us here.”
Liu Bei grew fond of him and wished to adopt him as a formal son. Liu Bi gladly agreed, and Kou Feng knelt to Liu Bei as father. Liu Bei gave him the new name Liu Feng, then brought him back and ordered him to call Guan Yu and Zhang Fei his uncles.

Guan Yu said, “My lord already has a son; why adopt this moth of a man? Disorder may come after.”
Liu Bei answered, “I will treat him as my son, and he must serve me as if I were his father. How could trouble come from that?”
Guan Yu was displeased.
Liu Bei consulted with Dan Fu and ordered Zhao Yun to lead a thousand men to guard Fan City. Then he led the rest back to Xinye.

Cao Ren and Li Dian returned to Xuchang and, kneeling on the earth before Cao Cao, sought forgiveness. They reported the losses in full.
Cao Cao said, “Victory and defeat are ordinary in war, but tell me: who devised strategy for Liu Bei?”

Li Dian said it was Dan Fu.
Cheng Yu smiled. “It is not Dan Fu. This man, as a child, loved study and swordplay. In the later years of Zhongping, he once avenged a blood debt by killing a man and then fled with hair wild and face smeared. Caught by the authorities, he would not give his name. The officers bound him to a cart and dragged him through the marketplace with drums, calling on the townsfolk to identify him. None dared to speak, though some did know him. A companion secretly freed him; he changed his name and escaped, then humbled himself and sought out great teachers. He once even debated with Sima Hui. He is indeed Xu Shu of Yingchuan, courtesy name Yuanzhi. Dan Fu is just his assumed name.”

Cao Cao asked, “How does Xu Shu’s talent compare with yours?”
Cheng Yu said, “Ten times yours.”
Cao Cao sighed. “It is a pity that such a worthy man has gone to Liu Bei. He has acquired both wings and feathers; how can we lose him?”
Cheng Yu said, “If Xu Shu is truly there, your request would easily bring him.”
Cao Cao asked, “How can we get him to come?”
Cheng Yu answered, “Xu Shu is deeply filial. His father is long dead. Only his old mother remains at home. His brother Xu Kang is already gone, and no one tends his mother. If the Chancellor orders her brought to Xuchang and has her write to him, Xu Shu will have no choice but to come.”

Cao Cao rejoiced and sent men through the night to fetch Xu Shu’s mother. Within a day they brought her. He honored her with proper care and said, “I have heard of you, Xu Yuanzhi, and know you are a singular talent under heaven. Now you are in Xinye, helping the rebel Liu Bei, turning his back on the court. It is like fine jade fallen in mire—truly a pity. Do us this kindness: write to him and call him back to Xuchang, and I will petition the Son of Heaven to grant you rich rewards.”

He then ordered attendants to bring the four pieces of the scholar’s studio and made his mother write. She asked, “What sort of man is Liu Bei?”
Cao Cao answered, “A small man of Pei Commandery, one who brazenly calls himself imperial uncle, without faith or righteousness. He looks like a cultured gentleman but is a petty man at heart.”
Xu’s mother shouted back, “How deeply you lie! I have long heard that Liu Bei is of the line of King Jing of Zhongshan, grandson of Emperor Wen, and his reputation for courtesy and humanity is already well known. Men of every rank—the yellow-haired boy, the gray-haired elder, the village steward, the woodcutter—know his name. He is truly a hero of this age. My son chose to assist him and found a worthy lord. You may wear the title of Chancellor of Han, but you are a bandit of Han in deed. Yet you dare call Liu Bei a rebel and seek to force my son from light into darkness. How could you not be ashamed?”

After she spoke, she took up a stone inkstone and struck Cao Cao.
Cao Cao, angry, ordered soldiers to seize her and bring her out to execution. Cheng Yu hurried him to stop.
He remonstrated, “Xu’s mother has offended the Chancellor; she invites death by her own act. If Your Lordship kills her, you win a reputation for injustice and her virtue will only be greater. Once she is dead, Xu Shu will surely die to avenge the wrong with Liu Bei. Better to keep her alive: then Xu Shu will be divided between heart and duty; even if he aids Liu Bei, he will not give his full strength. If she remains safe, I can still devise a way to bring Xu Shu here.”

So Cao Cao heeded him and spared her life, placing her in a separate room to be cared for.
Cheng Yu visited daily, falsely saying he had sworn brotherhood with Xu Shu and treated her as his own mother. He always sent gifts and included a written note by hand. She too began writing replies with hand-signed notes.
Cheng Yu used her handwriting to copy a family letter, forged in her hand, then sent a trusted officer with it straight to Xinye to ask for Dan Fu.

At Liu Bei’s camp, the officer asked for Dan Fu. The sentry brought Xu Shu out. Seeing that his mother had a family letter, Xu Shu called him in immediately.
The messenger said, “I am a servant from her household. Madam has sent words with this letter.” Xu Shu opened and read:

Your brother Kang has recently died, and there is no one left on earth for me to look to. In this time of grief, I never expected that Chancellor Cao’s men would be sent to bring me to Xuchang, saying you had betrayed him, and that I was confined in chains. If Xu Shu comes in, perhaps I can live. By this letter’s arrival, remember all your care for me and come at once through the night to fulfill filial duty; then afterward I may plan to return and farm our old fields. I will not survive if you do not save me. I have no more to say.

When Xu Shu had finished reading, tears poured down him like springs. He took the letter to Liu Bei and said, “I am Xu Shu of Yingchuan, courtesy name Yuanzhi. I changed my name to Dan Fu when I fled the turmoil. I had heard that Liu Jingsheng had gathered worthy men; I went to visit him. When we spoke, I came to know he was a person of little use. I wrote him a farewell note and at midnight went to Sima’s Water-Mirror manor with that letter, laying out my case.
The master at Water-Mirror severely rebuked me for not knowing my lord and said: ‘Liu Yu Province is here. Why do you not serve him?’ I then acted insane and sang like a madman in the market to move my lord. By Heaven’s favor he did not reject me and soon gave me high command. Only this old mother remains, and now Cao Cao has trapped her as part of a trick to summon me and has her confined, intending harm.
If my old mother has called me home in this way, I cannot in good conscience stay on.”

Liu Bei wept. “Parent and child are joined by nature. Yuanzhi need not think of himself. When we meet with the old lady, perhaps you may receive my guidance again.”
Sun Qian whispered to Liu Bei, “Yuanzhi is a man of extraordinary talent throughout the realm. He has known our camp in full—its strengths and weaknesses. If Cao Cao gains him, he will be used greatly and your danger is plain. Lord, hold him here and do not let him go. If he does not return, Cao Cao will have his mother killed. Learn this: if Yuanzhi learns his mother is dead, he will seek revenge with all his strength.”

Liu Bei answered, “No. To let him go after the king has ordered his mother executed would be cruel; to keep him here and cut him off from his mother and sonly duty would be unjust. I would rather die than commit either cruelty or injustice.” All men were moved by this.

Liu Bei invited Xu Shu to drink. Xu Shu answered, “I have just heard my mother is in custody. Even the finest golden-and-jade wine cannot pass my throat.”
Liu Bei said, “Since I hear you will leave, I feel as though I lose both right and left hands. Even if this wine were made of dragon livers and phoenix marrow, it would still have no taste.”

The two men sat facing each other and wept, waiting together for dawn. The generals had already arranged a farewell banquet outside the outer watch. Liu Bei and Xu Shu rode out together from the city gate and, at a long pavilion, dismounted and said their parting words.

Liu Bei raised his cup and said to Xu Shu, “My affection is shallow, my ties are little; I cannot hold you longer. I beg you now to serve your new lord well and become famous by succeeding.”
Xu Shu wept and said, “My talent is small, my intellect shallow. I owe deep gratitude to you for your favor. It is my misfortune to part in mid-course, but only for my mother’s sake. Even if Cao Cao pressures me, I will never devise a single stratagem for him.”
Liu Bei said, “Once you leave, I too will head far into the mountains and forests.”
Xu Shu replied, “The reason I worked with you on the matter of empire was this small heart within me. My mind is now in ruin because of my mother. Even if I remained, it would help no one. My lord should seek another worthy man to aid him. Why should you be so disheartened?”
Liu Bei answered, “Among this age’s worthies, none surpasses you.”
Xu Shu said, “I am only a poor block of timber and common timber. I do not dare receive such praise.”

As they prepared to part, Xu Shu turned to the generals: “Please all serve my lord well, that your names be remembered on silk and your merit marked in blue histories. Do not follow me in my own failure of constancy.”
None could hide their grief.

Liu Bei could not bear to part and sent him off for a stretch, then sent him off for another. Xu Shu finally begged, “Please do not trouble yourself to see me farther. I will part here.”
Liu Bei reached for his hand in the saddle and said, “When you go now, our destinies are parted beneath different skies. I do not know when we may meet.” His words ended in tears that fell like rain. Xu Shu too wept as they separated.

Liu Bei stayed mounted by a grove and watched Xu Shu ride away with his attendants in haste. He cried, “Yuanzhi is gone. What can I do?” He fixed his eyes on the road, but a screen of trees cut off his sight.
He tapped his whip against a tree trunk and said, “I want to cut down these trees.”
The men asked why.
Liu Bei said, “They block my view of Xu Yuanzhi.”

While he still watched, Xu Shu suddenly turned and came back at speed on horseback.
Liu Bei said, “Yuanzhi returned—does he not wish to stay?” and joyfully rode forward to meet him.
Xu Shu reined in and said, “My mind is in confusion like tangled hemp. I forgot to tell you one thing. There is a remarkable man twenty li west of Xiangyang, at Longzhong. Why not seek him out yourself? If you gain this man, it is no different from Zhou gaining Lü Wang, Han winning Zhang Liang.”

Liu Bei said, “Please, by all means, ask this man to come before me.”
Xu Shu said, “He cannot be dragged here at your command. Your lord should go in person to seek him. If we gain him, it is no different from Zu of Lü Wang and Han’s Zhang Liang.”
Liu Bei asked, “How does he compare with you in talent and virtue?”
Xu Shu said, “Compared with me, it is like a plow-horse beside a qilin, a carrion crow beside a pair of phoenixes. He often compares himself to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi; from where I stand, even Guan and Yue are not his match. He has the talent to measure heaven and map the earth. I think he is one in all under heaven.”

Liu Bei said with joy, “I want to hear his name.”
Xu Shu said, “He is of Langya, Yangdu. His surname is Zhuge, personal name Liang, courtesy name Kongming. He is descended from Zhuge Feng, Commandant of the Metropolitan Censors. His father was Gui, courtesy name Zigong, once the Magistrate of Taishan Commandery. His father died early. Liang lived with his uncle and in time followed old ties to Liu Jingsheng in Jingzhou; he therefore made his home at Xiangyang. After his uncle died, he and his younger brother, Zhuge Jun, returned to till fields by themselves in Nanyang. He was fond of singing old songs in the style of Liang Fu. The place where he resides has a rise called Wolong Hill, and so he calls himself Master Wolong. He is a genius without peer in this age. Your lord should, without delay, alter his route and meet him. If this man will assist, why should the kingdom not be set in order?”
Liu Bei said, “Water-Mirror once told me, ‘If one of Fulong and Fengchu can be gained, the world can be pacified.’ Could this be Fulong and Fengchu in person?”
Xu Shu said, “Fengchu is Pang Tong of Xiangyang. Fulong is indeed Zhuge Kongming.”

Liu Bei exclaimed, “Today I understand those words. How could I have lived blind-eyed if not for your counsel?”

Later generations praised this as the verse Xu Shu wrote when he rode to recommend Zhuge:

Bitter is it to meet such a worthy and never meet one like him again; at the roadside farewell, our two hearts were thick with sorrow.
Yet one brief word, like spring thunder, could awaken the Crouching Dragon of Nanyang.

Xu Shu recommended Kongming, bid Liu Bei farewell, and rode away again.
After Xu Shu’s words, Liu Bei suddenly understood Master Sima’s earlier counsel, as if waking from drunkenness, as if waking from a dream. He returned to Xinye with his men, prepared rich gifts, and sent Guan and Zhang ahead to summon Kongming in Nanyang.

When Xu Shu had left Liu Bei, he remained troubled by how much he had been loved and feared that Kongming might refuse to leave his mountain. So he pressed on in one ride to Wolong Ridge, entered the thatched cottage, and met Kongming.
Kongming asked the reason for his coming.

Xu Shu answered, “I wished to serve Liu Yuzhou. But my mother was seized by Cao Cao, and a letter came summoning me. So I had to leave. Before I went I spoke of you to my lord and praised you. Liu Bei is coming to make his full court before you at once. Please do not turn him away; if you will not reject him, may you display your life’s gifts and lend him your aid.”

Kongming’s face changed as he listened and said, “Do you take me for the sacrificial meat of a feast?” He brushed past with his sleeves and withdrew. Xu Shu, ashamed and embarrassed, turned away and spurred on for Xuchang to see his mother.

Thus it was:

Out of love for one’s lord, I spoke one faithful word,
Rode a thousand li to tend to my grieving heart and mother.
Who can say what comes after this,
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Xuande Takes Fan City by Stratagem; Yuanzhi Rides Off to Recommend Zhuge Liang

chapters.html:
Now Xu Shu hurried toward Xuchang. When Cao Cao heard that Xu Shu had arrived, he ordered Xun Yu, Cheng Yu, and a group of advisers to go out and receive him. Xu Shu entered the Chancellor's residence and made his obeisance before Cao Cao.

Cao Cao said, “You are a brilliant man. Why have you stooped so far as to serve Liu Bei?”

Xu Shu said, “I fled as a child from hardship and drifted on the rivers and roads until I happened to arrive at Xinye, where I became close with Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande. My mother remained at home. She spared me concern and kindness, and I am full of shame and gratitude.”

Cao Cao said, “Now that you are here, you can tend to your mother morning and evening, and I, too, may hear your clear counsel.”

Xu Shu bowed his thanks and withdrew. He rushed in to see his mother and knelt, weeping, at her feet. She was taken aback.

“Why have you come here now?” she asked.

Xu Shu said, “Not long ago I served Yuzhou’s governor and became close to Liu Bei. A letter came from my mother, so I rode by night and came at once.”

His mother suddenly grew furious and struck the table.

“After wandering in shame for so many years, I thought your studies had gone forward, but they have gone backward even beyond where you started. You have read and should know that loyalty and filial duty are not always both possible. Do you not know that Cao Cao is a villain who betrays his ruler and defies the throne? Liu Bei’s benevolence is spread through the four seas, and he is also a scion of the Han house. You already chose your master. Yet you believed a single false letter and, without inquiry, abandoned light for darkness. You have won yourself a bad name. You are a fool indeed. What face can I have when I look at you? You have brought disgrace on your ancestors and live only between heaven and earth for that shame!”

She cursed him so hard that Xu Shu collapsed to the ground and dared not lift his head. His mother moved behind the screen and left.

After a while, a servant came out to report, “The old lady has hanged herself from a beam.” Xu Shu rushed in panic to rescue her, but her spirit had already departed.

Later, people composed a eulogy for Mother Xu:

Worthy Mother Xu, your fragrance endures through ten thousand generations.
Her virtue remained unbroken, and she was a blessing to the household.
She taught her son through many disciplines and bore hardship in her own life.
Her spirit was mountain-like, and her righteousness rose from the marrow.
She praised Lord Yuzhou and exposed Wei Wudi’s crimes.
She feared not the cauldrons nor the axes.
She feared only that her descendants would dishonor their forebears.
She laid herself upon the sword and joined the faithful dead; her resolve was fit to stand beside the mother who cut the loom.
She earned her name in life and found fitting rest in death.
Worthy Mother Xu, your fragrance endures through ten thousand generations.

When Xu Shu saw his mother dead, he wept so hard he collapsed, and only after a long while did he recover. Cao Cao sent gifts with condolences and himself came to offer rites. Xu Shu buried his mother’s bier south of Xuchang and kept mourning at her grave. He declined everything that Cao Cao gave him.

At that time, Cao Cao wished to discuss a southern campaign, and Xun Yu remonstrated: “The weather is too cold now to march troops. Let us wait until spring warms before launching a great advance.” Cao Cao took his advice. He then drew water from the Zhang River into a pool he called Xuanwu Pool, and within it trained the water forces in preparation for the southward expedition.

Liu Bei, who was preparing gifts, was ready to head for Longzhong to pay a visit to Zhuge Liang, when someone reported, “A gentleman is at the gate: hat high, official attire broad and handsome, and carriage of a truly extraordinary man. He has come to make inquiries.”

Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, said, “Could this be Kongming?” and sent to meet him. He saw it was Sima Hui.

Liu Bei was delighted and invited him into the back hall and offered him a high seat. He bowed and asked, “These many days since I was separated from Heaven's face, my duties have been ceaseless and I missed my visit. To receive you now is a joy beyond words.”

Sima Hui said, “I heard that Xu Zizhi was here, so I came for a while.”

Liu Bei said, “Not long ago, because Cao Cao detained his mother, Master Xu had a messenger from his mother summon him to return to Xuchang.”

Sima Hui replied, “This is Cao Cao’s trick. I have long heard that Xu’s mother was the most virtuous. Even if she is in Cao Cao’s custody she would not write to summon her son. This letter must be false. If Master Xu leaves, he should not yet be gone if his mother is still alive. If he goes now, his mother will surely die.”

Liu Bei was startled and asked the reason. Sima Hui said, “Xu’s mother is of such high loyalty that she would rather die than look on her son in shame.”

Liu Bei said, “Before he leaves, he recommends this Zhuge Liang of Nanyang. What sort of man is he?”

Sima Hui laughed. “Master Xu, having wished to go, would go and be done with it. Why drag him out by force to cry out his heart and blood?”

Liu Bei asked, “Master, why do you say this?”

Sima Hui said, “Kongming is close with four men: Cui Zhou-ping of Bo-Ling, Shi Guangyuan of Yingchuan, Meng Gongwei of Rinan, and Xu Shu. All four pursued purity in conduct, but Kongming alone was known for great breadth of mind. He would sit with knees drawn up and sing long verses, then point to the four and say, ‘Each of you may rise to become an Inspector or a Commandery Administrator.’ When asked what ambition Kongming held, he only smiled and did not answer. He often compared himself with Guan Zhong and Yue Yi, and his talent could not be measured.”

Liu Bei said, “How can there be so much wisdom in Yingchuan?”

Sima Hui said, “In old times Yin Kui, master of celestial observation, said that where the stars gather in the Ying region, there will be many worthy men.”

Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, said at his side, “I have heard of Guan Zhong and Yue Yi: men of the Spring and Autumn and Warring States, their accomplishments covering the world. Is it not excessive for Kongming to compare himself to them?”

Sima Hui laughed. “By my view he should not be measured against these two. I would compare him with two others.”

Guan Yu asked, “Who are those two?”

Sima Hui said, “He may be compared with Jiang Ziya of Zhou and Zhang Zifang of early Han.”

Everyone was startled. Sima Hui rose from the steps and was about to depart. Liu Bei could not hold him. As he stepped out, he looked up to heaven and laughed aloud: “The Sleeping Dragon has found his lord but not his time. How regrettable!”

He then added, “He is indeed an upright recluse.”

The next day Liu Bei, together with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei—whose courtesy name was Yide—and his attendants, rode back to Longzhong. Nearing a hillside they saw several men carrying hoes across the fields and singing:

The dark sky spreads like a round parasol; the earth lies like a game board.
Men in the world split black and white, then trade honor and disgrace.
Those granted glory grow secure in themselves; those cast into disgrace are destined for drudgery.
In Nanyang there are hidden recluses who cannot rest in easy sleep.

When Liu Bei heard the song he pulled in his horse and asked the farmer who wrote it.

“It was made by Master Wolong,” the farmer answered.

Liu Bei asked, “Where does Master Wolong live?”

“The ridge to the south of here, one chain of high mounds—Wolong Slope. In the sparse woods by its front, in a thatched hut, that is where Master Zhuge lives in high repose,” the farmer replied.

Liu Bei thanked him and urged his horse on. In only a short distance he looked toward Wolong Slope and found the place unexpectedly serene and strange.

Later, a poem was composed to describe that place:

Twenty li west of Xiangyang town, a long ridge leans above flowing water.
The high ridge bends and presses the roots into the cloud-base; clear water babbles and chips at stone marrow.
Like a trapped dragon, the ground coils upon the rock; like a single phoenix it stands under the pine shade.
A reed gate hangs half-shut before a thatched hut where a high man does not rise or stir.
Tall bamboos, interlaced, form green screens; every season wild flowers scent the fence.
Scrolls of yellow paper are stacked by the bed; no common scribes cross the seat.
A grey ape at the door sometimes brings fruit; an old crane at the gate listens to sutras at night.
In his robe pouch rests a famous zither and, on the wall, a jewel-bright sword reflects pine grain.
The recluse in the hut is serene and elegant; on idle days he ploughs and sows himself.
Waiting only for spring thunder to startle him awake, with one long cry he can calm all under heaven.

When Liu Bei reached the estate and dismounted, he knocked on the thatched gate. A boy came out.

“The Han Left General, Marquis of Yicheng District, Governor of Yu Province, and Imperial Uncle Liu Bei has come to pay his respects to Master Zhuge,” Liu Bei said.

The boy replied, “I do not remember many names.”

“Just say Liu Bei has come to visit,” Liu Bei said.

The boy said, “The master already left earlier.”

Liu Bei asked, “Where has he gone?”

“The sign is unclear; I know not where,” the boy said.

Liu Bei said, “When will he return?”

The boy replied, “No fixed time. It may be three or five days, or ten days.”

Liu Bei grew desolate.

Zhang Fei said, “If we are not to meet him, let us return.”

Liu Bei said, “Wait a little while.”

Guan Yu said, “Better go home and send another runner to ask.”

Liu Bei accepted his suggestion and told the boy, “If the master returns, tell him Liu Bei sought him.” Then he mounted and rode on. After a few li he reined back and studied the Longzhong scenery. The hills were low and graceful, the water shallow and clear, the land small and level, the woods not large but lush; crane and monkeys kept company, pine and bamboo gave green shade. He stood for a long while, spellbound.

Then he saw a man approach along a lonely mountain path, handsome and elegant, head wrapped in a hat of a wandering-knight, body in plain black cloth, cane in hand.

Liu Bei said, “This must be Master Wolong.” He dismounted quickly and moved forward to pay his respects.

“What if the master is not Wolong?” he asked.

The man asked, “Which general are you?”

“I am Liu Bei,” Liu Bei replied.

“I am not Kongming. I am Kongming’s friend, Cui Zhou-ping of Bo-Ling.”

Liu Bei said, “Your fame has long reached me. I am fortunate to meet you. Please sit wherever there is room and permit one question.”

The two sat on a stone in the woods, and Guan Yu and Zhang Fei stood at their sides. Cui Zhou-ping asked, “Why does General Liu seek Kongming?”

Liu Bei replied, “The realm is in tumult and all quarters are in disorder. I want to see Kongming to ask for ways to bring peace to the state and settle the nation.”

Cui Zhou-ping laughed. “You seek order and are moved by a compassionate heart, but peace and disorder have never come in fixed sequence. From the uprising of Gaozu ending Qin's tyranny, this age of violence entered order. In the reigns of Ai and Ping, after two hundred years of peace, Wang Mang usurped and turned order back into chaos. Guangwu restored the realm and rebuilt the foundation, and in that too, order came out of disorder. For two hundred years the people have now known peace, and so weapons rise again. This is precisely the moment when order turns to disorder; it cannot be corrected overnight. You want Kongming to turn Heaven and Earth and patch the cosmos—hardly easy, only a waste of effort. Do you not hear it said, ‘He who follows Heaven endures ease; he who resists Heaven labors’? ‘If the number is where it is, law and reason cannot wrest it away; if destiny is where it is, man cannot force it.’”

Liu Bei said, “What you have said is truly keen sight. But as a scion of Han, I ought to restore the Han house and have no place yielding to number and fate.”

Cui Zhou-ping said, “A hill-man has little to say on statecraft. I answered too freely only because you asked with sincerity.”

Liu Bei said, “Master, your instruction is generous, but I do not know where Kongming has gone.”

Cui Zhou-ping said, “I also want to visit him and do not know where he is.”

Liu Bei said, “Come with me to my humble county. Will you?”

Cui Zhou-ping said, “My nature is fond of idling and I have long had no desire for rank or fame. Let us meet another day.” He bowed deeply and departed. Liu Bei with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei remounted.

Zhang Fei said, “Wolong was not found again, yet we met this dry scholar and talked idle words too long.”

Liu Bei said, “Even a recluse’s words may hold weight.”

After three men had returned to Xinye and days passed, Liu Bei sent for news of Kongming. They returned with word: “Master Wolong has already gone back.”

Liu Bei immediately urged his horse onward.

Zhang Fei said, “Why should brother ride alone for what a village laborer cannot do? Send someone and have him fetched.”

Liu Bei snapped, “Did you not hear Mengzi say, ‘One who wishes to see a worthy man but does not use his way is like trying to invite him through a closed gate while the gate is shut?’ Kongming is the greatest worthy man of this age. How can he be summoned?”

So he remounted and went again to seek Kongming, with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei riding with him.

It was deep winter; the weather was severe, and red clouds were packed together. They had ridden many li when a piercing north wind came, and drifting snow began in fine abundance. Mountains looked like clusters of jade, and the woods like silver beds.

Zhang Fei said, “The cold has frozen earth and frost. Since we are not to be fighting now, is there benefit to seeking someone so useless? Better to return to Xinye and avoid this wind and snow.”

Liu Bei said, “My wish is to show Kongming how earnestly I seek him. If the younger brothers fear the cold, you may return.”

Zhang Fei said, “I do not fear death, only the cold. I fear only that brother wastes his mind and heart.”

Liu Bei said, “Speak no more; continue with me.”

As they neared the thatched hut, they suddenly heard someone singing in a tavern by the roadside. Liu Bei dismounted and listened. The song said:

The brave one’s fame and rank are not yet fulfilled, alas, a long while no spring has come.
Have you not seen the old recluse by the Eastern Sea who left behind the thorns of Jing and then went in the second chariot to join King Wen?
Eight hundred lords never set out to meet; white fish boarded boats and crossed Mengjin.
At Muye they fought and blood ran in rivers of the pestle, and heroes of soaring spirit crowned the military ranks.
Did you not see the tavern-bonded master from Gaoyang, rising from the fields at Mangdang and bowing to Lord Zhongshun?
His grand speech on kingly ambition astounded the ears.
Seventy-two to the east of Qicheng; none under heaven can trace his path.
Two men are no longer of emperor's realm, and who in all the world can yet recognize heroes?

Afterward someone struck a zhuo and sang another song:

My lord lifts the sword to clear the all-soaking sea, founding a great enterprise to last four hundred years.
In Huan-Ling’s later era, virtue has burned away; evil ministers and treacherous sons stir cauldrons and furnaces.
A green snake flies down beside the imperial seat; again a strange rainbow descends into the jade hall.
Bandits gather in every direction like ants; a hundred ferocious scoundrels rise like hawks.
We beat our chests and cry aloud, but our hands only clap empty air;
we drink village wine in a village tavern with no one to hear.
If one can keep one’s own path and be at peace all day, why seek a name undying through the ages?

After the songs, both men pounded their tables and laughed. Liu Bei said, “Could Wolong be among them?”

He dismounted and entered the tavern. He saw two men leaning on the table and drinking together. The one above had a white face and long beard; the one below had an odd and ancient air.

Liu Bei bowed and asked, “Who of you is Master Wolong?”

The long-bearded man asked, “Who are you, and what is your purpose in seeking Wolong?”

Liu Bei said, “I am Liu Bei. I seek the master to ask for ways to bring peace to the people and secure the state.”

The long-bearded man said, “We are not Wolong. We are friends of Wolong. I am Shi Guangyuan of Yingchuan, and this is Meng Gongwei of Rinan.”

Liu Bei was delighted. “I have long heard your names. To meet you by accident is a blessing. I have good horses with me. Will you come and speak with me at Wolong’s estate?”

Guangyuan said, “We are all rustic and idle men who do not attend to statecraft or governance. Do not trouble yourself with that. Great lord, you should mount again and search for Wolong yourself.”

Liu Bei took their leave, mounted, and rode back to Wolong Ridge. At the estate gate he dismounted and asked the boy, “Is the master at the house today?”

The boy replied, “He is reading upstairs now.”

Liu Bei rejoiced and followed the boy inside.

In the inner gate, over the lintel was a pair of lines in large characters:

To clear the mind, keep simplicity; in quietness, seek the far.

As Liu Bei was looking, he suddenly heard someone reciting. He stood at the side of the gate and peered in. On the upper floor of the cottage, a young man sat by the brazier with knees hugged, singing:

A phoenix ranges among a thousand heights, yet never perches without a paulownia.
A worthy man dwells in one place and serves none but his lord.
I joyfully till and plough the ridges and furrows; I cherish my cottage.
I set my proud ease in qin and books, waiting for the right time of heaven.

When the song ended, Liu Bei entered and paid obeisance.

“I have long admired the master and lacked the chance for a meeting. Because Xu Yuzhi spoke highly of him, I came in haste and had an empty return. I have braved wind and snow on this journey to see him; to catch even one glimpse is a great grace.”

The young man replied in alarm, “General, are you not Liu Yuzhou? Do you want to see your elder brother?”

Liu Bei was surprised. “Are you not Master Wolong?”

The youth replied, “I am Zhuge Jun, Wolong’s brother. Of our three brothers, the eldest is Zhuge Jin, now in the service of Sun Zhongmou as a retainer. Kongming is our second brother.”

Liu Bei asked, “Is Wolong in the house today?”

Zhuge Jun said, “Yesterday, by appointment with Cui Zhou-ping, he went out to wander.”

Liu Bei asked, “Where has he gone wandering?”

Zhuge Jun replied, “At times he rows a small boat on rivers and lakes, at times he visits hermit monks and Daoist recluses on mountain peaks, at times he seeks friends from village to village, at times he delights in qin and chess in cave chambers. His movements are impossible to chart.”

Liu Bei sighed, “My fate is poor. Twice I have come hoping for this worthy man and missed him both times.”

Zhuge Jun said, “Sit and take some tea.”

Zhang Fei said, “Since the master is not here, let brother return to his horse.”

Liu Bei said, “Now that I have come this far, how can I leave without a word?”

He asked Zhuge Jun, “I have heard Master Kongming deeply knows strategy and studies the arts of war daily. Can I not ask whether this is true?”

Zhuge Jun answered, “I do not know.”

Zhang Fei said, “You ask and ask, yet in such wind and snow, better to return early.”

Liu Bei stopped him. Zhuge Jun said, “As my elder brother is not here, he would not wish a long stay by horse and armor. If you wish, return another day to make your respects.”

Liu Bei said, “How could I ask a master to ride out here in vain?”

“Within a few days I will come again. Let me borrow paper and brush so I may leave a letter for your elder brother showing my earnest intention.”

Zhuge Jun brought the writing tools. Liu Bei unsealed his reed brush, spread the cloud-colored paper, and wrote:

I have long longed for your renown. Twice, in haste, I came to pay respect and returned empty-handed, my heart heavy. I dare reflect that I am a scion of the Han line and have unworthily taken high title and rank. I look on courtly change and upheaval: state structure collapsing, the order broken, lords contending and the state in chaos, wicked men deceiving the ruler. My heart and courage are torn. Though I possess sincerity to aid, I truly lack strategies of governance. I turn in hope for your compassion, loyalty, and righteousness. Open widely your brilliance like Luwang and display your vast design like Zifang. The realm will be fortunate; the ancestral altars and state will be fortunate. Before this, I have laid my purpose before you. When you are done with your rites and purified by fasting and bathing, do me this favor: grant me your respectful audience, and accept this humble sincerity, hoping for your full consideration.

When he finished writing, Liu Bei gave it to Zhuge Jun, who took it and placed it aside. Liu Bei bowed and withdrew. Zhuge Jun escorted him out, and Liu Bei repeatedly expressed his earnest respects before leaving. As he was mounting again, a child waved from outside the fence and shouted, “The old master comes!”

Liu Bei looked and saw, west of a small bridge, a man with a fur cap pulled over his head, fox-fur robe covering him, riding a donkey with a young blue-clad boy behind, and carrying a gourd flask of wine. They crossed the small bridge through snow while he was reciting:

In one night the north wind bites; ten thousand li of heavy red cloud.
The sky is filled with drifting snow, and old mountains and rivers are remade.
Looking up into the void above, it seems as if jade dragons are battling.
Fins and scale-like armor whirl in thousands, and in an instant fill the whole heaven and earth.
On the donkey he crossed the small bridge, alone lamenting the thin plum blossoms.

Liu Bei cried out, “This is truly Wolong!” He dismounted and rushed forward with reverence.

“Master, it is not easy to brave this cold. Liu Bei has waited for you long.”

The man quickly dismounted, removed his hat, and returned Liu Bei’s bow.

Zhuge Jun said behind him, “This is not Master Wolong but his father-in-law, Huang Chengyan.”

Liu Bei said, “The verse you just sang is exquisite indeed.”

Huang Chengyan said, “At my young son-in-law’s house I have seen the Liangfu Chant, and I remember this piece. I happened to cross the bridge and saw plum blossoms between the fence, and was moved to recite it. I did not expect to be heard by an honored guest.”

Liu Bei asked, “Have you seen my worthy son-in-law?”

Huang Chengyan said, “It is I, the old man, come to visit him.”

Liu Bei said farewell, remounted, and returned home. Wind and snow were heavy again.

Looking back toward Wolong Ridge, he remained heavy in heart.

Later, there was a poem describing Liu Bei’s wind-and-snow visit to Kongming:

In one full day of wind and snow I sought the worthy, and returned with no meeting but a heart full of sorrow.
Ice crusted the creek bridge, and slick mountain stones made the way treacherous; cold pierced horse and rider, and the road stretched long.
In front, petals of pear blossom fell in sheets, and wild willow fluff struck the face in frenzy.
When he looked back and checked his rein, all he could see at a distance was Wolong Ridge, a heap of shining silver.

After Liu Bei returned to Xinye, time passed and it was already early spring. He ordered diviners to cast stalks and choose an auspicious day. After three days of fasting, cleansing, and changing robes, he again headed for Wolong Ridge to visit Kongming. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei heard this and were displeased, and together entered to remonstrate before Liu Bei.

The lofty worthy will not easily bear the ambition of heroes;
when virtue is constrained, rare men become the objects of doubt.
What he would say remained unknown.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Sima Hui Again Recommends the Worthy, and Liu Bei Visits the Thatched Cottage Three Times

chapters.html:
The plan at Longzhong sets the threefold division.\ War on the Yangtze brings retribution against the Sun house.

Later, Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, did not meet Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, on two visits and wished to visit him again. Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, said, “Your elder brother has gone in person twice now to pay him his respects, and the ceremony is excessive. I suspect this Zhuge is all reputation and little learning, so he avoids seeing you. Why are you so utterly deceived by this man?”

Liu Bei said, “No. In the time of Duke Huan of Qi, when he wished to meet a recluse in Dongguo, he had to ask and ask five times before they met once. How can I not seek out such a worthy man?”

Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, said, “Brother, you are mistaken. A mere villager—what sort of worthiness could he have? This time you need not go yourself. If he will not come, I will bind him with a single hemp rope and drag him here!”

Liu Bei rebuked him. “Have you never heard of King Wen of Zhou visiting Jiang Ziya? The king showed such reverence to talent. Why are you so rude? Do not go this time. I and Yunchang will go together.”

Zhang Fei said, “If both elder brothers go, how can I be left behind?”

Liu Bei said, “If you go with us, do not lose your manners.”

Zhang Fei assented. The three then rode out with retainers and reached Longzhong. Half a li from the thatched hut, Liu Bei got down and walked. As he arrived, he happened to meet Zhuge Jun. Liu Bei hurriedly paid respects and asked, “Is the elder brother in the cottage?”

Zhuge Jun replied, “He only came home last evening. General, today you may meet him.” He then drifted away.

Liu Bei said, “By good fortune, we are to see the Master this time!”

Zhang Fei said, “This man is insolent. He could have brought us to his dwelling anyway. Why did he leave us and go?”

Liu Bei replied, “He each had his own duties; how can we compel him?”

The three came to the gate and knocked. A page boy came out to ask. Liu Bei said, “Please tell the gentleman with all honor that Liu Bei has come to bow before him.”

The page boy said, “The Master is at home, but he still sleeps late in the thatched hall.”

Liu Bei said, “In that case, do not announce it.” He ordered Guan Yu and Zhang Fei to wait at the gate. He walked slowly in and saw the Master lying propped on a couch in the thatched hall. Liu Bei stood with hands folded on the lower steps.

After some time the Master still had not awakened. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei had been waiting outside and had not moved for a long while. They re-entered to report to Liu Bei but still remained standing. Zhang Fei, in great anger, said to Yunchang, “How proud this gentleman is! My brother stands waiting by the stair and he lies there propped up and ignores him. He has not even stirred from sleep! Let me go behind the house and set a fire to see if he wakes!”

Yunchang restrained him repeatedly. Liu Bei still ordered the two to stand outside and wait.

When he looked toward the hall, he saw the Master roll over as if to rise, then at once turn back toward the inner wall and fall asleep again. The page boy wished to report. Liu Bei said, “Do not startle him.” He waited another hour. At last Kongming awakened and chanted:

Who first awakens from the great dream? All my life, I alone have known.
Spring sleep is ample in the thatched hall; beyond the window, the sun moves slowly on.

When the poem was done, he turned over and asked the page, “Have any visitors come?”

The page boy said, “Liu the Imperial Uncle is here, waiting long.”

Kongming said, “Why did you not report him earlier? Let me change my clothing first.” He went into the rear hall. After some time, he properly dressed and came out to receive him.

Liu Bei saw him and thought him almost six feet tall, with a face like polished jade, a black cloth cap, and a white-feathered cloak, floating with an air as though he belonged among immortals. Liu Bei knelt and said, “I am an unworthy fool from Zhuo Commandery, a last sprigling of the Han line. I have long heard your great name as if thunder had passed through my ears. Twice before I made respectful approach and was not granted a single audience. I wrote my unworthy name at the writing table. I do not yet dare to hope you might read it.”

Kongming said, “I am a rustic from Nanyang whose nature is spare and lazy. General has ridden here many times in vain; this is shame enough.”

The two observed the rites of protocol and sat as host and guest. The page served tea. When the tea was finished, Kongming said, “By yesterday’s letters, your concern for the people and the state is clear. My regret is only that Kongming is young and his abilities are shallow, yet he dares still to ask.”

Liu Bei said, “Did not the words of Sima De-cao and Xun Yu mean something? I beg the Master not to abandon a humble and poor man, but grant your teaching.”

Kongming replied, “De-cao and Xun are eminent men of the age. I am only a man of the plow, how could I dare to speak of world affairs? The two gentlemen miss my nature. Why does the General cast away jade and seek a rough stone?”

Liu Bei said, “A true man carrying extraordinary talent for governing age is not meant to waste himself old and idle under groves and springs. Please, Master, have the world’s people in mind and open my dullness so I may be instructed.”

Kongming smiled and said, “I will hear the General’s ambition.”

Liu Bei motioned others back and said, “The Han house is collapsing. Treacherous ministers have usurped life itself. I am not up to this work; I wish to act on great righteousness in the realm, yet my schemes and calculations are shallow and short. Only if the Master lifts my ignorance and relieves this distress would be my great good fortune.”

Kongming said, “Since Dong Zhuo raised rebellion, all the great men of the realm have risen. Cao Cao did not originally surpass Yuan Shao, yet he defeated him not only through time and circumstance but also through counsel and design. Now Cao Cao already commands a hundred thousand men, holds the Son of Heaven to order the lords; this cannot truly be met head-on.

Sun Quan holds Jiangdong, already in three generations. The land is defensible and the people are attached; this can be used as an ally, but never as a target. Jing Province holds the Han and Mian to the north, and all its benefits reach to the South Sea. Its eastern reaches join to Wu Hui, and its western roads run to Ba and Shu. It is a place of arms and cannot be held by one who is not its rightful lord. Heaven has therefore supplied this to the General. Can he cast it aside?

Yi Province is rugged and guarded; its rich plains run for a thousand li, the realm of abundance. Through it, Gaozu established an imperial legacy. Now Liu Zhang is dull and weak, with a populous and wealthy land but no care to preserve it. Talented men wait for a clear ruler.

The General is a descendant of the imperial household; his trust and loyalty are known in all four seas. He gathers heroes and hungers for men of worth. If you first secure Jing and Yi, guard their mountain barriers, pacify the frontier tribes in the west, comfort the Yi and Yue in the south, make alliance with Sun Quan outside, and repair governance within; when upheaval touches the realm, send one foremost commander with Jing’s army toward Wan and Luo. Let the General lead Yi’s forces out toward Qinchuan. Will there be no common folk who would greet him with plain grain and jarred wine? If all this comes to pass, your great undertaking can be accomplished and the Han house raised again. That is my counsel for the General. The general should choose it.”

After he spoke, he told the page boy to bring out a scroll and hang it in the center hall. Pointing to it, he said to Liu Bei, “This is the map of the five-and-forty provinces of western Sichuan. If the General wishes to accomplish dominion, he must ignore the tides that favor Cao Cao in the north and the terrain advantage Sun Quan has in the south, then rely instead on human accord. First take Jing as your home, then take western Sichuan and set your foundations, forming the threefold tripod, and only then attempt Zhongyuan.”

When Liu Bei heard this, he rose from his seat, joined his palms, and said, “The Master’s words have ripped the straw mat from my ear and opened my view. I now see as if cloud and mist had been pushed aside. Yet Jing under Liu Biao and Yi under Liu Zhang are both kin of the Han house. How could I bear to wrest them from them?”

Kongming said, “By night I read the signs of heaven. Liu Biao will not live long. Liu Zhang is no lord fit to found an enduring order; eventually he will yield to the General.”

Liu Bei then knelt and thanked him. In that one exchange, Kongming, though he had not yet left the thatched hut, already knew the threefold division of the empire. Truly, no man in all ages could match him.

A later commentator praised the scene in verse:

That day Lord Yuzhou lamented his lonely straits—how fortunate that Nanyang held the Sleeping Dragon!
To see where the realm would one day divide like a tripod, the Master smiled and pointed within the map.

Liu Bei begged Kongming, “Though my name is small and my virtue thin, please do not refuse the poor and humble, but come down from the mountain and help. Liu Bei will listen in full to your wise instruction.”

Kongming said, “Kongming has long delighted in plow and hoe and has been lazy in answering the world. I cannot obey an order.”

Liu Bei wept and said, “If the Master does not come forth, what hope do the common people have?” When he finished, tears soaked his sleeves and collar.

Seeing the depth of his sincerity, Kongming said, “Since the General does not reject me, I am willing to labor like a dog and a horse.”

Liu Bei rejoiced and ordered Guan Yu and Zhang Fei to present gifts of gold and silk in proper ceremony.

Kongming refused firmly. Liu Bei said, “This is not a payment for a great worth, only a sign of Liu Bei’s sincerity.” Kongming then accepted.

That night Liu Bei and the others stayed in the manor together. On the next day, Zhuge Jun departed. Before leaving, Kongming instructed, “I have received from Liu the Imperial Uncle three visits of favor; I cannot decline to go. You should till here in person and never let the fields lie waste. When I finish my work and win success, then I shall return to retirement.”

A later poet wrote:

Before he had risen, he already thought of retreat; once merit was won, he should have recalled his words on leaving.
Only because the Former Lord entrusted him with his last charge, his star fell in the autumn wind at Wuzhang Plains.

There was also a piece in the Old Style:

The High Emperor raised a three-foot blade of snow; at Mangdang, the white serpent bled by night.
He pacified Qin, destroyed Chu, and entered Xianyang; two hundred years later, the line nearly broke.
Great Guangwu revived it at Luoyang; passed down to Huan and Ling, it split apart again.
Emperor Xian moved his court to Xuchang; throughout the four seas, heroes rose in throngs.
Cao Cao seized power and gained Heaven’s season; the Sun house in Jiangdong opened a mighty enterprise.
Lonely and poor, Xuande wandered the realm; dwelling alone at Xinye, he grieved for the people in peril.
Nanyang’s Sleeping Dragon cherished vast designs; within his breast, mighty armies divided orthodox and surprise.
Because of Xu Shu’s words as he departed, three visits to the thatched hut joined their hearts.
The Master was then twenty-seven years old; he gathered zither and books and left the furrowed fields.
First he would take Jing Province, then Sichuan, unfolding statecraft with hands that could mend Heaven.
On his tongue, the game roused wind and thunder; in easy talk, the stars themselves changed place.
Dragon-soaring and tiger-gazing, he settled earth and sky; through ten thousand ages, his name will never die.

Liu Bei and the others left Zhuge Jun and returned with Kongming to Xinye. Liu Bei treated him as his teacher; they ate at the same table and slept on the same couch, discussing affairs of the world all day long.

Kongming said, “Cao Cao is digging out an Xuanwu reservoir in Ji Province to train a fleet; he surely intends to move against the Jiangnan region. Send people quietly across the river to gather intelligence.”

Liu Bei followed this and sent men toward Jiangdong.

After Sun Ce died, Sun Quan held Jiangdong. Inheriting the legacy of his father and elder brother, he welcomed worthy scholars in great numbers. He opened a guest hall at Wuhui and appointed Gu Yong and Zhang Hong to receive guests from every quarter. Year after year men recommended one another. At that time these men came to Jiangdong: Kan Ze from Kuaiji, whose courtesy name was Derun; Yan Jun from Pengcheng, courtesy name Mancai; Xue Zong from Pei County, courtesy name Jingwen; Cheng Bing from Runan, courtesy name Dezhu; Zhu Huan of Wu Commandery, courtesy name Xiumu; Lu Ji, courtesy name Gongji; Zhang Wen, a man of Wu, courtesy name Huishu; Luo Tong from Kuaiji, courtesy name Gongxu; and Wu Can from Wucheng, courtesy name Kongxiu. Sun Quan honored all of them highly.

He also gained a number of formidable generals: Lu Meng of Ruyang, courtesy name Ziming; Lu Xun of Wu Commandery, courtesy name Boyan; Xu Sheng of Langye, courtesy name Wenxiang; Pan Zhang of Dongjing, courtesy name Wengui; and Ding Feng of Lujiang, courtesy name Chengyuan. Civil and military men together assisted him on all matters. From this, Jiangdong came to be praised for its abundance of talent.

In the seventh year of Jian’an, Cao Cao defeated Yuan Shao and sent envoys to Jiangdong ordering Sun Quan to send his son to court with the ruler. Sun Quan hesitated.

The Lady Wu of Jiangdong had Zhou Yu and Zhang Zhao deliberate together. Zhang Zhao said, “By sending our son to court, Cao Cao seeks to constrain the lords. If we refuse, he may gather troops and come against Jiangdong; then all is danger.”

Zhou Yu said, “You inherited six commanderies and all their men, with disciplined troops and full grain stores. With loyal soldiers so willing to obey you, what compulsion could make you surrender your hostages to him? If the son goes in, he must then be bound to Cao’s alliance and cannot disobey that summons. Better not to send him now, watch developments, and prepare separate counsels in good time.”

The Lady Wu said, “Gongjin’s words are right.” Sun Quan followed her counsel, apologized to the envoys, and did not send his son. From then onward Cao Cao fed thoughts of coming to the south, but the north was still unsettled and he had no time for a southern campaign.

In the eighth year of Jian’an, in the eleventh month, Sun Quan marched against Huang Zu and fought on the Great River. The Huang forces were broken. At the fore was his marshal Ling Cao in light boats; he cut through to Xiakou and was shot dead by one arrow from Gan Ning, a commander under Huang Zu. Ling Cao’s son, Ling Tong, only fifteen years of age, dashed out and retrieved his father’s body.

When the wind turned ill, Sun Quan withdrew and brought the army back to Dong Wu.

Now Sun Yi, Sun Quan’s brother, was the prefect of Danyang. Sun Yi was hard and hot-tempered, and after drink he sometimes whipped the soldiers. The Danyang commander Gei Lan and the county chief Daiyuan had long wished to kill Sun Yi. They conspired with one from Sun Yi’s staff, Bi Hong, and plotted murder.

At that time all county officers and magistrates were gathered at Danyang. Sun Yi held a large banquet.

Xu Shi, his wife, was beautiful and intelligent and excellent at divination. That day she drew a chart and found a figure of great misfortune. She urged Sun Yi not to attend. He would not listen and held a larger feast with everyone.

By evening, after the revelers dispersed, Bi Hong drew his sword and followed Sun Yi outside the gate. He immediately drew his blade and killed Sun Yi. Gei Lan and Daiyuan then blamed Bi Hong and had him beheaded in the market.

Those two then seized Sun Yi’s household goods and his concubines. Gei Lan saw Xu Shi’s beauty and said to her, “I avenged your husband. You must come with me. If you do not, you die.”

Xu Shi replied, “My husband has only just died. I cannot suddenly join you. Let me wait until the dark day of mourning and perform the rites of removal of mourning; marriage need not be delayed.”

Gei Lan agreed.

Xu Shi then secretly summoned Sun Gao, an old general loyal to Sun Yi, and Fu Ying, his trusted aide, into the residence. She knelt and wept. “While my husband lived, he spoke of the two lords’ loyalty and righteousness. Now these two villains, Gei Lan and Daiyuan, plotted to kill my husband, and then blamed only Bi Hong and beheaded him. They have divided all my household retainers and concubines among themselves. Gei Lan also seeks to seize me by force. I promised him only to keep him from immediate rage. Generals, please send one at once to the Son of Wu and arrange in secret a plan to punish these two villains, wash away this disgrace, and settle this enmity.”

After finishing, she bowed twice. Sun Gao and Fu Ying both wept and said, “While we were alive we survived only by the Lady’s kindness, waiting for this day to repay her. We dare not fail your command.”

So they sent a trusted messenger to Sun Quan in secret.

On the dark mourning day, Xu Shi first summoned Sun Gao and Fu Ying and hid them behind curtains in a side chamber. She then set up a memorial ceremony in the hall. After the rites, she removed the mourning garments, bathed, perfumed herself, and dressed in vivid ornaments, speaking and laughing as though nothing had happened.

When Gei Lan heard, he rejoiced. At night, Xu Shi sent a maid to invite him to the residence. She set a seat in the hall and served wine. Once he was drunk, Xu Shi invited Gei Lan into the inner chamber.

Gei Lan entered with pleasure and staggered in from intoxication. Xu Shi suddenly cried out, “Where are Sun Gao and Fu Ying?” The two men leapt out from behind the curtains, knives in hand.

Gei Lan was at a loss and was cut down by one stroke from Fu Ying. Sun Gao struck again, and he was killed at once.

Xu Shi then had Daiyuan invited again to another feast. He came into the mansion and was also killed in the hall by the two generals.

She then had guards execute the two villains’ households and their remaining accomplices.

Xu Shi changed back into mourning garb and presented the severed heads of Gei Lan and Daiyuan before Sun Yi’s spirit tablet. Not long after, Sun Quan rode out with his command in person to Danyang. Seeing what Xu Shi had done, he made Sun Gao and Fu Ying Gate Commanders to guard Danyang and ordered Xu Shi to return home and live in retirement.

The people of Jiangdong all praised her virtue. A later verse praised her:

No other age has seen such virtue joined with talent; in one stroke she rooted out the treacherous.
Craven ministers followed rebels while loyal ones died—not one could match this heroic woman of Eastern Wu.

Elsewhere in Jiangdong, mountain bandits had all been pacified. In the Great River there were more than seven thousand war junks.

Sun Quan appointed Zhou Yu as Chief Commander and made him direct all Jiangdong land-and-water forces and cavalry. In the twelfth year of Jian’an, in the winter month of ten, Sun Quan’s mother, the Lady Wu, fell gravely ill and summoned Zhou Yu and Zhang Zhao to her side.

She said, “I am of Wu. My father and mother died when I was young, and with my younger brother, I moved to the land of Yue. Later I married into the Sun house and bore four sons. When my eldest, Sun Ce, was born, I dreamt the moon entered my womb. Then I bore the second son, Sun Quan, and dreamt the sun entered my womb. The diviners said, ‘A child whose womb receives moon and sun will be made high and honored.’ Alas, Sun Ce died early. I now entrust Jiangdong’s foundation to Quan. Help him with one heart. I will not be forgotten when I die.”

She then instructed Sun Quan, “Treat Zibu and Gongjin as teachers and do not neglect them. My younger sister shared this husband of ours before your father, and she is also your mother after I am gone. Treat my sister as you would treat me. Your sister likewise should grant her good marriage and fosterage of a worthy husband.”

When she had finished, she died. Sun Quan wept and performed the funeral rites in full; no further telling is needed.

The next spring Sun Quan considered attacking Huang Zu. Zhang Zhao said, “You have not yet completed the mourning period, and cannot lead troops.”

Zhou Yu said, “To avenge grievances and reclaim honor, why wait for the mourning period?”

Sun Quan still hesitated.

Just then Lü Meng came and reported, saying, “Master, at Longqiu water gate there has suddenly come down to us Gan Ning of Huang Zu’s forces. I have spoken with him closely. His name is Xingba, and he is from Linjiang of Bajan. He is fairly learned in records and history, strong in body, and fond of the way of roaming heroes. He has at times gathered outlaws and roamed this world by river and lake. He hangs a bronze bell at his waist; when its sound is heard, all avoid him. He once used Sichuan brocade as a sail-cloth; therefore people called him the ‘Brocade-Sail Brigand.’

“After regretting his past wrongs, he turned to good conduct, moved his men, and came to serve Liu Biao. But seeing that Liu Biao could not complete anything, he then wished to come to Jiangdong but was held at Xiakou by Huang Zu.

“In the earlier fight when Jiangdong broke Huang’s force, Huang gained strength from Gan Ning and recovered Xiakou. Yet he treated Ning very harshly. General Sui Fei kept recommending him, and Huang replied, ‘Ning robbed this river; how can I dare employ him again?’ Ning bore that grudge. Sui Fei saw this and invited him home for a feast, saying, ‘Though I have recommended you many times, your lord would not use you. Time and the sun move on and life is short; one should chart for oneself a farther road. I will secure you as magistrate of E County, and then you may decide your own path.’

“Ning was therefore allowed through Xiakou and sought to cross into Jiangdong, but he feared that Jiangdong would remember that he had once rescued Huang and killed Ling Cao.”

“I spoke plainly to my lord, saying he thirsts for worthy men and does not keep old enmities. Each of us already serves our own sovereign, so why should resentment remain? Ning gladly brought his men across the river and came to see my lord. I beg you to command him as you see fit.”

Sun Quan said, “I welcome Xingba and from this time Huang Zu cannot stand. This is a jewel-and-gold argument indeed.” He ordered Lü Meng to bring Gan Ning before him.

When the formal greeting was complete, Sun Quan said, “Xingba, your coming has won my heart at once. There is no reason for old grievances to stand between us. Ask no one to doubt you. Teach me how to break Huang Zu.”

Ning said, “Heavenly mandate is weakening under the Han. Cao Cao will in the end seize it outright. The lands south of the Han are among those he must claim. Liu Biao has no far-sightedness; his son is foolish and cannot inherit and hold the state. The Master should prepare now. If he delays, Cao will plan first.

“Now it is best to strike Huang first. He is elderly and senile, caring only for profit. He exploits officials and peasants; all are resentful. His equipment is neglected and no discipline in the army. If you attack him, he will surely be broken. Once Huang is defeated, you can advance west, occupy Chuguan, and then set your eyes on Ba and Shu. The realm will be stabilized.”

Sun Quan said, “These are words of gold and jade!” He therefore named Zhou Yu Chief Commander of water-and-land armies. Lü Meng was made advance commander of the vanguard. Dong Xi and Gan Ning became deputies. Sun Quan himself led the main force of one hundred thousand men to subdue Huang Zu.

A scout returned with report that Huang was quickly gathering troops and summoning Sui Fei as commander, while Chen Jiu and Deng Long led the vanguard. They raised all soldiers of Jiangxia to receive the attack.

Chen Jiu and Deng Long each brought a group of mengchong to block Mian mouth, each of those towers fixed a thousand or more heavy bows and crossbows to the sides and anchored the boats with thick cables to the surface. When Jiangdong troops came up to the river, drums sounded from the mengchong and the bows and crossbows fired together. The soldiers could not advance and drew back several li over open water.

Gan Ning told Dong Xi, “Now matters have come to this. We must go forward.” He selected more than a hundred small boats, fifty men on each: twenty paddled and thirty wore armor with iron blades. Ignoring arrows and slingstones, they ran to the mengchong edge and cut the great cables. The anchored warboats then drifted loose.

Gan Ning leaped onto one mengchong and cut down Deng Long. Chen Jiu abandoned ship and fled.

When Lü Meng saw this, he sprang from his skiff, took up the paddle and paddle-hand himself, and rowed straight into the fleet, setting fire to the ships. As Chen Jiu hurried to shore, Lü Meng risked life and caught him, then with one chest stroke of the blade he felled him.

By the time Sui Fei brought troops to the bank to connect, Jiangdong soldiers surged all at once onto shore and the clash became impossible to withstand. Huang’s force was decisively defeated.

Sui Fei fled in disorder and happened to meet the Jiangdong great general Pan Zhang. Their horses collided and they fought for several exchanges, whereupon Pan Zhang took him alive and brought him straight to the fleet, where he presented him before Sun Quan.

Sun Quan ordered him put in a cage cart, to be kept alive until Huang was captured and then all be punished together. He drove the three armies on without pause by night or day to press the fight toward Xiakou.

It was thus:

Because he would not employ the Brocade-Sail fighter, his great cable-linked ships were broken through.
Whether Huang Zu would win or lose remained unknown.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Longzhong Strategy Sets the Three Kingdoms; War on the Yangtze for the Sun Clan’s Vengeance

chapters.html:
Now Sun Quan had gathered his men and driven them to attack Xiakou. Huang Zu’s troops were defeated and near ruin. Realizing he could not hold Jiangxia, he abandoned it and turned toward Jingzhou to flee. Gan Ning predicted that Huang Zu would go only to Jingzhou, so he laid an ambush outside the eastern gate.

Huang Zu rode out with a few dozen riders. As he was leaving, Gan Ning called out and blocked him. Huang Zu said from horseback,

“I have never treated you lightly before. Why do you force me this time?”

Ning shouted back,

“When I was in Jiangxia I won many merits. Yet you treated me as a river-bandit. What do you say to this now?”

Huang Zu knew escape was all that remained, so he turned his horse and rode. Ning pushed through the soldiers and drove straight after him. He then heard shouting behind him and saw several riders coming up. It was Cheng Pu. Fearful that Cheng Pu would steal his share of the glory, Ning hastily nocked an arrow and shot backward at Huang Zu from horseback. Huang Zu was hit, turned over, and fell from his horse. Ning took his head, returned, and joined Cheng Pu’s men, then went back to Sun Quan and presented Huang Zu’s severed head.

Sun Quan ordered it placed in a wooden chest, to be brought home to Jiangdong and offered before his late father’s spirit. He rewarded the armies and promoted Gan Ning to Commandant. The court discussed how to split the force and defend Jiangxia. Zhang Zhao said,

“A lone city cannot be held. Better to pull back to Jiangdong for now. Liu Biao will know we have broken Huang Zu and will surely come to seek revenge. Let him come and exhaust himself first. When he is spent, we can strike him and then take Jing and Xiang too.”

Sun Quan agreed. They abandoned Jiangxia and withdrew back to Jiangdong.

Su Fei, confined in a cage-cart, secretly sent word to Gan Ning begging for aid. Ning replied, “Fei has not said a word to me, but how could I forget him?” As the main army reached Wujui, Sun Quan ordered Su Fei’s head to be brought out and offered together with Huang Zu’s. Ning then entered court and knelt to report,

“If I had not found Su Fei, my bones would by now be filling ditches and ravines. How could I then have served your banner? His offense merits death, but I remember the kindness he once showed me and beg that I restore his rank and atone for him.”

Sun Quan said,

“He has done you good service once, and I forgive him for your sake. But if he flees, what then?”

Ning said,

“If he escapes death and receives pardon, he will still have no place to repay this grace. He would not run. If he ran, I would rather bring his head to these steps myself.”

Sun Quan pardoned Su Fei. He left out the sacrifice of Huang Zu’s head only. After the rites were done, there was a banquet to celebrate with all civil and military officers.

While they were drinking, one man in the hall suddenly wept, rose up with a drawn sword, and moved straight at Gan Ning. Ning quickly raised a stool to meet him. Sun Quan looked closely and saw it was Ling Tong. During the Jiangxia affair, Gan Ning had shot Ling Tong’s father, Ling Cao, and Ling Tong had come to avenge him.

Sun Quan hurriedly restrained him and said,

“Xingba killed Ling Cao while serving the man to whom he owed loyalty, and Ling Cao had none but that duty too. Now you are of one household. Could you still hold on to old enmity? Everything is in my hands.”

Ling Tong knelt and wept again,

“A grudge with whom we cannot share heaven and earth in common cannot remain unanswered.”

Sun Quan and the officials pleaded with him again and again, but Ling Tong kept his eyes furious. Sun Quan at once ordered Gan Ning to take five thousand soldiers and one hundred warships to Xiakou and garrison there to avoid Ling Tong. Ning thanked him, took command, and departed.

Sun Quan also conferred on Ling Tong the title of Commandant. Ling Tong had no choice but to swallow his resentment.

From then on, Eastern Wu built more warships in force and split troops to hold the riverbank; Sun Quan also ordered Sun Jing to guard one contingent at Wuhui. Sun Quan himself led the main army and encamped at Chaisang. Zhou Yu trained the water forces at Poyang Lake day after day to prepare for battle.

The narrative splits.

Meanwhile, Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, sent scouts for news of Jiangdong. They returned: Eastern Wu had already broken Huang Zu and now had troops posted at Chaisang. Liu Bei at once asked Zhuge Liang to deliberate. In the middle of this, a messenger from Liu Biao arrived requesting that Liu Bei come to Jingzhou for consultation.

Zhuge Liang said,

“This is certainly because the Jiangdong army broke Huang Zu and now calls this meeting to discuss vengeance. I will go with you, and at the moment we can find a good way.”

Liu Bei agreed. He left Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, at Xinye, and ordered Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, to lead five hundred horse and men to follow him to Jingzhou.

Liu Bei said to Zhuge Liang while on horseback,

“When we meet Liu Biao, what should I answer him first?”

Kongming replied,

“First, apologize for what happened at Xiangyang. If he asks you to raise an expedition against Jiangdong, refuse it. Say you must return to Xinye and arrange your troops.”

As instructed, Liu Bei reached Jingzhou and took lodging. He left Zhang Fei with a detachment outside the city. Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang then entered to meet Liu Biao. After the formal greetings, Liu Bei knelt and asked pardon.

Liu Biao said,

“I already know of the matter in which my junior brother was harmed. At the time I wished to behead Cai Mao’s head and offer it to your brother. But when the elders pleaded, I forgave him for now. Do not fear punishment.”

Liu Bei replied,

“It was not only General Cai’s doing. It must have been done by some of the attendants beneath him.”

Liu Biao said,

“Now Jiangxia has fallen, and Huang Zu is dead. I ask that my younger brother join me to discuss a plan of retaliation.”

Liu Bei replied,

“Huang Zu was violent and could not use capable men, which caused this disaster. If we raise troops for a southern expedition and Cao Cao advances from the north, what then?”

Liu Biao said,

“I am old and sick and cannot manage affairs anymore. You may come to assist me. After I die, you may take charge of Jingzhou.”

Liu Bei said,

“How can you say this, big brother? I do not dare to take so great a burden.”

Zhuge Liang looked at Liu Bei, and Liu Bei said,

“Let me consider carefully and find a better strategy.”

So they withdrew. When Liu Bei returned to the inn, Kongming said,

“Jingsheng proposes to entrust Jingzhou to your lordship. Why do you refuse?”

Liu Bei said,

“Jingsheng has shown us kindness beyond measure. How could I seize the province while his position is weak?”

Kongming sighed,

“He is truly a benevolent lord.”

As they were still discussing, Liu Qi came in. Liu Bei invited him to step forward. Liu Qi knelt and wept,

“My stepmother cannot bear me. My life hangs on tomorrow’s dawn. Please save me, uncle.”

Liu Bei answered,

“This is family business, and he asks me.”

Liu Bei then asked Zhuge Liang for counsel. Kongming said,

“This is a private matter of household blood, and I dare not involve myself.”

After a while, Liu Bei sent Liu Qi out and said in a low voice,

“Tomorrow I will send Kongming back to return your greeting. He will have a way to help.”

Liu Qi thanked him and left.

The next day Liu Bei pretended an ache in his stomach and ordered Zhuge Liang to go in his place to visit Liu Qi. Kongming agreed and rode to the young lord’s house. He dismounted before the gate and was received within.

Liu Qi invited him to the rear hall. After tea, he said,

“Liu Qi cannot find favor with his stepmother. I beg the Master to speak one word and save me.”

Zhuge Liang said,

“I am but your guest here. I dare not interfere with blood relations. If anything were revealed, the harm would not be light.”

He rose to leave, but Liu Qi said, “How can he who has honored me so highly wait on me with such formality?” and drew him into a private room to drink.

As they drank, Liu Qi said again,

“My stepmother still gives me no welcome. I beg the Master to save me.”

Zhuge Liang said,

“This is not a thing I dare to devise.”

After speaking he prepared to rise. Liu Qi said,

“If the Master remains silent, let him go. Why then leave at once?”

Kongming sat again.

Liu Qi then said,

“I keep an old book. Please, Master, look at it.”

He led him up into a small pavilion.

Kongming asked, “Where is the book kept?”

Liu Qi knelt and wept,

“My life is on the edge of dawn and dusk. My stepmother gives no welcome. If the Master says nothing, how can he save me?”
