Zhuge Liang rose and prepared to go, and at that moment the staircase had already been removed. Liu Qi said,

“I seek a true stratagem from the Master. The Master fears leakage and will not speak. Today I am between heaven and earth—if your mouth can open and his ear can hear, then I may receive the teaching.”

Zhuge Liang said,

“When one who is not intimate speaks to kin, how can Kongming counsel the prince?”

Liu Qi replied,

“Will the Master never teach me at all? My life cannot be kept. Let me die before you now.”

He drew his sword to stab himself. Zhuge Liang stopped him and said,

“I have already found a good plan.”

Liu Qi knelt and said,

“Then grant me instruction at once.”

Zhuge Liang said,

“Have you not heard of Shensheng and Chong’er? Shensheng died within while Chong’er survived by staying outside. Now Huang Zu has just fallen and Jiangxia has few men to guard it. Why does the young lord not speak up and request to station troops there? Then you may avoid disaster.”

Liu Qi knelt again in thanks and sent men to fetch a ladder and bring Zhuge Liang down.

Back with Liu Bei, Kongming recounted all that had happened. Liu Bei was overjoyed. The next day Liu Qi submitted a request to defend Jiangxia. Liu Biao hesitated, so he asked Liu Bei to discuss with him. Liu Bei said,

“Jiangxia is an important place and not for ordinary men to hold. It must be the prince himself who goes there. The southern matter should be borne by father and son there; for the northwest, I, Liu Bei, am willing to hold.”

Liu Biao said,

“I have heard that Cao Cao has made the Xuanwu Pond in Ye Commandery to train water troops and likely intends a southern expedition. We must prepare against that.”

Liu Bei replied,

“I know that. Do not worry.”

He then took his leave and returned to Xinye. Liu Biao ordered Liu Qi to bring three thousand soldiers and garrison Jiangxia.

Cao Cao, abolishing the offices of the Three Dukes, assumed the Chancellorship and appointed Mao Jie as Eastern Clerk of the Chancellor’s Office, Cui Yan as Western Clerk, and Sima Yi, whose courtesy name was Zhongda, as Literary Clerk. Sima Yi was from Wen in Henei. He was a grandson of Sima Juan, Administrator of Yingchuan; a son of Sima Fang, Intendant of Jingzhao; and a younger brother of Sima Lang, who served as a clerk. The civil office was now fully staffed, and Cao Cao gathered the generals to discuss a southern campaign.

Xiahou Dun proposed,

“I have heard that Liu Bei has been training his men daily at Xinye. He will become trouble later. We should plan against him early.”

Cao Cao immediately appointed Xiahou Dun as Chief Commander, with Yu Jin, Li Dian, Xiahou Lan, and Han Hao as deputies, and ordered him to lead one hundred thousand soldiers straight to Bowang to reconnoiter Xinye.

Xun Yu advised,

“Liu Bei is a hero, and now he has Zhuge Liang as his military adviser. We should not treat him lightly.”

Dun replied,

“Liu Bei is no more than a rat. I will surely capture him.”

Xu Shu said,

“Do not underestimate Liu Xuande, though he is called by that name. Since he has received Zhuge Liang, he is like a tiger with winged support.”

Cao Cao asked,

“Who is Zhuge Liang?”

Xu Shu answered,

“His name is Kongming, known as Master Wòlóng [Sleeping Dragon]. He has talents that map heaven and ground and strategies that enter beyond spirits. He is an exceptional man of this age, not one to be underestimated.”

Cao Cao said,

“What of yourself, then?”

Xu Shu said,

“This humble adviser has no right to compare with Kongming. I am but a firefly’s light; he is the moon’s clear brilliance.”

Xiahou Dun laughed and said,

“Yu, your words are mistaken. I look on Zhuge Liang as a blade of grass. Why should we fear him? If I do not capture Liu Bei alive and seize Zhuge Liang in one battle, I will offer their heads to the Chancellor.”

Cao Cao said,

“Report good news soon and ease my heart.”

Xiahou Dun rose at once, saluted, and left to march.

Liu Bei had received Kongming and treated him with due reverence. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei were displeased.

“He is young. What talent has he? Your devotion to him is too much. And we have yet to see him prove himself,” they said.

Liu Bei answered,

“Since I found Kongming, it is as a fish finding water. You two should not add further words.”

Guan Yu and Zhang Fei withdrew in silence.

One day, someone brought a buffalo tail to court. Liu Bei took the tail and tied it onto his cap himself. Zhuge Liang entered and said sharply,

“My lord, do you have no far ambition anymore, but only this task at hand?”

Liu Bei threw the cap onto the ground and apologized,

“I only put this on to set aside my worries.”

Zhuge Liang said,

“How does my lord measure yourself against Cao Cao?”

Liu Bei said,

“By no means equal.”

Zhuge Liang replied,

“Your men are but a few thousand. If Cao’s host comes, how can you meet it?”

Liu Bei said,

“That is what has been worrying me. I have no good plan.”

Zhuge Liang said,

“Recruit the local militia at once; let me train them. They can wait for the enemy.”

Liu Bei did so at Xinye and raised three thousand men. Kongming taught them formation and maneuvers day and night.

They soon heard that Xiahou Dun had arrived with one hundred thousand men from Cao Cao marching hard toward Xinye. When Zhang Fei heard, he said to Guan Yu,

“Brother, why not send ‘the strategist’ first?”

Liu Bei said,

“Our hopes rest on Kongming, and courage on my two brothers. I cannot lay all this aside.”

When Guan and Zhang had gone, Liu Bei requested Zhuge Liang to devise a plan.

Zhuge Liang said,

“I fear the two of you will not obey my orders. If my lord wishes for me to lead an army, please grant me your sword seal.”

Liu Bei gave the seal to Kongming. Zhuge Liang then assembled the assembled commanders and issued orders.

Zhang Fei said to Guan Yu,

“Let us listen and then go. Let us see how he directs them.”

Kongming ordered,

“To the left of Bowang is Yushan Mountain; to the right is a wood called Anlin. It is fit for concealing men and horse. Guanyu, send one thousand men to Yushan and set ambush first. Let the enemy arrive, and let him pass us by and wear himself down. Their baggage and grain will surely come behind. Watch for a blaze from the south, then send your men out to strike and burn their grain train. Yide [Zhang Fei], take one thousand men and hide in the valley behind the mountain at Anlin. Again, when fire rises from the south, ride out and burn what stores were previously stacked at Bowang where supplies were kept. Guan Ping and Liu Feng should bring five hundred and keep prepared burning materials on either side behind the Bowang slope, so that at the first watch, once the enemy troops arrive they can set fire. Also, recall Zhao Yun from Fan City and make him the vanguard. Instruct him not to seek a hard victory, but to keep yielding ground.”

“My lord should draw one army and hold as reserve. Each man must act by this plan without fail.”

Guan Yu asked,

“We all go out to meet the enemy. What is the master strategist to do?”

Kongming said,

“I will stay and defend this city.”

Zhang Fei laughed,

“We all go to fight while you sit at home and hold your seat?”

Kongming said,

“The sword seal is here. Whoever disobeys my order will be cut down.”

Liu Bei said,

“Have you not heard, ‘deciding and planning in the tent, settling victory a thousand li away’? You two must not disobey.”

Zhang Fei gave him a cold laugh and left.

Guan Yu said,

“Let us see if his plan works or not; we can ask him later.”

After they left, no one among the gathered commanders fully understood Kongming’s stratagem. Though they followed orders, all were uncertain.

Kongming told Liu Bei,

“Today, my lord, move and encamp at the foot of Bowang Mountain. Tomorrow at dusk the enemy will certainly arrive. Then my lord should abandon your camp and withdraw. When you see flames rise, return at once and kill in enclosure. I will go with Mi Zhu and Mi Fang leading five hundred to guard the county. Send Sun Qian and Jian Yong to prepare a celebratory feast and ready the rewards ledger.”

All these deployments were made, but Liu Bei still wavered.

Xiahou Dun and Yu Jin, with their forces, arrived at Bowang and split half of the picked troops as the vanguard, while the rest guarded the baggage wagons. In the autumn a wind slowly rose. As the men and horses ran, dust suddenly rose before them ahead. Xiahou Dun formed the troops and asked the local guide, “What place is this?”

The guide replied,

“Ahead is Bowang Slope. Behind lies Luochuan Pass.”

Xiahou Dun ordered Yu Jin and Li Dian to hold the line and went forward himself. He looked ahead at the approaching army and suddenly burst out laughing.

When the others asked why, he said,

“I laugh that Xu Yuan [Xun Yu] praised Zhuge Liang to the Chancellor as one among gods and men. Look how he now uses his troops in battle: these horses and riders would be just like dogs loosed against tigers and leopards! I boasted before the Chancellor that I would capture Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang alive. My words will be fulfilled now.”

He spurred directly forward.

Zhao Yun rode out.

Xiahou Dun shouted,

“You cling to Liu Bei as a lonely soul clings to a ghost!”

Zhao Yun, enraged, spurred forward to battle. The two horses met, exchanged only a few blows, and Liu Bei’s ally feigned retreat. Xiahou Dun chased.

After about ten li, Zhao Yun turned and fought again, then feigned retreat once more, and did this more than once. Han Hao rode up to intercede,

“Zhao Yun is luring the enemy. He must have laid a trap.”

Xiahou Dun said,

“Even if there were ten ambushes, what do I fear?”

He ignored Han Hao and pressed on to Bowang Slope.

A single heavy blast sounded. At that same moment, Liu Bei drove his army forward and came to join and exchange blows. Xiahou Dun said to Han Hao,

“That is the ambushed force indeed! I swear I will not stop killing until I take Xinye tonight!”

He drove the force onward.

Liu Bei and Zhao Yun withdrew and retreated.

Night had now fallen and dense clouds covered the sky. There was still no moon. The daytime wind had risen, and the night wind rose stronger. Xiahou Dun, intent only on pressing forward, drove the men to kill and chase.

Yu Jin and Li Dian reached a narrow place, with reeds on both sides. Li Dian said to Yu Jin,

“Those who rely on deception often lose. The south road is narrow, mountains and streams hem you in, trees are thick. If they use fire, what then?”

Yu Jin answered,

“You speak truly. I will go forward to warn the Chief Commander. You hold the rear army.”

Li Dian hauled back his horse and shouted, “Hold the rear ranks!” But no wall could have held them at that pace. Yu Jin then shouted harder, “The rear ranks of the commander’s column should slow their pace!”

As Xiahou Dun rode onward, he saw Yu Jin coming back from the rear and asked why.

Yu Jin said,

“The southern road is narrow. Mountains and water constrict it, and trees crowd together. They may use fire.”

Xiahou Dun suddenly realized this. He wheeled and ordered the cavalry to stop. He had not finished giving the order when a roar rose from behind. He turned and saw flames spreading at once. Soon the reeds on both sides were burning too. In a moment, all around was fire in every direction. With the wind high, the flames grew fierce.

Cao’s men trampled one another in panic; the dead were too many to count.

Zhao Yun countercharged and pursued, and Xiahou Dun rode through smoke and fire to escape.

Li Dian saw the tide turning badly and ran back to Bowang City. In the firelight a column blocked him. At its front was no other than Guan Yu.

Li Dian wheeled his horse into close fighting and forced through. Yu Jin saw that the baggage wagons and supplies were already burning and bolted down a side track.

Xiahou Lan and Han Hao came to recover the baggage, and met Zhang Fei. The two fought for only a few exchanges. Zhang Fei drove his spear through Xiahou Lan and downed him with the horse. Han Hao stole away.

The fighting continued until dawn before the army could be reassembled. Heaps of bodies lay in the fields, and blood ran like a river.

A later song said:

At Bowang, the lines held in fire attack, Their command and deployment came as easy as idle chat. At once it shook Cao Gong’s courage; This was the first merit of the thatched-cottage master.

Xiahou Dun gathered his remnant and returned to Xuchang.

Kongming then assembled his men. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei said,

“Kongming truly is a heroic man.”

After only a few li, they saw Mi Zhu and Mi Fang bringing a small formation, and in one wagon a man sat upright: it was Kongming.

Guan Yu and Zhang Fei dismounted and knelt before the wagon. Before long, Liu Bei, Zhao Yun, Liu Feng, Guan Ping, and the others arrived. They gathered the troops, assigned the seized grain and baggage, and distributed rewards to the soldiers before returning to Xinye.

The people of Xinye blocked the roads and bowed as the troops passed, saying,

“You all live because we live by your lord’s strength and by this worthy man!”

Returning within the county, Kongming told Liu Bei,

“Although Xiahou Dun has been beaten, Cao Cao will surely bring a great army himself.”

Liu Bei asked,

“How shall we respond?”

Zhuge Liang replied,

“I have one plan by which we can meet Cao’s army.”

So it was:

Though the enemy has been broken, the battle horses cannot yet rest; to evade pursuit, good strategy will again be required. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: In Jingzhou City the Prince Seeks Counsel Three Times, and at Bowang Slope the Military Strategist Takes His First Battle Command

chapters.html:
Liu Bei asked Zhuge Liang for a plan to repel Cao Cao’s force.

Zhuge Liang said, “Xinye is a small county. We cannot stay there long. I have recently heard that Liu Biao, whose personal name was Jing Sheng, is dangerously ill. This is a chance to take Jingzhou as a place to settle in, and perhaps then we can withstand Cao Cao.”

Liu Bei said, “Your reasoning is excellent. But I have enjoyed so much kindness from Jingsheng—how could I bear to turn it against him?”

Zhuge Liang said, “If we do not seize this chance now, how can we remedy our regret later?”

Liu Bei said, “I would sooner die than commit an unrighteous deed.”

Zhuge Liang said, “Let us discuss it once more.”

Xiahou Dun returned defeated to Xuchang, bound himself, and bowed to the ground before Cao Cao, asking to be put to death. Cao Cao spared him.

Xiahou Dun said, “Xiahou Dun was outwitted by Zhuge Liang’s ruse and my army was broken by a fire attack.”

Cao Cao said, “You have handled troops since you were young. How could you not know that narrow ground requires caution against fire?”

Xiahou Dun said, “Li Dian and Yu Jin had already warned me of this. My regret comes too late.”

Then Cao Cao rewarded both men.

Xiahou Dun said, “Liu Bei is that unruly; he is truly a grave threat in our midst and must be dealt with at once.”

Cao Cao said, “What I fear is only Liu Bei and Sun Quan. The rest are not worth my concern. Now is the time to sweep down and pacify Jiangnan.”

He gave orders to raise five hundred thousand men in five columns. Cao Ren and Cao Hong would be the first column, Zhang Liao and Zhang He the second, Xiahou Yuan and Xiahou Dun the third, Yu Jin and Li Dian the fourth, and Cao Cao himself led the fifth. Each column was to bring one hundred thousand soldiers.

He also made Xu Chu General of Breaking Through and ordered three thousand men as the vanguard.

On the bingwu day of the seventh month of the autumn in the thirteenth year of Jian’an, the expedition was launched.

Kong Rong, the Grand Councillor, offered a remonstrance: “Liu Bei and Liu Biao are both kinsmen of the Han house; they should not be attacked lightly. Sun Quan has made himself secure in six commanderies and holds the great River as a natural defense, so he is also not easily taken. Now the Chancellor has raised an unjust army in pursuit of them; it may ruin his fame before the world.”

Cao Cao was angry. “Liu Bei, Liu Biao, and Sun Quan are all ministers who disobey Heaven’s mandate. How could they be left unpunished?”

He shouted Kong Rong away and ordered that whoever remonstrated again should be beheaded.

Kong Rong left the hall and lifted his eyes to the sky, sighing, “Even one who is cruelly inhuman attacks one who is humane. How can he avoid ruin?”

At that moment an attendant of the Inspector Xi, Xi Lu, heard what had been said and reported it to him. Xi Lu had long been insulted by Kong Rong and deeply resented him. He used this moment to inform Cao Cao again: “In former days, Kong Rong repeatedly presumed with the Chancellor and was on cordial terms with Mi Heng. Mi Heng praised Kong Rong and said, ‘Confucius has not died.’ Kong Rong praised Mi Heng and said, ‘Yan Hui is reborn.’

And when Mi Heng once insulted the Chancellor, it was Kong Rong who urged him on.”

Cao Cao was furious and ordered the Imperial Censor to arrest Kong Rong.

Kong Rong had two sons, still quite young, then at home playing weiqi. His attendants rushed in and said, “Your lord is being taken by the Censor and is likely to be executed. Why do not the two young lords flee at once?”

They replied, “Under a fallen nest, where can there be one egg left unbroken?”

Before they could finish speaking, the Censor returned and seized all the household staff and both boys. All were executed, and the body of Kong Rong was displayed in the marketplace.

Wei Zhi Xi of Jingzhao stood by the corpse and wept. When Cao Cao heard, he raged and wanted to kill him too.

Xun Yu spoke: “I have heard that Zhi Xi has always remonstrated with Kong Rong, saying, ‘Your uprightness and bluntness go too far and are a path to disaster.’

Now Kong Rong has died and he came to mourn him. He is a righteous man; he cannot be killed.”

Cao Cao relented.

Zhi Xi gathered the bodies of Kong Rong and his sons and buried them all.

Later people composed this verse:

Kong Rong in Beihai,
Heroic spirit spanning a long rainbow.
His chamber always crowded with guests,
Never empty the cups in his vessels.
His prose stunned the common world,
His laughter and talk mocked lords and nobles.
The brush of history praised his loyalty and uprightness,
And preserved his name in the records of high office.

After Kong Rong’s death, Cao Cao ordered the five columns to set out in sequence, leaving Xun Yu and others behind to guard Xuchang.

Then Liu Biao of Jingzhou became gravely ill and sent for Liu Bei to entrust him with his orphaned house. Liu Bei arrived with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei.

Liu Biao said, “My illness has entered my marrow and I will not survive long. I entrust this matter to my worthy younger brother. My sons have no talent and will not sustain my inheritance. After I die, my brother may govern Jingzhou himself.”

Liu Bei knelt in tears and said, “I will devote all I can to assisting your honored nephew. How could I have any other intent?”

Just then someone reported that Cao Cao had taken command of a large army and was on the way. Liu Bei immediately took leave and raced back to Xinye by night.

Liu Biao heard this news and was shocked. He deliberated and drew up a testament making Liu Qi his heir in Jingzhou. Lady Cai, however, concealed the testament.

When Liu Qi of Jiangxia learned of his father’s crisis and arrived at Jingzhou to visit him, Cai Mai at the outer gate blocked him and said, “Your highness has been ordered by your father to hold Jiangxia. The charge is grave. If you do not shoulder this properly and Wu troops come from the east, what will you do? If you force your way inside before the lord, your lord’s temper will flare and his illness will worsen. It would not be filial. You should leave at once.”

Liu Qi stood outside the gate and wept bitterly, then mounted his horse and rode back to Jiangxia.

Liu Biao’s condition worsened. He looked for Liu Qi in vain as he failed to arrive; on the wufu day of the eighth month he cried out several times and died.

Later people composed this verse for Liu Biao:

Once I had heard the Yuans hold sway north of the Yellow River;
Now I saw Lord Liu seize and dominate Hanyang.
All for household and rank’s ruin
It is sad, and in little time all was gone.

After Liu Biao’s death, Cai Wife and Cai Mao and Zhang Yun conferred and forged a testament naming Liu Cong, the second son, ruler of Jingzhou. Then they performed the rites and announced the mourning.

Liu Cong was barely fourteen and fairly sharp. He gathered the officials and said, “My father is gone. My elder brother is in Jiangxia, and my uncle Liu Bei is in Xinye. You have all raised me as lord. If elder brother and uncle raise troops to punish this, how can we explain?”

Before the attendants could answer, Li Gui of the Secretariat replied, “Your Highness has spoken wisely. Now send an urgent mourning message to Jiangxia requesting the elder brother to govern Jingzhou, and order Liu Bei to administer affairs together with him. With this, we can resist Cao Cao in the north and hold against Sun Quan in the south. It is the wisest strategy.”

Cai Mao shouted, “Who are you, to speak and oppose my lord’s testament?”

Li Gui cursed him: “You and your associates inside and out, invoking my lord’s testament, have removed the elder and raised the younger so that all nine commanderies of Jing and Xiang fall into the hands of the Cai clan! If my late lord has any spirit, he will surely execute you.”

Cai Mao became furious and ordered his attendants to seize and execute Li Gui. Li Gui kept up his cursing until death.

So Cai Mao installed Liu Cong as ruler. The Cai family branches divided and took command of the troops of Jingzhou, and Deng Yi, the Governance Officer, and Liu Xian, an assistant director, were ordered to guard Jingzhou.

Lady Cai accompanied Liu Cong to Xiangyang and camped there to guard against Liu Qi and Liu Bei. They buried Liu Biao’s coffin east of Xiangyang near Hanyang.

They gave no formal mourning notice to Liu Qi or Liu Bei.

When Liu Cong reached Xiangyang and had scarcely dismounted, word arrived that Cao Cao was leading the main force straight for Xiangyang. He was terrified and summoned Kuai Yue and Cai Mao to discuss the situation.

Fu Xun, an imperial secretary in the eastern bureau, offered his opinion:

“Not only is Cao Cao’s army dangerous by itself. Now the elder brother is in Jiangxia and Liu Bei in Xinye. Neither has yet come to mourn. If he raises troops to punish us, Jing and Xiang are lost. I have one plan: surrender the nine commanderies of Jing and Xiang to Cao Cao. Cao Cao will then treat the ruler with high esteem.”

Liu Cong said, “What can this plan be?”

Fu Xun said, “It would be better to offer Jing and Xiang to him.”

Liu Cong barked, “What words are these! I have just inherited my father’s foundation and it is not yet firm. How can I now abandon it to another?”

Kuai Yue spoke: “The meaning is right. Order and disorder have their great principles, strength and weakness follow their fixed tides. At present Cao Cao is in the south for campaigns and in the north for repression, claiming to act for the court. If our lord refuses him, he will appear to be in the wrong. And with the lord newly installed, outside danger is not yet settled and inner trouble is about to come. The people of Jing and Xiang have heard Cao’s army is coming; before battle they already tremble. How could they face him?”

Liu Cong said, “Your words are not what I refuse, yet if this inheritance of my father is abandoned in one stroke to another man, the world will laugh at us.”

The discussion was still in progress when a figure stepped in, upright and proud: Wang Can, surname Wang, given name Can, courtesy name Zhongxuan, from Gaoping in Shanyang. He was short and slight in build. In childhood he had visited Chief Minister Cai Zhong (Cai Yong); Cai Yong, whose guests overflowed his hall, ordered his attendants to rise when Can entered. Every guest asked, “Why does Chief Minister Cai honor this child so?”

Yong replied, “This boy has uncommon talent. He is better than I am.”

Wang Can read widely and had a prodigious memory; few could match him. He could read inscriptions by the roadside and immediately recite them, and if he saw a chaotic go board, he could rearrange it perfectly.

He was also excellent at calculations. His writings and rhetoric were unrivaled in the age.

At seventeen he was invited to serve as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate but declined.

Later, fleeing disorder, he came to Jingxiang, where Liu Biao treated him as an honored guest.

That day he told Liu Cong, “General, how do you assess Cao Cao?”

Liu Cong said, “He is not to be compared.”

Wang Can said, “Cao Cao has strong troops, excellent generals, and deep intelligence. He captured Lü Bu at Xiangfu, crushed Yuan Shao at Guandu, drove Liu Bei to Longyou, and beat the Wuhuan at White Wolf. The men he has eliminated and crushed cannot be counted. If he comes with a great army to the south for Jing and Xiang, it will be impossible to withstand him. The plans of Fu Xun and Kuai Yue are indeed long strategy. The governor had better not delay and repent later.”

Liu Cong said, “Master, your counsel is fitting. But I still need to report this to my mother.”

At that moment Cai Fu came out from behind her screen and said to Liu Cong, “If Master Zhongxuan, Master Futi, and Master Yidu all agree, why must you report this to me first?”

Then Liu Cong settled his mind and wrote a letter of surrender. He sent Song Zhong to infiltrate and present it before Cao Cao’s camp.

Song Zhong accepted the mission and reached Wancheng, met Cao Cao, and presented the letter.

Cao Cao rejoiced greatly and rewarded him generously, then ordered him to return and tell Liu Cong to come out to receive him. He confirmed Liu Cong as forever ruler of Jingzhou.

After bowing and leaving Cao Cao, Song Zhong set out back to Jingxiang. He was about to cross the river when he saw a troop arriving. It was Guan Yu.

Song Zhong could not avoid it; Guan Yu called him in and questioned him closely about events in Jingzhou. At first Song Zhong concealed the truth, but Guan Yu persisted in his interrogation and he finally told him, in full, everything that had happened.

Guan Yu was greatly shocked and captured Song Zhong, bringing him to Liu Bei at Xinye.

Liu Bei was devastated and burst into tears.

Zhang Fei said, “It has come to this. We should first execute Song Zhong, then raise an army and cross the river, take back Xiangyang, kill the Cai clan and Liu Cong, and then meet Cao Cao in battle.”

Liu Bei said, “Keep your mouth closed. I will decide in time.”

Then he called to Song Zhong, “Now you know how everyone is acting, why did you not come straight to me sooner? Slaying you now will not change anything. Go quickly.”

Song Zhong bowed and left, clutching his head and slipping away.

Liu Bei was still weighed down by grief when a messenger arrived from his elder brother, Liu Qi.

Liu Bei thanked him deeply for rescuing him in earlier days and came down from the gate to receive him repeatedly.

He said, “The elder brother is in Jiangxia. He heard that Jingzhou had already passed away. Cai Wu and Cai Mao and the rest met together; they did not come to report the death and made Liu Cong ruler. When your highness sent men to Xiangyang to investigate, they returned with that report. Fearing you might not know, they have sent me with this letter of mourning and ask you to summon all your best troops, and all of us to Xiangyang to punish the usurpers.”

After reading the letter Liu Bei said to Song Zhong, “Master Yi only knew Liu Cong had usurped the office and did not know Liu Cong had already offered the nine commanderies of Jing and Xiang to Cao Cao.”

Song Zhong was shocked. “How did my lord learn this?”

Liu Bei explained how he captured and questioned Song Zhong.

Song Zhong said, “Then my lord should go to Xiangyang in mourning’s name, and lure Liu Cong out to meet you; then seize him and execute his followers. Jingzhou will return to my lord.”

Zhuge Liang said, “What Master Yi says is right. Lord, you can follow this.”

Liu Bei, tears still on his face, said, “My elder brother placed this burden on me in peril and I promised to aid him. If I seize his son and take this land, how can I ever face him on the day I die?”

Zhuge Liang said, “If you do not act, Cao’s army has already reached Wancheng. How will you resist?”

Liu Bei said, “Then we should move to Fan City to avoid them.”

While they were discussing, scouts reported that Cao’s army had reached Bowang.

Liu Bei hastily ordered Song Zhong back to Jiangxia, to organize horse and men. He and Zhuge Liang conferred again on a way to resist.

Zhuge Liang said, “Your Grace, calm yourself. Before, one fire had burnt most of Xiahou Dun’s men; now Cao’s army has come again. They will surely fall to this same plan. We cannot remain in Xinye. Let us go first to Fan City.”

He ordered notices posted at the four gates and messengers to tell the residents: “Men and women, old and young: whoever wishes to follow us should go with us to Fan City today to take temporary refuge. Do not delay.”

He sent Sun Qian to the river to gather boats and rescue civilians, and sent Mi Zhu to escort the families of the officials to Fan City.

He then assembled the officers and gave orders.

First he told Guan Yu to take one thousand men to conceal themselves at the upper reaches of the White River: each man should carry a cloth sack full of sand, damming the water; then at the third watch tomorrow, when someone downstream shouts and calls out horse cries, they should quickly tear up the sacks, release the water, and drown the pursuing army, then move downstream after them.

He told Zhang Fei to take one thousand men and ambush at Boling Ford. “The current here is slowest. When Cao’s soldiers are overwhelmed by flood and seek escape, they will pass this way. Strike them then.”

He told Zhao Yun to lead three thousand men and divide into four groups. He would lead one, while three groups would conceal themselves at the west, south, and north gates. At the same time he should hide in the rooftops of household homes within the city ample sulphur, saltpeter, and burning materials.

“When Cao’s men enter the city, they will surely dismount there. After dusk there will certainly be a great wind. As soon as the wind rises, let the units hidden at west, south, and north gates shoot flaming arrows into the city. Wait until flames spread in the city, then chant and shout from outside as if reinforcing yourselves. Leave only the east gate open for escape and strike them from behind when they emerge.

At dawn, join Guan Yu and Zhang Fei and withdraw the troops to Fan City.”

Then he ordered Mi Fang and Liu Feng to take two thousand men, half with red banners and half with blue banners, and camp thirty li outside Xinye before Qiewei Slope.

“As soon as Cao’s army arrives, red-banner troops on the left and blue-banner troops on the right. Their hearts will be uncertain and they will not dare to pursue. You two should then take separate ambushes. Wait until the fires break out in the city, then pursue and cut down the broken troops, and then return to the upper reach of the White River for reinforcement.”

Zhuge Liang finished arranging his deployments and then he and Liu Bei climbed to a height to watch and wait for victory news.

Cao Ren and Cao Hong led one hundred thousand men in the first column, with Xu Chu’s three-thousand iron-armored vanguard cutting the way before them. In one great surge they rushed toward Xinye.

At midday that day they reached Qiewei Slope and saw in front of it a massed force under blue and red banners. Xu Chu pressed the troops forward. Liu Feng and Mi Fang had split into four groups, with blue and red banners on opposite wings.

Xu Chu reined in and ordered, “Stop advancing. There must be ambushes ahead. My troops will hold here.”

On one horse he rode back and reported to Cao Ren.

Cao Ren said, “This is only a false alarm. Surely no ambush lies ahead. Advance quickly. I will order the rest to follow.”

Xu Chu returned to the slope and pushed ahead with his men. In the woods they searched but saw no one.

The sun had nearly set. As Xu Chu was about to advance again, a great clamor of gongs and drums rose from the mountain. He looked up and saw on the summit a cluster of banners and tents, with two umbrella canopies. On the left was Liu Bei; on the right, Zhuge Liang. The two sat opposite each other, drinking.

In rage, Xu Chu urged his army uphill. A great battering of timber-ram guns and stones came down from above, blocking any advance.

He then heard cries from behind the mountain so loud they shook the ground, and the troops searched for paths to continue fighting. Night had already darkened.

Cao Ren arrived with troops and ordered them to seize Xinye and dismount. When the soldiers reached the city gates, they found all four gates thrown open.

The Cao army burst in at once without resistance. No one remained within; the city was empty.

Cao Hong said, “This is a city stripped bare and desperate with no hope left, so all the people fled with it. Let us rest and then march on at dawn.”

By then all columns were exhausted and hungry, and everyone had set out to find food. Cao Ren and Cao Hong were resting inside the city hall.

Past the first watch of night, wild wind rose. A gate watchman reported that fires had started.

Cao Ren said, “This must be soldiers cooking badly and making careless fires. Let us not be alarmed.”

Not long after, several further reports arrived in quick succession. Fires were said to have started at the west, south, and north gates.

Cao Ren quickly ordered all generals to mount, and as he spoke the whole county burned. Flame ran up through the town, red from top to bottom. The fire that night outshone the fire at the Bowang camps of the previous day.

Later people composed this verse:

Cunning Cao Cao, keeper of the middle realm,
in the ninth month marched south to Hanchuan.
The Wind Lord came angry upon Xinye County;
Zhurong dropped his flames to scrape the sky.

Cao Ren and the other generals charged through smoke and fire, searching for a way out. As they ran, they heard that no fire burned at the east gate and hurried out through it.

Soldiers trampled one another in the rush; many died.

By the time Cao Ren and the others escaped the immediate danger, a cry rose from behind. Zhao Yun’s force came charging in mixed combat. The defeated host fled for life; few turned to stand and fight.

Still running, Mi Fang reached with his force and pressed in again. A sharp skirmish was fought, Cao Ren was badly defeated, and he tried to break through.

Liu Feng also came with another force to cut him off again.

By the fourth watch, men were spent and horses exhausted, most soldiers bruised and disordered. They reached the bank of the White River and found some relief: the river was not very deep, so men and horses went down to drink.

By then Guan Yu upstream had dammed the White River with his sacks.

Toward dusk he watched the fires in Xinye; by the fourth watch he suddenly heard shouts and horse cries from downstream. He immediately ordered his men to lift all sacks at once. The flood came rushing, swelling and roaring.

Cao’s soldiers and horses were all drowned in the water; many died.

Cao Ren led the remaining commanders to find the path where the current ran slowly. They reached Boling Ford, where shouts rose and one force blocked the way.

At its front stood Zhang Fei. He shouted, “Cao rebel, come and give us your life!”

The Cao soldiers were terrified.

It is said:

Inside the walls the red flames had just begun to spit out,
At the riverbank a black wind came again.
How Cao Ren’s life would fare is yet untold—
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Lady Cai Debates Surrendering Jing Province, and Zhuge Liang Burns Xinye

chapters.html:
Earlier, because Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, had released the men upstream, Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, pursued with his troops from downstream and slaughtered his way through to cut them off. He soon met Xu Chu, who came to close combat. Xu Chu did not dare to stay and tangle in battle, so he snatched his escape path and got away. Zhang Fei caught up, and then Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, and Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, proceeded together upriver. Liu Feng and Mi Fang had already arranged boats and waited, so they crossed together all at once and headed straight for Fan City. Zhuge Liang ordered the boats and rafts set aflame.

Cao Ren then gathered the shattered troops and set camp at Xinye. He sent Cao Hong to report everything to Cao Cao. The Chancellor flew into a rage and shouted, “That village peasant Zhuge--how dare he act this way?” He ordered all the army to move, sealing mountain and open country, and all arrived to set camp below Xinye. He ordered the soldiers to search the hills on one front and block the Baihe on another; he divided the main force into eight columns and directed them all to take Fan City at once. Liu Ye warned him: “Since the Chancellor has just arrived at Xiangyang, he must first win the people’s hearts. Now Liu Bei has moved all the people of Xinye into Fan City. If our troops advance directly, the two counties will be ground to flour. A better course is to send men first to win Liu Bei over.” If he refuses, then this will also show that we have concern for the people. If he comes over, we can secure Jing Province without a fight.

The Chancellor asked, “Who could serve as envoy?” Liu Ye replied, “Xu Shu is on very good terms with Liu Bei and is right there in camp. Why not have him go?” Cao Cao said, “If he goes, he may not return.” Liu Ye said, “If he does not return, they will mock him forever. Chancellor, do not doubt.” Cao Cao then summoned Xu Shu and said, “I want to take Fan City by force, yet I pity the life of the common people. You can go and tell Liu Bei this: if he comes to surrender, he will be pardoned and ennobled; if he persists in obstinacy, soldiers and civilians will all be put to the sword and all be burned alike. I know your loyalty and rectitude, and therefore send you so directly. Do not let me be disappointed.”

Xu Shu obeyed and went to Fan City. Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang received him and recalled their old friendship. Shu said, “The Chancellor sends me to recruit you as a ruse to buy the people’s heart. He has split his army into eight roads and filled the Baihe while advancing. Fan City will be hard to hold. You should make urgent plans at once.” Liu Bei wished to keep Xu Shu, but he thanked him and said, “If I fail to return, men will laugh at me. My mother is already dead and I have nursed my grievance to the end of my life. Though I stand with him, I will not devise one trick against him. You have the Sleeping Dragon as adviser; why need you fear the great undertaking will fail?” He asked to be excused. Liu Bei did not dare force him to stay.

Xu Shu returned to Cao Cao and reported that Liu Bei had no thoughts of surrender. Cao Cao grew furious and that same day pressed forward. Liu Bei consulted Kongming, who said, “You can abandon Fan City now and go to Xiangyang to rest for a while.” Liu Bei said, “I have had these people following me for such a long time. How can I bear to abandon them?”

Kongming answered, “Order these words proclaimed to the people: those who are willing to follow may go together, those unwilling may remain.” He first sent Yun Chang to the riverbank to organize boats and ordered Sun Qian and Jian Yong to spread the word in the city: “The Chao [Cao] troops are coming and this lone city cannot hold long. If the people are willing to follow, cross the river at once.”

The folk of both counties cried out together, “Though we may die, we will still follow our Lord!” They wept and set out that very day. Old and young were supported over shoulders, sons carried with daughters; they poured across the river in unceasing streams, and both banks rang with grief. Liu Bei on a boat looked on and wept bitterly. “Because of one man’s sake, I have made the people suffer this great calamity. Why should I still be alive?” He tried to cast himself into the river, and his attendants rushed to pull him back. All who heard him wept.

By the time the boats reached the southern bank, when he looked back toward the far side there were still many who had not crossed and now faced south in tears. Liu Bei ordered Yun Chang at once to hasten the boats over, and only then did he mount and ride on. As they came to Xiangyang’s east gate they saw banners flying across the walls everywhere and stakes packed tightly along the moats. Liu Bei reined in and cried out, “Liu Qiong, my worthy nephew, I come only to save the people. I have no other thought. Open the gate.”

When Liu Qiong heard Liu Bei had arrived, he trembled and did not come out. Cai Mao and Zhang Yun rode straight up to the enemy tower and shouted while a shower of arrows burst downward. All the civilians outside the city turned and wept toward the tower. Suddenly one of the officers climbed up with a few hundred men and shouted from the battlement: “Cai Mao, Zhang Yun—traitors who sell the state! Lord Liu is a man of benevolent virtue; he has come now to rescue the people. How can you still refuse him?”

The watching men recognized him as a man eight chi tall, face as full as a ripe jujube, a native of Yiyang named Wei Yan, courtesy name Wenchang.

Wei Yan swung his axe-saber and cut down the gate guards, opened the gate, dropped the hanging bridge, and shouted, “Imperial Uncle Liu, quickly lead your men into the city and strike the traitors who sold the state!” Zhang Fei leapt from his horse to enter. Liu Bei hurriedly stopped him: “Do not alarm the people!” Wei Yan kept calling for Liu Bei’s troops to file into the city.

Then an officer from within rode out and shouted, “What nameless drudge is Wei Yan, who dares to raise rebellion? Do you know General Wenpin?” Wei Yan was incensed. He planted his spear, vaulted into the saddle, and moved to meet him in battle.

At the city edge the two forces mixed in killing confusion, and the cries were deafening. Liu Bei said, “I meant to protect the people and have only harmed them! I do not wish to enter Xiangyang!” Kongming said, “Jiangling is the key of Jing Province; better take Jiangling first and make it your base.” Liu Bei replied, “That agrees exactly with my heart.” So he guided the people out, leaving Xiangyang entirely, and headed for Jiangling. Many civilians of Xiangyang, swept by chaos, fled out the city and followed Liu Bei.

Wei Yan and Wenpin fought from the hour of Si through the hour of Wei, and the men under Wei Yan were all cut down. He turned his horse to flee and later could no longer be found; in the end he went to the hands of Han Xuan, the Administrator of Changsha.

Liu Bei then, in company with more than one hundred thousand soldiers and civilians, with thousands upon thousands of carts and uncounted porters, passed by Liu Biao’s tomb. He ordered his senior commanders to bow before it and cried out, “I, the brother Liu Bei, have no merit and no talent, yet I have failed my brother’s trust; all the guilt is mine alone and the people are guiltless. May my brother’s spirit come to life and save the people of Jing and Xiang!” His cry was so raw that the troops and civilians all wept.

A horseman’s scout then reported, “Cao Cao’s main army has camped at Fan City. Men are already collecting the boats and rafts; today he means to cross and catch up.” All the commanders said, “Jiangling is strategic and can be held if we stand fast. We have now taken tens of thousands. A day’s march is only ten or more li. By the time this is all done, how soon can they reach us? If Cao’s troops arrive, how do we resist? Better to leave the civilians for now and ride out first.”

Liu Bei cried, “When one undertakes great matters, one must put the people first. Now these people have all come to me; how can I abandon them?” The civilians, hearing this, were deeply moved.

Later people praised it in a verse:

In calamity, humane in heart and full of care for the people, he boarded the boat and wept, stirring all three armies. Even now, at the Xiang River mouth they mourn; the elders still remember their Lord.

Liu Bei continued to move slowly with the civilians. Kongming said, “The pursuers will arrive soon. Send Yun Chang to Jiangxia for help from the young lord Liu Qi and tell him to raise troops and meet us at Jiangling.”

Liu Bei agreed, so he wrote a letter and ordered Yun Chang and Sun Qian to lead five hundred soldiers toward Jiangxia. He assigned Zhang Fei to hold the rear, Zhao Yun to protect the old and the children, and the rest to keep the civilians in order as they moved. They rode only ten or so li each day and then rested.

At that same time Cao Cao, encamped at Fan City, had men cross to Xiangyang and summon Liu Qiong to meet him. Qiong trembled and dared not go, so Cai Mao and Zhang Yun made the approach. Wang Wei whispered privately to Qiong, “General, once you have surrendered and Liu Bei has gone, Cao Cao will be lax and unprepared. If you can gather an extraordinary force and set an ambush in rough ground, you may strike and win. If we can capture Cao, the realm will quake, and even Central Plains, wide as it is, can be settled by an edict. This rare opening must not be missed.”

Qiong relayed those words to Cai Mao. Mao shouted at Wang Wei, “How dare you, who do not know Heaven’s decree, speak such nonsense?” Wei replied in fury, “I hate you, traitors who sold out the state—why were you not born for me to eat your flesh!” Mao moved to kill him, and Huai Yue advised restraint. Mao then went with Zhang Yun to Fan City and, with excessive deference, made their report before Cao Cao.

Cao asked, “How many troops, horses, grain, and silver are now in Jing Province?” Cai Mao answered, “Fifty thousand horsemen, one hundred fifty thousand infantry, and eighty thousand river troops: that makes two hundred eighty thousand. Most of the funds and grain are in Jiangling, and what remains in other places can supply a year’s campaign.”

Cao Cao said, “How many warboats are there, and who originally commanded them?” Cai Mao answered, “Including the small craft, there are more than seven thousand. Their command was originally in the hands of the two of us.”

Cao Cao then made Cai Mao Marquis of Zhennan and Naval Commander-in-Chief, and made Zhang Yun Assistant Marquis Zhenshun and Deputy Naval Commander. Both men rejoiced and bowed in thanks. Cao Cao added, “Liu Jingsheng is already dead, and his son Jiangshun is about to surrender. I will memorialize the Son of Heaven and have him kept forever as lord of Jingzhou.” The two rejoiced and withdrew.

Xun You said, “Cai Mao and Zhang Yun are flatterers both. Master, why then grant such open rank and also make them naval commanders?” Cao Cao laughed. “Do I not know people well? I only needed these two for now. The army from northern fields I command is not trained in river war, so I must use them for the time being. When things are complete, I will sort it out another way.”

Cai Mao and Zhang Yun returned to Liu Qiong and told him that Cao Cao would petition that he remain forever lord of Jing and Xiang. Qiong was overjoyed. The next day, with his mother by his side and carrying the seal, token, and military tally, he crossed the river himself to receive Cao Cao. After formal mourning rites, Cao Cao drew him close, then led the conquering troops and camped outside Xiangyang. Cai Mao and Zhang Yun ordered the civilians to burn incense and receive him in ceremony.

Cao Cao used good words to pacify them all, and once he had taken his seat in the official hall, he called Kuai Yue forward and spoke comfortingly: “I do not rejoice merely in obtaining Jing Province; I rejoice in having found Yidu.” He immediately ennobled Kuai Yue as Governor of Jiangling and Marquis of Fan City. Fu Xun and Wang Can were all made Marquises within the Passes, and Liu Qiong was made Inspector of Qing Province, and then ordered to depart.

When Qiong heard that order, he was deeply shocked. He begged off, saying, “I do not wish to hold office; I would rather keep the soil of my parents.” Cao Cao said, “Qing Province is close to the capital and protects you at court; thus you need not be harmed in Jing and Xiang.” Qiong refused again and again, but Cao Cao refused to relent. Qiong could only go with his mother to Qing Province. Only the old officer Wang Wei followed, while all the rest of the staff escorted them to the river mouth and returned. Cao Cao called Yu Jin and entrusted him with instructions: “Lead a light cavalry force at speed and kill Liu Qiong and his mother, so no future trouble can grow.”

Yu Jin obeyed and caught up with his men at speed, then shouted, “I carry the Chancellor’s order. Come submit your heads, mother and son!” Liu Qiong’s mother, Cai Furen, clutched her son and wept loudly. Yu Jin ordered the soldiers to seize the horse. Wang Wei raged and fought fiercely, but he was cut down by the crowd. The soldiers killed Liu Qiong and his mother. Yu Jin returned to Cao Cao, who rewarded him richly. He ordered men sent to search Longzhong for Zhuge Liang’s wife and children, but their whereabouts were unknown. In truth, Liang had already had them moved and hidden among the people of three rivers. Cao Cao’s resentment deepened.

Now that Xiangyang had been secured, Xun You advised, “Jiangling is the strategic center of Jing and Xiang and holds vast grain and coin. If Liu Bei holds it, the situation will be shaken by extreme danger.” Cao Cao replied, “Have I forgotten that?” He then ordered one officer from among the Xiangyang commanders to lead troops and make a path. None noticed Wenpin among the generals, and Cao Cao sent for him, and he only arrived afterward.

Cao Cao said, “Why are you so late?” Wenpin answered, “A servant ought to keep his lord’s land and borders safe; to fail in that is a humiliation that fills me with shame. I have no face to be seen quickly.” His words ended, and tears welled and fell. Cao Cao said, “You are a true loyal minister.” He made him Governor of Jiangxia and ennobled him as a Marquis within the Passes, and had him lead troops to open the route.

A scout then reported, “Liu Bei is bringing the civilians and is moving only ten or so li per day, with only about three hundred li on the road.” Cao Cao selected the finest five thousand horsemen, made them ride through the night, and ordered them to catch up in a day and a night.

Then Liu Bei, leading over ten thousand civilians and three thousand-some cavalry, advanced step by step toward Jiangling. Zhao Yun protected the old and young; Zhang Fei held the rear. Kongming said, “Yun Chang has gone to Jiangxia and there is no answer yet. We do not know what is to come.” Liu Bei said, “Please have the Master himself make a personal ride.” “Liu Qi is deeply grateful for your earlier instruction,” Kongming replied. “If he sees you in person, things will surely be settled.” He agreed, and went with Liu Feng and five hundred soldiers ahead to Jiangxia seeking help.

That very day Liu Bei traveled with Jian Yong, Mi Zhu, and Mi Fang. While they moved, a savage wind suddenly struck before their horses. Dust rose to the sky and screened the red sun. Liu Bei cried, “What omen is this?” Jian Yong, who knew some Yin-Yang, took out his divination slips and said, alarmed, “This is a major omen of disaster. It should occur tonight. The lord should quickly abandon the civilians and run.” Liu Bei said, “These people came from Xinye to follow me here. How can I abandon them?”

Jian Yong replied, “If the lord clings to them and does not abandon them, disaster is not far off.” Liu Bei asked, “What is ahead?” Men replied, “Ahead lies Dangyang County. There is a mountain called Jing Mountain.” Liu Bei ordered the column to halt and entrench there.

It was late autumn turning to winter; a raw cold wind cut through bone and skin. At dusk, cries spread across the fields. By the fourth watch, a roar came from the northwest. Liu Bei was greatly alarmed. He leapt on his horse and brought the core of his troops—just over two thousand warriors—to meet the enemy. Cao’s forces arrived masked in dust and proved impossible to hold. Liu Bei fought to the death. In his desperate extremity, he was saved by Zhang Fei arriving with troops, who opened a bloodway and pulled him eastward in retreat. Wenpin attempted to block him first. Liu Bei shouted, “Even traitor to your lord, how do you still have a face to be seen?” Wenpin, face full of shame, withdrew and rode northeast.

Zhang Fei kept close to Liu Bei, fighting and retreating. As dawn came and enemy cries ebbed, Liu Bei could finally halt. He looked over his accompanying men and found no more than a hundred riders. The civilians and old and young, along with Mi Zhu, Mi Fang, Jian Yong, Zhao Yun, and others were missing.

Liu Bei wailed, “Ten thousand souls are all drawn into disaster because they cling to me. Our generals and old and young alike—I do not know who lives or dies, and they are no less human than I.”

In his desolation, he saw Mi Fang stagger in with several arrows in him, crying, “Zhao Zilong has defected and gone to Cao Cao!” Liu Bei barked, “Zilong was my old companion. How dare he betray?” Zhang Fei said, “He sees us in this hard hour, nearly at the end of strength, and may well have gone to Cao Cao for rank.” Liu Bei said, “Zilong has been with me through hardship; his heart is iron and cannot be swayed by wealth or rank.” Mi Fang said, “I saw him myself turn northwest.” Zhang Fei said, “Let me go and look for him at once; if I run him down, one spear will end him.” Liu Bei said, “Do not jump to this suspicion. Did you not see how your two older brothers judged Yan and Wenchou? Zilong has gone off on purpose; he must have business that way and I believe he will not abandon me.”

Zhang Fei, regardless, gathered twenty-odd riders and rode to Changban Bridge. He saw a stretch of trees to the east of the bridge. He devised a plan: he had twenty riders cut branches and tie them to the tails of their horses, then run in and out of the grove, raising dust and giving the sound of a large force. He himself stood with a halberd planted on horseback on the bridge, looking westward.

Meanwhile, from the fourth watch onward, Zhao Yun fought and fought with Cao’s men, clashing forward and back until dawn. He still could not find Liu Bei, and then the lord and the old and young too were lost from him. He thought, “The lord has entrusted the two wives of the household, Gangu, and the young master A dou to me. If he does not find us in this scattering, how can I face him? Better to cast myself into a death-fight and at least find the lord’s wives and the young lord.”

Turning back, he saw only three or four dozen riders with him. He drove through the mêlée and heard the cries of men and women from two counties rising and shaking the sky. Many who had been struck by arrows and spears, cast down men and women and ran on. As he moved, he found Jian Yong lying in the grass and asked sharply, “Have you seen either lady of the household?” Jian Yong answered, “The two lords’ ladies abandoned their baggage, carrying A dou as they ran. I spurred my horse on, turned at a ridge, and a general struck me with one lance thrust, throwing me from my horse. My horse was taken. I could not fight him off, so I lie here.”

Zhao Yun gave his horse to Jian Yong and had two mounted men escort him first, telling them, “I will go until heaven and earth allow me, and by any means I will find my Lady and my young lord. If I cannot, let me die on this field.”

When he said this, he spurred toward Changban Slope. Someone cried out, “Where is General Zhao?” He reined in and asked, “Who are you?” The man said, “I was an escortman under Lord Liu’s tents, struck down by arrow and left here.” Zhao Yun asked, “Have you seen the two ladies?” He said, “I just saw Madam Gan and saw her barefoot, hair down, running with a few women and many civilians to the south.”

Zhao Yun did not spare the escortman and spurred south at full speed. Soon he saw several hundred civilians—men and women—walking in disorder. He shouted, “Is there Madam Gan among you?” The Lady looked back when she saw Zhao Yun and burst into tears. He dismounted, drove his spear into the earth, and said, with tears, “If I fail in this and my Lady’s household is parted, the fault is mine! Where is Madam Mi and the young lord?”

Madam Gan said, “Mi and I were driven out, leaving all baggage and mingling among the women and children on foot. Another troop burst in and scattered us. I do not know where Madam Mi and A dou have gone. I escaped alone only.”

At that moment the people were crying and another troop emerged from the noise. Zhao Yun planted his spear and rode out. In front of him sat a man with someone bound on horseback. It was Mi Zhu. Behind him rode a general who brandished a great blade and led a thousand men: Chu Yu Dao, a sub-commander of Cao Ren. He seized Mi Zhu and was preparing to dismount him for credit. Zhao Yun shouted, drove his spear, and charged straight for Chu Yu Dao. Chu Yu Dao could not withstand it. Zhao Yun’s single thrust put him off his horse, then he turned and rescued Mi Zhu, taking two good horses.

Zhao Yun bade Madam Gan mount up, tore open a corridor of blood, and sent them quickly toward Changban Slope. As he looked, Zhang Fei stood on horseback on the bridge with his halberd raised and shouted, “Zilong! How could you betray my brother?” Zhao Yun answered, “I did not see my Lady and the young master, so I lagged behind. Why should you call that betrayal?”

Zhang Fei said, “If Jian Yong had not first run to you with that report, I would not have yielded to your coming. Where is the lord now?” Zhao Yun said, “Not far ahead.” He told Mi Zhu, “Brother-in-law Mi, escort Madam Gan ahead first. I must ride back and find Madam Mi and the young lord.” He did so, drawing up several riders and turning back the way they had come.

As they went, they saw a general come charging, carrying a three-pointed spear and a sheathed sword, with a dozen riders. Zhao Yun said nothing and struck him directly. In a single rider-to-rider collision, the general was pinned with a spear and all his riders fled. That general was Xiahou En, a trusted sword-bearing officer of Cao Cao. Cao Cao had two treasured swords: one called Yi Tian and one called Qinggang. He wore Yi Tian himself and ordered Xiahou En to carry Qinggang. The Qinggang blade could shear iron like clay, sharper than any blade.

At that moment Xiahou En relied on his own strength and kept the sword behind him as he drove men to seize and plunder, not noticing Zhao Yun until they met. Zhao Yun killed him with one thrust and took the blade. When he saw the hilt inlaid with gold and the words “Qinggang,” he realized it was a prized sword.

Zhao Yun raised the sword and drove the spear forward again, cutting through the heavy ranks. Looking back, all the riders with him had vanished—he was alone. He had no thought of retreat and kept searching. Whenever he came upon civilians, he asked about Madam Mi.

A man pointed: “The Lady is hurt in the left leg by an arrow and cannot walk. She is seated by the break in the wall up ahead.”

Zhao Yun hurried there. One house had burned down and its clay wall had collapsed. There, by the edge of a dry well, Madam Mi sat holding A dou and weeping. He knelt to the ground in full respect.

She said, “General, I am glad to see you. As for A dou, he is still alive. He can only rely on your compassion. His father has been adrift half his life. He is this last bone and blood of my line. Please protect this child and make sure he sees his father. Then I can die without regret.”

Zhao Yun said, “Lady, you endured this. The fault was mine. Do not delay; please mount. I will march on foot and die by the road if needed, and carry your lady beyond this encirclement.” Madam Mi answered, “No. Could a general move without horse? This child depends on you alone. I am badly wounded and life has no value to me now. I beg you: take this child and hurry forward; do not make me your burden.”

Zhao Yun said, “The shouting is drawing close; the pursuers are near. Lady, mount immediately.” Madam Mi said, “I cannot move. Do not delay me long.” She then put A dou into Zhao Yun’s arms. “This child’s life is in your hands!”

Zhao Yun asked three, then five times for her to mount, but she still would not. As cries rose around all four sides, he shouted in anger, “Lady, if you ignore my words and the chasers arrive, what can be done?” Madam Mi finally dropped A dou on the ground, flipped herself over into the dry well, and died.

Later people praised this in verse:

With war, all he can do depends on horseflesh and speed, how can he bear the young lord on foot? Willing to die for the Liu heir in one final charge, brave and reckless, yet still she was called womanly by men.

When Zhao Yun saw that Madam Mi had died, fearing Cao’s soldiers would steal her body, he pushed down the clay wall and covered the dry well. When he had done so, he unbuckled his breast-plate straps and lowered his shielded heart-mirror, set A dou in his arms, and leapt on horseback.

A mounted officer was already there leading a detachment, Yanming of Cao Hong’s command, wielding a three-pronged double-edged saber. Zhao Yun did not allow three exchanges to pass before he killed him with one spear thrust, broke the pursuing soldiers apart, and broke out along a route.

As he rode, yet another troop of horsemen blocked the way ahead. At its front was a major general, clearly flagged, with a bold banner reading “Hejian Zhang He.” Zhao Yun did not answer but charged with his spear. After more than ten exchanges, he did not linger to trade blows and made off by force.

Zhang He pursued. Zhao Yun spurred on. Suddenly, with a thudding collapse, man and horse pitched together into a pit. Zhang He thrust with his spear. Suddenly a red flash rolled up out of the pit, the horse sprang straight into the air, and leapt out. Later people praised:

A red glow wrapped the body as a trapped dragon flew, the charging horse split open the encirclement on Changban. For forty-two years, this truly is the appointed ruler; by him did the general reveal his divine might.

Zhang He, seeing this, was greatly startled and withdrew. Zhao Yun drove forward still, but two generals behind him shouted, “Zhao Yun, do not run away!” Ahead two more generals rode out with two kinds of military weapons to block the road: Ma Yan and Zhang Yi came from the rear, while Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan blocked ahead—they were former officers who had served Yuan Shao. Zhao Yun fought all four with force. Cao’s army pressed in together.

Zhao Yun pulled out the Qinggang sword and hacked wildly. Wherever he struck, armor and clothing tore through and blood surged like a fountain. He broke back the encircling troops and the officers, cutting straight through.

Cao Cao, on the top of Jing Mountain, watched a general whose path none could withstand. He asked the men nearby who it was. Cao Hong rode down from the ridge and cried out, “In the ranks, give your name!” Zhao Yun answered at once, “I am Zhao Zilong of Changshan!”

Cao Hong reported this to Cao Cao. Cao Cao said, “He is truly a tiger-general! I must keep him alive.” He ordered horsemen to report in all directions: “If Zhao Yun comes, do not fire cold arrows. Only seize him alive.” That is why Zhao Yun escaped this trouble. It was also fortune from his role as guardian of the future lord.

In this slaughter Zhao Yun carried the young lord in his arms and cut through the heavy encirclement, chopping down two great banners and taking three spears. He thrust and stabbed, cut with sword and spear, and killed more than fifty renowned commanders of the Wei camps.

Later people praised in verse:

Blood stains his campaign robe, and through his armor runs red; Who in Dangyang dared contend with his charge? From old times to now, who in the line has rallied the peril-bound lord? Only Changshan’s Zhao Zilong.

When Zhao Yun had already broken entirely through the thick ranks and left the main array, all over with blood on his battle coat, he was descending the hill slope when he met two troops again. They were the Zuo brothers, Zhongjin and Zhongshen, sub-commanders under Xiahou Dun, one with a great axe and one with a halberd. One cried: “Zhao Yun, dismount and submit!”

He had just slipped out of the tiger’s den to live, and yet another dragon-pool of waves rose to meet him. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Liu Xuande Leads the People Across the River and Zhao Zilong Rescues His Lord Alone

chapters.html:
Zhong Jin and Zhong Shen blocked Zhao Yun and fought in close contact. Zhao Yun thrust with his spear. Zhong Jin was first to strike, swinging a great axe to meet him. The two horses collided, and after no more than three exchanges, Zhao Yun had already speared him from his saddle, sent him crashing down, and forced his way to escape.

Zhong Shen came up behind with a halberd. Their horse tails struck each other, and that halberd only cut a ghostly arc behind Zhao Yun’s back.

Zhao Yun sharply turned his horse; their chests struck together. With his left hand he deflected the halberd with his spear. With his right he drew the green-steel treasure sword and swung. Helm and skull came away together. Zhong Shen fell from the saddle and died, and the rest scattered.

Zhao Yun got free and ran for Changban Bridge. He heard a crashing roar behind him. It was Wen Pin, bringing troops forward. Zhao Yun reached the bridge, tired and with a spent horse.

He saw Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, upright in the saddle on the bridge with his spear held. Zhao Yun shouted, “Yide, aid me!”

Yide said, “Zilong, go quickly. I will hold the pursuers.”

Zhao Yun galloped across, and after more than twenty li he saw Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, and others resting beneath trees. Zhao Yun dismounted, knelt, and wept. Liu Bei wept too.

Catching his breath, Zhao Yun said, “My fault is so grave that I deserve to die ten thousand deaths. Lady Mi was grievously wounded, would not mount, and threw herself into a well and died. I could only cover her with an embankment of earth. Carrying the young lord, I crashed through layers of encirclement. By our lord’s fortune, I barely escaped.

Just now the child was still crying in my arms; when he was suddenly still, I feared there could be no rescue.” He then checked him.

It was A Dou, still asleep and not yet awake. Zhao Yun cried out in joy, “By Heaven’s mercy, the boy is unharmed!” He passed him to Liu Bei with both hands.

Liu Bei took him and set him down on the earth: “For this child of yours, I nearly lost one of my best generals.”

Zhao Yun hurriedly knelt to the ground, lifted A Dou again, and bowed while weeping, “Even if I laid down my life and blood, I still could not repay this grace.”

A later verse says:

A tiger breaks from Cao Cao’s troops and comes out; in Zhao Yun’s chest the little prince sleeps.\ with no way to soothe the loyal heart, he casts his own child before his horse.

Wen Pin pursued and brought his troops to Changban Bridge. He saw Zhang Fei, with his beard bristling and eyes round as lanterns, spear poised like a snake, standing on his horse atop the bridge. Beyond the trees on the east of the bridge he saw a great dust cloud rising and, suspecting an ambush, held his horse back.

Soon Cao Ren, Li Dian, Xiahou Dun, Xiahou Yuan, Yue Jin, Zhang Liao, Zhang He, Xu Chu, and others arrived. Seeing Yide with eyes like coals, a spear across and standing on the bridge, and fearing that it might be Zhuge Liang’s design, they all dared not approach closely. They planted their line and arrayed themselves in single file to the west of the bridge, sending a messenger to report to Cao Cao.

When Cao Cao heard, he rode up quickly from the rear. Zhang Fei’s round eyes still fixed on them, and far off he could faintly make out blue silk parasols and halberd banners from the rear troops arriving. He judged Cao Cao had, out of suspicion, come himself.

Yide shouted in a raised voice, “I am Yide of Yan! Who will settle a life-and-death fight with me?” His voice was like thunder. Every Wei soldier who heard it shivered.

Cao Cao ordered the parasol removed and said, looking to both sides, “I have heard Yunchang speak that Yide in the midst of ten thousand could seize the first officer of the vanguard as if lifting fruit from a basket. We meet him now; we must not take him lightly.”

Not yet done, Yide again cried out with eyes still wild, “Yide of Yan is here! Who comes to decide death against me?” Seeing such spirit in him, Cao Cao felt an impulse to withdraw. Yide saw Cao Cao’s rear formation begin to move, so he set his spear and shouted again, “You refuse to fight and refuse to retreat. Why is that?”

Before the cry ended, Xiahou Jie at Cao Cao’s side was so frightened that he nearly lost his composure and fell from his horse. Cao then wheeled and rode back.

One by one all the gathered commanders fled west. Then this is apt:

A yellow-mouthed child cannot hear thunder, how could he hear its split?\ a diseased woodcutter cannot bear the roar of tiger and leopard.

At that moment shields and helmets were abandoned in countless numbers. Men surged like tide, horses like landslides, trampling one another.

A later verse says:

At Changban Bridge, fury rises from the killing intent;\ With crossed spear and eyes wide open, Yide stands there.

One cry is like rolling thunder;\ one man alone drives back Cao’s million-strong army.

Cao Cao, fearing Yide’s might, spurred west in panic. His hairpins all came loose; he fled with flying hair.

Zhang Liao and Xu Chu caught up and pulled at his rein. Cao was in chaos.

Zhang Liao said, “Chancellor, do not fear. Could a single man like Yide truly cause such danger? If now we return and strike hard, Liu Bei can be caught.”

Only then Cao’s face steadied, and he again ordered Zhang Liao and Xu Chu to return to Changban Bridge and learn what had happened.

Zhang Fei saw Cao’s forces mass in retreat and not daring pursuit. He immediately called back the original two dozen riders, had the horse-tail and tree-branch obstacles removed, and ordered the bridge broken apart. Then he rode back to Liu Bei and reported the bridge’s destruction.

Xuande said, “My brother is brave indeed, but careless in reckoning.”

Yide asked why.

Liu Bei replied, “Cao Cao is greatly strategic. You should not tear down the bridge. He will surely come after us.”

Yide said, “He was driven back many li by my single shout. How can he dare to chase again?”

Liu Bei replied, “If we leave the bridge unbroken, he may think there is an ambush and dare not advance. Now if it is broken, he will think we are without troops and only hesitant, so he must pursue. He has a host of a hundred thousand; even if he crosses Jiang and Han, he can fill and pass. How could he fear one broken bridge?”

At once Liu Bei stood and took a small path, turning off sharply toward Han Ford and heading for the road to Mianyang.

Cao Cao had Zhang Liao and Xu Chu check Changban Bridge; they returned: “Yide has broken the bridge and left.”

Cao Cao said, “If he breaks a bridge and departs, that is fear.” He ordered ten thousand troops to build three floating bridges at once. They would cross tonight.

Li Dian said, “This likely is Zhuge Liang’s false design. Do not advance lightly.”

Cao Cao said, “Could a man of one brave stroke like Yide be planning deceit?!” and he sent the orders onward; the troops advanced in haste.

Liu Bei, coming near Han Ford, suddenly saw a great cloud of dust behind him, drums sounding through the sky, cries shaking the earth.

He said, “There is a great river ahead and enemy at our back. What are we to do?” He ordered Zhao Yun to ready for resistance.

Cao Cao gave an order to the army: “Liu Bei is a fish in the kettle, a tiger in the pit; if we do not seize him now, it is like releasing fish to the sea and allowing a tiger to return to the mountain. Let all commanders urge strength and chase forward.”

Each general gave his command and, one by one, pressed hard in pursuit.

Suddenly behind a ridge drums sounded again, and a troop of cavalry burst forth, crying, “We have waited for this long!”

At their head rode a great general holding a Green Dragon Blade on a chi-tu horse.

It was Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang. He had taken a force of ten thousand from Jiangxia and, knowing of the battle at Dangyang and at Changban, intentionally cut out by this road.

When Cao Cao saw Guan Yu, he pulled hard on the reins and looking back among his commanders said, “Again we have fallen into Zhuge Liang’s trap!” and ordered a quick retreat.

Guan Yu chased the force for more than ten li, then turned back to protect Liu Bei and the others, reaching Han Ford where boats waited. Guan Yu invited Liu Bei, Lady Gan, and A Dou aboard and seated them.

Guan Yu asked, “Where is your second sister?” Liu Bei related what happened at Dangyang.

Guan Yu sighed, “If, in those days at Xu Tian, we had done as I advised, this trouble would not have arisen.”

Liu Bei said, “Now I too must move with the utmost caution, lest striking the rat shatter the vessel.”

Just then, from the south bank war drums sounded in full. Boats like swarming ants came, sails full in the wind. Liu Bei was greatly alarmed.

When the boat drew near, a man in white robes and silver armor stood at the bow and called out, “Uncle, are you otherwise in health? Your nephew comes late with apology!”

Liu Bei saw and recognized him as Liu Qi. Liu Qi stepped aboard and knelt with tears: “When I heard my uncle was trapped before Cao Cao, your nephew came in haste to aid you.”

Liu Bei rejoiced. They gathered troops together and moved. While they were recounting events on the boat, suddenly a line of war vessels opened from the southwest and came swiftly with whistles in the wind.

Liu Qi said in alarm, “The troops from Jiangxia have all risen and arrived here. If warships now block the way, they are either Cao Cao’s army or that of Eastern Wu. What are we to do?”

Liu Bei stepped to the bow and saw a man in hemp scarf and plain robes sitting at the bow. It was Kongming, and behind him stood Sun Qian.

Liu Bei hurriedly invited him aboard and asked why he was here.

Kongming said, “Liang came to Jiangxia first and ordered Zilong to land at Han Ford to meet and receive. I judged Cao Cao would surely pursue and that the Lord would not come from Jiangling, but take a slant to Han Ford. So I specifically asked the young lord to come ahead and receive us, and then I returned to Xiakou and summoned all troops to come forward to assist.”

Liu Bei rejoiced. The three talked together to discuss breaking Cao’s force.

Kongming said, “Xiakou is a secure city and has adequate money and grain, enough to hold out for long. Please have my lord camp at Xiakou. Let the young lord return to Jiangxia to arrange the boats and repair the arms, creating an oblique, angular posture to withstand Cao Cao. If we all return together to Jiangxia, our position becomes isolated.”

Liu Qi said, “The Strategist speaks truly, but I think it wise to ask uncle to stop by Jiangxia briefly, to set horse and troops right, and then return to Xiakou without delay.”

Liu Bei answered, “My worthy nephew speaks truly as well.”

So he left Zilong with five thousand troops to hold Xiakou.

Liu Bei, Kongming, and Liu Qi then moved together toward Jiangxia.

When Cao Cao saw that Guan Yu had intercepted the land route, he suspected an ambush and dared not pursue. He also feared that the water route had already been taken at Jiangling by Liu Bei, so he hastened overnight and marched on toward Jiangling.

In Jingzhou, the city commander Deng Yi and the assistant minister Liu Xian already knew the matter at Xiangyang and judged they could not resist Cao Cao. Therefore they led Jingzhou’s troops and civilians out of the gates and surrendered.

Cao Cao entered the city, stabilized the populace, and freed Han Song from prison, promoting him to Grand Master of Ceremonies. All other officials received rewards.

Cao Cao discussed with his commanders, “Now Liu Bei has gone to Jiangxia. He may join with Eastern Wu, and this will spread dangerously. What plan shall we use to destroy this?”

Xun You said, “I shall now raise the army’s military prestige, send envoys with proclamations to Jiangdong, and ask Sun Quan to join in a hunt at Jiangxia so we may together capture Liu Bei and divide Jingzhou, forever securing alliance and favor. If Sun Quan comes in alarm and suspicion, he will come under submission, and our matter is done.”

Cao Cao accepted this plan. At one side he sent proclamations and envoys to Jiangdong. At the same time he counted out 830,000 horse, infantry, and river troops—claiming one million—and ordered a combined advance by land and water, horse and boat in two lines, moving down the river. In the west they linked Jingxia Gorge and in the east connected Qihuang, with stockades and fortifications linked for more than three hundred li.

At this point the story takes two routes.

Over in Jiangdong, Sun Quan kept his troops in Chaisan County. Hearing that Cao Cao’s huge army had reached Xiangyang, that Liu Qiong had already submitted, and that now he too had taken Jiangling by overnight routes, he gathered all his counselors and debated a defense.

Lu Su said, “Jingzhou borders our state, and rivers and passes are steep and secure; the people and wealth are rich. If we possess it, it is material for kings. Now that Liu Biao is newly dead and Liu Bei newly defeated, I request permission to carry condolences to Jiangxia and say to Liu Bei that he should pacify Liu Biao’s old officers and make them one heart. If he gladly agrees, this great affair may be accomplished.”

Sun Quan was happy and followed his counsel, sending Lu Su with gifts to Jiangxia in condolence.

When Liu Bei reached Jiangxia, he and Kongming and Liu Qi discussed a good stratagem.

Kongming said, “Cao Cao is mighty and impossible to oppose in haste. It is better to go to Eastern Wu and Sun Quan for aid. If north and south are locked in contention, we can profit from the middle. Why is that impossible?”

Liu Bei said, “The people of Jiangdong are many and surely have far-reaching plans. Why would they accept us?”

Kongming smiled, “Cao Cao has brought a million men and crouches across the Jiang and Han. How could Jiangdong fail to send someone to probe the true situation? If one comes, Liang, with a single favorable wind and a tongue that never fails, can sail straight to Jiangdong and with persuasion say that north and south are each trying to swallow the other. If the southern army wins, we punish Cao Cao together and take Jingzhou. If the northern army wins, then we can use the moment to take the south.”

Liu Bei said, “That argument is lofty. How do we get someone from Jiangdong here?”

Just then they were told that Sun Quan’s envoy Lu Su had arrived for condolences and moored his ship.

Kongming said, “This is excellent news.” He asked Liu Qi, “When Sun Ce died, did Xiangyang already send an envoy to condole?”
