Liu Qi answered, “Jiangdong owes my family a father-killing grudge; there is no occasion for celebratory mourning rites.”

Kongming said, “Then Lu Su has not come to pay condolences; he has come to inquire about military affairs.” He told Liu Bei, “If Lu Su asks about Cao Cao’s situation, my lord should simply say he does not know. If he asks again, say he should ask Zhuge Liang.”

With the plan fixed they sent men to welcome Lu Su. Lu Su entered the city to condole and receive gifts. Liu Qi asked him to meet Liu Bei. After rituals, he invited him into the back hall to drink.

Lu Su said, “Long have I known the fame of the Imperial Uncle but never met him. I am truly comforted to meet him now. Recently hearing that the Imperial Uncle fought with Cao Cao, you must know the enemy’s vulnerabilities. May I ask how many soldiers Cao has?”

Xuande said, “Our troops are small and commanders few. As soon as Cao came near, we withdrew. We do not know his vulnerabilities.”

Lu Su said, “I heard the Imperial Uncle using Zhuge Liang’s planning: two consecutive fires burned away Cao’s soul and made his courage collapse. How could he not know?”

Liu Bei said, “Only by asking Kongming can I know.”

Lu Su asked, “Where is Master Kongming? I ask to see him.”

Liu Bei had Zhuge Liang come forth.

When Lu Su met him and saw the ceremonial greeting complete, he said, “I long admired the teacher’s talent and virtue but had not yet met him. Now, to meet him now, I am glad. I wish to hear about our present safety and the matter of danger.”

Kongming replied, “Cao Cao’s deceit is known to me, but my strength is lacking. So I have waited and withdrawn for the moment.”

Lu Su said, “Will the Imperial Uncle now stop here long?”

Kongming said, “Your Highness has long had old ties with Wuchen, the Administrator of Cangwu; I mean to go there.”

Lu Su said, “Wuchen has little grain and few soldiers; he cannot hold himself, how can he shelter others?”

Kongming replied, “Wuchen’s dwelling is not enough for long residence. Yet for now we can stay there temporarily; I have another good plan.”

Lu Su said, “General Sun occupies six commanderies. His soldiers are excellent, his grain sufficient, and he highly respects worthy men and scholars; many heroes of Jiangdong attach to him. Now for Your Highness, it is best to send a trusted insider to connect with Eastern Wu and share a great undertaking.”

Kongming said, “Liu’s lord has never had prior ties with General Sun. I fear words would be spent in vain, and there is no one close and trusted I can send.”

Lu Su said, “The Master’s brother now serves as adviser in Jiangdong and waits daily to meet you. Though unworthy, I beg to go with you to meet General Sun and discuss this great matter.”

Liu Bei said, “Kongming is my master and teacher. How could he leave me even briefly?”

Lu Su persisted in asking Zhuge Liang to go.

Liu Bei pretended to refuse.

Kongming said, “The matter is urgent. I ask that I may go on this mission.”

Liu Bei finally consented.

Lu Su then left Liu Bei and Liu Qi and took to the boat with Zhuge Liang, heading for Chaisan County.

Then, as the saying goes:

Because Zhuge, in his small boat, moved away, Cao’s troops at once were given a rest. Who knows how this departure will end? Let the next chapter explain it.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhang Yide Rages at Changban Bridge; Liu Yuzhou Is Driven to Hanjin Ford

chapters.html:
Now Lu Su and Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, took leave of Liu Bei and Liu Qi and boarded a boat to Chaisang County. While in the boat the two discussed matters together. Lu Su said to Kongming, “When you meet General Sun, do not speak plainly about the full strength and spread of Cao Cao’s forces.” Kongming answered, “No need for your reminder, Zijing; I have words prepared.”

When the boat reached the bank, Lu Su asked Kongming to rest at the posthouse for a while, and he went first to report to Sun Quan. Sun Quan was already gathering civil and military officers in the hall for deliberation. Hearing that Lu Su had returned, he urgently summoned him and asked, “Zijing, you went to Jiangxia—what is the true state?”

Lu Su replied, “What I learned is partial and can be reported gradually.”

Sun Quan held up the summons sent from Cao Cao and said, “Cao just sent an envoy with this. I had first ordered a messenger out, but before that he arrived. We are all deliberating now and the consensus is not yet fixed.” Lu Su read it. It stated:

I now accept the emperor’s command and with the imperial decree move to punish offenders. My banners point south. Liu Qun has yielded his hands in surrender, and the people of Jing and Xiang, seeing the wind, have come to submit. I now command a host of one million men and a thousand senior commanders. I intend to meet the General at Jiangxia, to strike Liu Bei together, divide the land, and make an enduring alliance. Do not delay in waiting for me. Send your reply at once.

After reading it, Lu Su asked, “How does Your Majesty view this?”

Sun Quan said, “There is no final decision yet.”

Zhang Zhao said, “Cao Cao has a host of one million. He carries the Son of Heaven’s name and nameplate to levy arms against all quarters. If we do not follow, we refuse him. As for my lord’s chances against Cao, the great obstacle is the Yangtze. Since he has now taken Jing Province, the strength of the river now belongs to both sides of the conflict. It cannot be opposed by force. As a poor man’s plan, accepting his terms is the route to ten-thousandfold peace.”

All the strategists declared, “Zibu’s argument accords with Heaven’s will.”

Sun Quan stayed silent. Zhang Zhao added, “My lord need not doubt so much. If we submit to Cao, the people of Wu stay safe and the six southern commanderies are preserved.” Sun Quan lowered his head and said nothing.

Soon after, Sun Quan rose to change clothes. Lu Su followed behind him. Sensing Lu Su’s purpose, Sun Quan grasped his hand and said, “What do you think we should do?”

Lu Su answered, “What everyone said is mistaken. All of them can submit to Cao, only the general cannot.”

Sun Quan asked, “Why do you say so?”

Lu Su said, “Should men like me submit, we may still return to our home districts, and though stripped of office we do not lose all commanderies. But if my lord submits, where can he then go? At best he gets enfeoffed as a marquis, with no more than one carriage, one horse, and only a few attendants. How could he then face south and be called lord?”

“The thoughts of each here serve only their own interests,” he continued. “Do not listen to them. My lord must settle the larger plan at once.”

Sun Quan sighed, “Their arguments have missed my hopes. What you just said, Zijing, is exactly what I think, and it is as though heaven has bestowed that on me through you. Yet Cao Cao has only just absorbed Yuan Shao’s crowd, and has now gained Jing Province’s forces. I fear the momentum is too great for us to resist.”

Lu Su said, “I have already been to Jiangxia and brought Zhuge Liang, the younger brother of Zhuge Jin, so you may ask him directly and know the truth of it.”

Sun Quan asked, “Is the Hidden Dragon here?”

Lu Su said, “He is now resting at the relay station.”

Sun Quan said, “It is late today, and we have not yet met. Tomorrow gather the civil and military officials in the tents first. Let them behold the men of my domain, and then hold the formal council in the hall.”

Lu Su obeyed and left.

The next day, he came to the poststation and saw Kongming, reminding him again: “As agreed, do not state Cao’s actual troop strength in full before my lord.”

Kongming smiled. “I will match the moment and change my words. I will not err.”

Lu Su brought him into the pavilion. Zhang Zhao, Gu Yong, and over twenty officers were already seated, robes and crowns properly set, waiting upright. Kongming greeted each one, inquired each name, and after the courtesies were finished sat among the guests. Seeing his lofty, elegant appearance and commanding presence, Zhang Zhao thought, “This man is clearly here to persuade.”

Zhang Zhao began the questioning first. “I am but a minor man of Jiangdong. I have long heard Master had long withdrawn to Longzhong, comparing himself to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi. Is there truly cause for such words?”

Kongming replied, “That is but a small likeness of mine.”

Zhang Zhao said, “Recently it is heard that Liu Xuande made three visits to meet you at the thatched cottage, and with good fortune he has obtained you so you may be as fish in water. He was to roll through Jing and Xiang swiftly. Yet now, in one moment, he follows Cao Cao. Is this from your sense of right and wrong?”

Kongming thought inwardly: Zhang Zhao is the foremost counselor of my lord. If he is not first disarmed, how can I persuade Sun Quan?” he thought, and answered:

“From the moment I observe this world, the lands above Han are easy to take up as one turns over one’s palm. Liu Xuande practices benevolence and righteousness in his person and cannot bear to seize the base of his own clan, so he refuses repeatedly. Liu Qun, a simple fool, believed flattering words, surrendered in secret and let Cao Cao run rampant. Liu Xuande has now concentrated troops at Jiangxia; he has an unspoken design and this should not be treated lightly.”

Zhang Zhao objected, “Then your words and deeds contradict each other. You compared yourself to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi yourself. Guan Zhong served Duke Huan and dominated the lords, bringing the world under one rectification; Yue Yi raised weak Yan and brought down more than seventy cities of Qi. Those two men truly restored the world. In the cottage you only laughed at wind and moon, crossed your knees and sat in ease. Now you have taken up service under Liu Xuande, you should bring profit to life and eliminate evil men. Even before he found you, he had already ranged the realm and held cities; now that he has found you, all look up to him. Even a child of three feet, they would say, has wings like a tiger and will see Han restored and the Cao house destroyed. Former ministers and reclusive scholars alike keep their eyes fixed, saying this is the moment when the high heavens clear their clouds and the sun and moon recover their luster, rescuing the people from water and fire and setting the state upon a proper seat.

“So why, now that you have returned, when Cao’s army moves out, do you throw down armor and spears, run from the wind of rumor, abandon your post, abandon New Marsh, go to Fan City, be broken at Dangyang, and run to Xiakou with nowhere to stand? Did not Liu Xuande, once he had you, become less than at first?”

“Did Guan Zhong and Yue Yi ever do as you now claim?”

“Accept this blunt speech in simplicity.”

Kongming had no smile now and replied calmly:

“Can the soaring ambition of a roc over ten thousand li be known by ordinary birds? A person suffering deep damp disease must first be fed gruel and given medicine to soften the channels; once the spleen and bowels are in balance and the body slowly steady, only then should one use meat and stronger remedies. That is how the root of illness is removed and life returned. If one forces the strong medicine while the channels are not ready, seeking quick cure, the outcome is hard indeed.

“My lord Liu Xuande once suffered defeat at Ru-nan and took refuge with Liu Biao. His troops were under a thousand, only Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Zhao Yun as the core. That was the condition of one who had already weakened at root. New Marsh was a remote, small county, the people were few and grain scant. Would he truly sit there to hold forever?

“With weapons incomplete, city walls weak, troops untrained, and grain not enough day by day, yet by burning camp at Bowang and using the waters of Baihe he made Xiahou Dun and Cao Ren lose all nerve. I would say even Guan Zhong and Yue Yi might not have done better in such a use of force.

“As for Liu Qun’s surrender, Liu Xuande truly did not know the timing and still dared not seize his own clan’s base in disorder. That is great benevolence and great righteousness. In the defeat at Dangyang, Liu Xuande saw several tens of thousands of men of faith and followed old and young together, unwilling to leave them behind. He moved ten li a day, did not dare to press toward Jiangling, and shared defeat with all. That too is great benevolence and great righteousness.

“One cannot always triumph over overwhelming odds. In earlier times Gao Emperor lost repeatedly to Xiang Yu and only at Guanhai was he victorious; was that not Han Xin’s fine stratagem? Han Xin served the Great Emperor long and never counted victories lightly. Great state policy and dynastic safety depend on one true grand design, not on bragging men who trade in empty reputations, deceive people with words, and sit at leisure in debate. They cannot answer when circumstances change. Truly, this is a matter for laughter under heaven.”

Zhang Zhao could not answer once after this flow of words.

From the hall, one man shouted, “Cao Gong now has a million men and one thousand commanders; with dragon-and-tiger look, he intends to swallow Jiangxia in one sweep. What is your view?” Kongming looked up and saw it was Yu Fan.

Kongming said, “Cao Cao gathered Yuan Shao’s ant-like troops and forced together Liu Biao’s motley men. Though it were in the millions, it need not alarm us.”

Yu Fan sneered, “He was beaten at Dangyang, came to a dead end at Xiakou, then seeks help from others. To still say he is not to be feared is grand deceit.”

Kongming said, “Liu Xuande has only a few thousand of men rooted in benevolence and justice. How can he stand against Cao’s ferocious mass? He pulled back to Xiakou to await the proper time. Wu now has disciplined troops and enough grain, and has the advantage of the Yangtze. Yet you would still have your lord kneel for submission? What does this do to the shame of the empire?”

Yu Fan had no answer.

Another man from the assembly asked, “Does Kongming seek to act as the tongue of Su Qin and Zhang Yi, persuading Eastern Wu?” Kongming recognized him as Bu Zhi.

Kongming said, “Bu Zhi says Su Qin and Zhang Yi were called rhetoricians, but Su Qin and Zhang Yi were men of towering ability. Su Qin held six kingdoms’ seals; Zhang Yi served Qin twice. They had plans to set states right, not to fear those with blades and avoid swords as cowards.”

Bu Zhi said no more.

Another asked, “What is Cao like as a man?” Kongming looked and saw Xue Zong.

Kongming answered, “Cao Cao is a bandit of Han; why ask further?”

Xue Zong said, “Your words are wrong. Since Han’s cycle has reached the end, heaven’s order turns. Cao has already conquered two-thirds of the realm and all the people incline to him. Liu Xuande does not understand the timing and insists on fighting him—that is like striking stone with an egg. How can he avoid defeat?”

Kongming spoke sharply: “Xue Zong, how can you produce words without father or lord? A man in this world stands on loyalty and filial piety. If you are indeed a Han official and you see one who does not serve his lord, you should swear to strike him down together. That is a minister’s duty. Cao Cao has inherited Han grain and salary from his ancestors, yet he does not seek to repay it and harbors treasonous thoughts, which the world as a whole resents. You call this merely Heaven’s cycle and shift blame; what a man with no father, no lord! You should not continue. Enough.”

Xue Zong, filled with shame, could not answer.

Another from the hall asked next, “Though Cao has carried the Son of Heaven by force, he is still the grandson of Chancellor Cao Shen. Liu Xuande, though he claims descent from the Prince of Zhongshan, can scarcely be proved. He appears to me as a maker of reed mats and sandals. How can he contend with Cao?” Kongming saw it was Lu Ji.

Kongming said, “Are you not Lu, son of Jing’s district, who always carries oranges at others’ tables? Sit and listen first. If Cao Cao is indeed the son of Prime Minister Cao, then he is by status a Han minister. But now he monopolizes power, bullies fathers and lords alike. He is not only faithless to ruler and master, he also insults his ancestors. He is not only a traitor to Han, but even a rebel son of the Cao house.

“Liu Xuande is the scion of the imperial line, the emperor of the day, invested with title according to the genealogy. How can you call him unverified?

“Did not Gaozu rise from a village watch officer and yet end over all beneath heaven? Is making mats and sandals truly such shame? Your childish gaze is not fit to speak with men of lofty purpose.”

Lu Ji was silenced.

Another man spoke out: “All that Kongming says is forceful wordplay and not true argument; no need to continue. Tell us what texts he has studied.” Kongming saw him as Yan Jun.

Kongming replied, “To pluck phrases from chapters is the work of decay-ridden scholars. Can such men revive a realm and settle affairs? In former times, Yi Yin of the Xia dynasty, Jiang Ziya of Wei, Zhang Liang, Chen Ping and others, Deng Yu and Geng Yan— all held talent to set the world right. Why should we demand what classics they studied first? Are they mere scribes, confined to desk and brush, discussing black and yellow, playing with writing and ink?”

Yan Jun bowed his head, lost voice, and could not answer.

Again another called out in a loud tone: “You speak boldly, Master, but perhaps you lack real learning. You may become a scholar to be mocked.” Kongming saw it was Cheng Deshu of Runan.

Kongming said, “There is a difference between gentleman and petty scholar. A gentleman-scholar is loyal to ruler and devoted to state, upholds justice and hates evil, works so his benefits flow to his age and his name endures. The petty scholar cares only for carving insects, polishing brush and ink, composing verse as youth, and exhausting a lifetime in texts. Though a thousand words stand under his brush, one policy is absent in his breast. Think of Yang Xiong, famed for style, who served Wang Mang and still ended at the eaves. Even if he wrote ten thousand words a day, what is it worth?”

Cheng Deshu had no response.

All present saw that Kongming replied freely and fluidly, and all of them fell pale. At that moment two men, Zhang Wen and Luo Tong, wished to keep questioning. Just then one person entered from outside and shouted: “Kongming is an exceptional talent of this age. For men like you to cross-question with mere lips is in no way respectful hospitality to a guest!”

The man was Huang Gai, surnamed Huang, named Gai, courtesy name Gongfu, now Wu’s grain official.

He said to Kongming, “It is known that talking too much for gain is less useful than prudent silence. Why do you not speak of matters of iron and stone before my lord and continue your rhetoric with everyone here?”

Kongming answered, “These gentlemen do not understand affairs of the world, so they cross-question one another and must be answered.”

Then Huang Gai and Lu Su led Kongming in. At the middle gate they encountered Zhuge Jin. Kongming offered courtesy.

Zhuge Jin said, “Since my talented younger brother has come to Jiangdong, why has he not come to visit me?”

Kongming said, “My brother now serves in Xuande’s charge and first completes public duty before private ties. My public affairs are still not finished, so I have not dared to do otherwise. I ask my brother’s forbearance.”

Zhuge Jin said, “Your talented younger brother has seen Lord Wu; now come and talk.” He then withdrew.

Lu Su said, “What I warned at first: do not err. Kongming nodded. He then brought him to the hall.

Sun Quan descended the steps to receive him and treated him with great courtesy. After the exchange of greetings, he was given a seat. The officials stood in two rows around. Lu Su stood at Kongming’s side, watching him speak. After Kongming delivered Xuande’s intent, he glanced at Sun Quan: blue eyes, purple beard, a handsome, imposing presence. Kongming thought privately, “This man is extraordinary in appearance, capable of only being provoked, not reasoned into assent. Let him ask at the right moment and then I can spur him with words.”

After tea was served, Sun Quan said, “I have often heard Zijing speak of your talent. It is good fortune to meet you. May I seek instruction?”

Kongming said, “I am unworthy and not learned. I have brought shame to your inquiry.”

Sun Quan said, “You were recently in New Marsh, where you aided Liu Xuande against Cao. You must know well the true state of his army.”

Kongming said, “Liu Xuande had few men and scant officers. New Marsh is a small city, its grain poor. How could he withstand Cao?”

Sun Quan said, “How many troops does Cao have?”

Kongming said, “Cavalry, infantry, and river forces together are about one million and somewhat above.”

Sun Quan said, “Could this be feigned?”

Kongming said, “Not feigned. In Yan Province alone Cao already had two hundred thousand Qingzhou troops; after subduing Yuan Shao, he obtained another five to six hundred thousand; newly levied troops from the Central Plains number three to four hundred thousand; and now he has gained another two to three hundred thousand from Jing Province. By this reckoning it is not less than one million five hundred thousand. If I spoke in terms of a million, it was only to avoid frightening the men of Wu.”

Lu Su saw this and grew pale; he looked at Kongming, who pretended not to notice.

Sun Quan asked, “How many competent generals serve directly under Cao?”

Kongming said, “Men of genius and strategic brilliance, commanders used to battle, are surely not merely one or two thousand.”

Sun Quan said, “Since Cao has now pacified Jing and Chu, does he have a farther plan?”

Kongming said, “Right now, by the river he has set up camps and prepared warships. He does not yet aim to absorb Jiangdong; he awaits what he might take next.”

Sun Quan asked, “If he bears intention to absorb us, whether we fight or not, please decide for me.”

Kongming said, “I have one word, but I fear the general may not heed it.”

Sun Quan said, “Please speak your high opinion.”

Kongming said, “Earlier, when order in the state had collapsed, you rose in Jiangdong. Liu Xuande gathered benevolent men of the south and contested heaven and earth with Cao over the realm. Now Cao has cut down the great disorder and nearly levelled the crisis. He has now newly broken Jing and his prestige now shakes the world. There is no room for heroes to use their strength there. Therefore your lord has come here by retreat. Measure your strength and act accordingly.

“If you can resist China with Wu and Yue together, then better to cut ties with him now. If not, why not follow what the many counselors advise, keep your arms bound, and face north in service to him?”

Sun Quan said nothing at once.

Kongming continued, “Your lord bears outwardly the name of obedience, but inwardly you still harbor doubts. When urgency arrives and no break comes, disaster comes without end.”

Sun Quan asked, “If this is true, why did Liu Xuande not submit to Cao?”

Kongming said, “In old times Tian Heng, though a mere warrior of Qi, still kept loyalty unsullied. How much more Liu Xuande, the imperial scion and peerless talent, admired by all men. If this matter does not succeed, that is Heaven’s way; how then could he bend himself under another?”

When Sun Quan heard this, he abruptly reddened, rose, swept his robe aside, and retreated to the rear hall. The assembly laughed and drifted away.

Lu Su said to Kongming, “Why did you speak such words? It is fortunate my lord is broad and forbearant and does not rebuke you outright. Your words so far have deeply slighted my lord.”

Kongming looked up and smiled, “Is it wrong he cannot bear all who differ from him? I have my own plan to break Cao. If he does not ask me, I will not speak.”

Lu Su said, “If there is a good plan, I will ask my lord to seek instruction.”

Kongming said, “I regard Cao Cao’s million men as an ant heap. With one raised hand, they all become mere flour dust.”

Hearing this, Lu Su entered the rear hall and spoke with Sun Quan. The anger had not yet passed. Sun Quan, looking at him, said, “Kongming has offended me beyond measure.”

Lu Su said, “I too rebuked him for this. Yet Kongming smiles and says my lord cannot tolerate divergent thought; he will not casually expose his plan against Cao. Why does my lord not demand it?”

Sun Quan’s anger changed to joy and he said, “So there was indeed a sound stratagem in his words, using provocation. I had shallow sight and nearly ruined a major matter.” He then went out once more with Lu Su and invited Kongming back into the hall.

When Sun Quan saw him, he said, “I just committed an offense in insulting your dignity. Forgive me.”

Kongming bowed, “My words were impolite. I beg pardon.”

Sun Quan then invited him to the rear hall and served wine.

After circling through several rounds, Sun Quan said, “Cao’s lifelong dislikes are Lü Bu, Liu Biao, Yuan Shao, Yuan Shu, and Liu Xuande, and me. Now the five great have fallen, and only Liu Xuande and I remain. I cannot, as ruler of all Wu, be subordinate to one man. My decision is made. No one besides Liu Xuande can stand against Cao. Yet after Liu Xuande’s recent defeat, can he withstand this danger?”

Kongming said, “Though Liu Xuande was recently defeated, Guan Yu still leads one full ten thousand veterans, and Liu Qi commands the Jiangxia fighters, not less than ten thousand. Cao’s host has come far and is weary. As he pursued Liu Xuande, he rode light cavalry three hundred li in a single day and night. This is what people call ‘the power of a snapped crossbow at its end cannot pierce silk from Ru-sock’.

“Further, men from the north do not practice water warfare. The people and soldiers of Jing who serve Cao did so under compulsion, not from the heart. If General can truly unite heart and force with Liu Xuande, breaking Cao’s army is certain.

“If Cao’s army breaks, it must retreat north. Then the strength of Jing and Wu grows, and a three-legged balance will be formed. The point of success and failure is in this moment; the decision is in your lord’s hand.”

Sun Quan was greatly pleased and said, “Master’s words at last open my heart. My intent is fixed and no further doubt remains. From this day I will convene and raise troops to destroy Cao.” He ordered Lu Su to convey this to the civil and military officials, and sent Kongming back to the relay post to rest.

Zhang Zhao learned of Sun Quan’s intention to send troops and said at once, “He has fallen into Kongming’s scheme!” He rushed to report:

“Your lord plans to raise troops and clash with Cao. Compare it with Yuan Shao for a moment. When Cao had few men and few commanders, he could in one drumbeat strike Yuan Shao once; how can we now, with an army of a million, lightly oppose him? If Your Majesty moves by Kongming’s words, this is like setting fire to one’s own thatched house to save a burning field.”

Sun Quan only lowered his head and said nothing. Gu Yong said, “Liu Bei lost to Cao and now seeks to borrow Wu’s troops to resist him. Why should my lord be used by him? Please listen to Zijing.”

Sun Quan remained in thought. Zhang Zhao and others withdrew. Lu Su returned: “The counsel just now was again urging no movement and recommending submission. Those words came from men who seek to save only their own households. Your Majesty should not listen to them.”

Sun Quan was still undecided. Lu Su asked, “If Your Majesty delays, the crowd will surely mislead you.” Sun Quan said, “You should step aside for three moments while I think.” Lu Su stepped aside.

Some generals wanted battle, some civil officials wanted surrender; the arguments flew, none settled.

As for Sun Quan, he withdrew to the inner hall and ate and slept poorly, sleepless and unsettled, wavering all the while. Lady Wu, saw this and asked, “What is your mind, that food and sleep are abandoned?”

Sun Quan said, “Cao has camped between the Yangtze and the Han with intention to descend south. I asked the officials. Some urge submission, some urge war. If war is chosen, I fear I cannot withstand. If surrender is chosen, I fear Cao will not allow peace. That is why I hesitate.”

Wu Guotai said, “Do you remember what my sister spoke at death’s edge?”

Sun Quan seemed to wake from intoxication and start from a dream; at once he recalled those words. The verse was:

Remember your mother’s words on her deathbed; They raise General Zhou to stand and earn battle merit.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang Debates the Gathered Scholars; Lu Su Rejects the Crowd’s Counsel

chapters.html:
Lady Wu of Wu saw that Sun Quan was still uncertain. She said to him, “Our late sister’s parting words were: ‘Bofu, on his deathbed, said this: when there is doubt about internal matters, ask Zhang Zhao; when there is doubt about external matters, ask Zhou Yu.’ Why do you not ask Gongjin to advise you?” Sun Quan, much pleased, immediately sent a messenger to Poyang to invite Zhou Yu to discuss affairs.

Zhou Yu had been at Poyang Lake drilling the water force. When he heard that Cao Cao’s great army had arrived at Han Shore, he returned overnight to Chaisang Commandery to meet about war plans. By the time the envoy departed, Zhou Yu had already arrived. Lu Su, with whom Zhou Yu was closest, came first to receive him and gave him a full account of the matter already discussed. Zhou Yu said, “Zijing, do not worry. I have my own conclusions. Ask Master Kongming to come at once.”

Lu Su mounted and left.

Zhou Yu had scarcely settled to rest when news came that Zhang Zhao, Gu Yong, Zhang Hong, and Bu Zhi had come to seek him. He received them in the hall, and after the usual greetings he spoke briefly with them. Zhang Zhao said, “Does the Chief Commander know the stakes for Jiangdong?”

Zhou Yu said, “I do not yet.”

Zhang Zhao said, “Cao Cao has gathered a million men and is encamped on the Han River. The edict only arrived yesterday and asks the lord to hold a hunting gathering at Jiangxia. There is an intent to swallow us, though it is not yet fully exposed. Zhang Zhao and the others counseled the lord to surrender, hoping to spare Jiangdong from disaster. Yet Zijing, coming from Jiangxia with Liu Yu Zhou’s strategist Zhuge Liang, came here on his own account to wash away his frustration and spoke words to stir the lord. Zijing remains stubborn and has not awakened. We should await the Chief Commander and then decide.”

Zhou Yu said, “Do all your opinions agree?” Gu Yong and the others said, “The same as ours.”

Zhou Yu said, “I too have wanted to surrender for some time. You may go home. Tomorrow when we stand before the lord, there will be a final resolution.”

Zhang Zhao and the rest withdrew.

Soon after, Chéng Pu, Huang Gai, Han Dang, and others of the commanders arrived.

Zhou Yu welcomed them in and finished asking after each of them. Chéng Pu said, “Does the Chief Commander know whether Jiangdong is to fall to another by tomorrow or by this day’s end?”

Zhou Yu said, “I do not yet.”

Chéng Pu said, “We have followed the great general of Wu from the founding of this state; in a few hundred skirmishes of large and small, we have only just secured six commanderies and cities. Now the lord listens to strategists and wants to surrender to Cao Cao. This is truly a shame and a bitter regret. We commanders will rather die than submit. I ask the Chief Commander to press the lord toward raising arms. We are ready to die in battle.”

Zhou Yu said, “Do all the commanders share that view?”

Huang Gai rose in anger and struck his brow with his hand: “I would cut off my own head first; I swear not to submit to Cao Cao!”

The others all said, “None of us wish to surrender.”

Zhou Yu said, “I too intend to fight Cao Cao. How can I submit to him? Leave this matter with your Commander. Tomorrow, in the court, the decision will be made.”

Chéng Pu and the others withdrew.

Not long after, Zhuge Jin, Lu Fan, and another group of civil officials arrived. Zhou Yu greeted them and performed the proper courtesies.

Zhou Jin said, “My younger brother, Zhuge Liang, came from the Han River front and says that Governor Liu of Yu Province wishes to join Eastern Wu to strike Cao Cao, but the civil and military counselors have not yet reached a decision. As I have sent my brother as envoy, I cannot offer much. I have waited for the Chief Commander to settle this matter.”

Zhou Yu said, “What do you judge this as?”

Zhuge Jin said, “To surrender is easy and secure; to fight is hard to preserve.”

Zhou Yu laughed and said, “I have my own intention. Come tomorrow; we shall settle it together in the office.”

Zhuge Jin and the rest withdrew.

Again there was report that Lü Meng, Gan Ning, and others had come. Zhou Yu invited them in and discussed the matter with them as well. Some spoke for war; some spoke for surrender; and they argued back and forth. Zhou Yu said, “There is no need for further words. Come tomorrow, all of you, to the office and discuss this in public.” They then withdrew. Zhou Yu kept smiling with cold amusement and did not stop.

By evening, Lu Su came to fetch Kongming to make his salutation. Zhou Yu came through the middle gate to receive him. After formalities, they sat as host and guest.

Lu Su spoke first. “Now that Cao Cao drives his army southward, there are two policies before us: peace or battle. The lord cannot decide and listens to his generals. What is your view, General?”

Zhou Yu said, “Cao Cao claims the emperor’s name, and his troops cannot be refused. Moreover, his force is huge; we should not lightly oppose him. In battle we will surely lose; in surrender we are secure. My mind is decided. Tomorrow, when we face the lord, we will send an envoy to accept submission.”

Lu Su was taken aback: “Your words are wrong. The foundation of Jiangdong has passed through three generations. Can we abandon it to others in one day? Bofu’s bequest entrusted external matters to you. Now that this is the time to save the state through your strength, and to be the pillar against the hills, why do you now follow the counsel of a coward?”

Zhou Yu said, “Jiangdong has six commanderies. The number of living souls is limitless. If the calamity of war and uprising lands on them, all the blame will fall to me. Therefore I have decided to seek terms.”

Lu Su said, “No. With your valor and Wu’s defenses, Cao Cao is not certain to win his will.”

They argued with each other. Kongming only folded his sleeves and smiled coldly.

Zhou Yu said, “Master, why do you smile?”

Kongming said, “Bright One does not laugh at others; he laughs that Zijing does not understand the times.”

Lu Su said, “How can you laugh at my not understanding the times?”

Kongming said, “Master Gongjin’s intention to surrender to Cao Cao is very reasonable.”

Zhou Yu said, “Then Kongming is surely a man who understands the times and has only your consent.”

Lu Su said, “Kongming, why do you also speak this way?”

Kongming said, “Cao Cao is superb at using troops; in the world none would dare oppose him. Before he was checked, only Lü Bu, Yuan Shao, Yuan Shu, and Liu Biao dared to resist him. Those few men are now all destroyed by him, and there is no one left in the world. Only Liu Yu Zhou, not understanding the times, still insists on weighing himself against him. You are alone at Jiangxia; your survival is uncertain. If the commander chooses surrender to Cao Cao, he can protect wife and children and preserve wealth and rank. Dynastic fate has turned many times to heaven’s decree. Why should one grieve over what is assigned?”

Lu Su was furious: “You would teach my lord to kneel in humiliation before a traitor to the state!”

Kongming said, “I have one plan. You need not burden pack animals with hauling wine and gift vessels, nor present earth and seal; you need not even cross the river yourself. Send one common messenger, and in a skiff send two people to the riverbank. If Cao Cao receives these two, the whole million-strong host will lay down its armor and stack its flags to withdraw.”

Zhou Yu said, “What two could make Cao Cao withdraw his troops?”

Kongming said, “From the perspective of Jiangdong, these two are like a single leaf on a giant tree, lighter than a grain removed from granaries. Yet if Cao Cao gains them, he will be delighted and leave.”

Zhou Yu asked again, “Then exactly which two are to be used?”

Kongming said, “When Bright One stayed at Longzhong, he heard that Cao Cao built a new platform on the Zhang River and called it the Copper-Sparrow Platform. It is vast and splendid. He selected beauties from all over the realm to fill it. Cao Cao, by nature a lover of women, has long heard that in Jiangdong there are two daughters of Qiao, the elder called Great Qiao and the younger called Little Qiao, with beauty like fish under water and geese in flight, like moonlight behind clouds and flowers ashamed to be seen. Cao Cao once swore: ‘I have one wish: to sweep and pacify all four seas and complete an imperial undertaking. I have another: to get the two women of Jiangdong, place them in the Copper-Sparrow Platform, and spend my old age in delight. Even in death I would be without regret.’ Although he now comes with a million men and eyes south like a tiger, this is truly for those two women. Why does the Commander not go to Qiao-gong and, with a thousand pieces of gold, buy these two women and send them to Cao Cao? When he gets them, his heart will be satisfied and he will certainly call back his army. It is the tactic Fan Li used to give up Xishi—why not do it at once?”

Zhou Yu said, “How is it proven that Cao Cao wants the two Qiaos?”

Kongming said, “Cao Cao’s young son, Cao Zhi, courtesy name Zijian, writes with ease and speed. Cao Cao once ordered him to compose a prose-poem called Rhapsody on the Copper-Sparrow Platform. Its intent plainly states that he sees himself fit for the Son of Heaven and vows to take the two Qiaos.”

Zhou Yu said, “Can you recite it?”

Kongming said, “I love the beauty of its prose and verse, and once memorized part of it. I can recite it now.”

Zhou Yu said, “Then recite.” Kongming recited:

Following dawn, he went out to sport and roam, and climbed the tiered tower for pleasure. He beheld the broad hall where all was opened and saw the sacred virtue the sovereign had established. He raised lofty, steeping gates and built soaring structures, the twin towers floating in the highest height. He set an ornate terrace in heaven’s middle and linked flying pavilions to the western city. He looked across the long current of the Zhang River, and saw the garden and fruit thrive in abundance. He placed twin platforms to his left and right, with a jade dragon and a golden phoenix. He embraced the two Qiaos in the southeastern quarter, delighting in their morning and evening companionship. He looked down on the vast imperial city and gazed at cloud and drizzle drifting in the sky. He rejoiced that many talents gathered and that their favorable dreams flew together like a flying bear. He raised his face to the gentle spring wind and heard the sorrowful cries of hundreds of birds. Heaven’s clouds stretched across the whole sky as he stood there, and this family wished to gain both women. He spread benevolent transformation through the cosmos and made all in the upper capital stand in reverent order. Only Han Wen was so splendid—how could it compare with august brightness? Beautiful it is, beautiful it is! Its blessings and grace reach far. Together I aid my royal house and settle the four directions. Conforming to Heaven and Earth in measure, he matched the radiance of sun and moon. Forever elevated and honored without limit, his life was to be equal to the Eastern Deity’s years. He drove a dragon banner to wander and circle, and returned the phoenix carriage in a circling rhythm. His grace extended through all four seas, rare things flourished and the people prospered. May this pavilion stand firm forever; may its joy endure to the end, never exhausted.

After Kongming finished, Zhou Yu rose in furious anger, pointed north, and shouted, “That old villain has cheated and insulted me far beyond measure!”

Kongming hurriedly stepped forward to stop him and said, “In former days, when the Xiongnu pressed the frontiers again and again, the Son of Heaven offered a princess in marriage. Why should two private women of the realm now be so precious?”

Zhou Yu said, “You do not know this. Great Qiao is the principal wife of General Sun Bofu; Small Qiao is your own wife.”

Kongming, feigning alarm, said, “Bright One truly did not know! I spoke in error and upset my own mouth. Death is my punishment. Death is my punishment!”

Zhou Yu said, “With the old villain I swore not to coexist.”

Kongming said, “A matter like this needs three times of thought, else regret will follow.”

Zhou Yu replied, “I was entrusted by Bofu. I have no place in submitting myself to Cao Cao. What I said earlier was only to test you. From the day I left Poyang Lake I had already held a heart for marching north. Even if axe and halberd should fall on my head, that resolve will not be changed. Ask Kongming to aid one flank and we will break Cao Cao together.”

Kongming said, “If he does not reject me, I will render service like a horse and dog, and by morning and night be ready at the sound of your commands.”

Zhou Yu said, “Tomorrow we enter court and discuss raising troops with the lord.” Kongming and Lu Su withdrew and parted.

The next morning at dawn, Sun Quan mounted the hall. On the left stood over thirty civil officials, such as Zhang Zhao and Gu Yong; on the right were more than thirty military officers, including Cheng Pu and Huang Gai. Their robes and hats were neat and complete, their swords and sheaths clanged; each stood by rank.

After a short time Zhou Yu entered for audience. After all formalities were complete, Sun Quan greeted him with ritual courtesies.

Zhou Yu said, “I have heard that Cao Cao has advanced troops to the Han frontier and sent this edict here. What does Your Majesty intend?”

Sun Quan handed the edict to Zhou Yu. After reading it, Zhou Yu laughed and said, “The old villain takes us in Jiangdong for having no men, and so he dares such disrespect.”

Sun Quan said, “What is your thought?”

Zhou Yu said, “Did Your Majesty already confer with all civil and military men?”

Sun Quan said, “For several days they have debated this matter. Some urged surrender; others urged battle. My decision is not fixed; therefore I ask Gongjin to decide it.”

Zhou Yu said, “Who urged surrender?”

Sun Quan said, “Zhang Zibu and the rest all pushed that policy.”

Zhou Yu asked Zhang Zhao, “I wish to hear your reason for pressing surrender.”

Zhang Zhao said, “Cao Cao carries the Son of Heaven and campaigns in all directions, using court authority as pretense. He has just obtained Jing Province, and his strength has only increased. If we in Jiangdong can refuse him, it is because of the Yangtze. Yet his war junks alone are no mere hundreds—they are in the thousands. He advances by land and water. We cannot withstand this. Better to surrender and seek a later opportunity.”

Zhou Yu said, “This is the argument of an over-stretched scholar. Since Jiangdong was founded, we have now passed three generations. How can we discard it in one stroke?”

Sun Quan said, “If this plan is adopted, where does it end?”

Zhou Yu said, “Cao Cao may claim to be regent of Han, but in truth he is a Han traitor. The commander possesses divine strength and heroic talent. Relying on his father’s and elder brother’s legacy, he holds Jiangdong, with disciplined troops and enough grain. Now is the hour to stride through all under heaven, to remove remnant brutality and tyrannies. Why then submit to a bandit? Consider further: Cao Cao’s present approach breaks several principles of warfare. First, the northern lands are not pacified. Ma Teng and Han Sui remain dangers behind him, a deep rear threat. Second, his northern armies are unaccustomed to river battles; he has set aside his horse and saddle and depends on boats and oars against Eastern Wu. Second, this is late winter in bitter cold, and grass for the horses is scarce. Third, soldiers from the central lands are driven far across lakes and rivers, unfamiliar with this water country; many illnesses will take them. There are four such dangers. When an enemy runs into all of them, even with a great number he must fail. Capturing Cao Cao is ours for this day. Give me an elite force of several thousand and let me post it at Xiaokou; I will break him.”

Sun Quan raised his eyes in astonishment and said, “That old villain has long wished to usurp the Han and set himself up. What he fears now are only the two Yüans, Lü Bu, and Liu Biao—until now all three are gone. I alone remain. This old villain and I have sworn we will not coexist. If you press to punish him, it matches my intent. It is Heaven that entrusts this command to you.”

Zhou Yu said, “I, your servant, will decide one battle with blood, and I do not shrink from ten thousand deaths. I only fear Your Majesty might hesitate.”

Sun Quan drew his belt sword, chopped a corner off the document table before him, and said, “Any of the officials or commanders who again raise the matter of surrendering to Cao Cao will meet what you see in this cut corner.” He then handed that sword to Zhou Yu, and immediately bestowed on him the title of Chief Commander, made Cheng Pu Deputy Chief Commander, and made Lu Su Colonel Who Assists the Army.

For any civil or military officer who disobeyed commands, he would be put to death by this sword.

Receiving the sword, Zhou Yu said to those assembled, “I carry out Your Majesty’s order to lead the troops and break Cao Cao. Tomorrow all commanders and officers should come to the banks of the river for camp and follow commands. Should anyone delay, the seven legal orders and five-and-fifty penalties will be enforced.” After he had finished speaking, he thanked the lord and rose to leave the hall. The civil and military ranks parted silently.

Zhou Yu returned to his residence and then invited Kongming to discuss the matter. Kongming arrived.

Zhou Yu said, “The deliberation in court this day is settled. I need a good plan to break Cao Cao.”

Kongming said, “The Lord of Wu has not fully settled in mind and should not yet make the final decision.”

Zhou Yu asked, “What do you mean by an unsettled mind?”

Kongming replied, “He fears Cao’s many soldiers and suspects his own small strength against that multitude. Use your command to open this to him and make this clear beyond doubt, and then the great matter can succeed.”

Zhou Yu said, “Your argument is excellent.”

He returned again to see Sun Quan.

Sun Quan said, “Gongjin came at night. Surely there is some matter.”

Zhou Yu said, “Did Your Majesty already arrange for moving horses and troops? Are you still uncertain?”

Sun Quan said, “I only fear that Cao’s army is large and that our small number cannot meet it. He has no doubt in my mind.”

Zhou Yu laughed and said, “This is exactly why I came: to clarify him. Your Majesty saw in Cao’s edict an army of hundreds of thousands, both by river and land, so you doubt and fear, and so you fail to judge it correctly. Compare with the reality: his force from the central lands is not more than one hundred fifty to one hundred sixty thousand, and they are already worn out. The troops he obtained from the Yuans are only seventy to eighty thousand and still many are uncertain and unconvinced in allegiance. For an army long exhausted in battle, and for troops still in doubt, however many, they are not truly to be feared. I have fifty thousand troops. That is sufficient to break him. Do not let Your Majesty worry.”

Sun Quan patted Zhou Yu’s back and said, “Your words, Gongjin, are enough to clear my doubt. Zibu has no strategy and has deeply disappointed me. Only you and Zijing and Cheng Pu are of one mind with me. You and Zijing and Cheng Pu should select forces and move at once. I will send men and grain on behind you. If your advanced army is not favorable, return to me at once. I will then personally decide with the Cao traitor and end this with no further doubt.”

Zhou Yu thanked him and left.

He reflected quietly to himself: “Kongming had already foreseen the heart of the ruler of Wu. His plan is one move above mine. He will one day be a calamity for Jiangdong. I should simply kill him.” He had a man sent that very night to summon Lu Su into his quarters to arrange Kongming’s death.

Lu Su said, “You cannot. The enemy of Cao is not yet broken; to kill a worthy scholar now is to discard his help yourself.”

Zhou Yu said, “This man aids Liu Bei; he will be a threat to Jiangdong.”

Lu Su said, “Could not his elder brother, Zhuge Jin, be asked to bring this man into common service with Eastern Wu? Is that not better?”

Zhou Yu accepted his counsel.

At dawn the next day Zhou Yu went to the field camp and mounted the high seat of the central command tent. Armed men with swords and axes stood at his sides, and civil and military officers gathered to receive orders.

Cheng Pu was older than Zhou Yu, and now Zhou Yu held rank over him, so Cheng Pu’s heart was not pleased. That day he feigned illness and did not go out, sending his eldest son, Cheng Zi, instead.

Zhou Yu announced to the assembled: “The law of the realm is no private thing; each of you keep to your posts. Right now Cao Cao has abused authority, worse than Dong Zhuo when he held the Son of Heaven in Xuchang and arrayed unruly troops on our border. I am under orders to punish him; each of you must press forward with all strength. In every place where the army moves, civilians are not to be disturbed. Reward and punishment for reward and fault are alike; I will not spare favoritism.”

When he finished, he assigned Han Dang and Huang Gai to be the first guard as the vanguard, and they were to take their main fleet and depart at once to Sanjiangkou, to set camp there and await separate orders. Jiang Qin and Zhou Tai were the second unit; Ling Tong and Pan Zhang the third; Taishi Ci and Lü Meng the fourth; Lu Xun and Dong Xi the fifth; Lu Fan and Zhu Zhi were placed to command the patrol guards in all directions. In all, six teams of regular troops were ordered forward, land and water together, each pushing to the appointed rendezvous.

Once orders had been sent, each general gathered ship and weapons and set out.

Cheng Zi returned to his father, Cheng Pu, and described Zhou Yu’s military deployment and method. Cheng Pu was greatly startled.

“I have always underestimated the young lord, thinking him too mild to command,” he said. “Now to do this with such method is true command talent. How could I still not submit?”

He then went personally to the field camp and apologized.

Zhou Yu also returned the apology in turn.

The next day Zhou Yu asked Zhuge Jin to come.

Zhou Yu said, “Your younger brother Kongming has talent to be a royal counselor and support this state. How can such a man serve Liu Bei in humiliation? Now that he has come to Jiangdong, I wish your favor to request him, without concern for gossip, to leave Liu Bei and serve Eastern Wu. Then Your Majesty would have a worthy adviser, and you brothers could see one another again. Is that not good? You should act at once.”

Zhuge Jin said, “Since I came to Jiangdong, I have nothing with which to boast. The Chief Commander has given command. How can I not do him service?” He mounted his horse at once and rode straight to the relay pavilion to meet Kongming.

Kongming received him, knelt and bowed in tears, and each spoke at length of long-lost feelings.

Zhuge Jin wept and said, “Brother, do you know of Bo Yi and Shu Qi?”

Kongming thought inwardly, “This must be Zhou-lang’s setup to convince me,” then replied, “Bo Yi and Shu Qi were sages of antiquity.”

Zhuge Jin said, “Though Bo Yi and Shu Qi died of hunger under the Shouyang heights, those two brothers remained together at one place. I, who shared mother’s milk with you, now serve different lords, and we cannot meet morning and evening. With a view of Bo Yi and Shu Qi, can we remain without shame?”

Kongming said, “What you say is affection; what I keep is righteousness. You and I are both Han men. Now Liu Huangshu is the shield of the Han house. If brother can leave Eastern Wu and serve Liu Huangshu with me, we can stand upright as Han ministers and still be siblings who are reunited. This does both emotion and duty. I do not know how you will judge it.”

Zhuge Jin reflected, “I came to persuade him, but he has persuaded me instead.” He spoke no more, rose, and took his leave.

He returned to Zhou Yu and recounted Kongming’s words in detail.

Zhou Yu asked, “What is your judgment?”

Zhuge Jin said, “I have received great kindness from the General. How can I stand against my lord?”

Zhou Yu said, “Since you are sincerely loyal and do not need to speak further. I already have my trap for Kongming.”

Where wisdom meets wisdom, it should come to one accord; yet talent and talent still clash and refuse to yield. In the end, what stratagem will Zhou Yu use to trap Kongming?

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang Stirs Zhou Yu, and Sun Quan Decides to Move Against Cao Cao

chapters.html:
Cao Cao’s army is checked at the Three-River Ford. The assembly of heroes traps Jiang Gan.

Yet it is said that after Zhou Yu, whose courtesy name was Gongjin, heard Zhuge Jin, he turned his resentment against Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, and plotted to kill him. The next day he gave orders to line up the army commanders and entered audience with Sun Quan. Sun Quan said, “Go on first. I will raise the troops and follow.”

Zhou Yu withdrew and, with Cheng Pu and Lu Su, led the troops out and invited Kongming to accompany them. Kongming readily agreed, and together they boarded the boats, raised sail, and moved toward Xiakou in a steady drift. Fifty or sixty li south of the Three-River Ford, the ships, one after another, came to a halt and moored. Zhou Yu pitched camp in the middle of the line, and on the bank he established a camp below West Hill, stationing troops all around. Kongming settled aboard a single small boat.

Zhou Yu had already assigned the deployments and now sent someone to ask Kongming to discuss military affairs. Kongming arrived at the central command tent and exchanged formal courtesy. Zhou Yu said, “In former days, Cao Cao had fewer troops while Yuan Shao had many, yet Cao prevailed by using Xuyou’s plan and first cutting off the supplies at Wuchao. Now Cao has eight hundred and thirty thousand soldiers, while we have only fifty or sixty thousand. How can we resist him? We must first cut off Cao’s supplies, and only then can we break him. I have found that Cao’s stores of grain are all concentrated at Juite Shan. You have long lived at Han’s camp and know the terrain well. If you are willing, you and Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, and Zhao Yun and I will send in a thousand troops and go by night to Juite Shan to sever Cao’s food line. Each man would be serving his own lord, so do not fail him through over-caution.”

Kongming thought to himself, “He has said this to keep me from moving and to plan to trap me. If I refuse, I will be mocked. Better to agree, and then devise another plan.” So he answered pleasantly and accepted. Zhou Yu rejoiced greatly, and Kongming withdrew.

Lu Su spoke privately to Zhou Yu. “Why do you have Kongming break the supplies? What is your design?”

Zhou Yu answered, “I want to kill Kongming, but I fear ridicule. So I use Cao Cao’s hand to do it and end this future trouble at the source.”

When Lu Su heard this, he went to see Kongming and tried to read whether he knew what had passed. Kongming showed no sign of distress, and quietly arranged men and horses in readiness to move. Lu Su could not bear it and provocatively said, “Why has Gongjin sent you to seize Cao's grain? What is his intent?”

Kongming laughed. “I am competent in water fighting, foot fighting, horse fighting, and chariot fighting; why should I worry that my achievements will fail? I am not like men of Jiangdong—only you and Zhou there would claim such excellence.”

Lu Su said, “What do you mean, Master by saying that I and Zhou Liang are the only one truly able?”

Kongming replied, “I have heard a rhyme from children in Jiangnan: ‘At the crossing road, Rao Zijing holds the barrier; on river battle by the Yangtze, there is Zhou Lang.’ On land you only know how to block roads, and Master Zhou can only handle water fighting, not land fighting.”

Lu Su reported these words to Zhou Yu.

Zhou Yu grew angry. “Do you mean to pretend I cannot fight on land? I will not send him! I myself will lead ten thousand cavalry to Juite Shan and cut off Cao’s supply route.”

Lu Su again told Kongming what Zhou had said.

Kongming smiled. “By setting me to cut grain, General Zhou intends me to be killed by Cao Cao. I mocked him in passing, and he has no room to hold it in. At this critical time, I wish only that Lord Wu and Lord Liu act with one heart; then the enterprise can succeed. If each works to harm the other, then this major effort will end.”

“Cao, who is full of schemes, has always been used to cutting an enemy’s food line. How could he now not keep heavy troops ready? If General Zhou goes, he will be taken and captured. Now we must first resolve the river battle, exhaust the northern army’s sharpness, and then seek another clever way to break it. Please tell him this as kindly as you can.”

Lu Su returned overnight and recounted all Kongming had said. Zhou Yu shook his head and stomped his feet. “This man’s insight exceeds mine by tenfold. If we do not remove him now, he will become our country’s disaster in time!”

Lu Su said, “Now is not the moment for choosing and removing men. Let us put the state first. When Cao is defeated, there will still be time to deal with him.”

Zhou Yu accepted what Lu Su said.

It is said that Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, ordered Liu Qi to hold Jiangxia and personally led the other commanders south to Xiakou. From the riverbank he could see banners on Jiangnan’s bank barely visible, spears and halberds dense in rows; clearly, Eastern Wu had already moved troops. He moved all the Jiangxia forces to anchor at Fankou.

Liu Bei assembled everyone and said, “Since Kongming has been in that land for long and now intends to return, I have no news of him and do not know what has happened. Who can go and learn the true state of things and report back?” Mi Zhu said, “I volunteer to go.”

Liu Bei prepared sheep and wine gifts and told Mi Zhu to go to Eastern Wu. In name of offering rewards to the army, he was to gather true information.

Mi Zhu took his charge and, boarding a small boat, drifted downstream directly to the forward camp of Zhou Yu. A sentry reported him to the general. Yu summoned him in.

Mi Zhu bowed twice and conveyed Liu Bei’s respect. He presented the wine gifts. Zhou Yu accepted and gave him a formal banquet.

Mi Zhu said, “Kongming has stayed there for a long time. Now he wishes to return with us.”

Zhou Yu said, “Kongming is still plotting with me how to break Cao. How could he go at once? I also want to meet Governor Liu and discuss this matter, but I cannot leave at once while commanding the whole army. If he is willing, let him come in person; my joy would be complete.”

Mi Zhu agreed, bowed out, and returned. Lu Su asked Zhou Yu, “How did you wish to meet Liu Bei?”

Zhou Yu answered, “Liu Bei is a fierce predatory figure of the age and cannot be left alive. I mean to use this chance to lure him here and kill him for the state’s sake.”

Lu Su urged him repeatedly, but Zhou Yu would not listen. He sent a secret order: “When Liu Bei arrives, hide fifty axe-and-halberd men in the wall-clothes by the screen. Wait for my sign, the cup cast to the ground, and then strike.”

It is said that when Mi Zhu returned and told Liu Bei everything, Zhou Yu had wished him to come to a face-to-face meeting and had other designs. Liu Bei at once commanded the preparation of a fast boat. “Go at once,” he said.

Guan Yu, courtesy name Yunchang, protested: “Zhou Yu is clever and has no letter from Kongming. I fear there is a trick. We should not go lightly.”

Liu Bei said, “I have now allied with Eastern Wu to break Cao Cao together. If Zhou Lang wishes to see me and I refuse, it will not seem that we are allied. If suspicion grows between us, matters will never proceed in harmony.”

Guan Yu answered, “If Brother insists on going, I will go with him.”

Zhang Fei, courtesy name Yide, added, “I will go too.”

Liu Bei replied, “Only Yunchang will follow me. Yide and Zilong stay with the camp. Jian Yong should hold E County. I will return soon.”

After giving orders, he set off with Guan Yu by small boat with more than twenty attendants.

They crossed and soon reached Jiangdong. Liu Bei saw Eastern Wu’s tower war-junks, banners, and armored soldiers arranged in neat left-right ranks and was deeply pleased. The camp messengers rushed in: “Governor Liu has arrived.”

Zhou Yu asked, “How many boats with him?” The messenger replied, “Only one boat, with more than twenty attendants.”

Zhou Yu laughed. “This man’s life is almost finished.” He ordered the hidden blade-men set as planned and then dispatched men to welcome him.

Liu Bei brought Guan Yu and the rest, more than twenty, to the central command tent and exchanged formal courtesies. Zhou Yu invited Liu Bei to sit in the seat of honor. Liu Bei said, “Your reputation is known to the world. Though I am unworthy, why this heavy honor?” He made them sit as host and guest by custom, and Zhou Yu hosted him to a feast.

At that moment Kongming happened to come to the riverbank, and on hearing that Liu Bei had come to meet Zhou Yu, he was startled. He hurried into the central camp tent and quietly watched the scene. He saw Zhou Yu with killing intent in his face and, on both sides of the sleeves of the camp garments, rows of axe-and-halberd men concealed. Kongming gasped inwardly and said, “What can be done now?” and looked back at Liu Bei. Liu Bei sat chatting as if nothing had happened. Behind him stood a man with a drawn sword—Guan Yu.

Kongming said in relief, “My lord is safe,” then did not enter further. He returned to the riverbank and waited.

During the banquet Zhou Yu and Liu Bei drank. After several rounds of cups, Zhou Yu rose and lifted his cup. At once he clearly saw Guan Yu standing behind Liu Bei with his sword drawn. “Who is that man?” he asked urgently.

Liu Bei answered, “My brother is Guan Yu.”

Zhou Yu was startled. “Is he not the one who once cut down Yan Liang and Wen Chou?”

Liu Bei said, “He is.”

Zhou Yu was startled all over, sweat streaming down his back. He filled a cup and handed it to Guan Yu.

After some time Lu Su entered.

Liu Bei said, “Where is Kongming? I beg you, Excellency Zijing, ask him to come for a meeting.”

Zhou Yu replied, “After we break Cao, there will be time to meet Kongming, and there is no need now.”

Liu Bei did not press further. Guan Yu watched Liu Bei with his eyes. Liu Bei understood and stood to leave, saying to Zhou Yu, “I will take my leave for now. The moment the enemy is broken and success secured, I will certainly return to offer congratulations.” Zhou Yu did not detain him and accompanied him to the gate.

After parting from Zhou Yu, Liu Bei and Guan Yu returned to the riverbank and found Kongming already aboard the boat. Liu Bei was overjoyed.

Kongming asked, “My lord, do you know what danger lay in today’s situation?”

Liu Bei answered in surprise, “I do not.”

Kongming said, “Without Guan Yu, you would have been killed by Zhou Yu.”

Only then did Liu Bei fully realize the peril. He asked Kongming to return to Fankou together.

Kongming said, “Though I sit in a tiger’s mouth, I am still as calm as Mount Tai. My lord, prepare your ships and horses and hold them ready. Mark the day: after the twentieth day of the eleventh month, Jiazi. Tell Zilong to take a small boat and wait on the southern bank. Do not make any mistake.”

Liu Bei asked his meaning, but Kongming hurried him to set off at once. As soon as he finished speaking, he returned.

Liu Bei with Guan Yu and their attendants cast off. After they had gone only a few li, they saw fifty or sixty ships coming downstream in formation. On the prow of the foremost boat stood a captain with a cross spear: Zhang Fei.

Fearing Liu Bei might meet harm and Guan Yu be unable to stand it alone, Zhang Fei had come as support. So the three returned together to camp.

Now no further account is given there.

When Zhou Yu had seen Liu Bei off and returned to his camp, Lu Su entered and asked, “You lured Liu Bei here, so why did you not strike?”

Zhou Yu shook his head and stamped his feet. “Guan Yu is a tiger general of this age. He accompanied Liu Bei while seated and traveling together. If I struck now, he would come and ruin me.”

Lu Su was astonished.

A messenger arrived then: Cao Cao had dispatched an envoy with a letter. Zhou Yu summoned him. The messenger presented it; on the outside it was marked, “Han Great Chancellor to Commander Zhou.” Zhou Yu grew angry and would not even open it. He tore it apart and threw it to the ground, then ordered the envoy executed.

Lu Su said, “Between two states in conflict, an envoy is not killed.”

Zhou Yu said, “Beheading the envoy displays force,” and he had him slain, and he sent the head back with an orderly.

He ordered Gan Ning as vanguard, Han Dang on the left wing, Jiang Qin on the right, and he himself directed the rest of the generals to reinforce.

At dawn the next day they prepared provisions; at the fifth watch they would board, beat drums and shout, and advance.

It is said that when Cao Cao heard Zhou Yu had ruined the letter and executed the envoy, he was furious and called Cai Mao and Zhang Yun and other surrendered generals from Jing Province to the front.

Cao himself took command of the rear, drove the warships forward, and came to Three-Jiang Ford. He saw Eastern Wu vessels covering the river.

At their head a giant commander sat on the foredeck and shouted, “I am Gan Ning! Who dares come and settle battle with me?”

Cai Mao ordered his brother Cai Xun forward.

When the two ships drew near, Gan Ning drew bow and set an arrow. It struck Cai Xun as Cai Xun released his own; he fell. Gan Ning then drove his ship forward swiftly. Thousands of crossbow bolts rose and were loosed, and the Cao forces could not stand against it.

On the right sailed Jiang Qin; on the left advanced Han Dang. They drove straight into the Cao formation. Most of Cao’s troops were from Qing and Xu, unused to naval battle. In the vast waters of the Great River their ships could not keep footing.

Gan Ning’s three-way attack and his crews scattered through the water like wind. Zhou Yu sent additional ships to reinforce.

Many in Cao’s army were shot and struck by fire-tipped projectiles. From the fourth watch to the seventh watch, battle continued. Though Zhou Yu gained advantage, he still feared the small force against the overwhelming army and ordered the signal-gong to halt and recall ships.

The Cao army withdrew in defeat. Cao climbed the dry camp and reorganized the troops. He summoned Cai Mao and Zhang Yun and said, “Eastern Wu has fewer men, yet they have beaten you. The fault is your lack of effort!”

Cai Mao replied, “The Jing troops have not trained for long; and the Qing and Xu forces are unaccustomed to river fighting. That is why we were defeated. First set up a water camp, place Qing and Xu troops in the center, Jing troops outside. Have them train each day until they become exacting in skill before using them.”

Cao said, “Since you both are admirals of the water forces, you can carry out what is convenient. Why must you report to me for this?”

So the two of Cai Mao and Zhang Yun went off to train the water troops.

Along the river they opened twenty-four sluices. Large ships stood outwardly as walls; smaller vessels inside were used for passage. Night came with torches lit, and the sky reflected a red glow over the water. Three hundred or more li of dry camp along the banks burned with unbroken smoke and fire.

Meanwhile Zhou Yu returned victorious to camp and rewarded the three armies, then sent men to report the victory to Lord Wu.

That same night Zhou Yu climbed high and watched. He saw lights in the west, touching the sky. Those nearby reported, “These are the lights of the northern army.” Zhou Yu was startled.

The next day Zhou Yu wished to see Cao’s river camps with his own eyes. He ordered one tall decked ship to be prepared and carried drums and music, with several chosen generals each with powerful bows and crossbows, and all advanced together.

When they reached Cao’s camp edge, he ordered anchor-stones to be dropped and made drums and music sound together on the tower ship. Zhou Yu looked covertly at the water camp and was startled: “He has truly mastered the art of naval force.” He asked, “Who is the water-force admiral?” The attendants answered, “Cai Mao and Zhang Yun.”

Zhou Yu thought, “These two have long lived east of the river and are well versed in naval combat. I must devise a plan first to remove them, and then we can break Cao.”

Just as he watched, a Cao report reached him: Zhou Yu was peering into their camp. Cao ordered boats out to seize him.

Zhou Yu saw the banner and signal movement in Cao’s water camp; he ordered the anchor stones hauled up at once. On both sides all the oars struck together and the ship sped away like an arrow over the river.

By the time Cao’s camp boats launched in pursuit, Zhou Yu’s tower ship was already ten or more li away, beyond reach. He reported back to Cao.

Cao asked his generals, “Yesterday we lost one engagement and our sharpness was blunted; now we have again been deeply observed. What plan can I make now to break him?”

Before he had finished speaking, a man came out from among the attendants in the tent. “I grew up with Zhou Lang and have the persuasive tongue of one who never fails. Let me go to Jiangdong and speak to persuade this man to surrender.”

Cao was pleased and saw him: he was a man from Jiujiang, surname Jiang, given name Gan, courtesy name Ziyi. He served in his household as a court attendant.

Cao asked, “Do you share close ties with Master Zhou?”

Jiang Gan replied, “Trust the Chancellor. If Gan enters Jiangzuo, success is certain.”

Cao asked, “What must be taken with you?”

Gan replied, “Only one child attendant and two servants to row. Nothing more is needed.”

Cao was delighted and celebrated him with wine before sending him off.

Gan wore a felt cap and plain linen robe, took a small boat, and went straight to Zhou Yu’s camp. He had his approach announced: “Friend of old, Jiang Gan arrives.”

Zhou Yu was in council in his tent. Hearing Gan had come he laughed and told the generals, “A spokesman has arrived.” He whispered to them in low voice, “Thus and so.” They all obeyed and withdrew.

Zhou Yu dressed neatly and took several hundred attendants with him, all in brocade robes with flowered caps. They formed around him in a compact formation and came out front and rear.

Jiang Gan came with one blue-clad boy and strode in proudly. Zhou Yu bowed and received him.

Gan said, “Master Gongjin, you are in good health apart from my absence.”

Zhou Yu replied, “You have labored much, Ziyi. You have crossed broad waters to be emissary for the Cao house?”

Gan, startled, said, “I have not seen you for long; I came to renew our old friendship. Why would you suspect I am a spokesman?”

Zhou Yu laughed. “Though I do not match your cleverness in hearing, I can know intent from music and song.”

Gan said, “If this is how you treat an old friend, then ask me to leave.”

Zhou Yu laughed and took him by the arm. “I simply fear my brother is here as Cao’s spokesman. If his heart is pure, why should he go so quickly?”

And he brought him into the tent.

After courtesies were exchanged and they sat, Zhou Yu ordered all Jiangnan’s heroes to be summoned for meeting with Jiang Gan.

Soon scholars and officers entered, all in brocade dress; camp attendants and junior officers wore silver armor. They entered in two lines. After each paid respect and greeted him, Zhou Yu had them sit on both sides and spread a great banquet hall, played music from the army’s victory repertoire, and passed wine in turn.

Zhou Yu told the assembled officers, “This man is my schoolmate and old friend. Though he came from Jiangbei, he is not an emissary of the Cao house. Do not doubt him.”

Then he took off his belt-sword and handed it to Taishi Ci, saying, “Hold my sword while I watch over the wine. Today we feast as friends. If any man brings up Cao Cao and the campaigns of Eastern Wu, execute him at once.”

Taishi Ci agreed and took out his sword, seating himself at table.

Jiang Gan was startled and dared not speak much.

Zhou Yu said, “Since I have taken command I have not drunk a drop. To see an old friend and have no suspicion now, I will drink a full cup.” Speaking so, he laughed and drank deeply. Cups crossed in the hall.

At half-drunk Zhou Yu took Gan by the arm and walked out of the tent together. The guards all stood fully armed, belts tight, holding spears and halberds.

Zhou Yu asked, “My soldiers—isn’t their vigor and strength obvious?”

Gan answered, “They are indeed like tigers and bears.”

Zhou Yu drew Gan to the rear of the tent and showed him the mounds of supplies heaped like mountains.

Zhou Yu asked, “Are my food supplies sufficient?”

Gan answered, “The troops are disciplined and the stores sufficient, as the name claims.”

Feigning drunken laughter, Zhou Yu said, “When Zhou Yu studied with Ziyi, I never imagined this day.”

Gan replied, “With your talent, this does not exceed expectation.”

Zhou Yu clasped Gan’s hand and said, “When a man of high standing lives in the world, he must meet a sovereign who knows him, outwardly sustain lord and minister bonds, inwardly form bonds of flesh and blood. Words must be carried out, plans must be executed, fortune and ruin shared together. Even if Su Qin, Zhang Yi, Lu Jia, and Li Sheng returned again, with mouths like a hanging river and tongues like keen blades, how could they move my heart?” He ended with laughter.

Jiang Gan’s face turned ashen.

Zhou Yu led him back into the tent and continued drinking among the commanders, then pointed and said, “These are all the heroes of Jiangdong. This gathering can be called the Assembly of Heroes.”

After drinking until evening, he lit the lamps. Zhou Yu rose and danced with his sword while singing:

A man who lives in this world should establish merit and fame;
Establishing merit and fame brings solace to his life.
With life thus solaced, I shall drink my fill;
And in my drunkenness, burst into a wild song!

When the song ended, the whole hall laughed with joy. It was late into the night when Gan said, “I cannot withstand this wine.”

Zhou Yu dismissed the feast and let the generals leave. He said, “It has been long since I shared a bed with you. Tonight we sleep as we once did, deep and at ease.” Then he feigned great intoxication and took Gan into the tent to sleep together.

Zhou Yu and Gan lay covered under one covering. Zhou’s breathing came like thunder, and his clothing and bed were in disorder from vomit and weariness.

How could Gan sleep? He tucked his pillow and waited, and when he heard the second-watch drumming in the camp, he rose and saw that the lamp still burned. Looking at Zhou Yu, whose breathing sounded like drums, Gan noticed on the table in the tent a bundle of documents. He rose and secretly looked at it. They were all letters that had come and gone.

Among them was one sealed: “Reverently addressed from Cai Mao and Zhang Yun.” Gan was startled and read it covertly.

Its contents, roughly, said: “The two of us have joined Cao not for rank and profit but because we are forced by circumstance. We have already gained that the northern army is stuck in camp. If there is favorable timing, we will take the head of the bandit Cao and offer it to you. People will arrive morning and evening with news in turn. Do not raise suspicion. I respectfully return this first.”

Gan reasoned, “So this is what it is; Cai Mao and Zhang Yun have joined hands with Eastern Wu.” He hid the letter secretly in his clothing.

When he turned to examine the other letters, Zhou shifted in bed. Gan at once put out the lamp and lay down.

From Zhou’s mouth came a murmured mutter: “Ziyi, within these few days I will make you see the head of the bandit Cao!”

Gan forced an answer.

Zhou said, “Ziyi, hold! I will make you see the bandit Cao’s head!”

Gan asked, and Zhou had already fallen asleep.

Gan lay in bed. As dawn neared the fourth watch, he heard someone enter the tent calling, “Is the commander awake?”

In sleep, Zhou seemed to be waking and asked, “Who sleeps on the bed?”

The man answered, “The commander requested Ziyi to share your bed. How could you forget?”

Zhou, with shame and regret, said, “I do not drink drunk. The day before yesterday we drank and there may have been words I did not know I had uttered.”

The man answered, “Men from Jiangbei have arrived.”

Zhou hissed, “Keep your voice low!” and called, “Ziyi.”

Gan pretended to sleep still. Zhou stepped out of the tent in stealth.

Gan listened from under the bedding and heard someone outside say, “The two commanders, Cai Mao and Zhang Yun, say: ‘Do not act too quickly.’” The rest was low and unclear.

After a short while Zhou returned, called again for “Ziyi.” Gan still made no reply, covering his head and feigning sleep.

Zhou too took off his robes and lay down.

Gan considered, “Zhou Yu is a very careful man; if he could not find the plan by the Gate of Heaven, he must intend harm to me.”

Jiang Gan thought, "Zhou Yu is a meticulous man. If he wakes at dawn and finds the letter gone, he will surely kill me." Before the fifth watch, Gan called to Zhou, but the man was asleep.

Gan put on his hood and scarf, stepped silently out of the tent, and called the boy attendant. He came directly to the gate. A guard asked, “Where is the master going?”

Gan said, “I fear my stay here may hinder the commander’s business. I bid him farewell for now.”

The guard did not stop him.

Gan went down to the boat and rowed swiftly back to Cao Cao.

Cao asked, “How did matters go with Ziyi?”

Gan said, “Zhou Yu is of lofty character. Neither words nor persuasion can move him.”

Cao was angry: “Even now it did not work, and he mocks us!”

Gan said, “Though I cannot persuade Zhou Yu, I have heard one thing that may matter. Let me speak privately.”

Gan took out the letter and explained each item to Cao.

Cao grew furious: “These two traitors have shown such impudence!” He immediately summoned Cai Mao and Zhang Yun to his tent.

Cao said, “I wish you to lead an advance battalion forward.”

Cai Mao said, “The army has not yet been trained; it must not advance too rashly.”

Cao shouted in fury, “If the army had once been trained, my own head would be offered to Zhou Lang!”

Cai and Zhang did not know his meaning. They were frightened and could not answer. Cao called for the soldiers and had them executed.

Soon their heads were brought into the command tent. Cao then understood in full: “I have been outwitted.”

Later a poem was composed in lament:
