“Cao Cao, a crafty villain, cannot be faced; For one moment’s tricking, he is ensnared by Zhou. Cai and Zhang sold out their lord to save their own lives; Who could have thought they would this morning perish beneath the sword?”

The other generals, seeing Cai Mao and Zhang Yun executed, asked why.

Though Cao understood he had fallen into a stratagem, he would not admit it and told the generals, “They were careless and negligent of military law. That is why I executed them.”

The assembled commanders sighed repeatedly.

From among them Cao selected Mao Jie and Yu Jin to replace Cai Mao and Zhang Yun as admirals of the water troops.

A spy learned the report and carried it across the river to Eastern Wu. Zhou Yu rejoiced and said, “These are the two I feared most. Now that they are purged, I have no worries.”

Lu Su said, “When one wields troops this way, why should Cao’s army not fall?”

Zhou Yu said, “I suspect the other commanders do not understand this stratagem and that only Zhuge Liang saw through it and could not hide it. Ask Master Zijing to test his words—whether he knows or not—and report back.”

Thus it is said:

The stratagem of counterintelligence succeeds once more; Go, challenge the one who watched quietly from the side.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: At Three-River Ford, Cao Cao’s Army Is Checked and the Heroes’ Assembly Traps Jiang Gan

chapters.html:
A strange stratagem has Zhuge Liang borrow arrows;
A hidden design is offered, and Huang Gai receives punishment.

Afterwards, Lu Su, whose courtesy name was Zijing, had finished his business for Zhou Yu and went directly to meet Zhuge Liang by boat, and Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, stepped into a small craft to sit facing him.

“You have been all these days occupied with military duties and have failed to relay my instructions,” Lu Su said.

“That is also why I have not gone to congratulate the Commander-in-Chief,” said Zhuge Liang.

“What is there to celebrate?”

“That Gongjin has sent you to test whether I know this matter or not. That itself is something to celebrate.”

Startled, Lu Su’s face drained of color. “How did you know this?”

“This plan can only be carried through by Jiang Gan. Cao Cao was deceived for a moment, and he will surely awaken to it soon, though he will not admit he was wrong. Now that Cai Mao and Zhang are both dead, Jiangdong has no danger. Why should this not be cause for rejoicing? I hear that Cao Cao has made Mao Jie and Yu Jin commanders of the river forces; at any rate these two are now the ones to pay with their naval lives.”

Lu Su, unable to find words, stammered for a while before leaving and returning by himself. Zhuge Liang told him:

“Do not tell Gongjin before him that I already knew of this. I fear he will become jealous and look for ways to harm me.”

Lu Su agreed and then reported the whole affair faithfully to Zhou Yu.

Zhou Yu was startled. “This man can never be kept! I have decided to behead him.”

Lu Su urged, “If you execute Zhuge Liang, Cao Cao will laugh.”

Zhou Yu replied, “I will put him to death by right, and he will die without grievance.”

“By what right?”

“Do not ask. You will see tomorrow.”

The next day he gathered the gathered commanders beneath his tent and ordered Zhuge Liang to discuss strategy.

Zhuge Liang came gladly. Once seated, Zhou Yu asked, “When we fight Cao’s army across the river tomorrow, what weapon should be used first?”

“On the Yangtze, bows and arrows should go first,” Zhuge Liang answered.

“Your idea suits my dull mind exactly. Yet our troops are running short of arrows. I ask you to oversee the making of one hundred thousand arrows for use in battle. This is official business; I hope you will not refuse.”

“As the Commander-in-Chief commands, I will do my best,” Zhuge Liang said. “May I ask when these arrows are required?”

“How soon can we have them? Within ten days, can you finish?”

“Cao Cao’s army arrives today. If we wait ten days, we will miss the hour.”

“Then how many days do you need?”

“In three days at most, I can deliver the full one hundred thousand.”

“This is no place for idle words.”

“How dare I jest with the Commander! I will post the formal order: if I fail in three days, I will accept severe punishment.”

Joyful, Zhou Yu had the military clerk read out the document in front of him and raised a cup. “After the military business is done, there will be your reward.”

“It is already too late today,” Zhuge Liang said. “Work begins tomorrow. By the third day send five hundred light soldiers to the riverbank to carry off the arrows.” He drank several cups and withdrew.

Lu Su asked, “Could this man be an impostor?”

Zhou Yu said, “He sends himself to death; I am not forcing him. Today he obtained the order openly before everyone. He cannot flee now, even with both wings spread. I will tell the engineers to delay the work on purpose and leave all materials unfinished. Then, when the deadline passes, he will be at fault. We can then be sure the charge.”

Lu Su, taking his leave, went to see Zhuge Liang.

Zhuge Liang said, “I told you not to tell Gongjin because he would surely try to destroy me. Yet Zijing would not keep silent for me; now another trouble is made. How am I to make one hundred thousand arrows in three days? Zijing alone can save me from this peril.”

“If you have invited this fate yourself, how can I rescue you?” Lu Su replied.

“Please ask if he can lend me twenty ships, each with thirty soldiers. Each ship should have blue cloth canopies and a little over a thousand bundles of straw placed along both sides. I have a use for it. By the third day I will surely have one hundred thousand arrows. Just do not let Gongjin know this; if he learns it, my plan fails.”

Lu Su agreed, though he still did not understand his intent. He reported to Zhou Yu and did not mention the ships at all. He only said, “Zhuge Liang needs no arrow-shafts, feathers, or glue and varnish. He has his own method.” Zhou Yu was deeply doubtful: “Let us see how he answers me in three days.”

Lu Su secretly prepared twenty light, fast boats in advance, with thirty men on each ship, along with canopies and bundles of straw, all fully ready and waiting for Zhuge Liang to deploy them. The first day, there was no movement; the second day too passed in stillness.

At the fourth watch of the third day, Zhuge Liang quietly summoned Lu Su to the boat.

“Why have you called for me?” Lu Su asked.

“Zijing, come with me to take the arrows.”

“To where?”

“Ask no question; when we arrive, you will see.”

Zhuge Liang ordered the twenty boats linked by long ropes and set off straight for the north bank. That night the fog was thick over the river, denser than usual in midstream, and neither bank could see the other.

Zhuge Liang urged the boats onward. As it happened, it was indeed a great fog. A prose poem on that immense fog called “Great Fog over the Yangtze” says:

The Yangtze is vast; it joins Min and E in the west, controls the Three Wu in the south, and bears the Nine Rivers in the north.
It gathers a hundred streams into the sea and through ten thousand years tosses its waves high.
There appear Dragon-Lord, Sea-Lord, River-Maiden, Water Mother, whales of a thousand zhang, nine-headed sky-serpents, weird demons, all in attendance.
These are precisely the abodes of spirits and the ground where heroes fight and guard.
When yin and yang are in disorder, day and dawn lose their difference;
all at once the sky turns one color and great fog thickens in all quarters.
Though one may move cartloads of brushwood and still not see, only drum and gong can be heard.
At first the mountains to the south are only dim spots, like a leopard hidden;
then the dark mass swells and seems ready to blind the black water fowl of the North Sea.
At last heaven and earth join, the upper reaches sink, and thick vapor hangs down like earth.
Vastly dim, boundless and immeasurable.
Whale-beasts leap from the water and raise billowing waves;
coiled dragons sink and exhale steam from the deep.
Then it is as if damp rain settles, spring cold ferments;
mist thick as ink, flood-like and endless.
The bank near Chaisang vanishes, and no mountain of Xia-kou is seen.
Thousands of warships sink into ravines like boulders;
a fisherman’s small skiff only appears and disappears in the surging swells.
Again and again, the vault of heaven is lightless, and dawn loses its hue;
white noon turns dusk, and red hills become water-blue.
Even Yu the Great himself could not measure its depth;
could the moon of Li Lou distinguish what was near in a span’s breadth?
Then the Fenglies calmed their waves, and the sun and moon withdrew;
fish and turtles hid their tracks, birds and beasts withdrew their paths.
Cloud-islands in the distance were severed and sealed,
and the offices of Changhe were darkly enclosed.
Sudden, it surged and raced, as if rain were about to fall;
confused and crowded, like cold clouds ready to mass.
Then hidden vipers formed within, turning to miasma and pestilence.
Within lie monsters, and by clinging to them we cause harm.
They bring illness and misfortune to mankind, and raise storms and dust on the frontier.

Common people lose themselves when they meet this; the great men lament when they see it.
It is as if primeval qi is returning to the chaos, mixing heaven and earth into one vast mass.

At the fifth watch of that same night, the ships were near Cao Cao’s river encampment. Zhuge Liang ordered them arranged with their bows west and sterns east in one line, then to beat drums and shout. Lu Su said anxiously, “If Cao’s troops all come out, what are we to do?”

Zhuge Liang laughed. “I expect that in such thick fog, Cao Cao will not dare to move. We will keep drinking and cheering until the fog lifts and then return.”

In Cao Cao’s camp, hearing the drums and cries, Mao Jie and Yu Jin rushed to report.

Cao Cao gave the order: “The river is veiled by heavy fog. If their army has come suddenly, they must have an ambush. Do not move lightly. Dispatch river crossbowmen and shoot in disorder.”

He also sent for Zhang Liao and Xu Huang from the dry camp, each with three thousand crossbowmen, to come at once to the riverbank to assist the shooting.

By the time the orders arrived, Mao Jie and Yu Jin, fearing the southern force might break into the river camp, already had crossbowmen firing from in front.

Soon the archers and crossbowmen from the dry camp arrived, over ten thousand in all, all shooting into the river. Arrows fell like rain.

Zhuge Liang ordered the boats turned around, bows east and sterns west, and brought them close to the camp to receive arrows while drums and shouts continued. When the day rose and the fog broke, he ordered the boats pulled back at speed.

The two rows of boats, each packed with bundles of grass on both sides and loaded with arrow shafts, soon withdrew fifty li downstream; each had gathered five to six thousand arrows. They shouted together:

“Praise the Chancellor’s arrows!”

By the time Cao Cao heard the news from the camp, these boats had already slipped away quickly downstream more than twenty li; he could not pursue, and he regretted bitterly.

Back aboard, Zhuge Liang told Lu Su, “Each ship has about five or six thousand arrows. Without Jiangdong spending a single string, we have over one hundred thousand already. Tomorrow we can come and shoot at Cao’s troops. It should be convenient, is it not?”

Lu Su said, “You truly are a divine man! How did you know the fog would be this great?”

Zhuge Liang replied, “A commander who does not understand astronomy, terrain, the odd gates, yin and yang, battle charts, and army strength is a mediocre man. Three days ago I had calculated that today would bring a great fog, so I dared to accept a three-day limit. Gongjin gave me ten days; in my plan I knew the craftsmen and supplies would not come together in time. He was clearly seeking a fault that would make my death obvious. I have tied my life to Heaven; how can Gongjin harm me?”

Lu Su bowing acknowledged it.

When the boats reached shore, Zhou Yu had already sent five hundred soldiers to receive the arrows at the riverbank. Zhuge Liang told those aboard to disembark; more than one hundred thousand were taken and carried to the central command tent to be reported.

Lu Su entered and explained Zhuge Liang’s method to Zhou Yu.

Zhou Yu was astonished. “Zhuge Liang’s uncanny calculations surpass mine!” he exclaimed. “I cannot match it.” Later, one poem praised the feat:

One day of thick fog filled the Yangtze so that near and far were lost in a dim sea.
In sudden rain, locusts flew toward the warships—today Zhuge Liang conceals himself before Lord Zhou.

After a short while, Zhuge Liang came to camp to see Zhou Yu. Zhou Yu rose from his tent to receive him and said admiringly, “Master, your divination and calculation make all men revere you.”

Zhuge Liang answered, “A crooked little scheme is no miracle.”

Zhou Yu invited him in and shared more wine. “Yesterday I inspected Cao Cao's waterside camp. It is extremely disciplined and well ordered, no ordinary position to attack. I have thought of a plan but do not know whether it will work; please decide it for me.”

“Kongming is but a commonplace, clumsy man; where could such genius as yours be in me?”

“I saw Cao Cao’s river camp yesterday—rigorously ordered and impossible to break easily. If I could find a strategy, could you do something?” Zhou Yu asked.

“Do not speak of this now, Commander. Let us each write one character and compare. If they are not the same, I withdraw.”

Zhou Yu, delighted, brought out pen and ink and first wrote in secret, then passed it to Zhuge Liang.

Zhuge Liang also wrote in secret. The two drew close to the bed and each showed the character in his palm, then both laughed loudly.

It turned out that Zhou Yu had written the character 火 and Zhuge Liang had written the same.

Zhou Yu said, “Now that what we both saw is the same, there can be no doubt. Keep this from leaking.”

“This is no private matter between two states,” Zhuge Liang said. “Cao Cao has already suffered two rounds of this sort of plan, and he will not prepare for it again. Let the Commander carry it out.”

After they drank, they parted; the other generals did not know of any of it.

Cao Cao, having lost one hundred and fifty to one hundred sixty thousand arrows for nothing, was choked with rage. Xun Yu offered counsel: “In East Wu there are Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang, who can set a ruse beyond breaking. We must send agents to feign surrender so that they become inside informers and pass news back. Only then can we plan a response.”

Cao Cao said, “Your words are exactly as I thought. Who in your army can do this?”

Xun Yu replied, “Cai Mao has been executed, and the whole Cai clan is in your army. Cai Mao’s brothers, Cai Zhong and Cai He, are now deputy commanders. The Chancellor can win them with favors and send them to feign surrender. Eastern Wu will not suspect them.”

Cao Cao approved, summoned the two at night, and charged them:

“You two may bring a few soldiers, sail downriver and feign surrender to Eastern Wu. If anything stirs, report to me secretly. If this succeeds, your rewards will be great. Let there be no divided heart.”

“Our wives and children are all in Jing Province,” they answered. “How could we dare to keep a double mind? Do not mistrust us. We two swear to seize Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang and present them under your banner.”

Cao Cao rewarded them richly. The next day they came with five hundred soldiers in several boats, and with a favorable wind rowed toward the south bank.

At that moment Zhou Yu was discussing the advance when he was told that ships from the north had reached the river mouth, claiming to be Cai He and Cai Zhong, Cai Mao’s brothers, come to surrender. He summoned them.

The two fell and knelt in tears: “My elder brother was innocent. Killed by the villainous Cao. We two have come to avenge him by surrendering. Grant us acceptance, and we ask to serve at the vanguard.”

Zhou Yu rejoiced greatly and rewarded them, then ordered Gan Ning to lead troops as the vanguard. The two bowed in thanks and, while accepting, became what they were meant to be.

Zhou Yu privately summoned Gan Ning and instructed him: “These two came without families aboard and are no true defectors. They are sent by Cao Cao as double agents. I intend to let them run this counter-plan and let them report our situation. Guard the rear and be cordial; on the day of action, first kill those two as a sacrifice to the standards.”

Gan Ning bowed and took his orders.

Lu Su then came to see Zhou Yu: “Cai Zhong and Cai He’s surrender is likely feigned. They should not be accepted.”

Zhou Yu snapped, “Their brother was killed by Cao Cao. They come to repay that blood debt. How could this be trickery? If you remain so suspicious, how can you house men from all under heaven?”

Lu Su withdrew silently, then went to Zhuge Liang, who only smiled.

Lu Su asked, “Why do you laugh, Master?”

“I laughed that Zijing does not realize Gongjin’s use of devices,” Zhuge Liang said. “The river between us is broad; spies can scarcely pass. If Cao sends Cai Zhong and Cai He to feign surrender, he seeks to spy on our camp. By letting the scheme run forward, Gongjin will force them to report for us. War does not despise deceit; Gongjin’s design is just this.”

Lu Su came to understand.

Later that night Zhou Yu sat in his tent, and Huang Gai, whose courtesy name was Gongfu, came quietly to meet him.

Zhou Yu asked, “You arrive at night, so there must be good design to share.”

Huang Gai answered, “We are outnumbered. We should not hold on too long. Why not use fire attack?”

“Who taught you this?”

“My own thought, no one taught it.”

Zhou Yu replied, “I intended exactly that. That is why I kept the false deserters to pass messages. Yet I regret I have no one to carry out this feigned surrender.”

“I will carry it out.”

“Why would he accept a man who suffers pain?”

“I have been deeply indebted to the house of Sun. Even if my liver and brain were spilled across the ground, I would still have no regret.”

Zhou Yu bowed in thanks. “If you can carry this suffering-body stratagem, it will be Jiangdong’s fortune.”

Huang Gai answered, “Even if I die, I will not complain,” then withdrew.

The next day Zhou Yu beat drums and assembled the generals, with Zhuge Liang also present.

Zhou Yu said, “Cao has one million troops, linked along over three hundred li. We cannot break them in one day. For this reason every commander shall prepare three months of grain and fodder and ready for defense.”

Not yet done speaking, Huang Gai stepped forward and said, “Do not say three months. Even if we had thirty, it still would not suffice. If we do not break him this month, then by Zhang Zibu’s counsel we should throw down our armor and surrender northward!”

Zhou Yu’s color changed at once and he burned with anger. “By my lord’s command I drive these troops to break Cao. If anyone again dares to speak of surrender, I will execute him. In the face of two opposing armies, you dare to say this? You ruin our morale. If I do not behead you, no one will obey me.”

He ordered Huang Gai immediately executed and sent word.

Huang Gai too cried angrily, “I served the General Who Smashes the Caitiffs and have campaigned across the southeast through three generations of the Sun house. Where were you then, to speak to me like this?”

Gan Ning stepped forward, pleading, “Gongjin, you have long served Eastern Wu. Show mercy.”

Zhou Yu shouted, “How dare you add words and upset my regulations?”

He first shouted at Gan Ning and ordered the guards to drag him out and beat him with cudgels.

The commanders all knelt and begged: “Huang Gai’s crime deserves death, but his death harms the army. In pity, let the Commander show forbearance and set aside his sentence for now. After Cao is broken, your axe can still strike.”

Though his rage had not left him, the commanders begged repeatedly. Zhou Yu said, “If I do not mind the faces before you, I would surely behead him now. For now, I spare him from death.” He ordered the attendants to drag him out and strike him with a hundred rod-blows to set his guilt right.

They begged again. Zhou Yu overturned the table, drove them away, and ordered the beating again.

He stripped Huang Gai and dragged him to the ground, beating him with fifty strokes until he bled.

When the officers again begged for reprieve, Zhou Yu leaped up, pointed at Gai, and said, “You dare to despise me! Add five hundred? No—count this as fifty. If you offend again, both punishments will be counted.” His curse of hatred did not cease as he returned to the tent.

The officers raised Huang Gai, who had skin split and flesh torn, blood spurting in fresh spurts. They carried him to his own camp; he almost collapsed in unconsciousness twice.

Anyone who saw him wept. Lu Su, having gone to ask after him, then returned to Zhuge Liang’s boat.

“Today Gongjin struck Huang Gongfu in fury. We are all under him and dared not offend him with counsel. But you are a guest—why did you sit by in silence and speak no word?”

Zhuge Liang smiled. “Zijing, you have deceived me.”

“Since we crossed the river, Lu Su and you have never deceived each other in anything. Why this now?”

Zhuge Liang said, “Does Zijing not know that Gongjin’s harsh beating of Huang Gongfu is his plan? Why would I ask him to stop?”

Zijing only then understood.

“Do not say that I know this first,” Zhuge Liang continued. “Now Huang Gongfu must go on feigning surrender, so Cai Zhong and Cai He are now told to report the matter. When you see Gongjin, do not say that Master Kongming knew from the start. Say only that Kongming too grumbled at the Commander.”

Lu Su took leave, entered Zhou Yu’s tent, and was received.

“Why did you so harshly punish Huang Gongfu today?” Zhou Yu asked.

“Many are uneasy in their hearts,” Lu Su answered.

“What does Zhuge Liang think?”

“He too says the Commander is cold in feeling.”

Zhou Yu laughed. “Today I need to deceive him.”

“How?”

“This beating was a design. I want him to feign surrender; first he must employ a suffering-body plan, deceive Cao Cao, then strike by fire and win.”

Lu Su thought privately of Zhuge Liang’s high wisdom, but did not speak.

Huang Gai lay in his tent as all the commanders came asking after him. He made no words, only long sighs.

Suddenly Han Ze arrived to inquire. Huang Gai had him brought into the sick-chamber and sent others away.

Han Ze asked, “General, do you bear a private grudge against the Commander?”

“No,” Huang Gai replied.

“Then this punishment is surely a suffering-body scheme?”

“How did you know?”

“By watching Gongjin’s actions, I have understood nine-tenths of it.”

Huang Gai said, “I have received three generations of heavy kindness from the Prince of Wu and have no way to repay it. For that reason I present this scheme to break Cao Cao. Though I suffer, I have no resentment. I have looked over the army and found no one I can call my heart-man. Only you have long been known for loyalty and righteousness. I dare entrust you.”

Han Ze said, “What you asked me for is plainly the forged surrender letter.”

Huang Gai agreed. “That is so. Whether you will do it?”

Han Ze gladly accepted.

And this is the verse:

The brave are willing to stake their bodies for their lord’s return of duty;
Counsellors of state share one heart for the land.
No one yet knows what Han Ze will say,
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang’s Witty Stratagem: Borrowing Arrows, and Huang Gai’s Secret Plot

chapters.html:
Kan Ze quietly presents a hidden note of false surrender. Pang Tong skillfully introduces the linked-chain stratagem.

Kan Ze, whose courtesy name was Derun, came from Shanyin in Kuaiji. His family was poor, yet he loved learning and took day labor with others when needed. He would borrow books, study them once, and remember them without losing what he had read. His speech was sharp and convincing, and he had uncommon courage for his age. Sun Quan enlisted him as a military adviser, and he became closest to Huang Gai. Huang Gai recognized how boldly and artfully he spoke, so he asked him to deliver a feigned surrender letter.

Kan Ze agreed at once. “A man of stature should not live without making merit and helping to build our realm. Is it not better to be one thing in life than rot like brushwood and trees? You have already offered yourself in sacrifice for your lord. Why should I hesitate to throw away this little life?” Huang Gai rolled off his bed, knelt, and thanked him. Kan Ze said, “There must be no delay; I depart tonight.” Huang Gai replied, “The document is already drafted.”

Kan Ze took the letter and, that very night, dressed as a fisherman, climbed into a small boat and headed for the northern bank. That night the stars were cold and bright. By the third watch he had arrived early at Cao Cao’s waterside camp. A patrolling soldier of the river guards seized him and carried the news through the night to Cao Cao at once.

Cao Cao, whose courtesy name was Mengde, asked, “Could you be an enemy agent?”

The soldier said, “Only one fisherman, claiming to be Kan Ze, adviser of Eastern Wu, bringing urgent intelligence for a personal report.”

Cao Cao ordered him brought in. When the soldier led Kan Ze before him, Cao Cao was seated upright at a table in the torchlit command tent and asked, “If you are an adviser of Eastern Wu, what business brings you here?”

Kan Ze replied, “People say Chancellor Cao longs for talent as if he thirsted for water, yet this question fits him badly. As for Lord Huang, he too has mistaken the situation.”

Cao Cao said, “You and Eastern Wu have war with us at dawn and dusk. You travel here in secret. Why do you not ask first?”

Kan Ze answered, “Lord Huang Gai, a retainer whose family had served Eastern Wu for three generations, was cruelly beaten before all officers by Zhou Yu, whose courtesy name was Gongjin, without cause. He burns with grievance and wants to surrender to the Chancellor to take revenge. He sought my aid in conceiving this.”

“I and Lord Huang are as close as blood kin,” Kan Ze continued. “I have come directly to submit a secret note. I do not know whether the Chancellor will accept it.”

Cao Cao asked, “Where is the letter?”

Kan Ze handed it over. Cao Cao opened it and read beneath the lamp. The letter read:

I have long owed deep gratitude to Lord Sun; I ought not to hold divided loyalty in my heart. Yet by today’s circumstances, we all see it clearly: the troops of six commanderies in Jiangdong cannot face the million-strong armies in the center of the realm. Even the common soldiers and officials there know this is impossible. That boy Zhou Yu, narrow-minded and shallow, is swollen with conceit, and he dares to oppose stone with an egg. Worse, he acts arbitrarily, punishing the innocent and rewarding no one for merit. I, a man of long service, was insulted and broken without reason. I cannot hide my hatred. I have heard that the Chancellor receives men sincerely and with an open heart. Therefore I am prepared to lead men to surrender, in hope of earning merit and clearing our disgrace. Provisions and transport equipment will come aboard ship as tribute. I weep blood and kneel in submission. Let no one suspect anything else.

Cao Cao flipped and re-read the document over a dozen times on the desk. Then he suddenly struck the tablet, eyes wide, and shouted in fury, “So Huang Gai used the ‘bitter-meat strategy’ to hide treachery and sent you with this false surrender letter to mock me! Send him out and execute him!”

He ordered Kan Ze thrown out for immediate death. Kan Ze, however, remained calm and laughed up at the sky. Cao Cao had him dragged back and barked, “I have already seen through the plot. Why do you laugh?”

Kan Ze replied, “I am not laughing at you. I am laughing at Lord Huang Gai for failing to know people.”

Cao Cao demanded, “What does he fail to know?”

Kan Ze said, “If you intend to kill me, do so. Why ask so much?”

Cao Cao said, “I have long studied the military books since boyhood and understand deception and fraud well. Your scheme may deceive other men, but how could it deceive me?”

Kan Ze said, “Then explain which part of your own letter is deceptive.”

Cao Cao said, “I will tell you every flaw in your ruse so you may die without complaint. If you truly came in sincerity to surrender, why did you not specify a date for an agreed rendezvous? Now you ask me for what reasoning?”

Kan Ze laughed aloud. “You have no fear and dare to boast that you know war treatises! Should you not have withdrawn your troops in time? If battle comes, you will be taken by Zhou Yu. An unlearned one! How regrettable that I must be forced to die at your hands!”

Cao Cao asked, “How so unlearned?”

Kan Ze said, “You do not discern stratagems nor understand principle. Is that not ignorance?”

Cao Cao said, “Tell me where I am wrong.”

Kan Ze replied, “You do not know how to receive worthy men; I need not waste breath on it. I have only my life to spend.”

Cao Cao said, “If you make your case with reason, I will yield to it.”

Kan Ze said, “Have you not heard, ‘A loyal servant who turns coat has no fixed term’? If you set a date in advance and hurry, the chance slips. One must act only when opportunity appears; how could a date be fixed beforehand? You do not understand this principle, yet would wrongfully put an honorable man to death. Why should one set a meeting beforehand if he intends to make a move by opportunely seizing the moment?”

Cao Cao listened, then changed his expression, descended from his seat, and said, “I judged this wrongly and have offended you by my offense. Do not keep this in your heart.”

Kan Ze answered, “I and Lord Huang Gai are heartily prepared to surrender, like a child longing for its parents. Are there even now any signs of deceit?”

Cao Cao brightened. “If the two of you can win great achievements, when honors and rank are conferred, yours will stand above all others.”

Kan Ze answered, “My companions have not come for titles and salaries. We should follow Heaven’s decree and the hearts of men.”

Cao Cao then had wine brought.

After a short while, someone entered, leaned in by Cao Cao’s ear, and whispered. Cao Cao said, “Bring the letter for me to see.” The man presented a sealed note. Cao Cao read it and was visibly pleased.

Kan Ze thought to himself, “This must be news from Cai Zhong and Cai He that Huang Gai has been punished. Cao’s gladness proves he believes my surrender to be true.”

Kan Ze said, “Please return to Jiangdong once more and arrange with Lord Huang. Send the news across the river first. I will meet him there with troops.”

Kan Ze added, “I have already left Jiangdong and cannot go back again. Send only a trusted secret courier.”

Cao Cao said, “If another person goes, the matter may leak.”

Kan Ze refused repeatedly, then after a while said, “If I go, I dare not linger. I will leave at once.”

Cao Cao awarded him gold and silk, which Kan Ze did not take. After he took his leave and left the camp, he once again took a small boat and rowed back across the river. He returned to Huang Gai and explained everything in detail.

Huang Gai said, “Had you not been so able to argue, I would have only suffered this pain.”

Kan Ze answered, “I will now go to Gan Ning’s camp to learn what news Cai Zhong and Cai He have brought.”

Huang Gai said, “Very good.”

Kan Ze arrived at Gan Ning’s camp. Gan Ning greeted him. Kan Ze said, “General, yesterday you went out to rescue Lord Huang Gai and were insulted by Zhou Yu. I am very displeased.” Gan Ning laughed and did not answer.

As they were speaking, Cai He and Cai Zhong arrived. Kan Ze noticed them and nodded at Gan Ning.

Gan Ning understood and said, “Zhou Yu trusted only his own talent, never caring about us. After my humiliation, I can no longer face Jiangleft dignitaries.” He bit his teeth and spoke through clenched anger.

Kan Ze stepped close and spoke quietly to Gan Ning’s ear; Gan Ning lowered his head in silence and sighed heavily.

Cai He and Cai Zhong saw that both Kan Ze and Gan Ning seemed to incline the other way and provoked them: “General, why this trouble? What disturbs you, Master? What injustice wounds you?”

Kan Ze answered, “Would you know the bitterness in our bellies?”

Cai He said, “Could this be a plan to betray Wu and submit to Cao?”

Kan Ze turned pale.

Gan Ning drew his sword and stood.

“I have already seen through this,” he said. “It must be ended now, and we cannot leave his mouth open to leak the truth.”

Cai He and Cai Zhong, alarmed, replied, “My lord, do not worry. I, too, will tell you all in confidence.”

Gan Ning said, “Speak quickly.”

Cai He said, “Both of us are envoys of Lord Cao, sent as men of false surrender. If either of you truly wishes to submit, I can bring you forward.”

Gan Ning demanded, “Are your words true?”

Both answered, “How could we dare deceive?”

Gan Ning feigned delight. “If this is so, Heaven has given us a gate!”

Cai He and Cai Zhong added, “I already informed the Chancellor about how Lord Huang was insulted and humiliated.”

Kan Ze said, “I delivered my letter to him for Huang Gai already. I have come today only to meet Xingba and arrange our joint surrender.”

Gan Ning said, “A true man who has found a bright lord should lean his heart without reserve.”

So the four drank together and spoke openly. Cai He and Cai Zhong immediately wrote a secret letter, reporting that Gan Ning and some others were also inside collaborators.

Kan Ze separately wrote one and had someone send it in secret to Cao Cao. In the letter he specified: if Huang Gai came, he was to be identified by the signal of a blue-toothed flag flying at the bow of the boat.

When Cao Cao received two letters in succession, he remained uncertain and gathered strategists to debate.

He said, “Gan Ning of Jiangdong, disgraced by Zhou Yu, now offers himself as an inside ally. Huang Gai was blamed and sent Kan Ze in false surrender. Neither should be trusted. Who among us dares to slip directly into Zhou Yu’s camp and gather confirmed intelligence?”

Jiang Gan (Xiying) stepped forward: “Some time ago I went to Eastern Wu and failed. I still carry shame. I now offer my life and go again to bring back verified information.”

Cao Cao was delighted and immediately ordered Jiang Gan to board.

Jiang Gan rowed a small boat and reached the riverbank edge of Eastern Wu’s waterside camp at once, then sent word of his arrival.

When Zhou Yu heard that Jiang Gan had come again, he was overjoyed. “My success rests on this man alone,” he said. He then told Lu Su, “Please ask Pang Tong to come; he must advise us.”

Pang Tong, whose courtesy name was Shiyuan, had once moved to Jiangdong from Xiangyang when he avoided the turmoil. Lu Su had once recommended him to Zhou Yu, but they had not yet met. Zhou Yu, whose courtesy name was Gongjin, first asked Lu Su, whose courtesy name was Zijing, for a plan. “If we are to break Cao’s army,” he said, “what is your device?”

Pang Tong privately answered Lu Su, “To break Cao’s force, we must use fire attack. But if one ship burns, the rest will scatter across the great river. Only if they are bound in the linked-chain method will they remain in one mass, and then the task can be completed.”

Lu Su reported to Zhou Yu. Zhou Yu believed the argument deeply and said, “Only Pang Tong can carry this out for me.”

Lu Su said, “I fear Cao Cao is sly. How will you go?”

Zhou Yu hesitated and could find no opening, and then news came that Jiang Gan had returned.

Zhou Yu was glad. He once again told Pang Tong to use the plan and at once, sitting in his tent, had Jiang Gan summoned.

Jiang Gan, seeing no one come to welcome him, felt his suspicions rise. He told a boatman to moor in a secluded cove, then entered camp to see Zhou Yu.

Zhou Yu glared and said, “Why, Ziying, have you deceived me so far beyond measure?”

Jiang Gan laughed. “I remember us as old brothers and came to unburden matters. Why would we deceive each other?”

Zhou Yu said, “You ask me to surrender? Only when the seas dry up and the rocks wear away! The last time I recalled old ties and invited you to drink, kept you in the same bed. You stole my private papers and left without so much as asking leave, then returned to report to Cao Cao, killing Cai Mao and Zhang Yun and ruining my plans. Why come now? You do not come in good faith.”

“Old bonds do not move me,” he said. “Two blades can cut you in two! I had already planned to send you across, but within a day or two I must break Cao’s bandits. To keep you in the ranks will invite leakage.”

He ordered his attendants, “Send Ziying to rest in the hermitage behind Xishan. Once I have broken Cao Cao, I will take you across the river.”

When Jiang Gan tried again to speak, Zhou Yu had already gone into the tent and disappeared.

His guards gave him two horses to ride and sent him to the small retreat behind Xishan, where two soldiers were posted to attend him.

Inside the hut Jiang Gan was anxious and sleepless. That night, with stars spilled across the sky and bright dew in the air, he walked out behind the hut and heard voices from a distance reading aloud.

He wandered toward the sound and saw, by a rock face, a thatched hut with a lamp shining within. He peered inside and saw a man, with a sword hanging nearby, reading aloud a book of military strategy by Sun Wu and Wu Qi.

“Surely this is no ordinary man,” Jiang Gan thought, and knocked on the door.

The man opened and came out to greet him. He had a presence beyond common rank.

Jiang Gan asked his name. He replied, “My surname is Pang, my given name Tong, courtesy Shiyuan.”

Jiang Gan asked, “Could you be Master Fengchu?”

Pang Tong answered, “I am.”

Jiang Gan said, “I have long heard your name. Why live in such seclusion?”

Pang Tong replied, “Zhou Yu trusts only his own brilliance and can not bear other men. That is why I withdrew here.”

“And who are you?”

Jiang Gan said, “I am Jiang Gan.”

Pang Tong invited him into the hut. They sat and spoke at length.

Jiang Gan said, “With your ability, where can you not succeed? If you are willing to come to Cao, I can introduce you.”

Pang Tong replied, “I have long wished to leave Jiangdong. Since your intention is to bring me in, I will leave at once. If delayed, Zhou Yu will hear of it and likely see to my death.”

So they descended together under cover of night, reached the riverbank, found their original boat, and with urgent strokes crossed north.

Once they arrived at Cao’s camp, Jiang Gan entered first and explained everything. Cao listened to Pang Tong’s account and, hearing that Master Fengchu had come, personally came out of his tent to welcome him. He set host and guest seats. “Zhou Yu is young and relies on his talent to bully the crowd. He will not use good advice. For long I have heard your name and now receive your favor; I beg you to instruct me freely.”

Pang Tong said, “I have long heard the Chancellor commands war with method. Today I am honored to behold your array.”

Cao ordered his horse prepared and invited Pang Tong to ride high and view the dry encampment. They mounted together and looked over it from an elevation.

Pang Tong said, “You follow the hills and woods, with fore-and-aft movement and winding routes mutually guarded. Even if Sun Wu and Wu Qi were reborn, or Sima Rangju returned, they would not do better than this.”

Cao said, “Do not praise me so highly; still I welcome instruction.”

Then he took him to inspect the waterside camp.

There they saw twenty-four river gates to the south, each with armored warships arranged like city walls. Small craft were hidden inside them, lanes opened between, rise and fall in order.

Pang Tong laughed. “The Chancellor’s deployment is exactly as praised.” Pointing south across the river he said, “Zhoulang! Zhoulang! He will surely perish at the appointed time!”

Cao happily returned to camp, invited him into the tent, and set out wine. They drank together and discussed the matter of war. Pang Tong spoke forcefully and answered with ease. Cao held him in deep esteem and treated him with ceremony.

Pang Tong feigned inebriation and asked, “Do you have good physicians in the army?”

Cao asked, “For what purpose?”

Pang Tong said, “Your water troops are sickly and need good physicians.”

At that time Cao’s men did not thrive in the river climate and many suffered vomiting, with many dying. Cao had indeed been worried over this, so when Pang raised it he was alert.

“How did you know that?” Cao asked. “My way of training river troops is not poor, yet there is some flaw.”

Pang Tong said, “I have a method that can keep both large and small squadrons healthy.”

Cao eagerly asked for this skillful solution.

Pang Tong said, “In the Great River, the tide rises and falls, the wind and waves never cease. Men unused to boats grow ill when thrown in this rolling motion. If you lash large and small vessels together in groups—sometimes thirty to a row, sometimes fifty—connecting bow and stern with iron rings and laying wide planks across them, men can cross on them; even horses can pass. Go this way, and let wind, waves, and tide do what they can.”

Cao got up in disbelief and thanked him: “Without your excellent counsel, how could I have broken Eastern Wu?”

Pang Tong said, “My insight is shallow. The Chancellor will do as he sees fit.”

Cao at once ordered smiths summoned from the ranks and worked through the night to forge chain-fastened anchors and lock the ships together. The soldiers heard this and rejoiced.

There was later a verse about it:

Red Cliffs fights by fire and flame, every plan and stratagem agreeing, But for Pang Tong’s linked-chain design, could Gongjin have won such triumph?

Pang Tong then said to Cao, “I have observed the heroes of Jiangleft; many resent Zhou Yu. With my three-inch tongue I can persuade them to come over. Then Zhou Yu will stand isolated, and the Chancellor will capture him. If Zhou Yu is broken, Liu Bei will have no use left for those men.”

Cao said, “If you can truly achieve a great deed, I will report it to the Son of Heaven and enshrine you among the Three Excellencies.”

Pang Tong said, “I do not seek riches and rank. My only wish is to save ten thousand households. When the Chancellor crosses the river, take care not to harm the people.”

Cao said, “I uphold Heaven’s order in war. How could I bear to slaughter common people?”

Pang Tong requested a proclamation to secure his relatives. Cao asked, “Where do your family now live?”

Pang Tong answered, “They are only on the riverbank. If I hold this proclamation, that will keep them safe.”

Cao ordered the decree written and delivered. Pang Tong thanked him and said, “After we part, advance quickly. Do not wait for Zhoulang to sense anything.”

Cao assented.

Pang Tong bowed and departed. At the riverbank, just as he was about to board, he saw a man on the bank, in robes with a bamboo hat, who grabbed him by the arm and cried:

“Bold fool! Huang Gai used the bitter-meat stratagem and Kan Ze came with false surrender notes. Now you come with the linked-chain stratagem. I fear you will not carry the burning through to the end! Such vicious methods may deceive Cao Cao, but they cannot deceive me!”

Pang Tong was shaken to the core. Then came the close:

Do not say the southeast can alone win wars, nor that the northwest has no men. In the end who this person is, let the next chapter explain.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Kan Ze Secretly Submits a Feigned Surrender, and Pang Tong Cunningly Deploys the Linked-Chain Plan

chapters.html:
When Pang Tong heard this he was taken aback; he turned around quickly and saw who it was, and it proved to be Xu Shu. Seeing that he was an old friend, Pang Tong steadied his heart. He looked around and saw no one nearby, and said, “If you should reveal my plan, then all the people of Jiangnan, the eighty-one provinces, will have been delivered into danger through you.”

Xu Shu smiled and said, “There are eighty-three wan—eight hundred and thirty thousand—horse and men in this area. What is to become of their lives?”

Pang Tong said, “Yuanzhi, do you truly mean to spoil my plan?”

Xu Shu said, “I do not forget the deep grace of Imperial Uncle Liu; I have never once forgotten to repay it. Cao Cao drove my mother to death. I have already said that for the rest of my life I would not devise any stratagem. How could I now break your excellent scheme? Yet I am with this army; if the soldiers are defeated and jade and stone are mingled, who can escape danger? You must teach me a way to slip away, and then I will keep my mouth shut and hide myself far away.”

Pang Tong laughed and said, “With the far-sighted understanding you show here, how could there be any real difficulty in this?”

Xu Shu said, “Please, sir, instruct me.”

Pang Tong bent down and whispered several words into Xu Shu’s ear. Xu Shu was overjoyed and bowed to thank him. Pang Tong then let him depart from the boat and Xu Shu returned to the south.

That night Xu Shu secretly sent trusted men to each stockade, spreading rumors in secret. On the next day, in threes and fives, people whispered to each other in the camps. Early a scout reported to Cao Cao: “Rumors run in the army that Han Sui and Ma Teng of Liang Province have plotted rebellion and are fleeing toward Xuchang.” Cao Cao was greatly startled. He quickly gathered many advisers and said, “In leading the army south, my worries have been only Han Sui and Ma Teng. Though the rumor in camp has not yet been judged true or false, it is not something to neglect.”

Before he had finished speaking, Xu Shu stepped forward and said, “I have been taken into the Chancellor’s service yet still feel ashamed that I have rendered not one bit of service. Grant me three thousand horse and men, and I will go at once through the night by way of Sand Pass to hold the chokepoint. If emergency comes, I will report again.”

Cao Cao was pleased: “If I can send Yuanzhi away, I have no worries. There are already troops on Sand Pass, and you shall command them. Right now, dispatch three thousand troops, foot soldiers. Make Zang Ba the vanguard. Go by night without delay.”

Xu Shu withdrew from the audience, and with Zang Ba set out. That was Pang Tong’s rescue plan for Xu Shu.

A later verse says:

Cao Cao’s southern campaign was fretted day after day, Han Sui and Ma Teng raised spears and lances to rebel. Fengchu, with a single phrase, taught Xu Shu to leave; It was like a fish in water breaking loose from a hook.

After sending Xu Shu away, Cao Cao felt a little at ease, and he mounted his horse to inspect first the dry camps along the river, then the river camps. He ordered a single great warship to stand in the center, and raised on it a banner bearing the character “commander.” To both sides he lined up the water stockades. A thousand crossbows were hidden on the ship. Cao Cao took the center.

It was the fifteenth day of the eleventh month of winter in the twelfth year of Jian’an. The sky was clear, the wind mild, and the waves still. Cao Cao ordered, “Set wine and music aboard the great ship. This evening I will hold a banquet with the commanders.”

At dusk, the moon rose over Dongshan, shining as bright as day. All along the Yangtze it lay like a ribbon of white silk. Cao Cao sat aboard the great ship, with several hundred attendants on either side, all in brocaded robes and surcoats, carrying halberds and lances. Civil and military officials sat in order. As he looked around he saw the mountain colors of Nanping painted like a scroll, in the east the lands of Chaisang, in the west the river at Xiakou, to the south Mount Fan, and to the north Wulin. Looking all around over the open expanse, he rejoiced in his heart and said to the assembled officials, “Since I rose in rebellion with armed force, I have served the state in removing villains and dangers. I swore to clear the four seas and level all under heaven; only Jiangnan is not yet mine. Now I have one million-strong army, and with your commands my task will surely succeed. Once Jiangnan is brought under authority, all under heaven will be in order, and I can share wealth and honor with all of you, and we will enjoy peace together.”

All officials and officers stood and said in unison, “May we soon be able to offer triumphant victory songs. We all of us have lived by the Chancellor’s benevolent favor.” Cao Cao was much pleased and ordered his attendants to pass the wine.

By midnight the wine had gone deep; Cao Cao was drunk. He pointed south across the river and said, “Zhou Yu and Lu Su do not understand the times. Now that there has arrived one who has surrendered to us, he has become an inside troublemaker to them. This is Heaven’s help to me.”

Xun Yu replied, “Chancellor, do not speak so. There may be leaks.”

Cao Cao laughed broadly: “All those at my table and all close attendants are men of my heart. Why should there be obstruction to speech?” He pointed again toward Xiakou: “Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang—how could they expect, with the strength of ants, to shake Mount Tai? How foolish!”

Turning to the commanders, he said, “I am fifty-four years old this year. If I gain Jiangnan I would have reason to rejoice. In former days, the Jiaogong and I went as far as Qi, and I knew both of the two Qiao women were beauties of national renown. I did not expect them to be taken as wives by Sun Ce and Zhou Yu. I have just now built the Copper Sparrow Terrace over the Zhang River; if I gain Jiangnan, I will marry both Qiao and place them there for my old age to enjoy. That alone would satisfy me.” He finished and laughed.

Du Mu of the Tang later wrote:

My broken lance lies sunk in the sand, The iron of former days has not worn away. The east wind did not come to aid Zhou-lang; In deep spring the Copper Sparrow Terrace keeps the Two Qiaos chained.

While Cao Cao was still laughing, he suddenly heard crows flying south and crying. He asked, “Why is there cawing at night?” Attendants replied, “Because the moon is bright, the crows think it is dawn, so they leave the trees and cry.” Cao Cao laughed again.

By then he was already deeply drunk. He took up his spear and stood on the ship, poured wine into the river, drank all three cups, laid the spear across his lap, and told the commanders: “With this spear I broke the Yellow Turbans, captured Lü Bu, destroyed Yuan Shu, subdued Yuan Shao, rode deep into the northern frontier, struck as far as Liaodong, and moved freely beneath Heaven. I have not wholly failed my vow of a grand ambition. This scene stirs my spirit in a fine way. I shall sing, and you all should join in.”

He sang:

Sing while we drink: how many days are there in life? Like morning dew, yesterday departs and it is hard to endure its leaving. With heroic feeling, let one be fierce; sorrow and thought refuse to be forgotten. How does one shake off sorrow? Only Dukang can do so. My robe's collar is green and fresh, My heart wanders far and wide. The roe-deer calls—its voice low and tender— Feeding on wild waterside plants in the marsh. I have honored guests—I beat the zither and sound the flute. As bright as the moon, when may this end? The sorrow comes from within and will not cease. Beyond the village gate and past the footpath, What use was it for you and me to remain in memory? Far apart at the feast and in talk, The old favors are what my heart recalls. With scarce a star in the sky and a few moons visible, Magpies fly south, Sweeping around trees three times, No branch to rest upon. A mountain does not refuse height, Water does not refuse depth. When Duke Zhou offered out his bowls, Hearts of all under Heaven followed him to him.

When he had finished, the others sang with him and all laughed together. At that moment someone at the table stepped forward and said, “In this hour when the grand army should stand firm and soldiers should give their lives in obedience, why does the Chancellor speak such unlucky words?”

Cao Cao looked and saw that it was Liu Fu, Inspector of Yang Province, a native of Pei State, surname Liu, name Fu, courtesy name Yuanying. Fu had arrived from Hefei, set up a prefectural seat, gathered people scattered by war, founded schools, expanded state lands, and promoted learning. He had long served Cao Cao and accrued many merits. Cao Cao asked across the spear, “What is unlucky in my words?”

Fu answered, “‘With few stars in the sky and the magpies flying south, Sweeping around trees three times, And finding no branch on which to rest’—these are unlucky words.”

Cao Cao became furious: “How dare you ruin my momentum!” He raised the spear and stabbed Liu Fu to death.

All were aghast, and the banquet was dismissed.

The next day, when Cao Cao sobered, he regretted deeply and could not restrain it. Liu Fu’s son, Liu Xi, petitioned him for permission to return the body for burial. Cao Cao wept: “Yesterday, in my drunkenness, I injured your father by my hand. My remorse cannot be repented in time. You may bury him with honors proper to a funeral for one of the Three Dukes.” He ordered officers to escort the casket back with troops and to bury him that very day.

On the following day, water army commander Mao Jie and Yu Jin came to his tent and asked, “All the large and small boats have already been coupled in chain-link formations. Banners and weapons are all in readiness. Please direct the Chancellor to set marching orders for the appointed day.”

Cao Cao went to the central warship of the water army and took his seat, then called all the commanders together. Each listened to orders. The land and river forces were each assigned five banners by color. In the center of the water army, yellow banners to Mao Jie and Yu Jin; the vanguard red banner to Zhang He; rear black banner to Lü Qian; left blue banner to Wen Pin; right white banner to Lü Tong. For the cavalry-and-infantry vanguard under red banner was Xu Huang, rear under black banner Li Dian, left wing blue banner Yue Jin, right wing white banner Xiahou Yuan.

To connect the land and river routes and provide reinforcement he put Xiahou Dun and Cao Hong in charge. Xu Chu and Zhang Liao, to do the passing of protective watch, were assigned to guard and relay battle signals.

The rest of the brave generals lined up with their units in place.

When the orders were done, drums sounded three times within the water camp, and each team of warships filed out through its own gate.

That day a northwest wind rose suddenly. Each ship hauled up its sails, cleaving the waves into white surges, steady as on level ground. The northern army on the ships sprang forward with eager courage, using spears and swords. Before and behind, left and right, all banners kept cleanly separated by rank. More than fifty small boats moved back and forth, patrolling, urging and checking. Cao Cao stood on the command platform watching the drilling, and in his heart rejoiced greatly, taking it as a sign of certain victory. He ordered the sails and canopies hauled in, and every unit to return in order to the stockades.

When he had returned to his tent he said to the strategists, “If this did not have Heaven’s blessing, how could the trick of Fengchu have served me? With warboats linked by chains, crossing the Yangtze is truly as easy as walking on level ground.”

Cheng Yu said, “The boats are linked by chain and thus stable, yes. But if the enemy uses fire attack, it will be hard to evade. We must not leave room for that.”

Cao Cao laughed: “Cheng Zhongde, though his foresight is long, still he has places he cannot see.”

Xun Yu said, “Cheng Zhongde’s words are true. Why does the Chancellor laugh at him?”

Cao Cao said, “Any fire attack must borrow the force of wind. Now in deep winter there is only west wind and north wind. How could there be easterly or southerly wind? I sit to the northwest and their troops are all on the southern bank. If they should use fire, it is their own troops that burn first. Why should I fear it? If it were the tenth month’s little spring, I would have prepared long ago.”

All the ministers prostrated themselves and said, “The Chancellor has exceptional vision; others do not equal it.”

Cao Cao looked at his generals: “The men of Qing, Xu, Yan, and Dai are not practiced in rowing boats. If not for this plan, how could we cross the dangerous Jiang at all?”

Then from the line, two commanders stepped forward: “Though we are men of You and Yan, we can also row boats. We ask now to borrow twenty patrol boats and go straight to the mouth of North River, seize banner and drums, and return, so they can see that the northern army too can row boats.”

Cao Cao recognized them as Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, former officers under Yuan Shao. He said, “You both were raised in the north, so I fear rowing may not suit you. Men from Jiangnan ride and train on the water all the time and do so with great skill. Do not treat life lightly.”

Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan shouted, “If we fail, we are willing to endure military law.”

Cao Cao said, “The warships are all linked together; only the small boats remain free. Each small boat holds two dozen men, and I fear it is still difficult for close battle.”

Jiao Chu said, “What wonder is there in using a large ship? Grant us some twenty small boats. I and Zhang Nan will each lead half. Today we go straight to the Jiangnan water stockades and are to seize flags and behead commanders before returning.”

Cao Cao said, “I will assign five hundred picked soldiers with your two groups, all armed with long spears and hard crossbows. By dawn tomorrow when light appears, draw the great stockade ships out to the river face, to form a feint from afar. And assign Wen Pin to lead thirty patrol boats to support your return.”

Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan withdrew joyfully.

The next day before the fourth watch the soldiers were making their meals, and by the fifth watch all was ready and done. At once, from the camps drums resounded, with gongs in reply. All ships left the camps and took their stations on the water. Across the stretch of river the blue and red banners crossed and mingled. Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, leading twenty patrol boats, cut through the stockades and set out southward toward the river.

On the southern bank, they also heard the roar of drums and boom of gongs the next day. From far off they watched Cao Cao’s training of the navy; a scout reported it to Zhou Yu. Zhou Yu climbed to a ridge and gazed. Cao Cao’s army had already returned.

Then suddenly drums sounded again so loudly as to shake the sky. Soldiers hurried to high ground to watch. Small boats were seen charging through the waves, and they were instantly reported to the central command. Zhou Yu asked which officer in his tent dared to go out first. Han Dang and Zhou Tai both stepped forward and said, “One of us shall go as vanguard to break the enemy.”

Zhou Yu was pleased and ordered every stockade to guard carefully and not move lightly. Han Dang and Zhou Tai each took five patrol boats and moved out, one to the left and one to the right.

Meanwhile Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, trusting in courage alone, rowed their small boats onward with speed. Han Dang bared his chest and wore a shield over his heart, a long spear in his hand, standing at the bow.

Jiao Chu’s boat arrived first; he ordered his soldiers to fire arrows in a wild volley at Han Dang’s boat. Han Dang blocked with his shield. Jiao Chu lowered his long spear and engaged Han Dang in melee. Han Dang thrust once and speared Jiao Chu dead.

Zhang Nan came shouting and rushed up after. Zhou Tai’s boat came out at an angle.

Zhang Nan held a long spear on his bow while bows and arrows darkened both sides. Zhou Tai held a shield in one arm and a sabre in his hand. The two boats were seven or eight feet apart when Zhou Tai made a single leap, springing directly onto Zhang Nan’s boat. He raised his blade and cut him down into the water, then cut down the rowing men in confusion.

The other boats pulled hard and quickly returned. Han Dang and Zhou Tai ordered their boats in chase. Midway across the river they met the ships of Wen Pin, and combat between the two sides then formed fully.

At that time Zhou Yu had gathered his generals on a mountaintop and looked toward the northern waterfront. He saw in line were the Cao army’s covered warships, flags and standards arranged in order. He looked back and saw Wen Pin struggling with Han Dang and Zhou Tai. Han Dang and Zhou Tai fought with full strength; Wen Pin could not hold and turned his ship away. Zhou Yu and Han Dang urged their boats in pursuit at speed. Fearing that the two had pushed too deep into dangerous water, he raised the white banner and gave the signal, commanding all to beat gongs.

The two men then paddled back.

From the mountaintop Zhou Yu watched the opposing warships across the river pour entirely into the water stockades. He said to the gathered officers, “The northern warships are as dense as a bed of reeds. Cao has many stratagems. By what plan can we break them?” Before anyone could reply, he suddenly saw that the central yellow banner in Cao’s camps had been bent by the wind and had blown into the river.

He laughed: “This is a bad omen.”

Just as he watched, a violent wind rose at once. The waves struck hard on the banks. In a gust, the corner of a banner whipped across Zhou Yu’s face. A single thing flashed through his mind. He cried out once and then staggered backward, falling. He spat fresh blood.

When the generals rushed to treat him, he had already lost awareness.

And indeed:

One moment he laughed, the next he cried out; the southern army could not yet overthrow the north.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Cao Recites a Poem While Banqueting on the Yangtze; The Northern Army Fastens its Warships and Sets Out

chapters.html:
At the Seven-Star Altar, Zhuge invokes the wind; At Sanjiangkou, Zhou Yu releases fire.

Zhou Yu, whose courtesy name was Gongjin, stood on the mountain top and watched for a long while, then suddenly staggered backward, spat fresh blood, and lost consciousness. His attendants carried him back to his tent. All the generals came to ask after him, all astonished, and looked at one another: “A force of a million to the north of the river, tiger-sitting and swallowing all before it. Never had we imagined the commander like this. If Cao’s troops arrive, what then?” They hastily sent word to Sun Quan and called for doctors.

Later, Lu Su, whose courtesy name was Zijing, saw that Zhou Yu was still ill and came to Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, to report it. Zhuge said, “What do you think, minister?”

Lu Su said, “This is an illness of Cao Cao’s making, a disaster for Jiangdong.”

Zhuge smiled and said, “Your Master Gongjin’s illness, I can also treat.”

Lu Su said, “If that is true, the state is greatly fortunate.” He asked him to come at once to see Zhou Yu.

Lu Su entered first and found Zhou Yu covered to the eyes on his bedding.

Lu Su said, “How is the commander’s condition?”

Zhou Yu said, “My chest aches with churning pain, then I lose awareness.”

Lu Su asked, “What medicine has been taken?”

Zhou Yu said, “The heart is nauseated, and medicine cannot go down.”

Lu Su said, “I just told Kongming you were ill and can be treated. He waits outside the tent now. Ask him to come and tend you. What says the commander?”

Zhou Yu asked him in.

A servant was told to lift him and seat him on the bed. Zhuge said, “It has been many days since I saw your face. I never thought your body would become unwell.”

Zhou Yu said, “Fortune and misfortune turn with each dawn. Who can keep himself forever safe?”

Zhuge smiled: “Heaven gives unpredictable wind and cloud. Who can know their pattern?”

Hearing this, Zhou Yu grew pale and groaned.

Zhuge asked, “Does the chest still feel blocked and unsettled?”

Zhou Yu said, “Yes.”

Zhuge said, “You need cooling medicine first.”

Zhou Yu said, “I already took cooling medicine. It is wholly ineffective.”

Zhuge said, “We must first settle his qi. If the qi is smooth, recovery comes naturally with every breath.”

Zhou Yu, sensing that Zhuge’s meaning was deeper, said, “If he must settle the qi, what medicine should be used?”

Zhuge smiled, “I have one prescription to make the commander’s qi smooth.”

Zhou Yu said, “Master, grant instruction.”

Zhuge asked for paper and brush, sent everyone out, and secretly wrote sixteen words: “To break Cao Gong, we should use fire attack; everything is prepared, and only a southeast wind is lacking.” He handed the paper to Zhou Yu and said, “This is the source of the commander’s sickness.”

Zhou Yu, seeing it, was astonished and thought, How can Zhuge truly be such a man? He already knows my mind. I should report this plainly. He then smiled and said, “Master, you know already that this is the root of my malady. What medicine do you suggest? The matter is urgent; please instruct at once.”

Zhuge said, “Though I am not talented, I once met an extraordinary person and was taught the Heavenly Text of Qimen Dunjia, through which one may call wind and summon rain. If the commander wants a southeast wind, he should build a platform on Nánpíng Mountain and call it the Seven-Star Altar. Make it nine chi high in three tiers, and place one hundred and twenty men with banners around it to hold position. On the altar I can perform the rite to obtain southeast wind for three days and three nights and aid the commander’s campaign. What do you think?”

Zhou Yu said, “Do not mention three days and three nights. A single night of wind will make the great work. But the matter is before us now and cannot wait.”

Zhuge said, “On the jiazi day of the twentieth day of the eleventh month, we sacrifice to wind; by the bingyin day of the twenty-second, the wind will fall. What think you?”

Hearing this, Zhou Yu rejoiced and rose with sudden animation. He ordered five hundred hardy soldiers to build the altar on Nánpíng Mountain and one hundred and twenty to bear the flags and hold the circle, awaiting orders.

When Zhuge finished, he took leave and with Lu Su rode to Nánpíng Mountain to survey terrain. He ordered soldiers to bring southeast red earth for the altar. It was to be round to twenty-four zhang, three chi high at each tier, for a total height of nine chi.

On the lower tier he set twenty-eight banners in the form of the twenty-eight stars: eastward seven blue flags placed as Jiao, Kang, Di, Fang, Xin, Wei, and Ji in the shape of the Azure Dragon; northward seven black flags placed as Dou, Niu, Nu, Xu, Wei, Shi, and Bi like the Black Tortoise; westward seven white banners as Kui, Lou, Zhou, Mao, Bi, Zui, and Shen in the White Tiger’s force; southward seven red flags as Jing, Gui, Liu, Xing, Zhang, Yi, and Zhen to form the Vermilion Bird.

On the second tier, sixty-four yellow flags were set, arranged by the sixty-four trigrams and distributed across eight directions.

The upper tier had four men, each wearing a tied-hair crown, black robe, phoenix-patterned sash, and red square hemmed shoes. One stood front-left with a long pole, and at its tip he tied rooster feathers for wind signs. One stood front-right with a long pole bearing the seven-star badge to indicate the wind. One stood rear-left carrying a treasure sword. One stood rear-right carrying a censer. At the foot of the altar twenty-four men held banners, treasure canopies, halberds, long spears, yellow flags, white standards, scarlet pennons, and black streamers, circling all four sides.

On the jiazi day, under an auspicious hour, Zhuge fasted, bathed, donned ritual robes, went barefoot and loose-haired to the altar and told Lu Su, “Zijing, return and help the commander arrange his troops. If what I entreat does not answer, do not harbor fantasies.”

Lu Su left.

Zhuge then instructed the altar guards:

“Do not leave your station on your own. Do not whisper together. Do not speak idle words. Do not lose your composure and panic at strange things. Whoever disobeys will be executed.”

The men took this as command.

Zhuge moved slowly onto the altar, judged the directions, offered incense in the brazier, poured water into the basin, and prayed to heaven. He came down and rested briefly in the tent, ordering the soldiers to eat in shifts. That day he ascended and descended the altar three times. Not once did a southeast wind appear.

Meanwhile, Zhou Yu summoned Cheng Pu, Lu Su, and a group of officers, telling them to wait in the tent and watch only for the southeast wind, then move in at once. He also had someone send word to Sun Quan for support.

Huang Gai had already prepared twenty fire ships. Their bows were studded with large nails. The hulls were packed with dry reed and brush, flooded with fish oil, then topped with sulphur and match to catch flame; all was covered with dyed blue oil cloth. Each bow carried a Qinglong fang banner, and each stern was tied to a light skiff.

In the water camp, Gan Ning, Kan Ze, Wopan, Cai He, and Cai Zhong drank daily and let not one soldier set foot on shore. All around, Wu horse and foot troops controlled the riverbank and blocked the water passage. They all waited only for the commander’s order.

As Zhou Yu sat in council in the tent, scouts reported, “The boats stand eighty-five li beyond the stockade, moored and waiting only for the commander’s command.”

Zhou Yu immediately told Lu Su: “Tell all officers and soldiers under your command to gather ships, arms, sails, and paddles at once. When the order comes, do not fail by even a moment. Whoever errs will be punished by military law.”

The officers and men obeyed and every hand prepared to struggle hand to hand.

By evening the sky was clear and the wind still. Zhou Yu said to Lu Su, “Kongming is wrong. In midwinter, how can a southeast wind come?”

Lu Su said, “I believe Kongming never speaks falsely.”

Near the third watch, the wind suddenly came and banners were fluttering. Zhou Yu went out to look. At first the flags were drifting northwest, and in one instant the southeast wind roared up.

Zhou Yu said in alarm, “This man has arts that seize heaven and earth and twist providence. If such a one remains, he may become the root of Wu’s ruin. Kill him at once and avoid later sorrow.”

He quickly summoned the two captains in guard charge, Ding Feng and Xu Sheng: “Take a hundred men each. Xu Sheng, go by the river; Ding Feng, by the land route. Both of you go to the Seven-Star Altar. Do not argue over details. Seize Zhuge Liang and behead him. Bring me his head in reward.”

Both captains took the orders.

Xu Sheng boarded and with a hundred axemen cleared oars and drove on. Ding Feng rode out with a hundred crossbowmen. On the way, the southeast wind met them.

Later there was a verse on this:

The Crouching Dragon ascends the Seven-Star Altar, In one night a southeast wind makes the Yangtze waters surge. Without Kongming’s exquisite stratagem, How could Lord Zhou gain such success by strength alone?

Ding Feng reached first. He found the men around the altar standing to the wind. Ding Feng dismounted, drew his sword, and climbed up, but found no Zhuge. He asked in alarm, “Where is he?”

The guards said, “He has just descended from the altar.”

Ding Feng hurried back and began searching below while Xu Sheng’s boat arrived. The two met by the river.

A young soldier said, “A swift boat anchored at the front shoal last night. Some time ago I saw Zhuge Liang step ashore with unbound hair. That boat has since sailed out toward the upper water.”

Ding Feng and Xu Sheng then chased by land and by water. Xu Sheng ordered full sails and rode the wind.

As the boat drew near, he shouted, “Military adviser, do not go! The commander has issued orders for you!”

Zhuge Liang stood at the stern of his vessel and laughed, saying, “Convey this to the commander: use strategy well. Zhuge Liang will return temporarily to Xiakou; perhaps we shall meet again another day.”

Xu Sheng called, “Please pause. There is urgent business.”

Zhuge Liang said, “I have already concluded that the commander cannot tolerate me and intends harm. I have already ordered Zhao Zilong to meet you. The general need not pursue.”

Xu Sheng saw there was no canopy on the boat and pressed on. As he came close, Zhao Yun, whose courtesy name was Zilong, set arrow to bow and stood at the stern, shouting:

“I am Zhao Zilong of Changshan! I was sent to escort the military adviser. Why do you pursue? One shot from my bow should have ended you and spared both houses a feud. Now see my method!”

The arrow flew and snapped the canopy rope of Xu Sheng’s boat. The canvas collapsed into the river and the boat heeled over.

Zhao Yun then ordered his own men to raise full sail and take the wind. His boat flew and outpaced them.

On land, Ding Feng called Xu Sheng’s boat close and said,

“Zhuge Liang is truly beyond reach in cunning and calculation. And Zhao Zilong has courage beyond a thousand men. Did you think this is all? Go back and report.”

“Do you not remember Zhao Yun’s feat at Dangyang and Changban?” Ding Feng added.

The two then returned to Zhou Yu: they said that Zhuge had already arranged for Zhao Zilong to receive him.

Zhou Yu was startled and said, “This man’s many layers of thought give me no rest at night.”

Lu Su said, “Wait until Cao is broken. Then we can settle him.”

Zhou Yu took counsel with the first statement and summoned his officers.

First he ordered Gan Ning: “Take Cai Zhong and captured troops, and move along the south bank using the northern-battle standard as your signal. Go straight to Ulin, where Cao Cao stores grain. Penetrate deep into his camp and light the fire. Leave only Cai He in this camp; I have a use for him.”

Second he told Taishi Ci: “Command three thousand and move straight to the boundary of Huangzhou. Cut off any reinforcement arriving from He Fei and pressure Cao’s forces. Light fire as signal. Look for the red banner; that means Wu-hou’s support has arrived.”

These two columns were to set off earliest.

Third he gave command to Lü Meng: “Take three thousand men and go to Ulin to join Gan Ning and carry out the burning.”

Fourth he sent Ling Tong with three thousand: “Directly to Yiling’s boundary gate. Wait there for fire from Ulin.”

Fifth he ordered Dong Xi with three thousand: “Take the route to Hanyang and strike from Hanchuan into Cao Cao’s camp. Use white flags to signal.”

Sixth he ordered Pan Zhang with three thousand and all white flags to Hanyang to join Dong Xi’s force.

The six detachments then moved off in separate directions.

Meanwhile Huang Gai was ordered to set the fire ships and send runners to tell Cao Cao to surrender that night. He also dispatched four groups of warships to follow Huang Gai’s row: Han Dang at the first, Zhou Tai second, Jiang Qin third, and Chen Wu fourth; each group had three hundred battle ships and twenty fire ships in front.

Zhou Yu stayed on a large mengchong with Cheng Pu to direct battle; Xu Sheng and Ding Feng served as right and left escorts. He left Lu Su with Kan Ze and the other strategists to guard the camp. Cheng Pu respected Zhou Yu’s method of deployment.

At this point, Sun Quan sent an envoy bearing the military order: he had already sent Lü Xun as vanguard, advancing at Zhan-Huang ground, and the Wu-lord would come to support behind.

Zhou Yu then sent orders to fire signals from Western Mountain and raised flags at Nánpíng Altar. All was prepared and he waited for dusk.

Meanwhile at Xiakou, Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, waited for Zhuge Liang to return. A boat arrived; it was the prince Liu Qi come on a mission to hear the news. Liu Bei made him come up to the command tower and sat.

Liu Bei said, “The southeast wind has been rising long enough; Zilong went to fetch Zhuge Liang and still has not returned. I am deeply worried.”

A junior officer pointed to Fankou harbor: “One sailboat with wind and current at its back has come. It must be the military advisor.” Liu Bei and Liu Qi went down to meet them.

Soon Kongming and Zhao Yun came ashore. Liu Bei rejoiced.

After greetings, Kongming said, “No time for other matters. Are all troops and ships prepared as set out before?”

Liu Bei said, “All has long been made ready; we only awaited your order.”

Kongming sat in the tent with Liu Bei and Liu Qi and said to Zhao Yun,

“Zilong, take three thousand cavalry, cross the river, and by the short road to Ulin take position in ambush among dense trees and reeds. After the fourth watch, Cao will surely run by that route. When his horses pass midway, set fire. Even if you cannot kill him fully, kill half.”

Zilong asked, “Ulin has two roads: one to Nanjun, one to Jingzhou. Which road will he choose?”

Kongming said, “The road to Nanjun is tight with pressure. Cao will not take it. He must come through Jingzhou and then move with his main force to Xuchang.”

Zilong left on the order.

Kongming called Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide: “Yide, you can lead three thousand horse across the river and block the Yiling road. Go to the mouth of Hula valley and lie in ambush. Cao cannot take the southern Yiling route and will seek the northern. Tomorrow after the rain he will certainly set the pots to boil. When fire rises, light your own fires along the hillside. Even if you do not take Cao, your merit will not be small.”

Zhang Fei took the order and left.

Kongming called Mi Zhu, Mi Fang, and Liu Feng to each row boats. They were to sweep upriver, snare retreating troops, and seize equipment.

All three took their orders and left.

Kongming rose and said to Liu Qi,

“The stretch by Wuchang is most critical and narrow. Return and deploy your troops at the river mouth. When Cao is defeated, survivors will surely flee your way; seize them, but do not leave the city lightly.”

Liu Qi took leave and departed.

Kongming then told Liu Bei,

“My lord should station men at Fankou, keep higher ground, and watch. Sit and watch how Zhou the young lord wins today.”

Guan Yu had stood to one side, and Kongming ignored him. Guan Yu could not bear it and spoke aloud:

“For years, as my brother’s sworn companion, I have never lagged behind in any campaign. Today I face a great enemy and the military advisor does not assign me any task. What does this mean?”

Kongming smiled, “Do not blame me, Guan. I wanted to send you to the one most critical pass, but there were obstacles that made it impossible.”

Guan Yu said, “What obstacle?”

Kongming said, “Formerly, Cao treated you with kindness. You should repay him somehow. If he is routed, he will flee by Huarong Pass. If I sent you there, he would surely pass through and escape. That is why I did not send you.”

Guan Yu said, “The adviser is too cautious. In the past, when Cao favored me, I already beheaded Yan Liang and slew Wen Chou, then broke the White Horse encirclement—thus I repaid him. Now that we meet again, surely I will not spare him?”

Kongming said, “If he does pass there, what then?”

Guan Yu said, “I will obey military law.”

Kongming said, “Then draw up the military order.”

Guan Yu took the warrant.

He asked, “If Cao does not come by that route?”

Kongming said, “I have written that order too.”

Guan Yu was pleased.

Kongming said, “At the high hill above the smaller road in Huarong, pile firewood and raise a column of smoke. Draw him with that smoke.”
