Guan Yu asked, “If Cao sees the smoke, he will know there is ambush. Why would he come?”

Kongming smiled, “Do you not know the maxim: real and empty, strong and weak? In warfare there are such moves. Though Cao can command troops well, this can fool him. He will see smoke and think it is merely a false show, then come by that road. Do not be sentimental.”

Guan Yu took the order and with Guan Ping and Zhou Cang, and five hundred sword-bearing infantry, went to the Huarong pass to hide.

Liu Bei said, “My younger brother’s righteousness is profound. If Cao truly goes by Huarong, I fear he may not be detained.”

Kongming said, “This night I have read the signs: that treacherous Cao has not yet reached his destined end. If we keep this human feeling and let Guan handle it, it is also good.”

Liu Bei said, “Your forecasting is beyond common men.”

Kongming then went with Liu Bei to Fankou to watch Zhou Yu put this plan into action, leaving Sun Qian and Jian Yong to hold the city.

Cao Cao, in his main camp, held council with his officers and waited for news of Huang Gai. That day the southeast wind rose strong. Cheng Yu told him, “Today the southeast wind rises fiercely. We should strengthen defenses.”

Cao Cao laughed, “After winter solstice comes spring growth. If yang has returned, why would there be no southeast wind? Why be astonished?”

A guard then reported that a small ship had come from the Jiangdong side, bearing Huang Gai’s secret letter. Cao Cao quickly had him brought in; the letter was presented.

It read, “The commander’s lines are tightly guarded and there is no way for escape. There is now fresh grain from Poyang Lake arriving; Huang Gai is already patrolling and has found a way. Do your best to kill a famed general of Wu and bring his head in surrender. At tonight’s third watch, the ship with a Qinglong fang banner is the grain ship.”

Cao was overjoyed. He and the assembled commanders went to the great warship in the center of the waters to watch Huang Gai’s ship arrive.

Back in the south, near dusk, Zhou Yu ordered Cai He brought out, bound, and asked aloud, “No guilt!” then declared,

“Who are you to dare to feign surrender? I need lucky matter for the banners. I will borrow your head.”

Cai He denied at first and then shouted, “Kan Ze and Gan Ning were involved with this scheme too!”

Zhou Yu said, “They are as I sent them.”

Cai He regretted it too late.

Zhou Yu had him taken under the black banner by the river, offered wine, burned written papers, and beheaded him in one stroke. When the blood sacrifice for the banners was finished, he ordered the ships to depart.

On the third fire ship, Huang Gai, alone, wore a concealed breast-plate and held a sharp weapon in hand. On the bow was written in bold, “Vanguard Huang Gai.” He took the favorable wind and set out from the Red Cliffs.

By then the east wind was roaring, waves breaking high. Cao Cao in the center fleet looked across and saw the moon on the river, like ten thousand gold snakes and waves leaping and playing in sport.

He laughed, thinking himself victorious.

A watchman then shouted, “To the south, from far off, a cluster of sailcloths rides in on the wind.”

Cao Cao looked and said, “They all bear Qinglong fang banners, and one great banner with the words ‘Vanguard Huang Gai.’”

Cao Cao laughed: “Let him come as a surrendering enemy. Heaven even favors me.”

As they came nearer, Cheng Yu looked long and said to Cao Cao, “These boats are surely deceptive. Do not allow them near the camp.”

Cao asked, “How do you know?”

Cheng Yu replied, “If this were grain, they would be heavy and stable. But these are light and buoyant. And tonight the southeast wind is violent. If there is deceit, how can they hold?”

Cao understood and asked who should stop them.

Wen Pin said, “I know these waters well and volunteer to go.”

When he had spoken, he leapt into a small boat and pointed, and more than ten patrol boats followed.

Wen Pin stood at the bow and cried, “The Chancellor’s order: southern vessels must not approach the stockade. Stop and anchor in midstream.”

All soldiers shouted together, “Drop the awnings at once!”

Before the cry had ended, an arrow struck Wen Pin in the left arm and he fell into the boat. Chaos erupted, and men fled back.

The nearest enemy ship was only two li from Cao’s camp when Huang Gai raised a cutlass and signaled. The front ships all caught fire at once. Fanned by wind, they went like arrows. Smoke and flame filled the sky.

The twenty fire ships crashed into the water camp, and at once every ship in Cao’s anchorage caught fire. Iron rings and chains fixed together gave no room to run. Across the river cannon fire answered, and fire ships arrived from all around, making the three-river waters rise in a red, burning sky.

Cao looked toward shore and saw smoke and fires among his camps. He tried at once to jump ashore. Just then Zhang Liao brought a small skiff and helped him down. By that moment the great ship itself had already caught fire. Zhang Liao, with ten men, guarded Cao and ran toward the bank.

Huang Gai, seeing through smoke from a smaller boat with several men behind him, came forward, hoping to capture him. He saw a man stepping out in carmine robe and thought it was Cao Cao, so he shouted:

“Bandit Cao, do not run away! Huang Gai is here!”

Cao cried out in misery.

Zhang Liao set arrow to bow and watched Huang Gai drawing near, and loosed one shot. The wind was loud; in that firelight Huang Gai could not hear the bowstring. The arrow struck the hollow of his shoulder, and he turned over and fell into the water.

A last verse recorded this ending:

When the calamity of fire peaks, it is followed by water disaster. A bruise from a staff may heal, but a wound from metal still troubles.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Seven-Star Altar and the Fire at Sanjiangkou

chapters.html:
Yet that night, Zhang Liao shot an arrow that sent Huang Gai into the river. He brought Cao Cao to shore, and when Cao searched for a horse and moved on, the army was already in full disorder.

Han Dang drove through smoke and flame into the river camp. He heard a soldier report, “A man on the stern lookout is crying for my lord’s courtesy name.” Listening closely, he heard only the call, “Yi Gong, save me!” Han Dang said, “This is Huang Gongfu.” He ordered him raised at once. Huang Gai had taken the arrow in his side; he had bitten out the shaft and left the arrowhead buried in flesh. Han Dang quickly removed his wet coat, pried the arrowhead free with a knife, and tied it tightly with a strip cut from a banner. He gave Huang Gai his own battle robe and then sent him back to the main camp by another boat to receive treatment. Huang Gai understood the water well; even though he had gone into the river in heavy armor in the deep cold, he had still escaped with his life.

That same day, all along the Yang River the flames rolled, and cries shattered the earth. From the west bank of Chibi, Han Dang and Jiang Qin’s forces drove in. From the east side, Zhou Tai and Chen Wu came in from Red Cliff’s eastern flank. Through the center, the large flotilla of Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu, Xu Sheng, and Ding Feng arrived. The fire-shooting troops did their part, and armaments flared with blazing fury. This was true three-river water fighting, Chibi locked in a pitched struggle by water.

In the Cao armies, men were speared by arrows, burned by fire, and drowned; they were too many to count. Later ages preserved this verse:

Wei and Wu contested one another to decide victory and defeat; At Chibi the towered boats had their decks swept clean. The first fierce flames lit the cloud-sea;
Lord Zhou once broke Chancellor Cao here.

Another quatrain says:

Mountains towered and the moon stood small over endless water; Looking back, one laments how the old houses of the court once seized and held. The men of the south had no wish to welcome Wei Wu;
The eastern wind knowingly favored Zhou Lang.

Let us leave the river fight aside. Meanwhile, Gan Ning ordered Cai Zhong to drive deep into Cao Cao’s camp. He cut Cai Zhong down from his horse with one stroke and set fire to the grasses. Lü Meng, watching the center, raised ten fires of his own in support of Gan Ning. Pan Zhang and Dong Xi set fires in separate bands and shouted. Drumbeats thundered from all sides.

Cao Cao and Zhang Liao rode with more than a hundred horsemen through the thicket of flames, looking for a path forward but finding no opening. As they rode, Mao Jie came to Wei Peng’s rescue with a few dozen riders. Cao ordered the men to keep looking for a route. Zhang Liao pointed out, “Only Wu Forest is open—the ground there is broad enough to pass.” Cao Cao turned straight into Wu Forest.

Even as they passed, another force caught up from behind and shouted, “Wretch Cao, do not flee!” In the firelight he saw Lü Meng’s banner. Cao urged the cavalry forward, leaving Zhang Liao to cover his rear and face Lü Meng. Ahead, torches rose again. From a mountain pass a full force surged out with a cry: “Ling Tong is here!” Cao’s guts turned to ice. Then, suddenly from a skewed side, another detachment attacked and shouted, “Do not panic, Chancellor! Xu Huang is here!” There was a brief mêlée; Cao broke through, pushed northward.

Then he saw a body of cavalry drawn up before a mountain slope. Asking him, Xu Huang reported that it was Ma Yan and Zhang Yi, former officers of Yuan Shao, three thousand northern troops, camped together. All night they had seen fire in the sky and dared not move, but now they happened into Cao’s way. Cao ordered both generals to lead a thousand horse to clear a way, while the rest stayed to cover him. Grateful for this fresh force, Cao’s heart eased a little. Ma Yan and Zhang Yi rode ahead at speed. Within ten li, shouts arose, and a troop burst forth. The first commander cried, “I am Gan Xingba of Wu!” Ma Yan moved to meet him, but Gan Ning cut him down from horseback immediately. Zhang Yi came on with his spear. Gan Ning shouted once; Zhang Yi could not evade. The blow from Gan Ning sent him tumbling from the saddle.

Word flew back to Cao. At this moment Cao had hoped for relief at Hefei, but Sun Quan stood at the Hefei approach. Seeing fire across the water, he knew our troops had prevailed and ordered Lu Xun to raise the signal flames. Taishi Ci saw them and joined Lu Xun in one body of men to charge forward. Cao had no choice but to ride for Yiling. On the way he met Zhang He, and Cao left him to hold the rear.

Cao drove on at a gallop and by the fifth watch had run until the flames behind were fading. Then his mind settled, and he asked, “What place is this?” The reply was, “This is west of Wulin, north of Yidu.” Cao saw the massed woods and steep ridges. He threw back his head in his saddle and laughed uncontrollably. The officers asked, “Why does the Chancellors laugh?” Cao said, “I am not laughing at others. I laugh only at Zhou Yu’s poor planning and Zhuge Liang’s meager wit. Had I commanded this battle, I would have posted a force here beforehand. What else could I have done?”

He had not finished when drums roared from both sides and flames shot skyward, nearly throwing Cao from the saddle. From an oblique flank came a unit crying, “I, Zhao Zilong, stand by the Military Adviser’s command and have waited here long enough!” Cao told Xu Huang and Zhang He to take Zhao Yun together, while he cut through the smoke and fire himself. Zhao did not chase; he kept fighting over flags. Cao got away.

Daylight came faintly. Low black cloud covered the sky, and the southeast wind still blew. Then rain poured down in torrents, wetting armor and robes through. Cao and his men marched in the rain; many soldiers looked hungry. Cao ordered men to raid nearby villages for grain and seek embers. As they were about to cook, another unit arrived in haste from behind. Cao’s fear rose quickly. They turned out to be Li Dian and Xu Chu, bringing the rest of the officers with them.

Cao was deeply relieved. He told the cavalry to keep moving and asked, “What lies ahead?” The report came, “On one side lies the southern Yiling road, on the other the mountain road toward north Yiling.” “Which way is closer to Nan Commandery’s Jiangling?” he asked. The soldiers answered, “Going through southern Yiling over Hulu Pass is faster.” Cao ordered that route.

When they reached Hulu Pass, the army was hungry and exhausted. Many could barely walk, and the horses were spent, with many collapsing. Cao ordered a halt up ahead. Some had cooking pots, some had looted rice. They found dry ground by the mountain and set up fires, buried the pots, roasted and ate horseflesh. Everyone stripped off wet gear and set garments to dry in the wind. Saddles were removed from horses and left loose, and the animals nipped at grass roots.

Cao sat under sparse trees and laughed upward toward the sky. The officers asked, “Earlier Your Excellency laughed at Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang, and now it seems to have provoked Zhao Zilong and cost many men and horses. Why laugh again?” Cao said, “I laugh at Zhuge Liang and Zhou Yu, yet their strategy still lacked depth. If I had chosen this place and laid up cavalry in ambush as they should have done, we might still have lived, but not without grievous losses. They could not have foreseen this, and so I laughed.”

As he spoke, both front and rear guards shouted at once. Cao was suddenly alarmed and threw off his armor to mount. Many men failed to get their horses in time. Fire and smoke from all four sides now ringed the mountain pass. A force deployed itself in formation. At its head stood Zhang Yide of Yan, spear leveled on horseback. He cried, “Cao Cao, where do you think you are going?”

At the sight of Zhang Fei, Cao’s officers and soldiers lost heart. Xu Chu, riding bareback, went out to fight him; Zhang Liao and Xu Huang also spurred forward and attacked from either side. The two armies became locked in a confused battle. Cao Cao turned his horse and escaped first, and his generals each broke free after him. Zhang Fei pursued from the rear. Cao fled on until the pursuit gradually fell behind; when he looked back, most of his commanders were wounded.

As they went on, a soldier reported that two roads lay ahead. The broad road was level but more than fifty li longer; the narrow road through Huarong was fifty li shorter, but cramped, steep, and broken. Cao sent a man up the heights to look. The scout returned saying that smoke rose at several points beside the narrow road, while the broad road showed no movement. Cao ordered the vanguard onto the Huarong path. His generals objected that smoke must mark hidden troops, but Cao replied, “Have you not read in the military books: ‘Make the empty appear full, and the full appear empty’? Zhuge Liang has had smoke lit in the hills to frighten us from the narrow path while he waits in ambush on the broad road. I have seen through him.” The generals praised his calculation and followed the Huarong road.

Men fainted from hunger and horses were utterly spent. Those scorched about the head leaned on staffs; the arrow- and spear-wounded struggled onward. Clothes and armor were soaked and torn, weapons and banners in disorder. In the bitter midwinter cold, their misery was beyond telling. Rainwater had filled the ruts of the narrow mountain path and the horses sank in mud. Cao ordered the strong to carry earth, bind firewood, and fill the road, while the old and wounded followed slowly. Zhang Liao, Xu Chu, and Xu Huang took a hundred riders with drawn blades to behead any who lagged. Cries of anguish sounded without end, but Cao shouted that life and death were decreed by fate and threatened to execute anyone who wept again.

After they passed the worst ground, only some three hundred riders remained with Cao, none properly clothed or armored. The generals begged to rest their exhausted horses, but Cao urged them toward Jing Province. A few li farther on, he raised his whip and laughed again. “Everyone calls Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang men of great resource,” he said, “but to my mind they are incompetent. Had they placed even one detachment here in ambush, we would all have been taken bound.”

Before he finished, a single heavy blast sounded. Five hundred sword-bearing infantry deployed on both sides. At their head was Guan Yunchang, Green Dragon Crescent Blade raised as he rode the Red Hare, blocking the road.

When Cao’s troops saw him, their courage failed and they looked at each other in panic. Cao said, “Now that we have reached this place, we can only decide a fight to the death.” The officers replied, “Even if they do not dare, our horses are spent. How can we fight again?” Cheng Yu said, “I have known General Yunchang long: proud above all and unwilling to step upon the fallen; he tyrannizes only the strong and never insults the weak. He is clear in favor and against, and steadfast in loyalty. Your Excellency once owed him much. Go and tell him directly, and we may escape this strait.”

Cao took that counsel and rode ahead, leaning from the saddle to address Guan Yu: “General, have you been well since we last met?” Guan Yu bowed slightly and answered, “I, Guan, come under the Military Adviser’s order and have waited long for Your Excellency.” Cao said, “Cao Cao’s army is shattered and in peril, with no road left. I beg the general to weigh your old bond with me.” Guan Yu replied, “Though Your Excellency once showed me much grace, I have already returned it by slaying Yan Liang, beheading Wen Chou, and lifting the siege of Bailima. Could I now abandon public duty for private ties?” Cao said, “Do you not remember the time of the five mountain passes where generals were cut down? A true man values trust and righteousness above all. You understand the Spring and Autumn tradition, do you not? Do you not know Yu Gong’s pursuit of Zitong and his mercy toward Ziliu?”

Guan Yu was a man of loyalty as high as a mountain. He remembered all Cao Cao’s former kindness and also the deeds at the Five Passes, and he could not help but be moved. He saw the Cao men trembling on the brink of tears. His heart softened all the more. He pulled back his horse and told his troops, “Spread out.” It was clearly a sign to let Cao Cao pass. Cao saw Guan Yu turn his horse and drove ahead with all his commanders at once. By the time Guan Yu wheeled back, Cao and his men were already past. Guan Yu shouted once, and every man dismounted, crying and kneeling to the ground in a salute. Guan Yu, though torn, grew even more unwilling.

While he still hesitated, Zhang Liao rode in suddenly. Seeing him, Guan Yu’s old affinity stirred again. He exhaled heavily and released everyone. Later ages recorded this verse:

Cao Man fled in defeat through Hua Rong, and met Guan Gong in a narrow path; Only for their old favor and grace, he let the chained-claw dragon pass free.

Once Cao Cao escaped the trouble at Hua Rong and had gone as far as the ravine mouth, he looked back. He had only twenty-seven riders with him. By the time dusk came, he was near Nan Commandery. Torchlight came in full array before him; a band of horsemen blocked the way. Cao shouted in shock, “My life is finished!” But he soon recognized them as Cao Ren’s troops as scouts rode up in a rush. Cao was eased.

Cao Ren came alongside and said, “Though I knew you were defeated, I did not dare to move far away, so I came nearby to receive you.” Cao said, “How often I have gone without seeing you!”

He brought everyone into Nan Commandery to rest. Zhang Liao arrived soon after and spoke of Guan Yu’s virtue. Cao assessed his surviving officers and soldiers; the wounded were far too many, and he ordered all to rest. Cao Ren brought wine so Cao could unburden himself, and all his military advisers sat in attendance. Cao suddenly threw back his head and wailed aloud.

The councillors said, “When Your Excellency fled the Tiger Gully, there was no sign of fear. Now you are in city walls, with food for men and forage for horses, and should be drilling and reforming for reprisal. Why weep instead?” Cao replied, “I weep for Guo Fengxiao. If Fengxiao had been here, I would not have met such ruin.” He struck his chest and cried, “Alas, Fengxiao! Woe to Fengxiao! Regret, Fengxiao!” All the advisers sat in shameful silence.

The next day Cao summoned Cao Ren and said, “I will return briefly to Xuchang, gather and ready the cavalry and infantry, then come to exact vengeance. You hold Nan Commandery secure. I have a plan. Keep it hidden; do not open it unless urgent. Follow it, and Eastern Wu will not dare to eye Nan Commandery directly.” Cao Ren asked, “Who can defend Hefei and Xiangyang?” Cao said, “Jing Province you hold. I have assigned Xiahou Dun to guard Xiangyang. Hefei is the critical position. I appoint Zhang Liao as commander and Yue Jin and Li Dian as deputies. If there is urgency, fly orders to me at once.”

The dispositions were fixed. Cao mounted and rode out with the army, hastening back to Xu. The officials and soldiers that Jiang Province had surrendered, and who had already joined him, were sent back to Xu to continue in service. Cao Ren left Cao Hong in charge of Yiling and Nan Commandery to guard against Zhou Yu.

Then Guan Yu, who had let Cao Cao go, returned with his troops. While all roads’ troops had recovered horses, weapons, and grain and had already returned to Xia-kou, Guan Yu returned empty-handed, no man and no horse at all, and went in person to Liu Bei.

Kongming was in the act of exchanging congratulations with Xuande when a report came that Guan Yu had arrived. Kongming rose quickly from the seat and took up a cup to greet him: “All the more reason for joy, General. You have accomplished a deed surpassing generations and removed a great danger from beneath heaven. It is fitting we raise a long-distance celebration.”

Guan Yu was silent. Kongming said, “Is it that we, by not meeting you earlier, have offended you?” Turning to the others, he asked, “Why did you not send word first?” Guan Yu said, “Guan requests to die.” Kongming asked, “Did not Cao Cao pass through Hua Rong Road?” Guan Yu said, “He came from there. I was unable—by my own deficiency—to stop him.” Kongming said, “Did you seize any soldiers?” Guan Yu said, “I seized none.” Kongming said, “This is the kindness you still gave him for old mercies from before; he was released deliberately. But since this is in the general order, we must still carry it out by military law.” He shouted at the guards, and they were sent out to execute him.

Willing to die in one life to repay a trusted benefactor, he would have earned for ten thousand ages a name of enduring righteousness.

What became of Guan Yu’s life and death remained uncertain.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang’s Precise Stratagem at Hua Rong, and Guan Yu’s Righteous Release of Cao Cao

chapters.html:
Cao Ren wages war against the Eastern Wu army.
Zhuge Liang confronts Zhou Gongjin in one breath.

Zhuge Liang was prepared to execute Guan Yu. Liu Bei said, “When we three swore brotherhood, we promised to share life and death together. Now Guan Yu has broken the law, but I cannot betray our old oath. Ask Lord Sun to pardon him and let this service redeem the offense.” Only then did Kongming yield.

Zhou Yu gathered his troops and called over the commanders, had each man report his deeds, and sent a formal account to Lord Sun. All surrendered soldiers were sent across the river. He rewarded all three armies, then advanced to take Nan County. The vanguard reached the riverbank, made camp, and the host spread into five camps, with Zhou Yu in the center.

Zhou Yu was discussing the method of pressing the attack when he was suddenly informed: “Liu Bei has sent Sun Qian to present congratulations to the commander-in-chief.” Zhou Yu ordered him brought in. After Sun Qian paid his respects and said, “My lord Liu Bei sends word of thanks for your Great Virtue and brings a small token of courtesy.” Zhou Yu asked, “Where is Liu Bei now?” Sun Qian replied, “He has moved his troops and is now stationed at You River Mouth.” Zhou Yu cried out, “Then is Kongming at You River Mouth as well?” Sun Qian answered, “Kongming is with my lord at You River Mouth.” Zhou Yu said, “You return first. I myself will come to offer my thanks.”

After he passed on the gifts, Zhou Yu sent Sun Qian back ahead. Lu Su asked, “Why did the commander-in-chief just panic?” Zhou Yu answered, “Liu Bei has stationed troops at You River Mouth. He surely intends to take Nan County. We have spent so much money on men and horses; Nan County now lies ready to the hand. Their hearts hold no humanity; if a plunder is ripe, they take it. Someone may need to let Zhou Yu live by leaving him alive!”

Lu Su said, “What strategy should we use to make them go?” Zhou Yu answered, “I will go and speak with him myself. If all goes well, well and good. If not, we need not wait for him to take Nan County; we shall settle it with Liu Bei first.” Lu Su said, “I am willing to go with you.” So Zhou Yu and Lu Su rode out with three thousand light cavalry straight for You River Mouth.

After Sun Qian had returned to Liu Bei, he said that Zhou Yu would come in person to offer thanks. Liu Bei asked Zhuge Liang, “What does he mean by this?” Zhuge Liang laughed, “Why does he come for these trifles? He has come for Nan County.” Liu Bei asked, “If he brings troops, how should we meet him?” Zhuge Liang replied, “When he comes, answer him this way.” Liu Bei then arrayed his war boats at You River Mouth and lined cavalry along the bank.

A report came that Zhou Yu and Lu Su were arriving with troops. Kongming sent Zhao Yun to escort him with a few riders. When Zhou Yu saw the scale of Liu Bei’s force, his heart was uneasy. As they came outside the gate and entered camp, Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang received him. After formalities, they served a banquet and treated him as a guest. Liu Bei raised his cup to offer thanks for the battle arrangement.

After several rounds of wine, Zhou Yu said, “Why have your troops moved out of Yu Province? Is it to take Nan County?” Liu Bei answered, “Hearing that you intend to take Nan County, I came to assist. If you do not take it, I will take it.” Zhou Yu laughed, “For long ago, Eastern Wu wished to absorb the Han River region. Now Nan County is already in our grasp; how could we not take it?” Liu Bei said, “Victory and defeat cannot be predetermined. Cao Cao is near to leave the capital, and at places like Nan County he will surely have strange designs; besides, Cao Ren is fearless and hard to match. I only fear that you cannot take it.” Zhou Yu answered, “If I fail to take it, then by your leave let you take it.”

Liu Bei said, “Kongming and Zijing are here as witnesses. Do not regret it.” Lu Su hesitated, and Zhou Yu said, “When a man of standing has spoken, there is nothing to regret.” Zhuge Liang said, “That is common reason indeed. Let Eastern Wu take it first, and if you fail, my lord can take it. What difficulty is there in that?” Zhou Yu and Lu Su bade Liu Bei and Kongming farewell, mounted, and left.

When they had gone, Liu Bei said to Zhuge Liang, “You told me just now how to answer. Though we had spoken swiftly, the more I think on it, the less right it sounds. I am poor and homeless, lacking a place to stand. If I am to gain Nan County merely as refuge, then should Zhou Yu take it first, it will belong to Wu. How then can I hold it?” Zhuge Liang laughed heartily and said, “Did you not then ignore my old warning to take Jing Province?” Liu Bei said, “Before, it was Jing’s land under Jing Province, so I could not bear to seize it. Now it is Cao Cao’s land, and it is lawful to take it.” Zhuge Liang said, “Do not worry. Leave the fighting to Zhou Yu. Let him and you trade blows for a while; by morning or night your seat in the city of Nan County will be secure.” Liu Bei asked, “How will that plan unfold?” Zhuge Liang said, “Only just as I have laid it out.” Liu Bei rejoiced and remained stationed at the riverbank without moving further.

After Zhou Yu and Lu Su returned to their camp, Lu Su asked, “How could the commander even permit Liu Bei to take Nan County?” Zhou Yu said, “I could take Nan County at a snap of my fingers and yet leave a debt of favors in return.” He then asked his officers: “Who dare advance first toward Nan County?” One man stepped out at once: Jiang Qin. Zhou Yu said, “You will lead the vanguard. Xu Sheng and Ding Feng will be your deputy commanders. Take five thousand elite cavalry and infantry across the river first. I will follow with the main force.”

In Nan County, Cao Ren assigned Cao Hong to guard Yiling, using it as a hard-to-hit angle in the defense. A report came: “Wu soldiers have crossed the Han River.” Cao Ren said, “Hold fast and do not fight; this is best.” Niu Jin of the Fierce Cavalry leapt up and said, “When enemy troops stand under city walls and do not come out, that is cowardice. Our army has only just suffered loss; this is the moment to restore spirit. I ask leave to take five hundred picked troops and choose a decisive battle.”

Cao Ren agreed and ordered Niu Jin to lead the five hundred to fight. Ding Feng came on horse to meet him. After four or five exchanges, Ding Feng feigned defeat. Niu Jin chased him into the formation. Ding Feng then commanded his men to encircle Niu Jin in the heart of the field in an instant. Niu Jin and his attendants struggled, unable to break out. From the ramparts Cao Ren saw Niu Jin trapped in the center and threw off his armor, mounted, and led several hundred veterans out of the city, cutting down hard with his sword. He cut into the Wu formation. Xu Sheng met him but could not hold.

Cao Ren pressed into the center, broke out and rescued Niu Jin. Looking back, he saw dozens more riders trapped inside and unable to break out; he turned again, slashed and fought back in, and pulled them from the hard encirclement. At that moment Jiang Qin blocked the way. Cao Ren and Niu Jin drove through with all their strength. Cao Ren’s younger brother Cao Chun also came with reinforcements. There was a mingled clash, the Wu army broke and ran, and Cao Ren returned in victory.

Jiang Qin’s men were broken and he returned to Zhou Yu. Zhou Yu wanted to behead him, but his generals interceded.

Zhou Yu then ordered his troops to be inspected and prepared to decide battle personally with Cao Ren. Gan Ning said, “The commander-in-chief should not be rash. Cao Ren has ordered Cao Hong to guard Yiling, which serves as a protruding point to be fixed and then struck. I am prepared to take three thousand picked soldiers straight to Yiling; only then can you take Nan County, Commander-in-chief.” Zhou Yu accepted the argument and first ordered Gan Ning to lead three thousand men against Yiling. A spy had already sent news to Cao Ren. Cao Ren and Chen Qiao consulted. Chen Qiao said, “If Yiling is lost, Nan County cannot be held either. We should rush to save it.” Cao Ren therefore secretly ordered Cao Chun and Niu Jin to lead relief forces.

Cao Chun first reported to Cao Hong to lure the enemy out. When Gan Ning arrived at Yiling, Cao Hong rode out and fought him directly. After more than twenty rounds, Cao Hong was defeated and ran. Gan Ning seized Yiling. By dusk Cao Chun and Niu Jin arrived, joined with their troops, and besieged Yiling.

A fast rider rushed to Zhou Yu and reported that Gan Ning was trapped inside the city of Yiling. Zhou Yu was startled. Cheng Pu said, “We should quickly divide and send troops to rescue him.” Zhou Yu said, “This place is the key crossroads. If I split the force to rescue him and Cao Ren arrives with another wave, what then?” Lu Meng said, “Gan Ning, that famous hero of Jiangdong, cannot be left unaided.” Zhou Yu said, “I will go myself to rescue him, but who can stay here and bear my post?” Ling Tong said, “Leave Ling Gong to hold this command. I will lead the vanguard; Commander-in-chief, you stay behind and send victory news within ten days.”

Zhou Yu asked, “Will Ling Gong accept that he may hold for only ten days?” Ling Tong replied, “If ten days is the term, I can do it; beyond ten days, I cannot hold the responsibility.”

Zhou Yu was pleased. He left more than ten thousand troops under Ling Tong’s charge and immediately rode with the main force toward Yiling. Gan Ning said to Zhou Yu, “Yiling’s southern lanes and side paths are obscure and narrow, and this route makes Nan County extremely close. Send five hundred troops to cut down trees and block the road. If their force is broken, it will only be able to flee this way. Their horses will fail and they will dismount; then we can take their mounts.”

Zhou Yu did so. By the time the main host neared Yiling, he asked, “Who can break through and ride in to save Gan Ning?” Zhou Tai offered to go and instantly spurred forward, saber in hand. He cut through the Cao forces and reached the foot of the city. Gan Ning saw Zhou Tai arrive and came out to greet him. Tai said, “The commander-in-chief is coming with the army.” Ning passed the order for his men to eat well and don full armor and prepare for inside support.

Cao Hong, Cao Chun, and Niu Jin, hearing that Zhou Yu’s army was coming, sent men to Nan County to alert Cao Ren and split their force to meet the enemy. When the Wu army arrived, the Wei army met them. As battle joined, Gan Ning and Zhou Tai cut out on two fronts. Cao’s troops were thrown into disarray, and the Wu soldiers cut them down from all sides.

Cao Hong, Cao Chun, and Niu Jin indeed fled by a small side path. But that path was choked with felled brush, the horses could not pass, and all abandoned their mounts and ran. The Wu army captured more than five hundred horses.

Zhou Yu drove his men onward through the night and reached Nan County in time to meet Cao Ren’s force coming to rescue Yiling. The two armies crashed together once in a mixed melee. Night had already fallen, and both armies withdrew.

Cao Ren returned to the city and conferred with his men. Cao Hong said, “Now that Yiling has been lost, things are dangerous. Why not open the late chancellor’s hidden directive?” Cao Ren said, “What you say fits exactly my mind.” He opened the letter and read it. Greatly delighted, he gave orders that at dawn all troops and horses should be fed at first watch. By first light all cavalry and infantry should abandon the city; flags should be hung all along the walls to inflate appearances, and the army should leave by three gates in sequence.

Now Zhou Yu had rescued Gan Ning and arranged his lines outside Nan County. Seeing the Wei force break out through three gates, he climbed the command platform and scanned it all. He saw empty flags stuck along the city wall with no one guarding, and each soldier’s waist bound with spare packs. Zhou Yu guessed that Cao Ren had already prepared a route of escape, so he went down from the platform and issued orders: divide the army into right and left wings. If the vanguard wins, it should press straight forward and pursue only until the golden gong sounds, and only then may it pull back. He put Cheng Pu in charge of the rear, while Zhou Yu led the forward line toward the city.

The battle drums sounded. Cao Hong came out from the gate to lock in combat. Zhou Yu rode under the gate, then sent Han Dang out as well to trade blows with him. After more than thirty exchanges, Hong was routed and withdrew. Cao Ren himself rode out to engage next. Zhou Tai charged to meet him. After ten or more exchanges, Ren was also turned back, and the formation became confused.

With a signal Zhou Yu’s two wings burst forth, and the Wei army was badly beaten. Zhou Yu led his force in pursuit to the foot of Nan County’s walls. The Wei troops did not enter the city but fled toward the northwest. Han Dang and Zhou Tai led the front wings to chase with all strength.

At the city gate Zhou Yu saw it wide open and no one on the battlements, so he ordered all troops to rush in. Dozens of riders were first to enter. Zhou Yu galloped at the rear with his horse and spurred in hard, riding straight into Weng City. Chen Qiao, on an enemy tower, saw Zhou Yu himself enter and muttered quietly, “The Chancellor’s plan works like divination!”

Then a clapper rang. Arrows and crossbows fired together from both sides in a downpour. Those who rushed in first all plunged into pits. As Zhou Yu pulled his horse sharply back, he was struck by a heavy crossbow bolt squarely in his left ribs. He turned over, falling from the saddle. Niu Jin burst out from the city to seize Zhou Yu. Xu Sheng and Ding Feng threw themselves forward to save him.

Wei troops burst from within the city while Wu soldiers trampled over one another in panic, and countless men dropped into the pits. Just when Cheng Pu was trying to pull the force back in, Cao Hong and Cao Ren split and struck from two routes. The Wu army was utterly defeated. Fortunately Ling Tong came with one contingent through a diagonal hidden path and checked the Wei force. Cao Ren led the victorious cavalry into the city, and Cheng Pu withdrew the broken troops back to camp.

Xu Sheng and Ding Feng carried Zhou Yu to the command tent. A field surgeon with iron tongs pulled out the arrowhead, and gold-ointment plaster was laid over the wound. The pain was unbearable, and he could not eat or drink.

The surgeon said, “The tip of this arrow carries poison; it cannot be cured quickly. If he lets anger break through, the wound will break open again.” Cheng Pu had all three wings keep strict watch in each camp and forbid loose sorties.

Three days later Niu Jin returned with troops and skirmished. Cheng Pu kept his troops in place. Niu Jin cursed until dusk and withdrew. The next day he came again to curse and attack. Cheng Pu feared Zhou Yu’s temper and did not dare to report it. On the third day, Niu Jin came all the way to the gate and shouted abuse, saying only that he would capture Zhou Yu. Cheng Pu and the officers conferred and thought to withdraw for a time and report to Lord Sun.

Yet Zhou Yu, though in pain, had his own design in mind. He had already noticed that Wei soldiers came each day to the camp to rage and cuss yet saw no commander giving report. One day Cao Ren himself brought the main army, drums pounding and shouting, and came out for battle. Cheng Pu barred him out. Zhou Yu called for all the commanders into his tent and asked, “From where comes this racket of drumming?” The commanders replied, “The soldiers are merely exercising.” Zhou Yu shouted in anger, “How dare you deceive me! I have known those Wei men come to cuss before the camp. Cheng Demou who now controls command yet allows this?”

He ordered them to summon Cheng Pu into the tent and ask him directly. Cheng Pu said, “I see your own arrow wound, and the surgeon warned against excitement. So when the Wei men came to provoke, I did not dare report.” Zhou Yu asked, “If the commanders do not fight, what is your plan?” Cheng Pu said, “All officers wish to withdraw temporarily and return to Jiangdong. When your arrow wound has healed, we can make better arrangements.”

When Zhou Yu finished, he suddenly leaped from his bed and said, “A true gentleman who has eaten the ruler’s grain should die on the field and return with his body under horsehide. Better that! Could we abandon the kingdom’s great work for one man, even me?” Saying so, he put on his armor and mounted.

Every general and officer stared in alarm. He drew out a few hundred riders and rode ahead of camp. Looking out, he saw the Wei force already arrayed in battle ranks, and Cao Ren mounted at the gate with whip raised and cried out, “You brat Zhou Yu, you will surely die young. Never dare to face my army again!”

Before the curse had even finished, Zhou Yu suddenly burst forth from among the riders and cried, “Cao Ren, rogue and fool! Do you now see Zhou Lang?” The Wei soldiers, seeing this, were all startled.

Cao Ren looked back and told his officers, “Cry out at once!” The whole Wei line replied with loud curses. Zhou Yu flung into a great rage and ordered Pan Zhang forward. They had not yet traded blows when Zhou Yu suddenly screamed, blood spurting from his mouth, and he tumbled from his horse. Cao troops came surging in. The generals moved to resist, and in a savage clash Zhou Yu was pulled out and carried back to the camp.

Cheng Pu asked, “How is your state, Commander?” Zhou Yu whispered to him, “This is my scheme.” Cheng Pu asked, “Where is this scheme to go?”

Zhou Yu answered, “I am scarcely in pain at all. I did this so the Wei soldiers would know I am near death. They will then dare to attack more boldly. Send my trusted soldiers to enter the city and feign surrender, saying I have already died. This night Cao Ren will come to raid the camp. I will then lie in ambush on all sides and capture him in one stroke.”

Cheng Pu said, “This plan is excellent.” He then raised cries of mourning in the tent. All officers were shocked, and the news spread to every camp that the commander-in-chief’s arrow wound had broken open and he had died. Every camp wore mourning.

In the city, Cao Ren held counsel with his men and said, “Now that Zhou Yu has become enraged, his hot temper and broken gold wound shattered, blood spraying from his mouth before he falls—he cannot live long.” As they talked, a report came: “Several soldiers have come in surrender from Wu. Two of them were once captured by Wei soldiers.”

Cao Ren hastened to summon them. The soldiers said, “Today Zhou Yu’s arrow wound burst apart at the front ranks; he returned to camp and died immediately. All the officers hang mourning now. Because we were insulted by Cheng Pu, we returned to surrender now and report this.”

Cao Ren rejoiced and then resolved to raid the camp tonight, seize Zhou Yu’s corpse, cut off his head, and send it to Xuchang. Chen Qiao said, “This plan must be done at once. Do not delay.” Cao Ren ordered Niu Jin as vanguard, put himself in the center, and set Cao Hong and Cao Chun in support, leaving Chen Qiao with a few soldiers to hold the city while the rest all rode out.

At the first watch they moved out and headed straight for Zhou Yu’s camp. On reaching the gate, they saw not one man, only empty flags and spears. Realizing they had been tricked, they withdrew in haste. Trumpets and firing roared all around. On the east, Han Dang and Jiang Qin struck in; on the west, Zhou Tai and Pan Zhang struck in; on the south, Xu Sheng and Ding Feng struck in; on the north, Chen Wu and Lu Meng struck in. The Wei army was routed; all three routes of their force were broken and no front or rear could aid each other.

Cao Ren broke out with a dozen riders from the crush and happened to meet Cao Hong. He then drove the shattered remnant together and kept running. By dawn they had gone a short distance from Nan County when a drum sounded. Ling Tong again brought another unit and blocked the road, cutting them down in one engagement. Cao Ren broke out diagonally and fled again, and then met Gan Ning for another great slaughter.

Cao Ren dared not return to Nan County. He headed straight for the Xiangyang road. The Wu army gave chase for a while, then withdrew.

Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu steadied the troops, marched directly to the wall of Nan County, and saw flags spread everywhere. A captain on the enemy tower shouted, “Commander, pardon my presumption. I obey the order of the Chief Strategist and have taken the city. I am Zhao Zilong of Changshan.”

Zhou Yu grew furious and ordered an assault. Arrows rained in disordered bursts from above the wall. Zhou Yu recalled everyone briefly to discuss. He ordered Gan Ning to lead several thousand horse and men directly to Jing Province and Ling Tong to lead several thousand horse and men directly to Xiangyang; only then would retaking Nan County not be late.

At that moment a runner arrived: “Zhuge Liang has already won Nan County. He used a military tally to summon the Jing Province garrison by night, while ordering Zhang Fei to attack Jing Province.”

Another runner then arrived: “Xiahou Dun is at Xiangyang. Zhuge Liang sent men with a military tally pretending to be from Cao Ren and drew Dun out. Then Guan Yu attacked Xiangyang and took it.” Zhou Yu said, “How did Zhuge Liang get that tally?” Cheng Pu said, “He has captured Chen Qiao, so all the tallies naturally belong to him.”

Zhou Yu shouted once, and the old wound in his ribs tore open. And then it was said:

How many counties and city walls can any of us truly claim? I have worked with such pain for whom? What will become of us now?

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Ren Battles the Eastern Wu Army; Kongming Provokes Zhou Gongjin for the First Time

chapters.html:
Now as for Zhou Yu, whose courtesy name was Gongjin, when he saw that Zhuge Liang had taken Nan Commandery and later heard that he had also taken Jing and Xiang, how could he not be furious? His old arrow wound was angry again, and it was only after a while that he recovered. The generals repeatedly urged him to calm himself. Yu said, “If we do not kill that rustic fellow Zhuge, how can I still the resentment in my chest? Cheng Demou can help me attack Nan Commandery. We must recover it for Eastern Wu.”

While they were still discussing this, Lu Su, whose courtesy name was Zijing, arrived. Zhou Yu said to him, “I plan to raise troops and go with Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang to decide who is superior and to recover those lost cities. Zijing, I rely on you to help me.”

Lu Su said, “That cannot be done. At this hour Cao Cao still contests with us and the issue is not yet decided. My lord has just besieged Hefei and gained no victory. If we turn on one another and absorb one another’s strength, then if Cao’s soldiers seize the opening and come, our situation will be perilous. Moreover, Liu Xuande was once on good terms with Cao Cao. If we corner him now and make him surrender cities, and he then comes to help attack Eastern Wu, what then is our recourse?”

Yu said, “We devised plans and saved many soldiers and much grain, and he came to grasp what was already at hand. How could I not be angry?”

Zijing said, “Gongjin, please hold. Let me go and meet Xuande myself. I will try to reason with him. If he will not listen, it will not be too late to move troops then.” The generals replied, “Zijing’s words are very good.”

So Lu Su took his attendants and rode straight to Nan Commandery, calling at the gate. Zhao Yun, whose courtesy name was Zilong, came out to inquire. Zijing said, “I have matter for Liu Xuande to hear.”
Zhao Yun replied, “My lord and his strategist are inside the city of Jingzhou.”
Lu Su did not enter Nan Commandery. He rode straight to Jingzhou and saw the battle flags arranged in neat lines and the military array in full order. He thought to himself, “Kongming is truly no ordinary man!”
A soldier reported his arrival and said, “Lu Zijing wishes to be received.”
Zhuge Liang ordered the gates flung wide and had Zijing brought into the hall. After formal courtesy was exchanged, host and guest sat apart. When tea was done, Zijing said, “My lord, the Lord of Wu, and Commander-in-Chief Gongjin have sent me again and again to submit my thoughts on behalf of the Imperial Uncle.
Earlier, Cao Cao brought a host of a million and marched toward Jiangnan, truly with intent to seize the Imperial Uncle. It was only because Eastern Wu drove back Cao’s army that the Imperial Uncle was saved, and all nine commanderies of Jingzhou should therefore properly return to Eastern Wu. But Xuande has used trickery and seized Jing and Xiang; Jiangdong has spent money, grain, and troops for nothing, while the Imperial Uncle reaps the benefits. I doubt this accords with right.”

Zhuge Liang said, “How can Zijing, who is so far-sighted, utter such a line of argument? It is said, ‘What belongs to the lord must return to the lord.’ The nine commanderies of Jing and Xiang are not Eastern Wu’s land; they are the legacy of Liu Jingsheng. My lord is truly his brother. Jingsheng is dead, but his son yet lives. To take Jingzhou through one uncle and nephew—what is wrong with that?”

Zijing said, “If these districts were truly held by Prince Liu Qi, there would be room to explain it. But the prince is in Jiangxia; he is not here.”

Zhuge Liang said, “Does Zijing want to see the prince?” and ordered the attendants to bring him out.

Only two attendants came from behind the screen and raised Liu Qi, who had been seated there.
Liu Qi said to Lu Su, “My body is ill and cannot perform ceremony. Zijing, please forgive me.”
Lu Su was taken aback and fell silent. After some time he said, “If the prince is not present, then what should be done?”
Zhuge Liang said, “If the prince is here, he stays one day. If he is not here, we will decide another way.”
Zijing said, “If the prince is absent, we must return the city to Eastern Wu.”
Zhuge Liang said, “Zijing is correct.” and then held a banquet.

After the banquet Zijing took leave and rode out of the city overnight to his encampment and reported everything that had happened.

Yú said, “Liu Qi is still young and full of vigor. How could he die now? By what day will we recover Jingzhou?”

Zijing said, “Commander-in-Chief, put your trust in me. It rests on Lu Su alone. We must recover Jing and Xiang and return it to Eastern Wu.”
Yu said, “What wise idea do you have, Zijing?”

Zijing said, “I have observed Liu Qi. He has indulged in wine and women to excess, and the sickness has entered to the marrow. His face is already drawn, his breath is labored, and he even coughs blood. In no more than half a year that man must die. When that time comes, go and take Jingzhou then and do not let Liu Bei offer any pretext.”

Although Zhou Yu still smoldered with resentment, a messenger from Sun Quan arrived unexpectedly. Yu ordered him in.

The messenger said, “The Prince is besieging Hefei and has failed repeatedly in battle. He orders you to draw back the main force and send troops immediately to Hefei in aid.”

Zhou Yu could only disband and return to Chaisang to recover his health, ordering Cheng Pu to take command of the warships and soldiers and go to Hefei to serve as Sun Quan directed.

Liu Xuande, after taking Jingzhou, Nan Commandery, and Xiangyang, was greatly pleased and discussed matters of lasting strategy. Then one person came into the hall to present a plan. It was Yi Ji. Liu Bei respected him deeply for old kindness, treated him with full courtesy, sat and asked him.

Yi Ji said, “If you wish to know a long-term design for Jingzhou, why do you not seek a worthy man and ask?”
Liu Bei said, “Where is such a worthy man?”
Yi Ji said, “In the five brothers of the Ma family of Jing and Xiang, all have reputation. The youngest is named Shu and his courtesy name was Youchang. Most able among them is Liang, whose courtesy name was Jichang. A saying in the locality runs, ‘Of the five Ma, the one called Liang with white brows is best.’ Why do you not summon this man and plot with him?”

Liu Bei at once ordered him called in. When Ma Liang arrived, Liu Bei honored him and asked about a plan to hold Jing and Xiang.
Liang said, “Jing and Xiang is a place surrounded by enemies on four sides and hard to defend for long. Send Prince Liu Qi here to recover, and send him letters and orders to comfort old retainers so he holds it; then appoint the prince as Governor of Jing Province to steady the people’s hearts. After that go south to Wuling, Changsha, Guiyang, and Lingling, gather money and grain, and make this your base. That is the strategy for the long term.”

Liu Bei rejoiced and asked, “Of the four commanderies, which should be taken first?”

Liang said, “Lingling is nearest on the west bank of the Xiang River; it can be taken first. Next take Wuling. Then take Guiyang on the east bank of the Xiang. Let Changsha come last.”

Liu Bei made Ma Liang a staff aide and placed Yi Ji as his deputy, then asked Zhuge Liang to discuss sending Liu Qi back to Xiangyang and asking Guan Yu to return to Jingzhou. He then ordered up troops to take Lingling, appointing Zhang Fei as vanguard and Zhao Yun as support. Zhuge Liang and Liu Bei formed the center with fifteen thousand horse and men. He left Guan Yu to defend Jingzhou and ordered Mi Zhu and Liu Feng to hold Jiangling.

As for the Magistrate of Lingling, Liu Du, he heard that Liu Bei’s cavalry had arrived and discussed matters with his son Liu Xian.

Liu Xian said, “Father, do not worry. Though he has Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun in bravery, my local man Xing Dao-rong can meet ten thousand men and resist him.”

Liu Du therefore ordered Liu Xian and Xing Dao-rong to lead over ten thousand troops, leave the city three dozen li, settle by mountain and water, and pitch camp. A scout came and said, “Kongming has arrived, leading an army.” Dao-rong brought out the troops to battle.

The two formations stood facing each other in a full circle. Dao-rong came forward, took up a giant axe for breaking rocks, and cried out in a loud voice, “How dare rebels invade my territory?”

A cluster of yellow banners was seen in the opposing formation. Where the gate banner opened, a four-wheeled cart rolled out. Seated at its front was one man, his head wrapped in a silk kerchief, a crane-hued cloak on his shoulders, a feather fan in hand. He beckoned to Dao-rong and said, “I am Zhuge Liang of Nanyang. Cao Cao led a host of a million; I used a small stratagem and killed them so that none returned with even a scrap of armor. How can you stand against me? I have come to submit you to my terms. Why not surrender now?”

Dao-rong laughed loudly and said, “The battle at Red Cliffs was Zhou Lang’s stratagem. What matter is this to you? How dare you come and lie to us?”

He charged with that great axe. Zhuge Liang wheeled around his cart and withdrew to the rear of his formation, then the formation gate closed again. Dao-rong charged straight on and killed through, and the formation split in two and opened wide as it moved. Gazing from afar at the central cluster of yellow banners, he took that for Zhuge Liang and pressed on after it. When he reached the foot of the hill the yellow banners jammed fast; suddenly the center parted and vanished. The four-wheeled cart was gone, and there stood a general with a spear, leaping onto his horse and crying out as he came straight for Dao-rong. He was Zhang Yide.

Dao-rong brought his great axe to meet him. They fought but a few exchanges; his strength gave out, and he turned his horse and fled. Zhang Fei followed with a roar as a reserve burst from the flank on both sides. Dao-rong charged forward with a death rush, but before him stood another general blocking his way. That man shouted, “Do you recognize Zhao Zilong of Changshan?”

Realizing he could not withstand him and with no place to run, Dao-rong dismounted and surrendered. The two brought him into the camp and presented him before Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang. Liu Bei ordered him to be beheaded.

Zhuge Liang hurried to stop him and asked Dao-rong, “If you help us capture Liu Xian, I will allow you to submit.”

Dao-rong instantly offered to do so.

Zhuge Liang said, “By what method will you capture him?”

Dao-rong said, “If the Strategist permits me to return, I have a clever explanation ready. This night, the Strategist will lead men to seize the camp. I will be the inside accomplice and take Liu Xian alive to present to the Strategist. Once Liu Xian is captured, Liu Du will surely surrender.”

Liu Bei did not believe him.

Zhuge Liang said, “General Xing is not a vain speaker,” and released Dao-rong.

Dao-rong returned to camp and reported what had passed to Liu Xian.
Liu Xian asked, “What can we do now?”
Dao-rong said, “Counter with a counterstroke. This night place troops in ambush outside the camp. Raise false banners inside camp as a lure. When Zhuge Liang comes to seize the camp, capture him.”

Liu Xian followed the plan. At second watch of the night there truly came a band of soldiers to the camp gate, each carrying bundles of dry grass. They all set them alight at once. Liu Xian and Dao-rong rushed forward and killed at the gate. As the fire troops withdrew, Liu Xian and Dao-rong’s two forces pursued on the momentum and chased them for over ten li, then both commands disappeared.

Liu Xian and Dao-rong were startled and quickly rode back to their own camp. The flames still burned. From the camp a general stood out; he was Zhang Yide.

Liu Xian shouted to Dao-rong, “Do not go in. Go first and seize Kongming’s camp.”
So they turned back.

They had not gone ten li when Zhao Yun led a unit and burst out through a diagonal pass, driving a spear through Dao-rong’s horse and pinning him under it. Liu Xian then spurred away in haste. Behind him Zhang Fei came and leapt down from his horse, taking him alive and binding him before Zhuge Liang.
Xian confessed, “General Xing-rong gave me this course; it was not from my own heart.”

Zhuge Liang ordered his bonds undone, had him put on clothes, and gave him wine to settle him. He sent him back to the city with orders: tell his father to surrender; if he did not, the city would be stormed and the whole household exterminated.

Liu Xian rode back to Lingling and reported fully to his father Liu Du, praising Zhuge Liang’s virtue. He urged his father to surrender. Liu Du agreed. He raised a white flag on the city wall, flung wide the gates, and came out carrying seals and ribbons to submit to Liu Bei’s main camp.

Zhuge Liang kept Liu Du as prefect of the commandery, and Liu Xian was sent to Jingzhou to serve with the army. The residents of Lingling were altogether pleased.

When Liu Bei had finished pacifying the city and rewarding the three armies, he asked his commanders, “Lingling has been taken. Who now dares take Guiyang Commandery?”

Zhao Yun answered, “I am willing to go.”
Zhang Fei strode out and said, “I too am willing to go!”

The two argued. Zhuge Liang said, “After all, it is Zilong who volunteered first. Send only him.” Zhang Fei refused and insisted on going.

Zhuge Liang called for drawing lots. The lot fell to Zilong.
Again it fell to Zilong.
Zhang Fei shouted in anger, “I need no one to aid me; I can take the commandery with three thousand troops alone.”
Zhao Yun said, “I too will lead only three thousand troops. If I fail to take the city, I will answer the army’s order.”

Zhuge Liang was greatly pleased and drafted a formal order, selecting three thousand picked troops and assigning them to Zhao Yun. Zhang Fei still refused, and Liu Bei sent him away.

Zhao Yun, with three thousand men and horses, rode straight to Guiyang at speed.

An advance scout had already reported his arrival to Zhao Fan, magistrate of Guiyang. Fan quickly gathered the people and deliberated. The official colonels Chen Ying and Bao Long offered to lead troops into battle. It was said that both men were from hunting villages in the hills around Guiyang. Chen Ying could wield a flying trident; Bao Long had once shot two tigers. Proud of themselves in courage and strength, they told Zhao Fan, “If Liu Bei comes, the two of us will be the vanguard.”

Fan said, “I have heard Liu Xuande is the Imperial Uncle of the Great Han. On top of that, Kongming is clever, and Guan Yunchang and Zhang Yide are supremely brave. Zhao Zilong now comes leading troops. In this field of Dangyang the million-strong army at Changban as though it were empty ground. How many men have we in Guiyang? We should not meet him in battle; we should submit.”

Chen Ying said, “I ask leave to meet you on the field. If we cannot capture Zhao Yun then, no delay in surrendering the prefecture will follow.”

Zhao Fan could not press him and allowed them to go.

Chen Ying marched out with three thousand men. Soon he saw Zhao Yun’s army arriving. He arrayed his force and sent a horseman with a forked spear flying forth. Zhao Yun raised his spear and rode out.

“My lord Liu Bei is Liu Xuande, elder brother to Lord Jing. He has come with Kongming to comfort the people, while jointly governing Jingzhou with Prince Liu Qi. Why do you meet us with battle?” Zhao Yun shouted.

Chen Ying shouted back, “We acknowledge only Cao Chancellor. How can we yield to Liu Bei?”

Zhao Yun grew furious. He raised his spear, urged his horse hard, and charged straight at Chen Ying. Chen Ying twined his forked spear to receive him. Their horses met, and they fought for four or five exchanges. Chen Ying found he could not match him and turned his horse away. Zhao Yun pursued.

Chen Ying looked back at Zhao Yun’s nearing horse and threw his flying trident. Zhao Yun caught it and cast it back at Chen Ying. Chen Ying dodged, and Zhao Yun’s horse arrived first; he took Chen Ying alive off his horse and threw him to the ground, shouting to the soldiers to bind and return him to camp.

The defeated army scattered and fled.
Zhao Yun entered camp and roared at Chen Ying, “How dare you dare face us! I do not kill you now; go back and tell Zhao Fan: he should come in at once and submit.”

Chen Ying apologized and fled in shame, then returned to the city and told Zhao Fan everything.
Fan said, “I wanted to surrender, but you forced me to fight and caused this.”
He then sent Chen Ying away and, carrying the seals and ribbons, rode out with a dozen riders to surrender at the main camp.

Zhao Yun came out to receive him, entertained him as honored guest and poured wine to drink. They drank together.

When several rounds had passed, Fan said, “My general’s surname is Zhao; mine is also Zhao. Five hundred years ago we were one family. General is truly from Zhen Ding, and I am also from Zhen Ding; we share a native place as well. If you do not disdain this, it would be our good fortune to make brothers. That would be blessed.”

Zhao Yun was greatly pleased, and they exchanged age reckoning. Zhao and Fan had the same age. They were within about four months of each other, and Fan promptly swore brotherhood with Zhao. Being same town, same age, and same surname, the two fit one another well.

When the banquet ended, Fan left and returned to the city.

The next day Fan invited Zhao Yun into the city to pacify the people. Zhao Yun told his soldiers not to move and entered with only fifty riders. Residents held incense and knelt in the road to welcome him. After Zhao Yun settled the town, Fan invited him to drink in the official hall.

By the time the wine had worked to half measure, Fan called him back into a deeper chamber and refilled the cups. Zhao Yun, slightly drunk, saw that Fan had called in a woman, and he shared her cups as he drank. Zhao Yun noticed her beauty in plain white cloth and asked Fan, “Who is she?”

Fan answered, “That is my sister-in-law, Madam Fan.”

Zilong showed deference and changed his expression accordingly.

Fan asked her to retire from the inner chamber. Zhao Yun said, “Why must we trouble our brother-in-law to raise her cup?”
Fan laughed and said, “There is a reason. Pray do not object. My elder brother died three years ago, and my sister-in-law remains a widow. Her household is not settled. I have often urged her to remarry. She said, ‘Only if one man can satisfy three conditions will I marry. First, he must be master of both letters and arms and famed through the world. Second, he must have a stately appearance and distinguished deportment. Third, he must share my brother-in-law’s surname.’ Tell me, how can this happen so exactly in this world?
Now your imposing appearance and name shake all the lands under heaven, and you share the same surname as my brother-in-law. You match every condition exactly. If you do not despise my sister-in-law’s plain looks, I am ready to offer the match as bridewealth. Would this not make for ties across the generations?”

Zhao Yun rose in sudden rage and cried, “I have already made Fan my brother; his wife is therefore my sister-in-law. How can you make this outrage upon the order of kinship?”

Fan, ashamed and humiliated, his face flushed, replied, “I only meant to treat you well. How can this be so rude?”
He fixed his eyes on the attendants in a threatening way.

Zhao Yun saw it, struck him once, knocking him down, then walked out through the gate, mounted, and rode from the city.

Fan immediately summoned Chen Ying and Bao Long for consultation.

Chen Ying said, “This man left in anger. We only need to fight him and kill him.”
Fan said, “I fear I cannot defeat him.”
Bao Long said, “The two of us have already feigned surrender and entered his camp. The prefect has brought out troops to wrestle with us and we two were only waiting on the field to capture him. We must do it that way.”

Chen Ying said, “We must bring some soldiers with us.”
Bao Long said, “Five hundred riders are enough.”

That night both men led five hundred troops straight to Zhao Yun’s camp and surrendered.

Zhao Yun already suspected the trick and had them called in. The two commanders said under his tent, “Zhao Fan intended to use the beauty snare to lure the general. He was waiting for him to become drunk, then carry him into the inner hall and slay him and send your head to Cao Chancellor as a boast. This is inhuman. Because you heard the general grow angry and ride away, we were tainted by it and therefore came to surrender.”

Zhao Yun feigned joy and gave them wine to drink with him. When both were drunk, he had them bound in the tent and questioned their men. It proved a fake surrender.
Zhao Yun called in the five hundred soldiers, gave them food and wine, and ordered, “The would-be killers are Chen Ying and Bao Long; the rest are not to blame. Do what I say, and you shall all be richly rewarded.”
The soldiers bowed in thanks. He executed Chen and Bao on the spot and then ordered the five hundred to lead the way. Zhao Yun brought up one thousand soldiers behind them and by night reached Guiyang’s gate at a run.

The city watch heard and relayed that Chen and Bao had killed Zhao Yun and returned, asking the magistrate to confer. The men on the ramparts set the watch fires, but it was plainly their own troops that had arrived.

Fan hurried out of the city. Zhao Yun told the guards to seize him, then entered, calmed the people, and stabilized the situation before sending fast word to Liu Bei.

Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang came in person to Guiyang. Zhao Yun welcomed them into the city and pushed Zhao Fan down to the steps.

Zhuge Liang asked, “What happened? Tell me about the matter of your sister-in-law.”

Zhuge Liang said to Zhao Yun, “This is also a good thing, and yet why have you done so?”

Zhao Yun said, “If I marry Fan’s sister-in-law after he has made me brother, one, people would revile me. Two, that woman would remarry and lose her proper chastity. Three, Fan has just submitted and his heart is uncertain. Master, my lord has only newly settled the lands of Jianghan, and my bedding is not yet firm. How could I dare to forsake my lord’s great affairs for one woman?”

Liu Bei said, “Great matters have been decided today. Would you take her or not?”

Zhao Yun said, “There are many women in the world. I fear only that I cannot establish my reputation. What lack of wife and children would follow?”

Liu Bei said, “Zilong, you are a true man.”

He released Zhao Fan, kept him as magistrate of Guiyang, and greatly rewarded Zhao Yun.

Zhang Fei shouted, “All the merit was won by Zilong, while I am deemed useless! Give me three thousand troops and let me take Wuling. I will capture its prefect, Jin Xuan, and offer him in surrender!”

Zhuge Liang was pleased and said, “Yide, you may go if you wish, but you must obey one condition.”

The strategist won by many strange stratagems; the soldiers and officers competed to establish battle merit.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang's Clever Words to Lu Su, Zhao Zilong's Plan to Take Guiyang

chapters.html:
Guan Yu, by righteousness, pardons and releases Huang with the courtesy name Hansheng.
Sun Zhongmou wages a great battle with Zhang Wenyuan.

Earlier, Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, told Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, “When Zilong went to take Guiyang Commandery, he issued a military order first. Today Yide is going to take Wuling; he must also issue a military order if he is to lead soldiers away.”

So Zhang Fei drafted the order at once, and with pleasure he led three thousand soldiers, riding overnight into the Wuling border.

When Jin Xuan heard Zhang Fei had brought men, he gathered the officers and checked the fine weapons and armor before leading his troops out to meet him.

Gong Zhi, one of his attendants, advised, “Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, is the Han imperial uncle; benevolence and righteousness are spread through the world because of him. Besides, Zhang Yide is extraordinarily fierce and brave. Do not meet him in battle. Better to accept his surrender from the start.”

Jin Xuan grew angry. “Do you mean to make hidden correspondence with a bandit and bring treason from within?” he shouted, and ordered guards to be thrown out and beheaded.

All the officers pleaded at once, “If we execute our own man first, it will be harmful to the army.”

Jin Xuan dismissed Gong Zhi and brought out his soldiers himself. At twenty li beyond the city, they were just meeting Zhang Fei. Zhang Fei stood in his saddle with his spear raised and bellowed loud enough to shake the air.

Jin Xuan asked his officers, “Who dares to ride out first?” None of them dared approach.

Jin Xuan himself spurred forward, his horse prancing, and flourished his sword to fight.

Zhang Fei gave one mighty cry like thunder. Jin Xuan paled and would not dare to force a close clash. He turned his horse to flee. Zhang Fei pressed forward with his full army and struck him in pursuit.

When Jin Xuan reached the city gate, a confusion of arrows poured down from above. He looked around in alarm and saw Gong Zhi standing upon the wall.

“Because you did not follow Heaven’s timing, you have walked into ruin with your own head. I and the common people already surrendered to Liu yesterday,” Gong Zhi said.

Before the sentence was finished, an arrow struck Jin Xuan in the face and he fell from his horse. The soldiers cut off his head and offered it to Zhang Fei. Gong Zhi came out, surrendered, and was taken in.

Zhang Fei ordered Gong Zhi to carry the seal and tallies and go to Guiyang to meet Liu Bei. Liu Bei rejoiced greatly and immediately appointed him to Jin Xuan’s post.

Liu Bei then rode to Wuling to settle the people, and sent a rider to report to Guan Yu, saying, “You have each taken one commandery—Wing and Yide and Zilong. If this elder brother does not consider me unworthy, then let Guan this brother render that meritorious service well.”

Liu Bei ordered Zhang Fei to leave by night, to hold Jingzhou in place for Guan Yu, and told Guan to go and take Changsha.

When Guan Yu arrived, he appeared before Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang.

Zhuge Liang said, “Zilong took Guiyang; Yide took Wuling. Each moved with three thousand men. Changsha’s Administrator Han Xuan is not hard to defeat by force alone. But he has one formidable general, a man from Nanyang named Huang, courtesy name Hansheng, given name Zhong. He had once been a Zhonglang Jiang under Liu Biao and then guarded Changsha together with Liu Biao’s nephew Liu Pan. He now serves Han Xuan. Though he is near sixty years old, he has courage of ten thousand men. Do not lightly underestimate him. If Guan goes, he must bring many horsemen.”

Guan Yu replied, “Why does the Military Adviser dampen another’s sharpness and weaken his own authority? Can this old man really matter so much?”

“Guan does not need three thousand men. Five hundred of my own blade-men will do. I will definitely cut down Huang Zhong and Han Xuan’s head and bring them in as trophies for our banners.”

Liu Bei tried to block him. Guan Yu ignored him and departed with just five hundred blade-men.

Zhuge Liang said to Liu Bei, “Guan is underestimating Huang Zhong. I fear something might go wrong. My lord should go and support him.”

Liu Bei followed, then brought up the troops and set out toward Changsha.

Now Han Xuan, the Administrator of Changsha, was a man of quick temper and light hand in killing. His people all hated him.

When he heard Guan Yu’s army had arrived, he summoned his old general Huang Zhong at once.

Huang Zhong said, “Your lord need not worry. With my own blade and this one bow, one thousand men will come, one thousand men will die.”

Huang Zhong was in fact able to draw the two-shi bow and strike true a hundred times.

Before he finished speaking, a man from below the stair called out, “There is no need for the old general to ride out. Leave it to my hands to capture Guan alive.”

Han Xuan saw it was the commandant’s officer Yang Ling and was pleased. He ordered Yang Ling out with one thousand men to rush out from the city.

After about fifty li, they saw where the dust rose. Guan’s cavalry was already there.

Yang Ling lifted his spear in the saddle and stepped before the line, cursing and shouting for battle.

Guan Yu became furious and did not answer a word. He wheeled, spun his blade, and struck straight at Yang Ling. Yang Ling came forward with his spear.

Within three bouts, Guan’s blade came down and Yang Ling lay cut down at the horse’s feet.

He pursued the survivors and routed them all the way to the city’s foot.

Han Xuan was greatly startled, so he ordered Huang Zhong out to fight.

He watched from the top of the wall. Huang Zhong raised his blade, spurred his horse, and rode five hundred riders across the hanging bridge.

Seeing the old general ride out, Guan Yu recognized him. He spread the five hundred blade-men in one line, set his sword and raised his horse, and said, “Are you perhaps Huang Zhong, old general?”

Huang Zhong replied, “Since you already know my name, how dare you step on my ground?”

Guan answered, “I came specifically to take your head.”

With that, their two horses clashed in close combat and they fought for more than a hundred exchanges without any clear result.

Han Xuan feared Huang Zhong might lose, and sounded the drum to pull him back. Huang Zhong withdrew his men into the city.

Guan Yu also withdrew, setting camp ten li outside the gates. In his heart, he thought: “Old General Huang Zhong’s fame is no empty boast. We fought for a hundred rounds and found no flaw in him. On another day I will use the dragging-blade stratagem and cut him from the flank.”

The next morning, after breakfast, he returned to the city and resumed engagement.

Han Xuan sat on the wall and ordered Huang Zhong out again.

Huang Zhong rode across the hanging bridge with a few hundred riders and met Guan again.

They fought another fifty or sixty rounds, with no one winning. The two armies shouted themselves hoarse.

When the drumbeats surged, Guan feinted and turned away with his horse.

Huang Zhong chased after him. Just as Guan Yu raised his sword to strike, he heard a sharp sound behind his head. He turned and saw Huang Zhong unseated as the horse’s foreleg had slipped and he was thrown onto the ground.

Guan rode back and shouted with both hands raised, “I will spare your life! Change horses at once and meet me again to continue!”

Huang Zhong quickly lifted his horse by the stirrup, sprang into the saddle, and fled back into the city.

Han Xuan asked why.

Huang Zhong said, “This horse had not seen two battlefield rides for a long time, so it failed.”

Han said, “Your arrows are true in a hundred shots. Why did you not shoot?”

Huang Zhong replied, “Tomorrow there will be another battle. I must use deception. I will feign defeat and lure him to the hanging bridge, then shoot there.”

Liu Bei gave his own blue horse to Huang Zhong, who bowed and withdrew.

He thought to himself, “It is rare that Guan Yu has such righteous feeling. He could not bring himself to kill me; how can I then shoot him? If I do not shoot, I may be disobeying orders.”

That night he hesitated and could not settle his mind.

At dawn the next day, reports came that Guan was challenging another engagement.

Huang Zhong led out his men. Guan Yu, frustrated at two days’ stalemate, gathered himself and clashed with Huang again.

Not even thirty rounds had passed when Huang feigned defeat and pulled back. Guan charged in.

Huang, remembering yesterday’s mercy, did not dare to shoot. He checked his blade and only drew and released the bowstring. Guan dodged quickly, and no arrow came.

Guan charged again. Again Huang only pretended and drew the string with force but no arrow.

Guan dodged again. Thinking Huang could not shoot, he pressed forward, secure in himself.

Near the hanging bridge, Huang Zhong took position upon it, drew and released. The bowstring snapped like a thunderclap, and the arrow flew to strike exactly at the base of Guan’s helmet tassel.

The front rank of soldiers cried out in one voice.

Startled, Guan Yu took back the line of battle and returned to camp. Only then did he realize that Huang Zhong truly could shoot through one hundred paces; and today he had aimed only at his helmet tassel as repayment for yesterday’s mercy.

Guan withdrew with his army.

Huang Zhong rode into the city to report to Han Xuan.

Han Xuan shouted for him to be arrested. Huang Zhong cried out, “No guilt!”

Han Xuan grew angry: “I have watched these three days. You dare deceive me! The first day you did not fight hard, so your heart was not sincere. Yesterday your horse slipped, and he did not kill you. He certainly has secret ties with Guan. Today you gave two false draws of the bowstring, and the third arrow struck the center of his helmet exactly. If he is not beheaded, he will be a danger later!”

He ordered that a slayer with an axe be pushed outside the city gate and strike him down.

Some captains tried to speak in plea.

Han Xuan said, “If anyone asks that Huang be spared, that person is guilty of the same crime.”

Just as they had pushed him outside the gate, with the axe already raised, a general suddenly cut his way in and hacked down the executioner's swordsman. He pulled Huang Zhong up and shouted, “Huang Zhong, whose courtesy name was Hansheng, is the very pillar of Changsha. To kill him is to kill the people of Changsha. Han Xuan is cruel and lacking in humanity, he despises men of virtue. Let us execute him before all! Whoever wishes to follow me, come!”

Everyone saw him. His face was dark-red and his eyes shone like bright stars. He was Wei Yan of Yiyang.

He had chased after Liu Bei from Xiangyang and reached Han Xuan too late, then submitted. Liu Bei had found him arrogant and rude and refused to elevate him, and so he had been left constrained there.

On that day he rescued Huang Zhong. He called the citizens and, raising his bare arms with a shout, several hundred followed him.

Huang could not withstand them.

Wei Yan cut his way straight up to the city tower and in a single stroke split Han Xuan in two.

He took the head up on horseback, led the citizens out of the city, and bowed toward Guan Yu.

Guan Yu rejoiced and entered the city, finishing pacification, then invited Huang Zhong to meet him. Huang offered pretense of illness and did not come out.

Guan sent immediately for Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang.

Now Liu Bei, while Guan was coming to take Changsha, was pressing on behind with Zhuge Liang to dispatch men and support in time.

As he rode, a blue banner curled backward in the wind. A single crow flew from north to south, called three times, and passed on.
