Battle boats packed tightly upon the river, advancing one after another. As they came to Gong’an, not one warship was to be seen and not a man appeared to receive them. Zhou Yu urged the boats forward. Within ten li of Jing, the river lay flat and still.

A scout called back: “On the wall of Jing, two white flags are raised and no man’s shadow is to be seen.”

Zhou Yu suspected trouble. He had his boat pulled close to shore and disembarked himself. Taking Gan Ning, Xu Sheng, and Ding Feng, he led three thousand elite men and their attendants directly toward Jing.

When he arrived beneath the city wall, there was no movement.

Zhou Yu pulled up his horse and ordered a soldier to call at the gate.

The city asked, “Who comes?”

The Wu troops answered, “The Chief Commander of Eastern Wu, Zhou, comes in person.”

Before the reply was done, a clapper rang sharply. The city’s battlements sprang up with spears and blades.

From the gatehouse, Zhao Yun appeared.

“What is the reason for your arrival?” Zhou Yu called.

“Do you not yet know,” Zhao Yun said, “that Kongming has already seen your stratagem of using a false route to destroy Guo and kept Zhao Yun here?”

“My lord has said,” Zhao Yun continued, “that Liu Bei and I are both kinsmen in the Han household. Can we bear such betrayal and still take Xichuan? If your Eastern Wu truly intends to take Shu, I will tear my hair and flee to the hills before all the world, and I will not break my word.”

Hearing this, Zhou Yu reined in and rode back. At that moment a man bearing a command flag came before him, shouting at the horse:

“We have learned that four columns of troops are advancing together to seize you. Guan has come from Jiangling, Zhang Fei from Zigui, Huang Zhong from Gong’an, and Wei Yan from Yiling’s mountain pass. How many troops there are no one can tell. Their shouts are shaking the sound over the hundred li. They all say they come to capture Zhou Yu.”

Mounted there and then, Zhou Yu cried out in one voice. His bow and lance split apart and snapped, and he threw himself from the horse.

The rest is told like this:

A masterful move in chess makes opposition hard to match; all these calculations are now turned to empty wind.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Cao Holds a Great Banquet at Bronze Sparrow Terrace; Zhuge Liang Angers Zhou Gongjin Thrice

chapters.html:
Zhou Yu, whose courtesy name was Gongjin, had his anger fill his chest and fell from his horse. He was quickly rescued and brought back to the ship. Soldiers on his boat reported, “Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, are up on the ridge top ahead, drinking and enjoying themselves.” Zhou Yu snapped through clenched teeth, “You think I cannot take Xichuan? I swear I will take it.” Just then, he was told that Sun Quan had sent his brother Sun Yu.

Zhou Yu took him in and heard the matter. Sun Yu said, “I came on my brother’s command to assist the commander-in-chief.” He then ordered the army onward. They reached Bāqiū, and news came that Liu Feng and Guan Ping were leading troops there and had blocked the waterway. Zhou Yu grew all the more furious. Soon after, he heard that Kongming had sent a letter.

Zhou Yu broke the seal and read:

To the camp of Master Gongjin, the Eastern Wu Great Commander: From Zhuge Liang, the Han Army Advisor and General of the Imperial Guards,

Since we parted at Chaisang, I have not forgotten you once. I have heard that you intend to march for Xichuan; in my judgment, this is not feasible. Yizhou has fierce people and rough terrain. Although Liu Zhang is obscure and weak, he is enough to defend on his own. Now you have marched far to exert your strength and moved ten thousand li from home. Even if you are hoping to secure a complete victory, I do not think Wu Qi could plan it and Sun Wu could manage what comes after.

Cao Cao lost at Red Cliffs; is his ambition to forget his blood-feud so soon?

You now raise the army and go on this distant expedition; if Cao Cao seizes the opening and comes south, Jiangnan will surely be reduced to dust. I cannot bear to stand idle and watch.

Please accept this report in grace.

When Zhou Yu had finished reading, he let out one long sigh, called for paper and brush, and drafted a letter to Sun Quan.

He then gathered his officers and said, “I do not say that I do not want to serve loyally and repay the state, but heaven’s mandate has already been cut. Serve your Lord Wu well and complete the great work together.” He spoke and collapsed.

After a while, he regained his senses. Looking toward heaven, he sighed once more, “If Zhaolong was born, why was Kongming born too?” he called three or four times and then died. He was thirty-six years old.

Later, someone composed this elegiac verse:

Heroic glory remained after Red Cliffs, a youth with noble fame. Your lute and song knew noble feeling; the cup was raised in parting to men of worth. You once summoned three thousand measures, and often drove out an army of one hundred thousand. Baqiu was your last place of death, and lamentation there still bruises the heart.

Zhou Yu’s mourning lay at Baqiu. The officers bundled the letters he had left, sealed them, and sent riders to report to Sun Quan. When Sun Quan heard that Zhou Yu had died, he wailed. He opened the letter and then wrote a brief recommendation:

Gongjin’s talent was plain, yet he had been singled out for exceptional favor. He was trusted as a close attendant and placed in command of men and horses. How could he not have strained every limb and thought to make his contribution? But life and death are unpredictable and length is decreed by heaven. My designs are unfulfilled, and my meager body has already fallen—how great is the grief of what I left undone?

At this moment Cao Cao is in the north and the front is not at peace. Liu Bei is housed here like a tiger fed and kept warm; the affairs of all under heaven are still uncertain. This is the season when scholars of the morning and evening think late into the night, and it is fitting for the Son of Heaven to be worried.

Lu Su is faithful and heroic; he does not act carelessly in danger. He can take up this post in Zhou Yu’s place. “One whose death is near speaks with good intent.”

If he grants his kindness, Zhou Yu’s name will not perish.

Sun Quan read to the end and wept: “Gongjin had the talent of a royal adviser. To die so early and so suddenly—how can I rely on that now? He has already named Zijing in his final letter. How can I not obey?” That very day he appointed Lu Su as Great Commander and ordered him to take charge of all troops. At once he instructed that Zhou Yu’s coffin be returned for burial.

Elsewhere, in Jingzhou, Kongming observed the stars through the night and saw a star of command falling to earth. He said with a laugh, “Zhou Yu is dead.” At dawn he reported this to Liu Bei.

Liu Bei sent men to verify it and it proved true. He asked Kongming, “Now that Zhou Yu has died, what are we to do?”

Kongming replied, “He who should now command in place of Zhou Yu will certainly be Lu Su. The stars are gathering in the east. Let us go to Jiangdong on the pretext of mourning and make one tour there, then look for worthy men to assist our lord.”

Liu Bei said, “I fear only that officers in Wu might seize you.”

Kongming said, “While Zhou Yu was alive, I did not still hesitate. Now that he is gone, what need to fear?” He took Zhao Yun and five hundred soldiers, prepared mourning rites, stepped onto the riverboat, and sailed to Baqiu to attend the funeral.

On the way he had already heard that Sun Quan had named Lu Su as Great Commander and already sent Zhou Yu’s coffin back to Chaisang. Kongming went straight to Chaisang. Lu Su welcomed him with formality. The officers of Zhou Yu all wanted to kill Kongming, but seeing that Zhao Yun followed armed with sword in hand, they dared not strike.

Kongming ordered offerings placed before the spirit, poured wine himself, knelt on the ground, and read the mourning prose:

Alas, Master Gongjin! To die so young is not fortunate; life and death are heaven’s ordinance, and yet who could remain unhurt? My heart truly aches; I pour out this cup of libation. May you have spirit to receive it and share my heartfelt offering.

I mourn you, who as a youth won the friendship of Bofu for right conduct; you gave away wealth in righteousness, and gave up shelter with gracious ease. I mourn you, who at that tender age, like a roc spanning ten thousand li, set down a great enterprise and took possession of Jiangnan. I mourn you, with strength in full bloom, guarding Baqiu from afar; as Jing Sheng bore concern, he feared no trouble in quelling rebels. I mourn you, whose deportment was refined, and whose match with Little Qiao was worthy. As son-in-law to a Han officer, you did not fail your age. I mourn you, for your force of spirit and sense: in counsel you restrained what should be resisted and admitted what was right. Though in your beginning your wings were folded, in the end you could still spread them. I mourn you for Poyang, where Jiang Gan spoke; every movement was natural, and your breadth of mind and lofty aspiration were obvious.

I mourn you for your vast ability, in both civilian and martial planning. Through fire attack you shattered the enemy, turning strength into weakness. I remember you in former days, majestic and heroic; I grieve at your early death, and lie in the earth as if blood would run from me.

The heart of loyalty and righteousness, the breath of a heroic spirit; through three cycles of life your name will stretch across a hundred generations. I mourn you, my grief is keen, my entrails tied in a thousand knots. My loyal heart and true intentions have no end in their sorrow. The sky dimmed darkly, and three armies grew heavy-hearted. The lord wept in mourning, and friends cried tear upon tear.

Kǒngmíng is not talented, only begging for plans and counsel. I sought to help Wu resist Cao Cao, to aid Han and steady Liu. As mutually supporting wings, they answer each other from head to tail. Whether life or death comes to me, what fear is left then?

Alas, Master Gongjin—life and death part us forever! Preserve your chastity and uprightness in the dark and unseen. If your soul still has spirit, let it witness my heart. From this day onward there is no one in all the world who truly hears me. Alas! I beg your posthumous favor at this table!

After finishing, Kongming lay on the ground and wept bitterly, tears gushing like springs. His grief and crying did not end. All the officers and generals there said, “Everyone says Gongjin and Kongming were never in harmony; now seeing how he mourns him, all such talk is empty.” Lu Su, seeing how deeply Kongming wept, was himself moved and thought, “Kongming is naturally full of feeling, while Gongjin had narrow judgment. He brought his own death upon himself.”

There was also a later elegiac verse:

The Sleeping Dragon of Nanyang has not yet awakened, and the constellations gather again in Shuocheng. Since Heaven has already given us Gongjin, why does Kongming still need to appear in this world?

Lu Su hosted him in a banquet. After the banquet, Kongming took his leave and prepared to return. As he was about to step down to the boat, one man on the riverbank—robe, bamboo hat, black stringed belt, white shoes—gripped Kongming by the arm and laughed hard. “You rejoiced at Zhaolong’s death and now come to offer mourning. Do you think Eastern Wu has no people and that I am fooled?”

Kongming looked at him sharply and recognized him as Master Fengchou, Pang Tong. Kongming also laughed heartily. The two clasped hands and climbed into the boat, where they exchanged what weighed on their hearts.

Kongming gave him a letter and said, “I believe Sun Zhongmou can never fully employ you. If things become even slightly unfavorable, you can come to Jingzhou and help Liu Bei. This man is broad, humane, and generous, and he will not fail what he learned in all his life in fairness.” Pang Tong agreed and they parted. Kongming returned to Jingzhou.

Lu Su then sent Zhou Yu’s coffin to Wūhú, where Sun Quan met and mourned him and then ordered a full burial in his native place. Zhou Yu had two sons and one daughter—his eldest was Xun, and his second Yin. Sun Quan gave them generous aid.

Lu Su said, “I, Lu Su, am a tiresome and mediocre man. I have been overly praised by Gongjin and truly unfit for this office. I wish to recommend one man to aid our lord. He can master astronomy and understand terrain. His strategizing is not inferior to Guan or Yue; he can match Sun and Wu in matters of state at the pivot. Zhou Gong often used his words, and Kongming deeply respects his mind. Why in Jiangnan should we not make use of him?”

When Sun Quan heard this, he was glad and asked who the man was. Lu Su said, “This man is from Xiangyang, surname Pang, name Tong, courtesy name Shiyuan. His courtesy title is Master Fengchou.” Sun Quan said, “I have heard of him for a long time. Since he has already come, have him presented at once.”

So Lu Su invited Pang Tong to come before Sun Quan. After due ceremony, they presented themselves. Sun Quan saw him, with thick eyebrows, hooked nose, dark face, short black beard, and an odd countenance, and felt displeasure. He asked, “What is Master Zijing’s learning based upon?”

Pang replied, “Need not cling to one rule; one should respond according to changing circumstance.”

Sun Quan said, “How does your talent compare with Gongjin?”

Pang answered with a smile, “My own learning is very different from Gongjin’s.” Sun Quan, who had always loved Zhou Yu above all, looked down on Pang even more and said, “Then stand down for now. If ever your usefulness is needed, I will summon you.”

Pang took a long sigh and left.

Lu Su asked, “Lord, why do you not employ Shiyuan?”

Sun Quan said, “He is a wild man. What use is there in using him?”

Lu Su answered, “At Red Cliffs in that pitched battle, this man once offered the linked-wheel strategy, winning the first merit. Your lordship surely knows this.”

Sun Quan said, “At that moment it was Cao Cao who sought to burn his own ships, not this man’s merit. I swear I will not use him.”

After Lu Su had come out, he told Pang Tong, “Do not think it is that I do not recommend you; the ruler of Wu simply refuses you. You can only endure this for now.”

Pang bowed his head and sighed deeply.

Lu Su asked, “Does Master not mean to stay in Wu at all?”

Pang did not answer. Lu Su said, “You bear talent that could support the world and turn any direction to profit. Tell me plainly: where do you intend to go?”

Pang replied, “I intend to go to Cao Cao.”

Lu Su answered, “That is like throwing a bright pearl into the dark. Go instead to Jingzhou to assist Liu Bei. He will surely use you.”

Pang said, “It is truly my intention. Earlier I was jesting.”

Lu Su said, “I will send a letter recommending you. If you assist Xuande, then let both Wu and Liu never fight one another, and let both houses break Wei together.”

Pang said, “That is my lifelong ambition.” He asked for Lu Su’s letter and went straight to Jingzhou to meet Liu Bei.

Now Kongming had not yet returned from inspecting the four districts. A gate officer announced that Pang Tong, a famous scholar of Jiangdong, had come specially to offer himself. Liu Bei had long heard of him and asked him in.

When Pang Tong came to Liu Bei, he made a long bow and did not fully kneel. Liu Bei saw Pang’s coarse appearance and felt little pleasure, but asked, “For one who has come such a distance, it is no small matter.”

Pang did not produce Lu Su’s letter or Kongming’s recommendation from before; he only answered, “I heard Lord Liu invited worthy scholars and welcomed the learned. I came to offer myself.”

Liu Bei said, “Jingzhou and Chu are somewhat stabilized, but this is a time of scarcity of post and office. There is a county named Leiyang a few hundred li to the southeast, but the post is vacant. I appoint you there.”

“If there should later be a vacancy, you will be employed in greater place.”

Pang thought, Liu Bei had treated me too lightly; I should stir him with my learning. Seeing that Kongming was not there, he had no choice but to part after polite refusal and leave.

Pang reached Leiyang County, ignored office matters, and passed every day in drunken happiness. Every bill, grain issue, and petition case he did not attend.

One day someone reported this to Liu Bei and said that Pang Tong had entirely neglected Leiyang affairs. Liu Bei grew angry and said, “How dare such a shallow scholar disorder my laws?” He then called Zhang Fei and instructed: “Go. Take men to survey the counties to the south of Jing as far as you can. If anything unjust or unlawful is found, investigate on the spot. If anything remains unclear, take Sun Qian with you.”

Zhang Fei took the order and, with Sun Qian, went to Leiyang County. Military men and civilians, officials and clerks all came out of the walled city to receive him; only the county magistrate did not appear.

Zhang asked, “Where is the magistrate?”

A colleague replied, “Master Magistrate Pang has been on duty here for more than a hundred days, and there has been no attendance to county affairs. Every day he drinks from dawn to dark, living in drunken oblivion. He was still lying in bed this morning after not sobering off the previous night.”

Zhang Fei grew furious and wanted to seize him. Sun Qian said, “Shiyuan is a man of high brilliance, not to be treated lightly. Let us first go and ask him in the county hall. If he is truly unjust, punishment is still possible.”

So they entered the county hall and sat on the main dais. Zhang ordered the magistrate to present himself.

Pang came out in disordered clothes and with help rose in his drunkenness. Zhang said in anger, “I trusted you to be a county magistrate; how dare you completely neglect the government?”

Pang laughed and said, “General, what matters of the county have I neglected?”

Zhang replied, “You have been in post for over a hundred days. You stay in wine every day. How can not government be neglected?”

Pang answered, “For a county of a hundred li, its matters are small. Why should they be difficult to decide? Sit less, wait, and I will settle them.”

At once he summoned clerks and had all the business accumulated over one hundred days brought forth and spread out. The clerks, bustling, carried in stacks of case files to the hall, and all the litigants knelt around the steps in turn. With one hand he ruled by annotation, while his mouth issued decisions and his ears took testimony. Right and wrong were made clear, with no fault or ambiguity. The people all knelt and prostrated in thanks.

In less than half a day he settled all affairs from the previous hundred days. He dropped his brush to the ground and said to Zhang Fei, “Where are the things I neglected? Cao Cao and Sun Quan I can view as patterns traced on my palm. Can a county so small matter so much to me?”

Zhang was astonished and sat down to apologize. “Master, you are greatly talented. This youth has been disrespectful. I will do all I can to recommend you to my elder brother.”

Pang then produced Lu Su’s letter. Zhang said, “Why did you not show it at your first meeting with my brother?”

Pang said, “If I had presented it then, it would seem I came only by virtue of recommendation to make a show of courtesy.”

Zhang told Sun Qian, “Without this man, I should have lost a great talent.” He then returned to Jingzhou to meet Liu Bei and fully explained Pang Tong’s ability.

Liu Bei was greatly startled and said, “To treat the great man so poorly was my fault.” Zhang Fei presented Lu Su’s recommendation.

Liu Bei opened it and read:

Shiyuan is not merely a talent for a hundred-li domain. Put him first in the office of Internal Assistant to the Court, and he will then show his full strength. If one judges by appearance, one risks ruining what he has learned and letting him go to others’ service. This would be a grievous waste.

Liu Bei had nearly finished when he heard that Kongming had returned. He welcomed him and finished ceremony.

Kongming first asked, “How is Military Adviser Shiyuan lately?”

Liu Bei said, “Of late at Leiyang County he has indulged in wine and neglected his duty.”

Kongming smiled, “Shiyuan is no ordinary talent of a hundred li; his learning in the chest exceeds mine tenfold. Has his recommendation from Master Kongming reached your lordship?”

Liu Bei said, “Today I just received a letter from Zijing, and have not seen yours.”

Kongming said, “A great man in a small post is often clouded by wine and grows weary of state affairs.”

Liu Bei said, “Had it not been for my brother’s word, I might have nearly lost a great man.” He immediately ordered Zhang Fei to go to Leiyang and invite Pang Tong to Jingzhou and said to him from below the gate, asking pardon.

Pang had just brought out his letter from Kongming. When Liu Bei saw its intent, he remarked that it was now time to use Fengchou at once.

Liu Bei rejoiced, “Formerly Sima said: ‘Among the Fudragon and the Fengchou, if one of them is obtained, the world can be put in order.’ Now we have both. The Han dynasty may rise.”

He then appointed Pang Tong as Deputy Army Adviser and Colonel of the General Staff, to discuss plans with Kongming and to drill troops, waiting for campaign orders.

Soon someone reported to Xuchang: Liu Bei has Zhuge Liang and Pang Tong as his strategists, has been recruiting soldiers, buying horses, storing hay and grain, joining hands with Eastern Wu, and will likely mount a northern campaign soon. Cao Cao heard this and quickly gathered his advisors to discuss a southern expedition.

Xun Yu said, “Now that Zhou Yu is dead, perhaps we should first strike Sun Quan and then attack Liu Bei.”

Cao Cao said, “If I march far, I fear Ma Teng may strike Xuchang. At Red Cliffs, rumors once spread that Western Liang would invade. We must not leave that unguarded.”

Xun Yu said, “In my poor judgment, issue an edict naming Ma Teng as General Who Conquers the South and order him to subdue Sun Quan. Lure him toward the capital; once this man is removed, the southern campaign will have no worry.”

Cao Cao was pleased and at once sent men with the edict to summon Ma Teng to Xuchang.

Now Ma Teng, whose courtesy name was Shoucheng, was a descendant of Ma Yuan, the Han Fubo General. His father was Su, courtesy name Zishuo; in the time of Emperor Huan he was Langan County Commandant in Tianshui, and later lost his post and came to Longxi where he lived among and eventually married among the Qiang.

Ma Teng was eight chi tall, with an imposing appearance and genial nature; many respected him. In the later years of Emperor Ling there were many Qiang rebellions, and Ma Teng recruited citizen soldiers to crush them. In the initial Chuping period, thanks to success in suppressing bandits, he became General Who Conquers the West and was made brother-in-arms with the General Who Guards the West, Han Sui.

On receiving the edict, he discussed with his eldest son, Ma Chao: “From the day Dong Cheng received the belt-commission to summon us together with Liu Bei to strike bandits, and though Dong has died, Liu Bei has failed again and again. I have been confined to Western Liang and could not assist him. Now I hear he has gained Jingzhou; I am about to carry out the old ambition, yet Cao Cao has instead summoned me. How are we to interpret this?”

Ma Chao replied, “Cao Cao has called your father by imperial order. If he does not go, Cao Cao will accuse us of disobeying the Son of Heaven. We should obey the summons and go to the capital; in the middle of affairs, old ambition can still be fulfilled.”

Ma Dai, Ma Teng’s brother’s son, warned, “Cao Cao is hard to read. If Uncle comes, he may die by his guile.”

Chao said, “I am willing to raise all soldiers of Western Liang and march behind my father to Xuchang, to kill the danger and clear the world. What is impossible?”

Ma Teng replied, “You stay in Western Liang and keep the Qiang forces for me. Only Ma Xiu, Ma Tie, and nephew Ma Dai should go with me. Cao Cao, seeing you in Western Liang and with Han Sui at your side, will not dare harm me.”

Chao answered, “If father goes, do not enter the capital lightly. See and meet events as they come and respond by the moment.”

Ma Teng said, “I can make room for myself. Do not worry too much.”

Thus Ma Teng brought five thousand Western Liang soldiers forward, first appointing Ma Xiu and Ma Tie as the vanguard, leaving Ma Dai behind for support, and marched toward Xuchang. He camped for the army twenty li outside the city.

When Cao Cao learned Ma Teng had arrived, he called his secretary-in-attendance, Huang Kui, and instructed him, “Right now Ma Teng is coming south. Go ahead as campaign adviser to him and cheer the army. Tell him that the road from Western Liang is far, transport is hard, and he cannot bring many men and horses at once. I will send a bigger force to advance with him. In days ahead, have him enter the city and face the lord; I will then settle the matter of supplies.”

Kui took the order and visited Ma Teng, who received him with wine.

Halfway drunk, Kui spoke, “My father Huang Wan died in the turmoil of Li Jue and Guo Si. I have long carried pain and hatred. I did not expect to meet again the betrayer of the Son of Heaven.”

Ma Teng asked, “Who is the betrayer of the Son of Heaven?”

Kui answered, “The betrayer is Cao Cao. You do not know this and ask me?”

Ma Teng feared he might have been sent by Cao to probe, and quickly said, “There are too many ears nearby; do not speak nonsense.”

Kui barked, “Have you forgotten the edict tied on the belt?”

Ma Teng, seeing him speak plainly from the heart, confided the truth in secret.

Kui said, “Cao Cao will not invite you into the city to treat with no bad intent. Do not enter casually. Tomorrow, gather your troops outside the city. When Cao Cao comes out to inspect and line up the army, strike the decisive blow there and behead him. Our great matter will be done.”

Their plan was settled. Kui returned home with his anger still burning.

His wife asked repeatedly, but Kui would not tell. Unknown to him, his concubine Li Chunxiang was secretly in relations with Miao Ze, his wife’s brother. Miao Ze wanted Li Chunxiang and had no means to achieve it.

When she saw Kui’s anger, she told Miao Ze, “Sir Huang came back from military deliberations and is deeply angry. You do not know why, do you?”

Miao Ze said, “You can prod him by asking: ‘All men say Liu Xian Shu is benevolent and Cao Cao a villain. Why so?’ See what he says.”

That night Kui came to Chunxiang’s room. She raised that challenge. In drunkenness he answered, “You are a woman and still know right from wrong—what of me? What I hate, I want to kill Cao Cao.”

Chunxiang asked, “If you want to kill him, how will you do it?”

Kui said, “I have already arranged with General Ma that tomorrow, when he deploys troops outside the city, I will kill him there.”

She informed Miao Ze, who informed Cao Cao.

Cao Cao immediately summoned Huang Kui, while summoning Cao Hong and Xu Chu with instructions, and also Xiahou Yuan and Xu Huang with separate instructions. Each took their orders and left. At once Cao Cao had Kui’s household and children seized.

Next day Ma Teng led his Western Liang army and moved near the city. He saw in front of him a cluster of red flags flying the Chancellor’s standard. He only thought that Cao Cao had come himself to inspect troops and drove forward with urgency.

Then a loud blast rang out. Where the red flags had opened, bow and crossbow fire struck in unison. The first commander to charge was Cao Hong.

As Ma Teng wheeled his horse back in haste, cries rose again from both sides. On the left came Xu Chu to kill; on the right came Xiahou Yuan; from behind came Xu Huang with his force to close, cutting off the Western Liang cavalry and trapping father and son of Ma Teng in a killing ground.

Ma Teng saw there was no way out and fought with all his strength. Ma Tie had already been shot dead by wild arrows. Ma Xiu followed Ma Teng, charging left and right, unable to break through. Both father and son, heavily wounded, sat their horses and were shot down; both were captured.

Cao Cao ordered Huang Kui and the Ma father and son together to be bound and brought before him.

Huang Kui shouted, “No guilt!” Cao Cao ordered Miao Ze to verify by witness.

Ma Teng roared, “Wretch scholar ruined my great affair! Heaven itself forbade me from killing this traitor for the state!”

Cao Cao had them brought out. Ma Teng continued cursing and his son Ma Xiu too, and with Huang Kui all were executed.

Later, someone wrote a verse for Ma Teng:

Father and son burned together in great brilliance, loyalty and uprightness made known through one family. To cast away life and redeem the state, they swore themselves to die and repay lordly grace. With blood-chewed oaths they stood, and the record of punishing treachery remained. The famed son of Western Liang, in no way brought shame to Fubo’s grandson.

Miao Ze told Cao Cao, “I seek no reward. I only ask for Li Chunxiang as wife.”

Cao Cao laughed, “For one woman you ruined your own elder brother-in-law and household. What use is such an unjust man now?” He ordered Miao Ze, Li Chunxiang, and all of Huang Kui’s family to be executed in the market.

No one who saw it withheld a sigh.

Later someone penned a verse about Miao Ze:

Because of private evil, Miao Ze harmed his own servant-clan; Chunxiang did not prevail, and all was turned against him. Even a tyrant will not forgive this kind of treachery. He made himself small with a base design.

Cao Cao then issued instructions to the Western Liang troops: “Ma Teng and his sons plotted rebellion and touched no others’ matters.” At once he ordered guards to hold the passes so that Ma Dai would not escape.

Now Ma Dai, only taking one thousand men in rear, had scouts reporting outside Xuchang that soldiers had slipped back and returned. Ma Dai was startled and had to abandon the troops. He donned the guise of a merchant and fled through the night.

With Ma Teng and the others dead, Cao Cao resolved to march south. Then came word: “Liu Bei is drilling troops and tending horse, readying weapons and grain stores, and appears ready to seize Sichuan.” Cao Cao was alarmed: “If Liu Bei takes Sichuan, he will have wings. How shall I answer him?”

He had not finished when one man came forward and said, “I have one plan. Make Liu Bei and Sun Quan not wish to cooperate, and Jiangnan and Xichuan will both return to the Chancellor.”

The great heroes of Xichuan now face execution, and the heroes of the southern state again are struck by disaster. Who it is that brings this counsel, we shall see— How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: At Chaisang, Sleeping Dragon Mourns; In Leiyang, Young Phoenix Administers Affairs

chapters.html:
Now it was said that the man who offered the plan was Chen Qun, whose courtesy name was Changwen, an official censor in charge of documents. Cao Cao asked, “What good strategy does Changwen have?”

Chen Qun replied, “Now that Liu Bei and Sun Quan have become close as the lips to the teeth, if Liu Bei wants to take Xi Province, the Chancellor can send a leading general to raise troops, unite with the forces at Fei, and march straight into Jiangnan. Then Sun Quan will certainly ask Liu Bei for help. Since Liu Bei’s intention is on Xichuan, he will have no heart to save Sun Quan. If Sun Quan is not saved, his strength will fade and his army will weaken, and the lands of Jiangdong will surely come under the Chancellor’s control. If we gain Jiangdong, Jing Province can be leveled at one drumbeat. Once Jing is pacified, we can then take up Xichuan in due time, and the realm will be secure.”

Cao Cao said, “Changwen speaks exactly according to my thoughts.” He immediately raised three hundred thousand soldiers and moved down to Jiangnan at once. He ordered Zhang Liao to join at Fei and prepare grain so the army would have enough provisions.

A secret informant had already informed Sun Quan. Sun Quan gathered his men and consulted with them. Zhang Zhao said, “Dispatch a man to Lu Su and command him to hurry a letter to Jing Province, calling on Xuande to join in resisting Cao Cao. Lu Su owes Xuande deep favor, so he will surely heed this request. And since Xuande is now the Sun Quan’s son-in-law, he also cannot refuse by right. If Xuande comes to aid us, Jiangnan can be made free of trouble.”

Sun Quan accepted the advice and sent someone to order Lu Su to seek help from Liu Bei. Lu Su accepted the order and at once had a letter carried to Liu Bei.

When Liu Bei read the intent in Lu Su’s letter, he kept the messenger in a guest house and sent men to the South Commandery to ask for Kongming.

When Kongming reached Jing Province, Liu Bei had Lu Su’s letter shown to him. Kongming said, “There is no need to move troops in Jiangnan, and no need to move troops from Jing either. Let Cao Cao know that he dare not properly watch the southeast.” Then he wrote back to Lu Su and told him to rest easy. If only northern troops cross over, Imperial Uncle has ways to withdraw the army. The messenger left.

Liu Bei asked, “Cao Cao has raised a great force of three hundred thousand, joined with the host at Fei, and is coming in a single wave. What excellent plan does Master have to turn them back?”

Kongming said, “What Cao Cao has feared throughout his life is the western force from Xiliang. He has now killed Ma Teng, and his son Ma Chao now commands the troops of Xiliang; they are sure to grind their teeth against this brigand Cao. My lord should send a letter and bind with Ma Chao. If Ma Chao raises troops and enters Guanzhong, Cao Cao will have no leisure to march into Jiangnan.”

Liu Bei was overjoyed. He immediately drafted a letter and dispatched a trusted adviser straight to Xiliang.

As for Ma Chao in Xiliang, he felt a troubling dream that night: he was lying on snow, and a pack of tigers came to bite him. He woke in alarm. He wondered at heart what it signified and gathered the officers around his command tent and recounted the dream. One of his attendants answered immediately, “Such a dream is a bad omen.”

When the men looked at him, it was the trusted attendant and adjutant at the tent’s front, named Pang De, whose courtesy name was Lingming. Ma Chao asked, “How does Lingming interpret it?”

Pang De said, “A dream of lying in snow while tigers come is an ominous sign. Could it be that the old general has cause in Xuchang?” He had barely finished speaking when a man staggered in and fell to his knees crying, “My uncle and my brother are both dead!”

Ma Chao looked up and saw it was Ma Dai. Ma Chao, startled, asked. Ma Dai said, “My uncle and the imperial clerk Huang Kui conspired with him to kill Cao Cao. Unhappily their plot was exposed, and both were executed in the market. My second brother too was killed. Only I dressed as a traveler and fled under the stars overnight.”

When Ma Chao heard this, he cried out and fell to the ground. The officers pulled him back. He gritted his teeth in anger, hating the bandit Cao. At that moment, news arrived that Liu Bei, the Imperial Uncle, had sent a man bearing a letter.

Ma Chao opened it. The letter read, in brief: “Lend your ear to the misfortune of the Han house; this brigand Cao Cao monopolizes power, deceives the Son of Heaven, cheats above, and causes the masses to wither and waste away. Liu Bei once took the secret edict with your father and swore to execute this traitor. Now your father was killed by Cao Cao. He is no longer under one sky and one sun with you as a sworn enemy. If you can lead the Xiliang host to attack Cao Cao’s right flank, Liu Bei will raise the troops of Jing and Xiang to stop Cao’s advance. Then this rebel can be captured, the treacherous partisans destroyed, our grievance and shame avenged, and the Han house can rise again. The letter says no more and now waits for your reply.”

When Ma Chao finished reading it, he wept and immediately prepared a reply, sending the messenger back. Right after that, he raised the cavalry and soldiers of Xiliang. As he was about to depart, Han Sui, the administrator of Xiliang, sent someone to ask Ma Chao to come to see him.

When Ma Chao reached Han Sui’s residence, Han Sui brought out a letter from Cao Cao and showed it to him. The letter said, “If you seize Ma Chao and bring him to Xu, I will confer on you the title of Marquis of Xiliang.”

Ma Chao knelt to the ground and said, “Please, my uncle, arrest my two brothers and bring them to Xuchang, so you need not tire yourself with spear and halberd.”

Han Sui helped him up and said, “I made brothers with your father; how could I bear to harm you? If you raise troops, I will assist you.”

Ma Chao thanked him. Han Sui then had Cao Cao’s envoy brought out and beheaded.

He then summoned hand-picked cavalry units from eight commands. The eight were Hou Xuan, Cheng Yin, Li Kan, Zhang Heng, Liang Xing, Cheng Yi, Ma Wan, and Yang Qiu. The eight commanders joined with Han Sui and Ma Chao’s men, including Pang De and Ma Dai, and the two-hundred-thousand-strong force marched in full force toward Chang’an.

The Governor of Chang’an Commandery, Zhong Yao, flew a report to Cao Cao. He simultaneously led troops to oppose them and formed a battle array in the open field.

The vanguard of Xiliang, under Ma Dai, advanced with fifteen thousand men and came on in great waves, filling the hills and fields. Zhong Yao rode out and exchanged terms. Ma Dai clashed with him in a single stroke from a treasured saber. There was little to say by the time they met; Zhong Yao was routed in a great retreat. Ma Dai drew his saber and pursued.

Ma Chao and Han Sui brought up the main host and surrounded Chang’an, while Zhong Yao withdrew inside the city to defend it.

Chang’an, the old Han capital, had city walls made sturdy and deep moat ditches, impossible to be forced by hurried assault. They besieged for ten days in a row and could not break through. Pang De offered a plan: “The city has hard soil and brackish water, very hard to sustain; with no firewood at all, after ten days of siege the soldiers and civilians will be starving and desperate. Better to withdraw for now. Only in this way can Chang’an be taken by hand.”

Ma Chao said, “This is an excellent plan!” He immediately sent a “ming” command-banner through each division to order withdrawal. The commanders each pulled back, Ma Chao personally covering the rear, and the whole host gradually retreated.

The next day Zhong Yao climbed the walls and looked out. The army had all withdrawn, and he feared there might be a trick. He sent scouts and found they had in fact gone far, then only then did he relax. He let civilians and soldiers come out of the city for firewood and water and set the gates wide open for movement in and out.

On the fifth day, reports came that Ma Chao’s army had returned. Civilians and soldiers rushed into the city; Zhong Yao closed the gates again and kept a tight hold.

The account then turns to Zhong Jin, Zhong Yao’s brother, who guarded the West Gate. Near the deep of the night, a fire suddenly rose within the gate. Zhong Jin rushed to extinguish it. Around the city wall turned a man. He drew his saber, rode hard, and shouted, “Pang De is here!”

Zhong Jin was at a loss and could not react; Pang De cut him down in one stroke from horseback. He scattered the officers, cut locks of the gate chains, and let the troops of Ma Chao and Han Sui into the city. Zhong Yao abandoned the city through the East Gate and fled.

Ma Chao and Han Sui captured the city. They rewarded the armies.

Zhong Yao withdrew to Tongguan and informed Cao Cao. Cao Cao, having lost Chang’an, no longer dared to discuss the southern campaign. He called Cao Hong and Xu Huang and gave instructions: “Take ten thousand men and horses and ride out first and hold Tongguan in close guard. If this pass falls within ten days, both of you are to be beheaded. If beyond ten days, it is not your business. I will march the main army after you.”

The two accepted the orders and moved with all speed through the night.

Cao Ren offered remonstrance: “Cao Hong is hot-blooded and impetuous; I truly fear he will err.” Cao Cao said, “You and I must keep moving grain. Then follow with reinforcements.”

When Cao Hong and Xu Huang reached Tongguan and held it tightly with Zhong Yao, they did not go out to battle. Ma Chao’s army came to the gate day after day and abused Cao Cao in loud insults. Cao Hong became angry and wanted to lead his troops down to fight in close quarters.

Xu Huang remonstrated: “This is Ma Chao’s attempt to provoke the generals into killing. We must not fight. When the Chancellor’s main army arrives, he will have a settled plan.”

Ma Chao’s soldiers came in shifts each day and night to shout insults. Every time Cao Hong sought close battle, Xu Huang held him back.

On the ninth day, when they looked at the pass, the Xiliang army had left their horses on the field grass in front of the gate and sat. Many were exhausted and lay sleeping on the ground. Cao Hong then ordered the horses prepared and sent three thousand soldiers charging down the pass.

The Xiliang troops threw away their horses and spears and fled in confusion. Cao Hong pursued in loose, winding chases.

At that moment, Xu Huang was still checking grain at the pass and heard Cao Hong had plunged into a melee. He hurriedly led men after him in alarm and shouted at Cao Hong to turn his horse. Suddenly a great cry rose behind them and shook the ground: Ma Dai had come with his force to strike.

Cao Hong and Xu Huang wheeled back to retreat. At that instant a war drum sounded. From behind the hills, two armies emerged: on the left was Ma Chao, on the right Pang De. They mixed and wrought a murderous clash.

Cao Hong could not stand against it; he broke half his troops, crashed out of the encirclement, and ran to the gate. Xiliang troops followed on. Pang De pursued through Tongguan and collided with Cao Ren’s forces, rescuing Cao Hong’s army. Ma Chao then supported Pang De in entering the pass.

When Cao Hong had lost Tongguan, he came running to see Cao Cao. Cao Cao said, “I set you the ten-day limit. How is Tongguan lost in nine days?”

Cao Hong replied, “The Xiliang soldiers were endlessly abusive, and because we saw their forces slacken they took advantage to chase. I did not think to be trapped by the brigand’s trick.”

Cao Cao said, “Cao Hong is young and ferocious. Xu Huang, you must know these matters.”

Xu Huang said, “My repeated remonstrance was not heeded. When I was checking supplies at the pass, I learned only then that the young general had already gone down from the gate. I feared disaster, hurried after him, and then was caught in the same villain’s stratagem.”

Cao Cao, furious, ordered Cao Hong executed. The officials petitioned for clemency. Cao Hong served his sentence and withdrew.

Cao Cao moved the army straight to Tongguan. Cao Ren said, “You may first set up fixed stockades, and then the time to break the pass has not yet passed.”

Cao Cao ordered trees cut down and stockades built in line. He divided them into three camps: left camp for Cao Ren, right camp for Xiahou Yuan, and Cao Cao in the middle camp.

The next day, Cao Cao led commanders from all three camps and rode down to the pass. They came upon the Xiliang cavalry and arrayed both sides for battle.

Cao Cao looked from beneath his command banner. As he watched the Xiliang force, every man was strong and brave, and every man, heroic. He saw Ma Chao, whose face was as pale as ground rice, lips red as vermilion, whose waist was narrow and shoulders broad, who spoke with a loud voice and had giant strength. He wore a white robe and silver armor, holding a long spear, standing tall at the front of the formation, with Pang De in the front rank and Ma Dai in the rear.

Cao Cao marveled in secret and spoke to himself: “You are the grandson of a Han general of renown. Why have you turned to rebellion?”

Ma Chao gritted his teeth and cursed: “Cao the brigand deceives the Son of Heaven and cheats above; his crimes cannot be pardoned. He killed my father and my brothers; we are sworn enemies under no sky or sun! I will keep him alive and eat him with my own teeth!”

When he had spoken, he lifted his spear and charged straight to kill.

Yu Jin, from behind, rode out to receive him. The two horses clashed. They fought nine exchanges, and Yu Jin was beaten into retreat. Zhang He came out to meet him; after twenty rounds, he too was beaten away.

Li Tong came out, and Ma Chao, fierce and charging, fought in a series of rounds. In one of them, he thrust his spear into Li Tong while Li Tong was still on his horse.

Ma Chao pulled his spear back and made a feint, and the Xiliang troops surged together to strike. Cao Cao’s army was broken. When Ma Chao’s host arrived in such momentum, all officers in the wings could not stand against it.

Ma Chao, Pang De, and Ma Dai led more than a hundred riders straight into the middle camp to seize Cao Cao.

In the chaos, Cao Cao heard shouts from the Xiliang side: “The one in the red robe is Cao Cao!” Cao Cao quickly dismounted from his horse and stripped off that red robe. He then heard another shout: “The one with the long beard is Cao Cao!” Frightened, he drew his sword and cut off the beard at once.

A man from Cao Cao’s own army told Ma Chao of the beard-cutting. Ma Chao then ordered: “The one with the short beard is Cao Cao!”

When Cao Cao heard this, he pulled at the flag corner and fled. A poet later wrote:

At Tong Pass the army broke and fled with no wind to the back, while Mengde in panic cast off his brocade robe. A cut through the beard was meant to send his courage fleeing, yet Ma Chao’s renown rose and filled the sky.

While Cao Cao was in flight, a rider hurried up from behind. He turned and looked: it was Ma Chao himself. Cao Cao was greatly startled. Officers seeing Ma Chao in pursuit each fled for their own lives, leaving Cao Cao.

Ma Chao shouted at the top of his voice, “Cao Cao, do not run!” Cao Cao, alarmed, dropped his reins and his horsewhip.

He looked up, but Ma Chao had already caught up, and from behind thrust his spear. Cao Cao circled around a tree and fled. Ma Chao set his spear against the tree; when he pulled it free, Cao Cao had gone far.

Ma Chao spurred hard and rode on. On the mountain slope another commander appeared, cried out, “Do not hurt my lord! Cao Hong is here!” and with his broad saber at speed blocked Ma Chao’s horse.

With that, Cao Cao’s life was saved.

Cao Hong fought Ma Chao for forty to fifty exchanges. His movements grew disorderly and his strength declined. Xiahou Yuan came up with several dozen riders. Ma Chao, seeing himself alone, feared he had been reckoned; he turned his horse to withdraw. Xiahou Yuan did not pursue.

Cao Cao returned to camp. He found that Cao Ren had already stabilized the stockades, so he had lost little of his men. Back in his tent, he sighed, “If I had executed Cao Hong, I would surely have died by Ma Chao’s hand today!”

So he called Cao Hong back and showered him with rewards.

He gathered up the beaten force and held the camp firmly. Deep ditches and high walls went up, and no one was allowed to engage in open battle.

Ma Chao brought soldiers daily to taunt and strike at the camp. Cao Cao issued orders that the men must hold fast, and if anyone stirred recklessly they would be beheaded.

The officers said, “The Xiliang force uses long spears. If we let them come, we can meet them with crossbows and arrows.”

Cao Cao replied, “To fight or not to fight is in my hands, not in the brigand’s. Even if the thieves carry long spears, can they easily stab? All of you, stand the fortress and wait. The brigands will withdraw on their own.”

The generals muttered privately among themselves: “The Chancellor has always led campaigns in person and taken the lead, but now, after being defeated by Ma Chao, how weak he is.”

A few days later, a spy reported, “Ma Chao has brought in twenty thousand fresh Qiang warriors to aid him; they are Qiang clans.”

Cao Cao, hearing this, rejoiced. The officers said, “When Ma Chao gains troops, the Chancellor is pleased. How is that?”

Cao Cao said, “Wait until I defeat him, then I shall tell you.”

Three days later, another report came that fresh troops had again arrived on the pass. Cao Cao rejoiced again and held a victory banquet in his tent.

The officers all smiled darkly within.

Cao Cao said, “You all laugh that I have no scheme to break Ma Chao. What good strategy have you?”

Xu Huang spoke: “Now that Your Excellence’s army is fully stacked here, and the brigand’s men are all encamped at the pass, when they turn toward the northwestern side there will be no preparation. If we can send one force secretly across Pusan Ford to cut off their route home, Your Excellence can in turn cross the north bank and strike him. The brigand forces could not support each other and will surely be in danger.”

Cao Cao said, “Gongming speaks exactly as I thought.” He told Xu Huang to lead four thousand picked troops and, with Zhu Ling, go straight to Hexi and lie in ambush in the mountain valley. He ordered, “Wait until I cross northward over the He River, then strike together.”

Xu Huang and Zhu Ling followed orders, first leading the four thousand silently away.

Cao Cao then ordered Cao Hong to prepare boats and rafts at Pusan Ford, while Cao Ren was left to guard the camp. Cao Cao himself would lead the army across the Weihe River.

Earlier, a spy had already informed Ma Chao. Ma Chao said, “Now Cao Cao is not attacking Tongguan but is preparing boats and rafts to cross north of the river. He will surely cut off my rear. I will take one detachment across the river and block the northern bank. If Cao Cao’s army cannot cross, in no more than twenty days the grain on the eastern bank will run out, his army will be in disorder, and if I then strike him along the southern river course, Cao Cao can be captured.”

Han Sui replied, “No need for that. Do you not hear in military law that says, ‘Attack when the enemy is halfway across?’ Wait until Cao Cao’s army is half over and then strike at the south bank. His troops will all die inside the river.”

Ma Chao said, “My uncle’s words are very good.” He then sent scouts to learn when exactly Cao Cao would begin crossing.

Now Cao Cao had finished forming his ranks and divided the army into three stopping camps. The front crossed first along the Wei River. When men and horses reached within the riverbank and the first light of day came, Cao Cao first sent elite troops across to the north bank and set up a stockade there.

Cao Cao himself then took his personal guard of a hundred and rode to sit on the south bank with his sword while the army crossed.

Just then someone reported: “The white-robed general has arrived at the rear!” All recognized it as Ma Chao and all crowded down into boats.

At the river bank soldiers surged to board, and the noise would not cease. Cao Cao still sat and did not move, setting his sword aside and signaling a brief pause.

Then came shouts and hoofbeats; in a tide they arrived. A mounted man leapt ashore and cried, “The brigand has arrived! Pray, my lord, get off the boat!” Cao Cao saw it was Xu Chu.

Cao Cao said through his mouth only, “What matter if the brigand is here?” Turning, he saw Ma Chao less than a hundred paces away. Xu Chu hauled Cao Cao off the bank as the boat had already drifted more than a full meter from shore. He carried Cao Cao in one bound onto the vessel.

The following soldiers all leaped into the water. Holding the boat’s side, they struggled to clamber aboard in a panic. The boat began to overturn. Xu Chu cut in all directions with his sword; the hands at the boat’s sides were all severed and fell into the water, and he quickly thrust the boat into the current.

Xu Chu stood on the stern and hurriedly used a pole to steady it. Cao Cao lay at his feet.

When Ma Chao came up to the riverbank, he saw the boat already halfway in the river. He set arrow to bow and ordered his fierce riders to circle and shoot it. Arrows fell like rain.

Xu Chu, fearful that Cao Cao would be hit, raised a horse saddle in his left hand to shield him. Ma Chao did not miss with his shots; boatmen and riders answering the strings fell into the water. A score of men on the boat were shot down. The overloaded craft could barely keep. In the rapids it spun.

Xu Chu alone summoned extraordinary vigor, set his legs against the rudder to rock it, held the pole with one hand, and raised the saddle with the other to protect Cao Cao.

At that time, Ding Fei, magistrate of Weinan County, saw Ma Chao chasing so quickly from the heights of Nanshan. Fearing for Cao Cao’s life, he drove all the county’s cattle and horses out beyond the camp, so that the entire hills and open country seemed full of cattle and horses. The Xiliang troops saw this and turned back, all of them scrambling for the animals, no longer mindful to keep chasing.

Thus Cao Cao escaped.

After reaching the north bank, he sank the boats and rafts. When generals heard Cao Cao had barely escaped in the river, they rushed to save him. By the time they arrived, he had already reached the open camp. The men in full armor carried with them wounds and arrows all lodged in their plates.

The generals protected Cao Cao to the field camp and all knelt on the ground to offer respect.

Cao Cao laughed aloud: “Today I might have been trapped by such small thieves!”

Xu Chu said, “If not for one who drove out the horses and cattle, the brigand would have fought hard to force the crossing.”

Cao Cao asked, “Who is the one who drew the brigands?”

Someone knowing the matter replied, “It was Magistrate Ding Fei of Weinan County.”

Soon Ding Fei entered and made his report.

Cao Cao thanked him: “If not for your good design, I would have been captured by the brigands.” He awarded him the rank of Colonel in charge of the guards.

Ding Fei said, “Though the brigands are gone for now, they surely will return tomorrow. We must make a good plan to resist them.”

Cao Cao replied, “I have prepared for this.”

He called for commanders: “Each of you, separately along the river, build up causeways and prepare temporary camp-footings. If the brigands come, station the main army outside the causeways and leave only banners visible inside to appear like reserves. Then dig ditches along the river and lay light earth stockades over a hollow trench. Lure them inside the riverbank. If they come in haste, they will be trapped, and once trapped they can be captured.”

Ma Chao reported back to Han Sui: “I nearly caught Cao Cao. One general, with extraordinary courage, dismounted and carried him onto a boat, but I do not know who.”

Han Sui answered, “I have heard Cao Cao selects his strongest men as his camp guards, calls them the ‘Tiger Guards,’ and gives them to the valiant Dian Wei and Xu Chu. Dian Wei is dead. The one who saved Cao Cao now must indeed be Xu Chu. This man exceeds others in courage; everyone calls him the ‘Tiger Maniac.’ If you meet him, do not underestimate him.”

Ma Chao said, “I have heard that name long ago.”

Han Sui said, “Now Cao Cao is crossing the river and may threaten my rear. Attack him quickly; do not allow him to establish a camp. If he does, he will be hard to strike down.”

Ma Chao said, “As my nephew can judge, we should only hold the north bank and prevent him crossing; this is the highest strategy.”

Han Sui asked, “A worthy nephew keeps watch over the camp while I take men along the river to oppose Cao Cao; what do you think?”

Ma Chao said, “Put Pang De forward first and send him with Uncle before you.”

So Han Sui and Pang De took fifty thousand men and rode straight toward Weinan.

Cao Cao ordered all his generals to use the causeway flanks to lure them in. Pang De first brought forward more than a thousand men in heavy cavalry. They charged and clashed.

At the cry, man and horse together fell into a pit prepared for horses. Pang De leapt hard and sprang free of the pit into open ground, where he cut down several men and cut out a way on foot through the encircling force.

Han Sui had already been trapped in the center of a battlefield pit.

Pang De fought to free him on foot, and at that moment met Cao Ren’s subordinate commander, Cao Yong. He felled him with one saber stroke from horseback, took his horse, and opened a bloody path that freed Han Sui and let him ride southeast. Behind them, Cao troops came hard. Ma Chao led supporting troops and beat them back, routing the force and rescuing the bulk of the army. They fought until dusk and then withdrew.

After tallying men and mounts, they found they had lost commanders Cheng Yin and Zhang Heng and more than two hundred men who had died in the pits.

Ma Chao and Han Sui conferred: “If we linger too long, Cao Cao will set up a camp in Hebei and make it hard to push him off. Better, on this very night, ride light and capture the field camp.”

Han Sui said, “Then split the troops to support each other from front and rear.”

Thus Ma Chao made himself the vanguard, and ordered Pang De and Ma Dai to stand as rear support. They moved out at night.

Now Cao Cao collected his troops and bivouacked north of the Wei River. He told his officers: “The brigand’s men mocked me and found no camp built. They will surely come to sack our camp. Let everyone lay hidden traps in all directions and leave the center appearing weak. When the drums boom, the ambushes should rise at once. In one drum-beat they can all be captured.”

The officers followed the order, and the ambushes were complete.

That night Ma Chao first sent Cheng Yi with thirty riders ahead as scouts. Seeing no man or horse in sight, Cheng Yi rode straight into the main camp.

When Cao’s army saw Xiliang troops arrive, they sounded the drums and horns. Ambushes from all four sides emerged and surrounded all thirty riders. Cheng Yi was slain by Xiahou Yuan.

Yet Ma Chao himself came behind with Pang De and Ma Dai, dividing forces in three paths and rushing in with fierce speed.

And this was sung:

Even if ambushes can wait to catch an enemy, how can one valiant general race to seize first place? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Ma Chao Raises an Army to Settle His Grievance, and Cao Cao Cuts His Beard and Casts Off His Robe

chapters.html:
The two armies mixed in close combat that night until dawn, then each withdrew and drew back to camp. Ma Chao stationed his troops at Wei Mouth, shifting men by day and night and striking in waves. Cao Cao, on the Wei River, ordered boats and rafts chained into three floating bridges to connect across to the south bank. Cao Ren brought troops across, set up a stockade, and linked the grain wagons as a shield.

When Ma Chao heard this, he told his soldiers to carry a bundle of straw each with fire ready in hand. He and Han Sui drove forward together to the front of the camp, heaped the straw, and set it alight. Cao’s men could not withstand the flames and abandoned the camp. The horses, wagons, and the floating bridges were burned. The Xiliang army won decisively and cut the Wei. Cao Cao could not restore a camp and began to worry deeply.

Xun You, whose courtesy name was Wenruo, said, “Take the Weihe sands and earth and build an earthen wall. It can hold.” Cao sent thirty thousand soldiers to shoulder the soil and build. Ma Chao then ordered Pang De and Ma Dai, five hundred cavalry apiece, to trade charges repeatedly. Worse, the sandy soil was unstable. What was raised collapsed quickly. Cao had no immediate plan.

By then it was late September. The weather was violently cold; red-brown clouds closed over the sky and had not opened for days. Cao sat in the camp in a mood of bewilderment. Suddenly someone reported: “An old man has come to see the Chancellor and wishes to set out a strategy.” Cao invited him in.

He had a long-necked, crane-boned frame and a weathered face. It later emerged he was from Jingzhao, living in seclusion on Mount Zhongnan, surname Lou, courtesy name Zi Bo, and Daoist title Master Mengmei. Cao received him with a guest’s honors. Zi Bo said, “The Chancellor has long wanted to cross the Wei and settle in place. Why do you not do it now?”

Cao asked, “This is sandy ground; building a wall will not hold. What is your good strategy?”

Zi Bo replied, “The Chancellor fights like a god. Do you not know the weather? For many days overcast clouds and then wind out of the north are coming. There will be hard frost. Once the wind rises, order the men to carry soil and splash water. By dawn the earthen wall will be complete.”

Cao suddenly understood. He rewarded Zi Bo well, but the recluse refused and left.

That night the north wind rose in strength. Cao drove his men to carry water in cloth sacks for lack of proper containers, using it to wet the earth as it rose; they built while it froze. By the time dawn came, the soil was hard and the earthen wall was finished.

An agent reported it to Ma Chao. He inspected it and was astonished, suspecting divine aid. The next day he gathered his whole army, sounded drums, and advanced.

Cao himself rode out alone from camp, Xu Chu, whose courtesy name was Zhongkang, following.

Cao lifted his whip and shouted, “Mengde has come here on one horse. Ma Chao, come out and answer.”

Ma Chao rode out, spear raised. Cao said, “You have failed to break my camp. In one night, with weather’s help, it is built complete. Why did you not surrender early?”

Ma Chao burned with anger and aimed to dash forward and seize him. He saw behind Cao a man with fierce, startled eyes, standing with a steel knife in hand and reins taut, watching. Ma Chao wondered if it was Xu Chu and called, “Where is your Tiger Marquis in your army?”

Xu Chu called back, “I am Xu Chu of Qiao Commandery!” His eyes flashed, his presence awe-inspiring.

Ma Chao did not dare move. He reined back. Cao also drew Xu Chu back into camp.

All who watched were stunned. Cao told his officers, “The rebels even know Zhongkang is the Tiger Marquis.” From then on all the army called Xu Chu Tiger Marquis.

Xu Chu said, “On another day I will capture Ma Chao.”

Cao said, “Ma Chao is brave and cannot be lightly matched.”

Xu Chu said, “I swear I will fight to death!” He had a challenge written out for single combat on the next day between Xu Chu Tiger Marquis and Ma Chao.

Ma Chao read it and grew furious: “How dare anyone dare to trick me this way?” He replied in writing that he would kill the Tiger Idiot the next day.

Next day both armies rode out and arrayed their ranks. Ma Chao assigned Pang De to the left wing, Ma Dai to the right, and Han Sui the center. Ma Chao lowered his spear and rode upright before the lines, shouting, “Tiger Idiot, come out at once!”

Cao looked back from behind the gate and told the other generals, “Ma Chao is no less valiant than Lü Bu.” Before he had finished, Xu Chu beat with his horse and came out brandishing his sword.

Ma Chao and Xu Chu met in battle. They fought more than a hundred rounds, and the outcome could not be decided. The horses grew exhausted. Both withdrew to their units, changed mounts, and came out again. Again they fought for over a hundred rounds with no winner.

Xu Chu’s spirit rose. He returned to camp, cast off his armor, and came bare-shouldered with sword raised. He vaulted back onto his horse and charged to decide with Ma Chao.

Both armies were greatly startled. They battled again for over thirty exchanges. Xu Chu raised and swung his blade, striking Ma Chao.

Ma Chao dodged and thrust a spear toward Xu Chu’s chest.

Xu Chu dropped the sword and caught the spear. On horseback the two wrestled for it. Xu Chu, with force alone, snapped the shaft with one sharp crack, and each held a half while still riding, striking wildly.

Cao feared Xu Chu might lose. He ordered Xiahou Yuan, whose courtesy name was Miaocai, and Cao Hong to advance together and strike in from both sides. Pang De and Ma Dai saw the Chancellors ride out and sent their heavy cavalry in with a straight-on charge, colliding and slashing. Cao’s army became confused.

Xu Chu took two arrows to the upper arm.

The other generals in haste fell back into camp. Ma Chao drove straight to the riverbank, and Cao’s men were maimed and broken by a half. Cao ordered the camp to close up tightly and not come out.

Ma Chao returned to Wei Mouth and told Han Sui, “I have seen no one who can match Xu Chu in fierce battle. He is truly a Tiger Idiot.”

Cao Cao judged that Ma Chao could be broken by stratagem. He secretly ordered Xu Huang and Zhu Ling to cross fully to the west bank and set up camp to strike from both front and rear.

On one occasion Cao, standing atop the wall, saw Ma Chao lead several hundred riders straight up to the front of camp, coming and going as if flying. He watched for a long while, then threw his helmet to the ground and said, “If that horseman does not die, there will be no burial ground for me.”

Hearing this, Xiahou Yuan burned with anger and shouted, “I would rather die here than fail. I vow to wipe out Ma the bandit!” He led out over a thousand of his core unit and opened the gate wide to charge.

Cao could not restrain him; he mounted at once and rode forward to assist. When Ma Chao saw Cao’s troops close in, he made the front lines become the rear and the rear become vanguard, opening into one line. He reached Xiahou Yuan and fought him.

Among the chaotic troops, Ma Chao saw Cao and abandoned Xiahou, pressing straight toward Cao. Cao was shocked and wheeled away. The army broke.

Just as the chase began, there was sudden word: Cao had an army already crossed west and pitched camp there.

Ma Chao was startled and no longer chased. He drew back in dismay, pulled his men back to camp, and spoke with Han Sui: “Cao’s troops have crossed to the west bank while there was an opening. Our own forces are attacked in front and behind. How can we meet this?”

Officer Li Kan said, “Better to concede land and make peace, and let each side stop for now. Let us endure winter and make plans when spring warms.”

Han Sui said, “Li Kan speaks best. We should follow it.”

Still Ma Chao hesitated. Yang Qiu and Hou Xuan both pressed for peace. Han Sui therefore sent Yang Qiu as envoy and asked for a written separation and peace.

Cao replied, “Return to your camp. I will report back tomorrow.” Yang Qiu took leave.

Jia Xu, whose courtesy name was Wenhe, entered and said, “What is the Chancellor’s intent?” Cao asked, “And what do you see?”

Jia Xu answered, “War does not disdain deception. It may accept the proposal first, then use divided counsel to make Han and Ma suspect one another. Then one drumbeat can break them.”

Cao laughed and struck his palms. “Many in the world can observe this. Wenhe’s plan is exactly the one in my own thoughts.” He ordered a return message: “I will slowly withdraw, and restore your western bank to you.” At the same time he had the floating bridges raised as if preparing for withdrawal.

When Ma Chao got the reply, he told Han Sui, “Though Cao appears to consent, this villainous hero is hard to measure. If we are not prepared, we become trapped by him. Today I and my uncle will alternate our troops: today I face Cao while my uncle faces Xu Huang; tomorrow I face Cao and my uncle faces Xu Huang. We should prepare in separate parts against treachery.”

Han Sui followed this plan.

Before long a report reached Cao. He said to Jia Xu, “It is nearly settled. Who is to come out against us tomorrow?” The report came: Han Sui.

The next day Cao brought out all his commanders and surrounded the field. He alone rode in the center. Han Sui’s men, many not knowing Cao, came out to observe his formation. Cao cried, “Do your troops wish to see Chancellor Cao? I am still human. I have no four eyes and two mouths; I simply possess more stratagems.”

All the troops wore a look of fear.

Cao sent a messenger through the lines to Han Sui: “The Chancellor respectfully requests that General Han come and speak.” Han Sui rode out at once. Seeing Cao without armor and in light clothing, he too discarded his cuirass and rode out simply.

The two riders drew close and came with reins in hand, facing each other.

Cao said, “Your father and I shared the same civil service route. I once served him in my youth, like an uncle.”

He added, “Your and my offices came by the same road too. Years have passed beyond counting. How old are you now, General?”

Han Sui replied, “I am forty.”

Cao said, “Only recently in the capital you were still young. How strange that you are already in your middle years! How will the land ever be brought back to peace and shared joy?”

He spent the time recalling old events in detail without touching army matters. After a full hour they separated, turning back their horses and returning to their camps.

Soon after, someone reported this to Ma Chao. He came in haste asking Han Sui, “What was said by Cao in front of your lines?”

Han Sui answered, “Only old stories from the capital.”

Ma Chao said, “How can one not speak of military affairs?”

Han Sui replied, “Cao did not speak. Why should I alone speak?”

Ma Chao doubted still more and withdrew in silence.

Cao returned to camp and told Jia Xu, “Do you understand the meaning of our parley before the lines?”

Jia Xu said, “This is clever, but still it does not fully separate them. I have one scheme by which Han and Ma will kill each other.”

Cao asked for the plan.

Jia Xu said, “Ma Chao is a brave warrior and does not read hidden intent. The Chancellor should write one letter with his own hand to Han Sui, leave the crucial phrases blurred, then seal and send it. Let Ma Chao know it. He will ask for it to read.”

“If he sees blurred places, he will assume Han Sui, fearing that Ma Chao learned secrets, has altered those places himself. That matches the suspicion from yesterday’s single-horse talk. Suspicion gives rise to disorder. Then I will secretly sow division among Han Sui’s own officers. In that way Ma Chao can be taken apart.”

Cao said, “A most excellent stratagem.” He wrote a letter, blotted over every crucial place, sealed it, and had many riders carry it to Han Sui, then withdrew them.

Sure enough, Ma Chao was informed. His suspicion deepened. He came straight to Han Sui for the letter. Han Sui handed it to him.

When Ma Chao saw the blotched writing, he said, “How come this is all rubbed and blurred?” Han Sui said, “The original was like this. I do not know why.”

Ma Chao said, “Would anyone send a rough draft by messenger? Your uncle must fear I could know sensitive details. He must have altered the lines first. That is exactly why this is.”

Han Sui replied, “Could Cao accidentally have sent out a draft instead?”

Ma Chao said, “I do not believe it. Cao is precise in everything. Could he make such an error? I have fought beside my uncle as one to destroy this bandit. How can sudden treachery rise?”

Han Sui said, “If you do not trust me, tomorrow when I speak with Cao, break out from within and thrust a spear into him.”

Ma Chao answered, “If so, then I will know my uncle’s true heart.”

They fixed this.

The following day Han Sui sent Hou Xuan, Li Kan, Liang Xing, Ma Wan, and Yang Qiu out to form the line. Ma Chao concealed himself behind the gate.

Han Sui sent a man to Cao’s camp and shouted, “General Han asks the Chancellor to speak face-to-face.” Cao ordered Cao Hong to lead several dozen riders directly to meet Han Sui before the lines.

Their horses were only a few strides apart when Cao Hong bent low on horseback and said, “Last night the Chancellor conveyed this intention to you: do not misunderstand.”

He turned and returned.

Ma Chao heard this and was furious. He snapped his spear, spurred hard, and struck toward Han Sui. The five officers blocked him and urged him back into camp. Han Sui said, “Esteemed nephew, hold your doubts. I hold no evil intent.”

Ma Chao did not yield.

Han Sui then met with those five on how to explain the matter. Yang Qiu said, “Ma Chao leans on his courage and often harbors a heart above his lord. If he defeats Cao, will he yield anything? In my poor view, better to defect to Cao in secret. A future enfeoffment may still be yours.”

Han Sui said, “I and Ma Teng once made brotherhood vows. How could I be disloyal?”

Yang Qiu said, “When matters are this far advanced, there is no other path.”

Han Sui asked, “Who can carry this message?”

Yang Qiu answered, “I volunteer.”

Han Sui wrote a sealed letter and sent Yang Qiu to Cao’s camp, telling of surrender.

Cao was very glad. He promised Han Sui the Marquisate of Xiliang, Yang Qiu Administrator of Xiliang, and offices to the rest. They agreed the signal would be fire and that both within and without would cooperate.

Yang Qiu took leave and returned to Han Sui, reporting every detail:

“Tonight we are to light a fire. Inside and outside will move together.” Han Sui was delighted and ordered dry timber piled behind the central command tent, and the five generals to keep swords and blades unsheathed and ready.

Han Sui considered setting a banquet to invite Ma Chao and catch him there, but never reached final decision.

Ma Chao had already detected all of it. He had come ahead with his close guard and a few riders, carrying his sword, to the fore, and he told Pang De and Ma Dai to hold back for relief. He slipped into Han Sui’s tent. He found the five generals and Han Sui in close conference. All he heard from Yang Qiu’s mouth was, “This must not be delayed. Do it at once!”

Ma Chao grew enraged and shouted, “How can this gang of thieves dare to plot my death?” He drew his sword and entered in full force.

He all but cried, “A band of villains, how dare you.” The men all started in alarm. Ma Chao swung straight for Han Sui’s face.

Han Sui flung out his hand to parry. His left hand was cut away at once.

The five generals drew their own blades and rushed out together. Ma Chao stepped from the pavilion and the five closed around him. He alone swung his treasured sword against them. Where the blade flashed, blood splashed. He cut down Ma Wan and hacked Liang Xing; three of them fled. When Ma Chao went back toward Han Sui’s pavilion to finish him, Han Sui had been carried out by his own men.

A fire rose behind the pavilion and soldiers from all camps surged.

Ma Chao quickly mounted. Pang De and Ma Dai had arrived and joined the struggle. When Ma Chao cut out with his force, he found himself ringed by Cao’s troops: Xu Chu in front, Xu Huang in rear, Xiahou Yuan on the left, Cao Hong on the right. The Xiliang troops, being pressed together, began to kill one another.

Ma Chao no longer saw Pang De or Ma Dai and drew over one hundred riders to hold at Wei Bridge.

By first light he saw Li Kan leading a unit crossing beneath the bridge. Ma Chao lowered his spear and rushed. Li Kan ran while dragging his spear.

At that moment Yu Jin came running from behind Ma Chao and loosed an arrow. Ma Chao heard the bowstring and dodged in time, but the bolt hit Li Kan in front, killing him and sending him off his horse.

Ma Chao wheeled and came back to strike Yu Jin, but Yu Jin spurred away.

Ma Chao held at the bridgehead. Cao’s troops came on from all sides. The Tiger Guard was first, and arrows flew in crossing rain. Ma Chao deflected them with his spear so that the shafts came down all over the ground.

He ordered his riders to charge in and out, to kill and split through, but Cao’s lines were thick and held firm. They could not force a way through.

On the bridge, Ma Chao shouted, rode hard into the north bank, and cut toward safety; the riders following him were cut apart.

Ma Chao fought alone inside the press. He was struck down on horseback by a hidden crossbow bolt.

Ma Chao fell to the ground. Cao’s army closed in.

At that critical moment a band of soldiers came in from the northwest corner to strike—Pang De and Ma Dai.

The two saved Ma Chao. One with Ma Chao in hand of horse, heaved together through the blood. They turned and cut out a blood-licked path and rode northwest.

When Cao heard that Ma Chao had escaped, he ordered all his generals, “Pursue him night and day. Whoever brings Ma Chao’s head will receive a thousand pieces of gold and be enfeoffed as a marquis of ten thousand households. Whoever captures him alive shall be made General-in-Chief.”

The commands were carried out. All sought to outpace one another in pursuit.

Ma Chao, with no thought for the weariness of men and horses, kept running. His riders gradually scattered. Foot soldiers who could not keep pace were taken.

Only thirty-odd riders remained, and with Pang De and Ma Dai they fled toward Longxi and Lintao.

Cao pursued to Anding himself. Learning Ma Chao had gone far, he finally gathered his forces and returned to Chang’an.

The whole host assembled there. Han Sui’s left hand was gone. He had become an invalid. Cao ordered him kept in Chang’an to rest and granted him the title Marquis of Xiliang. Yang Qiu and Hou Xuan were made marquesses and placed at Wei Mouth.

Cao ordered the army to return to Xuchang.

Yang Fu, an assistant general from Liangzhou, courtesy name Yishan, arrived directly in Chang’an to see Cao.

Cao asked, “What do you hear?”

Yang Fu said, “Ma Chao has courage like Lü Bu and has deeply won the hearts of the Qiang. If Your Highness does not press and exterminate him now, in time he will gather force there, and the commanderies of Long can no longer be called ours. For now, please do not pull your troops back yet.”

Cao said, “I did intend to leave forces to punish him. But the Central Plains are in turmoil and the south not settled. I cannot stay long. You must guard it for me.”

Yang Fu obeyed, and again recommended Wei Kang as Inspector of Liangzhou. He was to command troops and camp at Jicheng to defend against Ma Chao.

As Yang Fu prepared to leave, he said, “Chang’an must hold heavy reserves there as fallback.”

Cao said, “I have already arranged that. Trust me.”

Yang Fu withdrew.

Other generals asked, “When the bandits first held Tongguan and the road north of the Wei was open, why did the Chancellor not strike Henan and destroy Fengyi, but instead return to defend Tongguan and then stay so long before crossing north to build this camp and fortify?”

Cao said, “At first the bandits held Tongguan. Had I gone at once, I would have taken Hedong. The rebels then would have divided, stationing each outpost at every ford, and then the west bank could not be crossed. So I gathered all my forces at Tongguan and made them hold southward, while west of the river they were unprepared. For this reason Xu Huang and Zhu Ling could cross.

I then crossed north, linked carts and stockades into causeways, raised an ice fortress, and let them believe I was weak so as to swell their pride and keep them unready. I then used the trick of reverse intelligence and the force of my soldiers in one stroke to crush them. As the saying goes: not even swift thunder can cover the ear.”

The generals asked, “The Chancellor rejoices whenever he hears that the bandits are bringing in more troops and men. Why is that?”

Cao said, “The Central Plain is far and hard to govern. If every bandit clings to a pass and rough ground, to pacify them takes one or two years. Now they have gathered all in one place.
