Their ranks are large, but their hearts are not one. They are easy to divide and one strike can wipe them out. That is why I am glad.”

The generals knelt and said, “No one in this world can equal the Chancellor’s divine design.” Cao replied, “It is due to the strength of your civil and military men too.” He rewarded them heavily.

He left Xiahou Yuan to garrison Chang’an. The surrendered soldiers were assigned by units.

Xiahou Yuan recommended a man from Fengyi named Zhang, surname Zhang, given name Ji, courtesy name Derong, a native of Gaoling, who served as Prefect of Jingzhao, to share the defense with him.

Cao then completed his march back to the capital. Emperor Xian drove out the ceremonial carriage and rode to the gate to welcome him. By decree he did not publicly announce Cao’s promotion; but when Cao entered court he did not kneel, and ascended with sword and boots, as in the old story of Chancellor Xiao He under Han. From then on his power shook the inner and outer realms.

News of this entered Hanzhong early and startled the Administrator of Hanning, Zhang Lu.

Zhang Lu had been a native of Feng in Pei. His ancestor, Zhang Ling, in West Sichuan made Daoist scriptures on Mount Huming and used them to mislead people. The people respected him. When he died, his son Zhang Heng carried it on. The people who studied the Way gave him five dou of grain in aid and were called “grain thieves.” After Zhang Heng’s death, Zhang Lu inherited it.

In Hanzhong Zhang Lu styled himself “Shijun.” Those who came for the Way were called “ghost soldiers.” The leaders among them were “ji jiu,” and those who commanded many were “zhitou da ji jiu.” Their order was founded on honesty. Fraud was forbidden. If one was ill, one was put in a quiet room to ponder one’s own offense and present one’s face before making prayer.

The official who conducted the prayers was titled the Superintending jijiu. For prayer, one wrote down the name and admission of guilt, then composed three documents called the “Three Officials’ Handscroll.” One was burned on a summit to report to Heaven, one was buried in the earth to report to Earth, and one was sunk in deep water to report to the Water Official.

Afterward, if recovered, they offered five dou of grain as thanks.

He also maintained charity halls, provisioned with rice, firewood, and meat, where travelers could eat as much as needed; if someone took too much, he was said to fall under Heaven’s punishment.

Within his domains, criminals were granted three chances to repent; only those who did not amend were punished. There were no official magistrates there. The entire administration was in the hands of the ji jiu.

Thus he held Hanzhong firmly for thirty years.

The state tolerated this because of distance, and made him General Who Defends the Southern Court and Administrator of Hanning, accepting tribute.

When he heard Cao had broken the Xiliang host and that the land trembled under this report, he gathered his men and discussed: “Ma Teng of Xiliang is dead, and Ma Chao has newly failed. Cao Cao will surely invade Hanzhong. I wish to call myself King of Hanning and set a force to block him. What should we do?”

Yan Pu said, “Hanzhong has over one hundred thousand households. Its wealth and grain are abundant. It is surrounded by strong passes on all four sides. Since Ma Chao has just failed, the people from Xiliang who fled into Hanzhong through Ziwu Valley number not less than tens of thousands. In my poor opinion, Liu Zhang in Yi Province is weak and foolish. Better to first secure the forty-one prefectures of Xichuan before taking the title.”

Zhang Lu was pleased, and discussed uprising with his brother Zhang Wei. Spies were already brought in from Sichuan.

Back in Yi Province, Liu Zhang, courtesy name Jiyu, was the son of Liu Yan and a descendant of King Gong of Lu of the Han house. In the Yuanhe era of Emperor Zhang, a cadet branch of the family was transferred in enfeoffment to Jingling and settled there. Liu Yan later rose to become Governor of Yi Province and died of an ulcer in the first year of Xingping. Senior officers of Yi Province, including Zhao Wei, then supported Liu Zhang as Governor. Liu Zhang had already killed Zhang Lu’s mother and younger brother, and the two sides were enemies.

Liu Zhang appointed Pang Xi as Administrator of Bashi to oppose Zhang Lu.

At that time Pang Xi learned Zhang Lu intended to raise troops and take Sichuan, so he rushed the message to Liu Zhang.

Liu Zhang, timid by nature, grew greatly anxious and quickly gathered his officers to discuss. Then one man stepped forward: “My lord, take heart. Though I am no able man, with a three-inch, never-failing tongue, I can keep Zhang Lu from looking at Sichuan head-on.”

As said:

Only because a strategist entered Shu, the heroes of Jingzhou have been drawn in.

Who this man is,

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Xu Chu, in Plain Garb, Fights Ma Chao; Cao Cao Blurs a Letter to Han Sui

chapters.html:
Zhang Song, whose courtesy name was Yongnian, came from Yi Province as its Assistant Biejia. He had a broad, bulging forehead, a pointed head, a flat-nosed face with teeth that showed, and a short body not reaching five chi. His voice was deep like that of a bronze bell. Liu Zhang asked, “You, who serve in this office, what sound strategy do you have that might save this place from Zhang Lu?”

Song replied, “I have heard that in Xudu, Chancellor Cao Cao has swept through the Central Plain. He has subdued Lü Bu and the two Yuans, and lately he has beaten back Ma Chao. Under heaven he has no equal. If my lord prepares tribute goods—gold, pearls, and brocade—and sends an envoy, I should go personally to Xudu and say this to Cao Cao: ‘Raise your troops and seize Hanzhong in pursuit of Zhang Lu, and we shall keep you busy there. With his army occupied, how would he dare to press into Shu again?’

Liu Zhang was pleased. He packed gold, pearls, and silk gifts and sent Zhang Song as envoy. Song secretly copied a map of Sichuan and hid it, then with only a few mounted attendants took the road for Xudu.

Word had already reached Jing Province. Zhuge Liang, who is called Kongming, then sent men to Xudu to gather news.

When Zhang Song reached the guest lodging at Xudu, he settled there and each day went to the Chancellery to report and seek an audience with Cao Cao. Cao had returned from breaking Ma Chao in triumph and, riding high on victory, held drinking parties daily and seldom went out. State business was all handled in the Chancellery.

Song waited three days before he could pass his name forward. Court attendants and close attendants first demanded bribes and only then was he brought in. Cao sat in the hall. After Song bowed, Cao asked, “Your lord Liu Zhang has not sent tribute for years. Why?”

Song replied, “The roads were difficult, Your Excellency, and bandits interrupted the traffic. We could not pass tribute through.”

Cao snapped, “I have swept the Central Plain. What bandits now?”

Song answered, “To the south there is Sun Quan, to the north Zhang Lu, and to the west Liu Bei. All three can each bring forth with tens of thousands of armored troops. How can one say all is peaceful now?”

Song’s appearance did not please Cao, and he disliked him from the start. He also found his speech biting and unruly, so he rose, waved off his sleeve, and moved to the rear hall.

An attendant rebuked Song: “You are here on an imperial mission. Why do you not know ceremony and always speak with insolence? He only spared you out of respect for your coming so far. Go home at once!”

Song laughed. “No one in my Sichuan does flattery.”

At that moment a loud voice from below called up, “If your land has no flatterers, do we in Zhongyuan have none either?”

Song looked up at the speaker. He had thin eyebrows, narrow eyes, a pale face, and clear spirit. He asked his name and learned this was Yang Xiu, courtesy name Dezu, son of Grand Commandant Yang Biao, now chief clerk under the Chancellor’s office, keeper of the treasury. He was widely learned, eloquent, and exceptional in understanding. Song realized that Yang Xiu was a man of verbal talent and difficult to defeat. Yang Xiu too trusted his own brilliance and looked down on other scholars.

When Yang saw Song’s mocking tone, he invited him outside into a study pavilion and set them as host and guest. “The road to Shu is rugged and far. You must have come with hardship,” Yang said.

Song replied, “By my lord’s order, even if I must walk through fire or wade in boiling water, I dare not refuse.”

Yang asked, “What is the terrain and weather of Shu like?”

Song replied, “Shu is known as the old West Commandery and is called Yi Province. The roads are perilous by the Jin River, and the land links to the mighty Jiange Pass. The route winds for 208 li and stretches over 30,000 li in width. Roosters crow and dogs bark in answer across the way. City lanes and neighborhoods never cease. The fields are rich, the land fertile, and there is no fear of flood or drought in the years. The state is wealthy and the people prosperous, and pipes and strings often sound at times of joy. Its products are piled like mountains. None in the world can match it.”

Yang asked, “And what men are there in Shu?”

Song replied, “In letters there is one like Xiangru; in arms one with the talent of Fubo. In medicine one like Zhongjing; in divination one like Lord Qing. Men of all Nine Schools and Three Teachings rise up, with only the best and the rarest beyond counting. Who could list them all?”

Yang asked, “Under today’s Lord Ji-yu, how many men like you remain?”

Song replied, “In both civility and war, in wisdom and courage, in loyalty and righteousness, there are hundreds. As for men as base as I am, I can scarcely count them by the cartload.”

Yang asked, “What post do you hold these days?”

Song replied, “I fill the post of Biejia in name, and it is most ill-suited to me. What high office do you hold in the Chancellery?”

Yang said, “I am now chief clerk in the Chancellery.”

Song replied, “I have long heard your family bears court caps from generation to generation. Why do you not stand in the hall of state to aid the Son of Heaven, instead of being but a low clerk under the Chancellery?”

Hearing this, Yang’s face flushed with shame, but he kept a straight front and answered, “Although I am low in office, the Chancellor has entrusted to me the weight of military finance. I receive his instruction day and night and have improved myself; so I keep this post.”

Song laughed, “I have heard that Chancellor Cao Mingde’s writings are ignorant of Confucian and Mencian thought and blind to the methods of Sun and Wu. His concern is only for dominance and coercion from a high post. How can he teach one here?”

Yang said, “How can you, coming from a border post, know the Chancellor’s greatness? Try reading this for yourself.” He ordered attendants to bring forth a volume from the casket and showed it to Song. Its title read Mengde’s New Writings.

Song read all thirteen chapters from beginning to end. They were all essentials of military strategy.

When he had finished, he asked, “What is this treatise, in your view?”

Yang answered, “This is a work Cao Cao made after weighing antiquity and the present, modeled on Sunzi’s thirteen chapters. You mocked the Chancellor’s lack of talent. Is this fit to pass to later ages?”

Song laughed loudly. “A mere child in Shu can recite this by heart; why call it ‘new writing’? This is a work from the Warring States by an unknown author. Cao Cao has stolen it and passed it as his own, only to deceive men like you.”

Yang protested, “Though this is a book kept secretly and now bound in volumes, it has not yet reached the world. You claim a little boy in Shu can memorize it. Why should I think you are deceitful?”

Song said, “If you doubt me, I can recite it.” He proceeded to recite all of Mengde’s New Writings from start to end with no single error.

Yang was greatly startled. “You read and remember at once. You are truly a rare genius under heaven.”

Later men put it this way:

Strange is your form and strange your face; spare, lofty air and countenance. Your voice flows like the waters of the Three Gorges; your eyes can take in ten lines at once. Your courage towers above West Shu; your prose pierces the boundless sky. Among the hundred lineages and all their schools, none remain when one glimpse of yours appears.

Song now wished to depart.

Yang said, “Stay in the pavilion for a while. Let me report to the Chancellor again and have him receive you.”

Song thanked him and withdrew. Yang then entered to see Cao and said, “Just now, why was Your Excellency so severe with Zhang Song?”

Cao replied, “His words were unsuited to ceremony. I was displeased.”

Yang said, “Yet Your Excellency welcomed Ni Heng. Why not receive this man?”

Cao replied, “I did not kill Ni Heng because his writing was famous in our day.”

Yang said, “As for Song’s abilities, leave that aside. He speaks like the hanging river and his eloquence meets no obstruction. I just showed him this new book you compiled. He read it once and recited it whole. Such learning and memorization are rare in all ages. He even says this book comes from an unknown Warring States hand and that children in Shu can recite it.”

Cao asked, “Could it be that an ancient man and I are in secret accord?” He ordered the book torn into pieces and burned.

Yang said, “This man can stand before you and witness the splendor of court and army.”

Cao said, “Tomorrow I will marshal forces at the western drill ground. You shall bring him in first, so he can see my host’s full strength and return to spread the truth that I have subdued Jiangnan and will soon come for Sichuan.”

Yang took his leave.

The next day he and Song went together to the western drill ground. Cao brought out fifty thousand of the Tiger Guards and set them there in formation. Their helmeted armor shone bright; robes flashed with color. Brass drums thundered to the sky, halberds and spears flashed in the sun. From four directions and eight points the units were distributed in ranks; banners and pennants streamed with color; horsemen and men were in the air with such vigor. Song looked sidelong.

After a while Cao called for Song and pointed out the display. “In your Shu have you ever seen heroes like these?”

Song answered, “I have never seen soldiers in armor in my Shu. In my land we govern by benevolence and justice.”

Cao’s complexion changed. Song did not flinch. Yang Xiu kept glancing at him.

Cao said, “In my eyes, upstarts in the realm are but weeds and chaff. Where my great army goes, battle is always won and fortresses always taken. Those who follow me live, and those who oppose me die. Do you understand?”

Song replied, “Your Excellency drives troops everywhere and always wins battles and captures cities. I have long known this. Yet in the battle at Puyang against Lü Bu, in the fight at Wan against Zhang Xiu, at Red Cliffs meeting Zhou Lang, at Huarong encountering Guan Yu, when your beard was shaved and your robe cast off at Tong Pass, and when you took a boat and dodged arrows on the Wei River, these were not all acts of an invincible man?”

Cao grew furious. “How dare this low scholar lay bare my faults!” He shouted and ordered Song’s immediate execution.

Yang Xiu intervened, saying, “Song can be executed if you wish, but he came through the road from Shu to offer tribute. If he is slain, we lose the goodwill of distant men.” Cao’s anger was still hot. Xun Yu also interceded, and only then Cao spared him and ordered him beaten out with a rough staff.

Song returned to his lodging and left the city overnight with his preparations, heading back toward Shu. He thought, “I came intending to present Sichuan and its commanderies to Cao Cao. How did I meet such contempt! Before I leave Liu Zhang, I spoke in boldness and was proud. Today I return bitterly, empty-handed, to be laughed at by the men of Shu. I have heard that in Jing Province Liu Xuande’s benevolence and righteousness have long been celebrated. Better to go by that route directly. Let me see what sort of man he is; then I will know what is right.”

So he mounted his horse and with his attendants watched his way back to the borders of Jing Province. Near the border of Yingzhou he saw a detachment of about five hundred cavalry, with a tall general in light gear riding first. The officer reined in and asked from the front, “Are you not Zhang Biejia?”

Song replied, “I am.”

The officer hurried down and bowed deeply. “Zhao Yun has waited long for you.”

Song dismounted and said, “Are you truly Zhao Zilong, the mountain?”

Zhao Yun said, “Yes. By order of my lord Liu Xuande, I have come as a master attendant on this distant mission. I have driven horse and saddle hard; I was ordered to bring you food and wine.”

When the words were done, soldiers knelt and offered food and wine; Zhao Yun respectfully presented it. Song thought, “They say Liu Xuande is broad in kindness toward guests; this is truly the case.” They drank several cups together and rode onward. When they reached the gate of the frontier for Jing Province late that day, they arrived at a relay inn. More than a hundred men stood outside the gate beating drums in a formal welcome.

One officer before the horse gave formal greeting, saying, “By my lord’s command, an attendant is ordered to sweep the inn grounds and prepare lodging.” Song dismounted and entered with Guan Yu and Zhao Yun. They greeted, sat in order, and spoke.

Soon they served wine and food. The two men urged each other repeatedly. They did not part from drinking until deep into the night, then ended the session and spent one night in lodging.

Next morning after early meal they mounted and rode three to five li when a group of horsemen arrived. It was Xuande himself, bringing Fuling and Fengchou, and had come in person to meet them. Seeing Zhang Song waiting below, already dismounted, Song quickly dismounted and came to greet him.

Xuande said, “I have long heard the master’s high reputation by repute alone. It is a shame we were so far apart that I could not hear your teaching. Now that we know you have returned from the road, I am honored to meet you. If you will not reject me, I will count it bliss to rest one while in this wilderness county and clear the longing in my heart.”

Song rejoiced and mounted with him into the city. In the hall each performed formal respect; hosts and guest sat in order, and a feast was arranged.

During the banquet Xuande spoke only of easy matters and never raised Western Sichuan. Song turned conversation and asked, “My lord, as imperial uncle holding Jing Province, how many commanderies do you have now?”

Kongming said, “Jing Province is only a temporary loan from Eastern Wu; he and they often send soldiers and tax men to trouble us. Since my lord is the son-in-law of Eastern Wu, he for now can only stay here at ease.”

Song replied, “Eastern Wu holds six commanderies and eighty-one counties. Its people are strong and its nation rich, and yet it is still not satisfied?”

Pang Shuoyuan said, “My lord is the Han imperial uncle and thus the Han family has no rightful grasp on these prefectures and commanderies. All others are bandits against the Han, relying on force to seize land. Only a wise man feels no peace.”

Xuande said, “Gentlemen, cease. What merit has this man? How dare I ask such of you?”

Song said, “No, your majesty, Han emperor’s kinsman, your benevolence fills the four seas. Do not speak only of taking commanderies and counties. Were one to replace the legitimate succession and sit the imperial seat, that would still be beyond my rightful measure.”

Xuande clasped his hands in thanks: “Your words overdo me. How could I dare to claim as much?”

From then on, Song remained for three days drinking and talking, still without touching the matter of Sichuan. He then took leave. Xuande hosted him with a feast at a pavilion ten li out and saw him off.

Xuande raised the cup and said to Song, “I thank the master greatly for three days of companionship. I do not know when we shall again have cause to hear your teaching.” When he finished he was nearly in tears. Song thought, “Such a broad-minded and generous host, how can one leave him? Better I speak plainly and press him to take Western Sichuan.”

He said, “I think continually of attending morning and evening, yet no chance has come. In what I have seen of Jing Province, Sun Quan on the east always harbors tiger-like ambition; to the north Cao Cao always seeks to swallow all. This is no place to stay long.”

Xuande said, “I know it is so, yet I have no secure foothold.”

Song said, “Yi Province is a fortress country, with fertile plains and a thousand li of wealth. Its people are abundant and its state rich. Men of intelligence there long to follow your humane governance. If you raise the people of Jing and Xiang, then ride straight west. Your hegemony can be made and the Han house restored.”

Xuande said, “How could I dare do this? Liu Yixu is also kin to the imperial line, and he has long dispensed beneficence through Shu. Who can unsettle him?”

Song said, “I do not come for rank or reward. Now that I meet your excellency, I cannot conceal my loyalty. Liu Ji-yu has land in Yi Province but weak nature and little strength to employ worthy men. With Zhang Lu pressing from the north and thinking often to invade, the people are scattered and wish for a true lord. I came only to bring gifts to Cao, but I met only arrogance and contempt from this villain, so I came to you deliberately. If your excellency first secures Western Shu as your base, then turn north for Hanzhong, and from there recover the Central Plain, rectifying Heaven’s court. Great name and achievement would be yours and unmatched. If you truly intend to take Western Shu, I am willing to spend even a dog’s and horse’s sweat to serve as an inside helper. I do not know your intent.”

Xuande said, “I deeply feel your deep-heartedness. Yet Liu Ji-yu and I share the same Liu line. If I attack him, the world will spit on me.”

Song replied, “A true man should strive first for merit and accomplishment and carry the whip forward. If it is not taken now, others will take it. Regret will come too late.”

Xuande said, “I have heard Shu’s roads are rugged and steep, with a thousand mountains and ten thousand waters. The carts cannot keep straight line and horses cannot keep rein in step. Even if I wished to take it, what good plan is there?”

Song took a map from his sleeve and gave it to Xuande. “Because you are so gracious, I dare submit this map. By studying it, you can know the ways of Shu at once.” Xuande unrolled it briefly and looked. It contained clear notes on routes, distances, topography, mountain passes, strong points, treasuries, and military stores.

Song said, “My lord should copy it quickly. I have two close and loyal friends: Fa Zheng and Meng Da. Both can aid you. When they arrive in Jing Province, let them discuss your intentions together.”

Xuande clasped his hands in thanks and said, “The mountains stay old, and green waters run long. If this is accomplished, I will reward you beyond measure.”

Song said, “Meeting a worthy ruler, I have revealed my mind fully. How could I expect reward?”

Then they parted. Kongming ordered Guan Yu and others to escort him for several dozen li.

When Zhang Song returned to Yi Province, he first met his friend Fa Zheng. Fa Zheng, courtesy name Xiaozhi, was a native of Fufeng Commandery and the right Fufeng county. He was the son of the worthy Fa Zhen. Song said everything to him. “Cao Cao is arrogant and scorns the worthy, fit only for shared worry and not shared joy. I have now handed Yi Province to Liu Xuande. I have come to confer with my brother.”

Fa Zheng said, “I have long judged Liu Zhang to be incapable and have long wished Liu Xuande for the realm. Since we have the same heart, what doubt can there be?”

Shortly after, Meng Da arrived. His courtesy name was Ziqing and he was from the same homeland as Fa Zheng. As soon as he entered and saw Zheng and Song in close conversation, he said, “I already know your meaning. Do you mean to deliver Yi Province?”

Song said, “That is what I hope for. Brother, try to guess to whom it should go.”

Meng Da said, “It cannot be anyone but Liu Xuande.”

The three laughed and slapped their hands together.

Song then said to Fa Zheng, “Tomorrow you must meet Liu Zhang and speak how.”

Song said, “I propose sending the two of you as envoys to the west of the river.” The two assented.

The next day Zhang Song saw Liu Zhang.

Liu Zhang asked, “How have your affairs progressed?”

Song said, “Cao is a traitor to the Han, intent on seizing the realm under heaven. He already has designs on taking the rivers and roads of Sichuan.”

Liu Zhang said, “If so, what can we do?”

Song said, “I have one stratagem so that neither Zhang Lu nor Cao Cao will dare to trespass in Western Shu easily.”

Liu Zhang said, “What plan?”

Song said, “Liu Xuande, the imperial uncle in Jing Province, is your kinsman. He is benevolent and expansive, with the manner of an elder. After the battle at Chibi, Cao heard of him and his courage failed. How much more so for Zhang Lu? Why do you not send an envoy to join hands with him so he will be your outside support? Then you can resist Cao and Lu.”

Liu Zhang said, “I have had this same thought for long. Who can go?”

Song said, “Fa Zheng and Meng Da cannot go.”

Liu Zhang immediately called both in. He wrote a missive and made Fa Zheng the envoy first to open good feelings. Then he ordered Meng Da to lead five thousand picked troops and welcome Xuande to Shu as aid.

As they discussed the matter, a man burst in from outside, all sweat-soaked. He shouted, “If my lord follows Song’s counsel, all forty-one commanderies and provinces will already belong to another.” Song was startled. Looking at him, he recognized a man of Ba in West Lang County, surname Huang, given name Quan, courtesy name Gongheng, and currently a clerk in Liu Zhang’s household.

Liu Zhang asked, “Xuande is my kinsman. I sought alliance with him for aid. Why do you speak this way?”

Song answered, “I have long known Liu Xuande to be broad in hospitality, soft in dealing yet strong in subduing force, and unmatched among heroes. He wins the people’s hearts and the favor of common folk. He is also advised by Zhuge Liang and Pang Shuoyuan, with Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Zhao Zilong, Huang Zhong, and Wei Yan as his wings. If you bring him into Shu and treat him as a mere subordinate, will he accept being made a lowling? If you treat him as an honored guest, one state cannot host two lords. If you listen to me, Sichuan can be as safe as Mount Tai; if not, your danger is like an egg nest ready to crack. Song came from Jing Province only yesterday. He must have conspired already. Slay him first, then cut Liu Xuande off, and all of Western Shu will be saved.”

Liu Zhang said, “If Cao and Zhang Lu come, how could we refuse them?”

Huang Quan said, “Do not do so. Instead close the passes and seal every border, dig deep ditches and raise high stockades, and wait until the times are clear.”

Liu Zhang said, “Bandits cross our borders in burning haste. If we wait for clean times, the calculation is too late.” He did not take Huang Quan’s words and ordered Fa Zheng to proceed.

Another man interposed, “No! no!” Liu Zhang looked and saw him as Wang Lei, a clerk from the pavilion.

Wang Lei knelt and said, “My lord, heeding Song’s advice brings ruin on your own head.”

Liu Zhang said, “No. I join with Liu Xuande to resist Zhang Lu.”

Wang Lei replied, “Zhang Lu is like a skin disease on this state’s body; Liu Xuande entering Sichuan is like a hidden, mortal illness. Liu Xuande is known as a predatory eagle. Before he was at Cao Cao and he plotted to kill; after he served Sun Quan he took Jing Province. Can such a heart stay in one place with yours? If he comes, Sichuan is lost.”

Liu Zhang shouted, “Stop this disorderly talk. Xuande is my kinsman; how could he steal my base?” He ordered both men from the pavilion. Then he ordered Fa Zheng onward.

Fa Zheng soon left Yi Province and traveled straight to Jing Province to meet Xuande. After paying homage, he presented Liu Zhang’s letter.

Our kinsman Liu Zhang, bowing again and again, writes this to the banner beneath General Xuande. I have long been at your command and, due to rough roads, failed to carry offerings on time; my remorse is profound. I once heard that in blessing and curse one must rescue one another and in disaster one must support one another. If brothers in friendship remain so, how much more between kinsmen? Now Zhang Lu stands in the north and at dawn and dusk gathers troops to invade my command, leaving me utterly unquiet. I have sent an urgent missive by messenger, begging Your Excellence to attend. If you remember blood-kin feeling and brotherly duty, then ride out today to exterminate the mad bandit and let us be as lips and teeth to each other. This little measure of a letter says not all; more must wait for your cavalry.

Xuande read it and rejoiced, then hosted Fa Zheng with a feast.

After several rounds of wine, Xuande dismissed others and quietly said, “I have long heard Xiaozhi’s brilliance. Zhang Biejia spoke much of your noble virtue. To receive your teaching now brings me great comfort.”

Fa Zheng replied, “A petty clerk from Shu has little to say. But when a noble horse meets a horse’s master, when a man meets a true understanding, he may even die. Song Biejia has spoken what he could. Does the general still have intent?”

Xuande said, “I, only a guest living by borrowed favor, have never lacked moments of sorrow and sighing. Even a finch keeps one branch and a rabbit three burrows. If I wished, I could take Shu’s abundant land, but I cannot harm Xuande, my own kinsman.”

Fa Zheng said, “Yi Province is a granary of heaven and earth and cannot be kept by one who governs with confusion. It cannot be held by an unfit lord. Today I entrust this to you; do not miss it. Have you not heard, ‘To hunt the rabbit, seize first?’ If you want it, I will serve unto death.”

Xuande clasped his hands and said, “We can still discuss it.”

When the session ended, Kongming himself escorted Fa Zheng back to his lodging. Xuande sat alone in thought. Pang Shuoyuan said, “A matter needing a decision but left undecided marks a fool. My lord is discerning. Why so much doubting?”

Xuande asked, “In your opinion, what should we do?”

Pang answered, “In the east of Jing Province is Sun Quan, in the north Cao Cao; to succeed in gaining one must resist both. Western Shu has a million households, soldiers and wealth enough for a great undertaking. Now that Song and Fa Zheng are within your inner circle, this is heaven’s gift. Why doubt?”

Xuande said, “My present foe with me in both water and fire is Cao Cao. He uses speed, I use forbearance. He uses force, I use benevolence. He uses deceit, I use loyalty. Against him I always do the opposite and so things may succeed. If for small gain I lose great righteousness in the world, I will not do it.”

Pang smiled, “My lord’s words agree with heavenly principle, but in this age of disorder, taking power by force is no single road. If one clings to ordinary doctrine, one cannot move an inch. We must bend by changing circumstance. Strike the weak while advancing from darkness, take and then defend; this is the way of Tang and Wu. If peace comes afterward, then answer with righteousness and reward him as a king. But to delay now is to let another take it. My lord should consider well.”

Xuande suddenly saw clearly and said, “Your words of gold and stone will be engraved in my lung and marrow.” He then called Kongming to join and decided on marching westward.

Kongming said, “Jing Province is a crucial place and must keep troops divided for defense.”

Xuande said, “I will go west with Pang Shuoyuan, Huang Zhong, and Wei Yan. Let the commander stay here: the Adviser with Guan Yu and Zhang Yide and Zhao Zilong for Jing Province.”

Kongming agreed.

So Kongming held Jing Province. Guan Yu blocked the key routes at Xiangyang, holding the pass at Qingni Slope. Zhang Fei patrolled the Yangtze for four commanderies. Zhao Zilong garrisoned Jiangling and held Anping. Xuande made Huang Zhong the vanguard and Wei Yan the rear. Xuande himself with Liu Feng and Guan Ping rode in the center, Pang Shuoyuan as strategist, and fifty thousand cavalry and infantry marched west.

When departure was near, Liao Hua led a force to submit. Xuande therefore ordered Liao Hua to assist Guan Yu in resisting Cao.

That winter, he set out. After only a few leagues, Meng Da arrived to salute and said that Liu Yixu had ordered some troops come to come from afar and welcome him. Xuande sent word into Yi Province first to Liu Zhang. Liu Zhang sent dispatches along the way to each prefecture and commandery to provide money and grain.

Liu Zhang wished to go out of Fucheng in person to meet Xuande, and issued orders that carriages, tents, banners, and armor be made bright and visible. Clerk Huang Quan entered to remonstrate, “My lord, if you go, you will surely be harmed by Liu Xuande. I have eaten your salary these many years; I can no longer bear to let your lord be trapped by another’s scheme. Think again three times.”

Song replied, “Quan’s words, though spoken in the name of blood-brotherhood, only nourish rebel power. This helps the lord nothing.”

Liu Zhang shouted, “My intent is set. Why do you oppose it?”

Huang Quan knocked his head and bled, then came forward biting Liu Zhang’s robe and remonstrating. Liu Zhang was enraged, pulled up his robe and rose. Quan did not let go and snapped both front teeth.

Liu Zhang roared and ordered attendants to escort Huang Quan out. Quan returned in tears.

As Liu Zhang prepared to depart, someone cried out at the gate, “My lord rejected Huang Gongheng’s loyal advice; he is going of his own death.” The man lay down before the stairs, and Liu Zhang saw him as Li Hui. He was from Yuyuan in Jianning, surname Li, given name Hui.

Li Hu bowed and remonstrated, “It is said, ‘When a ruler has a remonstrating minister, it is like a father with a remonstrating son.’ Hui’s loyal words must be heeded. If you admit Liu Xuande into Sichuan, it is like inviting a tiger through the gate.”

Liu Zhang said, “Xuande is my kinsman; why would he hurt me? Say this again and you die!” He shouted to attendants to throw Li Hui out.

Song said, “In Shu now the civil officials each guards wife and child, no longer serving my lord. The generals are proud of prior merit and each has separate intent. Without Liu Yixu, enemies will strike from outside and people from inside. This is the road to ruin.”

Liu Zhang said, “What you seek is beneficial to me.”

The next day he mounted at Yuchiao Gate. A report came: “The officer Wang Lei, having taken rope, hanged himself upside down at the gate, holding a memorial in one hand and a sword in the other. He cried that his remonstrance was ignored and then cut the rope himself, smashing his body here.”

Liu Zhang had his carried memorial read. Its brief text said:

Your servant Wang Lei, an Officer of Yi Province, bows with bloodied tears. I have heard it said: ‘Bitter medicines are good for illness, and harsh truths help good action.’ The Lord of Chu once rejected Qu Yuan’s words and, in joining covenant at Wuguan, was trapped by Qin. Now my lord lightly leaves the great province and wishes to welcome Liu Xuande to Fucheng, fearing there is nowhere to go yet no return path. If you can execute Zhang Song in the market and cut off your pact with Liu Xuande, both old and young in Sichuan will be saved, and my lord’s foundations saved also!

Liu Zhang read it and shouted, “I have met a true man like this as if he were kin’s elegant orchid. Why did he endure so many insults from me?”

Wang Lei cried out once more, cut his own rope, and crashed to death at the foot of the gate.

Later men set this in verse:

He hangs at the city gate, holding a memorial, hurling himself for Liu Zhang’s life; Huang Quan lost his teeth and finally submitted to Xuande—what of Wang Lei’s steadfast blade-like spirit?

Liu Zhang brought three thousand troops and horse to Fucheng.

The rear train carried money and bolts of silk in more than one thousand carts.

When Xuande’s vanguard had arrived at Shuju, provisions in Western Sichuan awaited it at every stop. His commands were severe: any taking even a small thing from the people would be death. So wherever they passed there was no plunder of even the finest hairs. Elderly people and small children came along the roads to watch, incense burning and bows offered. Xuande all along used kind words to reassure them.

Fa Zheng told Pang Shuoyuan quietly, “A secret letter from Song has arrived just now. It says if you can meet Liu Zhang at Fucheng, he can be taken then. Do not lose this chance.”

Pang answered, “Set this thought aside for now. Wait until the two Liu meet and then seize at convenience. If it leaks early, there could be trouble.”

Fa kept silent.

Fucheng lay three hundred sixty li from Chengdu. Liu Zhang had arrived and sent men to receive Xuande. Both armies camped over the Fu River. Xuande entered the city and met Liu Zhang, exchanging brotherly feeling. After formalities they spoke with tears.

After the banquet they each returned to their camps to rest.

Liu Zhang said to the assembled officials, “How laughable Huang Quan and Wang Lei were, not understanding the heart of my brother, and needlessly suspecting him. Today I have truly met a man of benevolence and righteousness. Now that I have him as outside aid, why should I still fear Cao Cao or Zhang Lu?”

He removed his green robe and five hundred taels of gold and sent them to Zhang Song through Chengdu.

At that time subordinates Liu Gui, Leng Bao, Zhang Ren, Deng Xian, and others said together, “My lord, do not rejoice yet. Liu Xuande may be soft in surface and hard in spirit. His heart cannot be measured. Continue to be on guard.” Liu Zhang laughed, “You all are overcareful. Does my brother have double intentions?” All withdrew with sighs.

When Xuande returned to his camp, Pang Shuoyuan entered and asked, “What did my lord see in Liu Ji-yu today?”

Xuande said, “Ji-yu is a sincere man.”

Pang said, “Though he is good, his officials Liu Gui and Zhang Ren all show displeasure; the omens in between are not secure. In my calculation, the plan should be this: tomorrow hold a banquet, invite Ji-yu to sit. Hide a hundred sword- and axe-men in the side tents and let my lord throw the cup as the signal, then strike him at the banquet. Then one charge into Chengdu: no sword need leave its scabbard nor bow be strung, and you can sit and settle all.”

Xuande said, “Ji-yu is kinsman to me. He receives me with sincerity, and when I first came to Shu the bonds of trust are not yet firm. If we do this, heaven will not permit it, and the people below will also resent. Even a hegemon would not do this.”

Pang said, “This is not my scheme. Xiaozhi has learned from Song’s secret letter that delay is dangerous; one must act soon.”

Before the matter ended, Fa Zheng entered and said, “We are not doing this for ourselves, but following Heaven’s mandate.”

Xuande said, “Liu Ji-yu is my kin. I cannot take him.”

Zheng said, “My lord is mistaken. If not, Zhang Lu and Shu will bring old-mother revenge and surely attack. You crossed mountains and rivers, pressed horse and men, and you are already here. If you advance you gain merit, if you turn back, nothing is gained. If you hold back with suspicion, delay day by day and lose the chance. The scheme may be discovered and counted by other men. Better to take advantage of this time when heaven and men are returning to you. Strike unexpectedly and establish a base early—that is the best policy.”

Pang also urged him repeatedly.

The chapter closes:

A man may keep to benevolence for many years, but a talented minister keeps his mind on advancing stratagems.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhang Yongnian Challenges Yang Xiu, Pang Shiyuan Debates Taking Western Shu

chapters.html:
It is said that Pang Tong, whose courtesy name was Shiyuan, and Fa Zheng, whose courtesy name was Xiaozhi, advised Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, to kill Liu Zhang on the spot while they sat together at table. Liu Bei replied, “This is not something I can do. I have only newly entered Shu, and my favor and trust are not yet established.” The two men pressed him again and again, but Liu Bei did not yield. The next day they again held a banquet with Liu Zhang in the city and spoke with one another in close and friendly conversation. By the time the wine had warmed both sides, Pang Tong and Fa Zheng conferred.

“Now the matter has reached this point. It is no longer possible to avoid action, my lord.”

They told Wei Yan to mount the hall steps and dance with his sword. As Liu Zhang entered the room, Wei Yan drew his blade and went forward, saying, “The banquet has offered no real amusement. Allow me to dance for pleasure.”

Pang Tong then called in the bodyguards and lined them below the hall, waiting for Wei Yan’s cue. When Liu Zhang’s own captains saw Wei Yan’s sword dance before the table, they saw too the guards below with blades drawn, and they fixed their eyes on the hall above. Zhang Ren also drew his sword and joined the dance, saying, “Swordplay needs an opponent. I will dance with Wei General.”

The two men danced together before the table. Wei Yan fixed his eye on Liu Feng, and Liu Feng drew his blade and assisted.

Then Liu Gui, Leng Bao, and Deng Xian all drew their swords and stepped forth saying, “We should dance in a group and make this a joyful occasion.”

Liu Bei was startled. He quickly drew the swords worn by the guards at his side and stood up at the table.

“Brothers are meant to meet and drink deeply in frank friendship. We bear no suspicion toward one another, and this is no banquet at Hongmen. Why all this swordplay? If any man draws steel without cause, he will be beheaded!”

Liu Zhang also shouted, “We are brothers in spirit. Why must we still carry swords?” He ordered his attendants to remove all their ceremonial blades.

The attendants withdrew in confusion. Liu Bei called his officers to the dais and gave them wine.

“I and my brothers are of one bloodline and one brotherhood. We have discussed a grave matter and have no divided heart. There is nothing here for you to suspect.”

All the officers bowed in thanks. Liu Zhang took Liu Bei’s hand and wept. “I shall never forget your kindness, my brother.”

The two men then drank until evening and parted. Liu Bei returned to his camp and said to Pang Tong, “How have you dared to urge me toward an unjust act? Never do this again.” Pang Tong sighed and withdrew.

When Liu Zhang returned to his camp, Liu Gui and the others said, “My lord, did you see how strange yesterday’s banquet appeared? It would be better to return home at once and prevent future trouble.”

Liu Zhang said, “My brother, Liu Xuande, is not like others.”

The generals replied, “Even if Xuande himself has no such design, those under his command all want to absorb West Shu and grasp riches.”

Liu Zhang said, “You are wrong to doubt my brotherly feeling. For this reason I will not listen.” He went on talking with Liu Bei cheerfully every day.

Soon a report came that Zhang Lu had been putting his troops in order and was preparing to strike at Jiameng Pass. Liu Zhang invited Liu Bei to go out and resist. Liu Bei agreed with feeling and moved at once with his own troops toward Jiameng Pass.

The commanders advised Liu Zhang that his chief generals should hold all passes closely, to guard against any treachery from Liu Bei. Liu Zhang at first refused, but later, at repeated entreaty, he ordered Yang Huai and Gao Pei to guard Fushui Pass. He then returned to Chengdu.

When Liu Bei arrived at Jiameng, he enforced strict discipline among his soldiers and extended generous favor to secure the people’s hearts.

A covert report had long reached Eastern Wu. Sun Quan, lord of Wu, convened his civil and military officers.

Gu Yong said, “Liu Bei has dispersed his army across difficult routes and far terrain. It will not be easy for him to return quickly. Why not send one force first to block the Sichuan approaches and cut his road home, then raise all of Wu’s troops and descend into Jingzhou in one rush? This opportunity must not be missed.”

Sun Quan said, “This is a fine plan!”

As they were discussing it, a voice shouted from behind a screen, “Whoever proposed this should be executed. Do you intend to kill my daughter?” The officials turned in shock. It was Sun Quan’s mother.

She was furious: “I have had only one daughter in my life. I married her to Liu Bei. If you move now, what is to become of her life?” Then she shouted at Sun Quan, “You bear your father’s and elder brother’s legacy and rule over eighty-one commanderies, and yet you are still not satisfied? You seek only small profit and forget your blood ties.”

Sun Quan answered repeatedly, “How could I violate my mother’s instruction?” He sent the officers away.

The Empress Dowager withdrew in displeasure. Sun Quan stood under his pavilion and thought to himself, “If this chance is lost, when will I ever take Jingzhou?”

While he still pondered, Zhang Zhao came in and asked, “What concerns Lord Sun?”

Sun Quan said, “I have been thinking about what just happened.”

Zhang Zhao said, “It is easy. Send one trusted general with only five hundred men, send him secretly into Jingzhou, and place a letter in the lady’s hands. Tell her that Madam Mother is seriously ill and wants to see her daughter. Have her return to Wu by night. Liu Bei has but one son—ask her to bring A-dou with her. In that case, Liu Bei will trade Jingzhou for his child. If he resists, then let us take up arms as planned.”

Sun Quan said, “This is excellent. I know one man named Zhou Shan. He is fearless, and from childhood he could slip in and out of houses and often followed my brother.”

Zhang Zhao said, “Use him at once and do not let the matter leak.”

So Sun Quan secretly ordered Zhou Shan to leave with five hundred men, disguised as merchants and divided into five boats. He also prepared counterfeit government documents for questioning, and hidden weapons were stowed within the boats.

Zhou Shan obeyed and came by water toward Jingzhou.

At a riverside landing he sent no alarm, entered Jingzhou, and asked the gate officers to summon Madam Sun. The gate officer reported to her. She ordered Zhou Shan admitted, and he presented the secret letter. On reading it, she burst into tears and asked anxiously.

Zhou Shan reported that Madam Mother had grown dangerously ill and longed constantly to see her daughter, and that, if delayed, she might not live to meet her.

Sun Furen said, “The Imperial Uncle has brought troops far from home. If I now go back, I must send word to our strategist first.”

Zhou Shan said, “What if the strategist answers that you are to wait for his command before leaving?”

Sun Furen replied, “If I simply leave without permission, there will surely be obstruction.”

Zhou Shan said, “A boat is already prepared on the river. Please climb aboard and leave at once.”

When she heard her mother was near death, Sun Furen was in no state to be calm. She placed seven-year-old A-dou in the carriage, and with thirty men bearing swords rode out with her.

With sword at each hip they set out from Jingzhou. Before anyone in the household could report to the city, Sun Furen had already reached Shatou and boarded the ship.

When Zhou Shan was about to cast off, he heard from shore a cry, “Do not set the ship adrift yet! Give the mistress leave to take leave!”

It was Zhao Yun.

Zhao Yun had just returned from patrol and, hearing the news, had ridden four or five horsemen with windlike speed along the riverbank. Zhou Shan held a long halberd in his hand and shouted, “Who are you, to confront the mistress?” He shouted to his soldiers, “Set the ship in motion and bring all weapons out.”

The wind was favorable and the current swift, so the ships drifted downstream.

Zhao Yun galloped along the riverbank for ten li. Then he saw a fishing boat moored on a slant of the bank. He dropped his horse and, spear in hand, leapt into that boat.

Two men rowed forward, while Sun Furen’s ship pressed on behind. Zhou Shan ordered his soldiers to shoot.

Zhao Yun turned away the arrows with his spear; the shafts splashed into the water.

Now the ships were separated by more than ten Chinese feet. Wu soldiers stabbed wildly with their spears. Zhao Yun threw the spear onto the fishing boat and drew the Qinggang sword at his belt.

He opened a narrow path with his thrust and, at once, springing from the boat, leapt aboard the larger ship. The Wu soldiers all recoiled in astonishment.

Inside that vessel, Sun Furen held A-dou in her arms. She cried out, “How dare you behave without decency!”

Zhao Yun bowed his sword and replied, “Your ladyship, where are you going? Why was no strategist informed?”

Sun Furen said, “My mother is on the edge of death. I have no time to report.”

Zhao Yun said, “Why is Your ladyship bringing the little master out when he is your child to visit illness?”

Sun Furen said, “A-dou is my son. Who at Jingzhou can watch him if I do not bring him?”

Zhao Yun said, “Your ladyship is mistaken. This is the last line of blood in his father’s life. I rescued him once amid the hundred-thousand-strong troops of Changyang’s Longban slope. How can you carry him away today?”

She said angrily, “You are only one foot-soldier beneath the standard. Who are you to meddle in my household?”

Zhao Yun said, “If Your ladyship insists on leaving, leave. But leave the little master.”

She shouted to a maid, and the woman moved forward to pull back the child.

Zhao Yun pushed her down and, taking A-dou from her arms, held him to his chest and moved to the bow.

She wished to go ashore, but there was no hand to assist her. She wished to do violence, but reason and principle held her back. She found herself trapped.

When Sun Furen again cried for a maid to seize A-dou, Zhao Yun held the child with one arm and supported himself on his sword in the other; nobody dared come near.

Zhou Shan at the stern held the rudder and kept the ship in midstream. The current was strong and the wind favorable; they moved with the flow toward deep water.

Zhao Yun had only one pair of hands and one arm to spare, but he could protect the child and could not bring the ship to land.

At that point of extreme peril, he saw more than ten ships come out of the headwater harbor below, banners flying and drums sounding.

Zhao Yun thought, “This is the Wu plan.”

On the lead ship a senior general, a long spear in hand, shouted, “Sister-in-law, leave the nephew with us!”

It was Zhang Fei, who had been on patrol. He had heard the news and rushed to the river mouth at Youjiang, colliding just then with the Wu vessel and blocking it.

Zhang Fei leapt over with sword in hand.

Zhou Shan saw him come aboard and drew his own blade in greeting. One stroke from Zhang Fei cut him down, and he flung the head at Sun Furen’s feet.

Sun Furen cried out, “Uncle, how is this not disrespect?”

Zhang Fei said, “Sister-in-law does not honor my elder brother, and she has gone home in secret. That is disrespect!”

Sun Furen replied, “My mother is in grave condition. If I wait for your brother’s return, my mother’s condition will worsen. If you do not let me go now, I will throw myself into the river.”

Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun considered together. Zhang Fei said, “To force Lady Sun is not the way for one of us. Let us only protect A-dou and get him across.”

He spoke to her, “My brother, the Imperial Uncle of the great Han, would never disgrace his sister-in-law. Now we part. If you remember his kindness, return quickly.”

Having said this, he took A-dou and returned with Zhao Yun to their boat, leaving five of Sun Furen’s vessels to continue.

Later there were verses praising Zi Long:

In former years I saved the master at Dangyang. Today I plunged from the bank into the great river. All the Wu soldiers aboard ship lost courage; Zi Long’s heroism has no equal beneath the world.

There were also verses praising Yi De:

On Changban Slope anger mounted like a roaring storm; with one tiger cry he drove back Cao’s army. This morning on the river he lifts a fallen lord; Let the annals bear his name for ten thousand years.

The two rejoiced as they returned to their ship. Before they had gone far, Zhuge Liang drew out a large escort of boats in succession.

When they saw A-dou safe in hand, he rejoiced greatly. The three men rode back together.

Kongming hastily sent a written dispatch to Jiameng Pass to report to Liu Bei.

Sun Furen later returned to Wu and described Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun killing Zhou Shan, seizing back A-dou, and intercepting the river crossing.

Sun Quan was furious: “My sister has returned, and relations are no longer warm. They have killed our Zhou Shan. If they can do that to a messenger, how can they go unpunished?” He gathered his civil and military staff and discussed launching an attack to seize Jingzhou.

No sooner had they begun arranging troop movements than a report arrived: Cao Cao had raised four hundred thousand troops to answer the wound from Red Cliffs. Sun Quan was greatly alarmed. He at once paused his Jingzhou drive and discussed meeting Cao Cao’s threat.

News then came that his chief counselor Zhang Hong had asked leave from illness to return home, and that he had in fact died, sending a memorial before he passed.

In it Zhang Hong advised Sun Quan to move the seat to Moling, saying that Moling’s hills and waters held the atmosphere of kingship and that he should transfer the capital there for a work meant to last ten thousand generations.

Sun Quan read the letter and wept before everyone, saying, “How could I fail to listen? Zhang Ziwang urges me to move to Moling.” He ordered a full transfer of government to Jianye and ordered the building of the Stone City.

Lü Meng said, “When Cao Cao’s army comes, we should build works at the Rusu mouth and meet him there.”

The other generals objected: “If he lands, we can charge on foot. Why build walls and fortifications?”

Lü Meng replied, “Armies have strength and sluggishness; no battle can be certain. If the enemy suddenly appears, if horse and foot press each other in close ground, there will be no time even to climb the ships.”

Sun Quan said, “‘One who does not plan from afar will surely meet worries nearby.’ Brother Ziming sees farther than the rest.”

He ordered several tens of thousands of troops and began building Rusu redoubt at once. Through one night of labor, the work was finished by the appointed day.

Cao Cao in Xu rose in authority and prestige. His chief adviser Dong Zhao spoke to him.

“Since ancient times,” he said, “no minister has achieved what the Chancellor has. Not even Zhou Gong or Lü Wang can rival him. For thirty years through wind and rain you have swept away unruly men and removed danger from the people so that the Han Court survived. Why should you stand beside your ministers as an equal? I recommend that you receive the title Wei Gong and accept the Nine Honours.”

He then recited:

  1. Horses and chariots
  2. Robes
  3. Music offices
  4. Vermilion gates
  5. the right to approach the steps
  6. Tiger Guards
  7. the battleaxe and halberd
  8. bows and arrows
  9. the juchang tripod and guizan jade implement

Palace Attendant Xun Yu, whose courtesy name was Wenruo, said, “No. The Chancellor raised troops in the name of righteousness and to support the Han Court. He should keep the resolve of loyalty and upright truth and hold the spirit of humility. A gentleman wins loyalty by virtue, not this display.”

Hearing him, Cao Cao’s face darkened.

Dong Zhao replied, “How can one man stand against the longing of all under heaven?” He filed a memorial urging Cao to be honored as Wei Gong and to receive the Nine Honours.

Xun Yu sighed, “I never expected to witness this.”

Cao Cao heard how deeply he resented him and concluded he was not assisting him. In the tenth month of Jian’an seventeenth year, Cao Cao raised troops and moved south.

Cao Cao ordered Xun Yu to accompany him, but Xun Yu, knowing Cao intended him harm, feigned illness and remained at Shouchun. Suddenly Cao sent him a gift box with a sealed note in Cao’s own hand.

When he opened it, there was nothing inside. He understood the meaning and took poison.

He was fifty years old. Later, people wrote:

Wenruo’s brilliance was famed throughout the world, Yet pity that he met ruin at a ruler’s gate. Men later likened him to Marquis Liu, Yet he died without being able to face the Son of Heaven.

Xun Yu’s son, Xun Yun, sent a letter of mourning to Cao Cao. Cao was deeply regretful, ordered a rich burial, and gave him the posthumous title "Marquis Jing."

Now Cao Cao’s main army arrived at Rusu. First he sent Cao Hong with thirty thousand iron-clad cavalry to scout, to the riverbank.

He reported, “From far upstream along the river there are countless banners; I cannot tell where the troops are concentrated.”

Cao Cao remained uneasy and marched personally with all his men. He deployed his forces at the mouth of Rusu.

He went up a hillock with a hundred retainers and surveyed the warships.

He ordered the battalions in five different arrays so that every band of troops and every weapon line was clear and distinct.

On the central great ship, beneath a blue gauze parasol, sat Sun Quan, with his civil and military officials standing on both sides.

Cao Cao pointed with his whip and shouted, “If one has a son, one should be like Sun Zhongmou! What kind of son is Liu Jingsheng’s? He has no better than dogs and piglets for sons!”

There was a sudden commotion and at once the southern ships surged forward together. Another force inside Rusu redoubt broke out and struck hard at Cao’s army.

The cavalry of Cao backed and withdrew. He could not hold them long.

Then hundreds of riders came up to the mountain flank. At their head sat a man with blue eyes and purple beard.

The men all recognized him as Sun Quan.

Sun Quan drew a cavalry force and came straight to strike Cao. Cao was startled and turned back. On the way out, Wu’s generals Han Dang and Zhou Tai rode in with two squadrons to strike.

Behind him, Xu Chu flung forward his horse and wielded his sword in a broad sweep, breaking the two commanders, and Cao Cao managed to escape into camp.

Xu Chu fought the two for thirty bouts and then returned.

Back in the camp, Cao Cao rewarded Xu Chu heavily, and blamed all the generals.

“Those who turn and retreat before the enemy sap my vigor. If this happens again, all of you will be executed by beheading.”

By the third watch of that night, a roar of shouting rose outside the camp. Cao Cao mounted at once.

He saw fires everywhere. He had already been seized into the great camp by Wu forces.

The fighting continued until dawn, and when morning came the Wei troops withdrew more than fifty li and set up camp downstream.

Cao Cao was heavy of heart. While he idly studied military writings, Cheng Yu said to him,

“Your Excellency knows warfare. Do you not know that in war, speed is king? You raised this host and delayed long, allowing Sun Quan enough time to prepare. If one seizes the Rusu crossing for fortification, attack becomes difficult. Better to withdraw and return to Xuchang, then make another plan.”

Cao Cao made no reply. Cheng Yu withdrew.

Cao Cao lay down on a raised cot. Suddenly he heard a roaring tide, as if ten thousand horses were breaking into a gallop.

He looked up and saw a red sun rising in the great river, its light blinding. Again he looked at the sky and saw two suns confronting one another.

Then the red sun in the river rose straight up and crashed into the mountain before camp, sounding like thunder.

He jolted awake and realized he had been dreaming in his tent.

From the watchword it was noon. Cao Cao ordered his mounts made ready and, with fifty riders, rode straight out of camp.

He rode to the spot where in his dream the sun had seemed to set upon the mountain. As he watched, he saw one group of horsemen coming, led by a man in gold helmet and gold armor.

It was Sun Quan.

Sun Quan saw Cao arriving and did not panic. From the mountain he reined in his horse and pointed his whip.

“The Chancellor sits among the center plains, with wealth and rank already at their peak. Why is your greed never satisfied, that you again invade my Jiangnan?”

Cao Cao replied, “You are a vassal under heaven. Why raise your head against the Han throne? I come by imperial command to attack you.”

Sun Quan laughed. “Does that not shame you? Does not all under Heaven know you seize the Son of Heaven and move the lords at your pleasure? I do not dishonor the Han Court. I have come precisely to punish you and set the realm right.”

Cao Cao raged and ordered his generals, and the mountain behind them was filled with a drumbeat.

Two groups of troops emerged: on the right Han Dang and Zhou Tai, on the left Chen Wu and Pan Zhang. Four generals led three thousand crossbow men who loosed arrows in rain.

Cao Cao hurriedly drew his men back and fled.

The four generals pursued him with speed. Halfway back, Xu Chu and his Tiger Guard cavalry blocked the pursuers and pulled Cao Cao to safety.

The Wu troops played victory songs in full chorus and returned to Rusu.

Back in camp, Cao Cao reflected, “Sun Quan is not an ordinary man. The sign of the red sun must in time make him emperor.” He decided to withdraw, but still feared mockery from Wu.

At that moment, still undecided, both sides remained in opposition for more than a month and fought several times, each side alternately gaining and losing.

Until the following January, with spring rains unbroken and river ports all flooded, soldiers stood in mud and water, suffering heavily.

When he was in camp, Cao Cao held a meeting with his advisers. Some urged immediate withdrawal, while some argued that the spring weather favored holding on and should not permit retreat.

Cao wavered.

There then came report that an envoy from Wu had arrived with a letter.

Cao Cao opened it. It read:

We are both ministers serving the Han court. The Chancellor does not think to secure the state and the people and so rashly takes up arms and massacres the living. Is this worthy of a humane man? Spring waters have just begun to rise. Leave at once, Your Excellency. If not, the calamity of Chibi will return.

On the reverse he wrote two lines:

If you do not die, I cannot find peace.

Cao Cao looked it over and laughed, “Zhongmou is no fool.”

He rewarded the envoy richly and issued orders for a full retreat.

He named the Administrator of Lujiang, Zhu Guang, to hold Wancheng, and he led the great army back to Xuchang.

Sun Quan also drew back to Moling. He and his commanders discussed.

“Although Cao Cao has withdrawn north, Liu Bei is still at Jiameng and has not yet returned. Why not take the force that resisted Cao and turn it on Jingzhou?”

Zhang Zhao offered a plan: “Do not move yet. I have one strategy that can keep Liu Bei from returning to Jingzhou again.”

That is to say:

Mengde’s mighty host only now turns north, Yet Zhongmou’s vast ambition rises again toward the south. How else might one measure the plan Zhang Zhao was about to reveal? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhao Yun Intercepts the River and Recovers A-dou; Sun Quan’s Secret Letter to Send Away Lao Man

chapters.html:
Zhang Zhao offered a stratagem and said, “Do not set troops in motion yet. If we raise an army, Cao Cao will surely return. Better to draft two letters. One to Liu Zhang: tell him that Liu Bei has joined with Sun Quan and is preparing to seize Xichuan, so Liu Zhang will become suspicious and attack Liu Bei. One to Zhang Lu: instruct him to advance and come to Jing Province. Then Liu Bei, with no way to save both ends, will not be able to answer. After that I will raise troops and take it. All this will work out.” Sun Quan approved, and he immediately sent messengers to both places.

Liu Bei, courtesy name Xuande, remained long at Jiayong Pass and won much of the people’s goodwill. He then received a document from Kongming and learned that Lady Sun had returned to Eastern Wu. He also heard that Cao Cao had raised troops and moved against Runshu, so he asked Pang Tong, whose courtesy name was Shiyuan, “Cao Cao attacks Sun Quan. If Sun Quan wins, he too will claim Jing Province. If Cao Cao wins, he will still take it. What is to be done?”

Pang Tong replied, “My lord, do not worry. With Kongming there, you may trust that Eastern Wu will not dare to invade Jing Province. My lord should send word to Liu Zhang and urge him to direct all force toward attacking Sun Quan. Sun Quan will cry out for aid from Jing Province; although my lord and Sun Quan share a bond like gums and teeth, we cannot refuse each other. Zhang Lu stays to guard his own lands and will not dare to cross our border. I want to pull back the main force to Jing Province and together we will crush Cao Cao. But we are short of men and grain. Rely on kinship among the same lineage and send three or four wan of elite troops and ten thousand hu of grain in aid. Please do not fail us. If horses, money, and grain come by another route, we can discuss the rest.”

Liu Bei accepted and sent men to Chengdu. When they reached the frontier, Yang Hui and Gao Pei heard of it and ordered Gao Pei to guard the pass while Yang Hui went with emissaries into Chengdu, presenting Liu Bei’s letter. Liu Zhang read it and asked why Yang Hui had also come.

Yang Hui said, “I came only for this letter. Since Liu Bei entered Shu, he has spread his benevolence to win the hearts of the people. His intent is most troubling. If he requests horses, troops, and grain, do not grant it. If you assist him, it is like adding fuel to fire.”

Liu Zhang asked, “I and Liu Bei are tied by the bond of elder and younger brothers. Can I really refuse him?”

One man spoke, “Liu Bei is a reckless hawk. He has long remained in Shu and not departed; it is like letting a tiger into a house. To help him now with troops, horses, and grain is no different from adding wings to a tiger.”

All in the hall turned their eyes on him and recognized him as Liu Ba of Zhenyang in Lingling commandery, surname Liu, courtesy name Zichu. Hearing Liu Ba’s words, Liu Zhang hesitated but could not settle his mind. Huang Quan persisted in his appeal.

Liu Zhang apportioned four thousand old and weak soldiers and ten thousand hu of rice, then sent a reply to Liu Bei saying he had to do so. He also ordered Yang Hui and Gao Pei to hold the pass tightly. A messenger reached Fu Pass with Liu Zhang’s reply.

Liu Bei grew furious: “I have spent my strength and troubled my heart to stand against the enemy for you. Now you save money and withhold reward. How then can soldiers fulfill their duty?” He tore up the letter in anger, cursed, and stood.

The messenger fled back to Chengdu.

Pang Tong said, “My lord has always placed righteousness and justice above all. By tearing this letter and rising in anger, what you had before is wholly cast aside.”

Liu Bei asked, “What should I do now?”

Pang Tong replied, “I have three plans. Let my lord choose and act.”

Liu Bei asked which were the three. Pang Tong said, “The upper plan is this: choose picked troops at once and make a day-and-night forced march to strike Chengdu directly.

Yang Hui and Gao Pei are famous commanders in Shu, each relying on sturdy troops to hold the pass. If my lord returns to Jing Province only in name, the two generals will receive word and come out to escort him. When they come out to see him off, arrest and kill them, seize the pass, take Fu City first, and only then turn toward Chengdu—that is the core of this plan.

The lower plan is this: return to Baidi by night and then go back to Jing Province to plot a slower advance.

If my lord hesitates and delays, we will be in grave danger and cannot be saved.”

Liu Bei said, “Your foremost plan is too quick, and your lowest plan too slow. I can take the middle and set it in motion.”

He then wrote to Liu Zhang, saying that Cao Cao had sent Colonel Yue Jin with troops to Qinni town, that all commanders could not hold against it, and that he himself would go in person to meet him. He could not arrive for audience and sent this as an apology. The letter arrived at Chengdu.

Zhang Song heard that Liu Xuan [Liu Bei] sought to return to Jing Province and believed it sincere. He drafted a letter of his own to send to Liu Bei. Just then, his sworn brother Zhang Su, the administrator of Guanghan, arrived. Zhang Song hurriedly hid the letter in his sleeve and stayed with Zhang Su to converse.

Zhang Su saw Zhang Song’s distracted face and grew suspicious. Zhang Song poured wine and drank with him. In the moment of toasting and serving, the letter slipped from Zhang Song’s hand to the ground, and Zhang Su’s attendant picked it up. After the gathering ended, the attendant delivered it to Zhang Su.

Zhang Su opened it. It read,

Yesterday, I told His Imperial Uncle of a matter not false or fabricated. Why do you still delay your departure? To oppose and then comply in turn is what the ancients honored. Now the enterprise already lies in our grasp; why would you abandon it and return to Jing Province? If Zhang Song hears of this, he will feel that something has been lost. On the day this reaches you, quickly advance your forces. Zhang Song is to act as an inside accomplice. Do not fail yourself!

Zhang Su, upon reading it, was astonished and said, “My brother is planning a house-clearing rebellion. The head must be struck first.” He brought the letter to Liu Zhang overnight and told him plainly: his brother Zhang Song had conspired with Liu Bei and intended to deliver the west of Shu.

Liu Zhang was enraged. “I have never treated him poorly, so why does he now seek rebellion?” He ordered Zhang Song and all his family seized and all beheaded in the market.

Later, a poet lamented:

Though rare from ancient days is one who can see all from afar, who would have guessed that letters would expose Heaven’s design? Before seeing Xuande raise a royal enterprise, blood already stained his own clothes in Chengdu.

After Liu Zhang executed Zhang Song, he assembled civil and military officers and asked how to handle Liu Bei’s seizure.

Huang Quan said, “Do not delay. Send riders immediately to every pass with orders to add troops and hold them. Do not allow even one rider or rider-to-rider from Jing Province to enter.” Liu Zhang followed this and dispatched orders through the night.

Liu Bei took troops back to Fu City and first ordered that Yang Hui and Gao Pei be summoned to the gate to part ways. Upon receiving the summons, Yang and Gao conferred.

Gao Pei said, “Liu Bei’s return must hide an intent. We each should hide blades upon ourselves and, at the parting point, stab him to eliminate our lord’s trouble.”

Yang Hui said, “This plan is excellent.” The two men took only two hundred attendants, crossed the gate to bid farewell, and left most troops behind while Liu Bei’s main force moved ahead.

As they reached the stream above Fu, Pang Tong, still mounted, said to Liu Bei, “If Yang Hui and Gao Pei come with cheerful faces, guard against it; if they do not come, then take up arms at once and seize this pass directly. Do not delay.”

At that moment a whirlwind rose and toppled the forward-command flag with the character “Shuai” on it. Liu Bei asked Pang Tong what it portended.

Pang Tong said, “It is a warning cry. Yang Hui and Gao Pei both mean to assassinate. We should be prepared.” Liu Bei put on heavy armor and buckled his treasure-sword.

A report came that Generals Yang Hui and Gao Pei were arriving to escort him. Liu Bei ordered the horses and troops to rest.

Pang Tong instructed Wei Yan and Huang Zhong: “Any soldiers who come from the gate, whether mounted or on foot, and whoever they are, do not let one of them return.”

As ordered, both men rode away.

Yang Hui and Gao Pei, each with hidden blades, brought two hundred soldiers each and slung wine jars on donkeys straight to Liu Bei’s front. Seeing no special preparation, they were secretly pleased, thinking the trap had sprung in their favor.

They entered the command pavilion and saw Liu Bei sitting with Pang Tong. The two generals bowed and said together, “Hearing that His Imperial Uncle has returned from afar, we brought this humble offering as farewell tribute.” They offered wine to Liu Bei.

Liu Bei said, “Guarding this pass has not been easy; first, please drink this cup.”

After the two generals had drunk, Liu Bei said, “I have matters of state to discuss with you. Let all others step away.” He then ordered the two hundred they had brought all driven out of the center camp.

Liu Bei shouted, “Seize those two traitors!” Liu Feng and Guan Ping came out at once from behind the screen.

Yang and Gao moved to resist, and Liu Feng and Guan Ping each seized one. Liu Bei cried, “I and your lord are blood brothers of the same clan. Why did you two conspire to sever that brotherhood?”

Pang Tong shouted for soldiers to search their bodies. They found a blade on each, one in either waist. Pang Tong then ordered them beheaded.

Liu Bei hesitated.

Pang Tong said, “These two intended to kill our lord. Their crime cannot be pardoned.”

He then ordered sword and axe men to execute Yang Hui and Gao Pei before the pavilion.

Huang Zhong and Wei Yan had already taken the two hundred escorting soldiers earlier and captured them before one could escape.

Liu Bei called them in, gave each a cup to steady their nerves, and said, “Yang Hui and Gao Pei sought to split the brotherhood and then hid blades for assassination. Therefore they are executed. You have no fault. Do not be alarmed.” All paid respects.

Pang Tong said, “I will now employ you to lead the road. Bring my army through the pass. There will be heavy rewards.”

All agreed.

That night the two hundred went first. The main army followed. At the pass they shouted to the walls, “The two generals have urgent business and have returned. Open the gate quickly.” The city heard his own men’s voices and opened at once.

The entire force poured through at once, without bloodshed, and seized Fu Pass. The Shu soldiers all surrendered. Liu Bei granted heavy rewards and deployed his troops in front and rear to hold positions.

The next morning, after laboring the men, he held a banquet in the public hall. Later, drunk, Liu Bei looked at Pang Tong and said, “Was today’s gathering worthy of joy?”

Pang Tong replied, “To invade another man’s state and call it joy is not the army of a righteous man.”

Liu Bei said, “Did not King Wu invade Zhou and make music to mark victory? Is that not also no army of a righteous man? What you said fits ill. Step out at once!”

Pang Tong rose and laughed.

His attendants helped Liu Bei to the rear hall to sleep until half the night, when he woke. His officers then relayed Pang Tong’s words to him.

Liu Bei felt great regret and the next morning, dressed and entering the hall, asked Pang Tong to pardon him. “Yesterday in drunkenness my words were indiscreet. Do not hold them against me.”

Pang Tong answered in calm good humor. Liu Bei said, “Yesterday’s words were my own failing.”

Pang Tong replied, “Both minister and lord have erred; why only the lord?”

Liu Bei laughed and the mood returned.

Later Liu Zhang learned that Liu Bei had killed Yang Hui and Gao Pei and seized Fu Pass. He was startled and said, “I did not expect this today!” He assembled officials and military men to debate retreat or resistance.

Huang Quan said, “Send troops through the night to garrison Luo City and block the throat road. Even if Liu Bei has selected troops and fierce generals, he cannot pass.” Liu Zhang ordered Liu Gui, Leng Bao, Zhang Ren, and Deng Xian to lead fifty thousand men and that night hold Luo City against Liu Bei.

As the four commanders marched, Liu Gui said, “I have heard there is an eccentric man in Jinping Mountain, called Master Zixu. He claims to know life and death and rank and fortune. We are now marching past that mountain. Why not ask him?”

Zhang Ren said, “Can a true man marching against the enemy ask directions from a mountain wanderer?”

Liu Gui said, “Not so. The sages said, ‘With true sincerity one may foresee.’ When we ask those of higher wisdom, we seek auspiciousness and avoid misfortune.”

So the four rode with fifty or sixty riders to the mountain’s foot and asked a woodcutter for the way. The woodcutter pointed to the summit where the elder dwelt.

The four climbed up to the hermitage and saw a young attendant there to receive them. After giving their names, they were brought inside. There sat Master Zixu on a rush mat on a low platform.

The four men knelt and asked about the prospects ahead.

Master Zixu said, “I am but a worthless man of the wilds and fields. How can I know what fortune brings?”

Liu Gui begged repeatedly. Master Zixu then ordered the attendant to fetch paper and brush and wrote eight lines, which he gave to Liu Gui.

Its text was:

The dragon on the left, the phoenix on the right, fly into Xichuan. The fledgling phoenix falls to earth; the lying-dragon rises to heaven. Gain and loss are both of Heaven’s tally. Act when the moment appears; lose not your way to the Nine Springs.

Liu Gui asked, “How stand the fortunes of our four men?”

Master Zixu said, “A fixed destiny cannot be escaped. Why ask again?”

Liu Gui pressed him once more. The old man lowered his brows and closed his eyes as if asleep and did not answer. The four men returned downhill.

Liu Gui said, “Words of an immortal should be trusted.”

Zhang Ren said, “He is a wild old fool. What use is this listening to?” They resumed their march.

When they reached Luo City and assigned men to the garrisons, Liu Gui said, “Luo City is Chengdu’s final refuge. If this is lost, Chengdu is hard to save. The four of us discussed together: two should hold the city; two should go ahead, one in front of Luo City, and with terrain to our side, build two major stockades in the hills. Do not let enemy troops come near the walls.”

Leng Bao and Deng Xian said, “One of us is willing to build the stockades.”

Liu Gui was pleased and divided two men each of 20,000, sending Leng Bao and Deng Xian to camp six tens of li south of the city. Liu Gui and Zhang Ren stayed to guard Luo City.

Liu Bei, having taken Fu Pass, then talked with Pang Tong about seizing Luo City. When he heard Liu Zhang had dispatched four commanders, he noted that same day Leng Bao and Deng Xian had each brought twenty thousand cavalry and infantry and had set two large camps.

Liu Bei called for volunteers to seize the two camps. The old commander Huang Zhong stepped forward at once.

Liu Bei said, “General Huang Zhong, lead your own men. If you take Leng Bao’s or Deng Xian’s stockade, there will be great reward.”

Huang Zhong rejoiced and prepared to depart.

A man in the courtyard stepped out and said, “General Huang Zhong is old and broad of frame. How can he go?”

It was Wei Yan.

Huang Zhong said, “I have already issued the order under you. How dare you interfere?”
