Wei Yan replied, “General Huang’s strength does not lie in sinew and bone. I have heard Leng Bao and Deng Xian are famous generals of Shu, young and vigorous. You may not capture them. Would that not risk my lord’s enterprise? This is my good intent, but I offer to trade with him.”

Huang Zhong shouted in anger, “You dare call me old and compare yourself in arms with me?”

Wei Yan said, “Why not try before the ruler himself? Whichever one wins may go. What say you?”

Huang Zhong stepped down and called for a lieutenant to bring his sword. Liu Bei quickly stopped him. “No. I now bring the troops to lead the army into Sichuan. I rely on both of you. If two tigers clash, one will be wounded. It would endanger my great task. Both of you should reconcile, and do not argue.”

Pang Tong said, “Neither of you should contest.

Lengt Bao and Deng Xian have set up two camps already. Let each of you take your own detachment and each strike a camp. Whoever captures first will be first to gain merit.”

So it was fixed: Huang Zhong would strike Leng Bao’s camp; Wei Yan would strike Deng Xian’s. The two each took command and left.

Pang Tong warned, “The two may brawl on the way. My lord, have you bring a reserve force in the rear.”

Liu Bei left Pang Tong to hold the city and himself with Liu Feng and Guan Ping took five thousand to follow.

Huang Zhong returned to camp and ordered that at the fourth watch of the next day they prepare food, and at the fifth watch halt all cooking and at dawn advance into battle, entering by the left ravine.

Wei Yan, however, had already sent men to observe when Huang Zhong would move. A scout returned: “Tomorrow at the fourth watch they will cook, and at the fifth they will begin.” Wei Yan was pleased. He told his soldiers at the second watch to prepare food and at the third watch to rise and move, so they would reach Deng Xian’s camp by daybreak.

The soldiers obeyed. They ate a full meal, took off their bells, carried staffs in their teeth, tied their standards, buckled armor, and slipped forth to seize the camps.

Near the third watch, they moved out. Halfway there, Wei Yan thought from the saddle, “If I go only against Deng Xian’s camp, my strength will not be shown. Better go first against Leng Bao’s camp, and then use those men to strike Deng Xian’s. I will collect the credit from both camps.” He instantly ordered his men toward the left mountain path.

By first light they were not far from Leng Bao’s camp and told his men to rest little and arrange drums, banners, standards, spears, and blades.

A courier of hidden troops had already ridden in reporting that Leng Bao had prepared defenses. At one blast of gunfire, all three lines mounted and sallied out.

Wei Yan galloped, sword drawn, and engaged Leng Bao. The two riders met. The fight ran about thirty exchanges before troops from the Sichuan side came from two roads in support. The Han army had marched half the night; men and horses were exhausted and could not endure. They withdrew in disorder and retreated. Wei Yan, hearing the rear formations break, abandoned Leng Bao, wheeled his horse and ran back.

The Sichuan troops followed and Han forces suffered a major defeat. They had not gone five li when, behind them from the mountain gorge, drums burst across the valley. Deng Xian led a clump of troops bursting through and shouted, “Wei Yan, dismount and surrender!”

Wei Yan spurred his horse full speed, but the beast suddenly slipped on its forehoof and both forelegs knelt, throwing him down.

Deng Xian burst there, leveled a spear at Wei Yan. Before the spear-point arrived, an archer’s string sang, and Deng Xian crashed down off his mount.

Only then did Leng Bao move to assist; from the slope a senior general leapt from horseback and cried out, “General Huang Zhong is here!” and whirled his sword straight toward Leng Bao.

Leng Bao could not stand the assault and turned his mount back in flight.

Huang Zhong pursued, and the Sichuan army was thrown into confusion.

A unit under Huang Zhong rescued Wei Yan, killed Deng Xian, and drove straight to the camp.

Leng Bao turned again to match Huang Zhong and fight, but within no more than ten exchanges, a full host of horse and foot came behind him. Left with no way out, he abandoned the left camp and fled defeated to the right camp.

The banners there were wholly different.

Leng Bao reined in at once and saw, in the front of the host, a great general in golden armor and brocade robes—Liu Bei himself. Liu Feng stood to his left and Guan Ping to his right.

He cried, “This camp is already ours. Where can you go now?”

It was indeed Liu Bei arriving from the rear to reinforce and ride the momentum that had broken the two camps.

With no path ahead, Leng Bao sought a hidden track through the hills to return to Luo City. He had not gone ten li when ambushes rose in a narrow pass, hooks and ropes all cast together and he was taken alive.

It was Wei Yan, now aware he had committed an offense and had no excuse. He had drawn the Shu troops into this place and laid an ambush here, then waited for the exact moment, binding Leng Bao with rope and leading him bound back to Liu Bei’s camp.

Liu Bei raised a flag of pardon, but ordered that Sichuan soldiers who had turned their spears and stripped their armor not be killed. Even if wounded, their lives were to be repaid. He also announced to the captives: “You of Sichuan all have fathers and mothers, wives and sons. Those who wish to surrender will serve as household troops; those who do not may return home.”

Great rejoicing rose from the earth.

Huang Zhong returned from camp and reported to Liu Bei that Wei Yan had disobeyed orders and should be beheaded.

Liu Bei immediately summoned Wei Yan. Wei Yan presented Leng Bao to him.

Liu Bei said, “Even though Wei Yan has offended, this merit can absolve him.” He instructed Wei Yan to thank Huang Zhong for saving his life, and said there should be no further rivalry.

Wei Yan knelt and confessed his fault.

Liu Bei greatly rewarded Huang Zhong.

He ordered Leng Bao brought before him and had his bonds removed. He gave him wine to calm his fear and asked, “Will you surrender?”

Leng Bao said, “Now that I have been spared from death, how could I not? Liu Gui and Zhang Ren are sworn blood companions of mine. If I may return, I will bring both to surrender and offer Luo City.”

Liu Bei rejoiced and gave him clothing and horse and saddle, then ordered him back to Luo City.

Wei Yan said, “This man cannot be released. If he slips away once, he will never return.”

Liu Bei said, “If I treat people with righteousness, people will not fail me.”

Leng Bao returned to Luo City and told Liu Gui and Zhang Ren nothing of his capture and release. He claimed he had only killed more than ten and escaped with stolen horses.

Liu Gui hurried men to Chengdu for aid.

When Liu Zhang heard that Deng Xian had been cut down, he was startled. He hurriedly gathered all and deliberated.

His eldest son, Liu Xun, offered, “My lord, I will lead troops there to guard Luo City.”

Liu Zhang asked, “Since my son is willing, whom shall I send as his support?”

One man stepped forth saying, “I will go.” Liu Zhang saw it was his brother-in-law, Wu Yi.

He said, “It is best that your honored uncle goes. Who can act as his deputy commander?”

Wu Yi appointed Wu Lan and Lei Tong as deputies and raised twenty thousand mounted and foot soldiers to Luo City.

Liu Gui and Zhang Ren arrived, giving a full account.

Wu Yi asked, “An army under the walls is hard to repel. What superior insight do you have?”

Leng Bao said, “This stretch here lies by Fu River, whose current runs fierce. The camps ahead are lowest on the mountain foot. I request five thousand men, each with shovel and spade, to go forward and dam the river. We can then release all of it and drown Liu Bei’s army completely.”

Wu Yi followed this and sent Leng Bao to prepare the waterworks. Wu Lan and Lei Tong moved their troops to join him.

Meanwhile Liu Bei ordered Huang Zhong and Wei Yan each to hold one stockade and returned to Fu City to consult with his strategist Pang Tong.

A scout reported, “Sun Quan of Eastern Wu has made peace with Zhang Lu and plans to attack Jiayong Pass.”

Liu Bei was alarmed: “If Jiayong Pass is lost, our rear is cut and I cannot advance or withdraw. What is to be done?”

Pang Tong told Meng Da, “You are from Shu and know the terrain. Go guard Jiayong Pass. How do you plan to do it?”

Meng Da said, “I will send one man with me and there will be no failure.”

Liu Bei asked who.

Meng Da answered, “That man served under Liu Biao in Jing Province as an zhonglang general. He is from the Zijiang commandery of Nanzhou. His surname is Huo and his name is Jun; courtesy name Zhongmiao.”

Liu Bei was glad and at once sent Meng Da and Huo Jun to the pass.

Pang Tong returned to his quarters. The gateman reported, “A guest has arrived to visit without prior notice.”

Pang Tong went out to receive him. The man was eight chi tall, extremely imposing; his hair was cut short and hung around his neck; his clothes were not very neat. Pang Tong asked, “Sir, who are you?”

The man did not answer. He went straight into the hall and stretched out on a couch.

Pang Tong grew suspicious and asked again and again.

The man said, “Wait a little. I will tell you about the great affairs of the world.” Pang Tong grew even more doubtful and ordered wine and food. The man rose, ate heartily, and asked no modesty. He ate much; when done, he slept again.

Pang Tong was in doubt, so he sent for Fa Zheng to look in case it was a spy. Fa Zheng came quickly.

Pang Tong greeted him and said, “There is a man like this before us.” Fa Zheng stared and asked, “Could this be Peng Yong?”

He climbed the steps and stood over him. The man rose and said, “How goes it, has Xiazhi stayed well?”

It was then that this verse came:

Only because a man of Shu met an old acquaintance, the flood of the Fu River was brought to rest. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Seizing Fu Pass: Yang Huai and Gao Pei Are Beheaded; Seizing Luo City, Huang Zhong and Wei Yan Strive for Merit

chapters.html:
When Counselor Fa Zheng met that man, the two laughed and clapped one another on the shoulders. Pang Tong asked, “Who is this person?”

Fa Zheng replied, “This man is from Guanghan. His family name is Peng, his given name was Yang, and his courtesy name was Yongyan. He is a distinguished warrior among Shu. He offended Liu Zhang by speaking too plainly, and Liu Zhang reduced him to household servitude, which is why his hair was cropped short. I received him as a guest and asked where he had come from.”

Peng Yang said, “I have come especially to save ten thousand of your soldiers from death. I can speak plainly only when I meet your general.”

Fa Zheng quickly reported to Liu Bei. Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, personally went to meet him and asked for the reason. Peng Yang asked, “How many riders and troops are there in your forward encampment, General?” Liu Bei answered straightforwardly, “Huang Zhong and Wei Yan are there.”

“Is that how a commander is supposed to act?” Peng Yang asked. “Can he not know the terrain? The forward encampment sits by the Fu River. If we release its waters and block the approaches with soldiers both in front and behind, not one man will be able to escape.”

Liu Bei suddenly understood. Peng Yang continued, “The star Kang is in the west, and Venus is directly above this place. Harm is due. You should be careful.”

Liu Bei made Peng Yang a guest among the tents at once, sent men quietly to Wei Yan and Huang Zhong, and instructed them to patrol morning and evening with full attention to prevent the water being let out. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan planned it together: one day on each watch; if enemy troops arrived, they would report to one another at once.

Leng Bao saw that the night brought wind and rain and moved five thousand troops along the riverbank, intending to seize the channel. As soon as he began to open the river, cries rose from behind.

Leng Bao knew preparations had been made and withdrew in haste. Behind him Wei Yan arrived in pursuit; men from the river units trampled one another in the rush. As Leng Bao fled, he collided with Wei Yan.

Their horses clashed only a few times, and Wei Yan took him alive.

By the time Wu Lan and Lei Tong came to reinforce, Huang Zhong’s force also came charging. Wei Yan brought Leng Bao in to Fu Pass.

Liu Bei reproached him: “I treated you with benevolence and let you go. How dare you now betray me! This offense is not to be excused.”

He had Leng Bao brought out and beheaded, then rewarded Wei Yan highly.

Liu Bei then held a banquet in honor of Peng Yang. Just then word arrived that Master Strategist Zhuge Liang of Jingzhou had sent Ma Liang by dispatch with a sealed letter.

Liu Bei summoned him in. After Ma Liang presented his respects he said, “Jingzhou is at peace. Do not trouble yourselves with concern.” Then he presented his master’s letter.

Liu Bei opened and read it. It said in part:

“Master Kongming has calculated the Taiyi numbers this night. This year is the guihai year cycle. Kang is in the west. Also by observing the heavenly signs, Venus descends on the sector of Luo City. The general-in-chief and field commander has more inauspicious signs than good ones. Extreme caution is required.”

After reading the letter, Liu Bei told Ma Liang to return first. “I will return to Jingzhou and talk this matter through there.”

Pang Tong thought privately, “Kongming fears that I will take Western Region and win renown, so he sent this letter to delay me on purpose.” He said aloud to Liu Bei: “I also cast the Taiyi numbers. I already know Kang is in the west, so your lordship ought to obtain Xichuan. It does not signify an ill omen. I observed the heavenly patterns as well and saw Venus over Luo City. We already beheaded Leng Bao, fulfilling the warning already. Do not doubt your mind; advance at once.”

After being pressed repeatedly by Pang Tong, Liu Bei moved his army forward. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan went ahead toward the encampment.

Pang Tong asked Fa Zheng, “How many routes lead to Luo City from here?”

Fa Zheng drew a map on the ground. Liu Bei compared it with the copy of the chart that Zhang Song had left behind; it matched exactly.

Fa Zheng explained, “To the north of the mountains there is one broad route, which should go directly to the east gate. To the south there is a small route, which leads to the west gate. Both routes can admit a force.”

Pang Tong said to Liu Bei, “Let Wei Yan be the vanguard. He should take the southern small road. You should send Huang Zhong in as vanguard along the northern broad road. Take both and break into Luo City together.”

Liu Bei said, “I learned to ride and draw a bow from childhood and can use smaller paths easily. The strategist should go by the broad road and take the east gate. I will take the west gate.”

Pang Tong replied, “If we use the broad road, the enemy will have a force waiting to intercept. Your lordship should lead the main body to meet it. I will take the small road.”

Liu Bei said, “No, strategist. I had a dream in the night: a spirit figure held an iron club and struck my right arm. When I woke, my arm still ached. This march may not be favorable.”

Pang Tong said, “A brave man is not killed by battle only because he enters it wounded. It is only a matter of nature. Why should you let a dream disturb your mind?”

Liu Bei said, “What I doubt is Kongming’s letter. Why should the strategist remain to guard Fu Pass?”

Pang Tong laughed and said, “Your lordship has been misled by Kongming. He does not want you to win this campaign alone and earn all the achievement, so he planted those words to cast doubt in your heart. Doubt brings dreams; if doubt is present, what misfortune can arise? I would lay my heart and mind to the ground to show my true loyalty. Do not press the matter any further. We move at once.”

On that day the order passed: the troops cooked at the dawn watch and mounted at first light. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan led the troops ahead.

Liu Bei and Pang Tong arranged to ride together again. As they sat down to mount, Liu Bei noticed something wrong in his horse’s gait and pulled Pang Tong from the saddle.

He leapt down and took the reins of that mount himself. He said, “Why are you riding this bad horse, Military Adviser?”

Pang Tong answered, “I have ridden this horse for a long time and it has never failed before.”

Liu Bei said, “A horse that stumbles before the battle can cost men their lives. Mine is a white horse, very tractable. You should ride it and there will be no misstep. I will ride this poor horse.”

Then they exchanged mounts. Pang Tong bowed. “My lord’s kindness is too great. Even ten thousand deaths could not repay it.”

They mounted and took the road forward. As Pang Tong rode away, Liu Bei felt no joy in his heart and moved forward in a heavy mood.

In Luo City, Wu Yi and Liu Gui heard that Leng Bao had been cut down. They consulted together with their officers. Zhang Ren said, “There is a narrow but crucial path in the southeast of the city’s hills. I will lead one force there myself. All remain tight on Luo City and allow nothing to slip.”

Just then word came that Han troops were coming in two columns to attack.

Zhang Ren quickly led three thousand men, came first to cut through the path, and lay an ambush. Seeing Wei Yan’s force pass, he ordered them to pass unhindered, making no noise.

When they later saw Pang Tong’s men coming, an officer in Zhang Ren’s ranks pointed and said, “The one on white horse must be Liu Bei.” Zhang Ren rejoiced and gave an order.

Pang Tong advanced slowly, looked up and saw narrow twin ridges and dense thickets. It was late summer, early autumn, and the foliage was still luxuriant. He grew increasingly uneasy and reined in his horse.

“What is this place called?” he asked.

A newly surrendered soldier in their ranks pointed and answered, “This place is called Luo Feng Slope.”

Pang Tong cried out in alarm, “I am nicknamed the Phoenix Chick. This place is called Fallen Phoenix Slope. It is not favorable to me.” He ordered the rear ranks to fall back at once.

A cannon-like report sounded ahead on the slope. Arrows came as thick as locusts, all aimed at the rider on the white horse. Poor Pang Tong was killed beneath the hail of arrows. He was thirty-six years old.

Years later, men wrote in verse:

Ancient spurs touch, the purple-green ridges pile high, Shiyuan’s house once clung to the hollow of the hill. Children knew by heart the Cuckoo Song; in the lanes they had heard him reveal the speed of a warhorse. He planned to cleave the three kingdoms as one and stride alone, a tall frame wandering for ten thousand li. Who could have foreseen the heavenly dog and falling star would deny the general his return in robes of brocade?

There had once been a folk rhyme in the southeast:

A phoenix and a dragon came together, moving as one toward Shu. Only halfway on the road, the phoenix fell on Luo’s eastern slope. Wind sends rain; rain sends wind, When Han’s rising age brings the road to Shu, and when it opens only the dragon may pass.

On the day Zhang Ren shot Pang Tong, the Han soldiers packed tightly shoulder to shoulder and could neither advance nor retreat; most were slain.

A runner reported to Wei Yan. Wei Yan immediately formed ranks and tried to return, but the mountain road was too narrow for close combat. Zhang Ren blocked their way home and at a high rise cut down on them with heavy bows and crossbows. Wei Yan grew uneasy.

One newly surrendered Shu soldier said, “Let us cut through and run straight into Luo City and take the broad road.”

Wei Yan followed this advice. He led the first break in the way and cut forward toward Luo City.

In the dust rise of their feet, a force appeared in front: it was the city’s defenders, Wu Lan and Lei Tong. Behind them Zhang Ren’s troops came in pursuit. Surrounded front and rear, Wei Yan was hemmed in the center.

Wei Yan fought hard and could not break free. He saw Wu Lan and Lei Tong’s rear force growing confused and disorderly. The two commanders turned their horses and rushed back to rescue.

Wei Yan seized the moment and rode on, the first commander in line, striking his horse and crying, “Wenchang! I have come to save you!” It was the old general Huang Zhong.

The two flanks fought together and defeated Wu and Lei, then drove straight toward the foot of Luo City. Liu Gui led troops out and met them, but Liu Bei was behind holding the line to cover their return. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan turned back at once.

Liu Bei’s cavalry, by the time it reached the camps, saw Zhang Ren’s cavalry break out from the small path. Liu Gui, Wu Lan, and Lei Tong came in hot pursuit. Liu Bei could not hold both camps and withdrew while fighting, then ran back to Fu Pass.

Shu troops won and chased on, and Liu Bei’s men came on in a chain. But his men were exhausted and his horses tired; there was no heart left for close fighting, only for flight.

As they neared Fu Pass, Zhang Ren’s army pursued close.

By good fortune, Liu Feng arrived on the left and Guan Ping on the right.

Liu Feng and Guan Ping on the left and right brought thirty thousand fresh soldiers and broke through, driving Zhang Ren back.

They pursued twenty li and reclaimed a great number of warhorses.

Liu Bei’s column of horses entered Fu Pass again. He asked for news of Pang Tong.

A soldier who had escaped from Luo Feng Slope reported, “The strategist and his horse were shot to death by wild arrows at the foot of the slope.”

When Liu Bei heard this, he turned westward and wept without ceasing, and made distant arrangements for a mourning rite. All commanders wept.

Huang Zhong said, “We have now lost Pang Tong, the strategist. Zhang Ren will surely come to strike Fu Pass. What are we to do? Send someone to Jingzhou and request Master Strategist Zhuge Liang to discuss how to secure Sichuan.”

Just then, while speaking, someone reported that Zhang Ren had brought troops and come straight beneath the city, contesting at the gate.

Huang Zhong and Wei Yan both moved to go out with force. Liu Bei said, “Our edge is newly blunted; we should hold fast and wait for the strategist to arrive.”

Huang Zhong and Wei Yan obeyed and held the city firmly.

Liu Bei wrote a letter and told Guan Ping to carry it: “You and I are going to Jingzhou to fetch the strategist.”

Guan Ping took the letter and rode through the night to Jingzhou.

Liu Bei himself held Fu Pass and did not go out to fight.

Meanwhile, Zhuge Liang was in Jingzhou. It was Qixi Festival and he had gathered his officers for a night banquet, all speaking of how to finish taking Sichuan, when one star appeared in the west above the horizon, huge as a dipper, and fell from heaven, scattering light.

Kongming was shaken, threw down his cup, covered his face, and wept.

“Alas! I am stricken!” he cried.

The officers, alarmed, asked why.

Kongming said, “I computed this year that Kang is in the west, so this expedition is unfavorable for me. The Heavenly Dog has struck my army, and Venus presides over Luo City. I already sent a letter to my lord and told him to be on guard. To think now a star from the west has fallen—Shiyuan’s life is finished.”

When he had spoken, he wept again: “Today my lord has lost one of his vital arms.”

The officers were all astonished and did not believe him at once.

Kongming said, “Within a few days there will be news.”

The wine and banquet that night did not reach joy before they parted.

A few days later, while Kongming and Yunzhang etc? Guan Yu sat together, a runner announced Guan Ping’s arrival.

All officers were startled. Guan Ping came and presented Liu Bei’s letter.

Kongming read, and inside it said, “On the seventh day of the seventh month this year, Strategist Pang was struck by arrows and killed by Zhang Ren before Luo Feng Slope.”

Kongming wept deeply, and all officers wept as well.

Kongming said, “Since my lord is in Fu Pass in a position of advance and retreat both difficult, I have no choice but to go.”

Guan Yu said, “If you go, who will guard Jingzhou? Jingzhou is no light matter.”

Kongming said, “Though my lord does not state a person plainly, I have understood his intention.”

He showed Liu Bei’s letter to everyone and said, “In the letter, he entrusts Jingzhou to me and asks me to assign duties as I judge fit. Though he wrote so, he has now sent Guan Ping with this message: he wants you, honored general of the Peach Garden oath, to take this heavy charge.”

Guan Yu said, “Our brotherly oath from the Peach Garden compels me; I can defend this place with all my strength.”

Kongming replied, “The responsibility is grave. You should strive to bear it.”

Guan Yu did not decline and accepted with composure.

Kongming set a banquet and handed over seal and badge. Guan Yu came forward and accepted with both hands.

Kongming raised the seal and said, “From this moment all this responsibility rests on you, General.”

Guan Yu said, “A great man who takes a heavy charge rests only in death.”

Kongming, seeing that he had uttered the word “death,” was displeased and wished to object, but the words had already gone out.

He asked, “If Cao Cao brings troops here, what will you do?”

Guan Yu answered, “Resist with force.”

Kongming asked, “If Cao Cao and Sun Quan rise together, what will you do?”

Guan Yu answered, “Split the army and resist them.”

Kongming said, “If so, Jingzhou is endangered. I have eight characters for you to hold and remember, and they can keep Jingzhou secure.”

Guan Yu asked what the eight characters were.

Kongming said, “‘Block Cao Cao in the north; make peace with Sun Quan in the east.’”

Guan Yu said, “Your words, Master Strategist, will be engraved in my lungs and marrow.”

Kongming then handed over the seals and symbols and ordered Ma Liang, Yi Ji, Xiang Lang, and Mi Zhu from the civil side, and Mi Fang, Liao Hua, Guan Ping, and Zhou Cang from the military side to aid Guan Yu in jointly defending Jingzhou.

At the same time he personally took command of the army entering Sichuan.

He first sent ten thousand veteran troops under Zhang Fei, saying, “Take the main road and cut hard to Ba Prefecture, then to the west of Luo City. He who arrives first wins the chief honor.”

He sent another detachment with Zhao Yun as vanguard to ride along the river upstream and join at Luo City.

Zhuge Liang then set out at once with Jian Yong and Jiang Wan and others. Jiang Wan’s courtesy name was Gongyan; he came from Lingling in Xiang. He was a noted literatus of Jingxiang and now served as a clerk.

That day Zhuge Liang led fifteen thousand troops, marching with Zhang Fei at the same hour.

Before departure, he charged Zhang Fei: “Many mighty men of Xichuan await you. Do not make light of them. On the way, bind and regulate your three armies. Do not seize and plunder the common people, else you will lose their hearts. Wherever we reach, keep to humane treatment and do not let soldiers strike people with reckless cruelty. I hope General, you will reach Luo City quickly and make no mistake.”

Zhang Fei cheerfully accepted and mounted to depart, advancing steadily.

Every place they passed, those who submitted were not harmed even by a hairsbreadth.

He headed directly along the Han River route.

When he arrived at Bazhou, scouts reported, “The Prefect of Bazhou is Yan Yan. He is a famous commander of Shu. Though old, he has not lost strength. He is skilled with a heavy bow and a great saber. He has courage beyond what ten thousand men can match. He is holding the city and has not raised a surrender flag.”

Zhang Fei made camp ten li outside the walls and sent men into the city: “Tell that old old fighter to come in and surrender quickly, and your city’s entire households’ lives will be spared. If you do not submit, I will flatten this city; neither young nor old will be spared.”

Yan Yan in Bazhou heard that Liu Bei had entered Sichuan at Liu Zhang’s request through Fa Zheng, and, clasping his chest, sighed: “He is one of those men who sits alone in a remote mountain and calls a tiger to guard himself!” Later he heard Liu Bei held Fu Pass and grew angry, repeatedly trying to raise troops for battle but fearing troops might come down this road as well.

That same day, hearing that Zhang Fei’s force was arriving, he called out five or six thousand of his own men and horses and prepared to meet them.

One adviser submitted a plan:

“Zhang Fei turned Cao Cao’s army of ten thousand on the battlefield at Changban with one shout and made them run. Cao Cao even heard of it and moved away in fear. We should not underestimate him. We should dig deep moats and build high stockades, hold fast and not sally out. His army has no provisions; within a month it must retreat. Moreover, Zhang Fei’s temperament is fiery and he likes to cane his men. If we do not fight, he will rage. Raged, he will meet his soldiers with savage violence. If his army’s spirit changes, the moment is ours to strike and Zhang Fei can be captured.”

Yan Yan followed this and ordered all soldiers to climb the walls and guard. Suddenly one soldier cried out, “Open the gate!”

Yan Yan ordered him let in and asked who it was.

That soldier reported he came on behalf of Commander Zhang and delivered Zhang Fei’s words faithfully.

Yan Yan grew furious: “How dare a rough soldier speak so without courtesy! Is Old General Yan a man to yield to thieves?” He called a warrior and had the soldier’s ears and nose cut off, then sent him back to camp.

The men returned to Zhang Fei and tearfully reported Yan Yan’s abuse. Zhang Fei was enraged, bared his teeth, and mounted in armor. He led a few hundred riders to a skirmish below Bazhou walls.

City soldiers above hurled insults at them in every way. Zhang Fei, quick-tempered, rode close several times to the bridge, hoping to cross the moat, but he was again driven back by a storm of arrows.

By evening no one had left the city. Zhang Fei swallowed his rage and returned to camp.

Early next morning he went out again to skirmish. Yan Yan, from the enemy wall, shot one arrow that struck Zhang Fei’s helmet.

Zhang Fei pointed and shouted in fury, “I will seize this old brute and eat your flesh with my own hands!”

By evening again they returned empty-handed.

On the third day Zhang Fei led the army along the city and railed aloud.

The city was a hill fort, ringed by broken mountains. Zhang Fei rode up and down, looked down from his horse into the city and saw soldiers all fully armed and arrayed in lines, lying hidden in the city, refusing to come out; he also saw common laborers passing back and forth carrying bricks and stones to aid the defense.

He ordered the cavalry to dismount and the infantry to sit. He drew them out against the walls, yet there was still no movement. He shouted all day and still returned with nothing.

In camp, Zhang Fei thought, “All day I only shout and insult him, and he still does not come out. What are we to do?”

Then he found a plan.

He ordered the whole army not to press close for skirmish, but to stand ready in camp and wait for melee in one place. He told only three to five dozen soldiers to go to the city base and keep shouting, in order to lure Yan Yan’s men out for close fighting.

Zhang Fei ground his palms and fists and waited for their arrival.

The small detachment shouted for three days and not one came out. Zhang Fei furrowed his brows and devised another plan.

He ordered the troops to scatter and chop at brush and brushwood, seeking paths, and not return to skirmish.

Yan Yan in the city, seeing no movement from Zhang Fei for several days, was puzzled. He took ten or so junior soldiers, disguised them as Zhang Fei’s woodcutters, sent them out quietly, hid them in the camp, and had them blend in to reconnoiter in the hills.

That day, when the armies returned to camp, Zhang Fei sat in the camp and stamped his feet shouting, “That old brute Yan Yan wastes his breath killing our men in vain!”

Three or four men before his tent said, “General, do not worry. These few days we have discovered a small path by which one might sneak across Bazhou.”

Zhang Fei purposely shouted, “If this way exists, why did you only bring it up today?”

They replied, “It was only now, these past few days, that scouting found it.”

Zhang Fei said, “Delay is not wise. Tonight at the second watch we cook, at third watch under the moonlight pull up the camp, carry grains in our mouths, tie the horse bells low, and move silently. I will open the way in front; the rest will follow in sequence.”

He gave the order and the whole camp was informed.

The scouting little troops heard this and hurried back into the city to tell Yan Yan.

Yan Yan rejoiced: “I am certain this brute cannot bear waiting. When this fellow takes the small path, his supply train will be behind him. I will cut off the road behind; how then can he escape? This fool has no foresight and has fallen into my plan!”

At once he ordered all soldiers to get ready for battle:

“At the second watch we will also cook. At the third, leave the city; lie hidden in the thickets. Wait till Zhang Fei reaches the hidden-necked path and has passed it. When the baggage train comes, listen for the drum, and all break out together.”

After the order, by near-nightfall, Yan Yan had all troops fully fed and armored. They slipped out quietly and scattered to hidden points in the woods. At a sign, Yan Yan himself led ten or so auxiliary officers, dismounted, and lay low under the trees.

About half past the third watch, far ahead they could just see Zhang Fei leading in person, spear in hand, drawing his horse slowly and silently forward. Not three or four li after, the baggage and horse-train began to follow in succession behind.

Yan Yan read it perfectly. He had the drums resound at once, and all the ambush troops sprang out from every side.

When they rushed in to seize the baggage train, a gong sounded from the rear and a squadron of cavalry crashed in. A commander’s cry rang out: “Old brigand, do not run! We have been waiting for you!”

Yan Yan turned sharply and saw at their front a commander with a tawny face-ringed head, an aquiline jaw, tiger whiskers, wielding a seven-foot spear on a deep black horse. It was Zhang Fei.

The four-way drums thundered, and soldiers surged on. Yan Yan froze, hand and arm stilled.

In the first clash of horse, Zhang Fei made a feint. Yan Yan struck with a single stroke; Zhang Fei dodged, slammed into him, tore at the seams of Yan Yan’s armor, and captured him alive, hurling him to the ground.

The soldiers surged forward and bound him with cords.

It had been a decoy that had gone ahead.

Yan Yan had thought the drum he sounded would be the signal; Zhang Fei had ordered the bronze gong as his sign. When the gong sounded, his troops all arrived and most of the Shu army threw down helmets and spears and surrendered.

Zhang Fei rode to the gate of Bazhou city. His rearguard had already entered.

He called for no killing of civilians and hung a proclamation to calm the people.

Hired swordsmen pushed Yan Yan forward.

Zhang Fei sat in the hall; Yan Yan refused to kneel.

The general shouted fiercely, teeth bared, “A commander has come this far. Why do you not surrender and dare to resist?”

Yan Yan did not show fear. He shouted back, “You are without righteousness, invading my commandery! I have but one fate: decapitation! I will not become a surrendering commander!”

Zhang Fei, angry, called for him to be cut down.

Yan Yan shouted, “Bandit! If you want to cut, cut. Why are you so angry?”

Seeing Yan Yan’s ringing voice and steady face, Zhang Fei’s anger faded. He turned as if to scold, then laughed, stepped down from the stage, and shouted his men back.

He untied the prisoner himself, removed his bindings, covered him with a cloak, and set him upright on a raised seat in the hall.

Then he lowered his head and bowed: “The words I spoke when you came were presumptuous. Please do not punish me for them. I always knew this old general was a hero among men.”

Yan Yan was moved by this kindness and submitted.

Later men wrote a poem praising him:

White-haired he dwells in western Shu; his clear fame shakes a great realm. His loyalty is like the clear sun; his vast spirit churns the Yangtze. Better to die with a severed head than kneel in surrender. In old age in Ba Prefecture, there is no second of him under Heaven.

Another poem praised Zhang Fei:

By capturing Yan Yan he found courage beyond compare, and only by righteousness won over both troops and households. To this day his altars in Ba and Shu remember, and at seasonal wine and sacrifice the chicken and pork are offered every spring.

Zhang Fei asked how to enter Sichuan. Yan Yan said, “A general of a beaten army is in your debt for your great grace; I can do nothing as repayment. Let me offer any labor of horse and hound. Do not lift bow or arrow. Go straight for Chengdu.”

It was said:

Only because one general gave his heart to honor, the whole city yielded as if handed over at a touch.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang Wept for Pang Tong; Zhang Fei Righteously Spared Yan Yan

chapters.html:
Zhang Fei, whose courtesy name was Yide, asked for counsel from Yan Yan. Yan said, “From here to Luocheng, all the defensive passes are under my command. The court forces are all within my control. I can never repay your grace, my lord. Let me take the van. Wherever we go, I will call out and make them surrender.” Zhang Fei thanked him repeatedly. So Yan Yan took the vanguard, with Zhang Fei following with the main column. Wherever they came, it was all within Yan Yan’s command, and he called out all who saw him to submit. If someone hesitated, Yan said, “I have already surrendered. Why should you not do the same?” From then on, all yielded at a glance. Not a single pitched battle was fought.

Kongming had already reported the departure date to Xuande, and ordered everyone to assemble at Luocheng. Liu Bei met with his officers: “Now Kongming and Yide are taking two routes for Chuan, and they will join at Luocheng before moving into Chengdu. Since the army left by water and overland on the twentieth day of the seventh month, now it should arrive soon. We can advance now.” Huang Zhong said, “Zhang Ren fights skirmishes every day. Seeing no sortie from the city and a loose enemy, whose troops are unprepared, this night is the moment. We should divide our forces, raid the camp, and win as if in broad daylight.” Liu Bei agreed and ordered Huang Zhong to take the left wing, Wei Yan to take the right, while Liu Bei himself took the center road. At the second watch, the three columns of horse and men set out together.

Zhang Ren really had made no preparations. The Han army pushed into the main camp, set fires, and the flames rose high. The Shu soldiers rode through the night to report at once to Luocheng, and troops from the city marched to reinforce inside. Liu Bei returned to the middle column and set his camp down; the next day he led the army to Luocheng and surrounded and attacked. Zhang Ren held back and did not fight outside. On the fourth day, Liu Bei personally led one detachment in assault against the west gate and ordered Huang Zhong and Wei Yan to strike the east gate, leaving the south and north gates open for troops to move through. The south gate led to mountain paths, and the north gate faced the Fu River; so neither was fully closed in.

When Zhang Ren saw Liu Bei at the west gate riding back and forth directing operations from the hours between Chen and Wei, horses and men were already growing fatigued. He ordered Wu Lan and Lei Tong to lead forces out by the north gate and wheel to the east gate to meet Huang Zhong and Wei Yan. He himself drew out troops by the south gate, wheeling to the west gate to meet Liu Bei alone. The people of the city sent everyone onto the walls and raised drums and shouting cries.

As the sun dropped westward, Liu Bei saw it and ordered the rear troops to withdraw first. They turned back, and from the walls came a single roar of battle cries as riders surged out through the south gate. Zhang Ren rode straight into the midst of Liu Bei’s force to seize him. Liu Bei’s command was thrown into confusion. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan were held by Wu Lan and Lei Tong, so neither could keep eye on the other. Liu Bei could not bear Zhang Ren’s pressure and turned his horse toward a little mountain road to slip away. Zhang Ren chased from behind, nearly catching him.

Liu Bei, exhausted and still pushing forward at full gallop, suddenly saw a troop burst from the mountain road ahead. From horseback he cried in distress, “There are ambushers ahead and pursuers behind. Heaven abandons me!” At the head of the arriving troops was a great commander: it was Zhang Fei. Zhang Fei had come with Yan Yan on that route; seeing the rising dust, they had known they had run into the Sichuan troops in combat. Zhang Fei came first and collided with Zhang Ren; they met on horseback. They fought for more than ten rounds. Yan Yan then brought a large force in from the rear. Zhang Ren quickly turned and ran. Zhang Fei drove straight to the city wall. Zhang Ren retired into it and hauled up the hanging bridge.

Zhang Fei returned to Liu Bei and said, “The strategist rowed upriver and had not yet arrived, yet I have taken the first merit.” Liu Bei asked, “On this road, with its dangerous passes, how did you arrive here so quickly without any delay?” Zhang Fei replied, “There were forty-five passes to clear, all through the efforts of old-general Yan Yan. That is why we came along this route without spending a coin of blood.” He then narrated everything about calling out Yan Yan and brought Yan Yan before Liu Bei. Liu Bei replied, “If it were not for you, old general, how could my younger brother have reached here?” He removed his golden chain-mail coat and gave it to him. Yan Yan bowed in thanks. As they were about to arrange a feast, a messenger on a relay horse arrived: “Huang Zhong and Wei Yan are fighting Wu Lan and Lei Tong; inside the city, Wuyi and Liu Gui have brought out troops to aid the fighting, and our lines are being pinched from two sides. Our armies cannot hold, and the two generals have broken and retreated eastward.” Hearing this, Zhang Fei asked Liu Bei to split the army into two routes and ride to rescue. So Zhang Fei took the left and Liu Bei the right, and they rode hard forward. Wuyi and Liu Gui, hearing the shout from behind, fled in panic back inside the city. Wu Lan and Lei Tong kept driving their troops to pursue Huang Zhong and Wei Yan, and then Liu Bei and Zhang Fei cut off their route back. Huang Zhong and Wei Yan wheeled their mounts and counterattacked. With no way to stand, Wu Lan and Lei Tong brought their main troops over and surrendered. Liu Bei accepted their capitulation and drew the troops to camp near the city.

Having lost two generals, Zhang Ren was uneasy. Wuyi and Liu Gui said, “Our troops are in danger. If we avoid a fight to the death, how can they retreat? Send a runner to Chengdu to urge our lord for emergency command, and in the meantime devise a trick against them.” Zhang Ren said, “Tomorrow I will lead a force out to skirmish and feign a retreat, then turn back toward the north side of the city. Inside, another force will sally out and cut off their line. We can win then.” Wuyi said, “General Liu (Wen) is supporting you in guarding the city. I will lead troops out to join the fight.”

The arrangement was made. The next day Zhang Ren led several thousand men, wreathed the banner, and shouted as he came out to skirmish. Zhang Fei mounted and rode out to meet him without speaking and faced him in combat. After no more than ten rounds, Zhang Ren feigned defeat and ran around the city. Zhang Fei pressed him hard in pursuit. Wuyi’s force blocked his way, and Zhang Ren turned his troops back, surrounding Zhang Fei in the center of the field, giving him no room to advance or retreat. Just when there seemed no remedy, a force burst from the riverbank. Leading it was a commanding figure, spear raised in the hand and horse leaping, who engaged Wuyi directly. In one clash he captured Wuyi alive, drove the enemy back, and saved Zhang Fei. When they saw it, it was Zhao Yun. Zhang Fei asked, “Where is the strategist now?” Zhao Yun said, “The strategist has arrived. He should by now have met the lord.” The two captured Wuyi and returned to camp. Zhang Ren withdrew inside through the east gate.

Zhang Fei and Zhao Yun returned to camp and found Kongming, Jian Yong, and Jiang Wan already in the tent. Zhang Fei dismounted and saluted the strategist. Kongming asked, surprised, “How did you arrive first?” Liu Bei explained in full how Yan Yan had been used. Kongming congratulated him: “General Zhang, being able to wage strategy as you did is all because of my lord’s great fortune.” Zhao Yun presented Wuyi to Liu Bei. “Have you surrendered?” Liu Bei asked. Wuyi replied, “Since I was captured alive, how can I not surrender?” Liu Bei rejoiced and personally removed his bonds.

Kongming asked, “How many men still hold the city?” Wuyi replied, “Liu Xun of the Liu family of Jiyu is Liu Xun; commanders Liu Gui and Zhang Ren are still here. Liu Gui is no matter of concern, but Zhang Ren is from Shu Commandery and very bold in spirit. He is not to be taken lightly.” Kongming said, “First capture Zhang Ren, and then take Luocheng.” He asked, “What is the name of this bridge to the east of the city?” Wuyi said, “The Golden Goose Bridge.”

Kongming then rode to the bridge and circled along the riverbank before returning to camp. He summoned Huang Zhong and Wei Yan to hear his orders: “Five or six li south of Golden Goose Bridge, both banks are thick with reed and rush. Make an ambush there. Wei Yan will lead a thousand spearmen to hide on the left and thrust at riders; Huang Zhong will lead a thousand axe-men to hide on the right and chop the horses down from the ground. Once we break Zhang Ren’s force, he will surely retreat along the little road to the east of the mountain. General Yide, take a thousand men there and catch him there.” Then he summoned Zhao Yun to lie in wait north of Golden Goose Bridge. “When I draw Zhang Ren across the bridge, you break the bridge. Keep troops posted on the north side to hold the appearance of a force, so he dares not run north and is forced to circle south. We will catch him in that very snare.”

Meanwhile, Liu Zhang sent Zhuo Ying and Zhang Yi to join the fight at Luocheng. Zhang Ren ordered Zhang Yi and Liu Gui to hold the city and paired with Zhuo Ying as front and rear teams, with Zhang Ren in front and Zhuo Ying behind, to ride out and repel. Kongming rode out across Golden Goose Bridge with a disorderly army to face Zhang Ren. He mounted a four-horse carriage, with a silk scarf and feather fan, and emerged with more than one hundred riders around him. He pointed at Zhang Ren and said, “Cao Cao, with his host of a million men, hears my name and flees in his tracks. Who are you, then, that dares not submit?”

Zhang Ren saw Kongming’s troops in disorder from afar and sneered from horseback, “People say Kongming commands war like a god. They have a name but no reality!” He thrust his spear and led all captains and men to charge at once. Kongming abandoned the four-wheeled carriage, mounted a horse, and withdrew across the bridge. Zhang Ren pursued him from behind. As he crossed Golden Goose Bridge he saw Liu Bei’s troops on the left and Yan Yan’s on the right, driving in. Realizing it was a stratagem, he turned back in haste, but by then the bridge had already been broken. He tried to go north, but Zhao Yun’s force blocked the opposite bank in a line, so he dared not and turned south to follow the river.

He had gone no more than five or six li when he already reached the patch of dense reeds. Wei Yan’s men rose up from within the reed bed and jabbed with long spears in all directions. Huang Zhong’s force had hidden in the reeds and, with long knives, cut down horse legs. The cavalry all fell and were bound. Where could their infantry have dared to go? Zhang Ren led a few dozen riders toward a mountain track, only to run straight into Zhang Fei. As Zhang Ren was trying to retreat, Zhang Fei shouted once, all the troops surged up at once, and Zhang Ren was taken alive. Unknown to him, Zhuo Ying, seeing his trap sprung, had already gone over to Zhao Yun’s side and surrendered. He reached the main camp the same day.

Liu Bei rewarded Zhuo Ying. Zhang Fei brought Zhang Ren before him, and Kongming was also seated in the tent. Liu Bei said to Zhang Ren, “The Shu generals are surrendering at the first sign of this wind. Why did you not surrender earlier?” Zhang Ren opened his eyes and shouted in anger, “How can a loyal minister serve two lords?” Liu Bei replied, “You do not understand the season of Heaven. If you surrender now, your life will be spared.” Zhang Ren said, “If I were to surrender today, I would still not surrender later. Kill me at once!” Liu Bei could not bring himself to kill him. Zhang Ren shouted fierce curses. Kongming ordered him beheaded to preserve his honor.

A later poem praised him:

A loyal hero would not consent to serve two lords; for Zhang Jun, to die was still to be alive. Clear and upright as the moon by Heaven’s rim, night after night its light shone on Luocheng.

Liu Bei could not stop himself from sighing. He ordered Zhang Ren’s remains collected and buried beside Golden Goose Bridge as witness to his loyalty.

The next day he ordered Yan Yan, Wuyi, and the other former Shu surrendering generals to lead the vanguard to Luocheng and proclaim loudly: “Open the gates at once and submit. Do not let this city and its people suffer further.” Liu Gui cursed violently in the city. Yan Yan was about to shoot arrows at him when an officer on the wall drew a sword, cut Liu Gui down, opened the gate, and surrendered. Liu Bei’s horsemen entered Luocheng. Liu Xun opened the west gate and fled, escaping to Chengdu. Liu Bei issued proclamations to reassure the people. It was Zhang Yi of Wuyang who had killed Liu Gui.

After taking Luocheng, Liu Bei rewarded all the generals heavily. Kongming said, “Luocheng is broken and Chengdu is at hand, yet we still fear unrest in the outer commanderies. Send Zhang Yi and Wuyi with Zhao Yun to pacify the river regions and settle Jiangyang and Qianwei and the attached commanderies. Send Yan Yan and Zhuo Ying with Yide to pacify Bazha and Deyang and the attached commanderies there, restore civil order, and then draw troops back to Chengdu to assemble our forces.” Zhang Yi and Zhao Yun accepted the orders and led away with their men separately.

Kongming asked the surrendered Shu generals, “Which pass lies ahead on this road?” One replied, “Only Mianzhou has heavy troops posted to guard it. If we get Mianzhou, Chengdu is at arm’s reach.”

Kongming then began planning the advance. Fa Zheng said, “Now that Luocheng is lost, Shu is in danger. Since the lord intends to rule by benevolence and virtue, do not yet advance. Let me write to Liu Zhang, setting out costs and benefits clearly. Once he sees this, he will naturally submit.” Kongming said, “Xiaozhi’s words are best.” He ordered a letter written and sent immediately straight to Chengdu.

Liu Xun returned and told his father Liu Zhang that Luocheng had fallen. Liu Zhang hurriedly gathered officials and consulted. The attendant Zheng Du offered a plan: “Although Liu Bei has attacked a city and seized land, his troops are not many, his men are not yet attached, and his stores are from field grain. He has no logistics. Better drive all people from Ba Xi and Zitong to the west of the Fu River. Burn grain barns and open fields, dig deep ditches and raise high stockades, and wait in stillness. If he seeks battle we should not give it. In no time, without supplies, he must leave within a hundred days. Then I can strike him.” Liu Zhang said, “No. I have heard that pacifying the people is to protect them from enemies, not to move the people to prepare for enemies. This is not a plan for preservation.”

In the middle of this discussion, someone reported that Fa Zheng’s letter had arrived. Liu Zhang summoned him, and the letter was presented. He tore it open and read:

We had sent envoys to befriend Jing Province. I did not expect that my lord’s aides were not worthy men, and it came to this. The former ties to Jing Province are old and enduring; the bonds of family are not forgotten. If my lord were to turn in whole and at once, he would not be treated harshly. Pray consider this with thought and decide.

Liu Zhang was furious, tore the letter apart, and shouted, “Fa Zheng is a traitor who sold his lord for glory and forgot grace and loyalty!” He drove the messenger out of the city. At once he sent his brother-in-law Fei Guan with troops forward to defend Mianzhou. Fei Guan promoted a man from Nanyang, whose surname was Li and who was named Yan, courtesy name Zhengfang. Together they took command. Fei Guan and Li Yan immediately brought thirty thousand men to guard Mianzhou.

Dong He, governor of Yi Province, a native of Zhiping in Nanyang Commandery, submitted a memorial to Liu Zhang asking to borrow troops from Hanzhong. Liu Zhang asked, “Zhang Lu has been my family enemy for generations. Why would he come to aid us?” He replied, “Though we have a feud, Liu Bei’s army is in Luocheng and in a perilous position. What threatens one tooth chills its neighbors. If you argue it by practical benefit he will surely come.” Liu Zhang therefore drafted a letter and sent an envoy to Hanzhong.

Elsewhere, Ma Chao had been in the Qiang lands since his defeat, and for more than two years had cultivated friendship with Qiang troops and taken Longxi commanderies. Everywhere he came, all surrendered, only Jicheng resisted. The inspector Wei Kang repeatedly sent men to Xiahou Yuan for aid. Yuan could not obtain orders from Cao Cao, and dared not move troops. Seeing no reinforcements come, Wei Kang discussed with his officers: “Better to surrender to Ma Chao.” Yang Fu, his staff officer, wept and protested: “These men who follow Chao have rebelled against the Son of Heaven. How can you surrender to them?” Wei Kang replied, “As matters stand now, why wait?” Yang Fu’s remonstrance did not move him. Wei Kang opened the city gates and surrendered. Ma Chao was furious. “You submit only because your situation became dire. It is not from the heart,” he said, and executed more than forty of Wei Kang and all of them.

Some said, “Yang Fu urged Wei Kang not to surrender. He should be put to death.” Ma Chao said, “This man held to the right thing. He should not be killed.” He restored Yang Fu to the post of staff officer and used him. Yang Fu recommended Liang Kuan and Zhao Qu, and Ma Chao used both as officers. Yang Fu told Ma Chao, “Fuy’s wife died at Linjiao. Grant me two months to go back and bury her before I return.” Ma Chao agreed.

Yang Fu passed through Licheng and came to General Fuyi, Jiang Xu. Jiang Xu and Yang Fu were cousins by their mothers. Jiang Xu’s mother was Yang Fu’s aunt and was eighty-two years old. That day Yang Fu entered Jiang Xu’s inner house, bowed to his aunt, and wept while saying: “I could not keep the city, and my lord died and I failed to die with him. I have no face to face you. Ma Chao has rebelled against his lord and murdered a prefect without cause. He has slaughtered all the men of a commandery’s people. Now my brother sits occupying Licheng with no desire to punish this bandit. Is this what a minister owes his lord?” Tears came bloodshot from him.

Jiang Xu’s mother, hearing this, called Jiang Xu in and said, “The killing of Wei Jianjun is also your fault. Yang Fu, you have already received favor and salary from this enemy. Why then do you nurse a wish to oppose him?” Yang Fu answered, “I followed this rebel only to stay alive, but now I seek to make amends to my lord.” Jiang Xu said, “Ma Chao is brave and fast; this is a difficult time.” Yang Fu replied, “Where there is courage without planning, he is easy to defeat. I have already arranged in secret with Liang Kuan and Zhao Qu. If your brother raises troops, those two will act as inside helpers.”

Jiang Xu’s mother said, “You did not move early enough; what else is there to wait for? Does no one die? If one dies for loyalty and righteousness, then death is in the right place. Do not think of me. If you will not follow what Your Lady of Righteousness says, I shall die first to sever your hesitation.”

Jiang Xu then consulted the regimental captain Yinfeng and Zhao Ang. Zhao Ang’s son Zhao Yue was currently serving Ma Chao as an auxiliary officer. When Zhao Ang agreed on that day, he returned home and told his wife Wang: “Today I discussed with Jiang Xu, Yang Fu, and Yinfeng about avenging Wei Kang’s death. Zhao Yue, our son, now follows Ma Chao. If I raise troops, Chao will certainly execute our son first. What should we do?” His wife replied sharply, “To restore honor to your father’s dishonor, even death is nothing to refuse. What then of one son? If you stay back out of concern for him, I will die first.” Zhao Ang decided at once. The next day they rose in arms together. Jiang Xu and Yang Fu pitched at Licheng; Yinfeng and Zhao Ang held Qishan. Wang herself handed over all her jewelry and silk gifts and personally went to the Qishan camp, rewarding the soldiers to hearten them.

When Ma Chao heard Jiang Xu and Yang Fu had joined Yinfeng and Zhao Ang and raised troops, he became furious and immediately beheaded Zhao Yue. He ordered Pang De and Ma Dai to mount and ride hard for Licheng. Jiang Xu and Yang Fu rode out. When their two formations came into circle, Yang Fu and Jiang Xu came out in white robes and shouted, “You rebels who have no loyalty to your lord!” Ma Chao, enraged, charged in. The two armies locked and fought hand to hand. How could Jiang Xu and Yang Fu withstand Ma Chao? They were routed and fled. Ma Chao drove after them, and then shouts rose behind as Yinfeng and Zhao Ang were charging in. Ma Chao hurriedly turned, and the enemy attacked from both sides, so he could not support front and rear at once.

In the midst of the battle, a large troop came in from the slanting path; it was Xiahou Yuan, who had received Cao Cao’s orders and now led an army to break Ma Chao. How could Chao withstand a three-pronged cavalry force? He was routed and fled back through the night. By dawn he reached Jicheng and called at the gate, where arrows rained from above in chaos. Liang Kuan and Zhao Qu stood on the wall, shouting and berating Ma Chao. They struck down his wife, Yangshi, from the wall with one slash and threw down her body. They then cut down Ma Chao’s three young sons and more than ten close kin from above, one stroke each.

Ma Chao choked with rage and breath caught in his chest, nearly falling from his horse. Xiahou Yuan pursued him from behind. Seeing the tide had turned, he did not linger in battle, and with Pang De and Ma Dai he cut open a way to escape. Ahead he crashed again into Jiang Xu and Yang Fu and fought a bout; then he burst past them, only to crash into Yinfeng and Zhao Ang and fight again. Broken and scattered, only fifty or sixty riders remained by night’s end. Around the fourth watch they reached below Licheng. The gate guards thought Jiang Xu’s army had returned and opened the gate wide to admit him. Ma Chao struck in from the south gate and massacred the townsfolk. He came to Jiang Xu’s house and dragged out the old mother. She showed no fear and pointed at Ma Chao, shouting abuse. In blind fury, he drew his sword and killed her. Yinfeng and Zhao Ang’s entire household, old and young, were also killed by Ma Chao. Zhao Ang’s wife, Wang, was in the army and was spared by chance.

The next day Xiahou Yuan’s main army arrived. Ma Chao abandoned the city and fled west. He could not ride more than twenty li before meeting a force drawn up ahead, headed by Yang Fu. Chao ground his teeth in hatred, spurring his horse and thrusting with his spear. Yang Fu’s seven brothers came to aid him at once. Ma Dai and Pang De held off the rear. Yang Fu’s seven brothers were all killed by Ma Chao. Yang Fu himself took five spears, yet he still fought to the death. When Xiahou Yuan’s main army came up behind, Ma Chao fled. Only Pang De and Ma Dai went after him with six or seven riders. Xiahou Yuan calmed the people of the western provinces, ordered Jiang Xu and others to take turns keeping the posts, and sent Yang Fu by cart to Xuchang to meet Cao Cao. Cao Cao enfeoffed Yang Fu as Marquis of the Inner Realm. Yang Fu said, “I have no merit of rescuing danger nor courage to die in danger. By law I ought to be executed. How can I accept an office?” Cao Cao approved, and still granted him his rank.

Ma Chao conferred with Pang De and Ma Dai and went straight to Hanzhong to seek aid from Zhang Lu. Zhang Lu rejoiced, believing that with Ma Chao he could swallow west Yi and hold east against Cao Cao. He discussed making a daughter-in-law match with him. The senior general Yang Bai advised, “Ma Chao’s wife and children were ruined by him; that is his own doing. How could the lord give him a daughter?” Zhang Lu accepted the advice and abandoned that marriage plan. Yang Bai’s words reached Ma Chao. Ma Chao grew furious and considered killing Yang Bai. Yang Bai understood him and, with his brother Yang Song, also plotted against Ma Chao’s intent.

Just then Liu Zhang sent an envoy begging aid from Zhang Lu, and Lu refused. There was then word that Liu Zhang had sent Huang Quan again. Huang Quan first went to Yang Song and said, “Eastern and western Sichuan are in a jaw-and-tooth relation; if west Sichuan falls, east Sichuan cannot hold. If you will help, it will be repaid with twenty commanderies.” Song was greatly pleased and brought Huang Quan to Zhang Lu, explaining the strategic dependence and offering twenty commanderies in thanks. Zhang Lu, delighted at the gain, agreed. Yan Pu from Bazha remonstrated, “Liu Zhang has been your sworn enemy for generations. He calls for help in urgency and offers to concede land falsely. Do not accept it.”

At the courtyard steps, someone suddenly stepped in and said, “Though I am not talented, I beg for one contingent of troops to take Liu Bei alive. I must have those lands cut and returned.”

This closes the chapter:

Just when one can see the true ruler come to western Shu, one sees the elite troops come out of Hanzhong. Who this man was remained to be seen.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Kongming devises a plan to catch Zhang Ren, and Yang Fu raises troops to crush Ma Chao

chapters.html:
Yan Pu was trying to persuade Zhang Lu not to aid Liu Zhang when Ma Chao stood up and declared, “General I owe the lord so much kindness that I can never repay it fully. I will take a full detachment and attack Jiameng Pass. I will capture Liu Bei alive if I can. See to it that Liu Zhang hands over twenty commanderies and returns them to my lord.”

Zhang Lu rejoiced. He first sent Huang Quan by the back road and immediately gathered twenty thousand men under Ma Chao. Pang De was bedridden and unable to move, so he remained in Hanzhong. Zhang Lu ordered Yang Bo to supervise the army. Ma Chao and his younger brother Ma Dai set out at once.

Liu Bei’s troops were in Luo City. A messenger from Fa Zheng returned with news: “Zheng Du advised Liu Zhang to burn every field of wild grain and every granary, move the people of Ba Xi to the west of the Fu River, dig deep ditches and raise high stockades, and never fight.”

Liu Bei, Kongming, that is, Zhuge Liang, were both greatly alarmed.

“Your camp is in danger if this plan is used,” Fa Zheng said with a laugh. “Do not worry. The stratagem is cruel, but Liu Zhang will not be able to carry it out.”

Within a day, word spread that Liu Zhang refused to move the people and did not follow Zheng Du’s advice. Liu Bei finally breathed easier.

Kongming said, “We should move quickly and take Mianzhu. Once we have that place, Chengdu will be easy.” He sent Huang Zhong and Wei Yan forward.

Fei Guan heard that Liu Bei’s army had come and ordered Li Yan out. Li Yan led three thousand men and deployed his troops. Huang Zhong charged out, fighting Li Yan for forty to fifty exchanges without a clear edge. In the midst of the line, Kongming rang the golden signal and called for withdrawal. Huang Zhong reformed his formation and asked, “I was waiting for the chance to take Li Yan. Why does the strategist pull us back?”

Kongming said, “I have already seen Li Yan’s skill. He cannot be taken by force. Fight again tomorrow. You can feign defeat, draw him into a valley, and win with a surprise force.”

Huang Zhong carried out the plan.

The next day Li Yan brought out the troops again. Huang Zhong went out to battle him and, after fewer than ten exchanges, feigned defeat and broke off. Li Yan pressed him hard, then chased into the valley before realizing what was happening. As he turned to retreat, Wei Yan appeared in front, having laid out his troops.

Kongming, who stood on the mountain, called out, “If you do not surrender, there are two prepared crossbow lines behind you, and you will be made to repay the debt owed to Pang Shiyuan. Do not force this further.”

Li Yan quickly dismounted, removed his armor, and surrendered. Kongming ordered no one among his men to harm him.

Kongming brought Li Yan to Liu Bei, who received him with great courtesy. Li Yan said, “Fei Guan is a relative of Yizhou and an old acquaintance. I am close to him. Let me go and speak with him.”

Liu Bei then ordered Li Yan back to Mianzhu to persuade Fei Guan to surrender.

When Li Yan entered Mianzhu, he praised Liu Bei’s humanity and benevolence. Fei Guan, persuaded, opened the gate and surrendered.

Liu Bei then entered Mianzhu and planned how to divide forces to take Chengdu. A messenger came in haste: “Meng Da and Huo Jun are guarding Jiaming Pass. At this moment, Ma Chao has arrived with Yang Bo and Ma Dai from Zhang Lu of Dongchuan to press the attack. If we delay, the strong pass will be lost.”

Liu Bei was alarmed. Kongming said, “Only Generals Zhang and Zhao can meet this opponent now.”

Liu Bei said, “Zilong is still outside and has not returned. Yide is here. I can send for him at once.” Kongming said, “My lord, do not speak yet. Let us let Liang stir him.”

When Zhang Fei heard that Ma Chao was attacking the pass, he burst in and shouted, “Let me leave my elder brother and go fight Ma Chao now!”

Kongming feigned not to hear and said to Liu Bei, “No one can meet Ma Chao at the gate now unless we bring Guan Yu from Jing Province. Then and only then could we stand against him.”

Zhang Fei said, “Why does the strategist look down on me? I once alone held off Cao Cao’s army of a million. How could I fear one horseman?”

Kongming replied, “Yide once held back crossing waters and burned bridges, but then Cao Cao did not know the facts. Had he known, he would not have given you such an easy chance. Ma Chao’s courage is known throughout the realm. At the battle of Weiqiao he forced Cao Cao to cut off his beard and cast off his cloak and nearly took his life. This is no ordinary contest. Even Yunchang may not beat him.”

Zhang Fei said, “I go now. If I cannot prevail against Ma Chao, I will submit to command as an obedient soldier.”

Kongming said, “If you are willing to write one order, you can lead the vanguard. Have my lord go once in person as well, and leave Kongming to hold Mianzhu. When Zilong returns, we will discuss.”

Wei Yan said, “I too am ready to go.”

Kongming ordered Wei Yan to ride ahead with five hundred cavalry scouts, Zhang Fei second, and Liu Bei with the rear guard. They set out for Jiameng Pass.

Wei Yan’s scouts arrived first beneath the pass and immediately met Yang Bo. Wei Yan fought Yang Bo, and within fewer than ten exchanges the latter fell back in retreat.

Wei Yan sought to seize all the credit from Zhang Fei and chased after him. Ahead a formation opened, and at its front was Ma Dai. Wei Yan believed him to be Ma Chao and, blade flashing, leapt from the saddle to meet him.

After fewer than ten exchanges Wei Yan was close to victory and Ma Dai turned and withdrew. Wei Yan chased, and Ma Dai shot him from the shoulder with a single arrow before Wei Yan could recover. He wheeled back and mounted fast.

Ma Dai rode to the pass entrance. There a man shouted like thunder and came galloping down over the parapet. It was Zhang Fei, who had just reached the pass. He had heard the clash below and gone to inspect; he saw Wei Yan wounded from the arrow, so he dismounted in haste and rode down to rescue him.

Zhang Fei called out, “Tell me your name first. Then we will continue this struggle!”

Ma Dai said, “I am Ma Dai of Xilang.”

Zhang Fei said, “So you are not Ma Chao. Go back at once! You are no opponent for me. Send word that Zhang Yixide, the Yanman, is here.”

Ma Dai, furious, said, “How dare you look down on me?” He lowered his spear, vaulted his horse, and drove straight at Zhang Fei. After fewer than ten exchanges, he was forced to retreat.

Zhang Fei set out in pursuit, but seeing Liu Bei arrive with horses at the pass, he checked his course.

“Brothers, stop pursuit!”

He turned back. Liu Bei had arrived.

Zhang Fei did not continue. Together they climbed into the pass.

Liu Bei said, “Because I feared your rash temper, I followed at a distance. Since you have already beaten Ma Dai, rest one night. Tomorrow we fight Ma Chao.”

At dawn the next day, drumbeats thundered at the gate. Ma Chao’s troops were already arriving.

From the top of the pass, Liu Bei looked down. In the flickering pennants, Ma Chao rode out with spear in hand, in a lion helmet with beast trappings, silver armor, white robe. In both appearance and bearing he was no ordinary man. Liu Bei sighed, “People call him ‘Brocade-Horse Ma Chao.’ The name is no exaggeration.”

Zhang Fei moved to descend, but Liu Bei quickly stopped him.

“Do not go yet. First let his sharpness blow past.”

At the foot of the gate, Ma Chao challenged Zhang Fei to meet him alone. Above, Zhang Fei, burning with fury and wanting to swallow Ma Chao whole, came up but was turned back by Liu Bei three or four times.

By mid-afternoon Liu Bei saw the men and horses in Ma Chao’s formation had grown tired. He chose five hundred riders, followed by Zhang Fei, and charged down from the gate.

Ma Chao saw Zhang Fei’s troops arrive, thrusted his spear backward once, and drew back to within one arrow’s distance. Zhang Fei’s horsemen all braced and stopped; troops came out one by one from the pass.

Zhang Fei rose in the saddle, spear in hand, and shouted, “Do you even recognize me, Yán-man Zhang Yide?”

Ma Chao answered, “My family has borne noble rank for generations. Would I meet a village roughneck like you?”

Zhang Fei roared with anger. The two charged. Both spears rose together. For more than a hundred exchanges they fought, with no sign of a winner. Liu Bei sighed in awe.

“Truly a tiger-general,” he said. “I fear Zhang Fei may lose his footing.” He ordered the brass signal to recall the lines.

The two withdrew.

Zhang Fei, once back in camp, only rested his horse briefly. Without helmet and with only a headcloth, he mounted again and rode out to match Ma Chao.

Ma Chao returned to meet him. Liu Bei, fearing another risk, removed his own armor and rode to the front of the formation. He watched Zhang Fei and Ma Chao for another hundred exchanges; both grew fiercer. Liu Bei again rang the gold and called the retreat.

The two commanders parted and returned to their own lines. The day had already fallen dark.

Liu Bei said to Zhang Fei, “Ma Chao is very valiant. Do not take him lightly. Go back to the gate and rest. We fight again tomorrow.”

Zhang Fei, inflamed, would not relent.

He shouted, “I swear I will not return!”

Liu Bei said, “Night has fallen. We cannot fight now.”

Zhang Fei replied, “Then light a hundred torches. We can fight through the night.”

Ma Chao, now on another horse, rode out and shouted, “Zhang Fei! Will you dare to fight at night?”

Zhang Fei stood up in his saddle, changed his seat, and charged out in a roar, “If I fail to catch you, I will not return to the gate!”

Ma Chao answered, “If I cannot beat you, I will not return to camp!”

The two armies screamed and raised hundreds of torches that made the night bright as noon. The two commanders returned to their front lines and locked in close battle. After more than twenty exchanges, Ma Chao reined up and turned away as if retreating.

“Where do you go?” Zhang Fei called.

In truth, Ma Chao knew he could not win a clean victory over Zhang Fei. A thought came to him. He deliberately feigned defeat and withdrawal to lure Zhang Fei in. When Zhang Fei charged, Ma Chao drew a bronze hammer with his other hand, twisted his body, and cut for him.

Zhang Fei had kept his guard up and slipped aside. The hammer passed so close to his ear that it hissed by.

As Zhang Fei brought his horse back, Ma Chao came on again. Zhang Fei steadied his mount and drew an arrow, firing at Ma Chao. Ma Chao sidestepped, and both returned to their own ranks.

From the front Liu Bei called out, “I have treated men with benevolence and do not use trickery. Ma Mengqi, halt your advance and rest. I will not pursue you while the moment is favorable.”

Hearing this, Ma Chao personally detached the rear guard and withdrew. As the rest of his troops gradually pulled back, Liu Bei also ordered a withdrawal up the pass.

The next day Zhang Fei wished once more to go down and fight Ma Chao. A messenger arrived saying the strategist had come.

Liu Bei welcomed Kongming.

Kongming said, “I have heard that Mengqi is a tiger among the generals of his age. If he fights Yide to the death, one of them will surely be gravely wounded. Therefore I left Zilong and Huang Zhong to hold Mianzhu and came here through the night.”

He then added, “We can use a small stratagem to bring Ma Chao to surrender to our lord.”

Liu Bei said, “I admire Ma Chao’s courage. But how can that be done?”

Kongming said, “I have heard that Zhang Lu of Dongchuan wants to proclaim himself King of Hanning. His chief adviser, Yang Song, is notorious for greed. We can send someone by a side road to Hanzhong, first befriend Yang Song with gold and silver, then send a letter to Zhang Lu saying,

I fight Liu Zhang for Xichuan and this is my way of avenging old injury against my father. Do not believe the words that divide us. After matters are settled, I will preserve your title as King of Hanning.

If he receives this, he will order Ma Chao to withdraw troops. Then when he pulls back, we can draw him to surrender.”

Liu Bei rejoiced and immediately drafted a letter. He sent Sun Qian to carry pearls by a side road to Hanzhong to present the gift to Yang Song.

Sun Qian presented the gold- and silver-laden message through him. Yang Song rejoiced and first brought Sun Qian before Zhang Lu, explaining how useful this was.

Zhang Lu said, “Liu Bei is only General of the Left. How can he preserve my title as King of Hanning?”

Yang Song answered, “Bei is the Imperial Uncle of Han. He is precisely suited to grant such a favor.”

Zhang Lu was pleased and sent word to have Ma Chao drop his campaign. Sun Qian waited at Yang Song’s home for the reply.

Before a day had passed, a messenger returned: “Ma Chao says the mission has not succeeded and he will not pull back.”

Zhang Lu sent people again. He refused once more. Three times he did not return.

Yang Song said, “This man has no habit of words matching his actions. He will not halt. His intention is surely to turn against us.” He spread the rumor that

Ma Chao intends to seize Xichuan, set himself up as lord of Shu, and avenge his father himself, and will not submit to Hanzhong.

When Zhang Lu heard this, he sought counsel.

Yang Song said, “At once send a message to Ma Chao: If you truly wish to succeed, take this one-month limit. Obey my three terms. If you can carry them out, there will be reward. If not, you must give me your head.”

He continued, “First, take all of Xichuan. Second, bring Liu Zhang’s head. Third, send the troops from Jingzhou away. If these three are not fulfilled, surrender your own head.”

At once he instructed Zhang Wei to station troops at the pass, guarding the approach in case Ma Chao mutinied.

Zhang Lu followed this, sent word to Ma Chao’s camp, and had the three demands read aloud. Ma Chao was greatly startled.

“How did it come to this?”

He consulted with Ma Dai: better to pull back the troops.

Yang Song then spread another rumour: if Ma Chao withdrew, he would still harbor rebellious intent. Zhang Wei then split his force into seven routes and blocked the approaches, holding the gate so Ma Chao could not enter with his men.

Ma Chao could neither advance nor retreat and had no plan left.

Kongming told Liu Bei, “Now Ma Chao is truly in a deadlock between advance and retreat. I will go myself, with my unbreakable tongue, and persuade him to surrender.”

Liu Bei said, “You are my right arm and loyal heart. If you misstep, what will become of me?”

Kongming persisted in his wish to go. Liu Bei refused repeatedly.

In the midst of hesitation, word came that Zhao Yun had sent a man from Xichuan and recommended him for surrender.

Liu Bei summoned him. He was Li Hui, from Yuyuan in Jianning. His surname was Li, personal name Hui, courtesy name De’ang.

Liu Bei asked, “I once heard you had taken great pains to remonstrate with Liu Zhang. Why have you come to me now?”

Li Hui replied, “They say, ‘A good hawk chooses a proper perch; a wise minister chooses his lord and then serves.’ I once remonstrated fully for Liu Yizhou in faithful service. Since I could not be heard, I know I would lose. Now your forbearance and mercy fill Shu, and I know success is in your hands. So I have come.”

Liu Bei said, “Your coming must help me.”

Li Hui said, “I have heard that Ma Chao is now trapped between advance and retreat. In Longxi I had one meeting with him once. I could go and persuade him to surrender, if you allow.”

Kongming said, “I have been hoping to send one man on this task. Tell me your wording.”

Li Hui explained his plan to Kongming at the ear. Kongming was pleased and immediately dispatched him.

When Li Hui reached Ma Chao’s camp, he first sent in word of his name and name. Ma Chao replied, “I know Li Hui is a polished rhetorician. He has certainly come to speak with me.” He summoned twenty halberd-ax bearers and laid them in the tent, ordering, “If he blunders, cut him up for meat paste.”

Soon Li Hui entered on his own.

Ma Chao sat unmoving on his couch and barked, “Why have you come?”

Li Hui said, “I have come as your guest.”

Ma Chao said, “My treasured sword is newly whetted. Speak your mind; if your argument is weak, test it on me.”

Li Hui smiled and said, “General, your disaster is near. I only suspect your freshly polished sword cannot test my head. I suspect you wish to test me first.”

Ma Chao said, “What disaster could you mean?”

Li Hui said, “Even the cleverest slanderer cannot conceal Xi Zi’s beauty, and even the cleverest praise cannot hide Wuyan’s ugliness. ‘When the sun reaches noon, it declines; when the moon is full, it wanes.’ Such is the constant principle of the world.
