Now you have a father-killing grudge against Cao Cao and a tooth-and-nail hatred toward Longxi. You could not rescue Liu Zhang and drive back the troops from Jing Province; afterward, you could not thwart Yang Song or gain an audience with Zhang Lu. At present, nowhere within the four seas will receive you, and you have no lord to serve. If you suffer another defeat at the Wei Bridge and another loss of Ji City, how will you show your face to the people of the world?”

Ma Chao bowed his head and thanked him. “Your words are excellent,” he said. “Yet I have no path to act on them.”

Li Hui said, “If you listened, why have axemen waited outside the tent?”

Ma Chao was ashamed and withdrew them at once.

Li Hui continued, “Liu the Imperial Uncle honors worthy men and low-born scholars equally. I know he must prevail, so I have left Liu Zhang and come to him. You are a respected elder. In past years you and he promised to punish the bandits together. Why do you not leave darkness and stand in light to repay your father’s injury and gain rank?”

Ma Chao was greatly delighted. He called for Yang Bo, cut him down with one sword stroke, and brought the head, together with Li Hui, to the pass to surrender to Liu Bei.

Liu Bei met him personally, gave him guest honors, and Ma Chao bowed and said, “I have found a sovereign like clear sky after fog and rain. My vision has cleared.”

Sun Qian had already returned. Liu Bei ordered Huo Jun and Meng Da to guard the pass, then withdrew his forces to take Chengdu.

Zhao Yun and Huang Zhong entered Mianzhu.

A report came: “The Shu commanders Liu Jun and Ma Han have arrived with their troops.”

Zilong said, “I volunteer to ride and capture these two.”

He had just mounted and led his troops out when Liu Bei in the city hall ordered refreshments for Ma Chao. Before he could even seat himself, Zilong had already cut off the heads of both and laid them at the table.

Ma Chao was astonished and his respect increased.

Ma Chao said, “Do not make slaughter here by the lord’s order. I can summon Liu Zhang myself and bring him in to surrender. If he refuses, then Ma and his brother Ma Dai will take Chengdu and bring it as tribute in both hands.”

Liu Bei rejoiced. He made everything a festival that day.

A defeated messenger returned to Yizhou to report to Liu Zhang. Liu Zhang was stunned and shut himself in the gates.

When it was reported that Ma Chao and Ma Dai had arrived as relief from the north, Liu Zhang dared to come onto the wall.

Seeing them below, he shouted, “Ask Liu Jiyu to answer.”

Liu Zhang called from the wall: “Who is this?”

Ma Chao, mounted, pointed his whip and said, “I came with Zhang Lu’s troops to defend Yizhou. I had never expected Zhang Lu, by Yang Song’s slander, to turn and seek my ruin. I have now surrendered to the Imperial Uncle of Han. Receive him and accept your surrender, and spare the people from further suffering. If you insist on stubbornness, then I will attack this city.”

Liu Zhang was so shocked that his face turned the color of earth and he nearly fainted atop the wall. His attendants revived him.

Liu Zhang said, “In my blindness, what can repentance do now? It is no use. I had better open the gates and surrender to save the whole city.”

Dong He said, “There are still more than thirty thousand soldiers inside the city, and we have money, silk, and grain enough for a year. Why surrender?”

Liu Zhang replied, “My father and I have remained in Shu over twenty years without bringing grace to the people. Three years of war has bled men and women across the wild fields. All this is my guilt. What peace can be mine? Better to surrender and spare the people.”

The men around him all wept at the words.

Suddenly someone stepped forward. “My lord’s words accord with Heaven’s will.” He was Qiao Zhou from Xichong, with the surname Qiao, personal name Zhou, courtesy name Yunnan. He was one who knew astronomy. Liu Zhang asked what sign he had seen.

He said, “For one night I watched the heavenly form and saw the stars clustered over Shu Commandery. The great star burned like moonlight: this is the sign of an emperor. One year ago a child’s rhyme said, ‘If one wants to taste fresh rice, one must wait for the First Lord to come.’ This is a forewarning. We cannot oppose the way of Heaven.”

Huang Quan and Liu Ba both raged and wanted him executed. Liu Zhang restrained them.

Then came word: “The Administrator of Shu Commandery, Xu Jing, has crossed the walls and defected.” Liu Zhang wept and returned to his residence.

The next day another report arrived: “Yun Gong Jian Yong, bearer from the Imperial Lord’s camp, waits below your gate and calls for entry.” Liu Zhang ordered the gates opened and Jian Yong received.

Jian Yong sat in his carriage with an air of haughtiness. Suddenly a man drew his sword and shouted, “A young man newly in favor acts as though no one is present. How dare you disdain figures in Shu?”

That man was Qin Mi of Mianzhu in Guanghan. Surname Qin, name Mi, courtesy name Zhi. He was proud of his courage.

Jian Yong smiled and said, “You do not know a worthy elder. Please do not fault me.” He then entered to meet Liu Zhang and described Liu Bei’s broad mercy and the lack of any intent to harm. Thus Liu Zhang resolved to surrender and treated Jian Yong generously.

The next day he personally carried the seal, edict, and records, and rode out with Jian Yong to surrender.

Liu Bei came out to receive him, clasped his hands, and wept, “It is not that I did not hold to benevolence and righteousness. Circumstance left me no way.”

They entered camp together, handed over seals and records, then entered the city.

When Liu Bei entered Chengdu, citizens lined the streets with flowers and candles and welcomed him at the gate. In the public hall he ascended and sat.

The county officials all knelt in the hall below, but only Huang Quan and Liu Ba kept their doors shut. The generals became angry and wished to kill them.

Liu Bei shouted, “Whoever harms these two will see three families erased!”

Liu Bei himself went to invite them out. They were moved by his generosity and appeared.

Kongming then said, “Now that Xichuan is pacified, this land can no longer accommodate two lords. Better to send Liu Zhang to Jing Province.”

Liu Bei said, “I have now only just received Shu, how can I send Jiyu away?”

Kongming answered, “Liu Zhang lost the foundations of his state because he was too weak. If my lord rules by a woman’s pity and cannot decide in a crisis, this land may not hold long.”

Liu Bei accepted and held a great banquet. He asked Liu Zhang to gather his property, take charge of the Marshal of Tremendous Might seal and credential, and send his wives and children, and all dependents, to Nanjun An’gang to rest. They would depart that day.

Liu Bei then personally assumed the office of Yizhou Governor.

As for the defeated officials who submitted, he gave them rewards and ranks at once:

  • Yan Yan as Grand General in the First Rank,
  • Fa Zheng as Administrator of Shu Commandery,
  • Dong He as Colonel of Central Military Personnel,
  • Xu Jing as chief clerk to the Left General,
  • Pang Xi as Camp Staff Officer,
  • Liu Ba as Left General,
  • Huang Quan as Right General.

Among the other officials and officers who had submitted as civilians and soldiers—Wu Yi, Fei Guan, Peng Yang, Zhuo Ying, Li Yan, Wu Lan, Lei Tong, Li Hui, Zhang Yi, Qin Mi, Qiao Zhou, Lü Yi, Huo Jun, Deng Zhi, Yang Hong, Zhou Qun, Fei Yi, Fei Shi, Meng Da—there were over sixty in all, and they were all promoted.

Zhuge Liang was appointed military adviser. Guan Yu was made General Who Subdues Bandits and Marquis of Hanshou Pavilion. Zhang Fei became General Who Conquers the Distant and Marquis of Xinting. Zhao Yun became General Who Guards the Distant. Huang Zhong became General Who Conquers the West. Wei Yan was made General Who Spreads Martial Courage. Ma Chao was made General Who Pacifies the West.

Sun Qian, Jian Yong, Mi Zhu, Mi Fang, Liu Feng, Wu Ban, Guan Ping, Zhou Cang, Liao Hua, Ma Liang, Ma Su, Jiang Wan, Yi Ji, and the officials of Jingxiang from earlier days all received rewards.

He sent envoys with 500 jin of gold, 1,000 jin of silver, fifty million cash, and one thousand bolts of Shu brocade to present to Guan Yu. Other officers received gifts according to rank.

Cattle and horses were slaughtered, soldiers lavishly rewarded, and granaries opened to relieve the people. Soldier and civilian alike rejoiced.

When Yizhou had been secured, Liu Bei intended to divide Chengdu’s famous houses and fields among his officers. Zhao Yun remonstrated.

“The people of Yizhou have been burned and ruined by war repeatedly. Their homes and fields are empty. We should return these back to the people and let them settle and resume their livelihoods. Only then will popular feeling harden into trust. It is improper to make them private gifts,” he said.

Liu Bei gladly agreed and asked Zhuge Liang to draft regulations for governing the state.

The laws were still quite severe.

Fa Zheng said, “In ancient times Gaozu gave only three edicts, and commoners all praised his virtue. Please ask the strategist to lighten punishments and ease statutes to satisfy public wishes.”

Kongming replied, “You know one thing and not the second. Qin used violent law and all the people resented him; Gaozu won them back through lenient benevolence. But Liu Zhang was blind and weak. Good governance was never raised; stern penalties were never enforced. The relationship of lord and minister has already turned upside down. Favor makes one proud when one rises too high; when favor exhausts itself, they become arrogant. So we arrived at this disorder by this path.”

“In this I will uphold law. When law is clear, men know grace. When rank is bounded, men know honor. When grace and honor are both present, each side keeps its station. That is the beginning of order.”

Fa Zheng listened and submitted.

From then on the people and soldiers were calm and secure.

The forty-one prefectures were assigned by force and garrisoned, and all were pacified.

Fa Zheng was made Administrator of Shu Commandery. Even a meal once owed by him and even the smallest grievance against him was repaid in justice.

Someone told Kongming, “Xiaozhi is too overbearing. You should restrain him somewhat.”

Kongming said, “When my lord was trapped in Jingzhou, fearing Cao Cao to the north and fearing Sun Quan to the east, he relied upon Xiaozhi’s support as his wing and staff and by sudden vigor took to the air. He can no longer be held by strict restraints. How can I now forbid Xiaozhi from acting according to his nature?”

He said no more.

Fa Zheng heard and also tempered himself.

One day Liu Bei was at leisure with Kongming when he received word that Guan Yu sent Guan Ping to thank him for the gifts of gold and silk.

Guan Ping saluted and handed a letter.

It said:

My father says Ma Chao’s martial skill is extraordinary and he wants to come into Sichuan to compare themselves in strength. I have informed my elder uncle of this matter.

Liu Bei was alarmed. “If Guan Yu enters Sichuan to face Mengqi, this will not end with both in peace.”

Kongming said, “No matter. The strategist will write back.”

Liu Bei feared Guan Yu’s impetuousness, so he had Kongming write and send him back by night.

When Guan Ping reached Jingzhou, Guan Yu asked, “I intend to match Mengqi. Did you mention it to your lord?”

Guan Ping answered, “The strategist has sent a letter; it is here.”

He opened it:

The strategist has heard that General wishes to test himself against Mengqi. Measured against him, Mengqi’s ferocity surpasses the ordinary, yet he is no more than men such as Kui Bu and Peng Yue. Even if he runs with Yunchang to take first place, he still does not approach the matchless standard of the Beardy-Whiskered Lord. Since you hold command in Jingzhou, do not think this rank is light. If once you enter Sichuan and Jingzhou suffers, your guilt is beyond measure. I only beg you to understand clearly.

After reading it, Guan Yu stroked his whiskers and laughed.

“Zhuge Liang understands my heart,” he said. He then showed the letter to all his guests and dropped any intention of entering Sichuan.

Meanwhile, Sun Quan of Eastern Wu learned that Liu Bei had absorbed Xichuan and had driven Liu Zhang to An’gang. He summoned Zhang Zhao and Gu Yong to discuss.

Sun Quan said, “When Liu Bei borrowed my Jingzhou, he said that if he secured Xichuan he would return Jingzhou. He has taken the forty-one prefectures of Bashu. He should now give back the commanderies north of the river. If he does not, we will take up arms.”

Zhang Zhao said, “Wu has only lately been in peace; do not mobilize troops. I have one plan: force Liu Bei to return Jingzhou with both hands to the lord.”

So it was:

In western Shu, a new sun and moon have only begun to shine; Eastern Wu now demands the old rivers and mountains back.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Ma Chao’s Great Battle at Jiameng Pass, and Liu Bei Assumes the Yizhou Governorship

chapters.html:
Guan Yu rides to the summons with a single blade,
Empress Fu gives herself up for the realm.

Sun Quan, whose courtesy name was Zhongmou, sought Jing Province. Zhang Zhao offered counsel.

“Liu Bei relies on Zhuge Liang above all. His elder brother, Zhuge Jin, now serves in Wu. Why not detain Jin and his household and send him to Sichuan to tell his younger brother to hand Jing back? If Liu Bei refuses, surely my old and young people here will be entangled.”
Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, heard this and thought of his blood tie and knew he would have to comply.

Sun Quan asked, “Zhuge Jin is a sincere and upright man. How can I make him detain a man's household?”
Zhang Zhao replied, “He is a loyal man who trusts us; he will not doubt the plan.”

Sun did as he said. He summoned Zhuge Jin and his household to be held under house guard in the capital, and at once drafted a memorial and sent Jin west to Sichuan.

Soon thereafter he reached Chengdu and had someone report to Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande.

Xuande asked, “Why did you come?”
Kongming answered, “To ask for Jing Province.”

“How am I to answer him?”
“Just answer exactly as I told you.”

The plan now fixed, Kongming met Zhuge Jin at the city gate. He did not go to the private residence but went straight to a guesthouse. After formal salutes, Jin burst out crying.

Kongming said, “If there is important business, tell me plainly. Why this lament?”
Jin said, “My old and young household has been detained.”
Kongming answered, “Could it be that the return of Jing Province is being delayed? For my brother’s sake you have held your own brother’s old and young. How can I remain at peace? Do not worry. I will have a plan to return Jing Province.”

Jin rejoiced, and he and Kongming went to see Xuande. Jin presented Sun Quan’s letter. Upon reading it, Xuande became furious and said, “Sun married his sister to me, and yet while I was absent from Jing he secretly took her away by stealth. I can hardly bear that. I was about to raise Sichuan troops and sweep Jiangnan to repay this hatred, and he comes asking for Jing now?”

Kongming knelt and wept.

“Wu’s marquis has taken Jin and his household. If Jing is not returned, my whole family will be beheaded. If I survive, can my brother, Guan Yu, live alone? Look upon my face and return Jing to Eastern Wu. Restore the brotherhood between my brothers.”

Xuande refused several times, and Kongming only pleaded, crying.

At last Xuande said slowly, “So be it. Because you asked so hard, I will return half, by ceding three commanderies at once: Changsha, Lingling, and Guiyang.”

Kongming said, “If he has given assent, write this letter now and let me send it to Yunzhang (Guan Yu) to hand over the three.”
Xuande said, “Let Ziyu (Zhuge Jin) go, but he must ask my brother with care. My brother is as fierce as fire; even now I fear him. You must be very careful.”

Jin took the letter, left Xuande, and took leave of Kongming. He then returned to Jing Province. Guan Yu invited him into the great hall for host and guest to speak as equals.

Jin presented Xuande’s letter: “The Imperial Uncle has promised first to return the three commanderies to Eastern Wu. I beg you to hand them over at once and allow me to return to my lord.”
Guan Yu’s face changed.
“I swore with my brother in Peach Garden to aid Han’s restoration. Jing Province is the land of Great Han. By what right can we give away even a handspan? ‘A commander in the field does not obey commands that reach him from afar.’ Though my brother has written, I will not return it.”

Jin said, “Wu’s marquis holds my old and young under restraint. If Jing is not returned, they will certainly be executed. I beg the general for compassion.”
Guan said, “This is a deceitful stratagem by Wu’s marquis. How could I be unaware of it?”

Jin asked, “How can you face me if you have no shame?”
Guan, sword already in hand, replied, “Speak no more. There is no room for shame on this blade.”

Guan Ping said, “His face is not fit to behold today, Father. Please calm your anger.”
Guan said, “If you do not look at his face, you will not get back to Eastern Wu!”

Humbled to the roots of his hair, Jin left in disgrace. He returned to Sichuan to see Kongming, who was already out on rounds. He could not see him again and returned once more to Xuande, crying and reporting that Guan Yu had meant to kill him.

Xuande said, “My brother is quick-tempered and hard to reason with. Ziyu, go back for now. Let me take Dongchuan and the Hanzhong commanderies and assign Guan Yu there to hold. Only then can I hand over Jing.”

Jin had no choice but to return to Eastern Wu and report everything to Sun.

Sun was enraged. “Since Ziyu went back and forth and back again, could this all be Kongming’s scheme?”
Jin said, “No. My brother also cried out to Xuande and agreed first to return the three commanderies, but Guan Yu would not yield, so it could not be done.”

Sun replied, “If Liu Bei has promised to return those three commanderies first, then send officials now to Changsha, Lingling, and Guiyang to take charge and see what happens.”

Jin said, “Your Highness is perfectly right.”

Sun ordered Jin to recover his household and at once posted officials to the three commanderies.

Within days those officials arrived and were all driven out in turn, reporting that Guan Yu would not accept any arrangement and had chased them off in one night; those delayed were told they would be killed.

Sun raged and sent for Lu Su, whose courtesy name was Zijing.

“You stood surety for Liu Bei once and borrowed Jing Province from him,” Sun said. “Now that he has obtained Sichuan he refuses to return it. How can you sit idle?”

Lu Su said, “I have thought of a way and was just about to report to you.”

“What is it?” Sun asked.

Lu Su said, “Station troops at Luxu and send someone to ask Guan Yu to come to a meeting. If he comes, persuade him with good words. If he refuses, use axe-men waiting in ambush and kill him. If he still refuses to come, then move immediately and settle it in battle; we shall then seize Jing.”

Sun said, “That fits my intention. Do it at once.”

Kan Ze advised, “It should not be done. Guan Yu is a tiger among generals, no ordinary man can match him. I fear this plan will not go smoothly and will rebound upon us.”

Sun, angry, answered, “If we do nothing, when will Jing ever be ours?” He commanded Lu Su to carry out the plan at once.

Lu Su thanked and left, reaching Luxu and summoning Lü Meng and Gan Ning to confer. A banquet was prepared on the riverside pavilion beyond the Luxu camp. He drafted a summons and chose one courtier with sharp speech as messenger, who crossed by boat to Jing.

Guan Ping received the envoy at the river bank and had him brought before Guan Yu, conveying Lu Su’s invitation. After reading the letter, Guan said, “Since Zijing has invited me, I will come tomorrow for the banquet. You may return now.”

The messenger withdrew.

Guan Ping said, “You know as well as I do that Zijing’s invitation is not sincere. Why would Father agree?”
Guan laughed. “Do I not understand? Zhuge Jin has indeed returned to report this to Sun. He told him I would not return three commanderies, so Lu Su gathered troops at Luxu and invited me to this feast in order to demand Jing Province. If I do not go, people will say I am afraid.”

Then he added, “Tomorrow I will go by myself in a small boat with no more than ten men. I will attend with a single sword; let us see how Lu Su dares approach me.”

Guan Ping pleaded, “How can your body, worth ten thousand pieces of gold, go into the lair of tigers and wolves? It may not be right to bear your uncle’s trust so lightly.”

Guan said, “In a hundred spears and ten thousand sabers, amid arrows and stones, I can ride alone like an open plain. Why should I fear a nest of Jiangdong rats?”

Ma Liang also remonstrated. “Lu Su has the manner of an elder, yet this is urgent. It should not be assumed there is no hidden intent. The general should not go lightly.”

Guan replied, “In Warring States times, a man named Xiangru of Zhao, though he lacked even the strength to tie a chicken, faced Qin at a great assembly and treated Qin’s lords and ministers as if they were nothing. What, then, is this compared to a man who has learned to oppose ten thousand? Once I promised, I cannot break my word.”

Ma Liang said, “Even if the general goes, he should prepare.”
Guan said, “Order my son to ready ten fast boats and hide five hundred good river troops on the river to stand ready. When he sees my red flag rise, let him come over.”

Guan Ping carried out the order and departed.

The envoy reported to Lu Su that Guan Yu had accepted eagerly and would come the next day.

Lu Su and Lü Meng conferred: “If he comes with force, let each of us lead one unit to the bank and fire signals, and stand ready to fight. If no force arrives, place fifty axe-men behind the pavilion and kill him there.”

Their arrangement was now fixed. The next day Lu Su had men watch from the bank. After midday he saw a single boat on the river, only a few rowers, showing a single red flag in the wind. The flag itself bore one huge character: 關. As it neared the bank, Guan Yu appeared in a green hood and green robe, seated aboard. At his side Zhou Cang held a huge blade; around him were eight or nine men from the west, each with a waist knife.

Lu Su, startled, invited him in.

After formalities, they sat and drank, cups offered each in turn. No one dared look Guan Yu in the face. Guan talked as if in a calm mood.

When wine was half-drunk, Lu Su said, “I have one matter to present; I beg your indulgence. Formerly the Imperial Uncle, on my lord’s behalf, borrowed Jing Province from you for temporary residence until he gained Sichuan. Now he has taken Sichuan and yet has not returned Jing. Can this be kept in good faith?”

Guan replied, “This is a matter of state; it should not be argued at a banquet.”

Lu Su said, “My lord had only a small tract in Jiangdong, and he dared to lend Jing to you because he pitied your troops and your lack of provisions after your defeat. Now that you hold Yi Province, Jing should of course be returned. Yet he has offered first three commanderies, and your lord still does not obey. It cannot be justified.”

Guan said, “At the battle of Wulin, the Left General himself braved arrows and stones and labored with all his strength to break the enemy. Must he now be denied even a single foot of land for such efforts? You return now and ask for land again?”

Lu Su said, “Not so. Your lord and the Imperial Uncle were broken at Changban and near exhaustion, determined to flee far away. My lord pitied him with no place to go and had no interest in land for himself. But if there is a place to rely on, he can plan future gains. Yet now Xuande has spent virtue and broken trust, gained Yi Province and taken Jing, greedy and unfaithful, and he will be shamed before the world. Look into it carefully.”

Guan replied, “These are my brother’s matters; they are not for me to argue.”

Lu Su said, “I have heard that you and the Imperial Uncle swore an oath of life and death at Peach Garden. The Imperial Uncle is you. How can you refuse?”

Before Guan could answer, Zhou Cang shouted from the steps, “Across all the land, only one with virtue can hold land. Is it only because you are in Wu that you may claim it?”

Guan’s face darkened; he rose, seized the great blade from Zhou Cang, and stood in the courtyard. He fixed Zhou Cang with a hard glance and roared, “This is a state matter. How dare you speak so much! Go away at once!”

Zhou Cang understood. He hurried to the bank and raised the red flag.

Guan Ping’s boat shot across like an arrow and sped back from the eastern bank.

With his right hand on the blade and his left gripping Lu Su’s, he pretended to stagger drunk and said, “You invited me to this feast; do not raise Jing Province now. I am already drunk and fear I will bruise our old friendship. Someday, if you send for me in Jing and invite me again, we can talk further.”

Lu Su could scarcely stand; he looked like a person with no soul. Lü Meng and Gan Ning drew up their own detachments, but seeing the blade in Guan’s hand and Luo (Lu Su) in his grasp, and fearing harm to their lord, they held back.

At the landing, Guan released his hand. He was already up on the bow, already leaving in the wind. Lu Su seemed dazed.

Afterward people made this verse in praise of Guan Yu:

I laughed at the ministers of Wu as if they were children,
yet came to the feast with a single sword; the heroics of that day surpass Xiangru at Mianchi.

Guan Yu returned to Jing Province.

Lu Su and Lü Meng discussed, “This plan failed. What are we to do now?”
Lü Meng said, “Report to the lord, and if need be, raise the army to settle this with Guan Yu.”
Lu Su did so and informed Sun Quan.

Sun, enraged, prepared to raise all state troops to seize Jing Province. Suddenly news came that Cao Cao was marching three hundred thousand more troops.

Sun was startled and ordered Lu Su to stop provoking Jing’s army, and instead shift forces toward Hefei and Ruxu to prepare to resist Cao Cao.

While Cao Cao prepared to march south, his aide Fu Gan, courtesy name Yancai, submitted a memorial:

My lord, I have heard: when war is used, strength must first appear; when culture is used, virtue must first appear. When might and virtue stand together, a kingdom is established.
The realm was once in chaos. Your Grace used force and regained order in nine parts out of ten. Now what face to heaven we meet is not yet secure under full command; there are still Wu and Shu. Wu has the barrier of the Yangtze, Shu the barriers of high mountains. They are hard to force in open battle. I advise therefore increasing civil virtue, repairing the armor and resting the troops, and moving only when the time is right.
If tens of thousands are gathered and posted along the Yangtze bank, and if bandits hide deep in terrain so that my horsemen cannot show their strength and no extraordinary maneuver can be used, then Heaven’s mandate is weakened. Please examine this carefully.

Cao read it and canceled the southern expedition. He opened schools and recruited scholars to ritual court. Then officials Wang Can, Du Xi, Wei Kai, and He Qia gathered and spoke of inviting Cao to take the title of King of Wei.

Xun Yu, Prefect of the Masters of Writing, said, “This should not be done. The Chancellor has already been made Duke of Wei with ninefold honors. His position is already at the limit; to elevate him to king now is not fitting in principle.”

Cao, hearing this, grew angry. “Does this man seek to imitate Xun Yu?” Xun Yu’s worry and anger turned to fever. He lay ill for many days and died at fifty-eight.

Cao gave him an honorable burial and abandoned the plan to make him King.

One day Cao entered the hall with a sword as Emperor Xian sat with Empress Fu.

Seeing Cao approach, the empress leapt to her feet. The emperor trembled at the sight.

Cao said, “Sun Quan and Liu Bei each rule a domain and do not honor court authority. What ought to be done?”

The emperor replied, “All rests with the duke’s management.”

Cao snapped, “If the Son of Heaven speaks so, outsiders will think I only pretend loyalty and deceive you.”

The emperor said, “If you are willing to aid me, that would be good. If not, grant me mercy and withdraw.”

When Cao left in anger, some officers reported, “Recently one hears that the duke intends to make himself king and will soon usurp the throne.” The emperor and empress wept.

The empress said, “My father, Fu Wan, has long wished to kill Cao. I will now draft a letter and send it to my father in secret.”

The emperor said, “When Dong Cheng served without caution he met calamity. Again we fear a leak; then your safety and mine are finished.”

She said, “Each day and night is like sitting on a mattress of needles. A man like this cannot endure; better to die at once. Of the inner attendants, none but Mu Shun can be trusted. Let me send this letter through him.”

She summoned Mu Shun to the rear screen, sent away the chamber attendants, and then she and the emperor wept together.

To Shun she said, “Cao means to raise himself as King of Wei and soon will seize the throne. I wish my father, by your help, to plan this traitor’s fall. Yet those around him are all his men, none trustworthy. You must carry my secret letter to Fu Wan. By your loyalty and righteousness, he cannot fail me.”

Shun wept and answered, “Your servant is deeply in the Emperor’s debt and dare not fail with my life. I will take it.”

The empress wrote out the letter and handed it to Shun. He hid it in his hair and slipped out of the forbidden court to Fu Wan’s house and presented it. Fu Wan saw it was in the empress’s own hand.

Fu Wan said to him, “Cao has many traitorous hearts. We cannot act too hastily. Only if Liu Bei in Shu and Sun Quan in Wu rise together from outside can we force him to move. He must then return here. Only with men in court who are still loyal can we discuss this inside. If we strike from both sides, there may be hope.”

Shun said, “Your Marquis should send back a letter to the emperor and empress, asking for a secret edict and secretly dispatching men to Wu and Shu to arrange revolt and rescue the lord.”

Fu Wan took paper and wrote the return letter, giving it to Shun, who once more hid it in his hair and returned to the capital.

At the gate, Cao was waiting. Shun met him on the way back.

“Where have you come from?” Cao asked.

Shun answered, “The empress is unwell and has sent me to seek a doctor.”

“Did you summon one yet?” Cao asked.

“Not yet.”

Cao ordered his men to search his clothing. Finding nothing, he let him pass. But the wind lifted Shun’s cap, and Cao called him back.

He took the cap and searched it, then found nothing and returned it. Shun put it on upside down.

Cao grew suspicious and ordered a search of Shun’s hair. They found Fu Wan’s letter.

He read it and saw that it spoke of joint action with Sun and Liu as external support. Cao flew into a rage. Shun was arrested and taken to an inner chamber for questioning; he refused to confess.

Cao that very night ordered three thousand soldiers to surround Fu Wan’s house. Old and young were all seized. The empress’s letter was found, and all three branches of the Fu clan were brought to prison.

At first light, Palace Guards Commander Xili entered with the emperor’s order and took the seal and jade-tassel tokens from the empress. Three hundred guards entered at once.

That day the emperor was in the outer hall. Seeing three hundred guards in formation and Xili entering directly, he asked, “What matter is this?”

Xili said, “I bear the duke’s command to collect the empress seal.”

The emperor knew the matter had leaked and his courage broke. Xili entered the rear palace first, where Empress Fu was now awake. He called for the keepers of the seal and jade and ordered them brought out.

Empress, sensing what had happened, hid within a cavity in the rear wall of the Pepper Chamber.

Presently, Chief Clerk Hua Xin entered with five hundred guards and asked the palace maids, “Where is Empress Fu?” They all claimed ignorance.

He told the guards to open the vermilion doors and search. Finding nothing, and suspecting she was in the wall, he shouted for soldiers to break through the wall.

Hua Xin himself pulled back the empress’s hair and dragged her out.

She cried, “Spare my life!”
Hua Xin shouted, “You will answer to the duke now!”

Her hair loose and bare feet, two guards pushed her out.

Hua Xin had once been famous for his literary reputation and was once close with Bing Yuan and Guan Ning. The three were praised as one dragon: Hua Xin as the dragon’s head, Bing Yuan as its belly, and Guan Ning as its tail.

One day he and Guan Ning were weeding a garden. As Guan lifted his hoe, he struck a buried coin. He paid no attention, while Hua picked it up, looked at it, and tossed it aside.

Another day they sat reading together, and heard raised cries of a noble carriage passing outside. Guan sat still and did not move; Hua set down his books and went to watch. From then on Guan despised him and moved their seats apart. He never resumed the friendship.

Later Guan Ning withdrew to Liaodong and was often seen with a white hat, living in one pavilion, never stepping on bare ground, and all his life he refused office in Wei.

Hua Xin, however, first served Sun Quan and later entered Cao’s service; now he came to seize the empress as we have seen.

Later men wrote:

Hua Xin loosed his cruel stratagem that day, broke the wall, and seized the Empress alive,
and for a thousand years he is mocked as the head of the dragon.

And also this verse about Guan Ning:

In Liaodong there is said to be Guan Ning’s pavilion: the owner is gone, the hall is empty, only his name remains.
Laughing at Zi Yu’s greed for rank and riches, how can one match the white-capped man’s free-flowing elegance?

Hua Xin then brought Empress Fu into the outer hall. The emperor saw her and ran down the steps, embraced her and wept.

Hua Xin said, “The duke’s command—go now.”

Empress cried to the emperor, “Can you not let me continue living?”
He said, “I do not even know when my own life is to end!”

Soldiers carried her away, and the emperor struck his breast in grief. Seeing Xili at his side, he said, “Great Excellency Xili, can this exist under heaven?” and fell to the ground in tears. Xili ordered attendants to carry him back.

Hua Xin delivered her to Cao.

Cao shouted, “I treated all of you sincerely, and you sought my harm. If I spare you, you would kill me.”

He ordered the guards to beat her to death. He then entered the hall and had the two sons of the empress poisoned. Before nightfall, more than two hundred members of Fu Wan’s and Mu Shun’s families were beheaded in the market.

Courtiers and commoners alike were stunned. It was the eleventh month of the nineteenth year of Jian’an. In later years people lamented:

Cao Man was cruel as no age has seen;
what became of Fu Wan’s loyal righteousness?
Pity! In separating lord and empress,
he had no pity even equal to common wives and husbands.

Since the empress’s death, Emperor Xian did not eat for days. Cao entered and said, “Your Majesty, do not grieve. I bear no other intent. Let Cao Guiren, your honored consort, be elevated as your principal empress. She is virtuous and filial.”

In the first month of the twentieth year of Jian’an, at the celebration of New Year’s first day, he established Cao Guiren as empress. No one below dared speak.

At this time Cao’s power grew ever greater. He convened ministers to discuss a campaign to finish Wu and then Shu. Jia Xu said, “You should summon Xiahou Dun and Cao Ren at once and confer.”

Cao sent urgent summons through the night. Xiahou Dun had not yet arrived when Cao Ren came first and entered the hall at once in the night. Cao was drunk and resting, and Xu Chu stood with sword at the hall door. Cao Ren tried to enter but was stopped.

Xu Chu said, “General, though you are of the clan, your office guards frontier command. I am only a lesser householder yet now stand in inner service. The lord lies asleep; he may not be disturbed.”

Cao heard this and praised, “Xu Chu is truly a loyal minister.”

Not long after, Xiahou Dun arrived and together they discussed an expedition.

Dun said, “Wu and Shu cannot be taken at once. We should first take Zhang Lu in Hanzhong. With an army fresh from victory we can strike into Shu in one swift effort.”

Cao said, “That exactly matches my thought.” He ordered troops to march west.

So it is written:

He now lays bare his murderous design, bullying a weak ruler and sending hard-fighting troops to sweep aside a border state;
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Guan Yu Meets the Summons with a Single Sword; Empress Fu Gives Her Life for the State

chapters.html:
Soon after, Cao Cao raised troops to campaign west, splitting his army into three corps: the vanguard under Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He, himself in the center with the principal generals, and the rear under Cao Ren and Xiahou Dun, which hauled the grain and forage. A spy had already reported from Hanzhong. Zhang Lu and his brother Zhang Wei discussed how to repel the invaders. Zhang Wei said, “Hanzhong is most dangerous and difficult to hold, and none is stronger than Yangping Pass. Put ten or more stockades on both sides of the pass by the hills and woods, and meet Cao’s army there. Brother, you remain at Hanning and send out as much grain and grain-fodder as needed.”

Zhang Lu followed that advice and sent the commanders Yang Ang and Yang Ren off with his brother at once. Their cavalry and mounted men reached Yangping Pass and finished setting camp. Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He of the forward corps arrived soon after and, hearing that Yangping Pass was already prepared, camped fifteen li away from it. That night the soldiers were exhausted and each unit lay down to rest.

Suddenly, from behind the camp arose a single sudden blaze. Yang Ang and Yang Ren came in along two routes, killing and looting through the camp. Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He rushed to their horses in alarm. Huge forces came up all around, and Cao’s men suffered a heavy defeat and withdrew before Cao Cao.

When they reported in, Cao Cao was furious: “You two have been marching for many a long year. Do you not know that when soldiers march far they become worn and weary, and one must guard against raids on the camp? Why did you make no such preparation?” He wanted to execute both men to set an example under military law. The officers begged for clemency.

The next day Cao Cao himself led the troops forward as the first line. Seeing the savage ridges, tangled woods, and no clear road, he feared an ambush and withdrew to camp. “If I had known this ground was so perilous, I would not have come out with troops,” he said as he addressed Xu Chu and Xu Huang.

Xu Chu said, “The army has already come this far, my lord, and it is no shame to bear hardship.”
The following day Cao Cao mounted up with only Xu Chu and Xu Huang and came to inspect Zhang Wei’s stockades. Three horses rounded the slope, and he saw Zhang Wei’s defenses at once.

Cao Cao raised his riding-whip and pointed from afar. “As they are now, these works are sturdy and hard to assail.”
He had not finished speaking when a shout rose from behind, and arrows came down like rain. Yang Ang and Yang Ren came charging from two directions.

Cao Cao was greatly startled. Xu Chu shouted, “I will confront the villains! Xu Gongming, stand by and protect my lord!” He drew his sword, leapt upon his horse, and rushed forward to oppose them. Yang Ang and Yang Ren could not match Xu Chu’s courage and turned back, while the rest dared not come on. Xu Huang kept close to Cao Cao as he rode over the slope; another unit arrived in front. When they arrived, it was Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He; hearing the battle cries, they came up in support. They drove back Yang Ang and Yang Ren and brought Cao Cao back to camp in safety.

Cao Cao gave the four generals great rewards. From then on both sides faced each other for more than fifty days without battle. Cao Cao then ordered a withdrawal. Jia Xu said, “We have not yet seen how strong or weak the enemy really is, why should Your Excellency retreat?” Cao Cao said, “I judge that the enemy is on daily alert and therefore hard to crush by direct attack. I will make this appear a retreat, let the enemy slacken its guard, and then send light cavalry to sweep through the rear. Then we will win.”

Jia Xu said, “The Chancellor’s stratagem is unfathomable.”

So he ordered Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He to split into two routes and lead three thousand light cavalry each along a side path, cutting behind Yangping Pass. Cao Cao ordered the main army to pull up camp in full. Yang Ang heard that Cao’s troops were withdrawing and spoke with Yang Ren, wanting to exploit the moment and strike. Yang Ren said, “Cao has too many tricks. We do not know if it is real. Do not give chase.” Yang Ang said, “If you will not go, I will go alone.” Yang Ren’s strong remonstration was ignored.

Yang Ang pushed all five-stockade units and the cavalry forward and left only a handful of soldiers to guard the stockade. That day fog was thick, and the two sides could not see each other. Halfway there, his force could not proceed and had to wait.

Meanwhile, Xiahou Yuan’s force, which had cut around the mountain, saw a heavy fog hanging in layers and heard voices and horsecalls; fearing an ambush, he urged everyone forward. In the thick fog he mistakenly rode into the front of Yang Ang’s stockade. The guard on watch there, hearing horse-hoof sounds, thought it was Yang Ang’s troops returning and opened the gate.

The Wei soldiers surged inside, found it an empty stockade, and set it alight. The five stockade troops abandoned their posts and fled. As the fog lifted, Yang Ren came with his men to rescue and fought Xiahou Yuan, but before they could gain much ground, Zhang He’s men arrived behind him. Yang Ren found a way out and ran back to Nanzheng. Yang Ang, when he tried to leave, discovered that Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He had already taken the stockades. At that same moment, Cao Cao’s main body came thundering up from behind. The Yuan army was caught on both sides with no road in any direction.

Yang Ang tried to break through the lines, but collided with Zhang He. The two fought; Zhang He killed him. His defeated men ran back to Yangping Pass to report to Zhang Wei. In fact, Zhang Wei had learned his two commanders had failed and that the camps were already lost; in the middle of the night he abandoned the pass and ran off.

Cao Cao now gained Yangping Pass and the other stockades.

Zhang Wei returned to Zhang Lu and said that the two commanders had lost the choke point and could no longer hold the pass. Zhang Lu grew furious and wanted to behead Yang Ren. Yang Ren said, “I had earlier remonstrated with Yang Ang and begged him not to pursue Cao’s soldiers. He refused to heed me, which brought this disaster. Permit me one more army to go forth and challenge them. I will cut down Cao Cao. If I fail, I will accept the penalty of command.”

Zhang Lu handed him the command order. Yang Ren mounted and led twenty thousand troops out from Nanzheng, leaving camp.

Now Cao Cao advanced again. First he ordered Xiahou Yuan with five thousand men to scout the Nanzheng route. There he met Yang Ren’s cavalry, and the two lines of soldiers deployed. Yang Ren sent his officer Chang Qi to challenge; they fought not three rounds before Xiahou Yuan cut him down from horseback. Yang Ren lifted his spear and entered the fight himself, trading with Xiahou Yuan for more than thirty rounds without clear result. Xiahou Yuan feigned defeat and withdrew; Yang Ren pursued from behind.

Xiahou Yuan then used a sweeping-sword trick and he was cut down beneath his horse. Yang Ren’s soldiers were routed and ran back.

Cao Cao learned that Xiahou Yuan had slain Yang Ren and immediately pushed forward to Nanzheng, reaching the bottom of the camp line. Zhang Lu gathered civilians and officials to discuss. Yan Pu said, “One man alone could match the commanders under your Excellency.” Zhang Lu asked who.

Yan Pu said, “Pang De of Nanan. He had once followed Ma Chao and then submitted to your Excellency. When Ma Chao went west to Sichuan, Pang De fell sick and could not move. Now that he is nourished by your Excellency’s kindness, why not send him?”

Zhang Lu rejoiced and summoned Pang De, rewarding him richly. He gave him an order for ten thousand horse and troops and told him out. Ten li beyond the city wall, they met Cao’s army face to face. Pang De rode out to grapple in battle.

At the Weiqu Bridge, Cao Cao had already learned of Pang De’s valor, and he instructed the officers, “Pang De is a brave general of Xiliang, once a follower of Ma Chao. Though he now serves Zhang Lu, it is not in his heart. I want this man. You must engage him gradually, wear his strength down, and then capture him.”

Zhang He moved first and, after a few exchanges, withdrew. Xiahou Yuan too fought for several passes and withdrew. Xu Huang also fought three to five rounds before withdrawing. Finally, even after more than fifty rounds, Xu Chu withdrew as well. Pang De fought hard against all four and showed no fear. Each general before Cao Cao praised Pang De’s martial art.

Cao Cao rejoiced in his heart and conferred with the officers, “How can we bring this man to submission?” Jia Xu said, “I know there is a strategist under Zhang Lu named Yang Song. He is very greedy for bribes. We can secretly send him gold and silks, and he will slander Pang De before Zhang Lu. Then we may act.”

Cao Cao said, “How can we get inside Nanzheng?” Jia Xu said, “Tomorrow in the clash, feign defeat and retreat, as if abandoning the camp; when Pang De takes our stockade, I will in the deep night lead troops to seize that stockade. Pang De will certainly retreat into the city. Then choose a soldier with a good voice, dress him in Han Commandery soldier garb and let him mingle in their ranks; he can slip into the city.”

Cao Cao accepted the plan and chose one excellent soldier, showered him with reward, and gave him a suit of gold-trimmed mail, telling him to wear it beneath the skin-tight layer and the outer uniform of Han Commandery soldiers. He waited halfway along the route. The next day Cao first sent two wings, Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He, off to hide far away. He then ordered Xu Huang to challenge; after only a few rounds he was routed and withdrew.

Pang De charged and struck all that he could; Cao’s soldiers all pulled back. Pang De seized Cao’s stockade. Seeing abundant grain and provisions there, he rejoiced and at once reported it to Zhang Lu and held a celebration feast in the stockade.

After the second watch that night, flames suddenly rose from three directions: directly in front were Xu Huang and Xu Chu; to the left Zhang He; to the right Xiahou Yuan. The three cavalry waves came together to loot the camp. Pang De had no time to prepare; he could only mount and break through while still fighting, then ride toward the city. Three routes of soldiers followed him.

Pang De shouted for the gates to be opened and led his force in a rush back inside.

Now spies had already mixed into the city and went straight to Yang Song’s residence to report. “The Duke of Wei, Chancellor Cao Cao, has long heard of your great virtue. He has specially sent me to deliver gold and armor as a token of good faith.” Yang Song’s face lit up. Reading the message, he said to the messenger, “Tell the Wei Chancellor that he may be at ease. I have a good scheme and will report it.” He sent the messenger back first and then entered Zhang Lu’s presence that night, saying Pang De had taken Cao’s bribe and sold this battle. Zhang Lu became furious, summoned Pang De, and shouted him down, wanting to execute him. Yan Pu remonstrated. Zhang Lu said, “If you fail tomorrow in battle you shall die by my hand!” Pang De withdrew in resentment.

The next day Cao’s soldiers attacked the city and Pang De rode out. Cao Cao ordered Xu Chu to engage. Xu Chu feigned defeat, and Pang De came after him. Cao Cao himself mounted on a slope and called out, “Pang De, why did you not submit to me earlier?”

Pang De thought, “If I can catch Cao Cao I might ransom a thousand commanders!” and spurred his horse up the slope. With a shout he leapt; the earth seemed to split. He and horse and rider tumbled into a pit. Hooks and ropes were cast at once, and he was taken alive and hauled up the slope.

Cao Cao dismounted, drove back the soldiers, and personally unbound him. He asked whether Pang De would submit. Pang De considered that Zhang Lu was no longer humane and preferred to swear allegiance. Cao Cao helped him back on his horse and returned deliberately in the opposite direction so that the city could witness him. He reported Pang De to Zhang Lu, saying he rode with Cao together.

Zhang Lu believed Yang Song’s earlier report more than ever.

The next day Cao Cao raised three ladders on all three faces and set up incendiary projectiles in attack. Zhang Lu saw the force had become critical and discussed with his brother Zhang Wei. Zhang Wei said, “Burn all storehouses and granaries and ride south to Ba Zhong for safety.” Yang Song said, “Better open the gates and surrender.” Zhang Lu hesitated.

Zhang Wei said, “If you burn them and leave, then go.”
Zhang Lu replied, “I at one time meant to return to the court, but my purpose has not been fulfilled. Now, if I have no choice but to flee, the storehouses and grain and coffers are of the state and can never be abandoned.” So he ordered all gates sealed.

That night in the second watch, Zhang Lu led his entire household and opened the south gate to break out. Cao Cao gave no command to chase. He entered Nanzheng and, seeing the sealed stores and granaries, was moved. He sent men to Ba Zhong to urge surrender.

Zhang Lu wished to yield, but Zhang Wei refused. Yang Song sent a secret letter to Cao Cao and arranged for internal coordination. Cao Cao received it and personally moved troops toward Ba Zhong. Zhang Lu sent his brother Wei out to engage, but he fought Xu Chu and was cut down from horseback. His defeated force returned and reported. Zhang Lu wanted to stand firm.

Yang Song said, “If you do not now come out, you will sit and die by waiting. I can hold the city; you, Your Majesty, must come out and decide this final battle.”
Zhang Lu followed him. Yan Pu remonstrated and asked Zhang Lu to stay in, but he did not listen and led his soldiers out to meet them.

Before they even clashed, the rear ranks had already fled. Zhang Lu hastily retreated, and the soldiers of Cao came up from behind. He reached the foot of the city walls, but Yang Song shut the gates and would not admit him. With no road left, Cao Cao himself followed close and called out, “Why did you not surrender in time?” Zhang Lu dismounted and prostrated himself.

Cao Cao was greatly pleased. Remembering his refusal to burn the stores, he treated him honorably and bestowed on him the title of General Who Guards the South. Yan Pu and others were all made marquises. Thus Hanzhong was fully pacified. Cao Cao ordered each commandery to establish Administrators and Chief Commanders and awarded the soldiery generously.

But Yang Song, who sold his lord for glory, Cao Cao had put to death before the camp gate as an example for all.

Later a poem was composed:

The traitor who sells a true man, boasting of strange exploits,
collects all the gold and silver, yet all of it is empty.
His family does not prosper; his body receives the axe;
for ten thousand years they will laugh at Yang Song.

After Cao Cao had taken Dong Chuan, Sima Yi said, “Liu Bei has taken Liu Zhang by force and deception, and the Shu people have not yet yielded their hearts. Now Your Excellency has gained Hanzhong; Yi Province is shaken. We should quickly push forward and attack; if we press now, it will surely collapse. Those who can take occasion are precious for seizing time; one must not miss the hour.” Cao Cao sighed and said, “People never know enough. After gaining Longyou, one wants Shu as well.”

Liu Ye said, “Sima Zhongda is right. If we are slow by even a little, Zhuge Liang, now wise in governance and a prime minister, and the valiant Guan and Zhang are the strongest in all three armies. The people of Shu will be settled, and they hold the mountain passes. It will not be easy to break through.”

Cao Cao said, “The soldiers have crossed far and are fatigued. We should care for them.” He therefore held his troops in readiness and did not advance.

In the western Sichuan countryside, when people heard Cao Cao had taken Dong Chuan and assumed he would next take West Sichuan, fear passed through them repeatedly in a single day. Liu Bei asked his military adviser for counsel. Zhuge Liang said, “Ming has a plan. Cao Cao will withdraw on his own.”

Liu Bei asked, “What is the plan?”
Zhuge Liang said, “Cao Cao has split his army and is garrisoning Hefei, fearing Sun Quan. If we now return Jiangxia, Changsha, and Guiyang commanderies to Wu and dispatch an eloquent envoy to explain the gains and dangers, and have Wu raise troops against Hefei, he will be forced to pull south.”

Liu Bei asked, “Who can go as envoy?”
Yi Ji said, “I volunteer.” Liu Bei rejoiced and prepared a letter with full ceremony, sending Yi Ji first to Jing Province to notify Yunchang, then onward to Wu.

Yi Ji went to Moleng and presented himself before Sun Quan, who had already been informed of his name. The king summoned him. After Yi Ji finished the rites, Sun Quan asked, “Why have you come here?”
Yi Ji said, “Yesterday I was entrusted by Master Ziyu to manage the handover of the three commanderies, and the military adviser is absent; the handover failed. I now bring word and return what is due. The southern commanderies of Jing Province and Lingling were to be sent back; but Cao Cao has taken Dong Chuan, leaving General Guan no place to stand. Hefei is now empty of force. I ask Your Majesty to take up arms and assault it, so that Cao Cao will turn his army south. If my lord takes Dong Chuan, then I will return all of Jingzang to him in full.”

Sun Quan said, “Return now to the guest hall. Let me consider this with my council.”

Yi Ji withdrew, and Sun Quan asked his strategists. Zhang Zhao said, “It is true Liu Bei fears Cao Cao taking West Sichuan, and therefore devised this stratagem. Still, since Cao Cao now stands at Hanzhong and can strike Hefei in momentum, this is best as a grand plan.” Sun Quan agreed.

He dismissed Yi Ji back to Shu and, while he finished, ordered troops to rise against Cao. He told Lu Su to take possession of Jiangxia, Changsha, and Guiyang commanderies and station them at Lukou; then called for Lü Meng and Gan Ning to return. He also ordered Ling Tong from Yu Hang.

Not many days passed before Lü Meng and Gan Ning arrived. Lü Meng proposed a plan: “Cao Cao has placed Zhu Guang, the Cangjiang governor of Lujiang, in Wan City; he has opened wide paddies and stored grain in Hefei, supplying the army. We should first take Wan City, then strike Hefei.”
Sun Quan said, “That plan matches my thought.” He sent Lü Meng and Gan Ning forward as the vanguard, Jiang Qin and Pan Zhang to follow, and Sun Quan himself led Zhou Tai, Chen Wu, Dong Xi, and Xu Sheng as the center. At the time, Cheng Pu, Huang Gai, and Han Dang were posted at various fortresses and did not join the campaign.

The army crossed the river, took Hezhou, and went straight to Wan City. The governor Zhu Guang sent men to Hefei to beg for relief and, while doing so, stood firm in the city and refused to move. When Sun Quan arrived below the walls, arrows rained down from above and struck the canopy over his banner. Sun Quan returned to camp and asked his lieutenants how to take the city.

Dong Xi said, “You may send soldiers to build an earthen mound and attack.”
Xu Sheng said, “We could erect ladders and build a rainbow bridge, then observe and press from above.”
Lü Meng said, “Those methods waste time and day by day, and Hefei’s relief force may arrive soon. Our men are newly arrived and fierce with fresh zeal. We should strike now. Tomorrow at dawn we advance, and by midday we will break the city.”

Sun Quan agreed. At dawn the next day, after the soldiers had taken their morning meal, the three armies advanced. Arrows and stones fell like rain from the ramparts. Gan Ning, gripping an iron chain, charged through the hail of weapons. Zhu Guang ordered his archers and crossbowmen to fire together at once; Gan Ning swiped aside the storm of arrows and with one sweep brought Zhu Guang down. Sun Quan personally struck the war drum. The soldiers surged forward and slashed down on the city walls with their broad sabers. Many enemy troops surrendered, and by just past noon they took Wan City. Zhang Liao arrived halfway and, when messengers said Wan City had fallen, he turned back to Hefei.

Sun Quan entered Wan City, and Ling Tong also arrived with his force. After words of thanks, Sun Quan rewarded the three armies and poured in praise and rewards for Lü Meng and Gan Ning and the generals, then held a triumph banquet.

Lü Meng stepped down to let Gan Ning sit above him and loudly praised his merit. When drink had reached half intoxication, Ling Tong recalled that Gan Ning had killed his father and saw Lü Meng praising him too highly. He glared at Gan Ning for a long while, then suddenly drew the sword at his side and stood at the table: “There is no music on this mat. Watch me with my sword.” Gan Ning understood and pushed away the table and stool, sprang up with both hands and took up two spears, then said, “I shall move the swords on this mat.” Lü Meng saw both men with ill intent. He drew his sword in one hand, his blade in the other, stepped between them, and said, “Though both gentlemen are able, neither surpasses my skill.” He then drew his knife and danced between the two.

Word reached Sun Quan promptly. He spurred his horse and hurried straight to the table. Seeing Sun Quan arrive, the generals set down their weapons. Sun Quan said, “I have told the two of you many times to forget old grudges. How can this be now?” Ling Tong knelt and wept. Sun Quan again and again exhorted him to refrain.

The next day he raised the army to continue the march against Hefei and sent the whole host onward.

Zhang Liao, for losing Wan City, returned to Hefei with a troubled heart. Cao Cao suddenly sent Xue Ti with a wooden casket bearing a sealed note: “Open this when the bandits arrive.” That day the report came that Sun Quan had brought one hundred thousand soldiers and was attacking Hefei. Zhang Liao opened the box and read the instruction within: “If Sun Quan arrives, let Generals Zhang and Li take the field. Let Yue General hold the city.”

He showed Li Dian and Yue Jin the note. Yue Jin asked, “What is Your Excellency’s thought?” Zhang Liao said, “Our lord is campaigning far afield. The Wu troops think we are certainly broken. We should send out forces to meet them, strike with force to dull their edge and steady the people, and then hold.”

Li Dian, who had never gotten along with Zhang Liao, heard this and answered nothing. When Yue Jin saw Li Dian fall silent, he said, “The enemy is many and we are few; it is hard to meet them in the open. Better to hold fast.” Zhang Liao said, “You both speak from private feeling and do not serve the state. I will go out and meet them now to decide this by force of blood.” He ordered his men to prepare his horse.

Li Dian rose in sorrow and said, “General, if you are thus, how could I, Mancheng, allow private resentment to make me neglect duty? I will take command.” Zhang Liao was pleased and said, “Since Mancheng can aid, tomorrow you will take one corps and lie in ambush north of Xiaoyao Ford. When Wu’s army charges across, cut Xiaoyao Bridge first; I and Le Wenqian will strike them.” Li Dian took his command and left to post the ambush.

Now Sun Quan ordered Lü Meng and Gan Ning forward as the vanguard, Ling Tong in the center. The other generals arrived in succession and came toward Hefei in attack. Lü Meng and Gan Ning’s forward troops met Yue Jin. Gan Ning rode out to face Yue Jin and after only a few passes Yue Jin feigned defeat and withdrew. Gan Ning called Lü Meng, and both brought their corps in pursuit.

Sun Quan, in the second line, heard the front had succeeded and drove men on toward the north of Xiaoyao Ford. At that moment, a rapid succession of signal blasts sounded: Zhang Liao’s army from the left and Li Dian’s from the right arrived. Sun Quan was in alarm and hurriedly ordered Lü Meng and Gan Ning back in rescue, but Zhang Liao’s men were already there. Ling Tong had only three hundred and some riders, and he could not stand against the massed Cao forces.

Ling Tong shouted, “My lord, hurry across Xiaoyao Bridge!”

Before he could finish, Zhang Liao came riding with more than two thousand men to strike first. Ling Tong turned and died fighting. Sun Quan spurred his horse onto the bridge; the south section of it had been torn apart by more than a zhang and no plank remained. Sun Quan stood frozen for a moment.

His guardsman Gu Li shouted, “My lord, pull back the horse and then let him go forward again. Make him leap over the broken bridge.” Sun Quan reeled the horse back three more zhang, then stood him and struck with the reins; the horse leapt over the broken span at the bridge’s south end.

Later people made this poem:

The hero once leaped the Tan Creek;
once again Wu Hou was defeated at Hefei.
After turning back, he flogged on the swift horse,
and above Xiaoyao Ford a jade-scaled dragon rose.

After Sun Quan leapt past the damaged bridge, Xu Sheng and Dong Xi met him by boat. Ling Tong and Gu Li blocked Zhang Liao. Lü Meng and Gan Ning turned back to rescue, but Yue Jin pursued from behind and Li Dian cut them off in close fighting. The Wu army lost nearly half.

The three hundred and more men under Ling Tong were all cut down. Ling Tong was pierced by many spears and fought to the bridge, but the bridge was already broken. He went around the river to escape. Sun Quan in a boat saw him and ordered Dong Xi to paddle over; he was ferried across.

Lü Meng and Gan Ning both fought desperately and escaped across to the river’s southern bank. This fight made everyone in Jiangnan frightened; hearing Zhang Liao’s great name, even children would no longer cry at night. Generals protected Sun Quan on the return to camp. Sun Quan rewarded Ling Tong and Gu Li and withdrew the armies to Ruxu, repairing ships and discussing a combined attack by water and land. He sent men to Jiangnan again to raise more men for the fight.

Zhang Liao learned Sun Quan was at Ruxu and wished to raise troops and march, fearing the city was too weak for a stand. He hastened to order Xue Ti, at once in the night, to run south to Hanzhong and report to Cao Cao, requesting reinforcements. Cao Cao discussed with his officers and asked whether this was the time to take West Sichuan. Liu said, “Shu is now somewhat settled and prepared; we cannot strike now. Better to withdraw from here and rush south to save Hefei.”

Cao Cao therefore left Xiahou Yuan guarding the mountain pass at Dingjun to hold Hanzhong, and left Zhang He at Mengtou Cliffs and the other chokepoints. The rest of the army pulled up camp and went swiftly to Ruxu.

It was just now:

Iron-clad riders can just flatten the Longyou frontier,
and banners once again point south to Jiangnan.
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Cao Pacifies Hanzhong, and Zhang Liao Strikes Fear at Xiaoyao Ford

chapters.html:
Sun Quan was making arrangements with his troops at Ruxu Ford when he heard that Cao Cao had led four hundred thousand men from Hanzhong in person to come to the relief of Hefei. Sun Quan met with his strategists. Zhang Zhao said, “Cao Cao has come far; he must first be checked before he can deploy his sharpest force.” Sun Quan then asked the captains, “Cao Cao has come from far away. Who dares strike first and break the enemy’s spirit?” Ling Tong came forward and said, “I volunteer.”

Sun Quan asked, “How many men should you take?” Ling Tong said, “Three thousand will be enough.” Gan Ning said, “Only one hundred riders are needed. Why send three thousand?” The two men at once argued before Sun Quan.

Sun Quan said, “The Wei force is vast; we must not take it lightly.” So he ordered Ling Tong to lead three thousand out to Rusu and scout ahead, and if they met Cao’s men, to fight.

Obeying orders, Ling Tong led three thousand horsemen away from the Rusu encampment. When dust rose ahead, Cao’s troops were already there. Zhang Liao of the vanguard met Ling Tong in combat, and the two fought fifty exchanges without decisive advantage. Sun Quan, fearing for Ling Tong, sent Lü Meng to reinforce.

Gan Ning saw Ling Tong return and said to Sun Quan, “Tonight I only need a hundred horsemen to strike the Wei camp. If we kill only a single man and horse, it is still no real merit.” Sun Quan admired the nerve in him and ordered one hundred picked cavalry sent from the camp to Gan Ning, plus fifty jars of wine and fifty jin of lamb for the soldiers.

Gan Ning returned to the palisade. He had one hundred men sit and take their places. He first poured out wine in silver bowls and drank two bowls himself. Then he told the men, “Tonight we are ordered to raid the camp. I ask each of you to drain your cup and push on with all your strength.” The men looked at each other in doubt. Gan Ning drew his sword and shouted angrily, “I, as your senior commander, do not care to hold back my life. Why do you hesitate?” The men, seeing Gan Ning’s expression, all rose and knelt, saying, “We are ready to die with you.”

Gan Ning and the one hundred shared the wine and meat together. After they had finished, it was around the second watch. He handed out one hundred white-goose plumes and fixed one on each helmet as a signal. All donned armor and mounted. They galloped to the edge of Cao Cao’s camp, tore open the horned barrier, and shouted together before riding in. They drove straight into the center of the camp, trying to strike Cao Cao.

In the center, the Wei troops had laid out chariot gear across the road and formed an interlocked barrier like iron tubs, so they could not be pierced at first. Gan Ning drove the hundred riders in sudden charges and swift turns. Cao’s men panicked, and not knowing how many enemies they faced, they were thrown into confusion. Gan Ning’s hundred in the camp wheeled and charged, killing whoever they met. Every camp sent out drums and shouting; fires rose like stars; their screams shook the air.

Gan Ning broke out through the southern gate of the camp; no one dared oppose him. Sun Quan ordered Zhou Tai to bring a unit forward in support. Gan Ning brought the hundred riders back to Rusu. Cao’s troops, fearing an ambush, dared not pursue.

A later poem praised the assault:

Drum and gong thundered and shook the earth; wherever Wu’s army moved, ghosts and spirits wailed. The hundred plumes cleaved the Wei camp at once; all of it proclaimed Gan Ning’s tiger-hearted generalship.

Gan Ning returned to camp without killing or losing a man or horse. At the gate he ordered the hundred to strike drums and play flutes, crying, “Long live!” Their cheers shook the air. Sun Quan himself came out to receive him. Gan Ning dismounted and knelt in submission. Sun Quan raised him and took his hand. “General, this trip alone made the old brigand quake,” he said. “I did not set you aside for fear of losing you. I only wanted to test your courage.”

He then rewarded him with one thousand bolts of silk and one hundred sharp blades. Gan Ning accepted and then divided rewards among the one hundred riders. Sun Quan told the generals, “Mengde has Zhang Liao, and I have Gan Xingba; that is enough to meet him.”

The next day Zhang Liao came out to strike.

Seeing Gan Ning’s success, Ling Tong said resolutely, “I wish to face Zhang Liao.” Sun Quan granted the request. Ling Tong then led five thousand men out of Rusu. Sun Quan brought Gan Ning with him to observe from the field.

At the line of battle, Zhang Liao came out on horseback, with Li Dian on his left and Yue Jin on his right. Ling Tong charged forward, horse and saber in hand, into the front line. Zhang Liao sent Yue Jin to meet him. The two fought for fifty rounds without a clear winner.

Cao Cao heard of it and rode himself to the banner line to watch. Seeing the two locked in fierce combat, he ordered Cao Xiu to fire a concealed arrow. Cao Xiu slipped behind Zhang Liao, drew his bow, and loosed one arrow that struck Ling Tong under him as he sat in the saddle. The horse reared and threw Ling Tong to the ground. Yue Jin came on with a spear to stab.

Before the spear landed, a bowstring snapped from the opposite side—a single arrow struck Yue Jin in the face, and he turned and came off his horse. Both armies came out together and each side rushed to rescue its own commander and withdrew, and the ringing of bells ended the fight.

Ling Tong returned to camp and thanked Sun Quan. Sun Quan said, “The one who shot to save you was Gan Ning.” Ling Tong knelt and saluted Gan Ning, saying, “I had not imagined the General would show such grace.” From then on they became friends for life and death, and never turned to evil again.

Later, when Cao Cao saw that Yue Jin had been hit, he returned to his tent to attend to him. The next day he divided his forces into five routes to strike Rusu: he led the center himself, the left one by Zhang Liao and the second left by Li Dian, the right one by Xu Huang and the second right by Pang De. Each route had ten thousand men and riders and ran to the riverbank.

At that time Dong Xi and Xu Sheng were on boats. When the five columns arrived, all ranks showed fear in their faces. Xu Sheng said, “To eat the ruler’s grain is to serve loyally. Why should we fear?” He led several hundred fierce men across in small boats and charged into Li Dian’s force.

Dong Xi stayed aboard the ship and ordered drums and shouts to raise the men’s spirits. Suddenly a fierce wind rose on the river; white waves lifted into the sky and the surge became violent. The soldiers saw their big boats might overturn, and they rushed down to smaller craft to flee.

Sword in hand, Dong Xi shouted, “You were ordered to hold the enemy. How dare you leave your ship?” He beheaded more than ten men who tried to disembark. Soon the wind grew and his boat turned over. Dong Xi died in the river mouth.

Xu Sheng fought amid the melee inside Li Dian’s line.

Chen Wu heard the river battle and brought out a unit. He met Pang De directly, and the two armies became a mixed melee. At Rusu, Sun Quan heard Cao’s troops had reached the riverbank and rode out with Zhou Tai to help.

It happened just as he saw Xu Sheng in Li Dian’s melee making a complete tangle of fighting. He waved troops in to reinforce. Then Zhang Liao and Xu Huang with two detached forces trapped Sun Quan at the center of the formation. From a high rise Cao Cao saw Sun Quan surrounded and urgently ordered Xu Chu to ride with sword and cut into the army, splitting Sun’s force into two so that they could not rescue each other.

Zhou Tai cut his way out and reached the riverbank. When he saw Sun Quan was not there, he pulled back and then reentered the circle, asking his unit, “Where is the lord?” They pointed toward where the fighting was densest and said, “The lord is in a close encirclement, in great danger.” Zhou Tai pushed forward and found Sun Quan. He said, “My lord, come with me and break out.”

Then Zhou Tai went ahead and Sun followed behind, fighting hard through the press. Zhou Tai reached the riverbank, looked back, and still saw no sign of Sun Quan, so he turned and again plunged into the encirclement and found him again.

Sun said, “With bow and crossbow firing together, we cannot get out. What can we do?” Zhou Tai replied, “My lord is in front, and I am behind. We can break through together.”

Sun charged forward. Zhou Tai shielded him on both sides. Spears struck him repeatedly; arrows pierced his heavy armor, yet he saved Sun. They reached the riverbank, where Lü Meng brought a branch of the water force to help them board.

Sun said, “By three times cutting in, Zhou Tai, I escaped this heavy encirclement. But Xu Sheng remains in the middle of it. How will he get out?” Zhou Tai answered, “I will go back again.” He turned and drove through once more, then entered the heavy encirclement and rescued Xu Sheng. Both men were heavily wounded. Lü Meng ordered the men to fire arrows in all directions at the troops on the bank and then pull the two commanders down to the boats.

Chen Wu fought against Pang De again. With no troops left behind him to reinforce, Pang De pressed him to a narrow pass by a dense wood. Chen Wu tried to turn and fight again, but a tree trunk caught his robe sleeve and he could not answer the charge. Pang De killed him.

When Cao Cao saw that Sun Quan had escaped, he drove his horse and pressed forward to the river edge to shoot and exchange missiles. Lü Meng had run out of arrows.

In the moment of panic, suddenly a group of ships arrived on the river. At their head was Lu Xun, Sun Ce’s son-in-law, bringing one hundred thousand troops. He led a heavy volley that drove Wei back. Then he took the chance to land, pursue, and recover several thousand warhorses. The Wei losses were innumerable, and they fled in a major rout. In the confusion they found Chen Wu’s body.

Sun learned that Chen Wu was dead and Dong Xi had also sunk into the river. He was struck with great grief and sent men to search the water for Dong Xi’s body, then buried the two together.

He also owed a deep debt to Zhou Tai for saving him. Sun held a banquet and honored him. Sun himself offered him a cup and patted his back, tears flowing, saying,

“Twice you rode in to rescue me and did not spare your life. You were pierced by dozens of spears, and your skin is marked like carved wood. Can a lord like me not return your bone-and-blood kindness by trusting you with soldiers and cavalry? You are my meritorious officer; I will share honor and ruin, joy and grief with you.”

When he had finished, Sun ordered Zhou Tai’s armor removed before the assembled officers. The skin and flesh were gouged with scars like knife marks, all through the body and deep to the roots. Sun pointed to each wound and asked about it. Zhou Tai told him where each had been struck in battle. The more wounds he named, the more cups he drank.

That day Zhou Tai was drunk from start to end. Sun awarded him a blue silk umbrella and ordered him to go in and out under a canopy so that his service would be made known.

Sun and Cao remained facing each other at Rusu for more than a month, and neither could win. Zhang Zhao and Gu Yong spoke up: “Cao Cao’s force is huge. We cannot force him. If the war drags on, too many soldiers will die. It is better to seek peace and keep the people safe.” Sun followed their counsel and sent Bu Zhi to Cao’s camp to ask for peace and promise yearly tribute.

Cao Cao saw that crossing into the south bank was not yet feasible, so he agreed and ordered, “Sun Quan should withdraw his troops first. I will then return home.” Bu Zhi returned. Sun left only Jiang Qin and Zhou Tai to hold Rusu and sent the main army aboard ships back to Moling.

Cao left Cao Ren and Zhang Liao to garrison Hefei and then withdrew to Xuchang. The civil and military officials all proposed that Cao Cao be made King of Wei. Cui Yan, the Prefect of the Masters of Writing, argued vehemently against it.

The others said, “Do you alone not see Xun Yu, then?” Cui Yan became furious. “Now! now! there will be a change! Do what you choose!” he cried. A man who had quarreled with Cui Yan reported him to Cao. Cao flew into rage, seized Cui Yan, and imprisoned him for questioning.

Cui Yan, with eyes like a tiger and beard curled like a dragon, still shouted out, “Cao Cao is a rogue who betrays the Son of Heaven.” The censor informed Cao, and Cao ordered him beaten to death with the penal staff in prison.

A later verse praised him:

Cui Yan of Qinghe—nature hard and unbending. Tiger eyes and whiskered muzzle, a heart of iron and stone. The evil and crooked give way before him; his upright voice rings high. Loyal to the Han lord, his name shines through ten thousand ages.

In the twenty-first year of Jian’an, in the fifth month, the ministers submitted memorials to the Son of Heaven praising Wei Lord Cao Cao’s achievements and merits, saying they reached the height of Heaven and Earth and outstripped even Yi and Zhou. They asked that his rank be advanced to king.

Emperor Xian ordered Zhong Yao to draft the decree, and Cao Cao was proclaimed King of Wei. Cao Cao submitted three memorials declining the honor. The decree refused him all three times. Then he accepted the grant of the Wei kingly title, receiving a crown with twelve tassels, riding in a gold-fitted carriage drawn by six horses, using the Son of Heaven’s carriage and ceremonial gear. He moved in and out at court with official process, and in Ye he established the Wei king’s palace and deliberated over the name of his designated heir.

Cao Cao’s principal wife, Lady Ding, did not attend. His concubine Liu gave birth to Cao Ang, who died at Wan City during the campaign against Zhang Xiu.

Lady Bian bore four sons: first, Cao Pi; then Cao Zhang; third, Cao Zhi; fourth, Cao Xiong. Thus Lady Ding was deposed, and Lady Bian was made principal consort of the King of Wei.

The third son was Cao Zhi, style name Zijian. He was exceptionally brilliant, and whenever he put brush to paper he wrote complete prose in one line. Cao Cao wanted to make him heir. As the eldest, Cao Pi feared he would not be chosen and consulted Jia Xu.

Jia Xu gave detailed advice. From then on, whenever Cao Cao went on campaign, all his sons accompanied him in farewell, but Cao Zhi would speak in polished phrases, praising merit and offering carefully formed words, while Cao Pi would only weep and kneel in silence before their father. All the onlookers were moved.

Cao Cao therefore began to suspect that Cao Zhi was artful but insincere compared with Cao Pi. Cao Pi then sent men to buy the confidence of close attendants, and they all praised Cao Pi’s virtue. Cao Cao still hesitated about naming an heir. He asked Jia Xu, “If I am to name a successor, whom should I choose?”

Jia Xu did not answer at once. When Cao Cao asked why, he said, “I have something weighing on my mind and cannot answer immediately.”

Cao Cao asked, “What do you mean?” Jia Xu replied, “I am thinking of Yuan Shao and Liu Biao, father and son.” Cao Cao laughed and then installed his eldest son Cao Pi as crown prince.

In the tenth month of winter, the Wei king’s palace in Ye was complete. People were sent out to collect rare flowers and fruits and set them in the rear garden. An envoy reached Wu and told Sun Quan that King Cao had ordered him to return once more to Wenzhou for mandarins.

At that time Sun Quan was already treating King Wei with respect and was making the required arrangements. He selected more than forty great loads of mandarins and sent them overnight to Ye.
