Midway, when the porters carrying the loads were exhausted and rested at the foot of a mountain, they met a strange man with one eye and one bad leg, wearing a white rattan crown and blue indigo robe. He bowed with his hand to the bearers and said, “You labors are hard. If you wish, I can carry one shoulder for you.”

The men rejoiced. The old man carried each load for five li, though every load he had carried before seemed lighter than the others, and the men grew uneasy with wonder and doubt. Before leaving he said to the officer in charge of the fruit, “I am an old acquaintance from the King’s countryside. My surname is Zuo, my given name is Ci, my courtesy name is Yuanfang, and my Daoist sobriquet is Master Wujiao. If you come to Ye, say that this is what Zuo Ci requests.” He then swept away his sleeve and vanished.

The bearers arrived at Ye with the fruit and presented the mandarins to Cao Cao. Cao Cao cut one open himself. It was only the shell, and there was no flesh inside.

“Find out where these loads came from,” he said. The bearers told him what had happened with Zuo Ci. Cao Cao still did not believe them. A gate guard then announced that a master calling himself Zuo Ci sought an audience with the King.

Cao Cao summoned him in. The bearers confirmed, “This is the same man we met on the road.” Cao Cao shouted, “By what sorcery did you seize my fine fruit?”

Zuo Ci smiled. “How could that be?” he said.

When he cut a mandarin, there was flesh, and it was sweet in taste. But the ones Cao Cao himself had opened had only shells.

Cao Cao was astonished, and he seated Zuo Ci. “What art do you have to make this happen?” he asked.

Zuo Ci asked for wine and meat. Cao Cao ordered it given to him. He drank five dou of wine and ate the entire sheep, yet still was not full.

Cao Cao asked, “How can you do this?”

Zuo Ci said, “I studied the Way for thirty years in Mount Emei of Jialing. One day I heard my name called from inside a rock wall and looked out, but I saw nothing. After this happened for several days, thunder split the rock wall and three volumes of the Book of Evasion appeared.

The upper volume was called Heavenly Evasion, the middle Earthly Evasion, and the lower Human Evasion. Heavenly Evasion can leap through clouds and cross wind to rise into the high emptiness. Earthly Evasion can pass through mountains and rock. Human Evasion can roam over the four seas, change one’s form, throw swords and knives, and take a person’s head. You sit above your ministers and below the Son of Heaven. Why not step down and follow me to Mount Emei to cultivate?

Here, take these three books as your ties.”

Cao Cao said, “I have long wished to retire in sudden haste, but the court has no suitable man ready.”

Zuo Ci laughed. “Liu Bei of Yizhou, courtesy name Xuande, is an heir to the imperial line. Why do you not leave this office to him? If not, I will throw my sword and take your head.”

Cao Cao exploded with anger. “So you are Liu Bei’s secret agent!” he said, and ordered men to seize him.

Zuo Ci kept laughing. Cao Cao ordered a dozen prison guards to take him and beat him. They strained and kicked him, but he seemed to be in deep sleep and felt no pain. Cao Cao ordered a heavy iron collar with iron nails and iron chains to be fixed to him and put him under close jail confinement.

At once the shackles and chains fell away and he lay on the ground without injury. After seven days in solitary jail without food or drink, he still sat upright when checked. His face had turned red.

A guard reported this to Cao Cao, who brought him out and asked him why.

Zuo Ci said, “I have not eaten for many decades. I can also eat a thousand sheep.”

That day, the officials all came for a great banquet at the royal palace. During the drinking, Zuo Ci, his wooden sandals sounding on the floor, stood near the edge of the table. All were startled.

Zuo Ci said, “The King has water and land banquets together today and gathered strange things from every quarter. Still, something is lacking. If Your Majesty permits, I will fetch it.”

Cao Cao said, “I want dragon liver soup. Can you take it?”

Zuo Ci replied, “What is difficult?”

He took up an ink brush and drew a dragon on the white wall, then gave the robe sleeve one sweep. The belly of the painted dragon opened. From its belly Zuo Ci withdrew two pieces of dragon liver, with blood still running.

Cao Cao did not believe it. He shouted, “You hid this in your sleeve beforehand.”

Zuo Ci said, “Today I can even make the grass and trees wither at the camp and in the grounds. If His Majesty wants certain flowers, he may choose.”

Cao Cao said, “I only want peonies.”

Zuo Ci said, “It is easy.” He had a large flowerpot brought to the front of the table and water poured over it.

In a moment a peony rose and bloomed with two blossoms. The officials were shocked, and Cao invited him to sit and share the meal.

After a short time, the cook brought fish slices.

Zuo Ci said, “Only Songjiang perch are worthy for this.”

Cao Cao said, “The distance is over a thousand li. How can you get it?”

Zuo Ci said, “What difficulty is there?” He had a fishing rod brought and ordered it used in the fish pool beneath the hall. In a moment he caught dozens of large perch and set them before the hall.

Cao Cao said, “These were already in my pool.”

Zuo Ci said, “Would Your Majesty trick me so? All perch in this world have two gills. Only Songjiang perch have four; this is how you can tell.” The officials examined them, and indeed they were four-gilled.

Zuo Ci said, “To cook a Songjiang perch, one must use the purple-sprout ginger.”

Cao Cao asked, “Can you bring that too?”

“It is easy,” Zuo Ci replied.

He ordered a gold basin placed and covered it with his robe. In a short time it was filled with purple-sprout ginger and presented before Cao Cao.

Cao Cao reached for some, and inside was a book titled Mengde’s New Book with every character exactly as in the text.

Cao asked, “Are these things genuine?”

Zuo Ci took the jade hairpin from the table and drew a line through the wine in the cup, dividing it into two halves. He drank one half and offered the other to Cao Cao, saying, “Drink this, and the King may live for a thousand years.”

Cao said, “You drink first.”

Cao shouted. Zuo Ci threw the cup into the air, and it turned into a white dove, circling the hall. All eyes looked upward. Zuo Ci was nowhere to be seen.

A guard then reported, “Zuo Ci has left through the palace gate.”

Cao Cao said, “If this is a demonic trickster, he must be eliminated, or he will bring harm.” He ordered Xu Chu to lead three hundred iron-armored troops to pursue him.

Xu Chu mounted and rode out with troops. When he saw Zuo Ci in front, walking slowly in wooden sandals, he urged mounted riders to pursue, but none could catch him.

He chased him right to a mountain where a shepherd boy came driving a flock of sheep. Zuo Ci walked into the flock.

Xu Chu shot arrows. Zuo Ci vanished.

The shepherd boy stood guard and wept over the sheep.

Then he saw one of the sheep heads on the ground speaking like a person, telling him, “You can gather all the sheep heads and stack them into the belly of the dead sheep.” The boy was terrified and covered his face and ran.

At once he heard someone call from behind, “Do not run in fear. I will give you back your living sheep.”

He looked back and saw Zuo Ci had placed the dead sheep together with life again and was driving the flock toward him.

The boy hurried forward, but by then Zuo Ci had already swept away his sleeve and gone. He moved like flying; suddenly he was gone.

The boy told his master, who did not dare conceal the matter and reported it to Cao Cao.

Cao Cao drew up shadowy portraits, and three to four hundred people appeared in town and in the countryside who had one eye, one lame foot, white rattan crown, blue indigo robe, and wooden sandals. All resembled him.

The whole city roiled. Cao Cao ordered several generals to douse them with pig and sheep blood and escort them to the southern city arena.

Cao Cao himself pulled in five hundred soldiers and had them all beheaded. From each severed throat rose a single streak of green vapour that climbed halfway to the sky. The vapours gathered into one Zuo Ci. He rode a white crane in the air and clapped his hands, then laughed loudly:

The rat of the earth follows a golden tiger; the treacherous tyrant will be cut down at once!

Cao Cao ordered everyone to shoot at him with bow and arrow. A sudden wild wind rose, hurling stones and sand.

Every severed corpse jumped up and picked up its own head in hand, running to the Martial Hall to strike at Cao Cao.

Civil and military officials covered their faces in shock and knocked down in confusion.

A saying closed the chapter:

A tyrant’s power and force can tilt a kingdom, and the Daoist’s immortal arts are stranger than any man. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Gan Ning and One Hundred Riders Raid the Wei Camp; Zuo Ci Throws a Cup at Cao Cao

chapters.html:
Later that day, Cao Cao saw the heads of many corpses rise up amid a black wind and was shocked to the ground. After a short while, the wind quieted and all the corpses vanished. His attendants supported him back to the palace, and in his fright he fell sick. Later, people recited this verse praising Zuo Ci:

He strode through the clouds and crossed the Nine Provinces, Alone he roamed by hidden arts of Dunjia calculation. At leisure he set up the arts of immortals, Yet by a single flash of awakening he could not turn Cao Man back.

Cao Cao’s illness did not improve with medicine. In due time Assistant Astronomer Xu Zhi came from Xuchang to see him. Cao Cao told Xu Zhi to perform zhou yi divination.

“Have you heard of the divine diviner Guan Lu?” Xu Zhi asked. "I have heard somewhat of his reputation, but not his method. Speak fully," said Cao.

"Guan Lu, whose courtesy name was Gongming, was a man of Pingyuan. His appearance was rough and unattractive; he liked wine and often seemed wild. His father had once been a local official, the district-chief of Langye. As a boy, Guan Lu liked to look up at the stars and could not sleep at night. His parents could not prevent him. He would say, ‘A house chicken and even a wild goose can sense the time; how much more should someone living among men know it?’

When he played with children from neighboring households he would draw the heavens on the ground and assign the sun, moon, and stars their places. As he grew older he came to master the zhou yi, studied wind and omen and direction, could calculate numbers with divine precision, and also mastered physiognomy.

"At that time, Dan Zichun, the Administrator of Langye, heard of him and asked Guan Lu to an audience. There were a hundred scholars there and all could speak with learning. Guan Lu told Zichun, ‘My courage is still unsteady because I am young. First get me three sheng of fine wine, and then I shall speak.’ Zichun marveled at this and ordered him three sheng of wine.

After he drank, Guan Lu asked Zichun, ‘Who here wishes to debate with me—are they men of your four-sided hall?’ Zichun said, ‘I stand at least equal to you.’ So they talked about the doctrines of the changes. Guan Lu spoke plainly and steadily, his words deep and subtle. Zichun raised objections, and Guan Lu answered as if he were on a stream. From dawn till dusk they did not stop for food. Zichun and every guest marveled and submitted themselves in admiration. From then on, people across the realm called him a ‘divine youth.’"

"Later, three brothers from one village, among them a man named Guo En, all stricken with lameness, asked Guan Lu to divine for them. Guan Lu said, ‘In your clan’s ancestral tomb there is the spirit of a dead woman: either your paternal aunt or your maternal aunt. In a year of famine they conspired over several sheng of grain, drew the profit into a well, and crushed her head with a large stone. In pain she cried to Heaven, and this is why your brothers suffer this reprisal. It cannot be exorcised.’ Guo En and the others wept and knelt in apology.

"The Administrator of Anping, Wang Ji, knew of Guan Lu’s divine divination and invited him home. By then Wang’s wife had long suffered from a wind sickness of the head, and his son had pain in the chest. He asked Guan Lu to divine. Guan said, ‘In the west corner of this hall there are two dead bodies, a man holding a spear and a man holding bow and arrows. The head is inside the wall and the feet are outside. The one with the spear strikes from the front—so this is the cause of the headache. The one with the bow and arrows strikes the chest and belly—so this is the cause of your son’s pain.’

He ordered a grave to be dug. Eight chi down, there were indeed two coffins. In one coffin lay a spear; in the other a horned bow and arrows. The wood had long since rotted. Guan told them to move the bones and bury them ten li outside the city walls, and the wife and son thereafter were unharmed.

"Zhuge Yuan, the Administrator of Guantao and newly transferred to Xinxing, summoned Guan Lu to see him off. Some guests did not believe Guan Lu could do shefu divination. Zhuge Yuan secretly took three things—a swallow egg, a wasp comb, and a spider—set them in three boxes, and had Guan divinate. Each time an oracle came up, Guan wrote four lines on the box.

The first read, ‘The vital breath must change. Depend on the hall and chamber. Male and female are distinguished by form; wings spread wide. This is the swallow egg.’ The second read, ‘House and home hang upside down; there are many doors. Essence is hidden, venom is nurtured, and only in autumn it is transformed. This is the wasp comb.’ The third read, ‘Long-legged and wary, it spits silk into a web. It roams for food in every net; it profits in the dark of night. This is the spider.’ The whole assembly was astonished.

"In a village an old woman had lost a cow and asked Guan to divine. He said, ‘On the north bank of the stream, seven men have been slaughtered for cooking. Go quickly and look for them; the flesh is still on the hide.’ She rushed out and found seven men behind a thatched hut boiling meat, with flesh still on the skin.

She reported this to the county magistrate Liu Bin, who had them arrested. When he asked how she knew, she said it was by Guan Lu’s divine divination. Liu Bin did not believe her and summoned Guan, putting a seal packet and junglefowl feather in a box for him to divine.

Guan divined once more. ‘Interior square, exterior round, five colors make pattern. It holds treasure and keeps faith; when it is brought out it bears seal marks. This is the seal packet.’ Then he said, ‘A high looming ridge, a bird with red body; black and yellow wings, and it never misses its dawn cry. This is the junglefowl feather.’ Liu Bin was shocked and then received him as an honored guest.

"One day Guan took a leisurely walk outside the city and saw a youth plowing in a field. He stood by the road to watch him. After a while he asked, ‘Young man, what is your surname and age?’ The youth answered, ‘I am Zhao Yan. I am nineteen years old. Who is the master?' Guan said, ‘I am Guan Lu. I see a death aura between your brows; within three days you must die. You are handsome, but your life is short.’

Zhao Yan hurried home and told his father. The father came in panic and knelt to the ground before Guan: ‘Please, save my son!’ Guan said, ‘This is fate. How can it be averted?’ The father replied, ‘I have this only son. I beg you, show mercy.’ Zhao Yan also wept and begged. Seeing how deeply father and son were attached, Guan said, ‘You may prepare one bottle of clean wine and a slice of deer dried meat. Tomorrow go into Mount Nanshan. Beneath a great tree there is a broad rock where two men are playing yì. One sits facing south in a white robe and has a hideous face. One sits facing north in a red robe and has a beautiful face.

At the height of their game, kneel and offer them the wine and deer meat. When they have finished eating and drinking, kneel on the ground and beg for an extension of years. Your fortune will improve. But do not in any way tell anyone that I told you.'"

The old father kept Guan in his house for the night. The next day, Zhao Yan took cup, tray, and meat up into Mount Nanshan. After five or six li of walking, he found two men indeed playing chess beneath a great pine tree on a large rock. Neither of them paid attention. Zhao Yan knelt and offered the wine and meat. The two men were so absorbed they did not notice they had emptied both vessels.

Zhao Yan knelt and wept, imploring a longer life. The two men were startled. "You must have come from Guan’s instruction," said the man in red. "We have both accepted your bribe, so we must take pity on you." The white-robed man took records from his side and examined them and said to Zhao Yan, "You are nineteen this year and should die. I will add the character for nine to your character for ten, and your life will be extended to ninety-nine years. Return to Guan Lu and tell him you must not reveal this heavenly matter. If you do, Heaven will punish you." The red-robed man wrote with a brush, and then a fragrant wind passed by. Both men transformed into white cranes and rose into the sky.

Zhao Yan returned to Guan and asked what they had been. Guan said, "The red-robed one was the Southern Dipper. The white-robed one was the Northern Dipper." Zhao Yan asked, "I know the Northern Dipper has nine stars. How could there be but one person?" Guan said, "Scattered they are nine; gathered they are one. The Northern Dipper governs death, the Southern Dipper governs life. I have already added years to your tally. Why should you still worry?" The father and son thanked him.

After that, Guan Lu feared exposing such heavenly matters and no longer readily divined for common people. He now lived in Pingyuan. The Great King asked, ‘If you have all this, why does he not summon him now to ask our fortunes?’

Cao Cao rejoiced, so he sent men to summon Guan Lu. Guan Lu came and after kowtowing, Cao had him divine. Guan said, “These are magician’s illusions. Why should you be anxious?” Cao felt relieved and slowly became healthier. Then he asked Guan to divine the state of the realm.

Guan divined: “A pattern of threes and eights runs across the board, a yellow boar meets a tiger; to the south of Dingjun camp, one major force will be broken.” He then read the length and brevity of the ruling house’s fate and added, “In the Lion’s Palace, set your spirit-place in peace. The Kingly Way will renew and your descendants will be greatly honored.” Cao asked him for details. Guan said, “The vast numbers of Heaven cannot be known in advance. We will see by what follows."

Cao Cao asked to appoint Guan Lu as a senior clerk, but Guan refused. “My fate is meager. I am not fit for this post and dare not accept.” Cao asked why. Guan replied, “My forehead has no leading bone, my eyes no watchful pupils, my nose no pillar, my feet no heavenly root. My back has no three Jia and my belly no three Ren. I can handle ghosts in Mount Tai style, but not govern living men.”

Cao Cao asked, “How do you assess me?” Guan said only, “You are already at the highest rank among ministers. Why must I assess further?” After repeating the question many times, Guan only smiled and did not answer.

Cao ordered him to assess his civil and military ministers and officials. Guan said, “They are ministers for a stable age.” Cao asked about their fortunes; he refused to elaborate.

Later, people composed this verse in praise of Guan Lu:

At daybreak the divine diviner Guan Gongming could reckon the stars, from the southern and northern stars with the patterns of heaven, Mastering the hidden lines of the eight trigrams and the oracular depth, He probed the mystery of the six lines in heaven’s court. He foresaw his own craft and expected no ordinary lifespan, and he himself sensed a heart-source of rare responsiveness. Yet these wondrous arts of that earlier age, no later generation has inherited and passed down.

Cao Cao ordered Guan to cast for East Wu and West Shu as well. Guan arranged an oracle that said, “In East Wu, one major commander of Lu-kou will die; in West Shu, troops are violating the border.” Cao did not believe him. Soon a messenger came in haste: the governor of Lu-kou in East Wu, Lu Su, had died.

Soon after came a report that Liu Xuanbei had sent Zhang Fei and Ma Chao to hold troops at Xiabian. Cao Cao became furious and was about to personally lead troops back into Hanzhong. He ordered Guan to divine, and Guan said, “My lord, do not act recklessly. In the coming spring, fire will break out in Xu.”

Because Guan’s words had already proved true before, Cao Cao did not dare to act lightly. He stayed in Bei County and had Cao Hong lead fifty thousand men to assist Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He in jointly defending Dongchuan. He also sent Xiahou Dun with thirty thousand men to patrol to and from Xu, in case of emergency, and ordered his Chief Clerk Wang Bi to command the Palace Cavalry and horse guards.

The clerk Sima Yi said, “Wang Bi likes wine and is broad in temper; I fear he cannot bear this role.” Cao Cao said, “Wang Bi has followed me through thorns and hardships. He is loyal and diligent, hard of heart as iron and stone. He alone is fit to hold this position.” Thus he made Wang Bi command the palace guard forces, stationing them outside Xuchang’s Donghua Gate.

At that time there was a man surnamed Geng and called Ji, style Jixing, from Luoyang. He had once been an assistant in the Chancellery, then appointed to palace attendant of the Office of Master of the Household, and he was very close with Wei Huang, an officer in the Secretariat. After Cao Cao received kingly enfeoffment and moved with imperial carriage and robes, Geng was inwardly angry.

In the spring of the twenty-third year of Jian’an, in the first month, Geng Ji and Wei Huang discussed together: “Cao’s treachery and villainy are worse day by day. He will surely perform usurpation. We are ministers of Han. How can we join hands with evil?” Wei Huang said, “I have a trusted man named Jin He. He is a descendant of Grand Minister Jin Ridi and has long nursed a desire to strike at Cao. He is also close with Wang Bi. If we can cooperate, this major task will be accomplished.”

Geng said, “Since he is so close with Wang Bi, why would he conspire with me?” Wei Huang said, “Let us go tell him first and see what comes of it.”

So the two went together to Jin He’s residence. Jin He received them in the hall. They sat.

Wei said, “I, Wei Huang, and Wang Bi’s chief clerk are close. We three have come to ask.” He asked, “What do you ask for?” Wei said, “We have heard that King Cao will soon receive abdication and mount the Great Throne; the two of you and Wang Bi will both rise in rank. We hope he does not cast us off and that his grace will lift us up; your favor is no shallow thing.”

Jin He swept his sleeve and stood. At that moment a servant came with tea, and he poured it upon the ground. Wei, feigning surprise, cried, “Why, friend so dear, why such coldness?” Jin He said, “I shared fortune and misfortune with you as a near friend. Because we are descendants of Han ministers, do you ask me now to aid one who rebels? What face do I keep to call us friends?”

Geng Ji said, “When Heaven’s numbers are thus, one must follow.” Jin He became furious. Geng Ji and Wei Huang saw that he did have loyal righteousness, and they then told their real intent: they had come to recruit him; their earlier words were only a test.

Jin He said, “I have been a Han minister for generations. How can I join a bandit? You say you would support the Han house. What high plan do you have?” Wei Huang said, “We have loyalty to the state but not a plan yet.” Jin He replied, “I will combine inner aid with outer alliance. Kill Wang Bi, seize command, and support the Son of Heaven; at the same time ally with Liu, the Imperial Uncle, as outside support. Then Cao the bandit will be annihilated.” The two men heard this and praised him.

Jin He said, “I have two men in my heart, living outside the city, who share Cao’s slays with fathers murdered by him. They can be our wings.” Geng Ji asked who they were. He answered, “The sons of imperial physician Ji Ping: the elder is Ji Miao, courtesy name Wenzan; the younger, Ji Mu, courtesy name Siran. Cao once served the secret memorial of Dongcheng in his waist-rope mission and once killed their father. The two fled to distant districts and escaped danger. They have now returned secretly to Xu. If we can use them to strike at the brigand, they will not fail us.”

Geng Ji and Wei Huang rejoiced greatly. Jin He then secretly called the two men. Soon they came. He explained the situation. The brothers, moved to tears, were filled with resentment and swore to kill the traitor of the state.

Jin He said, "On the fifteenth night of the first month, the whole city will hang great lanterns and celebrate the Lantern Festival. Geng Shaofu and Wei Siji, each of you take your household retainers and strike to Wang Bi’s camp. When fires rise in his camp, strike in through two routes. After killing Wang Bi, go straight with me into the inner city and ask the Son of Heaven to climb the Wufeng Tower and summon the officials to issue commands to eliminate the bandit.

The Ji brothers will enter from outside the city and set fires as signal. Each of them should then raise shouting, call on the citizens to kill the national bandit, and block the rescue army inside the city. When the Son of Heaven issues an edict announcing the pardoning and settling, then ride out to advance on Yecheng and capture Cao Cao, and send a royal edict to call Liu the Imperial Uncle. Our meeting is fixed. At the hour of the second watch we rise together. Do not repeat Dong Cheng’s self-brought ruin."

The five men swore to heaven and sealed their covenant with blood and returned to prepare horse and gear.

And so Geng Ji and Wei Huang each gathered three or four hundred household retainers as prepared men and gear. Ji Miao and Ji Mu also gathered three to four hundred people and arranged a hunt for the day. Jin He came early to the City Guard command and said, “The realm is for now a little calm. The King of Wei has awe over all under Heaven. On this Lantern Festival should not pass by without lanterns; let it show peace and order.” Wang Bi accepted his words and ordered the residents to hang lanterns and revel in the feast.

On the fifteenth night the sky was clear and the moon and stars shone together. In six streets and three markets, flower lanterns competed in brilliance. The watch was truly relaxed, and the night bell failed to chime. Wang Bi and the Palace-guard generals feasted in camp.

After the second watch there came a cry from the camp and men reported that fire had broken out behind it. Wang Bi hurried out of his tent to see and found wild rolling flames. He heard continuous shouts and knew there had been treachery in camp. He hurriedly mounted his horse, then met Geng Ji by chance. An arrow struck his shoulder and he nearly fell from the horse. He then ran toward the west gate. A cart came running from behind.

Wang Bi in panic abandoned his horse and went on foot to the main door of Jin He’s house, where he pounded in fear. In the meantime Jin He had set fire to the camp and personally led household retainers to join the fighting, leaving only the women at home. When those in the house heard Wang Bi’s knocking, they assumed Jin He had returned home. Jin He’s wife called through the door, “Has that rogue Wang Bi been killed?” Wang Bi was shocked. He suddenly understood that Jin He was co-conspirator. He went straight to the house of Cao Xiu and told him that Jin He, Geng Ji, and their confederates had plotted rebellion.

Cao Xiu hurriedly donned armor and went up on horseback, bringing more than a thousand men to resist within the city. Fires now burned in all directions, the Wufeng Tower caught fire, and the Emperor withdrew to the inner palace. The Cao house’s trusted inner retainers held the palace gates to the death, and all that the city heard was the cry, “Kill all Cao the brigand and restore the Han house!”

Unbeknownst to them, Xiahou Dun, under Cao Cao’s command, had been patrolling at Xu with three divisions and had camped five li from the city. That night, from afar, he saw the city in flames and immediately led his troops forward, surrounding Xu, and sending one branch of the army inside for reinforcement.

Cao Xiu fought straight through to dawn. No one came to aid Geng Ji or Wei Huang. Reports came that Jin He and the two Ji brothers had been reported dead. Geng Ji and Wei Huang broke out by force through the gates, only to meet Xiahou Dun’s encircling army. They were captured alive; over a hundred of their men were all killed. Xiahou Dun entered the city, quelled the remaining fires, and seized the old and young of the five households. He then sent a fast report to Cao Cao.

Cao Cao ordered that Geng Ji and Wei Huang and the five households of close families, old and young, all be beheaded in the market, and that all high and low officials in court be arrested and carried to Ye Commandery to await judgment.

When Xiahou Dun brought Geng Ji and Wei Huang to the market before Cao, Geng Ji shouted loudly, “Cao Aman, I could not kill you while alive. I will become a fierce ghost when I die and strike the brigand from the dead!” Executioners prodded their blades through his mouth and he bled all over the ground, cursing until he died. Wei Huang struck his cheek down to the ground and said, “How hateful! How hateful!” and as he bit his own teeth, they shattered and he died.

Later, people praised them in verse:

Geng Ji was upright and faithful; Wei Huang was wise. Each held empty hands and sought to uphold Heaven. How could they know Han fortune was nearly gone? Resentment filled their chests as they sank to the Nine Springs.

Xiahou Dun beheaded the five families of all their close households and sent the captured officials to Ye Commandery. Cao Cao set one red flag on his left and one white on his right in the military yard and ordered:

Geng Ji, Wei Huang, and those who rebelled with them set Xu afire. Among you, some rescued the fires, others shut their doors and went out. Stand under the red flag if you ever put out the fire; stand under the white flag if you did not.

All officials thought: surely those who rescued fire would be without fault, and they therefore ran under the red flag in multitudes. In all three divisions, only one line stood beneath the white.

Cao ordered all who had stood under red to be arrested. Every one of the officials said they were blameless. Cao said, “The heart you had at the time was not to rescue the fire; it was truly to aid the bandit.” He then ordered all of them dragged to the banks of the Zhang River and beheaded, three hundred and more dead.

Those who had stood beneath the white were all rewarded and sent back to Xu. By then Wang Bi had already died of infection from the arrow wound. Cao ordered that he be buried with honor. He made Cao Xiu oversee the Palace guards and horse troops, made Zhong Yao Chancellor, and Hua Xin Great Censor. He then formalized the peerage grades: eighteen levels of six ranks of marquisates, seventeen levels of Guanzhong marquisates—both with gold seals and violet sashes; then sixteen levels of inner-and-outer-Guanzhong marquises with silver seals, black turtle-knotted ribbons; and fifteen levels of five grand officers with bronze seals and linked-bronze cords.

He reformed the appointments in court and replaced another set of men with new ones. Cao Cao now grasped the truth of Guan Lu’s warning about the fire and therefore showered him with honors. Guan Lu accepted none.

Now Cao Hong reached Hanzhong, ordering Zhang He and Xiahou Yuan to hold all the key passes. Cao Hong himself advanced with troops to resist the enemy.

At that time Zhang Fei together with Lei Tong held Bashi. The cavalry reached Xiaobian, and he ordered Wu Lan to lead the vanguard, with a scouting column forward. Wu Lan met Cao Hong’s army and wanted to retreat. Yan General Ren Kui said, “The enemy cavalry has just arrived. If we do not first break its sharp edge, how can we look at Mengqi?”

So he spurred his horse and grabbed his spear and charged against Cao Hong. Cao Hong himself drew his knife and leapt on horseback. After three rounds of engagement he cut Ren Kui down beneath the horse and, with momentum, swept in with killing. Wu Lan was greatly defeated and returned to Ma Chao. Ma Chao rebuked him, "Why disobey my command and lightly meet them with such easy spirit?" Wu Lan said, “Ren Kui did not listen to my orders, and this is why we were defeated.” Ma Chao said, "Guard the pass closely and do not strike out in open engagement." He at once reported to Chengdu and waited for orders.

Cao Hong saw Ma Chao not advancing for days and feared some hidden design, so he withdrew his army back to Nanzheng. Zhang He came and asked him, "General, you already slew a commander. Why should we retreat?” Cao Hong replied, “Since he does not come out, I fear there is another design. I am in Ye Commandery, and I have heard Guan Lu, the divine diviner, say that at this place one major commander will be broken. I doubted it, and so I dare not advance lightly.”

Zhang He laughed and said, "I have lived half my life campaigning. Why now do you believe a diviner and let him cloud your mind? Though He is unfit, I, Zhang He, offer to take my own division and seize Bashi. If we take Bashi, the prefecture of Shu will fall easily." Cao Hong asked, “If we err, what then?” Zhang He answered, “I gladly accept the army’s order.” Cao Hong approved the written plan and Zhang He advanced.

As it was said:

Since ancient times, arrogant armies have often lost through pride. Those who underestimate the enemy rarely find success. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Guan Lu Divines the Turning Point; Five Loyal Ministers Die for the Han Cause

chapters.html:
Zhang Fei boldly takes Wakou Pass.
Elder Huang Zhong plots to seize Tiandang Mountain.

Zhang He had 30,000 soldiers stationed in three camps, each camp posted by a mountain danger point: one was Dangqu Camp, one was Mengtou Camp, and one was Dangshi Camp. That day, in each camp he split half of the soldiers, took the other half to march for Bashu, and left half to guard the camps. Early that day, scouts reported Zhang He’s coming march reached Baxi. Zhang Fei urgently called for Lei Tong to confer. Lei Tong said, “The land around Langzhong is rough and full of ravines, good for ambushes. If the General leads out the main force to battle, I will strike with a surprise detachment, and we can capture Zhang He.”

Zhang Fei sent 5,000 of his best troops with Lei Tong and set out. He himself led 10,000 soldiers out of Langzhong for 30 li and met Zhang He’s force. The two armies drew up in line, and Zhang Fei dismounted from his horse, reaching out to seize Zhang He alone. Zhang He, in full stride, vaulted from the saddle and charged out. They fought for more than thirty bouts before a shout rose from the rear. It turned out that the soldiers could see Shu banners and pennons behind the mountain, which threw the formations into confusion. Zhang He dared not stay in close combat and wheeled his horse to retreat. Zhang Fei pressed after him from behind. At the front, Lei Tong drove another force out of camp. The two-sided attack shattered Zhang He’s line, and his army was badly beaten.

Zhang Fei and Lei Tong pursued through the night and drove all the way to Dangqu Mountain. Zhang He still had his men distributed among the three camps and set many log-batteries and rolling stones in place. He held fast and did not fight. Zhang Fei withdrew his men to a large encampment 10 li below Dangqu. The next day he drew up his force for battle. Zhang He stood atop the mountain, drumming and shouting, drinking as he looked down, and never came down. Zhang Fei ordered his soldiers to curse him loudly; Zhang He still did not come out. Zhang Fei therefore had no choice but to return to camp.

The next day, Lei Tong again pressed combat from beneath the mountain. Zhang He still would not come out. Lei Tong drove his troops uphill. From the mountain top, log-rams and stones crashed down on them. Lei Tong suddenly withdrew. Troops from Dangshi Camp and Mengtou Camp came out and won against Lei Tong. The next day Zhang Fei tried again. Zhang He still did not leave the heights. Zhang Fei had his soldiers curse him in every possible way; from the mountain, Zhang He cursed back. Zhang Fei later thought hard and found himself without a way through. For more than fifty days the two sides remained facing each other. Zhang Fei made a great camp at the mountain foot and drank daily. He drank himself nearly senseless, sat before the hill, and kept up his taunts.

Liu Bei sent men with provisions to Zhang Fei, and seeing him drunk all day, the envoy reported back. Liu Bei was greatly alarmed and hurried to ask Zhuge Liang. The strategist laughed and said, “That is why. There is likely no good wine near the front. In Chengdu there is excellent brew in abundance; take fifty wine jars in three carts and send them to the front for Commander Zhang to drink.”

Liu Bei said, “My brother has long taken to drinking and to ruin. Why does the Master send more wine to him?”
Zhuge Liang smiled. “Lord, you and Yide have been brothers in arms for many years. Do you not know his nature? Yide has always been direct and hard, yet during the Sichuan campaign he mercifully released Yan Yan. That was no act of a cowardly man. Now he has faced Zhang He for over fifty days. Only after wine-drunk does he sit at the mountain’s edge and taunt everyone as though no one is present; this is no craving for the cup, but the tactic to break Zhang He.”

Liu Bei replied, “Even so, we should not place all reliance on one plan. Let Wei Yan help him.”
Zhuge Liang then ordered Wei Yan to bring the wine forward to the army. On the wagons he had yellow banners raised, each bearing large characters that read: “Good wine for the army before us.” Wei Yan obeyed and brought liquor to the camps. He met Zhang Fei and told him the lord had bestowed wine. Zhang Fei bowed and accepted. He ordered Wei Yan and Lei Tong each to lead a detachment as left and right wings, and to advance their troops as soon as they saw red flags rise among the army. He ordered the wines laid under the tents and the soldiers to let their drums and gongs thunder while they drank.

A scout came up the mountain. Zhang He had long watched from the summit. He saw Zhang Fei sit by the camp-fire in his pavilion, drinking; and ordered two young soldiers to wrestle in front of him for sport. “Zhang Fei mocks us to excess!” Zhang He said. He ordered that he would descend tonight and sack Zhang Fei’s camp. He told Mengtou and Dangshi camps to come out and serve as left and right reinforcements.

That night, with the moon only faintly bright, Zhang He rode down from the mountain side and straight into the camp front. He saw Zhang Fei’s bright lamps and the flicker of candles and banners as he sat in the pavilion drinking. Zhang He shouted first, and drums rolled from the heights to aid him as he drove straight into the center. Yet Zhang Fei sat fixed, unmoving. Zhang He spurred his horse straight to him and drove his spear, but it struck a stuffed straw man. He checked his horse to turn away, but then a chain-shot burst from behind the pavilion. A general came first, blocking the path. His eyes were round and glaring, his voice like thunder; it was Zhang Fei himself. He rose with spear in hand, vaulted on horseback, and went straight for Zhang He. The two generals fought in the firelight for thirty to fifty rounds. Zhang He watched anxiously for help from either camp, but those camp-rescue troops had already been killed and driven off by Wei Yan and Lei Tong, with those two camps lost in the same motion.

Zhang He could not see any rescue. Then he saw fire on the mountain: Zhang Fei’s rear troops had already seized the stockade posts. All three camps had fallen, and he could only run for Wakou Pass.

Zhang Fei gained a grand victory and reported it in Chengdu. Liu Bei rejoiced and came to understand that Yide’s drinking had been a stratagem—only a lure to drag Zhang He down from the ridge.

Zhang He had withdrawn behind Wakou Pass, and of his 30,000 men nearly 20,000 had fallen. He sent a request to Cao Hong for rescue. Cao Hong was furious. “You did not heed me,” he said. “You forced an advance, lost this crucial checkpoint, and now you come asking for aid!” He would not send reinforcements and instead had him hurried onward to the front again.

Zhang He, anxious and unsettled, decided at once to entrench in two groups near a secluded spot ahead of the pass. He ordered: “I will feign defeat. Zhang Fei will surely pursue, and you should cut off his way back.”

That day Zhang He led out in force and met Lei Tong at once. They fought only a few rounds before Zhang He broke and fled. Lei Tong pursued. The two armies came out again, and Zhang He, forcing his way, speared Lei Tong from beneath the horse. The beaten troops carried back the report to Zhang Fei. Zhang Fei rode forward to challenge, and Zhang He again faked defeat; Zhang Fei did not give chase. Zhang He resumed battle and again, after only a few exchanges, broke and fled. Zhang Fei recognized the tactic and withdrew with his troops. He conferred with Wei Yan. “Zhang He is using a concealed-rout plan, and he has already killed Lei Tong. He wants to snare me. Why not set a plan inside a plan?” he said.

Wei Yan asked, “How, then?”

Zhang Fei said, “Tomorrow I will first lead one army forward. You must bring elite troops behind. When the ambush comes out, split your force and strike it. Take ten or more carts loaded with brushwood and straw, block the small paths, and burn them. I will seize Zhang He, and then I can take revenge for Lei Tong.”

Wei Yan took the design. The next day Zhang Fei advanced. Zhang He’s army arrived and fought again. By the tenth exchange, Zhang He again faked a retreat. Zhang Fei drove both horse and foot to give chase. Zhang He fought and withdrew while running. He drew Zhang Fei across the valley mouth, then put his rear troops up front and made camp again to fight Zhang Fei once more.

He hoped the two ambush formations would strike, surrounding Zhang Fei. But Wei Yan’s elite troopers had already gone in first and rushed into the valley mouth, parking their carts across the mountain path and setting them alight. Wood and brush caught, and flame and smoke darkened the route. The Shu soldiers could no longer pass out.

Zhang Fei kept charging into the melee, and Zhang He was routed completely. He tore open a way through at all cost and climbed for Wakou Pass, gathering what was left of his troops and holding fast there without coming down.

Zhang Fei and Wei Yan attacked the pass for days without breaking it. Seeing no gain, Zhang Fei withdrew 20 li and, with Wei Yan, came with scores of riders to probe the side paths on both flanks. They saw several men—both men and women—with small bundles on their backs slipping along a hidden mountain track by clinging to vines and roots. Zhang Fei pointed from horseback with his whip and said to Wei Yan, “Wakou Pass is on the backs of these villagers.”

He called to his men and ordered, “Do not frighten them. Bring those villagers to us gently.” The soldiers hurried and brought them before the horse line. Zhang Fei spoke soothingly and asked why they had come.

The villagers answered, “We are all from Hanzhong. We wish to return home. When we heard the great armies fighting and saw the mountain roads sealed at Langzhong’s official way, we took another route: through Cangxi, past Zitong Mountain’s Guijian River, and into Hanzhong to go home.”

Zhang Fei asked, “How far is Wakou Pass by this road?”
The villagers said, “From Zitong Mountain’s hidden path, this is the way behind Wakou Pass.”
Zhang Fei rejoiced, brought the civilians into camp, gave them wine and food, and told Wei Yan to bring men and strike the pass. “I will personally lead light cavalry out through Zitong Mountain to attack from behind the gate.” He then had the villagers lead the way and selected 500 light riders to enter by the narrow path.

At this time, Zhang He, with no relief arriving, sat in frustration. Word came that Wei Yan was attacking at the foot of the gate. Zhang He donned his armor and mounted to go down the mountain, but an alarm rose: “Four or five fires are burning behind the pass. We know not where the soldiers come from.” Zhang He himself rode out to meet them. At the first view, he saw Zhang Fei’s banner. Zhang He was startled and hurried toward the side path to run, but his horse could not keep up. Zhang Fei chased hard behind him. Zhang He abandoned his horse and fled up the mountain by a bypath; only then did he break free.

Only ten or so men remained with him, and they walked into Nanzheng, where they appeared before Cao Hong. Cao Hong saw him with only ten or so men and shouted in rage, “Did I not tell you to hold and return a report? After spending your whole army, you should have died rather than return alive! For what purpose are you back?”

The marching adjutant, Guo Huai, interceded. “Three armies can be raised, but a good general is hard to find. Though Zhang He is guilty, he is loved deeply by the King of Wei. He should not be executed at once. Send him with five thousand troops straight to Jiameng Pass and pull in the forces from elsewhere. Hanzhong will stabilize itself. If he fails, punish him for both crimes.”

Cao Hong obeyed and sent another 5,000 with him, ordering Zhang He to recover Jiameng Pass. Zhang He accepted and set out.

At Jiameng Pass, the guardians Meng Da and Huo Jun learned that Zhang He was coming. Huo Jun wanted only to hold firm. Meng Da insisted on meeting him. He led his army down into the pass and did battle with Zhang He, but was badly beaten and had to return. Huo Jun quickly sent an urgent report to Chengdu. Liu Bei heard the news and asked Zhuge Liang to confer.

Zhuge Liang gathered the officers in the hall and asked, “Now Jiameng is critical. Liu Bei must first bring back Yide from Langzhong so that Zhang He can be driven off.”

Fa Zheng said, “Yide now has his army stationed at Wakou and is garrisoning Langzhong, another crucial point. He cannot be brought back now. Among the generals in camp, pick one man to break through Zhang He.”

Zhuge Liang smiled. “Zhang He is a famous general of Wei, not a man for casual challenge. Except Yide, there is no one fit for him.”
A man then stepped forward with a loud voice: “Why does the strategist look so lightly upon everyone? Though I am no able man, I volunteer to take Zhang He’s head and lay it at your foot.”

All eyes turned to him; it was old General Huang Zhong. Zhuge Liang said, “Though brave, Commander Hansheng is advanced in years; I fear he may not match Zhang He.” Huang Zhong bristled and spoke through his white beard:

“Though old, I can still draw a three-stone bow with both arms. My body still holds a thousand jins of strength. How could that be enough to face Zhang He, this common soldier of Wei?”

Zhuge Liang said, “Your generalship is near seventy; how can you not be old?”

Huang Zhong strode down from the hall, took a great sword from the rack, and twirled it like flight. He drew two hard bows from the wall and snapped both at once.

Zhuge Liang asked, “If you go, who will be your second?”
Huang Zhong answered, “Elder Yan Yan can go with me. But should there be any emergency, take this white head first.”

Liu Bei was pleased and immediately sent Yan Yan and Huang Zhong to fight Zhang He. Zhao Yun protested, “Now that Zhang He has entered Jiameng itself, Master Strategist, do not treat this as a game. If Jiameng falls, Yizhou is in grave danger. Why send two old men against so great an enemy?”

Zhuge Liang replied, “You think they are old and cannot accomplish this. I am certain Hanzhong can be won from the hands of these two.”

He and the others withdrew, smiling dryly.

Huang Zhong and Yan Yan reached the pass. Meng Da and Huo Jun saw them and laughed in their hearts, muttering that Zhuge Liang had no command: “At such a crucial place, how could he send two old men?”

Huang Zhong said to Yan Yan, “Did you see how those people move? They laugh at us for being old. Let us now accomplish an unusual feat to silence their hearts.”

Yan Yan said, “I will obey the General’s orders.”
The two settled their plan. Huang Zhong led his force down toward the pass and stood against Zhang He.

Zhang He mounted out to the field and seeing Huang Zhong said with contempt, “At your age, you have no shame; you still want to fight?”

Huang Zhong snapped back, “Whelp, you mock my age! The treasure saber in my hand is not old!” He struck his horse and charged. The two horses met. They fought for over twenty rounds. Then a cry rose behind them. Yan Yan had slipped through by a side path and struck Zhang He’s army from the rear. With both sides pressed from two sides, Zhang He was heavily defeated and ran through the night. He withdrew 80 to 90 li.

Huang Zhong and Yan Yan pulled back into camp and each held their ranks.

Cao Hong learned that Zhang He had been routed again and again and again again wished to punish him. Guo Huai said, “Zhang He has been pressed hard and likely to flee west into Shu. We can send commanders to assist him and place nearby supervision so he does not drift astray.”

Cao Hong assented and sent Xiahou Shang, nephew of Xiahou Dun, and Han Hao, the brother of the surrendered commander Han Xuan, each with 5,000 soldiers to reinforce him. The two commanders set out at once and arrived at Zhang He’s camp, asking of the tactical situation.

Zhang He said, “Elder Huang Zhong is truly heroic, and with Yan Yan assisting him, we must not underestimate him.”

Han Hao said, “I once knew this old brigand at Changsha and know his ferocity. He and Wei Yan surrendered a city and harmed my elder brother. Now that we meet, I must have revenge.”

So he and Xiahou Shang marched out with the new troops.

For several days Huang Zhong had patrolled and learned the roads. Yan Yan said, “The road ahead leads to Tiandang Mountain. There Cao Cao has stockpiled grain and straw there. If we seize that place, cut off their supplies, and Hanzhong will be ours.”

Huang Zhong replied, “That exactly matches my mind. Do it so.”

Yan Yan gave command and led a branch of troops as planned.

Huang Zhong later learned that Xiahou Shang and Han Hao had arrived and at once brought his cavalry and horsemen out of the camp. Han Hao, at the front of the formation, shouted at Huang Zhong: “Treacherous old bandit!” He reined and drove hard, bringing spear and horse to take Huang Zhong. Xiahou Shang then attacked from a flank.

Huang Zhong fought both commanders with force. The two fought more than ten rounds. Huang Zhong was routed and withdrew.

The two pursuers chased him 20 li and took Huang Zhong’s camp. He made a new camp and on the next day Xiahou Shang and Han Hao came again. Huang Zhong rode out once more. They exchanged a few rounds, and he was again forced to withdraw. The two chased him 20 li and seized his camp again, then called Zhang He to hold the rear camp.

Zhang He came to the forward camp and warned, “Huang Zhong has fallen back twice in two days; there must be trickery in the center.”

Xiahou Shang shouted at Zhang He, “You are so timid! You lose again and again now. Do not speak anymore; we will build merit tonight.”

Zhang He, ashamed, withdrew.

The next day the two commanders fought again. Huang Zhong withdrew another twenty li. They pursued in turn for another day until they pushed up near the pass and came under it. The two commanders settled below the gate; Huang Zhong held and did not go out.

Meng Da quietly sent word to Liu Bei: “Huang Zhong has been defeated many times and now rests at the pass.” Liu Bei anxiously asked Zhuge Liang. Zhuge Liang said, “This is the old general’s strategy of feigned retreat.”

Zhao Yun and the others did not believe him. Liu Bei sent Liu Feng to the pass to support Huang Zhong.

Huang Zhong met Liu Feng and asked, “Young general, why did you come to help in battle?”
Liu Feng said, “My father heard that the General has suffered repeated defeats, and he sent me.”
Huang Zhong laughed. “This is the old general’s proud retreat plan. In tonight’s assault we can recover all camps and take their grain and horses. This is only a borrowed camp to seize their stored supplies. Tonight leave Huo Jun to hold the pass; General Meng can help me with moving the forage; young general, look and see me break the enemy.”

At second watch that night, Huang Zhong led 5,000 troops and went straight through the gate downward.

In truth, Xiahou Shang and Han Hao had been complacent after seeing no battle from the pass for many days. Huang Zhong broke through the camp like lightning. Men and horses had no room for armor or saddle. The two commanders each fled for their lives; the mounts and troops stampeded one another, and dead bodies lay everywhere.

By dawn, Huang Zhong had taken three camps. What they left behind in the camps—arms, harness, and horse tack in countless numbers—he had Meng Da carry into the pass. Huang Zhong hurried the cavalry to follow closely.

Liu Feng said, “The soldiers are exhausted. We may rest a bit.”
Huang Zhong answered, “‘How is a tiger cub gained without entering the tiger’s lair?’” he said, and spurred ahead. The men all pressed forward hard. Zhang He’s troops, driven by their own routing men, could not keep formation and turned to flee; they abandoned many stockade posts and ran straight to the banks of the Han River.

Zhang He recognized where Xiahou Shang and Han Hao had gone. He spoke with counsel: “This Tiandang Mountain is the place for grain and hay. Near it lies Rice Granary Mountain; both are storehouses of supply. If they are neglected, Hanzhong falls. We must think how to protect them.”

Xiahou Shang said, “Rice Granary Mountain is guarded by my uncle Xiahou Yuan with troops and joins on to Dingjun Mountain; we need not worry for that. Tiandang is defended by my brother Xiahou De. We should ride to him and secure this mountain.”

So Zhang He and the two commanders rode through the night to Tiandang. There they met Xiahou De and told him all that had happened. Xiahou De said, “I have 100,000 soldiers stationed here; you may take them and take back the former posts.”
Zhang He replied, “We should only hold firm and not act rashly.”

Suddenly, drums and gongs shook the mountain front. Men reported, “Huang Zhong is arriving.”

Xiahou De laughed. “The old brigand knows no strategy; he only relies on courage.”
Zhang He said, “Huang Zhong has planning and is not just bold.”
De said, “The Shu soldiers have crossed far, and they are exhausted by long travel. Added to that, they have gone deep in enemy territory; this is not strategy.”
Zhang He said, “It still should not be despised. We must hold firm.”

Han Hao said, “Permit me to borrow 3,000 elite men and break him.”

Xiahou De then detached troops with Han Hao down the mountain. Huang Zhong drew up and marched to meet them. Liu Feng advised, “The sun has gone low; your soldiers have marched far and are spent. It is better to rest a little.”

Huang Zhong laughed. “No. This is heaven-bestowed singular fortune; to leave it undone would be to oppose Heaven.” He beat his drums and charged.

Han Hao brought his soldiers into battle. Huang Zhong swung his sword directly at Han Hao, and in one exchange he cut him down from his horse. Shu soldiers shouted loudly and surged up the mountain.

Zhang He and Xiahou Shang hurriedly brought their armies out to meet them. Then a shout rose from the mountain rear, and firelight burst into the sky, turning both upper and lower slopes red. Xiahou De, bringing troops to save the flames, came upon Yan Yan at that moment. Yan Yan raised his hand and with one sword stroke cut Xiahou De from his horse.

It was Huang Zhong’s old plan: he had previously had Yan Yan bring troops into hidden places in the mountain so that when Huang Zhong’s army arrived, they would ignite the stacked brushwood and set it all at once. Great flames shot up and lit the valley.

After Yan Yan took Xiahou De, he came down from the rear and slashed toward the enemy line. Zhang He and Xiahou Shang could neither aid nor look to each other, so they had to abandon Tiandang Mountain and run toward Dingjun Mountain, then to Xiahou Yuan.

Huang Zhong and Yan Yan held Tiandang, and word of success flew to Chengdu. Liu Bei heard it and, with all the commanders, celebrated.

Fa Zheng said, “In earlier days when Cao Cao marched against Zhang Lu and pacified the Han territory, he did not use that position to seize Ba-Shu; instead he left Xiahou Yuan and Zhang He to hold watch and himself pulled north again. That was a failed stratagem. Now Zhang He has just been defeated and Tiandang has fallen. If the lord seizes this moment and leads a full army in person, Hanzhong can be secured. Once Hanzhong is secured, we can drill troops and store grain, observing opportunities and seizing gaps, advancing to punish bandits and retreating to defend ourselves. Heaven has opened this hour. It must not be lost.”

Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang both agreed deeply and so sent orders for Zhao Yun and Zhang Fei to act as advanced guards. Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang personally led 100,000 troops and chose a lucky day to campaign on Hanzhong, sending proclamations everywhere and raising strict readiness.

It was the auspicious day in the seventh month of Jian’an Twenty-Three. Liu Bei’s main army set out and camped below Jiameng Pass. He summoned Huang Zhong and Yan Yan into camp and granted rich rewards.

Liu Bei said, “All call the General old, but only the strategist truly knows his strength. You have now done wondrous work. Yet Dingjun Mountain in Hanzhong is the seat of Nanzheng’s defense, where grain and grass are stored in number. If we take Dingjun, the route through Yangping is beyond worry.”

“Dare the general to take Dingjun Mountain now?” he asked.

Huang Zhong answered with readiness, “I will.”

Zhuge Liang moved him quickly. “Though the old general is brave, he should not go against Xiahou Yuan as Zhang He. Yuan is no lesser man and is not like any ordinary enemy. He reads deep stratagems and is keen to war’s shifts. Cao Cao relied on him as shield in Xiliang; once he garrisoned Chang’an to oppose Ma Chao; now he has also put him in Hanzhong. Cao Cao trusts him alone in this work because Yuan has command talent.”

“Huang Zhong may have won over Zhang He,” said Zhuge Liang, “but we cannot know if he can also win over Xiahou Yuan. I think we should select one person and send him to Jingzhou to bring the pass commander back; only then can we meet him.”

Huang Zhong answered heartily, “In his day, Lian Po at eighty still ate three-dou of grain and ten jin of meat and kept all feudal lords from crossing Zhao’s borders. How could Huang Zhong, not yet seventy, be less capable? The strategist says I am old, but I will not take an assistant. I will go with three thousand of my own troops and bring back Xiahou Yuan’s head under my banner.”

Zhuge Liang refused him repeatedly.

Huang Zhong only insisted on marching. Zhuge Liang said, “If you insist on going, I will send one man as supervising commander to go with you.”

This was it:

Please use the goad to spur the general on;
no young man can stand against a seasoned elder.
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhang Fei’s Sudden Victory at Wakou Pass and Elder Huang Zhong’s Plan for Tiandang Mountain

chapters.html:
Later, Kongming told Huang Zhong: “Since you are going, I will have Fa Zheng assist you. Think through every move before you act. I will send troops after you to come as support.” Huang Zhong agreed and took his main force off with Fa Zheng.

Kongming told Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande: “This old general will not be moved by coaxing words; he may not succeed through mere persuasion. Since he has already set out, send troops forward to reinforce him.” He then summoned Zhao Yun and gave him one company of troops, ordering him to move through the smaller path as a hidden force: “If Huang Zhong wins, do not ride out to engage. If Zhong encounters difficulty, go at once to relieve him.”

He also sent Liu Feng and Meng Da: “Lead three thousand soldiers to the precarious points in the hills, raise many banners, and swell the appearance of our strength, so the enemy becomes fearful and uncertain.” The three each took their men and went. He also sent instructions to Ma Chao, telling him to do the same. He further sent Yan Yan to Langzhong in Baxi to hold the pass there, so that, together with Zhang Fei and Wei Yan, he could jointly seize Hanzhong.

Zhang He and Xiahou Shang came to Xiahou Yuan and said, “Tiandang Mountain has already fallen; Xiahou De and Han Hao have been routed. Now Liu Bei has personally led troops against Hanzhong. Please report to the King of Wei at once, and dispatch selected troops and fierce officers to support us.” Xiahou Yuan immediately sent a messenger to Cao Hong.

Cao Hong rode all night to Xu, and reported to Cao Cao. Cao Cao was deeply alarmed. He quickly gathered his officials and generals to discuss sending troops to rescue Hanzhong. The Minister Liu Ye spoke up: “If Hanzhong is lost, the Central Plains will shake. Your Highness should not talk about the hardship of campaigning; you must personally lead the suppression.” Cao Cao regretted, “I wish I had listened to your advice before, or we would not be where we are now.”

He then issued orders without delay: four hundred thousand troops were to be raised for him to lead in person. It was autumn, the seventh month of the twenty-third year of Jianan. Cao Cao divided his forces into three routes. Xiahou Dun led the vanguard; Cao Cao took the center; Cao Xiu was ordered to command the rear. The three armies moved out in succession.

Cao Cao rode a white horse with a golden saddle, wearing a jade-belted brocade robe. The guards carried large red silk parasols edged in gilt. At his side were officials holding golden mace-heads, silver halberds, crossbars, and spears. Dragon-and-phoenix banners with sun-and-moon designs rippled above them. His personal guard, the Dragon-Tiger bodyguard, numbered twenty-five thousand, split into five squadrons of five thousand each, marked by blue, yellow, red, white, and black colors. Banners, pennons, armor, and horses all followed their own hue. The splendor was brilliant and imposing.

When the army passed Tong Pass, Cao Cao looked down from his horse and saw a dense, luxuriant grove. He asked one nearby, “What place is this?” “That is Lantian,” came the reply. “In the grove stands the estate of Cai Yong. His daughter, Cai Yan, now lives there with her husband Dongsi.”

In truth, Cao Cao and Cai Yong had long been close. In earlier days, Cai Yan had been the wife of Wei Daojie; she was then captured by the northern tribes, bore two sons in the northern lands, and composed the Eighteen Variations on the Hu Jia. She later drifted back to Zhongyuan. Cao Cao pitied her deeply and sent a thousand pieces of gold north to ransom her. Prince Xiao of Xian, fearing Cao Cao’s power, returned Cai Yan to Han lands. Cao Cao then married Yan to Dongsi.

When they arrived at the estate gate that day, Cao Cao, remembering Cai Yong, sent the main horsemen on ahead. He then rode with more than a hundred attendants and dismounted at the gate. Dongsi was away on official duty, so only Cai Yan was at home. Hearing that Cao Cao had come, she hurried out to receive him. In the hall, after she rose and took her places, she stood at his side.

Cao Cao happened to notice a painted stone inscription hanging on the wall. He stood up to see it and asked Yan about it. “This is the stele of Cao E,” she said. “During the reign of Emperor He, in Shangyu there was a shaman named Cao Xu who could call the spirits. On the fifth day of the fifth month, he drunkenly danced in a boat and fell into the river and died. The girl who was then fourteen went round the riverbank and wept for seven days and nights, then leapt into the water. Five days later, bearing her father’s corpse, she floated upon the river. The villagers buried her by the bank.

The commandery administrator, Du Shang, petitioned the court and recommended her as a filial daughter. Du Shang then had an able craftsman, Handan Chun, carve a stele to record the matter. At that time Handan Chun was only thirteen; without draft or correction, he finished it in one handstroke and set it beside the stone of her tomb. People were astonished. My father, Cai Yong, went there in the dusk. Unable to read the light, he felt the inscription by touch and somehow read the text. He then took up a brush and wrote eight large characters on its reverse. Later engravers copied the stone but did not carve those eight characters.”

Cao Cao read the eight characters as “黄絹幼婦，外孫齏臼.” He asked Yan, “Do you understand what this means?” She said, “Though my father once left these notes, I truly do not understand.”

He turned back to his advisers and asked, “Can any of you read this?” None could answer. From among them one man came forward: “I have understood it.” It was Yang Xiu, the bureau clerk. Cao Cao said, “Say nothing yet. Let me think.” He dismissed Cao Yan and withdrew with his attendants from the estate. After riding three li, he suddenly recalled the matter and laughed, saying, “Explain it now.” Yang Xiu answered, “This is a hidden reading. Add the thread of silk to 黃, and 色 with that thread becomes 絕. 幼婦 means a young maiden. Add the graph 少 beside 女 and it becomes 妙. 外孫 means one’s daughter’s child; add 子 to 女 and you get 好. 齏臼 is a vessel for the Five Aromatics. Add 辛 to it and you obtain 辭. In total, this yields the four characters 絕妙好辭.”

Cao Cao was astonished. “Exactly what I had thought!” he exclaimed. All praised Yang Xiu’s quick intellect.

After only a short time, the army reached Nanzheng. Cao Hong came up and reported to Cao Cao what Zhang He had done. Cao Cao said, “It is not Zhang He’s fault; victory and defeat are always constant in war.” Cao Hong said, “At present Liu Bei has assigned Huang Zhong to attack Dingjun Mountain. Xiahou Yuan knows Your Highness’s army has arrived, yet he holds fast and has not moved.” Cao Cao replied, “If he does not leave his lines, he is showing cowardice.” He immediately sent an envoy with commands to Dingjun Mountain instructing Xiahou Yuan to advance.

Liu Ye objected: “Yuan is too rigid by nature. He may be taken by a treacherous stratagem.” Cao Cao wrote out an order by hand and sent it under seal to him.

When the messenger entered Xiahou Yuan’s camp and delivered the order, Xiahou Yuan read it: “As one who would be general, one must combine firmness and flexibility and not rely only on courage. If one trusts to courage alone, one is no more than a single-man challenge. I have now encamped this great army at Nanzheng to see your ‘clever skill’; do not bring me shame.”

When Xiahou Yuan finished reading, he was very pleased. He sent the messenger back and then consulted Zhang He. “Now that His Highness has brought his main force to Nanzheng to punish Liu Bei, how can I and you hold this place forever and still earn merit? On the morrow I shall take the field. We must capture Huang Zhong alive.”

Zhang He answered, “Huang Zhong has both strategy and courage, and with Fa Zheng behind him this is no light foe. This mountain route is treacherous; we should hold fast.” “Then if another wins merit and praise, what face do you and I have before the King of Wei?” Xiahou Yuan said. “You defend the mountain; I will go out and fight.” He then ordered, “Who dares go forward on an outpost to entice the enemy?” Xiahou Shang answered, “I will go.” “Go then,” Xiahou Yuan said. “You are not to win when you meet Huang Zhong; you are to lose. I have a scheme, this and that.” Xiahou Shang accepted the order and marched three thousand troops from the forward camp at Dingjun Mountain’s great redoubt.

Meanwhile, Huang Zhong and Fa Zheng held at the gate of Dingjun Mountain and repeatedly challenged the enemy, but Xiahou Yuan held firm and refused to come out. Whenever he tried to attack, he feared the dangerous mountain roads and unable to know the foe, so he only kept his position. That day, word came that Wei troops had come down from the mountain to engage. Huang Zhong was about to lead out his troops, when the armored captain Chen Shi said, “General, do nothing yet. I will take this on.”

Huang Zhong was pleased and ordered Chen Shi to lead a thousand men out of the mountain gate and form ranks. Xiahou Shang arrived and exchanged blows. After only a few encounters, Shang feigned defeat and withdrew. Chen Shi chased after him. Halfway through, stone-throwing engines on both mountain sides began hurling rocks and he could not press forward. As he turned back, Xiahou Yuan sent troops out from behind and appeared upon the ridge. Chen Shi could not hold, and was taken alive by Xiahou Yuan. Many of his soldiers surrendered. The few who had broken out survived and returned to report Huang Zhong that Chen Shi had been captured.

Huang Zhong hurried to consult Fa Zheng. Fa Zheng said, “Yuan is a man of hasty impulse and hard courage with little planning. We should whip up our men, lift camp, and advance step by step, setting temporary camps along the way to lure him into battle and then seize him. It is the method of making the guest into the host.”

Huang Zhong used this plan. He distributed rewards equal to what each man had expected, and cheer rose through the valley. The army vowed to fight to the death. The same day he lifted camp and advanced, then settled each day at a temporary encampment and advanced again. Xiahou Yuan heard of this. He wanted to fight. “This is the ‘guest-becomes-host’ plan,” said Zhang He. “You should not advance; once you do, it will bring loss.” Xiahou Yuan refused, and ordered Xiahou Shang to lead several thousand men against the enemy, advancing as far as Huang Zhong’s camp. Huang Zhong mounted, drew his blade, and rode out to receive him. At the very first clash he captured Shang alive and brought him back to camp. The rest of Shang’s men fled in disorder and returned with the news. Xiahou Yuan quickly sent word to Huang Zhong, offering to exchange Chen Shi for Shang. The two fixed an agreement: they would trade at the front lines on the morrow.

Next day, both armies reached the wider part of a mountain valley and arrayed themselves. Huang Zhong and Xiahou Yuan each set their mounts beneath each main gate banner. Each carried Shang and Chen Shi with him. Neither wore his coat-and-armor, only a light body covering. A drum sounded once. Chen Shi and Xiahou Shang each turned and ran back to their own camps. When Shang reached the gate, Huang Zhong shot him with one arrow through the back. Shang staggered away with the arrow. Xiahou Yuan, furious, drove straight at Huang Zhong at once. Huang Zhong prepared to meet him in close combat. They charged horse to horse and fought for over twenty exchanges, but suddenly from within Cao’s camp a bronze-gong was struck to sound recall. Xiahou Yuan wheeled his horse back in confusion. Huang Zhong seized the moment and cut one full round into him. Back in his own lines, Xiahou Yuan asked the officer commanding camp, “Why did you sound the gong?” “He saw several banners inside a mountain hollow and thought there must be ambush troops,” came the answer. “He drew Your General back in haste.” Xiahou Yuan believed him and held firm, refusing to go out.

Huang Zhong pursued to below Dingjun Mountain and spoke with Fa Zheng. Fa Zheng pointed with his hand: “To the west of Dingjun Mountain stands a high peak, and all around it are hidden paths. From that peak one can look down and read the condition of Dingjun Mountain. If the General secures this mountain, Dingjun lies in the palm of your hand.”

Looking up, Huang Zhong saw a relatively level crest with a few troops on it. In the second watch of the night, he ordered his men to beat gongs and drums and rode straight up the hill to seize the peak. The peak was guarded by Du Xi, one of Xiahou Yuan’s generals, with barely more than a few hundred men. At first glance at Huang Zhong’s massed ascent, he had no choice but to abandon it and run. Huang Zhong took the summit, facing Dingjun Mountain opposite. Fa Zheng said, “You should hold half-way down. I will stay at the top. When Xiahou Yuan’s troops arrive, I will raise a white flag. Do not move. When they grow weary and careless, I will raise a red flag. Then you must descend and strike. Resting while he tires, our strategy is to meet him at leisure; we will surely win.” Huang Zhong approved it, and followed the plan.

Du Xi withdrew to Xiahou Yuan and reported that Huang Zhong had taken the opposing mountain. Xiahou Yuan roared with anger: “If Huang Zhong has occupied the opposing mountain, I cannot avoid battle.” Zhang He remonstrated: “This is Fa Zheng’s stratagem. General, you must not go out. Hold your lines.” “But if he has taken my opposite mountain and now sees through our defenses, how can I not fight?” Xiahou Yuan said. Zhang He repeated counsel with great insistence, but the general ignored him. He split his force and ringed the opposite peak, shouting threats and taunts. Fa Zheng raised the white flag on the summit. No matter how much Xiahou Yuan abused him, Huang Zhong did not engage. After midday, Fa Zheng saw the Wei troops growing weary, their sharpness already gone. Many dismounted and sat down to rest. He then unfurled the red flag. Drums and horns rang together, and loud shouts rolled across the valley. Huang Zhong, his horse foremost, rushed down the slope like a landslide.

Xiahou Yuan could not react in time. Huang Zhong drove him down to the standard’s banner, then gave a great shout, like thunder. Before Xiahou Yuan could meet him properly, Huang Zhong’s treasure-cutting saber landed, severing head and shoulder as one.

Afterward people of later times composed a poem:

His hoary head before a mighty enemy, his white beard flaunting divine fierceness; His strength snapped like a released bow; with the wind, the snowy blade whirled in his sweep; His voice roars like a tiger, his swift horse flies like a dragon; He offered severed heads for fame and merit of weight, he opened the borders and extended the imperial domain.

Huang Zhong killed Xiahou Yuan and Cao troops broke apart and fled in confusion. In the wake of that blow, Huang Zhong took Dingjun Mountain. Zhang He came to oppose him with troops. Huang Zhong and Chen Shi pressed from both flanks, slaughtering together for a while, and Zhang He broke and ran. Suddenly a body of men flashed from beside the mountain and blocked the retreat route. At their head was a towering commander who shouted, “Zhao Zilong of Changshan is here!” Zhang He was startled and drew out his broken troops, slipping away toward Dingjun Mountain. A detachment came forward to meet him; it was Du Xi. “Dingjun Mountain has now been taken by Liu Feng and Meng Da,” he said. Zhang He was shaken. He and Du Xi led the broken troops down to the Han River and set camp there. At once he sent a fast rider to Cao Cao with the news.

When Cao Cao heard of Yuan’s death, he shouted and wept openly. He finally remembered Guan Lu’s words: “three-eight in all directions” had meant the twenty-fourth year of Jianan; “the yellow pig meets the tiger” meant the year was Jihai and it was the first month, “south of Dingjun” meant south of Dingjun Mountain, and “one branch broken” meant that Yuan and Cao had once been as close as brothers.

He ordered men out in search of Guan Lu, but no one knew where he had gone.

Cao Cao deeply hated Huang Zhong. He personally led a great army to Dingjun Mountain to avenge his fallen kinsman and ordered Xu Huang to advance as the vanguard. As they came down to the Han River, Zhang He and Du Xi joined Cao Cao. The two generals advised, “Now that Dingjun Mountain is lost, we should move grain and fodder from Micang Mountain into the northern mountain camp for storage, and then push forward.” Cao Cao agreed.

Huang Zhong then returned with Xiahou Yuan’s head to Jiameng Pass and presented his achievement to Liu Bei. Liu Bei was delighted, promoted Huang Zhong to General Who Conquers the West, and set a banquet for celebration. Then an armored officer named Zhang Zhuo reported, “Cao Cao has brought two hundred thousand under his own hand to avenge the death of Xiahou Yuan. At present Zhang He is at Micang Mountain moving supplies to the foot of the mountain north of the Han River.”

Kongming said, “Since Cao Cao has brought such a force here, he may not push forward because supplies are insufficient. If one person can enter his camp, burn his grain, and seize his transport, Cao Cao’s sharpness will be blunted.” Huang Zhong said, “I will take that assignment.” Kongming said, “Cao Cao is not Xiahou Yuan; do not underestimate him.” Liu Bei said, “Though Xiahou Yuan was a grand commander, he was only a brave man. What of Zhang He? If you cut him down, it is worth ten times taking Xiahou Yuan.”

Huang Zhong spoke up with force: “Then I will go and do it.” Kongming answered, “Take one branch with Zhao Yun. In every matter, act only after proper planning and counsel. We will see who makes the greater merit.” Huang Zhong assented and set out. Kongming made Zhang Zhuo the deputy commander to accompany him.

Zhao Yun said to Huang Zhong, “Cao Cao has brought twenty thousand, split into ten camps. For you to seize grain before the Lord is watching is no small matter. What will you do?” Huang Zhong said, “Watch me go first.” Zuo Yun replied, “Then let me go first.” Huang Zhong said, “I am the commanding general, you my deputy. How can we argue over who goes first?” Zhao Yun answered, “We both serve the lord as one. Why count precedence? Let us draw lots; whoever draws first goes first.” Huang Zhong agreed. It was Huang Zhong who drew first.

Zhao Yun said, “Then since the General goes first, I shall assist.” They fixed a time. “If the General returns by noon, I will hold back. If he does not return by then, I will come in with reinforcements.” Huang Zhong said, “Your word is enough.” They fixed noon as the deadline. Zhao Yun returned to his own camp and told his chief captain, Zhang Yi: “Huang Hansheng has agreed to raid the grain tomorrow. If he fails to return by noon, I shall go to assist. My camp faces the Han River and the ground is dangerous. While I am away, you must guard the breastworks carefully and not move lightly.” Zhang Yi answered in assent.

Back in camp, Huang Zhong told deputy Zhang Zhuo, “I have cut down Xiahou Yuan and frightened Zhang He. At dawn tomorrow I will lead this charge for grain. Leave only five hundred to guard camp. You will help me.” “Tonight, at the third watch, feed everyone well and depart at the fourth with all men ready. We go first to seize Zhang He, and then to steal the grain.”

That is what Zhang Zhuo obeyed. That night Huang Zhong led the main body and Zhang Zhuo followed. They crossed the Han River in silence and reached the base of the northern mountain.
