By dawn they saw grain piled high like a mountain. A few sentries watched, but as soon as they saw the Shu troops they fled. Huang Zhong ordered his horsemen to dismount together and bring brushwood, covering the grain mounds. He was about to set it alight. At that moment Zhang He’s men arrived and a general melee broke out with Huang Zhong. Cao Cao heard of it and urgently ordered Xu Huang to send aid. Xu Huang marched forward and trapped Huang Zhong in the center of a battle-ring. Zhang Zhuo led three hundred men to break clear and began to return toward camp, when another enemy force burst out and blocked the way. At its head was the Wei general Wenpin. Behind him other Wei troops arrived and enveloped Zhang Zhuo.

Zhao Yun was in camp and waited until noon. He saw that Huang Zhong had not returned and quickly buckled on his armor and mounted, leading three thousand troops to reinforce. As he left, he told Zhang Yi, “Hold your camp firmly. Set many crossbows along both sides of the wall.” Zhang Yi answered repeatedly in assent. Zhao Yun surged forward with spear and reins in hand. The first commander to block him was Murong Lie, a subordinate of Wenpin. He struck and came in whirling his blade to meet Zhao Yun, but Zhao Yun thrust his spear once and killed him. The Wei troops broke and fled. Yun pressed in through the crushing ranks. Then another detachment cut him off; its leader was the Wei general Jiao Bing. Zhao Yun shouted, “Where are the Shu soldiers?” Jiao Bing replied, “All have been cut down.” Zhao Yun grew furious, spurred his horse, and with one spear thrust killed Jiao Bing again. He scattered the rest and hurried onward to the foot of the northern mountain, where he saw Huang Zhong and Zhang He, with Xu Huang, still surrounding the trapped General and with his men held in danger for a long while.

Zhao Yun gave one great shout, lowered his spear, and drove his horse forward. Left and right he broke through as if entering empty ground. His spear moved over his whole body, like dancing pear blossoms; the air around him seemed to drift with auspicious snow. Zhang He and Xu Huang trembled and dared not close with him. Zhao Yun rescued Huang Zhong and kept fighting while withdrawing, and wherever he rode, no one dared to stand in his way.

From a high place Cao Cao saw this and asked the assembled officers, “Who is this man?” A man who knew answered, “It is the Zhao Zilong of Changshan.” Cao Cao said, “So the hero of Changban still lives!” He shouted immediate orders: “Where he comes, do not treat him lightly.”

After Zhao Yun rescued Huang Zhong and tore open the encirclement, a soldier pointed out, “The man who was blocking the southeast outer ring must be Deputy Zhang Zhuo.” “Zhao Yun did not return to camp,” he said, and turned and rode southeast to kill his way through. In every place he arrived, he saw banners marked “Zhao Yun of Changshan.” Men who had heard of his courage at Changban and repeated stories of his valor all fled. Zhao Yun then rescued Zhang Zhuo.

When Cao Cao saw him charging east and west without obstruction, impossible to stand before, and having rescued both Huang Zhong and Zhang Zhuo, he grew indignant. He personally led the men near at hand to chase Zhao Yun. Zhao Yun had already cut his way back to camp. Zhang Yi came up behind him and saw dust rising behind them. “Pursuers are near,” he said. “Order the troops to close the camp gates and defend on the wall.” Zhao Yun shouted, “Do not close the gate! Do you not know, when I was at Changban in the past, I on spear and horse regarded Cao Cao’s eight hundred and thirty thousand as mere weeds? Now I have troops and generals with me—what fear have I?” He set archers and crossbowmen in ambush in the ditches beyond the gate, laid all flags and spears inside the camp in a prostrated position, and kept gong and drum silent. He stood by the camp gate on horseback, spear in hand.

Zhang He and Xu Huang chased to the Shu camp. It was already dusk. They saw the flags lowered and drums silent inside, and Zhao Yun alone on horseback and spear outside, with the gate wide open. The two generals did not dare to advance. Before they could make sense of it, Cao Cao himself arrived and urgently urged all soldiers forward. At the command, the men gave one cry and ran toward the camp front. Seeing Zhao Yun remain unmoving, the Wei troops immediately turned and ran back. Zhao Yun made one spear motion and the crossbows hidden in the ditch sent out a synchronized volley. It was dark, and no one knew how many Shu soldiers there were. Cao Cao turned his horse and rode away first. From behind came a great crash of shouting and horns, and the Shu troops came charging. The Wei army trammeled one another in panic. They reached the Han River edge, where many fell into the water and drowned. The number who perished is unknown.

Zhao Yun, Huang Zhong, and Zhang Zhuo each led a body of troops in heavy pursuit. While Cao Cao was running, Liu Feng and Meng Da came with two contingents along the Micang Mountain road and set fire to the supplies. Cao Cao abandoned his northern mountain grain, hurried back to Nanzheng, and Xu Huang and Zhang He, unable to set firm footing, also abandoned their own camps and withdrew. Zhao Yun captured the Wei camp. Huang Zhong took the grain. He gained huge quantities of arms at the Han River, and won a broad victory. He sent men to report to Liu Bei.

Liu Bei, with Kongming, went to the Han River and asked one of Zhao Yun’s captains, “How did Zilong fight it through?” The soldiers told in detail how Zhao Yun had rescued Huang Zhong and held against the river crossing. Liu Bei rejoiced. Looking at the steep and fierce roads ahead and behind him, he said with pleasure to Kongming, “Zilong is courage itself!”

Later men composed a poem for him:

Once he fought at Changban, and his majesty of mien had not diminished; He broke into formation and showed himself a hero, and while encircled he displayed boldness; Ghosts wailed and spirits cried out; heaven shuddered and earth was shaken; Zhao Zilong of Changshan—his whole body is made of courage.

Liu Bei therefore conferred upon Zilong the title Tiger-Warrior General, praised the soldiers greatly, and made a joyful feast late into the night.

A report came in: Cao Cao was sending a large army again by the slanting valley path to seize the Han River. Liu Bei laughed: “Cao Cao comes again yet he cannot do a thing. I can see we will take the Han River.” He led his troops to the west of the Han River to meet them.

Cao Cao made Xu Huang the vanguard to decide the battle. A man came out before the pavilion and said, “I know this terrain well. I wish to assist General Xu and break the Shu.” Cao Cao recognized him as Wang Ping of Dangqu in Baxi, with name Wang and courtesy name Zijun, and the rank of Guard Captain. Cao Cao was pleased and made Wang Ping the deputy vanguard, to assist Xu Huang.

Cao Cao encamped north of Dingjun Mountain. Xu Huang and Wang Ping led their men to the Han River. Xu Huang ordered the front guard to cross and form rank. Wang Ping said, “If the army has crossed and then must retreat quickly, what then?” Xu Huang replied, “General Han once formed his array with his back to water; this is what is called setting men in a dead-end so they can be reborn.” Wang Ping answered, “Not so. Han Xin used that only when he expected no cunning in the enemy. Can this General truly read the intentions of Zhao Yun and Huang Zhong?” Xu Huang said, “You lead the infantry to hold them off. I will bring the cavalry and break through.” He ordered a floating bridge raised and then crossed at once to meet the Shu forces.

It was then said:

The men of Wei foolishly invoke Han Xin, yet the Shu Prime Minister knows not Zi Fang; Who can yet tell how victory will be decided?

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Huang Zhong Takes the Opposing Mountain, and Zhao Yun Holds at the Han River

chapters.html:
Zhuge Liang wins Hanzhong by stratagem, Cao Amin’s army retreats at Xie Valley.

Now, it was reported that Xu Huang led his army across the Han River. Wang Ping repeatedly remonstrated to stop, but was not heeded, and he crossed and camped. Huang Zhong and Zhao Yun then told Liu Bei, “We should each lead our own troops and go out to meet Cao’s army.” Liu Bei agreed. The two set out with their troops. Huang Zhong said to Zhao Yun, “Xu Huang comes here relying on courage. Do not meet him yet. If we wait until dusk when the troops are tired, we can split our forces into two routes and strike.” Zhao Yun readily agreed, and each led a unit and held the stockades.

Xu Huang pushed the fight from the third watch until the ninth hour; the Shu soldiers did not move. Xu Huang ordered his bow and crossbow men forward to shoot toward the Shu camp. Huang Zhong said to Zhao Yun, “When Xu Huang sends out his bow and crossbow men, his army is bound to retire; we should strike at that moment.” Before he had finished speaking, news came that the rear of the Cao forces was already falling back. Shu drums and war drums thundered across camp. Huang Zhong led his troops out on the left, Zhao Yun on the right. They struck from both sides; Xu Huang was badly defeated. Soldiers pressed back toward the Han River, and the dead were uncounted. Xu Huang fought his way free and returned to camp, saying to Wang Ping, “You saw my army in danger and did not come to rescue me. Why?”

Wang Ping answered, “If I had come to help, this stockade also could not have been held. I had begged you to leave, but you refused to listen. This defeat is the result.” Xu Huang in fury wanted to kill Wang Ping. That night Wang Ping brought his own troops to camp and set fires through the lines. The Wei ranks were thrown into confusion, and Xu Huang abandoned camp and fled. Wang Ping crossed the Han River and came to Zhao Yun, who brought him before Liu Bei. Wang Ping reported in full on the terrain along the river. Liu Bei was delighted and said, “I have gained Wang Zijun; there is no doubt we can take Hanzhong.” He then appointed Wang Ping as a Deputy General and made him Guide Officer.

Later Xu Huang returned to report to Cao Cao that Wang Ping had defected and joined Liu Bei. Cao was furious. He personally led the main army to take back the Han River fortifications. Fearing his army stood alone, Zhao Yun withdrew to the west bank of the Han River. The two armies confronted each other across the water.

Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang came to observe the situation. Zhuge Liang saw upstream on the Han a stretch of earthworks where a thousand men could lie hidden, then returned to camp and instructed Zhao Yun: “Take five hundred men, all carrying drums and horns, and lie hidden under that earthen ridge. Whether at midnight or dusk, when you hear one signal blast from my camp, answer with one beating of the drums. Do not enter open battle.” Zilong carried out the plan. Zhuge Liang remained concealed on a high mountain and watched.

The next day Cao’s men came and tested for battle, but not one in the Shu camp came out, and not a single bow or crossbow was fired. The Wei troops withdrew on their own.

Late that night, when the lamps in Cao’s camp had almost gone out and soldiers were settling, Zhuge Liang sounded the alarm. Zhao Yun heard and ordered drums and horns to sound together. The Wei troops panicked, thinking their camp had been raided. When they emerged, they found no one. Just as they began to return in order to rest, the alarm sounded again, drums and horns roared again, and cries shook the valleys. The soldiers of Cao passed the entire night in anxiety. This continued for three nights. Fearful and shaken, Cao moved back thirty li to an open site.

Zhuge Liang laughed and said, “Though Cao Cao knows military arts, he does not know deception.” He then invited Liu Bei to cross the Han River himself and camp with his back to the water.

Liu Bei asked for the plan. Zhuge Liang said, “This can be done exactly so.”

When Cao Cao saw Liu Bei pitching camp with his back to the river, he was full of suspicion and sent someone with a war letter. Zhuge Liang wrote back, “Tomorrow will decide in battle.”

The following day the two armies met before Wujie Mountain in the middle path and formed up in array. Cao Cao mounted his horse, stood beneath the banner awning, arranged two lines beneath dragon-and-phoenix standards, and beat the drums three times, calling for Liu Bei’s response.

Liu Bei came out with Liu Feng, Meng Da, and the commanders from the river ranks. Cao Cao brandished his whip and shouted, “Liu Bei, ungrateful and treacherous traitor who betrays the court!” Liu Bei replied, “I am a kinsman of the Great Han, acting under edict to punish rebels. You killed your mother and empress, claimed the Son of Heaven’s carriage for yourself, and set yourself up as king. How is this anything but rebellion?”

Enraged, Cao ordered Xu Huang to ride out and fight. Liu Feng met him. As soon as the engagement began, Liu Bei rode into the lines first. Liu Feng could not hold against Xu Huang, turned his horse, and fled. Cao issued the order: “Catch Liu Bei, and make him King of Xichuan.” The whole army roared and surged forward across the lines.

The Shu soldiers turned and ran toward the Han River, abandoning camp and stockades and leaving horses and equipment strewn across the roads. All the Wei men rushed to seize the spoils. Cao urgently sounded the drums to recollect his army. His generals said, “We were waiting only to capture Liu Bei. Your Majesty, why do you order a retreat?” Cao said, “I saw that Shu men camped with their backs to the Han River—that is one suspicious sign. So many horses and pieces of equipment were abandoned—that is a second. Withdraw at once. Do not take their clothing or goods.”

His command was, “Whoever takes even one article will be beheaded. Withdraw the army at speed.” As the Wei turned their backs, Zhuge Liang raised his flags and signal horns. Liu Bei led the center troops out and came forward. Huang Zhong struck in on the left, Zhao Yun on the right. The Wei army broke and fled, and Zhuge Liang pursued through the night.

Cao ordered the army back toward Nanzheng. Suddenly fires rose on five roads. It turned out Wei Yan and Zhang Fei, having replaced Yanyan to guard Langzhong, had split their men and moved in; they had taken Nanzheng first. Cao was alarmed and withdrew toward Yangping Pass.

Liu Bei’s main army pursued to Nanzheng and Baozhou. When civil order had been restored, he asked Zhuge Liang, “Why did Cao Cao fail so quickly?”

Zhuge Liang replied, “All his life Cao has been a man of suspicion. Though he can command soldiers, suspicion makes him lose often. I have defeated him by deceptive warfare.” Liu Bei said, “Now Cao has retired to Yangping Pass with his strength isolated. How will we drive him back?”

Zhuge Liang answered, “The plan is already set. Send Zhang Fei and Wei Yan, each splitting the troops into two routes, to cut Cao Cao’s supply lines. Send Huang Zhong and Zhao Yun, each splitting their troops, to set fires in the hills. Each of the four columns then moved off with their local guides.”

When Cao retreated to Yangping Pass, he sent scouts to reconnoiter. They reported, “Shu troops have sealed every nearby and distant track. Places for cutting firewood have all been burned through. They are no longer in any place we can identify.” While Cao was still in confusion, another report came that Zhang Fei and Wei Yan had split their forces and were raiding supplies.

“Who dares face Zhang Fei?” said Xu Chu, “I volunteer.” Cao ordered Xu Chu to lead a thousand picked soldiers and go out the Yangping Pass route to escort food and straw.

The supply official who met them said, with relief, “Without your arrival, the grain and forage would never have reached Yangping.” He brought the cartloads of wine and meat and presented them to Xu Chu.

Xu Chu drank hard and was overtaken by drunkenness, then, in that inebriated giddiness, urged the supply carts forward. The supply official said, “It is already evening. Beyond here toward Baozhou the ground is treacherous, not yet safe to pass.”

Xu Chu replied, “I have the courage of ten thousand men. Why should I fear others? The moonlight is perfect tonight for moving the grain carts.” He rode first, sword drawn, horse at full speed, and led the force ahead.

After the second watch they were halfway toward Baozhou when, from a hollow in the hills, drums and horns sounded like thunder and a column of troops appeared before them. At its head was Zhang Fei. He couched a spear and charged on horseback straight at Xu Chu. Xu Chu drew his knife in return, but his drunkenness let him fail to withstand Zhang Fei. After only a few exchanges, Zhang Fei’s spear struck his shoulder; he turned over and fell from the saddle. His men quickly pulled him up and fled backward. Zhang Fei seized the supply carts and returned.

The other generals protected Xu Chu and brought him back to Cao Cao. Cao ordered physicians to treat the puncture wound and at once personally rode out with troops to do battle against Shu.

Liu Bei came out to meet him. The two formations closed opposite one another. Liu Bei ordered Liu Feng to ride out first. Cao shouted, “Wretched boy, you keep sending a substitute child to meet the enemy! If I call for Old Hairy-cheek, your substitute would be minced into paste!”

Liu Feng was enraged, lowered his spear and lashed his horse toward Cao. Cao ordered Xu Huang to meet him, and Liu Feng feigned defeat and withdrew. Cao pursued. Within the Shu camp, signal blasts and horn calls thundered from all sides. Fearing an ambush, Cao hastily ordered retreat. The Wei troops trampled one another in panic and many died. They ran back to Yangping Pass and barely rested.

Shu soldiers arrived under the walls: fire at the East gate with shouts at the West gate; fire at the South gate and drums at the North. Cao was in great fear and abandoned the pass and fled.

Shu troops attacked from behind. As Cao was running, Zhang Fei blocked his way with a troop at the front. Zhao Yun struck from the rear with another unit, and Huang Zhong came from Baozhou with yet another troop. Cao was routed. Officers protected Cao and fought a fighting retreat through the roads.

Just as he reached the boundary of Xie Valley, a swirl of dust rose ahead, and another unit appeared. Cao said, “If this is an ambush, we are finished.” But when the men drew nearer, it was his second son, Cao Zhang.

Cao Zhang, with courtesy name Ziwen, was, in youth, good at riding and archery; he had strength beyond ordinary men and could wrestle wild beasts. Cao had once cautioned him, “You do not read and prefer bow and horse. This rough courage of a common brute is not enough for honor.” Cao Zhang answered, “A true man ought to follow Wei Qing and Huo Qubing, making achievements in the desert, riding fast through tens of thousands of troops, cutting across the world. How could one become a doctor?”

Cao had once asked the ambitions of his sons. Cao Zhang said, “I wish to be a general.” Cao asked, “What kind of general would you be?” Cao Zhang answered, “Wearing armor, carrying sharp weapons, ignoring danger, leading in front of my men; rewards are given, and punishments are trustworthy.” Cao laughed.

In the twenty-third year of Jian’an, when the Wuhuan in Dai Commandery rebelled, Cao ordered Cao Zhang to lead fifty thousand troops against them. He warned him before departure: “In the home one is a father and son, in office one is lord and subject. The law does not follow emotion—you must keep this deeply in mind.”

At Dai, Cao Zhang charged at the head of the line and fought all the way to Sanggan; the northern frontier was pacified. Hearing of Cao’s defeat at Yangping, he came to help.

When Cao saw Cao Zhang arrive, he rejoiced: “My Yellow-Mustache boy has come. Liu Bei will surely be broken.” He ordered the army to return and camp again at the mouth of Xie Valley.

Someone reported to Liu Bei, saying Cao Zhang had come. Liu Bei asked, “Who will go against Cao Zhang?” Liu Feng said, “I will go.” Meng Da also offered to go.

Liu Bei said, “The two of you will go together. See who succeeds.” Each brought five thousand troops to meet him: Liu Feng in front, Meng Da behind.

Cao Zhang fought with Liu Feng, and in only three rounds Liu Feng was severely defeated and turned back. Meng Da brought his force forward and was just about to make contact when he saw the Wei ranks in confusion. Ma Chao and Wu Lan were charging together; that movement alone threw the Wei troops into panic. Meng Da pressed in and attacked from both sides.

Ma Chao’s men had held their sharpness for a long time; when they came, they made a show of armoring strength and were impossible to withstand. The Wei army broke and fled.

Cao Zhang met Wu Lan directly. They faced each other; in only a few passes, Cao Zhang thrust a halberd and pierced Wu Lan beneath the horse. The three armies crashed together in confused battle. Cao gathered his men and halted at the edge of Xie Valley.

Cao had camped too long and wanted to advance, but was blocked again by Ma Chao and forced to withdraw to his position. He wished to retire but feared laughter at Shu, and thus remained undecided.

At that time the cooking steward brought chicken soup. Cao saw the chicken bones in the bowl and was moved in thought. While he was brooding, Xiahou Dun entered and requested permission for a night watchword. Cao, thinking aloud, said, “Chicken ribs. Chicken ribs!”

Dun relayed the word through the camp: all officers were to salute with the same phrase, “Chicken ribs.” The campaign clerk Yang Xiu, seeing the two characters, ordered all the marching soldiers to begin packing their gear and preparing for departure.

Someone informed Xiahou Dun. He was startled and brought Yang Xiu into the command tent to ask, “Why are everyone collecting gear?” Yang Xiu said, “From the signal of this night, it is clear the Lord of Wei will withdraw soon. Chicken ribs means there is flavor in discarding something useless when there is no flesh in it. Since we cannot win tomorrow and retreating would be laughed at if delayed, it is better to go home early. Tomorrow Wei Wang will certainly order the return march, so the troops must pack now to avoid confusion on the move.”

Xiahou Dun said, “You truly understand the Chancellor’s heart and lungs!” and he too prepared his own gear. Then every commander and soldier in the camp prepared to return.

That night Cao was troubled and could not sleep. He took his steel axe in hand and walked around camp alone. He saw inside Xiahou Dun’s position all the soldiers packing to march. Cao was greatly alarmed and hurried back to call Dun to account.

Dun replied, “It was the clerk Yang Zhezhu, who sensed your intention to return.” Cao called for Yang Xiu. Xiu answered with the meaning of chicken ribs. Cao shouted in fury, “How dare you invent such words and confuse my army!” He ordered sword and axe men to drag him out and execute him at once. He had his head raised on display outside the gate.

Yang Xiu had already been a man proud of talent and often offended Cao’s taboos. Once Cao had built a garden pavilion. After touring it, Cao made no praise or blame, but took up a brush, wrote one character on the gate—“alive”—and left. No one understood his meaning.

Yang Xiu said, “Putting “alive” inside 門 makes the character “kō.” In modern script, it is “wide,” meaning ‘a gate too broad.’ The Chancellor dislikes a broad gate.” So they raised another wall around it. Once rebuilt, he again invited Cao to inspect. Cao was delighted and asked who had known his intent. The attendants said, “Yang Xiu.” Cao praised him outwardly but remained deeply suspicious.

Another day, a large box of su from the frontier was brought in. Cao himself wrote on the box three characters: “one helping of su.” He placed it on the table. Yang Xiu came in, took out a ladle, and distributed it to everyone. Cao asked why. Yang Xiu answered, “The box clearly says ‘one helping per person.’ How could I disobey the Chancellor’s command?” Cao smiled on the surface, but his dislike grew.

Cao feared men might plot against his life in secret and often told his attendants, “When I dream, I am eager to kill people. Whenever I sleep, do not come near.” On one day he had a daytime nap in his tent and the quilt slipped to the floor. A close attendant hurriedly pulled it up for him. Cao sprang up and drew his sword, beheading the attendant, then returned to bed.

After a while he rose, feigned surprise, and asked, “Who killed my attendant?” They answered truthfully. Cao wept aloud and ordered the man buried with honor. Everyone thought Cao had truly killed him in a dream. Only Yang Xiu understood and at the funeral pointed and sighed, “His Excellency is not the one in the dream; it is Your Majesty who is in the dream!” Cao heard this and disliked him more.

Cao Cao’s third son, Cao Zhi, loved Yang Xiu’s talent and often invited him to talk through the night. Cao met with his men and discussed appointing Zhi as crown prince.

Cao Pi learned of this and privately asked the gate master of Zhaoge, Wu Zhi, to enter the inner court to discuss. Fearing discovery, he hid Wu Zhi inside a large wicker basket and claimed only lengths of silk were inside before it was carried to the household. Yang Xiu learned this and came straight to Cao to report.

Cao ordered guards to watch Cao Pi’s gate. Cao Pi, alarmed, warned Wu Zhi. Wu Zhi said, “Do not worry. Tomorrow he will be brought in again in another big basket of silk to deceive him.” Cao Pi did as advised and entered carrying silk in a large basket. A messenger searched the basket, found only silk, and reported to Cao Cao. Cao thus suspected Yang Xiu was setting Cao Pi against Cao Zhi and his dislike deepened.

Cao Cao wished to test both Cao Pi and Cao Zhi’s abilities. One day he ordered each to leave the gate of Ye City, but he secretly instructed gate officers not to let them out. Cao Pi arrived first and was stopped at the gate, forced to turn back.

When Cao Zhi heard, he asked Yang Xiu. “You serve under the king’s command. If someone blocks your way, he should be cut down,” Xiu advised. Cao Zhi agreed and followed the same counsel. At the gate, officers blocked him as well.

Cao Zhi shouted, “I am acting under the ruler’s command—who dares to stop me?” and immediately beheaded the gate officer. Cao Cao recognized him as capable from then on.

Later someone reported to Cao Cao, “This was taught by Yang Xiu.” Cao became furious and now also withdrew his favor for Cao Zhi.

Yang Xiu had once drafted more than ten reply templates for Cao Zhi, and when Cao asked anything, Cao Zhi answered by following those templates. Cao asked military and state questions; Cao Zhi answered smoothly each time. Cao grew deeply suspicious.

Later, Cao Pi secretly bought Cao Zhi’s attendants and had them report that his brother used prepared answers.

When Cao saw this, he was furious: “How can a common fellow dare deceive me?” By then he already had intent to kill Yang Xiu; now he used the charge of disordering the army’s spirit and executed him. Yang Xiu died at thirty-four.

A later poem says:

The brilliant Yang Dezu of inherited jade plume, Dragons and snakes race beneath his brush, Brocade is made within his chest. One opening speech startled fourfold the hall, his quick replies crowned him among the worthy. He died through trusting his talent too far, not for wanting to turn back the army.

After Cao had killed Yang Xiu, he feigned anger at Xiahou Dun and also wished to behead him. The ministers interceded, and he spared Xiahou Dun.

Cao shouted Dun away and ordered the army to advance the next day.

The next day troops marched out from the mouth of Xie Valley. A force came out to meet them, with Wei Yan at its head.

Cao invited Wei Yan to surrender; Wei Yan shouted insults.

Cao ordered Pang De to fight. As the two generals engaged, fire broke out in Cao’s camp. Someone reported that Ma Chao had raided the middle and rear stockades. Cao drew his sword and shouted, “Any officer who falls back will be beheaded!” The generals drove forward fiercely.

Wei Yan feigned defeat and withdrew. Cao then hauled his troops back to fight Ma Chao himself, mounted on a high knoll and watched the two armies struggle. Suddenly a troop crashed straight toward him, crying, “Wei Yan is here!” He drew bow and loosed an arrow, striking Cao.

Cao toppled and fell from his horse. Wei Yan discarded bow and lance and leapt forward up the hillside to kill Cao. From the slanted ridge, a general dashed out crying, “Do not strike my lord!” It was Pang De. Pang De forced forward, fought and repelled Wei Yan, and protected Cao’s advance.

Ma Chao had withdrawn. Cao, wounded, returned to camp. He had been hit in the face by Wei Yan’s shot, breaking two front teeth. He ordered physicians to treat him at once. Then he remembered Yang Xiu’s words; he had the body of Xiu brought back and buried in honor. He then ordered a general withdrawal, leaving Pang De to cover the rear.

Cao lay in a felt cart, with Tiger Guards around him as he moved. News came that fires rose on both sides of Xie Valley, and ambush forces were coming down the mountain. Every Wei soldier grew frightened.

Dimly recalled is his peril once at Tong Pass; Once more it seems the danger he faced at Red Cliffs.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang Takes Hanzhong by Stratagem; Cao A'man Withdraws His Army through Xie Valley

chapters.html:
Yet there was talk that Cao Cao withdrew his army to Xie Valley. Kongming had already calculated that he would abandon Hanzhong and flee, so he sent Ma Chao and other generals, splitting the forces into more than ten routes and striking and looting from time to time. For this reason Cao Cao could not stay for long. Wei Yan also had shot him with an arrow, so he hurriedly ordered a retreat. The sharp edge of the whole army fell away. As soon as the forward detachment had only just set out, fires broke out on both sides; it was Ma Chao’s ambush in pursuit. Cao’s soldiers all lost heart. Cao Cao ordered the troops to move on in haste and they ran through the night without rest; only when they had reached Jingzhao did he begin to feel secure.

Meanwhile Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, ordered Liu Feng, Meng Da, and Wang Ping to take up the counties of Shangyong. When Shen Dan and others heard that Cao Cao had abandoned Hanzhong and left, they all surrendered. Once Liu Bei had settled the people and fixed governance, he gave great rewards to the whole army, and spirits rose among all. So every general in attendance wished to honor Liu Bei as emperor, but did not dare to raise the matter directly. They reported it to Zhuge Liang, whom everyone called the military adviser. Zhuge said, “I have already decided the matter.” He then led Fa Zheng in and requested an audience with Liu Bei.

“Cao Cao now monopolizes state authority, and the people have no lord. Your Majesty’s benevolence and justice are known throughout the world. You have now pacified and governed lands in both Sichuan; you can answer Heaven and win men’s support. You can take the imperial seat as the Han King, with lawful title and right order, to punish the traitor to the state. This must not be delayed; choose an auspicious day.”

Liu Bei was startled. “What the adviser says is wrong. Though Liu Bei is of the Han imperial lineage, he is a servant of the court; if I do this, it is rebellion against Han.” Zhuge said, “No. Today the realm is split apart. Heroes rise everywhere and each rules his own sphere. Men of merit across the Four Seas, abandoning life and choosing service under a ruler, all seek to climb a dragon and attach to a phoenix in order to make a name. Now, if Your Majesty refuses for the sake of scruple and righteousness, you risk losing the people’s expectations. Think again on it.”

Liu Bei replied, “If I dare to seize the august seat, I would not do so. Let us discuss a greater strategy again.” All the generals spoke at once: “If Your Majesty keeps refusing, the common people’s hearts will part in confusion.”

Zhuge said, “Your Majesty has always taken righteousness as your root and has not been eager to call yourself lord by a title. Now that Jing and Xiang and both Sichuan are in your control, you can for now take the title King of Han.” Liu Bei said, “You all may wish to honor me as king, but without the Son of Heaven’s edict it is usurpation.” Zhuge said, “Now we must proceed by expediency and not cling to strict convention.”

Zhang Fei shouted, “Men of different clans all seek to be lords. How much more so, with Brother as a lineal scion of the Han throne. Need we say merely King of Han? Why not imperial title?” Liu Bei rebuked, “Do not speak too much!” Zhuge said, “Your Majesty should follow flexible action. Take first the rank of King of Han, and then report it to the Son of Heaven; that is no delay.”

Liu Bei delayed again and again, and at last reluctantly consented. In the autumn of the twenty-fourth year of the Jian’an era, in the seventh month, he built an altar at Mianyang, nine li in circuit, arranged the five directions with banners and honors. All ministers lined up in formal order. Xu Jing and Fa Zheng invited Liu Bei to mount the platform, and after receiving crown, seal, and ribbons, he faced south and sat while civil and military officials congratulated him as King of Han. Liu Shan was established as crown prince of the king. Xu Jing was made Grand Tutor. Fa Zheng was made Prefect of the Masters of Writing. Zhuge Liang was appointed as military adviser, and made to manage all major state and military affairs. Guan Yu, Zhang Fei, Zhao Yun, Ma Chao, and Huang Zhong were enfeoffed as the Five Tiger Generals. Wei Yan was made Administrator of Hanzhong Commandery. The rest of the merits and ennoblements were settled according to service records.

Now that Liu Bei had become King of Han, he drafted a memorial and sent envoys to Xu.

The memorial read:

I, Liu Bei, have but a servant’s talent and yet was entrusted with the office above general. I was given command over three armies and served outside the court; I have not been able to sweep away bandit disorder, steady the royal house, and thus for many days have delayed the Son of Heaven’s teaching and governance. Within the Four Seas heaven is not yet at peace; I am only anxious over reversals and turning tides, as if a fever had taken hold in my head.

In former days Dong Zhuo had made himself a source of disorder. Since then, lawless men ran rampant and plundered the realm. By Your Majesty’s holy virtue and command, ministers answered together. Either loyal men rose in resistance, or Heaven’s punishment struck down the violent and rebellious, and they gradually withered. Only Cao Cao has remained unremoved, and he has long misappropriated state authority, yielding his heart to ruin.

Formerly I once planned with Dong Cheng, General of Chariots and Cavalry, to punish Cao Cao. The matter was not held with care, and Cheng was caught in a trap. My base then shifted and broke, loyal effort bore no fruit; thus Cao Cao was made to run full stride in his villainy. He slaughtered the Son of Heaven and the Empress and poisoned imperial sons. Though I tried to forge alliances, my intent was to fight hard, yet I was weak and not forceful. For many years it availed nothing. I always feared I might perish and betray the emperor’s grace; day and night I kept sighing, startled in my sleep and wakeful as one who heeds danger.

Now my councillors and I agree that in the old records one is taught to settle the nine clans so that royal rule may be clarified and the line of sovereigns pass on in order; this way must not be abandoned. In the two Zhou dynasties, though many consorts were raised, success still came with the aid of ministers Pu and Zheng. When the Great Ancestor’s dragon rose, he honored his brother the king, opened the Nine Provinces, and in the end beheaded Lü’s household to secure the grand clan.

Now Cao Cao is ugly in intent and corrupt in uprightness, full of violent followers, storing treachery in his heart. His theft and usurpation are already clear. Since the imperial house is weak and the royal lineage has no seat, by referring to ancient precedent and adjusting to present necessity I submit that I, your subject, be made Great Commandant and King of Han.

Bowing in all three courts, having received deep favor from the state and bearing charge over one region, I have spent myself with little effect; what I have gained is already beyond enough. It is not fitting to keep presuming high office again and incur grave guilt. Pressed by ministers and officials, I am driven by duty and meaning. If I look away, rebels remain unpunished and the national danger continues. The ancestral temple tilts and the state’s altar and foundation are near collapse; truly my heart feels cracked to pieces. If expediency is needed to change and still the Holy Court, even water and fire would not let me refuse. Therefore I followed the advice of the officials and accepted the seal and cords to raise and strengthen the state’s authority.

As I look up, I find my title to be lofty and honored; as I look down, I think on how I might repay these benefits. My worry is deep, my accountability heavy; fear and alertness keep me awake like one standing at a ravine. How could I fail to exert every strength, devote my loyalty, reward the six armies, unite all the righteous, and in accord with Heaven and the time, crush the ferocious traitors and pacify the realm? I humbly submit this memorial.

When the memorial reached Xu, Cao Cao in Ye received word that Liu Bei had proclaimed himself King of Han and was furious.

“Woven-mat brat,” he said. “How dare you do this! I swear I will wipe him out.”

He immediately sent orders to raise all the nation’s troops and move into both Sichuan to decide life and death with the King of Han.

One official stepped forward to remonstrate, “Your Majesty, do not, for a moment’s anger, drive the chariot in person for a distant campaign. I have one plan that needs no bow or arrow. Let Liu Bei be left to suffer in Shu. When his army weakens and his strength drains, just send one general against him and he can be easily taken.”

Cao Cao looked at the man. It was Sima Yi. Cao Cao asked with joy, “What high thought has Zhongda?”

Yi said, “Sun Quan of Jiangdong married his sister to Liu Bei and then took her back in secret; Liu Bei in turn holds Jingzhou and does not return it. They both carry the hatred of biting teeth. Now send a persuasive envoy with letters to Sun Quan. Let him raise troops to seize Jingzhou. Liu Bei will certainly send his soldiers from both Sichuan to defend it. Then Your Majesty can march against Hanchuan; Liu Bei will be unable to protect his front and rear at once. He will surely be trapped.”

Cao Cao was delighted and immediately sent Fan Chong as envoy. Fan hastened through the night to Jiangdong. When Sun Quan learned that Fan Chong had arrived, he conferred with his ministers.

Zhang Zhao said, “Wei and Wu were not enemies by nature. Because we followed Zhuge’s words before, this has made our two houses wage wars back to back. The people are burning and grinding under the fire. Since this envoy has come now, he must bear an intention of peace. Receive him with courtesy.” Sun Quan followed this, and ordered all strategists to welcome Fan into the city. After the ceremony, he greeted him with proper state hospitality and gave him chamberly rest.

Fan presented Cao Cao’s letter:

“Between Wei and Wu there has long been no enmity. It is Liu Bei’s fault that this rift and clash have continued for years without cease, and that the people suffer through it. The King of Wei sends me here to propose that Commander-in-chief you and he raise forces for Jingzhou. When your army and mine meet, Wei king will press in at Hanchuan and strike at both front and rear. After defeating Liu Bei, we will divide the territory and swear never to invade each other’s lands.”

After reading the letter, Sun Quan held a banquet for Fan and then sent him back to a guesthouse for rest.

Sun Quan then consulted the strategic circle.

Guo Yong said, “Though there is reason in this argument, we can do two things at once: send Fan back with a message for a coordinated strike from both sides, and at the same time send men across the river to report on Yun Chang’s condition.”

Zhuge Jin said, “I have heard that Guan Yu came to Jingzhou and that Liu Bei has taken a wife and set household. He has one son and then a daughter; the girl is still young and not yet betrothed. I wish to ask for her on behalf of Your Majesty’s heir. If Guan Yu agrees, we can discuss together how to destroy Cao Cao. If he refuses, then we may aid Cao in taking Jingzhou.” Sun Quan accepted the plan. He first sent Fan home to Xu; then he dispatched Zhuge Jin as envoy to Jingzhou.

Upon entering the city, Guan Yu received him with ceremony. Guan Yu said, “Why has Ziyu come?”

Zhuge Jin said with deference, “I have come only to ask for harmony between our two houses. My lord, the Prince of Wu, has a son, who is very intelligent. Hearing that the general has a daughter, I come to ask for a marriage. It is a fine matter for both families; Lord, please consider.” Guan Yu grew fierce. “Would my tiger-girl agree to marry a dog’s whelp? Do not let me see your face, and I will cut your head down at once. Say no more!” He then ordered attendants to drive him out.

Zhuge Jin slunk away, kept his head low, and returned to Sun Quan. He hid nothing and reported everything exactly. Sun Quan was furious. “How could he be so impertinent?” he said, then called Zhang Zhao and other martial officers to plan the taking of Jingzhou.

Bu Zhi said, “Cao Cao long desired to usurp Han, and what he fears most is Liu Bei. He has sent an envoy to stir Wu’s troops into swallowing Shu. This means he has loaded Wu with trouble.”

Sun Quan said, “I have wished to seize Jingzhou for long.”

Bu Zhi replied, “Cao Ren is now encamped at Xiangyang and Fancheng. Since there is no great river barrier there and the dry route is open, Jingzhou can be taken by land. Why should we wait and move our host? This alone shows his intent. Your Majesty should send an envoy to Xu to Cao Cao and urge that Cao Ren take up his forces by land and seize Jingzhou first. Guan Yu will move his own troops and take Fancheng. If Guan Yu stirs, Your Majesty can send one general and take Jingzhou in one move in secret.”

Sun Quan followed this. He at once dispatched an envoy across the river to inform Cao Cao. Cao Cao rejoiced, ordered the envoy back ahead, and then sent Fan Chong to Fancheng to serve as strategist for Cao Ren and plan operations. At the same time he sent urgent orders to Eastern Wu for troop movement by water in support, with Jingzhou as the target.

Now the King of Han had ordered Wei Yan to supervise cavalry and horse supply, and to defend Dongchuan. He summoned all officials back to Chengdu. He ordered works for a palace and guesthouses and established more than four hundred mail stations and lodgings from Chengdu to Baishui. He hoarded grain and made many weapons, preparing to advance into Central Plains.

When agents reported that Cao Cao had allied with Eastern Wu and meant to take Jingzhou, they flew the news into Shu. The King hurriedly consulted Zhuge Liang. Kongming said, “I already expected Cao Cao to have this plan. But there are many clever men in Wu, and he will surely order Cao Ren to raise troops first.”

The King asked, “In that case, what should we do?” Zhuge said, “Send an edict and command to Yun Chang immediately, ordering him to raise troops and take Fancheng first. If he does so, the enemy force will grow fearful and naturally break.”

The King rejoiced at this and sent Fei Shi, the Sima officer, as messenger, with the king’s edict to Jingzhou.

Guan Yu left the city gate and welcomed him inside. At the hall of audience, with formal greetings complete, Guan Yu asked, “What rank has the King of Han granted me?”

Shi said, “Chief of the Five Tiger Generals.”

“Which five?” Guan Yu asked.

He replied, “Guan, Zhang, Zhao, Ma, and Huang.”

Guan Yu bristled. “Yide is my younger brother; Mengqi is famed in his generation; Zilong has long followed my brother, too, and is like my younger brother. Their standing may be made equal to mine. But who is Huang Zhong, to stand in the same line as me? A true man will never stand with old drudges!” So he refused to accept the seal and ribbons.
Shi laughed and said, “General, you are mistaken. In former days, Xiao He and Cao Shen were among Emperor Gaozu’s closest men when great matters were undertaken. Yet Han Xin, once a doomed general of Chu, was still raised to a king above both Xiao and Cao, and none of them made it their grievance. Now though the King of Han has conferred the title of Chief of the Five Tiger Generals, he and you are bound as brothers. You are one body. The general is the King of Han, and the King of Han is the general. How is this alike ordinary men? You receive great grace from the King of Han; you must share joy and suffering, fortune and misfortune with him, and should not argue over the relative heights of titles. I urge you to ponder this well.”

Guan Yu came to clarity. He bowed twice and said, “Through my lack of understanding, and not through your instruction, this nearly caused great error. I accept the seal and ribbons.”
When the king’s command had just been delivered, Shi ordered Guan Yu to lead his troops and take Fancheng.

Guan Yu accepted the order and at once sent Fu Shiren and Mi Fang as vanguard captains. He also sent one army to encamp outside Jingzhou; at the same time he prepared a banquet in the city and entertained Shi. As they drank until the second watch, a sudden report came that fire had broken out among the outer sentry camps. Guan Yu donned his armor and mounted. He went out and saw that Fu Shiren and Mi Fang, drunk at their tents, had left embers behind; they had caught fire to the cannons, and the whole camp shuddered in flame, all camp weapons and provisions burning to ruin.

Guan Yu rode to put out the fire and by the fourth watch it was finally gone.

Back in the city, he summoned Fu Shiren and Mi Fang and said, “I ordered you two as vanguard. You have not even left the camp, and yet you burned our own weapons and grain, and burned the military engines that shot our mounts. This mistake in action — how could either of you be useful?” He shouted for their execution.

Shi intervened, “You have not even left camp; to cut down your superior generals now is bad for the army. Their fault should be set aside for the moment.”

Guan Yu’s anger did not cool. He shouted to the two men, “I will not look on Shi’s face. I will cut down both your heads!” He then ordered warriors to cane each of them forty strokes, removed their vanguard seals, and reassigned Mi Fang to guard Nanjun, and Fu Shiren to guard Gong’an. “If I return in victory,” he said, “and there is any shortfall at all, both offenders will be punished again.” The two men left in shame. Guan Yu then made Liao Hua vanguard and Guan Ping deputy commander. He took total command of the center, with Ma Liang and Yi Ji as military advisers, and led the assault together. Earlier, Hu Ban, son of Hu Hua, had come from Jingzhou to surrender to Guan Yu. Guan Yu remembered the aid Hu Hua had once given him and loved the man. He sent Hu Ban with Shi back into Shu to report the conferment. Hu Ban bid farewell and returned with him to Shu.

Elsewhere that day, Guan Yu raised the main battle banner and reclined briefly in camp. Suddenly he saw a black pig as large as an ox burst into the pavilion and bite his left foot. He grew furious and drew his sword to cut it down, the sound ringing like torn silk. At once he woke with a start. It had all been a dream. Yet his left foot throbbed faintly. Deeply unsettled, he summoned Guan Ping and reported the dream.

Guan Ping answered, “A pig may carry dragon features; when a dragon joins the leg it is an omen of ascent. Do not mistrust it.”

Guan Yu assembled his officers in the pavilion and reported the omen. Some called it auspicious, others inauspicious; opinion was divided. Guan Yu said, “A man of my age near sixty, what regret is there if I die?” As he spoke, an envoy from Shu arrived with a command from the King of Han. He was appointed General of the Vanguard, granted the token ribbon, and made Superintendent of the nine commanderies in Jing and Xiang. After receiving the edict, the officers congratulated him, saying, “This is proof that the pig-dragon was favorable.” He then cast off his hesitation and raised the army toward Xiangyang.

At that time Cao Ren was in the city when news came that Guan Yu had come in command of his troops. He was startled and wanted to hold firm and not venture out. Deputy commander Zhai Yuan said, “The King of Wei asked this general and Commander-in-chief Cao to coordinate with Eastern Wu to take Jingzhou. He has come now by himself; this is a move to offer himself to death. Why then avoid him?” Adviser Fan Chong remonstrated, “I have long known Guan Yu to be brave and clever. We must not underestimate him. The best course is to stand firm and hold.”

Brave commander Xiahou Cun said, “That is bookman talk only. Have you not heard, ‘When the waters are shallow and mud covers the ford, a coming army should be met in the open square’? Our army is fresh while his is tired by march; we can win.” Cao Ren agreed and ordered Fan Chong to hold Fancheng while he personally led troops to meet Guan Yu. Guan Yu heard the Wei forces approaching and summoned Guan Ping and Liao Hua to consult and advance.

Liao Hua rode out to engage in skirmish; Zhai Yuan came to receive him. The two generals fought a little. Liao Hua feigned defeat and turned his horse and fled. Zhai Yuan pursued from behind and the Jingzhou troops fell back twenty li. The next day they fought again. Xiahou Cun and Zhai Yuan both came out to meet them. Again the Jingzhou soldiers were repelled and chased over twenty li. Then they suddenly heard loud shouts behind them and drums and horns sounding as one. Cao Ren hurriedly ordered the front line to turn and run back; from behind, Guan Ping and Liao Hua were striking down toward them. The Wei army was thrown into confusion. Realizing he had been tricked, Cao Ren at once cut out one army and dashed for Xiangyang; several miles from the city, banners in bright silk snapped forward from the front, and Guan Yu reined in his horse sideways and blocked the road. Cao Ren was terrified, trembling in fear, and dared not make frontal contact. He slipped out along a slanting road toward Xiangyang. Guan Yu did not pursue. Soon Xiahou Cun’s force arrived and seeing Guan Yu, grew furious and engaged. In a single clash, Guan Yu killed him. Zhai Yuan fled, and Guan Ping caught up and cut him down in one stroke. In the press of pursuit, most of Cao’s men died in the Xiang River. Cao Ren retreated and withdrew to Fancheng.

After taking Xiangyang, Guan Yu rewarded the troops and pacified the people. Wang Pu, his chief clerk, said, “General, in one drum of time you brought down Xiangyang, and though Cao’s men are disoriented, my poor opinion is this: on the eastern side, Lü Meng is encamped at Lukou and often wants to swallow Jingzhou. If he advances straight toward it, how are we to meet that?”

Guan Yu said, “I have also thought of this. You can take this matter in hand. Along the river above and below, every twenty or thirty li choose high mounds and build signal towers. Put fifty soldiers in each tower. If Wu troops cross the river, burn bright fire at night and raise smoke by day as signals. I will ride to meet them myself.”
Wang Pu said, “Mi Fang and Fu Shiren hold the two passes and I fear they are not earnest enough. We need another to supervise all Jingzhou.”

Guan Yu said, “I already assigned Pan Jun to the inner office. Why this concern?”

Wang Pu said, “Pan Jun all his life has been cautious and fond of profit; he cannot be trusted with this charge. Send Zhaolei, deputy commander and logistics officer. Zhaolei is loyal, upright, and frugal. If we use him, there will be no failure.”
Guan Yu replied, “I have long known Pan Jun. Now he is already assigned; there is no need to change. Zhaolei now oversees grain and provisions; that too is an important matter. You need not suspect. Build the beacons and watchtowers only.”

Wang Pu bowed, still troubled, and left. Guan Yu ordered Guan Ping to prepare boats for crossing the Xiang River and to attack Fancheng.

Back at Fancheng, Cao Ren had lost two commanders and retired to the city. He told Fan Chong, “I did not follow your advice, and the army was lost and Xiangyang lost. How are we to endure?” Fan Chong said, “Guan Yu is a tiger general, ingenious and wise. He must not be underestimated. We should hold the city alone.” As this was being spoken, news came that Guan Yu had crossed the river and was coming to assault Fancheng. Cao Ren was alarmed. Fan said again, “We must keep firm.”

Deputy commander Lü Chang suddenly said, “Your servant asks for several thousand troops. I am willing to meet the enemy in the waters of Xiang River.” Fan remonstrated, “No.” Lü Chang grew angry. “You civil officials only repeat: ‘hold the city.’ How can that alone drive back the enemy? Have you not heard war doctrine: ‘When an army is halfway across a river, strike them then’? Guan Yu is halfway across the Xiang River now. Why not strike him? If he reaches the ramparts, he will be at the ditch and difficult to resist.”

Cao Ren took two thousand and sent Lü Chang out of Fancheng to meet battle. Lü Chang arrived at the river mouth and saw ahead the bright banners. Guan Yu, cross-sword raised in hand, came out. Lü Chang tried to come forward to engage. From behind, the rest of the army saw Guan Yu’s awe-inspiring vigor and began to retreat before striking; Lü Chang could not stop them. Guan Yu rushed on through mixed close-combat, and the Wei army was routed. The mounted and foot forces were broken in large part. The survivors fled in disarray into Fancheng. Cao Ren immediately sent for help and dispatched riders by night to Chang’an with a petition to Cao Cao: “Guan Yu has taken Xiangyang. Now he besieges Fancheng in grave urgency. Please send the Great General.”

Cao Cao pointed to a man in his staff and said, “You should go and break the siege.” The man came out at once. The onlookers saw it was Yu Jin. Yu Jin said, “I ask leave to act as vanguard with one general and take troops with me.” Cao asked the assembled, “Who dares be vanguard?” One man came forth. “I volunteer for this dangerous vanguard mission. I will capture General Guan alive and present him beneath your standard.” Cao Cao looked at him with joy.

It was said:

The lords of Wu have not yet come to watch for openings, yet first the forces of northern Wei send forth more troops.
Who this man is

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Liu Bei Ascends as King of Han and Yunchang Attacks Xiangyang Commandery

chapters.html:
Pang De lifts a coffin to fight to the death, Guan Yu unleashes the waters and drowns seven armies.

Cao Cao was preparing to send Yu Jin to Fancheng to relieve its danger. He asked among his generals who would dare to lead the vanguard. One man called out that he would go. When Cao Cao looked at him, it was Pang De. Cao Cao was overjoyed and said, “That Guan fellow has his reputation shaking all under heaven, but he has not yet met his match; this time he meets a proper rival.” Cao Cao appointed Yu Jin as General Who Conquers the South and made Pang De the western vanguard leader of seven divisions, and ordered them to advance on Fancheng. All seven divisions were troops of hard, northern-blooded men. The two officers in charge of the vanguard were named Dong Heng and Dong Chao. That day they were all called before Yu Jin to pay their respects. Dong Heng spoke, “My general takes seven solid masses of heavy troops to break through the peril at Fancheng and expects certain victory; yet making Pang De the vanguard seems an unwise choice.” Alarmed, Yu Jin asked why. Dong Heng replied, “Pang De was once a deputy under Ma Chao and had no choice but to submit to Wei. His former lord is in Shu and holds office as one of the Five Tiger Senior Generals. His elder brother Pang Rou is also an officer in Western Sichuan. If this man leads the vanguard, it is like pouring oil on a fire. Why not report this to the King of Wei and send another in his place?”

When Yu Jin heard this, he went straight to Cao Cao by night and reported it. Cao Cao understood at once, summoned Pang De to the steps, and ordered him to accept the vanguard token. Pang De was greatly startled and asked, “I wanted to exert myself for the Great King; why does he not make use of me?” Cao Cao replied, “I have no suspicion at all. But Ma Chao is now in the Western Lands, and your brother Pang Rou is in the Western Lands, both serving Liu Bei. Even if I trust you, what of the many voices outside?”

Hearing this, Pang De removed his cap, knelt, and knelt with blood at his lip, saying, “Since I came to surrender in Hanzhong, I have always remembered the Great King’s immense kindness; even if I spilled my liver and brains upon the earth, I still could not repay it. Why does the Great King doubt me? When I was still at my home, I lived with my brother; my sister-in-law was not easy at all, and in drunkenness I slew her. My brother’s hatred of me entered his very marrow; he swore never to meet me again; our bonds were already severed. My former lord Ma Chao had courage but no strategy; in defeat he lost his lands and went alone into Sichuan. Now each of us serves our own lord, and old loyalty is gone. I, who owe the Great King favor and grace, dare not allow any contrary thought to rise within me. Only may the Great King judge me.”

Cao Cao helped him up and reassured him. “I have always known your loyalty. I spoke earlier only to calm the hearts of others. You can strive to earn merit. You will not fail me, and I will not fail you.”

Pang De bowed in thanks and returned home. He ordered carpenters to make a wooden coffin. The next day he invited his close friends to a formal meal and set the coffin in the hall. All his kin and friends were shocked when they saw it and asked, “General, you are leading the army—why bring this ominous thing?” Taking a cup, Pang De told them, “I received the Great King’s deep mercy and swore to repay it with my life. Tomorrow I go to Fancheng to settle accounts with that Guan one-on-one. If I cannot kill him, he will kill me. If he does not kill me, then I shall kill myself. Therefore I prepare this coffin now so there is no shame of coming home empty-handed.”

All sighed. Pang De called his wife, Lady Li, and his son Pang Hui to come out. To his wife he said, “As vanguard, I should return death on the field. If I die, you must raise our son carefully. Our son has uncommon signs in him; when he grows, he will one day avenge me.” The wife and son wept terribly at parting. Pang De had them help carry the coffin.

He then told his officers, “I am going to give my life in battle against that Guan fellow. If I am killed by him, take my body at once and place it in this coffin. If I kill him, put his head here too and send it back to the King of Wei.” The five hundred officers and soldiers all said, “A general so loyal and brave as you—who among us would not spare no effort to assist?” They moved out with the army.

Someone reported these words to Cao Cao. Cao Cao said, “Pang De is so loyal and brave; why should I worry?” Jia Xu warned, “Pang De trusts to blood and courage and seeks a decisive struggle with that Guan fellow. I privately fear it.” Cao Cao accepted his point and ordered that this message be conveyed to Pang De: “That Guan is strong in wit as well as courage. Do not lightly challenge him. If he is attainable, take him; if not, you must hold fast.”

Upon hearing the command, Pang De told his officers, “What does the Great King value that man so highly for? I think on this mission I will crush him and shatter the thirty-year fame of his name.” Yu Jin said, “What the Wei king has said must be followed.” With an outburst of force, Pang De drove his troops forward to Fancheng and advanced with blare and drum.

Now Guan Gong sat in camp when a courier on horseback burst in with news: “Cao Cao has sent Yu Jin out and the seven iron-strong divisions have arrived. The vanguard, Pang De, carries a wooden coffin before his army and speaks with immodest words, vowing to decide this by a death match. He is still only thirty li from the city.” Hearing this, Guan Yu, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, went red, his fine beard tossing violently. In fury he cried, “Among all under Heaven, whoever hears my name bows in fear. How can this vulgar fool Pang De dare to ignore me? Guan Ping, you strike Fancheng from one side; I will go myself and behead this common brute to settle my grievance.”

Guan Ping said, “Father should not match himself against a stubborn rock with the weight of Mount Tai. Let me, your unworthy son, take your place and fight Pang De.” Guan Yu answered, “Go test him once; I will come immediately behind to assist.”

Guan Ping mounted, took up his blade, and led a force to meet Pang De. The two ranks faced each other. On the Wei side a black banner displayed four white words: “Nan’an Pang De.” Pang De, in a blue robe with silver armor and white horse, stood in front of his line. Behind him five hundred soldiers followed closely, and several footmen bore the coffin on their shoulders. Guan Ping shouted at him, “Traitor who betrayed your lord!”

Pang De asked his men, “Who is that?” One answered, “It is Guan Ping, the righteous son of Guan Gong.” De said, “I come by order of the King of Wei to fetch your father’s head. You are a miserable, pockmarked child; I will not kill you. Call your father at once!”

Guan Ping erupted with fury, spurred his horse, and drew his knife in a leap to take Pang De. Pang De crossed blades with him. They fought thirty passes and neither gained clear advantage, and both lines withdrew.

Some soon reported this to Guan Gong. He was furious and sent Liao Hua to attack Fancheng, while he himself rode out to face the vanguard. Guan Ping reported that he and Pang De had fought without either side winning. Guan Yu immediately rode out with his saber drawn and shouted, “Guan Yu is here. Why does Pang De not come sooner to die?” As drumbeats thundered, Pang De rode out and said, “By the King of Wei’s command I came especially to take your head. If you do not believe me, I have prepared this coffin. If you fear death, dismount now and surrender!” Guan Gong shouted back, “What can you fool do? You cannot stand before me! Shame to let this green-dragon blade of mine cut down a vermin-thief like you!” He spurred forward, saber in hand, to take Pang De. Pang De angled his blade to meet him. The two generals fought more than a hundred rounds; their spirits only seemed to swell. Those who watched on both sides gaped in stupefaction.

Wei troops, fearing Pang De might lose the edge, ordered the signal for recall. Guan Ping, fearing his father’s age, also ordered recall. The two withdrew. When Pang De returned to camp, he said to his men, “People have spoken of Guan Gong as a hero. Now only today do I truly believe it.” As he spoke, Yu Jin arrived.

After saluting, Yu Jin said, “I hear you fought Guan Gong and after hundred rounds no room for advantage has been won. Why not withdraw for now?” Pang De snapped, “The King of Wei has appointed me as a great general. Why should I be so weak? Tomorrow I will settle death with him; I swear I will not retreat.” Yu Jin did not dare to stop him and left.

Guan Yu rode back to camp and said to Guan Ping, “Pang De’s blade work is accustomed and measured. He is a true opponent for me.” Guan Ping replied, “It is said, ‘A calf newborn does not fear the tiger.’ Even if father severs this man’s head, he is only a petty trooper from Xiqiang. If even then there is carelessness, it would not honor Brother-in-law’s trust.” Guan Yu said, “If I do not kill him now, how can my grievance be cleared? My decision is made. Speak no more.”

The next day he mounted and led troops forward. Pang De also brought his men to meet him. The two armies lined opposite and both leaders rode out together without much exchange, meeting in direct charge. After more than fifty exchanges, Pang De turned his horse and made a sword-dragging retreat. Guan Yu drove after him in pursuit. Guan Ping, fearing some gap in the moment, followed right behind.

From horseback Guan Yu shouted, “Rogue, you are using that blade-drag trick. Am I frightened by you?” Unknown to them, Pang De had only feigned a dragging-sword retreat, then hooked his blade in the saddle rigging, secretly drew a bow, set an arrow, and loosed it.

Guan Ping’s eyes were quick. Seeing Pang De pulling the bow, he cried out, “Bandit general, do not release a cold arrow!” Guan Yu only then opened his eyes wide; the bowstring sounded and the arrow was already in flight. He had nowhere to dodge, and it struck his left arm squarely. Guan Ping rode up and carried his father back to camp.

Pang De wheeled his horse and came on, blade turning, then suddenly heard the great drums pounding from his own camp. Fearing disorder in the rear, he checked his horse and turned back. In truth, when Yu Jin saw Pang De had wounded Guan Yu, he feared this could bring too much merit to him and ruin Yu Jin’s standing with the ranks, so he signaled a recall. Pang De returned and asked why the recall had sounded.

Yu Jin said, “The King of Wei warned: Guan is perfect in both wit and courage. Although he is struck by an arrow, he may only be feigning; that is why the drums were sounded.” Pang De replied, “If I had not recalled, I would already have beheaded this man.” Yu Jin said, “There is no good in hurrying to a reckless pace. We must seek a more deliberate plan.” Pang De did not understand Yu Jin’s intent and regretted it bitterly.

Guan Yu returned to his camp and pulled out the arrowhead. It had not gone in deep, and he dressed the wound with gold medicine. Guan Yu blamed Pang De and told his officers, “I swear to repay this single arrow’s injury.” His officers answered, “General, rest for a few days, then fight is still not too late.” The next day a man reported that Pang De was pressing the battle. Guan Yu prepared to go out and fight. His officers restrained him. Pang De ordered a small detachment to hurl insults. Guan Ping blocked the pass and told his officers not to report to Guan Yu.

For more than ten days Pang De exchanged blows and no one dared to come out. He then discussed with Yu Jin and said, “I have seen Guan’s head wound from the arrow now break open and he can barely move. Why not use this chance, unite seven divisions, and surge in one wave into camp—thus breaking the siege of Fancheng?” Yu Jin, fearing that Pang De might truly succeed, only pushed back the King of Wei’s warning and refused to move troops.

Pang De repeatedly tried to move, and Yu Jin would not allow him. So they shifted the seven divisions around a mountain pass and camped ten li north of Fancheng, under a mountain. Yu Jin then took command of the main road and ordered Pang De to quarter his troops behind the valley, preventing him from making a successful advance.

When Guan Ping saw Guan Yu’s arrow wound had closed, he rejoiced greatly. He then heard that Yu Jin had moved the seven divisions to camp north of Fancheng ten li away and did not yet know its purpose. He reported this to Guan Yu. Guan Yu mounted and from a high mound with a few riders looked over. He saw the city flags at Fancheng in disorder and the soldiers inside in confusion; he saw horse and troops camped in the valley ten li north of the city, and the current of Xiangjiang running fiercely.

After looking for a while, he asked the local guide, “What is the name of that valley ten li north of Fancheng?” The guide replied, “It is Zengkou Creek.” Guan Yu cried out in joy, “Yu Jin is doomed and will be captured.” An officer asked, “How do you know?”

Guan Yu said, “Once fish enter a net-mouthed river trap, can they ever linger long?” The other generals did not believe him. Guan Yu returned to his own camp.

It was the autumn of the eighth lunar month; rain had come for several days. Guan Yu ordered boats and rafts prepared and all water gear readied.

Guan Ping asked, “Why need water gear while we are holding by land?”

Guan Yu said, “You do not understand. Yu Jin has not camped his seven divisions on open high ground but gathered them at the tight defile of Zengkou Creek. Now this autumn rains have been continuous and the Xiang River will surely rise. I have already sent men to dam each water intake. When the waters come up, I will go high with boats and release the flow. The soldiers of Fancheng and Zengkou Creek will be like fish and turtles in a single instant.”

Guan Ping saluted and acknowledged.

In the Wei camp at Zengkou Creek the rains did not cease for days. Cheng He, a supervising officer, reported to Yu Jin, “The main army camps at the river mouth where the land is low. Though there is a dirt embankment, it is far from camp. These autumn rains make life hard for the soldiers. This is what I heard: soldiers of Jing Province have moved to high mounds and prepared fighting rafts at the mouth of the Han River. If the Yangtze water rises, our army will be in peril. We should make a plan at once.”

Yu Jin shouted, “Are you a rogue trying to confuse my army’s heart? Speak again and you will be executed!” Cheng He, ashamed and humbled, withdrew, then came to Pang De and spoke of the report. Pang De said, “You have seen rightly. Yu Jin refuses to move the troops; tomorrow I will shift the camp elsewhere.” As the plan settled, a storm and wind broke out that night.

Pang De sat in his tent when he heard horses running in all directions and war drums rumbling like earth itself. He bolted out, mounted, and looked. Water surged in from every side; seven divisions fled in wild panic, and in some places whole waves carried men away. Flooded level ground was deep as seven feet or more. Yu Jin, Pang De, and the other generals all climbed low hills to escape the water.

By dawn, Guan Yu and his officers raised banners and drums and arrived on large ships. Yu Jin saw that there was no route to escape, with only five or six dozen men left beside him. He judged they could not flee and spoke of surrender. Guan Yu ordered everyone to strip off armor and clothing, then took them aboard and then came to seize Pang De.

At that time Pang De, together with the two Dongs and Cheng He and five hundred foot soldiers, all without armor, stood on the levee. When Guan Yu came, Pang De showed no fear and advanced proudly to meet battle. Guan Yu sealed the four sides of ships around them. Soldiers on all sides loosed arrows, killing more than half the Wei soldiers.

Dong Heng and Dong Chao saw the crisis and said to Pang De, “Most soldiers are badly wounded and broken, and there is no path out. Better to surrender.” Pang De was enraged: “I have received great favor from the Great King. Would I ever stoop in yielding submission?” He immediately executed Dong Heng and Dong Chao before the troops and shouted, “If anyone speaks of surrender again, let this be the example of these two!” Then all fought on with renewed force.

From dawn to noon, courage doubled. Guan Yu pressed attacks from all sides, while arrows and stones fell like rain. Pang De ordered his soldiers to use close weapons and meet him hand to hand. He turned to Cheng He, saying, “I have heard it said: ‘A brave commander does not fear death for safety. A stout warrior does not break his honor to save his life. This is the day I die.’ You should fight with all your strength.” Cheng He obeyed and moved forward. Guan Yu shot him with one arrow and he fell into the water.

All the Wei troops surrendered; only Pang De alone still resisted fiercely. Just then several men from Jing Province drove a small boat close to the levee. Pang De swung his saber, leaped and stood aboard, killing more than ten at once. The rest tossed their boat and leapt into the water to escape. Holding a saber in one hand and a short paddle in the other, Pang De tried to row toward Fancheng.

From upstream came another of their commanders on a broad raft. He crashed the small boat, and Pang De tumbled into the water. The commander jumped after him, and with skill in water and strength of arm from years spent in Jing Province, he captured Pang De and hauled him aboard.

All present saw that the man who seized Pang De was Zhou Cang. Yu Jin and the seven divisions he had commanded drowned in the water. Those swept by water with no route of escape all surrendered as well.

Later poets wrote:

At midnight, war drums thunder through heaven, and in Xiang and Fancheng the flat land becomes a deep abyss. Who can keep pace with Guan Gong’s stratagem? His fame across Hua Xia will be sung forever.

Guan Yu returned to the high mound, mounted, and sat in his tent. An executioner unit brought Yu Jin in chains. Yu Jin prostrated himself on the ground and begged for mercy.

Guan Yu said, “How dare you oppose me?”

Yu Jin answered, “The command came from the Son of Heaven; I had no choice. I beg Your Lordship for pity and swear to repay in death.”

Guan Yu laughed with a broad beard and said, “If I kill you, it is like killing a dog or a boar—only to soil my saber and axe in vain.” He ordered him bound and sent to the Jingshou jail to be held: “When I return, I will decide differently.” Then they sent Pang De in also.

Pang De, brows knitted and eyes fierce, stood upright and refused to kneel. Guan Yu said, “Your brother is now in Hanzhong. Your former lord Ma Chao is also a major general in Shu. Why did you not submit earlier?” Pang De, in rage, said, “I would sooner die beneath your blade than yield to you!” He did not stop cursing.

Guan Yu was furious and ordered the executioners to bring him forward and behead him at once. Pang De offered his neck to the punishment. Yet Guan Yu, with pity, gave him burial.

Because the waters had not yet ebbed, he then boarded warships again, bringing larger and smaller officers with him to attack Fancheng.

Meanwhile around Fancheng the waves were roiling, and the current only grew. The city walls grew wet and crumbled. Men and women carried earth and bricks to stuff and repair the breaches but could not stem it. Cao Ren’s assembled officers all lost heart and rushed to report.

Cao Ren said, “Today’s danger cannot be met by strength. We can still seize boats and flee by night before the enemy arrives. Even losing the city, we might yet preserve our lives.” As they were arranging this, Man Chong interjected, “Do not. The flood has surged with violence and cannot last forever; it will retreat in less than ten days. Though Guan has not yet attacked, he has sent separate generals down below Jiaxia. Why he does not rush forward is that he fears our striking at his rear. If we abandon this city now, all south of the Yellow River will no longer belong to Wei.”

Cao Ren folded his hands and thanked him. “Without your counsel, we might nearly have ruined the state’s affair.” He then mounted a white horse and went to the walls, gathering the officers to swear: “I received orders from the King of Wei to guard this city. Any man who speaks of abandonment will be beheaded.” All the officers said, “We are willing to hold and defend to death!” Cao Ren was overjoyed and set hundreds of crossbowmen atop the walls. Troops stood watch day and night and dared not slacken. Old and young civilians carried soil and stone to reinforce the walls.

In ten days the waters slowly retreated.

After Guan Yu had captured Yu Jin and others, Guan Yu’s prestige shook heaven and earth; no one was unmoved. At that time his second son Guan Xing came into camp to visit. Guan Yu ordered him to carry various petitions for promotion to Chengdu, before King Liu, and seek advancement for each officer. Guan Xing bade farewell to his father and headed straight to Chengdu.

Guan Yu then split the army in half and sent it directly to Jiaxia. He himself led the rest and attacked Fancheng from all four sides. That day he rode to the north gate, raised his whip in the air, and shouted, “You rat-like rabble, why do you still not submit? How much longer will you delay?”

As he spoke, Cao Ren happened to be on the enemy tower and saw Guan Yu with only a heart-covering shirt and vest draped over him, exposing a green cloak. He immediately called for five hundred archers, and they loosed arrows together. Guan Yu pulled his horse back sharply, and an arbalest bolt struck his right arm as he dismounted.

At that moment:

Water still held the seven divisions in fear, and one arrow within the city suddenly wounded him. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Pang De Raises a Coffin to Fight to the Death, and Guan Yu Unleashes the Flood to Swallow Seven Armies

chapters.html:
Later, Cao Ren saw Guan Yu fall from his horse and led troops in a charge out of the city. Guan Ping drove them back in one rush, rescued Guan Yu, and returned him to camp, then withdrew the arrow from his arm. The arrowhead was coated with poison; the toxin had penetrated into the bone. His right arm had swollen blue and could not be moved.

Guan Ping and the officers, all in a panic, conferred together. “If Father loses this arm, how can he face the enemy? It is better for him to return to Jing Province and recuperate for now.” With that agreement they entered Guan Yu’s tent. Guan Yu asked, “What has brought you all here?”

The officers answered, “Because we saw that my lord’s right arm is badly injured, we fear you may become angry in the field and that close combat will be difficult. The officers have decided it is best for you to pull back your campaign for now and return to Jing Province to treat the wound.”

Guan Yu growled, “I will take Fan City and it is but a short distance away. Once I have taken Fan City, I will drive the army forward and march straight to Xu City, wipe out the Wei rebels, and then pacify the Han court. How can a small wound be allowed to endanger the great work?”

The officers remained silent and withdrew.

Since he could not be persuaded to retire and the wound had not healed, he sent men in all directions to look for a famous physician. One day, somebody came from Jiangdong in a small boat and landed before the camp gate. A junior officer introduced him to Guan Ping. Guan Ping looked at him closely.

He wore a broad scarf and loose robe, with a blue medicine satchel strapped to his arm. He said, “My name is from Qiao Commandery in Pei State. My surname is Hua, my given name is Tuo, and my courtesy name is Yuanhua.”

He added, “I heard that General Guan is the heroic man of all beneath Heaven. Now that he has been poisoned by an arrow, I came especially to treat him.”

Guan Ping exclaimed, “Could you be the physician who once healed Zhou Tai of Eastern Wu?”

Hua Tuo replied, “I am.”
