Guan Ping was overjoyed and led Hua Tuo, together with the officers, into Guan Yu’s tent. Guan Yu, though in pain in his arm and fearing any delay to his soldiers, was then playing chess with Ma Liang. When he heard a doctor had arrived, he sent for him.

After the formalities, he was seated and given tea. After tea ended, Hua Tuo asked to examine his arm. Guan Yu removed part of his outer robe, stretched out the arm, and ordered him to inspect it.

Hua Tuo said, “This is an injury from a crossbow bolt, and the arrowhead contains poison of aconite. It has gone straight through to the bone. If not treated quickly, this arm will be useless.”

Guan Yu asked, “What shall be used to treat it?”

Hua Tuo said, “I have my own method, but I fear your lordship may be afraid.”

Guan Yu laughed. “I look at death as going home. What is there to fear?”

Hua Tuo replied, “In a quiet place, set up a tall post and fasten a large ring to it. Ask your lordship to pass his arm through the ring and tie it with rope. Then cover his head with a quilt. I will take a sharp knife and cut through the skin and flesh down to the bone, scrape away the poison from the bone, apply medicine, and stitch the wound shut with thread. Then all will be well. Again, I fear your lordship may be afraid.”

Guan Yu laughed again. “If it is so straightforward, why a post and ring at all?”

He ordered that a banquet be prepared.

After several cups of wine, Guan Yu resumed his game with Ma Liang, extended his arm, and asked Hua Tuo to make the cut.

Hua Tuo took a narrow knife in hand, told one junior officer to hold a large basin under the arm to catch blood, and said, “I will begin at once. Your lordship should not startle.”

Guan Yu replied, “Do as you wish. Am I like the ordinary men of this world who are afraid of pain?”

Then Hua Tuo cut through the skin and flesh to the bone; the bone was already stained blue. He scraped with his knife and heard a harsh, rasping sound. All who watched, both within and without the tent, covered their faces and turned pale.

Guan Yu drank his wine and ate meat, still chatting and laughing over chess without a sign of pain.

In a little while blood flowed in full measure. Hua Tuo scraped away all the poison, applied medicine, and stitched the wound. Guan Yu sat up and laughed.

He said to the officers, “The arm feels as free as before and there is no pain at all. You are truly a divine physician, Master.”

Hua Tuo said, “In my life I have never seen anything like this. My lord is truly heaven-endowed!”

Later, people made this poem:

In treatment, one must distinguish inner from outer wounds, For the world has few arts that surpass this craft. His divine authority can scarcely match General Guan, But the holy hand that heals can be only Hua Tuo.

After the arrow wound had healed, Guan Yu held a formal seat and thanked Hua Tuo. Hua Tuo said, “Your lord’s wound is healing, but it still requires care. Do not let anger touch and worsen it. After more than one hundred days, it will be as it was before.”

Guan Yu paid him one hundred taels of gold. Hua Tuo said, “I heard of my lord’s lofty righteousness and came only to treat him. Why should he expect a payment from me?” he refused and would not take it. He left a single prescription for medicine to be applied to the wound and left, bidding farewell.

Meanwhile, Guan Yu had captured Yu Jin and executed Pang De. His fame grew and shook all of Hua Xia, and all under the Central Plains were astonished. A courier arrived at Xu City.

Cao Cao was greatly alarmed. He gathered his civil and military officers and discussed the matter. “I have long known that Yunchang’s wisdom and courage fill the world. Now he has seized Jingzhou and Xiang province; like a tiger he has sprouted wings. Yu Jin has been captured and Pang De beheaded. If his forces then push directly on Xu City, what can we do? I wish to move the capital to escape him.”

Sima Yi remonstrated, “Do not do that. Yu Jin and the rest were swept by water, not defeated in battle. For the larger design of the state, this has not truly harmed us. Now Sun and Liu are out of favor with each other and Yunchang has risen. Sun Quan will not be pleased. Your Majesty can send a message east to Wu and explain the dangers; ask Sun Quan to raise troops in secret behind Yunchang’s lines. On the day the matter is settled, grant Sun land south of the river as a fief, and the peril at Fan City will dissolve.”

The registrar Jiang Ji said, “Zi-da’s words are sound. We can send a messenger to Eastern Wu immediately and need not move the capital with all the court.”

Cao Cao accepted the advice and did not move the capital. He sighed and said to the officers, “Yu Jin has served me for thirty years. How could he, in disaster, fail me more than Pang De?”

“He must have already been captured while crossing the river. At least he did not fall in battle,” he said, then added in frustration, “I will dispatch one message to Wu, and at the same time I must appoint a great general to blunt Yunchang’s edge.”

Before he had finished speaking, a junior commander shouted from below, “I volunteer.”

Cao Cao looked at him: it was Xu Huang.

Cao Cao rejoiced and immediately raised fifty thousand troops, appointing Xu Huang commander with Lu Jian as his deputy. They set out at dawn, advanced to the Yangling Marsh, and made camp. From there they waited for a fitting signal from the southeast before advancing.

When Sun Quan received Cao Cao’s letter, he read it and readily agreed. He had a reply prepared and sent it back by messenger, then gathered his ministers and officers for discussion.

Zhang Zhao said, “I just heard that Yunchang has captured Yu Jin and executed Pang De, shaking all the lands. Cao Cao now speaks of moving his capital to evade this thrust. Fan City is in danger, and he has asked for aid. After the matter is settled, he may turn and break his promise.”

Sun Quan had not yet spoken when he suddenly heard the report: Lü Meng had come in a small boat from Lukou with matters to present in person. He summoned him.

Lü Meng said, “Guan Yunchang has brought his army to besiege Fan City. This is a chance: he has moved far out. Strike into Jingzhou while he is absent.”

Sun Quan asked, “I had intended to seize Xu Province in the north. What do you think?”

Lü Meng replied, “Cao Cao is far away in Hebei and has no time to attend to the east. Xu Province has few guards and can be taken, but its terrain favors land warfare and does not favor water. Even if we take it, holding it will be difficult. Better to take Jingzhou first, hold the Yangtze fully, and then make better plans.”

Sun Quan said, “I did say I wanted Xu Province; I spoke to test you only. Draw my plan in writing as quickly as you can. I will raise troops thereafter.”

Lü Meng took leave and returned to Lukou. Soon scouts reported signals along the river, two or three tens of li apart, with beacons lit on raised mounds. They also heard that Jingzhou was already in strict order and seemingly preparing for contingencies. Lü Meng was startled. “If this is so, there is urgent reason to rethink! Before the Lord of Wu, I urged taking Jingzhou—what shall I do now?” He could find no answer.

He pretended to be sick, stayed indoors, and sent word back to Sun Quan of illness.

Hearing that Lü Meng was unwell, Sun Quan was pained and somewhat resentful. Lu Xun spoke, “Lu Ziming’s illness is a pretense, not real.”

Sun said, “Since Boyan already knows the pretense, he should go at once to inspect him.”

Lu Xun accepted the order and that night came to the camp at Lukou to see Lü Meng. As expected, he had no look of illness.

He said, “I am here on behalf of the lord of Wu to inquire respectfully about your valued health, General Ziming.”

Lü Meng answered, “My humble body is somewhat unwell. What need to worry?”

Lu Xun said, “The lord has entrusted you with heavy responsibility. You did not act in time and hold back your troops in resentment. Why is that?”

Lü Meng looked at Lu Xun for some time but said nothing.

Lu Xun continued, “I have a small remedy for the general’s sickness. Can it be used?”

Lü Meng dismissed his attendants and asked, “General Boyan has a sound method. Lend it to me at once.”

Lu Xun laughed. “Ziming’s illness is not in his body. It is because Jingzhou’s forces are fully drilled and beacons stand ready along the river. My idea is this: order all frontier officers along the Yangtze to be unable to raise beacon fires. Then the troops of Jingzhou will be left with no choice but to surrender. Can that be done?”

Lü Meng, startled, thanked him. “Those words cut through my lungs and entrails as if they were my own. I wish to hear the full stratagem.”

Lu Xun said, “Yunchang relies on his reputation and believes he is invincible; his only concern is this general. Use this moment. Feign illness and resign, leaving Lu-kou to another. Let that other praise Guan Yu in humble words and flatter him so that he becomes proud. He will pull all his Jingzhou troops toward Fan City. If Jingzhou has no precautions prepared, then with a single brigade and unusual tactics he can be struck. Jingzhou will then be in our grasp.”

Lü Meng was delighted. “It is excellent strategy.”

Following this, Lü Meng stayed in bed and submitted a petition of resignation. Lu Xun returned to Sun Quan and explained the full stratagem. Sun then recalled Lü Meng to Jianye to continue his recovery.

When Lü Meng arrived, he presented himself before Sun Quan. Sun said, “For the post of Lukou, Lord Zhou Jujin once recommended Lu Ziming’s predecessor, and Lu Ziming then recommended you in his place. Now you must recommend a man both reputable and respected to replace you here.”

Lü Meng said, “If a man of famous standing is chosen, Yunchang will become cautious. Lu Xun has deep thought but no wide name, and is no target for Yunchang’s suspicion. If he were put in my place immediately, it could do good.”

Sun Quan rejoiced and that very day appointed Lu Xun as Deputy General and Right Commander, replacing Lü Meng at Lukou.

Lu Xun bowed and said, “I am young and unlearned. I fear I am not equal to so great a responsibility.”

Sun Quan said, “Yiming, I cannot trust you to fail. Do not decline.”

Lu Xun accepted the token of office and rode through the night. The transfer of the mounted and naval forces was completed. He then drafted a letter and included names of horse, patterned brocade, wine, and gifts and asked a messenger to carry it to Fan City to greet Guan Yu.

At that time Guan Yu was really only resting his arrow wound and had not moved. A messenger announced: “The frontier commander of Lukou, Lü Meng, is critically ill. Sun has brought him back to recover. He has now made Lu Xun a commander, replacing Lü Meng. Today Lu Xun has dispatched messengers with gifts, to first congratulate your lordship and second seek peace between our two houses. Pray permit their stay.”

Guan Yu summoned the messenger and said, “Zhongmou’s insight is shallow; he puts this child in command!”

The messenger dropped to his knees and said, “General Lu has submitted a letter and honors, one for your lordship’s celebration and one to beg that friendship between the two households be restored. He begs mercy to let them stay in laughter at court.”

Guan Yu read the letter. Its wording was exceedingly humble. After he had finished reading it, he laughed aloud, then ordered the gifts returned and sent back through the envoy. The messenger, upon returning, told Lu Xun, “Guan says he is delighted and has no more concern about Jingdong at all.”

Lu Xun rejoiced. Quietly he sent men and confirmed that Guan Yu had in fact withdrawn the greater part of his Jingzhou army and marched to Fan City awaiting orders; once the arrow wound recovered, he would move forward.

Lu Xun understood the full details and sent word to Sun by night.

Sun discussed it with Lü Meng and said, “Now that Yunchang has pulled back most of the Jingzhou troops to attack Fan City, we can plan to seize Jingzhou at once. You and my brother Sun Jiao should lead the main forces ahead. What do you think?”

Sun Jiao, whose courtesy name was Shuming, was the second son of Sun Jing, the uncle of Sun Quan.

Lü Meng replied, “If your lordship thinks I am usable, use me alone. If he thinks Shuming usable, use him alone. Did not Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu once serve as joint right and left commanders? The matter was decided by You, but because Cheng Pu was an old retainer and stood below You, the two did not get on. Only later, after he saw Yu’s talent, did he truly respect him. My talent does not surpass Zhou Yu’s, and Uncle Shuming’s family ties exceed Cheng Pu’s; I do not think this can work either.”

Sun Quan understood at once and made Lü Meng Grand Commander, placing all Jiangdong armies under his command. He ordered Sun Jiao to follow in rear with supply support.

Lü Meng accepted and thanked him, then raised thirty thousand troops and above eighty fast boats. He chose swimmers and had them pose as merchants in white clothing.

On the boats, they rowed while concealing seasoned troops in the hulls. Then he summoned Han Dang, Jiang Qin, Zhu Ran, Pan Zhang, Zhou Tai, Xu Sheng, Ding Feng, to join in turn. The rest followed as reserves for joint support after the lord of Wu.

At the same time he sent word to Cao Cao, urging advance to strike Yunchang’s rear, then sent advance notice to Lu Xun, and only then dispatched the white-clad men in fast boats toward Xunyang River.

Day and night they rushed on and came directly to the north bank. When the guards at a beacon post on the Yangtze bank questioned the river troops, the men from Wu said, “We are only merchants. A wind barrier is blocking the river, so we have stopped here for shelter.” They sent gifts with goods to the watch troops. The soldiers accepted them and allowed them to tie up at the riverbank.

Around the second watch, all the hidden soldiers in the boats leapt out together. At once they seized the sentries at the beacon garrisons, then gave one concealed signal; in an instant the eighty-odd boats of elite troops rose up and moved.

They captured every soldier at key posts and loaded them into the boats. Not one escaped.

Then they rushed on and immediately moved straight for Jingzhou, where no one noticed. When they came before Jingzhou, Lü Meng took those garrison troops taken from the riverbank stations and pacified them with fair words, rewarding each richly.

He ordered them to open the city gate and to set fire to their signal stations as a signal. The entire army obeyed his order, and the vanguard advanced.

By the time it was half the night, Lü Meng shouted from before the gate. The gate guard recognized him as Jiangzhou troops and opened the gates. The whole force burst through with one cry, then raised signal fires within the city. Wu troops entered at once and attacked; Jingzhou was taken.

Lü Meng gave an order throughout the army: “Whoever kills a man without need, whoever takes a civilian possession without authority, will be punished under military law.”

The original officials all kept their former offices. He ordered Guan Yu’s family to be housed in a separate residence and forbade strangers to disturb them. Then he sent word to Sun Quan of the success.

One day there was heavy rain. Lü Meng mounted and with a few riders inspected all four gates. He saw a man using a reed hat from among the people to cover his armor. Lü Meng shouted for him to be seized and questioned. It was a fellow native of Lü Meng.

Lü Meng said, “Though you are one of my kinsmen in origin, my command has already gone out. You broke it by wearing this, and must be punished under military law.”

The man wept and said, “I feared my officer armor would get wet in the rain, so I took a cover. I did not do it for private use. I beg your general’s sympathy as one from the same native place.”

Lü Meng said, “I know you truly meant only to cover your armor, but you still should not have taken a civilian object.”

He shouted for his men to drag him down and execute him. He displayed the severed head as warning and then collected the corpse and buried it with tears.

From this time the whole army grew strict and orderly.

After not long, Sun Quan arrived at the city with his retinue.

Lü Meng came out beyond the gate to receive him at the yamen. After comforting him and praising him for the effort, Sun appointed Pan Jun as chief administrator and gave him charge of Jingzhou’s government. He ordered Yu Jin released from custody and sent back to Cao Cao. He settled the people and rewarded the soldiers, then held a feast to celebrate.

Sun asked Lü Meng, “Jingzhou is ours now, but what of Gong’an and Nanjun? What is the best way to recover these two places?”

Before he finished, someone stood forth and spoke: “It is not necessary to draw bow and fire arrow. By my unfailing tongue alone, I can bring Fu Shiren to surrender. Is that possible?”

All turned to him. He was Yu Fan.

Sun asked, “What good scheme has Zhongxiang to bring Fu Shiren under peace?”

Yu Fan said, “I have known Fu Shiren since we were boys. If I explain profit and danger to him clearly, he will return.”

Sun rejoiced and ordered Yu Fan to take five hundred troops and march directly to Gong’an.

When he heard that Jingzhou had been lost, Fu Shiren ordered the city gates shut and tightly defended. Yu Fan arrived and saw the gate firmly closed, so he wrote a letter and tied it to an arrow, shooting it into the city.

The sentry recovered it and presented it to Fu Shiren.

Fu Shiren opened it and saw it called for surrender. He read it and thought back on the resentment he had once held toward Guan. Better to submit now than delay.

He ordered the city gates opened widely and invited Yu Fan inside. The two finished ritual courtesy and spoke of old ties. Yu Fan praised Sun Quan as generous and broad-minded, one who honored worth and lowered himself to lesser men.

Fu Shiren was delighted and together with Yu Fan brought his official seal and commission, submitting himself at Jingzhou.

Sun rejoiced and kept him in charge at Gong’an.

Lü Meng told Sun privately, “Yunchang has not yet been captured. If Fu Shiren remains in Gong’an, there will surely be change in time. Better send him to Nanjun to recruit Mi Fang into surrender.”

Sun summoned Fu Shiren and said, “Your connection with Mi Fang is close. You may summon him. If you return him, I will reward you greatly.”

Fu Shiren accepted with emotion and led ten or more riders directly to Nanjun to invite Mi Fang and bring him over.

So it was:

This day in Gong’an there is no will to stand and defend; In former days, Wang Fu indeed spoke well. Who can yet know what lies ahead? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Guan Yu Scrapes the Bone to Cure Poison, and Lu Ziming Crosses the River in White Garb

chapters.html:
Xu Gongming battles along the Mian River. Guan Yunchang is routed from Maicheng.

Now Mi Fang heard that Jing Province had fallen and had no measure left. Just then word arrived that Fu Shiren, commander of the Gong’an garrison, was here. Mi Fang quickly received him into the city and asked about the matter. Fu Shiren said, “I am not disloyal; the position is dangerous and our strength is strained, so we cannot hold it. I have already surrendered to Eastern Wu. You, Excellency, should not delay your own surrender.” Mi Fang said, “We have all lived long under the great grace of the King of Han; how could we turn against him in a single morning?” Fu Shiren said, “Since Guan Gong departed, he has harbored bitter hatred for us two. If, on some future day, he returns in victory, there will be no mercy. Look into the matter closely.” Mi Fang said, “My brothers and I have served the King of Han for years. How can we abandon him in one day?”

While he was still hesitating, news came that Guan Gong had sent an envoy to the hall. The envoy announced, “General Guan’s army lacks grain. We have come from Nanjun and Gong’an to take one hundred thousand shi of white rice. You two generals are to ride through the night and deliver it. If you delay even briefly, he will be beheaded. Mi Fang was greatly shocked and said to Fu Shiren, “Jing Province has already fallen to Eastern Wu. How can this grain pass through?” Fu Shiren, in a sharp voice, said, “Do not be so suspicious.” He drew his sword and beheaded the envoy in the hall. Mi Fang asked in alarm, “What do we do now?” Fu Shiren said, “This is exactly Guan Gong’s intent. He now wants to execute us both. If we do not surrender to Eastern Wu at once, he will kill us.” Even as he spoke, news came that Lü Meng was riding with troops and had struck down to the city gate. Mi Fang was startled and, together with Fu Shiren, left the city to surrender. Lü Meng was overjoyed and had them brought before Sun Quan. Sun Quan awarded both men handsomely. After pacifying the city, he rewarded the three armies generously.

At this time Cao Cao was in Xudu, discussing Jing Province with his counselors, when word came that Eastern Wu had dispatched an envoy with a letter. Cao Cao summoned him in. The messenger presented the letter. Cao Cao opened it and read: Wu troops would attack Jing Province, and he was asked to mount a joint strike on Guan Gong; he was also instructed not to leak it so that Guan Gong would make preparations. Cao Cao consulted with his advisers. His clerk Dong Zhao said, “Now Fan City is besieged and straining at the neck for relief, waiting only for rescue. It is better to have someone shoot the letter into Fan City to steady the army’s hearts, and also let Guan Gong know that Eastern Wu intends to invade Jing Province. If he fears the loss of Jing, he will withdraw quickly. Then Xu Huang can strike with the opportunity and bring complete success.” Cao Cao accepted the plan. He sent men to urge Xu Huang to fight urgently. At the same time he personally led a large force and marched to the marshes south of Luoyang to station there and relieve Cao Ren.

Xu Huang was in his command tent when he was told that an envoy from the Wei king had arrived. Xu Huang received him. The envoy said, “The King of Wei has already moved his forces past Luoyang, and orders General Xu Huang to fight Guan Gong at once, and thus free Fan City from its crisis.” While they were speaking, a scout came in reporting, “Guan Ping has encamped at Yancheng, and Liao Hua at Sizhong. From front and rear there are twelve stockades linked without break.” Xu Huang then ordered his deputies Xu Shang and Lü Jian to go forward under Xu Huang’s banner and engage Guan Ping at Yancheng. Xu Huang himself led five hundred picked men and followed the Mian River to attack the rear of Yancheng.

Now Guan Ping, hearing that Xu Huang had advanced with his own force, raised his own troops to meet him. The two formations faced each other. Guan Ping went out first and exchanged weapons with Xu Shang. After only three bouts, Xu Shang was defeated and fled. Lü Jian came out to fight and was also defeated after six exchanges. Guan Ping pressed while they were in retreat for more than twenty li, when word came that fire had broken out in the city. Guan Ping realized he had been tricked and quickly beat back the troops to save Yancheng. As he rode in, he found a column of troops already arrayed. Xu Huang, on horseback beneath the battle banner, shouted, “Faithful nephew Guan Ping, do you not understand death? Jing Province has already been taken by Eastern Wu, and yet you still rage on here!” Guan Ping became furious, spurred his horse, and waved his blade straight at Xu Huang. After no more than three or four clashes, there was uproar from all three armies, and fire flared high across Yancheng. Guan Ping did not dare continue the duel, cut a broad path, and rode straight back to Sizhong. Liao Hua caught up with him. Liao Hua said, “It is said that Jing Province has fallen to Lü Meng. The troops are frightened and restless. What are we to do?” Guan Ping said, “This must be false talk. Any soldier who says it again will lose his life.”

A swift horse arrived with news that the northern first encampment was under attack by Xu Huang. Guan Ping said, “If the first encampment falls, how can the other camps remain secure? This place all leans on the Mian River, and enemy soldiers will not dare reach here. Come, you and I, and go at once to rescue it.” Liao Hua called his unit commanders and said, “You must hold this stockade tightly. If the enemy comes, raise the beacon fire at once.” A subcommander replied, “Sizhong Stockade has ten layers of antler defenses. Not even a flying bird can enter. Why should we fear enemy soldiers?” So Guan Ping and Liao Hua sent all the best troops of Sizhong and rushed to garrison at the first encampment. When Guan Ping saw the Wei troops camped on low hills, he said to Liao Hua, “Xu Huang has chosen bad ground. This night we can move troops and raid the stockade.” Liao Hua said, “The General may send half our men ahead; I will keep this stockade carefully.”

That night, Guan Ping led a detachment and broke into the Wei camp. No one was there. Realizing this was deception, he withdrew at speed. Xu Shang came in from the left, and Lü Jian from the right, and both attacked from two sides. Guan Ping suffered a severe defeat and returned to camp. Wei soldiers pressed in pursuit and came in from all four sides, surrounding him. Guan Ping and Liao Hua could not hold. They abandoned the first encampment and went straight to Sizhong. Already they saw flames in the stockade. As they arrived at the gate, they saw only Wei banners. The troops retreating with them ran in disorder to the main road toward Fan City. A force blocked the way. At its head was a great general—none other than Xu Huang. Guan Ping and Liao Hua fought with all they had, broke through, and made to escape. They returned to the main camp and reported to Guan Gong, “Xu Huang has taken Yancheng and the other positions. Cao Cao has also brought a large army himself and come by three routes to relieve Cao Ren. Many are saying Jing Province is already taken by Lü Meng.” Guan Gong cried, “These are enemy lies to shake our army’s spirit! Lü Meng is dying of illness, and the lad Lu Xun has replaced him; there is nothing to fear in that!”

Before this was done, word came that Xu Huang’s soldiers had arrived, and Guan Gong ordered his horses made ready. Guan Ping remonstrated, “Your body is not yet healed. You should not meet the enemy.” Guan Gong said, “I know Xu Huang well and know his strength. If he does not retreat, I will first behead him, so all Wei generals see a warning.” He donned his armor, took up his blade, mounted, and leapt out. The Wei troops saw him and all were struck with awe. He pulled the horse short and asked, “Where is Xu Gongming?” At the Wei camp gate, where the banners were being opened, Xu Huang rode out. He dipped his head and said, “Since we last parted, only a few years have flown. I had not imagined, General, that your hair and beard had turned so gray. I remember our youth when we traveled together. I never forgot your teachings. Now your military renown rings through under Heaven, and old allies hearing it can scarcely hold back envy. To have this meeting is fortune indeed, and it brings great comfort to my longing.” Guan Gong said, “Between you and me, Xu Gongming, there is old and deep fellowship, not like that with others. Why now do you keep threatening my life?” Xu Huang looked back at the ranks of his men and cried out, “Whoever secures General Yunchang’s head will receive one thousand gold pieces!” Guan Gong was shocked. “How can you say such a thing, Xu Gongming?” Xu Huang replied, “Today this is state business. I dare not, for private feeling, set aside duty to the realm.”

When he had spoken, he raised his great axe and charged straight at Guan Gong. Guan Gong raged and swung his own blade to meet him. They fought more than eighty rounds. Though Guan Gong’s martial arts were exceptional, his right arm was then weak. Liao Hua feared for his lord and rang the alarm gongs in haste. Guan Gong turned his horse back to the camp, and suddenly a roar surged from all quarters. It was Cao Ren from Fan City: on hearing that Cao Cao’s relief troops had arrived, he marched out and joined Xu Huang. The two armies attacked in a pincer and the Jing forces were thrown into confusion. Guan Gong mounted and urged the commanders forward, fleeing toward the upper reaches of the Xiang River. Wei soldiers pursued close behind. Guan Gong crossed Xiang River in haste and rode toward Xiangyang. A swift horse then arrived: “Jing Province has been taken by Lü Meng. The families have been captured.” Guan Gong was deeply alarmed and dared not run to Xiangyang. He pulled up his troops and turned toward Gong’an. A messenger came again: “Fu Shiren in Gong’an has already surrendered to Eastern Wu.” Guan Gong was enraged. At once, an officer connected to supplies arrived and reported, “Fu Shiren has gone to Nanjun, killed the messenger, and drawn all of Mi Fang over to Eastern Wu.”

Guan Gong heard this and his rage filled his throat. The wound in his body split and he fainted to the ground. His officers revived him. He said to Sima Wangfu, “I should have listened to you, and now this has happened.” He asked, “Why did no one along the river raise signal fires?” A scout answered, “Lü Meng ordered all boatmen to wear white and cross the river in merchant guise. He hid picked soldiers inside the boats and first seized the tower sentries, so no fire could be raised.” Guan Gong stamped and groaned, “I have fallen into a traitor’s trick. How can I face my elder brother now?” Zhao Lei, director of grain transport, said, “The matter is urgent. At once send men to Chengdu for aid, and from the land route take troops to recover Jing Province. Guan Gong agreed and sent Ma Liang and Yi Ji with three summons to Chengdu by night. At the same time he led troops to recover Jing Province. He led the vanguard himself and left Liao Hua and Guan Ping to cover the rear.

Now Fan City was relieved. Cao Ren came with all his officers before Cao Cao, wept and knelt, begging pardon. Cao Cao said, “This is the reckoning of Heaven, not your fault.” Cao Cao rewarded the three armies generously and rode in person to Sizhong. He made the rounds outside and then said to the assembled generals, “The Jing forces built layered stag-horn ditches and stockades, and Xu Gongming penetrated deeply into them and still achieved complete success. For over thirty years I have led armies and never dared a forced charge straight into an enemy ring. Gongming truly joins courage and wit.” The men all admired him. Cao Cao gave the order to return to camp and station at Mopi. Xu Huang arrived there; Cao Cao came out to meet him. Seeing Xu Huang’s army arranged in full order with no disorder, Cao Cao rejoiced, saying, “General Xu truly has the composure of Zhou Yafu!” He then made Xu Huang the General Who Pacifies the South, and appointed Xiahou Shang to co-defend Xiangyang, to block Guan Gong’s force. Because Jing Province was not settled, Cao Cao kept his troops stationed at Mopi, waiting for further news.

Now Guan Gong was on the road in Jing territory, with no way forward or back. He asked Zhao Lei, “Now Wu troops stand before us and Wei troops behind us. I am between them, and no relief has reached me. What is to be done?” Zhao Lei replied, “When Lü Meng was at Luku, he once sent a letter to your lord and both houses agreed to strike down bandit Cao together. Now they help Cao and assault us. This is a broken pledge. My lord should hold the army here for the time being. You may send a letter to Lü Meng and lay the blame before him. See how he answers.” Guan Gong agreed and wrote the letter, sending an envoy back to Jing Province.

Now Lü Meng, at Jing Province, issued this command: For all in Jing’s commanderies who had followed Guan Gong into battle, none of Wu’s soldiers were to disturb their households, granting grain each month. If anyone was ill, doctors were to be sent to treat them. The soldiers’ households, moved by this grace, stayed calm and did not depart. Soon came news that Guan Gong’s messenger had arrived. Lü Meng rode out to the gate, received him in the city, and welcomed him as a guest. The envoy handed him the letter. Lü Meng read it, then said, “My former good relations with General Guan were only my own private view. What happens today is the command from above, and I have no freedom in it. Please send word back that General Guan knows my respectful greetings.” He gave a feast, then escorted him in courteous fashion and sent him back to the rest-house to stay the night.

Afterwards, the families of troops who had marched with Guan came asking for messages. Some brought home letters, others brought spoken news. All reported their homes were not in danger and provisions were not lacking. The envoy took leave of Lü Meng and he himself escorted him out of the city. The envoy reported back to Guan Gong all that Lü Meng had said, and added that in Jingzhou, Your Lord’s family and the families of the commanders were all unharmed and their supplies did not lack. Guan Gong was enraged: “This is the villain’s design! If I do not kill this scoundrel while alive, I will surely kill him dead to clear my resentment.” He shouted the envoy away. When the envoy left camp, the officers all came asking about the homefront. He told them each household was well, that Lü Meng’s kindness was deep, and the letters were delivered to every commander. The officers rejoiced and lost all desire to fight.

Guan Gong marched on toward recovering Jing Province. As the army advanced, many soldiers slipped away and returned to Jing Province. Guan Gong’s anger only grew, and he pressed them onward. Suddenly a cry of battle thundered—one clump of troops blocked the way. At their head was Jiang Qin. He reined in and, spear in hand, shouted, “Why has Yunchang not surrendered already?” Guan Gong barked back, “I am a Han general. Would I bow to bandits?” He struck his horse and whirled his sword, riding straight on Jiang Qin. In less than three clashes, Jiang Qin turned and fled. Guan Gong pursued with raised blade for over twenty li when shouts rose again. On the left, Han Dang burst out with troops from a mountain ravine, and on the right Zhou Tai brought troops from another ravine. Jiang Qin returned to fight. It became a three-sided assault. Guan Gong withdrew in haste. After marching many li, they saw crowds gathering on Nan Mountain Ridge around white banners, one banner waving and marked with “People of Jing Province.” Everyone cried, “Submit here at once!” Guan Gong raged and set to ride up the ridge to execute them. Inside the hillside hollow, two more armies burst out: Ding Feng on the left and Xu Sheng on the right, with Jiang Qin joining them. The three columns merged, and the shouts and war horns shook the air, ringing Guan Gong into the center. His following soldiers gradually scattered.

When dusk came, Guan Gong looked toward the hills. Every ridge had Jing troops. From all sides came voices crying “brother,” “elder brother,” “mother,” “father,” and the calls did not stop. The army spirit had broken completely and all answered and fled. Guan Gong could not stop his shouting. Only a little over three hundred remained. He fought on until the third watch. From the east in the night came cries so loud they filled the sky— it was Guan Ping and Liao Hua, entering in two separate columns and breaking into the encirclement, bringing him out. Guan Ping said, “The troops’ morale is ruined. We must at least take shelter in a city and hold it awhile for reinforcements. Though small, Maicheng is defensible enough to hold temporarily.” Guan Gong agreed and hurried the shattered troops onward to Maicheng. He divided them to hold all four gates tightly and gathered his officers to confer. Zhao Lei said, “This place is near Shangyong, where Liu Feng and Meng Da now stand watch. We can quickly send men for help. If those troops arrive and Sichuan reinforcements come in full, the army will regain its heart.”

While they were still deliberating, news came that Wu troops had arrived and sealed the city from all four sides. The Lord asked, “Who dares break out now and ride to Shangyong for rescue?” Liao Hua said, “I am willing.” Guan Ping said, “I will escort you through the encirclement.” Guan Gong quickly wrote a letter and placed it with Liao Hua to carry, then fed him fully, had him mount, and opened the gate. He met Ding Feng, who blocked the way. Guan Ping struck with all his strength and killed him. Ding Feng fled. Liao Hua used the moment to break through and ride to Shangyong. Guan Ping returned and held the city, not venturing out again.

Now Liu Feng and Meng Da had just taken Shangyong, and Magistrate Shen Dan had surrendered with his men. The King of Han therefore promoted Liu Feng to Deputy General and with Meng Da put him in charge of Shangyong. That same day, as they discussed this and heard of Guan Gong’s defeat, word came that Liao Hua had arrived. Liu Feng ordered him to be admitted and asked after him. Liao Hua said, “Guan Gong was defeated and is in a desperate siege in Maicheng. No Shu force can arrive by tomorrow. He ordered me to break the encirclement and come here to ask for aid. If the two generals raise Shangyong troops at once, you may save this danger. If there is even slight delay, General will surely fall.” Liu Feng said, “General, wait. Let me think.”

Liao Hua then retired to the guesthouse to rest and wait for departure orders. Liu Feng said to Meng Da, “How could we let our uncle be trapped?” Meng Da said, “Wu soldiers are strong and full of brave commanders. Also, the nine commanderies of Jing are all in their hands. Only Maicheng remains, just a grain of a place. I hear Cao Cao personally commands four hundred to five hundred thousand troops at Mopi. How can our mountain-town garrison face the strongest forces of both states? We must not underestimate this danger.” Liu Feng said, “I know that too. Still, Guan Gong is my uncle. How can I sit still and not rescue him?” Meng Da laughed, “Though you honor Guan as uncle, fear that he does not treat you as nephew. I have heard that when the King first named you as heir, Guan Gong was not pleased. After the King ascended the throne and wished to appoint an heir, he asked Kongming. Kongming said, ‘This is a household matter. Ask Guan and Zhang.’ The King then sent men to Jing to ask him. Guan said your Highness is a son of Mingling, so you cannot usurp the throne; he urged the King to set you far at Shangyong Mountain City to prevent future trouble. Everyone knows this. How can you not know? Why now do you still cling to this notion of uncle and nephew and wish to risk careless action?”

Liu Feng said, “Your words are true. Yet how should I answer him?” Meng Da said, “Say only that this mountain city is newly submitted, and its people are not yet settled. You cannot raise troops in haste for fear of losing what is held.” Liu Feng followed this and the next day asked Liao Hua to come. He said, “This mountain city only recently submitted and cannot divide its forces to help.” Liao Hua was shocked, struck the ground with his head and said, “If this is so, then Guan Gong is finished!” Meng Da replied, “If I go now, can a single cup of water save a cartload of burning fuel? Let the General return and wait for Shu reinforcements to arrive.” Liao Hua cried out in grief. Liu Feng and Meng Da both swept their sleeves and withdrew. Liao Hua understood that matters could not be reconciled. He resolved to report to the King of Han for aid, and mounted up, leaving the city in bitter complaint, riding toward Chengdu.

Now, in Maicheng, Guan Gong waited for Shangyong’s troops, but no one came. Only five or six hundred men remained with him, most of them wounded. The city had no grain and suffered terribly. Suddenly a man from below the gate asked to fire cease, saying he carried a message to the lord. Guan Gong ordered him in. It was Zhuge Jin. After formal greetings and tea, Zhuge Jin said, “I come under the authority of Lord Wu to counsel the General. As the saying goes, ‘The man who discerns his times is a true hero.’ Now, the nine commanderies of Han under Heaven have all gone under other hands. Only this lone city remains. There is no grain within and no aid without; danger is at dawn. Why does not the General accept my counsel, submit to Lord Wu, and return to occupy Jing and Xiang, so you may secure your household?” Guan Gong answered flatly, “I am one plain and good soldier who bears this armor. My lord has treated me as a kinsman with his own hands. How could I cast aside loyalty and throw myself to an enemy state? If this city falls, I die. Jade may be shattered but cannot change its whiteness. Bamboo may burn but cannot destroy its virtue. Though the body falls, my name may endure on bamboo and silk. Speak no further. Ask him to withdraw. I will settle this with Lord Sun in a battle to the death.” Zhuge Jin said, “Lord Sun wishes only to ally with you as Qin and Jin did, join hands to destroy Cao and aid the Han. There is no other design. Why do you hold to stubbornness so?”

Before he finished, Guan Ping drew his sword and came forward to behead Zhuge Jin. Guan Gong stopped him: “His brother Kongming is in Shu, assisting your uncle. If you kill him now, you would hurt their brotherly bond.” He then ordered his attendants to escort Zhuge Jin out. Zhuge Jin, his face covered with shame, mounted and left the city, then reported to Sun Quan, “Guan’s heart is iron and stone and cannot be moved by words.” Sun Quan said, “He is a truly loyal officer. What else can be done?” Lü Fan said, “I ask to read his fortune and outcomes.” Sun Quan ordered him to do so. Lü Fan cast yarrow stalks and formed the hexagram Earth over Water. He also saw the image of the Dark Warrior in response, indicating the enemy would flee far. Sun Quan asked Lü Meng, “If that omen means the enemy runs far, what plan do you have to catch him?” Lü Meng smiled, “The omen matches my stratagem exactly. Though Guan has wings that rise to heaven, he cannot fly out of my net.”

Dragon through a ravine is mocked by a shrimp, Phoenix enters a cage to be mocked by birds.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Xu Gongming Battles on the Mian River and Guan Yunchang Is Routed from Maicheng

chapters.html:
Jade Spring Mountain reveals Guan Gong in manifested holiness.
Luoyang City awakens Cao Cao to the touch of divinity.

Sun Quan sought strategy from Lü Meng. Lü Meng said, “I judge that Guan the general has few men and cannot flee along the road. North of Maicheng, there is a steep, narrow path; he must go that way. Send Zhu Ran with five thousand picked soldiers to lie in ambush twenty li north of Maicheng. When the enemy comes, do not engage him directly; strike from behind after he leaves. His troops have no will to fight and will surely run toward Linju. Send Pan Zhang with five hundred picked soldiers to hide on a narrow back path at Linju Mountain. Then Guan can be captured. Now have the commanders attack through every gate except keep only the north gate open.”

Sun Quan heard this, then ordered Lu Fan to divine again. When the hexagram formed, Fan said, “This omen shows the enemy running to the northwest. Tonight at the Hai hour, he will certainly be taken.” Sun Quan rejoiced and ordered Zhu Ran and Pan Zhang to take their elite detachments and go to their ambushes at once.

In Maicheng, Guan Yu counted his horse-and-foot soldiers and found barely more than three hundred left; the grain was gone as well. That night, Wu soldiers outside called out unit names and passed over the wall in great numbers. Rescue troops did not appear. With no plan, he told Wang Fu, “I regret I did not listen to you before. Today in this crisis, what can be done?”

Wang Fu wept and said, “Even if Great Lord Jiang Ziya had come back to life, this cannot be solved today.”

Zhao Lei said, “No reinforcement reached us from Shangyong, because Liu Feng and Meng Da kept their forces still. Why not leave this isolated city, break into West Sichuan, rebuild the army, and then seek recovery?” Guan said, “I want to do that too.” Then he climbed the wall and asked the townspeople, “North of here, what is the land like?”

They answered, “It is all hidden lanes through hills; they lead toward West Sichuan.” Guan said, “We can go by that path tonight.” Wang Fu objected, “There are ambushes on the side path. Better to use the main road.” Guan replied, “Though there is an ambush, what is there for me to fear?”

He issued the order at once: mounted cavalry and foot troops were to stand in strict gear and prepare to leave the city. Wang Fu wept, “My lord, be careful on the road! A hundred or so of us will die on this city wall and never surrender. Though the city falls, we will not yield. We all await your quick rescue.”

Guan Yu likewise parted in tears. So he left Zhou Cang with Wang Fu to defend Maicheng. Guan Yu led Guan Ping and Zhao Lei with two hundred-odd survivors out by the north gate. Guan Yu advanced, slashing with his halberd. After the first watch, having marched over twenty li, they reached a small mountain hollow where drums and gongs sounded in one voice and the shouting resounded like thunder.

A mass of horsemen had already gathered there, led by Zhu Ran, who rode forward and cried, “Yunchang, do not run! Surrender now and avoid one needless death!” Guan Yu grew furious, spurred his horse, and drew his wheel-bladed axe to fight. Zhu Ran turned away and Guan Yu pressed him in pursuit. Then, at one stroke of drum, all the hidden troops rose at once. Guan Yu did not choose battle. He headed for the Linju path. Zhu Ran’s force followed and cut down whichever men they could.

The men with Guan Yu thinned away as he went. After four or five li, they heard shouting ahead and bright flames rose around them. Pan Zhang galloped in with sword raised. Guan Yu was furious, brought his weapon up to meet him; in only three exchanges Pan Zhang was broken and fled. Guan Yu refused another fight and rushed on toward the mountain track. Guan Ping came running behind, reporting that Zhao Lei had already died in the confusion. Guan Yu, unable to conceal his grief and panic, told Guan Ping to cover the rear while he drove forward. He ended with only ten men beside him.

When they reached Jie Rock, mountains rose on both sides, with reeds, dead grass, and thickets of trees along the slopes. It was near the fifth watch. Just as they moved forward, a cry went up. Ambush men emerged from both sides at once. Long-hooked lassoes were lifted together and first cast to trip Guan Yu from his seated horse.

He rolled off the horse. Ma Zhong, Pan Zhang’s officer, seized him. When Guan Ping learned his father had been taken, he rushed to rescue him. Pan Zhang and Zhu Ran arrived together with troops and surrounded Guan Ping on every side. Guan Ping fought on alone, and when his strength failed he too was captured.

By dawn, Sun Quan heard that Guan Yu and his son had both been caught and was very glad, gathering the officers in his tent.

After a while, Ma Zhong brought Guan Yu before him. Sun Quan said, “I have long admired the General’s excellence and wished to make peace between us like Qin and Jin. How did you leave it thus, that my hand now has you in chains?”

Guan Yu thundered back, “Blue-eyed boy, purple-bearded rat! I entered an oath at the Peach Garden with Liu the Imperial Uncle, and swore to uphold the Han house. How can I stand with one who has betrayed Han and plots with him? I have fallen by a treacherous scheme; I only have to die. What more is there to say?”

Sun Quan looked over the assembled officers and said, “Yunchang is the foremost hero of his age. I deeply esteem him. I want to treat him with respect and invite him to submit. What do you think?”

Zuo Xian, the prime registrar, said, “No, sire. When Cao Cao once took this man, he gave him rank and fiefs, held a small banquet every three days and a great one every fifth day. Each time Guan mounted his horse one coin of gold was raised, each time he dismounted one coin of silver: such grace would not keep him. In the end he left and slashed through our guards and generals, so close that we nearly moved the capital to avoid his spearhead. Now that the Lord has captured him, if he is not cut down at once, later trouble will surely follow.”

Sun Quan grew silent for a moment, then said, “Your words are right.” He ordered Guan and his son put to death.

So Guan Yu and his son met their end. It was winter, twelfth month of Jian’an twenty-four. Guan Yu was fifty-eight.

Later people sighed in verse:

No talent under late Han could equal this one, and Yunchang stood alone above the rest. His divine vigor can rouse valor; he also knew elegance in learning. His heart, bright as daylight, held a mirror that did not cloud; His justice, wider than spring and autumn, spread beyond envy. His fame shows through ten thousand ages, And he no longer stood merely first among three.

Another poem says:

Only once in a man’s age came such a worthy man, as Yunchang of Han; people and officials alike knelt in worship. Brothers and mates from one day in the Peach Garden, rulers and kings for ten thousand years in bronze vessels. His spirit bore storm and thunder with no equal, his purpose lit the sun and moon. Until today, his temple visage fills all under heaven, and old trees and black crows face evening light.

After Guan Yu had died, his red warhorse was taken by Ma Zhong and presented to Sun Quan. Sun Quan then allowed Ma Zhong to ride it. The horse would not eat grass or feed for several days and died.

Back in Maicheng, Wang Fu trembled with pain, then asked Zhou Cang, “Last night I dreamed my lord stood there all blood-soaked, facing me. I called out and suddenly woke in fright. I know nothing of its meaning.” Just then came word that Wu soldiers were below the city offering the heads of Guan Yu and his son for pacification. Wang Fu and Zhou Cang ran to the top of the wall and saw it indeed: the severed heads.

Wang Fu cried out once and fell to the ground to die. Zhou Cang drew his sword and killed himself. In this way Maicheng fell to Eastern Wu.

But Guan Yu’s spirit did not disperse. It roamed restlessly, and one day came to a mountain called Jade Spring in Dangyang County, Jingmen commandery. At the top lived an old monk named Pu Jing, dharma-name Pure Purity, formerly a senior monk from Zhi Guo Temple at Sishui Pass. Wandering through the world in former days, he had come here, seeing mountain and waters fair, and had built a hut of thatch where he meditated and practiced the Way each day, with only a young novice to sustain himself with alms.

On a night of bright moon and clear wind, after the third watch, Pu Jing sat in silent meditation when he heard someone in the air shout, “Give me back my head!” Pu Jing looked up and saw a man in the air, riding a red horse, carrying a Qinglong halberd, with a white-faced general on his left and a black-faced, curly-bearded man on his right. They all came together and settled at the summit of Jade Spring. Pu Jing recognized him as Guan Yu and struck the gate with his fly-whisk: “Where is Master Yunchang?”

The spirit of Guan Yu understood, then dismounted from the wind and came before the hut. Joining his hands, he asked, “Who are you, Master? I seek your Dharma name.” Pu Jing said, “I am the old monk Pu Jing. Once, at Zhen Guo Temple by Sishui Pass, you and the lord met me. Has all that truly been forgotten?”

Guan Yu said, “Your help and kindness are engraved in me. Now I have met disaster and died. I beg for true guidance to clear this lost path.”

Pu Jing replied, “Then and now are different. Do not argue from former causes to present results; what is meant to happen has come. You were slain by Lü Meng and cried, ‘Return my head!’ But then to whose heads, such as Yan Liang, Wen Chou, and the men called Five Passes and Six Generals, must you demand them from now?”

Guan Yu suddenly awakened to understanding. He knelt, bowed, took refuge, and departed. Thereafter he often showed himself as a holy one on Jade Spring Mountain, protecting the people. Villagers moved by his virtue built a shrine at the top and offered sacrifice in the four seasons. Later someone inscribed a couplet:

He who holds a red face and red heart rides the red mare in pursuit of wind, Chasing on, he never forgets the command of the Crimson Lord. Under a blue lamp he watches blue history, With the Green Dragon crescent he guards the hidden without shame beneath the blue sky.

Back in Jianye, after Sun Quan had caused Guan Yu’s death he took all the lands of Jing and Xiang, rewarded and supplied the three armies, held a great feast and banquet for his generals in celebration, and placed Lü Meng in command. He said to them, “I never truly possessed Jingzhou; now it is mine at a touch, all by Ziming’s achievement.”

Lü Meng repeatedly refused. Sun Quan said, “In former times Zhou Lang had talent beyond men, and at Red Cliffs he broke Cao Cao, but was unfortunate to die early. Lu Su took his place. From our first meeting, Lu Su saw the broad design of kings and emperors—that was one wisdom. When Cao Cao moved east, all others urged me to surrender, and only Lu Su urged me to call back Gongjin and strike him—that was second wisdom. But he erred once: he advised me to lend Jingzhou to Liu Bei. Today, through Ziming’s planning and execution, Jingzhou is secured, greater than Lu Su and Zhou Lang by many times.”

Then Sun Quan personally poured out wine for Lü Meng. As Lü Meng raised it to drink, he suddenly flung the cup down, seized Sun Quan’s arm, and cried in rage, “Blue-eyed boy! Purple-bearded rat! Do you recognize me now?”

Great panic spread among all the generals. When attendants tried to help, Lü Meng toppled Sun Quan, strode forward and sat in the ruler’s place, his brows drawn down and eyes wide, then roared, “Since I broke the Yellow Turbans, I have moved with my sword across the world for over thirty years. To be trapped in one day by your stratagem—if I live, I will never taste your flesh; if I die, I will pursue the spirit of that bandit Lü to the end! I am Guan Yunchang, Marquis of Hanshou District.”

Sun Quan was startled. He quickly gathered all senior and junior officers and had all of them kneel. Only when Lü Meng was on the ground with blood from his seven orifices did he die. All the generals feared him in awe. Sun Quan placed his corpse in a coffin with full honors and buried him, posthumously granting him the title Marquis of Chanling and the rank of Administrator of Nan Commandery; he ordered his son Lü Ba to inherit the marquisate. From then on, Sun Quan was perpetually unsettled by Guan Yu’s affair.

Suddenly Zhang Zhao came from Jianye, and Sun Quan called him in. Zhang Zhao said, “Now Your Majesty has harmed father and son Guan. The disaster of Jiangdong is not far. This man took the oath of life and death with Liu Bei in the Peach Garden. Now Liu Bei has troops in both Sichuan and another strong will; with Zhuge Liang’s plotting and the courage of Zhang, Huang, Ma, and Zhao, if he learns Guan and his son are dead, he will raise a state-level force and avenge it with all might. East Wu may not withstand it.”

Sun Quan said in alarm, “I miscalculated! What am I to do?”

Zhang Zhao said, “Do not fear. I have one scheme, and with it Wu and Jingzhou will be as secure as a table rock.”

Sun Quan asked, “What scheme?”

Zhang Zhao said, “Cao Cao now commands a hundred-thousand host, and eyes Hua Xia. Liu Bei, desperate for vengeance, must reconcile with him. If Wu and Shu strike together, East Wu is in danger. Better send a messenger with Guan’s severed head to Cao Cao by night. Have him told that this was done by Wei’s ruler, so Liu Bei will hate him and not turn on Wu, only on Wei. As for my reading, this is how victory can be seized in the middle.”

Sun Quan followed that advice and sent a messenger with a wooden casket carrying Guan Yu’s head to Cao Cao by night. Cao Cao was returning to Luoyang from Mobei with his main army withdrawn when he heard that East Wu had delivered Guan Yu’s head. He said in joy, “Yunchang is dead. Tonight I can sleep close to my mat.”

One man came from below and said, “This is the move to shift disaster from East Wu.”

Cao Cao asked why. It was his registrar Sima Yi, courtesy name Zhongda. Cao Cao asked his counsel. Sima Yi said, “When Liu, Guan, and Zhang made oath in the Peach Garden, they vowed life and death together. So because East Wu slew Guan, fearing his return, they now offer his head to the Great King, hoping Liu Bei will be enraged at Wu and turn against Cao Cao. Meanwhile he can exploit Shu’s zeal and intervene.”

Cao Cao said, “Your words are true. What is the solution?”

Sima Yi replied, “This is easy. Have the Great King carve a sandalwood figure to match Guan’s head, and bury it with high-official rites. When Liu Bei learns of it, he will deeply resent Sun Quan and advance south with all strength. I will watch the outcome: if Shu wins it hits Wu; if Wu wins it hits Shu. If either side gains one, the other cannot endure long.”

Cao Cao rejoiced and followed that plan. He then called the envoy of Wu in, who presented the casket.

When Cao Cao opened it, Guan Yu’s face appeared as in former days. Cao Cao laughed, “Yunchang-Gong still looks unharmed.” Before he finished speaking, Guan Yu’s mouth opened, his eyes moved, and his beard and hair bristled. Cao Cao dropped in fear. Officials rushed in to aid him, and after long time he rose and said to them, “General Guan truly is a heaven-sent spirit.”

The envoy then reported to Cao Cao how Guan had manifested and cursed Sun Quan for chasing him through Lü Meng. Cao Cao feared even more. He prepared altars and sweet wine, offered sacrifice, carved a sandalwood body, and buried it outside Luoyang’s south gate with the rites of a king. He ordered all officers to escort the coffin, offered rites himself, granted him the title King of Jing, assigned men to guard the tomb, and sent the Wu envoy back to Jiangdong.

The King of Han returned from Dongchuan to Chengdu. Fa Zheng, courtesy name Xiaozhi, said, “Your Majesty’s first empress is gone; your consort Sun has gone south and may not return. Family and human order cannot be neglected. You must take a queen and stabilize domestic affairs.” The King did so.

Fa Zheng spoke again, “There is a sister in the house of Wu Yi, beautiful and virtuous. A diviner once said: should she marry, she will be greatly exalted. She was once promised to Liu Yan’s son, Liu Mao, but he died young. She remains a widow. Your Majesty may take her as queen.”

The King replied, “Liu Mao and I are of one clan; this is not fitting.” Fa Zheng said, “In closeness of kin, is it different from Jin Wen and Huaiying?”

The King accepted and took Lady Wu. In time they had two sons: the elder Liu Yong, courtesy name Gongshi; and the second Liu Li, courtesy name Fengxiao.

As for the two Sichuan regions, the people were at peace and the state prosperous, with grain and millet flourishing. Then someone came from Jingzhou saying Eastern Wu sought marriage from Guan Yu and Guan rejected it with force. Zhuge Liang, courtesy name Kongming, said, “Jingzhou is in peril! Send someone immediately to report this to Guan.” While they discussed this, reports from Jingzhou came one after another.

Not long after, Guan Xing arrived and described the disaster at Shuan-embankment Seven Camps.

Then word came again from horse courier saying that Guan Yu had built many mounds and high banks by the river, so defenses were dense and secure with no breach. Xuande was reassured.

One day, Xuande suddenly felt a trembling through his body, unable to sit or stand. He could not sleep at night. He sat up in his inner room, holding a lamp and reading when his thoughts dimmed and he grew dazed, then lay back. In the room a cold wind suddenly rose; the lamp went out and lit again. He looked up and saw a figure at the lamp beneath.

He asked, “Who are you to come to my chamber at this late hour?” The man did not reply. Xuande stared and saw it was Guan Yu, slipping in and out of the lamplight.

Xuande said, “Brother, you have not been well for some time. To come so late, there must be grave reason. We were as one in blood. Why do you avoid me?”

Guan Yu answered in tears, “Let my brother raise troops and repay this brother’s grievance!” When he had spoken, a cold wind rose, and Guan Yu vanished.

Xuande suddenly found himself fully awake and recognized it as a dream. It was just before the third watch. Still uneasy, he quickly went to the front hall and ordered someone to summon Zhuge Liang.

Kongming entered and saw him. Xuande spoke in detail of the dream warning. Zhuge Liang said, “It is only your own mind, for your thought has stayed on Guan Yu. Why wonder at it so much?” Xuande remained doubtful; Zhuge Liang, with well-chosen words, explained it away.

When Zhuge Liang had withdrawn, he went to the middle gate where Xu Jing met him. Xu Jing said, “I just came from the military-adviser residence with confidential news, and heard you had entered the hall, so I came directly.”

Zhuge Liang asked, “What confidential matter?”

Xu Jing said, “I heard among outsiders that Lü Meng of East Wu has seized Jingzhou and killed Guan Yu. I came in secret to report this.”

Kongming said, “I watched the heavens last night and saw a war-star fall over Jing and Chu. I already knew Yunchang would be in danger, but I feared Your Majesty would be troubled, so I spoke nothing.”

Before they could continue, a close attendant announced from inside, “Ma Liang and Yiji are here.”

Xuande called them in. In deep grief, they reported the loss of Jingzhou and that Guan Yu had asked for aid after defeat in battle, presenting a memorial.

Before the document could be opened, an attendant again announced Liao Hua’s arrival from there. Xuande summoned him quickly. Liao Hua knelt and cried, then described in detail how Liu Feng and Meng Da had refused to send troops.

Xuande cried out in great alarm, “If this is true, my brother is doomed!”

Kongming said, “Liu Feng and Meng Da behaved with such offense their crime is above pardon. Your Majesty should keep your heart steady. I will personally lead one army at once for the urgent relief of Jingzhou.”

Xuande wept, “If Yunchang has fallen, I will not live alone. I will mount an army myself tomorrow and go to rescue Guan Yunchang.” He sent one party at once to Langzhong to report to Yide, and another to muster men.

Before dawn, report after report came in: Guan Yu had fled by night toward Linju and was taken by Wu officers, and he and his son kept their loyalty and honor and ascended as spirits.

Xuande listened and cried once, then collapsed unconscious.

For the grief he uttered:

“Remembering our old oath to die together, how has it come that today I alone live on, casting off my life? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Guan Yu Reveals His Sanctity at Jade Spring Mountain; Cao Cao Is Aware of the Divine in Luoyang

chapters.html:
The wind-fever is treated, and the divine physician dies.
A final command is transmitted, and the treacherous hero reaches his end.

Now it was told that Liu Bei, the King of Han, collapsed when he heard that Guan Yu and his son were dead. The civil and military officials rushed to summon help, and after some time he regained consciousness and was carried back into the inner hall. Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, advised, “My lord, worry less. In the old sayings it is said that life and death are in the order of Heaven. This disaster came to Guan Yu because of his daily inflexibility and pride. My lord should care for your own body and seek revenge only in time.”

Xuande, whose courtesy name was Xuan De, said, “When I and my sworn brothers Guan and Zhang made the oath at the Peach Garden, we swore to live and die together. Now Yunchang is gone; how can I alone enjoy rank and comfort?” He had not finished speaking when Guan Xing arrived, crying aloud. On seeing him, Xuande cried once and fainted again. The officials revived him. For a day he would faint and waken three or five times, and for three days he would not take gruel or water, only wailing. His tears soaked his collar and robe until the stains turned red like blood. Kongming and the other officials repeatedly urged him to pull back.

Xuande said, “I swore with the king of Eastern Wu that I would never share the same sun and moon.” Kongming said, “I hear that in Wu they offered Guan Gong’s severed head to Cao Cao, and Cao Cao buried him with courtly honors.”

Xuande said, “What does this mean?”

Kongming said, “It is Wu’s attempt to shift blame onto Cao Cao. Cao Cao saw through that plot, so he buried Guan Gong with rich honors and invited Your Majesty to place blame on Wu.”

Xuande said, “I will set out immediately with troops to punish Wu and wash away my grievance.”

Kongming remonstrated, “It cannot be done. Wu now asks me to attack Wei, and Wei also asks me to attack Wu. Both sides harbor hidden schemes and wait for a crack. My lord should hold your army still and hold the funeral for Guan Gong. When Wu and Wei quarrel with one another, seize the moment to strike them.” The officials remonstrated again. At last Xuande managed to take food. He issued an order that all officers and soldiers in Shu should wear mourning. The Han King came out himself at the southern gate to summon the spirit and conduct the funeral, and he cried out in grief the whole day.

Cao Cao was in Luoyang. After burying Guan Yu, each night whenever he closed his eyes he saw Guan Yu. He was deeply alarmed and asked the officials what to do. They said, “The old halls of the traveling palace in Luoyang are haunted; you may build a new hall.”

Cao Cao said, “I wish to raise a hall named Jian Shi Hall, but I have no fine carpenter for it.” Jia Xu said, “There is a master carpenter named Su Yue in Luoyang, famous for clever design.” Cao summoned him and asked him to draw plans. Su Yue presented a plan for a nine-bay great hall with covered galleries and pavilions before and behind. Cao inspected it and said, “You have drawn it very much as I wished; I fear only that there is no timber to carry this.”

Su Yue said, “About thirty li from the city lies a pond called Yuelong Pond. In front of it is a shrine called Yuelong Shrine. Beside the shrine stands a giant pear tree, over ten zhang high, straight and fit to supply the main beam of Jian Shi Hall.”

Cao rejoiced and ordered carpenters to go and cut it.

The next day they reported that the tree could not be sawn, the ax could not bite into it, and it could not be felled. Cao did not believe them, so he personally rode out with a few hundred riders to Yuelong Shrine and dismounted before it. He looked up at the tree, towering like a canopy and reaching into the clouds, without any bend in it. He ordered it cut down. A few local elders came forward to remonstrate: “This tree is already several hundred years old and is home to a spirit person. It is likely unfit to be cut.”

Cao roared, “I have traveled under heaven for forty years. From Son of Heaven to the common people, none has failed to fear me. What spirit dares to disobey my will?” Then he drew the sword he wore and cut it himself. There was a sharp ringing sound, and blood sprayed all over him. Cao startled and panicked. He cast down the sword, mounted, and returned to the palace.

That night, in the second watch, Cao could not sleep, though he sat in the hall and drifted into dozing at the screen. Suddenly a man in wild hair and a black robe, carrying a sword, came straight before him, pointed and shouted, “I am the spirit of this pear tree. You build Jian Shi Hall to seize the great charge, and now you come to fell my sacred wood. I know your life is at an end. I have come to kill you.” Cao shouted, “Where are the guards?” and the black-robed man moved to strike. Cao cried out, and suddenly realized he was awake: he had a pounding headache he could not bear. He sent orders throughout the hall for doctors; no treatment could cure him. Everyone feared for him.

Hua Xin said, “Your Highness, do you know the divine physician Hua Tuo?”

Cao said, “Is he the one called Zhou Tai from Jiangdong?”

Hua Xin said, “It is.”

Cao said, “Though I have heard his name, I do not know his craft.”

Hua Xin said, “Hua Tuo, courtesy name Yuanhua, was from Qiao in Pei. His medical art is rare in the world. If there is a patient, he cures him with medicine, with needles, or with moxibustion as needed. For sickness of the five organs and six bowels when medicine is useless, he gives Mai-fei decoction to make the patient as if drunk dead, then opens the abdomen with a sharp knife, washes the organs with medicine broth, and the patient feels little pain. When finished, he stitches the incision and applies medicine; in a month or in twenty days, the patient is restored. Such is his astonishing skill.

One day he was passing on the road and heard a person groaning. He said, ‘This is a disease in which food and drink refuse to descend.’ He asked and it proved true. He had him drink three sheng of garlic-juice, whereupon a snake two or three zhang long emerged; the man’s appetite immediately returned. Governor Chen Deng of Guangling had vexation and flushed face, could not eat or drink, and sought Hua Tuo’s treatment. Tuo gave him a medicine; he vomited three sheng of parasites, each with red heads and trembling fore and aft. Deng asked why. Tuo said, ‘You have overate fishy flesh and this is the poison.’ Though he recovered today, in three years it will surely return; then he cannot be saved.’ Later Chen Deng indeed died after three years.

Another person came with a boil between the brows, unbearably itchy. He asked him to inspect it. Tuo said, ‘There is an insect inside.’ The men laughed. Tuo split it open and a yellow magpie flew out; the patient was cured.

Another person’s toe had been bitten by a dog; at the end of the toes two lumps grew, one causing sharp pain, the other intolerable itching. Tuo said, ‘The pain is from ten needles inside; the itching from two black-and-white game pieces inside.’ None believed him. He cut it open and the signs proved true. This man was indeed in the line of Bianque and Cang Gong.

He now lives near Jincheng, not far from here. Why would Your Highness not summon him?”

Cao immediately sent men through the night to summon Hua Tuo inside and diagnose his pulse and illness. Tuo said, “Your Highness’s headache comes from a wind disorder. The root is in the head; wind-phlegm cannot be expelled. Decoctions alone will not cure this. I have one method: first he must drink the Mai-fei Decoction, then the sharp axe must open the cranium to remove the wind-phlegm from the brain.”

Cao was furious and said, “You would kill me!”

Tuo said, “Your Highness once had an arrow poisoned through the right arm, like Guan Gong. I scraped the poison and he scarcely flinched. But now your small illness should not invite such suspicion.”

Cao said, “To scrape is for arm pain; shall one open the head? You knew Guan Yu well and use this moment to repay him!” He ordered him seized and dragged to prison, then beaten and questioned.

Jia Xu remonstrated, “A physician of this caliber is rare in the world; he should not be discarded.” Cao shouted, “This man means to use his opportunity to harm me. He is no different from Jiping’s pattern.” He ordered him tortured at once.

In prison there was a guard surnamed Wu, who everyone called Wu the Jailer. He served Hua Tuo each day with wine and food. Tuo, moved by his kindness, said, “I am soon to die and regret leaving the Book of the Green Gourd untaught to the world. Because of your kindness, I have no way to repay you. I will write a book and send it home; bring it to me, and then return with the Book of the Green Gourd to continue my art.”

Wu was overjoyed and said, “If I can get this book, I will leave this post and heal the sick of the world, passing on the virtue of the teacher.” Tuo wrote at once and gave it to Wu the Jailer.

Wu traveled to Jincheng and asked Tuo’s wife to fetch the Qingnang Book. He returned to prison and returned it to Hua Tuo. They reviewed it, and Tuo immediately handed the book to Wu.

Wu carried it home and hid it. After ten days Hua Tuo died in prison. Wu bought a coffin and burial coffin and then left his assignment to return home, intending to study the Qingnang Book. He saw his wife burning the volume there. He cried out in alarm, rushed to seize it, but it was already burned to ash; only one or two leaves remained. Wu cursed and berated his wife. She said, “Even if one learns medicine as miraculous as Hua Tuo, if he has to die in jail, what use is it?” Wu sighed and stopped. So the Qingnang Book was never passed on to the world; only small arts about chickens and swine were later passed down, and those too were from one or two burned leaves.

A poem later lamented:

Hua Tuo’s immortal skill, like a great mulberry branch, Divine insight like peering through one span of wall, It is mournful that the man dies and the book is severed, Later ages will no longer behold the Green Gourd.

After Cao Cao murdered Hua Tuo, his illness only worsened, and he still worried about Wu and Shu. While he was fretting over this, close officers suddenly reported that Eastern Wu had sent envoys with a memorial. Cao took the document and read it. It said briefly:

Your servant Sun Quan has long known that Heaven’s mandate has returned to Your Majesty. In hope that the Great Office be corrected at the earliest, I beg that You dispatch generals to crush Liu Bei and level the Two Rivers; I and my men will then return in submission.

Cao read it and laughed broadly, then showed it to all ministers: “This boy means to set me upon the funeral pyre!” The Chamberlain Chen Qun and others answered, “The Han house has long decayed. Your Highness’s virtue and merit are towering, and the people look to you. Now Sun Quan kneels in submission. This is Heaven’s design, and all signs are in accord. Your Highness ought to follow Heaven and men and seize the proper office.”

Cao laughed: “I have served the Han for many years. Though I have merits and benefits for the people, I have only reached the rank of King and the highest fief available. How could I harbor other designs? If Heaven’s mandate lies with me, I am already King Wen of Zhou.”

Sima Yi said, “Now that Sun Quan has submitted, Your Highness should grant him an office and rank so that he denies Liu Bei.” Cao agreed and issued a memorial appointing Sun Quan as General of Agile Cavalry and Marquess of Nanchang, with the governorship of Jing Province. He at once sent the imperial edict to Wu.

Cao’s illness grew worse. One night he dreamt that three horses ate from one trough; on waking he asked Jia Xu, “Recently I dreamt three horses in one trough, and I suspect this means Ma Teng and his son bring disaster. Ma Teng is dead now, yet last night I dreamt it again. What does it portend?”

Jia Xu said, “The horse omen is lucky. The blessed horse returns to Cao. Why should the king of Cao be worried?” Cao accepted that and did not doubt it.

Later people wrote:

Three horses in one trough may be seen as suspicious, Yet few know whether this has planted the roots of Jin. Cao Man’s scheming was full of villainy, but who in court recognized the Master Sima?

That night Cao lay in his chamber. At the third watch, when he grew faint and dizzy with head and eyes, he rose and reclined again against the side chair. He heard the hall split as if torn. Startled, he looked and saw Empress Fu, Consort Dong, the two princes, and Fu Wan and Dong Cheng among twenty others, all with their whole bodies smeared blood, standing beneath dark sorrowful clouds, and low voices calling for their lives. Cao snatched his sword and swung it into the air. A loud crack sounded and the southwest corner of the hall collapsed.

Cao staggered and fell to the ground. Attendants pulled him out, moved him to another palace, and he recovered there. In the next watch they again heard endless crying from men and women outside the hall until dawn. At daylight Cao summoned ministers and said, “In thirty years of life in arms and campaigning I had never trusted strange omens or phantasms. Why is this happening today?”

The ministers answered, “Your Highness should have Daoist priests hold sacrificial rites and charms to avert what approaches.” Cao sighed, “The sages said: ‘If one has offended Heaven, there is no prayer that can help.’ Heaven’s mandate is already used up for me. What can be done?” He refused to allow rites.

The next day he felt heat in his qi rise to the upper burner and could not make out what he saw. He urgently consulted Xiahou Dun. When Dun reached the hall gate, he too saw Empress Fu, Consort Dong, the two princes, Fu Wan, and Dong Cheng standing within the dark clouds. He was horrified, collapsed, and after he was helped out he fell ill.

Cao summoned Cao Hong, Chen Qun, Jia Xu, Sima Yi, and others to come to his bed and entrust matters after him. They knelt and said, “Your Highness, cherish your body; recovery will come and you will rise suddenly.”

Cao said, “For more than thirty years I have been reckless across the land, and all rival lords are gone. Only Sun Quan in Wu and Liu Bei in Shu remain uncleared. I am now in dangerous illness and cannot again confer with you all, so I entrust family matters.

My eldest son Cao Ang, born of Lady Liu, died young in Wan City. Now Lady Bian has borne four sons: Pi, Zhang, Zhi, and Xiong. The third, Zhi, has been my favorite; he is graceful yet shallow and unreliable, given to wine and loose living, and so he has not been named heir. The second son, Zhang, is brave but lacking strategy. The fourth, Xiong, is often sick and unlikely to survive. Only the eldest, Cao Pi, is grave, reverent, and careful; he may inherit my work. You should support him.”

Cao Hong and the others wept and received the order before they left.

Cao ordered attendants to fetch the perfumes he kept in daily use and distribute them to all the palace women, bidding them, “After I die, you must learn weaving with diligence and make silk shoes in quantity; selling them will give you your own means.” He also ordered the rest to stay mostly in the Copper Sparrow Terrace, setting daily memorial meals, and always having female musicians sing at table.

He further ordered that at Zhande Prefecture’s Jiangwu City, outside the city walls where weapons were taught, seventy-two decoy burial mounds be raised, and none should learn my place of burial, lest people exhume it. After all the orders, he took one long breath and wept in torrents. In a moment his qi left him and he died.

He was sixty-six. It was the first month of spring in the twenty-fifth year of Jian'an.

Later there was a piece called Ode to Ye City, lamenting Cao Cao:

In Ye, at the waters of Ye City and Zhang waters, A strange man surely rises from here. Great designs and elegant writings mingle like text and meaning; Ruler and minister as kin, yet as father and son too. Heroic hearts did not house common thoughts, Where they rose and withdrew no one could read by the eye.
