He was both prime mover and great culprit—not two men; From one body came both stench and fragrance. Poetry with spirit and command with force— can such power be scattered among ordinary crowds? Across the taiping rivers he built his terrace by the Taihang ridge, His vigor and reason surged and fell against each other. Can such a man exist without rebellion? If he was not tyrant, he was no king by destiny. Great captains became sons and daughters in lament, Yet nothing could make this inner unrest cease. The lamp in the front chamber knows what harm there was not, The divided incense cannot be called compassionless. Alas! The ancients act with no act too small; Their lone magnificence carries meaning. Young scholars lightly mock those in the mound; The dead in the mound will laugh at your scholar’s heat.

When news of Cao Cao’s death arrived, all civil and military officers wore full mourning.

At once envoys were sent to inform Prince Cao Pi, Marquis of Yanling, Crown Prince Cao Zhang, Marquis of Linzi, and Prince Cao Zhi, Marquis of Linzi, and Cao Xiong, Marquis of Xiaohuai, of their loss.

Officers prepared a golden coffin and silver casket and put Cao’s body in preparation; before dawn they carried the coffin and spirit-banner to Yè Commandery overnight.

When Cao Pi heard of his father’s death, he wailed aloud and led all officials in and out of the city ten li to meet the procession, which halted in a side hall. Officials in mourning gathered and wept there.

Suddenly one man stepped forward and said, “Please, Crown Prince, restrain grief and discuss the momentous matter.” All eyes turned; it was Sima Fu, Director of the Inner Household.

Sima Fu said, “Since King Wei has passed, the realm is shaken. We should quickly establish a successor king to steady the people; crying alone is not enough.”

An official said, “The Crown Prince should indeed inherit, yet without an order from the Son of Heaven no one should act precipitously.”

Minister of War Chen Jiao then tore a sleeve from his robe with his sword and shouted, “This very day I will request that the Crown Prince inherit! If anyone here dares to object, let them take this sleeve as example!”

All officials were struck with awe. Then Hua Xin arrived from Xuchang on a flying horse. All were startled.

Soon Hua Xin entered. The officials asked the reason.

Hua Xin said, “Now that the King of Wei is gone, the realm is shaken. Why do we delay and install the Crown Prince?”

The officials replied, “We were only discussing that because we lacked the Son of Heaven’s edict we wished him, the empress and mother Lady Bian’s mercy, to establish the Crown Prince as king.”

Hua Xin said, “I have obtained the edict from the Han emperor; it is here.” Great cheering arose. He drew the edict from his breast and read it aloud.

It turned out Hua Xin had flatly flattered Wei and drafted this decree, pressuring the Present Emperor to submit. The emperor only obeyed, and the order thus decreed Cao Pi as King of Wei, Chancellor, and Governor of Ji Province. Cao Pi ascended the same day and accepted the ceremonial bows and dances of all officials.

Exactly when the court was celebrating and toasting, news came that Cao Zhang had arrived from Chang’an with one hundred thousand troops. Cao Pi was startled. He asked the ministers, “My younger brother with the yellow beard is rough by nature and deeply skilled in arms. He has come with an army from afar. He must be angling for the throne. What am I to do?”

At once a man below the steps answered, “I beg to go and meet the Marquis of Yanling and resolve this matter in a few words.” The officials said, “No one but a senior statesman can untangle this calamity.”

The chapter closed:

Watch the matter of Cao Pi and Cao Zhang and see how near it comes to a contention like the Yuan house before them; Who this man may be remains unknown.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Treating the Wind Illness, the Divine Physician Dies; Giving His Last Commands, the Treacherous Hero Meets His End

chapters.html:
Now it was said that Cao Pi heard Cao Zhang had raised troops and was coming toward the capital. He anxiously asked the officials, and one man stepped forward, volunteering to go and bring him into obedience. Those present recognized him as Jia Kui, Remonstrance Gentleman. Cao Pi was greatly pleased and ordered Jia Kui to go.

Jia Kui took the command and rode out of the city, where he met Cao Zhang. Cao Zhang asked, “Where are the former sovereign’s seals and insignia?” Jia Kui said sternly, “The state has a crown prince, and the realm has an heir apparent. The former sovereign’s seals and insignia are not for you to ask about.”

Cao Zhang stayed silent. He then entered the city together with Jia Kui. Near the gate of the palace, Jia Kui asked, “Did you come to attend mourning, or to contest the throne?” Cao Zhang replied, “I came for mourning only. I harbor no other thought.”

Jia Kui said, “If so, why did you bring troops into the capital?” Cao Zhang immediately shouted for his men on both sides to fall back and, alone, entered in alone. The two brothers embraced and wept aloud. Cao Zhang handed over all his troops and horses to Cao Pi. Cao Pi ordered him to return to Yanling and hold there.

Cao Zhang bowed and left.

So Cao Pi settled on the throne and changed the twenty-fifth year of Jian’an into the first year of Yankang. He ennobled Jia Xu as Grand Commandant, Hua Xin as Chancellor, and Wang Lang as Censor-in-Chief. Officials at every level were all promoted.

He conferred the posthumous title of Wu Wang on Cao Cao and buried him at Gaoling in Ye Commandery. He gave Yu Jin the charge of managing the tomb. When Yu Jin arrived, he saw on the whitewashed walls paintings of Guan Yunchang’s victory at Shuiyin Seven Encampments, where Yu Jin had been captured: Guan Yunchang sat upright and dignified, while Pang De raged in anger without yielding; Yu Jin knelt on the ground in humiliation, pleading for a release of life.

Cao Pi had had these scenes painted on the tomb wall to humiliate Yu Jin, for he considered it indecorous that Yu Jin had been defeated, had failed to preserve martial integrity, then returned after surrender. When Yu Jin saw this painting, he felt shame and anger. His rage turned to illness, and he died soon after.

A later poet lamented:

For thirty years I spoke of old loyalty, yet, when danger came, he was not faithful to Cao.
He had not truly known men in his own heart; now he paints a tiger from its very bones.

Hua Xin then reported to Cao Pi: “The Marquis of Yanzhou, Cao Zhang, surrendered his troops and returned home. But the Marquis of Linzi, Cao Zhi, and Marquis of Xiao Huai, Cao Xiong, did not come to mourning. They should be charged with crime.”

Cao Pi approved and sent two missions at once.

After a day passed, the messenger from Xiao Huai returned to report, “Cao Xiong, Marquis of Xiao Huai, fearing punishment, hanged himself.” Cao Pi ordered a sumptuous burial and posthumously elevated him to King.

The next day another envoy returned, saying: “The Marquis of Linzi, Cao Zhi, has every day drunk and banqueted with Ding Yi (Zhengli) and Ding Yi (Jingli). They became wild and disrespectful. When the mission arrived, the Marquis of Linzi sat motionless and unmoving. Ding Yi shouted: ‘In former times the late sovereign wanted our lord to be made heir, but malicious ministers blocked it. How can he now, before mourning is ended, question blood kin?’

Ding Yi (Jingli) shouted: ‘Our lord’s wisdom surpasses the world and should naturally inherit; how could he not do so? Why are you ministers of court and cannot recognize talent of this scale?’

The Marquis of Linzi grew angry and shouted at the guards, ordering a staff to beat the attendants and drive everyone out.”

When Cao Pi heard this he was very angry and ordered Xu Chu to lead three thousand Tiger Guard troops at speed to Linzi to arrest Cao Zhi and all his companions.

Xu Chu led the army to Linzi City. The local commander tried to block him. Xu Chu stood and beheaded him on the spot, then entered the city directly. No one dared to oppose his thrust. He went straight to the hall.

Cao Zhi, Ding Yi (Zhengli), Ding Yi (Jingli), and their men all lay drunk and senseless. Xu Chu bound them, loaded them onto carts, and arrested all their subordinate officers and staff under the household, bringing all to Ye Commandery to await Cao Pi’s judgment.

Cao Pi ordered Ding Yi (Zhengli) and Ding Yi (Jingli) to be executed outright. The two men, were men of Pei Commandery and among the renowned scholars of their time. When they were killed, many regretted it.

Hearing that Cao Xiong had hanged himself, Cao Pi’s mother Lady Bian was deeply grieved. When she then heard that Cao Zhi had been seized and his associates Ding Yi and others already executed, she was greatly startled.

She hurried out and summoned Cao Pi to see her. Cao Pi came out of the hall and bowed in panic. Lady Bian wept and said, “Your brother Zhi always loved drinking and recklessness, because he trusts too much in his own talent and so has been unrestrained. Remember your own blood kinship and spare his life. Then I can rest in peace even at my ninth day in the grave.”

Cao Pi said, “Your son also deeply loves his talent; why should he harm him? I only wish now to correct his conduct.”

Lady Bian left in tears. Cao Pi returned to the side hall and summoned Cao Zhi.

Hua Xin asked, “Was this because Your Majesty’s mother asked you not to kill Zijian?” Cao Pi replied, “Yes.”

Hua Xin said, “Zhi is full of talent and wit. He is no ordinary man. If he is not removed now, he will become a later harm.”

Cao Pi said, “I cannot disobey my mother’s command.” Hua Xin said, “Everyone says that Zhi can speak in perfect prose and verse, but I do not fully trust this. Your Majesty should summon him and test him in talent. If he fails, he should be executed; if he truly succeeds, then demote him and silence the literary men of the realm.”

Cao Pi followed this.

After a while Cao Zhi came to audience, fearful, knelt down and begged pardon. Cao Pi said, “Though brotherly affection links us, duty and rank place you as my subject. How can you, relying on talent, disdain protocol? In our late lord’s day, you often showed off writing to others; I have long doubted you used others to write for you. I now allow you seven steps to create a poem. If you succeed, you will be spared one death; if you fail, you will face heavy punishment and I will not grant leniency.”

Cao Zhi said, “I beg Your Majesty to give the subject a topic.”

A water-ink painting hung in the hall showed two bulls fighting under an earth wall, one falling into a well and dying. Cao Pi pointed to it and said, “Take this as your topic. Your verse must not include the wording ‘two bulls fighting under the wall, one bull falls into the well and dies.’”

Cao Zhi took seven steps and completed this poem:

Two oxen walk in perfect alignment; one carries a hollow ridge on its head.
Encountering each other at the bank’s slope, they suddenly collide and clash.
The two enemies were not equally hard-fated, and one lay in a pit of earth.
This was not weakness of strength, but that mighty force had not fully exhausted itself.

Cao Pi and the full court were all astonished.

Cao Pi said again, “Though you made the poem in seven steps, I still find it slow. Can you answer with a poem extemporaneously now?”

Cao Zhi said, “I beg for a topic immediately.”

Cao Pi said, “We are brothers. Let this be the topic. Do not include the character “brother.””

Cao Zhi did not pause to think and instantly spoke:

Beans boiling, bean vines burned as fuel, While beans in the pot weep. They share one root from the same mother-tree; Why must one be hastened to crush the other?

When Cao Pi heard it, tears came to his eyes. Lady Bian then came out from behind the hall and asked, “Why do you oppress your brother so far?”

Cao Pi hastily rose and left his seat, saying, “State law cannot be abandoned.” Then he demoted Cao Zhi to Marquis of Anxiang. Cao Zhi bowed and took up his horse to depart.

After Cao Pi had succeeded, he renewed laws and statutes. He pressured the Han emperor even more than his father had. Detail agents had already reported to Chengdu. Liu Bei, King of Hanzhong, heard this and was shocked. He consulted with his civil and military officers and said, “Cao Cao is dead and Cao Pi has succeeded him. He presses the Son of Heaven more harshly than Cao Cao ever did. Sun Quan of Eastern Wu has extended submission with folded hands. I wish first to punish Eastern Wu and avenge Guan Gong; next I wish to pacify the Central Plains and remove the rebel villains.”

Before he finished, Liao Hua rose up and bowed to the ground, crying, “Lord Guan and his son were killed because of Liu Feng and Meng Da. Grant my lord’s order to execute these two villains.”

Liu Bei was about to send men to capture them.

Kongming remonstrated: “Not now. We should first set a slower plan. If pressed now, disaster will break out at once. Promote both men to commandery posts and send them in different regions. Then they can be captured.”

Liu Bei obeyed and sent an order to promote Liu Feng to hold Mianzhu.

Indeed, Peng Yang and Meng Da were close allies. When they heard this, they quickly returned home and made a report to be sent, sending Peng Yang’s trusted man at once to Meng Da. The messenger had only just left the south gate when Ma Chao, on an inspection ride, apprehended him and brought him before Ma Chao.

Ma Chao understood the matter at once and went to see Peng Yang. Peng Yang welcomed him and set out wine. After several rounds, Ma Chao pried with words: “Formerly King Hanzhong was exceedingly generous to you; why have you grown cold?”

Peng Yang, drunk, cursed and said bitterly, “An old villainous fool— I will surely repay him!” Ma Chao pressed on: “I, too, have long harbored resentment.”

Peng Yang said, “Raise your own troops and join with Meng Da to support us from outside; I will lead the Sichuan troops as an inner response. Then a great undertaking can be achieved.”

Ma Chao said, “Your plan is fitting. We will discuss it further tomorrow.”

Ma Chao left and conveyed Peng Yang and the letter to Liu Bei, explaining everything in detail. Liu Bei was very angry and ordered Peng Yang seized and thrown in jail for interrogation.

In prison Peng Yang repented too late. Liu Bei asked Kongming, “Peng Yang had intent to rebel; how shall he be punished?” Kongming said, “Though he is a wild and unruly man, leaving him alive will surely produce disaster.” So Liu Bei gave Peng Yang death in jail.

After Peng Yang’s death, someone informed Meng Da. Meng Da was greatly startled. He lost his composure. Before long, an envoy arrived ordering Liu Feng to return to guard Mianzhu.

Meng Da panicked and urgently gathered with his brothers-in-arms Shen Dan and Shen Yi, the commanders of Shangyong, to discuss: “Meng Da and Fa Xiaozhi have both rendered service to the King of Han. Now Xiaozhi is dead, and the King of Han has forgotten my prior service, and wishes to harm me. What shall I do?”

Shen Dan said, “I have a scheme by which the King of Han cannot harm you.” Meng Da was overjoyed and quickly asked what scheme.

Shen Dan said, “My brothers and I have long wished to surrender to Wei. You can draft a memorial resigning from your service to the King of Han and go over to Wei King Cao Pi. Cao Pi will certainly make use of you fully. My two brothers and I will come to surrender after you.”

Meng Da suddenly understood and wrote such a memorial at once, giving it to the envoy. That same evening he rode out with more than fifty horsemen and surrendered to Wei.

The envoy returned to Chengdu and presented the memorial to Liu Bei, reporting Meng Da’s defection.

Liu Bei read it and was furious:

Your servant Da humbly submits: your Highness has set out to complete the enterprises of Yi and Lu and to pursue the achievements of Huan and Wen. Great work has only just been begun, and by seizing advantage from Wu and Chu, you have drawn to you men of enterprise, who have returned and submitted. Ever since I placed myself under you, I have accumulated errors unending; I know myself, and how much more so Your Highness? Now, since in Your Highness’s court talents gather like fish in full school, I have no aptitude inside for aiding you and no talent outside for commanding troops. When I stand among your meritorious ministers, I can truly only be ashamed of myself.

I have heard it said that Fanli perceived the slightest signs and drifted upon the Five Lakes; that Shangfan sought pardon and repaid offense on the riverbank. In this moment of conjunction, I ask to resign my life and plead for release: it is but a desire to cleanse and separate my obligations.

How, then, can I, who am base and poor, with neither great merits nor great service, yet still be bound by the times, but secretly long for former worthies and think on distant shame? In former times Shen Sheng was supremely filial yet doubted by kin; Zi Xun was supremely loyal yet put to death by his sovereign; Meng Tian enlarged borders and yet bore a great penalty; Yue Yi broke Qi and yet was slandered by smooth tongues. Each time I have read their records, tears have never failed me; when they happened before my eyes, grief only deepened.

Recently Jing Province was overthrown, and high ministers lost discipline; not one returned. But because of what has happened to me, I have gone to Fangling and Shangyong and then begged to be removed from office and released abroad. I hope Your Highness’s holy favor, with true understanding and pity, will grasp my heart and compassionately consider my act.

I am a truly small man and cannot keep constant loyalty from beginning to end. If I knew and still did it, how can I say I am without guilt? I have often heard it said: when friends part there is no evil report; those who depart carry no words of resentment. I, your servant, followed a gentleman’s instruction; I pray Your Highness will try to honor it.

Liu Bei finished reading and said, “How dare this commoner betray me and mock me with polished words?” He almost ordered an immediate campaign to capture him. Kongming said, “Then send Liu Feng at once with troops and let the two tigers combine. If Liu Feng gains merit or suffers defeat, he will return to Chengdu, and then he can be dealt with, avoiding two evils.” Liu Bei agreed and sent orders to Liu Feng.

Liu Feng obeyed, leading soldiers to arrest Meng Da.

Later, Cao Pi was in the capital gathering officials when a close retainer reported, “General Meng Da of Shu has come in surrender.” Cao Pi summoned him and asked, “You have come this time. Is it not possible you are pretending to submit?”

Meng Da replied, “I did not save Lord Guan in his danger; therefore the King of Han wishes to kill me. I have come in fear of punishment; I have no other intent.”

Though Cao Pi had not yet fully believed him, news came that Liu Feng was bringing five or more ten-thousand troops and was coming to seize Xiangyang to engage Meng Da in close battle.

Cao Pi said, “If your heart is truly sincere, you may go to Xiangyang and bring back Liu Feng’s head. Only then I will believe you.”

Meng Da said, “If benefits and harms are considered, there is no need to move the armies; Liu Feng himself can be made to submit.”

Cao Pi rejoiced and promoted Meng Da to Scattered Cavalry Gentleman, General Who Establishes Military Success, and Marquis of Pingyang Ting. He made him Administrator of Xincheng and assigned him to guard Xiangyang and Fancheng.

At that time Xiahou Shang and Xu Huang were already in Xiangyang, collecting the units from Shangyong. When Meng Da arrived, he paid due courtesy to the two generals. He learned that Liu Feng had camped fifty li beyond the city beneath a hill. Meng Da sent a letter inviting Liu Feng to surrender.

When Liu Feng read the letter, he was in such anger saying, “This traitor has violated the duty of uncle and nephew and sullied the relation between father and son, making me appear disloyal and unfilial!” He tore up the letter and beheaded its messenger.

The next day he marched out to engage in battle.

Meng Da, hearing what had happened, was outraged at once and led his army out.

The two formations closed and faced each other. Liu Feng, mounted beneath the gate banner, pointed his saber and shouted, “Traitor who betrays the state, how dare you so blaspheme?”

Meng Da replied, “Death stands before you already. Why do you still cling to denial?” Liu Feng grew furious, drove his horse forward and charged directly at Meng Da. The fight was brief; Meng Da broke and fled. Liu Feng chased for twenty or more li. His cry rose, and all the ambush troops came out at once.

Shanghou Shang came from the left, and Xu Huang from the right. Meng Da turned back and fought again. Three armies attacked in a pincer.

Liu Feng was badly defeated and retreated through the night to Shangyong. Wei troops pursued from behind. Liu Feng reached the city wall and called to be let in, but disorderly arrows came down from the battlements.

Shen Dan called from the enemy tower, “I have already surrendered to Wei!”

Liu Feng’s footing was unsteady; he had no choice but to flee toward Fangling. He saw the city now fully hung with Wei banners. Shen Yi on the opposing tower shook his banner. From behind the city a massed unit surged forth, bearing a banner that read in large script, “Right General Xu Huang.”

Liu Feng could no longer stand the onslaught and fled hoping to reach western Sichuan. Xu Huang pressed the pursuit. Liu Feng had only a hundred riders left. On arriving in Chengdu, he entered in front of the King of Han and knelt, weeping, to detail the former events.

Liu Bei was furious and said, “With what face has an unclean son returned to me?”

Liu Feng said, “Your uncle’s peril was such that no son should not have aided him; it was only because Meng Da’s counsel obstructed me.”

Liu Bei’s anger shifted. “You should eat human flesh and wear human robes. You are no mere wooden puppet! How could you listen to a slanderous villain’s obstruction?” He ordered attendants to drag him out and execute him.

Liu Bei had now executed Liu Feng. Later, when he heard that Meng Da had invited and then betrayed him and that he had torn up the letter and executed the envoy, he regretted it inwardly. He also grieved over Guan Gong and had become ill from that grief, so he stayed his armies.

Meanwhile Cao Pi, since assuming kingship, rewarded all civil and military officials once more. He then commanded three hundred thousand troops, touring south to Qiao County in Pei. He made a grand offering before the ancestral tomb. The elders of the nearby fields raised dust along the roads and presented cups of wine in attendance, reenacting Han Gaozu’s return to Pei.

A report arrived that General Xiahou Dun was gravely ill. Cao Pi immediately returned to Ye Commandery. By then Xiahou Dun had already died, so Cao Pi assumed mourning and arranged his burial with full honors.

In the eighth month of that year, there were reports that phoenix omens appeared in Shiyi County, a qilin was seen in Linzi City, and a yellow dragon appeared in Ye Commandery.

Thus Li Fu, Zhonglang General, and Xu Zhi, Assistant to the Grand Historian, deliberated: such auspicious signs were signs that Wei should replace Han, and a ceremony of transfer might be arranged, with the Son of Heaven handing heaven-mandated rule to Cao Pi.

Accordingly Hua Xin, Wang Lang, Xin Pi, Jia Xu, Liu Yi, Liu Ye, Chen Qiao, Chen Qun, and Huan Jie, with more than forty officials of civil and military rank, entered the inner hall together and presented the request before Emperor Xian that he cede the realm to Wei King Cao Pi.

The Cao household’s state altars are now close to being founded; the Han’s court and territory have already shifted.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Elder Brother Presses Younger Brother to Compose Verse; Nephew Entraps Uncle and Liu Feng Is Condemned

chapters.html:
Hua Xin and a group of civil and military officials came in to make an audience with Emperor Xian. Hua Xin reported: “Your Majesty, since you ascended the position, your virtue has spread across the four directions and your mercy has reached all beneath heaven. You have surpassed past ages and now exceed the present age. Though even Yao and Shun could not surpass this, still the ministers met together and determined that the Han mandate is exhausted. We urge Your Majesty to follow the ways of Yao and Shun, and for the sake of mountains, rivers, and altars of state, to transfer the mandate to the King of Wei. Let Heaven and the people be aligned. Then Your Majesty may enjoy a life of quiet retirement, and Your ancestors and the living will rejoice.”

When the report reached him, the emperor was greatly startled and stood silent for half a while. He looked across the gathered officials, wept, and said: “I remember my high ancestor, who took up a three-foot sword, beheaded the serpent revolt, subdued Qin, and crushed Chu; he founded this realm, and its inheritance has passed for four hundred years. Though I am not gifted, I have committed no grave evil. How could I lightly cast aside the great foundation of our forebears? Yet you officials all follow the same counsel.”

Hua Xin brought Li Fu and Xu Zhi forward and said: “If Your Majesty doubts this, ask these two.”

Li Fu said: “Ever since the King of Wei ascended, a qilin was born, phoenixes came in proper formation, a yellow dragon appeared, auspicious grain grew thickly, and sweet dew descended. These are signs from Heaven, showing that Wei is to replace Han.”

Xu Zhi added: “I am in charge of observing Heaven’s pattern, and by night I have studied the heavenly trigrams. The fate of Han’s flame has already ended, and Your Majesty’s star is dim and obscure. In Wei, the heavenly pattern and earthly signs are all clear, though difficult to state in full. There is, moreover, an omen chart that matches what was expected. It reads: ‘A ghost on the frontier, the linked ministers; Han should pass on, no one can deny it. The word lies eastward, the horse lies westward; two suns shine together and move above and below.’ If we read this, Your Majesty should abdicate at once. ‘Ghost on the frontier’ and ‘linked ministers’ together form the character Wei. ‘The word is east, the horse is west’ forms the character Xu. ‘Two suns shine together and move above and below’ forms the character Chang. This means Wei, at Xuchang, is to receive Han’s abdication. I beg Your Majesty to consider this.”

The emperor replied: “These auspicious signs and omens are all delusions. How can one accept such fictions and at once abandon my ancestors’ great foundation?”

Wang Lang then said: “Throughout history, rise is always followed by fall, and fullness by decline. Is there any country that does not fall, any house that does not fail? Han rule has passed down four hundred and some years and has reached Your Majesty; the appointed number is exhausted. Better to retreat early and avoid delay. Delay brings calamity.”

The emperor wept and withdrew into the inner hall. The officials smirked as they withdrew.

The next day, the official corps again gathered in the great hall, and eunuchs were sent to summon the Son of Heaven. The emperor, fearing what would happen, did not dare to come out. Cao Hong’s sister, Empress Cao, said: “The officials request that Your Majesty convene court. Why do you refuse to appear?”

He replied with tears, “Your brother seeks to usurp the throne, pressing the officials together to force me. That is why I do not come out.”

Empress Cao grew angry and said: “Why should my brother do this treacherous, rebellious deed?” Before she could finish, Cao Hong and Cao Xiu entered with drawn swords, asking the emperor to come out to the hall.

Empress Cao shouted: “All of you are rebels who sought wealth and rank and conspired together in treason! My father’s merit covered the realm, and he shook the world, yet he did not dare steal Heaven’s regalia. Now my brother has just succeeded and already seeks to seize Han. Heaven will not bless him!”

She stopped, then entered the palace in a great cry. The attendants around her sobbed and wept.

Cao Hong and Cao Xiu pleaded fiercely for the emperor’s appearance. Being unable to resist, the emperor changed clothing and came out to the fore hall. Hua Xin reported: “Your Majesty should follow what we deliberated yesterday, and thereby avoid disaster.”

The emperor wept again: “You have all eaten Han stipends for long. In between there are many sons and grandsons of Han powerholders. How could you do this, when your duty is to serve?”

Hua Xin answered: “If Your Majesty does not follow the court’s counsel, murder within the inner quarters may rise by dawn. This is no lack of loyalty.”

The emperor said: “Who dares to kill me?”

Hua Xin replied sharply: “All under heaven know that Your Majesty has no favor as Son of Heaven, and therefore disorder swells at all four corners. If the King of Wei were not present, how would only one person kill your person? You do not even understand the return of favor and gratitude. You would invite all under heaven to strike you down?”

The emperor, trembling, rose and stirred. Wang Lang watched him. Hua Xin strode forward, grasped the dragon robe, and, voice changed, said: “Permit or refuse—speak now!”

The emperor shook and could not answer. Cao Hong and Cao Xiu shouted for swords: “Where is Fubao Lang?”

Zu Bi answered from the back: “Fubao Lang is here!” Cao Hong asked for the jade seal.

Zu Bi shouted back: “The jade seal is the treasure of the Son of Heaven. How can one seize it by force?” Cao Hong shouted, and ordered the soldiers to drag him out and execute him.

Zu Bi went on cursing until he died.

Later generations composed a verse on him:

Treacherous usurpers seized power, and the house of Han perished; Falsely naming it abdication, they imitated Yu and Tang. Every lord at court bowed down before Wei; Only the Keeper of the Seals proved a loyal minister.

The emperor trembled without ceasing. He then saw, at the stair, hundreds of armored men with halberds, all Wei soldiers.

Through tears he told the officials: “I am willing to abdicate the realm to the King of Wei and keep only a few breaths to end my life.”

Jia Xu said: “The King of Wei will not betray Your Majesty. Your Majesty should issue the decree at once to calm all hearts.”

Reluctantly, Emperor Xian ordered Chen Qun to draft the edict of abdication and ordered Hua Xin to carry it with the imperial seal to the King of Wei’s palace.

Cao Pi was overjoyed. He read it:

I have ruled thirty-two years. Great disorder has overturned everything beneath heaven, and only by the spirit of my forebears I have been saved and restored. Now, looking up to the signs in Heaven and looking down at the minds of the people, I see that the qi of Han has reached its end, and Fortune has moved into the Cao house. Therefore, where the former king showed mighty heroism, the present king now shines in lofty virtue in answer to this appointed time. The pattern is clear. The Great Way, when it is fulfilled, belongs to all under heaven. Yao did not keep the mandate for his own sons, and his name spread without limit. I admire that. Now I follow Yao’s precedent and yield the realm to the Chancellor of Wei. King, do not decline to receive it.

When Cao Pi finished reading, he moved as if to receive the imperial mandate. Sima Yi remonstrated: “Do not do so yet. Though the seal and edict have arrived, Your Highness should first submit a memorial in humility, so as to end criticism from the world.”

Cao Pi followed him and ordered Wang Lang to draft an offering of modesty in which he described himself as unworthy and asked to look for greater worthies to inherit Heaven’s mandate.

The emperor read the memorial and was deeply anxious and doubtful. He asked his officials: “The King of Wei is so modest. What can we do?”

Hua Xin said: “When King Wu of Wei first accepted kingship, he refused three times and only then accepted after repeated summons. Your Majesty should send down another edict. The King of Wei will then have to accept.”

The emperor had no choice. He ordered Huan Ji to draft yet another edict and sent Zhang Yin, an envoy with a tally from the ancestral temple, carrying the jade seal to the King of Wei’s palace.

Cao Pi opened it and read:

Hear this, King of Wei: the Son of Heaven humbly withdraws, yet he fears that my reluctance has become a matter of shame. By the merit of the Martial King, who bore your family’s title, virtue has answered Heaven’s mandate; he raised divine vigor, cut down violent brigands, and quieted the realms of the Four Quarters. Now you, Pi, have continued that thread. Your virtue is resplendent, your moral teaching reaches the four seas, and benevolence touches the eight districts. Heaven’s pattern is truly borne by you in person. The Great Yu of old had accomplished flood work and so the Great Emperor Shun yielded the throne; Yu then received the Mandate. In the line of Han from Yao, there is propriety in such succession. With harmony to numinous spirits and in compliance with Heaven’s bright command, I send General Supervisory Envoy Zhang Yin with the imperial seal and ribbon. King, you should receive it.

Cao Pi took the response with joy and said to Jia Xu: “Though this comes twice, later ages may still brand me a usurper.”

Jia Xu said: “The matter is easy. Send Zhang Yin back with the seal and ribbon, then have Hua Xin bring the Son of Heaven to build a platform named the Platform of Abdication. Choose an auspicious day and fortunate hour, summon all high and low state ministers, gather them below the platform, and have the Son of Heaven personally hand over the seal and ribbon to You and yield the realm there. Then all doubts will be cleared and all argument will cease.”

Cao Pi was pleased. He ordered Zhang Yin to carry back the seal and ribbon, and at once again made a memorial of humility.

When Zhang Yin returned and reported, the emperor asked his ministers: “The King of Wei refuses again. What does this mean?”

Hua Xin said: “Your Majesty should build a platform called the Platform of Abdication, gather all great and small ministers and commoners, and publicly clarify the transfer. Then Your Majesty’s children and children’s children will surely receive Wei’s grace.”

The emperor agreed and sent officials of the Court of Rites to select a site at Fanyang. They built a three-tier high platform and chose, on a gengwu day in the tenth month, a yinsi hour, for the transfer.

At the appointed time, the Emperor Xian invited King of Wei Cao Pi to ascend the platform and receive the abdication. Four hundred and more officials assembled below, and more than three hundred thousand imperial guards of the Forbidden Guards in tiger-patterned armor stood by.

The emperor personally held the jade seal and presented it to Cao Pi. Cao Pi accepted it. The officials below knelt and recited the edict:

Hear this, King of Wei: of old, Yao of Tang yielded his seat to Shun, and Shun in turn passed the task to Yu. The Mandate of Heaven does not belong to constancy alone; it returns only to virtue. Han’s course has been long and has lost its sequence; since it reached my person, chaos has only deepened. The violent ones have run wild, and the world is upended. By the martial strength of the Martial King, this danger was answered from all quarters, and with clearness you have guarded the ancestral temples. Could one person alone set all in order for the nine regions and receive this favor? Now, King, you uphold the previous legacy and shine with your own virtue. You restored and expanded the great undertakings of writing and arms, and your deeds now reveal your father’s glorious accomplishments. Auspicious signs descended, and people and spirits bore witness; Heaven’s brilliance chose your mandate. Therefore all should agree you match Shun, and you should follow the example of Yao and respectfully descend from your station. Ah! Heaven’s historical sequence rests in your person. Do not fail in the great ritual. Offer it to all realms, and with reverence receive Heaven’s charge!

When the edict was fully read, King Cao Pi received the eight formal ceremonies and entered the throne.

Jia Xu led the major and minor officials in court. The first year of Yan Kang was changed to the first year of Huangchu. The state was named Great Wei. Cao Pi then issued an order and granted amnesty across the realm. He gave Cao Cao, his father, the posthumous title Grand Progenitor Wǔ Emperor.

Hua Xin said: “‘There is no man but one sun in heaven, and no two kings among the people.’ The Han Emperor has now yielded the world; he ought to retire to fiefdom. We ask Your Highness for a clear order: where should the Liu house be placed?”

After he spoke, he led the emperor to kneel at the base of the platform to hear the command. Cao Pi issued the order that the former emperor would be Marquis of Shanyang and was to move that very day.

Hua Xin drew himself up, pointed at the emperor with his sword, and spoke sharply: “To establish one emperor and remove one emperor is the old practice! Your Majesty is merciful and unwilling to do harm. You have made him Marquis of Shanyang; since this is the decision today, it is not fitting to summon him and then forbid his entrance to court.”

The former emperor thanked him through tears, mounted his horse, and left. The army and commoners in the assembly were moved and could not hide their grief.

Cao Pi said to the court: “I know what Yao and Yu did.” The ministers all cried out their acclamations.

Afterward, some observing this Platform of Abdication composed a verse:

The Two Han labored hard to build their realm, Yet in one morning lost their ancient rivers and hills. Huangchu sought to imitate Tang and Yu; The Sima clan would one day follow this example.

The officials requested that Cao Pi answer heaven and earth. As he knelt, a sudden strange wind whipped up before the platform. Sand and stones flew, rapid as driving rain, obscuring what lay before him. The platform lamps were all blown out. Cao Pi fell in a daze from the platform.

Officials rushed to rescue him down the steps, and after some time he woke.

Servants carried him into his offices; for several days he could not hold court. When his illness improved, he came out to receive the congratulations of the ministers.

Hua Xin was made Minister over the Masses, Wang Lang Minister of Works, and officials great and small received promotions and rewards.

Cao Pi was not fully recovered, and suspecting that the palace at Xuchang was inauspicious, he left Xuchang for Luoyang and began building grand halls.

News soon reached Chengdu: Cao Pi had made himself emperor of Great Wei, and while building his palaces at Luoyang people said the Han emperor had been killed. Hearing this, the King of Han deeply grieved and ordered all officials to wear mourning and raise memorial rites from afar. He bestowed the posthumous title Emperor Xiaomin upon the former emperor.

Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, therefore grew anxious and came down with fever, unable to manage affairs; all state business was left to Kongming.

Kongming, together with Grand Tutor Xu Jing and Master of the Household Qiao Zhou, discussed the matter and said that the realm could not remain without a lord for even one day. They urged the King of Han to assume the imperial seat. Qiao Zhou said, “There are recent signs—auspicious winds, celebratory clouds; in the northwest of Chengdu, for dozens of zhang, yellow vapors rose to the clouds. The emperor star appeared among Bei, Wei, and Mao, blazing like the moon. This is exactly when the King of Han should take the imperial seat and continue Han’s succession. What more doubt is there?”

Accordingly, Kongming and Xu Jing submitted an appeal from major and minor officials asking the King of Han to assume the emperor’s seat.

The king read the memorial and was shocked: “Do you want to make me a disloyal and unjust man?”

Kongming replied: “No, my lord. Cao Pi seized Han and made himself ruler. You, as scion of the Han house, ought by right to succeed and continue Han’s sacrifice.”

The King of Han flushed with anger and said: “Am I to do what a rebel usurper does?” He flung his sleeve aside and withdrew into the inner palace. All the officials dispersed.

Three days later, Kongming again brought a multitude of officials into court and requested that the King come out. All of them knelt in front of him.

Xu Jing spoke: “Now the Son of Heaven of Han has been done to death by Cao Pi. If Your Majesty does not immediately take the throne, and does not fight to punish the rebels with your ministers, you cannot be called loyal and righteous. The whole world wants Your Majesty to be emperor and to clear the grievance of Emperor Xiaomin. If you do not follow our submission, you will fail the will of the people.”

The King of Han said: “Though I am the grandson of Jingdi, I have not yet spread benevolence and virtue to the people. If I now enthrone myself, how is that different from usurpation?”

Kongming begged repeatedly, but the king persisted.

Then Kongming devised a stratagem: he told the officials, “In this way, and in this way.”

So Kongming feigned illness and did not leave his quarters.

When the king heard that Kongming’s illness had deepened, he came himself to the residence and at once went to his sickbed to ask: “What ailment has our strategist taken?” Kongming answered: “My mind burns with worry. My days are not long.”

The king asked: “What is he worrying about?” asking several times. Kongming only insisted his illness was severe and would not open his eyes to reply.

The king asked repeatedly. Kongming sighed and then spoke: “Since leaving my thatched hut, I have met Your Majesty and followed you. You have always listened and followed my plans. Now, thank Heaven, Your Majesty holds the lands of the two rivers and has not lost what I spoke before. At present, Cao Pi has usurped. Han’s sacrificial line is about to be severed. All civil and military officers and officials want to raise Your Majesty as emperor to destroy Wei and restore Liu’s house, and together seek in achievement and renown. Yet Your Majesty has firmly refused. Their loyalty now sours; they will not remain long. If civil and military officers scatter, Wei and Wu will attack; two rivers will be hard to hold. How can I not worry?”

The King of Han said: “I do not block the matter; I only fear the judgments of the world.”

Kongming replied: “The Master said, ‘When names are not correct, speech cannot be in order.’ Your name is correct and your speech now follows it. What is there to discuss?”

He added: “Have you not heard, ‘Heaven gives and one must take; if one refuses, one bears the blame’?”

The King said: “When your illness improves, it will not be too late.”

When Kongming heard this, he leapt from the couch, struck the screen, and the court officers, soldiers, and officials gathered outside came in and knelt, saying: “Since Your Majesty has permitted it, please set an auspicious day and perform the great rites.”

When the king looked out, the assembled officials were among the Grand Tutor Xu Jing, General Who Pacifies Han Mi Zhu, Marquis of Qingyi Shangju, Marquis of Yangquan Liu Bao, Assistant Zhao Zuo, Intendant-in-Charge Yang Hong, Counselors’ Director Du Qiong, Court Attendant Zhang Shuang, Minister of Rites Lai Gong, Master of Ceremonies Huang Quan, Vice Minister of Discipline He Zong, Academician Yin Mo, Clerk Qiao Zhou, Grand Marshal Yin Chun, Left General Zhang Yi, Treasurer Wang Mou, Scholar Yi Ji, and Officer Qin Mi.

The King of Han said: “You have dragged me into injustice; all of you are to blame.”

Kongming said: “Now that Your Majesty has consented, build the platform and choose an auspicious day, then proceed with due ceremony.”

At once they sent Liu Bei back to his palace while ordering the scholar Xu Ci and censor-in-waiting Meng Guang to oversee the rites. A platform was built south of Wudan in Chengdu. All preparations were completed, and officials in full order prepared the imperial carriage and invited the King of Han to ascend the altar and make offerings.

Qiao Zhou stood upon the altar and read aloud the sacrificial text in a loud, high voice:

On the 1st day of the bingwu month in the 26th year of Jian’an, and on ding-si, the twelfth day that follows, I, the emperor Bei, dare to announce to Heaven and Earth: the Han realm has an unbounded cycle. Formerly Wang Mang usurped and stole; Emperor Guangwu in wrath executed him and restored the altars of state. Now Cao Cao blocked troops with cruelty and killed a ruler and empress; his crimes are immeasurable. His son Pi, in full rebellion, has taken the regalia by theft. Ministers and soldiers below all think Han’s sacrifice has collapsed and fallen; to prolong it is fitting, that one should succeed two ancestral founders and personally bear Heaven’s punishment. I fear I am unworthy to occupy the throne; I asked the common people and, beyond them, lords in remote lands. All answered alike: Heaven’s mandate cannot go unanswered, ancestral inheritance cannot be abandoned for long, and the Four Seas cannot be without a ruler. All lands under heaven look toward one man. I fear Heaven’s clear decree and I fear that the undertakings of Emperors Gaozu and Guangwu will crash to the ground. Thus I have chosen an auspicious day, mounted the altar, and informed Heaven and Earth, receiving the imperial seal and ribbon so as to govern the four quarters. Let the spirits receive and preserve the Han house, and let its line rule forever and securely.

When the reading ended, Kongming led the officials to kneel and respectfully present the jade seal. The King of Han received it, held it on the altar, and again declined the seat: “I lack talent and virtue. Let one with talent and virtue receive it.”

Kongming replied: “Your Majesty has pacified the four seas and your merit is clear to all. As one of the Han imperial clan, you should now correct your position. You have already offered to Heaven and Earth. Why this further refusal?”

All civil and military officials called out long live.

After worship and dance rites were completed, the era name was changed to the first year of Zhangwu. Empress Wu was made empress, and your eldest son Liu Shan was made crown prince. Liu Yong, your second son, was made King of Lu, and Liu Li was made King of Liang. Zhuge Liang was made Chancellor and Xu Jing the Minister over the Masses. Great and small officials were rewarded one by one. Great amnesty was issued.

People of the two river commanderies rejoiced beyond measure.

The next day they held court. After all civil and military officials had taken their bows and lined up in their two ranks, the ruler issued an order: “From the Peach Garden I swore brotherhood with Guan and Zhang to live and die together. It is not my fortune that Zhang Yunchang, my second brother, was killed by Sun Quan of Eastern Wu. If I do not avenge this, I violate our oath. I wish to gather the weapons of the state and strike East Wu, seizing the rebel alive and repaying this resentment.”

Before he finished, one man among the ranks threw himself on the steps in a full bow and remonstrated: “Do not do it.”

The king looked and saw it was Zhao Yun, Tiger-Might General. It is right:

Before the sovereign could carry out Heaven’s punishment, A minister came forward with forthright counsel.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Pi Forces the Han Emperor to Yield the Throne, and the King of Han Restores the Lineage

chapters.html:
Hasting to avenge an elder brother, Zhang Fei meets his death. To wash away grief for a younger brother, the Lord of Shu raises his army.

Yet the Lord, Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, raised his force for an eastern campaign. Zhao Yun, whose courtesy name was Yunchang, remonstrated:

“Cao Cao is the rebel against the state, not Sun Quan. Now that Cao Pi has usurped the Han, Heaven and men alike are in righteous anger. Your Majesty should early make plans for Guanzhong and station troops on the upper reaches of the Wei River to punish the treacherous usurper. Then the men of principle in the lands east of the pass will saddle up, gather grain, and ride out to welcome the army of the Son of Heaven. If Your Majesty leaves Wei and attacks Wu, once armies meet can they be separated at once? Please inspect this matter carefully.”

The Lord replied, “Sun Quan harmed my younger brother. In addition, Fu Shiren, Mi Fang, Pan Zhang, and Ma Zhong are all among those whose teeth grind against me. To consume their flesh and erase their clans is what will quiet my resentment. Why do you still hinder this?”

Yun said, “The Han usurper’s wrong is the realm’s wrong; your brother’s wrong is a private matter. I beg Your Majesty to hold the kingdom above all.”

The Lord answered, “If I do not avenge my brother, even though I possessed ten thousand li of land from river to river, what nobility would that give me?”

He would not heed Zhao Yun’s counsel and ordered the troops to march against Wu. He also sent envoys to Wuxi for fifty thousand auxiliary troops to coordinate for support. At the same time, he dispatched another mission to Langzhong, promoting Zhang Fei to General of Agile Cavalry, appointing him Colonel of the Capital Censors, Marquis of Xixiang, and also Governor of Langzhong, with imperial decrees in hand.

When word reached Zhang Fei in Langzhong that Guan Yu had been killed by Eastern Wu, he cried out and wept morning and evening; his collar was soaked with blood from his own fury. The officers offered him wine to soothe him, but as he drank his rage increased. In his pavilion and camp any who offended him at all were immediately lashed, and many died under the whips. Each day he clenched his teeth and glared southward, sobbing without pause.

Suddenly an envoy arrived. Zhang Fei hurried to receive him and had him read the decree aloud. After receiving the command and paying court in obeisance, he set out a proper welcome with wine. After drinking once, he demanded:

“I have lost my brother; my vengeance is as deep as the sea. Why has not the court put forward its ministers to begin this campaign at once?”

The envoy answered, “There are many who urged Your Majesty to eliminate Wei first and only then punish Wu.”

Zhang Fei thundered, “What is this nonsense? In the peach orchard of our youth, the three of us swore brotherhood and shared life and death. Yet by ill fortune one of my two elder brothers has already gone on the way halfway through life. How can I alone enjoy rank and safety? I must see Your Majesty in person and ask to lead the vanguard, in mourning garb, against Wu, to take the traitor alive and report to my brothers so we may keep our former oath.”

Once he had spoken, he departed with the messenger toward Chengdu.

At home, the Lord continued to drill horses and men at the parade ground, preparing on an auspicious day, and was to lead the campaign personally. So all ministers gathered in the Chancellor’s residence and addressed Kongming: “Your Majesty has only just ascended to the throne; personally commanding all six armies is not fitting for the weight of altar and state. You hold the office of balancing the realm as Chancellor. Why do you not remonstrate?”

Kongming answered, “I have already given remonstrance many times, but I was not listened to. Today you all come with me to the drill field; we will remonstrate him there.”

He then brought all officials to the training yard and submitted to the Lord:

“Your Majesty has just ascended the great seat. If Your Majesty truly intends to march north and punish the Han usurper, thereby serving the greater justice under Heaven, then only then should You personally lead six armies. If You wish merely to attack Wu, a single senior commanding general would suffice to command. Why must you personally wear yourself with the holy carriage?”

The Lord, seeing Kongming’s repeated remonstration, let his thoughts soften somewhat. Word came that Zhang Fei had arrived. He immediately summoned him.

Zhang Fei entered the martial hall, threw himself to the ground before Liu Bei, and clung to the Lord’s feet while crying. The Lord also wept.

“Your Majesty is emperor now,” Zhang Fei said, “yet you have forgotten our oath of the Peach Garden! How can we not repay the blood-debt of my two elder brothers?”

The Lord said, “Many ministers oppose this; I did not dare to act lightly.”

Zhang Fei replied, “Do others know what oath we made in the days gone by? If Your Majesty does not go, I will give up this body to pay back my two brothers. If I cannot bring vengeance, I would rather die than see Your Majesty.”

The Lord responded, “I shall go with you. You will bring out your own troops from Langzhong. I will bring the chosen troops and join with you at Jiangzhou. We will together attack Eastern Wu and wipe out this grievance.”

As Zhang Fei was about to depart, the Lord warned him: “I have long known that after wine you become violently angry, that you lash men and then keep them at your side again; this is a road to disaster. From now on, be restrained and do not be as before.”

Zhang Fei bowed and withdrew.

The next day the Lord arranged his army and prepared to depart. The scholar Qin Mi submitted counsel:

“Your Majesty, with imperial dignity in Your chariot, to favor a petty cause is not behavior of the ancients. Please consider this.”

The Lord said, “Zhao Yun and I are still one body. The great righteousness remains; how can it be forgotten?”

Qin Mi, kneeling on the ground without rising, said, “Your Majesty does not follow Your servant’s words; I truly fear there will be loss.”

The Lord grew angry: “I have resolved to raise arms. Why can you utter such unpropitious words?” He ordered soldiers to drag him out and execute him.

Qin Mi kept his face unchanged, looked back at the Lord, and smiled:

“Your servant has no grievance in dying, only regret that the work newly built may be overturned.”

Many officials pleaded for Qin Mi’s release.

The Lord said, “For now, imprison him. After I return from vengeance, I will dispose of this affair.”

When Kongming heard of this, he submitted an urgent memorial:

Servant Kongming and others humbly submit that the treacherous wiles of the bandits of Wu caused the disaster in Jing Province and the ruin of our frontier. Our hearts have tumbled from the stars of Dipper and fallen like a broken pillar in Chu land; this grief is real and cannot be forgotten. Yet it was Cao Cao who moved the Han cauldron; it was Sun Quan who displaced Liu’s fortune. If Wei’s usurpers are removed, Wu will of itself fall into submission. If Your Majesty accepts Qin Mi’s stone-and-metal words and gathers the strength of the soldiers, another sound plan can be made, and the state will be fortunate—very fortunate indeed, and all under heaven will be fortunate.

After reading it, the Lord threw the memorial to the ground and said, “My decision is made. Do not counsel me again.”

He then ordered Chancellor Zhuge Liang to hold the crown prince and keep the two Rivers secure. The General of Chariots and Cavalry Ma Chao and his brother Ma Dai would assist Wei Yan, the General Who Guards the North, in Hanzhong to meet Wei troops. Zhao Yun, General of Tiger Might, was assigned as rear support and also to supervise provisions. Huang Quan and Cheng Ji served as strategists. Ma Liang and Chen Zhen managed documents. Huang Zhong was made leading vanguard. Feng Xi and Zhang Nan were made deputies. Fu Tong and Zhang Yi were middle-army captains. Zhao Rong and Liao Chun were made to combine the rear guard.

Several hundred Sichuan officers, together with allied troops from Wuxi, brought the total force to seven hundred and fifty thousand. The date was set for the bingyin day of the seventh month in the first year of the Zhengwu era, and the army would march.

Zhang Fei returned to Langzhong and ordered that within three days the whole command should be outfitted with white flags and white armor, all under mourning colors, and set forth against Wu. The next day two junior officers in his camp, Fan Qiang and Zhang Da, came into his quarters and reported, “The white flags and white armor cannot be completed at once; a short extension is necessary.”

Zhang Fei shouted with fury: “I long to repay my vengeance and regret not reaching the enemy lands by tomorrow. How dare you disobey my command?” He ordered soldiers to bind the two and strap them to a tree and lash each of their backs fifty times.

“Tomorrow both of you must have it done! If you miss the deadline, I will execute you both before all.”

When the punishment was done they bled from the mouth. They returned to the camp to confer.

Fan said, “We have already been punished today; how can we complete this by tomorrow? This man’s temper is like fire. If it is not completed, both of us will be killed.”

Zhang Da replied, “It is better that he kills me than that I kill him.”

Fan said, “Yet we cannot get near enough.”

Da said, “If we are not to die, he will fall drunk in bed tomorrow; and if we are to die, he will be sober.”

They resolved and waited.

As for Zhang Fei, his whole mind was confused and his motions unsteady, dazed and absent, so he asked a staff officer, “I feel my heart in alarm and my flesh trembling; I cannot sit or lie still. What does this mean?”

The officer answered, “My lord, it is your thoughts of Guan Yu that bring it about.”

Zhang Fei ordered wine brought and drank with the officer until he grew fully drunk, then fell into the pavilion. Fan and Zhang, learning of this and waiting for the first watch, each hid a short knife and entered the pavilion in secret, pretending to report a matter of grave military importance and pressing straight to the bedside.

Since Zhang Fei never slept with his eyes truly closed, the two villains saw his beard bristling and his eyes wide; they would not dare move at once. When they heard breath like thunder, they dared to approach and drove a short knife into his belly. Zhang Fei cried out once and was dead. He was then in his fifty-fifth year.

Later people composed a poem of lament:

It is said in Anxi that he once lashed an Inspector, The Yellow Turbans were swept as one and Liu was consumed by flame. At Hulao Pass, his roar sounded first, By the Changban bridge the water seemed to run backward. In righteousness he released Yan Yan and pacified Shu, By wisdom he deceived Zhang He and secured the Central Lands. He died before his campaign against Wu could be won; In Langzhong, autumn grasses grow and brood in sorrow.

That night Fan Qiang and Zhang Da cut off Zhang Fei’s head and then, with several dozen men, fled through the night to Eastern Wu.

The next day, when camp learned the news, the army set out in pursuit but could not catch them. At that time, a former subordinate of Zhang Fei, Wu Ban, came from Jing Province to report to the Lord. The Lord appointed him Guardian of the Palace Gate and made him co-responsible with Zhang Fei for guarding Langzhong.

First, Wu Ban submitted a written report to the Son of Heaven. He then ordered his elder son, Zhang Bao, to prepare a coffin-case and storage. He sent his younger brother Zhang Shao to hold Langzhong, while Zhang Bao himself came to report to the Lord, who was already choosing a marching date. All major and lesser officials accompanied Chancellor Kongming as far as ten li and returned.

When Kongming came back to Chengdu he was ill at ease. He told the officials, “Had Fa Xiaozhi still lived, he surely could have restrained His Majesty from marching east.”

That night the Lord woke trembling in fear and could not sleep. Looking at the sky from his pavilion he saw in the northwest a star as large as the constellation Dipper suddenly fall from heaven. Doubting it deeply, he sent for Kongming through the night.

Kongming reported back, “Within three days, an upper commander will be lost. Within three days we will receive warning.”

The Lord therefore held his troops in place.

A court official then reported, “Wu Ban, a battalion commander under Zhang Fei at Langzhong, has sent someone with an imperial memorial.”

The Lord stamped his feet and said, “Ah! my third brother is no more!” When he read the report, indeed it carried the terrible news of Zhang Fei’s death.

He screamed, then fainted.

Officials revived him. The next day a troop of riders arrived in a rushing wind. The Lord rode out to inspect. After a while, a young general in white robe and silver armor dismounted in rolling saddle and threw himself to the ground and wept. It was Zhang Bao.

Zhang Bao said, “Fan Qiang and Zhang Da have killed my father and carried his head and delivered it to Wu.”

The Lord was overwhelmed with grief and took no food. Courtiers remonstrated bitterly: “Your Majesty now seeks to take vengeance for your two brothers; how can you first break down your own body?”

Only then did the Lord take a little meal. He said to Zhang Bao, “You and Wu Ban, would you dare to bring your own troops forward as vanguard to avenge your father?”

Bao said, “For country and for father, I would not refuse even death!”

The Lord had just resolved to dispatch Bao, when yet another column came in with wind-driven speed. He ordered an attendant to investigate. In a while, an attendant led in a young general in a white robe and silver armor, who threw himself down in tears. The Lord looked and saw it was Guan Xing.

On seeing Guan Xing, memory of Guan Yu surged up; the Lord burst into tears again.

The officials urged him repeatedly to take comfort. He said:

“When I was still in plain clothes, I had bound myself with Guan and Zhang and sworn to live and die together. Now as emperor I would have wished to share wealth with both my brothers, but unluckily both are dead by untimely fate. How can I see these two young nephews and not break my heart?”

He spoke and cried again.

The officials said, “Let these two young generals withdraw. Allow the Son of Heaven to preserve his body.”

An attendant informed him, “Your Majesty is past sixty years old and should not indulge so deeply in grief.”

The Lord answered, “Both of my younger brothers are gone. How can I endure to live alone?” He ended by striking his head to the ground and crying.

Many officers deliberated. Ma Liang said, “If His Majesty personally leads the main army against Wu, and yet cries all day, it will not favor him in war.”

Chen Zhen said, “I have heard that to the west of Qingcheng Mountain there is a hermit named Li, called Li Yi. The world says this old man is over three hundred years old and can know men’s life and death, good and evil—he is called an immortal of this age. Why not inform the Son of Heaven to summon him and ask about fortune and misfortune? Better than our words.”

He submitted this.

The Lord approved and sent Chen Zhen with an imperial summons to Qingcheng Mountain.

That very night, Zhen arrived and was guided by a villager into a remote valley. Far off he glimpsed an immortal’s courtyard, where light clouds drifted and auspicious vapors seemed unusual. A small boy appeared and greeted him: “Is the one who comes no one other than Chen Xiaoqi?”

Zhen was startled: “How could this divine boy know my surname and given name?”

The boy said, “My master said last night, ‘Today there must be an imperial edict to arrive, and the envoy will be Chen Xiaoqi.’”

Zhen exclaimed, “A true immortal! The world does not lie.” He entered with the boy and met Li Yi, announcing the edict from the Son of Heaven.

Li Yi rose slowly and would not move to receive him. Zhen said, “His Majesty urgently wishes to see the elder immortal. Please do not withhold your carriage.” After repeated pleading, Li Yi finally came.

He arrived at the royal camp and entered in audience. The Lord saw Li Yi, whose hair was like an old crane’s feather and countenance like a child, eyes green and round and bright like polished jade, radiant, with a body like an ancient cypress, and understood him to be an odd man. He was treated with high courtesy.

Li Yi said, “I am but a village elder of wild mountains, unlearned and ignorant. I am ashamed to answer a summons from the Son of Heaven. What instruction would His Majesty have me give?”

The Lord said, “For more than thirty years I have held life-and-death friendship with Guan and Zhang, my brothers. Now both my brothers were harmed; I now lead the great army to avenge and know not where this will end. I have long heard that you understand the subtle mechanisms of fate. I ask for your instruction.”

Li Yi said, “This is Heaven’s allotment; not known by this old man.”

The Lord pressed him further. The hermit then asked for paper and ink and drew forty or more sketches of troops, horses, and military implements, then tore each up one by one. He drew a large figure of a person lying on his back on the ground, and beside it one man digging a pit and covering him with earth. Beside this he wrote a huge character, “white.” After bowing, he departed.

The Lord was displeased and said to the officials, “This mad old man cannot be trusted!” He had him burned in a fire and then hurried the army forward.

Zhang Bao submitted a memorial: “Wu Ban’s cavalry and horsemen have already arrived. This servant begs to be the vanguard.”

The Lord admired his zeal and handed him the vanguard seal. As Bao was about to bear it, another young commander suddenly stepped forward crying, “Leave the seal and give it to me!” He was Guan Xing.

Bao said, “I already have an imperial command.”

Guan Xing said, “What skill have you that you dare take this charge?”

Bao said, “I learned arms from boyhood. Not one of my arrows has missed.”

The Lord said, “I wish to test the prowess of my worthy nephews and decide who is superior.”

Bao ordered his unit to plant a banner one hundred paces away with a red heart drawn upon it. He drew three arrows and shot; all three struck the red heart. All praised his skill.

Guan Xing, bow in hand, said, “To strike the red heart, what is surprising in that?” As he spoke, a line of wild geese passed overhead. He pointed and said, “I shall shoot the third goose in that flight.” One shot and the goose fell to his string.

Civil and military officers all cried approval.

Bao, angered, leapt to his horse, brandishing the steel-tipped halberd his father had used, and shouted, “Do you dare to challenge my martial skill?”

Guan Xing also mounted, drew the great broad sabre passed down in his family, and said as he cantered, “You can wield a lance—am I then unable to wield a blade?”

The two commanders were about to clash when the Lord shouted, “The two of you, show no impropriety!”

The two dismounted in haste, threw down their weapons, and knelt in the dust to ask forgiveness.

The Lord said, “From my days in Zhuo Commandery I entered into sworn brotherhood with your fathers and became as kin by blood. You two now are of equal age as younger brothers. You ought to stand together with one heart to repay your fathers’ blood-debts. How can you compete and quarrel among yourselves, losing this great righteousness? The mourning for our fathers is not yet recent—what then of later days?”

The two again knelt and begged pardon.

The Lord asked, “Which of you is older?”

Bao said, “This servant is one year older than Guan Xing.”

The Lord then ordered Guan Xing to bow to Bao as elder brother.

The two took broken arrows before him and swore by them to aid and protect each other always.

The Lord then issued an edict making Wu Ban the vanguard and ordering Zhang Bao and Guan Xing to guard him. On water and land alike the campaign advanced with ships and cavalry together, a vast tide of men and horses driving toward Wu.

Now Fan Qiang and Zhang Da brought Zhang Fei’s head to the ruler of Wu as tribute and set forth in brief the events. Sun Quan listened and then detained the two. He said to the assembly:

“Liu Bei has now taken the imperial seat and, with over seven hundred thousand selected troops, leads the army in person. What response can we make now that his force is so great?”

All officials turned pale and stared at one another.

Zhuge Jin stepped forward and said, “I have long eaten from your household bounty, Lord of Wu. I can no longer offer useful service. I wish to cast off this remnant of life and go to the Shu lord to speak of advantage and peril, to bring the two states to harmony and together punish Cao Pi for his guilt.”

Sun Quan rejoiced and immediately sent Zhuge Jin as envoy to ask the Lord to cease hostilities.

That is:

Two kingdoms are at odds and rely on one envoy’s mission; by one word he may untie their knot.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Hastening to Avenge His Brother, Zhang Fei Meets His End; Redressing His Brother's Wrong, the Former Lord Raises an Army

chapters.html:
In the autumn of the eighth month of the first year of the Zhangwu era, Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, moved the main army to Kui Pass and set up camp at Baidi City. The vanguard cavalry had already reached Chuan Gate.

A close attendant reported, “An envoy from Wu has come, Zhuge Jin.”

Liu Bei ordered that he not be admitted yet. Huang Quan then suggested, “His younger brother serves as Chancellor in Shu. He must have come with a matter of importance. Why would Your Majesty shut him out? Summon him in and hear what he has to say. If what he says is acceptable, accept it. If it is not, let him deliver your reasons before Sun Quan, so there is a clear record of blame.”

Liu Bei followed that advice and summoned him into the city.

Zhuge Jin bowed and knelt on the ground. Liu Bei asked, “Ziyu, you have traveled a long way. What business brings you?”

Jin said, “I have long served Your Majesty, so I did not shrink from this post for fear of the blade. I came to report on Jing Province. Earlier, while Guan Yu was in Jing Province, the Lord of Wu sought relations with him several times, but Guan Yu refused. Later, when Guan Yu took Xiangyang, Cao Cao repeatedly wrote to the Lord of Wu and asked him to attack Jing Province. The Lord of Wu at first did not agree. Because he and Lü Meng had lost harmony, however, he raised troops on his own, and this caused a great disaster. He now regrets it beyond remedy.

It was Lü Meng’s fault, not the Lord of Wu’s. Lü Meng has since died, and that blood feud has ended. Lady Sun has all along wished to return. The Lord of Wu now sends me as envoy, asking to return her, and to bring back the surrendered generals, and to hand back Jing Province just as it was, so that the alliance and friendship between us might be secure forever and we might together destroy Cao Pi, thus righting the wrong of usurpation.”

Liu Bei, angry, said, “You from the East have injured my brother, and now you dare to come with smooth words?”

Jin said, “I beg leave to weigh what is heavy and what is light with Your Majesty. You are the Imperial Uncle of Han. The Han emperor has already been usurped by Cao Pi. Instead of eliminating him, you remain the ally of one of another surname and have bent your sovereign honor as Grand Chancellor; this is to abandon great righteousness for lesser concern. Jing Province and the two capitals are where the Great Han was founded. It is Your Majesty’s duty to take them, not to contend only for Jing Province. That is to discard the heavy and seize the light.

Everyone in the world knows that when Your Majesty takes office, you must revive Han and restore the realms and rivers. You now ignore Wei and instead seek to strike Wu. It is for Your Majesty’s interests to refrain from that.”

Liu Bei was enraged. “He who sought my brother’s blood is one with whom I can never share the heavens. If you ask me to halt my army, I will only rest when he is dead. You will not even see my Chancellor’s face; I will behead you first. For now, go back and tell Sun Quan to wash his neck and be ready for execution.”

Zhuge Jin saw that Liu Bei would not listen and had to make his return to Jiangnan.

Soon after, Zhang Zhao told Sun Quan, “Ziyu understands the strength of Shu’s army, and he has used the excuse of embassies to hide his intent to defect in secret. He will not return after this.”

Sun Quan said, “I have life-and-death obligations to Ziyu; I have never betrayed Ziyu, and Ziyu has never betrayed me. When Ziyu was at Chaisang, Kongming came to Wu, and I tried to keep him. Ziyu said, ‘My brother has pledged himself to Xuande and has no split loyalty. My not holding him is like Ziyu’s not coming here.’ His words still ring true. Could he now submit to Shu this day?”

At this point, someone at the edge of the assembly announced, “Zhuge Jin has returned.”

Sun Quan asked, “What did I say?”

Zhang Zhao, face flushed with shame, withdrew. Jin saw Sun Quan and reported that the ruler of Shu would not accept reconciliation.

Sun Quan cried out in alarm, “If this is so, Jiangnan is in peril.”

A man stepped forward from the floor and said, “I have one idea to remove this danger.” When Sun Quan looked, it was Senior Counselor Zhao Zi.

Sun Quan asked, “Zhi, what is this good plan?”

Zi said, “Your Majesty could send an imperial memorial to Wei. If I dare to be an envoy, I can speak to Emperor Cao Pi and explain this matter. If he should attack Hanzhong, Shu forces there will be endangered.”

Sun Quan was pleased. “This is best. But if you go, do not lose the bearing of Wu.”

Zi replied, “If I should make even a small error, I will throw myself in the river. How then could I face the people of Jiangnan?”

Sun Quan ordered him to compose the memorial on the spot and grant him a missive. He was sent as envoy.

He arrived in Xu by night and first presented himself to Grand Commandant Jia Xu and other senior and junior officials.

At morning audience, Jia Xu read aloud: “Eastern Wu has sent Grand Officer Zhao Zi to present a memorial.”

Cao Pi laughed. “This, I suppose, is to make Shu troops withdraw.” He ordered him in.

Zi bowed and knelt on the vermilion terrace.

Cao Pi read the memorial and then asked, “What manner of lord is the ruler of Wu?”

Zi replied, “A ruler of wisdom, benevolence, intelligence, and mighty force.”

Cao Pi laughed. “Isn’t your praise excessive?”

Zi answered, “I do not flatter him excessively. The Lord of Wu elevated Lu Su among ordinary officers, and that was wisdom. He drew Lü Meng forward in the ranks, and that was clarity. He captured Yu Jin and did not harm him, and that was benevolence. He took the Jing Province troops without spilling blood, and that was intelligence. He held the Three Rivers and watched the world from afar, and that was might. He bent in deference before Your Majesty, and that is his strategy. By this measure, is he not truly a lord of wisdom, benevolence, intelligence, and might?”

Cao Pi asked, “Does the Lord of Wu study the Classics?”

Zi said, “The Lord of Wu commands a hundred thousand armored troops across a million and can summon ships by the tens of thousands. He appoints the worthy and uses talent. In his spare hours he reads widely and surveys histories. He takes their broad principles, not simply searching text for text like a bookman seeking phrases.”

Cao Pi asked, “Do you think I could march on Wu?”

Zi replied, “A great state has the army for conquest; a smaller state has the means to defend.”

Cao Pi said, “Does Wu fear Wei?”

Zi answered, “With a million armored men, with the Jiang and Han Rivers as its moats, what fear could it have?”

Cao Pi asked, “How many men of talent does Wu have?”

Zi replied, “As to those with bright and penetrating minds, there are perhaps eighty or ninety. As for men like me, we are more than can be counted on the axles.”

Cao Pi sighed. “When an envoy is sent to the four quarters, he must not fail in his lord’s command. You are fit for this task.”

He then issued an edict and ordered the Minister of Ceremonies Xing Zhen to carry official tablets, enfeoffing Sun Quan as King of Wu and adding the Nine Seals.

Zi thanked him and was allowed to leave the city.

The courtier Liu Ye objected, “Now that Sun Quan came and submitted to Shu’s pressure, he does so from fear of your military force. In my poor view, if Wu and Shu fight, that is Heaven striking us. If we send a senior general with only tens of thousands across the river, Shu will attack from without and Wei from within. Wu will not fall slower than ten days. If Wu falls, Shu will stand alone. Why does Your Majesty not plan this earlier?”

Cao Pi said, “Sun Quan has shown courtesy to me. If I attack him, how could I discourage those who might otherwise submit? Better to take him in and make him ours.”

Liu Ye persisted, “Though Sun Quan has ability, he is merely Marquis of Nan Chang and Cavalier-General of the Han? (southern vanguard). In rank he is light and his influence is not yet deep; he still holds fear of the Central Plains. If you raise him to kingship, you only give the tiger added wings.”

Cao Pi said, “No. I will not assist Wu, but neither will I aid Shu. I will wait to see these two exhaust one another. If one kingdom falls and one survives, then it will be easy to remove it. My decision is fixed. Do not repeat this.”

He ordered Xing Zhen to go at once with the sealed gifts, and together with Zhao Zi to travel directly to Wu.

Sun Quan gathered the hundred officials and discussed how to meet Shu’s threat. A report arrived of Cao Pi’s enfeoffment of the Lord as king. Ritual protocol required a distant reception.

Gu Yong remonstrated, “Your Majesty should name yourself Grand General and Marquis of the Nine Provinces. It is not right to accept a title from the Wei emperor.”

Sun Quan replied, “On the day of Emperor Gaozu’s concession by Xiang Yu, it was all due to circumstance. Why should I decline now?”

He then went out with all the ministers to greet the delegation.

Xing Zhen relied on his status as envoy from the court above and came through the gate without stepping down from his carriage. Zhang Zhao was furious and shouted, “Ritual demands reverence, and the law permits no insolence. Yet you dare to carry yourself so proudly? Do you think Jiangnan has no blade honed to the finest point?”

Xing Zhen quickly dismounted and met Sun Quan, then entered the city. Behind him, one man shouted from the rear of the carriage, “How can we, who have not been able to hurl ourselves forth and die for our lord, now see him bowing to receive a peerage from another while we are expected to join in swallowing Wei and Wu? Is that not a disgrace?” Those heeded him were Xu Sheng.

Hearing this, Xing Zhen sighed. “Generals and ministers of Jiangdong like this will not be one who remains forever below others.”

Afterward Sun Quan, having accepted the title, received congratulations from all civil and military officers. He then ordered precious jade and pearls and other valuables gathered and sent men with thanks. A covert reporter had already carried word: Shu’s lord had brought out his native force, and with the barbarian king Shamo-ke there were tens of thousands of allied troops; Du Lu and Liu Ning, Han officers from Dongxi, had brought detachments as well. The attack by water and land advanced together, with the force on water already past Wukou and the land force already at Zigui.
