Though Sun Quan now wore kingship, Cao Pi had not given practical support, and he asked his officers, “Shu force is strong. What then should we do?” All were silent.

Sun Quan sighed. “After Zhou Yu there was Lu Su. After Lu Su there was Lü Meng. Now Lü Meng is dead, and there is no one beside me to share my anxiety.” Before he could finish, a youth from the ranks sprang forward and knelt at the foot of the platform, saying, “I am young, but I have studied military texts. Grant me tens of thousands and I will break Shu’s army.”

Sun Quan recognized him as Sun Huan, whose courtesy name was Shuwu. His father was He, of the Yu surname by birth, and Sun Ce had loved him and bestowed the surname Sun; thus he too belonged to Wu’s royal clan. He Huan was the eldest of He’s four sons. He was already adept at horse and bow, often accompanying the king of Wu in campaigns and earning repeated achievements. He held the post of Captain of the Imperial Guard. He was twenty-five years old.

Sun Quan asked, “What is your plan to defeat them?”

Sun Huan said, “I have two senior generals: one named Li Yi, one named Xie Jing. Each has courage equal to ten thousand men. Grant me ten thousand men and I will seize Liu Bei.”

Sun Quan said, “Though courageous for your age, a boy cannot do this alone. You need one more commander.”

The Tiger-Wheei General Zhu Ran came forward and said, “I volunteer to take the field with the Little General Sun Huan.”

Sun Quan granted permission. He raised fifty thousand men across land and water, appointed Sun Huan left chief commander and Zhu Ran right chief commander, and ordered them to march immediately. Scouts reported that Shu troops had already encamped below Yidu. Sun Huan brought twenty-five thousand cavalry and troops to the Yidu border, and split them into three camps front and rear to face the enemy.

Shu’s commander Wu Ban, holding the seal of vanguard, had since coming out from Sichuan seen all cities submit before his coming wind. He had not spilled blood. He arrived at Yidu; learning that Sun Huan had encamped there, he reported immediately to Liu Bei.

At that time Liu Bei had reached Zigui. At the report he was angry and said, “How does this child dare to stand against me?”

Guan Xing said, “Since Sun Quan has made this young man commander, there is no need for Your Majesty to send a great general. Let me go and capture him.”

Liu Bei said, “I have wanted to test your courage.” He ordered Guan Xing onward.

As Guan Xing prepared to leave, Zhang Bao stepped forward and said, “Now that Guan Xing goes to punish the invader, I volunteer to go with him.”

Liu Bei approved. “The two of you going together is excellent. Be careful. Do not act rashly.”

The two bowing sons then took leave and joined the vanguard together. They moved in array.

When Sun Huan heard that Shu’s army was close and the camps were newly made, he had the camp raised again in many places. The two formations faced each other broadly. Sun Huan rode under the gateway banner with Li Yi and Xie Jing. In Shu’s camp, two major generals appeared—both on silver helmets and silver cuirasses, one on white horse with white banner. Zhang Bao was foremost, with an eight-foot iron spear; beneath him Guan Xing carried a broad war knife.

Zhang Bao shouted abuse: “Son of a lout, Sun Huan! You still dare to resist Heaven’s armies, even knowing you will die now!”

Sun Huan replied, “Your father has already become a headless ghost. You have come again to court death. You are not wise at all.”

Zhang Bao grew furious and thrust his spear straight at Sun Huan. Behind him, Xie Jing turned and charged to meet him.

The two captains fought for more than three dozen exchanges. Xie Jing fell away, and Zhang Bao pressed his advantage in pursuit.

Li Yi saw Xie Jing routed and, in panic, wheeled and raised a golden axe to join the fray. Zhang Bao and Li Yi fought for more than twenty rounds with no clear victor.

Then Tan Xiong, a Wu sub-commander, seeing Guan Xing’s daring and that Li Yi could not win, loosed one cold-tipped arrow that struck the horse Zhang Bao was riding. The animal recoiled in pain and ran back toward its own camp; before it reached the banner it collapsed to the ground, throwing Zhang Bao off.

Li Yi rushed forward and raised his great axe at the horse’s hooves, aiming at Zhang Bao’s head.

At that instant, a red flash came and Li Yi’s head was already on the ground. Guan Xing had watched Zhang Bao’s horse turn and was waiting for a chance to intervene. On seeing Li Yi come forward, he shouted once and split him down from beneath his saddle, rescuing Zhang Bao and then cutting down many in the press.

Sun Huan was badly beaten and each side sounded the bronze to withdraw.

The next day Sun Huan came again with troops. Zhang Bao and Guan Xing rode out together. Guan Xing mounted before the line and challenged him directly. Sun Huan, in fury, rode forward, sword raised, and fought with Guan Xing for more than thirty exchanges, his strength failing and he retreated in defeat to his camp.

The two younger generals pursued the enemy into the camp. Wu Ban ordered Zhang Nan and Feng Xi to drive in soldiers and cover the kill. Zhang Bao rushed forward bravely and charged into the Wu army. He met Xie Jing in close combat and killed him with a spear thrust. The Wu soldiers broke and scattered in panic.

The Shu force took up the victory and withdrew, but Guan Xing was not to be found.

Zhang Bao exclaimed in alarm, “I have not lived to see the disaster of peace and order! I must go.” He shouted as he spurred, and mounted with a trident.

After a short distance he saw Guan Xing, left hand holding a blade, right hand seizing a living man.

Zhang Bao asked, “Who is this?”

Guan Xing answered with a laugh, “In the wild melee I ran into my nemesis and captured him alive.”

Looking closely, he recognized him as Tan Xiong. Zhang Bao rejoiced and with him they returned to camp, cut down the head, drained the blood, made offering for the dead horse, and immediately dispatched a courier to Liu Bei to report the victory.

Sun Huan had already slain Li Yi, Xie Jing, Tan Xiong, and many officers, so he was depleted and isolated, unable to resist for long. He sent for aid from Wu.

Wu commanders Zhang Nan and Feng Xi told Wu Ban, “Wu’s forces have just been broken. It is just now a good moment to rush their camp and loot it.”

Wu Ban replied, “Though Sun Huan has lost many officers, Zhu Ran with the water army is now camping on the river and has not yet been broken. If we go to loot the camp and his water army lands, they could cut off our route home. What then?”

Zhang Nan said, “It is simple. Send Generals Guan Xing and Zhang Bao each with five thousand men to lie in ambush in the mountain valley. If Zhu Ran comes to rescue, both wings attack together and we are certain to win.”

Wu Ban said, “Better first send a few common soldiers who pretend to have surrendered and tell Zhu Ran they are in danger of the camp-loot. When he sees the fires, he will come to rescue; let the ambush strike him, and our enterprise will succeed.”

Feng Xi and the others rejoiced, and they acted accordingly.

When Zhu Ran heard Sun Huan’s losses and the fall of his officers, he was preparing to come to the rescue when suddenly a handful of soldiers from the ambush unit boarded boats and surrendered.

He asked, “What is your report?”

They replied, “We are soldiers under Feng Xi. Because punishments were unclear, we have come to surrender and bring intelligence. Tonight Feng Xi intends to exploit open ground and seize Commander Sun Huan’s camp. The signal is agreed: fires are to be raised.”

When Zhu Ran finished hearing this, he sent it to Sun Huan immediately. The messenger was killed halfway by Guan Xing.

Zhu Ran considered and decided he should go to the rescue. Commander Cui Yu advised, “Do not trust the soldiers’ report completely. If it is a trap, both our water and land forces will be destroyed. You should hold your river camp steadily. I volunteer to lead a force for you.”

Zhu Ran accepted this, and told Cui Yu to take ten thousand men forward.

That night, Feng Xi, Zhang Nan, and Wu Ban split their troops into three routes and drove straight into Sun Huan’s camp. Fires rose in all directions.

Wu soldiers were thrown into confusion and ran in panic.

As Cui Yu was on the move, he too saw the fires rise and urged his men forward. He had just crossed the mountain when drums thundered in the valley; on the left was Guan Xing and on the right Zhang Bao, and the two wings struck together.

Cui Yu was alarmed and tried to flee, but met Zhang Bao. They fought once with matching horses before Zhang Bao captured him alive and brought him back.

Zhu Ran, seeing the urgency, sent his ships drifting downstream fifty to sixty li.

Sun Huan gathered his broken army and fled. He asked his officer where they might be in a city with strong walls and broad grain stores.

The officer answered, “If we go straight north, Yiling city can hold us.”

Sun Huan pushed on with the broken force toward Yiling. As soon as he entered, Wu Ban and others closed in with full encirclement.

Guan Xing and Zhang Bao brought Cui Yu to Zigui. Liu Bei was very pleased. He executed Cui Yu at once and rewarded the three armies lavishly. From then on, Wu’s commanders in Jiangnan were struck with fear by the force of Shu’s prestige.

Sun Huan asked Wu for aid from the king, and Sun Quan was greatly alarmed. He summoned ministers and officers to meet.

He asked, “Now Sun Huan is trapped at Yiling and Zhu Ran has been badly defeated in the river. Shu’s force is great. What now?”

Zhang Zhao proposed, “Though many commanders have already fallen, there are still over ten. Why worry over Liu Bei? Command Han Dang as main commander, Zhou Tai as deputy, Pan Zhang as vanguard, Ling Tong in support, and Gan Ning in reserve. Raise an army of one hundred thousand and resist him.”

Sun Quan acted on this advice and sent the generals at once. Gan Ning, at this moment, was sick with dysentery, but he marched despite his illness.

Liu Bei advanced from the Jianping in Wuxia Gorge and directly reached the Yiling line, where he linked over seventy li with more than forty encampments.

He praised the repeated major achievements of Guan Xing and Zhang Bao, saying, “Formerly, those generals from my side were old and useless. Now with two nephews so heroic, what reason have I to fear Sun Quan?”

As he spoke, he heard that Han Dang and Zhou Tai had arrived with troops. Liu Bei was preparing to send commanders to meet them when an attendant said, “The old general Huang Zhong has gone to Wu with five or six men.”

Liu Bei laughed. “Huang Zhong, with the sobriquet Hansheng, is no traitor. Because I carelessly said, once, that old men were no use, he must have taken it badly and gone to contend in earnest to prove me wrong. Call in Guan Xing and Zhang Bao. Huang Zhong is sure to make errors on this expedition. My worthy nephews must not refuse hardship. They may go to aid him. If there is even the smallest merit, then send him back. Do not let him fail.”

The two young commanders bowed, took leave of their teacher, and brought their own troops to assist Huang Zhong.

The old minister has always sworn a loyal purpose to his lord; Young men can render meritorious service to the realm.

What became of Huang Zhong remains to be seen.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Sun Quan Submits to Wei and Receives the Nine Seals; the Former Lord Marches on Wu and Rewards the Six Armies

chapters.html:
In the battle at Xiaoting, the Lord wins vengeance; in Jiangkou, a scholar is made a great general.

Now in the second year of Zhangwu, in the spring of the first month, Huang Zhong, the Wuwei Rear General, followed the Lord, Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, as he marched against Wu. Upon hearing that the Lord had said old generals were useless, he drew his sword, mounted, and with five or six attendants rode straight to camp at Yiling. Wu Ban, Zhang Nan, and Feng Xi met him and asked, “Old general, what has happened that you have come?” Huang Zhong replied, “From the time I followed the Son of Heaven from Changsha to now, I have borne too much labor. Though I am already over seventy, I can still eat ten jin of meat, pull a bow of two shi, and ride a thousand-li horse. I am not yet an old man. Yesterday Your Majesty spoke of me and other elders as useless. So I came here, to meet Wu and prove in open battle that even as an old man I still can behead generals.”

He spoke but, just then, word came that the Wu vanguard had already arrived and scouting riders were near the camp. Huang Zhong sprang up at once, left the pavilion, and mounted. Feng Xi and the others urged him, “Old general, hold back and do not press forward.” Huang Zhong would not listen and spurred forward. Wu Ban ordered Feng Xi to bring soldiers to assist. In front of the Wu formation Huang Zhong reined in, crossed his blade, and alone fought with Pan Zhang, who led the van. Pan Zhang sent out his subordinate Shi Ji. Ji despised the old general’s age and raised his spear to battle. After not even three exchanges, Huang Zhong cut him down in one stroke at the horse’s side. Pan Zhang grew furious and brandished Lord Guan’s Green Dragon Blade to fight Huang Zhong. They rode together for several bouts, neither gaining clear advantage. Huang Zhong fought fiercely, and Pan Zhang, seeing he could not master him, turned and rode away. Huang Zhong pursued and pressed the attack, killing freely before he returned in complete victory. On the way he met Guan Xing and Zhang Bao. Guan Xing said, “We came by imperial command to assist you; now that you have gained merit, please return quickly to camp.” Huang Zhong did not listen.

The next day Pan Zhang came again to wrestle. Huang Zhong mounted immediately. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao wanted to join the fight; Huang Zhong refused. Wu Ban offered help; Huang Zhong refused. He alone led out five thousand troops. They did not stay in full battle long; Pan Zhang pulled up his blade and fled. Huang Zhong rode hard after him and shouted in a harsh voice, “Rebel commander, do not run! Today I repay Lord Guan!” He chased him past thirty li. Shouts came from all around, and hidden troops came all out together. On the right was Zhou Tai; on the left, Han Dang. Pan Zhang was in front, Ling Tong behind. They trapped Huang Zhong in an encirclement. Suddenly a fierce wind rose. As he turned to withdraw, a bolt from the hillside struck him in the hollow of the shoulder, and he almost fell from his horse. The Wu soldiers, seeing Huang Zhong wounded, all charged at him. Suddenly cries rose from the rear. Two columns of troops came in, and the Wu lines broke apart. They moved to rescue Huang Zhong. They were Guan Xing and Zhang Bao. The two young commanders brought Huang Zhong straight back to the Lord’s pavilion. The old general’s blood had thinned and his wound was pain-ridden; he was in grave condition. The Lord came in person from the chariot to see him, and patted his back saying, “Your wound, old general, is the fault of Your Majesty.” Huang Zhong answered, “I am only a mere fighting man, made fortunate to have met Your Majesty. I am seventy-five years old; my life has run enough. Please, Your Majesty, guard Your dragon body and plan for recovery of the Central Plains.” When he had finished speaking, he lost consciousness and did not recover. That night he passed away in the imperial camp.

After him, men later recited this poem:

The old general Huang Zhong, who spoke little yet made great merit in Shu, clad in heavy gilded mail and drawing twin iron-bossed bows, his courage and temper shook Hebei, and his fearsome fame held down Shu. Even with hair white as snow on the day he was near death, he still displayed a hero’s form.

When the Lord saw Huang Zhong dead, he grieved without end. He ordered coffin and bier prepared and burial in Chengdu. The Lord sighed, “Of the Five Tiger Generals, three are now dead. I still have not avenged this. It is grievous beyond measure.” He then rode directly with the imperial guard to Xiaoting, summoned all the commanders, split the army into eight lines, and advanced by land and water together. At the riverine front was Huang Quan, and the Lord led the main army on the dry roads. This was the middle of the second month of the second year of Zhangwu.

Han Dang and Zhou Tai heard that the Lord was marching to punish Wu and brought soldiers out to greet him. The two formations faced each other. When Han Dang and Zhou Tai came out on horseback, at the gate of the Shu camp itself the Lord appeared. His yellow silk parasol was drawn, with white plumes and yellow blades at his side, gold-and-silver streamers circling before and behind. He shouted at once, “Your Majesty is now Lord of Shu. How do you ride out so lightly? If negligence has entered, what then of regret?” From afar the Lord pointed and yelled, “You Wu curs, you have wounded my hands and feet. I swear I will not stand with you under Heaven and Earth!” Turning back to his assembled men, he said, “Who dares to clash with the army of Shu?” The subordinate commander Xia Xun stepped out with spear raised. Behind the Lord, Zhang Bao raised a seven-and-a-half-foot spear and sprang on horseback, roaring once and riding straight at Xia Xun. When Xia Xun heard Bao’s voice like thunder, he was frightened in heart. As he was about to turn, Zhou Tai’s brother Zhou Ping saw Xia Xun unable to withstand the clash, took up sword, and rode forward. Guan Xing saw this and leapt up, drawing sword to meet him. Bao roared once and thrust once: Xia Xun was pierced by the spear and fell from his horse. Zhou Ping was astonished and taken unawares. Guan Xing cut him down at one stroke. Then the two young commanders shifted to capture Han Dang and Zhou Tai. Han and Zhou, in a panic, entered the lines. The Lord watched and sighed, “A tiger father has no cur sons.” He pointed with the imperial whip; all the Shu troops surged and closed at once, and the Wu force was badly defeated. The eight lines of battle rushed like springs welling up; they killed so many of Wu that their bodies lay across the field and blood ran in rivers.

Now Gan Ning, recovering from wounds in a boat, heard that Shu troops had come in great force. He leapt into the saddle in haste. At once he encountered a band of wild barbarians, all disheveled and bare-footed, all using bows, crossbows, long spears, and broad chopping blades and shields. At their head was the chieftain Shamo Ke, whose face was as if blood had surged through it, with bright blue eyes, and a drooping silkworm-like brow. He carried a bundle of iron caltrop blades at his waist, with two bows on his belt. His air was awe-inspiring. Gan Ning saw the force and did not dare to close in combat. He turned his horse away. Shamo Ke shot him with an arrow, and it struck Gan Ning’s head. Gan Ning rode on with the arrow in him until he reached Fuchi Pass. He sat beneath a great tree and died there. A few hundred crows were circling in the trees, gathering around his body. When the King of Wu heard it he was in immeasurable sorrow. He arranged proper rites, buried him with rich honors, and raised a temple for worship. Later men sighed in verse:

Gan Xingba of Wu Commandery, aboard a bright-brocaded barge on the Yangtze, for a true friend’s knowing recognition you have repaid dear kindness, turning former enmity back into former friendship; he rode swift cavalry to raided stockades, driving troops to drink from massive jars. The sacred crow made the divine manifest; his fragrance and incense may burn forever.

The Lord, seizing his momentum, pushed the pursuit and took Xiaoting. Wu soldiers scattered in all directions. When the Lord gathered his forces again, Guan Xing was nowhere to be seen. The Lord hurriedly ordered Zhang Bao and others to search in all four directions. Guan Xing had burst into the Wu formation and, in that very moment, encountered the enemy Pan Zhang and gave chase. Pan Zhang, startled, fled into a mountain ravine and vanished. Guan Xing thought he must be in the hills. He looked and searched, but could not find him. When night fell he lost the trail. Fortunately, by starlight and moonlight, he had some direction. He pursued until the third watch and reached the edge of a remote manor. At about two gēng in the night he dismounted and knocked on the gate. An elderly man came out to ask who he was. “I am a warrior who has lost the way; grant me a meal to quiet my hunger.” The old man brought him in. In the hall, lanterns were lit, and in the middle room was a painted image of Lord Guan. Guan Xing wept openly and kowtowed. The old man asked, “General, why do you weep and bow?” Guan Xing said, “This is my father.” On hearing that, the old man immediately knelt in respect. Guan Xing asked, “Why do you honor my father?” The old man replied, “This place is where one honors the deified ones. While he was alive, all households here served him; all the more so now that he is a spirit. Old man only hopes that the Shu army can soon repay what is owed. Now that you have come, this village is blessed.” He poured out wine to welcome him and had the horse fed and unstrapped.

After the third watch another knock came at the gate. The old man opened it. It was Pan Zhang of Wu, also seeking lodging. As soon as Pan Zhang entered the thatched hall, Guan Xing drew sword and shouted, “Rebel, do not run!” Pan Zhang turned and was ready to go out. Then one more person entered from outside. His face was like red jujube, with cinnabar eyes, drooping silkworm brows, and three strands of handsome beard. He wore a green robe and gold armor and entered with a drawn sword. Pan Zhang saw him as the manifest spirit of Lord Guan and screamed. He tried to turn away, but was already cut down by Guan Xing’s rising blade. His chest was cut and blood flowed on the earth. Guan Xing offered his heart’s blood before the image of Lord Guan. He took up his father’s Green Dragon Crescent Blade. He fastened Pan Zhang’s severed head beneath his horse’s collar, thanked the old man, and mounted the enemy horse to go toward camp. The old man himself hauled away Pan Zhang’s corpse and burned it.

Guan Xing rode for countless miles. Suddenly he heard men calling and horses neighing as another troop arrived. At its front was Ma Zhong, a commander under Pan Zhang. When Ma Zhong saw that Pan Zhang had been slain, his head slung beneath Guan Xing’s horse and the Green Dragon Crescent Blade in hand, he flared in fury and spurred forward to seize Guan Xing. Guan Xing saw in him the slayer of his father and his spirit rose high with righteous rage. He raised the Green Dragon Crescent Blade to strike Ma Zhong. Three hundred of Ma Zhong’s men rushed in all together and with one cry surrounded Guan Xing in a ring. Guan Xing stood with little support, his position perilous. Then from the northwest came a mass of troops. It was Zhang Bao. When Ma Zhong saw the rescue force arrive, he quickly drew out and retreated with his men. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao chased in together. In fewer than a few li they saw Mi Fang and Fu Shiren leading soldiers in pursuit of Ma Zhong. The two forces joined and a fierce fight broke out. With so few men, Zhang and Guan withdrew quickly and returned to Xiaoting. They presented the severed head and reported everything. The Lord was shocked and delighted by such news. He rewarded and supplied three whole armies.

Ma Zhong returned to Han Dang and Zhou Tai. He gathered the broken troops and set posts in divided groups. There were as many wounded among the soldiers as could not be counted. Ma Zhong with Fu Shiren and Mi Fang took position and camped on the riverbank. That night at the third watch the soldiers were weeping and could not still the cries. Mi Fang listened and heard one group say, “We are all Jingzhou men. Through Lü Meng’s trick, they sent our lord’s life into danger. Now Liu Bei, our lord’s uncle, has come in person to lead the campaign; soon Eastern Wu will end. What is our grief? it is Mi Fang and Fu Shiren. Why should we not kill those two traitors, go as it were to the Shu camp, and defect? It would be no small merit.” Another group of soldiers said, “Do not act rashly. Wait for a lull and then strike.” Hearing this, Mi Fang was greatly startled. He and Fu Shiren then discussed. Mi Fang said, “The mood of the soldiers shifts; our lives are unsafe. Now the Shu Lord’s hatred is centered on Ma Zhong. Why not kill him, take the head, and present it to the Lord, saying: ‘We had no choice but to surrender to Wu; they deceived us, saying Lord Guan had died, and opened the gate. Now that Your Majesty has come, we came to your camp to confess and seek pardon.’” Fu Shiren said, “No. We will surely bring calamity.” Mi Fang said, “The Shu Lord is generous and merciful. Now Crown Prince A Dou is my nephew by marriage; he only remembers our family ties. He would not dare harm us.”

Their scheme settled, they prepared the horses. At the third watch they entered the pavilion and killed Ma Zhong, cutting off his head. Mi Fang and Fu Shiren rode out with several dozen mounted men directly toward Xiaoting. Ambush troops on the road first brought them to Zhang Nan and Feng Xi, and they conveyed the full matter. Next day they came to the Lord’s pavilion, offering Ma Zhong’s head. Kneeling before him, they cried out, “We truly had no intent of treason. Lü Meng tricked us with the claim that Lord Guan was dead and thereby opened the gates. We had no choice but to submit to Wu. Now that the Holy Carriage has come, we have this way killed this traitor in order to settle Your Majesty’s grievance. Please forgive our crimes.”

The Lord was angry and said, “I left Chengdu long ago, and how could both of you not have come before to confess your crimes? Now, seeing the danger, you come with smooth words and seek only your own lives. If I spare you, how shall I face Lord Guan beyond the nine springs?” Then he ordered, in the imperial pavilion, that Guan Xing should set up a spirit tablet for Lord Guan. The Lord personally took up Ma Zhong’s severed head and went before it to offer sacrifice. He also ordered Guan Xing to strip Mi Fang and Fu Shiren, make them kneel before the spirit, and with his own knife flay them as sacrifice for Lord Guan. At that moment Zhang Bao entered, weeping and kneeling in front. “Both of my two paternal uncles’ enemies have been executed,” he said. “My father’s wrongful enemy—when will I be able to repay him?” The Lord answered, “Your virtuous nephew, do not worry. I will flatten Jiangnan and kill all the dogs of Wu. I will capture both of these villains and have you personally dismember them, so that you may offer them to your father.” Zhang Bao thanked him with tears and withdrew.

At this moment the Lord’s prestige thundered through all the southlands, and the people of Jiangnan trembled in fear, crying day and night. Han Dang and Zhou Tai were deeply alarmed. They rushed to Wu’s king and reported plainly that Mi Fang and Fu Shiren had killed Ma Zhong, defected to the Shu emperor, and in turn were slain by him. King Sun, shaken with fear, gathered civilians and generals and discussed. Bu Zhi said, “The enemies hated by the Shu Lord are Lü Meng, Pan Zhang, Ma Zhong, Mi Fang, and Fu Shiren. Now those are all dead. Only Fan Jiang and Zhang Da remain in Wu. Why not seize these two, together with Zhang Fei’s head, and send them back to Jingzhou to the lady, then submit a memorial seeking peace and the renewal of our prior accord, and then together target Wei so the Shu force will withdraw?” The king accepted this. He prepared a sandalwood casket scented with aloeswood, placed Zhang Fei’s head in it, bound Fan Jiang and Zhang Da as prisoners, and put them in a barred cart. He ordered Cheng Bing as envoy, carrying a state letter, to go toward Xiaoting.

Back at the camp, the Lord prepared to send troops farther. Then an inner officer announced, “Wu has sent an envoy with the head of the cavalry general Zhang and has delivered Fan Jiang and Zhang Da to us in chains.” The Lord placed both hands to his brow and said, “This is Heaven’s gift, won through the spirit of my third brother as well.” He ordered Zhang Bao to set Zhang Fei’s spirit tablet. When the Lord saw Zhang Fei’s head in the box, his face did not change. He cried out in full voice. Zhang Bao, wielding his sharp knife, cut and flayed Fan Jiang and Zhang Da in cruel succession, then performed the sacrifice before his father’s spirit. After that, the Lord’s anger did not lessen. He was fixed on destroying Wu. Ma Liang submitted, “All enemies have now been executed; resentment may be repaid. Wu official Cheng Bing has arrived. He brings back peace, asks that Jingzhou be returned and our lady restored, and seeks a renewed union to fight Wei. I kneel and beg your sacred command.” The Lord said angrily, “I am grinding my teeth in hatred. It is Sun Quan. If I accept peace now, it is to betray the pact made with my two younger brothers that day. First we destroy Wu, and then we move on Wei.” He reached for the executioner’s order. Many officials pleaded; only then he held back. Cheng Bing ducked and scraped for his life, then reported to the Wu king, “Shu will not accept peace and swears first to destroy Eastern Wu, and only afterward to break Wei. His ministers pleaded, but he did not listen. What is to be done?”

Sun was startled and lost his composure. Kan Ze came forward and said, “There is this column that could prop the sky—how can it be left unused?” Sun asked who he referred to. Kan Ze replied, “In former great affairs of Eastern Wu, all was in Zhou Lang’s hands. After him, Lu Zijing took his place. After Zijing’s death, all responsibility passed to Lü Ziming. Though Ziming is now gone, there is still a man in Jiangzhou called Lü Boyan. In my judgment he is not below Zhou Lang. Before, the breaking of Lord Guan was accomplished through his plotting. If Your Majesty can use him, Wu will surely break Shu. If there is failure, I will share the punishment with him.” Sun replied, “This is not De-run’s fault; I have made a great mistake.” Zhang Zhao said, “Lü Xun is only a scholar. He cannot contend with Liu Bei. I fear he is not usable.” Gu Yong also said, “Lü Xun is young; if all officers take him lightly, they may not obey him and it will bring disorder, ruining our great efforts.” Bu Zhi added, “Lü Xun is suitable to govern a commandery, not a great campaign.” Kan Ze shouted, “If you do not use Lü Boyan, Eastern Wu is finished! I will stake my whole family on this.” Sun said, “I have long known Lü Boyan to be a rare man. My decision is made. None of you should press this further.”

So he ordered him summoned. Lü Xun’s earlier name was Lü Yi and was later changed to Lü Xun; his courtesy name was Boyan. He was a native of Wu County, Wu, grandson of Lü Yu, gate captain of Hancheng, son of Lü Jun, defender of Jiujiang. He stood eight chi tall and had a face like polished jade. He held the office of General Who Guards the West. Lü Xun came at once and made obeisance. The king said, “Now, as Wu army and cavalry gather, I appoint you to marshal all troops and break Liu Bei.” Lü Xun replied, “The civil and martial men of Jiangdong are all ministers from our lord’s old retinue. I am without ability—how can I control them?” The king said, “Kan De-run has offered his family to guarantee you. I, too, have known your talent long. I now appoint you Grand Commander. Do not refuse.” Lü Xun asked, “If the civil and martial men do not obey, what is to be done?” The king gave him the sword at his side and said, “If anyone refuses the command, behead him first, then report.” Lü Xun replied, “I dare not refuse this heavy trust. But please, Your Majesty, gather all officers, and then confer. Kan Ze said, “In appointing a commander, one must build an altar and gather the hosts, then grant white plume and yellow battle ax, signets, seals, and military tally. Only then will orders carry force. Your Majesty should follow this rite, choose an auspicious day, build an altar, and appoint Boyan as Grand Commander. Give him the sign of command and tally; then all men will obey.” The king did so. He ordered an altar raised at once and all officials assembled. He invited Lü Xun to ascend and made him Grand Commander, Right Protector-General, General Who Guards the West. He advanced him to Marquis of Lou and gave him a precious sword and a silk sash. He made him hold six commanderies and eighty-one states, with the routes of Jing and Chu under his charge of armies and horses. The king said, “Within the inner gates, this is my domain; outside, they are yours to command.”

After receiving command from the altar, Lü Xun appointed Xu Sheng and Ding Feng to guard him and deployed the army the same day. He shifted troops along all routes and advanced by land and water together. Letters reached Xiaoting that Han Dang and Zhou Tai were alarmed: “How could our lord set a mere scholar in command?” When Lü Xun arrived, none obeyed. He held council in his pavilion. Men offered only reluctant greetings. Lü Xun said, “I was made Grand Commander by the king to drill the army and break Shu. The army has fixed law, and each should follow it. Whoever disobeys, royal law has no parent: let none pay for regret later.” All were silent. Zhou Tai said, “At present An-dong General Sun Huan, your nephew, is trapped in Yiling. There is no grain within, and no relief from outside. Please, Grand Commander, send a good measure at once and rescue Sun Huan, to still the Lord’s heart.” Lü Xun replied, “I have long known Sun An-dong can win men’s hearts and will hold firm. No rescue is needed. After I break Shu, he will come out on his own.” All left with hidden laughter. Han Dang said to Zhou Tai, “This scion made commander, and Eastern Wu is ruined. Did you see how he acts?” Zhou Tai said, “I only tested him with words and found no one strategy in him. How then can he break Shu?”

The next day Lü Xun issued orders: place guards at each pass and keep choke points secure; do not be light in enemy matters. All laughed at his caution and did not keep strict posts. The next day he called the officers to his pavilion again. He said, “I have this day and every day three times and five times repeated the king’s command. I ordered each of you to hold each pass and keep strict. Why was there no obedience?” Han Dang said, “I have fought with this command from Sun General through hundreds of battles, pacifying Jiangnan. The other generals, either under the General who Subdued the Rebel or serving the present king, are men sharpened in iron and brave to die. Now Your Majesty has made you Grand Commander to drive back Shu. You should have made plans early and shifted the troops, sending them forth by divide-and-advance for some great action. But you order us only to hold and not to fight. Do you intend us to wait for heaven to strike the bandits for us? I am not a man who clings to life and shuns death. How can you make me lose my fighting edge?” Then all the officers at his feet answered together, “General Han speaks correctly. We are willing to decide a final battle of life and death!” Lü Xun, drawing his sword and holding it in hand, shouted fiercely, “I may be only a junior scholar. But the king has entrusted me with weighty duty because I can endure shame and carry burden. All of you must hold your posts and keep the key points and do not act rashly. If anyone disobeys, he will be beheaded.” The assembled withdrew in muttered rage.

The Lord had already deployed army lines from Xiaoting to Chuan-kou in a chain of seven hundred li, with forty camps front and back. By day, banners shaded the sky; by night, firelight brightened heaven. A scout then reported, “Eastern Wu has made Lü Xun Grand Commander and placed all military command in his hand. Lü Xun has ordered each general to guard the key passes and not to sally forth.” The Lord asked, “What manner of man is Lü Xun?” Ma Liang replied, “Though Lü Xun is only a scholar from Wu, he is young and talented, deeply strategic. In the former campaign in Jing Province, all these devices were his devising.” The Lord grew angry, “A little brat with plotting schemes has harmed my two younger brothers. I will seize him now!” He ordered the advance. Ma Liang advised, “Lü Xun’s talent is not less than Zhou Lang. It should not be taken lightly.” The Lord said, “I am old in warfare. Is he better than a child of ten years?” He therefore personally led the vanguard and attacked each ford and choke point.

When Han Dang heard Shu armies coming, he sent word to Lü Xun. Fearing Han Dang would rush blindly, Lü Xun rode out swiftly to watch. He saw Han Dang on horseback atop a hill, gazing at the Shu army spread across mountain after mountain. Within their host there were indistinct yellow-robed canopy tops. Han Dang drew near with Lü Xun, and they looked together. Han Dang pointed and said, “There must be Liu Bei in their lines. I want to strike him.” Lü Xun said, “Liu Bei has moved his army east and won more than ten battles in a row. His momentum is at full force. Now he should hold high and guard the key heights. To come out now is not advantageous. But reward the soldiers and spread broad defensive measures. We must watch his changes. He now rides on the open plains and broad fields, proud in this gain. If we hold firm and do not move out, he cannot win battle. He will have to shift to mountain and woodland camps. Then I will defeat him with singular stratagem.” Han Dang nodded outwardly, but in his heart he still did not accept.

The Lord sent forward troops to skirmish and lashed him with a hundred taunts. Lü Xun ordered them to shut their ears and refuse pursuit. He personally traversed every checkpoint and spoke kindly to soldiers, ordering all to hold. As the Lord saw Wu’s troops not coming out, his mind became restless. Ma Liang said, “Lü Xun has deep strategy. Now Your Majesty has come from spring into summer to wage this war. His not coming out, I think, is to wait for change in our ranks. Please examine this.” The Lord replied, “What strategy does he have? Only fear of us. After suffering several defeats, how dare he come out again?” Vanguard commander Feng Xi reported, “The air is fiercely hot today. Our camps stand under burning heat. It is hard to fetch deep water.” The Lord then ordered each camp moved into shaded woods and dense trees near streams and ravines. He intended to pass summer into autumn and then press all forces together. Feng Xi carried out the order with exactness and moved all stockades into thick woodland shade. Ma Liang said, “If we move and then the Wu troops strike quickly, what then?” The Lord replied, “I have ordered Wu Ban with over ten thousand rough soldiers to camp on the flat ground near Wu’s posts. I selected eight thousand elite soldiers and set them hidden in mountain gorges. If Lü Xun learns that we moved, he must seize that chance and strike. Then he should find Wu Ban defeated in seeming flight. If he gives pursuit, I will break out and cut off his return. That boy can then be captured.” All ministers praised, saying, “Your Majesty’s divine calculations and stratagem are beyond even those of your ministers.”

Ma Liang said, “I have recently heard that Chancellor Zhuge in Dongchuan has set watch on each pass and fears Wei invasion. Why does Your Majesty not draw a map of each camp in these new positions and ask the Chancellor?” The Lord said, “I know military law already. Why ask the Chancellor again?” Ma Liang said, “As the old saying goes, ‘Many ears make seeing clear; one ear makes obstruction.’ Please, inspect this.” The Lord said, “You go and draw four-to-eight path maps of each camp. Ride to Dongchuan and ask the Chancellor yourself. If there is anything wrong, report quickly.” Ma Liang accepted. The Lord shifted his army into the shade of trees and water to avoid the heat. By then reports had already reached Han Dang and Zhou Tai that the camps had been moved. Hearing this, they were very glad and came before Lü Xun, “Now there are forty-some Shu camps, all moved into hills and dense woods, in shade near streams and ravines, resting cool by water. Would not the Grand Commander now strike at this opening?”

The Shu lord sets traps and ambushes; Wu soldiers eager for bravado will surely be captured.

Whether Lü Xun can obey these words remains to be seen. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Battle at Xiaoting: The Lord Wins Vengeance; at Jiangkou, a Scholar Is Made Great Commander

chapters.html:
Tiger tents discuss war by the Six Military Canons,
Scented bait is laid to draw the whale from the deep.
Among the three lands there are always gifted men,
And once more Luo of Jiangnan, Lu Xun, shows his worth.

Han Dang and Zhou Tai reported quickly that the Lord had moved camp and withdrawn toward Liang, then relayed the news to Lu Xun. Lu Xun rejoiced and led troops to observe the camp himself. He saw only a plain encampment of under ten thousand men, most of them old or weak, with a banner boldly marked “Vanguard Wu Ban.” Zhou Tai said, “I take these troops as a mere child’s play. I am willing to split off with General Han in two columns and strike. If we fail, I will obey the commandment as penalty.”

Lu Xun looked long at them, pointed with his whip, and said, “There is a sense of killing qi rising in the valley ahead. There must be an ambush below. Therefore, on level ground they have set these weak men to lure me. All of you must not leave.”

The generals all thought him timid.

The next day Wu Ban brought his men to the pass and invited a skirmish, posturing and blustering without ceasing, while insults flew. Many stripped off garments and armor, some even barefoot and bare-bodied, half sleeping, half sitting. Xu Sheng and Ding Feng entered the command pavilion and reported to Lu Xun: “Shu soldiers have greatly deceived us! We would all like to ride out and strike them!”

Lu Xun laughed. “You place your confidence in blood heat and brute courage, yet you do not know the military methods of Sun Wu. This is a plan to lure the enemy. After three days, we will see through the deceit.”

Xu Sheng asked, “If they have already shifted camp after three days, how can we strike them then?”

Lu Xun said, “I intend them to shift first.”

The commanders laughed derisively and withdrew.

After three days, the generals assembled at the pass and watched. They saw that Wu Ban’s soldiers had already pulled away. Lu Xun pointed and said, “Now the killing qi rises. Liu Bei must come out by the valley.”

Before he could finish speaking, all Shu soldiers appeared in full kit and harness, surrounding their lord and moving through. When Wu soldiers saw this, fear split them open.

Lu Xun said, “The reason I would not let you all strike the vanguard was for this. The ambush has now emerged; within ten days we will break Shu.”

The commanders said, “To break Shu should have been at first contact. We have camped for five or six hundred li, holding out seven or eight months; all key points are already fortified. How can we now break in?”

Lu Xun replied, “You do not know military law. Liu Bei is one of the foremost predatory heroes of this age, and he has far greater strategy. He assembled his army first with strict order. He has been waiting this long without giving us advantage; his soldiers are worn and his will hindered. The time to seize it is today.”

The commanders only then yielded in awe.

Later people praised him in verse:

Tigertent masters war by the Six Military Canons,
Laying fragrant bait to lure a whale from its bed.
Three states are indeed full of heroes,
Yet once again does Jiangnan’s Lu Xun stand high.

Lu Xun had already fixed his plan to shatter Shu, and he drafted a memorial to Sun Quan, reporting that the fall of Shu was to come the very next day.

Sun Quan read it and rejoiced: “Jiangdong has another extraordinary man after this; what cause have I to worry? Every general petitioned me saying he was cowardly, and I alone did not believe them. Now from his words he is surely not cowardly.”

He raised the full Wu force in support.

Now Liu Bei, at Xiao-ting, had driven the navy forward and down the river, following the current and camping at Zha camps along the Yangtze, penetrating Wu territory. Huang Quan remonstrated: “A fleet moving down the river can advance easily, but withdrawal is hard. Let me lead the vanguard. Your Majesty should stay in the rear ranks; then there is no chance of complete loss.”

Liu Bei said, “The Wu brigands have lost nerve. I shall charge ahead in full; what obstacle can stand?”

Many officials urged caution, but he refused, and split his troops in two routes. He ordered Huang Quan to command the troops on the north bank to guard against Wei raiders, and he personally led the Jiangnan force on the south bank, setting two lines of camps along the river to prepare for seizing ground.

Spies learned this and reported through the night to the Wei ruler, saying: “Shu’s army is invading Wu, tying stockades in extended camps, stretching in length across some seven hundred li, divided into more than forty camps, each beside mountain and woodland. Huang Quan now commands the army on the northern bank; each day he sends out patrols one hundred li or more, and we do not know his purpose.”

Hearing this, the ruler of Wei laughed upward and said, “Liu Bei will surely be defeated.”

The ministers asked why.

He said, “Liu Xuan­de does not understand the art of war: how can camps spanning seven hundred li hold back an enemy? To mass troops on terrain that blocks and binds itself is the great warning sign in war. Bei’de will lose to Lu Xun of Eastern Wu. Within ten days news will arrive.”

The ministers still did not believe him. They all asked that troops be dispatched against it.

Wei’s ruler said, “If Lu Xun wins, he will bring all Wu forces to seize Xichuan. If Wu army goes far, the realm is bare. I will withhold my troops now, and when the three columns strike in one moment, Wu will be taken in a trice.”

Everyone bowed and obeyed. He ordered Cao Ren to lead one force out through Nushu, Cao Xiu out through Dongkou, and Cao Zhen out through Nanjun: “Let this be the date when three columns of horse and men meet and strike Eastern Wu by stealth, while I follow behind to support.”

Arrangements done.

The narrative skips the Wei attack on Wu for now.

Ma Liang reached Shu and entered before Zhuge Liang, presenting the map and saying, “Now he has moved camps along both banks and crossed the river for over seven hundred li, with more than forty camps, each at the head of a stream and ravine, in places where woods are dense. His Lord ordered your plan map to be brought for the Chancellor to review.”

When Zhuge Liang had finished looking, he struck the table and cried, “Who taught his Lord to pitch this manner of camp? This man must die!”

Ma Liang said, “It was all done by his Lord himself, not another man’s scheme.”

Zhuge Liang sighed, “The mandate of Han has run out!”

Ma Liang asked the reason.

Zhuge Liang replied, “To block a valley and defend by the same obstacles is the great flaw in war. If they strike with fire, how could one answer it? And how can seven hundred li of linked camps refuse attack? Disaster is near. The reason Lu Xun holds and does not sortie is precisely this.”

“You must go quickly to see the Son of Heaven and change the camps. Not this way.”

Ma Liang asked, “If Wu men have now won, what then?”

Zhuge Liang said, “Lu Xun will not dare pursue. Chengdu can be kept safe.”

Ma Liang said, “Why does he not pursue?”

Zhuge Liang answered, “He fears Wei’s army striking his back. If his Lord suffers, we must withdraw to Baidi City. When I entered Shu, I already had ten thousand soldiers hidden at Yufupu.”

Ma Liang was startled. “I have gone to Yufupu many times and never saw a single soldier. Why would the Chancellor speak such a falsehood?”

Zhuge Liang: “Later it will be seen. Ask no further.”

Ma Liang obtained the memorial and raced back to the imperial camp.

Zhuge Liang returned to Chengdu and moved troops and horses to give support.

Lu Xun now saw that the Shu troops had become complacent and neglected to hold embankments and defenses. He gathered all officers and soldiers in the command, mounted and said, “Since my appointment I have not yet gone to battle. Now seeing Shu’s soldiers, I understand their motion and stillness; I want first to seize the fourth camp on the southern bank. Who dares go and take it?”

Before he finished speaking, Han Dang, Zhou Tai, and Ling Tong answered in turn: “We, for one, are willing.”

Lu Xun dismissed all of them and only summoned his lowest officer Chunyü Dan: “You and I, with five thousand troops, take the fourth camp on the southern bank, held by Shu commander Fu Tong. We must succeed tonight. I will bring reinforcements forward.” Chunyü Dan led his men off, and Lu Xun called Xu Sheng and Ding Feng: “Each of you takes three thousand men and camps five li outside the stockade. If Chunyü Dan returns in defeat and troops come rushing, you are to go out and rescue him. Do not chase farther.”

The two commanders went to their own battle fronts.

At dusk Chunyü Dan advanced with troops. By the time he reached the Shu camp it was after the third watch. He ordered his army’s drums and horns to thunder in. Fu Tong within the Shu camp rode out and charged, spear level, straight at Chunyü Dan. The officer could not hold and turned his horse to retreat.

Suddenly a roaring cry shook the air. A troop of soldiers intercepted the road; in front strode Commander Zhao Rong. Dan cut another way and lost half his force. As he was withdrawing, three roads of “barbarian” troops in the hills cut him off—at their head stood General Sha Mo Ke. Dan fought to break through and escaped only in hard slaughter; from behind, three columns came in hot pursuit.

When he was only five li from the camp, Wu generals Xu Sheng and Ding Feng came in from both sides and cut the Shu force away; they fled and rescued Chunyü Dan back to camp.

Dan entered before Lu Xun, bowing to confess guilt.

Lu Xun said, “It is not your fault. I only tested the enemy’s weakness and strength. My design to break Shu is fixed.”

Xu Sheng and Ding Feng said, “Their army is vast and hard to break; we only bleed and lose men.”

Lu Xun laughed: “My design here can fool no one but Zhuge Liang, and Heaven has favored me that this man was absent; thus I can make a great success.”

He assembled all officers and soldiers and ordered: send Zhu Ran by water to advance. Tomorrow afternoon, with the southeast wind rising, load the boats with haystraw and follow the plan. Han Dang leads one force to attack the north bank. Zhou Tai leads one to attack the south bank. Each man carries one bundle of straw, with sulphur and match powder hidden inside, each has a fire source, each holds spear or saber, and all mount and move at once.

But when they reached the Shu camp, with the wind in their favor they set the fire. Of the forty Shu camps, twenty burned; each pair of camp burned one camp. Every unit carried dry rations and was forbidden to fall back even for a moment.

Day and night they pursued and harried, stopping only when they had seized Liu Bei himself.

The generals heard the orders and left at once.

Liu Bei in the imperial pavilion pondered his plan to break Wu, when he saw the central military banner before the command tent collapse as if from no wind.

He asked Cheng Ji: “What omen is this?”

Ji said, “Not this night could Wu men come and plunder the camp?”

Liu Bei answered, “After last night’s slaughter, how dare they come again?”

Ji said, “If this is Lu Xun’s test of the enemy, what then?”

While speaking, a runner arrived saying that from the mountain top one could see Wu soldiers moving all along the ridge, all toward the east.

Liu Bei said, “This is a feinting force.” He ordered rest and said to Guan Xing and Zhang Bao: each should lead five hundred riders to patrol.

At dusk, Guan Xing returned and reported that fire had started in a north bank camp.

Liu Bei hurriedly sent Guan Xing toward the north bank and Zhang Bao toward the south to probe the truth. “If Wu troops arrive, return at once.”

The two followed command.

By the first watch, a sudden southeast wind rose. The left pavilion of the imperial camp burst into flame. As rescue was attempted, the right pavilion also burst. Wind tightened, the flames surged, trees all caught. Shouts thundered.

Two camps, horse and men, came out together and ran from the pavilion. Soldiers in the pavilion trampled one another; the dead were beyond count.

Behind them, Wu soldiers arrived, and no one could tell how many horse there were. Liu Bei mounted in haste and rode toward Feng Xi’s camp; in that camp fire and sparks rose to the sky. He looked south and east and saw the riverbank blazing like day, south and north equally.

Feng Xi, flustered, scrambled up and mounted, taking several dozen riders and running off. He met Ding Feng’s arrival and was held in hard fighting.

Liu Bei saw this and pulled his horse to flee westward. Ding Feng let go of Feng Xi and pushed troops in pursuit.

Liu Bei, in panic, saw ahead a column blocking his way; it was Wu commander Ding Feng. The two sides attacked together. The lord was struck with shock. With no road in four directions, he was trapped.

Then came a great cry. A unit of troops broke into the encirclement, and it was Zhang Bao, who rescued Liu Bei and drew the imperial bodyguard away running.

While they were still moving, another unit came up ahead: Shu commander Fu Tong as well. They joined troops in one mass. Wu soldiers pursued from the rear.

Liu Bei came to a hill called Ma’an Mountain. As Zhang Bao and Fu Tong urged Liu Bei up the slope, shouts rose from the foothills again: Lu Xun’s main force was encircling Ma’an. Zhang Bao and Fu Tong held the pass and the mountain gate. From above, Liu Bei looked over the entire field and saw unending firelight in all directions, with piled deadmen and the river choked below.

The next day Wu soldiers set fires all around the mountain, and soldiers in the ranks scattered in panic. Liu Bei was already in full panic when a figure broke through the flames with several riders and rode up the mountain. It was Guan Xing.

Guan Xing knelt low and said, “The fire from all sides closes in and cannot be endured. Your Majesty, ride quickly for Baidi City; then you may gather what troops you can.”

Liu Bei asked, “Who will cover the rear?”

Fu Tong reported, “Your servant volunteers to die for it.”

At dusk, Guan Xing rode in front, Zhang Bao in the middle, and Fu Tong held the rear and defended as Liu Bei withdrew off the mountain.

Wu soldiers saw Liu Bei fleeing and each vied for merit, each bringing greater force, sky- and earth-covering, all chasing to the west.

Liu Bei ordered his soldiers to remove all robes and armor, blocking paths and setting them alight to break up the pursuing rear guard. As they ran, a thunder of voices rose: Jiang commander Zhu Ran led a force down from the riverbank and blocked the way.

Liu Bei cried, “I will die here!”

Guan Xing and Zhang Bao leapt and charged and were struck back by a storm of arrows, each with grave wounds, unable to break through.

Again the cries rose behind: Lu Xun arrived with a great force from the valley.

In Liu Bei’s most anxious moment, dawn was near. He saw ahead a cry that shook the sky; Zhu Ran’s force fell into ravines and over rocks, and a troop surged in to rescue the royal carriage.

Liu Bei was overjoyed. Looking, he recognized Zhao Zilong of Changshan. Zhao Yun had been in Jiangzhou on the river, and when he heard of Wu and Shu joining battle, he had raised troops and advanced. Now, seeing the fire in the southeast as a wall into the sky, he had looked from afar and found Liu Bei trapped. He rode with desperate courage into the crush.

When Lu Xun learned it was Zhao Yun, he ordered his troops to pull back.

Zhao Yun, in the midst of killing, suddenly met Zhu Ran and exchanged blows. Before long they had not closed more than once before a single spear impaled Zhu Ran from beneath his horse, scattering the Wu soldiers and rescuing Liu Bei, then he turned toward Baidi City and escaped.

Liu Bei said, “Though I have escaped, what of my officers and men?”

Zhao Yun said, “The enemy remains in the rear; we cannot delay. Your Majesty should enter Baidi City to rest. I shall lead troops back now to rescue and support them.”

Only a little over a hundred men entered Baidi City with Liu Bei at first.

Later people praised Lu Xun in verse:

Straw raised in flames to break linked camps,
Xuande in flight at last to Baidi City.
One shout makes his name feared by Shu and Wei—
Does not the king of Wu now honor the scholar too?

Fu Tong, holding the rear, was besieged on all eight sides by Wu troops. Ding Feng shouted: “So many of you have fallen, and many have surrendered. Your lord Liu Bei is already captured. Why not submit now?”

Fu Tong barked, “I am a Han commander. How can I kneel to a dog of Wu?”

He threw spear and mounted, leading Shu soldiers in stubborn slaughter. For more than a hundred rounds he crossed and recrossed; he could not break free. Finally he sighed deeply, “Now I can rest.”

When he finished, he spewed blood and died among the Wu soldiers.

Later people composed a poem in praise of Fu Tong:

At Yiling, Wu and Shu fought in mighty battle;
Lu Xun’s design used fire to burn it down.
Even at death he still cursed the dogs of Wu—
Fu Tong did not betray the honor of a Han general.

Shu remonstrance minister Cheng Ji rode alone to the riverbank and called the navy to come into battle; Wu soldiers came on in pursuit, and the navy scattered in flight.

The commander of the Jiang division shouted, “Wu soldiers have arrived! Cheng Ji, run now!”

Cheng Ji answered in fury, “Since my lord took the field, I have never turned from battle and run!”

Before the words ended, Wu soldiers came in sharply. With nowhere to go, Cheng Ji drew his sword and slit his own throat.

Later people praised him in verse:

Fierce in courage, Shu’s Minister Cheng,
He leaves one blade to answer the king’s call.
In peril he never abandoned his old resolves—
Thus he won a name of unfading fragrance.

At this time Wu Ban and Zhang Nan had long besieged Yiling City. Feng Xi arrived then and reported Shu was defeated, and moved troops to rescue the Lord. Sun Huan had only just slipped away. As Sun Huan and Feng Xi rode, Wu soldiers came at them from the front, and from behind Sun Huan struck out from Yiling City, attacking from both sides. Zhang Nan and Feng Xi fought hard but could not break free. They died in the chaos.

Later people praised it in verse:

Feng Xi keeps one loyalty, Zhang Nan one fierce sense of right;
On the field each chooses battle and dies willingly.
Their names remain with fragrance through the histories.

Wu Ban broke through the siege and again met Wu pursuit. He was fortunate to be overtaken by Zhao Yun and was carried back to Baidi City.

At that time the barbarian king Sha Mo Ke, running one horse, met Zhou Tai; they fought for more than twenty rounds and were killed by Zhou Tai.

Shu commanders Du Lu and Liu Ning all surrendered to Wu. All Shu camps’ grain, equipment, and arms disappeared utterly; the surrendering soldiers were countless.

At this time Lady Sun was in Wu. Hearing of the defeat at Xiaoting, wild reports said the Lord had died in battle. She drove her carriage to the riverbank, looked west and wept aloud, then cast herself into the river and died.

Later they set a temple on the riverbank and called it Xiaojī Shrine. Later chroniclers wrote this verse:

The Lord’s troops return to Baidi City;
Wife hears of war, casts off life alone.
To this day a stone by the river remains,
Still bearing across ten thousand ages the name of a chaste wife.

Lu Xun, having gained complete victory, moved on with his winning force and pressed west in pursuit.

Not far beyond Kui Pass, Lu Xun was in the saddle and saw near the river by the mountain a mass of killing qi rise and crash toward heaven. He reined in and told his men, “There is surely an ambush ahead. The entire army must not advance lightly.”

He withdrew ten li and formed ranks on open ground to oppose enemy approach. He sent scouting riders forward. The scouts reported no camp there. Lu Xun doubted and dismounted, climbed a hill to look. The killing qi rose again.

He ordered another careful investigation. Riders returned: there was not one rider, not one soldier in front.

Seeing the sun near sinking west, with the threat rising, he felt uneasy and told his aide to inspect again. The report came: along the river there were only eighty or ninety piles of broken stones, no men or horse.

Lu Xun asked the local men why and what stone heaps carried this killing qi from within.

Some soon came. He asked, “Who piled these stones? How could killing qi rise from these piles?”

They answered, “This place is Yufupu. When Zhuge Liang entered Shu, he drove soldiers here and arranged the stones into formations on the sandbank. From then onward, there is often a qi like clouds rising from within.”

Lu Xun, after hearing, mounted and came with several riders to inspect the stone array. He set his horse on a hillside, and on all four sides he saw openings and doorways.

Lu Xun laughed: “This is only trickery to confound people. What use is it?”

He brought several riders down from the slope and entered the stone formation directly.

An officer said, “It is evening now, please, Commander, return soon.”

Lu Xun was about to leave when a wild gale struck. In a moment sand and stone flew, sky-dark and land-sealed. Strange stones stood jagged, jagged like swords; earthen ridges rose like hills; and the river roar roared like drumbeats of weapons.

Lu Xun cried in alarm: “I have fallen into Kongming’s calculation!” He tried to retreat, but there was no path.

In this panic, an old man appeared before his horse and said, smiling, “General, do you wish to leave this array?”

Lu Xun said, “I beg the elder to lead me out.”

The old man moved slowly with staff, passed directly through the stone array without obstruction, and escorted him to the hilltop.

Lu Xun asked, “Who are you, elder?”

The man answered, “I am Huang Chengyan, father-in-law of Zhuge Kongming. In the past, when this little son-in-law came into Shu, he laid this stone array here and called it the ‘Eight-Array Diagram.’ Repeating the eight gates of Dunjia—Xu, Sheng, Shang, Du, Jing, Si, Jing, and Kai—it changes with each season and hour and can rival ten thousand elite soldiers in force. Before he left he told me: ‘If later some commander from Eastern Wu becomes lost in it, do not bring him out.’”

“I happen to stand on this ridge and saw you enter by the gate of Death. I figured you would not know the array and would surely be entrapped. I am by nature kind and could not bear to see you sink into it, so I led you out by the birth gate.”

Lu Xun said, “Have you learned this array method?”

Huang Chengyan said, “Its changes are endless; one cannot learn it.”

Lu Xun hastily dismounted and, with bows of thanks, returned.

Later Du Gongbu made a poem:

Triumph covered three states, and fame became the Eight-Array map.
The river’s stones refuse to turn, a lingering sorrow: he failed to swallow Wu.

Returning to camp, Lu Xun sighed, “Kongming is truly a Sleeping Dragon. I could never reach him!”

He then ordered retreat.

His assistants said, “Liu Bei’s forces are beaten and cornered in a single city. This is the moment to strike while we have fortune. Why withdraw after seeing this stone array?”

Lu Xun replied, “It is not fear of the array that makes me withdraw. I calculate Cao Pi of Wei; his fraudulence and cunning are no less than his father’s. He will know I pursue Shu and then ride in on the gap. If I press deep into Xichuan, I will be hard pressed to return.”

So he assigned one officer to block the rear and led the main army home.

Within two days of beginning to withdraw, three separate messengers came flying: Cao Ren from Nushu, Cao Xiu from Dongkou, and Cao Zhen from Nanjun. Three routes, several hundred thousand men and horse, had arrived by night—purpose unknown.

Lu Xun laughed. “Exactly as I expected. I have already ordered troops to hold against it.”

And it is written:

His great heart longs to swallow Xichuan,
Yet still he must endure and defend the northern court.
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Lu Xun Camps and Burns Seven Hundred Li; Kongming Wields the Eight-Array Diagram

chapters.html:
Liu the Former Lord sends out his dying decree and entrusts the orphaned heir. Zhuge Liang stabilizes the household and repels five invading routes.

In the second year of the Zhangwu era, in the sixth month of summer, Lu Xun of Wu completely routed Shu troops at Xiaoting in the land of Yiling. The Lord of Shu, Liu Bei, whose courtesy name was Xuande, retreated back to Baidi City, and Zhao Yun, whose courtesy name was Zilong, led troops to defend it.

Suddenly Ma Liang arrived and saw that the main army had already been beaten. Too late to repent, he conveyed Zhuge Liang’s words to the Lord. Liu Bei sighed: “If I had followed the Chancellor’s counsel, this disaster would not have befallen us. How can I return to Chengdu and face the ministers?” He therefore ordered the court to camp at Baidi City, turning the relay station into Yong’an Palace.

An attendant later reported that Feng Xi, Zhang Nan, Fu Tong, Cheng Ji, and Sha Mo Ke had all died for the state. The Lord was deeply pained. Soon afterward another official reported, “Huang Quan brought his northern troops over from the bank and has submitted to Wei. Your Majesty, order us to bring his family before the censorate to be judged.”

Liu Bei answered, “Huang Quan was cut off on the north bank by Wu forces, and there was no road back to Shu. He surrendered because there was no alternative. It is I who failed him, not he failing me. Why punish his family as well?” He ordered grain and rations sent to sustain them.

Later, after Huang Quan had surrendered to Wei, officers led him into the presence of Cao Pi, whose courtesy name was Zihuan. Cao Pi said, “You have just surrendered to me today. Do you come now to imitate the famous ministers of Chen and Han?”

Huang Quan wept and said, “Your Majesty, the Lord of Shu had shown me exceptional favor and entrusted me with command of all our army north of the river, where Lu Xun cut off our retreat. I had no path to return to Shu. To surrender to Wu was impossible; so I came to submit to Your Majesty. A defeated commander might count survival as grace. How dare I now pretend to emulate men of old?”

Cao Pi was greatly pleased and immediately made Huang Quan the General Who Guards the South. Huang Quan humbly refused to accept. Just then, an official from a nearby office reported, “A covert reporter from Shu says that the Lord of Shu intends to execute all of Huang Quan’s household.”

Huang Quan replied, “I and the Lord of Shu share trust and sincerity. He knows my heart and would never consent to killing my family.” Cao Pi accepted this.

Later a verse was written censureing Huang Quan:

I cannot turn back to Wu once I have turned away; I cannot now turn to Cao. How can loyalty and righteousness serve two thrones at once? It is pity that Huang Quan would rather die than yield; even the hand that writes in the style of Ziyang is not easily soft.

Cao Pi asked Jia Xu, whose courtesy name was Wenhe, “I want to unify the realm in one stroke. Should I strike Shu first, or Wu first?”

Jia Xu replied, “Liu Bei has great talent, and Zhuge Liang governs Shu with uncommon skill. Wu’s Sun Quan judges strength and weakness as clearly as daylight. Lu Xun has already posted forces in difficult terrain and is prepared across river and lake. I doubt that even with Heaven’s authority over you this would be a complete victory. For now, hold fast and wait for change between the two states.”

Cao Pi said, “I have already sent three armies against Wu. How could this be a losing undertaking?”

The Minister of the Masters of Writing, Liu Ye, said, “Wu has just suffered repeated defeats by Shu; their momentum has collapsed, and they are easy to strike. Now they have won completely; their spirit is renewed tenfold. They are not yet ready for attack.”

Cao Pi said, “My intention is already fixed; do not counsel me on this again.” He went with the Imperial Guards to reinforce the three armies in person.

Scouts soon reported that Wu had already prepared. Lü Fan was ordered to stop Cao Xiu; Zhuge Jin to stop Cao Zhen at Nan Commandery; and Zhu Huan to hold Nu-Su against Cao Ren.

Liu Ye said, “Now that there is preparation on the Wu side, marching on will likely be of no benefit.” Cao Pi refused the warning and pressed on.

At that time Zhu Huan, age twenty-seven, was exceptionally brave and bold; Sun Quan loved him deeply. He was already commanding troops at Nu-Su. When he learned that Cao Ren had moved with a great army to Xiansi for Xianxi, he moved all his forces to guard Xianxi and left only five thousand cavalry in the city.

Suddenly there was news that Cao Ren had sent his vanguard, Changdiao, with Zhege Qian and Wang Shuang, along with fifty thousand picked troops, to rush Nu-Su. All the armies showed signs of alarm.

Zhu Huan drew his sword and said, “Victory belongs to the commander, not to numbers. As military law says, ‘When one side outnumbers the other two to one, the side with fewer troops may still defeat the larger host.’ Now Cao Ren has marched a thousand li and his men and horses are exhausted. My men and yours occupy the high ground, with the Yangtze to our south and mountain defenses behind us. We wait while preserving strength against a tired enemy; this is a posture to win a hundred battles. Even if Cao Pi himself were present, we need not fear; what chance does he have?”

He ordered everyone to lower flags and keep quiet, making it appear as though no one guarded the city.

At that moment Wei’s vanguard commander Changdiao came on ahead with his elite troops to take Nu-Su. Seeing no horses or infantry on the walls, he pushed the army forward. As soon as the city was still a short distance away, a cannon sounded and the banners went up together.

Zhu Huan leapt from horseback, cross-bladed sword in hand, and charged straight for Changdiao. The combat lasted less than three rounds. Zhu Huan cut down Changdiao under his horse with a single stroke. The Wu force followed the momentum, struck once, and Wei suffered a terrible rout.

Zhu Huan captured countless flags, armaments, and warhorses. Cao Ren came on with the main force shortly thereafter, only to be attacked as the Wu troops surged out from Xianxi. He suffered a great defeat and fell back. He returned to report to the Wei lord in detail. Cao Pi was startled.

As they conferred, a scout reported, “Cao Zhen and Xiahou Shang have been checked at Nan Commandery. Lu Xun ambushed them within and Zhuge Jin outside, and they were crushed between them.” Before he finished, another report arrived: “Cao Xiu too has also been beaten by Lü Fan.”

When Cao Pi heard all three roads had failed, he heaved a sigh: “I did not heed Jia Xu and Liu Ye’s counsel, and this defeat has come!” It was summer, and a severe epidemic spread in camp. Of horse and infantry, six or seven in ten died. He withdrew the army back to Luoyang. From that time, Wei and Wu lost harmony.

In the third year of Zhangwu, in the fourth month, the former Lord at Yong’an Palace fell gravely ill and gradually worsened.

Soon he sensed only his legs and arms failing; then he wept for his brothers Guan and Zhang and his illness deepened. He could barely see clearly, and he tired of his attendants. He shouted them away and lay alone on the dragon couch.

Suddenly, a wind rose in the dark hall, the lamps flickering, going out, and relighting. Beneath the lamp glow, two figures stood in attendance. The former Lord grew angry: “My heart is unsettled. I sent you away. Why have you come back?” They did not withdraw.

He stood and looked at them. At the top was Cloud-Long, and at the bottom Winged Virtue.

Liu Bei cried out in shock, “My two younger brothers are still here!”

Guan Yu said, “Your Majesty, we are not men; we are ghosts. The Son of Heaven sent us both as spirits because all our lives we kept faith and righteousness. Brother and brothers will not be apart much longer.”

Liu Bei collapsed into great weeping. He suddenly realized the figures were gone. He called to those near him, and it was the third watch of night.

He sighed: “I will not remain in this world long.”

He sent a courier to Chengdu for Chancellor Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, and Li Yan, Master of the Written Records, to come at once to Yong’an Palace and hear his final charge. Kongming and the crown prince Liu Shan, his son and ruler-in-waiting, along with Prince of Lu, Liu Yong, and Prince of Liang, Liu Li, came to the palace and the former Lord.

At this point only Liu Shan remained in Chengdu.

When Zhuge arrived at Yong’an Palace and saw the Lord close to death, he hurriedly knelt under the dragon couch.

Liu Bei ordered him to sit by the side of the couch and, placing a hand on his back, said, “I gained you as Chancellor and prospered the state. How could I have failed to follow your counsel and suffered this defeat through narrow-mindedness? That remorse has become illness, and I may die within a day or two. My successor is weak; I must therefore entrust him with matters of consequence.” He choked with tears.

Kongming wept and said, “May Your Majesty preserve Your holy body to meet Heaven’s charge for all under heaven.”

Liu Bei looked over and saw Ma Su, who was beside him, and ordered him to leave. Ma Su withdrew.

Liu Bei asked Kongming, “How would you judge Ma Su’s talent?”

Kongming replied, “He is among the outstanding men of this age.”

Liu Bei said, “No. I have observed him and found his words exceed his deeds. He should not be trusted with great office. Kongming, examine him deeply.”

After this, he summoned all ministers into the hall, gave paper and brush into Kongming’s hand, and had the final edict written, then handed it over and said with a sigh: “I cannot read deeply, but I know the larger outlines. The sages say, ‘The bird that is about to die cries bitterly; the man who is about to die speaks most clearly.’ I waited to end Cao’s rebels with you and to uphold the Han house together, but we are parting on the way. I ask Kongming to carry this edict to the Crown Prince Shan and let it not be treated as mere form. In everything, trust Kongming above all.”

Kongming and the officials knelt and said, “May Your Majesty rest Your body. We will expend every ounce of our strength and loyalty to repay the grace Your Majesty has shown us.”

Liu Bei had an attendant lift Kongming up. One hand wiped his tears; the other clasped his hand, and he said, “I am dying now. I have words for you from the heart.”

Kongming said, “What is Your Majesty’s command?”

The former Lord wept: “Your talent is ten times that of Cao Pi. You can settle the kingdom and secure the state. If the heir can be guided, guide him. If he is not worthy, you are the one to be lord of Chengdu.”

When Kongming heard this, he sweated all over, his hands and feet shook. He knelt and wept, saying, “How can I, with loyal bones and blood for marrow, not do all I can and uphold my lord to death?” He struck his head against the ground.

Liu Bei asked Kongming again to sit on the couch. He called Liu Yong and Liu Li forward and said, “Remember my words. After I am gone, all three of you must serve Kongming as if he were your father. Do not be remiss.”

After they had knelt, he ordered the two princes to bow before Kongming.

Kongming said, “Though I would spill my liver and brains upon the ground, I could never repay the grace of Your Majesty’s recognition.”

The former Lord addressed all officials: “I have entrusted the child to Kongming and ordered my successor to serve him as father. All of you, do not grow careless, so that you do not fail my hope.”

He also spoke privately to Zhao Yun, whose courtesy name was Zilong: “Through hardship and disaster, we were together until now, and now we part in this place. Recall my old friends. Watch over my sons morning and evening, and do not let me be in vain.”

Zhao Yun knelt and said, “I dare not fail to labor as a dog and horse would.”

The former Lord told all officials again: “I cannot individually instruct you all in detail. May you all take care of yourselves.”

Then he passed away. He was sixty-three years old. It was the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month of the third year of Zhangwu.

Later, poet and official Du Gongbu wrote this verse:

The Lord of Shu gazes toward Wu beyond the Three Gorges, and death comes in Yong’an Palace. His green carriage ought to be in the empty mountain beyond, while his jade hall now lies vacant in a wild chamber. In the ancestral shrine, cypress and pine and wild geese on the water share a sorrowful nest; in the time of the winter solstice, old village elders still walk their rounds. Near the temple of Wuhou, the houses stand side by side; one spirit is worshiped with lord and minister together.

After the former Lord’s passing, officials and soldiers alike wept deeply. Kongming led the whole courtly retinue back to Chengdu with the body in a shrine carriage.

Crown Prince Liu Shan went out to welcome the coffin and rested it in the main hall. After completing mourning rites and offering formal rites, they read the edict:

I was first ill only with flux, but now many diseases have come and gone without recovery. I have heard it said that a man should not die before the age of fifty. Now I am past sixty and have little cause for regret in death. It is my two sons I keep in my mind. Press onward. Press onward. Do not call an evil thing too small to do, and do not refuse a small good because it is small. Only merit and virtue can win men to follow. My own virtue was thin and not enough to copy. After I am gone, with the Chancellor serve in all affairs as sons with a father. Do not fail in this. Do not forget. As you continue, pursue distinction and clear achievement. This is my charge; this is my charge again!

When the reading ended, Kongming said, “The kingdom cannot be without a ruler even for one day. I beg the court to enthrone the heir, that he may inherit the Han line.” They enthroned the Crown Prince Liu Shan and bestowed the Imperial Title, adopting the era name Jianxing. Zhuge Liang was made Marquis of Wuxiang and Governor of Yi Province.

They buried the former Lord in Huiling and gave him the posthumous title Emperor Zhaolie. The empress dowager from the Sun family was raised as Empress Dowager. Lady Gan was made Empress Zhaolie. Lady Mi was also given posthumous title as Empress. The ministers were rewarded and the realm was granted a general amnesty.

Before many days had passed, the Wei army heard this matter and reported to the center. Court officers informed Cao Pi. He said, “Liu Bei has died. I have no cause for worry. Why should I not use this time when his state is headless to raise troops against it?”
