Jia Xu remonstrated: “Now that Liu Bei is gone, he has surely entrusted everything to Zhuge Liang. Kongming repays his grace and serves him without reserve, so he will defend the heir with his life. Your Majesty must not rush an attack.”

While he spoke, a man suddenly pushed out from the attendant ranks: it was Sima Yi.

Cao Pi was pleased and asked for counsel. Sima Yi said, “If only China’s armies move, it will be hard to secure victory quickly. Use five large columns and press from four sides so that Kongming cannot meet all at once, and then this can be done.”

Cao Pi asked, “What five routes?”

Sima Yi answered, “First, send one message to King Ke Binen of the Xianbei in Liaodong, bribe him with gold and silk, and order him to raise one hundred thousand Qiang troops from Liao West. They should advance by land first and strike Xianping Pass first.

Second, send orders with official rewards to the southern baron Meng Huo, telling him to raise one hundred thousand wild troops and attack the four commanderies of Yizhou, Yongchang, Zangke, and Yuejun, striking at the southern approaches of Xichuan.

Third, send envoys to Wu and seek alliance, promising land. Order Sun Quan to raise one hundred thousand troops and attack at the two-mouthed passes of Sichuan to take Fucheng.

Fourth, dispatch an envoy to the former defector Meng Da and order the one hundred thousand troops of Shangyong to rise and advance on Hanzhong.

Fifth, make Cao Zhen Supreme General-in-Chief and have him lead one hundred thousand troops out through Yangping Pass by the direct road to Xichuan.

These five columns total five hundred thousand men, with one hundred thousand in each route. Can Zhuge Liang, with the talent of Luwang, truly withstand this?”

Cao Pi was overjoyed and secretly sent four persuasive envoys on the mission. He also ordered Cao Zhen to be Supreme General-in-Chief and lead one hundred thousand men directly toward Yangping Pass.

At that time Zhang Liao and other veteran generals had all been made marquises. They were posted at Jizhou, Xuzhou, Qing Province, and He Fei guarding river crossings and passes, and therefore were not called out.

From then on, the Later Lord Liu Shan, soon enthroned, had many of his old ministers pass away, a number that cannot be detailed. For all court, legal, and fiscal matters, he let Chancellor Kongming adjudicate. Liu Shan had not yet taken an empress. Kongming and the ministers submitted: “A certain daughter of the former General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhang Fei is extremely capable. She is seventeen years old and may be taken as the principal empress.” Liu Shan did so.

In the first year of Jianxing, in the eighth month of autumn, a frontier report arrived: “Wei has raised five large armies to attack Xichuan.

The first route: Cao Zhen, made Great Commander and Supreme Commander, leads one hundred thousand men and comes through Yangping Pass.

The second route: the defector Meng Da raises one hundred thousand men from Shangyong and invades Hanzhong.

The third route: Wu’s Sun Quan raises one hundred thousand elite troops and enters Sichuan through the two gorge mouths.

The fourth route: the barbarian king Meng Huo raises one hundred thousand from the south to invade four commanderies of Yizhou.

The fifth route: the king Ke Binen of the Xianbei raises one hundred thousand Qiang troops and invades through Xianping Pass.

All five routes are grave and dangerous.”

The report had already reached Kongming, but he did not know what to make of it and did not attend court for several days.

The ruler heard this and was shocked. He sent an attendant with his order to summon Kongming to court. The messenger returned saying half the day after: “I have reported to Chancellor Kongming’s house, but Kongming says he is ill and cannot come out.”

The ruler grew frantic. The next day he sent Huangmen Secretary Dongyun and Counselors’ Office official Du Qiong to stand at Kongming’s bed and report this urgent state of affairs.

At their arrival before Kongming’s residence, they could not enter. Du Qiong said, “The former emperor entrusted the child heir to Kongming. The ruler has just ascended the throne and now Wei has sent five invasion columns against him. The emergency is severe. Why does the Chancellor avoid this and remain in bed?”

After some time, a doorkeeper relayed Kongming’s order: he was only slightly unwell and would appear in the Hall of the Capital at first light the next morning. Dongyun and Du Qiong sighed and withdrew.

The next morning, still more officials came and waited at his house and watched through the day and still did not see him emerge.

When the court remained unsettled, Du Qiong reported to the ruler: “Please, sire, descend from the palace and ask Kongming for a strategy in person.”

The ruler went with many officials to the palace and informed the empress dowager. The dowager was alarmed and said, “Why should the Chancellor act so, with the prior imperial charge now our life?” She said she would go herself.

Dongyun said, “The dowager should not go so lightly. I think Kongming has some profound design. Better to let the ruler go first. If he delays, then call for Kongming in the ancestral temple.” The dowager consented.

The next day the ruler made a direct visit to Kongming’s hall. The gatekeepers saw the royal chariot and hurriedly bowed on the ground in welcome.

The ruler asked, “Where is the Chancellor?”

The gatekeeper replied, “I do not know where he is. He has only ordered that officials be stopped from entering.”

He got down and walked alone to the third inner gate. There he saw Kongming leaning on a bamboo staff by a small pond, gazing at fish.

The ruler stood behind him for a while, then spoke softly, “Kongming, are you well?”

Kongming saw who it was, dropped his staff, and knelt: “I am worthy of ten thousand deaths, Your Majesty.” The ruler helped him up and asked, “Now that Cao Pi has split his armies in five routes, why do you not appear and take office?”

Kongming laughed and led him into the inner chamber, seating him, then said, “The five routes have all come. How could I not know? I have not been watching the fish. I have been thinking.”

The ruler asked, “How can this be?”

Kongming said, “King Ke Binen of the Qiang, King Meng Huo, the defector Meng Da, and Cao Zhen—these four roads of troops have already been sent away.

Only Wu’s route under Sun Quan remains. I have a plan for withdrawal, but I need one eloquent envoy to do it, and I have not yet found the right man. Think no more on this, sire.”

The ruler, hearing this, was startled and pleased in turn: “Truly, the Chancellor has a stratagem beyond heaven’s count! I want to hear how to turn back these enemies.”

Kongming answered, “The former Lord entrusted Chengming to me; how dare I be negligent for a day or a night? All the officials in Chengdu do not know the intricacies of military art. Their key is to make others not expect the unexpected. To expose our plan would be a mistake.

I learned earlier that King Ke Binen would lead troops through Xianping Pass. But my former ally Ma Chao, rooted in Xichuan and beloved by the Qiang, is treated by them as if he were a divine Great General. I have sent one messenger through the night to urge Ma Chao to guard Xianping closely and station four-way ambush forces, rotating each day and blocking every approach. That route is secure.

As for Meng Huo, he strikes from the four counties; I also sent Wei Yan with one force to enter and exit by left and right in the manner of a feigned force. The southern tribesmen are fierce and brave and inclined to suspicion; if they see a deceptive force, they will not advance. This route is also not cause for worry.

I learned Meng Da had led troops out of Hanzhong. He and Li Yan had once sworn life and death in friendship. When I returned to Chengdu, I left Li Yan in charge of Yong’an Palace. I already wrote one letter in Li Yan’s own hand and had it sent to Meng Da; he will certainly claim sickness and not march, delaying the army’s spirit. This route also is no longer to worry over.

I learned that Cao Zhen had brought troops through Yangping Pass. The terrain there is rugged and fit for defense, and I have ordered Zhao Yun to hold that pass with one force and not go out to battle. If he sees our army not striking first, Cao Zhen will withdraw soon on his own.

These four routes do not worry me. I have still sent Guan Xing and Zhang Bao with thirty thousand men each to key points as a further safeguard and reserve response. None of these deployments passed through Chengdu, so no one noticed. The only uncertain route is the one from Wu.

If four routes stand in danger, Wu will join and strike in a crisis. If four fail, it will not come to that. I believe Sun Quan still resents Cao Pi’s three-route invasion of Wu, and so he will not join their plan. Even so, we need one person with eloquent tongue to go directly to Wu and explain the peril clearly. That one man may force Wu to retreat first; then where could the other four frighten us? Until such a messenger is found, why should I trouble Your Majesty with the burden of a journey?”

The ruler replied, “The empress dowager also wanted to come to meet my Chancellor-father. After hearing your words, my confusion has lifted. What then remains to fear?”

Kongming drank several cups with the ruler and saw him out. The officials gathered outside the gates saw joy on the ruler’s face.

After taking leave of Kongming, the ruler entered his carriage and returned to court. The assembled officials were full of doubt.

Kongming noticed one officer outside standing beneath the sky and laughing with cheer. He had a bright expression. It was Deng Zhi, a man from Xiyang’s Xinye, surname Deng, name Zhi, courtesy name Bomei. He was now Minister of Revenue and a descendant of the Han officer Deng Yu.

Kongming quietly had Deng Zhi detained and asked him privately in the study. “Now Shu, Wei, and Wu are split across three realms. If we can first strike two and unite the land under one order, should we move against which state first?”

Deng Zhi said, “To my mind, Wei is indeed a bandit usurper, but its force is vast and hard to shake quickly. We should make a gradual plan. The ruler has just ascended and the people are not yet settled, so we should ally with Eastern Wu as close teeth and gums, and wash away old grievances with one imperial state. That is the long plan.”

Kongming laughed, “I have had these thoughts for a long time and could not find a man to speak it aloud. Today I have finally found you.”

Deng Zhi asked, “Who do you want to send, and for what?”

Kongming said, “I want one person to go to Wu and make this bond. Since you have grasped the point, you cannot fail this command. The mission to Wu is nothing but for you.”

Deng Zhi said, “I am shallow in talent and fear I cannot bear so heavy a charge.”

Kongming said, “Tomorrow I will report to the ruler and ask that you be sent. Do not refuse.”

Deng Zhi agreed and withdrew.

The next day Kongming reported to the ruler and appointed Deng Zhi for the mission. Deng Zhi bowed and departed toward Wu. In the words of the scene’s closing verse:

The people of Wu have only just seen the clash of arms to cease, and the envoy from Shu will return to exchange jade and silk. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Former Lord Liu Issues His Last Edict and Entrusts the Child-Heir; Zhuge Liang Calms and Guards Against Five Fronts

chapters.html:
After Lu Xun of Eastern Wu had routed the Wei soldiers, the Wu king appointed him General Who Aids the State, the Marquis of Jiangling, and the Governor of Jing Province. From then on, all military command was in Lu Xun’s hands. Zhang Zhao and Gu Yong petitioned the Wu king to adopt a new era name. Sun Quan approved, and the year was changed to the first year of Huangwu.

A message from Wei then arrived, and Sun Quan summoned the envoy in.

The envoy reported, “Shu recently sent people to ask for troops from Wei, but Wei was at first unsure how to answer, so it dispatched an army. It now deeply regrets that and intends to send four separate armies to seize Sichuan. Eastern Wu should come to assist. If Sichuan falls, each side will divide the territory in half.”

Hearing this, Sun Quan could not decide. He asked Zhang Zhao, Gu Yong, and the others. “Lu Boyan sees clearly and has very fine judgment,” Zhang Zhao said. “You can ask him.”

Sun Quan immediately summoned Lu Xun.

When Lu Xun arrived, he submitted, “Cao Pi is established in the Central Plains, and this is no time for loose planning. If we refuse, there will surely be enmity. I judge that neither Wei nor Wu has an opponent of Zhuge Liang’s caliber. For now, agree outwardly. Muster the army and prepare; meanwhile, explore how the four Wei advances are going. If the four armies win, Sichuan will be in danger and Zhuge Liang will not be able to come to relief in time. In that case, Your Majesty should send an expedition to respond, first taking Chengdu. That is the superior strategy. If the four armies lose, we should deliberate separately.”

Sun Quan agreed and told the Wei envoy, “Our army has not yet completed its preparations, but on an auspicious day we will depart at once.”

The envoy bowed and left.

Soon Sun Quan heard that the western barbarian troops had moved out of Xipin Pass and, on seeing Ma Chao, withdrew without fighting. In the south, Meng Huo raised troops and marched on four counties, but each was repelled by Wei Yan’s feint tactics and forced to retreat into caves. The Meng Da troops from Shangyong were halfway on the road when they suddenly fell ill and could not move. Cao Zhen’s force moved out through Yangping Pass, and Zhao Zilong held every difficult pass. As expected, one good commander at a narrow way could not be broken by ten thousand men. Cao Zhen camped on the route through Xia Valley, could not force victory, and withdrew.

When Sun Quan received this news, he said to the ministers and generals, “Lu Boyan is indeed a true mathematician of strategy. If I were to act rashly, I would again make enemies in Western Shu.”

At that moment came news that Western Shu had sent Deng Zhi.

Zhang Zhao said, “This is another design of Zhuge Liang to check the army and it has sent Deng Zhi as envoy.”

“Then how should we answer him?” asked Sun Quan.

“First, have a great cauldron prepared in the hall, and fill it with hundreds of jin of oil,” said Zhang Zhao. “Then heat it with charcoal. When the oil is boiling, choose a thousand tall, broad-faced warriors and have each carry a blade. Line them from the palace gate directly up to the hall, and summon Deng Zhi to appear. Before he can begin speech-making, rebuke him with the old Qi precedent of Li’s talk and execute him in this manner. Then we can see how he answers.”

Sun Quan accepted the suggestion and had the oil cauldron installed. He ordered the warriors to stand on both sides, blades in hand, and then summoned Deng Zhi.

Deng entered in full ceremonial dress. As he approached the palace gate, he saw two rows of armed men, stern in their bearing, each holding steel blades, great axes, long swords, and short halberds, all drawn up to the hall front.

He understood their intent and showed not a trace of fear; he advanced upright and proud. At the hall front, he again saw the cauldron of boiling oil. The warriors on both sides watched him with their eyes fixed there. Deng Zhi merely smiled faintly.

A near minister brought him near the curtain. Deng Zhi made a full respectful bow but did not kneel.

Sun Quan ordered the pearl curtain pulled up and roared, “Why do you not kneel?”

Deng replied with lifted chin, “Envoy from the Upper Country does not kneel before the lord of a minor state.”

Sun Quan snapped, “Do you think you can evade and prattle like Li’s ‘talking down Qi’ with your three-inch tongue? Go at once into the oil cauldron!”

Deng laughed aloud. “Everyone says Eastern Wu has many worthy men. Who would have thought anyone fears a scholar?”

Sun Quan turned with anger. “Do you suppose I fear a single common soldier like you?”

Deng said, “If you are not frightened by the old Deng Boyao, what is there to fear in what they have come to tell you?”

Sun Quan asked, “You have come to serve as Zhuge Liang’s spokesman to speak with me, have you not?”

Deng answered, “I am a small scholar from Shu, and I have come for the welfare of Wu. You set troops in place and the boiling cauldron to meet one envoy. How narrow is your mind, that it cannot contain another man?”

At those words Sun Quan was abashed. He shouted off the armed men, summoned Deng into the hall, offered him a seat, and asked,

“Tell me the advantages and dangers between Wu and Wei. Instruct me, Master.”

Deng said, “Does Your Majesty seek peace with Shu, or with Wei?”

“Your Majesty knows my heart,” said Sun Quan. “I want peace with the lord of Shu, but I fear Shu’s ruler is young and shallow and cannot keep faith from start to finish.”

Deng said, “You are one of the heroic men chosen by Heaven, and Zhuge Liang is also one of the outstanding worthies of this age. Shu has terrain strong with mountains and rivers; Wu has the triple river defenses. If the two states stay in close alliance and become as jaw and molars together, then advancing together one might absorb the world, and retreating together one might stand on three supports. If Your Majesty now submits and declares yourself a vassal to Wei, Wei will certainly call Your Majesty to court and demand a crown prince to serve as inner attendant. If this is refused, it will raise troops and attack. Shu will then advance with the current in support. Then the lands south of the Yangtze will no longer be yours. If Your Majesty rejects my counsel, as you say, this humble man will die before you here and thereby end the business of a would-be spokesman.”

When he had finished, he loosened his robe and stepped down from the hall, and would have leapt straight into the cauldron.

Sun Quan urgently ordered the men to stop him and invited him into a rear hall, where he treated him with guest-hospitality.

“Your words are exactly what I wished to hear,” Sun Quan said. “I now want to make a lasting peace with the lord of Shu. Will you introduce us?”

Deng said, “He who just now sought to cook a servant was Your Majesty. He who now would employ this servant is also Your Majesty. If Your Majesty remains doubtful, how can others trust you?”

Sun Quan said, “My will is fixed now. Do not doubt, Master.”

So Sun Quan kept Deng and summoned many officials. He said, “I command the eighty-one prefectures of Jiangnan and also the lands of Jing and Chu, yet this does not even compare to the remote reaches of Western Shu. Shu has Deng Zhi and he does not disgrace his lord. Wu has no one who can enter Shu and express my intentions.”

A man stepped forward and offered, “I will serve as envoy.”

All eyes turned to him. He was Zhang Wen of Wu Commandery, surname Zhang, given name Wen, courtesy name Huishu, presently the Colonel of the Zhonglang rank.

Sun Quan said, “I fear that if you go to Shu and see Zhuge Liang, you may fail to convey my intent.”

Zhang Wen answered, “Kongming is only a man, and why should I fear him?”

Sun Quan rejoiced and rewarded Zhang Wen richly, sending him with Deng Zhi to open relations with Shu.

Not long after Deng Zhi left, Zhuge Liang reported to the Later Lord,

“Once Deng Zhi is in his post, this task will certainly succeed,” he said. “Many capable men reside in Wu; surely someone has come to answer our gift. Your Majesty should treat them with courtesy and send him back so that our alliance may be restored. If Wu and Shu settle into peace, Wei will not dare to send troops against Shu. When Wu and Wei are both stable, I can campaign in the south, pacify the southern barbarians, and only then move against Wei. Once Wei is weakened, Eastern Wu cannot survive long by itself. Then the foundation for unity may be restored.”

The Later Lord assented.

Soon news arrived that Eastern Wu had sent Zhang Wen and Deng Zhi into Shu to return the courtesy visit. Liu Shan gathered the civil and military officers at the vermilion terrace and summoned Deng Zhi and Zhang Wen in.

Feeling he had found his opportunity, Zhang Wen ascended with head held high and performed a formal bow before Liu Shan.

The Later Lord granted him a brocade seat and placed him on the left of the hall and held a palace banquet for them.

Liu Shan was formal and courteous, but not overly familiar. After the banquet, all officials escorted Zhang Wen to his lodging.

The next day, Zhuge Liang held a banquet in his honor. He said to Zhang Wen,

“When our former ruler lived, Shu and Wu were not on good terms. He has now passed away. The present lord longs for the Wu king, and wishes to abandon old enmity and forge lasting alliance, and together break Wei. I hope Your Excellency will carry this back in your words.”

Zhang Wen acknowledged.

When the wine reached the middle of the cup, Zhang Wen still smiled cheerfully and seemed faintly proud.

The following day, the Later Lord gave Zhang Wen gold and silk and held another banquet at the pavilion south of the city, sending all officials to escort him.

Zhuge Liang earnestly urged him to drink more.

In the midst of drinking, a man staggered in on wine and entered with a lofty bow, then sat himself at the table.

Zhang Wen looked puzzled and asked Zhuge Liang, “Who is this man?”

Zhuge Liang replied, “His surname is Qin, name Mi, courtesy name Zilai; he is now a Yizhou Scholar.”

Zhang Wen smiled. “A ‘scholar’ by that name, and I do not know what books he may have studied.”

Qin Mi said sternly, “In Shu, children of three feet of height all still go to school. What of me should be unknown?”

Zhang Wen said, “Then Master, what have you studied?”

Qin Mi replied, “From Heaven and astronomy down to earth sciences, the Three Teachings and the Nine Disciplines, the various masters, and the hundred schools: all have I seen. The rise and fall of ages, the classics of sages and worthies, all have I read.”

Zhang Wen smiled. “Since you speak so grandly, answer me one thing. Does Heaven have a head?”

Qin Mi said, “It has one.”

“Where is the head?”

“It is in the west,” said Qin Mi. “The Book of Songs says, ‘There behold the westward face.’ Inference confirms the head is in the west.”

“Does Heaven have ears?”

“Yes.”

“Where is this evidence?”

“‘The cranes cry in the reeds at nine mounds, and their sound is heard in Heaven,’ says the Book of Songs. How could there be hearing without ears?”

“Does Heaven have feet?”

“It has feet.”

“‘Heaven walks with difficulty,’ says the Book of Songs. How could one walk without feet?”

“Does Heaven have a surname?”

“How could it have none?”

“Which surname?”

“It is Liu.”

“And how do you know?”

“The Son of Heaven’s surname is Liu, and so I know.”

Zhang Wen asked, “Does the sun rise in the east?”

Qin Mi replied, “It rises in the east, yet it sets in the west.”

By now Qin Mi’s answers were clear and flowing, and all seated were astonished. Zhang Wen had no answer.

Qin Mi then said,

“Master Zhang, since you have already raised such matters of Heaven, you must understand Heaven’s principles clearly. In the beginning, chaos was divided; yin and yang were separated. What is light and clear rose up as Heaven; what was heavy and turbid sank and condensed as Earth. Then, when Genggong was defeated, his head struck Mount Buzhou, the columns of Heaven broke, and the ties of Earth were torn. Heaven tilted northwest and Earth sank southeast. If Heaven is only light and clear, why did it tilt northwest? Apart from such light and clear, what else is there? Please teach me.”

Zhang Wen had nothing with which to answer. He withdrew from his seat and left, bowing to apologize.

All his eyes were widened. He said, “I had not expected Shu to produce such prodigies! I only thought, from this learned exchange, that the blockage in my understanding had suddenly cleared.”

Zhuge Liang, fearing Zhang Wen’s humiliation, explained, “The challenge at the table was but playful exchange. You know the ways of stabilizing a state and securing peace. What use is this sparring over lips and teeth?”

Zhang Wen acknowledged.

Zhuge Liang then ordered Deng Zhi to return to Wu with his courtesy gifts and to travel with Zhang Wen.

The two paid homage to Zhuge Liang and departed for Eastern Wu.

When Sun Quan heard that Zhang Wen had gone to Shu and had not yet returned, he gathered ministers and generals to deliberate. A courtier reported, “Shu has sent Deng Zhi together with Zhang Wen to return our courtesy visit.”

Sun Quan had him admitted.

Zhang Wen bowed before the hall and extolled Liu Shan and Zhuge Liang’s virtue. He said he wished for enduring alliance and that he had been sent by the Chief Minister for that purpose. Sun Quan rejoiced and gave him a banquet.

Sun Quan asked Deng Zhi, “If Wu and Shu unite and destroy Wei, and in time win all under heaven with peace, and each lord governs in two realms, would that not be joy?”

Deng said, quoting, “There are no two suns, and no two kings for one people. If Wei is destroyed, we still do not know by what Heaven will assign its charge. The one who governs must each cultivate his virtue; the one who serves must each keep his loyalty. Then only can war subside.”

Sun Quan laughed. “So this is your sincerity?”

He then rewarded Deng handsomely and sent him back to Shu. From then on, Wu and Shu were at peace.

A Wei undercover scout learned this and quickly carried the word to the capital. Cao Pi heard it and shouted in rage, “If Wu and Shu are now allied, they surely intend designs on the Central Plains. Better that I attack first.”

So he gathered ministers and discussed marching an army against Wu.

At this point, Grand Commandant Cao Ren and Grand Commandant Jia Xu were already dead.

Xin Pi stepped forward in court and said, “The plains of Zhongyuan are wide and thinly populated, and to send troops there has no clear advantage. The present plan should be to raise troops and settle into field agriculture for ten years, enough to supply men and grain, and only then use the army. Only then could Wu and Shu be broken.”

Cao Pi said angrily, “This is the argument of a backward Confucian pedant! Wu and Shu are now allied and will surely cross into our territory sooner or later. Where is the time to wait ten years?”

He issued the order to raise troops against Wu.

Sima Yi reported, “Wu has the hazard of the Yangtze; it cannot be crossed except by ship. Your Majesty should ride with the army in person. Choose small and large warships from Caizhong and Ying, enter through Huai, take Shouchun, then Guangling, cross at the estuary, and go straight to Nanxu. This is the superior strategy.”

Cao Pi adopted it. He had ten dragon boats built, each more than twenty zhang long and capable of holding over two thousand people, and prepared more than three thousand warships.

That autumn, in the fifth year of Huangchu, in the eighth month, he assembled all troops and ordered Cao Zhen to lead the vanguard, with Zhang Liao, Zhang He, Wen Ping, and Xu Huang as senior generals to advance first; Xu Chu and Lü Qian to protect the center; Cao Xiu to guard the rear; and Liu Ye and Jiang Ji as advisers. In total the land-and-water host numbered more than three hundred thousand cavalry and infantry.

At the next selected day they marched. He made Sima Yi the Prefect of the Masters of Writing and left him in Xuchang. All major state affairs were to be decided by Sima Yi.

The Wei army’s departure was not narrated. Yet Eastern Wu spies had learned of it and reported in:

“Now the Wei king Cao Pi himself rides the dragon boats, bringing both water and land forces of over three hundred thousand. From Cai and Ying he goes out through Huai, surely will take Guangling, cross the river mouth, and come down to Jiangnan. It is very dangerous.”

Sun Quan was alarmed and again gathered many civil and military officers.

Gu Yong said, “Since our lord has allied with Western Shu, write to Zhuge Kongming and have him raise troops out of Hanzhong to divide their strength. At the same time send one great commander and station troops at Nanxu to resist.”

Sun Quan replied, “No one but Lu Boyan can bear this heavy task.”

Gu Yong said, “Lu Boyan is holding Jing Province; he should not be moved lightly.”

Sun Quan said, “I do not deny that. But now there is no one to replace him.”

Before he finished, another spoke at once from the crowd: “Though unworthy, I am willing to lead an army against the Wei host. If Cao Pi himself crosses the Great River, I will capture him alive and offer him to Your Majesty. If he does not cross, I will still kill most of the Wei army and keep them from facing Wu directly.”

Sun Quan saw that it was Xu Sheng.

Sun Quan rejoiced: “If I have you hold this southern stretch of Jiangnan, what need then have I to fear?”

He thereby made Xu Sheng the General Who Guards the East, and ordered him to command the combined armies at Jianye and Nanxu. Xu Sheng thanked him, accepted the command, and withdrew. He then ordered all officers to prepare many weapons and raise many banners as part of the riverbank defense.

Again someone stepped out and said,

“Your Majesty has entrusted this heavy duty to this general and asked him to break the Wei army and capture Cao Pi. Why does he not advance early with cavalry and cross the river to meet the enemy at once at the land of Huainan? If he waits until Cao Pi’s soldiers arrive, it may be too late.”

Xu Sheng saw him and said, “That is my brother-in-law’s son, Sun Shao.”

Sun Shao, courtesy name Gongli, was a General Who Exalts Valor. He had once defended Guangling and though young was strong of spirit and extraordinarily brave.

Xu Sheng said, “Cao Pi’s force is vast, and he has renowned generals as his vanguard. It is not fit to cross the river and meet him there. If we let him gather all his ships on the north bank, I shall have a method to break them.”

Sun Shao replied, “I myself have three thousand horse and men under me, and I know Guangling roads and waters well. I wish to go north of the river and fight Cao Pi to death. If I fail, I shall accept the army’s judgment.”

Xu Sheng refused, but Sun Shao would not relent.

He repeated his request. Xu Sheng, angry, said, “If you defy commands this way, how can I control the other generals?” He shouted and ordered soldiers to remove Sun Shao.

Executioners seized Sun Shao and pulled him out beyond the gate, where he raised a black flag. One of his subordinates rode to report to Sun Quan.

When Sun Quan heard it he mounted at once and came to rescue him.

The executioners were just about to carry out the sentence when Sun Quan arrived. He shouted and dispersed them, saving Sun Shao. Sun Shao wept and presented himself: “In earlier years in Guangling I came to know the terrain deeply. If I had not gone there and fought Cao Pi, and instead waited until he had gone across the Yangtze, our doom would be near immediate for Eastern Wu.”

Sun Quan went straight into the camp. Xu Sheng welcomed him into his tent and reported,

“Your Majesty assigned me as chief commander to take up arms and resist Wei. Now this General Gongli has disobeyed the military law and should have been executed. Why has Your Majesty pardoned him?”

Sun Quan said, “His youth and fierceness gave him bloodshot courage, and he violated military law. I will allow him leniency.”

Xu Sheng said, “The law was not made by me. It is not made by Your Majesty alone. It is the statute of the state. If we spare one due to kinship, how can we govern the rest?”

Sun Quan replied, “He indeed broke the law and should be punished by this commander. Yet he was born of the Yu clan, and my elder brother loved him and bestowed on him the surname Sun; he has done me some service. If I kill him, I betray my brother’s favor.”

Xu Sheng said, “Still, look upon Your Majesty’s face and see the weight of this capital crime.”

Sun Quan ordered Sun Shao to apologize.

Sun Shao refused to kneel and shouted, “From what I see, one should simply lead troops and crush Cao Pi! If I die, I will not submit to your understanding!”

Xu Sheng’s color changed.

Sun Quan sent Sun Shao away and said to Xu Sheng, “If we remove this man, how much does it cost Wu? There is no need to use him again. Never let him be used.” He then returned.

That same night men reported to Xu Sheng that Sun Shao had quietly taken three thousand elite troops from his own unit and crossed the river in secret.

Fearing it would reflect badly before the king, Xu Sheng secretly told Ding Feng of his design, and ordered three thousand troops to cross the river in support.

Wei’s king rode the dragon boats to Guangling. In advance, Cao Zhen already had troops lined at the bank of the Great River.

Cao Pi asked, “How many of them on the far bank?”

Cao Zhen said, “From afar I can see no one on the opposite bank and no banners or camps.”

Cao Pi said, “This must be a ruse. I will go and inspect directly.”

He opened the river passage wide and sent his dragon boats straight to the Great River bank.

On ship stood banners of dragon, phoenix, sun, and moon in five colors. Courtly regalia surrounded him and flashed with fierce brilliance. Cao Pi sat upright in the boat and looked toward the south bank, where he saw no figure. He turned back to Liu Ye and Jiang Ji:

“Can we cross now?”

Liu Ye said, “In war, one must both hide and reveal. How could a large army arrive and leave itself unprepared? Your Majesty should not rush. In three or five days we can see their movements; then dispatch the vanguard to cross and scout.”

Cao Pi said, “You speak as I intended.”

That day the sky grew dark at dusk, and they camped on the river.

That night the moon was absent. The soldiers lit torches all around, so bright that the heavens and earth seemed day.

Looking toward the south bank, not a single glimmer of fire could be seen. Cao Pi asked those around him, “Why is this?”

A courtier said, “It is no doubt because they know Your Majesty’s army has arrived and have fled at the first alarm.”

Cao Pi laughed inwardly.

At dawn thick fog covered all. The opposite bank was invisible. Then wind rose and the mist thinned as the clouds parted. The south bank came into view. It was now a line of fortifications for miles on end; from city gate towers to military towers, spears and swords flashed in the light, and banners and flags were hung across every span.

Repeatedly messengers came reporting: “Along Nanxu beside the Yangtze, all the way to Stone City, there stretches for hundreds of li a continuous chain of city walls and towers. In one night carts and people have filled them without gap.”

Cao Pi was startled. What had happened was this: Xu Sheng had bound reeds into the shape of men, all wearing blue robes, carrying flags, and placing them upon false towers and decoy battlements.

When Wei soldiers saw so many men and horses above the walls, they could not but fear. Cao Pi sighed, “Though Wei has ten thousand warriors, there is no way to apply them. The people of Jiangnan are not to be underestimated.”

Even as he marveled, a violent wind rose at once. White waves lashed high; river spray soaked the dragon robes. Great vessels threatened to capsize. Cao Zhen hurriedly ordered Wen Ping to take a light boat and rush to rescue the command.

Men on the dragon boat could not stand steady.

Wen Ping leapt onto the dragon boat, shouldered Cao Pi down to a small craft, and ran into the river harbor. At that moment a messenger galloped in: “Zhao Yun has moved his forces out of Yangping Pass and is taking Chang’an directly.”

Cao Pi was amazed and terrified and gave orders to withdraw.

Troops scattered each on their own.

Behind them came Wu forces.

Cao Pi issued orders to abandon all court goods and retreat. As the dragon boats neared Huai, reeds in the river had beforehand been soaked in fish oil and set alight.

With wind at their backs the flames ran fierce and fast, and the fire rose across the water, cutting off the dragon craft.

Cao Pi, alarmed, jumped into a small boat. As he neared the shore, the dragon ship had already caught fire.

He quickly mounted in haste. On the bank a mass of enemy came; at its head stood Ding Feng.

Zhang Liao pounded in hard on horseback to come to him, but Ding Feng shot an arrow into his waist. Xu Huang rescued him and together they carried the Wei king away.

The army was broken in untold numbers. Behind, Sun Shao and Ding Feng seized horses, military transports, ships, and equipment beyond count.

The Wei army was badly defeated and withdrew. Xu Sheng gained complete merit and all honor from Wu. Sun Quan bestowed high rewards.

When Zhang Liao returned to Xuchang, the arrow wound split open and he died. Cao Pi buried him with great ceremony; further details are omitted.

After Zhao Yun had led troops to break out and kill through Yangping Pass, there suddenly came a memorial to the Chancellor: a prominent Yizhou elder, Yong Kai, had joined hands with the barbarian king Meng Huo, raised one hundred thousand of the southern tribes, and raided four counties. Therefore the Chancellor ordered Zhao Yun to withdraw his forces and Ma Chao to hold Yangping Pass firmly. The Chancellor wished to campaign south in person.

Zhao Yun gathered the army at speed and returned.

At this time Zhuge Liang in Chengdu was drilling troops and prepared to march south himself.

It was then that:

If one sees Eastern Wu oppose Wei to the north, and Shu in the west fighting the southern barbarians, Who can tell who will win and who will lose?

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Peril of Zhang Wen and Qin Mi in Heavenly Disputation; Xu Sheng’s Fire Attack on Cao Pi

chapters.html:
The Chancellor leads a great army to punish the southern tribes. The barbarian king is first taken captive.

Meanwhile, in Chengdu, Chancellor Zhuge Liang personally handled both great and small matters. The people of the Two Rivers rejoiced in peace, left their houses unbarred at night, and found no one on the roads who would steal. Harvests had been plentiful for years in a row, so old and young alike could fill their bellies and sing; whenever corvée labor was ordered, everyone vied to complete it early. Thus every item needed for the army was in perfect order; the granaries were full of rice, and the treasury was overflowing.

In the third year of Jianxing, a dispatch arrived from Yizhou: Meng Huo, king of the southern tribes, had raised one hundred thousand tribal troops and crossed the border to raid and plunder. Yongkai, the Administrator of Jianing and a descendant of Yongchi, the former marquis of Shifang, had allied himself with Meng Huo and revolted. The Administrators of Zangke Commandery, Zhu Bao, and Yuesui Commandery, Gao Ding, had both surrendered their cities. Only Wang Kang, the Administrator of Yongchang, refused to turn. Now Yongkai, Zhu Bao, and Gao Ding had all made their men and horsemen local guides for Meng Huo and were attacking Yongchang Commandery. Wang Kang, with his clerk Lü Kai, gathered the common people and held this city with a death grip; the situation was dire. Zhuge Liang presented the matter at court and told the later ruler, saying, “I have observed that the southern tribes are not yet obedient, and this is truly one of the state’s great troubles. I will personally lead a major army and march out to suppress them.” The ruler said, “East there is Sun Quan, north Cao Pi. Now, dear Prime Minister, you are going away from me. If Wu and Wei should attack, what would become of me?” Zhuge Liang said, “Eastern Wu is presently at peace with our state, so I expect no hidden agenda. If they do turn, Li Yan is in Baidi City and this man can stand in for Lu Xun. Cao Pi has just been defeated and has already lost his sharpness; he cannot yet project himself far, and in any case Ma Chao holds the Hanzhong passes. Besides, I have left Guan Xing, Zhang Bao, and others in two split commands as a force for relief, so Your Majesty need have no fear of loss. I will first sweep the southern borderlands, and then move north to campaign for the Central Plains, repaying the Three Visits of the late emperor and the heavy trust of my entrustment.” The ruler said, “My sovereign is young and ignorant. You alone should judge and act.”

Before this was finished, a man from within the troops spoke out: “Impossible! Impossible!” When the men turned, he was seen to be Wang Lian from Nanyang, surname Wang, given name Lian, courtesy name Wenyu, now serving as Remonstrance Official. He protested: “The south is a harsh, uncultivated land, a place of miasma and disease. You, Chancellor, bear the heavy balance of state; a remote expedition is not fitting. As for Yongkai and the rest, they are but a festering mange. You only need to send one great general against them, and success is certain.” Zhuge Liang replied, “The southern lands are far from the state and the people there are not yet used to imperial governance, so pacifying them is hard. I will personally go forth to subdue them. Sometimes one must be firm, sometimes soft, as appropriate; they require separate judgment and are not to be entrusted lightly.” Wang Lian urged him repeatedly, but Zhuge Liang did not yield.

That day, after bowing out to the ruler, Zhuge Liang appointed Jiang Wan as staff officer, Fei Wei as Chief Clerk, and Dong Jue and Fan Jian as assistant clerks. Zhao Yun and Wei Yan were named senior generals and made overall commanders of mounts and cavalry; Wang Ping and Zhang Yi were deputy generals. He also made dozens of Sichuan generals join, raising half a million Sichuan troops and marching toward Yizhou. At that time Guan Suo, the third son of Guan Yu, entered the army and met Zhuge Liang, saying: “I fell ill after fleeing the loss of Jingzhou and had stayed convalescing at Baojia village. Each time I wished to go to Shu and report my revenge to the late emperor, my wounds were not yet healed. Now they are healed; I have learned that the enemies in Eastern Wu have all been executed. I came west to see the emperor, and just happened to meet the troops going south. I have come to submit myself on this campaign.” When Zhuge Liang heard this, he was astonished and moved. At once he sent word to court and immediately appointed Guan Suo as the vanguard of the front divisions. Together they all marched south. The large units moved by the lines. They ate little, drank little, stayed only by night and moved at dawn. In all the places they passed, there was not a hair’s breadth of disorder.

Hearing that Zhuge Liang himself was commanding a major army, Yongkai consulted with Gao Ding and Zhu Bao and split his troops into three columns. Gao Ding took the center route, Yongkai the left, and Zhu Bao the right; each column brought fifty to sixty thousand troops to meet the enemy. So Gao Ding ordered E Huan to be the vanguard. E Huan was nine chi tall, with an ugly face, carried one Fangtian halberd, and had courage that not even ten thousand men could match. He led the forward detachment out of the main stockade to meet the Shu army.

When Zhuge Liang’s main army had already reached the Yizhou boundary, Wei Yan, with Zhang Yi and Wang Ping as deputies, entered the frontier pass and exactly met E Huan’s horse and foot soldiers. The two armies arrayed against one another. Wei Yan spurred his horse and shouted, “Rebel bandits, submit at once!” E Huan spurred his horse to engage Wei Yan directly. After a few clashes, Wei Yan feigned defeat and rode back. E Huan pursued. After only a few li, the shout of his men rose in the distance. Zhang Yi and Wang Ping’s two columns closed in from their routes and cut off his rear. Wei Yan turned around. The three commanders then jointly resisted. They captured E Huan alive and brought him to the main stockade, then presented him to Zhuge Liang. Zhuge Liang ordered his restraints removed and gave him wine and food. He asked, “From which command are you?” E Huan said, “I am a unit commander under Gao Ding.” Zhuge Liang said, “I know that Gao Ding is a loyal and upright man, but now misled by Yongkai, this is how it came to pass. I will release you and send you back, and urge Governor Gao to return and surrender immediately, lest great disaster come.” E Huan bowed and withdrew.

Returning to Gao Ding, he described Zhuge Liang’s virtue. Gao Ding too was deeply moved. The next day Yongkai came to the stockade. After formal greetings, he asked, “How did you send E Huan back?” Gao Ding said, “Zhuge Liang released him out of righteousness.” Yongkai said, “This is Zhuge Liang’s counter-intel tactic. He wants to divide us, and so he plotted this scheme.” He half believed and half doubted it, but his mind remained uncertain. Then a report came: the Shu commander had engaged and personally led thirty thousand troops out. They fought only a few rounds before turning their horses and running. Wei Yan pressed hard, and a pursuit went more than twenty li. The next day Yongkai once again raised troops to meet them. For three days Zhuge Liang did not come out. By the fourth day, Yongkai and Gao Ding each split their forces and came to take the Shu camp.

At that time, Zhuge Liang had Wei Yan watch and hold in ambush along both routes. As expected, when the troops of Yongkai and Gao Ding came in two columns, hidden soldiers cut down most of them and captured countless men alive, all of whom were brought to the main camp. Yongkai’s men were confined in one side, Gao Ding’s in another. The Chancellor then ordered the army to whisper this message: those from Gao Ding are spared, while all of Yongkai’s men are to be slain. All the troops heard this. After a while, Zhuge Liang summoned the men of Yongkai and asked, “To which command do you all belong?” They falsely answered, “Under Governor Gao Ding.” Zhuge Liang pardoned them all, gave them wine and food, and sent them out to the frontier and back toward camp. Then he called over the men of Gao Ding and questioned them. They all said, “We are truly soldiers from Gao Ding’s command.” Zhuge Liang also pardoned them all, giving wine, food, garments. He then declared, “Today Yongkai has come to surrender and offers your chief and Zhu Bao as severed heads for achievement. I cannot bear this. Since you are all under Gao Ding, I release you to return. Do not betray again. If you are ever taken again, there will be no easy mercy.”

All thanked him and left. Back in their own camps they reported the matter to Gao Ding. He secretly sent someone into Yongkai’s camp to gather intelligence. Then one of those returned men who had been spared spoke of Zhuge Liang’s benevolence. Therefore many in Yongkai’s ranks began to incline toward Gao Ding’s side. Even so, Gao Ding remained uneasy and sent another man into Zhuge Liang’s camp to probe for the truth. He was seized on the road and brought to Zhuge Liang. Zhuge Liang pretended he was a man of Yongkai and called him into the tent: “Your commander had already promised to surrender the heads of Gao Ding and Zhu Bao. Why did you miss the date? A scout should not be so careless. How could you have done reconnaissance with such poor attention?” The soldier mumbled assent. Zhuge Liang gave him food and drink, then wrote a sealed secret note and handed it to the soldier, saying, “You must carry this to Yongkai. Tell him to act quickly and not err.”

The spy thanked him and departed. Returning to Gao Ding, he presented Zhuge Liang’s letter and relayed what Yongkai had done. After reading it, Gao Ding raged: “I treated him in sincerity, yet he seeks to harm me. This cannot be tolerated!” He summoned E Huan to confer. E Huan said, “Zhuge Liang is humane. To turn against him brings only inauspiciousness. This treachery and evil are all Yongkai’s doing. Better to kill Yongkai and submit to Zhuge Liang.” Gao Ding asked, “How do we proceed?” E Huan said, “Set a banquet and send for Yongkai. If he has no deceit, he will come openly. If he fails to come, then he hides a different mind. You can then attack his front, while I lie hidden on a small rear path behind the camp. He can be captured.” Gao Ding followed this advice, prepared a banquet, and invited Yongkai. Sure enough, fearing the words from the spared men that had returned, Yongkai was startled and did not come. That night Gao Ding led his troops and struck Yongkai’s camp. All the men who had once been spared by Zhuge Liang and thought highly of him now aided the fight at the right moment. Yongkai’s army fell into disorder without a fight. Yongkai mounted and moved along the mountain path to escape. After only two li, as drums sounded, one body of troops surged forth. It was E Huan. He held high a Fangtian halberd and charged straight forward at full speed. Caught off guard, Yongkai was thrust down and at once his head was taken from his horse. His remaining soldiers all surrendered to Gao Ding.

Gao Ding led both columns in surrender to Zhuge Liang and presented Yongkai’s head at his tent. Zhuge Liang sat high in the command pavilion, and ordered his attendants to bring Gao Ding forward, then announced that Yongkai’s head had been delivered. Gao Ding said, “I am deeply moved by Your Excellency’s immense grace; I have now come with Yongkai’s head in surrender. Why do you have him executed?” Zhuge Liang laughed. “You came as if to surrender, but hoping to deceive me. How dare you try to hide it from me?” Gao Ding asked, “How did you know I was deceitful?” From his casket, Zhuge Liang drew out a sealed paper and said to Gao Ding, “Zhu Bao has already sent a secret surrender letter, saying you share a life-and-death bond with Yongkai. Would you really kill such a man at once? This is how I knew you were deceitful.” Gao Ding cried out in protest, “Zhu Bao’s word was only a trick to cause division. Prime Minister, this cannot be trusted!” Zhuge Liang said, “I cannot judge by one person’s report alone. If you truly are sincere, capture Zhu Bao and bring him to me.” Gao Ding said, “Do not doubt me. Let me go capture Zhu Bao and bring him here immediately.” Zhuge Liang said, “If you can do that, my suspicion will settle.”

Gao Ding at once led his unit commander E Huan and his own troops to Zhu Bao’s camp. When they were about ten li from camp, a body of troops came in from behind the mountain; they were Zhu Bao. When Zhu Bao saw Gao Ding’s men coming, he answered in alarm. Gao Ding shouted in fury, “How did you write to Prime Minister Zhuge Liang such a counter-intel stratagem to harm me?” Zhu Bao stared, wide-eyed, and could not answer. Suddenly E Huan wheeled around behind his horse and thrust a halberd into Zhu Bao at the horse’s feet. Gao Ding said sharply, “If you do not submit, all will be put to the sword!” Then all the troops immediately bowed and submitted.

Gao Ding brought both columns before Zhuge Liang and again offered Zhu Bao’s head. Zhuge Liang laughed and said, “I asked you on purpose to kill these two bandit leaders to show your loyalty.” He then appointed Gao Ding Administrator of Yizhou and placed him in charge of three commanderies, and made E Huan an assault officer. The armies of all three routes were thereby pacified.

Then the Administrator of Yongchang, Wang Kang, came out of the city to receive Zhuge Liang. After Zhuge Liang entered and the ceremony was complete, he asked, “Who has defended this city for you and kept it from danger?” Kang said, “Today this county is safe only because of Lü Kai of Yongchang, surname Lü, name Kai, courtesy name Jiping. It is all the strength of this man.” Zhuge Liang immediately asked Lü Kai to come. Lü Kai entered and was received with full formality. Zhuge Liang said, “I have long heard you as a distinguished man of Yongchang. Your defense of this city has brought great benefit. Now that I am to pacify the southern tribes, what key insight do you offer?” Lü Kai brought out a map and presented it to Zhuge Liang, “Since I have served in government for long, I have known that the southerners have long wished to rebel. I therefore sent people secretly into their lands to survey where they could entrench and fight, and drew this map. It is called the Chart for Subduing the Tribes. I dare present it to Your Excellency. If You examine it, it can help the expedition.” Zhuge Liang rejoiced greatly and made Lü Kai a marching tutor and also a local guide officer. Then he raised the army and moved deep into the southern tribal lands.

Just while he was marching, a report came: an imperial envoy from the Son of Heaven had arrived. Zhuge Liang requested him into the inner camp. A man in plain robes and white garments entered; it was Ma Su, now in mourning for his elder brother Ma Liang. He said, “By command of the ruler, I bring wine and silk to distribute among the troops.” When Zhuge Liang had finished transmitting the decree, he distributed everything according to order and kept Ma Su in his tent for conversation. Zhuge Liang asked, “I serve by Your Majesty’s decree to pacify the southern tribes. I have long heard that you, Master Young Constant, are keen-sighted; I hope you will grant instruction.” Ma Su answered, “I have a few words. Please consider them carefully. The southern tribes rely on remote mountains and rugged passes; they have long been disobedient. Though you may defeat them today, tomorrow they may rise again. When your main army reaches them, they can be subdued; but when you return north, you must turn to campaign against Cao Pi. If the tribal soldiers know your core is weak, their revolt will be swift. The principles of war are thus: “To strike the heart is superior; to strike the city is lesser. To fight by winning minds is superior; to fight by weapons is lesser.” If you only win the heart, that is enough.” Zhuge Liang sighed, “Young Constant surely knows the inmost of my intentions.” He then made Ma Su a staff officer and gave him command to take the vanguard of the main army.

After this, Meng Huo heard that Zhuge Liang had skillfully destroyed Yongkai and the others, so he gathered the three cave chiefs and discussed together. The first cave was headed by Jinhua Sange, the second by Dongtuna, the third by Ahainan. These three came before Meng Huo. Meng Huo said, “Now that Prime Minister Zhuge Liang leads a major army into our borders, we must unite and oppose him. You three should split your troops into three routes as ordered. Whoever wins should become the lord of that cave.” So they assigned Jinhua Sange to the center route, Dongtuna to the left, Ahainan to the right, each with fifty thousand tribal troops, and each followed the order.

As Zhuge Liang was still in camp discussing matters, a scout horse arrived in haste to report that the three cave commanders had divided into three routes and were coming. When Zhuge Liang heard this, he called Zhao Yun and Wei Yan, then did not assign either. He next summoned Wang Ping and Ma Zhong and said: “The barbarians are coming by three routes. I want Zilong and Wenchang to go, but those two do not know the terrain, so I dare not use them. Wang Ping should go to the left route to receive the enemy. Ma Zhong should go to the right route. I will send Zilong and Wenchang to reinforce behind.” They listened and departed. He also summoned Zhang Ni and Zhang Yi and assigned: “Both of you together command one force and go to the center route to receive the enemy. Rally the troops today; at dawn tomorrow meet with Wang Ping and Ma Zhong and advance. I want Zilong and Wenchang to take the enemy then, but those two do not know terrain, so I dare not use them.” Zhang Ni and Zhang Yi listened and left.

When Zhao Yun and Wei Yan saw that Zhuge Liang was not using them, both looked displeased. Zhuge Liang said, “I am not withholding your talents; I fear that if two middle-aged men confront this terrain, the barbarians may judge and blunt your edge.” Zhao Yun said, “If we only need to know the terrain, why should we not?” Zhuge Liang said, “You two must be careful and not act rashly.” They left in silence and frustration. Zhao Yun asked Wei Yan into his own camp to discuss: “Zilong and Wenchang have been set aside in front though they should be leading. How can we endure this?” Wei Yan said, “Let us mount at once and go directly to reconnoiter. If we catch local men, make them lead us in. If we engage the barbarians with them, this is a matter that can be accomplished.” Zhao Yun agreed. He then mounted and rode straight to the central route. After only a few li, from the mountain slope they looked and saw dust rising far ahead. They saw dozens of mounted tribesmen and rushed out in two lines. The barbarians, seeing them, were startled and turned to flee. Zhao Yun and Wei Yan each captured several alive and brought them back. They offered them wine and food, and then inquired carefully. The barbarians reported: “Ahead is the main stockade of Jinhua Sange. At the side of that camp, two routes run east and west, both leading behind the camps of Dongtuna and Ahainan after Wuxi Cave.”

Hearing this, Zhao Yun and Wei Yan selected five thousand of their best soldiers and made the captured tribesmen lead the way. By the time the force was ready to depart, it was the second watch of the night. The moon was bright, so they moved by moonlight. When they just reached Jinhua Sange’s camp at around the fourth watch, the tribal soldiers were just beginning to cook and preparing for dawn combat. Suddenly Zhao Yun and Wei Yan’s two detachments struck in. The barbarians were thrown into confusion. Zhao Yun rode straight into the center and met Jinhua Sange in person. They crossed weapons for only one exchange; he speared him from horseback and brought him down, then took his head from the horse. The rest of the army scattered. Wei Yan then split his men in half and moved toward the east path to strike Dongtuna’s stockade. Zhao Yun split his own in half and moved westward to strike Ahanan’s stockade. By the time they arrived at the tribal camps, dawn had broken.

It first speaks of Wei Yan’s charge to Dongtuna’s camp. When Dongtuna learned that troops had broken in behind his camp, he led soldiers out to resist. Suddenly a shout rose at the camp gate; the tribesmen were in full disorder. Wang Ping’s horsemen had already arrived. From both sides they attacked and the barbarians were routed. Dongtuna seized an opening to escape on the mountain route. Wei Yan could not catch up.

It says Zhao Yun led soldiers into the rear of Ahanan’s camp. By then Ma Zhong had already arrived before the gate. Again the two-sided attack broke them, and the barbarians were routed. Ahanan escaped through the turmoil. Each returned to report to Zhuge Liang. He asked, “Of the three cave forces, two cave lords have fled; where is the head of Jinhua Sange?” Zhao Yun presented it as achievement. All reported, “Dongtuna and Ahanan abandoned their horses and fled over the ridges, so no one could catch them.” Zhuge Liang laughed: “I have already captured those two.” Zhao Yun, Wei Yan, and the other generals all could not believe it.

After a short while, Zhang Ni brought in Dongtuna and Zhang Yi brought in Ahainan. All were astonished. Zhuge Liang said, “Using Lü Kai’s map, I already knew each of their camps. For that reason I intentionally stoked Zilong’s and Wenchang’s zeal and sent them deep into enemy ground, first shattering Jinhua Sange, then splitting and striking the rear of the side camps, while Wang Ping and Ma Zhong would respond. This task could not be assigned to anyone but Zilong and Wenchang. I judged that Dongtuna and Ahanan would choose to run by the mountain paths, so I sent Zhang Ni and Zhang Yi with ambushes to seize them, and ordered Guan Suo to come with troops in support. By this means these two are now ours.” All the generals knelt and said, “The Chancellor’s calculations are beyond demons and ghosts.” Zhuge Liang ordered Dongtuna and Ahanan to be brought under the tent, all restraints removed, and gave them food, drink, and clothing. He told each to return to his cave and not assist evil. Both wept and bowed, then slipped away by narrow paths.

Zhuge Liang said to his commanders, “On another day Meng Huo will certainly lead men personally and fight hand to hand. Then he can be captured here.” He called Zhao Yun and Wei Yan and shared his stratagem, then sent each away with five thousand soldiers. He also called Wang Ping and Guan Suo, commanding another force, and gave them instructions. When all distribution was complete, he sat in the command tent waiting.

At this time Meng Huo was seated in his own tent when a scout horse reported that all three cave commanders had been taken by Zhuge Liang and that their subordinates were in disorder. Meng Huo was deeply angry and raised his troops to advance. He ran into the army of Wang Ping. The two armies faced each other. When Wang Ping rode out and brandished his sword, only to gaze over the line, hundreds of southern mounted chiefs in two clusters stood open beside the banners. In the middle Meng Huo himself rode out. On his head he wore an inlaid purple-gold crown, over his body a red brocade robe tied with cords, at his waist a jade-lion girdle, on his feet green boots with eagle-snouted tips. He rode a curled-mane red horse, with two engraved green-knobbed swords hanging, and watched proudly. He looked back at his tribal commanders on either side and said, “People often say that Zhuge Liang is adept at war. Now look at this field: banners are mixed in disorder and the ranks are tangled; with these swords and spears and weapons, there is no one who can defeat me. I now know those words were mistaken. How much earlier I should have turned against him before. Who now dares to capture the Shu commander and restore the army’s spirit?”

Before he finished speaking, one officer answered immediately: it was Mang Yachang. He wielded a severed-headed great blade, rode a yellow-brown horse, and came for Wang Ping. The two generals exchanged battle for only a few exchanges, and Wang Ping withdrew. Meng Huo drove his troops forward and pursued in long sweep. Guan Suo skirmished and withdrew too, about twenty li or more. As Meng Huo was in hot pursuit, a roar rose at once. On the left came Zhang Ni; on the right came Zhang Yi. Troops surged from both paths and cut off his return. Wang Ping and Guan Suo turned and rejoined the fight. Encircled in front and rear, the barbarians were crushed. Meng Huo fought to the death with his lieutenants and escaped. He aimed for the Jinsashan mountains to flee. Three columns of troops came after in pursuit. As Meng Huo ran, ahead, voices rose and a troop mass blocked the way. Leading it was none other than Zhao Yun, Zhao Yun of Changshan. Meng Huo was struck with shock and fled along a small path in Jinsashan. Zilong broke through one hard clash, and the barbarian soldiers were routed, with captives taken in number. Meng Huo fled with only a few dozen riders into a mountain gorge. By the time pursuit came near from behind and the road ahead narrowed so his horse could not move, he abandoned his horse and ran up and over the ridges. Then he heard a drum in the gorge. It was Wei Yan, who had followed Zhuge Liang’s design and held five hundred foot soldiers in ambush there. Unable to withstand the assault, Meng Huo was captured alive. Those who had ridden with him all surrendered.

Wei Yan brought Meng Huo to Zhuge Liang’s main camp. Zhuge Liang had already slaughtered cattle and goats and arranged a banquet. In the tent he set seven ranks of executioners with blades, spears, halberds, and axes flashing like frost. He also ordered the ceremonial green-gold ax and curved-hand umbrella displayed, with palace guards in feathered breastplates and drums and pipes at fore and aft, and palace guards lined on the sides, all in strict array. Zhuge Liang sat upright. As the tribals kept arriving in numbers, he looked on. He called them into the tent and removed all their bindings. He spoke gently: “You are all good civilians. Unhappily, you were held by Meng Huo. Now you are frightened and in terror. I know your fathers, mothers, brothers, and wives and daughters are waiting by the gate. If you hear you have fallen in battle, their bellies will be cut and their ribs pulled. Blood will flow from your eyes. I release all of you to return home now, to comfort each of your fathers, brothers, wives, and children.” When he finished, he gave each food and grain and sent them off. The barbarians, deeply moved, knelt and wept as they left.

Zhuge Liang then ordered soldiers to bring in Meng Huo. Not long later, amid forward pressure and backward crowding, he arrived bound to the front of the tent. Meng Huo knelt below the command seat. Zhuge Liang said, “The late emperor did not treat you poorly. How dare you rebel?” Meng Huo answered, “The lands of the two rivers are all territory already occupied by others; Your Lord took them by force and now claims to be emperor. My family has long lived here; your men are uncivil and have invaded our land. Why do you call us rebels?” Zhuge Liang said, “I have captured you now. Do you yield your heart?” Meng Huo replied, “This was a remote, narrow land and rough road. I happened to fall into your hands. How could I submit?” Zhuge Liang said, “If you do not yield, I will send you back. How is that?” Meng Huo said, “If you send me back and I can arrange the troops again, then we will settle who is truly superior in battle. If you can capture me again then, I will yield.” Zhuge Liang removed his bonds. He gave him clothes and wine and food, provided horse and saddle, and sent him away by road directly back toward his own camp.

The episode ends:

The raider, captured in the Chancellor’s hand, was nevertheless released. The people dwelling beyond the wilds are not yet willing to submit.

Who can tell how they will fare when they meet again in battle?

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Chancellor Raises a Great Army to Pacify the Southern Rebels, and the Barbarian King Is Captured First

chapters.html:
Yet Zhuge Liang had released Meng Huo, and the officers came into his tent to ask, “Meng Huo is the chief of the southern tribes. Since he is now in our hands, the south is as good as pacified. Why did the Chancellor release him?” Zhuge Liang smiled and said, “I captured this man as easily as taking something from my sleeve. Once his mind submits, there will be peace naturally.” The officers heard this and still did not believe it.

That day Meng Huo reached the Lu River and at once ran into scattered remnants of the tribal soldiers, who came to scout. When they saw him, they were surprised and happy, and bowed and asked, “How did Your Highness get back?” Meng Huo replied, “Shu soldiers kept watch over me in camp, and I killed more than ten of them, then escaped in the dark of night. While traveling I met a scout cavalry unit, also killed it, and took this horse. That is how I got away.”

All of them rejoiced greatly. They carried Meng Huo across the Lu River and camped behind stockades, then assembled the chiefs of all their caves, calling in turn the tribal warriors he had released before. They gathered over one hundred thousand riders. At this time Dongtuna and A Huanan were already in their caves. Meng Huo sent for them; the two, frightened, had no choice but to bring their cave warriors as well.

Meng Huo issued orders: “I now understand Zhuge Liang’s plan. We must not fight. If we do, we will fall into his trick. The troops from the Central Plain have marched far and are worn out, and the heat is oppressive in these days. Could their men hold out for long? Here by the Lu River’s danger we will seize every raft and canoe and keep them on the south bank, then raise earth fortresses and deep moats, raised walls and high ramparts. Let us see how Zhuge Liang puts his plan into action!”

All the chiefs followed his order, hauling all boats and rafts to the south bank and raising earth fortifications. They chose ground by cliff and hillside and drove up high signal towers; atop those towers they placed crossbows, catapults, and stone-throwing devices, preparing to hold out for a long time. Grain and fodder were all supplied from each cave. Meng Huo thought this a perfect plan and felt entirely at ease.

Now Zhuge Liang advanced his troops swiftly. The forward detachment had already reached the Lu River when a scout horseman flew back: “There are no boats or rafts in the river. The current runs fast, and along the opposite bank they have built earth forts in a line, each with tribal guards.” It was in the fifth month, the heat pressing down, and in the southern lands the air was especially fierce and oppressive. The men’s armor, the horses’ gear, all of it was unbearable.

Zhuge Liang inspected the riverfront himself and returned to his own camp, where he gathered the generals in the tent and announced, “Meng Huo has stationed his men on the south bank, with deep moats and high walls to resist us. Now that we have marched here, how can I return empty-handed? Each of you lead your troops to the shade of hills and trees, choose the thickest stretches of forest, and keep your men and horses there to rest.”

He ordered Lu Kai, one hundred li from the Lu River, to pick cool spots and set up four camps. Wang Ping, Zhang Ni, Zhang Yi, and Guan Suo each guarded one camp. Inside and outside they raised grass shelters to cover the horses so both men and mounts could cool themselves and avoid the heat.

From among the staff, Jiang Wan looked and entered to ask Zhuge Liang, “I see these camps Lu Kai built are poor. They are exactly like the ground where the former emperor was defeated by Eastern Wu. If the tribal soldiers cross the Lu River at night and raid the camps, what then if they use fire? How could we rescue ourselves?” Zhuge Liang smiled and said, “Do not be so doubtful. I have a subtle calculation.” Jiang Wan and the others still did not understand.

Soon news came that Ma Dai had arrived from Shu with cooling draughts and grain. Zhuge Liang ordered him in. After saluting, Ma Dai distributed rice and medicine to the four camps. Zhuge Liang asked, “How many soldiers did you bring?”

Ma Dai answered, “Three thousand.”

Zhuge Liang said, “My army is spent and exhausted from repeated battles. I want to use your force, but I do not know whether you will go forward.”

Ma Dai said, “They are all imperial troops. What distinction is there between then and now? If the Chancellor wishes to use them, I will not refuse even if I must die.”

Zhuge Liang said, “Now Meng Huo blocks the Lu River and has no way to cross. I want to cut his supply route first and let his own force disorder itself.”

Ma Dai asked, “How can we cut it?”

Zhuge Liang said, “One hundred and fifty li from here, at the lower flow is Shakou. The water is slower there and can be crossed by rafts. Take your whole base force of three thousand and cross there, straight into the tribal caves, and first cut off their grain. Then join Dongtuna and A Huanan, the two cave lords, who will be our inner allies. Do not make a mistake.”

Ma Dai left joyfully and pushed ahead with his men to Shakou, driving them into the river and fording. The water was shallow, and most did not use rafts. Many crossed in their undershirts, and in passing many stumbled and drowned; blood came from mouth and nose as they were hauled back to shore.

Ma Dai was startled and returned overnight to report to Zhuge Liang. The Chancellor immediately called for local guides. One said, “These are the hot-season fumes of the Lu River. In daylight they are fierce. A man crossing is sure to inhale them and die. Even drinking this water can be fatal. If we must cross, wait for the stillness of night when the water cools and the fumes subside. If we cross after a full meal, no harm will come.”

So Zhuge Liang told the guides to lead the way and selected five to six hundred of the strongest soldiers to go with Ma Dai to Shakou. They built wooden rafts and crossed the river at midnight; indeed, there was no harm. Ma Dai led two thousand picked soldiers, followed by guides, taking the shortest route toward the supply choke point at the mountain cleft called Jia Shan Pass. Jia Shan Pass had steep walls on either side and only one track between them, wide enough for one horse at a time.

Ma Dai occupied Jia Shan Pass, arranged his troops, and raised an outpost fortification. The cave tribes did not know this. As they were bringing in grain supplies, Ma Dai intercepted them from front and rear, seized more than a hundred carts, and the tribesmen reported this to Meng Huo’s main camp.

At that time Meng Huo sat in camp and drank all day and took pleasure in himself, ignoring military affairs. He said to the chiefs, “If I face Zhuge Liang in battle, I will surely fall into his trickery. Now I rely on this danger from the Lu River, on the deep moats and high walls, and wait. Shu’s men cannot endure this cruel heat; they will surely retreat. Then we will strike from behind and capture Zhuge Liang.” He finished speaking and laughed harshly.

At once, a chief in his unit said, “Shakou is shallow; if Shu troops slip over there secretly, it will be very harmful. We should divide our army to guard it.”

Meng Huo laughed. “You are a local of this place; how could you not know? I am waiting for Shu to cross this water. If they cross, they will surely die in it.”

The chief said again, “If a local told us how to cross at night, what then?”

Meng Huo said, “No need for such suspicion. Who in my lands would help the enemy?” While he was still speaking, suddenly there was report: an unknown number of Shu troops had secretly crossed the Lu River and cut off the Jia Shan supply route. Their banner read “General Who Pacifies the North, Ma Dai.”

Meng Huo laughed, “How could this minor fellow be a matter of concern?” He ordered his deputy Mang Yachang to quickly lead three thousand men into Jia Shan Valley.

Now Ma Dai saw the tribal troops had arrived and put two thousand in front of the mountain. The two formations faced each other; Mang Yachang rode out to meet him. Their lines clashed once, and Ma Dai cut him down from horseback with one slash.

The tribesmen broke and ran back to report to Meng Huo. He called for all the commanders and asked, “Who dares go against Ma Dai?” Before anyone finished, Dongtuna stepped out and said, “I volunteer.”

Meng Huo rejoiced and set out with three thousand men. He feared someone else might cross the Lu River again, so he also sent A Huanan with three thousand to hold Shakou.

Now Dongtuna led his men to the lower camp of Jia Shan Pass. Ma Dai rode out to meet them. Men in the band recognized him and described his words and deeds to Ma Dai. Ma Dai drove his horse forward and shouted, “You traitor with no sense, no loyalty! The Chancellor spared your life, and you now betray him. How can you not be ashamed?”

Dongtuna’s face was covered with shame, and he had no answer. He withdrew without fighting. After only one skirmish, Ma Dai rode back.

When Dongtuna returned, he told Meng Huo, “Ma Dai is truly heroic; we cannot stand against him.”

Meng Huo grew furious: “I know you have benefited from Zhuge Liang’s mercy. That is why you did not fight and withdrew. It is a plan to sell the battle line!” He shouted and ordered him executed. The chiefs begged and begged again, and only then was his life spared, though he was beaten a hundred with clubs and sent back to his own camp.

Many chiefs came and told Dongtuna, “Though we live among the barbarian lands, we have never dared to offend China. China has never invaded us before either. Now, because of Meng Huo’s pressure, we were forced to rebel. How can we understand the mind of Zhuge Liang? Even Cao Cao and Sun Quan still fear him; what of us tribal folk? Besides, we all owe him our lives. We have nothing with which to repay it. If we surrender our lives and kill Meng Huo, then throw ourselves to Zhuge Liang, we can spare our villages and households from suffering.”

Dongtuna said, “I do not know what is in your hearts?” Among them were men who Zhuge Liang had once released, and together they answered with one voice, “We are willing.”

Then Dongtuna took up his steel sword, brought a hundred men, and rode straight for the great camp.

At that moment Meng Huo was heavily drunk in his own tent. Dongtuna came with his men, knives in hand. Two generals stood beneath the tent. Dongtuna pointed to them with his blade and said, “You too owe your lives to the Chancellor, and now should return him your service.”

The two replied, “It need not be done by you. I will capture Meng Huo alive and present him to the Chancellor.”

So they all entered the tent and seized Meng Huo. He was bound securely and taken to the Lu River bank. They boarded a boat and crossed to the north bank, sending word to Zhuge Liang first.

Zhuge Liang already had intelligence from spies and so had sent secret orders: he instructed all camp officers and soldiers to tidy their arms and armor, then bring the chief who captured Meng Huo forward while everyone else returned to their own camps to wait. Dongtuna entered the central command first and explained everything.

Zhuge Liang greatly praised him and rewarded him with kind words, then sent Dongtuna back with the chiefs while giving orders for axe-bearers to bring Meng Huo forward. Zhuge Liang smiled and asked, “Earlier you said: capture him once more and he will submit. What of him now?”

Meng Huo answered, “This is not your doing. It is because men under me slaughtered each other. How could I therefore submit?”

Zhuge Liang said, “Now I will release you again. What then?”

Meng Huo replied, “Though I am a tribesman, I know enough of warfare. If the Chancellor truly means to let me return to my cave, I will raise men and fight this matter out again. If he captures me this time, then I will submit with heart and entrails, and not dare to turn again.”

Zhuge Liang said, “This time if he is captured alive and still refuses to submit, there will be no leniency.” He told the men to remove his ropes and again gave him food and wine, seating him beside him in the tent.

Zhuge Liang said, “Since I left my thatched hut, I have won every battle and taken every stronghold. Why do your tribesmen not submit?”

Meng Huo was silent.

After drinking, Zhuge Liang called him to ride out with him. They looked over the outlying camps, stockades, stored grain and weapons. Zhuge Liang said, “You do not submit, and that is sheer folly. I have soldiers and warriors so fine, and so much grain and equipment. How can you ever beat me? If you submit now, I will report this to the Son of Heaven and have your position kept. Your sons and grandsons will forever keep peace in your lands.”

Meng Huo said, “Though I might submit, how do I make those in my caves accept it? If the Chancellor lets me return, I can call my own men home and then we can be all of one heart and breast.”

Zhuge Liang was pleased and again rode back to Meng Huo’s main camp. They drank until evening, and Meng Huo then took leave. Zhuge Liang personally escorted him to the Lu River bank and sent him back by boat to his camp.

Meng Huo returned and first stationed axe-men beneath his tent. He sent his inner retainers to Dongtuna’s and A Huanan’s camps and claimed that Zhuge Liang had a mission there. He lured both of them under the great camp’s tent and then killed them all, dumping the bodies in a ravine.
