Meng Huo immediately sent trusted men to guard the pass and then led his troops out of Jia Shan Pass to meet Ma Dai, but he found no one there. When he asked locals about the troops, they all said that the grain had been moved in the night, forded back across the Lu River, and returned to the great camp.

Meng Huo came back into his cave and discussed with his younger brother, Meng You: “Now I know Zhuge Liang’s strengths and deceit. You can do this and that.”

Meng You took his brother’s plan, led a hundred tribal soldiers, and loaded gold, jewels, treasures, ivory, and rhinoceros horn before crossing the Lu River and going straight to Zhuge Liang’s main camp.

As they just set foot across the river, drums and horns sounded all at once and a line of troops formed, with Ma Dai at their head. Meng You was shocked.

Ma Dai asked after them and ordered a report to be sent to Zhuge Liang. Zhuge Liang was in his tent with Ma Su, Lu Kai, Jiang Wan, and Fei Wei, discussing how best to pacify the tribes, when a man entered and reported that Meng Huo had sent his brother Meng You with gifts.

Looking back, Zhuge Liang asked Ma Su, “Do you know their purpose?”

Ma Su said, “I dare not state it plainly. Let me write in secret and present it to the Chancellor to see if it accords with his intent.”

Zhuge Liang agreed. After writing, Ma Su presented the note. Zhuge Liang read it, clapped his hands, and laughed aloud. “My plan to capture Meng Huo has already been set in motion. What you have now seen matches exactly what I intended.” He then called in Zhao Yun and whispered instructions at his ear, then called Wei Yan and whispered as well, then called Wang Ping and Ma Zhong and Guan Suo and gave each precise directions in secret.

Each received the plan and moved as instructed. Then they called Meng You into the tent.

Meng You knelt again before the tent and said, “My brother Meng Huo owes the Chancellor his life-grant and has nothing else to offer, so I have brought some gold, jewels, and treasures as provisions for rewarding the troops. Later, if this is accepted, I will bring more tribute appropriate for the Son of Heaven.”

Zhuge Liang said, “Where is your brother now?”

Meng You said, “To return the favor of the Chancellor’s mercy, he has gone straight to Yinkeng Mountain to gather more treasure. He will return soon.”

Zhuge Liang asked, “How many did you bring?”

Meng You replied, “I did not dare bring too many. Only a hundred and some men, all of them carriers of goods.”

Zhuge Liang ordered all of them into the tent. They were men with sharp eyes and dark faces, gray hair, purple-bearded, gold rings on their ears, wild hair, and bare feet, with tall, powerful bodies.

Zhuge Liang then had them sit with the guests, told the officers to urge wine, and received them with respectful courtesy.

Again, back in his own camp, Meng Huo watched only for a return message. Then word came that two men had returned. He summoned them and made them report: “Zhuge Liang was pleased with the gifts and brought all of the companions into his tent. He had oxen slaughtered, sheep killed, and set a banquet. The two great lords secretly told us: this second watch tonight, with inside and outside action, we will make the great event happen.”

Meng Huo heard this and rejoiced greatly, then ordered thirty thousand tribal soldiers divided into three teams. He told each cave chief, “All soldiers bring firebrands. Tonight when you reach the Shu camp, use fire as the signal. I will seize the central camp myself and take Zhuge Liang captive.”

Many tribal commanders carried out the plan. At dusk they crossed the Lu River in groups from the left side and came on. Meng Huo led one hundred of his most trusted men straight for Zhuge Liang’s main camp. On the way, no troop blocked them. When they reached the gate, Meng Huo and his men spurred straight into the camp.

But it was empty. Not a man could be seen. Meng Huo dashed into the central tent, where lamps still burned brightly. Meng You and the men of the tribes were all drunk and collapsed. In truth, Zhuge Liang had told Ma Su and Lu Kai to manage them, and actors had been set up to perform lively skits, with repeated invitations to drink; drugs had been mixed in the wine, and all had fallen into stupefaction, motionless like those dead drunk.

Meng Huo asked only among those who were still awake, and those only pointed with their mouths.

Recognizing he had fallen for the trap, he quickly rescued Meng You and all his men, and was on his way back to his detachment when a roar of voices broke out ahead and flames rose at once. A column of troops arrived: Shu general Wang Ping. Meng Huo was startled. As he ran for the left formation, flames shot up and another column came, led by Wei Yan. Then another wave of fire came as a third column arrived, led by Zhao Yun.

The three columns closed in together. With no way out on four sides, Meng Huo abandoned his soldiers and fled on horseback toward the Lu River. There he saw a few tribal men with a small boat waiting on the water. He ordered them near the bank. Just as men and horse were getting in, one war cry rose and he was seized. It was, indeed, Ma Dai, who had taken soldiers in our plan and, pretending to be tribesmen, rowed this boat and drawn in Meng Huo.

Then Zhuge Liang accepted the barbarians under surrender. Countless surrendered. Zhuge Liang comforted each one and harmed none.

He ordered all remaining fires put out.

Soon Ma Dai brought in Meng Huo. Zhao Yun brought Meng You. Wei Yan, Ma Zhong, Wang Ping, and Guan Suo brought in the cave lords.

Zhuge Liang pointed at Meng Huo and laughed. “You sent your brother first to feign surrender with ritual gifts; how could I be fooled by it?”

Meng Huo said, “It was my brother’s hunger and greed that misled him into poisoning. He spoiled this great undertaking. If I had come myself and he answered with force, it would surely have succeeded. This is bad fortune, not my inability. How can I still submit?”

Zhuge Liang said, “This is the third time. How can you still refuse?”

Meng Huo lowered his head in silence.

Zhuge Liang laughed again. “I will let you go once more.”

Meng Huo said, “If the Chancellor will release my brothers back, let me gather my household and close kin and then fight once with full force against him. If he captures me then, I will submit with full heart and entrails, without turning.”

Zhuge Liang replied, “If you are taken again, there will be no light mercy. You should attend carefully to the Art of War, and gather your trusted men and form good plans quickly, so you do not regret it later.”

So he ordered the guards to remove Meng Huo’s ropes, and also released Meng You and all cave chiefs together. They all bowed and thanked him before leaving.

By then the Shu troops had already crossed the Lu River. Once Meng Huo and the others had crossed, they saw ranks of troops and banners at the bank, dense with flags. When Meng Huo reached the front of the camp, Ma Dai sat high in his saddle and pointed with his sword, saying, “Now that you have been caught, there will be no easy release!”

When Meng Huo reached his own camp, Zhao Yun had already raided it and deployed the troops in order. He sat beneath the main banner and held his sword as he spoke: “The Chancellor treated you with such grace. Do not forget this great kindness!”

Meng Huo nodded repeatedly and withdrew. As he came out the boundary slope, Wei Yan led one thousand picked soldiers and formed a line on the hillside. He sat his horse and shouted in a loud voice, “We have already broken into your den and taken your strategic heights. You still cling to blindness and resist the grand army! This time you are taken and will be reduced to ten thousand pieces. I will not treat you lightly.”

Meng Huo and his men ducked their heads and ran for home.

Later people praised in verse:

In the fifth month I rode southward into unbroken lands, The moonlit Lu River swelled with ranking miasma. I vow to repay three summons with boldness and strength, Why should I fear seven hard expeditions against the southern tribes?

Yet when Zhuge Liang had crossed the Lu River, finished his encampment, and given his whole army a grand reward, he gathered the officers in his tent and said, “As he was taken the second time, I had wanted him to inspect each camp and test their weaknesses. I intended for him to come and raid the camp. I know Meng Huo understands military tactics fairly well. I showed off my troops, grain, and arms so that he would see where my lines were weak and try fire attack. By sending his brother in false surrender, he meant only internal coordination. I have captured him three times and not killed him because I truly wished for his heart to yield, not for his tribe to be destroyed.”

“I now tell you plainly. You need not hold back in your labor. Turn your hearts to serving the state.”

The officers knelt and said, “Chancellor, your wisdom, humanity, and courage are all complete. Not even Zi Ya and Zhang Liang can match you.”

Zhuge Liang said, “How could I dare to compare with the ancients? This success comes from your strength and our shared work.” The officers under his command listened and rejoiced.

Yet Meng Huo, stirred by the sting of three captures, returned in fury to the Silver Pit Cave and immediately sent trusted men with gold, jewels, and treasures to Bafan, Jiushansan Dian, and other tribal settlements and clans.

There, rugged tribal fighters armed with shields and blades—tens of thousands strong—massed from all sides, their columns pressing in like clouds and mist. The mountain-pass scouts learned of this and came to report. Zhuge Liang smiled and said, “I had wished to see all the tribesmen arrive so they might witness my strength.” He then mounted a small cart and rode out.

Thus it was:

If the cave lords were not fierce and commanding, how could the strategist’s methods be seen as supreme?

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Crossing the Lu River Again to Bind the Southern King, Detecting Feigned Surrender, and Capturing Meng Huo Three Times

chapters.html:
Wuxiang Marquis uses four stratagems.
The King of the Southern Barbarians is captured five times.

Kongming drove himself in a small cart and came with several hundred riders to scout the road. Ahead there was a river called Xi’er River. Its current was slow, and there was not a single boat or raft. Kongming ordered timber to be felled for rafts to cross, but every piece of wood sank the moment it touched the water. Kongming asked Lu Kai, and Lu Kai said, “I have heard that upstream on Xi’er River there is a mountain full of bamboo. The bamboo grows in great clumps. Send men to cut some, and they can build a bamboo bridge across the river so cavalry and troops may cross.” Kongming immediately dispatched thirty thousand men into the mountain. They felled tens of thousands of poles, floated them downstream, and at a narrow stretch of river built a bamboo bridge more than ten zhang wide. Then he camped his army on the north bank in one long line. The river itself became a moat, the floating bridge the gate, and earthen banks the walls; after crossing south the army laid out three great camps in a line and waited for the barbarian soldiers.

Later, Meng Huo came with tens of thousands of barbarian troops, angry and roaring. As he approached Xi’er River, Meng Huo led one force of ten thousand cave-clan fighters in front, directly bashing against the foremost camp. Kongming, with a linen kerchief on his head, a crane-feathered robe on his shoulders, and a feather fan in hand, rode out in a four-horse carriage, encircled by leading generals. Kongming saw Meng Huo in rhinoceros-hide armor, a vermilion helmet, a dao-pai in his left hand and a knife in his right, riding a red-maned bull and cursing aloud. With him were more than ten thousand cave troops all brandishing knives and shields, rushing forward and clashing in close mêlée. Kongming immediately ordered the troops back into their own camp, sealed all four sides shut, and forbade fighting out. The barbarians, bare-bodied and nearly bare, came to the gate and shouted insults.

The generals were furious and came to report, “We are willing to ride out and fight a death struggle!” Kongming refused. Again and again they sought to fight; Kongming said, “The southern barbarians do not follow court order. Their cruelty is at its peak now. We cannot meet them in open battle. We should hold fast for several days, wait until their arrogance is exhausted. I have a fine plan to break them.”

So the Shu army held firm for several days. On high ground, Kongming watched and saw the barbarians already growing careless. He gathered the generals and asked, “Do you dare to go out and fight?” They all gladly consented. Kongming first summoned Zhao Yun and Wei Yan into his tent, whispered the plan to them, and sent them forward first. He then summoned Wang Ping and Ma Zhong into his tent for the plan. He also summoned Ma Dai and instructed him, “I will abandon these three camps and withdraw across the north bank. As soon as my army retreats, you should tear apart the floating bridge, move it downstream, and then bring Zhao Yun’s and Wei Yan’s cavalry across the river to reinforce.” Ma Dai accepted the plan and left.

Kongming then summoned Zhang Yi: “When our whole army withdraws, leave many campfires burning in camp. Meng Huo will notice and surely pursue. You, then, cut off his rear.” Zhang Yi accepted and withdrew. Kongming only ordered Guan Suo to guard the carriage. The whole army withdrew, and many lights were left burning in camp. The barbarians saw this and did not dare to charge.

The next morning at first light, Meng Huo arrived with a large force at the Shu camp and saw three great camps, all without men or horses, with food carts and arms left inside in hundreds. Meng You said, “Kongming has abandoned camp and fled. Is there some plan behind this?” Meng Huo replied, “I judged that Kongming would not leave his baggage and go unless there was an urgent matter in the realm. If not Wu invading, then Wei must be attacking. He has feigned readiness for the sake of stratagem, leaving carts and armaments and burning lights as a decoy. We should pursue at once and not miss the chance.” So Meng Huo led his front line onward until he reached the bank of Xi’er River.

On the north bank he saw ranks of banners still in neat order and bright as embroidered silk, and along the river a woven city of stockades. The barbarians’ sentries saw this and none dared to advance. Meng Huo said to Meng You, “This is Kongming, frightened by our pursuit. He has come only this far to the north bank and will surely move on in one or two days.” He set the barbarians to camp at the bank, then sent men up the mountain to cut bamboo for rafts in case of crossing. He moved the fighting troops to the front of the camp. He did not yet know the Shu soldiers had already entered his own territory.

That day a fierce wind rose. Firelight flared in every watch and drums sounded; Shu troops struck suddenly. The cave-clan barbarians began to clash among themselves. Meng Huo was greatly startled and quickly ordered his kinsmen and cave men to cut a path and run straight back to the old camp. Suddenly a detachment broke out of the camp: Zhao Yun. Meng Huo then rushed back to Xi’er River and took a secluded mountain path to flee. Another mass of troops broke out: Ma Dai. Meng Huo now had only a few dozen broken soldiers left and fled toward the mountain valleys. Seeing torchlight and dust rising from the south, north, and west, he did not dare to go forward and instead ran east.

Not long after he rounded a mountain pass, in front of a great grove he saw a small cart with a few attendants. On the cart sat Kongming, laughing aloud: “Great King Meng Huo of the southern barbarians! Heaven’s fate has brought you this far; I have been waiting for you a long time!”

Meng Huo fumed. Looking about him, he said, “I have been caught by this man’s trick! I have been humiliated three times. Now we finally meet.” He commanded, “Men, push on! Cut him down with men and cart in one crash.” A number of riders charged hard. Meng Huo rode in front and shouted, but when he reached the place before the grove he stamped down, heard a crash, and collapsed. A pit had opened under his foot and the whole place gave way. All four sides collapsed with him. From within the grove Wei Yan emerged, brought out hundreds of troops, and bound them all with ropes.

Kongming then returned to camp, pacified the barbarians and the cave chiefs. By now most were already home. Apart from the dead and wounded, all others surrendered at once. Kongming met them with wine and meat, spoke gently, and sent everyone away.

Soon after, Zhang Yi brought in Meng You. Kongming said, “Your brother is a fool. You should have counseled him. You have now been captured by me four times. How can you show yourself before men again?”

Shame covered Meng You’s face. He knelt on the ground and begged not to die. Kongming said, “I will not kill you today. I will spare your life and urge you to counsel your brother.” He told the guards to unbind him and release Meng You.

Not long after, Wei Yan brought in Meng Huo. Kongming grew angry and said, “You are captured again this time. What excuse can you offer?” Meng Huo replied, “I was deceived by stratagem. I cannot die in peace.” Kongming shouted to the guards to bring him out and execute him. Meng Huo showed no fear. He looked at Kongming and said, “If you dare release me again, I will certainly settle the grievance of four humiliations.”

Kongming laughed, ordered him unbound, gave him wine to settle his mind, and had him sit in the tent. He asked, “I have treated you with ceremony four times, yet you still refuse to submit. Why?” Meng Huo replied, “Though I am from outside the court order, I do not think the Chancellor lays only deceitful plans; how could I submit?”

Kongming asked, “If I release you again, could you still fight?” Meng Huo said, “If you catch me again, then at that time I will yield sincerely, offer whatever this cave holds for your army’s supplies, and swear never to rebel.”

Kongming smiled and sent him away. Meng Huo gladly thanked him and left. He gathered several thousand strong men and headed southward. Soon he saw dust rising where a detachment appeared; it was his brother Meng You, who had regrouped the broken soldiers to come and avenge him. The two brothers embraced and wept, recounting what had happened.

Meng You said, “My army has lost again and again, and the Shu army has won again and again. We cannot stand against it. We should only withdraw into the caves and not come out; the Shu soldiers cannot endure this heat and will surely give up.” Meng Huo asked, “Where can we hide?” Meng You replied, “To the southwest there is a cave called Tulong Cave. Its lord is Great King Duo Si, and he is very close to our family. We could enter there.”

So Meng Huo first sent Meng You to Tulong Cave to meet Great King Duo Si. Duo Si hastily brought cave soldiers out to welcome him. When Meng Huo arrived, they saluted. He completed the formal respects and recounted what had happened. Duo Si said, “Great King, calm yourself. If the Shu soldiers come, not one will return home with horse and rider. They and Kongming will all die here.”

Meng Huo was delighted and asked for counsel. Duo Si said, “There are only two ways into this cave. One goes northeast, the road Meng Huo took. The ground there is level and firm, the water sweet, and both men and horses can pass. If we block the entrance with timber and stone, even one million cannot enter. The other way goes northwest, steep and difficult, with narrow tracks. Though there are little trails, venomous snakes and fierce scorpions hide there. At dusk, miasma rises in the wild, and it eases only around the Si and Wu hours. Only in the Wei, Shen, and You hours can one travel. The water there is undrinkable, and horses and men cannot move well. This place also has four poisoned springs. One is called Mute Spring; its water is somewhat sweet. Whoever drinks it loses his speech and in no more than ten days dies. Another is Extinguish Spring, and this water is no different from hot broth. Whoever bathes in it gets rotted skin and flesh, and when bone is seen, death follows. A third is Black Spring; its water is faintly clear, and anyone touched by it turns black in hands and feet and dies. The fourth is Soft Spring; its water is as cold as ice. If one drinks it, the throat has no warmth, the body grows soft like cotton, and death follows. Here there are no insects or birds. Only General Fubo once came here, and since then no one has.”

“Now we can fortify the northeast road and hold this very cave. If the Shu troops see this road blocked, they must come by the western path; once there and seeing those four springs, even one million troops will be lost. Why then use swords and lances?” Meng Huo asked. Duo Si then showed the way by pointing, “Today we have only this place to stand.” Meng Huo added, touching his forehead, “Now at least I have some place to stand. How could the divine calculations of Chancellor Zhuge fail to arrange this? These four waters can repay the grievances of those we have lost!” From then on, Meng Huo and Meng You held a feast with Great King Duo Si all day.

After several days without seeing Meng Huo’s forces, Kongming gave orders for the whole army to leave Xi’er River and move southward. It was June heat, and the heat was like fire. A later verse says:

Mountains and marshes are about to dry and wither, and radiant heat covers the great sky.
who can know what the heat is beyond earth and heaven?

Another verse says:

The Red Emperor holds office, and even shadowed clouds dare not rise.
Moist heat makes a lone crane gasp; sea-borne heat startles the giant sea-turtle.
I sit by the stream and hesitate to leave, and lazily toss my sleeves among bamboo.
How can a guest on the sands put on armor once more and march long?

Kongming led the army forward when a scout horse rode in and reported, “Meng Huo has retreated into Tulong Cave and not come out. He has blocked the approach with barricades; there are guards inside. The mountain is rough, the ridges high, and we cannot advance.” Kongming asked Lu Kai. Lu Kai said, “I once heard this cave has one path, but I do not know the details.” Jiang Wan said, “Meng Huo has already lost courage after being captured four times. How would he dare to come out again? With this heat, horses and men exhausted, marching on this is of no benefit; better to return to the country and disperse the army.” Kongming said, “If we do that, we would follow Meng Huo’s plan. Once we leave, he will seize the moment and pursue. We have come this far; there is no reason now to turn back.” So he ordered Wang Ping to lead several hundred troops as the vanguard. He also ordered newly surrendered barbarian soldiers to lead the route, enter by a northwest footpath, and bring the army in.

They came to one spring and men and horses were thirsty and all tried to drink. Wang Ping searched and reported the path. By the time he arrived at the large camp, none could speak; they could only point to their mouths.

Kongming was alarmed and, with a small carriage and a few people, rode forward to inspect. They came to a clear pool with no bottom in sight, cold mist rising from it, so that no soldier dared test it. Kongming dismounted, climbed high, and looked. Four sides of ridges and peaks enclosed the place; no bird or sparrow could be heard. He suddenly saw an ancient temple on a distant ridge. Clinging to vines and gorse he climbed there. In a stone chamber stood a general seated upright and a stone stele beside him; it was the temple of Han’s Fubo General Ma Yuan, whom the locals had established here when pacifying the barbarians.

Kongming knelt again and prayed: “I received the Late Emperor’s solemn charge and now bear an imperial command. I have come to pacify the barbarians. When the southern land is at peace, then I will punish Wei and swallow Wu, and set the Han house at rest. Now my soldiers do not know this land and by mistake drank poison; they have lost their voices. I beg you, divine one, remember the grace of our dynasty, reveal your spirit, and protect the three armies.”

After the prayer he went out in search of locals and, in the distance, noticed an old man coming from across the mountain, leaning on a staff. The old man looked strange. Kongming invited him into the temple, offered formal respect, and sat opposite on stone. Kongming asked, “What is your surname and name, elder?” The old man said, “This old man has long heard of the Han Chancellor’s splendor and is fortunate to see you. The southern barbarians have all survived by your mercy, and their gratitude is deep.”

Kongming asked about the springs, and the old man answered, “The water the troops drank was from Mute Spring. After drinking, speech fails and death comes in several days. Outside that are three other springs: one to the southeast where the water is coldest and, if drunk, the throat has no warmth and the body becomes weak and dies, called Soft Spring; one due south where the water splashed on the body makes hands and feet black and brings death, called Black Spring; one to the southwest where it boils like broth and if one bathes in it, skin and flesh peel away to death, called Extinguish Spring. These four springs gather poisonous air. No cure exists. A heavy miasma rises here; only in the Wei, Shen, and You hours may one move. In the other hours, miasma is dense and whoever touches it dies at once.”

Kongming said, “In this case the barbarian lands cannot be pacified. If they are not pacified, how can Wei and Wu be absorbed and the Han restored? Having failed my late emperor’s trust, I should die rather than live.” The old man said, “Chancellor, do not worry. I can point out a place that will remove this.” Kongming asked, “What insight do you have, elder? Please tell me.” The old man said, “A few li to the west there is a valley. Enter it another twenty li to a stream called Wanan Creek. At its head is a tall hermit called Wanan Yinzhe. He has left this stream for more than twenty years. Behind his hut is a spring called Anle Spring. Whoever is poisoned can drink it and be cured. If one has scabies or miasma, bathing in Wanan Creek is harmless. Also before the hut grows a herb called ‘Xieyeunxiang’: if one keeps one leaf in the mouth, miasma cannot cling. Chancellor, go quickly and ask for these things.” Kongming thanked him and asked, “I cannot repay the kindness that saves life. Tell me your surname.” The old man said, “I am the mountain spirit of this place, sent by General Fubo, and have come to guide you.”

After he finished, he stepped into the temple wall and vanished behind the rear stones. Kongming marveled but had no measure left, knelt again before the temple spirit, then took the old road back to the big camp.

The next day, Kongming prepared incense and gifts, brought Wang Ping and all the mute troops, and hurried day and night toward where the mountain spirit had said, winding along the path. In a small valley path they walked twenty li or more. They saw tall pines, great cypresses, and strange bamboo, surrounding a homestead. In a low fenced yard stood a few thatched huts, and a sweet fragrance rose in the air.

Kongming was rejoiced. At the front of the estate he knocked, and a small child came out. Kongming had not yet finished asking names when another man appeared, with a bamboo hat, grass sandals, white robe, and a yellow belt of ribbon. He had blue eyes and blond hair. Laughing, he said, “Are you not the Han Chancellor?” Kongming said with a smile, “How did the recluse know?” The recluse replied, “For long I have heard the Han Chancellor’s great banners marching south. How could I not know?” He invited Kongming into his grass hall. After greetings, they sat as hosts and guests.

Kongming said, “I have received the charge from Emperor Zhaolie and now bear my lord’s sacred command. I have brought a great army here to bring these southern lands under Han ways. But Meng Huo slipped into the caves, and my soldiers, by mistake, drank water from Mute Spring. Last night the spirit of General Fubo manifested and spoke clearly. He told that the hermit had a medicinal spring to cure this. Please have pity and grant sacred water to save what remains in my troops.” The recluse said, “This old wastrel of the hills has no standing. Why should you force the Chancellor’s journey? The spring is right behind this hut. Bring water and drink.”

So a child led Wang Ping and the others, including the mute soldiers, to the streambank. They drew water and drank; immediately foul saliva came out and they could speak again. The child then led all the army to bathe in Wanan Creek. In the hut, the recluse served ginkgo tea and pineflowers to wait on Kongming. He advised, “There are venomous snakes and fierce scorpions in these cave lands. Willow petals drift in the stream and spring water, and that water cannot be drunk. Dig out a fresh spring and draw from earth if one wants water.”

Kongming asked for Xieyeunxiang. The recluse told all troops to gather it freely: each person should hold one leaf in the mouth, and miasma will not invade. Kongming asked for the recluse’s name. He smiled and said, “I am Meng Jie, Meng Huo’s brother.”

Kongming was stunned. Meng Jie added, “Do not doubt, Chancellor. Allow me to say a few words: Our parents had three sons. The eldest is this old man Meng Jie, then Meng Huo, then Meng You. Our parents are dead. The two younger are fierce and unruly, not submitting to court order. I counseled and counseled, but they did not obey. So I changed my surname and name and withdrew into this reclusion. Now this younger brother has rebelled, and you have labored so far into an uncivilized land. To receive such a manhood, Meng Jie deserves ten thousand deaths. Therefore I ask to beg pardon before you first.”

Kongming sighed, “I have now seen true examples of Robber Zhi and Liu Xiahui again.” He said, “May I petition the Son of Heaven and make you a king?” Meng Jie answered, “I fled here to escape desire for office. Could I still be lured by wealth and rank?” Kongming gave him plenty of gold and silk, but Meng Jie resolutely refused.

Kongming lamented, gave him farewell bows, and went back.

Later, a verse was written:

A great recluse lives in secluded closed gates, where Wuhou once broke all the southern barbarians.
Even now, where no men live among ancient trees, cold smoke still locks the old mountain.

Back at the main camp, Kongming ordered digging for water. They dug twenty or more zhang, but there was not even a drop. In more than ten places it was the same. The army was alarmed. At midnight Kongming offered incense and implored Heaven:

“Your servant Liang is unworthy and only by the Han fortune has he been given life. He received the charge to pacify the barbarians. Now on the road we have no water; men and horses are parched with thirst. If Heaven does not remove Han’s blessing, then send us sweet spring water. If Fortune has ended, let us die here.”

The next dawn, every well he had ordered was full, with clear sweet water. Later, a verse says:

He led the great army to pacify the barbarian land, his heart set on the true way and fitting heaven’s decree.
Gently and reverently he bowed at the well, and the benign spring welled up in the night.

With water for horses and troops secured, the army entered Tulong Cave from a small path and set camp below it. The barbarians learned of this and reported to Meng Huo: “The Shu army is not infected by miasma, nor are they plagued by thirst. All the springs have no effect.” Great King Duo Si heard this but did not believe it. He and Meng Huo climbed to a high mountain and looked. They saw Shu troops in perfect health, with large tubs and small panniers carrying grain water and feed, feeding and watering horses and cooking.

Duo Si saw this and all his hair rose; he looked back at Meng Huo and said, “These are divine troops!” Meng Huo said, “You and your brother and I should settle this with a final death struggle. If we die in this field, who would accept surrender in chains?” Duo Si said, “If the Great King’s army is defeated, my wives and sons are finished as well. We should slaughter oxen and horses, reward cave soldiers, and charge directly against the Shu camp through fire and water without avoidance. Then we may win.”

So he granted rewards to all barbarians. As he was about to depart, news came that Yang Feng, lord of Yinye Cave and one of its twenty-one caves, had arrived with thirty thousand soldiers to help in battle. Meng Huo rejoiced and said, “With neighboring troops helping me, I must win.” He then met with Great King Duo Si and went out to greet them.

Yang Feng brought in his men and said, “I have thirty thousand elite soldiers, all in iron armor, able to cross mountains and leap ridges. They can oppose one million Shu troops. I have five sons, all with complete warrior training, and I wish to help the Great King.” He ordered his five sons to bow. Each had a hulking frame and tiger-like body, majestic with force.

Meng Huo rejoiced and set seats for Yang Feng and his sons. As the wine reached half full, Yang Feng said, “There is little joy in the army. I have a barbarian maiden who goes with the troops, dancing knife-and-shield, to aid some laughter.” Meng Huo was pleased and agreed. After a while, dozens of barbarian maidens in loose hair and bare feet entered dancing from outside the tents. The entire tribe clapped hands and sang in chorus. Yang Feng told two sons to carry cups. The two sons stepped to Meng Huo and Meng You with cups and approached. As they took the cups and were about to drink, Yang Feng shouted loudly once. Immediately the two sons dragged Meng Huo and Meng You from their seats. Great King Duo Si moved as if to leave, and was already seized by Yang Feng. The barbarian maidens barred the tents; no one dared come near.

Meng Huo said, “When a rabbit dies, foxes grieve, and all creatures pity their kind. You and I are lords of different caves and had no ancient rancor. Why have you harmed me?” Yang Feng answered, “My brothers, sons, and nephews all know the life given by Chancellor Zhuge and can only repay him. You have rebelled again. Why not capture and present you?”

So all cave barbarians returned to their homeland. Yang Feng and his men brought Meng Huo, Meng You, and Great King Duo Si to Kongming’s camp. He ordered them to be brought in and, kneeling under the tent, said, “All our sons and nephews feel indebted to the Chancellor’s grace. That is why we captured Meng Huo, Meng You, and others and presented them.”

Kongming rewarded him richly, then ordered Meng Huo brought forward. He laughed and said, “Are you persuaded this time?” Meng Huo answered, “I could not submit because your skill could not break us, but because my own cave people turned against each other. If you wish to kill me, kill me. I still do not submit.”

Kongming said, “You drew me into waterless land and set Mute Spring, Extinguish Spring, Black Spring, and Soft Spring, all toxic. Yet my army suffered no harm. Is that not Heaven’s will? Why do you remain so attached to stubbornness?” Meng Huo answered, “My ancestors reside in Silver Pit Mountain with three river dangers and strong mountain gates. If you capture me there, my family line will surrender with all its heart.”

Kongming said, “I release you again. Return, reorganize your army and troops, and meet me again for decisive battle. If I catch you then and you still do not submit, I will exterminate your nine clans.” He shouted for attendants, had him unbound, and released Meng Huo. Meng Huo knelt and left again. Kongming also released Meng You and Great King Duo Si, gave them wine and food to calm their fear. Neither dared to meet him directly, and he ordered horse and mount to take them back.

It is no easy matter to stand deep within dangerous ground, and extraordinary stratagems are not devised by chance.
How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Wuxiang Marquis Uses Four Stratagems, and the King of the Southern Barbarians Is Captured Five Times

chapters.html:
From the beginning,

Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, released Meng Huo and the other captives. Yang Feng and his son were each granted offices and titles, and the cave troops were heavily rewarded. Yang Feng and his companions thanked him and departed. Meng Huo and the others returned to Silver Pit Cave by night.

Outside the cave were three rivers: the Lu River, the Gannan River, and the Xicheng River. The three streams came together there, so the place was called Three Rivers. North of the cave lay nearly three hundred li of open plain, rich with all kinds of things. Two hundred li to the west was a salt well. Another two hundred li to the southwest reached the Lu and Gannan waters. Three hundred li to the south stood Liangdu Cave; within that cave system, mountains enclosed it. Silver ore came from those mountains, which is why it was called Silver Pit Mountain. In the mountains stood palaces and towers as the barbarian king’s stronghold. They built an ancestral hall and called it “Family Ghost.” It was used for cattle-killing and horse-slaughter sacrifices, with the rite called “Oracle Ghost.” Each year they also sacrificed and offered sacrifices to this spirit for the Shus and people from outer regions. When a person fell ill, he would refuse medicine and instead pray to wizard-shamans, a practice called “Medicine Ghost.” There were no formal criminal codes there, but crimes were still punished by beheading. When girls came of age, they bathed together in the streams with men and were free to pair as they wished; parents did not intervene. This custom was called “Learning by Arts.”

When the seasons and rains came in due order, they planted rice. If the grain did not ripen, they killed snakes for soup and cooked elephants for rice.

In each ward, the first household was called the cave lord, and the next one was the tribal chieftain. On the first and fifteenth of each lunar month, they all gathered in Three Rivers City to trade and barter. These were their customs.

Meng Huo gathered more than a thousand kinsmen and followers in the cave and said, “I have been humiliated by Shu soldiers many times, and I have sworn to repay them. What strong plan do you all have?” Before he finished, one man answered, “I can present one man who can break Zhuge Liang.” The men looked there. It was Meng Huo’s brother-in-law, now chief of the Eighth District, called Dailai Cave Lord. Meng Huo was overjoyed and asked quickly, “Who is he?”

Dailai Cave Lord said, “The chief beyond the southwest is King Mùlù of the Banyan Cave. He is deep in rites and sorcery. When he sets out, he rides an elephant and can summon wind and rain. Tigers, leopards, wolves, poisonous snakes, and venomous scorpions always follow him. He also commands thirty thousand divine soldiers, all ferocious. If he sends a formal letter and receives respectful treatment, I can go in person to petition him. If this man grants support, what fear is there of Shu soldiers?”

Meng Huo rejoiced and ordered his uncle by marriage to write and go. Then he ordered King Duosi to guard Three Rivers City as a forward barrier.

Kongming then marched with troops straight to Three Rivers City. He saw at a distance that the city was bounded by the river on three sides and open on the fourth by dry land, so he sent Wei Yan and Zhao Yun, whose courtesy name was Zilong, each with a corps, to assault the dry approach. When the army reached the city foot, the barbarians on the walls loosed crossbow and ballista volleys all at once. There were many bowmen in the cave; each crossbow released ten bolts at once, every arrowhead poisoned. Anyone struck saw skin and flesh rot until the five viscera were exposed, and then died. Zhao Yun and Wei Yan could not win. They returned to Kongming and reported the poisoned arrows.

Kongming rode in a small cart to the front, examined the situation, and then ordered the army to pull back several li to camp. The barbarians watched the Shu army retreat far away, laughed loudly and rejoiced, and assumed the Shus had retreated in fear. So they slept deeply and securely that night, sending no sentries on reconnaissance.

After the withdrawal, Kongming kept the camp closed and gave no orders for five days. Toward dusk on the fifth, a slight wind rose from the left. Kongming sent the order: “Every unit must bring one strip of collar cloth and answer check at the first watch hour. Anyone without one will be beheaded.” All the commanders were perplexed, but the troops prepared.

At the first watch hour, he sent another order: “Every unit must bring one bundle of earth. Anyone without one will be beheaded.” Again they were all confused, but all prepared.

Kongming gave yet another order: “All units, bring your earth bundles to the foot of Three Rivers City for handover. The first to arrive will be rewarded.” Hearing this, the army quickly packed clean soil and hurried to the city foot. Kongming had all the soil piled into a sloped ramp. Those who gained the wall first would receive first merit. So over ten thousand Shus, plus more than ten thousand newly enrolled men, cast their soil together at once before the wall. In a moment, the heaps became a mound and pressed up to the city wall. At a hidden signal, all Shu soldiers climbed in. The barbarians sent out their crossbows only to be mostly seized, and the rest fled and abandoned the city. King Duosi was killed in the chaos.

Kongming’s Shus separated the routes and slaughtered through. He took Three Rivers City; all treasure taken there was distributed to the army. A shattered band of barbarians fled back to tell Meng Huo, “King Duosi is dead. Three Rivers City is lost.”

Meng Huo was in dread. While he was still worrying, word came that the Shu soldiers had already crossed the river and camped before his own cave.

Suddenly, a single laugh rang out from behind the screen as one figure emerged: “If you are truly a man, how could you lack intelligence? I am a woman, yet I will fight with you.”

Meng Huo looked and saw it was his wife, Lady Zhu Rong. She had long lived in the southern barbarians and was of the Zhu Rong lineage; she was famed for her flying knives, never missing.

Meng Huo rose and thanked her. Lady Zhu Rong rejoiced, mounted, and led several hundred fierce chiefs and fifty thousand cave soldiers from Silver Pit Palace to oppose the Shus. As they had barely turned out of the cave mouth, a contingent stopped them; at its front rode the Shu general Zhang Ni. When the barbarians saw him, they spread out in two lines.

Lady Zhu Rong had five throwing knives tucked behind her, and held a long spearstaff nearly eight chi in length. She sat her curly-mane horse, red-bay in color. Zhang Ni admired the sight in silence. They charged and engaged at speed. After only a few turns of battle, Lady Zhu Rong turned her horse and withdrew.

Zhang Ni chased. In midair one flying knife dropped. He raised his arm to block, and it struck his left arm. He spun and fell from horseback. The barbarians shouted once, seized Zhang Ni, and took him away.

When Ma Zhong heard Zhang Ni had been captured, he moved in and was at once bound as well. Seeing Lady Zhu Rong standing with spear upright and horse reined in, Ma Zhong, burning with rage, rushed forward and was about to fight, but he tripped from his mount and was also captured. Then all were taken into the cave to meet Meng Huo.

Meng Huo offered them seats and celebrated. Lady Zhu Rong barked for the axe and sword men to bring out Zhang Ni and Ma Zhong for execution. Meng Huo stopped her: “Kongming once released me five times. If I were to kill these generals now, that would be unrighteous. Also, they were captured and surrendered in this cave. I did not refuse then. Since this was all an arrangement, we can execute them later after taking Kongming himself.”

Lady Zhu Rong obeyed his words and drank and feasted.

The shattered barbarian survivors came to report this to Kongming. He immediately summoned Ma Dai, Zhao Yun, and Wei Yan and gave each his plan. The next day the barbarians reported they had entered the cave. They said Zhao Yun was waiting for battle. Lady Zhu Rong mounted and rode out to meet him.

The two clashed in a few passes. Zhao Yun turned his horse and withdrew. Lady Zhu Rong feared an ambush and turned back with her men. Later, Wei Yan came and led troops into combat. Lady Zhu Rong urged her horse forward and met him in battle. As the engagement tightened, Wei Yan pretended to lose and broke away; Lady Zhu Rong did not pursue.

The next day Zhao Yun again brought troops and fought her. She met him and after only a few passes he again feigned retreat. She did not chase and instead began to withdraw to the cave, but then Wei Yan sent his whole force forward with loud insults. Lady Zhu Rong instantly drew her staff to strike him. Wei Yan turned his horse and rode away.

In fury she chased him. Wei Yan then spurred through a mountain-side side track. Suddenly there was a loud sound behind him. He looked back and saw Lady Zhu Rong off her saddle and falling. Ma Dai had been hiding there and used a strap rope to trip her. He captured her and took her back to the main camp.

The barbarians from the cave came to rescue, but Zhao Yun scattered them with one fierce attack.

Kongming sat upright in the command tent. Ma Dai brought Lady Zhu Rong in and Kongming ordered soldiers to untie her and seat her in a separate tent with wine to steady her. He then dispatched a messenger to Meng Huo, proposing to trade Lady Zhu Rong for Zhang Ni and Ma Zhong.

Meng Huo agreed and released Zhang Ni and Ma Zhong, returning him. Kongming then sent Lady Zhu Rong back into the cave.

Meng Huo received him with joy and anger together. Then came word that the Daini Cave Lord had arrived. Meng Huo went out to receive him. The man rode a white elephant, wearing gold-and-pearl cords and two large swords at his waist, and was surrounded by men who fed tigers, leopards, and wolves. Upon seeing him, Meng Huo knelt and wept to beg for help.

He narrated the events. King Mulu promised revenge. Meng Huo was overjoyed and held a feast.

The next day King Mulu led his cave troops and fierce beasts out. Hearing the barbarians were coming, Zhao Yun and Wei Yan formed their troops into array.

The two commanders stood side by side before the line and watched. The barbarians’ banners and equipment were unlike anything else: many wore no armor at all, bare and naked. Each carried four sharpened knives. No drums or horns sounded among them; instead they used metal sieves as signals. King Mulu had two treasured swords at his waist and held a bronze gong in his hand, riding a white elephant beneath the grand standard.

Zhao Yun said to Wei Yan, “In all the days I have stood in formation, I have never seen such figures.” As they were still pondering, King Mulu muttered spells no one could understand and shook his bell. Suddenly the wind rose violently; sand and stone flew as if in sudden rain. A war-horn sounded. Tigers, leopards, wolves, and poisonous snakes were all loosed by the wind, fangs and claws bared, charging toward them.

How could the Shu stand against them? They fell back. The barbarians pursued in a slaughtering rush, and only on the border road near Three Rivers did they turn back.

Zhao Yun and Wei Yan gathered the defeated and came before Kongming to apologize, explaining everything. Kongming laughed and said, “It was not your fault. Before I left my thatched hut, I knew the southern barbarians had a beast-mobilizing method. I prepared in Shu already the means to break this formation: There were twenty carts in the army, all sealed within. Today use half; leave half for later use.” He ordered ten carts painted red with oil containers brought under his tent, leaving ten black-oil carts in reserve.

No one knew his meaning. Kongming opened the chests: they held carved wooden and painted giant beasts, each covered in five-colored woolen threads for fur and fitted with iron claws, each large enough for ten men to ride.

He selected over a thousand stout soldiers and selected one hundred men to carry concealed smoke-fire compounds among the troops.

Next day Kongming drove the army forward swiftly and set in formation at the cave mouth. The barbarians discovered this and reported to their king. Proud in his own invulnerability, King Mulu went out with Meng Huo and the cave army.

Kongming sat on his cart, wearing a silk kerchief and fan, clad in a robe of the Way, upright and composed.

Meng Huo pointed. “The one in the cart is Zhuge Liang. If we take this man, all is decided.”

King Mulu chanted a spell and shook his bell. In an instant a violent wind rose and the beasts leapt out. Kongming stirred his fan once; the wind reversed and drove back into their own lines. Fake beasts from Shu burst forth.

To the Shus, the barbarian beasts appeared with fire in their mouths, black smoke from their nostrils, and bronze bells ringing on their bodies. They bared teeth and claws and rushed forward. The wicked beasts in their own ranks did not dare advance but fled back into the cave, crashing through and knocking down thousands of barbarians. Kongming drove the army onward; horns and drums roared as they chased and killed.

King Mulu died in the melee. Inside the cave, Meng Huo’s followers abandoned the palace halls and fled over mountains and ridges. Kongming’s main force occupied Silver Pit Cave.

The next day Kongming was preparing to split forces and capture Meng Huo when news arrived: “King Mulu of the band—wife-brother brought and called Dailai Cave Lord—has persuaded Meng Huo to surrender, but he refused. Now he has brought Meng Huo, Lady Zhu Rong, and more than a hundred kinsmen in chains to present to the Chancellor.”

Kongming gave immediate orders. He summoned Zhang Ni and Ma Zhong and instructed them to do exactly as laid out. The two generals took two thousand picked men and took positions concealed in two corridors. Kongming ordered the gate guards to let the prisoners enter.

Dailai Cave Lord led axe-and-sword men and unbound Meng Huo and the others. Around a hundred of them were brought before him.

Kongming shouted, “Seize them!” The men in both corridors came out together, each taking one captive. They were all bound.

Kongming laughed: “How can your little trick hide from me? The two times you came into this cave and were captured to force surrender, I harmed you not. You believed I was sincere, so you tried deceitful surrender to lure me inside and kill me!”

He shouted to the guards, “Search their sides; of course they each carried sharp knives.”

Turning to Meng Huo, Kongming asked, “You said you would submit only when you were captured in your own hall. Today, then?”

Meng Huo replied, “This is our own prepared march to death. It is not your doing. My heart is not yet surrendered.”

Kongming said, “I have captured you six times and you still do not submit. When will that time come?”

Meng Huo answered, “When you have captured me the seventh time, then only then will I surrender from the heart and never rebel again.”

Kongming said, “The nest is broken. What need have I to worry?” and ordered the guards to remove their bonds. He shouted, “This time you are captured. If you evade again, there will be no mercy.”

Meng Huo and his company fled with heads tucked, slipping like rats.

There were more than a thousand battered barbarians left. Most were injured and fleeing. They came upon King Meng Huo. Meng Huo gathered the defeated troops and felt some ease, then consulted with Dailai Cave Lord.

“Now our cave domain has been taken by Shu soldiers,” he said. “Where can we find secure ground?”

Dailai Cave Lord answered, “There is only one kingdom that can break the Shus.”

Meng Huo asked, “Where can I go?”

Dailai Cave Lord said, “Seven hundred li to the southeast is a kingdom called Ugo. Its lord is Wutugu. He is two zhang and two chi tall, eats no grain, and lives on snakes and wild beasts. He has scales on his body, and swords and arrows cannot pierce him. His soldiers all wear rattan armor. The rattan grows in mountain gullies and hangs on stone walls. The people cut it, soak it in oil, and dry it out for six months; then they dry and soak it again, repeating it over a dozen times before making armor. Once worn it does not sink when crossing water, does not wet in water, and cannot be pierced by blade or arrow. Therefore they are called the Rattan Armor Army. The king can go now and seek him. If he helps, taking Zhuge Liang will be like slicing bamboo with a sharp knife.”

Meng Huo rejoiced and went to Ugo to meet Wutugu.

The Ugo cave had no houses or halls; everyone lived inside earthen pits. Entering the cave, Meng Huo knelt and wept as he explained what had happened. Wutugu said, “I raise my cave forces for your vengeance.” Meng Huo joyfully bowed and thanked him.

So Wutugu called two subordinate captains: one named Tuan An, the other Xini. He raised thirty thousand soldiers, all in rattan armor, and set out toward the northeast from Ugo.

They crossed one river, Taohuashui, called Peach Blossom River. Both banks were lined with peach trees, and each year their fallen leaves floated on the water. If outsiders drank it they died at once, but Ugo people who drank became even more vigorous.

Wutugu’s army camped at Peach Blossom Ford to wait for Shu troops.

Kongming sent scouts and got news: “Meng Huo has called the lord of Ugo and now thirty thousand rattan-armored soldiers are encamped at Peach Blossom Ford. Meng Huo has also gathered tribes in each band and is resisting.” Kongming heard and marched in force to the ford.

From the opposite bank they saw the barbarians; they looked less than human, terrible and ugly. Asked a local, they said the peach leaves were falling that day and the water was undrinkable. Kongming pulled his army back five li and camped, leaving Wei Yan to guard.

The next day the lord of Ugo brought a contingent of rattan-armored warriors across the river. Gold and drums thundered. Wei Yan led troops out to meet them. The barbarians rolled over the ground. Shu arrows struck the armor but could not pierce; they fell to the ground. Blades and spears also failed to enter.

The barbarians swung their sharp knives and steel hooks, and the Shu could not stand against them; they all fled. Wutugu did not chase and then withdrew.

Wei Yan returned, chasing on to Peach Blossom Ford. He saw barbarian troops crossing with armor; the exhausted among them removed their armor and sat it on the water surface to cross. Wei Yan hurried back to camp and reported all to Kongming.

Kongming asked Lü Kai and the local guides. Lü Kai said, “I have long heard of an Ugo kingdom among the southern barbarians, where there are no civilized rules. Its rattan body armor is hard to wound. There is also the evil water of peach leaves: native people drink and become stronger, while outsiders who drink die. Facing such a barbary formation, even victory would give no real gain. Better to withdraw in good order.”

Kongming smiled. “Have I gone this far only to leave? Tomorrow I will have a strategy to pacify them.” He ordered Zhao Yun to assist Wei Yan in guarding camp and told him not to venture out lightly.

The next day Kongming rode with local guides in a small cart to an out-of-sight place on the northern bank at Peach Blossom Ford and surveyed the terrain thoroughly. When the cart could no longer pass over a steep, dangerous ridge, Kongming dismounted and walked on. He came to a mountain and saw a valley like a coiled serpent, with sheer stone walls and no trees. A broad road ran through the middle.

Kongming asked the local men, “What is this valley called?”

They answered, “This place is called Coiled-Serpent Valley. Coming out leads to the Three Rivers main road. In front of the valley’s mouth is Talan Meadow.”

Kongming rejoiced. “This is Heaven-given for my success!” he said.

He returned to the old road, climbed onto the cart, and rode back to camp. He called Ma Dai and instructed: “You have my ten black-oil casks. You will need a thousand bamboo poles. Do so with these things exactly. Use your main troops to hold both ends of Coiled-Serpent Valley and move as I said.

You have half a month. Make all this complete. If anything leaks, military law will apply.” Ma Dai received the plan and departed.

He then called Zhao Yun: “You will hold the Three Rivers Road junction behind Coiled-Serpent Valley. Prepare these materials by the appointed day.” Zhao Yun accepted.

He called Wei Yan: “Lead your core troops to camp at the Peach Blossom Ford bank. If the barbarians cross and attack, abandon the camp and run to the white-banner position. In half a month you must lose fifteen engagements and abandon seven stockades. If you lose only fourteen, do not come back to me.”

Wei Yan received the order and left, resentful. Kongming then called Zhang Yi and had him set up stockades as instructed elsewhere. He also ordered Zhang Ni and Ma Zhong, the surrendered men from the caves, to accompany and act as arranged.

Meng Huo then told Wutugu king, “Zhuge Liang has many clever stratagems; he is all ambush. Hereafter in battle, issue this order to all six armies: do not enter forested places in valleys lightly. The terrain is treacherous.”

Wutugu said, “Your thought is right. I know Chinese soldiers use deceitful plans. Let us follow this now. I will fight in front; you, lord, will teach from the rear.” Their plan was made.

A report soon came that Shu troops had set up camp on the north bank of Peach Blossom Ford. Wutugu sent two captains and crossed the rattan army over the river to fight. Before two rounds, Wei Yan broke and fled.

The barbarians, fearing an ambush, did not pursue and returned.

The next day Wei Yan made camp again. Their sentries saw this, and the barbarians crossed again to fight. Wei Yan rode out. He broke on the second engagement and fled again.

The barbarians chased for over ten li. Seeing no movement around, they then camped in the Shu camp.

The next day two captains again asked Wutugu to come. They explained this and the matter. Wutugu led his men in and gave chase, pursuing Wei Yan for one round. Shu soldiers dropped their armor and cast away spears and ran, finding a white banner ahead. Wei Yan brought only the survivors to the white-banner place; there was already a camp there, and he made his men hold it.

Wutugu pressed in pursuit. Wei Yan withdrew and abandoned that camp. The barbarians gained it.

The next day Wei Yan fought again and retreated again, running only toward the white-banner point. There was another camp there; he halted in it. The day after, they came once more. Wei Yan fought briefly and left again. The barbarians occupied another Shu camp.

To avoid repetition, Wei Yan, while fighting and retreating, had now failed fifteen engagements and abandoned seven camps. The barbarians surged after him with vigor. Wutugu, while breaking enemies ahead, saw heavy woodland in the roads and therefore would not advance; yet he had men look ahead. From the tree shadows they saw flags fluttering. Wutugu said to Meng Huo, “You have guessed exactly.”

Meng Huo laughed. “Zhuge Liang has now been exposed. Day after day he has won him one victory; he has taken seven camps and seven losses by our force. The Shu soldiers have run with the wind and fled. Zhuge Liang has no more stratagems left. With this one push all will be decided.”

Wutugu rejoiced and no longer thought much about the Shus.

On the sixteenth day Wei Yan, with the shattered remnant force, met the rattan army again. Wutugu led on, mounted on an elephant. His hat bore sun and moon wolf-whisker design, and his robe was netted with gold-beaded strands. Armor scales emerged below both ribs; there was a light gleam in his eyes. He shouted at Wei Yan.

Wei Yan turned and fled. The barbarians closed in hard behind.

Wei Yan took his men around Coiled-Serpent Valley and withdrew toward the white-banner. Wutugu led the massing force in hot pursuit. Seeing no woods or brush on the mountain, he believed there was no ambush and chased with confidence.

When he reached the valley, he saw dozens of black-oil casks across the road.

The barbarians shouted, “This is a Shu supply route. The king has come and abandoned the grain carts.”

Wutugu rejoiced and pushed harder. When he emerged from the valley mouth, Shu troops were nowhere in sight. Instead, logs and loose stones tumbled down, sealing the mouth.

Wutugu ordered a road cut to push through. Suddenly he saw larger and smaller vehicles ahead, loaded with dry timber, all afire. He ordered a retreat, but only then the rear ranks shouted that the valley entrance was blocked by burning timber piles. The carts were in fact filled with gunpowder and had all ignited together.

Wutugu felt no fear from no grass or trees in view and told soldiers to seek their way, but suddenly men atop the mountain hurled firebrands in every direction. Fires leapt along fuses set in the earth. Cannons flared up everywhere. Firelight roiled through the whole valley. Every rattan-armored body was hit.

The men of Wutugu and his thirty thousand rattan-armored troops were burned together while clinging together, and many died in Coiled-Serpent Valley.

From the mountain, Kongming looked down and saw the barbarians flailing in flames, hands outstretched and legs splayed. Most had had their heads and faces shattered by cannon fire. All had died in the valley; the stench was unbearable. Kongming wept and said, “Though I have done my duty for the state, this will surely shorten my life.”

His officers and soldiers all sighed with him.

Back at the camp, Meng Huo was waiting for reports when suddenly over a thousand men knelt and laughed before him. They said, “Ugo’s troops have fought the Shu army and encircled Zhuge Liang in Coiled-Serpent Valley. The king is requested to come and provide support. We were all cave folk and were forced to submit to Shu. Now knowing the king has come, we have come to help.”

Meng Huo rejoiced, leading his followers and gathered tribes, and set out by night on horseback. He ordered barbarians to guide.

As they reached Coiled-Serpent Valley, they saw flames rising and foul smoke everywhere. Realizing the trap, Meng Huo withdrew his troops, when to his left was Zhang Ni and to his right Ma Zhong, with two armies bursting out.

Meng Huo tried to meet the enemy. At one shout, most of the barbarians around him were actually Shu soldiers, and they captured Meng Huo and his gathered tribal men all at once.

Meng Huo rode out alone and broke from the encirclement, heading for a mountain path.

At that moment, a group at a hollow in the mountain, from earth and field, pushed forward a small cart. In it sat a single figure in a green-black turban, holding a feather fan, wearing a Daoist robe: it was Kongming.

Kongming shouted, “Rebel Meng Huo, what now?” Meng Huo turned his horse to run. A general flashed by and blocked the way. It was Ma Dai.

Catching him off guard, Ma Dai seized him alive.

At that time Wang Ping and Zhang Yi had already brought one army to the barbarian camp and captured Lady Zhu Rong and all old and young of that band alive.

Kongming returned to camp, ascended the command tent, and sat. He told all generals,

“Only after necessity did I use this plan, and it has cost me in virtue. I guessed they would think I had set many ambushes among the woods, while in truth I kept only banners there, no soldiers and no horses, to test their hearts. I ordered Wei Wenchang to lose fifteen engagements so as to harden his will. I saw Coiled-Serpent Valley had only one path. On both sides were bare stone and no trees; below it was sand. So I had Ma Dai lay the black-oil carts in the valley.

Inside each cart there were pre-made fire cannons, called earth mines, each containing nine smaller guns, buried at intervals of thirty paces. Bamboo segments connected them for fuses. When one ignited, the mountain cracked and split stone. I also had Zhao Zilong prepare hay carts and place them in the valley. I set large logs and loose rock on the slopes above.

I then had Wei Yan lure Wutugu and the rattan army into the valley, and once Wei Yan was released, I blocked their way and burned them. I have heard, ‘What harms water wins against fire.’ The rattan armor, though impervious to blade and arrow, is oil-soaked; fire takes it. How else could such recalcitrant barbarians be defeated?

If no one of the Wutugu folk remained alive, that is my great fault.”

All the generals knelt and said, “The Chancellor’s insight is beyond the stars and spirits to measure.”

Kongming ordered him brought in. Meng Huo knelt in the tent. Kongming ordered his bonds removed and had him taken to another tent with food and wine to calm him. He then told the steward of food and drink to sit near the couch and gave precise instructions before leaving.

Meng Huo, Lady Zhu Rong, Meng You, and Dailai Cave Lord sat drinking in the separate tent with all the household and kinsmen. Suddenly one man came in and told Meng Huo, “The Chancellor is ashamed to meet you. He has sent me to send you back, and then to summon men and horses to decide this once more.”

Meng Huo wiped tears and said, “There has never before been one captured seven times and released seven times. Though I am of outer lands, I know ritual and propriety. Is this not shameful?”

Then he and his brothers, wife, children, and all kin-knots knelt and rubbed their bare chests in apology: “By the Heavenly authority of the Chancellor, the southern people will never rebel again.”

Kongming said, “Do you now submit?”

Meng Huo wept and thanked him: “My sons and grandsons owe me for the grace that preserves life; how could they not submit?”

Kongming asked him to come to the main tent and held a celebration. He appointed him forever as Cave Lord. All captured lands were returned.

Meng Huo and his clansmen, and all barbarians present, were deeply moved and all joyfully rejoiced in leaving.

Later poets praised Zhuge Liang in verse:

With feather fan and silk kerchief, he raises the blue banner with calm command,
With seven captures he masters the barbarian king through wondrous stratagems.
His power and grace are still told in stream and cave,
And on high plains, people raise shrines to honor him.

The Chancellor’s Chief Clerk, Fei Hui, came to remonstrate:

“Chancellor, you have personally led troops into rough lands and subdued these southern peoples. Now that the barbarian king has submitted, why not place officials there and have Meng Huo guard with him?”

Kongming replied, “There are three reasons this is not easy. One: if we leave outsiders and do not leave troops, there is no food to sustain a garrison—that is the first difficulty. Two: if we leave outsiders with soldiers but no supplies, disaster becomes certain. Three: the barbarians have a long history of killing and betrayal; if outsiders stay, they will never fully trust us. So it is not easy either. Now I will leave no civilians there, bring no grain, and keep peace in the absence of strife.”

All agreed.

Thus all the barbarians felt Kongming’s kindness and raised a living temple for him. They offered seasonal sacrifices, and all called him a paternal lord. They each sent pearls, gold and jewels, red lacquer medicines, plowing oxen, and war horses for military supply, swearing not to rebel again.

The south was settled.

Kongming had finished rewarding the army, and the force withdrew to Shu, appointing Wei Yan to lead the main body as advanced guard.

Wei Yan’s army had only just reached the Lu River when dark clouds sealed above, and a fierce wind rose from nowhere over the water; sand and stones shot about and the army could not advance. He withdrew and reported to Kongming. Kongming then asked Meng Huo. It was the prelude:

The barbarian tribes beyond the frontier were only recently submitting, yet ghost soldiers by the water still ran rampant.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Driving the Giant Beasts and Breaking the Barbarians in Six Encounters, Burning the Rattan Armor, and Capturing Meng Huo Seven Times

chapters.html:
After Chancellor Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, returned from the southern campaign and was set to go home, Meng Huo led the chiefs and clan elders of the tribes, both great and small, to accompany him partway and bid him farewell.

When the vanguard reached the Lu River in the autumn of the ninth month, dark clouds suddenly gathered overhead, and a wild wind rose at once; the army could not cross, so they reported to Zhuge Liang. He asked Meng Huo why this had happened. Meng Huo answered, “Long ago this river was troubled by a water demon. All who cross it now and then are cursed by it.”

Zhuge Liang asked, “What is fitting for the sacrifice?”

Meng Huo replied, “In former times, because this vengeful spirit caused disaster, men offered seven times seven—forty-nine human heads—and one black ox and one white sheep. Only then did the wind quiet and the waves still, and the region enjoyed harvests for years.”

Zhuge Liang said, “My campaigns are now settled. How could I take an innocent life just for that?” He walked himself to the Lu River bank and looked. As if on cue, dark winds rose and waves surged wildly, making men and horses cry out in alarm.

Zhuge Liang grew suspicious and sought out local elders. They said, “Ever since the Chancellor passed this way, the riverbank has echoed every night with ghostly cries from dusk until dawn. In the drifting fog there are countless hungry spirits. Because of that, all avoid crossing.”

Zhuge Liang said, “This is my guilt and fault. Earlier I led over a thousand troops of Shu here under Ma Dai, and they all died in the water. Worse, we slew the southern men and left them at this very bank. Their enraged souls and restless ghosts cannot be calmed; this is why this happens. Tonight I will personally go and make our expiation.”

A local elder said, “According to the old custom, forty-nine human heads must be offered for the angry spirits to be dispersed.”

Zhuge Liang answered, “It is because one life became an angry ghost that we have this plight now; how can we answer it by killing another life? I have another way.” He ordered the kitchens to slaughter cattle and horses. Their flesh was mixed with flour and shaped into the form of heads, called mantou.

That night at the Lu Riverbank he set out an altar of incense, laid out the offering dishes, put up forty-nine lamps, and raised banners to summon the spirits. He arranged the mantou and other foods on the ground. At the third watch, in crown and crane-cloak, Zhuge Liang performed the rite himself and had Dong Jue read the sacrificial text:

In the first day of the ninth month of autumn, in the third year of Jianxing, I, the Wuxiang Marquis, Governor of Yi Province, and the Chancellor, Zhuge Liang, humbly present this rite and offer it to the wandering spirits of those who died in service to Shu and the southern dead in mourning.

Our Great Han emperor, whose power surpassed the Five Hegemons and who clearly continued the Three Rulers, was attacked from afar by foreign ways that rose in arms. They let wicked spirits loose and indulged in unruly violence. I, under the emperor’s orders, went out to punish the distant wild places; with fierce troops I swept through, removing ants and vermin. As our mighty army gathered like cloud, the raging raiders melted like ice. The crack of the war-crook was heard once, and the fury of the marauders collapsed.

All the soldiers and young lads were peers among the heroes of the nine provinces. Officers and clerks alike were among the brave in the four seas. Trained in warfare and sworn to service, all answered a single command and fought with one mind. By such resolve together we made seven great captures. All of you stood firm in loyalty to the state, and all of you shared zeal for serving the lord.

Alas that you were taken unawares by the enemy’s schemes—one by a stray arrow and swallowed by water, one by a blade and your spirits sent into endless night. Though alive, you had courage; though dead, you gained renown.

Now the songs of triumph are ready to return. You are all still bright spirits; we are sure our prayer is heard. Come with our banners, follow our troops, and return to your homelands. May each of you recognize your native place, receive flesh-and-bone and filial offerings among your own families, and live on in the remembrance of household rites. Do not drift in foreign lands as lonely ghosts, only to become souls of strange places.

I will report this to the Son of Heaven. Each of your kin will all receive his share of grace and yearly clothing and grain; each month, a grain stipend as well. I ask only this in return, to soothe your hearts.

As for the local gods of this land and the dead of the south, blood-offerings are their due, and they have never gone far from this place. If the living tremble at Heaven’s authority, even the dead return to the emperor’s governance. Keep your minds at peace, and do not break into cries of lament.

This is my sincere devotion, and respectfully offered, this sacrifice.

Alas, mourning indeed! May all now still receive our libation.

When he finished reading, Zhuge Liang sobbed out loud, in anguish so deep that the whole army was shaken and all men wept. Meng Huo and his followers all cried too.

Out of the moaning clouds and mourning mist, thousands of ghostly spirits were faintly visible, and then drifted away with the wind. Zhuge Liang then ordered all the ritual items cast into the Lu River.

The next day he brought the whole army to the southern bank of the river. The clouds had cleared, the mist had vanished, and wind and waves were still. The soldiers of Shu crossed the Lu River in perfect safety. Truly, as if in fulfillment of the old saying: whips struck bronze buckles with ringing sound, and men sang songs of victory as they returned.

When they reached Yongchang, Zhuge Liang left Wang Kang and Lü Kai to guard the four commanderies. He assigned Meng Huo to return home with his men and exhorted him to govern diligently, care for the people well, and do not neglect the fields. Meng Huo wept and bowed in parting and departed.

Zhuge Liang then led the main force home to Chengdu. The Later Ruler held the court carriage, rode out thirty li beyond the city gate to receive him, and set up a palace stand by the roadside to honor the Marquis, calling him out.

Zhuge Liang leapt down in panic and prostrated himself, saying, “Your servant has failed to pacify the south swiftly and has made Your Majesty bear anxiety. That is my guilt.”

The ruler lifted him up, returned with him in the same carriage, and arranged a banquet of peace. He bestowed great rewards on the three armies. From then on, more than two hundred distant polities sent tribute to court.

Zhuge Liang reported that all the families of those dead in imperial service be granted every grace. The people were happy, and the court and world settled into tranquility.

At the Wei court, Cao Pi, the Wei sovereign, was in the seventh year of his reign, which was also the fourth year of Jianxing in Shu.

Cao Pi had first taken Lady Zhen as his consort. She had once been Yuan Xi’s wife, the second son of Yuan Shao, taken when Ye was first taken in battle. Later he had one son, Rui, whose courtesy name was Yuanzhong. From childhood Rui was quick-minded, and Cao Pi loved him deeply.

Cao Pi then also took the daughter of Guo Yong from Guangzong in Anping as an honored consort, and she was very handsome. Her father once said, “My daughter is a queen among women,” and so she was called the Queen.

When Lady Guo entered the palace, Lady Zhen lost favor. Lady Guo sought to become empress and plotted with trusted official Zhang Tao. While Cao Pi was ill, Tao claimed he had found a wooden figurine of paulownia wood in Lady Zhen’s quarters; inside was a written note naming the date and time for the rites of enthralment and suggesting rites of demon-binding. Cao Pi was furious and ordered Lady Zhen to die, then established Lady Guo as empress.

As there was no other issue, he raised Cao Rui as his son. Though he loved him very much, he did not name him heir.

When Rui reached fifteen, he was a practiced archer and rider. In that spring’s second month, Cao Pi went hunting with Rui. In a mountain ravine they drove off a doe and a stag. Cao Pi shot down the mother; when he turned, he saw a fawn racing before Rui’s horse.

Cao Pi shouted, “Why did my son not shoot it?”

Rui, in tears, replied from his mount, “Your Majesty has just killed its mother. How could I bear to kill its child as well?”

Cao Pi heard this and threw down his bow: “My son is truly a ruler of benevolent virtue!” He then made Rui Prince of Pingyuan.

In the fifth month of summer, Cao Pi was seized by an illness of cold and weakness, and doctors could not cure him. He summoned Grand General of the Central Army Cao Zhen, General Who Guards the Armies Chen Qun, and General Who Pacifies the Armies Sima Yi, to the inner palace.

Cao Pi called Cao Rui forward and said to Cao Zhen and the rest, “My illness is now heavy and grave. I shall not recover. This child is still young. The three of you must support him well and not disappoint my heart.”

All three answered, “Your Majesty, what makes you speak so? We are ready to expend all we have for Your Majesty, from the first to the tenth thousand years.”

Cao Pi said, “This year the city gates of Xuchang collapsed without cause. It is an ominous sign. I know in my bones that I must die.”

As he spoke, an inner attendant announced that the General Who Conquers the East, Cao Xiu, had come to ask after him. Cao Pi summoned him and said, “You are among the pillars of the state. If you can join in helping my son, I can die in peace.”

When he finished, he wept and died. He was forty years old and had reigned seven years.

Then Cao Zhen, Chen Qun, Sima Yi, and Cao Xiu one and all raised mourning and enthroned Cao Rui as Emperor of Wei in the same act.

They posthumously titled Cao Pi as Emperor Wen and Lady Zhen as Empress Wen Zhao.

Zhong Yao was made Grand Tutor, Cao Zhen Grand General, Cao Xiu Grand Marshal, Hua Xin Grand Commandant, Wang Lang Minister over the Masses, Chen Qun Minister of Works, and Sima Yi Grand General of Agile Cavalry.

Other civil and military ministers were each granted posthumous enfeoffments.

An amnesty was proclaimed across the realm.

At that time the frontiers of Yong and Liang lacked men to hold command. Sima Yi submitted a memorial requesting command of forces in the West and the Western part of Liang. Cao Rui approved and named him Inspector of military affairs there.

Soon messengers from the front reached Shu. Zhuge Liang was greatly alarmed: “Cao Pi is dead, and the boy Cao Rui has ascended. We need not fear everything else. Sima Yi has deep cunning, and if he trains those troops in Yong and Liang, he will one day become a great threat to Shu. Better to advance troops first.”
