Cao Pi’s old campaigner Ma Su said, “Now that the Chancellor has returned from the south, the horses and soldiers are exhausted and worn. We should care for them, not march so far again. I have a plan: make Sima Yi die by Cao Rui’s own hand. I am not sure whether the Chancellor approves it.”

Zhuge Liang asked what plan he had.

Ma Su answered, “Though Sima Yi is a senior minister of Wei, Cao Rui already distrusts him. Why not quietly send men to Luoyang and Ye and spread rumor that this man plots revolt; then craft an edict in Sima Yi’s name and paste a poster across the realm. Let Rui’s doubts rise. Then he will certainly execute him.”

Zhuge Liang agreed and sent men to carry out the ruse in secret.

In Ye City, one day a notice appeared pasted up on the gate. A guard removed it and brought it to Cao Rui.

Cao Rui read it:

General of Agile Cavalry Sima Yi, in charge of the forces and troops of Yong and Liang, makes this faithful proclamation to the people under Heaven:

The Martial Emperor of the Late Ancestors, Great Founder, established this realm and first intended to enthrone Prince Chen Si as lord of the altars and the state. Through years of slander and intrigue, a hidden dragon has long coiled in silence. The Son of Heaven Cao Rui, naturally without virtue, has dared to claim dignity for himself and has betrayed the late founder’s will.

In Heaven’s mandate and in response to the people, I now march at an auspicious day to satisfy the realm’s many wishes. From the day this notice reaches you, all are to submit at once to the new lord. Those who do not obey this order and remain alien to it will lose even their nine generations.

All this having been announced, I hope all know what must be done.

After Cao Rui finished reading he was stunned and pallid, and he asked the court ministers.

Grand Commandant Hua Xin said, “Sima Yi’s memorial to hold Yong and Liang already aimed at this. Long ago the Martial Emperor, the Great Founder, told me, ‘Sima Yi has an eagle’s eye and a wolf’s regard. Do not trust him with military command; he will surely become disaster in time.’ His rebellious intent is now manifest. He must be executed quickly.”

Wang Lang said, “Sima Yi deeply understands strategy, knows troops well, and has long harbored great ambition. If he is not removed now, he will surely become a calamity.”

Cao Rui then issued an order, considering a campaign in person. At that moment, Grand General Cao Zhen stepped forth from the guard rank and said, “No.

Emperor Wen entrusted his young heir to several of us. We know Sima Yi, style Zhongda, bears no rebel intent. We do not yet know whether this is true. If we immediately send troops in haste, we force him into rebellion. It may be that crafty men of Shu and Wu have spread double-dealing slanders to divide ruler and ministers.

If our lord and ministers fall into disorder, they may then strike from the opening and attack. Your Majesty should examine this well.”

Cao Rui asked, “If Sima Yi does plot treason, how then?”

Cao Zhen said, “If Your Majesty doubts him, imitate the Han Emperor Gao’s stratagem at Yunmeng. Let the Son of Heaven make an inspection at Anyi. Sima Yi will surely come to meet you; observe his conduct and seize him on the road before the carriages.”

Cao Rui followed this. He made Cao Zhen regent, took direct command of ten thousand imperial guards, and rode straight to Anyi.

Sima Yi did not know why the summons had come. Wanting to convey the Son of Heaven’s majesty, he gathered and arrayed his troops and came forward with several ten-thousands of armored men.

When a close courtier reported to him that Sima Yi had indeed brought ten or more ten-thousands and was coming to resist, clearly showing treason, Cao Rui hurriedly ordered Cao Xiu to lead troops out first to receive him.

When Sima Yi saw the troops advancing, he thought only that the Son of Heaven himself had arrived, so he descended in a ready stance by the road and rode forward to meet him. Cao Xiu said, “You bear the late emperor’s charge of entrustment. Why do you rebel?”

Sima Yi was greatly startled and sweated all over, then asked what it was for.

Cao Xiu explained the charge.

Sima Yi said, “This is a crafty plot from spies of Wu and Shu to drive our ruler and ministers into mutual destruction, so they may strike while we are divided. I shall present myself before the Son of Heaven and let him judge.”

He immediately withdrew his force and came before the carriage, knelt in front of the Son of Heaven and cried out in tears, “My lord, I received the late emperor’s entrustment. How could I have any different intent? It must be a rogue plan of Wu and Shu. Allow me to take one touring force, first defeat Shu and then strike Wu, thereby repaying the late emperor and Your Majesty so our loyalty is clear.”

Cao Rui’s doubts did not wholly end. Hua Xin said, “Do not give him military command. He should be dismissed at once and returned to the countryside.”

Cao Rui obeyed this counsel. He removed Sima Yi from office and sent him back to the fields, and appointed Cao Xiu to supervise Yong and Liang’s military forces.

Cao Rui then returned to Luoyang.

A spy soon learned this and reported it in Shu. When Zhuge Liang heard, he was very pleased: “I have long wished to march against Wei, but Sima Yi held the troops of Yong and Liang. He has now been trapped and demoted—what concern remains for me now?”

The next morning the ruler held a court morning audience. Ministers assembled, and Zhuge Liang submitted his memorial.

The text was:

I, your servant, say: The late emperor left his career unfinished, and before it was half complete his life broke in midstream. Today Heaven has divided the realm into three, and Shu’s Yi Province lies ruined. This is truly the critical moment of survival and ruin.

Yet officials serving at court are never lax within; men of loyal purpose and resolute hearts are willing to spend their lives in action outside, for they remember the late emperor’s exceptional favor and seek to repay it before Your Majesty. Therefore Your Majesty must open Your holy hearing, display the late emperor’s residual virtues, and restore the spirits of men of purpose, not belittle yourself without cause. Do not, in idle self-abasement, stretch a comparison to the point of losing meaning and thereby block up paths of loyal remonstrance.

Palace and government are one body; merit and fault in both should be judged by the same standards.

If someone commits treachery or breaks law, if one is loyal and good, this, too, must be passed to the proper offices for punishment and reward. Then Your Majesty’s impartial governance will be manifest. Do not incline to partiality so that inside and outside the court have different laws.

Guo Youzhi, Fei Yi, Dong Yun and the others among the court attendants and ministers are upright men, steadfast and true in thought and loyal in intention. This is why the late emperor selected them and left them in trust for Your Majesty. I believe all court and internal matters, large and small, should be referred to their counsel before implementation.

Then what is lacking can be supplied and shortcomings corrected, and the realm will benefit.

General Xiang Chong, with steady and proper conduct, is clear in military affairs and when he has served before he has been praised by the late emperor as competent. He was therefore widely recommended to serve as general supervisor. I think if all matters in camp are handled by him, all tasks large and small will be managed. The troops will move in rhythm and the worthy and unworthy be assigned as they ought.

One should honor the capable minister and keep distant the petty and corrupt; this made the earlier Han flourish.

One keeps the wicked near and the worthy far, and thus the later Han declined. While the late emperor ruled, he discussed this with me every time and never failed to sigh in pain and anger over Huan and Ling.

The Grand Master, Master of the Secretariat, Head Gentleman, and junior staff are all upright men who kept their vows; if Your Majesty gives faith to them and trusts them, then Han’s restoration can be expected soon.

I was once a commoner and plowed my own fields in Nanyang.

In this age of chaos I sought only to preserve my life, not to seek renown among other lords.

The late emperor did not dismiss me as low and base, but by force bent himself low and sought me three times in my thatched cottage to consult me on the affairs of this age. Because of this, I became stirred and moved and afterward agreed to drive him in times of crisis.

Later, when the world was overturned, I accepted responsibility at the edge of defeat, and in this great danger I have carried his command for over twenty years.

The late emperor knew my carefulness. Therefore, in danger he entrusted me with great affairs.

Since being given command, I have spent day and night in worry, fearing my reliance would fail and hurt the late emperor’s brilliance. So I crossed the Lu in the fifth month, and went deep into lands without growth. Now the south is secure, and the troops and supplies are sufficient.

I must reward these men and lead three armies, set our banner northward, and secure the Central Plains in our native way, that I may exhaust my meager ability to remove villains and restore Han, and bring the court back to the old capital.

This is how I would serve both the late emperor’s charge and Your Majesty’s role.

As for weighing and balancing what gains and losses, and giving all the full force of loyal speech, these matters are the charge of Guo Youzhi, Fei Yi, and Dong Yun.

If Your Majesty entrusts me with success in suppressing rebels and restoring the realm, then I am fulfilled. If I do not, then punish me for my failure, and report it to the late emperor’s spirit.

If there are no words of restoration, then hold Guo Youzhi, Fei Yi, Dong Yun, and the rest responsible, so that their arrogance may be exposed.

Your Majesty should also plan for yourself; seek counsel from men of good ways, receive restrained words, and pursue deeply the late emperor’s final edict. I cannot bear the honor and favor in full measure and have no words, for I weep as I present this memorial at such distance.

The ruler read it and said, “The Chancellor has gone far south and crossed many hardships. He has only just returned and not yet steadied his seat; he now asks to march north again. This may wear out spirit and thought.”

Zhuge Liang said, “Your servant has never slacked in either night or day under the late emperor’s charge. The south is now pacified. There need be no worry of inward concerns, for if this is not the time to punish rebels and recover Zhongyuan, when will it be?”

At that moment the court astronomer Qiao Zhou stepped forward and reported, “I have observed the heavenly signs all night. The rising force is strong in the north, and the stars are brighter than usual. It is not yet time.” He then looked at Zhuge Liang, asking, “The Chancellor understands astronomy deeply. Why force this?”

Zhuge Liang answered, “The Way of Heaven changes and is never fixed. How can we cling to fixed signs? I will first encamp in Hanzhong, observe the signs there, and then proceed.”

Qiao Zhou argued earnestly but without success. So Zhuge Liang left Guo Youzhi, Dong Yun, Fei Yi, and the rest as Grand Attendants to handle affairs in the inner court. He kept Xiang Chong as Grand General to supervise the imperial guard. Chen Zhen was made a Palace Attendant, Jiang Wan an Army Adviser, and Zhang Ye chief clerk in charge of Zhuge Liang’s chancellery.

Du Qiong became Remonstrance Minister; Du Wei and Yang Hong were made secretaries of the Ministry of Works. Meng Guang and Lai Min served as preceptors in the state school. Yin Mo and Li Zuan became scholars. Xi Zheng and Fei Shi were his secretaries. Qiao Zhou was made Grand Astrologer.

More than one hundred civil and military officials inside and outside therefore managed Shu’s government.

After receiving the imperial order to depart, Zhuge Liang gathered his generals and issued assignments:

  • Front commander of the vanguard: Wei Yan, who was General Who Guards the North, Inspector of Liang Province, and Marquis of Duting.
  • Commander of the forward army: Zhang Yi, who was also Administrator of Fufeng.
  • Yamen General, Auxiliary General: Wang Ping.
  • Commander of the rear army: Li Hui, who was General Who Pacifies the Han, Administrator of Jianing; deputy commander, Liu Yi, who was General Who Stabilizes the Far Frontier, Administrator of Hanzhong.
  • Left logistics commander of transport, simultaneously General Who Pacifies the North and Marquis of Chencang: Ma Dai. Deputy: Liao Hua, Flying Guard General.
  • Right commander: Ma Zhong, who was General Who Brings Courage and Marquis of Boyang, as the army commander.
  • General Who Pacifies the Barbarians, Marquis of Guannei: Zhang Ni.
  • Chief strategist in the middle: Liu Yan, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry, Marquis of Duxiang.
  • Central monitor: Deng Zhi, General Who Raises Arms.
  • Central staff officer: Ma Su, General Who Quiets the Far West.
  • Front general: Yuan Zhen, Marquis of Duting.
  • Left General: Wu Yi, Marquis of Gaoyang.
  • Right General: Gao Xiang, Marquis of Xuandu.
  • Rear General: Wu Ban, Marquis of Anle.
  • Chief clerk: Yang Yi, General Who Pacifies the Armies.
  • Front general: Liu Ba, General Who Conquers the South.
  • Front palace guard: Xu Yun, Auxiliary General and Marquis of Hancheng.
  • Left palace guard: Ding Xian, Gentleman of the Household Guard.
  • Right palace guard: Liu Zhi, Auxiliary General.
  • Rear palace guard: Guan Yong, Colonel of Army Registers.
  • Acting staff officers: Hu Ji, General of Zhaowu Middle Office; Yan Yan, General of Remonstrance; Cuan Xi, Auxiliary General; Du Yi, Auxiliary General; Du Qi, Military Strategist General; and Sheng Bo, Commander Who Pacifies the Barbarians.
  • Assistant officer: Fan Qi, Military Strategist General.
  • Register clerk: Fan Jian, a Clerk of Military Records.
  • Chancellor’s secretary: Dong Jue.
  • Commander before the pavilion, left court guard: Guan Xing, General Who Rides the Dragon Banner.
  • Right court guard: Zhang Bao, General of the Tiger Wing.

All these officers accompanied Zhuge Liang, now in his full charge as Beiping Great Inspector, Chancellor, Wuxiang Marquis, Governor of Yi Province, and Director of Internal and External Affairs.

After the deployment was set, he issued orders to Li Yan and others to hold the Shucou passes and guard against Eastern Wu.

On the bingyin day of the third month of spring in Jianxing year five, he launched the northern expedition.

Then an elder general stepped forward from the camp rank and spoke in a raised voice, “Though I am now old, I still have the courage of Lian Po and the vigor of Ma Yuan. Both these elders would not yield to age. Why do you not use me?”

The assembly recognized him as Zhao Yun.

Zhuge Liang said, “Since I returned from pacifying the south, Ma Mengqi has died. I regret him greatly and count it as losing one arm. The general is already advanced in years. If he is slightly out of step, even for a moment, it would shake his lifetime reputation and dull Shu’s sharp edge.”

Zhao Yun shouted back: “Since following our former ruler, I have never retreated in battle. When I face an enemy, I go first. A true man has it as good fortune to die on the field. What grievance could I have? I ask only to serve as the leading vanguard of the front.”

Zhuge Liang tried hard to dissuade him twice, but could not.

Zhao Yun replied, “If you do not assign me to be the vanguard, then I will die crashing at your gate!”

Zhuge Liang said, “If General Zhao Yun must be the vanguard, he must have one man to go with him.”

Before he finished, one man answered, “Though I am not worthy, I am willing to go first with the old general and lead a force to break the enemy.”

Zhuge Liang saw this was Deng Zhi. He rejoiced and assigned five thousand elite troops and ten deputy officers to accompany Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi.

When Zhuge Liang went on campaign, the Later Ruler, with a hundred officials, accompanied him out to ten li beyond the northern gate.

Zhuge Liang took leave of the ruler, then with banners covering the fields and spears and halberds thick as a forest, he and the army marched toward Hanzhong, winding forward in long lines.

Back at the border, this fact was reported in Luoyang. It was the day Cao Rui held court when attendants informed him: “The border officers report that Zhuge Liang has taken more than three hundred thousand men and encamped at Hanzhong. He has sent Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi as the leading vanguard of the front to force an invasion.”

Cao Rui was greatly startled and asked the ministers, “Who can lead against them?”

A man answered aloud. “My father died in Hanzhong, and I have a grudge bitten to the teeth that has never been repaid. Now that Shu troops have invaded the border, I wish to take my own division’s fierce horsemen and ask Your Majesty to grant me the troops of Guanzhong, so I may go and break the Shu army. In this way I can serve the state above and repay my father’s vengeance below. I will die ten thousand times with no regret.”

The court saw him and recognized him as Xiahou Mao, son of Xiahou Yuan.

Xiahou Mao’s courtesy name was Zixiu. He was quick-tempered and very stingy. From childhood he was raised alongside Xiahou Dun’s sons. After Xiahou Yuan had been slain by Huang Zhong, Cao Cao pitied him and by taking Lady Qinghe princess married him in as his son-in-law. Therefore he had great respect in court.

Though he wielded military command, he had never once set foot in battle. When he now requested expedition, Cao Rui made him Great Commander and sent out the Guanzhong routes’ armies—more than twenty wan troops—to meet Shu.

It was the perfect time for caution.

Wang Lang submitted remonstrance: “No.

He is an heir by marriage to Xiahou Yuan and has never known battle. This is too great a task for him. Moreover, Zhuge Liang is astute and resourceful and deeply learned in strategy. He is not to be lightly opposed.”

Xiahou Mao shouted, “Is the Minister of Works aligning with Zhuge Liang as an internal accomplice for this?”

“My upbringing with my father taught me deep stratagem and thorough art of war. How dare you call me young and inexperience? If I do not capture Zhuge Liang alive, I swear I will not face the Son of Heaven again!”

Wang Lang and the others did not dare respond. Xiahou Mao left the Wei ruler and rode through the night to Chang’an, mustering and directing troops from Guanzhong routes—more than two hundred thousand—to oppose Zhuge Liang.

The scene ended:

He longs to command the soldiers with a white plume, yet he leaves the reins of the army to Huangwen.

Who will prevail remains unknown.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Sacrificing at the Lu River, the Han Chancellor Returns His Army; Marching on the Central Plains, the Marquis of Wuhou Presents His Memorial

chapters.html:
Zhao Yun slays five generals;
Zhuge Liang takes three cities through stratagem.

Now Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, brought his soldiers forward to Mian County. As he passed Ma Chao’s tomb, he ordered his brother Ma Dai to hang mourning cloth and personally offered sacrifices there. After the rites, he returned to camp to discuss an advance. A scouting horseman then reported:

“Emperor of Wei, Cao Rui, has sent his son-in-law, Xiahou Mao, transferring troops from all the routes of Guanzhong to come and block the enemy.”

Wei Yan entered the front tent and presented a plan. “Xiahou Mao is a pampered noble scion, timid and poor in judgment,” he said. “If I can have five thousand elite troops, I can take the road out through Baozhong, go east along the Qinling, and by Ziwu Valley swing north. In no more than ten days, we can arrive at Chang’an. If word reaches Xiahou Mao that I am coming, he will abandon the city and flee through the western gate. Since I came this way from the east, the Chancellor can drive out troops and horses and strike hard through Xiagu Valley. In this way, Xianyang and everything west of it can be settled in one move.”

Zhuge Liang smiled. “This is no all-sided plan. You underrate the men of the Central Plains, saying there are no worthy men there. If you let someone suggest this and we move through a secluded mountain pass, five thousand men might be cut down and our spirit of the charge broken. It must not be used.”

Wei Yan added, “If the Chancellor advances by the great road, he will pull out all the Guanzhong troops to meet us on that route, and then the conflict will drag on. How then can we reach the Central Plains?”

Zhuge Liang answered, “I am advancing along the broad, level road from the upper Long plateau under regulation, and moving as ordered. Why should we fail?” He did not use Wei Yan’s plan. Wei Yan felt chagrined. Zhuge Liang sent Zhao Yun forward.

Meanwhile Xiahou Mao gathered troops from many routes at Chang’an. Among them came Han De, a major general of Xiliang, who was excellent at wielding a mountain-splitting axe and whose courage no ten thousand men could match. He brought eighty thousand Qiang soldiers from western paths and appeared before Xiahou Mao. When Xiahou Mao saw him, he rewarded him heavily and set him as the vanguard. Han De had four sons, all highly skilled in martial arts and equally gifted at bow and horse: Han Ying, Han Yao, Han Qiong, and Han Qi.

Han De came with his four sons and the eighty thousand Xiliang troops, taking the way to Fengming Mountain, where he met the Shu soldiers. The two formations faced each other. Han De mounted and placed his four sons on both flanks. Han De bellowed in scorn, “You traitor to the state, how dare you violate our borders!”

Zhao Yun flew into a rage, raised his spear, and spurred his horse, engaging Han De in single combat. Han Ying charged first on horseback. Before three exchanges, Zhao Yun thrust him through with one spear thrust and killed him under the horse. Seeing this, Han Yao spurred forward and swung a saber at the field. Zhao Yun summoned his old tiger vigor and steeled himself; Yao could not stand against him.

Han Qiong next charged with a raised Fangtian halberd. Zhao Yun did not yield, and his spear work never wavered. Then Han Qi, seeing his two elder brothers fail against Zhao Yun, also spurred out with two day-and-moon blades raised, and closed in to surround him. In the center, Zhao Yun alone fought three generals. After some time, Zhao Yun’s spear caught Han Qi and sent him from the saddle. A flank officer of Han’s army rushed out in haste to save him, and Zhao Yun pulled his spear and moved on. Han Qiong set down his halberd and shot three arrows in quick succession; all were knocked aside by Zhao Yun’s spear.

Han Qiong then grew furious, raised his Fangtian halberd again, and spurred ahead. Zhao Yun shot him in the face and he fell from his horse and died. Han Yao raised a precious saber and tried to chop Zhao Yun down. Zhao Yun dropped his spear, sidestepped the blade, captured Han Yao alive and brought him back through the lines, then mounted again and seized a spear to kill his way through the formation.

Han De saw all four sons lost to Zhao Yun and said his heart and guts were torn apart. He withdrew into the ranks. The Xiliang troops, who had long known Zhao Yun’s name, now seeing his old prowess alive before their eyes, dared not engage. Wherever Zhao Yun’s horse reached, ranks gave way. On his own he fought in and out through the lines with one spear, as if riding through an empty field.

Later, people praised him in a poem:

Once more I recall Zhao Zilong of Changshan; at seventy he still built rare deeds. Alone he cuts down four generals in the charge, as when he rescued the lord at Dangyang.

When Deng Zhi saw Zhao Yun’s overwhelming victory, he led Shu troops to strike in support. The Xiliang soldiers were badly beaten and ran. Han De had been nearly captured by Zhao Yun, and escaped only by casting off his armor and fleeing on foot. Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi then withdrew and pulled their men back to camp.

Deng bowed and said, “General, your age is seventy, yet your bravery remains as before. Today to behead four generals before the lines is a rarity in the world.”

Zhao Yun said, “The Chancellor, because he thinks I am old, does not seek to employ me. So I offer this only in token of myself.” He then ordered a messenger to untie Han Yao and send a dispatch about the victory to Zhuge Liang.

Afterward Han De returned with his broken army to report to Xiahou Mao and wept over his losses. Xiahou Mao, after gathering his forces himself, marched to meet Zhao Yun. When scouts reported to the Shu camp that Xiahou Mao was approaching, Zhao Yun took up his spear, mounted with more than a thousand men, and formed ranks before Fengming Mountain. That day Xiahou Mao wore a gilded helmet, sat on a white horse, held a great cleaver in hand, and stood beneath a gate-banner.

He saw Zhao Yun leaping from horse to horse and racing from side to side; Xiahou Mao wanted to fight him himself. Han De said, “I am the one who lost my four sons. How can I not return the blood for blood?” He mounted with a giant mountain-splitting axe, heading straight for Zhao Yun.

Zhao Yun gathered his fury and thrust forward with his spear. Before three exchanges, he skewered Han De in the chest and killed him beneath his horse, then wheeled to charge toward Xiahou Mao. Xiahou Mao hurriedly dodged back into his own line. Deng Zhi drove men in to kill from close range, and the Wei troops bent another line and withdrew more than ten li below the mountain.

That night Xiahou Mao conferred with his commanders and said, “Long have I heard of Zhao Yun, never having seen him; today, though old, the hero still lives. I now believe the event at Dangyang truly happened. Since there is none to meet him here, what are we to do?”

Army Adviser Cheng Wu, a son of Cheng Yu, advised, “I judge that Zhao Yun has courage but not stratagem and thus need not trouble us. Tomorrow, when the commander advances troops again, he should deploy both lines to the left and right. The commander can feign retreat at first, drawing Zhao Yun toward an ambush. Then he can climb the slope, command cavalry on all sides, and overlap to encircle him. Zhao Yun can then be captured.”

Xiahou Mao accepted this and sent Dongxi with thirty thousand to lie in wait on the left and Xue Ze with another thirty thousand to lie in wait on the right. The ambush was set.

The next day Xiahou Mao rallied drums, banners, and standards and marched out again. Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi rode out to meet him. On horseback Deng warned him, “Last night the Wei troops were beaten and fled; they have returned today, so there must be deceit. Guard yourself, old general.”

Zhao Yun replied, “How can this milk-toothed boy mean anything? Today I will surely capture him!” He leapt from his horse and rushed out. Wei general Pan Sui came out to face him. They fought less than three passes, and then Pan Sui turned and rode away. Zhao Yun pursued, and eight Wei commanders came together from the line. Xiahou Mao slipped away ahead; the eight generals came running in turn. Zhao Yun used the moment to press the kill and Deng Zhi pushed reinforcements forward.

Zhao Yun rode deep into dangerous ground, then heard a great roar of cries from all four sides. Deng Zhi urgently pulled back troops and withdrew. Left was Dongxi, right was Xue Ze, and both streams of soldiers closed in. Deng Zhi had too few men to rescue him. Zhao Yun was trapped in the center of the field, pushing east and west, while the Wei lines grew thicker and tighter.

Zhao Yun had only a little over a thousand men with him. He cut down enemies down to the foot of the slope and saw Xiahou Mao on the mountain directing three armies. He signaled east, then west, right and left, but found no gap. He then drew his men and tried to climb the mountain.

From midmorning until the hour of the rooster, heavy logs and stone-throwers struck down from above, and he could not gain the slope. From the hour of the Dragon he fought until the hour of the Rooster and could not break free. He dismounted at last and sat briefly in his armor, waiting for moonlight before fighting again.

When the moon had only just risen, firelight suddenly blazed in all directions, drums thundered, and arrows and stones fell like rain. Wei troops came on, all crying, “Zhao Yun, surrender now!” He leapt onto his horse to meet them. Encircling cavalry drew ever closer on all sides. Arbalests and bows shot from every direction with terrible speed; men and horses could not move forward. Zhao Yun looked to the sky and sighed, “I refuse to bow to old age, yet I am to die here!”

At that moment a great outcry rose from the northeast corner and the Wei troops began to break and scatter. A mass of troops came thundering in, led by a tall officer with an eight-foot steel spear, a severed head hanging beneath his horse’s neck. Zhao Yun recognized him as Zhang Bao.

Zhang Bao spoke: “The Chancellor fears the old general may fail; he sent me with five thousand troops to aid you. When I heard you were trapped, I cut a way through, and at once I have killed Wei commander Xue Ze. I can show his head here.”

Zhao Yun was very glad and fought his way out through the northwest corner with Zhang Bao. The Wei soldiers dropped spears and ran. Another group burst in from outside, led by a general carrying a crescent-green-dragon blade and dragging a severed head in his hands. Zhao Yun saw that he was Guan Xing.

Guan Xing said, “At the Chancellor’s command, fearing that the old general might fail, I brought five thousand troops to aid this rescue. As I came onto the field I met Wei commander Dongxi, and I cut him down. His head is hanging here. The Chancellor will arrive soon after.”

Zhao Yun said, “Both of you have already done extraordinary merit. Will you not seize Xiahou Mao today and settle the matter?”

Hearing this, Zhang Bao drew his men away to pursue his part. Guan Xing said, “I too go for merit,” and went with his men. Zhao Yun turned to his side: “Those two are like sons and nephews to me, and yet they still rush forward to make merit; but I, a senior general of the state and old court servant, should I not do no less than these younger men? I will stake my old life to repay my lord’s grace!”

He then led men in a three-route attack that night and broke one of the Wei lines. Deng Zhi came in support. The field was strewn with corpses, and blood ran like a river. Xiahou Mao was a man without strategy and, being young, untried in war. Seeing the army in collapse, he took more than a hundred picked men from his tent and fled toward Nan’an Commandery. The rest of the army, seeing no commander, all ran in all directions. When Guan Xing and Zhang Bao heard Xiahou Mao had gone toward Nan’an, they rode through the night to pursue.

Xiahou Mao entered the city and ordered the gates tightly shut, then drove the troops to defend. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao arrived and laid siege to it; Zhao Yun came soon after. It was a three-sided attack. Some time later Deng Zhi also arrived with men. For ten days they besieged and attacked without taking it.

A report then came that the Chancellor had left the rear army at Mianyang, stationed the left army at Yangping, stationed the right army at Shicheng, and had brought up the central force himself. Zhao Yun, Deng Zhi, Guan Xing, and Zhang Bao all came to bow before Zhuge Liang and report that several days of attack had not broken the city. Zhuge Liang rode in a light cart to the city’s edge, walked around it once, then returned and sat up in his pavilion. All the commanders stood around to hear orders.

Zhuge Liang said, “This commandery has deep moats and steep walls; it is not easy to take. Our real task is not this city. If you all keep attacking, then if Wei troops break out and head for Hanzhong, our army will be in danger.”

Deng Zhi said, “Xiahou Mao is Wei’s son-in-law. To capture this one man is equal to beheading a hundred generals. Since we are trapped here, can we simply abandon him?”

Zhuge Liang said, “I have a plan already. This is west of Tianshui commandery, bordering Anding Commandery to the north. Who are the two administrators?” A scout answered, “The Tianshui administrator is Ma Zun; the Anding administrator is Cui Liang.”

Zhuge Liang was delighted, then called Wei Yan and gave him instructions; then he also called Guan Xing and Zhang Bao and gave them instructions; then he summoned two trusted officers and gave each instructions as well. He sent them all off with orders.

Zhuge Liang himself remained outside Nan’an and had the army stack brushwood under the city wall, saying they were preparing to burn the city. The Wei soldiers heard and laughed without fear.

Meanwhile, in An Ding, commander Cui Liang heard that Shu troops were surrounding Nan’an and had trapped Xiahou Mao. He was in great panic. He rallied roughly four thousand men to defend the city. Soon he saw a man coming from due south, saying he had urgent confidential news. Cui Liang called him in.

The man said, “I am Pei Xu, an intimate officer under commander Xiahou. By order of the commander, I have come to request help from the two commanderies of Tianshui and An Ding. Nan’an is in urgent danger; each day they light fires on the walls as a signal and rely only on aid from both commanderies, but none has arrived. So I have slipped out through the encirclement to bring this warning. If you can raise troops in the night and offer forceful outside support, then when the commander sees reinforcements from both commanderies, he will open the gate to receive them.”

Cui Liang asked, “Do you have the commander’s orders?” Pei Xu took out the written command from where it was pasted under his flesh; it was wet with sweat. He read just a portion and urgently ordered his men to change horses, then left the city and rode toward Tianshui.

Two days later a courier arrived again: “The Tianshui commander has already raised troops to rescue Nan’an and has ordered An Ding to join.” Cui Liang consulted his officials. Many said, “If we do not go, losing Nan’an and surrendering Xiahou Mao will be our two commanderies’ fault. We must go.” Cui Liang at once rallied troops and left the city, leaving civil officers to hold it.

Cui Liang drove his men toward the road to Nan’an. From afar there was firelight in the sky and he spurred men onward through the night. With fifty li still before Nan’an, he suddenly heard loud cries from front and rear. A scout rode in: “Guan Xing blocks the road in front; Zhang Bao is striking from behind!” The soldiers of An Ding scattered in panic.

Greatly alarmed, Cui Liang led a hundred of his men onto a side path and fought his way back to survive, returning at speed to An Ding. As soon as they reached the city ditch, arrows flew in a wild rain from above. A Shu officer on the wall, Wei Yan, shouted, “The city has already been taken. Why do you not surrender now?”

It was indeed Wei Yan, masquerading as An Ding troops, who had worked through the night and opened the gate. Shu soldiers poured in and thus took An Ding.

Cui Liang fled in confusion back toward Tianshui. He had not gone far when a full troop array deployed before him. Beneath a great banner sat a man in black silk headcloth, feather fan, robe and crane-cape, calmly seated in a cart. Cui Liang recognized him as Zhuge Liang and turned his horse back in haste, attempting to flee. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao pressed in on two converging fronts, only calling, “Surrender at once!”

Surrounded on all sides and seeing no way out, Cui Liang surrendered and returned with the main camp. Zhuge Liang treated him as an honored guest.

Zhuge Liang asked, “What is your relation with Yangling of Nan’an?”

Cui Liang answered, “This man is Yang Ling, younger kinsman of Yang Fu. He is close to your neighboring commandery.”

Zhuge Liang said, “I now need you to enter the city and ask whether Yang Ling can capture Xiahou Mao.”

Cui Liang said, “If the Chancellor wishes, I can retreat the armies a short distance and make room for me to enter the city and speak with him.”

Zhuge Liang agreed and ordered all four sides of the army to pull back twenty li to camp.

Single-hearted, Cui Liang arrived at the city wall and called for the gate to be opened. Inside, after formal greetings with Yang Ling, he quietly explained the matter. Yang Ling said, “We have all received great grace from the Wei ruler. How could we betray it? Let us turn the ruse against itself.” He then led Cui Liang to Xiahou Mao and explained everything in detail.

Xiahou Mao asked, “What plan should be used?”

Yang Ling replied, “If I alone offer the gate, luring the Shu troops in, we can kill them in the city.”

Cui Liang followed that plan back to Zhuge Liang and reported, “Yang Ling says he will offer the gate to bring in the Shu army, and then kill them within the city, but his own warriors are few and he dares not move too quickly.”

Zhuge Liang said, “This is easy enough. You now have over a hundred surrendered men. We can hide in them the trusted Shu officers disguised as An Ding soldiers and bring them inside. They will lie in wait beneath Xiahou Mao’s estate. But inside we will secretly coordinate with Yang Ling: at midnight, you open the gates, and while we move inside, I will join with you and capture him.”

Cui Liang thought it over: if he brought no Shu officer in, Zhuge Liang might suspect; if he brought them in and then killed them inside, he could also light the signal fire and lure Zhuge Liang in to be killed. He therefore agreed.

Zhuge Liang added, “I send trusted Guan Xing and Zhang Bao to go with you first. Have them forceful as rescue troops and enter the city so Xiahou Mao feels steadied. But once the fire signal is raised, I will enter myself to take him.”

At dusk, Guan Xing and Zhang Bao received Zhuge Liang’s secret instructions, donned armor, mounted and carried weapons, and mingled into An Ding soldiers. They followed Cui Liang back to the gate of Nan’an. Yang Ling stood on the wall on a suspended board, bracing his chest against a rail, and asked, “From where are these troops?”

Cui Liang answered, “The Tianshui relief force has arrived.”

Cui Liang first fired a signal arrow into the city; tied to it was a secret note reading, “Zhuge Liang has already sent two generals to lie in wait inside the city, for joint work from within and without. Do not make the slightest noise, lest our design be leaked. Let them enter the yamen first; examine the matter there.”

Yang Ling showed the note to Xiahou Mao, explaining it fully. Xiahou Mao said, “Since Zhuge Liang has fallen for it, have one hundred ax-and-hammer men lie in wait in the estate. If the two generals arrive with Governor Cui and dismount, close the gate and kill them. At the same time, raise the signal fire on the wall and lure Zhuge Liang inside. Then the ambush can all come out and seize him.”

When preparations were complete, Yang Ling returned to the wall and reported, “Since these are relief troops from An Ding, they may be admitted.” Guan Xing went first with Cui Liang, with Zhang Bao behind.

Yang Ling descended and came to the gate to receive them. As the two were near, Guan Xing raised his sword and cut Yang Ling down at the horse’s feet. Cui Liang was startled and immediately wheeled his horse to flee. At the bridge called Diao, Zhang Bao shouted, “You wretch, do not run! You were hiding this trick—how could you think to deceive the Chancellor?” and thrust a spear into Cui Liang, killing him.

Guan Xing had already reached the city and raised the signal fire. Shu soldiers from all sides poured in. Xiahou Mao, caught off guard, opened the south gate and tried to force his way out with all his strength. A troop met him from the front; its leading general was Wang Ping. With only one clash of horses, Wang Ping fought hand-to-hand and took Xiahou Mao alive, still mounted. The rest were all killed.

Zhuge Liang entered Nan’an, proclaimed peace to the soldiers and citizens, and harmed no one, not even an ear of grain. Each commander offered his own account of merit. Zhuge Liang had Xiahou Mao placed in confinement in a cart.

Deng Zhi asked, “How did the Chancellor know Cui Liang was deceitful from the beginning?”

Zhuge Liang replied, “I already knew this man had no intention of surrender, so I intentionally led him in. He was determined to report everything to Xiahou Mao and to proceed with the counter-plot. In such a situation, I understood his deceit and still sent the two generals along, to steady his mind. If he had truly meant sincere loyalty, he would surely block this at once. If he joyfully lets us go together, he may suspect no design. In his mind he figured our two generals would enter and kill him before we moved; meanwhile he would have my army on borrowed ground and feel at ease to press on. I have already secretly told those two generals to act beneath the gate. The city will have no preparation. When my army comes right behind, they will be struck unawares.”

Zhuge Liang continued, “It was Cui Liang I deceived by sending a trusted man to impersonate Wei officer Pei Xu. I had also gone to draw in the Tianshui commandery, and I still have not arrived there, and I do not know why. We should now take advantage and seize it.” He then ordered Wu Yi to hold Nan’an, Liu Yan to hold An Ding, and sent Wei Yan’s force out to take Tianshui Commandery.

That said, in Tianshui, the commander Ma Zun heard that Xiahou Mao was trapped in Nan’an. He assembled civil and military officials to discuss it. The audit clerk Liang Xu, the clerk Yin Shang, the recorder Liang Qian, and others said, “Xiahou Mao is the Wei ruler’s son-in-law, a branch of the imperial tree. If there is any lapse, we cannot hide from the crime. How can we sit still as a governor while this is so?”

Ma Zun was still hesitating when suddenly an aide from Xiahou arrived: Pei Xu from within the command. He entered the hall and delivered an official document: “The commander seeks troops from both Tianshui and An Ding and has ordered immediate aid through the night.” After giving the document, he left in haste.

The next day another horseman arrived with the same report: “An Ding’s troops have already gone first and ordered your governor to hurry and join.” As Ma Zun was preparing to mobilize, a man came in from outside shouting, “Governor Ma, you have fallen into Zhuge Liang’s plan!”

The man was Jiang Wei of Gansu. “My family name is Jiang, personal name Wei, courtesy name Boyue,” the officer later introduced. His father, Jiong, had once been an administrative clerk in Tianshui Commandery and had died in state turmoil among the Qiang. Since youth Jiang Wei studied widely in books and mastered military strategy and martial arts; no discipline was beyond him. Filial to his mother, he was respected by the people, and later became a General of the Central Army and served with local troops.

That day Jiang Wei said to Ma Zun, “I have heard that Zhuge Liang has beaten Xiahou Mao and that he is now trapped at Nan’an with no route for supply; how could a man truly break through a heavy encirclement and then return out? Moreover, Pei Xu is an officer without any established rank. I have never seen him. Besides, there is no official document with the report from An Ding. From this I judge this person is not a Shu general posing as a Wei officer. He has lured the governor outside; once he sees the city without preparation, he has likely hidden troops nearby and intends to seize Tianshui through the opening.”

Ma Zun suddenly understood. “Without Boyue’s words, we would have fallen for this wicked plan.”

Jiang Wei answered calmly, “Governor, do not worry. I have a plan that can capture Zhuge Liang and lift the danger at Nan’an.”

Then was sung:

Strategy and maneuver meet another master hand, In intellectual combat he finds another unexpected opponent.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhao Yun Slays Five Generals; Zhuge Liang Takes Three Cities by Stratagem

chapters.html:
Jiang Wei, whose courtesy name was Boyue, presented his plan to Ma Zun:

“Zhuge Liang will set an ambush behind the commandery and draw my army out of the city, then strike while we are out. I ask leave for three thousand elite troops to lie in wait along the key roads. The Administrator can send the main force out afterward, but he must not push far. Return after thirty li. Wait for the signal of raised fire, and then attack from front and rear for a great victory. If Zhuge Liang comes himself, he is certainly one I can take alive.”

Ma Zun used the plan and sent three thousand carefully selected men with Jiang Wei. Then he and Liang Qian brought out troops and waited by themselves outside the city, leaving Liang Xu and Yin Shang to hold the city.

As expected, Zhuge Liang had already ordered Zhao Yun to hide one army in a secluded mountain pass, waiting until the Tianshui troops marched out before striking. That day a scout reported to him that Ma Zun had sent troops out and left only civil officials inside the walls. Zhao Yun rejoiced and sent word to Zhang Yi and Gao Xiang to set an ambush on the main roads to cut down Ma Zun. Those two detachments had been prepared beforehand by Zhuge Liang.

Later, Zhao Yun led five thousand troops and came straight beneath Tianshui Commandery. He shouted, “I am Zilong of Changshan. You have been tricked. Surrender the city now and live.”

From the wall, Liang Xu laughed: “You are still pretending not to know you have fallen into my plan with Jiang Boyue, are you?”

When Zhao Yun was ready to storm the city, a tremendous cry rose and flames roared from all sides. A young commander rode forward with a spear and said, “Have you seen Jiang Boyue of Tianshui?”

Zhao Yun thrust his spear and rode straight at Jiang Wei. Their fight lasted only a few rounds, and Jiang Wei’s strength seemed to surge beyond ordinary limits.

Zhao Yun was startled: “Who would think such a figure was waiting here?”

At that instant, both flanks struck hard. It was Ma Zun and Liang Qian returning with their troops. Zhao Yun could not hold both front and rear. He cut a path through and withdrew with battered men, while Jiang Wei closed in. He was saved by Zhang Yi and Gao Xiang’s forces bursting out from two other approaches.

When Zhao Yun returned to Zhuge Liang, he admitted the enemy plot had succeeded. Zhuge Liang asked in surprise, “Who is this man who reads my scheme so clearly?” A man from Nan’an reported:

“His family name is Jiang, given name Wei, courtesy name Boyue, and he is from Jizhou. He is extraordinarily filial to his mother, complete in both letters and arms, with both wisdom and courage; he is truly one of the worthies of this age.”

Zhao Yun added that Jiang Wei’s spearwork was unlike any he had seen. Zhuge Liang said, “I did not expect to meet such a man when I marched into Tianshui.” He then led the main army forward.

Once more Jiang Wei returned to Ma Zun and reported: “Zhao Yun has been driven back, so Zhuge Liang will come in person. He will expect my army to be in the city. Divide our men into four formations. I will send one branch to lie east of the city and intercept the enemy if they arrive. The Administrator and Liang Qian and Yin Shang each bring one branch to lie in ambush outside the walls. Liang Xu should keep the wall defenses with the civilians.”

The distribution was fixed.

Because Zhuge Liang feared Jiang Wei, he commanded the vanguard and headed toward Tianshui. As he neared, he said, “In every siege, on the first day the armies must be roused and driven forward with shouting and drums. If the assault is delayed too long, morale collapses and the chance to break through is lost.”

So the main force went directly beneath the walls. He saw the gate banners on the city in good order and did not dare a light assault. At midnight, fire suddenly flared in four directions and a roar of voices shook the earth. No one could tell where the troops came from. From the city too came drum and shout in answer, and the Shu men scattered in confusion.

Zhuge Liang mounted in haste, guarded by Guan Xing and Zhang Bao, cut through the thickest press, and looked back. Eastward rose a line of cavalry and horsemen, a long stretch of firelight like a serpent.

He ordered Guan Xing to scout. The return was swift: “It is Jiang Wei’s force.”

Zhuge Liang sighed. “A force is not won by numbers but by deployment. This man truly is a general of talent.”

He withdrew to camp, thought long, then called for a man from Anding:

“Where is Jiang Wei’s mother now?”

The answer came: “Wei is now in Jixian.”

Kongming told Wei Yan:

“Take a detachment and make noise as if for an assault. Fake a strike on Jixian. If Jiang Wei comes, let him enter the city. Tell me: where is the key point here?”

The man of Anding said, “Tianshui’s grain and supplies are all at Shanggu. If Shanggu falls, his supply road is cut.”

Kongming was delighted. He sent Zhao Yun with a detachment to seize Shanggu.

He camped three thousand li from the city.

Soon word reached Tianshui that the Shu army had split into three groups: one remained to hold this commandery, one moved on Shanggu, and one on Jicheng. Hearing this, Jiang Wei asked Ma Zun desperately:

“Mother is now in Jicheng. I fear her safety. I beg one branch to run to that city and guard my mother.”

Ma Zun consented, and so ordered Jiang Wei with three thousand troops to guard Jicheng while Liang Qian took three thousand to Shanggu.

Jiang Wei reached Jicheng. A mass of troops lined the front, with Wei Yan commanding at its head. After several rounds of clash, Wei Yan feigned defeat and withdrew.

Wei Wei entered the gates, shut them, and held his men to defend inside. He paid respects to his mother and did not go out to battle.

Zhao Yun also let Liang Qian pass and move on to Shanggu city.

Zhuge Liang then ordered that a man from Nanan bring Xiahou Mao to camp.

He asked him, “Do you fear death?”

Xiahou Mao threw himself down and begged for life.

Zhuge Liang said, “Jiang Wei now holds Jizhou. He has sent a message saying, ‘If the son-in-law is here, I am willing to submit.’ I will spare your life if you persuade him to surrender. Will you do so?”

Xiahou Mao said, “I am willing to submit.”

Then Zhuge Liang gave him clothing and horsegear and sent him out without attendants.

Xiahou Mao slipped from camp and tried to make his way, but he did not know the roads. As he rode, he ran into several hurried townsfolk.

He asked where they were going.

“They are Jixian villagers,” they replied. “Jiang Wei has yielded the city and surrendered to Zhuge Liang. Wei Yan, a Shu officer, set fires and plundered goods, so we fled from our homes and now run toward Shanggu.”

Xiahou Mao asked, “Who holds Tianshui city now?”

“They say it is held by your Administrator, Ma.”

When he heard this he spurred toward Tianshui. He also passed groups of men and women with children and heard the same report.

At the base of Tianshui city he called to the gate. The townspeople recognized him as Xiahou Mao and hurriedly opened the gate to receive him. Ma Zun hurried forward in salutation.

Xiahou Mao gave a careful account of Jiang Wei’s actions and the villagers’ report.

Ma Zun sighed, “I did not expect Jiang Wei truly to join Shu.”

Liang Xu said, “He meant to rescue the Commander in chief, so he used this as a pretext for a false submission.”

Xiahou Mao said, “Now he has already surrendered. How can it be a pretense?”

While they hesitated, it had already become the first watch. Shu troops came again to attack the city.

In the firelight appeared Jiang Wei beneath the walls, spear in hand and horse forward, shouting, “Call on Xiahou Commander to answer me!”

Xiahou Mao and Ma Zun went up to the wall. Seeing Jiang Wei in martial display and loudness, he shouted:

“I surrendered as a Commander. What did you do to break your promise?”

Xiahou Mao answered, “You accepted Wei’s grace and then surrendered to Shu. What promise had you made?”

Jiang Wei replied, “Did you send me a letter to surrender to Shu? Why do you speak this now? You sought a way to slip away, but you entangled me! I have now submitted to Shu and been raised among the foremost ranks. How could I return to Wei now?”

After speaking, he drove his men against the walls and withdrew only at dawn.

It became clear in hindsight that the man seen as Jiang Wei that night had been a decoy arranged by Zhuge Liang— soldiers made to resemble him, made up in his likeness. In the fire and confusion, none could tell true from false.

Kongming then led his army on Jicheng. Food inside was already short. Jiang Wei watched from the walls as Shu carts carrying grain moved into Wei Yan’s camp. He led three thousand men out of the city and came straight to seize the supplies.

The Shu troops abandoned their wagons and fled when they saw it. Jiang Wei gained the grain and tried to return to the city, only to be stopped by a mass of soldiers with Zhang Yi in front. They fought a few rounds. Then Wang Ping arrived with another force. The two sides pressed from both sides.

Wei Yan’s strength failed; he could not withstand and took back-road course to the city. The Shu flag was already raised on the walls: they had already been overtaken by Wei Yan.

Wei Wei fled, with only ten riders left. He met Zhang Bao and cut down one engagement. Then only one horse and one spear remained, and he came to the base of Tianshui city, crying for the gate.

The soldiers on the walls recognized him as Jiang Wei and shouted alarm to Ma Zun.

“This is Jiang Wei come to trick my gate,” said Ma Zun, and ordered volleys of arrows down into the city.

Jiang Wei looked back and saw Shu troops already close. He spurred for Shanggu.

On the wall at Shanggu, Liang Qian saw him and shouted abuse: “You traitor who betrayed the state, how dare you try to trick my city? I already know you have surrendered to Shu!”

Then another hail of arrows came down.

Wei Wei could not speak for himself and cried out to heaven as he rode, tears running down his face, and turned his horse toward Chang’an.

After only a few li, he reached a dense grove by a great tree. A shout rose, and thousands of troops rushed out. In front rode Guan Xing and blocked the way.

Wei Wei, with horse and body exhausted, could not stand against it. He wheeled his horse and turned to run. Suddenly a small cart came from a slope in the mountain.

Its occupant wore a kerchief and a crane-cloak and held a feather fan. It was Zhuge Liang.

Kongming called, “Boyue, why do you still delay your submission?”

After long thought, with Zhuge Liang before him, Guan Xing behind and no road left, he dismounted and surrendered.

Kongming at once leapt from the cart and approached him. “Since leaving my thatched hut, I have searched everywhere for worthy men to whom I might pass on a lifetime of learning, but regretted that I had found no one fit. Now to meet you, Boyue, is enough for me.”

Jiang Wei joyfully bowed and gave thanks.

Kongming returned with Jiang Wei to the camp and discussed how to take Tianshui and Shanggu.

Wei Wei said, “In Tianshui city, Liang Xu and Yin Shang are very loyal to me. Let me write two secret letters and shoot them into the city. If the city is thrown into disorder, we can take it.”

Kongming agreed.

Jiang Wei wrote two secret letters, tied them to arrows, rode down to the base of the walls, and shot them in.

A junior officer retrieved the arrows and presented them to Ma Zun.

Ma Zun became highly doubtful and discussed with Xiahou Mao, “Liang Xu and Yin Shang may have joined with Jiang Wei and be ready to respond from within. The governor should decide quickly.”

Xiahou Mao said, “They can both be put to death.”

Yin Shang, hearing this, told Liang Xu, “Better to accept surrender to Shu and seek further gain.”

That night Xiahou Mao sent men many times requesting Liang Xu and Yin Shang to come speak. The two saw that matters had become urgent. They donned armor and mounted, each leading his own troops. They opened the gates widely and brought Shu soldiers in.

Xiahou Mao and Ma Zun were shaken. They took only a few hundred and left by the west gate, abandoning the city and escaping toward Qiang Zhong.

Liang Xu and Yin Shang welcomed Zhuge Liang inside the walls.

After pacifying the populace, Kongming asked who would handle Shanggu. Liang Xu said, “That city is held by my own younger brother Liang Qian. I hope to bring him over.”

Kongming was pleased. Liang Xu later went to Shanggu, called Liang Qian out to surrender.

Kongming granted heavy rewards and made Liang Xu Administrator of Tianshui, Yin Shang Magistrate of Jicheng, and Liang Qian Magistrate of Shanggu.

When his dispositions were set, he drew up the army and advanced.

The generals asked, “Why does the Chancellor not pursue and capture Xiahou Mao?”

Kongming said, “I let Xiahou Mao go as easily as releasing a duck. Now I have Boyue. I have gained a phoenix.”

After securing three cities, his renown roared outward; provinces and commanderies near and far yielded in fear and followed him. Zhuge Liang adjusted his armies, rallied the troops from Hanzhong, and moved out toward Qishan. The army came to the west of the Wei River.

A scout entered Luoyang with the report.

It was now the first year of the Taihe era. Cao Rui, the Wei ruler, ascended the throne and convened court. A close courtier reported: “Xiahou Mao has lost three commanderies and has fled into Qiang Zhong. Shu troops have reached Qishan; the forward force stands on the west bank of the Wei River. We should send troops at once to break them.”

Cao Rui was greatly startled and asked the ministers, “Who can drive the Shu force away?”

Wang Lang, the Minister over the Masses, spoke: “My lord, I observed your father’s rule: wherever Great General-in-Chief Cao Zhen went, he prevailed. Why does Your Majesty not appoint him as Great Commander to send back the Shu?”

Cao Rui approved and called Cao Zhen.

“This was the arrangement made by the late ruler,” he said, “who charged all these to you. Now Shu troops have invaded the heartland. Could you bear to sit idle?”

Cao Zhen replied humbly: “My abilities are shallow and my insight limited; I am not equal to the post.”

Wang Lang said, “General, you are a minister of the state’s foundations. You may not refuse. Though I am old and dull, I will follow you.”

Cao Zhen bowed again: “I have received great favor; how can I refuse? I only ask for one deputy.”

Cao Rui said, “You may choose.”

Cao Zhen named Guo Huai, a native of Yangqu in Taiyuan, surname Guo, name Huai, courtesy name Boji, marquis of Sheting and Inspector of Yong Province.

Cao Rui assented and appointed Cao Zhen Great Commander, giving him the insignia of authority. Guo Huai was made deputy commander and Wang Lang served as military adviser. Wang Lang was already seventy-six years old.

He drew and deployed two hundred thousand troops and horses from both eastern and western metropolitan armies for Cao Zhen.

Cao Zhen appointed his brother Cao Zun as vanguard and Zhu Zan, General Who Suppresses Bandits, as deputy vanguard.

In the eleventh month he marched out. Cao Rui himself accompanied them past the west gate before returning.

Cao Zhen led the main force to Chang’an and camped on the west side of the Wei River. Cao Zhen, Wang Lang, and Guo Huai discussed how to drive back the army.

Wang Lang said, “Tomorrow, make the ranks clean and raise full banners. I will only need one speech, for I alone can make him lay down his arms and return. If I speak, Zhuge Liang will bow and retreat.”

Cao Zhen was pleased. That night he ordered that tomorrow at the fourth watch the troops wake and by dawn the ranks be exact, with proper horse and men, banners, drums, and horns in proper sequence.

He sent out a formal challenge first.

The next day the two armies faced one another, arrayed before Qishan.

Shu soldiers saw the Wei force and its splendor and found it utterly different from Xiahou Mao’s.

When the drums and horns of both armies had ceased, Wang Lang rode out. At the head stood Commander-in-Chief Cao Zhen, behind him the deputy commander Guo Huai; the two vanguard elements held the wings.

A scout on horse came before the lines and called, “Let the leading commanders on both sides answer.”

In the opening of the Shu gate banners, Guan Xing and Zhang Bao came out on right and left, each taking horse. Then squads of fierce commanders came out in line. Under the shadow of the gate flags, in the center there was a four-wheeled cart. Zhuge Liang sat upright within it, wearing a cloth kerchief and feather fan, plain garments and blue sash, and moved out like a drifting cloud.

Kongming looked toward the first three military banners and saw one central white-bearded old man. It was Wang Lang, the Minister of Masses.

He thought to himself: “Wang Lang will deliver a set speech; I shall answer as occasion demands.” He told his guards to bring the cart forward outside the formation and sent the bodyguard to announce, “Han Chancellor and Minister of Masses will speak.”

Wang Lang rode out.

Kongming bowed from the cart; Wang Lang in his saddle lowered himself in return.

Wang Lang said, “For many days I have heard your great reputation. We are fortunate to meet at last. Since you understand Heaven’s order and know the times, why raise an unknown host?”

Kongming answered, “I obey the imperial commands to punish rebels. How can you call that an unknown host?”

Wang Lang continued: “Changes in Heaven’s decrees move dynasties; Heaven’s mandate passes to men of virtue. Since Huan and Ling, the Yellow Turban banners rose and the realm was torn. From early Ping and Jian’an to the present, Dong Zhuo rebelled, then Kuai and Zhi continued oppression; Yuan Shu usurped at Shouchun, Yuan Shao rose in power at Ye; Liu Biao occupied Jingzhou, while Lü Bu swallowed Xuzhou like a tiger’s maw. Bandits rose, ambitious warlords soared, and the state stood in danger of collapsing like eggs on a fragile nest, the people hanging by a thread.

“My Great Father and Ancestor, Martial Emperor, swept through all under heaven and rolled over all the wilds. The myriad households were moved and all quarters admired his virtue. This was not seized by force alone but came as Heaven’s will. My Great Grandfather, Emperor Wen, by sacred learning and warcraft received the Great Unification, in harmony with heaven and with men. He followed Yao and Shun and brought order to China, ruling all with justice. Is that not the heart of heaven and people combined?

“Now you, possessing grand talent and a great vessel, have the audacity to compare yourself to Guan Le and Qi. Why do you force this against Heaven’s law and against human feeling?

“Have you not heard the old saying: “He who follows Heaven prospers; he who defies Heaven dies.”

“Our Wei now fields a million armored troops and has a thousand worthy generals. How can the light of fireflies in rotten grass match the bright moon of Heaven’s mind? Cast down your arms and submit in ceremony. You will not lose your grant of marquis rank. With peace in the realm and joy for the people, what could be better?”

Kongming laughed broadly from the cart: “I thought the Senior Han minister would speak in lofty words; I did not expect this coarse speech.

“I have one word. Let all troops stand still and hear: In the days of Huan and Ling the Han mandate was overturned, eunuchs provoked disaster, famines and calamities shook the years, and the four quarters were in confusion. After the Yellow Turban tumult, Dong Zhuo, Kuai, and Zhi rose one after another, displacing the Han emperor and brutalizing the people.

“Because the court had fallen to rotten wood and the court steps fed beasts, jackals and hounds ran everywhere. Dog-faced flatterers and kneeling maids wielded office. Thus state altars became mounds, and the people burned. I have long known your conduct. Born on the shores of the Eastern Sea, you began as a local xiào lián and entered office rightly to rectify and aid your sovereign, to support Han and restore the House of Liu. How then did you become helper to rebel traitors and co-conspirator in usurpation?

“Your guilt is deep and Heaven cannot tolerate it. The people of the world wish to eat your flesh. Since Heaven has not ended the Han flame, and Emperor Zhaolie has inherited the line in western Sichuan, I now follow the command of the heir and raise soldiers to campaign against rebels. As a sycophantic courtier, you should hide yourself and live for your belly and clothing. How dare you stand in this army’s front rank and claim to know Heaven’s mandate?

“You old gray-haired man! You old bearded traitor! You will go today beneath the Nine Springs and have no face to stand before the twenty-four emperors. Retire at once, and call on the rebel ministers to settle victory and defeat with me!”

Wang Lang, on hearing this, clenched in rage, bellowed once, and was thrown from his horse and killed.

Later some people later wrote a verse praising Zhuge Liang:

The troops and horses rode out from Western Qin, strong enough to face ten thousand men; With but a three-inch tongue lightly stirred, they cursed the old traitor and sent him dead.

Kongming pointed with his fan to Cao Zhen and said, “I will not press you. Mend your ranks and horses and meet me in battle tomorrow.”

When he had finished, he returned to his cart.

So both armies withdrew.

Cao Zhen had Wang Lang’s corpse put in a coffin and sent back to Chang’an.

Deputy Commander Guo Huai said, “If we have lost a commander in mourning, Zhuge Liang will surely come to plunder our camp tonight. Divide the troops in four roads: two through secluded mountain tracks to strike our camp suddenly; two to lie outside our camp and strike from both sides.”

Cao Zhen agreed warmly. “This is very much the same as my thought.” He ordered Cao Zun and Zhu Zan, the two vanguards, to each take ten thousand troops and move behind Qishan. “As soon as you see the Shu force moving toward our camp, strike and plunder. If the Shu force stays still, withdraw at once. Do not push too hard.”

The two obeyed and rode out.

Cao Zhen told Guo Huai, “The two of us each bring one branch of troops and lie outside the camp. Keep only a few men inside and heaped brushwood there. If the Shu troops arrive, raise fire as the signal.”

Each general then prepared himself on left and right.

Back in camp, Zhuge Liang called Zhao Yun and Wei Yan and gave instructions.

Kongming said, “Each of you take your own main formation and go to loot the Wei camp.”

Wei Yan objected, “Cao Zhen deeply understands military method. He surely expects us to go for the camp. Did he not prepare for this?”

Kongming smiled. “It is exactly what I want him to think. He will lie with an ambush behind Qishan, waiting for us to pass. Then he will strike our camp. That is why I send you both along a path around the foot of the mountains, far enough down the encampment, to stand ready for when the Wei force moves to plunder us.

“When fire rises, divide into two routes. Wenchang hold the mountain pass. Zilong, lead your men back. When you meet Wei forces, let them think they are driving you off and then press on to attack them. They will come and cut each other down. We will gain a complete victory.”

The two generals accepted the plan and set out.

Kongming also called Guan Xing and Zhang Bao and told them: “Both of you take a force and lie on the main road at Qishan. Let the Wei army pass, then return by their trail and run hard toward Wei camp.”

They obeyed and went.

He ordered Ma Dai, Wang Ping, Zhang Yi, and Zhang Ni to lie outside the camp and stand ready to strike from four sides.

Kongming then built a hollow stockade before the camp, piling brushwood in the center to be used for the signal of flames. He withdrew all commanders to the back of camp and watched for movement.

Cao Zhen’s vanguard Cao Zun and Zhu Zan left camp at dusk. Near the second watch, they saw troops moving in the distance before the mountain.

Cao Zun thought, “Deputy Guo has truly divine understanding,” and pushed his men forward in haste.

They were within reach of the Shu camp at the third watch. Cao Zun entered first and found an empty camp. There was no one there, and he knew he had been deceived. He withdrew quickly.

At once the camp fire was raised.

Then Zhu Zan arrived and his men cut one another down in confusion, trampling men and horses into disorder.

When Cao Zun and Zhu Zan realized this they reined to one another and saw the mess. They tried to gather their strength. Suddenly a great roar rose from all four sides. Wang Ping, Ma Dai, Zhang Ni, and Zhang Yi had arrived.

Cao Zun and Zhu Zan each drew away with no more than a hundred close riders and ran for the main road.

Suddenly horns and drums rang all at once. A body of troops blocked their route. At its head was Commander Zilong of Changshan, calling, “Wicked general, where are you running? Be ready to die now!”

Cao Zun and Zhu Zan tried to force their way through, only to be driven back.

Then another cry rose, and Wei Yan led another troop into the field.

The two generals suffered a major defeat and ran ten li back to their camp.

The sentries inside thought the Shu army had come to plunder and, in panic, raised the fire-signs.

On the left, Cao Zhen rode in; on the right, Guo Huai rode in, and each side struck into the other.

From the rear, three routes of Shu force arrived: in the center Wei Yan, on the left Guan Xing, on the right Zhang Bao. A great slaughter followed.

Wei troops fled for more than ten li. Their losses were heavy.

Kongming won complete victory, then gathered his forces.

Cao Zhen and Guo Huai collected their scattered army and returned to camp. They spoke: “Now Wei’s force is isolated and Shu’s is swollen. How should we retreat?”

Guo Huai said, “Victory and loss are common in war and not enough to trouble us. I have one plan: separate their front and rear so they can no longer support each other. They will surely scatter.”

It goes on:

Pity that the Wei commanders cannot bring this off; They reach out westward for aid.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Jiang Wei Joins Zhuge Liang; The Marquis of Wuxiang Curses Wang Lang to Death

chapters.html:
Guo Huai told Cao Zhen, “The Xiyang Qiang have sent tribute year after year since Taizu’s time. Even Emperor Wen bestowed favor on them. We can now hold the mountain passes, send riders by a lesser route directly into Qiang lands, and promise marriage alliance. The Qiang people will surely rise and strike at Shu after they are invited. Why not then smash them with heavy troops, crushing from front and rear? It would be a great victory.”

Cao Zhen agreed and immediately sent men at night with letters into the Qiang lands.

Now in the lands of the Western Qiang, King Cheliji had also sent tribute every year since the time of Cao Cao. He had under him one civil official and one military official: Yadan as the chancellor and Yueji as the marshal. One time, a Wei envoy came with gold and pearls and a written message, entering first to see Yadan and bringing gifts in hand.

He explained that he had come to seek help. Yadan presented him to the king. Cheliji read the letter and called a council of elders. Yadan said, “Since we have always traded amicably with Wei, if the Wei commander asks for aid and offers marriage alliance, our duty is to comply.”

Cheliji followed his counsel and ordered Yadan and Marshal Yueji to raise one hundred and fifty thousand Qiang troops at once. They were all trained in bow and crossbow, spear and saber, javelin and flail. They had war wagons too, iron-plated and rimmed with nails, loaded with grain, weapons, and military stores. Some wagons were drawn by camels, some by mules and donkeys. They were known as “iron-cart troops.”

After bidding farewell to the king, the two men led the army straight toward Xiping Pass.

At the pass the Shu garrison commander Han Zheng sent men at once to report to Kongming. When Zhuge Liang heard the news, he asked the assembled officers, “Who will go to drive off the Qiang troops?” Zhang Bao and Guan Xing both said, “I volunteer to go.”

Kongming replied, “You two should not go as you are; the roads are unfamiliar.” He then called Ma Dai: “You have long known the way and understand the Qiang nature. Go as local guide.”

He raised a selected force of fifty thousand and sent it out with Xing and Bao. Their soldiers marched away together.

After some days of movement they met the Qiang force at daybreak. Guan Xing first rode out with a hundred riders to scout a hill slope. There he saw the Qiang carts linked head to tail in a long chain, every place marked by stockades, the carts carrying spears and bows and blades on every tier, like moving fortresses. Guan Xing studied the arrangement for a long time and found no easy way to break it. He returned to camp to confer with Zhang Bao and Ma Dai.

Ma Dai said, “Wait until tomorrow. Let us see their ranks and note where they are weak, then plan again.”

The next day he divided the force into three divisions. Guan Xing held the center, Zhang Bao the left, and Ma Dai the right. All three advanced together.

In the Qiang formation, Marshal Yueji gripped his iron flail, a precious carved bow at his waist, and spurred out with a shout. Guan Xing ordered all three columns straight ahead.

Then, on both sides of the field, the Qiang opened their ranks and sent forth the iron carts as if they were a flood. The crossbows were fired all at once. Shu’s army broke badly.

Ma Dai and Zhang Bao were forced to retreat first. Guan Xing’s force was then encircled on all sides and pushed to the northwest corner.

In the center of that crush, Guan Xing pushed left and right but could not break away. The iron carts closed around him like walls of a city. The Shu troops could not aid one another.

Guan Xing looked for a path in the valley below. At dusk he saw one dense cluster of black banners rushing in. A Qiang officer rode forward, lifting an iron flail, shouting, “Young master, do not run! I am Marshal Yueji!”

Guan Xing pushed his horse hard and charged to meet him. At the edge of a ravine he reined and turned, then turned back into battle. Yueji kept after him and struck once with the flail. Guan Xing dodged, but the blow struck his horse’s hip. The horse toppled toward the ravine and Guan Xing was thrown into the water.

At that same instant came a crash behind him. Yueji, horse and rider both, tumbled into the water as well.

Guan Xing struggled up in the stream and saw, on the bank, a Qiang officer still cutting down retreating enemies. He drew his sword to strike Yueji, but Yueji jumped into the water and escaped.

Guan Xing took Yueji’s horse, pulled it to shore, reined it in, mounted, and resumed command. He saw that same officer still pursuing at front.

Reflecting that the man had saved his life, he pressed hard after him. Through the mist of cloud and fog he caught sight of a tall general: face dark as a dried jujube, brows like curled silkworms, green silk robe and gold armor, he wielded a Green Dragon saber and rode a scarlet-chested horse, his handsome beard flaring in the wind.

Guan Xing recognized him at once: it was his father, Lord Guan. He was startled.

Guan Yu pointed southeast and shouted, “Go this way at once. I will stay and cover your return.” Then he was gone.

Guan Xing turned and rode rapidly southeast. Near midnight another troop burst upon him: it was Zhang Bao. He asked, “Have you seen your second uncle?”

Guan Xing answered, “How do you know?”

Bao said, “I was pressed by the iron-carts. Suddenly your uncle came down from nowhere, frightened the Qiang troops, and pointed at me, saying, ‘Go this way and rescue my son.’ So he led troops straight on in your direction.”

Guan Xing then told him what had happened; they lamented together at the strange turn and rode back into camp.

Ma Dai came up behind and said, “This force has no way out. I will hold the stockade. You two go to the Chancellor and report. He will decide the remedy.”

Accordingly Guan Xing and Zhang Bao came before Zhuge Liang by night and reported everything.

Zhuge Liang ordered Zhao Yun and Wei Yan to go out and lay ambushes, then brought out thirty thousand men and rode with Jiang Wei, Zhang Yi, Guan Xing, and Zhang Bao himself to rest at Ma Dai’s camp.

The next day from the high ridge he watched the enemy: the iron-cart line was unbroken, men and horses darting and crashing. Zhuge Liang said, “This is not difficult to break.” He called for Ma Dai and Zhang Yi and gave each of them detailed instructions. After they departed, he called Jiang Wei.

“Boyue,” he said, “do you know the way to break the carts?”

Jiang Wei answered, “The Qiang rely only on brute force and bravery. They know nothing of subtlety.”

Zhuge Liang smiled. “You understand my thought. Now the sky is full of dense cirrus clouds, the north wind is sharp, and snow is about to fall. Now is the moment.”

He ordered Guan Xing and Zhang Bao again to withdraw and lay hidden. Then he ordered Jiang Wei to take the force out. Whenever the iron-cart troops advanced, he was to fall back. At the gate he was to leave only banners, no mounts or formed cavalry. The arrangement was finished.

It was late in the twelfth month; as promised, great snow fell.

Jiang Wei led his troops out, and Marshal Yueji brought the iron-carts forward. Jiang Wei withdrew at once. As the Qiang pursued to the stockade, Jiang Wei moved around to the rear of the camp and vanished. From outside, the Qiang watched in perplexity. From the stockade came the sound of zithers and lutes, and tall banners stood empty around the four walls. They reported this back to Yueji.

Yueji hesitated; he did not dare to charge straight in.

Yadan said, “This is Kongming’s trick, setting empty forces in front. You can attack.”

Yueji then brought his force to the stockade. Zhuge Liang appeared and rode with his zither in hand. He and a few riders entered the stockade, turned and rode out.

The Qiang rushed in through the gates and chased past the mountain pass. They saw small carts turning out of sight into the woods. Yadan said, “Even if this is an ambush, there is no need to fear it.”

He therefore drove the main force in pursuit. They saw Jiang Wei’s troops all running in the snow. Yueji grew enraged and pressed them hard.

The mountain road was covered in snow and seemed broad and open. As they rushed on, a report came: Shu troops were emerging from the rear of the mountain.

Yadan said, “Even with this small ambush, what is there to fear?” and kept driving the horses and chariots forward.

Suddenly there was a crash like a mountain collapsing, and the Qiang cavalry fell into pits and ditches all at once. The iron-carts behind them, moving at speed, could not stop in time, and they piled up and trampled one another.

When the rear ranks tried to turn back, Zhang Bao appeared on the right and Guan Xing on the left and charged forward, while ten thousand crossbows fired together. From behind came Jiang Wei, Ma Dai, and Zhang Yi in three directions.

The iron-cart soldiers scattered into confusion.
