Marshal Yueji saw that way and tried to flee down the mountain valley, where he met Guan Xing. The two horses came shoulder to shoulder. With one shout Guan Xing raised his blade and cut the marshal down from horseback.

Yadan was captured alive by Ma Dai and brought in. Zhuge Liang ordered his ties removed, gave him wine, and spoke reassuring words in kindness.

Yadan was deeply moved by his humanity.

Kongming said, “My lord is the Emperor of the Great Han. I have been ordered by him to punish rebels. Why have you helped the enemy instead of him? I send you back now. Tell your lord that ours are neighboring states. Let there be an everlasting alliance. Do not listen to the voice of rebellion.”

He ordered all captured Qiang men, carts, and materiel returned, and let them all go home.

All bowed in thanks and left. Zhuge Liang then marched the two armies through the night to the Great Qishan stockade. He ordered Guan Xing and Zhang Bao to go ahead.

At the same time he sent a report to court of the victory.

Cao Zhen had been waiting for news of the Qiang force day after day. At last a patrolman arrived to report: “Shu troops have withdrawn from their camp and are moving on.”

Guo Huai rejoiced. “It is because the Qiang attacked, so the enemy retreated.” He dispatched pursuit with two routes.

The Shu front was in disarray and Wei troops followed hard.

At the vanguard, General Cao Zun pushed after them when suddenly the drums thundered and a sudden body of troops burst from nowhere.

The leading general was Wei Yan, crying, “Rebel, do not run!” Cao Zun was startled. He pressed his horse to meet him. In less than three passes the two were in melee, and Wei Yan cut him down from the saddle.

The sub-vanguard, Zhu Zan, rushed after. Again a troop broke out, with Zhao Yun at the head. Zhu Zan had no time to answer; Zhao Yun skewered him through with one spear.

Cao Zhen and Guo Huai saw the failure of both lead wings and tried to regroup the army to withdraw. But from behind came a terrible roar of shouts and the combined blasts of horn and drum.

Guan Xing and Zhang Bao charged out from two separate wings and closed around Cao Zhen and Guo Huai, killing heavily.

Cao and Guo escaped only by forcing their battered troops through a gap and running on.

The Shu army won completely. They pursued as far as the Wei River and seized a Wei stockade.

Cao Zhen had lost two of his vanguard commanders and was full of grief; he could only submit an urgent memorial pleading for reinforcements.

Cao Rui held court and heard his ministers.

“Great Commander Cao Zhen has failed repeatedly against Shu and has lost two of his vanguard commanders. The Qiang have also been broken in great numbers. The situation is urgent. He begs for help. How should Your Majesty decide?”

Cao Rui was alarmed. He immediately asked for a plan to draw back the army.

Hua Xin said, “Only if Your Majesty rides in person and gathers the rulers of the states can this be done. If not, Chang’an will be lost and Guanzhong endangered.”

Cao Rui called for Grand Tutor Zhong Yao. He said, “A commander who knows the enemy also knows himself can control men. Master Sun said, ‘Know the enemy and know yourself, and in a hundred battles one can win in a hundred.’ I estimate this: although Cao Zhen has seen war for long, he is no match for Zhuge Liang. Could Your Majesty allow one man to stand forth so the host may be saved?”

Zhong Yao replied, “I have just held this thought. Great Minister, should I recommend that man, this is my all-in recommendation.”

The emperor said, “You are our venerable and senior advisor. Whom do you recommend?”

Zhong Yao answered, “Formerly, when Zhuge Liang first mobilized an invading army, the only thing keeping him back from the throne was fear of this man. He spread rumors that Your Majesty should dismiss him, so that Kongming would dare to press ahead. If we use him again, Zhuge Liang will retreat from fear.”

Cao Rui said regretfully, “That is true; I have regretted this.”

“Where is Zhongda now?”

Zhong Yao said, “I heard recently he is resting in Wan City.”

Cao Rui issued an edict at once, ordered the envoy to carry the decree, restored Sima Yi to office, appointed him Great Commander for Pacifying the West, and gathered troops from the routes of Nanyang to come to Chang’an.

The emperor ordered that he would lead an imperial expedition with cavalry and that Sima Yi was to arrive at the appointed day for a conference.

He then dispatched the commission, and it reached Wan City before long.

Meanwhile Zhuge Liang, from the start of this campaign, had amassed repeated victories and was heartily pleased. He was in the Qishan camp discussing strategy when a report arrived that Li Yan had sent his son Li Feng from Yong’an.

Kongming assumed at once that Eastern Wu had invaded and was startled. He ordered him into the pavilion and asked, “What is it?”

Li Feng said, “I bring good news.”

“What good news?”

He replied, “In former days, Meng Da’s surrender to Wei was forced by circumstance. Cao Pi, who valued him, gave him excellent horses and pearls, held him like a companion in the sedan, made him a Palace Gentleman Attendant on horseback, and appointed him Administrator of Xincheng, with postings at Shangyong and Jincheng. Since Cao Pi died, Cao Rui has succeeded the throne. Many at court now resent him. Meng Da has not been at ease for nights and days and has often told his generals, ‘I was once a Shu general; events have forced me here.’

He has now sent trusted men again to bring letters home to his old father and ordered them to report without delay: when the armies from the five routes descended the river country there had already been this intent; now in Xincheng, he has heard that the Chancellor plans to strike Wei, and he wishes to raise armies from Jincheng, Xincheng, and Shangyong to strike out at once, seizing Luoyang directly. If you can take Chang’an, both capitals of the empire will be secured. He now brings to you several trusted envoys and many letters.”

Kongming was very pleased and rewarded Li Feng and the men. Then a private courier entered and reported, “Emperor Cao Rui has gone to Chang’an in person. He also ordered Sima Yi restored, made Great Commander for Pacifying the West, and ordered armies from their native stations to converge at Chang’an.”

Kongming was alarmed.

Field Officer Ma Su asked, “How can one even begin to mention Cao Rui? If he comes to Chang’an, we could seize him at once. Why are you astonished?”

Kongming replied, “I do not fear Cao Rui. My fear is only Sima Yi alone. Meng Da now plans a great uprising. If he meets Sima Yi, he will fail surely. Meng Da is no equal for Sima Yi and will be captured. Should he be killed, no one will recover the Central Plains easily.”

Ma Su said, “Why not immediately write and tell Meng Da to prepare defenses?”

Kongming agreed and immediately drafted a letter instructing the envoys to report back at once by night.

Meng Da was in Xincheng and was waiting only for his trusted men to return. One day they came and presented Zhuge Liang’s letter.

Meng Da opened it:

“Now I have received your letter and know you still bear loyalty and righteousness and have not forgotten old comradeship. That reassures me greatly.

If this succeeds, you will accomplish one of the greatest services of restoring the Han. Yet you must act with utmost secrecy and never trust information delivered by ordinary men.

Take care! Be alert!

It is rumoured that Cao Rui has again ordered Sima Yi to muster troops from Wan and Luo. Should you rise, he will surely arrive first. Make complete preparation and do not treat this as idle talk.”

Meng Da finished reading and smiled. “People have said Kongming has a complicated mind; now I can see why.” He dictated a return letter and sent his trusted men back.

When they entered Zhuge Liang’s pavilion with the reply, he opened and read it.

“I can only accept your instruction now, and dare not be negligent. I have lately heard that Cao Rui has again ordered Sima Yi to raise the troops of Wan and Luo. If he hears that you have risen, he will surely arrive first. Wan is about eight hundred li from Luo, and Xincheng is about twelve hundred li. If Sima Yi hears of your uprising, he will send a memorial and in one month’s travel return he could be at your gates. By then your defenses are firm and your generals and soldiers are in deep and difficult ground. Once Sima Yi arrives, what is there left for you to fear? Chancellor, be broad-hearted. Do not wait for victory messages only to celebrate.”

Kongming flung the letter down, stamped his feet, and said, “Meng Da will die by the hand of Sima Yi!”

Ma Su asked, “What do you mean by that, Chancellor?”

Kongming said, “The Art of War says: ‘Attack where he is unprepared, strike where he is unexpecting.’ Can a man rely on a full month to think this out? Since Cao Rui has already given Sima Yi command, he will strike as soon as he hears of trouble, without waiting for paperwork. If Meng Da rebels, in less than ten days the army will arrive. How can he answer in time?”

All the officers acknowledged this.

Kongming sent the envoys back urgently and ordered, “If he has not risen yet, tell him not to let anyone else know. If one soul knows, he is lost.”

They withdrew and returned to Xincheng.

Sima Yi stayed at Wan City and heard of Wei troops falling repeatedly against Shu. He lifted his face and sighed long.

His eldest son Sima Shi and second son Sima Zhao were already ambitious and learned in military studies. While he stood beside them they asked, “Father, why this sigh?”

Sima Yi replied, “Do you not know this is no ordinary matter?”

Sima Shi asked, “Is it because Your Majesty fails to employ you?”

Sima Zhao laughed, “Sooner or later he will call you back with decree.”

Before he could continue, a messenger with dispatch arrived.

After reading the imperial command, Sima Yi promptly arranged his troops from all roads of Wan City.

A second message soon came: a man from Jincheng’s household guard, an officer of the Shen family, sought urgent meeting.

Sima Yi brought him into a private room and asked the matter through. He explained in detail Meng Da’s plans to rise. He also said that Meng Da’s confidant Li Fu and his nephew Deng Xian had come out together to accuse him.

Sima Yi struck his hand to his brow and said, “This is the Son of Heaven’s heavenly blessing! Zhuge Liang’s army at Qishan has broken the hearts of men inside and out. The emperor had to come to Chang’an unwillingly. If he does not move at once, both capitals fall in a single day. This rebel surely coordinates with Zhuge Liang. I must strike first, and then Zhuge Liang will surely feel fear and pull back his army.”

Sima Shi said, “Father, send an urgent memorial to the Son of Heaven now.”

Sima Yi replied, “If we wait for the edict, in a month the matter is gone.” He ordered the riders and horse teams to set out at a speed of two days’ march per day, on pain of death for delay. At the same time he had his staff officer Liang Ji carry a dispatch to Xincheng by night, telling Meng Da to prepare for full campaign and remain unalarmed.

Liang Ji rode ahead. Sima Yi moved after him with the army.

After two days of marching, a force came down from the slope. It was Right General Xu Huang. He dismounted and asked, “His Majesty has come to Chang’an and is personally facing Shu. Where does Commander Sima travel?”

Sima Yi replied quietly, “Meng Da has rebelled. I ride to arrest him.”

Xu Huang said, “Then I ask leave to be vanguard.”

Sima Yi rejoiced and merged the troops. Xu Huang took the front, Sima Yi the center, and the two sons the rear.

After two more days of marching, an advanced scouting horse brought in one of Meng Da’s confidants. They searched him and found Kongming’s return letter.

The man was brought before Sima Yi. He read and asked where it came from. “From Meng Da,” the man answered.

Sima Yi said, “I will not kill you. Tell me everything from beginning to end.”

The man recounted in detail the exchange between Kongming and Meng Da.

Sima Yi read Kongming’s letter and was greatly shaken. “Everything a talented man sees is one and the same. My plan has been read by Kongming already. Fortunately heaven favored the Son of Heaven, and I have this message in time. Meng Da has no capacity now.”

He ordered a night march and pressed the troops forward.

Meanwhile Meng Da in Xincheng set a date with Jincheng Administrator Shen Yi and Shangyong Administrator Shen Dan, that he would rise on an appointed day.

Shen Dan and Shen Yi both feigned agreement and each day trained horse and men, waiting for Wei troops to arrive to aid them. But it was all news to Meng Da that their weapons and grain were still unprepared. He did not doubt this and trusted them.

Then Liang Ji arrived in person.

Meng Da welcomed him in and offered hospitality, then sent him out of the city.

Meng Da then informed Shen Yi and Shen Dan: tomorrow we rise, raise the Great Han banners, mobilize all troops, and march directly for Luoyang.

A report then came that a storm of dust rose outside the city. Meng Da climbed the wall to look. He saw a body of troops carrying the banner “Right General Xu Huang” and thundering down toward the gate.

He was startled. He had the drawbridge hauled up.

Xu Huang dismounted and came to the ditch, crying, “Rebel Meng Da! Surrender at once!”

Meng Da, enraged, drew a bow and shot at him. The arrow struck Xu Huang in the forehead, and the Wei general was carried away by his guards.

Arrows rained from the city ramparts, and the Wei troops withdrew.

As Meng Da prepared to open the gate and pursue, banners covered the sky in all directions. Sima Yi’s army had arrived.

Meng Da looked to the sky and sighed, “It has happened exactly as Kongming predicted!” He shut the gates and held fast.

When Xu Huang was taken down by Meng Da’s arrow, the Wei general’s soldiers carried him back to camp, removed the arrowhead, and summoned a physician, but he died by nightfall at age fifty-nine.

Sima Yi’s men brought his body back and had it carried toward Luoyang for burial.

The next morning Meng Da toured the city. He saw Wei troops encircling on all sides like iron jars. He was restless and uncertain.

All at once he saw troops advancing from two routes. Their banners bore, in large characters, “Shen Dan” and “Shen Yi.”

Meng Da believed these were relief troops and rushed to open the city gate and charge.

The two shouted at once, “Rebel, do not run! Surrender now and die!”

As the situation turned, Meng Da seized his horse and made for the interior of the city, but arrows flew from above in chaos.

Li Fu and Deng Xian cried out from the walls: “We have already delivered this city!”

Meng Da cut through whatever route he could. Shen Dan caught up and thrust him from horseback with a spear. He beheaded Meng Da.

The remaining troops surrendered.

Li Fu and Deng Xian opened the gate wide and received Sima Yi into the city.

After seeing the people calmed and rewarding the troops, they dispatched a report to Emperor Cao Rui.

The emperor rejoiced and ordered Meng Da’s head brought to Luoyang as warning to all.

He promoted Shen Dan and Shen Yi and ordered them to follow Sima Yi into further operations. Li Fu and Deng Xian were ordered to hold Xincheng and Shangyong.

Sima Yi then brought his army to camp outside Chang’an. He entered the city and came before the emperor.

Cao Rui said, with relief, “I was confused for a while and was deceived by the enemies’ misinformation. It cannot be repaired now. Had Meng Da’s uprising not been suppressed by you and your men, the two capitals would have perished.”

Sima Yi answered, “I heard Shen Yi and Shen Dan report the matter in secret to me first and feared delay. Therefore I went without waiting for an edict. If we waited to report back, we would have entered Zhuge Liang’s trap.”

He then presented Kongming’s secret letter to Meng Da and the emperor read it.

Cao Rui said, “Your understanding surpasses that of Sun Wu and Wu.” and laughed.

He gave him a pair of golden battle-axes and instructed: for future secret matters of state there was no need to report first, and he might act on suitable judgment.

He ordered Sima Yi to leave the pass and break Shu’s armies.

Sima Yi then asked, “I can name one great general to serve as first assault commander.”

Cao Rui said, “Who is it?”

Sima Yi said, “Right General Zhang He can take that post.”

The emperor smiled. “I intended to use him.”

So he appointed Zhang He as the forward vanguard and ordered him to march with Sima Yi out of Chang’an to break the Shu troops.

It is said:

“One strategist is present and can wield his wit; another asks for a fierce general to give force.

How this battle is decided remains unknown. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang Uses Snow to Break the Qiang Forces; Sima Yi Arrives in Time to Capture Meng Da

chapters.html:
Yet the Wei sovereign Cao Rui ordered Zhang He to serve as vanguard with Sima Yi advancing together, and at the same time ordered Xin Pi and Sun Li to lead fifty thousand men to reinforce Cao Zhen. The two took up the order and set out.

A vanguard had been sent, and Sima Yi led two hundred thousand soldiers, left the mountain pass, and pitched camp. He sent for Zhang He to come to his tent and said, “Zhuge Liang is generally cautious and never rash in action. Had I moved earlier against him, I could have taken Chang’an quickly by the Ziwu Valley long ago. He is not lacking in strategy, but he fears making mistakes and thus avoids dangerous moves. I must now go through the slanting pass and take Mei City. If we take Mei City, we will split forces in two, and one column will capture Jigu. I have already sent a written command to Zidan to hold Mei and not to engage if the enemy approaches. I ordered Sun Li and Xin Pi to block the Jigu road gate; if Wei soldiers come, they are to strike with a surprise detachment.”

Zhang He asked, “Where should the main force advance now, Master?”

Sima Yi replied, “I have known for some time that to the west of the Qinling there is one road, the pass of Jieting, with a small city near it called Lie Liu City. These two points are both throatways of Hanzhong. Zhuge Liang underestimates Zidan and will commit through this route. I and you will go directly for Jieting; Yangping Pass is not far away. If he realizes I have cut the artery at Jieting and severed his supply, then throughout Longxi this region cannot hold; he must flee back to Hanzhong in one night. If he turns and advances, I will engage him on a narrow track and win outright. If he does not return, then I will block every mountain track and hold them all with troops. In a month without grain, Shu troops will starve, and Zhuge Liang will be captured by me.”

Zhang He rose in understanding and knelt to the ground, saying, “Brilliant foresight, Commander!”

Sima Yi said, “All that said, Zhuge Liang is not Meng Da. As vanguard commander, you must not advance lightly. Send word to all generals: scout far along the western mountain road and keep distant patrols ahead. Only if no ambush is found may you move forward. If you grow careless, his plan will catch you.”

Zhang He accepted the counsel and marched his force.

Now back in the Qishan camp, Kongming suddenly received a report from a deep scout arriving from Xincheng. He immediately called him in. The scout said, “Sima Yi has pressed hard and in eight days reached Xincheng. Meng Da was unprepared. Also through the collusion of Shen Dan, Shen Yi, Li Fu, and Deng Xian, Meng Da was killed by his own confederate soldiers. Sima Yi has now withdrawn to Chang’an, reported to the Wei sovereign, then with Zhang He brought his troops out through the pass to oppose our army.”

Kongming startled, “Meng Da did not keep his work secure; his death was inevitable. Now that Sima Yi has left the pass he will surely take Jieting and cut our own throat-way. Who will go to defend Jieting?”

Before his sentence was complete, the staff officer Ma Su stepped forward. “I volunteer to go.”

Kongming said, “Though Jieting is small, it is critical. If Jieting falls, my whole army is undone. You have deep knowledge of strategy; yet this place has no city walls, no fortifications. To defend it will be difficult.”

Ma Su replied, “I have read the classics since childhood and know military law well. How could Jieting not be held?”

Kongming said, “Sima Yi is not an ordinary foe, and besides you will face Zhang He, Wei’s famous general. I fear you cannot oppose him.”

Ma Su said, “Do not speak of Sima Yi and Zhang He. Even if Cao Rui himself comes, what is there to fear? If there is any failure, may my whole family be executed.”

Kongming said, “There is no room for idle words in camp.”

Ma Su said, “Then record my military order.”

Kongming agreed.

Ma Su wrote the order and submitted it.

Kongming said, “I will send twenty-five thousand of my best men with you, and another senior commander to assist.” He called Wang Ping and gave him instructions: “I have long known your carefulness, so I entrust this heavy charge to you. Be very vigilant. This place is a camp-ground and must be a key route; thus the enemy troops cannot slip through quickly. After the camp is established, draw out four to eight maps of the terrain and show them to me. Consult everything carefully before acting; do not move rashly. If this defense stands firm, it is the first victory on the road to Chang’an. Take this warning to heart! Take it to heart!”

The two offered deep bows, took their troops, and departed.

Kongming then reflected with concern that the two might falter and called Gao Xiang: “To the northeast of Jieting there is a city called Lie Liu City, a small and remote track through the hills. This can be used as a troop encampment. Go there with ten thousand men to establish a camp, and if Jieting is in danger you can move to support it.” Gao Xiang led his men away.

Kongming thought further. Gao Xiang was no match for Zhang He; there must be a major general stationed at Jieting’s right flank for defense. So he summoned Wei Yan: “Bring your battalion to camp behind Jieting.”

Wei Yan said, “If I have the front, it is fitting that I break the enemy first. Why do you place me in a quiet posting?”

Kongming replied, “Breaking the enemy in the front is the task of an auxiliary wing. Now you are ordered to support Jieting. You must hold Yangping Pass and secure the throat of Hanzhong. This is a great charge, not an easy one. How could it be called quiet work? Do not treat this as trivial and lose my major plan. Be mindful.”

Wei Yan, pleased, led his troops away.

When his heart was at last eased, Kongming called Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi and said, “Now that Sima Yi has moved, this is unlike previous campaigns. You two each lead one army out through Jigu and serve as feigned forces. If you meet Wei troops, either fight or withdraw as needed to unsettle their thoughts. I will command the main army by the slanting pass and go straight for Mei City. If we seize Mei City, Chang’an may fall.”

They obeyed and left. Kongming assigned Jiang Wei as vanguard and sent the troops through Xie Valley.

Now Ma Su and Wang Ping reached Jieting and inspected the ground. Ma Su laughed, “Why is the Chancellor so anxious? Looking at this remote hill, how could the Wei soldiers dare approach?”

Wang Ping said, “Though they may not dare come, we should still camp at the convergence of the five approaches and order the soldiers to fell trees and build palisades for a long defense.”

Ma Su said, “Is a crossing a place for a campsite? This is a lone hill at the edge, with all around inaccessible, and the trees are dense. This is heaven’s own advantage. We can station troops on the hill-top.”

Wang Ping answered, “The officer is wrong to think so. If we camp directly on the road and build an earthen wall, even ten thousand raiders could not get through. If you abandon this key path and place troops on the hill, and if Wei soldiers arrive suddenly, they could encircle us on four sides. How then can we save ourselves?”

Ma Su laughed aloud. “You truly see only as a woman. The Art of War says, ‘From the heights one can look below as if wood were cleft in two.’ If Wei comes, not one piece of his armor will return!”

Wang Ping said, “I have followed the Chancellor through every battle line. Wherever we went, he advised me throughout. This hill is an exposed place. If Wei blocks our water draws, the soldiers will scatter in disorder without fighting.”

Ma Su snapped, “Do not confuse the road. Master Sun said: ‘Set men in a position of death, then they will be reborn with life.’ If Wei cuts our water supply, should the Shu soldiers not fight to the death, one against a hundred? I have always studied military texts, and the Chancellor asks me about all things; why do you hinder me?”

Wang Ping said, “If the staff-officer wishes to camp below on the path, we can split forces: let half come down west of the hill and form a cornered position. If Wei comes, we can aid each other.”

Ma Su refused.

Suddenly, clusters of hill villagers came running in from the woods, reporting that Wei troops had already arrived. Wang Ping moved to leave. Ma Su said, “Since you will not follow my order, go with five thousand and camp below.” Then he added, “When I have beaten Wei’s army, the credit may not be measured when we stand before the Chancellor.”

Wang Ping led his men ten li down from the hill and drew a map, then in the night sent men to report to Kongming, explaining fully that Ma Su had camped on the heights.

Now Sima Yi, in the city, ordered his second son Sima Zhao to reconnoiter the front road; if troops were defending Jieting, he was to hold position. Sima Zhao obeyed and returned to his father: “Jieting is defended.”

Sima Yi sighed. “Zhuge Liang is truly a divine strategist. I am no match.”

Sima Zhao laughed. “Father, why lower your spirits so much? I expect Jieting can be taken with little strain.”

Sima Yi asked, “How dare you speak so boldly?”

Sima Zhao said, “I observed it with my own eyes: troops are encamped on the hill, and there are no camps or walls on the road. They can be broken.”

Sima Yi rejoiced, “If they truly camp on the hill, Heaven has prepared this victory for me.” He changed his clothing, rode with over a hundred cavalry himself to inspect. That night the sky was clear and bright, and he went down to the base of the hill, patrolled the perimeter once, then returned.

Ma Su, seeing him above, laughed. “If he is permitted to act, he will not encircle the hill.” He ordered the commanders: “If the army arrives, then when a red banner flaps at the summit, everyone must descend on all sides at once.”

Meanwhile Sima Yi returned to camp and asked who commanded at Jieting. The report said, “It is Ma Su, brother of Ma Liang.”

Sima Yi laughed. “A man with empty reputation, a mere incompetent! If Zhuge Liang uses such a person, how could he not bring failure?”

He asked, “Any other troops to left or right of Jieting?”

The scout replied, “Wang Ping camped ten li away on the far side.”

Sima Yi then ordered Zhang He to lead one force and hold Wang Ping’s route. He also sent Shen Dan and Shen Yi on two lines to surround the hill and first cut the water-drawing path. When the Shu troops became disordered, only then strike. The dispositions were settled that same night.

At dawn, Zhang He first moved with one column behind and went around. Sima Yi drove the cavalry hard in one mass and pushed forward, surrounding the mountain on all sides. When Ma Su watched, he saw Wei soldiers spread over every slope, banners and ranks tightly ordered. Shu troops, seeing them, all lost nerve and dared not descend. Ma Su signaled the red flag; his own officers pushed one another back and forth, and not one dared move. In anger Ma Su executed two commanders. The rest, shaken by fear, could only force themselves down the mountain to strike at the Wei troops.

The Wei soldiers stood unmoving. The Shu troops withdrew again to the hill. Ma Su saw things not aligning and ordered the camp gate held tight, waiting only for outside support.

Now Wang Ping saw Wei arrive and drove in, colliding with Zhang He. They fought for many rounds. When Wang Ping was exhausted and isolated, he withdrew. Wei soldiers pressed from the hour of Chen until the hour of Xu; with no water on the mountain and no grain in camp, disorder spread through the camp. In the middle of the night, the Shu forces on the southern slope flung open the camp gate and descended to surrender. Ma Su could not prevent it.

Sima Yi then ordered fires along the mountain line. The Shu men above became more and more disordered. Judging that Jieting could not be held, Ma Su had no choice but to drive what remained of his troops down and flee west.

Sima Yi opened a broad road to let Ma Su pass. Behind them, Zhang He rode hard in pursuit. After thirty li, a battle cry rose ahead and a detachment burst out, blocking Zhang He while letting Ma Su through. It was Wei Yan, who drew his sword and leapt forward on horseback straight for Zhang He. Zhang He wheeled and fled.

Wei Yan came after and regained Jieting. At fifty li out, a shout rang out and ambushes opened on both sides—Sima Yi on the left and Sima Zhao on the right—cutting behind Wei Yan and trapping him in a circle. Zhang He returned, and three columns converged. Wei Yan rushed left and right, unable to break free, losing nearly half his force. In that desperate moment another unit burst in: Wang Ping. Wei Yan was overjoyed. “I am alive!” he cried. The two commanders joined forces and made one killing blow before the Wei withdrew. They hurried back toward camp, only to see Wei banners now filled the camp. Shen Dan and Shen Yi burst out from within.

Wang Ping and Wei Yan rode straight for Lie Liu City and went to Gao Xiang.

As soon as Gao Xiang heard that Jieting had been lost, he roused all forces in Lie Liu City and marched to render aid. He met Wei Yan and Wang Ping there and heard the events. Gao Xiang said, “Tonight we should storm Wei camp and recover Jieting.” The three generals discussed this on the hillside and fixed the plan. When dusk came, he divided the army into three routes.

Wei Yan advanced first and came directly to Jieting. He saw no one and, suspicious, did not go in recklessly but lay in wait at the track mouth. Gao Xiang’s men arrived; the two of them exchanged quick words about where Wei troops were. Still there was no one to hear, and still they did not see Wang Ping’s force. Suddenly there was cannon thunder, fire rose skyward, and drumbeats shook the ground. The Wei army came out all at once and surrounded Wei Yan and Gao Xiang in the middle of the field.

The two struggled fiercely and could not break through. From the slope behind came a cry like thunder and a mounted band entered—Wang Ping again—who rescued both. They ran straight to Lie Liu City.

Just as they reached the city gate, a force had already arrived and the banner showed in large letters: “Inspector Guo Huai of Wei.” Guo Huai had consulted with Cao Zhen. Fearing that Sima Yi would receive all the credit, he had split off to take Jieting. Hearing that Sima Yi and Zhang He had won this success, he now rode directly against Lie Liu City. He met the three commanders at once and they fought fiercely together. Shu losses were severe.

Wei Yan, fearing loss at Yangping Pass, hurried with Wang Ping and Gao Xiang toward Yangping Pass.

Now Guo Huai gathered horse and men and told his officers, “Though I have not taken Jieting, I did take Lie Liu City. That is still a great merit.” He led his force straight to the foot of the city and called for the gate to open. One cannon blast sounded atop the wall; the flags were all raised. Above them, an upper banner read: “Sima Yi, Commander Who Pacifies the West.”

Guo Huai looked up and saw the man there: Sima Yi, holding up a hanging plank and leaning upon a breast-support rail, laughing broadly: “Why did Guo Boji arrive so late?”

Guo Huai stammered, “The clever stratagem of Zhongda surpasses me.” He entered.

After the audience, Sima Yi said, “Now that Jieting is lost, Zhuge Liang must retreat. Move at once with Zidan, and pursue him through the night.” Guo Huai did as told and left.

Sima Yi then called Zhang He. “Zidan and Boji came for this city because they feared I had taken complete success. I did not come to win alone; I only happened to have fortune. I think Wei Yan, Wang Ping, Ma Su, and Gao Xiang will first go to occupy Yangping Pass. If I go for that pass, Zhuge Liang will return to strike and follow my ambush. Sun Tzu says: ‘When returning from victory, do not cover your retreat; when hunting a cornered enemy, do not pursue.’ So you may withdraw from Jieting through the smaller route in Jigu Valley. I will lead the main army along Xie Valley. If they turn and run, do not block them; just intercept midway, and all their baggage and supplies will fall to us.”

Zhang He received the plan and led half the force away.

Sima Yi ordered, “Take the Xie Valley directly and enter by West City. Though West City is a small and remote county, it is where Shu stores grain. It is also the junction for Nanan, Tianshui, and Anding commanderies. If we take this city, those three commanderies are restored.”

Thus Sima Yi left Shen Dan and Shen Yi to hold Lie Liu City and marched with the main army through Xie Valley.

Kongming, after assigning Ma Su and the others to defend Jieting, had been wavering still. Now he received Wang Ping’s map in person. He called him in and had the map presented. On the desk, he opened and viewed it, then struck the table in astonishment: “Ma Su is ignorant. He has trapped our army!”

The attendants asked, “Why this alarm, Chancellor?”

He said, “From this map he has lost the key route and camped on a mountain. If Wei arrives in force and surrounds from four sides and cuts the water path, the army will break in no more than two days. If Jieting falls, how are we to return?”

Yang Yi, the chief clerk, said, “Though I am not talented, let me replace Ma Youchang.”

Kongming then explained in detail the method of camp arrangement to Yang Yi. He was just preparing to leave when a horseman arrived: “Jieting and Lie Liu City are both lost.”

Kongming stamped and sighed deeply, “The great matter is gone. This is my fault!” He called Guan Xing and Zhang Bao and said, “Each of you lead three thousand picked soldiers and go by the Wugong Mountain path. If you meet Wei soldiers, do not give a decisive battle; beat drums and shout to sound like a feigned force. Let them fear and turn away. Do not pursue them. When all troops have fallen back, head for Yangping Pass.”

He also ordered Zhang Yi ahead with troops to repair Jian Ge in readiness for the way home. He issued secret instructions that the main army silently pack as if ready to depart.

He ordered Ma Dai and Jiang Wei to hold the rear, to lie first in the mountain valley, and only after all troops had gone clear themselves from the field.

He had trusted agents split roads to invite officials and soldiery from Tianshui, Nanan, and Anding to enter Hanzhong.

He also instructed trusted men to take Jiang Wei’s mother from Ji County to Hanzhong.

Kongming’s deployment complete, he first led five thousand men to Xicheng County to move supplies. Suddenly messengers arrived repeatedly, as many as ten at once, reporting that Sima Yi had brought one hundred and fifty thousand men and marched in two columns, swarming toward Xicheng County.

Kongming now had no major generals at his side, only a group of civil officials; the five thousand soldiers he had taken were already split, half of them sent ahead with supplies. Only two thousand five hundred remained in the city. The officers around him grew pale on hearing the report.

Kongming climbed the city rampart and saw dust rising like skyfall: the Wei force was advancing toward Xicheng County by two routes. He ordered all banners to be hidden. Each general was to hold posts within the city. If anyone moved in and out or spoke too loudly, they would be put to death. The four gates were opened wide; at each gate, twenty soldiers dressed as civilians swept the streets. “When the Wei come, no one may act without order. I have a plan,” he said.

Then Kongming donned a crane mantle and linen headcloth, took two young attendants, one carrying a zither and one a feather whisk, and sat beside the balustrade on the enemy-facing tower while incense burned and he played.

Now Sima Yi’s forward scouts reached the foot of the city and saw this scene; none dared to step forward. They reported to him. He laughed in disbelief but held the command to stop the three armies and rode out, watching from far away.

He saw clearly. Kongming sat on the city tower, smiling serenely, incense smoke rising, playing the qin. On his left stood a boy carrying a treasure sword; on his right a boy held a fly-whisk. More than twenty ordinary-looking civilians moved about the gates, sweeping in silence. Sima Yi, after seeing this, grew deeply suspicious and, in the main camp, ordered the rear to move forward and the vanguard to fall back, then withdrew along the northern mountain route.

His second son Sima Zhao said, “Could it be that Zhuge Liang has no army and thus is making such a show? Why must you pull back?”

Sima Yi said, “Zhuge Liang has always been cautious and never took reckless hazards. He has opened the gates wide today; there must be an ambush. If my troops enter, we fall into his trap. Do you know this? We should withdraw quickly.”

Thus both columns withdrew.

When the Wei army withdrew out of sight, Kongming tapped his hands and laughed. The officers were astounded.

Someone asked, “Sima Yi is Wei’s renowned general. He led one hundred and fifty thousand and seeing the Chancellor withdrew immediately. Why?”

Kongming said, “He has judged my long habit of caution and believes I do not take risks. Seeing this posture, he suspects ambush and therefore withdrew. I did not seek risk; I used it out of necessity. This man will take his army toward the small northern mountain route. Xing and Bao are already waiting there.”

All were struck with admiration: “Your mysterious insight is beyond ghosts and spirits. If it were by us, we would have abandoned the city in flight.”

Kongming said, “I have only two thousand five hundred men left in the city. If I abandon the city and run, we cannot get very far. Could we avoid being captured by Sima Yi?”

Later critics praised this in a verse:

The three-foot qin surpasses a mighty host; when Zhuge in West City sent enemies retreating. One hundred and fifty thousand men turned their horses there; to this day, later readers still wonder.

Then he said with a clap and laughter, “If I were Sima Yi, I would not find retreat so convenient.” He ordered the civilians of West City to move with the army toward Hanzhong; Sima Yi would surely come again.

So Kongming left West City and moved toward Hanzhong. The officers and soldiers of Tianshui, Anding, and Nanan arrived in succession.

Now Sima Yi withdrew along the Wugong Mountain path. Suddenly cries from behind the slope rose to the sky and drums shook the earth. He turned and said to his sons, “If I do not leave now, I will surely be caught in Zhuge Liang’s design.” A single army advanced on the main road, the banner on high pole reading, “Right Guarding Commander, General of Tiger Wing, Zhang Bao.” The Wei troops cast aside their armor and spears and ran.

No sooner had he gone a short distance when in the valley the calls roared and drums blared. Ahead was a tall banner reading, “Left Guarding Commander, General of Dragon Soaring, Guan Xing.” The valley echoed in answer. Not knowing how many Shu men there were, and already uneasy, the Wei soldiers dared not linger. They cast off baggage and forage and fled.

Both Xing and Bao obeyed their orders and did not press pursuit, bringing back much military gear and grain.

Seeing that the valley was full of Shu soldiers, Sima Yi dared not take the broad road and thus returned to Jieting. At that moment Cao Zhen learned Kongming was withdrawing and hastened out in pursuit.

A cannon blast sounded from behind the hill; Shu troops surged across the slopes, and at their head was Jiang Wei with Ma Dai. Cao Zhen startled and quickly withdrew. His vanguard, Chen Zuo, had already been cut down by Ma Dai. Cao Zhen drew his troops back in panic, while all night the Shu forces all rushed toward Hanzhong.

Now Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi lay in ambush in Jigu Valley. After Kongming’s order to retreat, Zhao told Deng, “If Wei learns we are pulling back, they will chase. I will lead one army to wait behind them; you, keep signaling with our banners and fall back slowly. At each step they will think you cover me.”

Now Guo Huai rode out and re-entered Jigu Valley again, calling the vanguard Suyong to him. “Zhao Yun of Shu is peerless in valor,” he said. “Guard carefully. If this army retreats, there will be stratagems.”

Suyong answered readily, “If the commander supports this, I will capture Zhao Yun alive.”

He led three thousand men in the front and rushed into Jigu Valley. He ran into the Shu force so quickly that a red flag with white letters flashed from the back slope, bearing the words “Zhao Yun.”

Suyong pulled back and retreated.

After only a few li, a great shout sounded and a unit crashed out. At the front rode the tall commander, spear raised, horse clear, shouting, “Do you know who this is? Zhao Zilong?”

Suyong was startled: “How can there be another Zhao Yun here?” Unprepared, he was skewered by Zhao Yun’s lance from his horse. The remaining forces scattered.

Zhao Yun advanced by circuit. Behind him another army came—the corps under Wan Zheng, a subordinate of Guo Huai. Seeing Wei pursue him, Zhao checked his mount, planted his spear, and waited at the roadhead for close contact. The Shu army was already thirty li ahead.

Wan Zheng recognized Zhao Yun and did not advance. As dusk came, Zhao slowly withdrew. When Guo Huai’s troops came up, Wan told him Zhao Yun was as brave as ever and therefore he kept distance.

Huai ordered his general to press hard; hundreds of mounted heroes raced forward. Reaching a great forest, they heard a shout from behind: “Zhao Zilong is here!” It terrified more than a hundred who lost their seats from horse. The rest fled over ridges.

Wan mustered and came out to meet him, but Zhao Yun shot him with an arrow through helmet ties and he fell into a ravine. Zhao pointed his spear and said, “I spare your life. Go! Tell Guo Huai to hasten!”

Wan escaped with life and returned. Zhao escorted the baggage and horses and headed for Hanzhong, and no losses occurred on the way.

Cao Zhen and Guo Huai later took back the three commanderies and counted it as their own merit.

Now Sima Yi again advanced in columns, but all Shu forces had already returned to Hanzhong. He led one army back to West City and inquired among the inhabitants and remote hill folk. All said Zhuge Liang had only two thousand five hundred men in the city, and no general of rank, only a handful of civil officials, with no ambush at all.

A villager of Wugong Mountain said, “Guan Xing and Zhang Bao each have three thousand soldiers. They only cried from the hills and beat drums. They made no separate forces and did not remain to close with the enemy.”

Sima Yi lamented too late and, raising his face to the sky, sighed, “I am not as good as Zhuge Liang.” He soothed the officers and civilians, then withdrew by direct way to Chang’an and came before the Wei sovereign.

Cao Rui said, “Today we have again taken back the commanderies of Longxi. All this is your merit.”

Sima Yi reported, “Shu forces are all in Hanzhong and not yet fully annihilated. I beg that the main armies combine to gather and subdue Sichuan to repay Your Majesty.” Cao Rui rejoiced and ordered Sima Yi to raise troops at once.

At that moment a man in the court stood to report: “Your servant has a plan that could settle Shu and aid us against Wu.”

Then it was written:

The ministers and generals of Shu have now returned to their country, and in Wei’s lands the lord and ministers again unleash their schemes. Who offered this strategy, we do not yet know. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Ma Su Rejects Counsel and Loses Jieting; the Marquis of Wuhou Plays the Qin to Send Back Sima Yi

chapters.html:
Kongming weeps and beheads Ma Shu. Zhou Fang cuts his hair and tricks Cao Xiu.

Now the man giving a plan was Sun Zi of the Shangshu office. Cao Rui asked, “What excellent scheme have you?” Sun Zi submitted, “When the martial Emperor Taizu subdued Zhang Lu, he helped him only after a brush with ruin; he once told all ministers, ‘The lands of Nanzheng are truly a heavenly prison.’ Middle-slanting Valley is five hundred li of rocky ravines and is not ground for military use. Now, if we mobilize all soldiers in the realm to strike at Shu, then Eastern Wu will raid as well. Better to keep the present army divided, assigning major generals to hold critical fortresses and preserve strength and resolve. In a few years, Zhongguo will grow stronger; Wu and Shu must wear each other down by then. At that time, if we move, is it not surely a winning chance? I beg Your Majesty to decide.”

Cao Rui then asked Sima Yi, “How do you judge this?” Sima Yi reported, “The Minister Sun’s words are entirely sound.” Cao Rui followed him, ordered Sima Yi to dispatch the generals to hold key passes, left Guo Zhun and Zhang He in charge of Chang'an, gave them three full carts of reward, then turned back to Luoyang.

Now Kongming returned to Hanzhong and took the roll of his soldiers. Only Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi were still unaccounted for, and his heart was greatly troubled. He ordered Guan Xing and Zhang Bao, each commanding one force, to move as reinforcements. As the two were about to depart, it was reported that Zhao Yun and Deng Zhi had arrived, and had not lost a single man or horse; no supplies or baggage were missing. Kongming was very happy and personally led the officers out to meet them.

Zhao Yun hurried down and knelt, saying, “Why should the Chancellor come so far to receive the commander of a broken army?” Kongming at once helped him up and took his hand, saying, “This is my fault for not knowing who was able or unable. Other commanders suffered losses, yet you, Zilong, did not lose one man or horse. Why so?”

Deng Zhi said, “I led the army forward first; Zilong held back alone, cutting officers and gaining merit. The enemy was startled and frightened. Therefore we did not abandon a single supply or object.”

Kongming said, “You are truly a general.” He gave Zhao Yun fifty jin of gold and ten thousand bolts of silk for Yun’s soldiers. Zhao Yun said, “Three armies have not gained a single inch of service. We all share blame. If I now take a reward, the Chancellor’s rewards and punishments would be unclear. Also, please put it in storage and, when winter comes, distribute it to all the armies. That would not be late.” Kongming sighed, “The late emperor, while he lived, often praised Zilong’s virtue. It is just so now.” He then doubled his respect and reverence for him.

Soon there came word that Ma Shu, Wang Ping, Wei Yan, and Gao Xiang had arrived. Kongming first called Wang Ping into his tent and rebuked him: “I had ordered you and Ma Shu together to guard Jieting. Why did you not remonstrate with him, resulting in this disaster?”

Wang Ping said, “I twice urged that we fortify and hold the road with an earth wall. The staff officer was furious and refused. So I took five thousand men down the mountain ten li to camp. Wei troops arrived in a rush and closed around us on all four sides. I charged out to break through more than ten times, but none entered.

The next day the earthwork collapsed. Countless men surrendered. I could not hold alone with my force, so I sought help from Wei Wenchang (Wei Yan). Halfway, we were trapped in a mountain valley by Wei troops; I fought my way out with my life. When we reached our camp, the Wei army had already occupied it. As we moved on toward Liucheng, we met Gao Xiang, so I split into three columns to raid a Wei camp and hoped to recover Jieting. Then I saw Jieting had no reserve troops; my heart was doubtful.

From the heights I looked out and saw Wei Yan and Gao Xiang both surrounded by Wei troops. I cut into the encirclement and saved the two generals, then I and the staff officer gathered together. I feared to lose Yangping Pass, so I returned immediately to hold it. This was not because I had not remonstrated. If the Chancellor will not believe me, let him question the commanders of all divisions.”

Kongming sent him away, then called Ma Shu. Ma Shu had bound his own hands and knelt at the front of the tent.

Kongming’s face changed. “You grew up reading military books and knowing war methods well. I have warned and admonished you repeatedly. Jieting is my foundation. I gave you this heavy duty under penalty of your whole family. If you had listened earlier to Wang Ping, could this misfortune have happened? Now our army is defeated, officers are slain, ground is lost, and a fortress is occupied. All this is your fault. If you do not understand proper military law, how can you lead men? You have broken the law; do not resent me. After your death, your household is poor; I will provide grain pay each month. You need not worry.” He shouted for the attendants to bring him out and behead him.

Ma Shu wept, “The Chancellor has treated me like a son; I have regarded the Chancellor as a father. My capital crime is truly inescapable. I beg Your Excellency to remember Emperor Shun punishing Gun and Yü’s righteousness; even in death, I will have no resentment!” He ended and wept bitterly.

Kongming, with tears in his eyes, said, “I stand with you in brotherhood, and your son is my son. You need not burden me with words.”

The attendants took Ma Shu outside the chariot gate and set to behead him. Jiang Wan had come from Chengdu. Seeing soldiers ready to execute Ma Shu, he was greatly alarmed and urgently called out to stop them, then entered and said to Kongming, “In the old state of Chu, Chancellor Wen rejoiced at killing a loyal minister. The realm is still unsettled, and here is a man of strategic mind. Should we not be reluctant to shed him?”

With tears, Kongming replied, “In former times, Sun Wu was able to win the world through clear law. In these days, the four regions are in chaos and war has just begun. If law were discarded when needed, how could we suppress the enemies? He must be executed.”

Before long an executioner brought in Ma Shu’s severed head and set it under the stairs.

Kongming wept without ceasing. Jiang Wan asked, “Young as I am, I have often erred. Now that military law has been correctly enforced, why does the Chancellor weep?”

Kongming said, “I do not weep for Ma Shu. At Baidi City, when the late emperor faced danger he once told me, ‘Ma Shu speaks beyond his true ability and should not be employed heavily.’ That now proves true. I deeply blame myself for not understanding, and I remember the late emperor’s clarity, and that is why I cry.”

Every general and soldier, whether high or low, wept. Ma Shu’s age was thirty-nine. It was the fifth month of the sixth year of Jianxing.

Later people wrote:

Losing Jieting was no light guilt; Ma Shu talked of war in vain. Beheading at the chariot gate follows strict military law; even through tears he still remembered the late emperor’s clarity.

So Kongming, having executed Ma Shu, showed the severed head to each camp, sewed it back onto his body with thread, prepared a coffin, and buried him. He drafted and recited a sacrificial text in his rites. He gave comfort and monthly stipends of grain and pay to Ma Shu’s poor household.

Then Kongming drafted a memorial and ordered Jiang Wan to submit it to the latter ruler, asking to step down one rank from Chancellor.

Jiang Wan returned to Chengdu and entered the audience hall before the ruler, presenting Kongming’s memorial. The ruler opened it and read:

I am by no means exceptional, yet I seized office through presumption. I personally held command and disciplined the three armies. I could not properly instruct the statutes, and when matters arose I misplanned, so that at Jieting I disobeyed command and at Jigu I failed to give warning. All blame is mine: I am not clear and I do not know men; in judging affairs I was dark. On the season of inquiry and accountability, where can sin escape? I beg to demote myself three grades and examine this grave failing. Shame cannot be borne by me. I bow and await the command.

The ruler finished reading and said, “Victory and defeat are ordinary in war. Why does the Chancellor speak this way?” Court Attendant Fei Yi replied, “I have heard it said: the one who governs a state must value law above all. If law is not enforced, how can men be controlled? The Chancellor has failed in battle; he should demote himself, and that is proper.”

The ruler accepted this and issued an edict: Kongming would be reduced to Right General, but continue to carry out Chancellor business and, as before, command all horses and troops. He ordered Fei Yi to issue the decree in Hanzhong. After the edict of demotion reached him, Fei Yi, fearing Kongming might be ashamed, offered congratulations: “The people of Shu know the Chancellor once recovered the four commanderies and rejoice deeply.”

Kongming’s face grew dark. “What words are those? To regain and to lose are alike. If you congratulate me for this, it is enough to make me ashamed.” Fei Yi said, “I hear now that the Chancellor has obtained Jiang Wei; the Son of Heaven is greatly pleased.”

Kongming said angrily, “My fault is great: after a defeated army returns, not even a span of land was won. What loss to Wei in taking one Jiang Wei?” Fei Yi asked, “Could the Chancellor once again lead a northern invasion against Wei?”

Kongming replied, “When the great army was stationed at Qishan and Jigu, our troops were more than the enemy’s, but we could not break them; instead we were broken. This was not a question of numbers but of the commanding general. Now we should reduce troops and remove generals, punish ourselves clearly, and think out ways to adapt for the future. If not, what use has a great army? From now on, if there are anyone in the state with far-reaching concern, let them concentrate on exposing my failings and pointing out my shortcomings. Then the affair can be settled, the enemy destroyed, and accomplishment will stand ready.”

All of Fei Yi’s generals accepted the argument. Fei Yi returned to Chengdu. In Hanzhong, Kongming, mindful of soldiers and people, urged training and weapons drills, built siege engines and river-crossing devices, gathered grain, and prepared boats for future plans.

A covert observer reported all this in Luoyang.

When Cao Rui heard it, he at once summoned Sima Yi to discuss taking back Sichuan. Sima Yi said, “Shu cannot be attacked now. At present the realm is in midsummer heat; Shu soldiers will not venture out. If our army goes deep into their land, they will hold their strong points and be very hard to force down.”

Cao Rui said, “If the army comes again to raid, what then?”

Sima Yi said, “I have already calculated that this time Zhuge Liang will repeat Han Xin’s covert crossing at Chen Cang. Send one man to the Chen Cang road gate and have him build defenses there; that will never fail. He is nine chi tall, ape-armed, and excellent with the bow, and he has deep stratagem in him. If Zhuge Liang invades, this one alone can meet him.”

Cao Rui asked happily, “Who is this man?” Sima Yi said, “He is from Taiyuan, surname Hao, named Zhaodao, courtesy name Baodao. He is now General Zaba and garrisoned at Hexi.”

Cao Rui accepted this and promoted Hao Zhaodao as General Who Guards the West, commanding him to hold the Chen Cang road gate. He sent an order immediately.

Then a report came in: Cao Xiu, Army Marshal and Grand Commander of Yangzhou, had submitted a memorial saying that Zhou Fang, Administrator of Shenyang, wished to surrender his commandery. He had secretly conveyed seven points. He said Wu could be broken and asked for immediate dispatch of troops to seize him.

Cao Rui, on the imperial bed, opened it and read it with Sima Yi.

Sima Yi said, “This is very reasonable, and Wu will fall. I will take a force and assist Cao Xiu.” A man in the ranks then reported, “The words from Wu are inconsistent and unreliable; Zhou Fang is a man of plotting and strategy and would never truly surrender. This is only a ploy to lure troops.” It was General Jianwei, Jia Kui.

Sima Yi said, “This warning too cannot be ignored, and the opportunity can also not be missed.” Cao Rui said, “Zhongda should aid Jia Kui in helping Cao Xiu.” The two departed with orders.

Then Cao Xiu led a major army straight to Wancheng. Jia Kui brought General Man Chong and Hu Zhi, Administrator of Dongwan, and moved on to Yangcheng, straight toward Dongguan; Sima Yi took his main force and went straight for Jiangling.

Now Sun Quan, at Wuchang East Pass, gathered many officials and discussed: “Now Zhou Fang of Shenyang has submitted a secret memorial saying that Cao Xiu, Supreme Commander of Yangzhou, means to invade. Zhou Fang, with deceitful words, has presented seven points by secret message, drawing Wei troops deep so that an ambush may catch them. Wei troops now come by three routes. What is your high suggestion, each of you?”

Gu Yong said, “Such a great responsibility would be more than even Lu Boyan would dare undertake.” Sun Quan rejoiced, summoned Lu Xun, made him General Who Assists the State and Supreme Commander for Pacifying the North, gave him full command of the main army, and entrusted him with sovereign affairs in this matter. He handed him the white-feathered yellow battle-sceptre; all civil and military officials were to obey him. Sun Quan himself held the reins and ran with him.

After ritual thanks, Sun Quan asked him for two adjutants. Lu Xun said, “General Zhu Huan and General Quan Cong are suitable for assistance.” Sun Quan approved and ordered Zhu Huan as left grand commander and Quan Cong as right grand commander. Therefore Lu Xun led the southern eighty-one commanderies and the Jinghu regions, more than seven hundred thousand men. He placed Zhu Huan on the left, Quan Cong on the right, and kept himself in the center, advancing by three routes.

Zhu Huan offered: “Cao Xiu is trusted by personal appointment, but he is no general of intelligence and courage. If we let Zhou Fang’s baiting words stand and let him go deep into important terrain, your commander-in-chief will strike and he will surely be defeated. After his defeat he will have only two exits: Jiaoshi on the left and Guiche on the right. Those two paths are mountain shortcuts and tiny tracks, steep and perilous.

I ask to have me and Quan Cong each lead a corps, lie in ambush on the heights, first block those routes with timber and heavy stones, and capture Cao Xiu. If he is taken, we can ride fast and directly reach Shouzhou; this is an age-defining moment to take a long look toward Xu and Luoyang.”

Lu Xun said, “This is not the best plan. I have my own way.” Thus Zhu Huan retired in displeasure.

Lu Xun ordered Zhuge Jin and the rest to hold Jiangling and resist Sima Yi. All routes were adjusted into place.

Now Cao Xiu’s army reached Anhcheng. Zhou Fang came out to greet him and came straight to his command tent.

Cao Xiu asked, “I have received your written words. The seven points you presented are profound and proper, and I have transmitted them to the Son of Heaven; therefore I have set out a great army in three routes. If you obtain land in Jiangdong, your merit is no small thing. Some say you are full of schemes, and truly I fear your words may be untrue. I assume you are not deceiving me.”

Zhou Fang burst into tears and quickly drew the sword from his attendant, intending to slash his own throat. Cao Xiu hastily stopped him.

Zhou Fang held the sword and said, “The seven matters I put forward I could not bring myself to express with my heart and liver. Since this doubt appears, surely some man from Wu has set me up for a ruse. If I were to accept this and listen, I would have to die. Only Heaven can prove my loyalty.” He finished, and again tried to cut himself.

Cao Xiu panicked and held him: “I only spoke playfully. Why would you do this?”

Zhou Fang used the sword to cut his hair and throw it to the ground, saying, “I serve your peace with a loyal heart. If you take this as a jest, I cut the hair left by my parents as a witness of this heart.”

Cao Xiu now fully believed and arranged a banquet. After it ended, Zhou Fang took leave.

Soon there came word that General Jianwei, Jia Kui, had arrived to see him. Cao Xiu admitted him and asked, “Why have you come?”

Jia Kui replied, “I estimate that Wu troops will all garrison at Anhcheng. The inspector should not rush in. Wait for me to strike in two flanking attacks, and the enemy army can be broken.”

Cao Xiu shouted angrily, “Do you want to steal my merit?” Jia Kui said, “I have also heard Zhou Fang’s hair-cut vow. This is deceit. In old days, Yao Li cut off his arm to stab Qingji; still we did not trust such a move.”

Cao Xiu grew angry: “I was already preparing to mobilize; with this speech you slow my army’s spirit!” He shouted for attendants and ordered Jia Kui beheaded.

The other generals reported, “Before we even march, to execute one of our generals is harmful for the army. Please allow him to remain.” Cao Xiu agreed, kept Jia Kui’s troops in camp for use, and himself took one army to take Dongguan.

When Zhou Fang heard that Jia Kui had been stripped of command authority, he rejoiced privately, saying, “If Cao Xiu had listened to Jia Kui, Wu would lose! Today he makes me victorious.” He quietly sent a messenger to Anhcheng to tell Lu Xun.

Lu Xun called his generals and gave orders: “The Shiting pass in front is only mountain road but enough for ambush. Go now to occupy the broader spots and form battle arrays there to meet the Wei army.” He ordered Xu Sheng as vanguard and sent him forward.

Now Cao Xiu ordered Zhou Fang to advance.

While on the road, Cao Xiu asked, “Where is the way ahead?” Zhou Fang answered, “Ahead lies Shiting. It is fit to post troops.” Cao Xiu followed; he moved the entire army, chariots and equipment to Shiting and made camp.

The next day scouts reported, “Ahead there are unknown Wu troops, holding the mountain mouth.” Cao Xiu was greatly startled: “Zhou Fang said there were no troops. Why are they now prepared?” He urgently asked for Zhou Fang, and a report came that Zhou Fang, who had only brought several tens of men, had gone somewhere unknown.

Cao Xiu deeply regretted: “I have fallen into the enemy’s scheme. Even so, I need not still fear.” He ordered Zhang Pu as vanguard, with several thousand men to fight the Wu troops.

The two lines met face to face. Zhang Pu spoke from horseback, “Bandit general, surrender at once!” Xu Sheng rode out to meet him. They fought many rounds. Zhang Pu could not hold his line and wheeled back his horse, then reported to Cao Xiu that Xu Sheng was not to be overcome.

Cao Xiu said, “I shall defeat him with unexpected force.” He ordered Zhang Pu to take twenty thousand men and hide to the south of Shiting. He ordered Xue Qiao to take another twenty thousand and hide to the north of Shiting.

“Tomorrow I myself will bring one thousand men into a sharp fight, then feign defeat and lure them forward before Beishan. When the signal cannon is fired, we strike from three sides. We will gain a great victory.” The two generals, having understood the plan, took twenty thousand each and sank into ambush that night.

Now Lu Xun called Zhu Huan and Quan Cong and said, “Both of you take three thousand men. Move by the Shiting mountains and circle behind Cao Xiu’s camp, using fire as signal. I will lead the main army along the middle route and capture Cao Xiu.” At dusk the two obeyed and advanced.

By the second watch, Zhu Huan’s force, having come straight to Wei’s camp rear, encountered Zhang Pu’s hidden troops. Zhang Pu, not knowing they were Wu, came asking who they were and was cut down in one blow from horse to horse. The Wei troops ran, while Zhu Huan ordered the rear unit to raise fire.

Quan Cong’s force then circled to the rear of the Wei camp and collided directly with Xue Qiao’s formation, where they fought hard at once. Xue Qiao lost and fled; the Wei army suffered heavy losses and retreated to its camp. Behind them, both Zhu Huan and Quan Cong closed in with killing.

In Cao Xiu’s camp all became disorderly; men struck one another. Cao Xiu mounted and fled along the Jiachi route. Xu Sheng charged a main body of cavalry and horsemen straight along the direct route.

Wei deadmen were uncountable; those who fled cast away armor and clothing. Cao Xiu was in great fear. In the Jiachi gorge he ran in agony. Suddenly a band of troops surged from a side path with a great general in the lead—Jia Kui.

Cao Xiu, breathless, said to himself, “I ignored your words, and this defeat has truly come.”

Jia Kui said, “The Inspector must leave this path quickly. If the Wu block it with timber and stones, we all are in danger.” Cao Xiu then spurred hard and galloped on, Jia Kui trailing behind.

In a place where trees were lush and the path steep and narrow, Jia Kui set up many banner flags as false troops. When Xu Sheng arrived, he saw flash of flags from the hillside and thought ambush waited there. He did not dare to chase, but drew his men back. So Cao Xiu was saved. Sima Yi, hearing of Cao Xiu’s defeat, withdrew as well.

Now Lu Xun was waiting for good news. Soon Xu Sheng, Zhu Huan, and Quan Cong all arrived with chariots, horse teams, donkeys and mules, supplies and weapons beyond counting, and tens of thousands of defectors.

Lu Xun rejoiced greatly and then returned with Zhou Fang and the generals to Wu, disbanding and withdrawing the forces.

Sun Quan sent civil and military officials from Wuchang out to receive him and, with a ceremonial canopy, brought him into the city. He promoted all the generals. Seeing Zhou Fang with no hair left, Sun Quan comforted him: “You cut your hair and made this great matter happen; your merit belongs in bamboo and silk.” He made Zhou Fang Marquis within the Pass and held a grand feast to reward the troops.

Lu Xun submitted, “Now that Cao Xiu has been defeated badly and Wei soldiers are shaken, we may repair the state letters and send envoys into Shu ordering Zhuge Liang to advance and strike at Wei again.” Sun Quan approved and sent messengers with letters into Sichuan.

As it is: Because the Eastern realm can lay such designs, West Sichuan must again raise troops for war. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Kongming Weeps and Beheads Ma Shu; Zhou Fang Cuts His Hair to Trick Cao Xiu

chapters.html:
In the autumn of the ninth month in the sixth year of Jianxing under Shu-Han, Cao Xiu, chief military commander of Wei, was heavily defeated by Lu Xun of Eastern Wu at Shiting. The carriages, horses, provisions, and armaments were exhausted. Cao Xiu was so alarmed that fear became an illness; he reached Luoyang, fell ill with fever in his back, and died. Cao Rui of Wei ordered him to be buried with honor. Sima Yi withdrew with his forces.

As the officers came in, they asked him, “A defeated commander in Wei under the generalissimo’s responsibility usually means serious fault. Why did you retire so suddenly?”

Sima Yi said, “I judged that Zhuge Liang would know we had been defeated and would ride the opening to seize Chang’an. If Longxi faced urgency, who would come to its aid? I returned for that reason.”

The whole army took it for cowardice and laughed at him as he left.

Soon Eastern Wu sent an envoy to Shu with a letter requesting troops against Wei, praising the great victory over Cao Xiu as proof both of martial strength and of goodwill between the allies. The Later Ruler rejoiced and sent the letter on to Hanzhong to report it to Kongming. At that moment Zhuge Liang’s army was strong, horses were sound, grain was ample, and every kind of materiel was complete. He was preparing to set out already. On hearing this message he hosted a feast and assembled the generals to discuss an expedition. Suddenly a gust rose from the northeast, breaking pines in front of the courtyard. All were startled. Kongming consulted it by divination and said, “This wind foretells the loss of a great general.”

The generals did not believe him. While they were still drinking, a messenger came: Zhao Yun’s sons, Zhao Tong, the elder, and Zhao Guang, the younger, had arrived to see the chancellor. Kongming was deeply shocked and dropped his cup to the ground. “Zilong is gone,” he said.

When the two young men entered and knelt to cry out their news, they said, “Our father died in the middle of last night, in the third watch.”

Kongming stamped his foot and wept. “With Zilong dead, the state has lost a main pillar. It is as if one of my two arms were gone!” All the generals wept.

He ordered the two brothers to go to Chengdu and formally report the bereavement to the court. Upon hearing of Zhao Yun’s death, the Later Ruler cried out and wept aloud. “When I was young and helpless, if it had not been for Zilong, I would have died amid riotous ranks.” Then he issued an edict: Zhao Yun was to be posthumously made Great General, granted the marquisate title of Shunping, buried to the east of Jinping Mountain at Chengdu, and enshrined in a hall where he would be sacrificially remembered in all seasons.

There was a verse that later people made of him:

A tiger-general from Mount Chang, In cleverness and courage he matched Guan Zhang, His merits on the Han River stood in the record, At Dangyang his name and deeds blazed.

Twice he raised the young lord, In one thought he answered the late emperor. The clear histories praised his loyalty and courage; The chronicles shall record his loyalty and valor, whose fragrance will endure a hundred generations.

The Later Ruler, remembering Zhao Yun’s past service, arranged elaborate burial honors for him. He enfeoffed Zhao Tong as Colonel of the Tiger Guards, and Zhao Guang as a gate-guard general, then ordered them to guard the tomb. Both bowed and withdrew.

Soon an attendant reported: the divisions for an expedition had already been allocated by Chancellor Zhuge Liang, and he would set out that very day against Wei.

The Later Ruler asked the ministers in court, but many counseled against moving so lightly. The ruler’s doubts were not settled. Then an attendant announced that the chancellor had dispatched Yang Yi with a memorial for mobilization. The ruler ordered him in and Yang Yi presented the memorial. The ruler took it and opened it at the table before him.

The memorial read:

The late emperor feared that rebels and the imperial house could not both remain and that the royal charge could never be secured by mere partial peace; thus he entrusted me with punishing the rebels. With the late emperor’s clear understanding and by weighing my ability, he knew I was weaker than the foe. Yet if I did not punish them, the state’s enterprise would perish. To sit idle and await ruin—would that fare better than marching out? Therefore he entrusted me and never wavered in his trust.

From the day I received command, I have known no ease of rest and no appetite at table. I reflected that to go north we should first pass through the south; therefore in the fifth month I crossed the Lu River, pressing deep into the rough lands where we ate at all hours. I did not spare my own life for such hardship.

Yet I cannot hold to mere safety in Shu capital city, so at risk to myself I have carried out the late emperor’s intention, though some called this not a sound plan. Now the enemy is exhausted in the west and engaged in the east as well. In war, one should strike an enemy who labors; this is the time to advance in force. I therefore submit the matter as follows:

Gaozu and Ming were both clear as day and moon, yet their strategists were deep as abyssal waters. Only by risking danger and injury did they reach safety. Now Your Majesty has not yet Liu Bang’s brilliance, and the strategists are no stronger than Liang and Ping, yet you hope to prevail through long strategy and settle all under heaven. This is one thing I do not yet understand.

Liu Yao and Wang Lang each hold provinces and commanderies. I have put forth counsels of peace and prudence, but doubts and objections fill the hall. If we neither fight this year nor campaign next year, Wu’s Sun Quan will grow, and in time he will absorb Jiangdong. This is another matter I do not yet understand.

Cao Cao possessed intelligence and schemes beyond the common man, and his use of military force resembled Sun Wu in appearance. Yet he was forced into difficult straits at Nanyang, in peril at Wuchao, pressured at Qilian, hemmed in at Liyang, nearly defeated at Beishan, and nearly dead at Tongguan; he settled things but briefly at a time, then moved on. How then can I, with my lesser talent, hope to settle him at little risk? This is still beyond my understanding.

Cao Cao attacked Changba five times and did not break it, and crossed Chaohu four times without success. He employed Li Fu, and Li Fu turned his favor toward treason; he entrusted Xiahou, and Xiahou was defeated and ruined. The late emperor often called Cao an able man, and yet this was one failure in him; how much less can I, dull as I am, be certain of victory? This is another matter beyond my grasp.

Since arriving at Hanzhong, only just over a year has passed, yet in that time we have lost Zhao Yun, Yang Qun, Ma Yu, Yan Zhi, Ding Li, Bai Shou, Liu He, Deng Tong, and more than seventy officers of the Quchang Tun division. Also came Tu commanders, Wuqian, Congsou, Qingjiang, and over one thousand scattered and armored riders. These are the finest troops gathered from all quarters over decades, not drawn from one province alone. Had we waited a few more years, we would lose two-thirds of them. By what method then can we hope to oppose the enemy? This is another matter I do not understand.

The people are poor and the army fatigued, yet affairs admit no pause. If they cannot pause, we cannot stay in place or move at ease—both spend equal cost. If we fail to plan early and instead seek to endure with only one province against the enemy, this is another thing I do not understand.

A foe hard to subdue, yes, is always like this. In former days, when the late emperor lost a battle at Chu, Cao Cao struck his palm and said the realm was already pacified. Yet afterward the late emperor allied with Wu in the east and took Ba and Shu in the west, raised banners northward, and won the capture of Xiahou by the time he marched. That was Cao’s miscalculation, and Han’s cause was then close to fulfillment. Yet Wu then broke the alliance, Guan Yu was ruined in defeat, Zigui suffered collapse, and Cao Pi took the throne. Events proceed like this and are difficult to reverse.

I have bent my back until all strength is spent and will not stop until I die. As for victory or loss, success or failure, whether my calculations are sound, I cannot claim foreknowledge beyond my own clarity.

The Later Ruler was delighted by the memorial and immediately issued orders for Zhuge Liang to take the field. Receiving the command, Kongming raised three hundred thousand troops. He ordered Wei Yan to command the vanguard and run straight along the Chen Village Pass route.

The first detailed report had already reached Luoyang. Sima Yi informed the Wei ruler, and ministers and officers gathered to deliberate. Generalissimo Cao Zhen stood to report: “I guarded Longxi till now, with small achievements but great blame; I am deeply fearful. Now I beg leave to lead a great army and seize Zhuge Liang. I have recently met a great general from Qingshui, sixty-jin broad sword, riding a thousand-li horse, carrying an iron-bow that could hold two stones, and secretly hiding three meteor hammers. His courage cannot be measured by ten thousand men. He is a northern Longxi Didao man, surname Wang, given name Shuang, style Ziquan. I keep this man as my vanguard.”

Cao Rui was delighted and summoned Wang Shuang to the hall. When he appeared, he was nine chi tall, dark-faced and light-brown, with a broad waist and tiger-like shoulders. Cao Rui laughed and said, “I have obtained this great general; what need have I to worry?” He then bestowed brocade robes and gold cuirass, and made Wang Shuang the Tiger-Guards General and commander of the Great Vanguard in front. Cao Zhen was made Chief Commander.

After expressing thanks, Cao Zhen led out and drew one hundred and fifty thousand elite soldiers to join with Guo Huai and Zhang He in controlling the mountain passes.

Meanwhile the Shu vanguard scouts reached Chen Cang and reported back to Zhuge Liang. “The gate at Chen Cang Pass has already been turned into a fortress,” they said. “General Hao Zhao is inside. The moat is deep, the walls are tall, and it is studded all around with antler-like battlements. Guard is strict in every direction. Better to abandon this city and march by the route over Taibai Ridge’s mountain path and through Qishan.”

Kongming said, “Directly north of Chen Cang is Jie Ting, and we must take this city before we can advance.” He ordered Wei Yan to bring the army to the foot of the walls and assault from four sides. For several days they could not break through. Wei Yan returned with the same report of failure.

Kongming grew angry and said, “I would have him beheaded.” At that moment a man from among the attendants informed him, “Though I have no talent, I have served the chancellor for many years and have never repaid him with any achievement. Permit me to go into Chen Cang and urge Hao Zhao to surrender. I need no bow or arrow.” They recognized him as the retainer Yin Xiang.

Kongming asked, “What argument will you use to persuade him?”

Yin answered in detail: “Hao Zhao and I are both from Longxi and have been companions since childhood. If I go now and appeal to him about benefit and peril, he will surely surrender.”

Kongming instructed him to go.

Yin Shuang hastened his horse and rode straight to the walls, crying out, “It is Yin Xiang, Hao Bo, old friend from home, come to see you.” People on the walls informed Hao Zhao.

Hao Zhao ordered the gate opened for him to enter and came up to meet him atop the wall.

Hao asked, “Old companion, why have you come here?”

Xiang said, “I serve under Kongming in Hanzhong-Southwest and attend to military matters. The chancellor has commanded me to pay you guest honors. I am only now dispatched to bear words I must tell you.”

Hao Zhao’s face changed at once. “Kongming is the enemy of my state and my feud enemy! I serve Wei; you serve Shu—each serves one’s own lord. Once we were two clans together, now we are sworn enemies. Speak no more. Please leave the city!”

Xiang tried again, but Hao already moved to the enemy tower. The Wei troops pressed the horses and rushed him out beyond the gate. As he looked back, he saw Hao standing by the protective breast-rail of the heart post. He checked his horse, struck with his whip, and pointed: “Honorable elder Hao, why is your loyalty so shallow?”
