Hao replied, “You know the law of Wei. I owe a debt to this state; I have only death to give. You need not try persuasion words. Return quickly to Zhuge Liang and tell him to come on and attack; I do not fear him!”

Yin Xiang returned to Kongming and said, “Hao Zhao blocked me before I could even begin to speak.”

Kongming said, “Go again. Convince him again with benefit and peril.”

Yin returned to the walls and requested the other audience. Hao came out onto the enemy tower. Yin reined in his horse and shouted loudly, “O righteous brother, listen to one honest word. You hold one isolated city. How can you refuse the multitude of hundreds of thousands? If you do not surrender now, remorse will come too late. Why do you not serve the Great Han, instead serving treacherous Wei? If you fail to know Heaven’s mandate, to distinguish clear from impure, what more can I say? Reflect on this, Hao.”

Hao Zhao flew into rage, took up bow and arrow, pointed at Yin, and shouted, “My earlier words stand. You have no need to say more. Withdraw now. I will not even shoot you.”

Yin reported to Kongming exactly this state of Hao Zhao. Kongming was furious and said, “How can this fellow lack all decorum? Does he think I cannot break this city?” He immediately asked the locals, “How many men and horses are in Chen Cang?”

They answered, “I do not know exactly, but around three thousand.”

Kongming smiled, “Measure this little city—how could it withstand us? Let the relief troops come, and then strike at once.”

So the troops built one hundred cloud-ladders. One could hold a dozen men, and the sides were covered by wooden planking. Each soldier took a short ladder and a soft rope. At the drumbeat through the camp, all charged up at once.

From the enemy tower Hao Zhao saw the ladders being raised from all sides and ordered three thousand men with fire-arrows to line all four sides. When the ladders came near the wall he ordered all fire them together. Kongming had assumed the city stood undefended, so he had built many ladders and urged all three armies forward with a roar. Unexpectedly, the archer fire from above rained down all at once. The ladders burned and many soldiers on them were burned alive. Arrows and stones from above fell like rain; the Shu troops withdrew.

Kongming said angrily, “You burn my ladders; I will answer with the rams!”

That night he arranged battering rams. The next day the armies again advanced to drum and shout from four sides. Hao Zhao ordered, in urgency, stones to be split for drilling, then tied grappling cords and crossbows to strike; the rams were all broken.

Kongming then ordered that dirt be hauled in to fill the defensive moat. He told Liao Hua to lead three thousand men carrying picks and spades to tunnel from the night and enter the city secretly. Hao Zhao himself then dug a deep cross moat inside the walls to cut off that assault path.

Thus through day and night there was assault for more than twenty days with no way to break through. Kongming’s mind grew troubled. Suddenly news arrived: “A relief force has come from the east. Their banner announces, ‘General Wang Shuang, Great Vanguard of Wei.’”

Kongming asked, “Who will go out to receive him?”

Wei Yan said, “I volunteer.”

Kongming replied, “You are the great vanguard commander. You must not go lightly.”

He asked, “Who else dares to meet him?”

Assistant general Xie Xiong stepped forth and cried out at once.

Kongming then sent three thousand men with him.

Kongming asked, “Who goes again?”

Another assistant general, Gong Qi, stepped out at once to go. Kongming sent him with three thousand as well.

Kongming feared Hao Zhao might charge out from the city, and so moved the forces back twenty li and encamped.

Xie Xiong, leading his division, encountered Wang Shuang. They fought for less than three exchanges before Wang Shuang cut him in one stroke.

Shu troops broke and scattered. Wang Shuang pursued. Gong Qi followed after, and after just three exchanges had his horse exchange and was also cut down. The broken troops reported back to Kongming.

Kongming was startled and urgently ordered Liao Hua, Wang Ping, and Zhang Ni to go out to meet them. The two armies came face to face. Zhang Ni rode foremost. Wang Ping and Liao Hua held the battle corners.

Wang Shuang surged his horse and exchanged with Zhang Ni several times, neither yielding. Then Shuang feigned defeat and withdrew. Zhang Ni chased after him. Wang Ping saw that Zhang Ni had walked into a trap and shouted, “Do not pursue!”

When Zhang Ni quickly turned his horse, Wang Shuang’s meteor hammer came early and struck him in the back. Zhang Ni slid from his saddle and fled. Wang Shuang wheeled his horse to pursue. Wang Ping and Liao Hua cut him off and rescued Zhang Ni back into formation.

Wang Shuang drove his troops to kill in one sweep; Shu suffered many losses, and Zhang Ni coughed blood several times before reporting to Kongming: “Wang Shuang is a peerless hero. Now twenty thousand troops have camped outside Chen Cang. They have raised stockades and heavy walls on all four sides and dug a deep defensive moat.”

Kongming, seeing two commanders wounded and Zhang Ni hurt, called for Jiang Wei: “The Chen Cang route cannot be carried. Is there another plan?”

Wei said, “Chen Cang is strongly fortified and Hao Zhao defends it with care; with Wang Shuang at his side, it cannot be taken. Better to send one great general to the mountains and waters and hold camp firmly, then pin down Cao Zhen.”

Kongming agreed. He ordered Wang Ping and Li Hui to guard the small road at Jie Ting with two thousand men, and Wei Yan to take one army to guard the Chen Cang pass. Ma Dai would lead the vanguard, with Guan Xing and Zhang Bao in forward-and-rear response positions.

From a small path they went through a slanting valley and advanced toward Qishan.

Cao Zhen, still recalling how his credit had been taken by Sima Yi before, had already assigned Guo Huai and Sun Li to hold the eastern and western gates out by Luokou. Learning that Chen Cang had signaled in alarm, he sent Wang Shuang to help; when he heard of Wang Shuang’s beheading of commanders and new merit, he rejoiced. He made Fei Yao, the middle bodyguard general, act in the interim as commander of the front division, and each general took station at his assigned pass.

A local informer captured in the mountains was suddenly brought before him, so Cao Zhen had him tied and brought to the command tent and knelt down before the command. The man said, “I am no spy or traitor, only one bringing secret orders. I was mistakenly seized by a hidden-ridge unit; please release me from chains.”

Cao Zhen ordered the bonds removed and had his attendants withdraw. The man said, “I am a trusted intimate of Jiang Wei and was sent by your lord with a secret letter.”

“Where is it?” Cao Zhen asked.

The man drew out a folded paper from within his quilted jacket and gave it.

Cao Zhen broke it open and read:

“The guilty officer Jiang Wei bows a hundred times and presents this to the Great Commander of Wei. Though I grew up on Wei stipends and now guard the front of the cities, I have swallowed heavy favor and have no way to repay it. Yesterday by mischance I was ensnared by Zhuge Liang’s deceit and nearly fell into a precipice. Can one ever forget one’s old state? No. Today Shu forces move westward, and Zhuge Liang is not suspicious of me. I rely on your lord bringing great forces; if you meet the enemy, you may act as if in defeat. If I remain at the rear, my signal will be fire. Burn first the Shu grain first and then turn the main army to cover the retreat; Zhuge Liang can then be captured. I desire not fame or reward, only to atone for my prior crimes.

If Your Excellency notices this, please issue orders quickly as stated.”

After reading it, Cao Zhen was delighted: “Heaven itself is granting me success!” He rewarded the messenger heavily and ordered him sent back to the meeting point.

Cao Zhen told Fei Yao to deliberate. “Now Jiang Wei has secretly presented a secret letter, directing me to act thus.”

Fei Yao said, “Zhuge Liang is many-stratagemed and Jiang Wei is broad of wit. Perhaps this is indeed what Zhuge has set in motion; there may be deceit in it.”

Cao Zhen replied, “He was originally a man of Wei, forced by circumstance to go over to Shu. Why should I suspect him?”

Fei Yao said, “Do not advance rashly, governor. Hold this true camp. I will lead one army to meet Jiang Wei; if success is ours, it is yours; if deceit lies in it, I will bear the blame.”

Cao Zhen was pleased and ordered Fei Yao to lead fifty thousand troops and advance toward the slanting valley. After two or three journeys he camped with mounted and foot soldiers and sent lookouts. At the seventh watch (afternoon, third period), he reported: “Shu troops are approaching from the slanting valley.” Fei Yao hurried on.

Shu troops withdrew before contact; Fei Yao ordered pursuit. The Shu forces returned, only then to form for battle; they withdrew again. This happened three times. Late toward the next afternoon, after a day and night the Wei army did not dare rest, fearing sudden attack from Shu. When the troops prepared a cooking pot one day, a sudden uproar of shouts rose from all sides and war horns sounded together. Shu troops came pouring over the entire hills and hillsides.

At the gate standard’s opening, a four-wheeled carriage rolled out. Zhuge Liang sat within, and asked that the Wei field commander answer him.

Fei Yao spurred his horse forward and saw Zhuge Liang. Secretly glad in his heart, he looked over his shoulder and said, “If Shu attacks in force, we withdraw and move back. If fire rises behind the mountain, then we reverse and break through—our troops will come in to join.” He finished his orders.

The horse moved out, and he rode up calling out, “A failed general from before—what business brings you hurrying again?”

Kongming replied coldly, “Call the Chief Commander Cao Zhen out to answer me.”

Fei Yao cursed, “The commander of Wei is a gold branch and jade trunk—how could he deign to meet a rebel?”

Kongming grew enraged, lifted his feathered fan with one motion. On his left was Ma Dai, on his right Zhang Ni. Troops surged out on two routes. The Wei troops broke and ran.

After less than thirty li the Shu forces met fire erupting behind them and unending shouts. The two armies closed in; on the left was Guan Xing, and on the right was Zhang Bao. Arrows and stones came down like rain from the mountain side. The Wei army was defeated in rout.

Fei Yao knew he had been tricked. Gathering the retiring formation, he aimed toward the valley to run, but men and horses were exhausted and disordered. Behind him, Guan Xing led an energized detachment to press forward. The Wei ranks stepped upon one another and were forced over cliffs into ravines, and the dead count could not be known.

Fei Yao fled for life and at that moment met a large host at the hillside mouth. It was Jiang Wei.

Fei Yao shouted in anger, “Rebels have no trustworthiness. Unhappily I have fallen for your treachery!”

Jiang Wei said with a smile, “I sought to capture Cao Zhen; by that plan I have mistaken only your losses. Dismount at once and surrender!”

Fei Yao leapt from his horse to cut for escape and ran into the valley. At once mountain fire roared upward, and chasing soldiers came from behind. He slew himself on the spot.

All remaining forces surrendered. Under cover of night, Kongming pressed on to the slope before Qishan, camped and held the mounted troops in place.

He rewarded Jiang Wei highly.

Jiang Wei said, “I wished I could have killed Cao Zhen.”

Kongming said too, “A grand design was spoiled by over-familiar timing.”

Cao Zhen, hearing Fei Yao had been lost, repented too late. He and Guo Huai discussed a plan of retreat. That night Sun Li and Xin Pi prepared a memorial and presented it to the Wei ruler, reporting that Shu forces had once again moved out to Qishan and Cao Zhen had suffered losses and lost commanders; his situation was precarious.

Cao Rui was startled and called Sima Yi inside, saying, “Cao Zhen has suffered heavy losses and lost commanders, and now Shu has come again to Qishan. What plan do you have to pull back?”

Sima Yi replied, “I already have a plan to withdraw from Zhuge Liang. Do not rely on Wei’s display of power and martial splendor; Shu forces will walk away on their own.”

Then came the closing lines:

Already, we have seen Zi Dan has no unbeatable stratagem; the whole matter rests on Zhongda’s good counsel.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Wuhou Submits Another Memorial to Attack Wei; Jiang Wei Deceives with a False Letter

chapters.html:
The Han army is pursued, and Wang Shuang is executed. Chen Cang is struck, and Wuhou prevails.

Sima Yi submitted his report. “I have already informed Your Majesty that Kongming must leave Chen Cang, so I ordered Hao Zhao to hold it. It has proved true. If they come from Chen Cang to raid, supplying grain would be very convenient. Now, fortunately, Hao Zhao and Wang Shuang are stationed here, so they do not dare to transport grain by this route; the other side roads are hard and difficult to use for movement. I calculate that Shu provisions will last only one month, so speed in battle is to our advantage. Our army should only hold and endure. Your Majesty should issue an edict ordering Cao Zhen to hold every pass and not seek battle. In less than a month the Shu army will have to withdraw. Then, when they are weak from marching, we can strike at them. Kongming would then be within reach.”

Cao Rui answered with satisfaction, “If you had such foreknowledge, why did you not lead a detachment yourself and strike first?”

Sima Yi replied, “I do not treasure life above my duty, and I truly wish to keep this force for guarding against Eastern Wu’s Lu Xun. Sun Quan will not be long before he assumes a pretended imperial title. If that happens and he proclaims himself the august ruler, I fear Your Majesty will move against him, giving him the excuse to invade us first. That is why I want to hold the army in readiness.”

At that moment an attendant arrived in haste: “Cao Commander reports the military situation.”

Sima Yi ordered, “Your Majesty should immediately send word to Cao Zhen: whenever you pursue the Shu forces, observe their true strength before acting; do not advance deep into hostile ground, lest you fall into Kongming’s trap.”

Cao Rui issued the order at once and sent Han Ji, the Minister of Ceremonies, with the imperial token. “Do not fight,” it read. “Defend carefully and hold the lines. Wait until the Shu army pulls back, then strike only then.”

When Han Ji was at the city gate, Sima Yi summoned him and said, “I entrust this merit to Zidan. When you meet him, say nothing that this was my advice. Let him think only that the Son of Heaven has commanded that defense takes precedence. In pursuit, commanders must watch closely; do not send rash men, hot-blooded and impatient, to chase.”

Han Ji withdrew.

Cao Zhen had just resumed council in his command tent when news came that the Son of Heaven had sent Han Ji with the imperial token. Cao Zhen went out to receive him. After he had done obeisance and retired from the command tent with Guo Huai and Sun Li to deliberate.

Guo Huai laughed. “This is exactly Zhongda’s reading.”

Cao Zhen asked, “In what way?”

Guo Huai replied, “He clearly understands how Kongming handles armies. If anyone can endure a prolonged defense against Shu troops, it is Zhongda.”

Cao Zhen said, “If the Shu force does not retreat, what then?”

Guo Huai answered, “Send Wang Shuang quietly to patrol on a side route with a light force. Then they will not dare to run grain there. Wait until their supply runs out and they must retreat. Then seize the moment and pursue; we can turn it into a complete victory.”

Sun Li said, “I can dress up troops as a grain convoy from Qishan. We load all the wagons with dry reed and brushwood and fill them with brimstone and saltpeter. Then I will have a fake dispatch saying grain transport from Longxi has arrived. If the Shu army is short of supplies, it will certainly rush in to seize it. Once they enter, we set fire to the wagons. Reserve troops outside will fall upon them and win.”

Cao Zhen praised it as excellent and ordered Sun Li to execute the plan exactly. He also sent men to tell Wang Shuang to patrol and report along side tracks, while Guo Huai ordered troops to move through Jigu Valley and Jieting, with troops and horses from each route posted at the critical ridges. Cao Zhen then assigned Zhang Hu, son of Zhang Liao, as advance guard and Lechen, son of Yue Jin, as deputy. They shared the forward encampment and were forbidden to take battle.

Meanwhile Kongming in the Qishan camp challenged the Wei troops every day, but the Wei army held firm and never came out. He called for Jiang Wei to plan. “Wei holds the position and refuses to advance,” Kongming said. “They are counting on the fact that our grain is nearly gone. With Chen Cang blocked, other side routes are difficult. I estimate our supplies cannot last more than a month. What are we to do?”

As he hesitated, news arrived that several thousand supply wagons from Longxi had come toward the west of Qishan. The officer in charge was none other than Sun Li.

Kongming asked, “Who is that man?”

A Wei informant said, “He once accompanied the Wei ruler on a hunt at Dashi Mountain. A fierce tiger leaped forward straight at the carriage. Sun Li dismounted, drew his sword, and severed it. From then on he was made General-in-Chief. He is close to Cao Zhen.”

Kongming smiled. “That is it. Wei expects us to be short of grain, and has devised this scheme. These wagons surely carry only straw and fire powder. I have always favored fire attack; and now they try to draw me into that very snare. If he suspects I will raid their grain train, he will come to raid my camp first. Let us meet plan with counterplan.”

He summoned Ma Dai and ordered him: “Take three thousand men directly to the Wei depot. Do not enter the camp. From above the windward ridge, set it alight. If the wagons burn, Wei soldiers will come to surround our camp.” He then dispatched Ma Zhong and Zhang Ni, five thousand each, to hold outside and close both hands of the field. They departed.

He then summoned Guan Xing and Zhang Bao. “The Wei forward camp controls four connecting roads. If fire rises on the west ridge tonight, Wei troops will rush to relieve me. You two hide beside the Wei camp, one on each side. Wait until their force moves out, then strike.”

He also summoned Wu Ban and Wu Yi. “Each of you lead a corps and lie in wait outside the camp. If Wei troops arrive, cut off their path home.” They too set out. Kongming had finished his dispositions and sat above Qishan, watching from the heights.

Wei scouts learned that the Shu force intended to raid the grain wagons and hurriedly informed Sun Li, who immediately signaled Cao Zhen by courier. Cao Zhen ordered men at the head camp to instruct Zhang Hu and Lechen: “When fire rises on the western mountain tonight, the Shu will come to relieve the camp. Then we can deploy; do so as I have indicated.”

Both took the instruction and climbed the towers to watch for the signal fires.

Sun Li posted his army on the west of the mountain and waited for the Shu to come. At the second watch, Ma Dai arrived with three thousand men. The men held arrows in their mouths and their horses had muzzles bound tight. He marched straight to the western heights, where wagon trains were massed in layers upon layers, crowded into a ringed camp with banners half-planted among them. At that moment a southwest wind rose. Ma Dai ordered his men to go to the southern edge and set fires. Every wagon burned, and the flames rose skyward.

Sun Li thought the Shu had reached Wei camp and set war cries from within. He rushed all troops to cover the position. Horns and drums exploded from behind him, two streams of troops came in. One was Ma Zhong and Zhang Ni, who had already encircled the Wei army at the heart of its camp. The other was Ma Dai bursting from the edge of the fire and noise. Under attack from both outside and inside, the Wei force collapsed. Wind and flame whipped the smoke; men and horses bolted in confusion; the dead were countless. Sun Li, hit in the body, cut his way through fire and smoke and fled.

Zhang Hu, in the main camp, saw the blazing fire and threw open the gate. He and Lechen rode out with all their troops, charging for the Shu camp. The camp was empty. As he pulled troops back, two roads of troops led by Wu Ban and Wu Yi burst out and cut their return lines. Zhang and Le sprang through the encirclement to run back to their own camp, only to see arrows raining on the earthen wall like locusts descending. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao had struck their camp. The Wei force was routed and all withdrew to Cao Zhen’s main camp.

As they were about to enter, a squad of shattered men rushed in. It was Sun Li.

Cao Zhen and the others entered to hear their report of being deceived. He kept only the great camp and did not fight further. The Shu victory having been won, they returned to Kongming.

Kongming quietly conveyed instructions to Wei Yan. “Raise the camp and prepare to withdraw as one.”

Yang Yi objected, “Now that we have a great victory and have broken the Wei spirit, why do you want to draw troops back?”

Kongming said, “Our army is short of grain. Haste favors us only in battle. Now Wei holds back and will not come out; the Shu force suffers by remaining. Even if they are defeated for the moment, they will have reinforcements from the Central Plains. If light cavalry strikes our supply road, we cannot return. Since Wei has just lost face, it will not dare to look straight at Shu. We can leave without being seen and withdraw on that very opening. My only concern is this: Wei Yan’s corps, at the Chen Cang gate, is blocked by Wang Shuang and cannot disengage. I have already issued secret orders: kill Wang Shuang, and no Wei men should dare pursue. The rearguard only should move first.”

That night Kongming left only gongs and drums in camp for the night watch. By dawn the whole army had withdrawn, leaving only an empty encampment.

Cao Zhen was still in his camp, troubled and gloomy, when suddenly Zhang He, General of the Left, arrived. He dismounted and entered the command tent: “I was ordered by imperial command to hear your adjustment.”

Cao Zhen asked, “Did Zhongda send a separate message?”

Zhang He answered, “He instructed: ‘If we win, the Shu army cannot leave easily; if we lose, it will leave at once.’ Since we have just suffered, have any scouts been sent from our side to sound out the Shu force?”

Cao Zhen admitted they had not.

He sent men at once to reconnoiter and found the camp to be empty by design: only several dozen banners remained planted, and the soldiers had departed two days earlier.

Cao Zhen bitterly regretted it too late.

Wei Yan carried out the secret plan and at the second watch raised camp and hurried back to Hanzhong. Earlier, a covert agent had already informed Wang Shuang. Wang Shuang drove his troops and horse at full speed in pursuit, reaching a little beyond twenty li before nearly catching him. Wei Yan’s banner was in front, and he shouted, “Wei Yan does not flee!”

The Shu troops did not turn back. Wang Shuang spurred forward, but behind him Wei soldiers called out, “Fire is burning in the outer camp; it must be a trap they set for us!”

He pulled his horse hard and rode back. Suddenly flames rose to the sky. He hurriedly turned his forces to retreat. As he moved along the left of a slope, a rider suddenly burst from the woods and cried, “Wei Yan is here!” Wang Shuang was startled and could not react; Wei Yan cut him down from under the horse in one stroke.

Wei soldiers, fearing an ambush, scattered in all directions. Wei Yan had only thirty riders at hand; they advanced slowly toward Hanzhong.

A later poem praised him:

Kongming’s wondrous reckoning outwits Sun and Pang, a guiding star shining over one realm. He moves with perfect judgment in advance and retreat, and at the gate of Chen Cang he slays Wang Shuang.

In truth, Wei Yan had carried out Kongming’s cunning design. He first left only thirty horse behind to lie in wait near Wang Shuang’s camp, only to burn his camp when he rode out in force. When Wang Shuang returned, the ambush struck without warning. Wei Yan beheaded him and returned to Hanzhong, handing back men and horses to Kongming.

Kongming hosted a grand banquet; the account goes no further here.

Zhang He gave up pursuit of the Shu and returned to his camp. Hao Zhao then sent word from Chen Cang: Wang Shuang had been beheaded.

Cao Zhen heard this and was overwhelmed with grief. Illness seized him from his sorrow, so he returned to Luoyang and ordered Guo Huai, Sun Li, and Zhang He to hold all routes toward Chang’an.

Now Sun Quan held court. An agent reported, “Shu’s Prime Minister Kongming has marched out twice; Cao Zhen’s forces are near collapse.”

Many ministers urged King of Wu to raise troops against Wei and make for the Central Plains, but Sun Quan hesitated. Zhang Zhao submitted: “Recently at Wuchang’s Eastern Mountain there were signs of the phoenix; in the Great River, yellow dragons appear repeatedly. Your lordship’s virtue matches that of Yao and Shun, and your brightness matches Wen and Wu. You can assume the emperor’s seat immediately, and only then launch a campaign.”

Many officials agreed: “What Zhang Zhao said is right.” They fixed the bing-chen day in the fourth month of summer and built a platform on Wuchang’s southern outskirts.

That day, ministers begged Sun Quan to mount the altar and take the throne. The eighth year of Huangwu was renamed the first year of Huanglong. Sun Jian was posthumously titled Emperor Wu. Lady Sun was named Empress Wu Lie. Sun Ce was titled King Huan of Changsha. Sun Deng was installed as Crown Prince. Zhuge Ke, Zhuge Jin’s eldest son, became Left Guardian to the Crown Prince, and Zhang Xiu, Zhang Zhao’s second son, became Right Attendant.

Zhuge Ke, whose courtesy name was Yuansun, was tall and highly intelligent and quick of response. He was six years old when this happened. At a banquet in Eastern Wu, he sat at his father’s side. Sun Quan noticed the length of Zhuge Jin’s face and ordered a donkey to be brought forward, then with chalk wrote two characters across its face: “Zhuge Ziyu.”

Everyone laughed loudly. Zhuge Ke came up, took the chalk, and wrote below: “The donkey of Zhuge Ziyu.” The whole hall was astonished.

Sun Quan was delighted and gave him the donkey. On another occasion at a great banquet, Sun Quan ordered Ke to pass the cup. As he came to Zhang Zhao, the latter refused to drink and said, “This is not proper for honoring old age.”

Sun Quan said, “Can you force Zi Bu to drink?” Ke accepted the command and answered Zhang Zhao, “Formerly Jiang Shangfu at ninety held banner and axe and still never called himself old. Today, when battle comes, you stand behind the line; on this day of drinking, you stand before me. How do you call this the ritual of old age?”

Zhang Zhao had no reply and had to drink in the end. Sun Quan, therefore, loved him deeply and made him tutor to the crown prince. He was already above the Three Dukes as a pillar at court, so his son Zhang Xiu was made Right Attendant to the prince. Sun Quan also appointed Gu Yong as Chancellor, Lu Xun as Grand General, and made them all guard Wuchang for the prince. Sun then returned to Jianye.

The ministers discussed strategy against Wei again. Zhang Zhao advised, “Your Majesty has only just ascended the throne; it is not yet time to raise armies. You should cultivate learning and restrain arms, set up more schools, and steady the hearts of the people. Send an envoy to Shu to renew alliance and divide the realm gradually.”

Sun followed the advice and sent an envoy in the night to Hanzhong to report to the Backing Lord. Formal greetings completed, he quietly presented the matter. Liu Shan consulted his court. Most argued that Sun Quan was a usurper and the alliance should be broken.

Jiang Wan said, “Inquire of the Prime Minister.” The Backing Lord sent a messenger to Hanzhong to ask Zhuge Liang. Zhuge responded, “Have someone bring gifts and present congratulations in Wu, requesting that Lu Xun raise troops and attack Wei. Wei will surely order Sima Yi to oppose. If Sima blocks Wu in the south, I will again march to Qishan and set my sights on Chang’an.”

Liu Shan followed this counsel and sent the Grand Commandant Yang Zhen with a famous horse and gifts of jade and gold ornaments into Wu as a congratulatory visit. When Yang Zhen arrived and presented the letters, Sun Quan rejoiced, held a feast, and sent him back in honor.

Sun then summoned Lu Xun and told him of the pact with Shu to attack Wei.

Lu Xun said, “This is Zhuge’s maneuver, fearing Sima Yi’s designs. Although he shares war plans with them, he does not truly wish to swallow Wu. They are feigning an alliance while waiting for a chance, and their purpose is to watch and choose. If Kongming presses Wei hard, I can then exploit the opening and strike for the Central Plains.” He immediately ordered training of men and horses in Jingxiang and all districts to prepare and choose an auspicious date for mobilization.

When Chen Zhen returned to Hanzhong and reported to Kongming, Kongming still worried about advancing into Chen Cang hastily. He sent scouts ahead. They returned: “Hao Zhao is gravely ill in the city of Chen Cang.”

Kongming said, “The matter is won.” He summoned Wei Yan and Jiang Wei and ordered, “Each of you take five thousand men and ride through the night toward the foot of Chen Cang. If you see fires rising, join and attack the city at once.” They did not fully trust this and asked, “When may we depart?”

Kongming answered, “Everything must be ready in three days. Do not ask my leave again; move at once.”

Both left. He then called Guan Xing and Zhang Bao privately and instructed them in whispers. Each took the secret plan and departed.

Guo Huai heard of Hao Zhao’s illness and spoke with Zhang He: “Since Hao Zhao is sick, you should hurry to replace him. I will write a memorial to the court and separately decide what must be done.”

Zhang He led three thousand men and came in haste to relieve him. That night, while Hao Zhao was indeed near death and moaning in the city, word came that the Shu army had reached the city walls. Hao Zhao ordered his men to man the battlements.

Fire rose on each gate and chaos swept the city. Hao Zhao heard it all and shook in panic. The Shu masses stormed in at once.

Wei Yan and Jiang Wei rode up to the foot of Chen Cang and saw no banners and no sentries. They were alarmed and did not dare assault.

Suddenly they heard cannon thunder, and banners rose on every side. A man in a silk kerchief, feather fan, and high-robed crane-cloak cried out, “You two have come too late!”

They recognized him as Kongming.

They leapt from horseback and knelt. “Your calculations are indeed marvelous,” they said.

Kongming told them to enter the city and explained: “I had learned that Hao Zhao was close to death. I ordered you to seize the city within three days so as to steady everyone’s hearts. I also told Guan Xing and Zhang Bao to send only a small detachment out of Hanzhong, while I remained hidden among the army and rode by back roads to the city without delay, so he could not shift troops. I had agents in the city set fires and raise calls to help. Their troops became confused and fearful. A force without a commander will disorder itself. Thus it came into my hands as if it were mere palm work. The Art of War says: ‘Attack where they are unprepared; strike when they are not ready. This is what this means.’”

Wei Yan and Jiang Wei knelt.

Kongming, in pity for Hao Zhao’s death, ordered that his wife and children return his spirit with proper rites and send the spirit tablet back to Wei to show his loyalty.

Kongming then told Wei Yan and Jiang Wei, “Neither of you should yet remove your armor. Bring troops and strike at San Pass. Whoever holds the pass will surely flee if they know your force has come. If you delay, Wei troops from the other road will arrive and the assault becomes harder.”

They obeyed and reached the pass. The gate guards indeed all fled when they saw the army coming. After Wei Yan and Jiang Wei began to unbuckle, they saw dust rise at the mountain’s edge and Wei soldiers approaching.

The two men said together, “The Chancellor’s calculations are not fathomable.” They climbed and watched. The Wei general was Zhang He.

They divided their troops and held the difficult paths. Seeing the Shu block the key road, Zhang He ordered retreat. Wei Yan pursued and engaged once. The Wei dead were innumerable; Zhang He withdrew in defeat.

Wei Yan returned to the pass and reported to Kongming. Kongming himself first took troops out from Chen Cang by way of Xie Valley and captured Jianwei. The rest of the Shu army followed in sequence.

The Backing Lord again ordered General Chen Shi to provide assistance. Kongming drove out a great army from Qishan once more and established camp. Gathering his men, he spoke:

“I have come to Qishan twice before and gained no clear advantage. Now I return again and believe the Wei army will defend in the same places and oppose us there as before. They will suspect I intend to take Yong and Mei and therefore post troops to deny me. I observe that Wudu and Yinping connect to Han. If we can take both commanderies, we can split their forces. Who among you dares to take them?”

Jiang Wei said, “I volunteer to go.”

Wang Ping also said, “I volunteer.”

Kongming rejoiced and ordered Jiang Wei with ten thousand men to take Wudu and Wang Ping with ten thousand to take Yinping.

Zhang He returned to Chang’an and told Guo Huai and Sun Li, “Chen Cang is lost, Hao Zhao is dead, and the pass of San has also been taken. If this continues, they will certainly seize Yong and Mei.”

Heeding the danger, Guo Huai assigned Zhang He to stay and defend Chang’an and ordered Sun Li to hold Yong. Guo Huai then brought his own troops through the night to defend Mi city, and meanwhile sent an urgent memorial to Luoyang.

Cao Rui held court and heard repeated reports: “Chen Cang has fallen, Hao Zhao is dead, and Kongming has again gone to Qishan; San Pass has also been taken.” He was alarmed. A memorial from Man Zhong and others arrived saying: “Sun Quan of Eastern Wu has usurped imperial title and allied with Shu. He has dispatched Lu Xun to Wuchang, training men and horses in preparation. The attack will begin at once.”

Hearing of danger from both fronts, the emperor grew uncertain and panicked. At that time Cao Zhen’s illness had not fully recovered, so he summoned Sima Yi for consultation.

Yi said, “In my poor judgment, Eastern Wu will not actually take up arms.”

Cao Rui asked, “How can you know that?”

Sima Yi replied, “I think Kongming still seeks revenge for Xiaoting and does not truly wish to swallow Wu. He fears that if he attacks now, Wei might strike Wu by exploiting the opening. Therefore he temporarily joins with Wu. Lu Xun also sees this and feigns mobilization to answer it, really only to wait and watch success or failure. Your Majesty need not defend against Wu; you must only guard against Shu.”

Cao Rui praised him. “You truly have keen vision.” He then made Sima Yi Grand Commander and placed him in charge of all Longxi front armies, ordering an official to fetch the commanding seal from Cao Zhen.

Yi said, “I will go and take it myself.”

He then bowed and left the court immediately, going directly to Cao Zhen’s residence. He had a report sent ahead before he entered.

After inquiring about the illness, Sima Yi said, “Eastern Wu and Shu in the west have formed a joint invasion. Kongming has once again moved from Qishan and made camp below. Did Your Excellency know of this?”

Cao Zhen was astonished. “The household has known I was unwell and did not let me know. In such a state of crisis, why did you not beg Zhongda to be your commander, to drive off Shu?”

Sima Yi said, “I am unworthy in talent and intelligence to hold so high an office.”

Cao Zhen said, “Take the seal and give it to Zhongda.”

Sima Yi replied, “A commander must be careful. I only wish to lend one arm of strength; I dare not accept that seal.”

Cao Zhen sprang up: “If Zhongda does not accept this office, all of China is lost. I will live in my illness before heaven to hold it safe!”

Sima Yi said, “Your Majesty has already granted this favor, but I dare not accept.”

Cao Zhen was overjoyed and said, “Now that Zhongda takes this command, he can drive back the Shu army.”

Sima Yi saw Cao Zhen yield again and then accepted the seal. He took leave of the Son of Heaven and marched with troops toward Chang’an to settle with Kongming.

Then it was set down:

A former commander’s seal passes to a new commander; Of two lines of troops, only one now comes. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Wang Shuang Is Executed, and Wuhou Triumphs at Chen Cang

chapters.html:
In the seventh year of the Jianxing era of Shu-Han, in the fourth month, Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, had his army at Qishan, split into three camps, waiting only for the Wei army.

Then Sima Yi marched his troops to Chang’an. He met with Zhang He, and Zhang He reported what had happened before. Sima Yi ordered Zhang He to serve as the vanguard and Dai Ling as his deputy commander, and took one hundred thousand men to Qishan, setting camp on the south of the Weishui River. Guo Huai and Sun Li entered the camp to report in person.

Sima Yi asked, “Have either of you met the Shu army in battle?”

The two answered, “Not yet.”

“Shu soldiers have come a thousand li. They profit from a quick engagement. Since they do not fight when they arrived here, they must have a design,” Sima Yi said. “Have any reports come from the roads out of Longxi?”

Guo Huai said, “Our agents have already learned in all the commanderies that everyone is on watch day and night and there is nothing unusual. Only at Wudu and Yinping there has been no report.”

“Once I have fought with Zhuge Liang, you two are to rush by the lesser roads to those two commanderies,” Sima Yi ordered. “Then hide behind the Shu army. It will certainly be disrupted.”

The two took his instructions, and led five thousand men through the smaller roads of Longxi to come to Wudu and Yinping and strike at the Shu army from behind. On the road, Guo Huai said to Sun Li,

“Zhongda or Kongming—which is more capable?”

Li said, “Kongming surpasses Zhongda by far.”

“Even so,” Guo Huai said. “This plan alone already shows Zhongda his exceptional wit. If the Shu army were to strike both commanderies directly, and we come around their rear, would they not become confused?”

Just then, a scouting horseman came with news: “Yinping has already been broken by Wang Ping. Wudu has already fallen to Jiang Wei. The Shu army is not far ahead.”

Li said, “If the Shu army has already broken through the cities, how could they array in front of them? It must be deception. Better to withdraw quickly.” Guo Huai agreed.

While he was giving orders for retreat, a cannon boomed out of nowhere. A detachment of cavalry flashed out from behind a hill, bearing a banner with great black letters: “Han Chancellor Zhuge Liang.” In the center stood a four-wheeled carriage, and Zhuge Liang sat upright upon it. On his left was Guan Xing, on his right Zhang Bao.

The two men, Guo and Sun, were terrified.

Kongming laughed aloud. “Guo Huai, Sun Li, do not run. How could Sima Yi’s scheme escape my notice? He has one unit fight in front each day, yet sends you to strike our rear. I have already taken Wudu and Yinping. Since you two did not come in time to surrender, you meant to drive your troops to a final fight with me, then?”

When Guo Huai and Sun Li heard this, they were in utter dismay. At that moment, shouts of attack and cries of pursuit rose from behind; Wang Ping and Jiang Wei came with troops from the rear. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao also led men and attacked from in front.

Attacked from both sides, the Wei forces were heavily routed. Guo and Sun cast down their horses and fled uphill on foot. Zhang Bao saw this and spurred off on horseback in pursuit; unexpectedly, with horse and rider together he slipped into a ravine. The rear troops rushed to rescue him, but his head had already struck against stone. He was sent back to Chengdu by Zhuge Liang’s men to recover.

Then Guo and Sun escaped and reported to Sima Yi:

“Wudu and Yinping are lost. Zhongyi [Kongming] waited on the main road, attacking from both front and rear, and so we were routed. He dismounted to go on foot and survived only by running away.”

Sima Yi said, “That is not your fault. Kongming was clever before I arrived. Let each of you bring new troops and hold the cities of Yong and Mei. Do not engage in battle. I have a way to break the enemy.”

The two took leave and withdrew. Sima Yi then summoned Zhang He and Dai Ling and assigned them:

“Kongming has taken Wudu and Yinping. He is surely pacifying the people to steady their hearts, and so he is not in camp. You two take ten thousand picked men each and set off tonight. Slip behind the Shu army and strike hard at the enemy all at once. I will array my forces in front. When the Shu formation breaks, I will drive the cavalry in and press through. The two armies together may seize their camp. If we hold this ground, what could toppling this army be?”

The two obeyed and marched away. Dai Ling rode on the left, Zhang He on the right. They took the side roads into the night, going deep into the Shu rear.

At the third watch, they came to the main road, where the two forces met and joined. They still moved on from the Shu rear. They had not traveled thirty li when the front line stopped.

Both Zhang and Dai reined up and looked. They saw hundreds of carts loaded with fodder crossing the road, blocking it.

Zhang said, “This must be prepared in advance. We should ride back at once.”

The order to withdraw had barely gone out when all the mountain slopes flared at once with firelight. Drums boomed loudly. Ambushes burst from all around, enclosing both men.

From the heights above Qishan, Kongming called out,

“Dai Ling, Zhang He, hear me. Sima Yi assumed I was pacifying the people at Wudu and Yinping and so not in camp, so he ordered both of you to raid my camp. He has fallen into my design. You two are commanders without fame and standing. I will not kill you. Dismount, and surrender now.”

Zhang He grew furious and pointed at Kongming. He cursed,

“You are a mountain villager and mere peasant, invading the borders of our great realm. How dare you speak so? If I catch you, I will tear your body into ten thousand pieces!”

When he finished, he drove hard, lowered his lance, and rode up the mountain. Arrows and stones fell like rain. He could not gain the heights.

He struck the horse, brandished his spear, and burst from the thickest press. None dared stand against him. At the same time, Shu soldiers trapped Dai Ling at the center of the field. Zhang He broke out. He did not see Dai Ling at first; then, braving everything, he turned back, charged in again through the thick ring, pulled Dai Ling out, and withdrew.

Kongming on the ridge saw Zhang He amid ten thousand men, clashing in and out. His courage had doubled. He told his attendants,

“Once I have heard that Zhang Yide once fought Zhang He and people were all struck with fear. Only today I have seen him truly. He is truly brave. If we leave this man alive, he will remain a danger to Shu. He must be removed.”

He gathered his army and withdrew to camp.

Then Sima Yi arrayed his army in formation and waited for the Shu forces to stir before striking at once. He saw Zhang He and Dai Ling arriving in disorder and reporting,

“Kongming had already built such preparations, so we were routed and came back.”

Sima Yi was startled.

“Zhuge Liang is truly otherworldly,” he said. “Let us withdraw for now.” He immediately ordered the main army to return to its own camp and hold fast, giving no battle.

Kongming won a great victory and took arms, mounts, and gear in countless amount. He led his army back to camp. For every day he ordered Wei Yan to issue challenges, but the Wei army did not come out. For one and a half months, no battle occurred.

Kongming was in council in his tent when word came: the Son of Heaven’s envoy Fei Xi arrived bearing an edict.

Kongming welcomed him into camp, burned incense, offered the required respects, and read the edict aloud:

The failure at Jieting was due to Ma Su; your own transgression had led to it, and you have humbled yourself deeply in shame. You disobeyed the Son of Heaven’s will too often and followed what was convenient. In the previous year’s campaign, you carried it to victory and severed Wang Shuang’s head; this year, on campaign again, Guo Huai fled. You induced the Di and Qiang to descend and restored the two commanderies. You made the wicked tremble, and your merit is plainly visible. The world is now all in turmoil; the old evil still prowls, and your charge is high and the weight of the state rests on you. To keep yourself subdued for so long is not how the former brilliance should be displayed. I therefore restore you as Chancellor. Do not refuse.

When Kongming had finished hearing the edict, he told Fei Xi,

“My state is not yet put in order; how can I resume the office of Chancellor?”

He refused earnestly.

Fei Xi said, “If the Chancellor refuses this appointment, he rejects the will of the Son of Heaven and coldly weakens the soldiers’ spirits. Receive the post, at least for now.”

Kongming only then accepted and bowed.

Fei Xi left.

Seeing that Sima Yi did not move, Kongming devised another plan and ordered all outposts to lift camp and rise up.

When scouts later reported to him, Sima Yi was told Kongming was withdrawing. Sima Yi said,

“Kongming has surely a major plan. Do not move lightly.”

Zhang He said,

“This must be because he ran out of food. Why not pursue?”

Sima Yi replied,

“I judge that last year he collected heavily, and now the grain is ripe and supplies are plentiful. Though transport is difficult, it can be stretched for six months. Would he leave so easily? He has seen us not battling day after day, and now he uses this stratagem to lure us. Send scouts far ahead.”

A scout returned to report,

“Kongming is thirty li away at a lower camp.”

Sima Yi said, “I still think Kongming did not leave. Keep the palisades strong and guard the camps. Do not advance carelessly.”

They waited ten days with no sign, and no Shu commanders appeared to fight. Sima Yi sent scouts again.

The report came back, “The Shu army has stood up and moved again to a lower camp, thirty li away.”

He still did not trust it. He changed his clothes, mixed with the troops, and came in person to inspect. He truly saw that the army had again withdrawn another thirty li.

Returning to camp, he said to Zhang He,

“This is Kongming’s design as well. We must not give chase.”

After another ten days, scouts were sent again.

They reported again, “The Shu army has withdrawn another thirty li to a lower camp.”

Zhang He said,

“Kongming is employing a slowing stratagem, gradually retreating toward Hanzhong. Why does the Governor suspect and not pursue? I am willing to go and force a battle.”

Sima Yi said,

“Kongming has innumerable schemes. A single misstep will ruin our advantage. We must not go forward lightly.”

Zhang He said,

“If I fail, I will accept your command and die for it.”

Sima Yi replied,

“If you are determined to go, split your force in two columns. You lead one ahead. Fight with full zeal and fight to the death. I will follow to reinforce and guard against ambush. Halt for the night by mid-route on the next day, and engage in battle on the following day so the troops are not exhausted.”

He divided the forces.

The next day, Zhang He and Dai Ling took several deputy commanders and thirty thousand picked men, and with great heart advanced first, camping halfway. Sima Yi left many horses to hold the camps and brought out five thousand picked soldiers to follow.

Meanwhile, Kongming had quietly sent scouts ahead and seen the Wei army halt halfway.

That night he called the assembled generals and said,

“Now that Wei comes in pursuit, they will fight to the death. Each of you must face ten against one. I will use an ambush to cut off their rear. This is no post for officers who lack either wisdom or courage.”

When he finished, he fixed his eyes on Wei Yan. Wei Yan lowered his head and said nothing.

Wang Ping spoke,

“I volunteer to do it.”

Kongming said,

“If failure comes, what then?”

Wang Ping said,

“I volunteer for the order.”

Kongming sighed,

“Wang Ping is willing to offer his life and expose himself to arrows and stones. He is truly a loyal minister. Yet even so, because Wei will come in two columns from front and rear, one ambush to split them may be cut off in the middle. If Ping fights bravely and wisely, he can only hold one head at once. He cannot split himself in two. It would be best to send another general with him.

Yet there is no one left in the army willing to stake life first and foremost.”

Before he had finished, one general stepped forward,

“I will go.”

Kongming looked at him and recognized him as Zhang Yi.

Kongming said,

“Zhang He is a famous Wei general whose strength could defy ten thousand men. You are not an equal foe for him.”

Yi answered,

“If anything goes wrong, I shall present my head in your camp.”

Kongming said,

“If you dare go, then Wang Ping and you each lead ten thousand picked men and lie concealed in a mountain pass. When the Wei army closes, let them pass first, then strike their rear from hiding. If Sima Yi follows hard after them, divide into two: Zhang Yi takes one force and holds the rear while Wang Ping takes one and cuts off the vanguard. Both columns must be prepared for a death battle. I have other plans to aid both of you.”

Both took the orders and set out.

Kongming then called Jiang Wei and Liao Hua and ordered them,

“Each of you has one brocadeed case. Take three thousand picked men, lower your flags and still your drums, and hide above the forward mountain. If you see Wei soldiers surround Wang Ping and Zhang Yi in extreme danger, do not come rushing to save them. Open the brocadeed case and look within. You will find a way out.”

Both obeyed and took their men.

He then ordered Wu Ban, Wu Yi, Ma Zhong, and Zhang Ni, in confidence,

“When tomorrow the Wei force comes and their momentum is strong, do not meet them at once. Fight while giving way. When you see Guan Xing ride out to raid the formation, then turn and strike in hard pursuit. I will have troops to reinforce.”

Those four also took their orders.

He summoned Guan Xing and said,

“You will take five thousand picked men and hide in a mountain ravine. Only when the red banner on the ridge snaps in the wind should you ride out to strike.”

Guan Xing obeyed and set off.

Then Zhang He and Dai Ling came leading soldiers like storm and rain.

Ma Zhong, Zhang Ni, Wu Yi, and Wu Ban came behind to meet them and rode out in combat. Zhang He became furious and drove his men to pursue.

The Shu soldiers fought and withdrew in turn.

Wei soldiers chased for more than twenty li. It was June, and the heat was crushing. Sweat poured off men and horses as if flung water.

They had gone fifty li when everyone in Wei was breathless. From the ridge, Kongming lifted a red flag once, and Guan Xing burst from cover with his men.

Ma Zhong and the other four generals all returned to strike in sudden support. Zhang He and Dai Ling fought to the death and did not retreat.

Suddenly a roar rose like thunder. Two lines of troops came out in pursuit, and they were Wang Ping and Zhang Yi. Each charged fiercely and pressed on, closing the enemy’s rear.

Zhang He shouted to his commanders,

“When you have arrived, if you will not decide in a death battle, when then will we do so?”

Wei soldiers struck forward with all their power and could not break away.

Suddenly drum and horn sounded from the rear; Sima Yi himself rode in at the head of selected troops.

Sima Yi directed the generals and pinned Wang Ping and Zhang Yi in the center of the field.

Zhang Yi cried,

“The Chancellor is truly a divine strategist. The plan is already made; good counsels lie behind it. We must decide and die in battle!”

He split his force in two routes. Wang Ping took one detachment and blocked Zhang He and Dai Ling; Zhang Yi took one and faced Sima Yi directly.

Both fronts fought to the death with cries filling the air.

Jiang Wei and Liao Hua watched from the ridge. Seeing that Wei’s momentum was enormous and Shu’s strength in danger, and that it grew hard to stand, Wei Yan said,

“Then this danger is severe; we should open the brocadeed case and see the plan.”

Liao Hua agreed.

They tore it open and read:

If Sima Yi’s soldiers come and encircle Wang Ping and Zhang Yi in an emergency, you two should divide your force in two, strike straight at Sima Yi’s camp, and then force him to retreat. While he turns back, you may attack in confusion. Even if we do not take the camp, there will still be an entire victory.

The two rejoiced and divided their force in two routes, heading straight for Sima Yi’s encampment.

Sima Yi, too, feared he had fallen into Kongming’s design and sent messages constantly from the front. While he was pressing the battle, a fast horseman arrived with news that Shu troops had taken the main camp from two sides.

Sima Yi turned white with shock.

“Had I not said Kongming had plans?” he cried. “You all did not believe and pressed the chase, and the great matter is now in danger.”

He ordered the troops to pull back in haste.

The army was in turmoil and broke apart in panic. Zhang Yi then struck from behind, and the Wei army was badly defeated.

Zhang He and Dai Ling, seeing the situation cut off, sought escape by a lonely mountain track. The Shu victory was complete. Behind them, Guan Xing rode in with troops to join all routes.

Sima Yi was routed in one engagement and ran into camp. By then the Shu army had already withdrawn.

Sima Yi gathered the scattered troops and berated the generals,

“You do not know the laws of war. You rely only on hot blood and raw courage, demanding battle. That has brought this defeat. Hereafter do not move rashly, and again if you disregard command, I will punish by military law.”

All withdrew, ashamed.

In this engagement, the Wei dead were very many, and men abandoned countless horses and arms.

Kongming brought his victorious army home and prepared to rise and advance.

A man arrived from Chengdu reporting that Zhang Bao was dead.

When Kongming heard, he cried out, and blood came from his mouth. He collapsed in faint.

The others revived him.

After this, Kongming was sick, lay on his bed, and could not rise. All the generals were deeply moved.

People later composed a verse of lament:

Fierce, brave Zhang Bao meant to achieve great fame; alas, Heaven offered him no aid. Lord Zhuge scatters tears into the west wind, grieving that none remains to bow and aid him.

After ten days, Kongming summoned Dong Jue, Fan Jian, and others into his tent and said,

“I feel heavy and clouded in spirit and can no longer govern affairs. Better to return to Hanzhong and nurse my illness, and later make my plans anew. See that no one leaks this. If Sima Yi knows, he will come to strike.”

He then sent orders that at night the camp should be silently lifted and all return to Hanzhong. Five days after Kongming had left, Sima Yi only then learned it and sighed deeply,

“Kongming truly has stratagems that appear and vanish like spirits. I cannot match them.”

Thus Sima Yi left his generals at the camp and sent detachments to hold each pass, and Sima Yi himself retired.

Kongming then encamped the main army at Hanzhong and returned to Chengdu to recover, too. Civil and military officials came out to welcome him; they drove him into the Chancellor’s residence. The Later Emperor rode in himself to ask after his health and ordered court doctors to treat him. Day by day he improved.

In the autumn of the eighth year of Jianxing, in the seventh month, Cao Zhen, Great General of Wei, fell sick but submitted a memorial:

The Shu troops have invaded our borders several times and repeatedly crossed the Central Plains. If we do not sweep them out, they will become a grave danger. Now is autumn’s cool season and men and horses are at ease; it is the right time to mount an expedition. I wish to lead a great army with Sima Yi into Hanzhong and extinguish that traitorous clique, thereby clearing the frontier.

Wei’s lord was greatly pleased. He asked the Court Attendant Liu Ye,

“Zi Dan advised me to punish Shu. What say you?”

Ye submitted,

“The Great General speaks truly. If we do not extinguish them now, they will indeed become a great danger later. Your Majesty should proceed.”

the Wei emperor nodded.

When Ye returned inside to go home, many high ministers were already asking,

“We heard the Son of Heaven and the Lord of Marriages discussed a campaign against Shu. What becomes of it?”

Ye answered,

“There is nothing to it. Shu has mountain and river defenses. It is not easy to predict, and any campaign would only waste horses and men, helping no one.”

The ministers withdrew in silence.

Yang Ji entered and reported inside,

“Yesterday I heard that you urged His Majesty to punish Shu. Today at court you again spoke against it and said to seize nothing. This is deceiving the Son of Heaven. Why not summon him and question him?”

the Wei emperor ordered Liu Ye in.

He asked,

“You urged me to punish Shu. Yet today you say it cannot be done. Why?”

Ye said,

“Your servant examined carefully: Shu cannot be attacked.”

the Wei emperor laughed.

A short while later, Yang Ji left the inner hall.

Ye then said,

“Yesterday I urged Your Majesty to punish Shu because it was a matter of state. How could such an undertaking be leaked so casually to others? War is a way of guile: before anything is declared, it should remain hidden.”

the Wei emperor said suddenly,

“You have said truly.”

From that point, his respect for him increased.

Within ten days Sima Yi entered court. The Wei lord asked Cao Zhen to report the matter. He spoke through every point.

Sima Yi submitted,

“I judge that Eastern Wu will not dare to raise troops. This is now the moment to ride west against Shu.”

the Wei emperor immediately appointed Cao Zhen as Grand Marshal and Commander Leading the Western Expedition, Sima Yi as General-in-Chief and Deputy Commander of the Western Campaign, and Liu Ye as military advisor. The three paid their respects and, taking leave of the Wei ruler, brought out four hundred thousand troops.

They marched to Chang’an and then straight for Jiange Pass to take Hanzhong. Guo Huai, Sun Li, and others each took a route.

People in Hanzhong reported to Chengdu.

Kongming, already much recovered, practiced drills each day, and trained horse and men in the art of the Eight Formations. His men were all accomplished. He wished to take the Central Plains. Upon hearing this, he called Zhang Ni and Wang Ping and said,

“The two of you first lead a thousand men to guard the old post at Chencang and meet whatever Wei force comes. I will bring the main army and come to reinforce.”

They replied,

“They report a Wei army of four hundred thousand, feigning eighty thousand and a vast appearance. How can only one thousand go to hold such a pass? If Wei comes in force, how will we resist?”

Kongming said,

“If I send too many, the soldiers will only suffer hardship.”

Zhang Ni and Wang Ping looked at each other and dared not leave.

Kongming said,

“If there is any fault, it is not yours. Say no more. You may leave at once.”

The two again pleaded,

“If the Chancellor wants to kill us both, please do so now. We dare not go.”

Kongming laughed.

“How foolish! If I send you, you have your own understanding to use. I am no fool. Last night I observed the heavens and saw Venus encroaching upon the Net mansion; within this month there must be a great pouring rain. Even if Wei has four hundred thousand troops, how can it venture deep into these mountain defenses? That is why few troops are enough, and no one will be harmed.

Let the main army all stay at Hanzhong and settle for one month. When the Wei troops retreat, I will break out then with all forces to strike and shelter the main army while we rest. By waiting while fresh against their fatigue, my one hundred thousand can defeat their four hundred thousand.”

The two were delighted and took leave.

Kongming led the main army out of Hanzhong and ordered all mountain passes to prepare dried firewood, brush, and light grain, enough for one month for men and horses, against the autumn rains. He gave the entire army one extra month of provisioning before departure.

As for Cao Zhen and Sima Yi, now leading the great army, they arrived straight at Chencang city and found not a single house standing. They questioned local farmers, who all said Kongming had burned everything on his departure.

Cao Zhen moved to advance by the Chencang road at once.

Sima Yi said,

“We must not enter lightly. I observed the heavens and saw the Comet Bit moving in the seat of Great Darkness; within this month there must be heavy rain. If we go deep into rough ground, and even if we win, if there is any oversight men and horses will suffer and withdrawal will be hard.

Let us first build shelters in the city and fortify there for the coming rains.”

Cao Zhen followed him.

Before half a month passed, rain fell in torrents and did not cease. Outside Chencang the ground water reached three chi deep. All weapons grew wet, and men could not sleep. Day and night were equally unsettled. Rain fell for thirty days. There was no grass for horses. Dead men were countless. Complaints from the soldiers never ceased.

Word reached Luoyang. The Wei ruler ordered ritual petitions for clear weather. He was unable to gain a reprieve.

Wang Su, the Gentleman of the Palace, submitted a memorial:

The records say: On campaigns across a thousand li with freighted grain, soldiers wear the face of hunger. After fires are made and cooking vessels carried, the army cannot stay full overnight.

That is what is said for those on the road in campaign. For one entering broken terrain, cutting roads as they go, their labor is multiplied by a hundred. Add now relentless rains, steep slippery slopes, cramped ranks unable to spread, and food and grain too far to sustain; this is truly the great forbidden state for marching armies. We hear that Cao Zhen has been on the move for over a month yet has gone only halfway through the valley, though road works have consumed much of his strength and every soldier is spent. He is therefore gaining the advantage of awaiting and resting while you force him into fatigue. That is what captains fear. Looking back to earlier ages, King Wu campaigned against Zhou; he returned after passing the pass. Looking at nearby days, Wu and Wen besieged Jian and failed at the Yangtze. Were these not men who knew the season and adapted by flexibility? I beg Your Majesty to consider how severe the water and rain have become for the troops, and allow them rest. If tomorrow an opportunity for offense comes, then use time to strike.

The ruler read the memorial and was still wavering.

Yang Fu and Hua Xin also submitted memorials of remonstrance.

Wei’s ruler then issued an edict ordering that envoys summon Cao Zhen and Sima Yi back to the court.

Cao Zhen and Sima Yi discussed,

“Now we have had three consecutive intervals of rain for thirty days. The army has no spirit for war and everyone longs to go home. How can we prevent that?”

Sima Yi said,

“It is better to return.”

Cao Zhen said,

“If Kongming chases us, how should we withdraw?”

Sima Yi said,

“We can only retreat if our second and first lines can cover our backs.”

While they were still arguing, a summons arrived.

The two reversed the army so that the front became rear and the rear became front, and withdrew slowly.

Kongming calculated that the autumn rains for one month would end and that the skies would still not be clear. He brought one army to Chenggu and ordered the entire force to assemble and camp at Chipo Hill.

He called the assembled commanders in his tent and said,

“I judge Wei will withdraw, and Wei’s Son of Heaven will soon issue an edict to have Cao Zhen and Sima Yi return. If they come, we can answer with our own preparation. Better to let them go now. I will make new plans later.”

Wang Ping then reported that Wei had already turned back.

Kongming instructed him and others,

“Do not pursue them.”

“I have a way to destroy the Wei force.”

Then comes the closing couplet:

Even if the Wei troops can hide in ambush, the Chancellor of Han is not one to chase. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang Crushes the Wei Army and Sima Yi Ravages Western Shu

chapters.html:
Yet all the commanders, hearing that Zhuge Liang had not given chase to the Wei troops, entered the pavilion together and reported: “The Wei army was soaked by the hard rain and could not set up an orderly camp, so it has turned back. This is the moment to press them, why does the Chancellor not pursue?”

Zhuge Liang said, “Sima Yi is very good at using troops. Now that the army has withdrawn, there must be an ambush. If I pursue, I will be walking into his trap. Better to let him go far away. I will split the forces and go straight through Xie Valley, then seize Qishan. In that way, the Wei men will have no defenses.”

A commander asked, “To take the lands of Chang’an there is another route. Why does the Chancellor insist only on Qishan?”

Zhuge Liang replied, “Qishan is the front gate of Chang’an. If troops from the Longxi commanderies come, they must pass this place. More, it faces the Wei River, depends on Xie Valley behind, can exit to one side and enter on the other, and is a place where one can lie in wait. It is exactly a place fit for war. That is why I want to take it first and gain the advantage of terrain.” The generals all bowed in agreement.

Zhuge Liang ordered Wei Yan, Zhang Ni, Du Qiong, and Chen Shi to take Jī Valley; Ma Dai, Wang Ping, Zhang Yi, and Ma Zhong to take Xie Valley. They were all to unite at Qishan. With the dispositions set, Zhuge Liang himself brought the main force and, with Guan Xing and Liao Hua as vanguard, advanced.

Now Cao Zhen and Sima Yi were in the rear, overseeing the army and horses. Cao Zhen ordered a detachment along the old road through Chencang to reconnoiter, and they reported no approach of Shu troops. After another ten days, the troops holding ambush all returned and said there was no news of Shu at all.

Cao Zhen said, “The autumn rains have come in one stretch; boardwalk roads have given way. How could the Shu know we have withdrawn?”

Sima Yi answered, “The Wei troops will come out behind us shortly.”

Cao Zhen asked, “How do you know?”

Sima Yi said, “There have been clear days for two days, yet the Shu do not press hard. That means they expect I have an ambush; they let our army go far out, then when our troops pass the point, they will seize Qishan.”

Cao Zhen did not believe him.

Sima Yi said, “How can Zidan not believe? I think Zhuge Liang will come by both valleys. I and Zidan will guard each pass in turn. We have ten days to measure this. If no Shu comes, I shall paint my face with rouge, wear women’s clothing, and come into camp to take the blame.”

Cao Zhen said, “If there is Shu, I will give you one jade sash of imperial bestowal and one imperial horse.”

Then the troops separated into two routes. Cao Zhen brought his men to camp at the west of Qishan at the mouth of Xie Valley. Sima Yi brought his army to the east of Qishan at the mouth of Jī Valley.

The camps were all set.

Sima Yi first led a detachment into a mountain ravine and hid them there; all the rest of the cavalry and troops camped at key roads. Sima Yi changed his clothing, mixed among the troops, and inspected each encampment in turn.

By chance he came to one camp and one officer muttered up to heaven in complaint: “We have been soaked by rain for so long, we refused to return; now we are held here again and compelled to gamble—who in the army does this not feel?”

Sima Yi heard this and went back to camp. He called the senior commanders to the pavilion and ordered the officer to be brought forward.

Sima Yi shouted, “The court has fed the army for a thousand days to use in one moment. How dare you grumble and weaken soldiers’ resolve?”

The man did not yield.

Sima Yi called two of his companions to testify. The officer still could not deny it.

Sima Yi said, “I did not force gambling. If we defeat the Shu, each of you will return to court with merit. Instead you have dared to complain. You invite punishment yourself!” He ordered the guards to bring him out and execute him.

In a short while, the head was delivered before the pavilion. The commanders trembled.

Sima Yi said, “You all should guard against the Shu with all your mind and heart. When you hear the cannon from the center, all of you must advance from all four sides.” The commanders obeyed and withdrew.

Now Wei Yan, Zhang Ni, Chen Shi, and Du Qiong, with twenty thousand troops, went through Jī Valley and pressed on. While they were moving, there came news that Adviser Deng Zhi had arrived.

The four generals asked why.

Deng Zhi said, “The Chancellor ordered: when moving out through Jī Valley, guard against a Wei ambush and do not advance recklessly.”

Chen Shi said, “How can the Chancellor be so suspicious? This rain has ruined our Wei troops’ armor and clothing; they surely wish to return quickly. How could there be an ambush now? My troops are moving on a second road and can win a great victory—why do you still order us to halt?”

Deng said, “The Chancellor’s calculations never fail; his plans do not come up short. How can you dare disobey?”

Chen Shi laughed, “If the Chancellor really had deeper stratagems, this would not have happened at Jieting.”

Wei Yan recalled that Zhuge Liang had not followed his advice before, and he too laughed: “If only the Chancellor had listened to me then and gone straight by Ziwu Valley, this could have taken Chang’an and even Luoyang. Now he has fixed to leave by Qishan. What benefit is that? He has ordered us to advance, then he orders us to halt—what confusion of command is this?”

Chen Shi said, “I have five thousand troops of my own. I will go straight out through Jī Valley, get to the foot of Qishan first, and see whether the Chancellor feels ashamed or not.”

Deng Zhi blocked him again and again. Chen Shi still refused and led out his five thousand through Jī Valley at once. Deng had no choice but to fly back and report to Zhuge Liang.

Chen Shi had gone only a few li when he heard a cannon blast, and ambushes emerged from all four sides at once. He tried to retreat, but Wei troops filled the mouth of the valley and enclosed him as if in an iron kettle. He thrust left and right in desperation and could not break out. Suddenly a great cry rose, and a great band of soldiers surged in—it was Wei Yan, who rescued him.

Chen Shi returned to the valley with them. Of his five thousand, only four or five hundred wounded men and horses were left.

Wei troops came from the rear in pursuit. Only then did Du Qiong and Zhang Ni bring reinforcements; the Wei forces then withdrew.

Chen and Wei at last understood that Zhuge Liang had seen through events like a spirit and regretted too late.

Deng Zhi then returned and reported to Zhuge Liang that Wei Yan and Chen Shi had behaved without courtesy.

Zhuge Liang laughed and said, “Wei Yan has naturally harbored disloyal feeling toward others. I know he has long carried resentment. I used him because of his courage. In time he will become a source of harm.”

At that moment there came fast riders with news: “Chen Shi has lost more than four thousand men and has only four or five hundred wounded among men and horses left, camped in the valley.”

Zhuge Liang ordered Deng Zhi to return to Jī Valley again to comfort Chen Shi so he should not turn treacherous. He then called Ma Dai and Wang Ping and gave them separate orders: “If Wei troops guard Xie Valley, the two of you lead your units over the mountain ridge, move by night, lie in wait by day, and break out to the left side of Qishan. Use fire as signal.”

He called Ma Zhong and Zhang Yi and said, “You too take a side path through the hills, move by day in concealment and by night in motion, come out on the right side of Qishan, and use fire as signal. Join Guan Xing and Ma Dai, and together raid Cao Zhen’s camp. I will attack in three directions from within the valley; then the Wei force can be broken.”

The four took their commands and each led troops away.

Zhuge Liang told Guan Xing and Liao Hua much the same and they, after receiving secret instructions, set off with their troops. Zhuge Liang himself took an elite force and moved by a separate route.

Meanwhile Cao Zhen and Sima Yi remained unconvinced that Shu troops would come, so they grew negligent and let the soldiers rest. They intended to wait ten days without incident and then mock Sima Yi.

After seven days, they were still unaware; then a report came that some small Shu force had broken out of the valley. Cao Zhen ordered his deputy, Qin Liang, to take five thousand men on reconnaissance and not allow Shu forces to near the boundary.

Qin Liang obeyed. As soon as he reached the valley, he saw the Shu troops turning away. He raced back, and after traveling fifty or sixty li saw no Shu troops. Puzzled, he told the men to dismount and rest. Just then a scout horse cried: “There is Shu ambush ahead!”

When he mounted and looked, he saw dust rising in the mountain, and he ordered the troops to take position for defense at once. Before long, shouts thundered from all sides: Wu Ban and Wu Yi broke out frontally with troops; Guan Xing and Liao Hua came charging from behind.

The mountains were on both sides, with no road to escape. Shu soldiers on the heights shouted, “Dismount and surrender, and you will not die!” Most of the Wei army surrendered.

Qin Liang fought to the end and was cut down by Liao Hua with one stroke beneath his horse.

Zhuge Liang held the surrendered soldiers in the rear camp. He then gave Wei armor and horse armor to five thousand of his men and had them dress as Wei troops. Then he ordered Guan Xing, Liao Hua, Wu Ban, and Wu Yi to lead those five thousand and rush straight for Cao Zhen’s camp.

First he had a rider report in, “Only a few small Shu troops came, and we all drove them off.” Cao Zhen was overjoyed.

Suddenly there arrived Sima Yi’s trusted man from camp headquarters. Cao Zhen called him in and asked what he brought.

He said, “Shu troops are using an ambush plan and have killed more than four thousand Wei soldiers. Sima Yi sends this warning: do not think only of your gambling, be careful and guard well.”

Cao Zhen said, “There is not one Shu soldier in this place.” He sent the man away.

Again there arrived a report that Qin Liang had returned with his force. Cao Zhen came out of the pavilion to receive him. As he came to the encampment, reports came of fires rising at both front and rear.

Cao Zhen hurried back and looked. Guan Xing, Liao Hua, Wu Ban, and Wu Yi came charging into the front of the camp. Ma Dai and Wang Ping came in from the rear. Ma Zhong and Zhang Yi also arrived with troops. The Wei soldiers were at a loss and ran in all directions to survive. Their commanders protected Cao Zhen and ran eastward while Shu soldiers pursued behind.

As Cao Zhen ran in panic, a roar shook the air, and a whole unit crashed down upon them. He trembled and looking saw it was Sima Yi.

A hard struggle followed once. The Shu then withdrew.

Cao Zhen escaped, ashamed and humiliated.

Sima Yi said, “Zhuge Liang has taken the position of Qishan. We should not remain here long. We ought to camp along the Wei bank and plan further.”

Cao Zhen asked, “How did you know I had suffered so great a defeat?”

Sima Yi said, “Those messengers saying that Zidan saw no Shu soldiers made me suspect that Zhuge Liang had entered silently to raid the camp. That is why I came to match him. My forecast was right. Do not speak of gambling now. Let us stand united and serve the state.”

Cao Zhen was greatly alarmed and ashamed. His anger became illness; he lay in bed and did not rise.

Sima Yi kept the troops camped on the Wei bank, fearing disorder in morale, and did not dare to tell Cao Zhen to move the force.

Meanwhile Zhuge Liang drove the men and horses hard once more and returned from Qishan.

The camp inspection was done. Wei Yan, Chen Shi, Du Qiong, and Zhang Ni entered and knelt to confess fault. Zhuge Liang said, “Who caused this breach?”

Wei Yan replied, “Chen Shi disobeyed orders and slipped into the valley mouth and this is why there was such a great loss.”

Chen Shi said, “Chen Shi says this is by Wei Yan’s instruction.”

Zhuge Liang said, “He did rescue you, and yet you run to him. You have broken command and need no clever excuses.” He ordered the guards to bring Chen Shi out and execute him.

In a short while, the head was hung before the pavilion as a warning.

At this time Zhuge Liang did not execute Wei Yan, so that he could keep him for later use.

As soon as Chen Shi was beheaded, Zhuge Liang was considering further advance when a scout reported that Cao Zhen was ill in bed and being treated in camp.

Zhuge Liang was rejoiced. He told the commanders, “If Cao Zhen recovers soon, he will surely return to Chang’an. If the Wei force does not truly withdraw, he must be gravely ill and remain here, which will steady our men. I will write a letter and have the men who surrendered from Qin Liang carry it to him. If he sees it, he will die of anger.”

He called the surrendered Wei men to his pavilion and asked, “You are all Wei troops; your parents and wives are mostly in the Central Plains, and it is not right for you to stay in Shu. If I release you to return home, what do you say?”

All soldiers wept and knelt in thanks.

Zhuge Liang said, “Cao Zidan and I have an understanding. I have a letter. You all must take it back and deliver it to Zidan. Great rewards await you.”

The Wei men took it and ran back to their old camp and presented Zhuge Liang’s letter to Cao Zhen.

Cao Zhen rose from bed with great effort, broke the seal, and read:

To the Grand Marshal Cao Zidan, from the Chancellor of Han, Marquis of Wuxiang, Zhuge Liang.

A general ought to know when to withdraw and when to stand, when to be soft and when to be hard; to advance and to retreat, to be gentle and to be stern. He should be immovable as mountains, subtle as the alternation of yin and yang, boundless as heaven and earth, full as the great granary, vast as the Four Seas, brilliant as the three lights.

He knows, beforehand, drought and flood from the stars and the condition of ground and ease of terrain. He judges when formations meet and measures an enemy’s strengths and weaknesses.
