Alas, you are unlearned and behind in the arts. You have rebelled against Heaven, aided the usurping rebel who wrongs the empire, and proclaimed yourself ruler in Luoyang. Your straggling troops have run to Xie Valley and endured drenching rain in Chencang. You are exhausted in both water and land transport, and men and horses are out of control. You fling spears and armor into the fields of Yingjiao, leaving swords and halberds strewn everywhere.

Your commander's heart has broken and courage shivered; the general scurries like a rat and rushes like a wolf. You dare not face the elders of Guanzhong, nor show your face in the halls of the Secretariat. Historians will write it down and the people will spread it with their mouths.

Zhongda will tremble upon hearing the battle line; Zidan will stare into the wind and be at a loss.

My troops are strong and my horses sturdy. Great generals rise like tigers and surge forth like dragons. We will sweep Qinchuan into a level plain and turn Wei into waste and ruin.

When Cao Zhen had read it, rage filled his chest. He died in camp that evening.

Sima Yi used a wagon and had him sent to Luoyang for burial.

When the Wei ruler learned that Cao Zhen had died, he issued an edict at once urging Sima Yi to go to battle. Sima Yi brought out the main army to face Zhuge Liang and sent formal declarations on the next day.

Zhuge Liang told the commanders, “Cao Zhen is surely dead.” He marked for a response and arranged for the engagement to begin the next day.

The envoy left.

That night Zhuge Liang gave Jiang Wei secret orders and then dispatched him as instructed. He also called Guan Xing and gave him instructions in secret. As they were setting out, he summoned Wu Ban and Wu Yi, gave them a separate secret plan, and sent them ahead with troops as well. The next day Zhuge Liang brought all force from Qishan to the Wei bank: one side river, the other mountain, and in the center an open plain and broad field—good ground for battle.

The two armies came face to face and loosed arrows at the corners of each formation. After three drumbeats, and the gate flag in Wei’s camp lifting open, Sima Yi rode out with his generals.

Zhuge Liang sat upright in a four-wheeled war carriage, fanning with a feather fan.

Sima Yi said, “My lord follows Yao and Shun in governing by virtue, passing on the Son of Heaven’s office from two emperors and holding Zhongyuan. He has allowed your Shu and Wu to remain because he is merciful and broad-minded, fearing injury to the people. You are a southern farmer from Nanyang, ignorant of heaven’s pattern, and yet you insist on invading. It is proper that we exterminate you. If you truly repent in your heart, return early, each keeping to the frontier, forming a stable three-legged balance and sparing all living creatures from ruin. Then you all will live.”

Zhuge Liang laughed: “I was entrusted with the late emperor’s charge as guardian; how could I not with all my heart and every strength go to suppress the traitors? The Cao house will not be long in being destroyed by Han. Your grandfathers were all Han ministers who lived on Han stipend and yet did not serve in return, but aided the usurping treachery. Are they not ashamed?”

Sima Yi, flushed with shame, said, “I will settle the matter with you as to who prevails. If you can win, I swear I will not be called Great General. If you fail, return quickly to your homeland; I will not harm you.”

Zhuge Liang said, “Do you want to duel generals, duel soldiers, or duel arrays?”

Sima Yi said, “First, the battle array.”

Zhuge Liang said, “Then watch me set array first.”

Sima Yi entered the central camp, a yellow flag raised in hand, signaling both sides to move and arrange into formation. He remounted and rode out, asking, “Do you know my arrangement?”

Zhuge Liang laughed: “Even the lowly in my own ranks can form one. This is the Hunyuan One Breath Array.”

Sima Yi said, “What of mine? You call this the Eight Trigram Array, how could you not know it?”

Zhuge Liang said, “If you recognize it, dare you attack mine?”

Sima Yi replied, “Now that I recognize it, how could I not?”

Zhuge Liang said, “Then just come on and strike.”

Returning to his own camp, Sima Yi called Dai Ling, Zhang Hu, and Le Lin, and ordered: “The array Zhuge has set has eight gates: Rest, Life, Injury, Block, Sorrow, Death, Alarm, Open. You three can enter by the central east Sheng gate, break out through the southwest Xiu gate, then from the true north Open gate strike in. This array can be broken. Pay close attention!”

So Dai Ling was in the center, Zhang Hu in front, Le Lin behind. Each led thirty riders. They entered through the Sheng gate. Both armies shouted and aided. The three entered the Shu array and saw it like a walled city—after collision they could not get out.

The three riders hurriedly turned and rode around the array corner, charging southwest. They were then shot at by Shu soldiers and again trapped. In that formation there were layered gates upon gates; there was no real east, west, south, or north to separate. The three could not even see one another and simply battered on at random. The air thickened in clouds of sorrow and haze. As their cries rose, Wei soldiers were each bound and sent back to the center camp.

Zhuge Liang was in the pavilion. Around him, Zhang Hu, Dai Ling, and Le Lin along with ninety soldiers had been all tied and brought before the pavilion. Zhuge Liang laughed: “To capture such men as you is no wonder for me. I will release you and have you return to Sima Yi. Tell him to read military treatises again and weigh warfare more closely; when he is ready, he may come and settle who is superior. Since you have been spared your lives, leave behind the arms and war horses.”

He then had their uniforms and armor removed, rubbed ink on their faces, and had them march out on foot from the array.

When Sima Yi saw this he was furious. Looking back on his commanders, he said, “So this defeat has weakened your sharpness—by what face can you return before the ministers of the Central Plains?” He then led three armies and urged the fiercest on the charge.

With sword drawn, he brought more than a hundred chosen captains and drove the charge. The armies had hardly met when suddenly drums and horns sounded from the rear in unison and great shouts arose. A great band of troops struck from the southwest: it was Guan Xing.

Sima Yi sent the rear to meet him and then drove his army again into close slaughter. Suddenly the Wei ranks broke into chaos. That had been Jiang Wei, who had led another force to strike quietly.

Shu troops attacked on three fronts and Sima Yi was deeply alarmed. He quickly withdrew the army. Shu soldiers closed around on all sides, and Sima Yi led three armies southward and charged hard to break through.

The Wei suffered six or seven wounded out of ten. Sima Yi withdrew and camped on the south bank of the Wei River, holding firm and refusing to go out.

When Zhuge Liang had taken the troops he could call victory, he returned to Qishan. Li Yan had Captain Ji An deliver grain and rice to the army. Ji An loved liquor and, while on the way, delayed and exceeded the ten-day limit.

Zhuge Liang was angry: “In our army, supplies are the utmost matter. If delayed three days one should be beheaded. You delayed ten days. What excuse is there?” He ordered him brought out for execution.

Chief Clerk Yang Yi said, “Ji An is a man appointed by Li Yan and also handles money and grain for Sichuan. If this one is killed, there will be none left willing to bring provisions.”

Zhuge Liang shouted for soldiers to free him, unbound him, and release him with eighty lashes.

Ji An was punished with words and nursed grudge. In one night he rode out with five or six retainers and went straight to a Wei camp to surrender.

Sima Yi called him in. Ji An explained the earlier matter.

Sima Yi said, “Though what you bring is true, still Zhuge Liang is too crafty for this to be fully believed. If you can do one great deed for me, I shall at once petition the Son of Heaven and have you made a high commander.”

Ji An said, “If there is anything, I shall serve.”

Sima Yi said, “You can go back to Chengdu and spread rumor that Zhuge Liang bears hatred toward the Son of Heaven and intends every day or night to claim the throne, and then ask the imperial edict to summon him. That will be your achievement.”

Ji An promised and returned straight to Chengdu. He saw court eunuchs and spread the rumor that Zhuge Liang relied on his success and would one day usurp the state.

When the eunuchs heard, they were greatly alarmed and promptly presented it to the emperor. The Emperor, surprised, said, “How is this to be handled?”

The eunuch said, “Issue an edict to recall him to Chengdu, reduce his control of military power, and avert rebellion.”

The emperor issued the order and conveyed that Zhuge Liang should return to court. Jiang Wan presented a memorial: “Since the Chancellor first marched out, he has built success after success. Why summon him home now?”

The emperor said, “The Son of Heaven has a private matter that must be discussed face to face with the Chancellor.” He sent a messenger with the edict through the night.

The mission reached the great camp at Qishan without delay. Zhuge Liang received it and, after reading fully, looked toward heaven and sighed: “The ruler is young; there must be sycophants at his side. I was just seeking to secure merit—why am I called back now? If I do not return, I am deceiving him. If I do return in obedience, I may never have this opportunity again.”

Jiang Wei asked, “If the main army withdraws, and Sima Yi strikes then, what happens?”

Zhuge Liang said, “If we now retire, we should withdraw by five routes. Today we pull out this camp. If there are a thousand soldiers inside, we dig two thousand stove-pits. Today we dig three thousand; tomorrow four thousand; each day we retreat and move forward with the stove count increasing.”

Yang Yi asked, “General Sun Bin once captured Pang Juan using a method of adding troops while reducing stoves. Why should the Chancellor increase stoves while retreating?”

Zhuge Liang said, “Sima Yi is capable with troops. He will know we are withdrawing and naturally pursue. He suspects hidden force and will choose a few places in our old camps to watch closely. If he sees the number of stove-pits increasing, thinking the army neither truly withdrawn nor still, he will dare not give chase. If we pull back slowly, we can lose no men.” He ordered the retreat.

Sima Yi, for his part, calculated Ji An’s scheme would be in place and waited only for Shu’s withdrawal to strike all at once. As he hesitated, a report came that the Shu camp was empty, men and horses all gone.

Because he was cautious about Zhuge Liang’s layered designs, he did not pursue. He led more than a hundred riders into the old Shu camp to inspect, had soldiers count the stove-pits, then returned to his own camp. The next day he again sent soldiers to that camp to check the count.

The report returned: “The number of stove-pits here has increased by one more than before.”

Sima Yi told his commanders, “I had thought Zhuge Liang very crafty. Now the pits truly increase with each step. If I pursue, I will surely fall into his plan. Better to turn back and make new plans.” He withdrew, making no pursuit.

Zhuge Liang did not lose a single person and turned his force toward Chengdu.

Later the Sichuan mouth locals reported to Sima Yi that when Zhuge Liang withdrew, they had seen no added troops, only additional stove-pits.

Sima Yi looked to heaven and sighed long: “Zhuge Liang used Yu Xiu’s method and tricked me. I do not match his stratagems.” He then withdrew the great army back to Luoyang.

The meeting of equal enemies cannot be easily won; a commander who has outmatched a fine general should not boast. Who knows how Zhuge Liang will return to Chengdu? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Han Troops Raid the Camp and Defeat Cao Zhen; Wuhou Tests Formations and Humiliates Zhongda

chapters.html:
He takes on a spirit-like form above Longshang;\ He rides for Jianmen while Zhang He falls for the ruse.

Zhuge Liang, whose courtesy name was Kongming, used the stratagem of reducing the army while increasing the cooking fire-points and withdrew to Hanzhong. Sima Yi, fearing an ambush, did not dare to pursue and also withdrew his army to Chang'an. As a result, not a single man of Shu was lost. After rewarding the entire army, Kongming returned to Chengdu and came before the Son of Heaven, saying, “I had marched beyond Qishan to take Chang'an when, in the end, I received Your Majesty’s decree to return. I do not know what grave matter called me back.” The Son of Heaven had no reply. After a long pause he said, “I have not seen the Chancellor for a long time and have missed him greatly; for that reason, I issued a special order for him to return. There was no other cause.” Kongming said, “This is not Your Majesty’s true intent. There must be treacherous ministers who slander me and claim I have rebel intentions.” The Son of Heaven was silent.

Kongming said, “Your servant received great grace from the late emperor and swore to serve with my life. If evil ministers are active inside the court, how can I, in the outer lands, punish them?” The Son of Heaven said, “I was misled by eunuchs’ words and once summoned you back in haste. Today the blockage in my ears is lifted, and my regret is beyond repair.”

Kongming then summoned all the eunuchs for examination and discovered only a base rumor. He had men seize the guilty parties, but most had already fled into Wei. He ordered execution for the eunuchs who had presented false reports and banished the rest from the palace. He sternly rebuked Jiang Wan and Fei Yi for failing to perceive the evil and for not remonstrating with the Son of Heaven. The two acknowledged their fault and submitted to blame.

After taking leave of the Son of Heaven, Kongming returned to Hanzhong. He issued an edict to Li Yan to handle grain supply and continue to send it to the forward army, and at the same time he resumed discussing another expedition. Yang Yi advised, “The army has been raised several times already, and our troops are exhausted and our grain stores cannot be replenished. It would be better to divide the army into two wings and use a three-month term. If we deploy only one of two hundred thousand as far as Qishan, let them stay there for three months and then have that one hundred thousand rotate back, to be replaced in turn. Then our strength will not run dry. We can then advance slowly. The Central Plains can be taken.” Kongming approved. “What you said accords exactly with my mind. My war against the Central Plains is not a matter of one day or one night. This is the long design that should be adopted.” He then ordered the split and the rotation with a one-hundred-day period; any unit that missed its term was to be punished under military law.

In the spring, second month of the ninth year of Jianxing, Kongming again marched out to invade Wei. It was also the fifth year of Taihe in Wei. When news of Kongming’s renewed advance reached Wei, Cao Rui, now ruler of Wei, summoned Sima Yi to consult. Sima Yi said, “Zi Dan has perished. I will pour out all my strength and wipe out the invading rabble to repay Your Majesty.” Cao Rui rejoiced and held a banquet for him. The next day, news came that the Shu army had raided in force. Cao Rui immediately ordered Sima Yi to ride out against the enemy and drove his carriage from the palace himself.

After reporting at court, Sima Yi went straight to Chang'an, assembled commanders from all the routes, and discussed plans to break the Shu forces. Zhang He said, “I am willing to lead a contingent to guard Ying and Mei and block the Shu.” Sima Yi replied, “Our forward army cannot stand against Zhuge Liang’s host alone, and if we split into advance and rear, victory is unlikely. It is better to leave troops to guard Shanggui and send the rest to Qishan. Are you willing to take command of the vanguard?” Zhang He said with joy, “I have long carried loyalty and righteousness and wished to repay the state with all my heart, but I have not yet met one who truly recognized me. Now that the commander-in-chief entrusts such a heavy charge to me, I will not shrink back even at the cost of my life.”

So Sima Yi made Zhang He the vanguard commander and overall commander of the main army, and gave Guo Huai the task of guarding the commanderies of Longxi. He sent other major generals along separate routes. Scout riders from the advance force then reported: “Kongming has brought his great army beyond Qishan. The advance vanguard of Wang Ping and Zhang Ni went straight out from Chencang, through Jiange, past Sanguan, and came by Xie Valley.” Sima Yi told Zhang He, “Now Kongming’s army is pushing rapidly forward. He will certainly cut the spring wheat in Longxi to provision himself. You should set your camp on Qishan. I will go with Guo Huai to inspect the Tianshui commanderies and guard against this cutting party.” Zhang He agreed, then took forty thousand troops to hold Qishan. Sima Yi moved the main army toward Longxi.

Kongming’s army reached Qishan. Their camp had already been established, and seeing Wei troops prepared on the Wei bank, he told the commanders, “This must be Sima Yi. The camp is already short of grain. I have repeatedly ordered men to hurry to Li Yan for grain deliveries, but he has not arrived. The wheat on Longshang should be ripe; we can discreetly draw soldiers there to cut it.” So he left Wang Ping, Zhang Ni, Wu Ban, and Wu Yi to guard the Qishan camp and led Jiang Wei and Wei Yan, together with other generals, toward Lu City.

Lu City’s commander, who already knew Kongming well, hurried to open the gates and surrender. After soothing him and his men, Kongming asked, “Where is the wheat ripe now?” The commander said, “The wheat atop Longshang is mature.” Kongming then left Zhang Yi and Ma Zhong to guard Lu City and led the generals and the entire army toward Longshang.

The vanguard reported back that Sima Yi had brought his troops here. Kongming cried out, “This man knows I will come to cut wheat!” He bathed, changed his robes, and brought forward several carts. All three had matching decorations. These were carts prepared in Shu in advance.

He ordered Jiang Wei to take one thousand men to guard one cart and five hundred drummers to wait behind Shanggui; Ma Dai on the left, Wei Yan on the right, each with one thousand men and five hundred drummers for another cart. For each of the carts, twenty-four men were assigned, dressed in black with bare feet and loosened hair, swords in hand, carrying seven-star black banners as they pushed each vehicle. The three commanders received their separate orders, and all moved the carts forward. Kongming also ordered thirty thousand soldiers to carry sickles and carry-rope cords, waiting to harvest wheat. He then selected twenty-four sturdy men and clad each in black with unbound hair and swords, a body of escorts around a four-wheeled cart. He had Guan Xing arranged as if in the form of a sky-borne attendant, holding a seven-star black banner and walking before the cart.

Kongming sat upright in the cart and moved toward the Wei camp.

When the scouts saw this, they were astonished and could not tell whether these were men or spirits. They reported quickly to Sima Yi. Sima Yi rode out to observe and saw Kongming wearing a tall cap and crane-feathered robe, one hand moving a feather fan, seated upright in the cart; on either side stood twenty-four men with loosened hair and drawn swords; in front, one man held a black banner. In the distance he resembled a heavenly spirit. Sima Yi said, “This is another trick by Kongming.” He then ordered two thousand riders: “Go now and catch that cart and men, every one of them, if you can.” The Wei soldiers obeyed and charged at once.

Seeing the Wei cavalry come hard after him, Kongming ordered the cart to turn back and slowly move away. The Wei troops spurred their horses in pursuit, yet though wind stirred in cold gusts and a damp mist spread thickly, after a long run they still could not catch the first cart, though it had moved three dozen li ahead. Confused, they checked their horses and said, “How strange! We rode hard for thirty li, yet he still stays ahead. What are we to do now?”

Kongming saw they did not close. He again had a cart reverse and return, then move slowly toward the Wei soldiers. Again he let the Wei forces chase him. Again they covered twenty more li but could not make up the distance; they stared in bewilderment. Kongming ordered the cart to turn again and reverse direction. The Wei cavalry pursued once more. From behind, Sima Yi arrived with a fresh host and sent the order: “Kongming is skilled in the arts of the Eight Openings and Nine Closings, and he can command the six ding and six jia spirits. This is the ‘shortening distance’ method from the Six Jia heavenly text. No army is to continue pursuit.”

At the same time the cavalry were coming to a halt. A war-drum boomed from the left; a full strike of troops came crashing in. Sima Yi ordered the lines to hold and resist.

From inside the storm of soldiers came one of the false processions: two dozen black-clad, bare-footed, disheveled, sword-bearing men shoved out a four-wheeled cart. Kongming sat upright at its center, in cap and crane-feathered robe, feather fan raised. Sima Yi exclaimed, “The one we chased for fifty li was Kongming and could not be caught. How can he be here again? This is strange indeed, strange indeed!”

Before he could finish speaking, a drum cracked again on the right front and another group came at speed. There too sat Kongming in a four-wheeled cart, again with twenty-four black-clad attendants and bare feet and swords pushing it forward.

Sima Yi was in deep doubt; he turned to his commanders and said, “This must be spirit troops!” The rank and file hearts collapsed, and none dared to close with them; all began to run.

Before any could settle, a fresh drum burst out and still another unit came rushing. At their front was a four-wheeled cart with Kongming seated upright, with the same kind of two-sided cart carriers. The Wei troops were transfixed. Sima Yi still did not know whether he looked upon men or spirits, nor how many Shu soldiers were behind him. He grew utterly frightened and hurried the army back into Shanggui, shutting the gates.

By then Kongming had earlier ordered three thousand elite troops to cut the wheat on Longshang and cart it back to Lu City to dry. Sima Yi stayed inside the city for three days and did not venture out. When the Shu troops withdrew, he finally sent out scouts. On the road they seized a Shu soldier and brought him in. Sima Yi asked him. The man said, “I was one of the wheat-cutting parties. I lost my horse and was caught.” “Who were those spirit-troops earlier?” asked Sima Yi. The man replied, “They were three hidden forces, and none of them were Kongming; they were Jiang Wei, Ma Dai, and Wei Yan. Each route had only one thousand soldiers guarding a cart and five hundred drummers. Only the cart that first baited your camp had Kongming on it.”

Sima Yi sighed up toward heaven. “Kongming has an art of appearing and vanishing like a ghost.”

At that moment, Guo Huai, the deputy commander-in-chief, arrived for audience. After formal greetings, he said, “I have heard that the Shu force is small. If it is now cutting wheat at Lu City, we may strike.” Sima Yi told him what had just happened. Guo Huai laughed: “It only deceived you for a while. Now you have seen through it. So what?” He said, “I will lead one army against its rear, and you one against its front. Lu City can fall; Kongming can be captured.” Sima Yi agreed and split his force into two columns.

Kongming brought his troops to Lu City and set to drying the cut wheat. He then called the generals and said, “Tonight the enemy must come to attack the city. I judge the east and west wheat fields outside can serve as an ambush. Which among you dares to go first for me?” Jiang Wei, Wei Yan, Ma Dai, and Ma Zhong volunteered all at once.

Kongming said with satisfaction, “Good.” He ordered Jiang Wei and Wei Yan to lead two thousand men each and lie in wait in the southeast and northwest. Ma Dai and Ma Zhong led two thousand each and lay in the southwest and northeast. “Wait for the boom of cannon and let all four wings strike together.” The four generals left with their troops.

Kongming himself led just over a hundred men, each with firearms, out of the city and hid in the wheat fields to wait.

Sima Yi brought his troops directly before Lu City. Night had already deepened when he said to the commanders, “If we attack by daylight, the city will be prepared. Let us strike now in darkness. The city walls are low and the moat shallow; we can break through easily.” They arrayed outside the walls. At the first watch, Guo Huai also brought his force in. Their two lines combined, and to one drumbeat they wrapped Lu City on all four sides in a ring like a great iron barrel. From the walls, ten thousand crossbows opened together and arrows fell like rain, and the Wei soldiers could not step forward.

Suddenly cannonfire rang repeatedly through the Wei ranks, startling all three divisions and no one could tell where the enemy came from. While Guo Huai had men search the wheat fields, flames burst from the four corners and loud cries rolled; Shu forces from four directions charged all at once. Lu City’s four gates opened wide and soldiers from inside surged out. A blow was dealt from within and without; a single mass of killing went through the night. Wei soldiers died in countless numbers. Sima Yi drew off the shaken survivors and broke through by force to hold a hilltop; Guo Huai too brought his survivors to form a post behind the hill.

Kongming entered the city and ordered the four generals to set camp at each of the four corners.

Guo Huai told Sima Yi, “We have held against Shu for a long while and found no way to push them out. Now we have already lost more than three thousand in one repulse. If we do not devise an exit now, we will fail to withdraw later.” Sima Yi asked, “How then?” Guo Huai said, “Issue an edict summoning troops from Yong and Liang to join in the hunt. I would lead a force to Jianmen to cut off their return, and then their grain line will collapse and their ranks will panic. In that moment strike again, and they can be annihilated.” Sima Yi accepted.

The edict was sent in one night. In no time, Senior General Sun Li arrived with men from several commanderies. Sima Yi then ordered Sun Li to rendezvous with Guo Huai and strike Jianmen.

Kongming had held against Lu City for a long time and saw no new Wei troops in open battle. He called Ma Dai and Jiang Wei back into the city and said, “Now the Wei troops hold the mountain passes and refuse to meet us. First, they mean to exhaust our grain, and second, they have sent men to Jianmen to cut our supply road. You two lead ten thousand each and take these key positions. When the Wei troops perceive this, they will naturally withdraw.”

As they marched, Chief Clerk Yang Yi entered the tent and said, “The Chancellor ordered every one-hundred-day exchange of main troops. The period is now complete. Hanzhong troops have come out at Chukou. The orders for reassembly have arrived; only the troop exchange remains. There are now eighty thousand men, with forty thousand remaining. The next forty thousand are due to rotate in.” Kongming said, “If that order has already been issued, act at once.”

The entire army heard this and began to pack for departure. Word then came that Sun Li was bringing twenty thousand cavalry and troops from Yong and Liang to aid the attack on Jianmen and that Sima Yi was coming himself from the rear to assault Lu City. The Shu army was struck with astonishment and fear. Yang Yi entered and reported to Kongming, “The Wei troops are coming quickly. It would be better if the retiring units stay behind to block them and then the new troops can take their place.” Kongming said, “No.”

“My campaigns rely first on trust, and that is my doctrine. If there is an order first and I then break it, what is my word worth? Every man slated to leave would like to return home to his parents, wife, and children who wait by the gate. But now there is a grave danger, and I will not keep him back.” He then gave the order to the departing contingents to depart that same day.

When the soldiers heard him, they cried out in unison, “The Chancellor shows such grace; we cannot retreat now. We are ready to give our lives and cut down Wei to repay him!” Kongming said, “Your duty is to return home. How can you stay here again?” Yet all said they wanted battle and refused to retreat.

Kongming said, “If you want to fight with me, go out and pitch camp and wait. When the Wei troops arrive, do not wait for them to recover breath. Attack at once. This is the method of waiting with advantage.” The soldiers took command and set out in gladness, forming ranks and waiting.

Meanwhile, the troops from Xiliang arrived at speed, tired from the forced pace. As they had just wished to camp and rest, the Shu army surged forward in one crash. Every soldier rallied, and the front ranks fought with vigor. The forces from Yong and Liang could not stand against it and fell back. The Shu soldiers pursued fiercely and cut them down until their dead lay thick across the field and blood ran in channels.

Kongming came out of the city and gathered his victorious men, then returned inside to reward them. A letter from Li Yan arrived from Yong’an in urgency.

“I have recently heard that agents from Eastern Wu have entered Luoyang and made peace with Wei. Wei has asked Wu to serve in Shu’s place; fortunately Wu has not yet taken up arms. I have heard this through scouts and trust this reaches the Chancellor.”

Kongming read it with great alarm. He gathered the commanders and said, “If Eastern Wu rises and invades Shu, I must return at once.” He ordered the Qishan main camp to retreat toward Xichuan: “Now that Sima Yi knows our camp here, he will not dare to pursue.” So Wang Ping, Zhang Ni, Wu Ban, and Wu Yi divided into two routes and slowly retired westward into Xichuan.

When Zhang He saw the Shu army retreating, he feared there was another scheme and did not dare pursue. He approached Sima Yi and asked, “The Shu army is withdrawing. Who can tell its meaning?” Sima Yi said, “Kongming has many guileful stratagems and must not be moved against lightly. Better to hold fast and wait. He will run out of grain in time and go away.” Wei commander Wei Ping said, “The Shu army is leaving Qishan’s camp. This is exactly the moment to pursue with advantage. If the Commander-in-Chief refuses to move, he flees in fear like a tiger, and all under heaven will laugh.” Sima Yi still held firm.

Kongming, knowing his Qishan troops had withdrawn, called Ma Zhong and Yang Yi into audience and gave a secret plan. He ordered them to lead ten thousand crossbowmen to the Wooden Gate route and prepare ambushes on both sides. If Wei forces pursued to that place, they were to wait for a cannon signal, then quickly roll down wood and stones to block the path and shoot from both ends. The two men departed.

He also ordered Wei Yan and Guan Xing to screen the rear. The city raised banners at all four corners, stacked brushwood messily within, and let smoke rise as if preparations were lax. He sent most of the army toward the Wooden Gate path.

A patrol from the Wei camp reported to Sima Yi, “The Shu force withdrew as a large body, but we do not know how many remain within the city.” Sima Yi rode there and saw banners flying on the ramparts and smoke rising from within, so he laughed, “This is an empty city.” He sent scouts; it was indeed empty. He rejoiced and said, “Kongming has gone. Who dare to pursue?”

Vanguard commander Zhang He said, “I would go.” Sima Yi tried to restrain him: “Your nature is rash; you should not.” Zhang He said, “When the Commander-in-Chief went out through the passes, he appointed me vanguard. This is today’s chance for merit, and yet you leave me idle?” Sima Yi said, “Where the Shu withdrew, there will be ambush in the rough ground. One must be cautious before pursuit.” Zhang He said, “I already understand; do not worry.” Sima Yi answered, “If you insist on going, take five thousand first.”

“Yet send Wei Ping with twenty thousand horse and infantry behind, and I myself will bring three thousand to support.”

Zhang He accepted the command and pursued quickly. After thirty li, a cry from the rear sounded like thunder and a force burst from the trees. At its head rode a commander with a broad sword, who cried, “Where are you leading the troops, traitor?” Zhang He turned, and it was Wei Yan. Zhang He was enraged and reined in to meet him. In less than ten exchanges, Wei Yan feigned a rout and fled.

Zhang He chased him thirty more li, then reined back to look around—no ambush. He then turned forward again. As they came over a slope, a shout rose again and another force appeared from the edge of trees, again with a senior commander at its head. It was Guan Xing, who drew his great horse and cried, “Zhang He, do not run! I stand here!” Zhang He reined in and fought him. In less than ten exchanges, Guan Xing wheeled around and withdrew. Zhang He pursued.

They raced into thick woodland. Zhang He, uneasy, sent scouts in all directions; no ambush was found. Assured again, he pursued on. Again Wei Yan appeared ahead. Again they fought more than ten rounds. Wei Yan feigned defeat and fled. Zhang He came in furious anger again, and once more Guan Xing intercepted him.

Zhang He’s anger rose still higher. He spurred into direct collision. They fought ten times; the Shu dropped armor, helmets, and other gear along the road, filling it thickly. Wei troops dismounted and fought for the pieces.

Wei Yan and Guan Xing alternated the combat while Zhang He chased them with mounting fury. As darkness deepened, they reached the gate of the Wooden Door Pass. Wei Yan snapped his horse around and shouted:

“Zhang He, traitor! I need not stand with you! You have chased me only this far. Now I will finish this and meet you in single combat!”

Zhang He was deeply angry, threw his spear and drove his horse straight at Wei Yan. Wei Yan answered with his blade. They met again for fewer than ten exchanges. Wei Yan was badly beaten, and he abandoned his armor, helmet, and even his horse, withdrawing in retreat toward the Wooden Gate. Zhang He, bloodly determined, spurred after him again.

By then it was dark. A cannonblast sounded. Fire leapt from the hilltop. Great stones and burning timber rolled down and blocked the way. “I have been tricked!” Zhang He cried. He wheeled his horse back, only to find his rear already packed with wood and rock and only one strip of open ground between cliffs. He had no room to advance or retreat.

At that moment a clapper sounded, and on both sides ten thousand crossbows fired together, striking down Zhang He and over a hundred officers in the pass.

伏弩齊飛萬點星，木門道上射雄兵。\ 至今劍閣行人過，猶說軍師舊日名。

When this poem is translated:

Bolts from crossbows flew in myriads, like ten thousand stars. On the Wooden Gate road, a host of heroes was shot down. Even to this day, travelers through Jianmen still speak of the Master’s former name.

Zhang He had fallen. The Wei troops came up behind and seeing the road blocked, understood he had been tricked. They drew rein and withdrew hurriedly. From the heights came a great cry: “Chancellor Zhuge is here!” The whole army looked upward. Kongming stood amid torchlight and pointed to the soldiers and said, “Today I set out to hunt one horse, but I accidentally shot a roe deer instead. Go safely, each of you, and report to Zhongda that sooner or later he will surely be captured by me.”

The Wei soldiers went back to report to Sima Yi. He was deeply grief-stricken. He lifted his face to the sky and sighed, “Zhang He, loyal and upright, has died by my fault.” He gathered the army and withdrew to Luoyang.

When Cao Rui heard of Zhang He’s death, he sent tears and sighed deeply, ordering that Zhang He’s body be retrieved and buried with honors.

Kongming returned to Hanzhong and prepared to go to Chengdu to see the Son of Heaven. The imperial guard Li Yan submitted an advance report saying, “My lord, I have prepared grain and it is now about to be carried to the Chancellor’s front. I do not know why the Chancellor suddenly returned.” The Son of Heaven, on hearing this, ordered the Chancellor of the Masters of Writing, Fei Yi, to go to Hanzhong and ask the reason for the retirement. Fei Yi went and conveyed the Son of Heaven’s intent. Kongming was alarmed and said, “Li Yan sent this urgent message saying Eastern Wu would raise troops against Shu, and thus I returned.” Fei Yi replied, “Li Yan’s report said the grain was ready; the Chancellor has withdrawn without cause, so Your Majesty sent me only to ask why.”

Kongming was furious. He investigated. He found Li Yan had feared punishment for failure in grain supply and therefore fabricated the message to recall the Chancellor, then made a false report to the emperor to hide his fault. Kongming said, “A common man, for his own sake, has neglected the state’s great affairs!” He summoned him for execution.

Fei Yi pleaded, “The Chancellor should remember the late emperor’s entrustment and forgive him for now.” Kongming agreed. Fei Yi drafted a memorial for the emperor. The Son of Heaven read it and was furious, shouted to the guards to bring out Li Yan and execute him. Participating colonel Jiang Wan then presented his official objection: “Li Yan was entrusted as a minister to raise and protect the state by the late emperor. I beg Your Majesty for clemency.” The Son of Heaven granted the plea, reducing him to a commoner and exiling him to the remote parts of Zitong Commandery.

Kongming returned to Chengdu and made Li Feng, Li Yan’s son, his chief clerk. He stacked grass and stored grain, drilled formations, taught military arts, repaired arms, and cared for the soldiers. For three years he remained before another campaign. The people and soldiers of both Sichuan and Hanzhong all relied on his benevolence.

Seasons passed unheeded; three years vanished. In the spring, second month of the twelfth year of Jianxing, Kongming came to court and said, “For three years I have nursed and preserved the army. Grain is ample, weapons are complete, men and horses are strong. We can attack Wei. If this time I do not clear away treacherous ministers and recover the Central Plains, I will not dare to see Your Majesty again.”

The Son of Heaven said, “The realm now stands as three equal powers, and neither Wu nor Wei has raided us. Why should Your Lordship not enjoy peace?”

Kongming replied, “I received the late emperor’s favor; in sleep and in waking I have never ceased devising ways to campaign against Wei. To exert my strength and complete loyal duty by winning back the Central Plains and restoring Han is my sole wish.” He had not finished speaking when a man from the ranks stepped out: “The Chancellor should not raise troops.” The company saw him: he was Qiao Zhou.

The chapter ended with this couplet:

The Martial Duke has worn himself out through all he has done, only to worry for the realm. The court astronomer sees the moment and reads Heaven again. What counsel Qiao Zhou now offers, we do not yet know.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Appears in Spirit-like Guise Above Longshang; Zhang He Is Caught Off Guard at Jianmen Pass

chapters.html:
Sima Yi takes position at Beiyuan’s Wei Bridge. Zhuge Liang builds the wooden oxen and flowing horses.

Now Qiao Zhou, who served in charge of astronomy and was well versed in the stars, learned that Kongming was preparing to campaign again and submitted a memorial to the Son of Heaven:

I am charged with the duties of the celestial observatory, and whenever I see omens of disaster and blessing, I must report them. Recently, tens of thousands of birds flew in from the south and died in the Han River. This is an ominous sign. I have also observed the heavens and seen the star Kui in the course of Venus, with its strong qi in the north. It does not favor marching against Wei. In Chengdu, everyone now reports hearing the cypresses cry out at night. With these several signs, the Chancellor should only act with caution and not make a reckless move.

Kongming replied, “I bear the late emperor’s charge to protect him, and I must apply all my strength to subduing the rebels. Shall I allow a mood of foreboding to halt a matter of state?”

He then ordered the officials to set up a grand sacrificial feast at the temple of Emperor Zhaolie, wept, and bowed as he made his report:

In five campaigns at Qishan I have gained no inch of land. My guilt is no light matter. Now I have once again mustered the full army and returned to Qishan. I vow to devote my whole strength and heart, to exterminate the Han usurpers and restore the Central Plains, to exhaust my body and efforts to the end, and not to rest before I die.

After the rite, he took leave of the Son of Heaven and rode through the night to Hanzhong, gathering the generals to discuss the campaign. Suddenly a report arrived: Guan Xing had died of illness. Kongming cried out loudly, then collapsed to the ground, only reviving after half a watch. The generals begged him to steady himself repeatedly. Kongming sighed:

“Alas for loyal and righteous men—Heaven does not grant them long lives. This is another major general I lose this time I take to the field.”

A verse was later composed in lament:

The course of life and death is ordinary, and mayflies are brief in the air. If loyalty, filial duty, and integrity remain, why must one live long like the tall pine?

Kongming led three hundred and forty thousand Shu soldiers in five columns forward, sending Jiang Wei and Wei Yan as the vanguard to take Qi Mountain; he ordered Li Hui to pre-position supplies at the Xia Valley crossing in advance.

In Wei, there had been in a prior year a Green Dragon rising from the bottom of a well at Moping, and the court altered the era to Green Dragon. Now it was the second month of the second year of that era. Nearby officials reported:

Scouts from the frontier report over three hundred thousand Shu troops, now divided into five columns, have again left for Qishan.

Cao Rui, ruler of Wei, was startled and immediately summoned Sima Yi, saying, “Shu has not raided for three years. Now Zhuge Liang goes out to Qishan again. What are we to do?”

Sima Yi reported,

“I watched the heavens in the night; I saw the qi in the Central Plains at its height, while Kui violated its course under Venus and the strong qi was in the north. This does not favor Xichuan. Kongming trusts his own brilliance and will act against Heaven; he is choosing ruin. Entrusting in your august blessing, I will go and break them. I wish the four of them to accompany me.”

“Four of whom?” the emperor asked.

Sima Yi replied, “Xiahou Yuan has four sons: the eldest Ba, courtesy name Zhongquan; the second Wei, courtesy name Jiquan; the third Hui, courtesy name Yaq quan; the fourth He, courtesy name Yiquan. Ba and Wei are long practiced in bow and horse; Hui and He know stratagems well. These four have long wished to avenge their father. I propose taking Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei as forward commanders, and Xiahou Hui and Xiahou He as campaign vice-commanders to coordinate operations and help force back Shu forces.”

“The father in this case was Xiahou Mao,” Cao Rui said. “Did he not violate orders and disgrace himself by losing large numbers of men and horses, and still not recover his honor? Are these four like him too?”

Sima Yi answered, “These four are not to be compared with Mao.”

Cao Rui agreed and appointed Sima Yi as Grand Commander. He ordered that all officers and soldiers should be assigned by merit, and that every unit should obey deployment orders.

Sima Yi bowed and accepted the edict, then left the court that day. Cao Rui also issued a hand memorial to him:

When you reach the Wei shoreline, hold firm behind strong fortifications and keep your position secure. Do not engage in open battle. Shu’s soldiers, finding no gain, will likely feign retreat and lure the enemy; do not chase. Wait until their grain runs out, and they will move of their own accord. Then attack only at the right moment and your victory will be easy, and your men and horses will not be worn out. There is no better plan than this.

Sima Yi, kneeling, took the order and within the day arrived at Chang’an to gather the armies from every command. Four hundred thousand were assembled there and all camped along the Wei banks. He also ordered fifty thousand troops along the Wei River to build nine pontoon bridges, and told the forward commanders Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei to cross first and establish camps. Behind the main camp, he had an inner wall erected at Dongyuan to guard against the unexpected.

While he was still deliberating with his generals, word came that Guo Huai and Sun Li sought audience. Sima Yi received them and heard their report.

Guo said, “Shu now has all its armies at Qishan. If they cross the Wei and move up onto the ridge, then link by the northern hills and cut off the Long Road, they may threaten us greatly.”

Sima Yi replied, “What you say is correct. You will now assume command of the Longxi troops, camp in the north plain, dig deep ditches and raise high ramparts, and hold fast without moving. Wait until they have no grain, then we can strike.”

Given the order, Guo Huai and Sun Li took men and camped below.

Kongming again led out at Qishan and established five large camps in a formation: left, right, front, rear, and center. From Xia Valley to Jianmen Pass he laid fourteen additional large camps in one line, rotating forces with the intention to stay the long term and sending scouts every day. Then word arrived that Guo Huai and Sun Li had moved the Longxi army to camp at Beiyuan.

Kongming said to his commanders, “The Wei troops camp at Beiyuan to block our route and shut the Long Road. I will make a feigned attack on Beiyuan, but move secretly on the Wei bank. Have a hundred raft boats prepared and loaded with bundled straw; choose five thousand skilled boatmen to man them. I will attack Beiyuan only overnight. Sima Yi will have to come to relieve it. If he suffers a small defeat, I will send the rear army across at once, and then send forward troops into the rafts. They must not disembark, but let the current carry them to the floating bridges and then set those bridges aflame so they burn through. I will bring one army directly at the gate of the forward camp. Once we gain the southern bank of the Wei, advancing troops becomes straightforward.” The commanders carried out his commands.

Before long, patrol scouts rode in to report that Sima Yi was near. Sima Yi called a council and said,

“Kongming has set this up with calculation. He makes it seem he is taking Beiyuan, but the plan is to use the current, burn our bridges, create confusion in our rear, and then attack our front.”

He then ordered Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei:

If you hear shouts from Beiyuan, immediately bring your troops into the southern hills on the Wei and await the Shu approach, then strike.”

He also ordered Zhang Hu and Le Chen to hide two thousand bowmen and crossbowmen on the northern bank of the Wei bridges:

If the Shu troops come downstream on rafts, shoot together and never allow them near the bridges.”

Next he told Guo Huai and Sun Li:

Kongming will cross in secret to the north of the bank. Your new camp has few men and horses. Hide and fall back along the road. If the Shu cross in the afternoon, by dusk they will surely attack you. Stage a retreat; the enemy will pursue. All of you must shoot with bow and crossbow. I will strike by water and land together. If the Shu forces are too many, watch my commands and strike in concert.”

After all orders were issued, Sima Yi sent his two sons Sima Shi and Sima Zhao with troops to support the forward camp. He personally led a column to Beiyuan.

Kongming then ordered Wei Yan and Ma Dai to cross the Wei and attack Beiyuan; he ordered Wu Ban and Wu Yi to send the raft troops to burn the bridges; he assigned Wang Ping and Zhang Ni to the vanguard, Jiang Wei and Ma Zhong to the middle, and Liao Hua and Zhang Yi to the rear, dividing the attack into three columns aimed at the Wei dry camp. At the hour of noon the men and horses left the large camp and fully crossed the Wei, forming ranks and moving slowly forward.

When Wei Yan and Ma Dai reached near Beiyuan, dusk had already fallen. Sun Li sighted them and abandoned his camp in flight. Wei Yan, sensing the enemy had prepared, rushed back. Four directions erupted in cries. On the left was Sima Yi; on the right, Guo Huai, and both columns moved to strike. Wei Yan and Ma Dai fought hard to break out. Most of the Shu troops went down into the water; the survivors tried to flee but found no way out. Then Wu Yi’s force arrived and rescued the broken troops, holding them as they crossed back to the bank.

Wu Ban split half his men to man rafts and run downstream to burn the bridges, but they were pinned by arrows from Zhang Hu and Le Chen on the bank. Wu Ban was struck and drowned. The remaining men leapt into the water and fled; the rafts were all seized by Wei troops.

Meanwhile, Wang Ping and Zhang Ni, not knowing the Beiyuan force had failed, pushed straight for the Wei camp. It was already after two gongs of the night watch when all around them shouts arose. Wang Ping said to Zhang Ni, “Our troops are attacking Beiyuan; we do not yet know the result. The camp on the southern bank is before us, and not one Wei soldier is in sight. Does Sima Yi already know and prepare? Let us wait until we see the bridges fire up before we move.” The two checked their horses. Suddenly a rider came up behind with this report: “The Chancellor orders the army to hurry back. The Beiyuan troops and the bridge troops are both lost.” Wang Ping and Zhang Ni were startled and turned back in haste. They were then intercepted from behind by Wei soldiers. A cannon blast sounded, and both sides closed in. Wang Ping and Zhang Ni met them in battle. The two armies clashed in close combat. The two broke through with valiant effort, but more than half the Shu force was shattered. Kongming returned to the Qishan camp, gathered the remnants—somewhere over ten thousand men—and withdrew to his own lines, deeply troubled.

Then Fei Yi arrived from Chengdu to report to the Chancellor. After he was received, Kongming said,

“I have a letter and planned to ask you to carry it to Eastern Wu. Will you take it?”

Fei Yi replied, “How could I refuse your command?”

Kongming then had the letter written and sent him off.

Fei Yi took it straight to Jianye and presented it to the Wu lord Sun Quan, with all due ceremony.

Sun Quan read the text, which ran:

The Han house is unfortunate. Court order has failed. The Wei traitors have usurped and overthrown. Their misrule spreads to the present day. General Kongming, entrusted by Emperor Zhaolie with a great charge, can only strain every power and devotion. The great army is already assembled at Qishan; the raging raider is about to be destroyed at the Wei River. I beg Your Majesty to honor our alliance and send armies north to reclaim the Central Plains and divide the realm together. The letter cannot include all I mean. May I have Your Majesty’s indulgent hearing.

After reading it, Sun Quan rejoiced and said to Fei Yi,

“Long have I wished to raise troops but not find the chance to meet Kongming. Now that this letter has come, I myself will mobilize today: I will advance at once to Jiaomen and seize Xinye New City. I will then dispatch Lu Xun and Zhuge Jin to garrison Jiangxia and Miankou and take Xiangyang. Sun Shao and Zhang Cheng, etc., shall move on Guangling and seize Huaiyang and related places. Three routes together, one campaign of three hundred thousand, set to start at the chosen day.”

Fei Yi thanked him. During the banquet Sun Quan asked,

“Who do you think will lead the first shock in battle before Kongming?”

Fei Yi answered, “Wei Yan.”

Sun Quan smiled and said, “This man has courage in excess but is not upright of heart. Should Kongming fall, he will become the realm’s ruin. Does Kongming not know this?”

Fei Yi answered, “Your Majesty is entirely correct. I will report this to him as soon as I return.”

After thanking Sun Quan, Fei Yi rode back to Qishan and told Kongming: Wu had raised three hundred thousand and Sun Quan himself would lead a three-pronged campaign.

Kongming asked, “Did the Son of Heaven speak of anything else?”

Fei Yi then repeated Sun Quan’s judgment of Wei Yan.

Kongming sighed, “He is a most sagacious lord, and I am not unaware of this man. I do employ him only because he is useful and brave.”

Fei Yi urged, “Then you should assign him with care.”

Kongming answered, “I have my own methods.”

Fei Yi left and returned to Chengdu.

Kongming was again conferring with his generals when he received word of a Wei commander surrendering. He called him in and asked why. The man answered,

“I am Zheng Wen, a Wei provincial colonel. Not long ago I served with Qin Lang over the same force and was assigned by Sima Yi under his command. Yet Sima Yi has favored me unfairly with bias and promoted Qin Lang to forerunner general while treating me like chaff. In resentment, I have come to submit to you. Grant me a place in your service.”

Before he had finished speaking, a messenger announced that Qin Lang had ridden out and was sparring with troops outside camp.

Kongming asked, “How does his fighting compare to yours?”

Zheng Wen said, “I would rather cut him down at once.”

Kongming replied, “If you first kill Qin Lang, only then will I accept you.”

Grateful, Zheng Wen mounted and rode out to fight. Kongming watched from camp. Qin Lang advanced with spear raised, cursing,

“Traitor, you have stolen my war horse and come here. Return it at once!”

Then he charged straight at Zheng Wen. The newcomer met him with horse-whirling swordplay. In one pass he severed Qin Lang’s head while still in the saddle. The Wei troops fled in all directions. Zheng Wen carried the head to camp.

Back in his tent Kongming seated himself and summoned him. He grew furious and shouted to his attendants, “He must be beheaded.”

Zheng Wen said, “I am innocent!”

Kongming replied, “I knew Qin Lang before. The one you killed is not him. How could you deceive me?”

Zheng Wen then knelt and declared, “He was Qin Ming, Qin Lang’s brother.”

Kongming laughed. “So Sima Yi sent you to feign surrender and strike in the middle; how could I be fooled! If what you say is false, you die.”

Zheng Wen could only confess it was an attempt to deceive and pleaded for mercy.

Kongming said, “If you truly wish to live, write one letter and summon Sima Yi himself to seize this camp. If you bring him in, that will be your merit, and I will then reward you greatly.”

Reluctantly, Zheng Wen wrote a letter and handed it over. Kongming ordered him confined under watch.

When Fan Jian asked, “How did you know he was deceitful?” Kongming answered,

“Sima Yi does not promote men lightly. If Qin Lang had really been made forward commander, he must be a man with excellent military skills. Yet in horse battle Zheng Wen slew him in one exchange. He is certainly not Qin Lang. Therefore I knew this was a ruse.”

The surrounding officers agreed.

Kongming chose one tactician-soldier, gave him a whispered order, and sent him at once with the letter to seek Sima Yi’s presence at the Wei camp.

Sima Yi read the letter and asked,

“Who are you?”

The man said, “I am from the Central Plains, now a drifter in Shu. Zheng Wen is from my native place as well. Kongming has promoted him through his exploits as a forward commander and entrusted him with this role. He asked me to present this letter to you and begs that tonight at dusk he raise fires for signals and invite your commander-in-chief to lead the main force and overrun his camp, where he will coordinate from inside.”

Sima Yi cross-examined him repeatedly and examined the letter again in detail. It proved true. He gave the soldier food and wine and said,

“The second watch tonight is our signal. I will come to overrun the camp. If this succeeds, you will be rewarded heavily.”

The soldier departed. Kongming, having taken up his sword and finished his divinatory prayers, summoned Wang Ping and Zhang Ni, issuing precise instructions, then Jiang Wei and Ma Zhong, then Wei Yan likewise. He brought a few dozen men, climbed to a high hill, and directed the whole army from there.

When Sima Yi saw the letter from Zheng Wen, he planned to bring his two sons and lead the entire force to seize the Shu camp. His eldest son, Sima Shi, counseled, “Why does Father ride into a deep place on one sheet of paper? If there is danger or a misstep, what then? Better send another general first and hold Father back in reserve.”

Sima Yi agreed and ordered Qin Lang to lead ten thousand to seize the Shu camp while he followed with supporting troops.

At the first watch of that night the wind was clear and the moon bright. Around the second watch, dark clouds suddenly gathered and black vapors filled the sky so that nothing was visible across the river. Sima Yi rejoiced, “Heaven aids my success!” Everyone bit down on arrowheads and bridle lines and drove forward in one rush.

Qin Lang took the lead with ten thousand, charging straight into the Shu camp, and saw no one in sight. Realizing he had been trapped, he shouted for withdrawal. Torches flared everywhere, cries split the air, and at the left came Wang Ping and Zhang Ni, at the right Wei Yan and Ma Zhong. They both rushed to slaughter. Qin Lang fought to the death and could not escape.

Behind them Sima Yi saw the Shu camp ablaze and cries unending; unaware of his own side’s state he only drove his troops forward to support, charging toward the fire. Then a cry rose. War horns blared, drums thundered. On the left came Wei Yan; on the right Jiang Wei. A battle erupted. The Wei force was badly defeated, with perhaps nine-tenths killed. They scattered in panic. At that moment Qin Lang’s ten thousand had all been enveloped by Shu soldiers; arrows fell like locusts. He died in the confusion, and Sima Yi pulled back with survivors into his own camp.

After the third watch, the sky cleared again. Kongming, on the hilltop, sounded the signal gong and gave the order to collect troops. The earlier darkening of the sky had come from his own art of concealed array. Once battle was over and he withdrew, the sky cleared. The movement had been his casting of six ding six jia to sweep away the clouds.

Kongming then won back and returned to camp and ordered Zheng Wen executed, then returned to the plan for the Wei south bank. Each day he set small engagements, but the Wei army still would not come out.

Kongming rode in a light cart around the terrain on both sides of the Wei at Qishan, and found a valley shaped like a calabash: it could hold over a thousand men; two hills merged into another valley capable of four or five hundred. Behind, two surrounding ridges left only space for one rider and mount. He rejoiced inwardly and asked the local guide,

“What is this valley called?”

The guide replied, “This is called Shangfang Valley, also called Hulu Valley.”

Kongming returned to camp and summoned the junior officers Du Rui and Hu Zhong, whispering a secret plan. He ordered more than a thousand accompanying artisans to enter Hulu Valley and manufacture the wooden-ox and flowing-horse devices. He assigned Ma Dai to hold the valley entrance with five hundred men.

He told Ma Dai,

“The artisan crews are not to be let out, and no outsiders are to be let in. I will come often to inspect. The whole scheme against Sima Yi rests on this. You must keep this from leaking.”

Ma Dai obeyed and departed. Du Rui and Hu Zhong were left to supervise the craftworkers in the valley. Kongming visited each day with instructions.

One day, Chief Clerk Yang Yi reported,

“Now that grain supplies are all at Jianmen, men and horses are hard to move. How do we solve this?”

Kongming smiled,

“I have already prepared this scheme for a long while. The timber we accumulated was all sourced in Xichuan and shaped beforehand, so that we can use these for wooden oxen and flowing horses to move grain. It is far more convenient. Because these devices require no fodder or drinking water, transport can run continuously day and night.”

All were astonished:

“From antiquity to now, no one has heard of such wooden oxen and flowing horses. We do not know by what wonderful method the Chancellor has conceived this marvel.”

Kongming replied,

“It is already made according to my plans though not yet finished. I will write out the dimensions and shapes clearly, and you may read them now.”

The men gathered and took turns reading. The method for the wooden ox is given as follows:

Curved body, bent shanks, one body and four legs. The head goes through the mouth opening, and the tongue lies to the belly. It carries much while moving little. A single one travels tens of li; a crowd can go thirty li. Curved ones are the ox heads; paired ones are the hoofs. The cross members are the ox neck; rotating ones are the ox feet. The covering is the ox back; the square one is the ox belly. Dangling parts are the ox tongue; curved parts the ox ribs. Carvings are the ox teeth; upright projections are the ox horns. Fine rigging is the ox yoke; reins are the ox traces. The driver sits on twin yokebars. A man can walk six feet, and the ox travels four paces. The men are not greatly exhausted, and the ox needs no fodder or water.

The method for the flowing horse is as follows:

Ribs are three chi and five cun long, three cun wide, two cun and five fen thick. The same at left and right. From the front axle socket to its head is four cun; the hole is middle-sized at two cun. From the front foot socket to its head is four cun and five fen, length one cun and five fen, breadth one cun. From the front axle socket to the front shaft-socket is three cun and seven fen, with depth two cun and breadth one cun. From the front shaft-socket to the rear axle socket is one chi and five cun, and the rear axle is the same size as the front. From the rear foot-socket to the rear axle socket is one cun and two fen, with depth three cun and five fen, and size the same as the front. From the rear shaft-socket to the rear foot-socket is two cun and seven fen; the rear load is removed and from the rear shaft to load-bearing line is four cun and five fen. The front shaft is one chi and eight cun long, two cun wide, one chi and five fen thick. The rear shaft is the same. Two square boxes, each eight fen thick, two chi and seven cun long, one chi and six cun high, one chi and six cun wide, can each hold two hu and three dou of grain. From the upper shaft socket to the underside rib is seven cun, front and back alike. From the upper shaft socket to the lower shaft socket is one chi and three cun, hole length one cun and five fen, width seven fen; eight such holes alike. The four front and rear feet are each two cun wide and one chi and five fen thick. Its form resembles an elephant; canopy is four cun long, and the mouth is four cun and three fen across. Across the center shaft, three foot-bars run, each two chi and one cun long, one chi and five fen wide, one chi and four fen thick.

Every officer who read it knelt and praised,

“The Chancellor is truly a godly man.”

Within several days the wooden oxen and flowing horses were complete and moved as if living, climbing hills and descending ridges with ease. The whole army saw them and rejoiced.

Kongming ordered the right general, Gao Xiang, to take one thousand men and drive the devices from Jianmen straight to the Qishan main camp, hauling grain continually to supply the Shu army.

A later verse praised this method:

The Jianmen cliffs and steep heights are tamed by the flowing horse, The Xia Valley’s rough way is crossed by the wooden ox. If later ages use this method, who will still fret over transport?

At this time Sima Yi, while worried and uncertain, received a patrol report:

“The Shu are transferring grain with wooden oxen and flowing horses. Men need little labor, and horses and cattle need no feed.”

Sima Yi was shocked.

“Why have I held on as firmly as this? It was to starve him out and wait for him to collapse. If he uses this, he has a long design. I cannot withdraw now. What should I do?”

He immediately called Zhang Hu and Le Chen and ordered,

“You two each lead five hundred troops from the Xia Valley by a minor path. When the Shu drive the wooden oxen and flowing horses through, let all pass and then strike as one. Do not steal many—just seize three or five each and return.”

They obeyed and each took five hundred men, disguising themselves as Shu troops, and slipped by night through the valley path to ambush. They saw Gao Xiang driving the wooden oxen and flowing horses with soldiers. As that procession passed, both sides burst into shouts and slaughtered as one. The Shu men were caught unprepared and left several devices behind; Zhang Hu and Le Chen were delighted and drove back to their camp.

Sima Yi saw those machines, clearly made as if alive, and smiled,

“You have figured out how to use this—why should I not do the same?”

He ordered more than a hundred skilled artisans to dismantle them in front of everyone and instructed them, by the same measurements, length, breadth, and thickness, to build wooden oxen and flowing horses in the same way. In less than half a month he had over two thousand made, made by the same rules as Kongming’s and able to run as well. He then ordered Zhenyuan General Cen Wei to take one thousand troops and drive them to move grain in Longxi. Their operations never ceased.

The Wei camp army rejoiced.

When Gao Xiang returned and reported to Kongming that Wei troops had seized three to five of the wooden oxen and flowing horses, Kongming smiled.

“That is just what I intended. I only let a few of mine be taken, and soon I will gain substantial aid from the army all over.”

The commanders asked, “How did the Chancellor know that?”

Kongming said,

“Once Sima Yi sees the wooden oxen, he will certainly imitate the method and make his own in like form. That is where my next scheme applies.”

After several days, word arrived that Wei now had also begun making and using wooden oxen and flowing horses to carry grain to Longxi. Kongming rejoiced.

“This is not beyond my count.” He called Wang Ping and told him:

“You bring one thousand men and disguise yourselves as Wei troops. At night slip over Beiyuan and claim to be an escort grain train, mixing among his transport columns. Kill all the grain guards and drive the wooden oxen and flowing horses back, then immediately return over Beiyuan. There the Wei soldiers must give chase. Twist the tongues in each device backward, so horse and ox cannot move. Then you will discard them and run. The pursuers will reach them but cannot drag them out or shoulder them. When I bring more men, turn your tongues forward again and drive away at full speed. The Wei troops will think it a marvel.”

Wang Ping followed the plan and left.

Kongming then called Zhang Ni and said,

“You bring five hundred men dressed as the six ding six jia warrior spirits, with ghostly heads and beastly bodies, painted in five colors and made to look like all sorts of wonders. Carry embroidered flags in one hand and a jeweled sword in the other. Hang gourds at your waists with fire devices concealed inside, and hide by mountain sides. When the wooden oxen and flowing horses arrive, raise those fire devices, surge out together, and drive the oxen and horses along. Seeing this, the Wei troops will think they are spirits and will not dare to pursue.”

Zhang Ni obeyed and departed.

Kongming also called Jiang Wei and Wei Yan,

“You two take ten thousand and go to the Beiyuan camp mouth to support the wooden oxen and flowing horses and prevent battle.”

He then called Liao Hua and Zhang Yi,

“You two take five thousand and cut off Sima Yi’s route.”

And called Ma Zhong and Ma Dai,

“You two bring two thousand to grapple with the enemy on the Wei south bank.”

Each of the six carried out their orders.

Now General Cen Wei had taken the transport force in front, with grain loaded, when he learned that patrol troops were in front. He sent scouts and found they were Wei soldiers and continued his march in relief. When both forces were together, cries rose from within the line and Shu soldiers struck from their own ranks, shouting,

“Great General Wang Ping is here!”

The Wei troops, taken by surprise, were cut down in large numbers. Cen Wei, who fled to regroup, was cut down by a single stroke from Wang Ping, and the rest broke apart.

Wang Ping drove the soldiers and forced all the wooden oxen and flowing horses to return as fast as possible. The fleeing men rushed into Beiyuan to report. Guo Huai, hearing that military grain had been robbed, hurried out with troops to assist.

Wang Ping ordered his men to twist the tongues on the devices and leave them on the road, fighting as they fell back. Guo Huai said, “Do not chase; just seize back the grain oxen and horses.” All the troops drove them onward, yet somehow could not drive them. Guo Huai was baffled by this. At that moment war horns exploded and shouts rose; soldiers of two columns struck in together. It was Wei Yan and Jiang Wei. Wang Ping drove back again. With three-way pressure, Guo Huai was defeated and withdrew.

Wang Ping ordered the men to reverse the tongue pivots and drive the devices onward. As Guo Hui looked to turn back and chase, he saw smoke rise from behind the mountain. A troop of ghostly soldiers emerged all at once, each carrying a flag and sword in strange forms, driving the wooden oxen and flowing horses as if by wind.

Guo Huai exclaimed, “It must be divine assistance!” The whole army saw them and were filled with fear, so none dared to pursue.

Now Sima Yi, hearing of the Beiyuan defeat, hurried to come in relief. He was only halfway there when a resounding signal blast sounded, and from a steep place two columns cut loose. Their cries shook the earth. The banners bore the writing: “Han General Zhang Yi and Liao Hua.”

When he saw it, Sima Yi was startled. The Wei army faltered and scattered.

The final verse stood thus:

Their route meets a divine general, and the grain transport is lost; strange troops strike, and life hangs in peril. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Sima Yi Fortifies Beiyuan’s Wei Bridge, and Zhuge Liang Builds Wooden Oxen and Flowing Horses

chapters.html:
In Shangfang Valley, Sima is trapped. On Wuzhang Plain, Zhuge Liang wards off the stars.

Now it was said that Sima Yi was defeated by Zhang Yi and Liao Hua in one bout, and, mounted on a single horse with a single spear, he rode toward the dense woodland. Zhang Yi held back his rear guard, while Liao Hua pressed hard in pursuit. When he closed in, Sima Yi swerved and circled the trees in panic. Liao Hua struck once, but his blade struck a trunk. By the time he drew the weapon out, Sima Yi had already gone out of the woods. Liao Hua followed, yet he could not tell where the enemy had gone; in the eastern trees he noticed a gold helmet lying on the ground. He picked up the helmet from his horse and continued east in pursuit. In truth Sima Yi had abandoned his helmet to the east and turned back west.

Liao Hao chased a long way, found no trace, and broke out at the mouth of the valley, where he met Jiang Wei. The two returned to camp and reported to Kongming. Zhang Ni had already driven the wooden oxen and flow-horses into camp. The handover was complete, and they had obtained more than ten thousand shi of grain. Liao presented the gold helmet and logged it as his leading merit. Wei Yan, displeased, made grumbling remarks, while Kongming merely looked as if he had not heard.

Now it was said Sima Yi returned to camp in deep vexation. He received an edict: the Eastern Wu army had invaded in three columns, and the court had already decided to appoint troops to oppose them, ordering him to hold fast and avoid battle. Sima Yi took the command and, while deep ditches and high ramparts were dug, held his position and did not sortie.

At that time Cao Rui heard that Sun Quan had divided his troops into three columns to come forward. He, too, raised three columns to meet them: he ordered Liu Shao to lead troops to rescue Jiangxia, Tian Yu to lead troops to rescue Xiangyang, and rode himself with Man Chong to lead a main force to Hefei.

Man Chong first led one column to Chao Lake mouth and saw countless warships on the opposite bank, their standards orderly and fine. He said in his field command, “The Wu men will surely underestimate us for coming so far; they are not prepared. We can seize their river camps tonight and win outright.” The monarch replied, “You speak exactly as I intend.” He then ordered the valiant general Zhang Qiu to lead 5,000 soldiers, each with fire gear, from the lake mouth; Man Chong took 5,000 soldiers and advanced from the eastern bank.

At the second watch that night, Zhang Qiu and Man Chong each secretly moved toward the lake mouth. As they came near the water camps, all at once they shouted and charged in together. The Wu soldiers were thrown into confusion and fled without fighting. The Wei troops set fires all around and burned the warships, grain, and equipment by the numberless count. Zhuge Jin, leading retreating troops, fled down to Miankou. Wei’s army returned in a sweeping victory.

The next day the scouts reported to Lu Xun. He assembled his generals and said, “I will send a memorial to the ruler and ask that we lift the siege of Xincheng. We should use troops to cut off the Wei army’s line of retreat. I will lead all men to strike them in front. Their forces are loose at front and back, so one drumbeat may break them.” The men approved his words. Lu Xun drafted the memorial and gave it in secret to a junior officer to send to Xincheng.

The officer took his orders and carried the petition as he went to the ferry, but unexpectedly he was seized on an ambush by Wei soldiers, then brought before Wei Rui, Cao Rui. The ruler searched out Lu Xun’s memorial, read it through, and sighed, “Lu Xun of Wu, truly ingenious.” He immediately ordered the Wu prisoners set to guard and ordered Liu Shao to prepare carefully against Sun Quan’s rear troops.

Yet Zhuge Jin had also suffered a great defeat and, in the heat of summer, his men and mounts developed many illnesses. He wrote a letter urging retreat and return home. When Lu Xun read it, he told the envoy, “Tell the Commander-in-Chief that I have my own design.” The envoy took it back to Zhuge Jin.

Zhuge Jin asked, “What did Commander Lu do?”

The envoy replied, “I only saw Commander Lu urge everyone outside camp to sow beans and other grain, while he and the generals sported at the gate with archery practice.”

Zhuge Jin was greatly startled and went personally to Lu Xun’s camp. “Now Cao Rui is present himself, and his forces are strong,” he asked. “How will you withstand him?”

Lu Xun said, “I sent my memorial to the ruler earlier, but it was taken by the enemy and read. Our plan is exposed; he must know our defense. Battle would be useless. We should withdraw for now. I have already sent men with a petition asking the ruler to let us slowly pull back.”

“Then if this is your intent,” Zhuge Jin said, “you should do so at once and not delay.”

Lu Xun said, “If we withdraw, we must move gradually. If we retreat now the Wei men will pursue us and this would be the path to defeat. You should first drill your ships as though determined to resist. I will move all men and horses toward Xiangyang, as a feint to confuse the enemy; then we shall draw back slowly to Jiangdong. Wei troops will not dare to come near.”

Zhuge Jin obeyed this plan. Lu Xun formally withdrew to his home camp, arranged the ships, and prepared to set out. He ordered the troops into disciplined order, raised martial display, and moved toward Xiangyang.

Spies had already informed the ruler that Wu troops were moving and that defenses must be prepared. The Wei generals, hearing this, all wished to fight. But the ruler knew Lu Xun’s ability and told them, “Lu Xun has strategy; this is probably a stratagem to lure us. Do not move lightly.” The generals quieted.

Several days later a scout came to report that all three Wu columns had withdrawn. Cao Rui did not believe it at once and sent men again to reconnoiter. The return was firm: indeed all had gone back. The ruler sighed, “Lu Xun’s command is not inferior to Sun Wu’s. The southeast is not yet pacified.” He then ordered each general to hold the key passes while he himself drew the main army to Hefei to watch for changes.

Now this was as Zhuge Liang intended in Qishan. He set Shu soldiers and Wei civilians to mixed-field cultivation, one part as troops and two parts as civilians, and forbade encroachment. With that arrangement, the Wei people all settled into content labor.

Sima Shi brought this to his father: “Shu soldiers have taken much of our grain. Now they again make Shu troops labor beside our people and till fields on the Wei bank for long-term purposes. This is truly a grave danger to the state. Why does Father not set a date with Kongming and give him one decisive field battle?”

Yi said, “I serve by imperial command to hold firmly and not move.” While they still discussed, a report came that Wei Yan had come on behalf of our marshal, bearing the helm lost the previous day, and was cursing and shouting. The generals were angry and all wished to fight. Sima Yi laughed and said, “The sages say, ‘If one cannot bear small provocations, one ruins the great design.’ To hold firm is best now.” They obeyed and did not sortie. Wei Yan cursed long enough, then withdrew.

Seeing that Sima Yi would not come out, Kongming quietly ordered Ma Dai to erect a stockade of timber, dig a deep trench, and stockpile dry fuel and fire gear. On the surrounding hills he laid brush and thatch and built flimsy huts for concealment, and placed hidden earth mines both inside and out. When all was ready he whispered at close ear, “Cut off the rear path of Hulugu Valley and hide troops there. If Sima Yi pursues, let him enter the valley, and then set all the prepared dry brush and stores ablaze at once.”

He ordered soldiers by day to raise seven-star banners at the valley mouth, and at night to set seven bright lamps on the hills as coded signals.

Ma Dai took command and moved out with troops. Kongming then called Wei Yan and ordered him, “Go with 500 soldiers to attack Wei camp and tempt Sima Yi to battle. Do not win—only feign defeat. Sima Yi will chase. Keep to the seven-star flag by day and to the seven lights by night. As long as you can draw Sima Yi into Hulugu Valley, I have a way to seize him.”

Wei Yan took the plan and moved out.
