Kongming also summoned Gao Xiang and told him, “Take a group of thirty wooden oxen and flow-horses, or forty or fifty at a time, each carrying grain, and move them back and forth along the mountain roads. If Wei troops seize them, that is your merit.”

Gao Xiang understood and drove the wagons away.

Kongming then dispersed the Qishan army entirely and allowed only land cultivation. He gave this instruction: “If other forces come to battle, feign retreat only. If Sima Yi himself comes, then unite all forces and only strike south of the Wei to cut his line of retreat.”

When all was arranged, he led one force to camp below the upper valley of Shangfang.

Xiahou Hui and Xiahou He entered camp and told Sima Yi, “Shu troops are dispersed in many small camps, each at different points and each tilling long-term. If we do not strike now, even if they sit still, they will sink roots and become hard to move.”

Yi said, “This must be another of Kongming’s schemes.”

The two replied, “If the commander-in-chief still doubts, when will the brigand enemy be crushed? We, your brothers, will risk all and strike a final battle to repay the state’s grace.”

Yi said, “Then go forth and each bring your force out.” He ordered Xiahou Hui and Xiahou He, each with 5,000 soldiers.

Zhuge Liang then waited for word.

Now Xiahou Hui and Xiahou He split into two columns and, as they moved, unexpectedly saw Shu soldiers driving wooden oxen and flow-horses. Both rushed at once and killed the forward guard. The Shu troops were routed; they ran. The wooden oxen and flow-horses were all taken and captured, then sent to Sima Yi’s camp. The next day they also raided and captured over a hundred men and mounts.

Yi took the captives for examination and hearing. They said, “Kongming expects the commander-in-chief to hold and not move, then sends us all to till fields far apart as a long-term plan. We never expected to be taken.” Sima Yi set all these Shu soldiers free.

Xiahou He said, “Why not kill them?”

Yi replied, “These are low soldiers. Killing them helps nothing. Return them to camp and let it be known that Wei generals are broad and merciful and release them. This is like Lü Meng’s taking of Jingzhou.”

So he ordered that henceforth whenever anyone captured a Shu soldier, he should send them home and reward officers who performed well. The generals all accepted and returned to their stations.

Kongming then ordered Gao Xiang to feign supply transport, driving the wooden oxen and flow-horses back and forth through Shangfang Valley. Xiahou Hui and the others periodically intercepted and were cut down; in half a month they won in several skirmishes. Sima Yi saw Shu repeatedly beaten and rejoiced in his heart.

One day he captured several dozen Shu men again. He asked under his canopy where Kongming was now. They answered, “Chancellor Zhuge is no longer in Qishan. He camps on the west side of Shangfang Valley, ten li away. Daily he is carrying grain into Shangfang.”

Yi inquired no further and sent those men home. He then called the generals and told them: “Kongming is not in Qishan now; he is camped at Shangfang. Tomorrow you shall all join forces and take the Qishan great camp together. I will bring troops in support.”

The generals prepared to move. Sima Shi asked, “Father, why now turn to attacking their rear?”

Yi said, “Qishan is Shu’s root. When they see our forces attack it, every camp will come to rescue. In that moment I will burn their supplies at Shangfang and cut them in two; they will be routed decisively.”

Sima Shi submitted.

Yi then issued orders and started out with troops, sending Zhang Hu and Lechen each with 5,000 soldiers to provide rear support.

Kongming, watching from Qishan, saw Wei troops moving in groups of three to five thousand, then one to two thousand, uncertain streams of men, looking ahead and back. He concluded they were surely coming for Qishan’s great camp. He discreetly told all his generals: “If Sima Yi comes in person, you go at once and loot the Wei camp, seizing Weinan.”

Then the Wei army all ran toward the Qishan camp. Shu troops ran in all directions together and raised loud cries, making the appearance of a rescue force. Seeing Shu troops all heading to Qishan, Sima Yi brought his two sons and central escort and charged for Shangfang Valley.

Wei Yan stood at the valley mouth, waiting for Sima Yi’s arrival. Suddenly one Wei soldier came running up. Wei Yan drove hard and looked to see it was Sima Yi himself. He shouted, “Sima Yi, do not run!” and met him with a sword in hand. Sima Yi raised his spear and joined in combat.

Not three rounds were struck when Wei Yan pulled back his horse and fled. Sima Yi followed closely. Wei Yan ran toward the seven-star flag.

Sima Yi, seeing Wei Yan alone with few troops and no horse force, felt at ease and pursued. He told Sima Shi to move left, Sima Zhao to move right, and he kept the center as he charged with the others. Wei Yan withdrew all 500 soldiers into the valley.

When Yi reached the valley mouth, he first sent men in to scout. They returned that there was no ambush; the hills held only straw huts. “This must be a grain stockpile,” he said, and drove horses and men in deep. He suddenly saw all the hill huts full of dry brush; in front of him Wei Yan had vanished.

His heart suspicious, he asked his two sons, “If our troops are cut off at the mouth, what then?” Before he could finish speaking, a shattering shout rose from all sides. At once men on the hills threw down torches and the valley mouth blazed with fire. With no path to flee, the Wei soldiers could not run. Fire arrows fell from the heights; the earth mines sprang together; the dry brush in every hut caught at once. The wind ripped and rattled, and flame climbed to the sky.

Sima Yi floundered in panic, dismounted, and gathered his two sons, crying, “My son and I—all three of us die here!” As he wept, a gale suddenly rose, black cloud spread through the sky, and thunder cracked. Immediately a wall of rain poured down. The whole valley fire was extinguished; the mines did not detonate, and the fire weapons were useless.

Sima Yi rejoiced and said, “Not until now have we a chance to break out—why wait?” He spurred the troops and drove hard through battle. Zhang Hu and Lechen each came with reinforcements. Ma Dai’s force was small and did not dare pursue. Sima Yi, his two sons, Zhang Hu, and Lechen joined together and returned to the Weinan great camp.

Yet the palisade there had already been taken by Shu soldiers. Guo Huai and Sun Li were already fighting Shu forces from the floating bridge. Sima Yi and his men came up, and the Shu withdrew. He burned the bridge and held the north bank.

Meanwhile, while Wei soldiers fought at Qishan to take the Shu camp, they learned of Sima Yi’s crushing defeat and the loss of Weinan’s camp. Their army was in panic and withdrew in haste. As they pulled back, Shu soldiers collided upon them from all sides. The Wei troops suffered a crushing defeat: eight or nine out of every ten were wounded or killed, and only a remnant survived by fleeing across the north bank of the Wei.

On the mountain, Kongming saw Wei Yan’s lure draw Sima Yi into the valley, and for one instant there was a great flare of flame. His heart rejoiced and he thought Sima Yi must surely be dead. Unexpectedly the sky gave a sudden rain and the fire would not hold, and a scouting report said Sima Yi and his sons had escaped. Kongming sighed, “To plan is for men; to make it happen is Heaven. One cannot force it.”

Later, people later composed this verse:

At the mouth of the valley the wind raged, wild flames drifted; who could have expected a sudden rain to fall from the blue heavens? If Wuhou’s wondrous stratagem could truly take, how could the mountains and rivers belong to the Jin court?

Sima Yi, now in the Weibei camp, issued this order: “The Weinan stockade has been lost. If any general dares to speak of fighting again, he will be beheaded.” The generals obeyed and held their positions without going out.

Guo Huai came in report: “Recently Kongming has been patrolling; he will select ground to encamp.”

Yi said, “If Kongming comes out at Wugong and moves east along the mountain, we are in danger. If he advances from Weinan and goes west, then to Wuzhang Plain, we may be safe.” He sent men to reconnoiter. They returned that enemy forces had indeed camped at Wuzhang Plain. Yi put his hand on his brow and said, “By the great fortune of the Wei emperor!” and then ordered all the generals to hold firm and not sortie. Their force would turn by itself in time.

Kongming brought one force and camped at Wuzhang Plain. Again and again he pressed for skirmishes, but Wei soldiers would not come out. He then took women’s scarves and plain mourning robes, packed them in a large chest, and wrote a letter. He sent a messenger to Wei camp. The generals could not conceal it and brought the envoy to Sima Yi.

Sima Yi stood before all and opened the chest. Within was the women’s scarf and white gown and a letter.

He opened it and read:

Zhongda has already become a great general, commanding the people of the Central Plains. You do not think to strip your armor and grip a sharp sword to decide life or death, yet you gladly hide in a dirt nest and avoid blade and arrow—how is that different from a woman? I send these women’s scarves and plain robes to you. If you will not go out to fight, bow and receive them again. If your sense of shame has not faded and you still have a man’s heart, return them at once, and come to meet the enemy at the appointed time.

After reading, Sima Yi grew very angry, then laughed thinly: “Does Kongming take me for a woman?” He took him in and ordered the envoy treated with honor.

Yi asked, “How fares the Chancellor in sleep and in daily work?”

The messenger replied, “The Chancellor rises before dawn and stays awake through the night; even punishments of twenty or more, he personally inspects each. His daily rations are no more than several sheng.”

Yi said to all the generals, “Kongming eats little and keeps matters close. How could such endurance last?”

The envoy withdrew and returned to Wuzhang, where he saw Kongming and gave a full report: “Sima Yi accepted the women’s scarf and read the letter. He showed no anger, and asked only of the Chancellor’s daily habits. He did not raise military matters at all. He answered, ‘Few food, busy with affairs—how can that continue forever?’”

Kongming sighed, “He knows me well.”

The registrar Yang Yong then said, “I often see the Chancellor checking accounts himself, and dare say this: in governance there is due order. One should not intrude where one should not, from top to bottom.

In household management, it is required that the farmer be set at the plow and the maid at the stove; the private industry must be complete, and every need supplied, while the householder remains composed and eats and drinks in ease. If the master must personally manage everything, his form fatigues, his spirit is exhausted, and no matter becomes complete. Is he therefore less wise than slave or maid? That would miss the way of holding a house.

That is why the ancients said: to sit and discuss principles was called Three Dukes; to act and do was called scholar-official.

In former days Bingji was troubled by a cow with a blocked breath and yet did not ask about a man dead in the street; Chen Ping was not aware of grain and coin accounts and said, ‘The Master has them.’ Now the Chancellor personally tends every minute matter, and sweats day after day. Is this not taxing?”

“She says his words are truly pointed.”

Kongming began to weep: “It is not that I am ignorant, but I bear the late emperor’s trust as guardian, and only fear others will not serve with heart as I do.” All men wept.

From that time Kongming felt his mind and spirit unsettled; thus, none dared push the army forward.

The Wei generals all knew that Kongming had insulted Sima Yi by sending the women’s scarf and that he had not gone out to fight. Entering camp, they all angrily reported: “We are all great generals of the state. How can we endure this humiliation from Shu men? We beg to advance and settle this matter in battle.”

Yi said, “I am not unwilling to fight, nor do I welcome this shame. But the Son of Heaven has commanded us to hold and not move. If I leave lightly now, I violate his order.”

The generals were full of anger and still dissatisfied.

Yi said, “Since you all wish to ride out, allow me to petition for the ruler’s approval. Then we can join and meet the enemy together. Why not?”

The generals assented. Yi then wrote a memorial and sent an envoy straight to Cao Rui’s command at Hefei.

He read:

I am weak in talent and bear a heavy office, yet by heaven’s favor I have received the clear command. I have held firm and not fought, waiting for Shu’s self-humbling; but now Zhuge Liang has left me women’s scarf and treats me as a woman. My humiliation is complete. I humbly beg Your Majesty to understand my intent: at dawn or dusk I will fight to the point of death, repay the state’s grace, and wash away the shame of the three armies. I cannot hold back this grief and fervor.

Cao Rui read and said to his officials, “Sima Yi has held firm and avoided battle. Why does he now submit this petition asking to fight?”

The Grand Commandant Xun Pi said, “Sima Yi has no desire to fight now. It must be that Kongming’s insult and the generals’ rage moved him, and this petition is to seek another imperial command to hold back the men.”

Cao Rui took this as true and ordered Xun Pi with imperial token to transmit directly to Weibei camp: no one was to sortie.

When Sima Yi received the edict, Xun Pi announced: “If anyone dares to speak of going out to battle again, it will be judged as disobedience of command.” They complied.

Sima Yi said softly to Xun Pi, “You truly know my heart.” He then spread the word through camp: the Son of Heaven has sent Xun Pi with token to forbid Sima Yi from fighting.

Shu heard this and reported it to Kongming. Kongming laughed: “This is how Sima Yi keeps his three armies calm.”

Jiang Wei asked, “How do you know this, Chancellor?”

Kongming said, “He had no wish to fight in earnest; he asked to fight to show courage before the men. Have you not heard, ‘A commander in the field may ignore an order’? Can one in ten thousand li ask for battle for mere pride?

This is Sima Yi using the generals’ anger and borrowing the emperor’s intention to control them. Now he spreads that saying to weaken our troops as well.”

While they still spoke, they learned Fei Yi had arrived.

Fei Yi was invited in, and said: “Cao Rui heard that Sun Quan advanced in three columns and personally brought the main army to Hefei. He ordered Man Chong, Tian Yu, and Liu Shao to take three columns to meet them. Man Chong devised a plan and burned all Wu grain and war gear. The Wu men became sick in great number. Lu Xun sent a memorial to Wu king asking for coordinated attack on both sides, but the messenger carrying it was captured by Wei troops before he arrived. Thus the secret leaked, and Wu troops returned without profit.”

When Kongming heard this, he sighed heavily and fainted to the ground. The generals rushed to help him; only after a long time did he revive.

He sighed, “My mind is clouded; an old illness has returned. I may not live!”

That night Kongming, ill, left the tent and looked up at the stars in alarm. Back in the tent he told Jiang Wei: “My life is near its end.”

Wei Wei said, “Why not use methods to ward off death?”

Kongming said, “I have known these arts long ago, but I do not know Heaven’s will. Take forty-nine armored men, each with a black banner, each in black robes, and circle outside the tent. I will perform rites to appease the Northern Dipper from within. If the main lamp does not go out within seven days, my life may gain another decade. If the lamp goes out, I surely die. Do not let common men pass in. Only two small boys should carry everything needed.”

Jiang Wei obeyed.

It was mid-autumn of the eighth month. That night, the Milky Way shone, and the dew settled low. Standards did not move, and the drums were still. Outside the tent Jiang Wei kept forty-nine men posted.

Kongming, in his tent, set out incense and flowers for worship. On the ground he laid out seven great lamps, with forty-nine small lamps around, and one life-lamp inside. He bowed and offered blessing:

I, born in an age of disorder, gladly grew old among wood and spring waters. Under the Three Visits of the august Emperor Zhaolie, and under the burden of a lone guardian, I dare not fail in the devotion of a humble servant. I swore to punish those who betray the state. Yet now my command star is said to fall and my yang longevity seems near its end. I write one strip of silk to report to the upper vault of Heaven. Please look with compassion and extend this servant’s reckoning, so I may still repay the emperor’s grace and rescue the people, recovering what was ours and lengthening the Han sacrifice for ever. I do not pray arrogantly; I speak from deep feeling.

Kongming ended the rite and waited inside through the night for dawn.

The next day, though sick, he handled government affairs, spitting blood without ceasing. By day he discussed military affairs, and by night he stepped the stars on the Earthly Canopy.

Now Sima Yi held firm in camp. One night, gazing at the sky, he rejoiced and said to Xiahou Ba: “I have seen the general star out of its station. Kongming must be ill and near death. Send 1,000 men to Wuzhang to scout. If Shu troops are turbulent and do not come out to fight, he must surely be sick. Then we can strike.”

Xiahou Ba moved with his force.

After six nights of Kongming’s rites, he saw the main lamp still bright and rejoiced greatly. Jiang Wei entered and saw Kongming with loose hair and sword in hand, performing star-stepping rites and suppressing the guiding star.

Heard then a cry outside the camp. Before he could ask someone to inspect, Wei Yan burst in at full speed and at that moment put out the main lamp.

Kongming set the sword down and sighed, “Life and death are by decree; they cannot be averted by warding.” Wei Yan knelt in fear and begged forgiveness. Jiang Wei was enraged and drew his sword to kill Wei Yan.

All things are not ruled by human command; One heart cannot keep pace with destiny.

Unknown how Wei Yan’s life will end. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Sima Is Trapped in Shangfang Valley; Zhuge Liang Wards Off the Stars on Wuzhang Plain

chapters.html:
A Great Star falls; the Han Chancellor returns to Heaven.
The Wooden Effigy is seen; the Wei Commander-in-Chief loses his nerve.

Jiang Wei saw Wei Yan stamp out the lamps and was filled with anger. He drew his sword, intent on killing him. Zhuge Liang stopped him and said, “This is my life that is about to be cut off. It is not Wenchang’s fault.” Wei Yan then lowered his sword.

Zhuge Liang spat blood several times, collapsed onto the bed, and told Wei Yan, “This is Sima Yi’s judgment that I am sick. He has sent men to test what remains of me. You should go out quickly and meet the enemy.”

Wei Yan obeyed, left for the gate, mounted his horse, and led his men out of the stockade. When Xiahou Ba saw Wei Yan, he hurriedly withdrew his army. Wei Yan pursued for over twenty li and only then returned. Zhuge Liang ordered Wei Yan to go back to his own camp and hold it.

Jiang Wei entered and went straight to Zhuge Liang’s bed to ask after his condition. Zhuge Liang said, “I meant to offer my loyalty and strength to recover the Central Plain and restore Han. But Heaven has arranged it otherwise; I will die soon.

Over my life I have written twenty-four treatises, totaling one hundred and four thousand one hundred and twelve characters, containing the Eight Duties, Seven Prohibitions, Six Fears, and Five Dreads.

I have reviewed all our generals and found no one fit to receive them except you. Take this and pass it on. Do not treat it lightly.”

Wei Yan knelt and wept as he accepted.

Zhuge Liang said again, “I have the method of the repeating crossbow, but I have never used it. In this method the arrow is eight cun long and one bow can shoot ten shafts. I have drawn all the diagrams. You should reproduce and employ it as set down.”

Wei Yan also bowed and accepted.

“Shu’s mountain roads need not be overly worried over,” Zhuge Liang said. “Only in Yinping the land must be examined very closely. Though it is steep and difficult, in time it will surely be lost.” He then called Ma Dai into the tent, spoke low by the ear, and gave him a secret plan. “After my death, carry out this plan.” Ma Dai took it and left.

After a while Yang Yi arrived. Zhuge Liang called him to the bed and gave him a silk packet, then whispered privately: “When I die, Wei Yan will rebel. When he rebels, open this only while you stand in line before him. There will then be men to kill him.”

All arrangements done, Zhuge Liang soon fainted. By evening he woke and rode by night to send a memorial to the sovereign. When the ruler heard it, he was greatly startled and ordered Shangshu Li Fu to ride through the night and go to camp to ask after him and the after-affairs. Li Fu obeyed and hurried to Wuzhang Plains, entered and conveyed the sovereign’s command. After offering greetings, Zhuge Liang burst into tears: “I am unfortunate to die midway, leaving the great matters of state unattended and offending the realm.

After I die, you all must expend your loyalty in support of the lord. The old state order must not be changed. The men I used cannot be lightly dismissed. I have given all military teaching to Jiang Wei; only he can carry on my will and exert himself for the state.

My life hangs by a thread and a final memorial must be presented at once to the Son of Heaven.”

Li Fu took in these words and left in haste.

By effort, Zhuge Liang held on, ordered attendants to place him in a small cart, and ride through each camp. As he felt the autumn wind on his face, cold ran through his bones. He sighed, “I can no longer ride the battle line to strike the invaders! Vast and distant is Heaven—where is its edge?”

He sighed long, returned to the tent, and his illness sank deeper. He then called Yang Yi and handed down further instructions: “Ma Dai, Wang Ping, Liao Hua, Zhang Yi, and Zhang Ni are men of loyalty and virtue, long tested in battle and heavy with service; they can be relied on. After I die, continue all matters according to former practice. Withdraw step by step, not in haste.

You know counsel deeply; no need for much telling. Jiang Boyue is complete in wisdom and courage; he can hold the rear.”

Yang Yi knelt and accepted.

Zhuge Liang then asked for his writing set, and on the bed wrote the posthumous memorial to be delivered to the sovereign:

I have come to hear that life and death are always present and one cannot evade fixed decrees. As death comes near, may I exhaust my foolish loyalty. I, your servant Liang, by nature are stupid and dull; in a time of hardship I carried seal and tally, held sway over state offices, raised armies for northern campaign, and did not win success. I did not expect illness in my innermost veins, life close to end, and not enough time to complete Your Majesty’s affairs; this brings boundless remorse.

My prayer to Your Majesty: calm your heart and reduce desire; govern yourself and care for the people.

Bring filial devotion to the former emperor; spread humaneness and grace beneath Heaven.

Promote hidden worth and advance good and honorable men.

Exclude evil and corrupt men so that customs become sound.

In my home in Chengdu I have eight hundred mulberry trees and fifteen qing of poor fields; my children and descendants’ food and clothing can be supplied from these.

As for my years serving away from home, there are no other allowances. Everything for my food and clothing has depended on office; no private livelihood has been arranged for me.

On the day I die, let there be no extra silk at home and no illicit gain outside, so I do not burden Your Majesty.

When finished, Zhuge Liang told Yang Yi again: “After I die, do not announce mourning. Make one large k'an and seat my body inside it. Put seven grains of rice in my mouth, and a bright lamp at my feet. Keep the army quiet as usual; raise no mourning.

Then the Commander Star will not fall. My lingering spirit will rise and remain here. Sima Yi, seeing the Commander Star not fallen, will surely be startled in doubt.

Let the rear camp go first, and then each camp withdraw slowly in turn.

If Sima Yi comes in pursuit, you may lay out ranks, turn banners, and reverse the drums. When he comes, put out the wooden image I had carved before, place it on a cart, and bring it to the front of the army. Place the officers and soldiers in rank to left and right. Sima Yi seeing it will surely panic and flee.”

Yang Yi received all instructions.

That night Zhuge Liang was helped outside and looked toward the Big Dipper. From afar he pointed to one star: “That is my Commander Star.” The men saw it dim, ashen, swaying as if falling. Zhuge Liang pointed with his sword and chanted spells. After finishing, he hurried back into the tent and lost awareness.

Just when the officers were in great confusion, Li Fu arrived again. Seeing Zhuge Liang in collapse, unable to speak, he wept loudly, “I have betrayed the state in a great matter!”

After a little while, Zhuge Liang woke and opened his eyes, looking at Li Fu standing at the bed. “Now I know the reason you came again.”

Li Fu answered, “Fu comes with the Son of Heaven’s command to ask who can take the major duties after the Chancellor is gone. Because of my haste, I failed in proper consultation, so I came again.”

Zhuge Liang said, “After I die, who can take great affairs: Jiang Gongyan is fitting.”

Li Fu asked, “After Gongyan, who should follow?”

Zhuge Liang replied, “Fei Yi can follow.”

Li Fu asked, “After Wenye, who should then follow?”

Zhuge Liang said nothing.

The officers drew nearer and already he had died.

It was the twenty-third day of the eighth month in autumn, in the twelfth year of Jianxing. He was fifty-four.

Du Gongbu later wrote:

The Great Star last night fell before the forward camp, and today the report of the Master’s death tipped the world. In the Tiger Camp no command is heard, yet at Lintai his meritorious fame still stands out. Three thousand guests alone remain under the gate, and I bear within my breast the burden of one hundred thousand soldiers. In the clear noon of green shade, there is no longer the song of elegant voices.

Bai Juyi also wrote:

The Master’s trace withdrew in silence to mountains and groves, and three visits seeking the Son of Heaven were never returned. Fish reaches Nanyang before it finds water; when the dragon soars in Heaven’s Han, it becomes rain.

Entrusting and finishing the rites to guard the heir, he poured out loyalty to the state to the end. The departure memorials from the campaigns are all still present, and anyone reading them sees tears on the sleeve.

First there was Liao Li, commander in Shu for water transport, who claimed he should be Zhuge Liang’s deputy. He had thought his post free and idle and was full of resentment and blame. Therefore Zhuge Liang demoted him to commoner and moved him to Mount Wenshan.

When he heard of Zhuge Liang’s death, he cried, “I end up as a wronged left-over sleeve!” Li Yan heard him, and he too wept and died.

Indeed, Li Yan had wished to live to see Zhuge recall him and return him for his former fault; now that Zhuge was gone, no one in this world could use him.

Yuan Weizhi then praised:

Restoring disorder and guarding the perilous lord, he received the entrusted charge with all humility. His brilliance surpassed that of Guan Le, and his subtle stratagem surpassed Sun Wu. His Departure Memorial was majestic, his Eight-formation diagram truly grand. With such complete virtue as his, past and future ages have cause to exclaim in awe.

That night heaven and earth were heavy with grief, and the moon was without light. Zhuge Liang suddenly returned to Heaven.

Jiang Wei and Yang Yi, obeying his orders, did not raise lamentation; they prepared the corpse as instructed and set him in the k'an. They posted three hundred trusted men to guard it and transmitted his sealed orders so Wei Yan held the rear while each camp withdrew in turn.

Now, Sima Yi at night watched the sky and saw a great red star, with an aura of horns, moving from the northeast to the southwest and falling within the Shu camp. It seemed to strike three times and rise again twice, with a faint sound.

Sima Yi, pleased and astonished, said, “Zhuge Liang is dead!” and at once sent out the main forces in pursuit.

As he was about to step beyond the stockade gate, doubt returned: “Zhuge Liang is skilled in six Ding, six Jia arts. Since I have not gone to battle long, he has used such arts to fake death and entice me. If I pursue now, I will surely walk into his plan.”

So he reined in and returned to camp. He ordered Xiahou Ba alone to lead a few dozen riders to the remote outposts around Wuzhang and check the news.

Wei Yan in his camp dreamed that two horns had suddenly grown on his head. He woke deeply disturbed.

The next day the marches officer Zhao Zhi came to him. Wei Yan asked him in, saying, “For long I have known you to understand the principles of the Yi. In the night I dreamt my head had two horns. I do not know whether this is good or evil. Pray decide it for me.”

Zhao Zhi thought for a while and answered, “This is an auspicious sign: a qilin has horns on its head, and a blue dragon has horns on its head; it is an image of changing and taking flight.”

Wei Yan rejoiced, “As you said, I will repay you heavily.” Zhao Zhi left. A few li later he met Shangshu Fei Yi.

Fei Yi asked, “Where from?”

“I just came from Wei Wenchang’s camp,” Zhao Zhi said. “Wenchang dreamt horns on his head and asked me to judge good and evil. This is not really good fortune, but fearing to shock him, I explained with qilin and dragon symbols.”

Fei Yi asked, “How do you know it is not good?”

Zhao Zhi said, “The shape of the character for horns is the character use (yong) under a knife. A knife below yong is dire misfortune.”

Fei Yi said, “Do not speak of this.” Zhao Zhi departed.

Fei Yi came to Wei Yan’s camp, sent everyone away, and said, “By the third watch the Chancellor has already left. Before he died, he repeated and repeated that he entrusted with you that Yang Yi should meet Sima Yi at the rear and withdraw slowly; do not raise mourning. This command tally is with me, so you may take command now.”

Wei Yan said, “Though the Chancellor has died, I still stand. Yang Yi is only a chief clerk—how can he manage the Chancellor’s great affairs? He should only carry the bier into Shu and bury it. I will lead great troops against Sima Yi and win. Could one, for one man, cast aside the state’s great business?”

Fei Yi said, “The Chancellor ordered that we should withdraw for now. Do not violate it.”

Wei Yan shouted in anger, “If the Chancellor had followed my plan he would have already taken Chang’an! I now hold the rank of Front General, General Who Conquers the West, Marquis of Nanzheng; how can I accept a chief clerk covering the rear?”

Fei Yi replied, “Though your words are true, you should not move rashly and make the enemy laugh. Let me go to Yang Yi and argue in terms of profit and danger; I will have him yield command to you. Is that not best?”

Wei Yan agreed.

Fei Yi left and quickly came to the main camp to report this to Yang Yi. Yang Yi said, “The Chancellor privately entrusted me before dying: ‘Wei Yan will hold strange intentions.’ I carried the tally to test his mind; now it matches the Chancellor’s warning. I have already set Jiang Boyue to cover the rear.”

So Yang Yi led out the bier first and ordered Jiang Wei to cover the rear, then withdrew by degrees according to Zhuge Liang’s instruction.

Wei Yan, in his own camp, did not see Fei Yi return. In suspicion he ordered Ma Dai with a dozen riders to scout.

They returned saying, “The rear army is under Jiang Wei; most of the forward army has already gone into the valley.”

Wei Yan cried, “How can this lowly scholar dare deceive me! I will kill him!” Then he asked Ma Dai, “Will you assist?”

Ma Dai said, “I have long resented Yang Yi. I now wish to help you attack him.” Wei Yan rejoiced, broke camp, and led his main force south.

Xiahou Ba then led troops to Wuzhang and found no one. He hurried back to Sima Yi, saying, “Shu troops have completely withdrawn.”

Sima Yi stamped and said, “Zhuge Liang is truly dead! Pursue quickly!”

Xiahou Ba said, “The Commander should not pursue quickly. Send forward detachments first.”

Sima Yi replied, “In this turn I myself must go.” He set out with two sons and both rushed in close pursuit toward Wuzhang.

When he came shouting with flags and drums, he found himself at the gate of the camp, only to find it empty.

He told his two sons, “Drive the troops quickly and overtake. I will lead the vanguard.”

Sima Shi and Sima Zhao urged the forces from behind. Sima Yi himself led at the front, pursued down to the mountain foot, and when he saw Shu troops not far off, he redoubled the chase.

Then came a great blast from behind the mountain, and cries shattered the air. They saw the Shu ranks turning banners and drums backward. In the shadows of trees floated the main flag of the center, with one line: “Han Chancellor, Lord of Wuxiang, Zhuge Liang.”

Sima Yi was struck dumb with shock. As his eyes fixed, he saw in the middle dozens of senior commanders bringing a four-wheeled cart. On it sat Zhuge Liang upright, with silk kerchief, feather fan, and crane-feather robe with a black sash.

Sima Yi cried, “Zhuge Liang is alive! I entered this deep place too lightly and have stepped into his trick!” He pulled the reins and ran.

Behind him Jiang Wei shouted, “Bandit commander, do not run! You are in my Chancellor’s trap!”

Wei troops were terrified, panic-stricken. They threw off armor and helmets, dropped spears and halberds, and fled each by each. Countless were killed.

Sima Yi ran for fifty li and more. Two Wei commanders caught him up, holding his horse. “Commander, do not fear,” they said.

He touched his own head and asked, “Did I still keep my head?”

The two answered, “Fear nothing, commander; the Shu troops are already far away.”

After several breaths and his features settled, he recognized them as Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Hui. He then slowly pulled the reins and, with the two, took a small path back to the main camp, while ordering everyone to send units out to scout in many directions.

After two days, villagers ran in to report: “When the Shu troops withdrew into the valley, wails shook the earth. A white banner rose in their camp. Zhuge Liang truly has died. Only Jiang Wei remains with one thousand troops covering the rear.

The Zhuge on the cart before was a wooden figure.”

Sima Yi sighed, “I can foresee his life, but not his death.” Thus among people of Shu it was said: “Only after Zhuge dies can one make it through life under Zhongda.”

Another poem later said:

The long star at midnight fell by the pivot of heaven, it rushed by so quickly one still wonders if Liang had really died. Even beyond the frontier, men still laugh with coldness to this day, asking with their heads whether there is agreement or not.

When Sima Yi knew for sure of the report of Zhuge’s death, he again ordered pursuit. He reached Chihan Slope and found the Shu troops far away; he then turned back. Looking at the assembled generals he said, “Now that Zhuge Liang is dead, we can all sleep secure.”

They executed a return march.

On the road he saw everywhere Zhuge Liang had camped and how each station had been established in proper order. Sima Yi sighed, “This was a talent beyond the world.” He then returned to Chang’an, assigned and relocated generals to the frontier passes, and eventually returned to Luoyang to report at court.

Yang Yi and Jiang Wei formed their lines, withdrew slowly through the gate to the stockade road, then changed into mourning and raised banners with lamentation.

Shu soldiers bumped and collided as they wept; some died in their crying.

When the forward command of Shu soldiers had just returned to the stockade-road mouth, they suddenly saw flames rising skyward, cries shaking the ground, and a band of troops blocking the way.

The senior officers were alarmed and hastened to report to Yang Yi.

So:

Already it is seen that the officers of the Wei camp have gone; who can know what force from Shu comes near? Unknown from where this horse and army arrive; How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: A Great Star Falls; the Han Chancellor Returns to Heaven, and a Wooden Effigy Makes the Wei Commander-in-Chief Lose His Nerve

chapters.html:
Yang Yi learned that soldiers were blocking the way ahead, so he hurried to send scouts. They reported that Wei Yan had burned the plank road and moved troops to cut off the route. Yang Yi was alarmed.

“While the Chancellor was alive, I always calculated this man would eventually rebel. Who had expected it to happen today? My road home has now been severed. What are we to do?” Fei Yi said, “This man must have first drafted a memorial to the Son of Heaven, falsely accusing us of rebellion; therefore he burned the plank road and blocked the way back. We should also submit a memorial to the Son of Heaven, setting out Wei Yan’s treacherous intent, and only then make plans.” Jiang Wei added, “There is a small path here called Chashan. Although it is rough and dangerous, we can pass behind the burnt road by it. Write a memorial and report to the Son of Heaven at once, and set men and horses moving by that Chashan path.”

Back in Chengdu, the Emperor was restless and sleepless. He could neither eat nor lie still in peace. One night he dreamed that Jinping Mountain in Chengdu had collapsed. He awoke in terror, sat up and kept vigil till dawn, gathered civil and military officials, and brought the dream before the morning court. Qiao Zhou said, “Your servant watched the stars last night and saw a red star with horned radiance fall from the northeast to the southwest. It indicates a great calamity concerning the Chancellor. Your Majesty’s dream of the mountain collapsing is exactly in accord with this omen.”

The Emperor became even more fearful. Soon word came that Li Fu had arrived, and the Emperor quickly summoned him. Li Fu knelt and wept as he spoke, saying the Chancellor had died and reciting in detail his last words. The Emperor cried, “Heaven has abandoned me!” and collapsed on the dragon couch.

Attendants carried him to the inner palace. Empress Wu also heard and cried out without ceasing. All officials mourned; all the people wept. For several days the Emperor was so grief-stricken he could not hold court.

A report then came that Wei Yan had submitted a memorial accusing Yang Yi of rebellion. The ministers were shocked. They entered the palace and reported to the Emperor, with Empress Wu also present. The Emperor, greatly startled, ordered a close minister to break open and read it.

Its contents said:

I, Wei Yan, General Who Conquers the West and Marquis of Nanzheng, in utmost fear and trembling, kneel and report: Yang Yi has assumed command authority, raised his troops, and rebelled; he seized the late Chancellor’s spirit-carriage and intends to usher enemies into our borders. I first burned through the plank road and placed troops to defend. I respectfully submit this report.

When the reading was finished, the Emperor said, “Wei Yan is a brave general and well suited to meet Yang Yi’s men in open battle. Why then did he burn the plank road?” Empress Wu said, “It was said the late emperor once remarked that Kongming understood that Wei Yan’s heart held rebellion and often wished to behead him, yet spared him for his bravery. What was reported just now cannot be accepted so quickly. Yang Yi is a learned man, and the Chancellor entrusted him with the office of Chief Clerk. He is not one who could be dismissed so easily. If we heed this one report alone, Yang Yi and his men will certainly throw in to Wei. In this matter we must think far and long and not act in haste.”

While the ministers were still discussing, another urgent memorial from Chief Clerk Yang Yi arrived. A close official tore it open and read:

I, Yang Yi, General Who Pacifies the Armies and Chief Clerk, with utmost fear and reverence, kneeling, respectfully submit: when the Chancellor lay dying he entrusted major matters to me and ordered me to follow old procedure without altering anything; Wei Yan was to hold the rear, with Jiang Wei next in command. Now Wei Yan has ignored the Chancellor’s final words, taken his own troops, first entered Hanzhong, set fire and burned the plank road, seized the late Chancellor’s funeral cart, and plotted treachery. The turmoil rose suddenly; I submit this urgent memorial.

After hearing this, the Empress Dowager asked, “What do your eyes see?” Jiang Wan said, “By my poor judgment, Yang Yi is indeed quick-tempered and not easy to tolerate, yet he has for a long time assisted the Chancellor in grain accounts, military matters, and strategy. If the Chancellor now dead entrusted him with major affairs, he could not have been a traitor. Wei Yan, relying on former merit, has long felt insulted by everyone but Yang Yi. Since Yang Yi disdains him, his heart holds resentment; now he has burned the road, cut off the way home, and spread slander to trap him. I dare not fully guarantee we can guard against his scheme.” Dong Yun also spoke: “Wei Yan trusts his own exploits too much and often voiced grievance. He has not rebelled before because he feared the Chancellor. Now the Chancellor has just died; seizing the moment to disturb the state is inevitable. If Yang Yi were truly inept and dull-witted, the Chancellor would not have placed him there in any case.”

The Emperor asked, “If Wei Yan truly rebels, what is the strategy to meet him?” Jiang Wan said, “The Chancellor has long doubted him and surely had left instructions to Yang Yi. If Yang Yi had not trusted those instructions, could Wei Yan have withdrawn into the valley mouth? He will take the bait.”

Not long after, Wei Yan submitted yet another memorial, charging that Yang Yi had rebelled. In the midst of reading it, Yang Yi sent another memorial, claiming Wei Yan had turned traitor. The two presented counterarguments in succession. Then Fei Yi arrived. The Emperor called him in, and Fei Yi recounted fully how Wei Yan had been disloyal.

The Emperor said, “Then let Dong Yun go with command and, with good words, attempt to win him over.” Dong Yun obeyed the edict and left.

Wei Yan burned the road, stationed men at South Valley, and blocked the pass; he believed the move had succeeded. He did not expect Yang Yi and Jiang Wei to slip past the road at night and come up behind South Valley.

Fearing for Hanzhong, Yang Yi ordered the vanguard commander, He Ping, to advance with three thousand men first. Then Yang Yi and Jiang Wei led their troops and the casket toward Hanzhong.

He Ping’s men came straight to the rear of South Valley, beating drums and crying out. A sentry horse reported to Wei Yan that Yang Yi had sent He Ping via Chashan’s small path to meet in battle from behind. Enraged, Wei Yan quickly buckled on his harness, mounted, drew his saber, and came out to intercept.

The two formations closed in a circle. He Ping rode forward and shouted, “Rebel Wei Yan, where are you?”

Wei Yan shouted back, “You helped Yang Yi rebel and yet dare to curse me?”

He Ping said, “The Chancellor is newly dead and his bones still warm. How dare you rebel?” Then he raised his whip and pointed to the soldiers, “All of you are men of Xichuan; in Sichuan dwell your parents, wives, and children, brothers, and old friends. When the Chancellor ruled, he never treated you harshly. Now do not aid the rebel. Each should return to your hometown and await reward.”

The troops heard this and shouted together; most of them broke apart.

Wei Yan grew furious, whipped his horse and charged directly toward He Ping. He Ping set his spear to meet him. The battle lasted only a few exchanges. He feigned a retreat, then turned to run. Wei Yan chased him hard. A hail of bows and crossbow bolts flew from the other soldiers. Wei Yan turned his horse back. As the army broke up in confusion, Wei Yan was wild with rage, surged forward, and killed several men, but he could not stop them all. Only the three hundred men under Ma Dai remained unmoved.

Wei Yan said to Ma Dai, “Master, if you truly aid me in your heart, I will repay you after the matter is done.” Then he and Ma Dai pursued He Ping.

He Ping led his men to a quick withdrawal. Wei Yan gathered the shattered troops and spoke with Ma Dai:

“If we turn to Wei, what then?”

Ma Dai replied, “My lord’s words are not wise at all. Why should a great man kneel to another when he can shape his own fortune of domination? In my judgment your wisdom and courage are whole enough. Who in the two Sichuan regions dares resist you? I swear that together we first take Hanzhong, then strike into the Two Sichuan regions.”

Wei Yan rejoiced, and with Ma Dai pressed his men straight toward Nanzheng. Jiang Wei was on the city walls there and saw Wei Yan and Ma Dai displaying their martial prowess as they surged forward like a driving wind.

Jiang Wei at once ordered the hanging bridge hauled up. Wei Yan and Ma Dai shouted together, “Surrender at once!”

Jiang Wei sent word to Yang Yi, “Wei Yan is fierce, and Ma Dai’s assistance makes him formidable. Though our troops are few, what path can turn him back?”

Yang Yi said, “Before he died, the Chancellor left a secret pouch and warned: ‘When facing Wei Yan in battle, only then may it be opened.’ We must take it out and read now.”

When the pouch was taken out and unsealed, it said: “When you confront Wei Yan, you may open this only while on horseback.”

Jiang Wei rejoiced. “Since the Chancellor has made this warning, Chief Clerk may carry it out. I will lead the troops out and form our ranks. You may come then.”

Jiang Wei buckled on his armor and took up his spear. He led three thousand troops, opened the gate, and charged out in one surge. The drumming thundered; ranks formed.

He stood with spear leveled beneath the gate banner and shouted,

“Rebel Wei Yan! The Chancellor never wronged you. Why rebel now?”

Wei Yan sat his horse with a crossed blade and answered, “Boyue, this concerns you not. Send only Yang Yi!”

Behind the gate banner’s shadow, Yang Yi took out and opened the secret pouch. As he read, he said, “The Chancellor has long known that someday he would rebel. He left me ready. This is exactly the moment.” He rode a light horse forward, stood before the formation, pointed at Wei Yan, and laughed,

“When the Chancellor was alive, he told me you would in time betray him. He taught me to prepare, and now he has been vindicated. If you can cry out three times from horseback, ‘Who dares to kill me?’ then you can call yourself a true man of courage. I will even give you Hanzhong city.”

Wei Yan laughed. “Yang Yi, you little bastard, listen: when Kongming was alive, even then I still feared him one third. Now he is dead. Who in all under Heaven dares contest me? Do not speak of three times; shout thirty thousand times if you wish. What is difficult?”

He raised his saber, pulled the reins, and roared from his horse, “Who dares to kill me?” Before he finished the first shout, a voice from behind shouted, “I dare to kill you!” He struck up and down in one motion, and Wei Yan was cut down from the saddle.

The whole host was astonished. The one who had slain Wei Yan was Ma Dai.

In truth, when Kongming was near death he had entrusted Ma Dai with this secret plan and said to strike Wei Yan at the instant he called out. When Yang Yi had read the hidden plan, he already knew Ma Dai lay in ambush there. He acted accordingly, and thus Wei Yan was killed.

A verse later said:

Zhuge discerned Wei Yan before time and knew he would eventually rise against Xichuan. The secret-pouch strategy is hard to foresee, yet in the end success waited in front of the horse.

Not yet had Dong Yun reached Nanzheng when Ma Dai killed Wei Yan. He joined forces with Jiang Wei. Yang Yi reported all to the Emperor without delay through the night. The Emperor issued an order,

His crimes now are made clear, and yet in memory of his former service, grant him coffin and burial.

Yang Yi and the others carried Kongming’s casket back to Chengdu. The Emperor summoned all civil and military officials and officials of the court, all dressed in mourning, and led them out twenty li from the city to receive it. The Emperor cried aloud.

From the highest ministers to the scholar-officials, to officials, commoners of mountain and forest, men and women, young and old, all wept. The cries of grief shook the earth.

The Emperor ordered the casket brought into the city and set in the Chancellor’s residence. Zhuge Zhan, his son, observed mourning and entered widowlike bereavement.

When the Emperor returned to court, Yang Yi came forward in shackles and pleaded for punishment. The Emperor told an attendant to remove the bonds.

“If it were not that you could follow the Chancellor’s final instruction, when would this funeral cart have returned? And how then would Wei Yan have been suppressed? It is all your strength that preserved the great matters.”

He then named Yang Yi Central Army Adviser. Ma Dai, for his merit in defeating the rebel, was granted Wei Yan’s marquisate. Yang Yi presented the late Chancellor’s memorial letter. The Emperor read it and wept, then decreed burial plans.

Fei Yi argued, “On the Chancellor’s deathbed, he ordered him buried at Mount Dingjun, without city wall or bricks, and with no ritual offerings at all.” The Emperor approved. On an auspicious day in the tenth month of that year, he personally sent off the casket and buried him at Dingjun Mountain.

The Emperor issued an order for sacrifice and conferred the posthumous title Loyal and Martial Marquis. He ordered a temple built at Mianyang for the four seasonal offerings.

Another poem by Du Fu then appeared:

Where now may one find the Chancellor’s shrine? Beyond Jinguan’s walls stand the cypresses in dense ranks. Emerald grass by the steps wears spring’s own hue; beyond the leaves, orioles sing their lovely notes in vain. Three visits framed the realm’s great plan; through two reigns the old minister gave his heart to open the way and bring relief. Before victory came he had died in person, and to this day heroes weep with sleeves full of tears.

Another poem by Du Fu:

Zhuge’s great name reaches through the universe under heaven; the ancestral minister’s image is austere and clear. Through three-way division, he devised all strategy; one feather in the clouds of ten-thousand ages. Between peers, he confronted Liu and Lu; if command were fixed, even Xiao and Cao would be cast away. Han’s Mandate has turned by fate and cannot be restored; with resolve fixed, he spent his life in the exhaustion of war duty.

When the Emperor returned to Chengdu, an attendant reported, “A border dispatch has arrived. Sun Quan of Wu has led General Zuanzong, with ten thousand men, to camp at Baqiu frontier pass. Their intent is unclear.”

The Emperor asked in alarm, “The Chancellor has just died; now the former ally Eastern Wu violates trust and invades our borders. What can be done?” Jiang Wan said, “I dare to state that Wang Ping and Zhang Ni have already brought ten thousand to Yong’an to prevent sudden turns. Let Your Majesty send one more emissary to Wu to offer mourning and to sound out the truth.”

“Let one man with eloquence go,” the Emperor said. A man came forward immediately, “Your servant volunteers.” All looked at him. He was a man from Nanyang, surname Zong, given name Yu, courtesy name Deyan, serving as Army Adviser, Right Gentleman-Guard General. The Emperor was greatly pleased and ordered Zong Yu to report mourning in Eastern Wu and at the same time test its real intention.

Zong Yu took up the command and went directly to Jinling, where he paid court audience to Wu ruler Sun Quan. After formal greetings he saw everyone there clothed in white.

Sun Quan, with sharp expression, said, “Shu and Wu have become one household. Why is your lord increasing the guard at Baidi?”

Zong Yu replied, “In my view, reinforcing Baidi and increasing the guard at Bada is simply appropriate to the present situation and does not require exchange of questions.”

Sun Quan laughed. “You are no less than Deng Zhi.” He then spoke to Zong Yu,

“I hear that Chancellor Zhuge has returned to heaven and that every day your ruler weeps and has all officials in mourning. I fear that Wei will use your grief and invade, so I increased the force at Baqiu by ten thousand as aid and nothing else.”

Zong Yu knelt and bowed in thanks.

Sun Quan said, “I have pledged alliance. How then can I violate righteousness?” Zong Yu said, “The Son of Heaven, because the Chancellor has just died, has specially ordered me to report this death.”

Sun Quan therefore took up an arrow of gold-pointed shaft and split it in two, saying, “If I violate our old alliance, may my descendants be cut off.” He also ordered that gifts of incense and silk and ritual vessels be sent so that sacrifices might be offered in Shu.

After bowing and taking leave, Zong Yu returned with Wu envoys to Chengdu and reported all before the Emperor.

“The Wu ruler,” he said, “also wept after the Chancellor died; he ordered all his court to mourn. As for sending reinforcements to Baqiu, I judge he did so only fearing Wei might take advantage; he swears no other intention. He has given this oath with the broken arrow.”

The Emperor rejoiced and rewarded Zong Yu richly and treated the Wu envoys well.

He then followed the Chancellor’s last instruction and promoted Jiang Wan as Chancellor and General-in-Chief, and made him take charge of the Secretariat; promoted Fei Yi to Prefect of the Masters of Writing to share in managing the Chancellor’s duties; promoted Wu Yi to General of Chariots and Cavalry and gave him authority to command in Hanzhong. Jiang Wei was made General Who Assists Han and Marquis of Pingxiang, and appointed to oversee personnel and troops in all regions. He was ordered to go out with Wu Yi and station in Hanzhong to prevent a Wei advance; all other generals and officers were assigned according to former offices.

Yang Yi thought himself older in service than Jiang Wan yet below him in rank; he also trusted in his own great merit and yet received no major reward. He spoke bitter words to Fei Yi: “In the first days after the Chancellor’s death, if I had delivered the whole army to Wei, would I now be sitting in such loneliness?” Fei Yi gave this in a secret memorial.

The Emperor grew angry and commanded Yang Yi sent to jail and interrogated, intending to execute him. Jiang Wan spoke, “Yi has committed a fault, but these last days he achieved much while serving the late Chancellor. He should not be beheaded. Let him be demoted to commoner.”

The Emperor accepted this. Yang Yi was punished to exile in Jia County of Hanzhong as a commoner. He, ashamed and grieved, cut his own throat.

In Shu-Han’s thirteenth year of Jianxing, Wei’s Cao Rui’s third year of Qinglong, and Eastern Wu’s fourth year of Jiahe, none of the three kingdoms raised armies.

For the moment, talk turned to Wei: Cao Rui had made Sima Yi Grand Commandant, assigning him the command of troops and horse and to calm the frontiers. Sima Yi thanked him and returned to Luoyang.

At Xuchang, the Wei ruler undertook vast earthwork and timber work, building official halls. At Luoyang he erected Chaoyang Hall and Taiji Hall, and built Zongzhang Pavilion. Each rose ten zhang high. He also erected Chonghua Hall, Qingxiao Pavilion, Phoenix Tower, and Jiulong Pond, with Doctor Ma Jun supervising these works. They were all exquisitely carved, painted, roofed in blue tile and gilded brick, and blazed with light. He selected more than thirty thousand artisans and over three hundred thousand manual laborers, and they worked day and night without rest. The people were exhausted and complaints never ceased.

Cao Rui then issued an order to undertake more earthwork in Shanglin Garden, forcing all civil and military elites to carry soil and wood into it.

Minister Dong Xun submitted a memorial of urgent rebuke:

From Jian'an onward, in field battles deaths have emptied houses and ruined families; if any survive, they leave behind orphans, the elderly, and the weak. Though imperial halls are already narrow, to enlarge them should be done according to time and season, and not at the expense of the fields. Is there any benefit to useless making? Since Your Majesty honors your ministers, clothing them in crowns and embroidery and loading them in splendid carriages, making you unlike common men for this very reason, how can you now make all of them carry timber and soil, staining body and feet, draining the brilliance of the state to build useless things? Confucius said, “When the ruler treats ministers with ritual, ministers serve with loyalty.” Without loyalty and ritual how does a realm stand? I know this report may end in my death; yet I am but one hair on a cattle’s ear: life brings no worth, and death brings no loss. My brush flows with tears as I part from the world. I have eight sons. If I die, my burden falls on Your Majesty. I cannot suppress my fear and trembling.

When Cao Rui read it, he exploded, “Does Dong Xun not fear death?” His attendants urged execution.

The ruler said, “This man has always had loyalty and righteousness. Let him be demoted to commoner now. If there is another foolish word, he dies.” At this same time, Prince’s Retainer Zhang Mao, courtesy name Yancai, also memorialized, and Cao Rui ordered him executed as well.

The same day Cao Rui summoned Ma Jun and said, “I want high terraces and steep pavilions so I may converse with immortals and find the way to long life without old age.”

Jun replied, “In Han there were twenty-four emperors. Of them, Emperor Wu ruled the longest. His span was great, perhaps because he took in the qi of sunlight and moonlight. In the Chang’an palace, there is the Bailiang Terrace. Upon it stood a bronze man holding a dish called the Chenglu Disc, said to receive the vapor from the Northern Dipper at the third watch, called heavenly juice and also sweet dew. If one ground this with fine jade powder and consumed it, one could return to youth and reverse old age.”

Cao Rui was delighted. “Go now with men at night to Chang’an,” he said. “Take down the bronze man and move him to Shanglin Garden.”

Jun obeyed. He took ten thousand men to Chang’an and had wooden scaffolds built around the terrace. In no time, five thousand men with ropes and hooks were climbing and circling. The Bailiang Terrace was twenty zhang tall; the bronze column was ten chi across.

Jun first directed them to dismantle the bronze figure. In one effort they pulled it down. They saw that tears were forming in its bronze eyes and falling. All were startled. Suddenly a fierce wind struck the terrace; sand and stones flew in torrents, quickly as sudden rain. There was a single great crash as if heaven cracked and earth split. The platform tilted, columns fell, and more than one thousand were crushed.

Jun took the bronze man and the golden disc back to Luoyang and presented them to Cao Rui.

The ruler asked, “Where is the bronze pillar?”

Jun said, “The column weighs a million jin; it cannot be moved.”

The Emperor ordered the bronze column broken apart and transported to Luoyang, then melted and cast as two bronze figures named Wengzhong and set outside Sima Gate; he cast also two bronze animals, dragon and phoenix. The dragon stood four zhang high and the phoenix over three zhang, and they were placed before the hall.

Within Shanglin Garden, he also ordered strange flowers and odd trees planted and rare birds and beasts raised.

Grand Tutor Yang Fu then memorialized:

I have heard that Yao still kept a straw-and-mat house; Shun dwelt in simple halls, and all realms were at peace. Yü and Wen also lived plain, yet the empire was at rest and worked in harmony. In the past even in Yin and Zhou one could set halls with only three feet and nine mats. The virtuous and enlightened rulers of old never ruined their people by building grand residences; not even once did they spend beyond the people’s strength. Jie made jade halls and elephant stables; Zhou Xuan built tilted palaces and stables for deer, and both met ruin. King Ling of Chu raised the Zhanghua halls and brought collapse upon himself and his dynasty; Qin Shi Huang built Epang Palace, and disaster struck his son in turn, so Qin collapsed in two generations. Whoever does not measure the people’s strength and follows only private desire of eye and ear—none of those has avoided ruin. Let Your Majesty take Yao, Shun, Yü, Tang, Wen, and Wu as law, and use Jie, Zhou, Chu, and Qin as warning; but this one instead seeks indulgence in buildings, as if delighting in ornament, and will surely invite danger. A ruler is the head of the state; ministers are its shoulders and arms. Life and death are one, and gain and loss are shared. Though I am clumsy and timid, can I fail in speaking as a remonstrating minister? My words are not keen enough to awaken Your Majesty. I wet my mourning garments and stand ready for severe punishment.

When the memorial came in, Cao Rui did not heed it. He kept pressing Ma Jun to finish the high terraces, install the bronze man, and place the Chenglu Disc.

He again decreed that hundreds of beautiful women across the land be recruited into Shanglin Garden.

Officials submitted repeated objections and memorials, but Cao Rui listened to none.

Cao Rui’s empress, Lady Mao, came from Henan. In earlier days, while Cao Rui was still Prince Pingyuan, she was deeply favored. After he became emperor he made her empress. Later he became infatuated with Lady Guo, and Lady Mao lost favor. Lady Guo was beautiful and clever; Cao Rui was much taken with her, daily seeking amusement with her. He did not leave the inner palace for a month.

In that spring, in the third month, flowers thronged Shanglin Garden. Cao Rui and Lady Guo went there to enjoy them and drink. Lady Guo said, “Why do you not invite the Empress to join us?”

Cao Rui said, “If she were present I could not swallow even a drop.” He ordered palace attendants in secret not to let Lady Mao know.

When Lady Mao heard that the Emperor had spent a month outside the main palace, she took more than ten women and went to the Cuilihall. She sat there and heard clear music in the distance, and asked, “Where is this music being played?” A palace official replied, “It is your Majesty with Lady Guo in the imperial garden, enjoying flowers and wine.”

Lady Mao was upset and returned to the palace. The next day, in a small carriage, she went out, and happened to meet Cao Rui in a winding corridor.

She smiled and said, “Your Majesty’s outing to the North Garden was no slight joy.”

Cao Rui grew angry, had all attendants from the previous day captured and cried, “Yesterday in the North Garden I ordered that no one tell Lady Mao of what was happening. How has this been spoken aloud?” He ordered all attendants from that outing to be executed.

Lady Mao was greatly shocked and returned to the palace. Cao Rui immediately issued an edict granting Lady Mao death and elevating Lady Guo to empress. No court official dared to intercede.

One day, the Inspector of Youzhou, Guanqiu Jian, submitted a memorial reporting that in Liaodong, Gongsun Yuan had rebelled, taking the title King of Yan and establishing the era Shao-Han, first year. He had built a palace, made offices, raised troops, and invaded, stirring the northern border.

Cao Rui was startled, immediately gathered civil and military officials, and discussed mobilizing troops to drive back Yuan.

It came to this:

They had only begun to exhaust China with earthwork and timber, and already saw war rise from the outer marches. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhuge Liang Prepares a Preemptive Secret-Pouch Stratagem, and the Wei Emperor Removes the Dewy Disc

chapters.html:
Gongsun Yuan’s soldiers are broken at Xiangping, and Sima Yi feigns illness to gain advantage over Cao Shuang.

Now it is told that Gongsun Yuan was the grandson of Gongsun Du of Liaodong and the son of Gongsun Kang. In the twelfth year of Jianan, when Cao Cao pursued Yuan Shang and had not yet arrived in Liaodong, Kang cut off Yuan Shang’s head and offered it to Cao Cao. Cao Cao made Kang the Marquis of Xiangping. Kang later died, leaving two young sons, the elder called Huang and the younger called Yuan. Kang’s brother, Gongsun Gong, inherited the office. In Cao Pi’s time, Gong was made Cavalry Commandant and Marquis of Xiangping. In the second year of Taihe, Yuan had grown up, combining learning and martial skill, with a hard and combative nature. He wrested his uncle Gongsun Gong’s position from him, and Cao Rui made him General of Yangle and the Administrator of Liaodong.

Later Sun Quan sent Zhang Mi and Xu Yan with gold, treasures, and jewels to Liaodong and bestowed on Yuan the title of King of Yan. Fearing the Central Plains, Yuan had those two executed and sent their heads to Cao Rui. Cao Rui then made Yuan Grand Marshal and Marquis of Lelang. Still unsatisfied, he consulted his men, proclaimed himself King of Yan, and changed the era name to Shaohan.

His deputy general Jia Fan remonstrated: “In the Central Plains, Your Grace is treated no lower than an exalted marquis. It is not fitting for you to rebel now. Moreover, Sima Yi knows how to use troops well. Even your illustrious general Marquis Wu of Shu—cannot yet win over all of Shu. How can one like your Grace prevail?”

Yuan flew into a rage and shouted for his guards to bind Jia Fan and execute him. Assistant military official Lun Zhi remonstrated in turn: “Deputy General Jia Fan speaks truly. The wise say, ‘Where a kingdom is about to fall, monsters and portents appear.’ Our realm has recently seen strange omens. A man recently appeared wearing a white cloth on his head and a red robe, walking on the rooftop as if climbing walls with his legs tucked up. In the southern quarter of the city, villagers boiled rice and suddenly a child was steamed alive inside the pot. In the north market of Xiangping, the ground sank suddenly and a patch of flesh, several chi across, rose from the earth, complete with face, eyes, ears, mouth, and nose but no hands or feet. Arrows and blades could not wound it. No one knows what creature it was. Diviners said, ‘It has form but no shape, a mouth yet no voice; the realm is fated to fall, and this form appears for that reason.’ These three omens are all inauspicious. Your Grace should turn from evil and pursue what is fortunate; do not act rashly.”

Yuan became even more enraged. He shouted for soldiers to bind Lun Zhi as well and executed him in the market, and ordered that Great Commander Bi Yan become overall commander, Yang Zuo lead the vanguard, and a force of 150,000 Liaodong troops should march on the Central Plains.

A frontier officer reported this to Wei ruler Cao Rui. Cao Rui was greatly alarmed and summoned Sima Yi for deliberation. Sima said, “My mounted and foot units total 40,000. That is enough to break the bandit.”

Cao Rui replied, “Your troops are few and your route long. I fear recovery may be difficult.”

Yi answered, “Victory does not lie in numbers; it lies in devising stratagems and using intelligence. Trust in Your Majesty’s heavenly blessing, and I will surely capture Gongsun Yuan to present him to Your Majesty.”

“How do you think Yuan will act?” Cao Rui asked.

“He may abandon the city and run out first—that is his highest-level plan. To stay in Liaodong and oppose the main army is his middle plan. To sit and defend Xiangping is his lower plan, and then I will surely capture him,” Sima said.

Cao Rui asked, “How long for the march and return?”

“Four thousand li. A hundred days to arrive, a hundred to strike, and sixty days to rest. About one year will suffice,” Sima said.

“What if Wu and Shu both raid at once?” Cao Rui asked.

“Defense measures are already fixed,” Sima replied. “Do not worry.”

Cao Rui approved immediately and ordered Sima Yi to raise an army and suppress Gongsun Yuan. Sima Yi took leave of court and set out, assigning Hu Zun as vanguard and ordering him to send troops quickly to Liaodong and establish a camp. A courier horse later reached Yuan. He ordered Bi Yan and Yang Zuo to station 80,000 troops in the Liaozui pass, digging a trench around the defenses for more than twenty li and surrounding the stag horns as tightly as possible.

Hu Zun sent word to Sima Yi. Sima smiled and said, “The rebel will not fight us; he wishes to wear out our troops. I estimate that most of the enemy are here, while their nest is emptied. Better to abandon this place and push straight for Xiangping. He will go to defend it, and he will be struck down on the way. We will win full victory.” He then ordered the army to take the smaller route and advance on Xiangping.

Bi Yan and Yang Zuo discussed, “If Wei troops come to attack, we should not engage. They have marched a thousand li, and supply cannot keep pace; they cannot last long. Once their food is gone they must withdraw. When they turn back, we can launch an unexpected strike and capture Sima Yi. It is the same now as when Sima Yi faced Shu troops and held steadfast at Weinan, while Kongming ended by dying in his own camp.”

They were still speaking when a courier arrived: “Wei forces are moving south.”

Bi Yan was startled: “They know our force at Xiangping is small, and now they are raiding our old camp. If Xiangping is lost, there is no point in holding this position.” He pulled down the camp and followed after.

Hu Zun had already sent a rider back to Sima Yi. Sima smiled. “He has fallen into my plan!” he said. He ordered Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei to move one division each and lie in wait on the banks of Ji River: “If Liaodong troops arrive, strike out from both sides together.” They took their stations.

Soon they saw Bi Yan and Yang Zuo moving forward with troops. At one cannon blast, both camp flags roared; drums thundered and banners shook. Xiahou Ba on the left, Xiahou Wei on the right, both charged out together.

Bi Yan and Yang Zuo had no mind to stand and fight. They cut a path and fled, reaching first mountain, where they met Gongsun Yuan’s arriving force. The two forces joined and turned horse, fighting the Wei troops again.

Bi Yan rode out and shouted at the invaders, “Rebel general, do not play tricks. Do you dare to enter battle?” Xiahou Ba spurred his horse and drew his sword to meet him. After only a few rounds, Xiahou Ba severed Bi Yan from below the saddle, and Liaodong ranks broke. Xiahou Ba drove his men in to kill while Gongsun Yuan led his broken force back into Xiangping and shut the gates, holding fast and refusing to come out. Wei troops surrounded the city on all sides.

The season was deep in autumn rains that did not stop for a full moon. The plain became three chi deep in water, and supply boats could row from the mouth of Liao River straight to below Xiangping. Wei soldiers stood and rode in the water all day, never comfortable. Left commander Pei Jing entered Sima’s tent and reported, “The rain does not stop. The ground in the camp is all mud and the army cannot hold. I ask to move the camp to higher hills in front.”

Sima shouted back, “The capture of Gongsun Yuan is within a day or two. How can we shift camp now? If anyone mentions moving the camp again, they will be executed.” Pei Jing bowed and withdrew.

After a short while, Right commander Qiu Lian also came with the same request: “The soldiers suffer from the water. We ask Your Excellency to move the camp to higher ground.” Sima roared, “My order has already been given. How dare you oppose it?” He ordered him seized and executed, then hung him outside the south gate. The whole army was shaken.

Sima then ordered both forward camps pulled back twenty li to give the city’s soldiers and civilians opportunity to leave for wood-gathering and to graze cattle and horses. Chief adjutant Sima Chenqun said, “Earlier, when Your Excellency besieged Shangyong, the army split into eight routes and arrived beneath the city in eight days, and you captured Meng Da in a great victory. Now you have four thousand armored men, and coming from hundreds of li away, you do not order an assault on the walls and instead keep us in mud for so long while allowing the enemy their firewood and grazing. I truly do not know what Your Excellency intends.”

Sima smiled. “Do you not know the laws of war? Meng Da had more provisions and fewer troops than I, so we had to strike swiftly and unexpectedly if we were to win. Now Liaodong has many men; I have fewer. The enemy is hungry and our camp is better supplied. Why must we force a direct attack? It is enough to let them move as they wish, then strike at the right moment. I open a road for them and do not block their firewood and grazing so that they may leave by themselves.”

Chenqun bowed in submission.

Sima Yi then dispatched men to Luoyang to urge grain to be sent out. Cao Rui convened a court. Court officials all spoke: “Recently the autumn rains have lasted for a full month and soldiers and horses are exhausted. It would be prudent to call back Sima Yi and suspend operations.”

Cao Rui said, “Sima Yi is good at warfare; under danger he changes the field and often has brilliant stratagems. He awaits the right hour to capture Gongsun Yuan. Why should you all worry?” He ignored their remonstrance and sent grain directly to Sima Yi’s front.

After several more days in camp, the rain stopped and the sky cleared. That night Sima walked out of his tent and looked up at the heavens. Suddenly he saw a star, as large as a Dipper, trailing its light for several chi; from northeast of Shoushan it fell to the southeast of Xiangping. All the captains and soldiers were awed and alarmed. Sima was delighted. He told the assembled officers, “Five days hence, at the place where the star falls, Gongsun Yuan will be beheaded. Tomorrow we will attack the city with all our strength.”

At his command, the next morning before dawn, the four-facing force surrounded the walls, built earthen mounds, dug tunnels, set gun platforms, and raised ladders. They attacked day and night without pause, arrows falling like heavy rain into the city.

Within Xiangping, grain had run out. Everyone slaughtered cattle and horses for food. The men were each resentful and had no heart to defend. Some said they should cut off Yuan’s head and surrender the city. Yuan heard of this and was greatly frightened. He quickly ordered the Chancellor Wang Jian and the censor Li Fu to go to the Wei camp and submit surrender.

They tied ropes over the wall and descended to report to Sima Yi: “Grant Your Excellency two camps’ width retreat, and my lord and I will come in to surrender.”

Sima yelled with anger, “Why does Gongsun Yuan not come himself? This is most unreasonable!” He ordered them seized and executed, and gave their heads to attendants.

The attendants reported this. Yuan was shaken and sent the court attendant Wei Yan to Wei camp. Sima ordered his tent raised and the generals stood in two lines. Wei Yan knelt and crawled forward, then knelt at the foot of the tent. “Let Your Excellency release the thunderbolt of your anger,” he said. “Should auspicious day come first, we will offer Your Majesty’s grandson Gongsun Xiu as a pledge. After that, my lord and his ministers will bind themselves and come down to surrender.”

Sima replied, “There are five main principles in war: when one can fight, one must fight; when one cannot, one must hold; when one cannot hold, one must run; when one cannot run, one must surrender; when one cannot surrender, one must die. Why must a son be sent as hostages before I can settle him?”

He ordered Wei Yan to return the message to Gongsun Yuan. Wei Yan lowered his head and fled away. Back before him, Yuan was in dismay.

Yuan then held a secret council with his son Gongsun Xiu, chose one thousand horsemen, and at the middle of the second night-watch opened the southern gate and fled southeast.

Seeing no pursuers, he rejoiced inwardly. They had not yet gone ten li when a cannon shot sounded from the mountain, horns blew together, and one force blocked the road ahead. Sima stood at the center, with Sima Shi at his left and Sima Zhao at his right. Both shouted, “Turned rebel, do not run!” Yuan was startled and pushed his horse to search a route for flight. But Hu Zun’s troops had already arrived—Xiahou Ba and Xiahou Wei on the left, Zhang Hu and Lechen on the right—four sides enclosing them like iron hoops.

The father and son, Gongsun Yuan and Gongsun Xiu, could only dismount and surrender. On horseback Sima said, “The previous night in bingyin I saw a great star fall at this spot. Tonight in ren-shen, the appointed day has come.”

The assembled officers praised him. “The Grand Commandant truly moves with divine art!” they cried. Sima gave orders to execute them. Gongsun Yuan and his son were both killed facing each other.

Sima then raised the army to retake Xiangping. Before they even reached the city gates, Hu Zun had already brought troops inside. The people burned incense and welcomed them. Wei troops fully entered the city. Sima sat in the administrative hall and had Yuan’s clan, together with officials who had plotted with him, all killed, seventy-odd heads in all. He issued proclamations to pacify the people.

Someone informed him: “Jia Fan and Lun Zhi had begged Yuan not to revolt, and both were killed by him.”

Sima honored their graves and conferred rewards upon their sons and grandsons. From the storehouses he took treasure and rewarded the three armies, then retired from the campaign and returned to Luoyang.

At the palace that night, Cao Rui lay in his chambers. At the third watch, a gust of dark wind suddenly extinguished all lights. Empress Mao came with dozens of palace women crying at his seat and begged for mercy, and Cao Rui fell gravely ill. As his illness worsened, he entrusted all affairs of the Privy Secretariat to the Shizhong and Guanglu Dafu Liu Fang and Sun Zi, and also summoned the crown prince’s uncle, Prince of Yan, Cao Yu, making him Grand Commander to assist Prince Cao Fang in governing.

Cao Yu, a man of modesty, frugality, and mildness, refused the charge and repeatedly declined. Cao Rui asked Liu Fang and Sun Zi, “Within the clan, who is fit for this?” The two had long received favors from Cao Zhen, and together they submitted, “Only Cao Shuang, son of Cao Zidan, is suitable.”

Cao Rui accepted. They then proposed, “If Cao Shuang is to be used, the Prince of Yan should first be sent home.” Cao Rui accepted this too. They requested a decree and delivered it to Cao Yu: “The Son of Heaven has issued an edict: the Prince of Yan must return home immediately; on no condition may he enter court without an edict.” Cao Yu wept and left.
