Cao Rui therefore made Cao Shuang Grand Commander and entrusted him with oversight of the court.

As Cao Rui worsened, he ordered an edict commanding Sima Yi to return to court. Sima Yi obeyed and came directly to Xuchang, where he was admitted to audience.

“Only by your presence do I feel at peace. Today to see you means I have no regrets,” Cao Rui said.

Sima knelt and answered, “When I learned my sovereign’s health was unwell on the road, I wished I had wings to fly to the gate of the hall. To behold Your Majesty now is my good fortune.”

Cao Rui then summoned Crown Prince Cao Fang, Grand Commander Cao Shuang, Liu Fang, Sun Zi and others to stand before the imperial couch. He took Sima Yi’s hands and said, “When Liu Xuan-de, at Baidi City, lay on the brink of death and entrusted his little son Liu Shan to Zhuge Kongming, it was by that gentleman’s wholehearted loyalty and tireless service that the matter was settled. How much more so for a great state! My son Cao Fang is only eight years old and cannot yet manage the state. I rely on you, Grand Commandant, and my elder coeval, Chancellor Yuanhun, the old ministers, to assist him fully. Do not fail me.”

Then he called to Cao Fang, “Zhongda and I are one body. You are to honor him greatly.” So he ordered Sima to draw Cao Fang closer. Cao Fang embraced Sima’s neck and refused to let go.

“Grand Commandant, do not forget the affection this child bears for you this day,” Cao Rui said.

Sima knelt and wept. Wei’s sovereign sank into confusion; his mouth could no longer speak. He only pointed at the crown prince. Soon he died. He had reigned thirteen years and was thirty-six years old, it being late in the first month of spring in the third year of Jingchu.

At once, Sima Yi and Cao Shuang lifted Cao Fang to the throne. His name was Cao Fang, courtesy name Lanqing; he had been one of Cao Rui’s secret sons, raised secretly in the palace, and no one knew his true origin. Cao Fang posthumously honored Cao Rui as Emperor Ming, buried him at Gaoping Mausoleum, raised Empress Guo to Empress Dowager, and changed the reign era to Zhengshi one.

Cao Shuang and Sima Yi served as co-regents. Cao Shuang treated Sima with great caution and brought all major matters to him first. Shuang’s courtesy name was Zhaobo. He had grown up moving in and out of the palace; Emperor Ming liked him for this careful manner. Under Cao Shuang there were five men he trusted as close guests, among five hundred under his roof. Among them, He Yan was fifth: courtesy name Pingshu. Deng Yang, courtesy name Xuanmao, a descendant of Deng Yu; Li Sheng, courtesy name Gongzhao; Ding Mi, courtesy name Yanjing; and Bi Gui, courtesy name Zhaoxian. Also Minister of Revenue Han Fan, courtesy name Yuanzu, was considered a strategist and many called him the “Council of Wisdom.”

He Yan said, “My lord now has great power. It must not be entrusted to others or trouble will come later.”

Cao Shuang answered, “I and Sima Yi both received the late emperor’s charge to nurture you. How could I betray it?”

Yan replied, “In former days, when the old one and Zhongda fought Shu, he suffered repeated insults from this man and eventually died because of it. Why do you not investigate?”

A jolt of understanding struck Cao Shuang. He then conferred with various officers and submitted a memorial to Cao Fang: “Sima Yi has meritorious service and virtue. He may be added as Grand Tutor.” Cao Fang accepted. From then on all military command passed into Shuang’s hands.

Cao Shuang made his brother Cao Xi Middle Commanding General, Cao Xun Weapony Guard General, and Cao Yan Gentle Gentleman Attendant, each with 3,000 imperial guard cavalry to enter and leave the Forbidden Court at will. He appointed He Yan, Deng Yang, and Ding Mi as Secretaries, Bi Gui as Director of the Capital Censors, and Li Sheng as Inspector of Henan; these five met with Cao Shuang day and night to discuss policy.

Thus, guest traffic around Cao Shuang flourished. Sima Yi withdrew, feigning illness and never going out, and both his sons also retired from office and lived apart. Cao Shuang drank and caroused daily with He Yan and the rest. Whatever clothing or vessels he used matched those of the court. At every place they sent gifts of fine curios and rare treasures, taking the best ones first for himself before passing them to the palace. He filled his residence with beautiful women and performers—three or four dozen talented sons and daughters of musical homes. He built high towers and painted pavilions and ordered hundreds of fine craftsmen to work by day and night on gold and silver vessels.

He Yan later heard that the master Guanlu of Pingyuan was skilled in numerology and asked him to discuss the changes of the arts. Deng Yang was present and asked Guanlu, “You claim to understand these changes, yet you do not explain their meanings. Why?”

Guanlu replied, “One who truly understands such teachings does not talk endlessly about them.”

He Yan laughed and praised him: “He is one who says only what is needed.” He said to Guanlu, “Cast a divination for me. Can I rise to the three offices? And again, I have repeated dreams in which dozens of green flies gather upon my nose. What omen is this?”

Guanlu said, “Yuan Kai served Shun and Zhougong aided Zhou. Both gained many blessings because they practiced harmony and humility and were courteous in conduct. In your case, your rank is high and your influence heavy; yet those who are virtuous are few and those who fear your authority are many. This is not the right way to secure blessings. The nose is like a mountain. The higher the mountain stands, the longer it can keep a high place. Now these foul flies gather there in stench, and one whose station is lofty may be overturned. You should not be reckless in what you do. If you increase little and reduce much, and refuse to step where it is not proper, then you may indeed attain the Three Excellencies and drive away the green flies.”

Deng Yang, angry, said, “These are only the common talk of an old man.”

Guanlu answered, “An old man has no life to lose; a common talker has nothing to discuss.” He then swept away and left. The two laughed together: “What a wild scholar.”

Returning home, Guanlu told his uncle. The uncle was greatly startled and said, “He and Deng Yang are both extremely powerful. How can you offend them?”

Guanlu replied, “I speak with those already dead; what is there to fear?”

His uncle asked why. Guanlu said, “Look at Deng Yang’s gait—his muscles do not restrain the bones, his pulses do not control the flesh, and when he rises he sways as if lacking hands and feet. That is the look of ‘ghost-frenzy.’ As for He Yan’s appearance, his aura does not hold the household, his blood lacks color, his spirit floats like thin smoke, his face withers like dead wood. That is ‘ghost-silence.’ These two will surely die soon by bloodshed. Why should one fear them?”

His uncle left without scolding him as mad.

Cao Shuang once went hunting with He Yan, Deng Yang, and others. His brother Cao Xi remonstrated: “Brother, you wield overwhelming power and delight in roaming and hunting. If someone has already calculated against you, regret will be too late.” Cao Shuang shouted, “The military command is in my hands. What is there to fear?” Minister Han Fan also remonstrated, but Shuang did not listen.

Around this time, Cao Fang entered the tenth year of Zhengshi, which was changed to Jia Ping first year. Cao Shuang had held authority throughout and did not know Zhongda’s true condition. The Wei sovereign, seeing this, removed Li Sheng as Inspector of Jingzhou and immediately ordered him to present himself before Zhongda and gather news.

Li Sheng came straight to the Secretariat’s outer office. A gate guard had already reported his arrival. Sima said to his two sons, “This is Cao Shuang’s envoy to test the weakness of my illness.”

So Sima removed his cap, left his hair loose, went to sit on the bed with blanket wrapped about him, then had two young women support his elbow. Only then did he summon Li Sheng.

When Li arrived, he knelt by the bed and said, “I have not seen the Grand Preceptor for some time. I did not think his condition so serious. The Son of Heaven has appointed you Inspector of Jingzhou, and you have come to pay farewell.”

Sima answered with pretense, “Bingzhou is near Shuofu and one must prepare for it.”

Li Sheng said, “My appointment is to Jingzhou, not Bingzhou.”

Sima laughed: “So you have come from Bingzhou?”

Li replied, “I come from Qingzhou in Shandong.”

Sima laughed, “You have come from Qingzhou, too.”

Li said, “How serious is the illness of the Grand Preceptor?”

One attendant answered, “The Grand Preceptor is deaf.”

Li: “May I have paper and a brush?”

A servant handed him paper and brush. Li wrote and presented it.

Sima read it and smiled. “My ears are indeed deaf,” he said. “Take care on your journey home.” He then pointed to his mouth.

A serving maid brought in broth. Sima tipped his mouth into it; broth spilled over his robe and he made a choking gurgling sound. “This old body is withered and weak. Death is at hand. My two sons are unworthy; I ask you to teach them. If you meet the Grand Commander, protect my two sons beyond all else!”

After speaking he collapsed back in bed, voice strained, breath labored. Li Sheng retired and again reported to Cao Shuang what he had seen. Cao Shuang rejoiced: “If this old man dies, I have nothing to fear.”

When Sima saw Li Sheng depart, he rose and told his sons, “Li Sheng has gone to report. When he reaches Cao Shuang, he will think no longer suspicious of me. It will be only when he is out hunting outside the city that we can act.”

In less than a day, Cao Shuang invited Emperor Ming to visit Gaoping Mausoleum and offer sacrifice to the late emperor. All levels of officials rode out with him.

Cao Shuang brought his third brother and trusted men including He Yan, with the Imperial Guard forming his escort. Minister Han Fan dismounted and remonstrated, “Your lordship commands the Imperial garrison. All brothers should not leave the city. If something changes in the capital, what then?”

Cao Shuang struck his whip and shouted, “Who dares to rebel? Never speak so nonsense again!”

When Sima Yi saw Cao Shuang leave the city that day, he was full of joy. He gathered old men from his former days who had broken enemies in battle, along with a number of family officers, and with his two sons mounted their horses and went straight to set out on Cao Shuang’s murder.

What followed is told:

Shutting the gate, fortune is bound to turn, and from this day on the soldiers will vent their fierce, triumphant wind. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Gongsun Yuan is Defeated at Xiangping and Sima Yi Feigns Illness to Outwit Cao Shuang

chapters.html:
The Wei lord restores authority to the Sima household; Jiang Wei’s army is defeated at Niutou Mountain.

Sima Yi, whose courtesy name was Zhongda, heard that Cao Shuang and his younger brothers Cao Xi and Cao Xun, along with his close advisers He Yan, Deng Yang, Ding Mi, Bi Fan, Li Sheng, and his Imperial Guard, had gone out of the city with Emperor Cao Fang to pay respect at Emperor Ming’s tomb and then to hunt. Sima Yi was delighted. He returned to the Palace offices, had Grand Commandant Jiang Ji and Prefect of the Masters of Writing Sima Fu draft a memorial together, and sent it out by a eunuch directly to the emperor. He ordered Minister over the Masses Gao Rou, gave him a halberd token to exercise the powers of the General-in-Chief, and sent him first to take possession of Cao Shuang’s camp; he also ordered Wang Guan of the Stables to assume middle command and occupy Cao Xi’s camp.

Sima Yi then entered the inner palace to report to Empress Dowager Guo: “Cao Shuang has betrayed the late emperor’s trust in leaving an orphaned throne to him. Through deceit and corruption he has thrown the realm into chaos. His crimes deserve dismissal.” The empress was shocked and asked, “The Son of Heaven is away. What can we do?” Sima Yi replied, “I have drafted a memorial for the Son of Heaven and a plan to execute treacherous ministers. Your Majesty need not worry.” In fear, the empress gave no choice.

Sima Yi hurriedly sent Grand Commandant Jiang Ji and Prefect of the Masters of Writing Sima Fu to write and submit another report. He ordered eunuchs to carry it out of the city at once and go directly before the Son of Heaven. Sima Yi moved his main force to the armories.

News reached Cao Shuang’s household quickly. His wife Liu Shi hurried to the front hall and asked the gate official, “Our lord is out of the city. Why has Zhongda raised the army?” Pan Ju, the gate captain, answered, “Lady, do not be alarmed; I will inquire.” He then brought dozens of bow and crossbow men to the gate tower and stared out. Just then he saw Sima Yi approaching with troops passing in front of the residence, so he signaled a random volley. Arrows rained down and Sima Yi could not pass. At that moment Sun Qian, a flank commander, shouted from behind: “Grand Tutor’s matter is urgent state business. Do not fire!” He stopped him three times, and only then did Pan Ju refrain.

Sima Zhao shielded his father, Sima Yi, as they passed. He led his troops out of the city and camped on the Luo River, taking the pontoon bridge.

Meanwhile, Sima Lu-Zhi, who served under Cao Shuang, saw turmoil inside the city and met with staff officer Xin Chang to discuss what to do. “How can we respond to Zhongda’s upheaval?” he asked.

“Take out your regular forces and ride outside the city to meet the Son of Heaven,” Xin Chang replied.

Lu-Zhi accepted his counsel. Xin Chang rushed into the rear hall. His sister Xianying saw him and asked, “What has happened, and why such haste?”

Xin Chang said, “The Son of Heaven is outside the city, and the Grand Tutor has closed the gates. He surely intends treason.”

Xianying replied, “Grand Tutor Sima may not be plotting treason; he may only wish to execute the Grand General.”

Xin Chang was startled. “Then what do we do?”

Xianying answered, “The Grand General was never equal to Zhongda. He will lose.”

Xin Chang said, “Was it truly possible the day Sima Yi told me to join him, I had no way to refuse?”

Xianying replied, “A person’s service is his duty. Even in crisis, one may still have compassion. To drop the whip and abandon one’s charge is the greatest inauspicious act.”

Heeded, Lu-Zhi followed her advice and broke through the gate with him, riding out with only a few dozen men.

Word reached Sima Yi. He feared that Huan Fan might have fled and sent for him at once. Huan Fan conferred with his son. His son said, “The imperial carriage is out of town. Better to go out by the southern road.” Huan Fan agreed and rode to Pingchang Gate. The gate was already shut. The gate captain, the old retainer Si Fan, blocked him.

From his sleeves Huan Fan drew out a bamboo order and said, “The empress dowager has issued an edict. The gate may be opened now.”

Si Fan said, “Please verify the edict.”

Huan Fan shouted, “You are my old subordinate. How dare you delay?”

Si Fan reluctantly opened the gate. Huan Fan rode out and called after him, “Grand Tutor has plotted rebellion. You should follow me at once.”

Si Fan was alarmed and pursued but could not catch up. He reported this to Sima Yi.

Sima Yi was startled. “The stratagem has been exposed! What are we to do?” Jiang Ji replied with an idiom: “A horse grown soft on stall-feed cannot do its work.”

Sima Yi summoned Xu Yun and Chen Tai. “Go to Cao Shuang and say the Grand Tutor has no other intention. He seeks only to reduce your brothers’ military power.”

The two departed.

He also summoned the palace officer Yin Da-mu, had Jiang Ji write a letter, and sent him to Cao Shuang. Sima Yi instructed him, “You and Cao Shuang have been close. You can take this mission. Tell him I and Jiang Ji have sworn an oath at the Luo River. I have no other motive beyond matters of military command.”

Yin Da-mu followed the order and departed.

At that time Cao Shuang, while chasing hawks and hounds, was suddenly informed that the city had changed and that the Grand Tutor had submitted a memorial. He was terrified, nearly falling from his horse. A eunuch held the memorial on his knees before the Son of Heaven. Cao Shuang took it, broke the seal, and ordered his close court attendants to read it aloud.

The memorial said:

Your servant Sima Yi, Grand Tutor and Grand Commander Who Conquers the West, humbly and with dread submits this report:

When I returned from Liaodong, the late emperor summoned Your Majesty and Prince of Qin and my fellow officials up onto his couch and, gripping my arm, spoke earnestly of later affairs. Now Grand General Cao Shuang has cast aside the late emperor’s charge; he has disrupted state precedent. Within the court he has presumptuously usurped the court’s forms, and without, he has monopolized authority. He made Zhang Dang of the eunuchs his supervisor and made him command all reports and connections, watching over the Son of Heaven and attending the sacred regalia. He has sown division between the Two Palaces and wounded the ties of flesh and blood. Across the realm all is in uproar; the people live in fear. This is not what the late emperor charged me with, nor what he entrusted to Your Majesty.

Though I am old and decayed, can I forget what I once spoke? Grand Commandant Jiang Ji and Prefect of the Masters of Writing Sima Fu all deem Cao Shuang to carry himself with no loyalty to his lord. Brothers should not command the guard units and escort troops. I therefore now submit this to Empress Dowager Yongning, requesting a command to act.

I have already ordered his men, Cao Xi’s men, and Cao Xun’s men to be dismissed from service so that each may return to his household and not wander beyond. Should they linger, they are to be punished by military law. I immediately hastened with my troops and camped at the pontoon bridge on the Luo River to observe signs of disorder.

I submit this respectfully for Your Majesty’s Holy hearing.

Cao Fang listened and then called for Cao Shuang. “This is what the Grand Tutor has written. How will you judge it?”

Cao Shuang, hands and feet gone slack, looked to his two younger brothers. “What are we to do?”

Cao Xi replied, “Your younger brother once remonstrated with you, but brother would not listen and now this has come to pass. Sima Yi is without equal in deceit. Even Kongming could not defeat him—how then for us? Better to surrender and present yourselves to him now, to avoid a swift death.”

Before he finished, Xin Chang and Sima Lu-Zhi arrived. Cao Shuang asked what they had seen.

They said, “Inside the city, the gates are taken up like iron-bound tubs. The Grand Tutor has stationed his army at the Luo River pontoon bridge; recovery seems unlikely. We should settle our plan at once.”

At that very moment Censor Huan Fan came at speed. He said to Cao Shuang, “The Grand Tutor has already moved. Why not ask the Son of Heaven to remain at Xuchang and bring outside troops to punish him?”

Cao Shuang asked, “Our whole family is inside the city. How could we seek aid elsewhere?”

Fan answered, “A mere man in distress still hopes to live! Your lord is at the Son of Heaven’s side and may issue commands to all under heaven. Who would disobey? Why cast yourselves into a place of certain death?”

Cao Shuang remained indecisive, only weeping.

Fan continued, “It is no more than half a night’s ride to Xuchang. The city stores can support several years. Your private cavalry camp is near the city gate and can come at once. A seal of the Grand Commander is still here. Your Excellency should hurry. To delay now is to rest in danger.”

“Do not urge too hard,” Cao Shuang said at last. “Let me think this through.”

After a while, Attendant-in-Waiting Xu Yun and Prefect of the Masters of Writing Chen Tai arrived. They told him, “The Grand Tutor wants only to cut your military power. He has no other intent. You should return early to the residence.”

Cao Shuang remained silent.

Then palace officer Yin Da-mu arrived. He said, “The Grand Tutor swore by the Luo River and has no other intent. The letter from Grand Commandant Jiang Ji is here. General, you should surrender your command authority and return to the Secretariat.”

Cao Shuang took it for honest advice. Fan repeated urgently, “The matter is urgent. Do not listen to men outside and choose death.”

That night Cao Shuang could not decide. He drew his sword and stood with it in hand, sighing and thinking. From dusk until dawn he wept and remained torn by suspicion. Huan Fan entered his tent and urged him: “Your Excellency has hesitated all day and all night. Why still cannot you decide?”

Cao Shuang threw down his sword and sighed. “If I do not raise troops and do not submit a petition, I can at least retire from office and live as a wealthy householder.”

Fan wept loudly and left the tent: “Cao Zi-dan has boasted so of strategy and wit; the three brothers are only fattened piglets!”

Xu Yun and Chen Tai then urged Cao Shuang to first hand over his seals of office and command regalia to Sima Yi. Cao Shuang ordered that they be sent.

His clerk Yang Zong caught and held the seals and regalia, crying: “Your Excellency, if you surrender your military authority and submit yourself now, you will surely be flayed in the eastern market.”

Cao Shuang answered, “The Grand Tutor will not break faith with me.”

Thus Cao Shuang handed over his seals and regalia through Xu Yun and Chen Tai. The rest of his army, seeing no one left with command authority, all drifted apart. Only a few dozen official riders remained at his side. At the pontoon bridge, Sima Yi’s orders arrived: the three brothers were told to return at once to their private mansions; everyone else was to be detained and wait for instruction. When Cao Shuang and his brothers entered the city, not one attendant accompanied them.

Huan Fan reached the bridge bank, where Sima Yi was mounted. He struck with his whip and asked, “Master Huan, why have you done this?” Fan lowered his head and said nothing, then returned to the city.

Then Sima Yi invited His Majesty to break camp and enter Luoyang. After the three brothers returned home, Sima Yi had a great lock fasten the gates and ordered eight hundred residents to guard their household.

Cao Shuang was tormented with worry. Cao Xi said, “Our stores are running low. Brother, write to the Grand Tutor and ask him for grain. If he is willing to lend us grain, he cannot intend harm.”

Cao Shuang wrote and sent it out.

Sima Yi read it and had grain delivered—one hundred hu—to Cao Shuang’s residence.

Cao Shuang rejoiced: “Grand Tutor Sima has no intention of hurting me.” He relaxed at once.

Sima Yi had already seized Zhang Dang, the eunuch, and held him for interrogation. Zhang Dang admitted, “Not only me. He Yan, Deng Yang, Li Sheng, Bi Fan, and Ding Mi are all among the five who planned rebellion.” Sima Yi took Zhang Dang’s statement and then arrested He Yan and the others, pressing them until the matter was clear. All confessed, saying that they had planned revolt over the last three months. Sima Yi placed heavy iron shackles on them.

Gate captain Si Fan reported that Huan Fan had forged an edict to leave the city, claiming the Grand Tutor plotted treason. Sima Yi said, “Falsely accusing an innocent man of treason is itself a treasonous offense. He, too, must answer for slander and is to be punished.” He imprisoned Huan Fan and the others as well. Then Cao Shuang, his two brothers, and all their associates were all brought out and beheaded in the market, and their three households were extinguished. Their property and all household goods were entirely confiscated.

At that time there was the wife of Cao Shuang’s younger cousin Wen Shu, who had been a daughter of Xiahou’s commander. She was widowed early and had no son. Her father wished to remarry her away, and she had once cut off her own ear as a vow. When Cao Shuang was executed, her father again sought to marry her off, and she cut off her own nose as well. Her family, shaken by fear and grief, asked her, “In this world life is as light as dust on brittle grass. Why punish yourself so? Moreover, your husband’s entire family has been exterminated by the Sima clan. For whom do you mean to preserve yourself?”

She wept and replied, “I have heard: ‘The humane do not alter their conduct with rise or fall; the righteous do not change loyalty with life or death.’ When the Cao family flourished, they still sought to preserve the end. Now that they are ruined, how could I abandon them? This is no act of a beast; how could I do it?”

Sima Yi heard and admired her. He allowed her to be spared, to raise her son, and to continue the Cao line.

Later people wrote:

弱草微塵盡達觀，夏侯有女義如山。 丈夫不及裙釵節，自顧鬚眉亦汗顏。

The grass is thin and dust is fine, yet it all accepts the way of things; Xiahou’s daughter keeps her righteousness like a mountain. A husband’s tie has not even reached the knot of hairpin and skirt, yet I myself blush, beard and brows wet with shame.

When Sima Yi had Cao Shuang beheaded, Grand Commandant Jiang Ji said, “Still there are Sima Lu-Zhi and Xin Chang, who broke through the gates and forced a way out, and Yang Zong, who seized the seals and did not hand them over. None should be spared.”

Sima Yi replied, “Each did what was right by his own lord. They are men of righteousness.” He restored each to old position.

Xin Chang sighed: “If I had not consulted my sister, I would have abandoned my duty of fidelity.”

Later people wrote in praise of Xin Xianying:

為臣食祿當思報，事主臨危合盡忠。 辛氏憲英曾勸弟，古今千載頌高風。

A servant who eats a ruler’s stipend must remember to repay it; when a lord is in peril, loyalty must be total. Xianying Xin once advised her brother, and through a thousand years the ages praise that lofty spirit.

Sima Yi pardoned Xin Chang and the rest and issued a public bulletin: All under Cao Shuang who served under him should be spared death. Any officials should return to their former appointments. Military and civilian households should keep their trades and lands. Within and without, order held.

He Yan and Deng Yang later died by extraordinary misfortune, as if their fate had already been foreknown in Guan Lu’s saying.

Later people wrote in praise of Guan Lu:

傳得聖賢真妙訣，平原管輅相通神。 鬼幽鬼躁分何鄧，未喪先知是死人。

He carried forward the true subtle teaching of the sages; Guan Lu of Pingyuan understood the breath of spirits. He discerned He Yan and Deng Yang before ruin took them, knowing them dead before their deaths arrived.

Thereafter Emperor Cao Fang named Sima Yi Chancellor and granted him Nine Bestowals. Sima Yi refused firmly. Cao Fang did not allow it and ordered father and sons together to oversee state affairs.

Sima Yi suddenly thought: Cao Shuang’s whole family had been destroyed, yet Xiahou Ba of the garrison in Yong Province and others were still there and related to them. If they were to rebel suddenly, how could we prepare? He must be handled.

He issued an edict commanding him to come to Yong Province and bring General Who Conquers the West Xiahou Ba to Luoyang for consultation.

When Xiahou Ba heard this, he was greatly startled and immediately assembled his own three thousand men to rise in revolt. The Inspector of Yong Province, Guo Huai, did likewise upon hearing of Xiahou Ba’s rebellion: he gathered his own force and fought him. Guo Huai spurred out and shouted in rage, “You are a great Wei kin and the Son of Heaven has never wronged you. Why do you now turn against the state?”

Xiahou Ba answered with equal fury, “My grandfather has rendered many services to the state. What sort of man is Sima Yi, extinguishing the family of the Cao line and then coming for me as well? He has long sought the throne and has been waiting for this moment. Is this my treason because I rise with justice against a bandit?”

Guo Huai grew angry and galloped forward with his spear. Xiahou Ba raised his blade and charged. After fewer than ten rounds the battle was lost for Guo Huai, and he turned and fled. Xiahou Ba chased him. Suddenly a shout came from rear troops. Realizing he was caught, Xiahou Ba turned back and Chen Tai arrived with troops and attacked. Guo Huai returned as well.

Pressed by both sides, Xiahou Ba was badly defeated and lost much of his force. Finding no path, he withdrew to Hanzhong and surrendered to the later lord.

Someone reported this to Jiang Wei. He did not trust it at once and sent an agent to verify, then admitted Xiahou Ba. Xiahou Ba came to bow and wept as he reported the events. Jiang Wei said, “Once when Weizi withdrew from Zhou, he became a model for ten thousand years. You have preserved the Han house without shame before the ancients.” He held a feast in his honor.

At table Jiang Wei asked, “Now that Sima Yi and his sons control all power, do they have eyes on our state?”

Xiahou Ba answered, “The old brigand is already plotting another overthrow and has no mind to attend outside matters. Yet in Wei there are now two men in the prime of their youth. If they receive military command, they would be a great threat to Wu and Shu alike.”

Jiang Wei asked, “Who are those two?”

Ba replied: “One is called a secretary clerk. He is from Changshe in Ying Province; surname Zhong, personal name Hui, courtesy name Shiji, son of Grand Tutor Zhong Yao. From youth he had courage and wit. When he and his brother were taken to court by Emperor Wen, they were seven and eight years old. When the emperor asked Yiu why he had been sweating, Yiu said, ‘I am frightened and my sweat runs in streams.’ When he asked Hui why not, Hui answered, ‘I am shaking all the time, yet my sweat dares not come out.’ The emperor admired him at once. As he grew, he loved military books and understood stratagems deeply. Sima Yi and Jiang Ji both praised his talent.

He has one other title: in the court he is treated as a clerkly assistant, and he is from Yiyang. His surname is Deng, personal name Ai, courtesy name Shizai. Orphaned young, he was born with strong ambition. Wherever he saw high mountains and broad marshlands, he drew maps and inspected whether there was place to station troops, where to stock grain, where to set ambushes. People laughed at him. Only Sima Yi recognized the talent, and therefore made him a military aide.

Ai stammered when he spoke and in counsel he always said, ‘Ai, Ai.’ Sima Yi once joked, ‘If you keep saying Ai-Ai, how many reeds are you naming?’ Ai answered at once, ‘Phoenix, Phoenix — in truth it is one phoenix.’ In nature he was quick and sharp; the two of them are truly daunting.”

Jiang Wei laughed, “Such children and we speak so seriously of them?”

Thereafter he brought Xiahou Ba to Chengdu and introduced him to the later lord. Jiang Wei reported: “Sima Yi slew Cao Shuang and then seized Xiahou Ba. In doing so he made clear his designs on our side. At present Sima Yi and his sons hold all power, and Cao Fang is weak; Wei is in danger. I have spent years in Hanzhong; the troops are seasoned and provisions are sufficient. I request command of the royal troops. Let Xiahou Ba be appointed a township guide and assigned, and then we will push forward into the Central Plain, restore Han rule, and repay Your Majesty’s grace and complete the former chancellor’s wish.”

The Minister of the Secretariat Fei Yi remonstrated: “Recently Jiang Wan and Dong Yun have died in succession; there is no one to govern inwardly. Lord Boyue should wait and watch the time, not move hastily.”

Jiang Wei replied, “No. Life slips by like a white colt through a narrow pass. If we keep delaying, when will we return the Central Plain?”

Fei Yi said again, “Sun Tzu taught: if one knows both oneself and the enemy, one wins every battle. We are all far below the chancellor; if even he could not recover the Central Plain, how could we?”

Jiang Wei answered, “I have lived long upon the Longzhong heights and know the heart of the Qiang. If we can ally with the Qiang as support, even if we do not recover the Central Plain now, we can still hold ground west of Longzhong.”

The later lord said, “If you seek to strike Wei, then give your whole heart and strength. Do not lose your edge and fail His command.”

So Jiang Wei, following the imperial decree, rode out with Xiahou Ba and traveled directly to Hanzhong to make war plans. He said, “First send envoys to the Qiang lands to establish alliance, then advance to Xiping and then near Yong Province. Build two fortresses first below Qushan, and let troops hold them as flanking horns. In all of Sichuan’s mouths, expend our grain in full, and then advance step by step by the former procedure of the chancellor.”

That year in the eighth month of autumn, he first sent generals Ju An and Li Xin with fifteen thousand men to the front of Qushan to build two adjacent fortresses. Ju An garrisoned the east, Li Xin the west.

There was already a spy report for Inspector Guo Huai of Yong Province. Guo Huai at once reported to Luoyang and sent his deputy Chen Tai with fifty thousand men to Qushan to fight the Shu troops.

Ju An and Li Xin each led one force to meet him in the field, but because they were too few they retreated into the fortresses. Chen Tai ordered his men to surround on four sides and cut off the supply road from Hanzhong.

Ju An and Li Xin had no water in the fortresses.

Guo Huai arrived with his own force as well. After he assessed the terrain, he rejoiced inwardly. Returning to camp, he and Chen Tai planned: “The city rises high on the slope and is short of water. We must fight outside to secure water. If we cut off its upper stream, Shu troops will die of thirst.” So he ordered soldiers to dig an earthen dam and break the upper flow.

As expected, the fortresses had no water.

Li Xin brought men out to fetch water, but the force from Yong Province surrounded him in desperate pressure. He fought and could not break out, so he retreated into the city.

The city under Ju An also had no water. He joined Li Xin and led troops out together. A fierce battle lasted long, and they again lost and returned into the fortresses. The soldiers were drying up from thirst.

Ju An and Li Xin said, “General Jiang’s force has not arrived yet. I do not know why.”

Xin answered, “I shall die if I must and cut a path out in exchange for rescue.” He led out several dozen riders, broke the gates, and charged forth.

The troops of Yong Province surrounded him on all sides. He broke through in a wild charge and only escaped with his life, though badly wounded; he alone survived while the rest were swallowed by the confusion.

That night a strong north wind rose, dark clouds covered the sky, and heavy snow fell. By that fortune the men in the fortresses ground the snow and shared it for food.

Li Xin did break the encirclement and for two days moved by a side path over the western ridge. He arrived precisely where Jiang Wei’s forces were gathered and knelt to the ground as he dismounted: “Both fortresses at Qushan are now fully encircled by Wei troops and cut off from water. Only by the heavy snow did they survive by grinding it for food. It is perilous indeed.”

Jiang Wei said, “I did not fail in haste; it was because the Qiang force had not arrived.” He ordered Li Xin treated in the river town.

Then he asked Xiahou Ba, “The Qiang force has not arrived, and Wei’s siege at Qushan is severe. What is your strongest opinion?”

Xiahou Ba answered, “When the Qiang arrive at Qushan both fortresses will fall. I expect all the Yong Province forces will come there to press the attack. Yongzhou city will then stand empty in the rear. General, ride to Niutou Mountain and strike from behind. Guo Huai and Chen Tai must return to save Yongzhou; then the encirclement at Qushan will lift.”

Jiang Wei rejoiced: “That is the best course.” He led his troops toward Niutou Mountain.

When Chen Tai saw that Li Xin had broken out, he told Guo Huai, “If Li Xin has sent an emergency message to Jiang Wei, he will think most of our troops are at Qushan and attempt to cut off his rear at Niutou Mountain. His Excellency should send one army to capture the Tao River and cut Shu’s supply route. I will send half our force straight to Niutou Mountain and strike.” Guo Huai agreed and sent one army to take the Tao waters by a hidden route. Chen Tai marched with one force toward Niutou Mountain.

When Jiang Wei’s troops reached Niutou Mountain, they suddenly heard their vanguard shouting that Wei soldiers had blocked the route. Jiang Wei rushed to the front and inspected. Chen Tai shouted: “So you want to strike us in Yongzhou? I have waited long enough!” Jiang Wei grew furious, raised his spear and spurred his horse straight at Chen Tai.

Chen Tai met him with his blade. After fewer than three exchanges, he withdrew in defeat. Jiang Wei closed and fought until Wei troops began retreating, pulling back to the ridge.

Jiang Wei drew up his camp below Niutou Mountain. Each day he ordered constant skirmishes that yielded neither victory nor defeat.

Xiahou Ba said to Jiang Wei, “This is no place for long entrenchment. Repeated fighting with no clear result is a maneuver to draw troops in. There is another plan behind it. Better to retreat for now and make fresh calculations.”

While they spoke, reports arrived: Guo Huai had taken an army and captured the Tao River, cutting off supplies.

Jiang Wei was shocked. He ordered Xiahou Ba to withdraw first. Jiang Wei covered the rear himself.

Chen Tai split his army into five routes and chased after them.

Jiang Wei held all five avenues alone and stopped Wei’s troops. Chen Tai then arranged for troops to climb the ridge, where arrows and stones came down like rain. In haste Jiang Wei withdrew toward the Tao waters, and Guo Huai rode in with his men. Jiang Wei sent his troops into rapid collision. The Wei lines blocked their path, close as an iron vat. He fought desperately to break through, losing half his men and finally bolting for Yangping Pass.

Another army reached the front next. At its head a major general rode out, sitting his horse crosswise with a sword drawn. The man had a round face and broad ears, a thick-lipped mouth, a left eye with a black swelling, and several black hairs rising from the swelling. He was Sima Shi, General of Agile Cavalry, the eldest son of Sima Yi.

Jiang Wei thundered, “How dare this mere boy block my way home?” He pressed his horse, raised his spear, and rode straight at him. Sima Shi met him with his blade. In only three exchanges Jiang Wei broke through and cut Sima Shi down. He slipped away and ran for Yangping Pass.

Those in the city opened the gates for Jiang Wei’s entry.

Sima Shi came to seize the gate as well. Both sides loosed crossbow fire. One release cast ten bolts: this was the repeated-bolt device left as Master Wuhou’s parting inheritance.

The final verse of the chapter is:

難支此日三軍敗，獨賴當年十矢傳。

This day no force could hold back the three armies from breaking, and only by the old ten-bolt shaft does one still endure.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Power under the Wei Lord Returns to the Sima Clan; Jiang Wei Is Defeated at Niutou Mountain

chapters.html:
Ding Feng draws his short weapons in the snow.
Sun Jun works a close-knit stratagem in the hall.

Jiang Wei was just setting out when he ran into Sima Shi with troops raised to intercept him. When he had captured Yong Province, Guo Huai had flown in to report at court. The Wei Emperor and Sima Yi had already settled counsel together. Sima Yi sent his eldest son, Sima Shi, with fifty thousand troops to come to Yong Province to aid the campaign. When Sima Shi heard that Guo Huai had driven back the Shu army, he judged the Shu forces weak and moved out midway to strike them. He rode straight to Yangping Pass, but there Jiang Wei applied the linked-bolt method passed down by Wuhou: more than a hundred hidden linked crossbows were set on both sides, each machine discharging ten bolts at once, all of them poison shafts. As both sides loosed together, the front ranks of men and horses fell by the tens of thousands. In the confusion, Sima Shi fled for his life and turned back.

In Qushan City, the Shu general Ju An, seeing that reinforcements would not arrive, opened the gates and surrendered to Wei. Jiang Wei had his battalions broken apart in the tens of thousands, then led the broken troops back to Hanzhong and encamped. Sima Shi returned to Luoyang. In the autumn of the third year of Jia Ping, Sima Yi sickened and worsened, and called his two sons to his bedside to charge them.

“Over the years I have served Wei, and I have been made Grand Tutor; a position above ordinary ministerial rank. Others all suspect I harbor some hidden design, and I have long feared that suspicion. After my death, you two must govern the state well. Be vigilant! Be vigilant!”

When he had spoken, he died. The eldest, Sima Shi, and the second, Sima Zhao, both reported to Emperor Cao Fang. The emperor granted him full rites, enhanced honors, and posthumous title. He made Shi Grand General, with overall charge of confidential matters in the Secretariat, and made Zhao Great General of Agile Cavalry.

As for Wu’s ruler Sun Quan, he had first made Sun Deng his crown prince; Sun Deng was born to Lady Xu and had died in the fourth year of Chiwu. He then established his second son Sun He, born to the Lady of Langye, as crown prince. Because Sun He fell out with Princess Quan, the princess slandered him, and Sun Quan deposed him. Sun He died in bitterness and resentment. Sun Quan then made his third son Sun Liang his crown prince; Sun Liang was born to Lady Pan. At this time both Lu Xun and Zhuge Jin had already died, and all major and minor affairs of state fell to Zhuge Ke.

On the first day of the eighth month of the first year of Taihe, a fierce wind suddenly rose; the seas of Jiang and the estuary heaved. Water reached eight chi deep on level ground. All the pines and cypresses Sun Quan had planted over the years were torn up, carried all the way and stuck upright in the road outside Jianye’s south gate. Alarmed by this, Sun Quan became ill. By the end of that August, his illness had deepened. He summoned Grand Tutor Zhuge Ke and Grand Commandant Lü Dai to his bedside to entrust the realm’s future. He died after finishing his charges.

He reigned twenty-four years and died at seventy-one years of age. That was in the fifteenth year of Yānxi in Shu-Han. Later writers put it in verse:

“Blue-black-bearded, blue-eyed, all call him a hero;\ Only he could make ministers and retainers serve with loyalty to the end.\ For twenty-four years he raised a mighty enterprise,\ Dragon coiled and tiger crouched firm in Jiangdong.”

After Sun Quan died, Zhuge Ke enthroned Sun Liang as emperor, issued a general amnesty, and changed the era to Da Xing Yuan; Sun Quan was given the posthumous title Great Emperor and buried at Jiangling. Agents had already entered this news quickly and sent it to Luoyang. When Sima Shi learned Sun Quan was dead, he proposed raising forces against Wu. The Prefect of the Secretariat, Fu Jia, replied,

“Wu has the natural advantage of the Yangtze. The late emperor attacked there again and again but could not force success. It is better to hold each frontier. That is the highest strategy.”

Shi said, “Heaven’s pattern changes every thirty years; can war always remain with the two powers at a standstill? I intend to strike Wu.”

Sima Zhao added, “Sun Quan has just died, and Sun Liang is young and weak; this opening can surely be exploited.”

So Sima Shi ordered the General Who Conquers the South, Wang Chang, to lead one hundred thousand men against Nanjun, the General Who Conquers the East, Hu Zun, to lead one hundred thousand against Dongxing, and the Inspector Who Guards the South, Guanqiu Jian, to lead one hundred thousand against Wuchang. They moved out on three routes. He also sent his brother Sima Zhao as Great Commander to take overall control of all three armies.

In the tenth month of winter that year, Sima Zhao’s force reached the Wu border, where they camped. He called Wang Chang, Hu Zun, and Guanqiu Jian into his command tent to plan and said, “The most critical point in eastern Wu is Dongxing Commandery. They have raised a great embankment there and two fortresses at either side, to block an attack from behind Chaohu Lake. The generals here must study this carefully.”

He then ordered Wang Chang and Guanqiu Jian each to lead ten thousand troops to the flanks and refrain from advancing; when Dongxing was taken, then all would move together. The two obeyed and withdrew. Zhao then made Hu Zun the vanguard over all three forces, ordered him forward to build a floating bridge first and seize the great embankment at Dongxing. If he could take the two side fortresses, it would be a great feat.

Hu Zun obeyed and brought his troops to construct the floating bridge.

Over in Wu, Grand Tutor Zhuge Ke heard that Wei’s three columns were coming and assembled his officers to deliberate. The General Who Pacifies the North, Ding Feng, said, “Dongxing is the key place in eastern Wu. If we lose it, Nanjun and Wuchang are in danger.”

Zhuge Ke said, “That is well said. You may take three thousand water troops down the river. I will then order Lü Qu, Tang Zi, and Liu Zuan each to bring ten thousand infantry from three routes to relieve them. When the chain-cannon sounds in unison, you are to advance together. I myself will bring the main force behind them.”

Ding Feng took the command and led three thousand soldiers by water, dividing them into thirty ships and moving toward Dongxing.

Hu Zun crossed the floating bridge and camped on the embankment. He sent Huan Jia and Han Zong to attack the two cities. In the left city stood the Wu general Quan Yi on guard; in the right city, General Liu Lue. These two cities were high and strong, and pressed attack could not break them. Quan and Liu, seeing the great Wei force, dared not sortie, and held their walls.

Hu Zun camped the army under a temporary fort at Xuzhou. It was midwinter, and snow fell heavily. He and his commanders sat down in the snow for an enormous banquet. Suddenly there came word that thirty warships had arrived on the water. Hu Zun rode out from camp to inspect. He saw the ships mooring one after another along the bank, about a hundred men aboard each. He returned to the pavilion and told his commanders,

“It is only three thousand men; why should we fear it?”

He merely ordered scouting detachments forward and kept drinking before him. Ding Feng cast his ships out upon the water in a single line. Then he told his captains,

“A true man of worth must seize fame and rank today!”

He ordered his men to strip off armor and helmets, leaving long spears and halberds behind and carrying only short blades. The Wei troops laughed at the sight and made no further preparation.

When the chain-cannon thundered three times in a row, Ding Feng drew his saber first and leapt onto the bank. All the men unsheathed their short swords and followed him ashore, cutting into the Wei camp. The Wei soldiers were unready. Han Zong rushed out a great halberd from before the command tent to meet them, but Ding Feng seized him, drove blade downward, and cut him over in one stroke.

Huan Jia broke out from the left flank and quickly thrust with his spear at Ding Feng; Ding Feng caught the shaft and held it. Huan Jia dropped the spear and ran. Ding Feng’s blade flew out and struck him on the left shoulder. Huan Jia staggered a little and then fell. Ding Feng closed and stabbed him with a spear. Three thousand Wu soldiers surged in the Wei encampment, rushing this way and that.

Hu Zun mounted in haste and rode off, forcing a way through. The Wei soldiers ran together up the floating bridge, but the bridge was already broken; most went into the water and drowned. How many died in the snow, no one could count. Their carriages, mounts, horses, and military stores all fell into Wu hands.

When Sima Zhao, Wang Chang, and Guanqiu Jian heard of the defeat at Dongxing, they too set their troops to withdrawal.

Returning, Zhuge Ke’s forces reached Dongxing, and after disbanding and rewarding the men he gathered his generals.

“Sima Zhao has been beaten and has turned back north. This is the right moment to press into the Central Plains.” He dispatched one party with letters to Shu, asking Jiang Wei to advance north to attack and offering to divide the realm in two. At the same time he raised two hundred thousand troops to strike the Central Plains.

When they were ready to march, a single strip of white vapor rose from the earth, blocking the three armies and concealing the opposite side.

Jiang Yan said, “That is white-rainbow omen. It presages the loss of soldiers and a broken army. Great Tutor, you should return to court; do not attack Wei.”

Zhuge Ke flew into a rage.

“How dare you speak inauspiciously and dampen my soldiers’ spirit?” he shouted, and shouted down a warrior to execute him.

All begged for mercy; Zhuge Ke then demoted Jiang Yan to commoner status. He pressed the army onward. Ding Feng said,

“Since Wei holds Xincheng as the key choke point, if we take this city first, Sima Zhao will lose heart.”

Zhuge Ke rejoiced and drove forward to Xincheng. Zhang Te, governor of the gate, saw the Wu host arriving in force, shut his gates and held firm. Zhuge Ke ordered his men to encircle the city on all sides.

A swift messenger had already reported at Luoyang. The clerk Yu Song told Sima Shi,

“Zhuge Ke is now besieging Xincheng and it is not yet time to give him open battle. Wu troops have marched far, they are short of provisions, and they will turn back when grain is gone. If we wait for them to begin withdrawing, then strike, we shall win utterly. We must still guard against possible incursions by Shu across the border.”

Shi accepted the point. He ordered Sima Zhao to lead one division to aid Guo Huai in guarding against Jiang Wei while Guanqiu Jian and Hu Zun held Wu back.

Zhuge Ke kept the siege of Xincheng going month after month without success. He ordered all his generals to throw themselves at the walls, and any who were slow were executed on the spot. His men attacked with full effort, and the northeastern corner of the city was about to fall.

Inside the city, Zhang Te had worked out a stratagem. He sent a man who was clever in argument, carrying bound registers, into the Wu camp to meet Zhuge Ke and report,

“In Wei law, if a besieged city has resisted one hundred days with no relief force arriving and then the commander breaks out to surrender, his household is not punished. Your General has been besieging this city for more than ninety days. Grant us a few more days’ delay, and I, together with the city’s command, will bring out soldiers and townspeople and surrender. I have here prepared the registers of the households.”

Zhuge Ke believed him fully and withdrew men and mounts, thus suspending the assault. The truth was that Zhang Te’s delaying measure merely drew Wu’s men away. He then broke down houses inside the city, repaired the breaches, and when they were sound he climbed the walls and shouted, “We still have grain for half a year. How could we surrender to Wu’s dogs? Let us fight through all!”

Zhuge Ke was furious and drove the army harder. Arrows flew chaotically from below. One struck him in the center of the forehead, and he flipped backward from his horse. His officers brought him back to camp. The wound, a severe puncture, broke open and bled.

The men had no fighting spirit, and the weather was hot and oppressive; soldiers fell sick by the multitude. When the wound cooled somewhat, he tried to urge another attack. The quartermaster reported,

“Everyone is sick. How can they fight?”

Zhuge Ke shouted in fury,

“Any man who speaks again of sickness will be beheaded!”

Hearing this, numbers slipped away in terror. A report then came in that Commander Cai Lin had taken his own detachment and defected to Wei. Zhuge Ke was greatly shaken. He mounted and rode through each camp; indeed every soldier’s face was yellowed and swollen with illness. He ordered a full withdrawal back toward Wu.

A courier from the interior had already informed Guanqiu Jian. Jian raised all his force and then ambushed, and the Wu army was badly beaten as it fell back.

Shamed deeply, Zhuge Ke feigned illness and stayed away from court. Sun Liang himself went to his house to inquire after him. Civil and military officials all came to make their respects. Fearing gossip, Zhuge Ke first searched for every officer and general’s fault. Minor mistakes meant banishment to the frontiers, and grave ones meant execution by beheading before all.

So every official within and without was in fear. He then set his trusted men Zhang Yue and Zhu En to command the palace guard as his sharp teeth and claws.

Now Sun Jun, whose courtesy name was Ziyuan, was a great-grandson of Sun Jing, a younger brother of Sun Jian, and was the son of Sun Gong. Sun Quan had loved him greatly in his day and had put him in charge of the palace cavalry. When he learned that Zhuge Ke had made Zhang Yue and Zhu En command the palace cavalry and taken his authority away, his heart burned with anger.

Teng Yin, Grand Minister of Rites, had long been at odds with Zhuge Ke and took his moment to tell Sun Jun,

“Zhuge Ke monopolizes power and abuses cruelty. He kills gentlemen and ministers, and clearly intends to be disloyal. You are imperial kin. Why not act first?”

Sun Jun answered,

“I have harbored this intent for a long while. I will now submit it to the Son of Heaven and ask for an order to execute him.”

So Sun Jun and Teng Yin appeared before Emperor Sun Liang and confidentially reported the matter.

The emperor said,

“I also find this man most terrifying. I have often wished to remove him but had not found a chance. If you are truly loyal, plot this in secret.”

Teng Yin replied,

“Your Majesty may summon Zhuge Ke here with an official audience. Conceal warriors under their armor. Let them stand ready at the first cry of a clinked cup, and kill him in his seat, so later trouble is cut off.”

The Son of Heaven agreed.

Meanwhile, after the defeat and return, Zhuge Ke had stayed home pretending to be ill and was feverish in his thoughts. One day he happened to go into the central hall, when he saw a man in coarse mourning cloth walk in. He barked at him; the man was stunned and confused. Zhuge Ke seized and interrogated him, and the man said,

“I came because my father has just died and I entered the city to find a monk to plead my case. I happened upon this shrine and entered, and did not know it was the residence of the Grand Tutor. How I have come here, I do not know.”

Zhuge Ke was angry and summoned the gate soldiers for questioning.

They told him,

“We are only dozens; we all held spears and guarded the gate, never leaving, and saw no one enter.”

Furious, he beheaded them all that instant.

That night Zhuge Ke did not sleep well. He suddenly heard a sound in the front hall like thunderclap. He came out to see. The central beam had split in two. He staggered in fear into his sleeping room. Then, when a cold wind rose, he saw the slain mourner in coarse robes and dozens of the gate soldiers he had beheaded, each with a severed head, demanding his life. Zhuge Ke collapsed, stunned, and only after some time came to himself.

The next morning, as he washed his face, he noticed that the water smelled strongly of blood. He ordered his maidservants to bring fresh tubs and replace them by the score, yet every one smelled the same.

Even as he sat in this dread, news came that the Son of Heaven had sent an envoy calling the Grand Tutor to a banquet. Zhuge Ke made ready his carriage train. As he was about to leave, a yellow dog seized his robe and whined as if crying. Zhuge Ke snapped, “Is this beast mocking me?” and shouted servants away from it. He then took his seat in the carriage and rolled out.

After only a few paces, he saw before the cart a white streak of vapor rising from the earth and climbing like a white ribbon into the sky. He was greatly unsettled. His trusted officer Zhang Yue stepped ahead to the carriage and warned in a low voice,

“Today the palace has made this banquet. I do not know good or ill. My lord should not enter lightly.”

When Zhuge Ke heard this, he ordered the carriage back. In fewer than ten paces, Sun Jun and Teng Yin rode up to it and asked,

“Why does the Grand Tutor turn back so soon?”

Zhuge Ke said,

“Sudden illness in my belly; I cannot appear before the Son of Heaven.”

Teng Yin said,

“The court has arranged this gathering because your service to the realm leaves you unaccounted for at headquarters; they called you to this banquet to discuss matters of state. Even with your pain, you must force yourself to come.”

Zhuge Ke accepted his words and entered the palace with Sun Jun and Teng Yin. Zhang Yue followed as well.

When Zhuge Ke came before Emperor Sun Liang, after saluting he took his seat. The emperor ordered another round of wine. Zhuge Ke was wary and declined,

“My frail body cannot endure drinking.”

Sun Jun said,

“The Grand Tutor keeps medicinal wine at his residence. Could it be brought?”

Zhuge Ke replied,

“Yes.”

He sent a servant back to fetch the wine he had prepared himself; only then did he drink with confidence.

After several rounds the emperor rose first, claiming other business. Sun Jun came down from the hall, removed his formal robes, put on a short jacket under ringed mail, and drew a fine weapon. Ascending again, he shouted,

“The Son of Heaven orders the execution of this traitorous rebel!”

Zhuge Ke was terrified. He flung down his cup and tried to draw his sword, but his head had already fallen from his body.

When Zhang Yue saw Sun Jun kill Zhuge Ke, he swung his saber forward to meet him. Sun Jun sidestepped the blade edge and grazed his left finger. Sun Jun turned and cut Zhang Yue’s right arm. The palace guards surged in together and cut Zhang Yue down, hacking him to meat pulp. Sun Jun at once ordered his men to seize Zhuge Ke’s household, and ordered one to wrap the heads of Zhang Yue and Zhuge Ke in a rush-mat and load them on a small cart, then carry them out and cast them into the disorderly pit of tombs at Shizigang outside the city’s south gate.

Now Zhuge Ke’s wife, in her chamber, was unsettled and restless in every motion and stillness. Suddenly a maid entered and asked, “Why does your whole body smell of blood?”

The maid abruptly bared her teeth in feral anger, leapt up, and struck her head against the beam, then screamed in a loud voice,

“I am Zhuge Ke! Sun Jun the traitorous villain has plotted my death!”

Zhuge Ke’s whole household, old and young, was overtaken by panic and weeping.

Before long, troops arrived and surrounded the estate. They bound all of Zhuge Ke’s household, old and young alike, and took them to the city prison offices to be beheaded.

That was in the tenth month of winter, the second year of Jianxing.

In the past, when Zhuge Jin was alive, he had seen how Zhuge Ke’s brilliance burned brightest in public and sighed,

“This one is no man to guard his own household!”

Also Wei’s Director of Civil Appointments, Zhang Ji, had once told Sima Shi,

“Zhuge Ke will not live long.”

Shi asked why, and Ji replied,

“He threatens to overawe his lord; how can he last long?”

And now this had proved his words.

After Sun Jun killed Zhuge Ke, Emperor Sun Liang made Sun Jun Chancellor and Grand General and titled him Marquis of Fuchun, and made him head of all military affairs both inside and out. From then on, authority and command of arms returned entirely to Sun Jun.

Now Jiang Wei was in Chengdu when he received Zhuge Ke’s letter asking for help to strike Wei. He entered court, obtained the Later Ruler’s approval, and raised a great army again, then launched another northern campaign.

It is fittingly put:

The field is raised once, but no victory is yet won;\ twice the rebels are fought and still sought to be vanquished.\ How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Ding Feng Draws His Short Weapons in the Snow, Sun Jun Sets a Covert Plot in the Hall

chapters.html:
To lay a strange stratagem that entangles Sima amid the Han generals; to depose Cao Fang and bring retribution on the house of Wei.

In the sixteenth year of Yanxi in Shu-Han, in the autumn, Jiang Wei raised an army of two hundred thousand and sent Liao Hua and Zhang Yi forward as left and right vanguards, Xiahou Ba as his adviser, and Zhang Ni as the supply officer. The main force marched out through Yangping Pass to strike Wei.

Jiang Wei conferred with Xiahou Ba. “Earlier we marched against Yong Province, failed, and withdrew. If we go out again now, they will be ready. What better course do you have?”

Xiahou Ba replied, “Among the commanderies above Long Pass, only Nan’an has the broadest stores of grain and silver. If we take it first, it is enough to secure our base. We failed before because the Qiang did not arrive. Send men now to meet the Qiang on the right of the Longs, then advance from Shiying and strike straight for Nanan.”

Jiang Wei was greatly pleased. “Your suggestion is excellent.” He then dispatched Qizheng as envoy with gold, jewels, and Shu silk to the Qiang and made peace with the Qiang king. Min-dang, delighted by the gifts, raised five thousand troops and had his general E He Shaoge lead a huge vanguard, then marched south toward Nanan.

When Guihai, the Left General of Wei, learned the report, he sent a flying dispatch to Luoyang. Sima Shi asked the assembled officers, “Who is willing to advance against the Shu forces?” Fuguo General Xu Zhi answered, “I volunteer.” Sima Shi had long known Xu Zhi to be exceptionally brave; in his heart, he was greatly pleased. He appointed Xu Zhi vanguard and named Sima Zhao chief commander-in-chief, commanding the army west toward Longxi.

When their army reached Dongting, they met Jiang Wei and the two armies immediately formed battle lines. Xu Zhi brandished a mountain-cleaving great axe, rode out, and called for single combat. Liao Hua rode to meet him in the Shu lines. After not many exchanges, Liao Hua was thrown off in retreat, while Zhang Yi pressed forward with his horse and spear; after not many exchanges, he too was driven out into the ranks. Xu Zhi drove his troops to envelop and slaughter, and the Shu army was routed and withdrew more than thirty li. Sima Zhao also called his men back and withdrew each to his camp.

Jiang Wei conferred with Xiahou Ba again. “Xu Zhi is exceedingly brave. By what plan can we capture him?”

Xiahou Ba said, “Tomorrow, feign a defeat and win him with an ambush.”

Jiang Wei replied, “Sima Zhao is Zhongda’s son. Does he not know the laws of war? If he sees the terrain shielding him, he will not dare pursuit. I have seen the Wei soldiers cut our supply lines more than once. If we use this stratagem now and draw him in, we can behead Xu Zhi.”

He called for Liao Hua and gave him specific instructions, then did the same with Zhang Yi, and both officers took their troops away. At the same time he ordered the soldiers to scatter iron caltrops along the road and to stack many deer antler stakes outside the camp, as if making a long plan.

For several days, Xu Zhi repeatedly drew out his men and prodded at skirmishes while the Shu troops did not come out. A scouting rider reported to Sima Zhao, “The Shu troops are behind Iron-Cage Pass, using wooden oxen and flow horses to move grain. They seem to be making long-term preparations and are only waiting for Qiang support.”

Sima Zhao summoned Xu Zhi. “When we won against Shu before, it was because we cut their supply route. Now the Shu are carrying supplies behind Iron-Cage Pass. Tonight you are to lead five thousand men and cut their supply road. The Shu troops will then withdraw on their own.”

Xu Zhi took the order. Near the first watch of the night, he moved toward Iron-Cage Pass. He truly saw more than two hundred Shu soldiers driving over a hundred wooden oxen and flow horses loaded with provisions.

At one command the Wei force shouted and Xu Zhi immediately blocked them. The Shu dropped all the grain and fled. Xu Zhi split his men in half: one half escorted the captured grain back to camp, and he led the other half in pursuit.

Within ten li they could not catch them. In front, chariot engines suddenly blocked the road. Xu Zhi ordered his men to dismount and break apart the heavy carts. Instantly, fire sprang up on both sides. He hauled back his horse and turned away.

Behind him, at another narrow and steep place in the mountain, another line of cart engines also blocked the way, and another flash of fire burst forth. Through smoke and fire they plunged forward, horses and men erupting through. A loud signal report came from afar. Two lines of troops surged in: Liao Hua on the left, Zhang Yi on the right. They slaughtered for a stretch, and the Wei force was routed.

Xu Zhi fought on in desperation and alone. His men were exhausted, his horse spent. As he ran, a detachment of troops reached him from ahead—Jiang Wei himself.

Xu Zhi was shocked and at a loss. Jiang Wei drove his spear through him, pitching him off the saddle; he fell backward from the horse, and the press of blades from the surrounding soldiers cut him down. The men Xu Zhi had left to escort the grain were also captured by Xiahou Ba and all surrendered. Xiahou Ba ordered the Wei soldiers to put on Shu armor and ride with horses, then told them to sit in harness, wave Wei battle flags, and slip back to Wei camp by a side route. The Wei troops, seeing their own men return, opened the gate and brought them in. The Shu men then slaughtered within the camp.

Sima Zhao was greatly shocked. He mounted in haste and turned to leave, but Liao Hua came at him head-on. Sima Zhao could not push forward. As he tried to retreat, Jiang Wei was already leading men in through the side path.

With no way to flee in any direction, Sima Zhao could only order his men to hold and defend atop Iron-Cage Mountain. That mountain had only one road, and all other sides were steep and hard to climb. At its top there was but one spring that could barely water a hundred men. At that moment, six thousand men stood under Zhao, and Jiang Wei had cut off all the passes. The spring water atop the mountain was not enough; men and horses were dried with thirst.

Looking up at the sky, Sima Zhao sighed deeply: “I will die on this ground.”

A later poet wrote:

Jiang Wei’s wonderful design does not wait idly; the Wei army is trapped in Iron-Cage. When Pang Juan first entered Maling Way, Xiang Yu first encircled Jiuli Mountain.

Master Clerk Wang Tao interjected, “Formerly Geng Gong was trapped and knelt at a well to find its spring. Why does the general not do the same?”

Zhao followed his counsel. He climbed to the top spring, knelt again, and prayed:

“I, Zhao, come by imperial order to drive away the Shu army. If death comes to me here, let the Sweet Spring run dry. I will then sever my own throat and command all my troops to surrender at once. If Heaven has not ended my years, may it send up the Sweet Spring at once and preserve my men’s lives.”

The prayer ended; the water surged up, and no one could say it would not run dry. Thus they did not die.

Meanwhile Jiang Wei held the Wei force trapped below and told his officers, “Once upon a time, Chancellor Zhuge Liang in Shangfang Valley failed to capture Sima Yi. I have long rued it. Now Sima Zhao must surely be caught by me.”

When Guihai heard that Sima Zhao was besieged on Iron-Cage Mountain, he prepared to bring troops. Chen Tai said, “Jiang Wei has already joined with the Qiang and intends to seize Nanan first. The Qiang have now arrived. If General Guihai now withdraws to rescue him, they will use the opening to strike our rear. Let us first send men to feign surrender to the Qiang and win from within. Only after this troop is removed can we rescue the siege on Iron-Cage.”

Guihai agreed. He ordered Chen Tai to lead five thousand men straight into the Qiang king’s camp, unarmored, and kneel in tears.

“Guo Huai has falsely grown proud and always had a heart to kill Tai. For that reason, I have come to surrender. The strength and weakness of Guo Huai’s army are all known to me. Tonight I would be able to lead one force to sack your camp. Then it will surely succeed. Once we reach the Wei camp, there will already be accomplices inside.”

Min-dang rejoiced. He therefore ordered E He Shaoge to accompany Chen Tai in leading the raid on Wei camp.

E He Shaoge told Tai’s men to follow behind and had Tai lead the Qiang vanguard. In the second watch of the night they all reached the Wei camp. Its gates were flung open. Tai entered first on horseback.

As E He Shaoge rode hard with spear aloft into the camp, he called out only one cry of pain and, with horse and body, fell headlong into a pit. Tai charged in from behind. Guihai came from the left, and the Qiang ranks descended into confusion. They trampled one another in panic; the dead were countless, and those who lived all surrendered. E He Shaoge cut his own throat.

Guihai and Chen Tai drove their men straight to the Qiang camp. When the Great King Min-dang hurried out of his tent and mounted, he was taken alive by Wei soldiers and brought before Guihai.

Guihai leaped from the saddle, personally unbound himand spoke gently: “The court has ever regarded you as loyal and upright. Why, then, aid the men of Shu?” Min-dang was ashamed and confessed guilt.

Guihai said, “You, in your role as vanguard, now go and break the encirclement on Iron-Cage. Disperse the Shu army, and when you have done so I will petition the Son of Heaven to grant you rich rewards.”

Min-dang obeyed. He led the Qiang in front and the Wei soldiers in the rear and rushed straight to Iron-Cage Mountain.

It was the third watch. He sent men ahead first to report to Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei was overjoyed and ordered him to enter and be received.

Most Wei soldiers were mixed among the Qiang ranks; by the time they reached the Shu camp, Jiang Wei had ordered the main force to encamp outside the camp. Min-dang then led more than one hundred men to the center-tent. Jiang Wei and Xiahou Ba came out to welcome them. Before the Qiang king could begin to speak, a Wei general struck from behind and sprang up to kill. Jiang Wei was shocked and quickly mounted and fled.

Qiang and Wei soldiers entered together; the Shu army tore itself apart in confusion and each man fled to save himself.

Jiang Wei had no weapon at hand. Only a bow and a quiver at his waist. In his haste, his arrows all fell away, leaving the quiver empty. He ran toward the hills. Behind him Guihai advanced, driving troops. Seeing Jiang Wei with no blade or spear, he spurred his horse and chased him with steel spear in hand.

As they came near, Jiang Wei pulled the bowstring as if loading it, and for more than ten times it twanged. Guihai dodged several times and could not see an arrow strike; realizing Jiang Wei had no arrows, he hooked his steel spear, set arrowhead and bow to it, and shot.

Jiang Wei darted away sharply, caught it in a motion, and pulled it back against the bowstring. When Guihai closed in, Jiang Wei aimed at the front of his face and loosed with all his strength. Guihai was hit in the string and tumbled from the horse.

Jiang Wei wheeled his horse back to strike Guihai. Wei troops surged up. There was no time for him to finish the stroke. He only managed to wrench out Guihai’s spear and ride on. Wei soldiers did not dare to chase further; they carried Guihai back to camp and pulled out the arrowhead. Blood would not stop and he died.

Sima Zhao came down from the mountain and pursued, then returned halfway.

Xiahou Ba escaped shortly afterward and fled with Jiang Wei together. Jiang Wei had broken many men and horses on the way; he could not keep his forces assembled and withdrew back to Hanzhong. Though he had been defeated in battle, he had shot and killed Guo Huai, slain Xu Zhi, and struck fear into the Wei state, compensating for some of his failures with merit.

Later Sima Zhao rewarded the Qiang soldiers and dispatched them home, then returned to Luoyang. He and his brother Sima Shi then monopolized the court, and all ministers dared not disobey.

Whenever Cao Fang, the Son of Heaven, saw Shi enter court, he shuddered uncontrollably, as if pricked by a needle in the back. One day when he convened court, he saw Sima Shi arriving with his sword hung on his waist on the main hall platform and hurried from his seat to receive him.

Shi laughed. “There is no ritual for a ruler to welcome one who serves him as a subject. Please remain at ease.”

Soon, when officials presented matters, Sima Shi settled each individually and offered no report to Cao Fang. After a short while he withdrew, stepped proud from the hall, and took his carriage out of the inner court. He was surrounded before and behind by not fewer than several thousand armed men and horsemen. Cao Fang returned to the rear hall. Looking around, only three attendants remained at his side: Xiàxiu (Xiahou Xuan), Grand Minister of Rites, Li Feng, director of the Central Secretariat, and Zhang Ji, Grand Master of the Imperial Household. Zhang Ji was Empress Zhang’s father, and thus Cao Fang’s father-in-law.

Fang drove away nearby attendants and spoke in seclusion with the three. He took Zhang Ji’s hand and wept. “Sima Shi treats me like a child, and he tramples the hundred officials like weeds. The realm and altars surely will pass to him before long!” After speaking, he wept aloud.

Li Feng pleaded, “Your Majesty need not worry. Though I am not accomplished, I will obey your decree and gather the virtuous and strong of all quarters to wipe out this traitor.”

Xiahou Xuan added, “My brother Xiahou Ba surrendered to Shu because he feared Sima brothers plotting him. If we now exterminate this traitor, my brother will surely return. I am an old kinsman of the state. How could I stand by while treacherous usurpers disturb the realm? I am ready to join your edict and pursue him.”

Cao Fang said, “I only fear we cannot do it.”

The three together wept and declared, “We swear to unite in heart and suppress this rebel bandit, and report our loyalty to Your Majesty.”

Cao Fang removed his dragon-and-phoenix silk robe, bit his fingertip, and wrote a blood edict, giving it to Zhang Ji with this charge: “My ancestor Emperor Wu executed Dong Cheng, because he did not keep matters close. You must be cautious and not let this slip outside.”

Li Feng said, “How can Your Majesty now speak such dangerous words? We are not men of Dong Cheng’s sort, and Sima Shi does not compare with the founder Wu. Do not doubt us.”

The three withdrew to the left of Donghua Gate. There they met Sima Shi coming with sword drawn and with hundreds of armed men at his back and side.

The three stood by the roadside. Shi asked, “Why are you three delayed in withdrawing from audience?”

Li Feng replied, “His Majesty is in the inner court reading, and the three of us were merely attending to reading with him.”

Shi asked, “What book did he read?”

Li Feng answered, “Books of the Xia, Shang, and Zhou dynasties.”

Shi said, “What does the Son of Heaven ask of those stories?”

Li Feng answered, “His Majesty asks: when Yi Yin steadied Shang and Duke of Zhou governed for regency, we all submitted that Sima Dajiang jun is both Yi Yin and Duke of Zhou.”

Shi laughed coldly. “Do you truly compare me with Yi Yin and Duke of Zhou? Your hearts in truth point to me as Wang Mang and Dong Zhuo!”

The three said, “We are all men under your command. How could we speak so?”

Shi was greatly angered. “You are all people of face-serving flattery! What was the crying in the intimate chamber with the Son of Heaven?”

The three answered, “It is not so.”

Shi barked, “Your eyes are still red with tears. How can you deny it?”

Xiahou Xuan knew the matter had leaked and shouted angrily, “What we wept for was the terror you brought upon your ruler. We feared you planned a usurpation!”

Shi in fury shouted for guards to seize Xiahou Xuan. Xiahou Xuan bared his sleeve, drew back his fists, and struck directly at Sima Shi but was caught by soldiers.

Shi ordered all three searched. Near Zhang Ji’s side a dragon-and-phoenix silk robe was found with blood writing on it. Presenting it to Shi, he saw that it was indeed the secret edict.

The edict read:

Sima Shi and my brother together hold the greater power and plot a usurpation. All the decrees issued by them are not by my will. All officials and officers in every command and camp, join in loyal duty and righteous service, overthrow these rebel ministers, and uphold the state. Great rewards will follow the accomplishment of this task.

On reading it, Sima Shi leapt in fury. “So you truly wished to plot the destruction of my brother and me! This cannot be endured!” He ordered all three to be beheaded by the waist in the market and for their three lineages to be exterminated. They never stopped cursing.

When brought to the eastern market, their teeth were all knocked out; each muttered curses until death.

Shi entered straight into the inner palace. Cao Fang was then speaking with Empress Zhang on the matter. Empress Zhang said, “There are many ears and eyes in the inner court; if this becomes known, it will endanger my rank and ranklessness in disgrace.” While she spoke, they saw Shi arrive; Empress Zhang was greatly startled.

Pressing his sword, Shi told Fang, “My father established Your Majesty as ruler; our merit is no less than that of Duke of Zhou. In serving Your Majesty, how am I different from Yi Yin? Yet now you return your grace into enmity and call merit a fault, gathering two or three minor ministers to plot against my brothers. Why?”

Fang replied, “I had no such intention.”

Shi drew from his sleeve the silk robe and cast it to the ground. “Who made this?”

Fang recoiled as if cast from heaven, color drained from him, and trembled as he answered, “These words were forced from me by others. How could I have dared this thought?”

Shi asked, “What penalty is for slandering a minister with false charges of revolt?”

Fang knelt and pleaded, “If I have any fault, I beg the Great General to pardon me.”

Shi replied, “Your Majesty, please rise. State law cannot be set aside.”

He then pointed toward Empress Zhang. “She is Zhang Ji’s daughter and must be removed.”

Fang wept and begged for mercy, but Shi refused. He shouted to his attendants to seize Empress Zhang. She was taken inside Donghua Gate and strangled to death with white silk cord.

A later poet wrote:

In former days the fallen Empress left the palace gate, Barefoot, she lamented, parting from the supreme one. Sima follows her precedent today; Heaven gives return in sons and grandsons for what was sown.

The next day Sima Shi convened the ministers in full court. “His Majesty is now licentious and without way, degraded by courtesans and favorites, listening to slander and closing the road of the worthy. His crime is worse than that of the Han’s Changyi; he cannot rule all under heaven. I shall, in accordance with the examples of Yi Yin and Huo Guang, set a new sovereign to preserve the state and pacify all beneath heaven. What say you?”

All responded, “Great General, to act as Yi Yin and Huo Guang did is to follow Heaven and the people. Who would dare to disobey?”
