Shi then, with many officials, entered Yongning Palace and reported to the Empress Dowager.

She asked, “For whom does Great General seek to enthrone as ruler?”

Shi replied, “I have watched Prince Cao Ju of Pengcheng; he is intelligent and compassionate and filial, and can be lord of the world.”

The empress dowager answered, “Prince Pengcheng is my old mother’s uncle. How can I set him as ruler? We have Gaozu of Gaoguixiang, Cao Mao, who is the Son of Wen Emperor and grandson as it should be. He is calm, respectful, and easy to yield. He can be established. All ministers, consider this carefully and at length.”

One official spoke, “Her words are correct. He can be established.”

They all turned to Sima Shi’s clan uncle, Sima Fu. Shi then sent an envoy to Yuancheng, summoning Cao Mao. He ordered the Empress Dowager to ascend Taiji Hall and summon Cao Fang, to rebuke:

“You are promiscuous and unrestrained in your debauchery, and lewdly keep close with courtesans and singers. You cannot bear the mandate of heaven. Submit the jade seals and belt immediately, recover the rank of King of Qi, and set out at once. Do not enter court until officially called.”

Fang knelt and wept before the Empress Dowager, gave over the regalia, mounted a royal carriage, and left in tears. Only a few loyal and righteous ministers accompanied him with sorrow.

A later poet wrote:

In former days Cao Man served Han and cheated the widows and orphans. Who would guess, more than forty years later, the widows and orphans would also be cheated?

In truth Cao Mao, style Yanshi, was a grandson of Emperor Wen and son of Ding Wang of Donghai, Lin. On that day, by Sima Shi’s order and with the empress dowager’s command, civil and military officials and guards assembled in full array outside Xiye Gate to greet him.

As Cao Mao arrived, he hurriedly offered respectful ritual. Grand Commandant Wang Su said, “Your Majesty should not be receiving ritual greetings.” Cao Mao said, “I am also a subject and how could I fail to offer the proper greetings?”

Officials and soldiers helped Cao Mao ascend the litter into the palace. He said, "I do not know why Her Excellency called me in this manner; how dare I ride in the carriage?" and then chose to walk on foot to the east hall of Taiji.

Sima Shi greeted him there, and Cao Mao prostrated first. Shi quickly helped him rise. Formalities being exchanged, Sima Shi introduced him to the empress dowager.

She said, “I saw in your youth the signs of a Son of Heaven. Now you may be lord of all under heaven. Be reverent and frugal, measure your means, spread virtue, and exercise benevolence. Do not dishonor your forefather.”

Cao Mao declined again and again. Shi ordered the ministers to escort him out of Taiji Hall. That day he was established as the new ruler; the Jianping Sixth Year became the first year of Zhengyuan. A general amnesty was issued for all under heaven. Sima Shi was granted the jade ceremonial ax as Great General. He entered court without dismounting, submitted memorials without naming to the throne, and carried his sword to the hall. All civil and military officials received titles and gifts.

In the spring of the second year of Zhengyuan, in the first month, a secret informer arrived in flight, reporting that Zhendong General Guanqiu Jian and Yangzhou Inspector Wen Qin had raised troops under the pretext of deposing this ruler.

Sima Shi was startled.

It was this:

Han ministers once carried a zeal to aid the Son of Heaven; yet Wei generals rise again to crush the rebel commander. How this will fare when meeting the enemy, How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: To Trap Sima, a Han General Uses a Wondrous Stratagem; Cao Fang Is Deposed, Requiting the House of Wei

chapters.html:
Wenyang rides alone against the host, and Jiang Wei lines his force with its back to the river and shatters the great enemy.

Yet in the second year of Zhengyuan, in the first month, Guanquiu Jian, courtesy name Zhonggong, a native of Wenxi in Henan, was Governor of Yang Province and Commander Who Guards the East, with command over the Huainan army and cavalry. When he heard that Sima Shi had usurped the authority to depose and enthrone, his heart burned with anger. His eldest son, Guanquiu Dian, said: “You hold the command in this region, Sima Shi has monopolized power and deposed the ruler; the state is in a dangerously brittle state. How can we sit idle in comfort?” Jian said, “My son speaks truly.” So he invited Governor Wen Qin to consult. Wen Qin had once been under Cao Shuang. On hearing that Jian invited him, he came at once to pay his visit. Jian brought him into the rear hall, and after the formalities were finished, as they spoke, Jian could not stop crying. Wen Qin asked the reason. Jian said, “Sima Shi acts on his own authority to depose and enthrone; can heaven and earth truly turn so, and not break my heart?” Wen Qin said, “If the Commander Who Guards the East is willing to act righteously and suppress the rebels, I am ready to give my life in support. My younger son, Wen Shu, called Ayang, has courage beyond ten thousand men and often wishes to kill Sima Shi and his brothers to avenge Cao Shuang. He may be used as the vanguard now.” Jian rejoiced and they swore an oath immediately by libation. The two then claimed that the Empress Dowager had issued a secret edict and ordered all Huainan officers and soldiers, both major and minor, to enter Shouchun and set up an altar in the west quarter. They slaughtered a white horse and drank blood in oath, and announced: Sima Shi had committed cruel and outrageous disorder. “Now, in obedience to the Empress Dowager’s secret decree, let all Huainan forces rise and punish the traitors in loyalty.” The troops all assented. Jian raised sixty thousand troops and stationed them at Xiangcheng. Wen Qin led twenty thousand troops as a roaming support force outside to coordinate. Jian sent summonses to the commanderies, ordering each to raise troops in support.

Yet now Sima Shi’s left eye was diseased, with painful swelling and itching. He ordered the physicians to cut it out and seal it with medicine, and he stayed in his office pavilion, nursing the wound for several days. Suddenly, news arrived that Huainan had raised the alarm. He called Grand Commandant Wang Su to consult. Wang Su said, “In earlier times, when Guan Yu’s might shook all beneath heaven, Sun Quan sent Lü Meng to take Jing Province and then tended the soldiers’ families. In that way, Guan’s troops collapsed. Now, the families of the Huainan soldiers all reside in the Central Plains. If we comfort them quickly and cut off their lines of return, their army will inevitably collapse.” Shi said, “Your words are exactly right. But I have only just had this eye tumor removed, and I cannot go on my own. If another goes, my heart will still be unsettled.” At his side, Secretary of the Secretariat Zhong Hui spoke up: “The Huai-Chu armies are strong and their edge is sharp. If another is sent to lead and retreat them, the result is mostly disadvantage. If one moment of slackness is allowed, the whole matter fails.” Shi stood suddenly and said, “If I do not go, I cannot break this treason.” He left his brother Sima Zhao behind in Luoyang to oversee the affairs of court. Sima Shi then took up a padded litter and, though unwell, rode east. He ordered the Commander Who Guards the East, Zhuge Dan, to supervise all Yu Province armies and advance from Anfeng Ford toward Shouchun. He ordered the General Who Conquers the East, Hu Zun, to command Qingzhou troops, advance through Qiaosong lands, and cut off their road of retreat. He also dispatched Yu Province Inspector Wang Ji, commanding the advanced battalion, to seize Zhennan first. Shi stationed his large army at Xiangyang and gathered civil and military officials in the camp for consultation.

Guanglu Xun Zheng Bao said, “Guanqiu Jian is good at plotting but lacks decisiveness; Wen Qin has valor but no wisdom. Now the large force is moving against him unexpectedly. Jiang and Huai foot soldiers are at their fiercest, and they should not be fought lightly. We should dig a deep ditch and raise high stockades to blunt that vigor. This is exactly General Yue’s strength of counsel.” Monitor Wang Ji said, “No. Huainan’s revolt is not the spontaneous unrest of soldier and commoner. It is all because they were forced by Guanquiu Jian’s power, and obeyed unwillingly. If the main force appears, they will surely crumble.” Shi said, “That is subtle counsel.” He then moved his force to the Yin River, setting the central camp at Yin Bridge. Wang Ji said, “Nanton is excellent ground to camp. You can seize it by night if you act quickly; if you delay, Guanquiu Jian will arrive first.” So Shi ordered Wang Ji to lead the vanguard down and encamp beneath Nanton city.

Now in Xiangcheng, Guanquiu Jian heard Sima Shi had already come and assembled his followers. Vanguard Ge Yong said, “Nanton is excellent: close to mountain and river, superb for camp. If Wei troops occupy it first, it will be hard to drive them out. Better seize it quickly.” Jian followed his suggestion and raised the troops to march on Nanton. As they were on the move, an outpost horseman from ahead reported that camp had already been established below Nanton. Jian did not trust the report at first; he went forward to inspect. As expected, banners filled the fields and the camp had been laid in ordered lines. When he returned to camp, he had no plan to respond. Just then a scout rider reported in breathless speed: “Commander Sun Jun of Eastern Wu has raised troops and crossed the river; he is attacking Shouchun.” Jian was greatly alarmed: “If Shouchun is lost, where can I return?” That night he withdrew his forces to Xiangcheng. When Sima Shi saw Guanquiu Jian’s troops withdraw, he gathered many officials for a meeting. The Imperial Clerk Fu Gu said, “Jian has withdrawn because he fears an attack by Wu. He will surely turn back to Xiangcheng and split his men to defend. The general should send one army to capture Lejia City, one to take Xiangcheng, and one to seize Shouchun. Then Huainan’s soldiers will all retreat. Deng Ai, Governor of Yanzhou, is quick-minded and talented. If he takes Lejia with force while we send heavy troops with him, defeating these rebels will not be difficult.” Shi approved and sent out envoys with orders: Deng Ai was to raise Yanzhou soldiers and take Lejia City; Shi would follow with his force to join him.

Still in Xiangcheng, Guanquiu Jian again sent riders to scout Lejia, fearing reinforcements. He asked Wen Qin to come to camp for counsel. Wen Qin said, “Commander, worry not. I and my rough son Wen Yang need only five thousand men to hold Lejia.” Jian rejoiced. Wen Qin and his son brought five thousand men to Lejia. The front troops reported: “To the west of Lejia City are all Wei troops, about ten thousand and more. From afar, I can see the central camp: white-horse banners and yellow battle-axes, black canopies and vermilion pennants, crowded around tiger tents. In the middle is a blackened lacquered officer banner with the commander’s title; this must be Sima Shi. The camp has not yet been completely set up.” Wen Yang, whip in hand, stood beside his father. Hearing this he said, “Since their camp is not complete, we can split into two, strike from both sides, and surely win completely.” Wen Qin asked, “When should we go?” Wen Yang said, “This evening at dusk, father should lead two thousand five hundred by the south gate and strike in. I will lead two thousand five hundred from the north gate. At the third watch we should meet in the Wei camp.” Wen Qin obeyed, and that night divided the army in two. Wen Yang, only eighteen, stood eight chi tall. He wore full scale armor, had a steel whip at his waist, and a long spear in hand as he rode out, gazing toward the Wei camp.

That night, Sima Shi’s army arrived at Lejia, set camp, and waited for Deng Ai’s arrival. The wound in his left eye still burned from the operation. He lay in his tent while a few hundred armored men stood in a ring around him. At the third watch, a roar of shouting shook the camp; horse and men were thrown into uproar. Sima Shi asked what it was. One soldier reported, “A force has cut straight through the northern enclosure and entered; at its head is one commander, impossible for any to match.” Sima Shi was startled. His heart flared like flame. His eyeball burst from the wound and blood poured onto the ground; the pain was unbearable. Fearing that he would shake the army’s morale, he bit down on the head of his blanket and endured, tearing it to shreds. It was then that Wen Yang’s horsemen reached first. They surged forward in one rush. Through the Wei camp they charged and countercharged; wherever they arrived, no one dared to meet them. Wherever resistance appeared, spear-stabs and whip blows fell, and none survived. Wen Yang could see only for his father and thought he had come from outside to answer him, but he saw none. After several assaults on the center, each time the men were driven back by bow and crossbow fire. Wen Yang kept fighting all the way until dawn, when he heard drums and horns raging from the north. Wen Yang looked back at the men with him and said, “Father is not here to aid from the south. He has instead come from the north; why is this?” He checked the horse’s pace and saw a force running forward like a wild wind; at its head was Deng Ai. Deng Ai leapt from his horse and, sword in hand, cried out, “Turning rebels, do not run!” Wen Yang was furious and drove forward with raised spear. They fought for fifty rounds with no clear outcome. Mid-fight, Wei troops advanced in great numbers, pressing from front and rear. Wen Yang’s followers fled in all directions; he alone remained mounted, cutting through the Wei troops and riding south. A few hundred Wei commanders gathered spirit and chased him hard. Just as they reached the Lejia bridge and nearly overtook him, Wen Yang suddenly reined back sharply, shouted once, and drove straight into the Wei commanders’ ranks. Where his steel whip rose, men dropped from their mounts, then withdrew in panic. Wen Yang resumed riding slowly onward. Wei commanders grouped in one place and said, astonished, “How can this man still dare to split us in this way?” “Let us combine and pursue him all together!” So a hundred Wei commanders came in to chase him again. Wen Yang was ablaze with anger: “How can these rat-like men not spend a life to the end?” He flicked his whip, wheeled the horse, and plunged again into the command group, striking down several with the whip; then he returned to a slower pace and continued riding. Wei commanders chased four or five times, and each time were beaten back by the lone man. A later poet wrote:

Wen Yang had once alone met Cao at Changban; From then onward Zilong displayed his bold magnificence. Where the battle roared in Lejia City’s heart, There one again saw Wen Yang’s bold courage.

Wen Qin, by this time, had been thrown by the rough mountain road and had strayed into a valley. He wandered for half the night, and when he found a way out it was already dawn. Still, Wen Yang’s mounted troop and its direction could no longer be seen. Wei troops were winning in force, and Wen Qin withdrew without fighting. Wei forces pressed hard and Wen Qin drew his men toward Shouchun.

Now Wei Palace Captain Yin Damu, who had been a close man of Cao Shuang, was present in the palace court. Sima Shi had inherited a heart to kill for Shuang’s death and had long wished vengeance, and he had been intimate with Wen Qin. Seeing Sima Shi now helpless with his eye tumor exposed and no ability to move, he entered the camp and said, “Wen Qin had no intention to rebel. He was forced by Guanquiu Jian into this condition. If I go and speak, he will surely come in to surrender.” Sima Shi agreed. Yin Damu donned helmet and full armor, mounted, and rode after Wen Qin. As he closed in, he cried, “Does Governor Wen Qin know Yin Damu?” Wen Qin turned and looked. Damu removed his helmet and set it in front of the saddle, then pointed with his whip and said, “Governor Wen Qin, why could you not endure only a few more days?” This was because Damu already knew Sima Shi would soon die and so had come to keep Wen Qin. Wen Qin did not understand the intention, and in rage shouted abuse and moved to draw his bow. Yin Damu wept and turned back. While Wen Qin was gathering men to charge toward Shouchun, it had already been taken by troops brought by Zhuge Dan. When he returned to Xiangcheng, troops under Hu Zun, Wang Ji, and Deng Ai had all arrived from three directions. Seeing his situation turn desperate, he defected and left for Sun Jun of Eastern Wu.

Now in Xiangcheng, Guanquiu Jian heard Shouchun had already been lost, Wen Qin’s cause broken, and three-way Wei troops had come to the walls. He ordered all troops in the city to come out and fight. He met Deng Ai on the field. Guanquiu Jian sent Ge Yong first. The two engaged, and did not stand long. Deng Ai cut him down with one stroke and drove his men through the lines. Guanqiu Jian still resisted to the end. The Jiang-Huai troops were thrown into great disorder. Hu Zun and Wang Ji brought their forces to a four-sided squeeze. Unable to withstand, Guanquiu Jian fought his way out with no less than ten riders. When they reached below Shencounty, the county magistrate Song Bai opened the gate and received him. He had seats prepared. Jian was deeply drunk, and Song Bai had him killed. The Wei army received his severed head. Thus Huainan was pacified.

Sima Shi still lay too ill to rise. He summoned Zhuge Dan into the tent, bestowed seal and emblems, and made him Great General Who Conquers the East and Chief Commander of all armies and forces of Yang Province. At the same time he ordered a return to Xuchang. His eye pain did not cease; each night he saw only Li Feng, Zhang Ji, and Xiahou Xuan standing by his bed. His spirit wavered and he believed he could not survive. He ordered men to bring Sima Zhao from Luoyang. Sima Zhao arrived and knelt, crying, at the foot of the bed. Sima Shi’s parting words were, “I now hold heavy authority. Though I would like to set my shoulders free, I cannot. You inherit this charge for me and do not entrust this great affair to another, lest he bring ruin to the clan.” He finished speaking and handed over the seal and insignia, eyes brimming with tears. As Sima Zhao was about to ask a question, Sima Shi cried out once; his eye burst from the growth and he died. It was the second month of the second year of Zhengyuan. So Sima Zhao carried the body home and reported to Emperor Cao Mao. Cao Mao sent an envoy with an imperial decree to Xuchang and ordered Sima Zhao temporarily to remain there with his army to guard against Eastern Wu. Sima Zhao still hesitated. Zhong Hui said, “The Great General has only just died, and the people’s hearts are not yet steady. If the commander stays here and the court is thrown into tumult, there will be no way to remedy it.” Sima Zhao followed this advice and raised troops, returning to camp south of the Luo River. When Cao Mao heard of this he was greatly startled. Grand Commandant Wang Su submitted, “Since Sima Zhao has inherited his brother’s command of great authority, Your Majesty should confer rank upon him for stability.” So Cao Mao sent Wang Su with an edict, granting Sima Zhao the title of Great General and recording the affairs of the Privy Council. Sima Zhao entered court and offered thanks upon completion of the ceremony. From then on, all important matters inside and outside the realm were entrusted to him.

Meanwhile secret informants from Western Shu reported the matter in Chengdu. Jiang Wei then addressed the Later Lord: “Sima Shi has just died. Sima Zhao has only just taken heavy authority and cannot in reality leave Luoyang on his own. I request permission to strike Wei now and recover the Central Plains.” The Later Lord agreed, and sent Jiang Wei to raise the army and campaign against Wei. When Jiang Wei reached Hanzhong, he put the troops in order. Great General Who Conquers the West Zhang Yi said, “Shu’s territory is narrow and poor in grain, unsuited for distant campaigns. Better to hold defensible positions and preserve both soldiers and people. That is the way to protect the state.” Jiang Wei said, “No. Before the Chancellor left his thatched cottage, he had already fixed the realm into three parts and planned six advances against Qishan. Yet he died midway and his achievements were left unfinished. Now I have received his posthumous charge. I must be loyal and faithful and continue his will, even if I die without regret. Wei now has a weakness we can use. If we do not strike now, what other time should we wait for?” Xiahou Ba said, “The general speaks truly. Send light cavalry ahead through Fuhan. If we secure the lands west of Tao and Nanan, all commanderies can be settled.” Zhang Yi said, “The earlier failure to return was because the march was so slow. The art of war says, ‘Attack where there is no readiness; strike where there is no anticipation.’ If we move at once and make Wei unable to prepare defenses, we must win completely.”

So Jiang Wei led fifty thousand men out toward Fuhan. When his army reached the Tao River, the frontier troops reported that Wang Jing, Inspector of Yongzhou, and General Who Conquers the West Chen Tai had arrived. Wang Jing had already called out seventy thousand horse and foot and come to meet him. Jiang Wei gave instructions to Zhang Yi and Xiahou Ba; they understood and took their commands. He then personally arranged his main army in rank with its back to the Tao River. Wang Jing sent out the four commanders Zhang Ming, Hua Yong, Liu Da, and Zhu Fang. He said, “Wei, Wu, and Shu have become a three-pronged order now. Why do you repeatedly raid us?” Jiang Wei replied, “Sima Shi overthrew his ruler without cause. A neighboring state may ask for justice, and what need of enmity then? Even more, this is an enemy to be answered.” Wang Jing looked back at the four and said, “Shu troops are formed with their backs to water; if they fail, they perish in the water. Jiang Wei is courageous and bold. You four can engage him. If he moves to withdraw, pursue.” The four men split left and right and came out to battle. Jiang Wei fought a few exchanges and then wheeled his horse back toward his own camp and withdrew. Wang Jing pressed horse and men hard and came on in one rush. Jiang Wei drew his troops toward Tao West and ran. When he neared the water, he shouted to his soldiers, “The situation is urgent. How much more effort can be mustered?” All commanders rushed back with all their strength, and Wei troops were greatly defeated. Zhang Yi and Xiahou Ba chased behind the Wei army on both flanks, splitting into two, and trapped the enemy in an enclosed killing ground. Jiang Wei roared with force, drove his men into the Wei center, and charged left and right; Wei troops became disordered and trampled one another. Most of them died. Vast numbers were driven into the Tao River. More than ten thousand heads were cut down, and the piled corpses stretched for miles. Wang Jing took one hundred horse of the broken force and broke out with desperate vigor, fleeing straight to Didao City and entering behind closed gates. Jiang Wei achieved full success. After he finished rewarding his troops, he prepared to march on Didao City. Zhang Yi remonstrated, “Your achievements are complete. Your reputation has become formidable enough; you may stop now. If we go farther and the result is not good, it would be adding snake feet.” Jiang Wei said, “No. After a defeat in Wei ranks one may still seek advance and crossing. In today’s battle on the Tao River Wei itself was shocked through and through. I think Didao is now within easy grasp. Do not let your spirit sink.” Zhang Yi urged him again and again; Jiang Wei would not yield and ordered the troops to move on for Didao City.

Now Chen Tai, General Who Conquers the West of Yongzhou, had intended to raise troops and avenge Wang Jing’s defeat when Deng Ai arrived leading Yanzhou troops. He received him and the forms were completed. Deng Ai said, “Now under the Grand General’s command I have come only to aid you and destroy the enemy.” Chen Tai asked him for strategy. Deng Ai replied, “Your victory at Tao River could become dangerous if we recruit Qiang masses and then rush east to seize Guanzhong and send edicts across four commanderies. Wei’s troops are not thinking in that way now; they are focusing on Didao City. Its walls are thick and strong and hard to take; it will only waste men and energy. Now I will deploy at Xiangling. Then I will advance against Didao and the Shu force must lose.” Chen Tai said, “This is an excellent analysis.” He first sent out twenty companies, each fifty men, all with banners, horns, and beacon fires. By day they lay hidden, by night they moved. They ambushed in the deep ravines and high ground southeast of Didao City. As soon as the enemy came they were to sound drums and horns together and by night raise fires and shoot cannon to strike panic. When all arrangements were set, he waited for the Shu army to arrive. Chen Tai and Deng Ai then each led twenty thousand troops and advanced in sequence.

Jiang Wei had besieged Didao and ordered eight-direction attacks, but after several days without success he was troubled with no plan. That dusk, there were three reports from the horsemen of flowing stars: “Two bodies of troops are coming, each with bold banners. One is General Who Conquers the West Chen Tai, and one is Governor of Yanzhou Deng Ai.” Jiang Wei was startled and consulted with Xiahou Ba. Xiahou Ba said, “I told the general before: Deng Ai has from childhood understood the art of war and knows geography well. Now that he has arrived with his army, he is a strong enemy.” Jiang Wei said, “Their force has come so far. If we do not let him take a stand, we can strike now.” He left Zhang Yi to continue the siege and ordered Xiahou Ba to bring men to meet Chen Tai. Jiang Wei drew his own force to face Deng Ai. When he had not gone five li, a cannon sounded from the southeast, drums split the earth, and fire blazed into the sky. Jiang Wei wheeled and looked: all around, Wei banners filled the field. He was startled and said, “We are caught in Deng Ai’s scheme!” He sent orders for Xiahou Ba and Zhang Yi each to leave Didao and retreat. Thus all Shu troops withdrew to Hanzhong. Jiang Wei covered the rear, and only then heard drums still booming behind him. By the time he withdrew through Jian Ge Pass, he knew that all those twenty-odd fires and drums were mere ruses. Jiang Wei drew up and withdrew to camp at Zhongdi.

After this, the Later Lord, because Jiang Wei had achieved success at the west of Tao, issued an edict and conferred the title of Great General upon him. Jiang Wei accepted the appointment, sent an memorial of thanks, and then discussed again the campaign plan against Wei.

Success needs no added serpent-foot embellishment. In chastising rebels, one still seeks to unleash tiger-strength. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Wenyang Alone Turns Back the Great Army; Jiang Wei Breaks the Great Enemy at the River’s Back

chapters.html:
Now Jiang Wei withdrew his troops and camped at Zhongdi, while the Wei army had encamped outside Didao City.

Wang Jing went out to welcome Chen Tai and Deng Ai into the city, thanked them for ending the encirclement, and hosted a banquet to treat them and reward the Three Armies. Chen Tai submitted a memorial praising Deng Ai’s service to Wei ruler Cao Mao. In reply, Cao Mao enfeoffed Deng Ai as General Who Pacifies the West, gave him temporary authority to command the Cavalry Commandant Guarding the Eastern Qiang, and ordered him to camp with Chen Tai in Yong, Liang, and other places.

After presenting thanks to Cao Mao, Deng Ai was also welcomed by Chen Tai at banquet, who said, “Jiang Wei has fled by night. His strength is gone; he will not dare to ride out again.”

Deng Ai laughed. “I judged that the Shu soldiers must come out in five ways.” Chen Tai asked why.

Deng Ai said, “Though the Shu force withdrew, they still have the momentum of victory; and my troops carry the reality of weakness. So they must come out one way. The Shu soldiers were all trained under Kongming’s instruction and are elite troops, easy to maneuver. I do not rotate mine as often, and my soldiers are not fully trained in field exercise; so they must come out a second way. Most of the Shu men move by boat, while my army is all on dry land and so has different levels of hardship and rest; that is a third reason. Didao, Longxi, Nan'an, and Qishan are all places where one can stand and fight; the Shu may feint east while striking west, point north while aiming south. My troops would have to hold several passes with divided columns. If the Shu come together as one body, then one part against our four parts, that is the fourth way. If the Shu march from Nan’an or Longxi, they can seize grain from the Qiang for food; if they come out at Qishan, they can harvest wheat. They have ready victuals. That is the fifth way.”

Chen Tai exclaimed in admiration, “Your estimate of the enemy is like a god’s; what has Jiang Wei to fear from us?” From then on, Chen Tai and Deng Ai became intimate friends despite the difference in their ages. Deng Ai then drilled the troops in Yong, Liang, and other outposts every day. At every mountain pass, he raised stockades and entrenchments to guard against the unexpected.

Now Jiang Wei held a great feast at Zhongdi, bringing together his generals to discuss raiding Wei. His adjutant Fan Jian cautioned him, “General, you have gone out again and gained no complete victory. In today’s battle of Taoxi, the Wei men already bent to your power. Why do you want to campaign again? If things turn poorly, your past achievements may be thrown away in one stroke.”

Jiang Wei said, “You all only know that Wei has vast land and many people and cannot be easily conquered. Yet you do not know that one who attacks Wei can win in five ways.” The others asked how.

Wei replied, “First, at Taoxi they suffered a defeat that broke their elan. Though my army withdrew, it did not suffer real damage. If we now advance, I can win that way. Second, my army will march by boats and suffer little exhaustion, while their troops come from dry ground to meet us; that is a second way. Third, my men are a force long-trained under discipline; theirs are merely a rabble gathered from various places and know no order, so this is the third way. Fourth, my troops can go out from Qishan and forage the autumn grain for food. Fifth, though their soldiers are distributed across defensive positions and scattered in force, if my army goes as one mass, how can they send aid?”

He leaned forward and said, “If we do not strike Wei now, when else will we?”

Xiahou Ba said, “Though Deng Ai is young, his strategic thinking is deep. Since he was just appointed General Who Pacifies the West, he has made preparations everywhere. He is no longer as he was in former days.”

Jiang Wei raised his voice, “What is there for me to fear from him? All of you should stop praising the enemy’s sharpness and speak instead of our own vigor. My decision is made. We must first seize Longxi.” No one dared to remonstrate.

Jiang Wei led the vanguard himself and ordered the others to follow behind. Thus all the Shu soldiers left Zhongdi and rushed toward Qishan.

A scout horseman reported that Wei troops had already occupied nine barracks at Qishan. Jiang Wei refused to believe it and mounted with several riders to inspect from high ground. He indeed saw the nine encampments at Qishan stretching out like a long serpent, head and tail watching each other. Jiang Wei looked back at those around him. “Xiahou Ba spoke truly. The arrangement of these stockades is excellent. Only our Chancellor of Shu, Kongming, could devise such a disposition. Observing Deng Ai’s actions now, he is not one step behind my Chancellor.”

He returned to his own encampment and called his generals, saying, “Since the Wei already prepared, they must know I am coming. I expect Deng Ai to be somewhere in this region. You must show a false flag display of my standards. Occupy this valley-mouth below and post a hundred or so horsemen for scouting each day. Each scouting sortie should return before changing to another set of armor and livery. The banners should be exchanged through the five directional colors—blue, yellow, red, white, black. I, meanwhile, will quietly lead the main army out through Dongting and strike straight for Nan’an.”

Deng Ai was then left to hold Qishan’s mouth.

Now as Deng Ai learned the Shu army had come out to Qishan, he had already camped with Chen Tai in readiness. He saw that the Shu forces did not come to skirmish for several days; one day he sent out five rounds of horse scouts, each ranging ten or fifteen li. After reaching a high point and looking out, he hurried into his command tent and said to Chen Tai, “Jiang Wei is not here. He has gone for Dongting and will attack Nan’an. These sortie riders are only a handful. They wear different armor each time, and the scouting horses are already worn out. Their commander cannot have strength. General Chen should lead one army against this camp and the stockades can be broken. Once the barricades fall, send troops to the road toward Dongting and first cut off Jiang Wei’s rear.”

“I will first bring one army to relieve Nan’an and then go straight to Wucheng Mountain. Whoever controls that hill first, Jiang Wei will certainly go to Shanggui. At Shanggui there is a valley called Duan Valley, narrow and hemmed by mountains, perfect for an ambush. When he comes to contest Wucheng Mountain, I will first set two armies hidden in Duan Valley and then break Jiang Wei for sure.”

Chen Tai said, “I have guarded Longxi for two or three decades and have never seen geography judged so clearly. What you say is truly divinatory strategy. Go at once. I will attack this line of barracks.”

So Deng Ai led his soldiers by night, doubled on another road, and went straight to Wucheng Mountain. He settled the camp; before the Shu forces arrived he ordered Deng Zhong and the captain-by-the-tent, Shi Zuan, each with five thousand troops, to go first to Duan Valley and lie in ambush. They departed with exactly this plan in mind. Deng Ai ordered the banners lowered and drums silent and waited for the Shu army.

Now Jiang Wei came from Dongting toward Nan’an and reached before Wucheng Mountain. He said to Xiahou Ba, “There is a mountain near Nan’an called Wucheng. If we secure it first, we can seize the advantage at Nan’an. I only fear Deng Ai has many devices and will block the crossing ahead.”

Just as doubt hung over him, suddenly from up the mountain came a single thunderous cannon report. Loud shouts rose; war horns blared in unison, and banners were raised all over—Wei troops. A yellow banner streamed in the middle wind with the large characters “Deng Ai” written on it.

The Shu soldiers were startled. Elite troops poured down from several points on the mountain; they were unstoppable. The forward lines were badly beaten. When Jiang Wei rushed the center troops to come to the rescue, the Wei had already withdrawn. Jiang Wei came straight down to Wucheng Mountain foot to meet Deng Ai in battle. The Wei on the heights did not descend.

Jiang Wei ordered soldiers to hurl insults and taunts. Near evening he intended to retire the army, but mountain horns and drums sounded again and still no Wei came down. Jiang Wei tried to rush up the mountain and charge through, but the bombardment of cannon stones on the heights was severe, and he could not advance.

The watch lasted until the third watch; he began to withdraw. Again the horns above sounded. He moved his troops down the mountain and camped, and only after ordering wood and earth carried to build stockades did he begin to raise them. The horns sounded once more from above, and Wei forces arrived in a rush. The Shu troops broke in confusion, trampling one another and falling back to their old camp.

The next day Jiang Wei ordered troops with supply carts to Wucheng Mountain, setting them in connected lines, hoping to raise fortifications and make a new garrison. At second watch that night, Deng Ai sent five hundred men, each carrying torchlight, down by two routes to burn the supply wagons. The two armies then slaughtered one another through the night, and the stockades could not be completed again.

Jiang Wei rallied and withdrew his force once more. Again he discussed it with Xiahou Ba, saying, “Nan’an is not yet gained. Better to take Shanggui first. Shanggui is where the grain for Nan’an is stored; if I take Shanggui, Nan’an is in danger.”

He left Xiahou Ba in garrison at Wucheng Mountain and brought all his elite troops and fierce commanders to go straight for Shanggui. They marched through one night; dawn came and, seeing steep, narrow ridges and rough roads, he asked the local guide, “What is this place called?”

He answered, “Duan Valley.” Jiang Wei was shocked. “That is an ominous name: Duan can mean a cut-off valley. If someone cuts off its mouth, what then?”

Exactly as he hesitated, a report came that the vanguard was sounding from behind: dust rose heavily in the rear and there was certainly an ambush. Jiang Wei ordered a withdrawal at once. Shi Zuan and Deng Zhong burst out with their forces in battle.

Jiang Wei fought while he withdrew. In front, loud war-cries rose; Deng Ai came with troops and closed in. Attacked from three directions, the Shu army was routed. Fortune favored them only because Xiahou Ba arrived with troops; only then the Wei troops withdrew and saved Jiang Wei, who aimed to return toward Qishan.

Xiahou Ba said, “The Qishan stockades have already been broken by Chen Tai, and Bao Su has been killed. All his men have withdrawn back to Hanzhong.”

Jiang Wei dared not take Dongting and hurried back by a small mountain path. Deng Ai pursued hard from behind. Jiang Wei ordered the divisions forward and himself to hold the rear guard. As they were moving, a detachment suddenly emerged from the hills: it was Wei general Chen Tai.

The Wei soldiers raised one shout and Jiang Wei was at their center. His men and horses were worn and tired; with blows to the left and right they could not break out. Zhang Ni, the General Who Quells Rebels, heard that Jiang Wei was trapped and led several hundred riders into the heavy encirclement. Taking advantage of the moment, Jiang Wei fought his way out.

Zhang Ni was struck down by a shower of Wei arrows. Once Jiang Wei had escaped the encirclement and returned to Hanzhong, he remembered Zhang Yi’s loyalty and courage—who had died in service to the state—and submitted a memorial commending his sons and descendants.

In the Shu army many had fallen, and all the blame was laid on Jiang Wei. Following the precedent from Zhuge Liang’s old battle at Jieting, Jiang Wei submitted a memorial and demoted himself to Rear General and Acting General-in-Chief.

When Deng Ai saw the Shu forces completely withdrawn, he held a feast with Chen Tai and generously rewarded the three armies. Chen Tai praised Deng Ai’s achievements, and Sima Zhao sent an envoy with the seal and orders, adding to Deng Ai’s rank, conferring office and honor, and also ennobling his son Deng Zhong as a Marquis of a District.

At this time, in the third year of the corrected first year of Zhongyuan, it became the first year of the Ganting era for Wei ruler Cao Mao.

Since Sima Zhao had made himself the Grand Commander of all troops and armies under heaven, he constantly ordered three thousand iron-clad valiant riders to surround him in front and behind as an escort. He handled all matters himself, not submitting them to the court, and made all judgments in his own residence.

From then on he constantly harbored a usurping intention; he only feared that the people in south and north had not yet all yielded their hearts. Among his close associates was Jia Chong, courtesy name Gonglu, son of former Jianwei General Jia Kui, and long-serving as a subordinate scribe under Sima Zhao.

Jia Chong said to Sima Zhao, “Now you hold the great weight of state. The people in the four directions cannot be entirely at peace. If so, we should first quietly probe, and then in time we may plot the major matter.”

Zhao said, “I intend just that. You can go east for me. Put forward the pretext that you are gathering troops to reward troops gone on campaign, and use that as cover to gather reports.”

Jia Chong took command and went straight to Huainan, and presented himself before General Who Guards the East, Zhuge Dan.

Zhuge Dan’s courtesy name was Gongxiu. He was from Langya, Nanyang, and was a cousin of Zhuge Liang. He had served Wei first; because of his relation to Zhuge Liang in Shu, he had not been heavily promoted. Later, after Zhuge Liang’s death, Dan rose through heavy posts in Wei, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gaoping, and administered the armies and horsemen of both Jiang region. On that day Jia Chong took the name of rewarding exhausted troops as pretext and came to Huainan to see Zhuge Dan.

Zhuge Dan hosted him at a banquet. When the wine had reached half-intoxication, Jia Chong provoked him in speech:

“Recently all the worthy men of Luoyang say the ruler is timid and too weak to be emperor. The Grand Commander Sima, who has for three generations supported the state, has accomplishments and virtue beyond measure and can receive transfer of Wei’s rule. What is your private opinion?”

Zhuge Dan was furious. “You are Jia, son of Yuezhou—descended by family on Wei salary. How dare you utter such disorderly words?”

Jia Chong said, “I am only relaying what others have said to you.”

Zhuge Dan said, “When the court is in peril, I will answer with my life.” Jia Chong held his tongue.

Later, after taking leave, he relayed the matter in detail to Sima Zhao. Zhao was enraged and shouted, “A rat-born commoner dares speak like that!”

Jia Chong said, “Dan in Huainan has deep support among people and will surely become dangerous in time; he should be removed quickly.”

Sima Zhao then sent a secret letter to Yue Lei, Inspector of Yang Province, and at the same time dispatched an envoy bearing a decree to summon Zhuge Dan as Minister of Works.

When Dan received the edict, he already knew it was a report planted by Jia Chong. He seized the arriving envoy and interrogated him.

The envoy said, “This matter Yue Lei knows.”

Dan asked, “How did he know?”

The envoy said, “Sima Commander has already sent someone to Yang Province with the sealed letter to Yue Lei.”

Dan was furious and shouted to his men, then immediately had the envoy beheaded. He then assembled a thousand soldiers under his command and charged for Yang Province.

When he arrived at the south gate, the city gate had been closed and the pontoon bridge pulled up. Dan called from under the walls, but no one on the walls answered.

He roared, “How dare Yue Lei, a single common man, do this?”

He ordered his officers to beat the walls. More than ten picked riders dismounted and waded across the river, leaping up to the city, scattering the guards and opening the gate.

Then Zhuge Dan led the troops into the city, set fires with the wind, and drove to Yue Lei’s residence. Yue Lei had scrambled up to an upper floor to hide.

Dan drew his sword and mounted the stairs, shouting: “Your father Le Jìn once received great grace from Wei. Will you not think of your old obligations and instead choose to align with Sima Zhao?”

Yue Lei had no time to reply before Dan slew him.

At the same time he drafted a memorial listing Sima Zhao’s crimes and sent it to be presented in Luoyang. He also gathered more than ten thousand households of registered settlers from the two river regions, and more than forty thousand newly surrendered men from Yang Province, stacked grass and provisions, and prepared for advance.

He ordered his chief clerk Wu Gang to send Zhuge Liang’s son, Zhuge Li, into Wu as a hostage and asked for aid, demanding all allied troops to join in punishing Sima Zhao.

At this time Eastern Wu Chancellor Sun Jun had died in illness, and his cousin Sun Chen was handling administration. Sun Chen’s courtesy name was Zitong; he was a violent and overbearing man. He killed grand marshal Teng Yin, General Lu Ju, and Wang Dun, and therefore all authority came into his hands.

Wu ruler Sun Liang, though intelligent, could not resist it. Wu Gang then escorted Zhuge Li to Shitou City and presented him before Sun Chen.

Sun Chen asked the reason for the visit.

Gang said, “Zhuge Dan is Zhuge Liang’s cousin, the brother in Shu-Han. He formerly served Wei. He now sees Sima Zhao deceive the Son of Heaven, discard the ruler, and usurp power, and wishes to muster arms against him but lacks strength. So he has come to surrender, bringing his own son Zhuge Li as a hostage as proof of sincerity. I beg you to send troops to assist.”

Sun Chen agreed and then dispatched General Quanyi and Quandu as main commanders, Yuquan as reserve commander, Zhu Yi and Tang Zi as vanguard, and Wen Qin as local guide. He raised seventy thousand soldiers and sent them forward in three divisions.

Wu Gang returned to Shouchun and reported to Zhuge Dan. Dan rejoiced and put his forces in order.

Now Zhuge Dan submitted a memorial to Luoyang. When Sima Zhao saw it, he was furious and wanted to go out personally to chastise him.

Jia Chong remonstrated, “Your Excellency inherited your father and elder brothers’ foundations; your benevolence has not yet reached all under Heaven. If you now abandon the Son of Heaven and go forth, then if any change comes in one morning, what remedy would there be? Better to petition that both Empress Dowager and emperor make the expedition together, and only then will there be no risk.”

Zhao was pleased: “This is exactly in line with my thought.” He then memorialized the Empress Dowager, “Zhuge Dan plans revolt; I have discussed this matter with both civil and military officials, and the plans are settled. I respectfully request that Her Majesty and the Son of Heaven personally ride out to campaign and thereby carry out the late emperor’s intent.”

The empress dowager, frightened, could only comply.

The next day Sima Zhao requested Wei ruler Cao Mao to set out. Cao Mao said, “You are the Grand Commander of armies and horses of all under heaven and command them in appointment and movement. Why must I come in person as well?”

Zhao said, “No, this is not so. In former times, Emperor Wu ranged across the four seas, and Emperors Wen and Ming held universal ambition and the intent to encompass the world. Whenever a grave enemy rises, the emperor himself must go in person. Your Majesty should pursue the will of your ancestors, sweep away wicked traitors, why shrink now?”

Fearful of Zhao’s power, Cao Mao reluctantly assented.

Zhao then issued orders mobilizing the two capital armies of two hundred and sixty thousand, naming General Who Guards the South Wang Ji as principal vanguard, General Who Pacifies the East Chen Qian as assistant vanguard, military supervisor Shi Bao as left wing, and Ji Province Administrator Zhou Tai as right wing. He protected the imperial carriage as they set forth in force and surged onward, heading to Huainan.

Eastern Wu vanguard commander Zhu Yi went out to meet them. The two armies faced one another.

Wang Ji rode forward, and Zhu Yi came out to answer. In less than three rounds of battle, Zhu Yi was defeated and broken. Tang Zi rode out; again before three rounds there was heavy defeat and rout. Wang Ji drove on with his troops and cut down the fleeing army. Wu soldiers were utterly routed and retreated fifty li to make camp, then withdrew into Shouchun.

Zhuge Dan himself led his own picked force and joined with Wen Qin and his two sons, Wen Yang and Wen Hu, a force of tens of thousands, to meet Sima Zhao.

Then it was that:

At just this moment, the Wu army’s sharp spirit began to collapse, and fresh and powerful Wei forces rode hard in.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Deng Shizai Cleverly Captures Jiang Boyue; Zhuge Dan Righteously Punishes Sima Zhao

chapters.html:
Save Shou-chun as Yuquan keeps faith to death;\ Take Longcheng while Boryue wages a grim battle.

Sima Zhao heard that Zhuge Dan had joined Wu troops and prepared for a decisive engagement, so he summoned Pei Xiu, Scattered Cavalry Gentleman, and Zhong Hui, Palace Gentleman of the Yellow Gates, to discuss a plan to break the enemy. Zhong Hui said, “Wu aid to Zhuge Dan is real gain. If we lure them with advantage, we will surely win.” Sima Zhao followed his advice. He ordered Shi Bao and Zhou Tai to march their armies in advance and lie in ambush at Shitou City. Wang Ji and Chen Qian led an elite force in the rear. He also ordered the subordinate general Cheng Cui to take several tens of thousands of soldiers forward to tease the enemy first. Chen Jun was told to gather wheeled gear, arms, horses, cattle, donkeys, and mules, load them with prize goods, and bunch them around the formation on all sides to abandon at once if the enemy came.

That day, Zhuge Dan posted Zhu Yi on the left and Wen Qin on the right. Seeing that the Wei ranks and men were not in order, Dan drove infantry and cavalry straight forward in a rush. Cheng Cui withdrew, and Dan charged to strike through. Seeing the plain carpeted with oxen, horses, donkeys, and mules, the southern troops scrambled to seize them and had no heart to remain in battle. A cannon boomed suddenly, and from two directions troops came in to kill. On the left was Shi Bao, on the right Zhou Tai. When Dan was startled and tried to fall back in haste, Wang Ji and Chen Qian’s elite arrived in a killing rush. Dan’s army was decisively beaten. Sima Zhao then brought in more troops to reinforce. Dan withdrew with his ruined force into Shou-chun, shut the gates, and held fast. Sima Zhao ordered the army to surround him on all four sides and press the city together.

Meanwhile the Wu troops withdrew to encamp at Anfeng, while the Wei sovereign’s mobile court was at Xiangcheng. Zhong Hui said, “Zhuge Dan may have suffered defeat, yet food stores inside Shou-chun are still abundant. Worse still, Wu forces are still posted at Anfeng as a flanking position. If Wu besieges on all four sides, if they are slow they will hold; if they rush they will fight to die. If they later join from two sides, our army gains nothing. Better we besiege Shou-chun on three sides and leave the southern gate road so the enemy may break out; when he runs, we strike him and gain full victory. Those Wu troops came from far away, and their supplies will not hold. If I lead light cavalry behind them, they can collapse without one real battle.” Sima Zhao patted his shoulder and said, “You are truly my own Zifang.” He ordered Wang Ji to pull back the troops of the south gate.

At Anfeng, where Wu troops were stationed, Sun Chen called Zhu Yi and reproached him, “Shou-chun cannot be saved by one push alone. How could one think to seize all the Central Plains on such a basis? If there is no victory again, he will be executed.” Zhu Yi went back to his own camp to consult.

Yuquan said, “The south gate of Shou-chun is not yet under close encirclement. I am willing to lead one army through it to enter and help Zhuge Dan defend the city. You engage Sima's army and test them; I will break out from within and strike from both sides. Then the Wei troops can be broken.” Zhu Yi accepted those words. Quán Yi, Quán Duan, Wen Qin, and others all volunteered to enter Shou-chun. So they entered together with Yuquan, a force of ten thousand, through the south gate.

Wei soldiers had no clear command and did not dare to be reckless. They let Wu soldiers enter and then reported it to Sima Zhao. He said, “This is intended to strike us from inside and outside together.” He summoned Wang Ji and Chen Qian and said, “You may take five thousand men, cut off Zhu Yi’s route, and strike him from behind.” The two obeyed and set out.

When Zhu Yi was bringing his troops forward, shouts rose violently from behind. From the left came Wang Ji, from the right Chen Qian, and two columns of armies rushed in. The Wu army was smashed. Zhu Yi returned to Sun Chen. Sun Chen grew furious: “For a general already beaten again and again, of what use are you?” He shouted at the soldiers to drag him out and execute him. He also scolded Quán Yí, son of Quán Duan: “If you cannot get away from Wei’s troops, you and your father need not come before me again!” So Sun Chen returned to Jianye.

Zhong Hui told Sima Zhao, “Now that Sun Chen has withdrawn and no rescuer is outside, the city can be fully besieged.” Sima Zhao followed this and ordered the army to press the encirclement.

Quán Yi led his men into Shou-chun, saw the overwhelming force of Wei and found himself with no way out, and submitted to Sima Zhao. Sima Zhao promoted Yi to Deputy General. Feeling his mercy, Yi wrote a family letter to Quán Duan and his uncle Quán Yí, saying Sun Chen had no humanity and that it was better to surrender to Wei, then shot the letter into the city.

Quán Yí received the letter and then with his father Quán Duan opened the gate for several thousand men and surrendered. Zhuge Dan was depressed in the city. Strategist Jiang Ban and Jiao Yi spoke up: “The city has little grain and too many soldiers, and cannot endure long. We should take the combined Wu and Chu troops out and force a life-ending battle with Wei.”

Dan snapped, “I want to hold, you want battle—must one of you have a different heart? Speak again and I will execute you.” The two raised their eyes to the sky and sighed, “Dan is doomed to fall. It is better we surrender early and avoid one complete death!” On the second watch of that night, Jiang Ban and Jiao Yi climbed over the walls and surrendered to Wei. Sima Zhao used them heavily, so though there were still men in the city willing to fight, none dared to speak of battle.

In the city, Dan saw Wei soldiers building earthen embankments all around, blocking the Huai, and looked only to flooding water to break them and drive his troops against it. Yet from autumn into winter there was no continuous rain, and the Huai did not flood.

Soon granaries ran dry. Wen Qin and his two sons held out inside the minor fort, and as soldiers gradually fainted from hunger they had no choice but to report to Dan: “Food is exhausted; soldiers waste away from hunger. Better to send the northern troops out entirely to reduce consumption.” Dan roared in anger, “You ask me to release all northern soldiers. Are you plotting against me?” He kicked one out and had him executed.

Wen Yang and Wen Hu saw their father killed. Each drew a short saber, cut down several people at once, leapt onto the wall, jumped down, crossed the ditch, and surrendered at the Wei camp. Sima Zhao still remembered Wen Yang’s single-handed retreat earlier and wanted to execute him. Zhong Hui remonstrated: “The guilt is Wen Qin’s. Wen Qin is dead, and these two have come in only out of desperation. If you kill surrendered generals, the city’s defenders will only grow firmer.”

Sima Zhao agreed and summoned Wen Yang and Wen Hu to camp, calmed them with kind words, rewarded them with swift horses and brocade robes, made them Deputy Generals, and enfeoffed them as Marquises within the Pass. The two bowed and thanked him, mounted their horses, and rode around the city shouting, “We two have received amnesty and ennoblement from the Great General. Why do you not surrender early?” The men inside heard and discussed among themselves. “Even Wen Yang, who was an enemy of the Sima clan, was used again; how could we be treated differently?” they said. All then wanted to surrender. Zhuge Dan, hearing this, became furious and patrolled wall and gate day and night, ruling by killing.

Zhong Hui saw how city hearts had already turned and entered camp to tell Sima Zhao, “This is the time to attack.” Sima Zhao was delighted and immediately called all four armies together in one surge. The defending commander Zeng Xuan opened the northern gate and admitted Wei soldiers. Dan saw Wei soldiers had entered and in panic led a few hundred under his banners through a side path out of the city to Diqiao bridge, where he collided with Hu Zun. Hu Zun raised the blade and struck; Dan was cut from the saddle. Hundreds were bound.

Wang Ji led troops to the west gate and ran into Wu general Yuquan.

“Why not surrender early?” Wang Ji shouted.

“Given orders, I set out to answer disaster for the living. If I cannot save and yet submit to another, that is not righteousness!” Yuquan threw his helmet to the ground and shouted, “To live in this world and die on the field is the one fortune! My life is enough!” He then wielded his saber and fought with fury for over three dozen exchanges. As man and horse tired, he was killed by the disorderly ranks.

Later people wrote poems in praise:

Sima once besieged Shou-chun, and the countless surrendered ran to kiss the dust of his chariot. East Wu may have heroes in abundance, but who among them would die when Yuquan chose death?

When Sima Zhao entered Shou-chun, he had the old and young of Zhuge Dan all beheaded and exterminated three of his clans. Wei officers brought with them several hundred of Dan’s captured soldiers, bound.

Sima Zhao asked, “Will you surrender?”

All shouted, “We wish to die with Lord Zhuge and not surrender to you.”

Sima Zhao grew furious and ordered the guards to drag all of them outside the city and question each one in turn: “Those who surrender will be spared.” Not one spoke of surrender. He killed them all until none remained. Sima Zhao gave a long, repeated sigh and ordered them all buried.

Later people wrote poems of lament:

Loyal to the lord with unbending will, they choose no stolen life but death beside General Zhuge’s ranks. The song of onions and dew would not yet have ceased; the trail left behind seems only to follow Tian Heng.

Later, most of the Wu soldiers surrendered to Wei. Fei Xiu told Sima Zhao, “These Wu men include old and young, and all are now in the southeastern lands by the Yangtze and Huai. If we keep them, they will become rebellion in time. Better to bury them all.”

Zhong Hui said, “No. In war, the well-governed state comes first: strike at the root of great evil and only that. If we bury all of them, it is not humane. Better release them back south to show the breadth of the Son of Heaven’s magnanimity.”

Sima Zhao said, “This is a fine argument.” He released all the Wu soldiers and sent them home. Tang Zi, fearing Sun Chen, dared not return to his own country and also came over to Wei. Sima Zhao used them all well and stationed them across Sanhe. Nanhan was pacified.

He was about to pull back when there came news that Jiang Wei from Shu was marching to take Changcheng to intercept supplies. Sima Zhao was greatly startled and consulted many officials on how to withdraw troops.

It was the twentieth year of Yanxi under Shu-Han, later changed to the first year of Jingyao. Jiang Wei in Hanzhong had chosen two river commanders, Jiang Shu and Fu Qian, and trained men and horses with them daily. He favored both greatly.

News came that in Huainan Zhuge Dan had raised troops against Sima Zhao and had Sun Chen of Wu helping him. Sima Zhao drew up two Huai armies and brought both the Wei empress dowager and the Wei sovereign on campaign.

Jiang Wei rejoiced, “This time I have truly accomplished a great task!” He petitioned the later ruler and wished to raise troops against Wei. Qiao Zhou, a Gentleman of the Court and Internal Attendants, heard of it and sighed, “Lately the court is sunk in wine and lust, trusting mid-level nobles like Huang Hao and ignoring state affairs for mere pleasure. Boyue has long sought punitive war and does not care for soldiers. The state is in danger!” He then composed an essay, Essay on Vengeful Wars, and sent it to Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei opened it and read.

The argument said:

One may ask: how did the weak in the past triumph over the strong? The answer: in a great state with few concerns, arrogance grows; in a small state with burdens, one learns to pursue prudence. Arrogance breeds disorder; prudence brings order. This is the constant order of things. So King Wen of Zhou nourished the people and overcame the many with the few; Goujian cared for the common people and from weakness brought down strength. This is the method.

Another asks: once Chu was strong and Han weak, and they divided by the Honggou agreement. Zhang Liang held that once the people's purpose was fixed, it could not be moved. He gathered troops to pursue Yue and finally overthrew the house of Xiang. Was this only a matter like King Wen and Goujian?

Again: in the time between Shang and Zhou, lords and kings enjoyed hereditary power and the bond between ruler and minister was fixed. In such times, even if there were Han, how could one seize all under heaven with sword alone? Yet after Qin removed lords and set commanders, the people were exhausted by Qin labor, the realm collapsed in pieces, and heroes contested alike. As for us and them, dynasties have already changed hands repeatedly. This is not a Qin-end frenzy; there are truly six kingdoms holding ground together. Therefore one may become like Wenwang, hard to become like the Founding Emperor of Han. Move only when the hour is right and raise arms after several combinations of strength. Thus Tang and Wu’s armies did not need a second campaign to conquer all. It was truly a matter of respecting the people’s burden and judging the time. If one presses into full-blown military arrogance, and misfortune comes, even the clever cannot devise a way through.

Jiang Wei, after reading, burst with anger: “This is the discourse of a corrupt scholar!” He threw it to the floor, then raised his river troops to march to the Central Plains.

He then asked Fu Qian, “By your reckoning, from where should we strike first?”

Fu Qian said, “Wei’s grain stockpiles are all at Longcheng. We can go straight for Luogu. Cross Mount Shenling to Longcheng, burn the supplies first, then ride directly to Qinchuan. Then the Central Plains can be taken in days.”

Wei said, “Your view and my plan are in accord.” He immediately led his force to Luogu, crossed Shenling, and came toward Longcheng.

The general stationed to defend Changcheng, Sima Wang, was in fact Sima Zhao’s uncle by clan. The city had much grain, but few men and horses. When Sima Wang heard of the Shu army’s arrival, he hurried with generals Wang Zhen and Li Peng to set camp twenty li outside. The next day the Shu army arrived, and Sima Wang brought out the two generals to face them in formation.

Jiang Wei mounted and addressed Sima Wang, saying, “Now that Sima Zhao has moved the lord to the army, there must be intent like Li Jue and Guo Si. I come now by imperial order to punish an offense. You should surrender at once. If you still cling to delusion, all your household will be exterminated!”

Wang Zhen answered loudly, “You are rude. You have violated the sovereign state repeatedly. If you do not withdraw at once, not a coat sleeve of yours will return.”

He had not finished when Sima Wang’s man Wang Zhen lunged his spear forward from behind. Fu Qian of the Shu formation stepped out to receive. Before ten exchanges they gave him an opening. Wang Zhen immediately thrust again. Fu Qian dodged and captured him alive from horseback, then returned to his own formation.

Li Peng grew furious and spurred his horse in with a wheel-like saber.

Fu Qian feigned slowness; when Li Peng came near, he hurled a heavy effort and threw him down. He had also prepared a four-pronged iron dart in his hand. Li Peng gained ground and raised his saber to strike, but Fu Qian twisted back, looked over his shoulder, and sent one short iron dart into Li Peng’s face. It burst from his eyes and he died at the horse’s feet. Wang Zhen was then pierced by a disorderly thrust from the Shu line and killed.

Jiang Wei drove his force hard forward. Sima Wang abandoned camp and entered the city, shutting his gate and not coming out.

Wei ordered, “This night the soldiers are to rest one night and gather sharpness. Tomorrow we must enter the city.”

At dawn the next day Shu soldiers rushed in in a mass and reached the walls. Fire arrows and fire-lances were sent into the city. The thatched structures on the walls blazed, and the Wei troops were thrown into confusion. Wei then ordered piles of dry brush packed beneath the walls and set them all afire at once; towering flames rose into the sky. The city was close to collapse, and Wei soldiers cried out in rage inside. Their screams were heard across the fields.

Just as they were attacking, a massive shout came from behind. Jiang Wei drew rein and looked back. Wei troops stamped and waved banners, surging toward him. He ordered the rear contingents to move forward as the front. He held under the gate banner to receive them.

A young Wei officer then rode out fully armed with armor and sash, about twenty years old, his face white like talcum, lips red as drawn cinnabar. He shouted in fierce voice, “Can you identify General Deng?”

Wei thought, “This must be Deng Ai.” The young officer rode forward with spear in hand. Both stirred themselves to full force and fought for thirty or forty exchanges with no clear advantage. The young general’s spearmanship had not a trace of slackness. Wei thought, “Without this plan, how could we win?” He turned his horse toward a mountain path on the left. The young officer chased hard. Wei hooked his steel spear and silently took out a crossbow and feathered bolt and shot. The young officer moved with sharp foresight. He had seen it already; with the twang of string he leaned forward and let the arrow pass.

Wei looked back to see the young man had arrived and thrust his spear; Wei dodged. The spear passed by his side, and Wei caught it. The young officer dropped his spear and ran back toward his own ranks.

Wei sighed, “Alas, alas!” and urged his horse to chase again. At the command gate he met an officer wading through with a saber raised:

“Jiang Wei, to chase my son is not fitting! Deng Ai is here!” Wei was startled. The young officer was indeed Deng Ai’s son, Deng Zhong.

Wei inwardly admired him in surprise. He wanted to fight Deng Ai but feared his horse was exhausted. He pointed loosely toward Ai and said, “Today I know you and your father. Withdraw for now and we will settle it in battle tomorrow.”

Ai saw the field not in his favor and also checked his horse in agreement: “So be it. Each of us should withdraw. One who hides an ambush is no man.”

So both armies withdrew. Deng Ai held camp below the Weishui, and Jiang Wei camped at the crossing between two mountains. Seeing the Shu troops’ terrain, Ai wrote to Sima Wang, “We must not fight at all; we should hold fast. When troops from Guanzhong arrive, the Shu grain will be gone and their supply will fail, and with a three-sided attack there is no victory for them. I am sending my eldest son, Deng Zhong, to help guard the city.” He also sent men to request aid from Sima Zhao.

Back at the forward camp, Jiang Wei sent a challenge letter demanding battle next day, and Deng Ai pretended to respond. At the fifth watch before dawn the next day Wei instructed the three armies to prepare food; by dawn they formed ranks and waited. The Ai camp hoisted its banners in silence and seemed as if no one remained. Wei only returned by evening.

The next day he sent another battle letter again accusing him of missing the set time. Deng Ai received him with wine and food and said, “My small body suffers slight illness; our timing has not held. We meet in battle tomorrow.”

The next day Jiang Wei again brought troops, and Ai still refused to come out.

After five or six such rounds, Fu Jian told Wei, “This must be a trick. We should guard against it.”

Wei said, “Certainly they will endure until Guanzhong troops arrive and then strike us from three sides. I will now send a letter to Sun Chen of Wu so that he joins our attack.”

Just then a courier galloped in: Sima Zhao had moved on Shou-chun, killed Zhuge Dan, and all Wu soldiers had surrendered. Sima Zhao was returning to Luoyang and intended to bring troops to rescue Changcheng. Wei was greatly startled: “This campaign against Wei has become a painted scheme again. We should instead retreat for now.”

Already mourning four attempts and failing to secure worthy achievements, and sighing for five campaigns that have still not succeeded. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: At the Rescue of Shouchun, Yu Quan Dies for Honor; At the Great Wall, Boyue Wages Fierce Battle

chapters.html:
Jiang Wei, fearing that relief troops might arrive, withdrew the command wagons, war chariots, and all military stores first. He sent the foot soldiers back first, and then had the cavalry pull back and close the rear.

A covert agent reported this to Deng Ai. Deng Ai laughed: “Jiang Wei knows that the Great General is arriving, so he withdraws first. Do not pursue him. If you do, you will fall into his design.” He then sent scouts, and they reported that at the narrow pass of Luogu he had piled up brushwood and prepared it to burn pursuing troops. Everyone praised him: “The General is truly a master of calculation!” He sent a memorial in a messenger. Sima Zhao rejoiced greatly and once again rewarded Deng Ai.

But the Grand General of Eastern Wu, Sun Chen, upon hearing that Quan Duan, Tang Zi, and the others had submitted to Wei, flew into a rage and had all of them beheaded, along with their households. Their young lord, Sun Liang, was then seventeen years old. Seeing Sun Chen’s slaughter was excessive, he felt deeply uneasy. One day he went out to the western garden, ate fresh plum fruit, and ordered the palace attendant to fetch honey. Soon it was brought. Inside, there were several clumps of mouse dung. He summoned the court storekeeper and questioned him. The attendant kowtowed and said, “My lord, I locked the storehouse securely. How could any mouse dung have gotten in?”

Sun Liang said, “Have you asked this attendant for honey before?”

The storekeeper said, “A few days ago he did ask for honey. I dared not give him any.”

Sun Liang pointed to the attendant and said, “He must have gotten angry at your refusing him, and put dung in the honey to implicate you.”

The attendant refused to concede.

Sun Liang said, “This matter is plain enough. If dung had been in honey for long, both outside and inside would be wet. If it was put in just now, the outside will be moist and the inside dry.” He ordered it to be cut open. Indeed, the inside was dry. The attendant confessed his guilt.

Much of Sun Liang’s shrewdness was like this. Yet he was controlled by Sun Chen and could not assert himself. Sun Chen’s brother, the Great General at Weiyuan, Sun Ju, entered Canglong and was assigned the palace guard duty. General of the Wu Guard, Sun En; Associate General, Sun Gan; and Changshui Captain, Sun Kai, were stationed separately in the camps.

One day Sun Liang sat in silent frustration, while his court attendant Quan Ji stood at his side. Quan Ji was his father-in-law’s family relative. Sun Liang wept and said, “Sun Chen has monopolized authority and kills without restraint. He has deceived me beyond measure. If this is not met, it will become trouble for the future.”

Quandi replied, “If Your Majesty has use for your servant, I am ready to die a thousand times.”

Sun Liang said, “Now you can quietly raise the palace guard and have Commander Liu Cheng hold each city gate with his men. I will go out myself and kill Sun Chen. This must not be known to your mother. Your mother is Sun Chen’s sister. If it leaks out, it is not a small error.”

Quandi said, “Please let Your Majesty draft an edict for me.”

He continued, “When the time comes for me to move, I will show the edict to everyone so that Sun Chen’s followers dare not act rashly.”

Sun Liang agreed and had a secret edict written and delivered to Quandi. Quandi returned home and quietly told his father, Quan Shang. Shang understood the matter and told his wife, “In three days Sun Chen will be killed.” She answered, “Then kill him.” Although she answered so, she secretly had the letter carried to Sun Chen. Sun Chen grew furious and that very night called his brothers and four brothers-in-arms, raised the elite troops, first surrounding the inner palace. At the same time he had Quan Shang, Liu Cheng, and their families seized.

By dawn, Sun Liang heard the great din of bronze drums and gongs outside the palace gates. A palace attendant hurried in to report, “Sun Chen has brought troops and has encircled the inner garden.” Sun Liang was furious and pointed at Empress Quan, scolding, “Your father and brother have ruined great matters for me!” He drew his sword and tried to go out.

Empress Quan, with attendants and close officials, clung to his robes and wept, refusing to let him leave.

Sun Chen first executed Quan Shang, Liu Cheng, and their household. Then he summoned all civil and military officials into the hall and issued orders:

The Son of Heaven has fallen into indulgence and illness for long, and, confused and unworthy, has ruled without order. He is not fit to offer incense to the ancestral temple. We therefore depose him. If any among you dare not obey, it is treason by rebellion.

The officials all trembled and answered, “We are willing to follow the General’s command.”

Senior Secretary Huan Yi was furious. From among the body of officials he strode forth and pointed at Sun Chen, shouting: “Our present sovereign is a wise lord. How dare you speak such disorderly words! I would rather die than obey a rebel.”

Sun Chen was furious. He drew his sword and beheaded him, then entered the inner hall, pointed at Sun Liang, and shouted, “A wicked and deluded ruler deserves death and mutilation, to satisfy Heaven and men. By the late sovereign’s face, I depose you to King of Kuaiji. I will choose a worthy one and enthrone him!”

He shouted at Mid-level Secretary Li Chong, seized his seals and title, and ordered Deng Cheng to arrest him. Sun Liang wept loudly and withdrew.

In later years, people sang a lament:

The traitors defame Yi Yin, while wicked ministers fill Huo Guang’s role.

Pity the sovereign of wit, denied the hall of court.

Sun Chen sent the Court Master, Sun Kai, and Mid-level Secretary Dong Chao to Hulin to invite Prince of Langye, Sun Xiu, to come. Sun Xiu had the courtesy name Zilie and was Sun Quan’s sixth son. In Hulin, he had a dream at night: he rode a dragon up to Heaven and, glancing back, saw that he could no longer see the dragon’s tail, and awakened in terror. The next day, Sun Kai and Dong Chao arrived and begged him to return to the capital.

As they passed Quya, an elderly man, surname Gan, name Xiu, knelt and said, “Change is certain when things endure too long. Your Highness should hurry.” Sun Xiu thanked him. On reaching Busei Pavilion, General Sun En drove out to welcome him. Sun Xiu dared not ride a palanquin, but entered in a small cart. Ministers and officials lined the road and bowing as he passed. Sun Chen came out and helped him up, inviting him inside. In the main hall he was led to the imperial seat as Son of Heaven.

Sun Xiu twice refused with formal humility before finally receiving the Jade Seal.

After the ceremonies of civil and military officers were complete, Sun Xiu issued a general amnesty over the realm and proclaimed the first year of Yong’an. He appointed Sun Chen as Chancellor and Governor of Jing Province. Many officers received offices and rewards. He also made Sun Hao, son of his brother, Marquis of Wucheng. The Sun family became five marquesses in all, each commanding the palace guard, and their power tilted the court toward themselves. Under Emperor Sun Xiu, though he feared inner treachery, he outwardly bestowed grace while quietly setting precautions. Sun Chen’s arrogance grew more and more.

In the twelfth month, Sun Chen brought beef and wine into the palace to offer congratulations for Sun Xiu’s life and longevity. Sun Xiu refused to receive them. Angered, Sun Chen went in a drunken state to the residence of General Zhang Bu and drank there. When he was very drunk he said, “When I deposed the King of Kuaiji, everyone urged me to take the throne. I did not, because Your Majesty is worthy. I therefore set him up. Yet today I come to offer your life-congratulatory drink and am refused; this treats me like a lesser man. I will make you learn how we should meet, sooner or later.”

Zhang Bu only assented. The next day he reported this to Sun Xiu in secret. Sun Xiu, greatly frightened, was uneasy day and night.

Within days Sun Chen sent Mid-level Secretary Meng Zong and assigned fifteen thousand of the Central Camp’s best troops to station at Wuchang, and gave them all the military gear from the armory.

Generals Wei Miao and the Wu Guard Officer Shi Shuo secretly reported to Sun Xiu: “Sun Chen has moved troops outward and moved out all weapons from the armory. Before long, he is certain to stage another coup.”

Sun Xiu was alarmed. He quickly summoned Zhang Bu to confer.

Boastingly, Bu said, “The veteran General Ding Feng has a mind keener than most and can decide grave matters. Invite him to meet us.”

Sun Xiu then summoned Ding Feng inside. Ding Feng reported, “Your Majesty need not worry. I have one stratagem to remove this danger from the state.” Sun Xiu asked what it was.

Ding Feng said, “On the coming year-end sacrificial day, summon all ministers together and call Sun Chen to sit with them. I will handle the rest of the arrangements.” Sun Xiu was delighted.

Ding Feng ordered Wei Miao and Shi Shuo to handle external matters, and Zhang Bu to stand ready within.

That night, wild wind came up. Sand and pebbles flew, old trees were torn out by the roots. By dawn when the wind settled, an envoy arrived with an imperial order: Sun Chen was to come to the palace for a banquet.

Sun Chen had just risen; as if someone had pushed him flat on level ground, and his mood soured. More than ten envoys crowded around and entered with him. His household tried to stop him: “All night, there has been storm and wind. This morning he rose without cause and stumbled as if stumbling without reason. We fear this is no good sign. Do not go.”

Sun Chen said, “My brothers and I jointly command the palace guard. Who dares to come near me? If there is any movement, raise signal fire in my residence.” After issuing this instruction, he mounted and entered.

Sun Xiu anxiously came down from the throne to receive him and asked him to sit high.

After several rounds of drinking, many cried out in alarm, “There is fire rising outside the palace!” Sun Chen tried to rise. Sun Xiu stopped him: “Chancellor, sit steady. There are many outer troops. Why need you fear?”

Before he could finish speaking, Left General Zhang Bu drew his sword, thirty soldiers at his back, and rushed onto the hall. With raised voice, he cried, “There is an edict to arrest the rebel Sun Chen!”

When Sun Chen suddenly tried to run, soldiers already had him. He knelt and begged, “Please, send me to Jiaozhou to return to my fields.”
