Sun Xiu shouted at him, “Why did you not send Teng Yin, Lu Ju, and Wang Dun there?” and ordered him pushed down and beheaded.

Then Zhang Bu pulled Sun Chen down the hall and beheaded him. None of his followers dared to move.

Zhang Bu read out an edict: “The guilt rests on Sun Chen alone. Let the others go unpunished.” The crowd then calmed.

Zhang Bu asked Sun Xiu to ascend Wufeng Tower. Ding Feng, Wei Miao, and Shi Shuo brought Sun Chen’s brothers and household in, and Sun Xiu ordered all of them beheaded in the city market.

Among those linked to the clique, several hundred died and three lineages were annihilated. Sun Xiu ordered soldiers to dig open Sun Jun’s grave and slay his head corpse. For the families of the already executed, such as Zhuge Ke, Teng Yin, Lu Ju, and Wang Dun, he ordered their tombs rebuilt to show their loyalty.

As for those whose ties were distant but who had fled, he pardoned them and sent them back to their hometowns. Ding Feng was rewarded heavily.

A dispatch reached Chengdu. Liu Shan, the Later Lord, sent an envoy in return congratulations, and the Wu envoy Xue Xu replied in kind. Xue Xu came back from Shu, and Sun Xiu asked what had been happening in Shu lately.

Xue Xu reported, “Of late, the eunuch Huang Hao has run affairs at court, and all ministers have followed him. In his court no one speaks frankly; outside, the people look thin-faced and pale. As the saying goes, swallows roost in the main hall unaware that the high hall is about to burn.”

Sun Xiu sighed, “If only Zhuge Wuhou had been alive, how could things have come to this?”

He then wrote an official state letter and had it delivered to Chengdu. In it he said Sima Zhao would in no long time seize Wei and then invade Wu and Shu for display of force, so each should make preparations.

When Jiang Wei heard this missive, he rejoiced and submitted another memorial, pressing again for an expedition against Wei. In the winter of the first year of Jingyao, Jiang Wei, Great General of Shu, led Liao Hua and Zhang Yi as the vanguard, Wang Han and Jiang Bin as the left army, Jiang Shu and Fu Qian as the right army, and Hu Ji as the reserve. Jiang Wei and Xiahou Ba served as central commanders-in-chief over two hundred thousand Shu troops. After taking leave of the Later Lord, he went straight to Hanzhong. There he conferred with Xiahou Ba about which place to strike first.

Xiahou Ba said, “Qishan is the place where weapons are matched and war is done. It was there that the Grand Chancellor once advanced his army six times. Other fields are not open for us now.” Jiang Wei followed his advice, ordered all three wings to advance toward Qishan together, and set camp at the valley pass.

At that time Deng Ai was already in the Qishan camps, organizing troops from Longyou. All of a sudden a horseman came rushing with news that the Shu army had set down three camps at the valley entrance. Deng Ai saw this and, ascending to a high point to look, returned to his camp and sat in his pavilion. He exclaimed in great delight, “It is just as I had expected!”

In truth, Deng Ai had already measured the veins of the ground and so left this area for Shu to set camp. From earth to Qishan camp all the way to Shu camps, he had dug an underground passage, waiting for the Shu troops to arrive and then to strike from within.

By then, Jiang Wei had come to the valley entrance and split his forces into three camps. The tunnel lay in the left camp, where Wang Han and Jiang Bin had camped.

Deng Ai ordered his son Deng Zhong and Shi Zuan each to lead ten thousand men, one to the left and one to the right, to strike in force. He then ordered his deputy commander, Zheng Lun, and five hundred sappers to move at the second watch of the night through the tunnel straight to the left camp and emerge from beneath the camp after it from the rear.

Wang Han and Jiang Bin, for their part, had only just raised camp and feared the Wei troops would swoop in, so they could not even take off their armor to sleep. Hearing in the middle camp that the formation was in confusion, they quickly armed their mounts and drew weapons. At the camp’s edge Deng Zhong marched in with troops.

They were attacked from inside and outside at once. The two commanders Wang and Jiang fought desperately but could not withstand it; they abandoned their camps and fled.

Jiang Wei, in the main pavilion, heard the cries from the left camp and understood there were troops from both within and without attacking together. He immediately mounted his horse and stood before the central tent, ordering, “If anyone makes a disorderly move, execute him. If enemy troops have reached the edge of camp, ask no questions: have them all shot with bow and crossbow.”

At the same time he instructed the right camp likewise and allowed no impulsive movement. In truth Wei troops made more than ten charges, each rebuffed and turned away by arrows. They struck only into dawn, and the Wei troops dared not break into the camp.

When Deng Ai drew his men back, he sighed in admiration and said, “Jiang Wei has learned thoroughly the method of Wu Hou! Though stationed in the night, he did not panic; he heard the change and did not fall into disorder. He is truly a commander of quality.”

The next day Wang Han and Jiang Bin gathered their broken men and knelt before the great camp to plead for pardon.

Jiang Wei said, “This is not your fault. It is because I did not understand the terrain.”

He then sent away the cavalry and ordered the two commanders to settle down and establish the camp. He had the badly wounded dead and killed men filled into the tunnel, then covered with earth.

He sent a single challenge letter to ask Deng Ai to meet in battle the next day. Deng Ai was pleased and accepted.

The next day both armies lined up before Qishan. Jiang Wei, following the Eight Formations of Master Kongming, had arranged deployment according to Heaven, Earth, Wind, Clouds, Bird, Snake, Dragon, and Tiger.

When Deng Ai came riding out and saw Jiang Wei spread in eight-trigram form, he arranged himself likewise, with front, back, left, right, and gates all similar. Jiang Wei held his spear and, shouting over the mounted ranks, said, “You copied my Eight Formation. Can you also change it?”

Deng Ai laughed, “Do you think only you can lay such a formation? If I know how to lay one, how could I not know how to transform it?”

He then checked his horse and entered the formation. He ordered the judges of standards to wave the flags left and right, transforming it into sixty-four gates in an 8-by-8 arrangement. Before leaving, he asked, “What do you make of this transformation?”

Jiang Wei said, “Though close enough, do you dare encircle me within your own array?”

Deng Ai replied, “Why should I not?”

Both armies advanced in rank and file. Deng Ai directed his force from the central command. When they collided, neither array deviated from position.

Jiang Wei moved into the center and with a sudden flag signal changed it into the “Long-Serpent Earth-rolling Formation,” trapping Deng Ai at the core, while shouts shook the four sides.

Deng Ai did not know this formation and was alarmed. The Shu troops steadily pressed in. Deng Ai ordered his commanders to keep clashing, and no one could break out.

Then everyone heard the Shu troops cry together, “Deng Ai, surrender at once!”

Looking at the sky, Deng Ai sighed: “I sought to show my talent for one moment and at once I have fallen into Jiang Wei’s scheme.”

Suddenly a squad from the northwest broke in. Seeing it was Wei troops, Deng Ai seized the moment and cut through. The one who came to rescue him was Sima Wang.

When this occurred, all nine camps at Qishan had been taken by Shu. Deng Ai withdrew with the remnants and retreated to his camp south of the Wei River.

Deng Ai said to Sima Wang, “How did you know this formation well enough to rescue me?”

Sima Wang said, “In my youth I studied in Jingnan. I was friends with Cui Zhouping and Shi Guangyuan, and we discussed this formation. What Jiang Wei changed was the Long-Serpent Earth-rolling Formation. If one presses it in the usual places, it cannot be broken. I saw its head at the northwest and so struck from the northwest. It broke of itself.”

Deng Ai said in thanks, “Though I have learned formation, I truly do not know the transforms. If I know this one now, how shall we retake the Qishan stockades tomorrow?”

Sima Wang replied, “My learning may not cover what Jiang Wei has mastered.”

Deng Ai said, “Tomorrow you fight him in formation, and I will lead one force to strike at the rear of Qishan. If we throw them into a two-front melee, we can recover the old camps.”

He then gave command for Zheng Lun to lead the vanguard, while he led the main army to strike the rear of the mountain. At the same time he sent a challenge for Jiang Wei to fight formation tactics again the next day.

Jiang Wei sent back his brief reply. He said to all the commanders, “I inherited the secret text of Wuhou, where this formation can be transformed three hundred sixty-five times, matching the number of the weekly cycle. What he has challenged me to is merely ‘showing a blade at the gate.’ But there must be deceit in its middle, do you all understand?”

Liao Hua said, “This must be him trying to bait our array and bring another force against our rear.”

Jiang Wei smiled, “That is exactly what I thought.” He ordered Zhang Yi and Liao Hua to lead ten thousand soldiers to hide behind the mountain.

The next day Jiang Wei gathered all nine camps and arrayed them before Qishan. Sima Wang marched out from the south bank of the Wei River and, riding forward, took position before Jiang Wei to answer him.

Jiang Wei said, “You challenged me to a battle of formation. Show me your array first.”

Wang set out the eight-trigram form.

Jiang Wei said, “This is the same form as my Eight Formation. You now copied my method; how is that astonishing?”

Wang said, “You too have stolen others’ methods.”

Jiang Wei said, “How many changes does this formation have?”

Wang laughed: “If I can lay it, can I not change it? This formation has eighty-one changes.”

Jiang Wei said with a smile, “Try then.”

Wang transformed several times and then came out asking, “Do you know my transformations?”

Jiang Wei smiled, “Mine has three hundred sixty-five by the cycle of Zhou heaven. You are a frog in a well: how can you fathom the mysterious depths?”

Wang knew he had not fully mastered this art and, forcing his voice, argued defensively: “I do not believe it. Try your own transformations.”

Jiang Wei replied, “Call out Deng Ai. I will lay it for him to see.”

Wang said, “General Deng has sound strategy and does not care for formations.”

Jiang Wei laughed broadly. “What sound strategy? It is only this: to trick me into arraying here while he takes troops against my rear.”

Sima Wang was alarmed and was about to move into close battle when Jiang Wei pointed at the left and right wings with the tip of his whip handle. The two wings advanced first, and the Wei soldiers who had come threw down armor and cast away spears, each fleeing to save their lives.

Deng Ai, meanwhile, ordered Vanguarding Commander Zheng Lun to rush the mountain rear. Just as Zheng Lun turned the mountain’s edge, there was suddenly a cannon report and trumpet blasts, and a hidden force surged out; the leading general was Liao Hua.

Before either side exchanged words, horse met horse and Liao Hua struck in one cut, beheading Zheng Lun under his horse.

Deng Ai, greatly startled, pressed hard on the reins and tried to pull back his force, but Zhang Yi came charging with another army. The two sides attacked from both sides. The Wei troops were badly defeated. Deng Ai barely broke free, but his body had taken four arrows.

When he reached the camp south of the Wei River, Sima Wang had also arrived. They discussed how to withdraw.

Sima Wang said, “Recently our Shu lord Liu Shan has favored the noble Huang Hao and passes his days in wine and girls. We can use counterintelligence and summon Jiang Wei back to Shu. This encirclement can then be lifted.”

Deng Ai asked the assembled strategists, “Who can go into Shu to contact Huang Hao?”

Before the discussion ended, one man called out, “I will go.” Deng Ai saw him and knew him as Dang Jun of Xiangyang.

Deng Ai was delighted. He ordered Dang Jun with jewels and gold, send him straight to Chengdu to ingratiate himself with Huang Hao, and spread rumors that Jiang Wei harbored resentment toward the Son of Heaven and would soon defect to Wei. Word quickly spread through Chengdu that this was what everyone believed.

Huang Hao reported to the Later Lord, who ordered an all-night dispatch to summon Jiang Wei to court.

Jiang Wei had challenged Deng Ai to battle day after day, while Deng Ai held firm and would not come out. Jiang Wei grew deeply doubtful. Suddenly an order of summons arrived, calling him into court. He did not know the reason, so he had to retreat from the field and return to the capital.

Deng Ai and Sima Wang knew that Jiang Wei had fallen into the stratagem. They withdrew the Wei River south forces and then ambushed him on the road after they left.

It was so:

Le Yi’s campaign against Qi was blocked by intrigue,

Yue Fei broke the enemy only to be recalled by slander.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Ding Feng Devises a Plan and Executes Sun Chen; Jiang Wei Contests Formations and Defeats Deng Ai

chapters.html:
Later, Jiang Wei ordered the troops to withdraw. Liao Hua said, “A commander in the field is not bound to obey every order from the court. Though we have an imperial edict now, we should not act yet.”

Zhang Yi said, “The people of Shu have seen the Grand General raise troops year after year and have many grievances. Better to use this moment of victory to gather them back and steady their hearts before making further plans.”

Jiang Wei said, “Good.” He ordered each army to retire by procedure, and sent Liao Hua and Zhang Yi to hold the rear and prepare for any pursuit from Wei.

Deng Ai then set out in pursuit. He saw in front of him that the Shu banners were in orderly lines and the cavalry withdrew slowly. He exclaimed, “Jiang Wei has truly mastered Wuhou’s methods!” He therefore did not pursue and drew up his forces back to Qishan camp.

Jiang Wei arrived in Chengdu and entered audience with the Son of Heaven to ask why he had been recalled. The Son of Heaven said, “You have been on the frontier for a long time with no return of the army. I feared your soldiers were exhausted by campaigning, so I issued the order for you to return to the court. I had no other intent.”

Jiang Wei said, “I had already reached Qishan camp and was prepared to conclude the operation, and did not expect to have it abandoned halfway through. This must be Deng Ai’s counter-ploting scheme.” The Son of Heaven was silent.

Jiang Wei offered another memorial: “I have sworn to attack the rebels and repay my debt to the state. Your Majesty should not listen to petty men and bring this doubt upon yourself.” After a long pause, the Son of Heaven finally said, “I do not doubt you. Return to Hanzhong and wait for change in Wei; then you may campaign again.”

Jiang Wei sighed and left the court, then returned to Hanzhong.

At that time, Dang Jun returned to Qishan camp and reported all this. Deng Ai and Sima Wang said, “When lord and minister are out of accord, internal treachery is certain.” They then sent Dang Jun to Luoyang to report to Sima Zhao.

Sima Zhao rejoiced and let his thoughts turn toward attacking Shu. He asked Zhonghu Jun, Jia Chong, “How can we take Shu now?”

Jia Chong said, “Not yet. The Son of Heaven still doubts his lord, and if you venture out lightly, an internal crisis will surely erupt.”

“Last year in the spring, two appearances of a yellow dragon were seen in Lingling well. The ministers submitted congratulations and called it a good omen. The Son of Heaven said: ‘Not a good omen. A dragon is a symbol of a ruler: it is neither in heaven above nor in the fields below, but in a well. That is a sign of confinement and humiliation.’ So he composed a poem called Hidden Dragon.

Its meaning made plain what the Son of Heaven intended. The poem says:

Alas, the dragon is constrained and cannot leap into the deep abyss. It flies not through the Han sky above, nor is seen in the fields below. It coils at the bottom of the well as eels and loaches dance before it. It hides its fangs, wraps its claws inside shell; alas, I am in the same plight.

When Sima Zhao heard this, he grew furious and told Jia Chong, “This man seeks to imitate Cao Fang. If we do not plan early, he will surely strike us down.”

Jia Chong said, “I am ready to scheme for the lord, morning and night.”

Now in the fifth year of Ganlu, in the fourth month, Sima Zhao came with sword drawn and entered the hall. Cao Mao came out to receive him. The court officials presented one petition after another: “The Grand General’s merit is lofty. It is fitting to make you Duke of Jin and grant nine honors.”

Cao Mao lowered his head and did not answer.

Sima Zhao spoke in a loud voice: “My father and brothers in all three of us have earned great merit for Wei. Now that I am Duke of Jin, is that not fitting?”

Cao Mao replied, “Who would dare to fail your order?”

Sima Zhao said, “In the Hidden Dragon poem, your phrase treats us as eels and loaches. What courtesy is this?”

Cao Mao could not answer. Sima Zhao laughed coldly and descended from the hall. The officials were solemn.

Back in the inner palace, Cao Mao summoned court attendant Wang Shen, Master of Writing Wang Jing, and Gentleman-in-Attendance Wang Ye, and they debated together in private.

Cao Mao wept: “Sima Zhao will attempt to usurp the throne. Everyone knows this. I will not sit and endure humiliation. Can you help me bring him down?”

Wang Jing said, “Impossible. In the past, Duke Zhaogong of Lu did not restrain the Ji clan and lost his state; now heavy power has long been in the Sima house. Every official inside and out has bent to this wicked clan; there is not one of us who stands on principle. Your Majesty’s household guards are too few and men of command are lacking. If Your Majesty does not endure, great disaster will follow. We must proceed slowly and not act rashly.”

Cao Mao said, “What can be borne? what cannot? My mind is made. Why should I fear death?”

After speaking, he went at once to the Empress Dowager and conveyed his plan.

Wang Shen and Wang Ye said to Wang Jing, “It is urgent. We must not invite ruin upon our families by our own choices. We should go to Sima Gong’s residence and submit ourselves there so as to avoid even a single death.”

Wang Jing became furious: “My lord suffers, and a servant suffers with him. My lord is disgraced, and a servant may die for him. How can I harbor a divided heart?”

Seeing Wang Jing refused, Wang Shen and Wang Ye went straight to report to Sima Zhao.

After some time, the Son of Heaven, Cao Mao, came out from the inner court, ordered the guard Jiao Bo to gather more than three hundred rough guards from the hall, and with drums and shouting they marched out. Cao Mao, sword in hand, mounted his sedan and shouted at those nearby, then headed straight toward Nanque.

Wang Jing lay before the sedan, weeping, and remonstrated: “Your Majesty leads several hundred men against Zhao. You are driving sheep into a tiger’s den, and it will be empty death. I do not value my life; I truly see this as impossible.”

Cao Mao answered, “My troops are already on the move, minister. You cannot hinder me.” He kept on toward Longmen.

They then saw Jia Chong in armor on horseback, Cheng Cui on his left and Cheng Ji on his right, with several thousand iron-clad palace guards in battle cry and rush.

Cao Mao raised his sword and shouted, “I am the Son of Heaven. You have broken into the court grounds. Are you trying to slay your lord?”

When the guards saw Cao Mao, none dared to move. Jia Chong called out to Cheng Ji: “What did Master Sima raise you for if not this day?”

Cheng Ji stood with a pike and looked back at Jia Chong: “Shall we kill? Or bind?” Jia Chong said, “Master Sima has ordered it: all must die.”

Cheng Ji raised his pike and rushed straight to the Son of Heaven’s sedan. Cao Mao shouted, “A common soldier, do you have no decency?” Before the words were done, Cheng Ji had already driven a pike through Cao Mao’s chest and hurled him from the sedan. A second stroke went through his back and he died at the carriage side.

Jiao Bo ran forward with a spear, but Cheng Ji skewered him through. The crowd fled.

Wang Jing came close behind, then shouted at Jia Chong, “Wicked rebel! How dare you kill the Son of Heaven!” Jia Chong grew angry and ordered him seized. He was brought to Sima Zhao.

Sima Zhao entered and saw the dead emperor. He feigned great shock, crying with his head on the sedan frame and summoning all ministers to report the event.

At that moment Tai Fu, Sima Fu, entered the hall, saw Cao Mao’s corpse, and knelt with his hand on his thigh as he wept: “I am the one at fault for this regicide.” He placed the corpse in a coffin and set it in the west of a side hall.

Sima Zhao then called a council of ministers in the hall. All came, except for Shangshu Puxi Chen Tai, who did not appear. Sima Zhao ordered Xun Yi, the Chancellor and uncle of Chen Tai, to summon him.

Tai, crying bitterly, said, “They used to compare him to his uncle; now the uncle is truly no better than Tai.” He entered in funeral cloth and mourning sash and paid respects before the spirit.

Sima Zhao, feigning mourning, asked, “How should we deal with this matter?”

Chen Tai said, “If only execute Jia Chong, it may at least satisfy the world.”

Sima Zhao was silent for a long while, then asked again: “Think further?”

Tai said, “Whoever has entered this hall has done so without knowing what comes after.”

Sima Zhao replied, “Cheng Ji’s treason is complete. He can be dismembered, and all three branches of his clan exterminated.”

Cheng Ji shouted at Sima Zhao, “This is not my fault; Jia Chong conveyed your command to me!” Sima Zhao ordered that his tongue be cut first. Until death, Cheng Ji never ceased crying innocence. Cheng Cui was also beheaded at the market, and his three clans were entirely exterminated.

A poem later lamented:

It was Sima who once ordered Jia Chong; a robe of red mud stained at Nanque for the slain ruler. Yet Cheng Ji was put to death and three clans destroyed; only the soldiers and people seemed deaf.

Sima Zhao had Wang Jing’s entire household seized and sent to prison. Wang Jing was in the prison court when he suddenly saw his mother brought in bound. He prostrated himself and wept, “An unfilial son has dragged his mother into this.”

His mother laughed: “Who does not die? I only feared they might not let us die in the right way. To lay down our lives for this—what regret is there?”

The next day, the whole family of Wang Jing was marched to the eastern market. Mother and son accepted punishment with smiles. In the city all scholars and commoners alike wept.

A later poem said:

In the early Han, they praised a hidden sword. At the end of Han, we saw Wang Jing. His true fierceness of heart did not change; his will was all the more clear and hard. His integrity weighed as heavy as Mount Tai, his life as light as a feather. The fame of mother and son remains. May it stand and tilt heaven and earth together.

The Grand Tutor Sima Fu asked to bury Cao Mao with the rites of a king. Sima Zhao allowed this.

Jia Chong and others then urged Sima Zhao to accept the Wei transfer of power and become emperor. Sima Zhao replied, “Formerly King Wen held two-thirds of the realm while serving the Yin house and was praised as supremely virtuous. Emperor Wudi of Wei refused to receive the edict from Han; it is no different from my refusal now to accept an edict from Wei.”

Jia Chong and the others already knew that Sima Zhao had his mind on Sima Yan. They no longer pressed him on succession.

In that year, sixth month, Sima Zhao enthroned Cao Huang, Marquis of Changdao Township, as emperor and changed the era name to Jingyuan, first year.

Cao Huang took the name Cao Huan, courtesy name Jingzhao. He was Cao Cao’s grandson and the son of Prince Cao Yu of Yan.

Huan made Sima Zhao Chancellor, Duke of Jin, and gave him one hundred thousand qin of silver and ten thousand bolts of silk. He bestowed numerous offices and rewards on ministers and commanders.

There had long been informers reporting into Shu. When Jiang Wei heard that Sima Zhao had killed Cao Mao and enthroned Cao Huan, he said with joy, “I have gained a name beyond all for my campaign against Wei today.”

He sent a letter to Wu and ordered troops raised to demand why Sima Zhao had slain the Son of Heaven. At the same time, he petitioned the Son of Heaven and raised one hundred and fifty thousand men. Thousands of wagons were prepared, each carrying board-crates on top. He appointed Liao Hua and Zhang Yi as the vanguard.

Liao Hua was assigned Zixia Valley, Zhang Yi Lop Valley, and Jiang Wei himself Xie Valley. All three were to pass by Qishan before turning to Qi. The three columns advanced in force and came dashing toward Qishan.

At that time Deng Ai was in the mountain fort, training men and horses. He heard the report that three Shu columns were advancing and gathered his officers to debate.

Army Adviser Wang Guan presented a plan: “I have one stratagem that cannot be spoken aloud. I have written it down and humbly submit it for the general’s inspection.” He handed it over.

When Deng Ai read it through, he laughed. “This plan is good, but I fear it will not deceive Jiang Wei.”

Wang Guan said, “I am willing to lay down my life to go.”

Deng Ai replied, “If your resolve is firm, you can certainly make it succeed.” He sent him five thousand men.

At night Wang Guan came from Xie Valley at once and collided directly with the forward pickets of the Shu vanguard. He called out, “I am a deserter from Wei. I can report to the field commander.”

The pickets reported to Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei ordered the remaining men to block and told the one in charge to come forward.

Wang Guan knelt on the ground and said, “I am Wang Guan, nephew of Wang Jing. I recently saw Sima Zhao slay the Son of Heaven and have seen his whole family exterminated. I grieve to the bone. Now, since Your Excellency has risen in arms to punish him, I have brought this branch of my troops, five thousand in all, to surrender. I beg to be posted where I may serve, destroy the traitors, and repay my uncle’s death.”

Jiang Wei was greatly pleased and said, “If you have come in earnest, I must also receive you in earnest. The one thing my army lacks is grain. The stores are at Chuan Gate; you may carry them to Qishan. I only need to go and take Qishan camp now.”

Inwardly Wang Guan rejoiced, thinking he had taken the bait, and gladly accepted. Jiang Wei said, “You need not bring all five thousand to carry grain. Take three thousand with you and leave two thousand behind as guides and to strike at Qishan.”

Fearing Jiang Wei still suspected him, Wang Guan took only three thousand men.

Jiang Wei told Fu Qian to bring two thousand former Wei soldiers to follow and obey later orders.

A moment later, Xiahou Ba arrived. Xiahou Ba said, “How did the Commander trust Wang Guan so quickly? Though I am in Wei and do not know every detail, I have not heard that Wang Guan is truly Wang Jing’s nephew. There is much deceit here, please inspect him closely.”

Jiang Wei laughed. “I already know Wang Guan is deceit. That is why I split his strength and use his own plan against him.”

Xiahou Ba said, “Tell me your reading.”

Jiang Wei replied, “Sima Zhao is as a villainous hero like Cao Cao: he killed Wang Jing and wiped out three clans. How could he spare his own nephew in a frontier garrison? Hence I know it is a ruse. My companion Zhongquan has seen this with me.”

Thus Jiang Wei did not leave Xie Valley. He sent soldiers to lie in ambush along the roads in preparation for Wang Guan’s trick. In less than ten days, the ambush did indeed seize Wang Guan and a messenger bringing letters to Deng Ai. The latter came to report everything.

Jiang Wei examined the matter in detail and searched out the private letter. The letter fixed an appointment for the twentieth day of the eighth month, by a small path, to transport supplies home to the main camp and had also instructed Deng Ai to send troops to Tan mountain valley to meet them.

Jiang Wei had the messenger killed, then changed the contents to order a meet on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, and for Deng Ai to bring his main force to Tan mountain valley.

He then sent men, dressed as Wei soldiers, to the Wei camp with a fresh letter. At the same time, he had hundreds of supply wagons unloaded of grain and filled with dry brushwood and kindling to make an igniting load, covered in blue cloth.

Fu Qian was ordered to lead two thousand former Wei men in the guise of grain transport.

Jiang Wei and Xiahou Ba each took a force into the valley to lie hidden. He also ordered Jiang Shu out through Xie Valley while Liao Hua and Zhang Yi each pushed forward to capture Qishan.

Deng Ai received Wang Guan’s letter and rejoiced. He hastily drafted a reply and sent the envoy back. On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, Deng Ai led fifty thousand elite troops straight to Tan mountain valley.

He sent men to a rise to reconnoiter. From afar they saw endless grain wagons, one after another, coming through a mountain hollow.

Deng Ai reined in and watched. It seemed truly all Wei soldiers. His men said, “It is already dusk and getting dark. Dispatch one quickly to Tan valley to support Wang Guan at the exit.”

Deng Ai replied, “The mountain in front covers the ground. If there is an ambush ahead, retreat will be hard. We should wait here.”

As he spoke, two riders came at speed: “General Wang has grain crossing the frontier and his rear is driving up; they look to us for quick aid.”

Deng Ai was greatly startled and urged his men forward in haste. It was the first watch and the moon shone like day.

Then they heard shouting from the mountains behind, as though Wang Guan himself was striking there. He rode straight past the mountain’s back when suddenly a thicket of troops burst from the trees. The commander was Fu Qian, leading on horseback.

Fu Qian cried out, “Deng Ai, you wretch! You are already caught in my lord’s net. Why not dismount and die?”

Deng Ai panicked, turned and rode back. He fled.

The wagons were instantly lit as signal fires. Both lines of Shu troops poured out together and cut down the Wei soldiers—seven out of eight, nearly all. From the valley floor to the peaks came cries: “Seize Deng Ai and receive a thousand jin; grant him the title of marquis of ten thousand households!”

Deng Ai dropped his armor and cast off his helmet. He leapt down from horseback and mingled in the infantry, scrambling over the ridges and ridges and escaping over the hills.

Jiang Wei and Xiahou Ba moved at the head of their horsemen to capture him, but not expecting him to escape on foot, Deng Ai vanished from the mounted pursuit.

Jiang Wei sent victorious troops to seize Wang Guan’s supply wagons.

Afterwards, Wang Guan had secretly arranged with Deng Ai to have the grain carts already in rank and fully prepared before raising the uprising. Then an insider reported: “The secret is exposed. General Deng has suffered a great defeat; we do not know whether he yet lives.”

Wang Guan had scouts sent out. They reported that three Shu columns were closing in from all sides and that rising dust still came from behind; there was no road left for escape. Wang Guan shouted at his men to set fire to the wagons and burn all the grain cars.

At once flames leapt up; a fierce fire blazed into the sky.

Wang Guan cried out, “The matter is urgent! You must die fighting!” He then led his men westward to break out.

Jiang Wei pursued from behind with all three columns.

Jiang Wei thought Wang Guan was fighting himself to save his life and return to Wei, and he did not expect Wang Guan instead to force his way into Hanzhong. Wang Guan feared the pursuers would catch him, so he burned bridges and mountain passes alike.

Jiang Wei, fearing for Hanzhong, stopped and did not pursue Deng Ai. He gathered men and took the night side road in chase of Wang Guan.

Wang Guan was attacked from all four sides by Shu troops and threw himself into Black Dragon River, where he died. The remainder of his soldiers were all put to death by Jiang Wei’s forces.

Though Jiang Wei had defeated Deng Ai, he had lost many grain stores and had destroyed the mountain roads, so he withdrew his force back to Hanzhong.

Deng Ai took his shattered men and fled back to Qishan camp, submitting a memorial and asking punishment in return; he requested demotion.

Sima Zhao, seeing that Deng Ai had done great service several times already, could not bring himself to demote him and again gave him rich rewards.

Deng Ai distributed all gifts he had already received to the bereaved families of fallen officers.

Fearful that Shu troops might yet march out again, Sima Zhao added fifty thousand men and stationed them with Deng Ai to hold defense.

Jiang Wei repaired the roads and ladders through the night, and then again proposed another campaign.

He repairs the roads and ladders, and the troops keep coming out in one force. If they do not conquer the Middle Kingdom, they will not rest before death. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Cao Mao Rides Out and Dies at Nanque; Jiang Wei Abandons Grain and Defeats Wei Troops

chapters.html:
In the fifth year of Jingyao in Shu-Han, in the tenth month of winter, the General-in-Chief Jiang Wei had men repairing the plank roads through the night, and he had the army stores and weapons put in order; he also shifted boats along the Hanzhong waterways. Everything was then complete. He submitted a memorial to the Latter Ruler saying,

“Though I have gone out on campaign repeatedly and have not won a great victory, I have already shaken Wei’s courage. Now, with soldiers kept too long in reserve, idleness will make them dull, and dullness will make them sick. As it is, the army thinks only of dying in service and wishes to risk its lives. If I do not prevail, I should bear the death penalty.”

The Latter Ruler read the memorial and hesitated. Qiao Zhou stepped out of his place and reported,

“I watched the heavens last night. In the land of Western Shu, the star of command was dim and not clear. Since the General-in-Chief wants to march again, this expedition is very ill-favored. Your Majesty should issue an edict and order him to stop.”

The Latter Ruler said,

“Let us see how this campaign turns out. If it is truly a failure, then I will stop it.”

Qiao Zhou remonstrated repeatedly and was not heard. He went home and sighing deeply, began claiming illness and did not come out.

When Jiang Wei was preparing to raise the army, he asked Liao Hua,

“Now that I take the field, I have sworn to recover the Central Plains. Which place should we take first?”

Liao Hua replied,

“Years of constant campaigning have unsettled the people. Wei has Deng Ai as well, ingenious and clever, not men of trivial caliber. Since the General is determined to do what is difficult, I do not dare to oppose him.”

Jiang Wei grew angry in an instant and said,

“Formerly the Chancellor rode out to Qishan six times, and that was also for the realm. I have attacked Wei eight times. Was it for one man’s private gain? We should take Taoyang first. Whoever opposes me will be executed.”

He left Liao Hua behind to guard Hanzhong and, with his commanders, he marched out with three hundred thousand men straight for Taoyang.

Soon after, men from Sichuan Gate arrived and reported to the stockade at Qishan. At that time Deng Ai was speaking of military matters with Sima Wang. When this news arrived, he sent scouts to verify it, and they reported that the Shu soldiers had all gone out through Taoyang.

Sima Wang said,

“Jiang Wei is very calculating. Could he be feinting Taoyang while truly aiming for Qishan?”

Deng Ai replied,

“It is so: Jiang Wei has truly taken the way out through Taoyang. If he knew us only of the grain in that area, he would expect us to hold Qishan and ignore Taoyang. He has therefore struck at Taoyang directly. If he takes this city, he can stock grain and forage, connect with the Qiang, and plan for a long affair.”

Sima Wang asked,

“What then should be done?”

Deng Ai said,

“We can withdraw all soldiers from here and split into two routes to go to Taoyang. Twenty-five li from Taoyang lies the small city of Houhe, the throat of that area. You take one army and hide at Taoyang. Lower flags and drum signals, open all four gates as if unguarded, and then act just so. I will take one army and hide at Houhe; we will win a great victory.”

Plans were fixed, and everyone acted accordingly. Only the subordinate commander Shizuan remained at the Qishan stockade.

Jiang Wei made Xiahou Ba lead the vanguard and set out with one force first toward Taoyang. As Xiahou Ba advanced, he saw no single banner on the city walls and all four gates stood open. Uncertain, he did not dare enter and turned to his commanders,

“Could this be deception?”

The commanders replied,

“We can see that it is an empty city. There are only a few common people in it. Having heard the General-in-Chief had come, they have all abandoned it and fled.”

Xiahou Ba did not trust them. He rode south of the city to scout. He saw countless old men and children all fleeing toward the northwest.

Xiahou Ba rejoiced,

“It truly is an empty city.”

He entered first, with the rest following behind. As they came up to the city wall, a sudden signal blast rang out. Drums and horns sounded together on the walls, standards were raised everywhere, and a bridge was hauled out.

Xiahou Ba was alarmed,

“I have been tricked!”

When he tried to withdraw, arrow and slingstone fell from above like rain. The pitiful Xiahou Ba and five hundred soldiers all died at the wall’s foot.

Later generations sighed in a verse:

Great was Jiang Wei’s boldness; his stratagems were long and subtle. Who knows that Deng Ai lay in hidden watch? Pity is Xiahou Ba, who dashed for Taoyang, slain in an instant beneath the city arrows.

Sima Wang broke out from the inner fort; Shu soldiers were utterly defeated and fled. Shortly afterward Jiang Wei arrived with the relieving force, drove back Sima Wang, and camped below the city. When he learned that Xiahou Ba had been shot dead, he grieved deeply.

At the second watch of that night, Deng Ai, from within Houhe city, secretly led one army by hidden ways into the Shu camp. Shu ranks were thrown into confusion, and Jiang Wei could not hold them. The ramparts above roared with drums and horns. Sima Wang brought out his troops. Clashing from both sides, the Shu army was overwhelmed.

Jiang Wei broke in on one side and surged on the other, fought and escaped only with difficulty, then withdrew more than twenty li and camped again. After two defeats in succession, the Shu troops trembled in heart. Jiang Wei told his commanders,

“Victory and defeat are common in war. Though we have lost men and officers today, there is no need for alarm. The matter of success and failure will be decided in this one turn. Do not change your hearts. If any man says we should retreat, he will be executed on the spot.”

Zhang Yi submitted,

“All Wei troops are here; Qishan must surely be empty. Let the General battle Deng Ai and hold him, and attack Taoyang and Houhe. I will take one force to take Qishan. If we take the Nine Camps of Qishan, then drive on Chang’an. That is the best plan.”

Jiang Wei agreed and ordered Zhang Yi to take the rear force and go straight to Qishan.

Jiang Wei brought his troops to Houhe and fought Deng Ai. Deng Ai led his army out to meet him. The two forces faced in formation, and the two armies faced one another, and their champions exchanged blows for several dozen rounds without deciding victory. Both withdrew and returned to camp.

The next day Jiang Wei again brought his force to challenge. Deng Ai held his troops and did not come out. Jiang Wei ordered his army to taunt the enemy. Deng Ai considered,

“The Shu men were nearly annihilated in one encounter and yet did not retreat, but returned day after day for close fighting. They must mean to split forces to strike the Qishan stockade. Commander Shizuan there is few and weak in wisdom, so he will fail for sure. I must go myself to save him.”

He called Deng Zhong and instructed,

“You must hold this post carefully and endure these skirmishes. Do not venture out lightly. Tonight I will take troops to Qishan to give aid.”

At the second watch that night, while Jiang Wei was planning in camp, a roar rose from outside, and drums and horns filled the air. Men reported that Deng Ai had brought three thousand picked troops for a night assault and the commanders intended to sally out.

Jiang Wei restrained them:

“Do not move rashly.”

In truth Deng Ai had already ridden to the forward pickets of the Shu camp, reconnoitered the position, and taken the chance to go help Qishan. Deng Zhong slipped back into the city.

Jiang Wei summoned his commanders,

“Deng Ai is making a fake display of a night fight. He must be going to save the Qishan stockade.”

He then called for Fuxian and told him,

“You hold this camp and do not lightly engage the enemy.”

After dispatching him, Jiang Wei took three thousand soldiers himself to aid Zhang Yi.

Zhang Yi had already arrived and was attacking Qishan. Commander Shizuan, with too few men, could not hold it long. As he waited to be broken, Deng Ai’s troops suddenly arrived and charged through one round. The Shu soldiers were badly defeated, and Zhang Yi was cut off behind the mountain with his path of return blocked.

In the middle of panic, a loud cry rose and horns thundered. It was seen that Wei troops were repeatedly falling back.

An officer reported,

“The General-in-Chief Jiang Boyue has arrived.”

Riding this moment, Zhang Yi drove his force forward to link with him. From both sides they attacked in tandem. Deng Ai was broken in one engagement and withdrew in haste up to the Qishan stockade, where he did not emerge.

Jiang Wei ordered the troops to surround from all four sides.

The story now splits in two threads. In Chengdu, the Latter Ruler, listening to the eunuch Huang Hao and sunk in drink and lust, neglected court affairs. In those days, Liu Yan’s wife, Hu Shi, was exceedingly beautiful. She entered the palace to receive an audience with the Empress; Hu Shi remained in the palace for a month before leaving.

Liu Yan suspected that his wife had private dealings with the Latter Ruler. He ordered five hundred household soldiers, lined up before him, and had his wife bound and beaten with the soles of shoes across her face repeatedly by each, so that she nearly died and came back again.

When the Latter Ruler heard this he was enraged and instructed the ministries to debate Liu Yan’s guilt. The ministers concluded: Liu Yan had no right to flog his wife, and the face was not a lawful place for such punishment; he should be exposed for execution in the market. He was therefore beheaded.

From then on, officials no longer allowed wives to enter court. Yet many literati, already uneasy with the Latter Ruler’s dissoluteness, nurtured resentment. The upright withdrew gradually, the petty-men advanced day by day.

Right General Yan Yu had gained no accomplishments at all. Because he attached himself to Huang Hao, he gained high rank. Hearing that Jiang Wei still commanded troops at Qishan, he told Huang Hao to tell the Latter Ruler,

“Jiang Wei has fought repeatedly without victory. You can appoint Yan Yu in his place.”

The Latter Ruler accepted this counsel and sent an edict to summon Jiang Wei back. At that time Jiang Wei was pressing the stockades at Qishan when, on one day, three edicts arrived ordering him to retreat.

He obeyed. He first ordered the Taoyang detachment to withdraw, then withdrew with Zhang Yi slowly.

Deng Ai was in the stockade and heard nothing but drums and horns through the night, not knowing what it meant. At dawn the report came that the Shu army had completely withdrawn, leaving only an empty camp. Deng Ai had suspected a stratagem and did not dare to pursue.

Jiang Wei marched directly to Hanzhong, rested men and horses, and with his envoys rode into Chengdu to see the Latter Ruler. For ten days in a row, the Latter Ruler did not hold court. Jiang Wei inwardly was puzzled.

That day near the East Flower Gate he met Xizheng, a Secretary Gentleman. Jiang Wei asked,

“Do you know why Your Majesty has summoned the General to return?”

Xizheng laughed,

“Why does your Highness not understand it yet, General? Huang Hao wishes Yan Yu to gain merit; he has already memorialized the court and obtained this edict to recall you. Later he heard that Deng Ai can handle the army well, so this matter has been set aside.”

Jiang Wei was furious:

“I must kill this eunuch.”

Xizheng restrained him,

“As one who has taken up Master Zhuge’s work and bears a great charge, you cannot act hastily. If the Son of Heaven does not permit it, it will be ugly indeed.”

Jiang Wei acknowledged,

“Master, your words are true.”

The next day, the Latter Ruler and Huang Hao were feasting in the rear garden when Jiang Wei entered with a few men. Someone reported Huang Hao in time; he hurried to hide at the side of Lake Mountain.

Jiang Wei came beneath the pavilion, bowed to the Latter Ruler, and with tears submitted a memorial,

“I have pinned Deng Ai at Qishan, and Your Majesty has sent three edicts calling me back. I do not yet understand Your Majesty’s intent.”

The Latter Ruler was silent.

Jiang Wei spoke again,

“Huang Hao is a clever and overreaching eunuch. He was one of the Ten Attendants in Emperor Ling’s time. If Your Majesty were to use his nearness to Zhangrang and his remoteness from Zhao Gao as examples, you would see what can happen. If this man is put to death now, the court will quickly clear and the Central Plains may return.”

The Latter Ruler smiled,

“Though Huang Hao is an intimate of my chamber, if he monopolizes authority, he still is not able to do harm. Dongyun’s former biting hatred of him was odd to me. Why do you insist on it?”

Jiang Wei knelt and submitted,

“Your Majesty, if Huang Hao is not put to death today, calamity is not far off.”

The Latter Ruler said,

“‘To love a man, one wishes him to live; to hate him, one wishes him to die.’ Why can you not bear one eunuch?”

He ordered the attendants near Lake Mountain to summon Huang Hao to the pavilion and told him to kneel before Jiang Wei and beg for mercy.

Huang Hao came crying, kneeling and bowing before Jiang Wei,

“I have always merely waited to attend on the Son of Heaven, and have not involved myself in state affairs. Do not listen to outsiders and seek to kill me. If your General ties me up, only ask for mercy.”

He finished the words, knelt again, and wept.

Jiang Wei left in a rage and went to see Xizheng, explaining the whole incident. Xizheng said,

“The General is in grave danger. If he falls, the state will fall with him.”

Jiang Wei replied,

“Master, you have thankfully taught me a way to save state and person.”

Xizheng said,

“In Longxi there is a place called Tazhong. It is exceedingly rich and sturdy. Why should the General not follow Master Kongming’s example and ask Your Majesty to allow him to go to Tazhong for Tuntian? First, he can use the wheat harvest there to support the army’s stores; second, he can fully survey the commanderies on the right of Liang; third, the men of Wei will not dare openly face Hanzhong; fourth, while the General holds the forces in the field, none can move against him, and he can avoid disaster. This is a strategy for preserving state and life. He should do it soon.”

Jiang Wei rejoiced and said,

“Master’s words are like gold and jade.”

The next day Jiang Wei memorialized the Latter Ruler requesting permission for Tuntian at Tazhong in imitation of Master Kongming’s precedent. The Latter Ruler approved.

Jiang Wei returned to Hanzhong and gathered his generals:

“I have gone out many times and, because grain was short, have not succeeded. Now I have eight wan men and go to Tazhong to sow wheat and camp for a long plan. We have long suffered in battle and hardship. Today we gather and consolidate men and grain and withdraw to defend Hanzhong. Wei troops must carry supply for a thousand li and cross mountain ridges and passes, so they will naturally tire. When they tire they must retreat; then we can pursue the opening and they will all lose.”

He then appointed Hu Ji to guard Hanshou City, Wang Han to guard Le City, Jiang Bin to guard Han City, and Jiang Shu and Fuxian to hold the mountain passes together.

When distribution was complete, Jiang Wei led eight wan soldiers to Tazhong and sowed wheat there for a long plan.

Deng Ai heard that Jiang Wei was conducting Tuntian at Tazhong. He saw that for more than forty camps there were lined up along the road in unbroken chain like a long serpent. He ordered spies to examine the terrain, sketched a map, and submitted an illustrated report.

Sima Zhao of Wei, seeing it, grew furious:

“Jiang Wei has violated the Central Plains repeatedly and cannot be exterminated. He is an ache in my own heart.”

Jia Chong said,

“Jiang Wei learned deeply from Kongming. It is hard to drive him off. Only a commander of wit and courage should be sent to stab him and spare the labor of moving troops.”

Xun Xu, Gentleman of the Court of Works, said,

“That is not right. Liu Shan of Shu is sunk in wine and lust, trusts Huang Hao, and all major ministers seek only to escape calamity. Jiang Wei’s Tuntian at Tazhong is exactly his plan to avoid disaster. If the principal command is used against him, there is no case where we do not prevail. Why need an assassin?”

Sima Zhao laughed,

“That is the best argument. Who can lead in the invasion of Shu?”

Xun Xu replied,

“Deng Ai is a talented man of this age, and with Zhong Hui as his deputy, the matter will be accomplished.”

Sima Zhao was delighted:

“Your words agree exactly with my thought.”

He summoned Zhong Hui and asked,

“I wish to appoint you as commander in chief. Will you go to punish Eastern Wu?”

Zhong Hui said,

“Your intent, my lord, is not in fact to punish Wu but to punish Shu.”

Sima Zhao laughed,

“You truly understand my heart. But if you go to punish Shu, what is your plan?”

Zhong Hui said,

“I understand Your intent, and the map is already here with Your Lordship.”

He spread it out. The map showed in detail where a route should camp and build stockades, where to store grain and forage, and from where to advance and from where to withdraw.

Sima Zhao saw it and praised him greatly,

“You are truly a good general. How is it if you join forces with Deng Ai and take Shu?”

Zhong Hui said,

“The roads in Shu are broad. We cannot advance in a single route. Let Deng Ai divide troops and advance in multiple directions.”

So Sima Zhao made Zhong Hui the General Who Guards the West, invested him with seal and command badge, made him Chief Commander of the Guanzhong cavalry and horsemen, and summoned contingents from Qing, Yan, Yu, Jing, and Yang Provinces. At the same time he sent an envoy with command and appointed Deng Ai as General Who Conquers the West, commander over the Long ridges beyond the passes to set the time and move against Shu.

The next day Sima Zhao discussed this matter at court. Former General Deng Dun said,

“Jiang Wei has attacked the Central Plains repeatedly. Our soldiers have suffered grave losses. At present, even defense is not secure. Why should we enter distant mountains and dangerous country and invite trouble for ourselves?”

Sima Zhao became angry,

“I wish to lead a righteous and benevolent army against an unrighteous ruler. How can you dare to oppose my intent?”

He shouted an officer to him who immediately beheaded Deng Dun and dragged him forward. In moments later Deng Dun’s head was presented below the steps. All present turned pale.

Sima Zhao said,

“Since I began the campaign eastward, I have rested six years and repaired troops and armaments. I have long wished to punish Wu and Shu. Now, first fix Western Shu, ride the stream-wind current and strike by land and water in one advance, and absorb Eastern Wu after. It is the way to overthrow Guo and seize Yu. I judge that Shu now fields eight or nine wan men at Chengdu, and on the frontier four or five wan at most. Jiang Wei’s Tuntian has not more than six or seven wan soldiers.

I have already ordered Deng Ai to bring in more than ten wan men from beyond Liangshan and bind Jiang Wei at Tazhong so he cannot look eastward. I have ordered Zhong Hui to lead from Guanzhong two or three wan men straight to Luogu. Three paths together will strike Hanzhong. Liu Shan of Shu is drunk in darkness; his frontier cities break outwardly and men and women tremble inwardly. Its fall is certain.”

All present obeyed and bowed.

When Zhong Hui received the seal and rank of General Who Guards the West, he raised the army against Shu. Fearing that intelligence might leak, he spoke of punishing Eastern Wu and so ordered the five regions of Qing, Yan, Yu, Jing, and Yang to each build large ships. He also sent Tangzi to gather coastal vessels at Deng and Lai commanderies.

Sima Zhao did not know his intent and asked him,

“You have come to collect grain by the dry road into Sichuan. Why build ships?”

Zhong Hui replied,

“If Shu hears that our army advances in strength, it will seek rescue from Eastern Wu. Therefore I raise this appearance first, displaying the forms of punishing Wu; Wu will then not dare to act rashly. In a year Shu will be broken and the ships will be ready, and then punishing Wu will be exactly in order.”

Sima Zhao was overjoyed and chose a date to dispatch the army.

In the fourth year of Wei Jingyuan, on the third day of the seventh month of autumn, Zhong Hui departed on campaign. Sima Zhao escorted him to ten li beyond the city and then returned.

Shao Ti, the secretary of the Western Ministry, spoke privately to Sima Zhao,

“The Great Lord has sent Zhong Hui with ten wan troops to attack Shu; I suspect his ambition is great and his heart high. He cannot be allowed to hold all authority alone.”

Sima Zhao laughed,

“Do I not know that?”

Shao Ti replied,

“Since you know it, why do you not appoint someone to share the command?”

Sima Zhao spoke many words that eased Shao Ti’s suspicion.

Thus it was:

As horses and men gallop in that day, one may recognize the general’s overbearing spirit. How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: The Latter Ruler Believes Slanderous Counsel and Orders a Recall, and Jiang Wei Dodges Disaster Through Tuntian

chapters.html:
Zhong Hui divides the forces along the roads to Hanzhong. Zhuge the Master makes His holy virtue manifest at Dingjun Mountain.

Yet Sima Zhao said to the western bureau clerk Shao Ti, “All court officials say that Shu is not yet ready to be attacked; that is because their hearts are timid. If they were to force a hard battle, it would be the way of defeat. Now Zhong Hui alone has proposed an expedition against Shu. His heart does not tremble. A heart that does not tremble means Shu will surely fall. Once Shu is broken, its people’s hearts and courage will be ripped open. ‘A defeated commander should not speak of courage; a minister of a doomed state cannot seek to save himself.’ Zhong Hui has a different purpose in mind; how could the people of Shu help him then? As for Wei soldiers who have won and long to return home, they will not follow Zhong Hui in betrayal. You and I have no need to worry about that. Keep this between us and do not let it leak out.” Shao Ti bowed in assent.

After Zhong Hui had finished setting up his camp, he ascended the command pavilion and gathered all the generals for orders. Among the officers present were military supervisor Wei Guan, escort general Hu Lie, and, among more than eighty in all, the senior generals Tian Xu, Pang Hui, Tian Zhang, Yuanxun, Qiu Jian, Xiahou Xian, Wang Jia, Huangfu Kai, Ju An, and others. Zhong Hui said, “There must be one senior general to act as vanguard. Who dares to do it?” One man answered at once: “I offer to go.” Zhong Hui looked at him and saw that it was Xu Yi, son of the famous warrior Xu Chu. All said at once, “No one but this man can be vanguard.” Zhong Hui called him and said, “You are Xu Yi, whose strength is like a tiger’s and whose arms are like those of an ape; your father and mother are both known for their merit to the court. All the other generals are protecting you as well. Hang the vanguard seal and take five thousand cavalry and one thousand foot soldiers, driving straight for Hanzhong. I divide the force into three routes: you lead the center through Xie Valley, the left army through Luo Valley, and the right army through Ziwu Valley. These are all rugged, rough, and steep places. Have the troops fill and level the roads, repair the bridges, hew through the mountains, and break rock for passage, so there is no obstruction. If this is disobeyed, enforce the laws of war.” Xu Yi accepted the charge and led the troops forward. Zhong Hui followed with more than one hundred thousand men, and by night he set out.

Deng Ai was in Longxi. As soon as he had received the order to campaign against Shu, he first sent Sima Wang to block the Qiang. He also dispatched Yongzhou Inspector Zhuge Xu, Tianshui Administrator Wang Qi, Longxi Administrator Qian Hong, and Jincheng Administrator Yang Xin, each bringing their own local troops to receive instructions. As the troops and horses gathered in number, Deng Ai had a dream in the middle of the night. He saw himself climbing a high mountain and looking toward Hanzhong when suddenly a spring burst from under his feet and surged upward. He woke in shock, drenched in sweat, and sat awake until dawn. He then called his bodyguard Shao Huan and asked him what it meant. Shao Huan, who understood the Yijing well, listened as Ai explained the dream. Huan replied, “The text says, ‘Where water appears on a mountain, it is the hexagram Jian. Jian means one prospers in advancing to the southwest and does not profit in advancing to the northeast; its way there is exhausted.’ Master Kongming also says, ‘Jian gains by advancing to the southwest; it wins by advancing and does not prosper in advancing to the northeast, where its road comes to an end.’ Your expedition will surely conquer Shu. Only this: your progress is blocked and you may not return.” Deng Ai heard this and became uneasy. Then Zhong Hui’s summons arrived, commanding him to raise troops and move on Hanzhong. Ai therefore ordered Guo Shu’s subordinate Yongzhou Cishi Zhuge Xu to lead fifteen thousand troops to cut off Jiang Wei’s line of return first. Next, he sent Wang Qi, Tianshui Administrator, with fifteen thousand to attack from the left toward Dazhong. Qian Hong, Longxi Administrator, with fifteen thousand came from the right toward Dazhong. He also sent Yang Xin, Jincheng Administrator, with fifteen thousand to intercept Jiang Wei from behind at Gansong. Ai himself brought thirty thousand to move back and forth in support.

When Zhong Hui took the field, all the officials saw him out of the city gates: banners blotted out the sun, and armor flashed like frost. Men were strong, horses massive. His air and demeanor made everyone tremble with envy, except Liu Shi, Assistant to the Chancellor, who gave no reply and only smiled faintly. Grand Commandant Wang Xiang saw this and, while mounted, took him by the hand and asked, “With Zhong and Deng setting out together, will Shu surely be pacified?” Xiang Shi said, “Shu will certainly fall. I only fear they may not all return to the capital.” Wang Xiang asked why, and Liu Shi smiled without answering. Xiang did not ask again.

Wei soldiers had already marched out when spies got to Dazhong and reported it to Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei immediately submitted a memorial to the Later Lord, pleading for an edict and dispatching Left General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhang Yi to hold Yangping Pass and Right General of Chariots and Cavalry Liao Hua to defend the bridge at Yinping, saying, “These two are the most crucial points. If we lose them, Hanzhong cannot be secured.” He added that at the same time envoys should be sent to Wu to request aid, while he raised troops from Dazhong to meet the enemy.

In that year Liu Shan changed the era name from Jǐngyào Five to Yánxīng First. Day after day he was in the palace with the eunuch Huang Hao, sports and delighting in pleasure. When Jiang Wei’s memorial arrived, he summoned Huang Hao and asked, “Now that Wei has raised both Zhong Hui and Deng Ai and has split its armies to come by several routes, what should we do?” Huang Hao answered, “This is only Jiang Wei seeking merit and fame, and he put up this memorial for that reason. Your Majesty, calm your heart and do not become suspicious. I have heard there is a shrine maid in the city who serves a spirit and can tell fortune. Bring her in.” The Later Lord followed his advice. In the rear hall he arranged incense, flowers, paper and candles, and made offerings. He ordered Huang Hao to bring her in a small carriage to the palace and seat her on the Dragon Bed. After the emperor burned incense and finished the rites, the shrine maid burst into the hall with hair down and bare feet, dancing dozens of times across the platform. Huang Hao declared, “The spirit man has descended. Your Majesty may dismiss everyone but your closest attendants and pray directly.”

The emperor withdrew all court officials and bowed in prayer again. The shrine maid cried out, “I am the earth spirit of the western lands. Your Majesty delights in peace; why do you seek out other omens? After several years, Wei’s lands will also return to your rule. Do not worry.” As she finished speaking, she collapsed to the ground unconscious. After some time she revived. The Later Lord rejoiced and rewarded her lavishly. From then on he believed her words completely, and he no longer listened to Jiang Wei’s repeated warnings. He spent each day only in drinking and celebration within the palace. Jiang Wei submitted many urgent memorials, all hidden by Huang Hao, and the great matter was thereby lost.

Zhong Hui’s army moved onward toward Hanzhong in a spreading line. The vanguard under Xu Yi, determined to win first blood, marched to Nanzheng Pass first. Xu Yi told his subordinates, “Once we pass this gate, we are in Hanzhong. There are not many troops here on the gate, so we can charge it with all our strength.” The officers took their orders, and all pressed forward together.

In fact, the Shu commander guarding the gate, Lu Xun, had known that Wei soldiers would be coming. Before the wooden bridge at the gate he had hidden troops on both sides and mounted ten-arrow crossbow mechanisms left by Master Kongmingming. When Xu Yi’s men came charging for the gate, he signaled once, and darts and stones rained down. Xu Yi withdrew in haste, and already dozens of riders had been shot. The Wei troops were badly beaten. He reported back to Zhong Hui. Zhong Hui himself came with over a hundred heavy-armored riders to inspect and saw at once that crossbow bolts had fallen all at once. He wheeled his horse and rode back at once. At the gate, Lu Xun came out with five hundred men and attacked.

Zhong Hui rode over the bridge, where the soil had sunk and caught his horse’s hooves; he nearly went over the edge. The horse could not be freed, and Zhong Hui dismounted to ride on foot. As he ran down the bridge, Lu Xun caught him and thrust with a spear, but a Wei soldier, Xun Kai from the ranks, turned and loosed one arrow, sending Lu Xun from his horse. Zhong Hui and his men surged forward and took the mountain gate. There were soldiers of Shu already in front of it, so they did not dare to shoot arrows. Zhong Hui had the force dispersed and the mountain pass seized. He made Xun Kai an escort general and gave him a complete set of saddle, horse, and full armor. Zhong Hui summoned Xu Yi and said, “You were the vanguard. Your duty was to encounter mountain and water first, clear difficult roads, repair bridges, dig out the mountain roads, and break stone, so the army could move. I just came to the bridge and my horse’s hooves sank so my mount almost toppled. If not for Xun Kai, I would already be dead. You disobeyed your military orders; punish you according to law.” He ordered Xu Yi thrown out by attendants for execution.

Some of the generals argued, “Xu Yi’s father, Xu Chu, has done great service for the court. We beg, Commander, to spare him.” Zhong Hui snapped, “If law in the army is unclear, how can I command others?” and ordered him beheaded in public. All the generals stood in alarm.

Meanwhile Shu general Wang Han held Le City and Jiang Bin held Han City. Seeing the sheer weight of the Wei forces, they dared not fight in the field and kept their gates shut. Zhong Hui gave the order, “In war speed is precious; we must not pause.” He sent Li Fu with the forward army to besiege Le City, and Xun Kai with the escort troops to besiege Han City, while he personally led the main host against Yangping Pass.

At the gate, Shu commander Fu Qian and his deputy Jiang Shu were deciding how to defend it. Jiang Shu said, “The Wei troops are so many; we cannot stand against this. It is best to hold firmly.” Fu Qian replied, “No. They have come a long way and must be tired; although they are many, we need not fear. If we do not descend the pass to fight now, both Han and Le are still safe.” Jiang Shu fell silent.

Just then a report said the Wei army had arrived in large formation before the gate. Both Fu Qian and Jiang Shu went up to it. Zhong Hui snapped his whip and shouted, “I lead over one hundred thousand men to stand here. If you surrender quickly, each of you will be promoted according to rank. If you stubbornly refuse, I will break the gateworks and burn you and your fortress in one flame.” Fu Qian, furious, ordered Jiang Shu to hold the gate and led three thousand soldiers down to fight. Zhong Hui immediately broke off, and the Wei soldiers withdrew all at once. Fu Qian pressed forward, but the Wei troops then reformed. When Fu Qian tried to retreat, a Wei flag was already raised on the gate. Jiang Shu shouted, “I have surrendered to Wei already!” Fu Qian was enraged and shouted back, “Traitor who forgets mercy and turns against righteousness—how dare you dare see the Son of Heaven?” He wheeled his horse back and resumed battle with the Wei army.

The Wei soldiers closed in all sides and hemmed Fu Qian in. He charged and rushed in every direction, fighting hand to hand and back again, and he could not break out. Ten of every nine men under him were wounded. Then Fu Qian looked to heaven and sighed, “I was born a minister of Shu; if I die, I should die as a Shu ghost.” He mounted again and drove straight into the enemy, receiving many spears. Blood filled his robes and armor; he sat down in the saddle and fell from his horse, then took his own life. Later people wrote a verse:

One day he poured out loyal fury, and for a thousand years his righteous name is praised. Let it be Fu Qian who dies rather than Jiang Shu who lives.

Zhong Hui captured Yangping Pass. Inside, supplies and arms were abundant. He rejoiced and rewarded the three armies. That night the Wei troops camped in Yang’an City. Suddenly from the southwest came a thunderous shouting that shook the air. Zhong Hui hurried out of his tent to investigate and found nothing. The Wei army did not sleep a wink the whole night. At the second watch, the southwest cry rose again. He woke with suspicion and sent men to reconnoiter at dawn. They reported, “At a distant watch point more than ten li away, there is not one person there.” Zhong Hui still felt unsteady and, fully armed with his troops and about a hundred riders, rode out to patrol toward the southwest.

When he reached a mountain, a killing aura rose on all sides. Mournful clouds closed in and mist ringed the peak. Zhong Hui drew rein and asked a local guide, “What mountain is this?” He replied, “This is Dingjun Mountain, where in former times Xiahou Yuan died.” Hearing this, Zhong Hui grew sorrowful and turned back. As he passed the slope of the mountain, a sudden fierce wind rose. From behind, thousands of riders burst out and came at speed with it. Zhong Hui was terrified and turned his men and rode hard away. The number of generals who fell from their horses was beyond count. By the time they reached Yangping Pass not a single man or horse had lost its life, yet many had faces gouged and helmets torn off.

Everyone said, “We only saw men and horses charging through gloomy cloud. Only when they drew near did no one get wounded; it was only a whirl of wind.” Zhong Hui asked the surrendered Jiang Shu, “Is there a temple here on Dingjun Mountain?” Jiang Shu said, “There is no temple. There is only General Zhuge’s tomb.” Zhong Hui exclaimed, “This must be the manifested sanctity of Master Kongming. I should go in person and make an offering.”

The next day, Zhong Hui made proper sacrifices and offered the great sacrificial set, then rode to Zhuge’s tomb and knelt before it in a second offering. When the rite ended, the gale instantly stopped. The dark clouds dispersed. Then a gentle wind came and a light rain fell. After the air cleared, the troops rejoiced and all returned to camp.

That night Zhong Hui reclined and slept in his pavilion. Suddenly, as a clear wind passed, he saw a man in a black sash and feather fan, wearing a white-feathered gown, plain shoes with black straps, skin like polished jade, lips like vermilion, and bright clear eyes. The man was tall and stood tall, with the air of an immortal. He entered the pavilion and walked in. Zhong Hui rose and greeted him: “Who are you, sir?” The man said, “I was favored with this audience this morning. I have a word to tell you. Although the Han fortune has declined and Heaven’s decree is hard to resist, the living in the Two Rivers have been torn by war. They are truly pitiful. Now that you have entered this land, do not, at any cost, slaughter the people.” He said no more, then brushed his sleeve aside and left. Zhong Hui tried to detain him, but then suddenly woke up. It had all been a dream.

He knew then that it had been Master Kongmingming’s spirit, and was astonished. So he ordered the vanguard to raise a white flag with four characters: “Protect the State, Safeguard the People.” Wherever they went, any person who killed one person without cause was to pay with his own life. Therefore the people of Hanzhong all came out of their cities to bow and welcome him. Zhong Hui calmed everyone and did not harm so much as a single hair of the people.

Thousands of hidden soldiers ring Dingjun, and made Zhong Hui kneel to honor the spirit. Having once been able to choose victory and sustain the Liu house, even in death he still bequeathed the command to protect the Shu people.

In Dazhong, Jiang Wei heard the Wei army had arrived in force. He sent edicts to Liao Hua, Zhang Yi, and Dong Jue to raise troops for aid, and arranged his own officers to meet them. Suddenly there was word: Wei troops had come. He rode out to engage them. The foremost commander in the Wei lines was Wang Qi, Tianshui Administrator. Wang Qi cried from his saddle, “I now have one million troops under command and a thousand high commanders, advancing by twenty routes and already reaching Chengdu. If you do not think to surrender early, you still wish to resist—do you not know Heaven’s decree?”

Jiang Wei flew into a rage, raised his spear and spurred forward straight at Wang Qi. They fought for less than three exchanges. Wang Qi was routed and fled. Jiang Wei drove his men to pursue for twenty li, and then heard drums and gongs in unison. A column opened with a banner reading clearly, “Qian Hong, Cishi of Longxi.” Jiang Wei laughed, “Such pests are no opponent of mine!” and pressed his men onward in pursuit.

Ten li further on, he ran into Deng Ai with his army. The two armies mixed in close melee. Jiang Wei rallied himself and fought Deng Ai for ten or more exchanges with no winner. Behind them, the drums sounded again. As he withdrew he was told, “All the outposts at Gansong have been burned by Jincheng Administrator Yang Xin.” Jiang Wei started in alarm and ordered his deputy to raise decoy banners and hold Deng Ai, while he pulled back his rear army and rode overnight to rescue Gansong. He came upon Yang Xin. Yang Xin did not dare to give battle, and turned and fled along the mountain road.

Jiang Wei chased after him. By a cliff-side they were met by hail of wood and stone, and he could not advance. By the time he had ridden back halfway, his Shu troops had already been defeated by Deng Ai; Wei main force came and surrounded him. Jiang Wei cut through the encirclement with mounted men and retreated into a grand encampment to hold, waiting for reinforcements.

Suddenly an outrider arrived and said, “Zhong Hui has broken through Yangping Pass. Commander Jiang Shu has surrendered; Fu Qian is dead in battle, and Hanzhong is now held by Wei. Governor Wang Han of Le City and Jiang Bin of Han City, knowing Hanzhong is lost, have also opened their gates and surrendered. Hu Ji could not stand against the enemy and fled back to Chengdu to ask for aid.”

Jiang Wei was greatly shocked and ordered a withdrawal. That night at the mouth of Jiangchuan, a Wei force appeared in front: at its head was Yang Xin. Jiang Wei was furious, charged and fought in close combat. In a single round Yang Xin broke and fled. Jiang Wei took up his bow and shot three arrows, none striking. He then grew angry, snapped his bow, thrust forward with his spear, but his horse stumbled and threw him. Yang Xin rode back to kill him.

Jiang Wei leapt up and drove his spear into Yang Xin’s horse’s brain. Wei soldiers suddenly arrived from the rear and rescued Yang Xin. Jiang Wei mounted and was about to pursue when a report came that Deng Ai’s soldiers had arrived behind. Unable to watch front and rear at once, he ordered troops back to reclaim Hanzhong.

A scout shouted, “Yongzhou Cishi Zhuge Xu has already cut off the road of retreat.” Jiang Wei made camp at the mountain pass. Wei troops were already at the head of Yinping Bridge. With no path to come or go, he gave a long sigh: “Heaven has taken me!”

Ning Sui, his deputy, said, “Though the Wei troops have cut Yinping Bridge, Yongzhou’s army is surely small there. If the general takes Kong Hangu Pass and marches straight for Yongzhou, Zhuge Xu must withdraw his bridge force to defend Yongzhou. If then the general rides in to defend Sword Pass, Hanzhong can be restored.”

Jiang Wei agreed and sent out troops through Kong Hangu Pass in order to feign taking Yongzhou. A spy told Zhuge Xu of it. Zhuge Xu started in alarm: “Yongzhou is the place where we intended to concentrate our forces. If we lose grip, the court will surely punish me.” He quickly withdrew the main body and moved south to save Yongzhou, leaving only a branch force guarding the bridgehead. Jiang Wei entered by the northern road and rode about thirty li, then, sensing Wei troops on the move, turned his men back to the rear and fronted them to meet. They reached the bridgehead and, as he suspected, only a few minor troops remained there, having moved with the rest. He cut them down in a single onslaught and burned their camp and stockades.

When Zhuge Xu heard the bridgehead burning and saw the fire, he brought soldiers back. But by then Jiang Wei had already been gone for more than half a day and they dared not chase.

Jiang Wei then marched his army past the bridgehead. As he advanced, a force appeared in front: Left General of Chariots and Cavalry Zhang Yi and Right General of Chariots and Cavalry Liao Hua. Jiang Wei asked after what had happened. Zhang Yi said, “Huang Hao has believed a witch and refuses to send troops. I have raised troops from Hanzhong myself, and by the time this reached me, Yangping Pass was already taken by Zhong Hui. Hearing the commander is in extremity, I came for help.” Liao Hua added, “We are encircled on all sides; grain and roads are blocked; better to withdraw to Sword Pass and plan there.” Jiang Wei still wavered.

Suddenly word arrived that Zhong Hui and Deng Ai were coming on separate routes in ten or more lines. Jiang Wei wanted to split and meet them all. Liao Hua said, “Whitewater is narrow and full of bad roads, not a place for open battle. Better to withdraw and at once go to save Sword Pass. If Sword Pass is lost, all routes are cut off.” Jiang Wei followed this advice and moved his troops to Sword Pass.

As they neared the gate, drums and horns all sounded at once, cries rose loudly, and banners flew everywhere. A unit had already taken a position blocking the gate. It was just then that he said:

Hanzhong is so steep and perilous there is no measure of it; and now sudden storm and waves rise again at Sword Pass.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Zhong Hui Splits His Forces Toward Hanzhong; Zhuge the Master Shows His Sacred Presence at Dingjun Mountain

chapters.html:
Now the Grand General Who Aids the State, Dong Jue, heard that Wei troops in ten or more columns had entered the border lands. He therefore led twenty thousand men to hold Jian'ge. That day a great rise of dust appeared on the horizon, and he feared it was Wei soldiers, so he hurriedly brought troops to block the pass. Dong Jue personally inspected the front in advance and saw that it was Jiang Wei, Liao Hua, and Zhang Yi.

Dong Jue was greatly pleased, brought them in through the gate, completed courtesy welcome, and in tears gave his account of the later sovereign and Huang Hao.

Jiang Wei said, “Do not worry, my lord. So long as I remain, I will not let Wei swallow Shu. Hold Jian'ge, and slowly we shall seek to drive the enemy back.”

Dong Jue said, “Though this pass is defensible, Chengdu has no one to spare. If the enemy reaches it, the whole situation will collapse.”

Jiang Wei said, “Chengdu is steep and rugged, not easy to take. There is no need to worry.”

While they were still speaking, a report arrived that Zhuge Xun was leading his troops down to the pass. Jiang Wei grew furious, and at once hurried five thousand troops to strike. He charged straight into the Wei formation, thrusting left and right, and forced Zhuge Xun to a great defeat. Xun withdrew twenty or so li and camped down. Wei losses were countless. The Shu soldiers seized many horses and military gear. Jiang Wei then withdrew and returned to the pass.

Now Zhong Hui was already camped twenty-five li below Jian'ge when Zhuge Xun came and yielded himself. Zhong Hui shouted, “I ordered you to hold the bridgehead at Yinping and cut off Jiang Wei’s line of retreat. How did you let it be lost? Again, without my order you advanced, and this defeat is the result!”
