Zhuge Xun said, “Jiang Wei has many stratagems. He feigned a move in Yong Province, and I feared the province had been compromised, so I drew troops to rescue it. He used the opening to slip away. I then chased him to the foot of the pass, and did not expect to be defeated again.”

Zhong Hui grew enraged and shouted for his execution.

The staff officer Wei Guan spoke: “Though he has sinned, he is the man once supervised by Dong the Western General. This is not fitting for you to kill him, and it may injure good morale.”

Zhong Hui replied, “I carry out the Son of Heaven’s clear edict and Jin Gong Jun’s command in this campaign against Shu. Even if Deng Ai were guilty, he too should be beheaded.”

The whole company urged him repeatedly.

So Zhong Hui had Zhuge Xun put in a caged cart and sent him to Luoyang, to be disposed of by Lord Jin. He also reassigned the troops under Xun under his subordinates.

News was brought to Deng Ai.

Deng Ai was greatly angered: “You and I are equal in rank. I have long guarded the frontier and labored much for the state. How dare you presume so much?”

His son Deng Zhong interceded, saying, “‘He who is not patient in small matters will ruin the great design.’ If father does not tolerate him, he will confuse the state’s grand affair. For now please bear with him.”

Deng Ai listened and kept his temper, but still with resentment in his heart. He then brought ten-some horsemen and went to see Zhong Hui.

When Zhong Hui heard he had arrived, he asked the attendants, “How many troops did Deng Ai bring?”

They answered, “Only ten-some horsemen.”

Zhong Hui ordered several hundred armed men to line his pavilion and inner camp. Deng Ai dismounted and entered to meet him. Zhong Hui welcomed him with formalities and all courtesies.

When Deng Ai saw the strictness of the military setup, he felt uneasy, then tested him in words:

“General, to secure Hanzhong for the throne is indeed a great fortune. Now settle your strategy and take Jian'ge at once.”

Zhong Hui asked, “How does the general judge this?”

Deng Ai repeatedly pretended he was not capable. Zhong Hui pressed him.

Deng Ai answered, “By my poor sense, you may take one army by the lesser path at Yinping, pass from Hanzhong through Deyang Pavilion, and use a surprise force to reach Chengdu directly. Jiang Wei will surely withdraw troops to meet it. Then you will seize Jian'ge while the opportunity is open, and win complete success.”

Zhong Hui was very pleased: “This plan is marvelous. Go at once. I will remain here and await the good report.”

The two parted after drinking.

Back at his own pavilion, Zhong Hui told the generals, “People have all said Deng Ai is able. But today, seeing him, he is merely a mediocre man.”

When they asked why, Zhong Hui said, “The smaller road at Yinping is all high mountain and rugged ridge. If Shu holds the key points with a hundred men and blocks his line of retreat, then Deng Ai’s whole army would starve. Since I am proceeding on the straightforward road, why should I fear that Shu land cannot be broken?”

He therefore set up climbing ladders and cannon platforms and continued the attack on Jian'ge.

Deng Ai then rode out from the gate and looked back at his men, asking, “How does Zhong Hui treat me?”

One replied, “From his words and expression he does not truly accept your words; he merely nods as if with force of mouth.”

Deng Ai laughed: “He believes I cannot take Chengdu. I, however, want to take it.”

Returning to his own camp, Shizuan, Deng Zhong, and several captains asked, “What remarkable matter did you discuss today with Zhong Zhenxi?”

Deng Ai said, “I spoke honestly and openly. He takes me for a mediocre man. Since taking Hanzhong, he deems it the greatest merit. Yet had I not pinned Jiang Wei at Dunda, could he have succeeded? If I now take Chengdu, I surpass Hanzhong.”

That night he gave orders. All were to abandon the camp and move via the Yinping side-path. They set out seven hundred li below Jian'ge.

Someone reported to Zhong Hui, “Deng Ai is now heading to take Chengdu.” Zhong Hui laughed at Deng Ai’s recklessness.

Deng Ai in the meantime drafted a secret letter and sent it by courier to Sima Zhao. He then assembled his officers in the tent and asked,

“With the moment before us, I will take advantage of the opening and seize Chengdu, creating undying renown together with all of you. Do you follow?”

The officers answered, “We are willing to obey orders and do not fear ten thousand deaths.”

Deng Ai first ordered his son Deng Zhong to lead five thousand picked troops, unarmored, each carrying hatchets and chisels and tools. Wherever the way was steep and perilous they were to carve through the mountain and build bridges and platforms to keep the army moving.

He selected three thousand men with dry rations and ropes and advanced them.

After about a hundred li he left three thousand to camp there. After another hundred li, he again selected three thousand and established a camp there.

In the tenth month, he marched from Yinping to the middle of cliff and steep valley, for over twenty days, over seven hundred li, all through empty land with no people.

The Wei troops had set down a number of camps along the way and were left with only two thousand men and horses.

Ahead rose a ridge named Mo Tian Ridge. The horses could not proceed, so Deng Ai went up the ridge on foot. He saw Deng Zhong and the men cutting through the road all crying.

Deng Ai asked why.

Deng Zhong explained, “The western back of this ridge is a sheer cliff face. It cannot be cut open, and all our previous labor was wasted, so they cry.”

Deng Ai said, “Our army has now passed more than seven hundred li to this place. Beyond it lies Jiangyou. How can we turn back now?”

He called the officers and men: “‘Who does not enter the tiger’s den cannot catch the tiger’s cub.’ We have all come this far. If we succeed, we share the riches and honor.”

All replied, “We will follow your command.”

Deng Ai ordered the equipment engineers to go first.

He wrapped himself in felt and was the first to roll down.

Among the deputies, those with felt robes also wrapped themselves and rolled down. Those without felt used rope to gird their waists, clinging to trees and vines, advancing in fish-file.

Deng Ai and Deng Zhong, along with two thousand soldiers and the men who hacked the mountain path, crossed Mo Tian Ridge.

When they had just regained their gear and clothing and moved forward, they saw by the roadside a stone stele engraved:

“By Chancellor Zhuge Wuhou.”

Its words read:

“Before the two fires first rose, one crossed this place. When two gentlemen vied for balance, they soon died of it.”

After reading it, Deng Ai was greatly startled. He immediately knelt before the stele and said, “Wuhou was truly a man of spirit. I cannot be his disciple. Alas!”

A later poem said:

Yinping’s towering ridge rises level with heaven; a ghostly crane circles and still dares not to fly. Deng Ai, wrapped in felt, came down here—who could know that Zhuge had set a prior stratagem?

Deng Ai moved by a hidden route across Yinping. As he marched again, they encountered a large empty camp.

His attendants reported, “During Wuhou’s days, he assigned a thousand men to guard this treacherous pass. Now the Shu lord Liu Shan has dismissed it.”

Deng Ai, unable to keep himself from exclaiming, said to all,

“We have a road to come, but no road to return. Ahead lie Jiangyou and its stores. If you advance you may live, if you fall back you die. We must join our strength and take it.”

All answered, “We are willing to fight here to the death.”

Deng Ai marched on foot, led just over two thousand, and at daybreak and after, doubled the pace to strike Jiangyou.

The commander of Jiangyou, Ma Miao, had heard that Dong Province was lost. Though he had prepared defenses, he only guarded the main roads and banks. And relying on Jiang Wei and the whole army holding Jian'ge, he still did not treat the danger as severe.

That day, after training horses and men, he returned home and drank by the hearth with his wife Lady Li.

His wife asked, “I hear repeatedly that the frontier is in grave danger. Why does the general show no worry?”

Ma Miao replied, “The great matter belongs to the Lord and to Jiang Bo Yao; what is it to me?”

Lady Li said, “Even so, this fortress city you guard is not an unimportant place.”

Ma Miao said, “The Son of Heaven listens to Huang Hao and revels in wine and lust. I think disaster is not far. When Wei troops arrive, surrendering is the best. Why should we need to be anxious?”

Lady Li became furious, spit on Ma Miao’s face, and said, “You are a man in this world, yet your heart is already not loyal and not righteous. You enjoy the state’s rank and emoluments falsely. How can I face you?”

Shamed and unable to answer, Ma Miao was left speechless.

A household messenger rushed in, crying, “Wei General Deng Ai came by way no one knows, and with more than two thousand men has entered the city in one push!”

Ma Miao was greatly alarmed. He hurried out and surrendered. He knelt under the public hall and wept:

“I have long wished to submit. I now invite all the civilians and my troops to submit to the general as well.”

Deng Ai approved the surrender. He gathered Jiangyou’s soldiers and horses under his own command and assigned Ma Miao to serve as local guide.

Then news came that Ma Miao’s wife had hanged herself.

Deng Ai inquired, and Ma Miao spoke the truth. Deng Ai respected her ability and ordered rich burial honors. He personally went to offer sacrifice. The Wei men who heard of this all could not help but sigh in pity.

A later poem praised her:

The later sovereign, confusion plunged the Han dynasty into ruin; Heaven sent Deng Ai to seize Xichuan. Yet none was as worthy as Lady Li of Jiangyou.

After taking Jiangyou, Deng Ai then brought in all the troops of the Yinping side-path, and all arrived at Jiangyou. He moved straight against Fucheng.

Officer Tian Xu said, “Our army has come through this danger and is greatly weary. We should rest some days before advancing.”

Deng Ai shouted in anger, “The army values speed above all. How dare you disorder the army’s heart?”

He ordered him pulled out and killed.

The other generals all begged, and only then was he spared.

Deng Ai drove the troops to Fucheng himself.

Inside the city, officials, soldiers, and civilians, thinking it came from heaven, all surrendered.

Shu messengers flew in to report to Chengdu.

When the later emperor learned it, he quickly summoned Huang Hao and asked.

Huang Hao replied, “This is a false message. Men of divinity would not so deceive Your Majesty.”

The emperor summoned Shipo, but he did not know at what place Shipo had gone.

Now urgent reports from near and far came in at once, like snowflakes, and messengers and documents went and came without rest.

The emperor held court and deliberation; many officials looked at one another in silence and spoke no word.

Xi Zheng stepped forward and said, “The matter is urgent. Your Majesty should announce Wuhou’s son and consult him on how to retreat from this danger.”

In fact, that was Zhuge Zhan, courtesy name Siyuan, son of Wuhou. His mother was Madam Huang, daughter of Huang Chengyan. She was of unattractive appearance, yet of brilliant ability: she understood celestial patterns above and landforms below; and in all books of stratagem, hidden-army formations, and military devices, she knew everything.

When Wuhou was in Nanyang, hearing her talent he sought her as spouse. During Wuhou’s studies, Madam Huang had helped him much. After he died, she soon followed him in death. On her deathbed she left this single instruction: to urge her son, with loyalty and filial piety.

Zhuge Zhan had been astute since childhood. He then married to the later emperor’s daughter and served as Imperial Son-in-law Colonel. Later he inherited his father’s title of Marquis of Wuxiang. In the fourth year of Jingyao he was moved to the office of General Who Leads Army Escorts.

At this time Huang Hao had the ear of the court, and so Zhan had feigned illness and stayed away.

Now, as if hearing Xi Zheng’s words, the later emperor at once issued three decrees one after another and summoned Zhan to the hall.

The emperor, in tears, said, “Deng Ai’s troops are now encamped at Fucheng. Chengdu is in danger. Looking at the late lord’s face, save my life!”

Zhan too wept as he reported, “Your servant and his line owe the late ruler deep grace, and Your Majesty has treated him exceptionally. Even if I paint liver and brain on the ground, I cannot repay it. Please marshal all Chengdu soldiers and let me lead them for one battle, even to death.”

The emperor immediately allocated seventy thousand of Chengdu’s troops for Zhan.

After receiving leave, Zhan arranged horse and troops, gathered all generals, and asked, “Who dares serve as vanguard?”

Before the words were complete, one young general stepped forward: “My father now holds all authority, so your servant will be the vanguard.”

All turned their eyes toward him. He was Zhan’s eldest son, Zhuge Shang.

Zhuge Shang was nineteen years old, well read in military books, and trained broadly in martial arts. Zhan rejoiced and appointed Shang as vanguard.

That day the main army left Chengdu and marched to meet Wei.

Deng Ai had received from Ma Miao a map of the terrain, one hundred and sixty li from Fucheng to Chengdu, plainly set out with mountains, waters, roads, passes, and dangerous ridges.

After reading it, Deng Ai cried out in alarm:

“I have only held Fucheng. If Shu forces hold the forward mountain and the passes, how can I succeed? If I delay, when Jiang Wei arrives our army is in danger.”

He immediately summoned Shizuan and Deng Zhong and gave orders:

“You two may each take an army and by night go straight to Mianzhu to block the Shu forces. I will arrive right after. Do not delay at all. If you allow them to seize the strategic point first, I will cut off your heads!”

Shizuan and Deng Zhong brought an army and came to Mianzhu. They soon met Shu troops.

The two armies deployed and formed ranks.

At the gate banner, Shizuan and Deng Zhong reined in their horses. They saw the Shu troops arranged in eight lines of formation. After three drumbeats, the gate flags split apart in two. Around forty officers crowded around a four-wheeled wagon. On it sat one man with a silk kerchief, feather fan, and broad hem of court robe.

A yellow banner above him read, “Han Chancellor Zhuge Wuhou.”

Shizuan and Deng Zhong broke out in sweat all over. Looking back at their soldiers they said, “Kongming still lives. We are rescued!”

They hurried their troops back. The Shu soldiers then came out in ambush and attacked. Wei soldiers were defeated and fled for over twenty li.

The Shu troops pursued for more than twenty li, then encountered Deng Ai’s reinforcements coming to meet them; only then did both sides withdraw and regroup.

Deng Ai ascended his command and sat. He called in Shizuan and Deng Zhong and asked, “Why did you two retreat without a fight?”

Zhong answered, “I saw that Zhuge Kongming was leading the Shu troops and therefore ran back.”

Deng Ai was furious: “Even if Kongming were alive again, what should I fear? Your easy retreat has caused this defeat. You must be executed quickly to enforce discipline.”

All pleaded hard, and only then did he calm.

Scouts reported that it was not Kongming. Zhuge Zhan was the main general, and Zhuge Shang the vanguard. The man on the cart had been only a carved wooden image of Zhuge Wuhou.

When Deng Ai heard, he addressed Shizuan and Deng Zhong: “The moment of victory and defeat rests on this one move. If you two do not win this time, your heads are certain.”

So Shizuan and Deng Zhong brought another ten thousand soldiers to battle.

Zhuge Shang, on horseback with one spear, recovered his spirit and drove both of them back in combat. Zhuge Zhan then commanded both right and left wings to break out and crash into the Wei formation. He charged left and right, and through repeated close fighting slew a great number.

Wei troops were badly defeated; the dead were beyond count. Shizuan and Deng Zhong were wounded and fled.

Zhan pursued with horse and men; after another twenty li he encamped and held in opposition.

Shizuan and Deng Zhong returned to Deng Ai and reported. Deng Ai saw both wounded and did not punish them immediately. He convened the generals and said,

“Shu has Zhuge Zhan, who continues his father’s will. He has twice this day killed more than ten thousand of our men and horses. If we do not break this force at once, calamity will follow.”

Qiu Ben, the inspector, said, “Why not write a letter to lure him out?”

Deng Ai followed this advice. He drafted a letter and sent a messenger into the Shu camp.

The gate captain brought it into his pavilion and presented it.

Zhan opened the seal and read:

To Deng Ai, General Who Conquers the West, from Zhuge Siyuan, who commands as General Who Leads Army Escorts:

Of recent worthies, few are there whose parent matches you in honor. From the moment you left your thatched hut, a single utterance already divided the three kingdoms, cleared Jing and Yi, and made your hegemony. Such an achievement is rare in ancient and modern times.

As for your six expeditions to Qishan, it was not lack of ability. It was only Heaven’s timing.

Now the later sovereign is dim and weak, and the royal mandate has ended. Under the Son of Heaven’s order, I have come with a great army to attack Shu and have already won all its lands. Chengdu is in danger by dawn. Why do you not obey Heaven and men alike and return with righteous mind?

I am prepared to confer on you the title King of Langye so your ancestors may shine. This is spoken in truth. Keep this as matter of record.

When Zhan finished, he grew intensely angry. He tore the letter to shreds, and shouted for soldiers to execute the messenger at once. He told an attendant to carry the severed head back to Deng Ai.

Deng Ai, in anger, almost charged out to battle.

Qiu Ben remonstrated: “General should not go out lightly. We should win through surprise tactics.”

Deng Ai followed his advice and ordered Wang Qi, Governor of Tianshui, and Qian Hong, Governor of Longxi, to hold two hidden armies behind.

Deng Ai then led his own troops forward.

Zhuge Zhan at that moment was readying to force battle when word arrived that Deng Ai had come leading troops.

Zhan became furious, led out his men, and went straight to break into the Wei formation. Deng Ai was forced to retreat.

Then Zhan followed with a crushing counterattack. Suddenly two ambush units broke out at both flanks; the Shu army was defeated and retreated into Mianzhu.

Deng Ai ordered it surrounded. Wei troops all shouted together; Mianzhu was ringed as if with an iron tub.

Within the city, Zhan saw the enemy force closing in. He ordered Peng He to carry a letter out and seek aid from Eastern Wu.

Peng He reached Wu and presented his urgent dispatch to Sun Xiu.

After reading it, the Wu lord conferred with his ministers and said, “Since Shu is in danger, how can I sit and watch and not save it?”

He therefore designated the old general Ding Feng as commander and Ding Feng and Sun Yi as his deputies, ordered fifty thousand to go. Ding Feng’s deputies each led twenty thousand and advanced toward Mianzhong, while Ding Feng led thirty thousand toward Shouzhou. The force split into three columns to assist.

Zhan saw no relief arriving and told his generals, “Long defense is not a good plan.” He left Shang and Administrator Zhang Zun to defend the city, and personally donned armor, mounted, and with three commands drove out through three gates.

When Deng Ai saw the troops come out, he withdrew his own.

Zhan struck furiously in pursuit. Suddenly a cannon sounded. Troops from all directions converged and surrounded him in the center.

Zhan drove his troops with left and right assaults, killing hundreds.

Deng Ai had the general troops shoot arrows at him, and the Shu soldiers scattered.

Zhan was hit by arrows, lost his horse, and cried, “My strength is spent; I shall answer the country with one death!” He drew his sword and killed himself.

His son, Zhuge Shang, saw his father die in battle from the city wall and rose in fierce wrath. He dressed and mounted.

Zhang Zun remonstrated, “Young general, you must not charge out lightly.”

Shang sighed, “My father, my son and my descendants have all received this country’s deep grace. My father is dead at the enemy’s hand—how may I remain alive?”

He then drove his horse forward and died in the field.

A later poem praised father and son Zhuge Zhan and Shang:

It is not only that loyal ministers are few in strategy; heaven seems intent on ending the Liu line. In the days of old, Zhen (Zhuge) left downline blood in the world— true virtue and righteousness worthy to follow Wuhou.

Deng Ai, moved by their loyalty, had father and son buried together. He then used the opening to strike Mianzhu.

Zhang Zun, Huang Chong, and Li Qiu each led one army and charged out.

Shu men were few, Wei men were many. The three all died in battle, and therefore Deng Ai gained Mianzhu.

After finishing labor and rest, he came to seize Chengdu.

It was then said:

If one studies the day when the later sovereign faces peril, it is no different from when Liu Zhang was once coerced. How Chengdu will survive this onslaught is unknown for now—watch in the next section.

How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Deng Shizai Slips Across Yinping; Zhuge Zhan Dies at Mianzhu

chapters.html:
Tears rise at the ancestral shrine, one king dies in filial devotion. One man in western Xichuan seeks to recover, two worthy men contend for merit.

Back in Chengdu, the Later Han emperor Liu Shan, whose courtesy name was Gongsi, heard that Deng Ai had taken Mianzhu and that Zhuge Zhan and his son had perished. He was greatly alarmed and hurriedly summoned civil and military officials to discuss the crisis.

A close court attendant reported: “Outside the city, the civilians are supporting old men and carrying children. Their cries are deafening. All are fleeing to save their lives.”

The emperor was frantic and at a loss. Just then a scouting rider arrived and announced that the Wei forces were close to the city walls.

Many officials then said, “Our troops are few and commanders are few; we cannot meet the enemy. It is best to abandon Chengdu at once, flee to the seven commanderies of Nanzhong. That land is rugged and defensible, so we can hold out there and then, with the aid of barbarian soldiers, come back to reclaim it before it is too late.”

Guanglu Dafu Qiao Zhou said, “That cannot be done. The southern non-Han peoples have long been prone to revolt and have never shown much loyalty. If we throw ourselves upon them, we will surely face calamity.”

Many officials again submitted, “Shu and Wu are already allied. In this emergency, we may submit to Wu.”

Qiao Zhou again remonstrated: “There has never, in all ages, been an emperor who gave himself into another state as a dependent ruler. I judge that Wei can swallow Wu, but Wu cannot swallow Wei. If we submit to Wu now, that is one humiliation. If Wu is later swallowed by Wei, and Your Majesty then submits to Wei, that will be a humiliation twice over. Better than throwing ourselves to Wu is to surrender to Wei. Wei will certainly divide up the land and enfeoff Your Majesty, so you may defend the ancestral temple above and secure the people below. Think on this.”

The emperor did not decide and withdrew into the palace.

The next day the debates were again crowded with arguments. Seeing the urgency, Qiao Zhou again submitted a memorial and again spoke out against surrender. The emperor followed Qiao Zhou’s counsel. He was about to go out in surrender when a man stepped from behind the screen and shouted at Qiao Zhou in a harsh voice: “A life-preserving rotten scholar—how dare you raise such reckless words in state affairs? Was there ever before an emperor who submitted?”

The emperor looked and saw it was his fifth son, Prince of Beidi, Liu Chen.

The emperor had seven sons: his first was Liu Xuan, his second Liu Yao, his third Liu Cong, his fourth Liu Zan, the fifth was Prince of Beidi Liu Chen, the sixth Liu Xun, and the seventh Liu Qu. Of those seven, only Liu Chen had been brilliant and keen since childhood; the rest were weak and compliant.

The emperor said to Liu Chen: “All my ministers urge surrender. Why do you alone rely on hot-blooded courage and wish the whole city to run with blood?”

Liu Chen said, “When the former emperor was alive, Qiao Zhou never interfered in state administration. Now he dares to talk of affairs of state and repeatedly raises disorderly words. This is utterly unreasonable. I privately judge that Shu’s remaining forces number in the tens of thousands. Jiang Wei has all his men in Jian'ge Pass. If he learns that Wei has entered the capital, he will come to the rescue. If we strike from within and without, we can gain complete victory. Could we follow this decayed scholar’s words and lightly discard the foundation laid by the former emperor?”

The emperor snapped at him: “You child, how could you read the signs of Heaven?”

Liu Chen knelt, struck his forehead, and wept: “If our strength fails and disaster comes, we should both, fathers and sons and lord and minister, make a last stand in the capital and die with the state so as to honor the former emperor. Why should we surrender?”

The emperor would not listen. Liu Chen cried out in a great voice: “The former emperor did not establish this realm with ease; now if we abandon it in an instant, I would rather die than live in disgrace!”

The emperor ordered attendants to escort him out from the palace. He then commanded Qiao Zhou to draft a surrender memorial and dispatch a private court gentleman-in-waiting Zhang Shao and Captain-in-Attendance Deng Liang, with Qiao Zhou, carrying the Jade seal to Luo City to submit surrender.

Each day Deng Ai had sent out several hundred armored riders to scout near Chengdu. When he saw that surrender flags had been raised, he was overjoyed.

Not long afterward Zhang Shao and the others arrived. Deng Ai ordered them welcomed inside. The three men knelt at the staircase and presented the surrender petition and the Jade seal. Deng Ai opened the memorial and rejoiced. He received the seal and treated Zhang Shao, Qiao Zhou, Deng Liang, and the others with great favor.

Deng Ai drafted a reply and gave the three men a copy to carry back to Chengdu in order to reassure the people.

The three men took leave of Deng Ai and returned straight to Chengdu. They entered before the emperor and presented the reply, explaining in detail how well Deng Ai had received them.

The emperor opened the letter, rejoiced, and immediately ordered Grand Equerry Jiang Xian to carry an edict commanding Jiang Wei to surrender early. He also dispatched the junior clerk Li Hu with administrative records for Deng Ai.

In total there were 280,000 households, 940,000 men and women, 120,000 fully armed soldiers, 40,000 officials, more than 400,000 stocks of grain, 3,000 jins of gold and silver, and 200,000 bolts each of brocade and dyed silk. What remained in the granaries was too many to itemize.

He chose the first day of the twelfth month for the sovereign and officials to go out and submit.

When Prince Liu Chen learned this, fury surged through him. He went into the palace with sword in hand. His wife, Lady Cui, asked, “Why is the king so changed in face today?”

Liu Chen said, “Wei forces are near. Our father emperor has already submitted the surrender petition. Tomorrow the king and ministers will go out and surrender, and our state will perish from here. I want to die first and face the former emperor in the ground, not kneel before others.”

Lady Cui said, “Excellent! Excellent! Then you can die now, and your death is not far.”

Liu Chen asked, “Why should you die?”

Lady Cui answered, “If a husband dies, it is right for the wife to die; what is there to ask?”

When she finished speaking, she struck a pillar and died.

Liu Chen then killed his three sons, then cut off his wife’s head, carried both to the Zhaolie Temple, knelt upon the ground and cried:

“Ministerial shame fills me to have seen our foundation abandoned to others. Therefore I first killed my wife and sons to sever all thought of worldly ties, then I shall repay my ancestors with this one life. If our ancestor has spirit, let him know my heart!”

After a great outburst of weeping and blood streaming from his eyes, he committed suicide by slitting his throat. The people of Shu heard and were all overwhelmed with grief.

Later people praised him in a verse:

A king and his ministers gladly bend and submit, yet one son alone is left to grieve. Xichuan’s work is gone from us now, how mighty was the Prince of Beidi! He fell to reward his revered ancestors, clawing his head and crying to the sky. A man of fierce upright spirit seems still present; who says Han has truly vanished?

When the later ruler heard of Liu Chen’s self-slashing, he ordered his burial.

The next day the Wei army arrived in force. The emperor went out with crown prince and royal sons, with more than sixty ministers and officials, faces bound and draped in funeral cloths, and traveled ten li north of the gate to surrender.

Deng Ai helped the emperor rise, personally untied his bindings, burned the funeral drapes, and brought him into the city in his carriage.

Later people sighed in verse:

Tens of thousands of Wei soldiers marched into Sichuan, yet the emperor escaped only by sacrificing his own judgment. Huang Hao long survived by deceiving the empire’s will, and Jiang Wei shouldered talent in saving the age in vain. Loyal men of upright principle, how fierce was their zeal, and King Sun’s resolve to keep his post is now a pity. What Zhaolie of Shu built was no light work, in one dawn that labor turned to ash.

Thus all the people of Chengdu brought fragrant flowers and welcome offerings. Deng Ai ennobled the former emperor as General of Agile Cavalry and then allowed all civil and military officials, one by one according to rank, to be granted offices. He ordered that the former emperor return to his palace, issue edicts to pacify the people, hand over the warehouses, and also appointed the Master of Rites Zhang Jun and Yizhou Deputy Administrator Zhang Shao to invite by amnesty every commandery’s military and civilians to submit.

He also sent word that Jiang Wei should come in and surrender.

At the same time he dispatched messengers to Luoyang to report victory.

When Deng Ai heard of Huang Hao’s treachery, he wished to execute him. Huang Hao bribed those near him with precious metal and therefore escaped.

From this point, Han had fallen.

Later people, reflecting on Han’s collapse, composed a verse:

Even ape and bird know to fear the decree-street message; wind and cloud seem to protect Shou Xu’s estate. The high commander labored with divine brush for nothing, and in the end the humbled king rides away in a public cart. Guan Yu had talent and did not bring shame, yet what path remained for Guan and Zhang? In later years, when you pass through brocade-lane shrines, you will hear Father Liang’s songs still full of sorrow.

Jiang Xian, the Grand Equerry, arrived at Jian'ge and entered before Jiang Wei, bearing the former emperor’s command and telling him of the surrender order. Jiang Wei was shocked and speechless.

When the officers under his command learned of it, they all grieved and complained together, gnashing their teeth and glaring, their hair standing on end. They drew their swords and struck at stone, crying out, “We fought for a war to the death. Why should we surrender first?” Their cries of lament were heard for dozens of li.

Seeing that the troops’ hearts still longed for Han, Jiang Wei used gentle words to soothe them: “Do not despair, generals. I have one plan that can restore Han’s house.”

The generals asked him. Jiang Wei and several officers bent near his ear and whispered their plan.

He then ordered surrender flags raised all along Jian'ge Pass. First he sent word into Zhong Hui’s camp that Jiang Wei was bringing Zhang Yi, Liao Hua, Dong Jue, and others to surrender. Zhong Hui rejoiced and sent men to receive Jiang Wei in his tent.

Zhong Hui said, “Why did Boyue arrive so late?”

Jiang Wei answered gravely, tears flowing, “The whole state’s armed force is under my command; coming as far as this is already swift enough.”

Zhong Hui was astonished and rose from his seat to bow and receive him as a high guest. Jiang Wei said to him:

“General Zhonghui, I have heard that since you came from Huainan, you have no obvious stratagem without flaw. If Cao Wei reaches this height, it is by Your Excellency’s own strength. I gladly submit and bow my head. Had I faced Deng Shizai, I would have fought him to the death. How could I have surrendered to him?”

Zhong Hui then broke an arrow as an oath and swore brotherly brotherhood with Jiang Wei, and their bond became close. He still ordered Jiang Wei to keep command of his troops as before.

Jiang Wei rejoiced inwardly and therefore had Jiang Xian return to Chengdu.

Now Deng Ai made Shi Zuan the Inspector of Yizhou, Qian Hong and Wang Qi other provincial commanders, and so on. At Mianzhu he built a raised platform to advertise his victory and summoned all surviving Shu officials to a banquet.

Deng Ai had drunk to near-saturation and, gesturing to the assembled officials, said, “You are fortunate to meet me, and so you have this day. Had it been any other general, all of you would have been destroyed by now.”

The officials rose and bowing thanked him. Just then Jiang Xian arrived and told them that Jiang Wei had surrendered to Zhonghui’s western command. Thus Deng Ai grew resentful of Zhong Hui and drafted a memorial to be carried to Luoyang for Sima Zhao.

Ai wrote:

I, Deng Ai, venture to suggest this: one must first make a sign and then bring substance to bear. Now, because we have just subdued Shu, this is the moment to sweep and subdue Wu. Yet after a major campaign the troops are exhausted and cannot be immediately employed. Keep 20,000 troops from Longxi and 20,000 Shu soldiers; begin salt-making and metallurgy, and build ships to prepare for a plan of going with the current waters. Then we can send envoys to explain advantage and danger, and Wu can perhaps be brought down without a campaign. Treat Liu Shan with great honor so as to win Sun Xiu’s submission. If we send him to the capital at once, the people of Wu will be suspicious and less moved toward yielding. Hold him in Shu for now, and let him come to the capital in winter next year. Grant him now the fief of Fufeng King, provide gifts and money, give stipends to his attendants, and make his sons ministers, so that his submission appears sincere. Then the people of Wu will fear our power and admire our virtue and will yield at once.

Sima Zhao read it through and deeply doubted that Deng Ai harbored intentions to act alone. He first sent a private memorial to Wei Guan, and afterward sent the surrender ennobling edict to him, written in his own hand:

General Who Conquers the West Deng Ai: your brilliance in the display of prestige and the vigor of arms drove deep into enemy lands, dragging the usurping ruler by the neck to surrender; your army never moved beyond time, your battles did not last through a day. Like the wind, you rolled up and swept all and settled both Ba and Shu. Even Bai Qi at the height of Chu and Han Xin in fierce Zhao cannot match your meritorious deed. Therefore you are named Grand Commandant. Your fief is raised by 20,000 households. Your two sons are made district marquises, each to hold a thousand households.

When Deng Ai finished receiving the decree, Weiguan, the monitor general, took out Sima Zhao’s own-letter and presented it to him. It said that Deng Ai’s proposals were to be held for formal report and not acted upon at once. Deng Ai replied, “The general is outside; a ministerial order from the ruler is not always one that must be accepted.” Since he had taken command as an envoy-for-haste, how could he be stopped? He drafted yet another letter and sent it by envoy to Luoyang.

At that time, all at court said that Deng Ai certainly had rebel intent. Sima Zhao grew even more suspicious. A messenger then returned and presented Deng Ai’s new letter.

Sima Zhao broke the seal and read:

Ai has been commissioned to campaign west. The once-entrenched enemies have been brought low; this is the hour when he should act with expedience to settle newly attached lands. If we wait for commands from court, we lose the travel days in going and returning. In government principle, when an official ministers abroad and there is a measure that can settle the realm and benefit the state, he may act on his own. Wu has not yet paid homage and still links with Shu; if we stand on custom, we may lose the opportunity for action. In warfare one advances not for praise and retreats not to avoid blame. Though Ai lacks the restraint of ancient men, he will never blush to use what harms the state. The matters already set forth are submitted for implementation.

Sima Zhao, after reading, was in a shock. He huddled with Jia Chong and said, “Deng Ai is haughty on account of his achievements and acts at will; his intention to rebel is revealed.”

Jia Chong replied, “My Lord, why not enfeoff Zhong Hui to keep him in check?”

Sima Zhao accepted that idea, dispatched an envoy with an edict naming Zhonghui as Minister over the Masses, and ordered Wei Guan to oversee both routes of the armies. He placed in Wei Guan’s hands a private order that he was to watch Zhonghui and Deng Ai carefully and prevent any revolt. Zhonghui read the order aloud:

General Who Guards the West Zhonghui: where you go you know no defeat. Before you, there is no strong rival; you regulate a number of city-states and collect fleeing men into your net. The commanders of Shu have come before you with bound faces to submit. No stratagem is unmade by you; no effort lacks accomplishment. Therefore you are appointed Minister over the Masses, promoted to county marquis, your fief increased by 10,000 households, and your two sons made district marquises, each to hold a thousand households.

Since Zhonghui had just been enfeoffed, he at once asked Jiang Wei for counsel:

“Deng Ai’s achievements seem greater than mine, and he now holds the Grand Commandant’s office. Now Master Sima suspects that Ai will rebel, and so has ordered Wei Guan to supervise him and commands me to restrain him. What counsel does Boyue have?”

Jiang Wei replied, “I heard that Deng Ai came from very modest origins; in childhood he was raised in a farming household to tend calves. By fortunate fortune he slipped through Yinping by a slant path, climbing trees and cliffs, and gained this great success. It is not pure good strategy, but the great blessing of the state at work. If not that Your Excellency and I blocked him at Jian'ge, how could Ai have made this achievement?

Now he seeks to enfeoff the Shu lord as King of Fufeng to bind the Shu people tightly to him. His rebellious heart is plain and need not be spoken. Sima-gong’s suspicions are correct.”

Zhonghui highly praised what he heard. Jiang Wei said, “Please send your attendants away; I have a confidential matter.”

He told Zhonghui to clear attendants. Jiang Wei took a map from his sleeve and said, “In former days Master Wuhou came from that thatched cabin and presented this map to the former emperor and said: ‘The land of Yizhou has broad fertile fields for miles, abundant people and rich state; it can become a hegemony.’ The former emperor therefore founded Chengdu.”

Jiang Wei unrolled the map and explained it point by point as Zhonghui inquired about rivers and terrain.

“Riding Sima’s present suspicion and jealousy, you must urgently submit a memorial saying that Ai is displaying signs of revolt. Sima will certainly order Your Excellency to punish him, and in one stroke you can capture him.”

Zhonghui followed that advice, sending an envoy with a memorial to Luoyang describing Ai’s self-assertive, uncontrolled command and his closeness to Shu men, warning that he would rebel at dawn or dusk.

Thus the whole court’s civil and military officers were alarmed. Zhonghui then had his men stop Deng Ai’s memorial while he was en route, then by imitating Ai’s hand, rewrote haughty phrases into his own words that supported reality.

When Sima Zhao saw Deng Ai’s petition, he was furious and sent men to Zhonghui’s camp ordering him to arrest Ai. He also sent Jia Chong with thirty thousand soldiers into Xie Valley. Then Sima Zao traveled in person with Wei emperor Cao Huan.

Xiao Cao, Assistant Clerk of the Right in the western department, Shàotì, remonstrated: “Zhonghui’s troops are six times larger than Deng Ai’s. As it now stands, arresting Ai is enough. Why does Your Lordship go yourself?”

Zhao laughed: “Have you forgotten your old words? You once said Zhonghui would rebel; this journey is not for Ai, it is for Zhonghui himself.”

Shàotì then laughed and said, “I fear Your Lordship has forgotten, so I ask. Now that this is the intention, it must be kept secret. Let it not leak.”

Zhao accepted those words and led his great force onward.

At that time Jia Chong also suspected Zhonghui of change and secretly informed Sima Zhao. Zhao said, “If I were to send you, would I also suspect you? When I reach Chang’an, all will be made clear.”

A secret informant had already told Zhonghui: Zhao had reached Chang’an. In a panic, Zhonghui sought Jiang Wei’s counsel on how best to bring Ai down.

Just then:

Just then a newly surrendered general from Western Shu is seen, and Chang’an is now in motion with vast forces. Who can say how Boyue will break Ai? How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: A King Dies of Filial Loyalty, and Two Men in Western Shu Compete for Merit

chapters.html:
A feigned surrender, with clever design, becomes hollow talk. Again accepting abdication, one traces another pattern in imitation.

Zhong Hui asked Jiang Wei to plan together for how to arrest Deng Ai.

Jiang Wei replied, ‘It is best first to have Inspector Wei Guan take custody of Deng Ai. If Ai attempts to kill Wei Guan, then his treachery is obvious. The General may then raise troops to punish him, which is also possible.’

Zhong Hui rejoiced and ordered Wei Guan with several dozen men to enter Chengdu and arrest Deng Ai and his son. Wei Guan’s soldiers tried to stop him, saying, ‘This is an order from Chancellor Zhong: Deng Zhenxi should be seized, for his changeable intent is criminal. It must not be done.’

Wei Guan answered, ‘I have my own device,’ and first issued two or three dozen proclamations. One of the orders read:

By imperial command, take into custody Deng Ai. Ask no questions about anything else. If he comes in early and submits, rewards and ranks will be added. If he refuses to come out, all three of his lineages will be exterminated.

Wei Guan prepared two cart cages and came toward Chengdu through the night.

By rooster crow, each of Deng Ai’s officers who read the proclamations came and knelt at Wei Guan’s horse. Deng Ai had not yet risen in his residence. Wei Guan burst in with several dozen men and shouted, ‘By command, arrest Deng Ai and his son!’

Deng Ai was stunned and rolled out of bed. Wei Guan shouted at the guards and had him bound and put on the cart. Deng Zhong came out to ask questions and was also seized and bound to the cart.

The officers in the estate were greatly alarmed and prepared to seize them by force, but at once a great cloud of dust rose and a scouting horseman reported that Chancellor Zhong’s host had arrived. All men scattered and ran in all directions.

Zhong Hui and Jiang Wei dismounted and entered the residence. They saw Deng Ai and his son already tied. Zhong Hui struck Deng Ai on the head with a whip and shouted, ‘A young fool reared like a calf, how dare you do this!’ Jiang Wei also shouted, ‘A mere adventurer taking reckless risks has brought about this day!’ Deng Ai cursed out loudly.

Zhong Hui sent father and son to Luoyang. After arriving in Chengdu he took all of Deng Ai’s soldiers and horses, and his prestige and terror spread greatly.

He told Jiang Wei, ‘Only today I have fulfilled this wish of my life.’

Jiang Wei said, ‘In old days, Han Xin refused Kui Tong’s advice and so suffered disaster at Weiyang Palace. Lord Dai did not follow Fan Li at Wuhu and in the end fell upon his sword and died. Are not these two men famous in achievement and name? Yet because they did not understand harm and benefit in time, they failed to seize the proper moment. Your Excellency has now obtained great merit and strikes fear into your lord. Why not board a boat, cut off all traces, climb Emei Ridge, and roam with Master Chisongzi?’

Zhong Hui laughed. ‘Your words are off course. I am not yet forty. I am only now intent on pressing forward. Could I ever do the lazy retirement you propose?’

Jiang Wei answered, ‘If retirement is not intended, then you must at once seek sound plans. This is all within Your Excellency’s own talents and strength; you need not burden an old man with my words.’

Zhong Hui clapped his hands and laughed. ‘Boyue understands my heart,’ he said. From then on the two discussed great affairs each day.

In private Jiang Wei wrote to the Later Lord: ‘Please endure a few days of humiliation. I will bring the state from danger back to peace, from darkness to light again. The Han house will not perish completely.’

Now Zhong Hui was already plotting rebellion with Jiang Wei, when news came that Sima Zhao had sent a letter. Zhong Hui read it: ‘I fear Zhong Hui cannot take Ai as ordered. I have therefore stationed troops in Chang’an for consultation on the matter. I report this first because we are already near.’

Zhong Hui was greatly alarmed. ‘My troops are many times Deng Ai’s. If he wanted only Ai’s arrest, Prince of Jin knew I could do it alone; Sima Zhao coming with troops today means he already suspects me.’

He conferred again with Jiang Wei. Jiang Wei said, ‘If Your Excellency doubts me, then I must die. Have you not seen Deng Ai?’

Zhong Hui said, ‘My resolution is fixed. If the matter succeeds, we gain the realm; if it fails, we retreat to western Shu. Even that is no loss to being called Liu Bei.’

Jiang Wei said, ‘I have just heard Empress Dowager Guo died. We can claim a posthumous order from her commanding Sima Zhao to be executed, to redress the crime of regicide, and declare that he will soon seize power from Wei. By Your Excellency’s talent, the Central Plains can be swept into submission.’

Zhong Hui said, ‘Boyue must act as the vanguard. Once this is done, we share rich and high fortunes together.’

Jiang Wei replied, ‘I can offer dog-and-horse service for a small effort. I only fear the other generals will not obey.’

Zhong Hui said, ‘Tomorrow is the Lantern Festival. The palace will hang great lanterns. I will invite the generals to a drink and feast. Anyone who refuses will be beheaded.’

Jiang Wei was inwardly glad.

The next day Zhong Hui and Jiang Wei invited the generals to drink. After circling the hall several times, Zhong Hui took the cup and cried out in grief.

The generals, alarmed, asked why.

Zhong Hui said, ‘I have a posthumous command from Empress Dowager Guo in my hands: she instructed that Sima Zhao was to strike down the Son of Heaven in Nanyue, a monstrous treason of patricide and conspiracy. He will soon usurp. She orders him to be punished. Each of you shall sign your names and complete this together.’

Everyone was stunned and stared at one another. Zhong Hui drew his sword and said, ‘Whoever disobeys this order will be executed.’

All were terrified and had no choice but to follow. After signatures were completed Zhong Hui confined them in the palace and strictly guarded every gate with troops.

Jiang Wei said, ‘I have seen they will not obey. I ask that they be driven into pits.’

Zhong Hui said, ‘I have already ordered a pit to be dug in the palace and set out thousands of great cudgels. If anyone refuses, he will be beaten to death in it.’

At the side stood Qiu Jian, trusted by the heart. Qiu Jian had once served as a subordinate of the palace guard Hu Lie; Hu Lie too was kept under watch in the palace. Qiu Jian secretly told Hu Lie all that Zhong Hui had said.

Hu Lie was greatly startled and sobbed as he said, ‘My son Hu Yuan leads troops outside; how could he know that Zhong has such intent? Think of the relationship we have had till now and pass this message through. If I die there will be no regret.’

Qiu Jian said, ‘My lord need not worry. Allow me to handle this.’

He then reported to Zhong Hui, ‘My lord keeps the generals in the palace; food and water are hard to come by. Allow one person to go back and forth carrying messages.’

Zhong Hui, who had long trusted Qiu Jian, entrusted him this mission and said, ‘I entrust a weighty matter to you. Do not allow it to leak.’

Qiu Jian, in secret, had a trusted person of Hu Lie enter inward. Hu Lie gave that man a secret letter. The man ran swiftly to Hu Yuan’s camp and explained the matter in detail, handing over the letter.

Hu Yuan was startled at once. He showed it throughout the camps.

Commanders grew furious. They assembled urgently and said, ‘Even if we die, would we follow a traitorous minister?’

Hu Yuan said, ‘On the eighteenth of the first month, at midday we can suddenly enter inside and do this.’

Inspector Wei Guan, hearing of Hu Yuan’s plan, greatly rejoiced. He prepared men and horses, and had Qiu Jian relay the instructions to Hu Lie, and Hu Lie informed the other commanders.

Again Zhong Hui asked Jiang Wei, ‘I dreamed last night of thousands of huge snakes biting me. Does this mean good or ill fortune?’

Jiang Wei replied, ‘To dream of dragons and snakes is an omen of good things.’

Zhong Hui believed him, and said, ‘Our weapons and regalia are prepared. I shall send forth the generals and ask what they say?’

Jiang Wei said, ‘These men all carry disloyal hearts. In time they will become harmful. It is best to execute them early.’

Zhong Hui followed this and ordered Jiang Wei to lead soldiers and kill the Wei generals.

Jiang Wei took command and was about to depart when a sudden chest pain struck him and he collapsed. His attendants raised him; after some time he came to.

Then people’s voices rose in tumult outside. Zhong Hui sent someone to investigate. The shouting was immense and troops arrived from all sides. Jiang Wei said, ‘This must be the generals’ revolt. Let us kill them first.’

At that moment word arrived that troops had already entered inside.

Zhong Hui ordered the hall doors shut. He had guards climb to the hall roof and strike down with roof tiles. They killed one another by the dozens.

Outside, fires rose on four sides, and from beyond the walls troops split open the palace gate and rushed in. Zhong Hui drew his sword and stood killing a number of men, but a hail of arrows knocked him down. The commanders seized and beheaded him.

Jiang Wei drew his sword up into the hall and surged in and out striking hard. His chest pain worsened.

Looking upward, he shouted, ‘My scheme has failed; this is the will of Heaven.’ He then cut his throat himself. He was fifty-nine.

A few hundred men died in the palace.

Wei Guan said, ‘Each unit of the army should return to its camp and await the king’s command.’

The Wei troops, eager for revenge, together opened Jiang Wei’s belly; his courage was no bigger than a chicken egg. Then all the commanders took the whole family of Jiang Wei and killed them.

When Deng Ai’s men saw that Zhong Hui and Jiang Wei were dead, they rode that night to chase and seize Deng Ai. One came and reported to Wei Guan.

Wei Guan said, ‘It was I who detained Deng Ai. If I let him go now, I have no place left to bury myself.’

The palace guard Tian Xu said, ‘When Deng Ai took Jiangyou, he wanted to kill me. He was pardoned through the intercession of numerous officials. Today we must return this grievance.’

Wei Guan was pleased and sent Tian Xu with five hundred troops to Mianzhu. Exactly there they met Deng Ai and his son, released from the cart cage on their way back to Chengdu. Deng Ai thought they were men of his own camp and made no preparation. As he moved to inquire, Tian Xu cut him down in one stroke. Deng Zhong was also slain in the disorder.

There were later poems lamenting Deng Ai:

From youth he could devise and plan, In counsel and in war he was skillful. By one glance he read land and river, With lifted face he read the stars. One ride and the mountain root was severed, At the soldiers’ coming the stone paths split. Great achievement was done, and yet he died by a blade, His spirit turns among the Han River clouds.

There were later poems lamenting Zhong Hui:

In early years he was praised as quick and wise, He once served as a secretarial gentleman. His clever plans tipped Sima Mai, In his time men called him Zifang. In Shouchun many praised his plans, At Sword Ridge his heroic spirit rose. He did not learn to withdraw like Tao Zhu, And his wandering soul mourns his old home.

There were later poems lamenting Jiang Wei:

Tianshui boasted fine talents and beauty, Liang Province gave birth to unusual ability. He left Shangfu’s line and came, He bore skill and pledged it to Kongming. His bold mind knew no fear, His broad will would not turn away. On the day he died in Chengdu, The Han generals had sorrow left over.

As Zhong Hui, Jiang Wei, and Deng Ai were all dead, Zhang Yi too died in the same chaos. The crown prince Liu Xuan and the Marquis of Hanshou, Guan Yi, were both killed by Wei soldiers.

The soldiers and people were in uproar. They trampled one another in disorder; the dead were beyond count.

After ten days, Jia Chong arrived first and posted proclamations to calm the people; only then did things begin to settle.

Wei Guan was left to guard Chengdu, and then the Later Lord was brought to Luoyang. Only a few stayed with him: Prefect of the Masters of Writing Fan Jian, Palace Attendant Zhang Shao, Grand Master of Ceremonies Qiao Zhou, and Secretary Xi Zheng.

Liao Hua and Dong Jue both feigned sickness and did not rise. In time both died of grief.

In the fifth year of the Jingyuan era of Wei, it became the first year of Xianxi. In the third month, Ding Feng of Wu saw that Shu had fallen and so gathered his troops and returned to Wu.

In the Secretariat, Chenghua He presented an account to Emperor Sun Xiu of Wu.

‘Wu and Shu are like lips and teeth. If the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold. I believe Sima Zhao’s invasion of Wu is near. Your Majesty should strengthen the defenses.’

Sun Xiu accepted this and appointed Lu Kang, Lu Xun’s son, as General Who Guards the East and Governor of Jing Province to defend Jiangkou. General of the Left Sun Yi took posts at the mountain passes in south Xu Province. Along the riverfront several hundred camps were raised, and the old general Ding Feng was made overall commander to guard against Wei forces.

Huo Ge, Administrator of Jianing, heard that Chengdu had not been defended. He wore plain mourning robes and cried toward the west for three days.

The commanders all said, ‘Since the Han ruler has lost his position, why not surrender at once?’

Huo Ge wept and said, ‘The roads are blocked, and no one knows whether our lord is safe or not. If Wei’s lord treats him with rites, then to surrender the whole city is not too late. If there is danger to our lord’s honor, then to surrender is impossible; this is our duty and death.’

All accepted his words and sent men to Luoyang to ask about the Later Lord’s fate.

Now that the Later Lord had arrived at Luoyang, Sima Zhao had already returned to court. Sima Zhao said, ‘You were given to lust and licentiousness, you discarded worthy ministers and ruined governance. You deserve death.’ The Later Lord’s face turned to the color of earth, and he knew not what was happening.

The civil and military officials together submitted memorials saying, ‘Shu’s lord has lost court order. He surrendered early and should be pardoned.’

So Sima Zhao enfeoffed him as Duke of Anle, gave him residence, monthly allowances, ten thousand bolts of silk, and a hundred household servants and bondsmen.

The son Liu Yao and ministers Fan Jian, Qiao Zhou, and Xi Zheng all were enfeoffed.

The Later Lord gave thanks and returned inward.

Because Huang Hao had ruined the state and harmed the people, Sima Zhao ordered soldiers to escort him outside the market hall and execute him by slow slicing.

At this time, Huo Ge learned that the Later Lord had been enfeoffed and he led his troops to surrender.

The next day, the Later Lord personally went to Sima Zhao’s residence and bowed to give thanks. Sima Zhao arranged a banquet. First he staged Wei music and dance in front. Shu officials wept in sorrow; only the Later Lord seemed happy and composed.

Sima Zhao ordered Shu men to perform Shu music before him; all Shu officials collapsed in tears, while the Later Lord laughed and smiled as if at ease.

When the wine was half-way and all drank deep, Sima Zhao said to Jia Chong, ‘Humankind has become so cruel! Even if Kongming himself were here, he could not keep him intact for long; how much less Jiang Wei.’ Then he asked the Later Lord, ‘Do you miss Shu?’

The Later Lord answered, ‘In this place of entertainment, I do not miss Shu.’

Soon after, the Later Lord rose and changed his clothes. Xi Zheng followed and said, from near the side screen, ‘Why did Your Majesty answer so that you do not miss Shu? If he asks again, reply with tears, “The ancestors’ graves lie far in Shu. My heart faces westward in sorrow; every day I remember it.” Then the Jin Prince will surely release you back to Shu.’

The Later Lord took this into his heart and held it.

The wine had made him only slightly drunk when Sima Zhao asked again, ‘Do you miss Shu?’ The Later Lord answered as Xi Zheng had taught him, trying to weep but with no tears, and kept his eyes closed.

Sima Zhao asked, ‘Why does this sound like Xi Zheng’s speech?’

The Later Lord opened his eyes in alarm and said, ‘It is exactly according to Your Excellency’s command.’

Sima Zhao and all those beside him laughed. He was pleased by the Later Lord’s sincerity and no longer suspected him.

A later poem lamented him:

He laughed among revelry and music with open face, Thinking of ruin there was not one point of grief. In distant joy he forgot the old court, Then we came to know the Later Lord was a fool.

After ministers of court praised Sima Zhao for his success in receiving Shu, they elevated him as king and remonstrated to Wei’s Emperor Cao Huan. Cao Huan in name was Son of Heaven, but he could not truly rule; Sima affairs governed all, and none dared refuse.

Thus they made Sima Zhao King of Jin, and in memorials named posthumously Sima Yi as Duke Xuan, and his brother Sima Shi as Duke Jing.

Sima Zhao’s wife was Wang Su’s daughter; she bore two sons. The elder was Sima Yan, of lofty build; when born, his hair hung nearly to the ground, his hands could reach beyond the knees; he was sharp, brilliant, and martial, and his courage beyond ordinary limits. The younger was Sima You, mild in temperament, reverent, frugal, filial; Sima Zhao loved him greatly. Because Sima Shi had no son, succession was to pass through You.

Sima Zhao used to say, ‘This world belongs to my elder brother’s world.’

After Sima Zhao had been made King of Jin, he wished to name Sima You as heir. Shan Tao remonstrated, saying, ‘To put the younger above the elder violates the rites and brings inauspiciousness.’ Jia Chong, He Zeng, and Pei Xiu also remonstrated: ‘The elder son is intelligent and heroic, with talent beyond the world. The people’s esteem is full, and heaven displays this; he is not fit to be treated as a mere minister.’

Sima Zhao hesitated. Grand Commandant Wang Xiang and Minister over the Masses Xun Yi also remonstrated: ‘In former ages, naming the younger to succeed often brought disorder to states. May Your Highness reflect on this.’

So Sima Zhao made his eldest son Sima Yan crown prince.

Officials memorialized:

A man descended from Heaven appeared once in Xiangwu County. He was over two zhang tall, his footprints three chi two cun long, with white hair and dark beard, wearing a yellow undershirt and a yellow headcloth, leaning on a staff. He declared, ‘I am the king of the commoners. I come to tell you that the dynasty will change and peace will appear.’ He wandered in the city for three days and then suddenly disappeared.

That was an omen for Your Highness. You may wear a crown with twenty tassels, set out imperial banners, move in and out under guard, ride in a carriage with gold axle and six horses, make your prince wife queen, and appoint a crown prince.’

Sima Zhao’s heart rejoiced secretly. When he returned to the palace and was about to drink, he suddenly suffered a stroke and lost speech.

The next day, as he lay critically ill, Grand Commandant Wang Xiang, Minister of Works He Zeng, Sima Xun Yi, and the other ministers entered to inquire. Sima Zhao could not speak and pointed toward crown prince Sima Yan. It was the xinsmao day of the eighth month.

He Zeng said, ‘All state affairs now rest with the King of Jin. Let the crown prince become King of Jin first, and then conduct burial rites.’

On that day Sima Yan became King of Jin. He appointed He Zeng as King’s Grand Chancellor, Sima Wang as Grand Minister over the Masses, Shi Bao as General of Agile Cavalry, and Chen Qian as General of Chariots and Cavalry. He gave his father posthumous title of Duke Wen.

When the burials were finished, Sima Yan summoned Jia Chong and Pei Xiu and asked, ‘Did Cao Cao truly once say, “If Heaven’s mandate is with me, then am I worthy of being King Wen of Zhou?”?’

Jia Chong said, ‘Cao Cao, who always held Han stipend, feared men would accuse him of usurpation. So he uttered that phrase to prepare Cao Pi to become Son of Heaven.’

Sima Yan asked, ‘How does my late father king compare with Cao Cao?’

Jia Chong answered, ‘Though Cao Cao’s achievements covered all Hua Xia, the common people feared his power but did not follow his virtue. Cao Pi succeeded him with hard toil and constant journeys east and west, and had no years of peace. My father King Xuan and my uncle King Jing then won repeated great victories, distributed mercy, and compassion, and the world has long entrusted itself to them. King Wen absorbed western Shu and his accomplishments were equal to the universe; how could they be compared?’

Sima Yan said, ‘Cao Pi still claimed to continue Han succession. Why should I not continue Wei succession?’

Jia Chong and Pei Xiu together knelt and reported, ‘Your Highness should follow Cao Pi’s example and continue Han’s former succession for Wei: rebuild the abdication platform and announce to all under heaven that you now assume the great seat.’

Sima Yan was greatly pleased. The next day he entered the inner court with a sword.

At that time Emperor Cao Huan had not held court for many days and had been absent-minded, his movements unsteady. Sima Yan entered the inner hall directly; Cao Huan hurriedly descended from the imperial couch and came out.

After Sima Yan sat, he asked, ‘Whose power is the realm of Wei?’

Cao Huan replied, ‘It was bestowed by my father, the King of Jin’s father and ancestors.’

Sima Yan laughed and said, ‘I see Your Majesty can speak of texts but not govern by the Way or by statecraft. Why not yield authority to one with talent and virtue?’

At once Zhang Jie shouted, ‘The words of the King of Jin are wrong! In old days, Great Founder, King Wu of the Martial Emperor, swept east and west and fought in all directions, south and north—this domain was no easy gain. Today, if Your Majesty has virtue and no fault, why give the realm to another?’

Sima Yan grew angry. ‘This state is in fact the state of great Han,’ he said. ‘Cao Cao used the Son of Heaven to command all lords and installed himself as King of Wei, thus seizing the Han house. My ancestors for three generations have aided Wei; those who obtained the realm were not the Cao house but the Sima house. The four seas all know this. Why should I not inherit the realm of Wei today?’

Zhang Jie added, ‘To seek this is the act of a traitor to the state.’

Sima Yan grew angry and shouted, ‘I seek to make recompense to the Han line. What is wrong in this?’ He ordered a guard to beat Zhang Jie to death with cudgels before him.

Cao Huan wept and knelt in petition.

Sima Yan rose and left the hall.

Cao Huan asked Jia Chong and Pei Xiu, ‘Matters have become urgent. What can be done?’

Jia Chong said, ‘The numerals of Heaven are at their limit. Your Majesty must not resist Heaven. Follow the example of Emperor Xian of Han: rebuild the abdication platform with full ceremony and give the throne to the King of Jin. If Heaven and the people approve, Your Majesty will be safe.’

Cao Huan agreed and ordered Jia Chong to construct the platform.

On a jiazi day of the twelfth month, Cao Huan himself held the imperial seal and stepped onto the platform. He assembled all officials.

A poem was later made:

Wei swallowed Han, and Jin swallowed Cao; Heavenly turns of history cannot be avoided. A pity to Zhang Jie who died for the state, How can a fist block Mount Tai?

Then he requested King of Jin Sima Yan to mount the platform and receive the great rites.

Cao Huan descended, wore court mourning clothes, and stood at the front rank. Sima Yan sat upright on the platform. Jia Chong and Pei Xiu stood on either side with swords drawn and ordered Cao Huan to kneel and listen to the command.

Jia Chong said, ‘Since the twenty-fifth year of Jian’an, Wei has received Han’s throne for forty-five years. Today the mandate reaches its end; Heaven and Man both now grant it to Jin. The Sima house has power and virtue that surpass heaven and earth, and can now take the imperial seat and continue Wei’s succession.’

He continued, ‘Before this Your Majesty must go to your new enfeoffment as King of Chenliu and take up residence at Jinyong City. Before you depart you may not enter the capital except under an imperial decree.’

After these words, Cao Huan wept in thanks and left.

Minister Sima Fu of the Taichuan said, with a bow before Cao Huan, ‘I am a Wei servant and will never betray Wei.’ Seeing this, Sima Yan ennobled Sima Fu as Duke of Anping. Sima Fu refused and withdrew.

That day all civil and military officials, knelt twice below the platform and cried out “Long live” in ten-thousand chorus.

Sima Yan inherited Wei’s mandate and founded Great Jin, changing the era name to Taishi. A general amnesty was issued across the realm. Wei was gone.

A later poem lamented:

Jin’s frame is vast like that of Wei’s king, The traces of Chenliu resemble Shanyang. Though this ceremony of transfer was done again, Looking back on those former days, one can only grieve.

King of Jin Sima Yan posthumously enfeoffed Sima Yi as Emperor Xuan, uncle Sima Shi as Emperor Jing, and his father Sima Zhao as Emperor Wen. He built seven ancestral temples to honor his forebears.

These were: General Who Conquers the West Sima Jun, his son Governor of Yuzhang Sima Liang, his son Governor of Yingchuan Sima Juan, his son Jingzhao Governor Sima Fang, his son Emperor Xuan Sima Yi, whose sons were Emperor Jing Sima Shi and Emperor Wen Sima Zhao.

With great affairs now settled, each day he discussed with his court strategy against Wu.

A fitting couplet now concluded the chapter:

Han courts and walls are no longer as before, Wu’s mountains and rivers will soon be changed. How they will break the state of Wu is yet to be seen— How this turned out will be told in the next chapter.
chapters.title: Feigned Surrender and Crafty Stratagems, Empty Words; Accepting the Mandate Again by Copying the Old Pattern

chapters.html:
Wu lord Sun Xiu heard that Sima Yan had already usurped Wei. Knowing he would surely move against Wu, he became worried and fell seriously ill. He summoned Chancellor Puyang Xing and ordered Crown Prince Sun Wan to enter for audience. Sun Xiu placed his hand on Xing’s arm, pointed to the crown prince, and then died.

Xing consulted the ministers on setting the crown prince as ruler. Commander Wan Yu said, “The prince is too young to govern alone. Better to set up the Marquis of Wucheng, Sun Hao.” Left General Zhang Bu also said, “Hao is clear-minded and decisive; he can serve as emperor.” Puyang Xing could not decide and reported to Empress Dowager Zhu. She replied, “I am only a widow; how can I know affairs of state and kingdom? You may deliberate and determine this yourselves.” Xing therefore brought Hao to the throne.

Hao, styled Yuanzong, was the son of the crown prince Sun He and grandson of Great Emperor Sun Quan. In the seventh month of that year he mounted the throne and changed the era to Yuanxing, its first year. He made Crown Prince Sun Wan the Prince of Yuzhang, posthumously honored his father as Emperor Wen, and raised Lady He to Empress Dowager. He promoted Ding Feng to Left and Right Grand Commander. The next year it became Ganlu.

Hao’s cruelty and violence increased by the day. He was heavily immersed in wine and lust and favored the eunuch Cen Hun. Puyang Xing and Zhang Bu remonstrated, and Hao angrily beheaded both, exterminating their three clans. From then on, ministers in court held their tongues and did not dare remonstrate again.

He again changed the era to Baoding, and made Lu Kai and Wan Yu Left and Right Chancellors. At this time Hao stayed at Wuchang. The people of Yang Province, sending grain by boat, suffered greatly and grumbled. He also spent lavishly and allowed no distinction between public and private scarcity.

Wan Yu submitted a memorial:

I am distressed. Though there is no current disaster, the people’s lives are nearly exhausted; without any effort the state granaries are empty. When the Han house had declined, the Three Houses contended; now Cao and Liu have lost the Way, and everything is to Jin. This is manifest proof before our eyes. I, only for Your Majesty’s sake, grieve for the state. Wuchang is rough and barren land, not fit for a ruler’s capital. I hear in folk songs: “Better to drink the water of Jianye and not eat Wuchang fish. Better to return to Jianye dead than live on in Wuchang.” This is enough to show both the people’s mind and Heaven’s intention. The state has not a year’s store; there is rot at the root. Officers are oppressive and overbearing, and none cares. In the Great Emperor’s time, women in the inner court were under one hundred; since the age of Emperor Jing, they are in the thousands. This is the greatest source of cost. Those beside Your Majesty are not worthy men; court cliques seize and obstruct, harming loyal ministers and hiding talent. These are the state’s diseases and the people’s burdens. If Your Majesty will reduce the burdens, cease extortion, dismiss palace women, and select proper officials, Heaven will be pleased, the people will attach themselves, and the state will be secure.

Hao disliked the memorial. He enlarged building works and began building Zhaoming Palace, ordering all civil and military officials to cut timber in the mountains. He also summoned diviner Shang Guang and asked him to read the stalks concerning the realm. Shang answered, “Your Majesty gains an auspicious omen. In a Gengzi year, a green canopy will enter Luoyang.”

Hao rejoiced and said to Hua He, deputy of the Secretariat, “Earlier the late emperor heeded you, sending generals by division to station hundreds of camps along the Yangtze, and he made old Commander Ding Feng in overall charge. I intend to recover Han lands and take revenge for Shu’s lord. Which place should be taken first?”

Hua He remonstrated, “At present Chengdu is not held and the royal state has collapsed. Sima Yan surely intends to swallow Wu. Your Majesty should first rectify your virtue and stabilize Wu people; that is the best strategy. If we now move arms and armor, it is like attempting to save a fire by spreading hay; it will only make us burn ourselves.”

Hao raged. “I intend to restore our former undertaking when the time comes. You speak only contrary words. If I do not look upon your former-service face, I should have your head chopped for bringing this speech,” and he shouted for guards to drag Hua He out.

Hua He said on leaving, “How regrettable that this brocaded state will soon belong to another,” and retired in seclusion.

Hao then ordered the General Who Guards the East, Lu Kang, to station troops at the river mouth and plan for Xiangyang.

Soon news reached Luoyang. Near officials informed Sima Yan that Lu Kang was attacking Xiangyang. Jia Chong stepped forward and said, “I hear that Sun Hao in Wu governs no virtue and acts lawlessly. You may issue an edict to Commander Yang Hu. When disorder appears in Wu and Heaven and earth grant opportunity, take and capture; Eastern Wu can be taken in a moment.” Sima Yan rejoiced, issued an edict, and sent it to Yang Hu.

Hu accepted and inspected the army, preparing to meet the enemy. Since then, while Yu stationed at Xiangyang, he won the heart of soldiers and people alike. Wu men who wished to submit were allowed. He reduced patrol troops and used them to reclaim over eight hundred qing of fields. When he first arrived, the army had not even a hundred days’ grain; by next year it held ten years’ grain.

In camp Hu dressed in light robes and broad belt, without armor and helmet; before his tent he had only around ten attendants.

One day a unit commander reported, “Scouts say Wu troops are lax; we can strike now and gain a great victory in surprise.” Hu laughed. “Do you all underestimate Lu Kang? The man is clever and versatile. Not long ago His Majesty ordered him to attack Xiling; he beheaded Bu Chan and dozens of his soldiers and I could not arrive to rescue him. As a commander he is no fool; we should only hold our borders and wait. If trouble appears inside him, we can seize then. If we push without testing affairs, it is the path to defeat.” The officers were convinced and held their positions.

On one occasion Hu led his generals hunting. Lu Kang likewise went out to hunt that day. Hu ordered, “My troops may not cross the border.” The commanders obeyed and hunted only in Jin land. Lu Kang watched from afar and sighed, “General Hu’s troops have discipline and may not be violated.” They withdrew at dusk.

Hu returned and inspected the game. Animals first wounded by Wu archers were all returned. The Wu were pleased and reported this to Lu Kang. He summoned the envoy, asked, “Can your commander drink?” The man answered, “If there is fine wine, he can.”

Kang laughed. “I have a dou of wine kept from long ago. Take it to him and present it. This is wine I myself brewed for my own drinking. This one ladle is from yesterday’s hunt.”

His officers asked, “General, why send wine to him?”

Kang replied, “He has shown grace to me; how can I not repay?”

When the envoy returned and gave report to Hu, Hu laughed. “Does he also know I can drink?” he said, and ordered the cask opened. Commander Chen Yuan said, “There may be guile in this; the grand commander should sip slowly.” Hu replied, “Kang is no poisoner; no suspicion is needed,” and drank it all. Thereafter they kept regular communication.

One day Kang asked after Hu by messenger. Hu asked, “How fares General Lu?”

The envoy said, “The commander has been sick in bed for several days and has not come out.”

Hu said, “His illness seems to match mine. I have already prepared a mature medicine. Send it for him.” The envoy carried it back. The commanders said, “Hu is our enemy; this medicine is surely not harmless.” Kang said, “Could Master Yang Hu poison men? Do not doubt,” and he took it. The next day his illness was gone. His officers congratulated him.

Kang said, “He subdues me with kindness while I subdue him with force. Now he submits without fighting. Each of you must hold your frontier and seek no small gain.”

Soon Wu’s envoy arrived. Kang received him and asked: “Why have you come?” The envoy said, “The Son of Heaven orders the general to make swift advance and not allow Jin men to enter first.”

Kang replied, “You first return. I will send a memorial.” The envoy withdrew. Kang sent a memorial to Jianye.

Hao read it through and was greatly angry: “I heard that Kang had contact with the enemy. This is now proven!” He removed Kang from command, reduced him to Sima, and appointed Left General Sun Ji to lead his troops. All ministers feared to remonstrate.

Hao changed the era to Jianheng and then to Phoenix Year One. He was willful and excessive, keeping soldiers in camp without end; all below groaned in complaint. Chancellors Wan Yu, General Liu Ping, and Minister of Revenue Lou Xuan all spoke against him plainly and were all executed. In the previous ten years he had killed over forty loyal ministers.

Hao moved with fifty thousand cavalry whenever he entered or left the palace, and officials were too terrified to resist.

Yang Hu, hearing of Kang’s removal and Hao’s depravity, saw a chance and sent to Luoyang requesting campaign against Wu with this memorial:

Even if the turn of fortune is bestowed by Heaven, achievement must still come through men. The defenses from the Yangtze and Huai are not like Jia-ge Pass. Sun Hao is cruel beyond Liu Shan. Wu people are in greater distress than Ba and Shu. Jin force is now far stronger than before. If our forces now hold back and keep soldiers facing one another, the realm will be exhausted by levy and campaign and cannot be sustained.

Sima Yan read the memorial and rejoiced. He was ready to raise troops, but Jia Chong, Xun Xu, and Feng Chun argued strongly against it, and he did not proceed.

When Hu heard the court did not approve, he sighed, “Not as one wishes is the result of the world. To have the moment but miss it is a great regret.”

In Xianning’s fourth year Hu came to court and petitioned to return and nurse his illness. Sima Yan asked, “What policy have you for preserving the state that I may learn?”

Hu said, “Sun Hao’s brutality has gone too far. He can be subdued without battle now. If Hao dies and a worthy ruler is later enthroned, Wu cannot be won.” Sima Yan understood at once, “If you were to move now and lead, what would you do?” Hu answered, “I am old and ill and cannot bear this task. Select another wise and brave man.”

He then left court. That November Hu fell ill and died. Sima Yan himself rode to his home in carriage to ask after him. At the bedside Hu said through tears, “I have ten thousand deaths and still cannot repay Your Majesty.” Sima Yan also wept, “I regret I did not let you attack Wu. Who now can carry your intent?”

Hu replied, “I am dead and dare not keep silent in my loyalty. The right General Du Yu can be trusted. If Your Majesty intends to strike Wu, he is the man.”

Sima Yan said, “To present merit and recommend the worthy is indeed good. Why did you keep your memorial private and burn it so no one knew?” Hu answered, “I do not accept private rewards; I cannot bow for my own honor.” He died after speaking.
